{"request_id":"ca3c1e3561f2856045116fc4","rewritten_text":"“I have to go now, and I don’t know what will happen to me. But I will come back here, or join your group, as soon as I can. One word, one look, will be enough to decide whether I come into your father’s house this evening—or never.”

Such a letter would not be soon forgotten. A half hour alone with her thoughts might have calmed her, but the ten minutes that passed before she was interrupted—while she still had to follow all the rules of her situation—did nothing to make her feel calm. Every moment only brought new agitation. It was overwhelming happiness. And before she had even reached the first full wave of feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta came in.

She had to keep up the act of being herself, and that caused an immediate struggle. After a while, she could not follow a word they said. She had to pretend she was unwell and excuse herself. Then they could see she looked very sick. They were shocked and worried, and they would not leave her for anything. This was awful. If they had only gone away and left her alone in that room, it might have helped her recover. But having them all standing around her was too distracting. In desperation, she said she would go home.

“By all means, my dear,” Mrs Musgrove cried, “go home at once and take care of yourself, so you’ll be well enough for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I’m not a doctor. Charles, ring for a chair. She must not walk.”

But a chair would not do. Worse than everything! She could not bear the thought of losing the chance to say two words to Captain Wentworth while she made her quiet, solitary way up the town—especially since she felt almost certain she would meet him. She protested strongly against the chair. Mrs Musgrove, who was only thinking about one kind of illness, reassured herself with some anxiety that there had been no fall. She was sure Anne had not slipped down at any time lately, and hit her head. She was perfectly convinced there had been no fall. She could let Anne go cheerfully and trust that she would be better by night.

Still, anxious not to miss any precaution, Anne struggled to speak and said—

“I’m afraid, ma’am, that it isn’t quite understood. Please be so kind as to tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your whole party this evening. I’m afraid there was some mistake. And I want you especially to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh! my dear, it is quite understood. I give you my word.”"}

{"request_id":"c2f5bb761d6d8667a4a656d4","rewritten_text":"But it is of little importance.”

“I might as well ask,” she replied, “why, with such an obvious plan to offend and insult me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your judgment, and even against your character. Was that not an excuse for rudeness, if I was rude? But I have other reasons to be provoked. You know I do. If my own feelings had not already turned against you—if they had been indifferent, or even favorable—do you think any consideration would have tempted me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a sister I love most dearly?”

As she said this, Mr. Darcy changed color; but the emotion passed quickly. He listened without trying to interrupt her while she went on—

“I have every reason in the world to think badly of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you played there. You can’t deny it—you dare not, you cannot deny that you were the principal, if not the only, means of driving them apart: exposing one to the world’s censure for caprice and instability, the other to its ridicule for disappointed hopes, and dragging them both into the most acute misery.”

She paused, and with no small indignation saw that he was listening with an expression that showed he felt no remorse at all. He even looked at her with a smile that seemed to be made for disbelief.

“Can you deny that you did it?” she repeated.

With an air of practiced calm, he answered, “I have no wish to deny that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am pleased with the result. Toward him I have been kinder than toward myself.”

Elizabeth refused to pretend she had noticed the polite remark, but its meaning did not escape her, nor was it likely to soften her.

“But it is not only this matter,” she continued. “My dislike is based on more than what happened then. Long before it took place, my opinion of you was already formed. Your character was laid out in the account I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On that subject, what do you have to say? What imaginary act of friendship could you use here to defend yourself? Or what misrepresentation could you use here to mislead others?”

“You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s affairs,” Darcy said, in a less steady tone, with his color heightened.

“Who wouldn’t feel concerned for him, knowing what his misfortunes have been?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated contemptuously. “Yes, his misfortunes have been very great indeed.”

“And the harm you’ve done him,” Elizabeth cried with force. “You’ve reduced him to his present condition—comparative poverty.”"}

{"request_id":"059dfba1f6500818a8fa2fac","rewritten_text":"Other chances to observe them would not fail to come. Anne soon found herself often in the company of all four together, enough to form an opinion, though she was too wise to admit it at home, where it would have satisfied neither husband nor wife. She thought Louisa was the favorite, but she also believed—at least as far as she dared judge from what she remembered and had seen—that Captain Wentworth was not truly in love with either of them. They were more in love with him, but it was not love. It was a kind of fever of admiration, and it might, and probably must, turn into love.

Charles Hayter seemed to feel that he was being slighted, and yet Henrietta sometimes looked as if she were pulled in two directions between him and the others. Anne wished she had the power to tell them all what they were doing, and to point out the dangers they were bringing on themselves. She did not think anyone was being dishonest. The greatest comfort to her was to believe that Captain Wentworth was not in the least aware of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph in his manner, and no cruel kind of triumph either. He had probably never heard, and certainly had never considered, any claims that Charles Hayter might have. He was only wrong in accepting—accepting, that must be the word—the attention of two young women at once.

After a short struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to give up. Three days passed without his coming once to Uppercross, which was a clear change. He even refused one regular invitation to dinner. And when Mr Musgrove found him on that occasion with several large books in front of him, Mr and Mrs Musgrove were sure that something could not be right. They spoke gravely about his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had given him a clear dismissal, and her husband lived with the constant expectation of seeing him the next day. Anne could only think that Charles Hayter was wise.

One morning, at about this time, when Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth had gone shooting together, the sisters in the Cottage were sitting quietly at their work when the sisters from the Mansion-house came to the window.

It was a fine November day. The Miss Musgroves walked through the small grounds and stopped only to say that they were going on a long walk, so they decided Mary would not want to go with them. When Mary answered at once, with a touch of jealousy that they did not think her a good walker—“Oh, yes, I should like to join you very much. I am very fond of a long walk”—Anne felt, from the look on the two girls’ faces, that this was exactly what they did not want. She admired again the kind of necessity that seemed to come from the family habits: that everything had to be shared, and everything had to be done together, even when it was unwanted and inconvenient."}

{"request_id":"1c9a67a99a2674e083d49baf","rewritten_text":"And I summon you, spirits of the dead, and you, wandering ministers of vengeance, to help and lead me in what I must do. Let the accursed, infernal monster drink deep of agony; let him taste the despair that now torments me.”

I began my appeal with solemnity and a reverence so strong that I almost believed the shades of my murdered friends were listening and approving my devotion, but the furies seized me as I finished, and fury choked my words.

Through the stillness of night I was answered by a loud, devilish laugh. It struck my ears and lingered, heavy and long; the mountains rang it back, and it seemed to me that all of hell pressed around me with mockery and laughter. I might, in that instant, have been driven mad and ended my wretched life, were it not that my vow was heard and that I was kept for vengeance. The laughter faded, and then, with a voice well known and loathed—seemingly right beside my ear—came an audible whisper: “I am content, miserable wretch! You have chosen to go on living, and I am content.”

I sprang toward the place from which the sound came, but the devil slipped beyond my reach. At once the broad face of the moon rose and shone full upon his ghastly, twisted form as he fled with speed beyond anything mortal.

I followed him, and for many months this has been my work. With only a slight hint to guide me, I traced the windings of the Rhone, but in vain. The blue Mediterranean opened before me, and by some strange turn I saw the fiend enter by night and conceal himself in a vessel bound for the Black Sea. I took passage on the same ship, yet he escaped—how, I cannot say.

Even through the wilds of Tartary and Russia, though he still slips away from me, I have never ceased to pursue his trail. At times the peasants, frightened by this dreadful apparition, told me where he had gone; at times it was he himself, fearing that if I lost all trace of him I would fall into despair and die, who left some sign to steer me on. Snow has fallen upon my head, and on the white plain I have seen the mark of his huge step. Tell me, you who are just beginning life, to whom worry is new and agony still unknown—how could you understand what I have suffered, and what I still suffer? Cold, hunger, and fatigue were the smallest of the torments I was meant to endure; I was cursed by some devil, and I carried my eternal hell with me. Yet even then, a spirit of good kept watch over my path and, when I most complained, would suddenly free me from difficulties that seemed utterly beyond my power. Sometimes, when hunger overcame my strength and I sank into exhaustion, a meal was laid out for me in the desert—food that restored me and set my spirit moving again."}

{"request_id":"09c8ccadb112fbab8f3d8631","rewritten_text":"“Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—no, Sir Simon—are you hungry? I’ve got a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?”

“No, thank you. I don’t eat anything anymore; but it’s very thoughtful of you all the same, and you’re far nicer than the rest of your dreadful, impolite, common, dishonest family.”

“Stop!” Virginia snapped, stamping her foot. “You’re the rude one—horrid and vulgar besides. And as for dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to spruce up that ridiculous blood-stain in the library. First you took all my reds, even the vermilion, so I couldn’t paint any more sunsets; then you grabbed the emerald-green and the chrome-yellow, and in the end I was left with nothing but indigo and Chinese white. That meant I could only manage moonlight pictures, which are always miserable to look at and quite hard to paint. I never reported you, though I was very annoyed, and the whole business was absurd—who ever heard of emerald-green blood?”

“Well, really,” said the Ghost, sounding rather subdued, “what was I supposed to do? Getting real blood is a very difficult business these days, and since your brother started it all with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason why I shouldn’t use your paints. And as for colour, that’s always a question of taste. The Cantervilles, for instance, have blue blood—the bluest in England; but I know you Americans don’t care much for such things.”

“You know nothing about it. The best you can do is emigrate and improve your mind. My father would be only too glad to give you a free passage, and although there’s a heavy duty on spirits of every sort, there won’t be any trouble at the Custom House, since the officers are all Democrats. Once you’re in New York, you’re bound to be a great success. I know plenty of people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars just to have a grandfather—and far more than that for a family Ghost.”

“I don’t think I’d care for America.”

“I suppose it’s because we have no ruins and no curiosities,” Virginia said with a touch of satire.

“No ruins! No curiosities!” the Ghost replied. “You’ve got your navy and your manners.”

“Good evening. I’ll go and ask papa to give the twins an extra week’s holiday.”

“Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,” he cried. “I’m so lonely and so miserable, and I truly don’t know what to do. I want to go to sleep, and I can’t.”

“That’s nonsense! You only have to go to bed and blow out the candle.”"}

{"request_id":"567d205c2123be10745e911b","rewritten_text":"“April 19th. This morning, to my great joy, at about nine o’clock, the moon’s surface was frightfully close, and my fears were at their highest point. At last, my condenser pump showed clear signs that the air around me had changed. By ten, I had good reason to think the air had become much denser. By eleven, the apparatus needed very little work. At twelve o’clock, with some hesitation, I unscrewed the tourniquet. Finding no trouble from doing so, I finally opened the gum-elastic chamber and took it off the car.

As you might expect, spasms and a violent headache were the immediate results of such a sudden, dangerous experiment. But although breathing was difficult, it was not so bad that I was in danger of losing my life. I decided to endure it as best I could, because I would leave these problems behind me as I moved into the denser air near the moon. Still, my descent was extremely fast. Soon it became painfully clear that, even if I had not been wrong to expect an atmosphere denser in proportion to the moon’s mass, I had been wrong about how dense it was—at even the surface. It was not enough to hold up the great weight in the car of my balloon.

This should have been true, just as it is on Earth: the actual gravity of bodies on either planet should match the ratio of atmospheric condensation. But since it was not, my sudden fall proved it. The only explanation I can give is that there must be geological disturbances of the kind I mentioned earlier. In any case, I was now very close to the planet and coming down with terrifying force.

I wasted no time. I threw overboard my ballast first, then my water-kegs, then my condensing apparatus and the gum-elastic chamber, and finally everything else in the car. It made no difference. I kept falling with horrible speed, and I was now less than half a mile from the surface. So, as a last resort, I got rid of my coat, hat, and boots. Then I cut the car loose from the balloon itself, even though it was heavy. Holding on with both hands to the netting, I barely had time to see that the land, as far as I could see, was covered with tiny houses. Before I could take in more, I tumbled headlong into the middle of a strange-looking city, right into a vast crowd of ugly little people. None of them said a word or even tried to help me. They just stood there like a bunch of idiots, grinning in a ridiculous way, and staring at me and my balloon from the side, with their arms stuck akimbo.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"eaf99e2faba4082ad26fe811","rewritten_text":"Poor Jack was later shot in a duel by Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara died of a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year had run out; so, in every respect, it had been a great success. Still, it was an exceedingly trying “make-up,” if I may borrow a theatrical phrase for one of the greatest mysteries of the supernatural, or, in a more scientific vein, of the higher-natural world, and it kept him busy for a full three hours while he made his preparations. At last everything was in readiness, and he was pleased enough with how he looked. The big leather riding-boots that belonged with the costume were just a touch too large, and he could only turn up one of the two horse-pistols; yet, on the whole, he felt fairly satisfied, and at a quarter past one he slipped out of the wainscoting and stole down the corridor. Reaching the room occupied by the twins—which, I should add, was called the Blue Bed Chamber because of the colour of its hangings—he found the door left slightly ajar. Hoping to make a striking entrance, he threw it wide, only for a heavy jug of water to tumble straight down on him, soaking him to the skin and missing his left shoulder by a couple of inches. At the same instant he heard muffled shrieks of laughter coming from the four-post bed. The shock to his nerves was so severe that he bolted back to his room as fast as he could, and the following day he was laid up with a bad cold. The only thing that in any way comforted him afterward was that he had not brought his head along; had he done so, the results might well have been far more serious.\n\nHe now abandoned any real expectation of frightening this impudent American family, and for the most part contented himself with skulking through the passages in list slippers, a thick red muffler about his throat to guard against draughts, and a small arquebuse in case the twins should come at him. The last blow fell on the 19th of September. He had gone down to the great entrance-hall, confident that there, at least, he would not be bothered, and he amused himself by tossing off satirical remarks at the large Saroni photographs of the United States Minister and his wife, which had now replaced the Canterville family portraits. He was dressed plainly but neatly in a long shroud, flecked with churchyard mould, had bound his jaw with a strip of yellow linen, and carried a small lantern and a sexton’s spade."}

{"request_id":"bca0b86cf039fa70efdf348c","rewritten_text":"Dear me, she was a master at talking. It would not do for me to remark that it was getting very late, that I was worn out, and that I felt heavy with sleep. I only wished I had gone to bed when I still might. Now I had to endure it; there was no other course. So she went on, tinkling along and along, through the otherwise deep and ghostly hush of the sleeping castle, until presently there came—seemingly from far below us—a distant sound, like a muffled shriek, and with an expression of agony in it that made my skin creep. The queen halted, and her eyes brightened with delight; she bent her graceful head the way a bird does when it listens. The noise worked its way back up through the stillness.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is truly a stubborn soul, and endureth long. It is many hours now.”

“Endureth what?”

“The rack. Come—ye shall see a blithe sight. If he yield not his secret now, ye shall see him torn asunder.”

What a sleek, smooth little hellion she was; and yet how steady and calm she seemed, while the cords all down my legs were aching in sympathy with that man’s suffering. With mailed guards, torches flaring, we marched through echoing corridors and down stone stairways that were dank and dripping, all the while smelling of mould and of ages of imprisoned night—a cold, uncanny journey, and a long one, made no shorter or pleasanter by the sorceress’s talk, which concerned this sufferer and his crime. He had been accused by an anonymous informer of killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

“Anonymous testimony isn’t the right thing, your Highness. It would be fairer to set the accused face-to-face with the accuser.”

“I had not considered it, as though it were of little consequence. But if I would, I could not; for the accuser came masked by night, told the forester, and straightway got him taken away again, so that the forester knoweth him not.”

“Then is this Unknown the only person who saw the stag killed?”

“Marry, no man saw the killing, but this Unknown saw this hardy wretch near to the spot where the stag lay, and came with right loyal zeal and betrayed him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag, too? Isn’t it possible he did the killing himself? His loyal zeal—behind a mask—looks just a shade suspicious. But what is your highness’s notion for racking the prisoner? Where is the gain?”

“He will not confess, else; and then were his soul lost. For his crime his life is forfeited by the law—and of a surety will I see that he payeth it!—but it were peril to my own soul to let him die unconfessed and unabsolved.”"}

{"request_id":"6f808974e875a701edbd6bfc","rewritten_text":"The insect’s weight was truly surprising, and, after thinking it all through, I could hardly blame Jupiter for his opinion about it. Still, I couldn’t understand why Legrand agreed with that opinion, and I couldn’t figure it out, no matter how hard I tried.

“I sent for you,” he said in a grand, dramatic voice, after I finished examining the beetle. “I sent for you so I could have your advice and help in carrying out Fate’s plans—and the plans of the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I interrupted, “you must be sick. You should take some precautions. Go to bed, and I’ll stay with you for a few days until you feel better. You’re feverish, and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I did, and honestly, I found no sign of fever at all.

“But you could still be ill without having a fever. Let me prescribe for you just this once. First, go to bed. Next—”

“You’re wrong,” he cut in. “I’m as well as I can be, considering the excitement I’m feeling. If you truly want to help me, you’ll calm this excitement.”

“And how would we do that?”

“Very simply. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills, out on the mainland. In this trip, we’ll need someone we can trust. You are the only person we can rely on. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you see in me will be just as quickly settled.”

“I’ll do what I can to help,” I said. “But are you saying that this awful beetle has anything to do with your trip into the hills?”

“It does.”

“Then, Legrand, I can’t take part in something so ridiculous.”

“I’m sorry—very sorry,” he said. “We’ll have to try it on our own.”

“Try it yourselves? The man must be out of his mind!—but wait. How long do you plan to be gone?”

“Probably all night. We’ll leave right away, and we’ll be back by sunrise, at the latest.”

“And will you promise me, on your honor, that when your little scheme is finished—and the bug business (good God!) is settled the way you want—you’ll return home and follow my advice exactly, as if it came from your physician?”

“Yes. I promise. Now come on—we have no time to waste.”

With a heavy heart, I went with him. We left at about four o’clock: Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and me. Jupiter brought the scythe and the spades, and he insisted on carrying all of them. It seemed to me he did it less out of hard work or willingness to help, and more out of fear that his master might not be able to be trusted with the tools within reach."}

{"request_id":"9b0f60c3e7144a9b58a82cdc","rewritten_text":"Sandy and I were back on the road the next morning, bright and early. It felt wonderful to open my lungs and breathe in great, rich barrels of the blessed God’s clean, dew-made, woodland-scented air again, after being stuck for two days and nights in the moral and physical stink of that unbearable old buzzard-roost. I mean, for me. Of course the place was fine enough for Sandy, because she had been used to high life all her days.

Poor girl—her jaws had had a long rest for a while, and I expected to pay for it. I was right, but she had stood by me in the castle and supported me with huge, foolish things. Those helped more in that moment than wisdom would have, even if it were twice as big. So I thought she had earned the right to run her mill for a while, if she wanted to, and I didn’t feel any sting when she started:

“Now turn we unto Sir Marhaus that rode with the damsel of thirty winter of age southward—”

“Are you going to see if you can work up another half-stretch on the trail of the cowboys, Sandy?”

“Even so, fair my lord.”

“Go ahead, then. I won’t interrupt this time, if I can help it. Start over again. Begin fresh, shake out all your reefs, and I’ll load my pipe and pay close attention.”

“Now turn we unto Sir Marhaus that rode with the damsel of thirty winter of age southward. And so they came into a deep forest, and by fortune they were nighted, and rode along in a deep way, and at the last they came into a courtelage where abode the duke of South Marches, and there they asked harbour. And on the morn the duke sent unto Sir Marhaus, and bad him make him ready. And so Sir Marhaus arose and armed him, and there was a mass sung afore him, and he brake his fast, and so mounted on horseback in the court of the castle, there they should do the battle. So there was the duke already on horseback, clean armed, and his six sons by him, and every each had a spear in his hand, and so they encountered, whereas the duke and his two sons brake their spears upon him, but Sir Marhaus held up his spear and touched none of them. Then came the four sons by couples, and two of them brake their spears, and so did the other two. And all this while Sir Marhaus touched them not. Then Sir Marhaus ran to the duke, and smote him with his spear that horse and man fell to the earth.”}"}

{"request_id":"37b03a2fe67a2b507932ade1","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is astonishing! I simply have to see Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose from his seat and paced the garden. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “to me Dorian Gray is nothing more than a spur to art. You may see nothing in him; I see everything. He is never more alive in my work than when there is no picture of him there. As I’ve said, he is a hint of a new manner. I catch him in the sweep of certain lines, in the grace and fine distinctions of certain colours. That’s all.”

“Then why not show his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I’ve slipped into it some trace of all this odd artistic worship—of which, naturally, I’ve never cared to tell him. He knows nothing of it. He shall never know. Still, the world might suspect it, and I won’t lay my soul bare to their shallow curiosity. My heart will never be set beneath their microscope. There’s too much of me in it, Harry—too much of me!”

“Poets aren’t nearly as delicate as you,” said Henry. “They know how useful passion is for getting printed. These days a broken heart will find its way into countless editions.”

“I despise them for it,” Hallward burst out. “An artist ought to make beautiful things, but put nothing of his own life into them. We live in an age where men treat art as though it were meant to be a kind of autobiography. We’ve lost the pure sense of beauty. Someday I’ll show the world what it is; and for that reason the world shall never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you’re mistaken, Basil, though I won’t argue with you. Only the intellectually stranded ever argue. Tell me—does Dorian Gray care much for you?”

The painter paused, weighing his words. “He likes me,” he answered at last, “I’m sure he likes me. Of course I flatter him shamelessly. I take a peculiar satisfaction in telling him things I know I’ll regret saying. Most of the time he is charming to me, and we sit in the studio and talk of a thousand matters. But now and then, he is dreadfully thoughtless, and it seems he truly enjoys hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I’ve given away my entire soul to someone who treats it as if it were a flower to pin on his coat—just decoration to feed his vanity, an ornament for a summer day.”"}

{"request_id":"36ba7e4ad186fe4844d74638","rewritten_text":"But then, how was I—this poor, dazed village boy—to steer clear of that splendid contradiction into which even the best and wisest men slip day after day?

“It may be all true enough,” I told Biddy, “but I can’t help admiring her dreadfully.”

In any case, when that thought came over me, I turned right over on my face, seized a handful of hair on either side of my head, and yanked it hard. All the while I knew the folly of my own heart—so frantic, so misplaced—that I was fully aware it would have been justice if I’d lifted my face by the hair and knocked it against the pebbles as punishment for being such an idiot.

Biddy was the wisest of girls, and she made no further attempt to argue with me. She laid her hand on mine—steady and comfortable, though roughened by work—and drew them gently out of my hair, one after another. Then, with my face still pressed against my sleeve, she gave my shoulder a soft pat meant to soothe, and I cried a little, just as I had done in the brewery yard, feeling—somehow, dimly—that I’d been ill-used by someone, or by everyone; I couldn’t say which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” said Biddy. “That you’ve felt you could trust me, Pip. And I’m glad of another: that you know you can rely on my keeping it safe, and on my always deserving that trust so far as I can. If your first teacher—dear me, such a poor one, and so much in need of being taught herself—had been your teacher at this very time, she thinks she’d know what lesson she’d set. But it would be a hard one to learn, and you’ve already gone past her, so it’s no use now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank. Then, with a fresh and pleasant shift in her voice, she asked, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, as I got up, slipped my arm around her neck, and kissed her, “I shall always tell you everything.”

“Only till you’re a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I never shall be—so that’s settled. And besides, I don’t have to tell you anything, because you already know everything I know, as I told you the other night at home.”

“Ah!” said Biddy, in a whisper, as she looked off toward the ships. Then, with that same former pleasant change, she asked again, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon faded into summer evening, and it was truly beautiful."}

{"request_id":"2d0e06111a30ef98f5bd4d3d","rewritten_text":"“Is that all? It isn’t much at all. Many people are unhappy with the Republic, and have to stare out of a small window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?”

“I am he. Of course, since I’m the last.”

Jarvis Lorry is the one who has answered every question so far. He has stepped down from the coach and now stands with his hand on the coach door, answering a group of officials. They walk around the carriage slowly and then climb up to the box slowly, to see the little luggage it carries on the roof. Country people gather nearby, press close to the coach doors, and stare greedily inside. A small child, held by its mother, has its short arm stretched out so it can touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry. They are countersigned.”

“One can leave, citizen?”

“One can leave. Forward, my postilions! Have a good trip!”

“I salute you, citizens. And the first danger is over!”

These are again Jarvis Lorry’s words. He clasps his hands and looks upward. Inside the carriage there is terror, there is crying, and there is the heavy breathing of the traveler who cannot feel what is happening.

“Are we not going too slowly? Can’t they be made to go faster?” Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

“It would feel like running away, my dear. I must not push them too hard, or it will make them suspicious.”

“Look back, look back, and see if we are being followed!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, we are not being followed.”

Houses pass by in groups of two and three. There are lonely farms and ruined buildings, dye-works, tanneries, and the like. Then it opens out into the countryside, with avenues of leafless trees. The hard, uneven road is under us, while soft, deep mud lies on both sides. Sometimes we move into the edge of the mud to avoid the stones that rattle and shake the coach. Sometimes we get stuck in ruts and deep tracks. When that happens, our impatience becomes unbearable. In our panic and hurry, we want to get out and run—hide—do anything except keep sitting still.

We leave the open country again and go back among ruined buildings, lonely farms, dye-works, tanneries, and the like. There are cottages in groups of two and three, and avenues of leafless trees. Have these men tricked us and taken us back by another road? Isn’t this the same place twice? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see if we are being followed! Hush! The posting-house.

Slowly, our four horses are taken out. Slowly, the coach stands in the small street without horses, with no chance of moving again. Slowly, the new horses appear, one by one. Slowly, the new postilions come after them, pulling and braiding the lashes of their whips. Slowly, the old postilions count their money, make the wrong sums, and end up with results that leave them dissatisfied."}

{"request_id":"76655b0749de6b1b475c57d4","rewritten_text":"In the days of my youth, discontent never once took hold of my thoughts; and if _ennui_ ever did assail me, the sight of whatever is beautiful in nature, or the contemplation of what is excellent and sublime in the works of mankind, would still draw my heart toward it and give a kind of spring to my spirits. But I am now a blasted tree: the bolt has entered my soul. Then I understood that I should live only to show what I shall soon no longer be—a wretched spectacle of ruined humanity, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent a considerable time at Oxford, wandering through its neighbourhood and trying to mark out every place that could be connected with the most stirring period of English history. These small excursions of discovery were often prolonged by the successive objects that kept presenting themselves. We went to the tomb of the illustrious Hampden, and to the field where that patriot fell. For a moment my soul rose above its degrading, miserable fears, to dwell on the divine notions of liberty and self-sacrifice which those scenes served as monuments and reminders. For an instant I dared to cast off my chains and survey my surroundings with a freer, higher spirit; yet the iron had already eaten into my flesh, and I sank again, trembling and hopeless, back into my wretched self.

We quitted Oxford with regret, and made our next resting-place Matlock. The countryside about this village bore, in a still greater degree, the look of Switzerland; only everything there is on a smaller scale, and the green hills lack the crown of far-off white Alps that always attend the pine-clad mountains of my native land. We visited the remarkable cave and the little cabinets of natural history, where the curiosities are arranged in the same fashion as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. The very last name made me shudder when Henry pronounced it, and I was eager to leave Matlock, since that dreadful scene was thus bound up with it.

From Derby, continuing northward, we remained two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could now almost persuade myself that I was among the Swiss mountains. The small remnants of snow that still lingered on the northern slopes, the lakes, and the dash of the rocky streams were sights at once familiar and dear to me. Here, too, we formed some acquaintances, who nearly managed to lure me into happiness. Clerval’s pleasure was, in proportion, greater than mine; his mind widened in the company of men of talent, and he discovered in his own nature larger powers and resources than he had ever supposed he possessed while he kept to those beneath him."}

{"request_id":"618a5985204ed9822a342326","rewritten_text":"The next day the ghost was very weak and exhausted. The terrible excitement of the last four weeks was starting to show. His nerves were completely shattered, and he startled at the smallest sound. For five days he kept to his room, and at last he decided to drop the whole point of the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family didn’t want it, then clearly they didn’t deserve it. They were evidently people living on a low, material level of existence, and quite incapable of appreciating the symbolic value of sensuous phenomena. The question of phantasmal apparitions, and the development of astral bodies, was, of course, a different matter—something really not under his control. It was his solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week, and to gibber from the large oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of every month, and he couldn’t see how he could honorably escape those obligations.

It was true that his life had been very evil, but on the other hand he was most conscientious in everything connected with the supernatural. For the next three Saturdays, accordingly, he walked the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every possible precaution to make sure he was neither heard nor seen. He removed his boots, stepped as lightly as he could on the old worm-eaten boards, wore a large black velvet cloak, and made sure to use the Rising Sun Lubricator for oiling his chains. I have to admit it took him quite a bit of effort to get himself to adopt this last method of protection. Still, one night, while the family were at dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and stole the bottle. At first he felt a little humiliated, but later he was sensible enough to see that there was a lot to be said for the invention, and that—at least to a certain degree—it served his purpose.

Even so, he wasn’t left entirely unbothered. Strings were continually being stretched across the corridor, over which he tripped in the dark; and on one occasion, while he was dressed for the part of “Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,” he suffered a severe fall after stepping on a butter-slide the twins had set up from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber to the top of the oak staircase. This last insult enraged him so much that he resolved to make one final effort to assert his dignity and social standing, and decided to visit the insolent young Etonians the next night in his celebrated role of “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.”

He hadn’t appeared in this disguise for more than seventy years—in fact, not since he had frightened pretty Lady Barbara Modish so badly with it that she abruptly broke off her engagement with the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather, and ran away to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton, declaring that nothing in the world would make her marry into a family that allowed such a horrible phantom to pace up and down the terrace at twilight."}

content.text: {"request_id":"f6c8142f89ef874f2d6dbedf","rewritten_text":"The shock and amazement I felt at this unusual change in how things stood was, perhaps, the part of the adventure that was hardest to explain. The change itself was not only natural and unavoidable, but it had been expected for a long time. I should reach the exact point in my trip where the pull of the planet would be replaced by the pull of the satellite. More precisely, the balloon’s pull toward the earth would become weaker than its pull toward the moon. I woke from a deep sleep with all my senses confused. I sat up to look at a very surprising sight—one that I had expected, but not in that moment. The shift must have happened slowly and smoothly. Even if I had been awake when it occurred, it is not clear that I would have noticed it from anything inside me—no discomfort or trouble with my body or with my equipment.\n\nWhen I finally understood where I was and came out of the terror that had taken over every part of my mind, my attention turned first to the moon’s overall appearance. It lay beneath me like a map. Even though I still thought it was at a considerable distance, I could see the details of its surface with a sharpness that was both striking and hard to explain. At first glance, the most extraordinary thing about its geology was the complete absence of any ocean or sea, and also of any lake, river, or other body of water. Still, in a strange twist, I saw wide, flat regions that looked clearly alluvial. Yet most of the hemisphere I could see was covered with countless volcanic mountains. They were cone-shaped and looked more like man-made structures than natural hills. The tallest of them did not rise more than three and three-quarters miles straight up. But a map of the volcanic districts of the Campi Phlegraei would show your Excellencies their general shape better than any poor description I could try to give. Most of these mountains were clearly erupting. Their violence and power frightened me as the repeated thunder of the so-called “meteoric stones” rose upward by the balloon. The sound came more and more often, with a frequency that grew more and more terrifying."}

{"request_id":"961552928a8f74427086b1c4","rewritten_text":"You won’t, won’t you? Oh, you precious little flat!”

“It’s naughty, isn’t it, Oliver?” Charley Bates asked. “He’ll end up getting scragged, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that means,” Oliver replied.

“Something like that, old fellow,” Charley said. As he spoke, Master Bates caught hold of the end of his neckerchief; holding it upright in the air, he dropped his head onto his shoulder, jerked it, and made a strange sound through his teeth—showing, with a lively bit of pantomime, that scragging and hanging were the same thing.

“That’s what it means,” Charley said. “Look how he stares, Jack! I never saw such top-notch company as that boy—he’ll be the death of me, I know he will.” Master Charley Bates laughed heartily again, then went back to his pipe, tears in his eyes.

“You were brought up badly,” the Dodger said, looking over Oliver’s polished boots with satisfaction. “Fagin will make something of you, though—if not, you’ll be the first one he ever had that turned out unprofitable. You’d better start right away, because you’ll be in the trade long before you even think about it, and you’re only wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates backed up this advice with a string of moral lectures of his own; once those were exhausted, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins launched into a glowing description of the many pleasures that came with the life they led. They sprinkled it with hints to Oliver that the best thing he could do would be to win Fagin’s favor without delay, using the same methods they themselves had used to get it.

“And always put this in your pipe, Nolly,” the Dodger said, as the Jew was heard unlocking the door upstairs. “If you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the point of talking like that?” Master Bates interrupted. “He doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take pocket-handkerchers and watches,” the Dodger said, bringing his talk down to Oliver’s level, “some other guy will; and then the fellows who lose ’em will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off too, and nobody’ll be half a ha’p’orth better—except the chaps who get them. And you’ve got just as much right to them as they have.”

“Sure, sure!” said the Jew, who had entered without Oliver noticing. “It all lies in a nutshell, my dear—in a nutshell. Take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the catechism of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands together gleefully as he confirmed the Dodger’s reasoning in those terms, chuckling with delight at how well his pupil had learned.

The conversation didn’t go any farther then, because the Jew had gone back home with Miss Betsy and a gentleman Oliver had never seen before. The Dodger addressed him as Tom Chitling. After lingering on the stairs to exchange a few gallantries with the lady, he finally appeared."}

{"request_id":"70ca4c81ed22ca5237a70d2b","rewritten_text":"He slipped out of the wall paneling, wearing an evil smile on his cruel, wrinkled mouth. The moon hid behind a cloud as he crept past the big oriel window, where his own arms and those of his murdered wife were shown in blue and gold. He kept gliding on, like an evil shadow, and even the darkness seemed to hate him as he went by. Once he thought he heard someone call, so he stopped. But it was only a dog barking from the Red Farm, and he went on, muttering strange curses from the sixteenth century. Now and then he waved a rusty dagger through the night air.

At last he reached the corner of the passage that led to luckless Washington’s room. He paused there for a moment. The wind stirred his long gray hair, and it twisted around his head, making the nameless horror of the dead man’s shroud look even more twisted and unreal. Then the clock struck the quarter, and he felt the time had come. He chuckled to himself and turned the corner. But the moment he did, he let out a terrified wail, stumbled backward, and hid his pale face in his long, bony hands.

Right in front of him stood a horrible spectre, perfectly still, like something carved in stone, and monstrous, like a madman’s dream. Its head was bald and shining. Its face was round, fat, and white. Its hideous laughter seemed to twist its features into a grin that would never end. From its eyes, red rays streamed out. Its mouth was a wide pit of fire. A dreadful garment, like his own, wrapped its Titan-sized body in silent snow. On its chest was a placard with strange writing in old characters—something like a scroll of shame, a record of wild sins, or an awful calendar of crime. With its right hand, it held up a gleaming falchion.

He had never seen a ghost before, so of course he was terrified. After a quick look at the phantom, he ran back to his room. He tripped over his long winding-sheet as he hurried down the corridor, and finally he dropped the rusty dagger into the Minister’s jack-boots. The butler found it the next morning. Once he was alone in his own apartment, he threw himself onto a small pallet-bed and covered his face with the clothes.

After a time, though, the brave old Canterville spirit took over again. He decided he would go and speak to the other ghost as soon as it was daylight. So, just as dawn began to touch the hills with silver, he returned toward the spot where he had first seen the grisly phantom. After all, he thought, two ghosts were better than one, and with the help of his new friend, he might be able to deal with the twins safely."}

{"request_id":"1a18071829c944258d94ccf4","rewritten_text":"“I’m going, Mr. Will—honestly, I am,” the man replied at once—“I’m out to the end now.”

“_Out to the end!_” Legrand fairly screamed. “Do you mean you’re out to the end of that limb?”

“Soon to the end, sir—o-o-o-o-oh! Lor-gol-a-marcy! what is this up on the tree?”

“Well!” Legrand cried, delighted. “What is it?”

“Nothing but a skull, sir—someone left it with its head up in the tree, and the crows have gobbled every bit of the meat off.”

“A skull, you say!—all right—how is it fastened to the limb?—what holds it on?”

“Sure enough, sir; I gotta look. Why, this is a strange thing, I swear—there’s a big nail in the skull that fastens it to the tree.”

“Well now, Jupiter, do exactly what I tell you—do you hear me?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Pay attention, then—find the skull’s left eye.”

“Hum! hoo! that’s good! why there ain’t no eye left at all.”

“Curse your stupidity! Do you know your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I knows that—knows all about that—’tis my left hand what I chop the wood with.”

“Of course! You’re left-handed; and your left eye would be on the same side as your left hand. Now, I suppose, you can find the skull’s left eye—or where the left eye used to be. Have you found it?”

There was a long pause. At last the man asked,

“Is the skull’s left eye on the same side as the skull’s left hand, too?—’cause the skull don’t have any hand at all—never mind! I got the left eye now—here’s the left eye! what do I do with it?”

“Let the beetle drop through it, as far as the string will reach—but be careful not to let go of the string.”

“All done, Mr. Will; that’s mighty easy—just put the bug through the hole—watch out for him down there!”

During this exchange, no part of Jupiter’s body could be seen; but the beetle he had let down was now visible at the end of the string, and it glistened, like a globe of burnished gold, in the last rays of the setting sun, some of which still faintly lit the height where we stood. The _scarabæus_ hung clear of any branches, and if it were allowed to fall, it would have fallen at our feet. Legrand immediately took the scythe and cleared, with it, a circular space three or four yards across directly beneath the insect; then, having done so, he ordered Jupiter to let go the string and come down from the tree."}

{"request_id":"2fbeefd4a8ca4df1346b345a","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. I’ll be late for lunch if I stay any longer. Thanks for giving me the information I wanted. I always like to know everything about my new friends, and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I’ve asked myself and Mr. Gray. He is her latest _protégé_.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, not to bother me any more with her charity appeals. I’m sick of them. The good woman seems to think I have nothing to do but write cheques for her silly causes.”

“All right, Uncle George, I’ll tell her, but it won’t make any difference. Philanthropic people lose all sense of humanity. It’s their defining trait.”

The old gentleman growled approvingly and rang the bell for his servant. Lord Henry walked past the low arcade into Burlington Street and turned his steps toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s parentage. Even though it had been told to him in such a crude way, it still stirred him with the suggestion of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a mad passion. A few wild weeks of happiness cut short by a hideous, treacherous crime. Months of voiceless agony, and then a child born in pain. The mother snatched away by death, the boy left to solitude and the tyranny of an old, loveless man. Yes; it was an interesting background. It shaped the boy, made him, in a sense, even more perfect. Behind every exquisite thing that exists, there is something tragic. Worlds have to be in turmoil, so that even the meanest flower can bloom.... And how charming he had been at dinner the night before—how, with startled eyes and lips parted in frightened pleasure, he had sat opposite him at the club, the red candle shades staining the awakening wonder of his face to a richer rose. Talking to him was like playing on an exquisite violin. He responded to every touch and thrill of the bow.... There was something terribly enthralling in the act of exerting influence. No other activity was like it. To project one’s soul into some gracious form, and let it linger there for a moment; to hear one’s own intellectual views echoed back with all the added music of passion and youth; to pour one’s temperament into another as though it were a subtle fluid or a strange perfume—there was real joy in that, perhaps the most satisfying joy left to us in an age so limited and vulgar as our own, an age grossly given to the flesh in its pleasures, and grossly common in its aims.... He was a marvelous type, too—this lad whom, by such a curious chance, he had met in Basil’s studio, or could, at any rate, be fashioned into a marvelous type."}

{"request_id":"4cfaec41ec11d8084bf7b081","rewritten_text":"“I’m with you. It’s the best thing. Just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh no, not for this. That’s fine for little, trashy common things—especially with girls, because they always turn on you anyway, and they blab if they get mad—but there ought to be writing about a big thing like this. And blood.”

Tom’s whole self seemed to applaud the idea. It was deep, and dark, and awful; the hour, the circumstances, the surroundings, all matched it. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, took a little fragment of “red keel” from his pocket, set the moon on his work, and painfully scratched out these lines, pressing each slow down-stroke by clamping his tongue between his teeth, then easing up on the up-strokes.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry was filled with admiration for Tom’s skill in writing, and for the grandeur of his language. He immediately took a pin from his lapel and was about to prick his flesh, but Tom said:

“Wait! Don’t do that. A pin’s brass. It might have verdigris on it.”

“What’s verdigris?”

“It’s poison. That’s what it is. You swallow some of it once—you’ll see.”

So Tom unwound the thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked the ball of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After many squeezes, Tom finally managed to sign his initials, using the ball of his little finger as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to make an H and an F, and the oath was complete. They buried the shingle close to the wall, with grim ceremonies and chants, and the fetters that bound their tongues were considered locked, with the key thrown away.

A figure crept stealthily through a break at the other end of the ruined building, but they didn’t notice it.

“Tom,” whispered Huckleberry, “does this stop us from ever telling—always?”

“Of course it does. It doesn’t matter what happens—we have to keep mum. We’d drop down dead—don’t you know that?”

“Yes, I guess that’s true.”

They kept whispering for a little while. Then, just outside—within ten feet of them—a dog let out a long, mournful howl. The boys clutched each other suddenly, in agony from fear.

“Which of us does he mean?” gasped Huckleberry.

“I don’t know—peek through the crack. Quick!”

“No, you, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t do it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"b2acf08472680fb38f333c7e","rewritten_text":"It was at that instant that my eyes—and his as well—rested on a bit of parchment, which I at the time took for paper. It lay half covered by the sand, with one corner jutting up. Close to where we came upon it, I noticed the remains of the hull of what seemed to have been a ship’s long boat. The wreck must have been there a very great while; the likeness to boat timbers could scarcely be made out.

“Well, Jupiter took up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Not long after, we set out for home, and on the way we met Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he begged me to let him carry it to the fort. When I agreed, he at once put it into his waistcoat pocket—without the parchment that had wrapped it, which I kept holding in my hand while he examined it. Perhaps he feared I might change my mind, and thought it safer to secure the prize at once; you know how eager he is about everything connected with Natural History. Yet, without my being aware of it, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket at the same time.

“You recall that when I went to the table, intending to make a sketch of the beetle, I found no paper where it was usually kept. I looked in the drawer, and there was none. I searched my pockets, hoping to come across an old letter, when my hand struck the parchment. I set down the exact way it came into my possession, because the circumstances impressed me with unusual force.

“No doubt you’ll call me fanciful—but I had already formed a sort of connexion. I had joined together two links of a great chain. There was a boat lying on a sea-coast, and not far from it a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn upon it. You will, of course, ask, ‘where is the connexion?’ I answer that the skull, or death’s-head, is the well-known emblem of the pirate. The death’s-head flag is raised in all their engagements.

“I have said the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment is lasting—almost imperishable. Things of little consequence are seldom committed to parchment; for ordinary drawing or writing, it is not nearly so suitable as paper. This thought led me to suspect some meaning—some relevancy—in the death’s-head. I did not overlook, either, the shape of the parchment. Though one of its corners had been destroyed by some accident, it could be seen that the original form was oblong.”"}

{"request_id":"1909ba4205944b22c49ba2f6","rewritten_text":"“But when I saw you become the object of someone else’s love, when I pictured that you might be loved in a way other than as a sacred symbol of beauty and excellence, or that you might love someone else with a stronger, hotter feeling than you ever had for me, then the fiend in me woke up. I pushed your lover away, and from that moment I have had no peace. I have searched in vain for sleep and rest. My eyes would not close, and my blood has been in constant turmoil. I woke to a new life, like someone who dies with hope and then wakes in Hell. I will not dirty your mind by telling you about my fights with myself, my anger at my own heart, and my despair. Let a veil cover the things no one can imagine that a guilty father feels. The secrets of a heart that has suffered so much should not be made common. Everything was chaos—crime, remorse, and hate—yet still there was the tenderest love. What first made me firmly decide to control my passion and to bring your father back to my child was the sight of your bitter, sympathetic sorrow. That is what brought me here. I thought that if I could wake again in my heart the grief I felt when I lost your mother, and the memories of her that had been sleeping for seventeen years, then all love for her child would finally die out.

“In a burst of heroic resolve, I decided to go alone. I would leave you, the life of my life, and not see you again until I could do it without guilt. But it did not work. I judged my strength too highly, or my love too low. I would surely have died if you had not hurried to me. If only I had truly been extinguished!

“And now, Mathilda, I must make you my final confession. I have been terribly wrong to think I could conquer my love for you. I never can. Seeing this house, these fields, and these woods—the places where my first love lived—seems only to have made it stronger. In my madness I even told myself, ‘Diana died to give you life. Her mother’s spirit was put into your body, and you should be Diana to me.’ No matter how hard I try to throw this love off, it clings even closer. This guilty love is more unnatural than hate. It destroys your hopes and destroys me forever.

Better to love despair, and safer to kiss her.

No time or distance can take from my soul what is part of it. Since I arrived here, I have not stopped feeling the Hell of passion that has been planted in me—to burn until everything is cold, stiff, and dead.”"}

{"request_id":"992e83964d71bb5ffca7657d","rewritten_text":"But it is very remarkable that she should always hear Jane better than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she will not find her grandmama any less deaf than she was two years ago. That is saying a great deal at my mother’s age, and it really has been a full two years since she was here. We have never gone so long without seeing her, and as I was telling Mrs. Cole, we shall hardly know how to make enough of her now.”

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax here soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Indeed!—that must be a very great pleasure.”

“Thank you. You are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone says the same nice things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends at Highbury as they can be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot say which, because Colonel Campbell will want the carriage for himself on one of those days. It is so good of them to send her the whole way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes, Friday or Saturday next. That is what she writes about. That is why she writes out of her usual schedule, as we call it; because, in the normal way of things, we would not have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, so I imagined. I was afraid there might be little chance of my hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today.”

“So kind of you! No, we would not have heard, if it had not been for this particular reason—her being on her way here so soon. My mother is delighted—for she will be with us for at least three months. Three months, she says, positively, and I am going to have the pleasure of reading to you. The situation is this: the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her father and mother to come over and see her right away. They had not planned to go until the summer, but she is so eager to see them again. Since she married last October, she has never been away from them for more than a week, which must make it very strange to be in different kingdoms—though I mean different countries. So she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father, I truly do not know which it was, but we will see when Jane’s letter arrives. She wrote in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, to urge their coming over directly. They will meet them in Dublin and then take them back to their country home, Baly-craig, a beautiful place, I imagine.”"}

{"request_id":"d318603836ff7fad9aa69dd4","rewritten_text":"Not a single word, however, passed his lips in reference to it, until their visitor had taken his leave for the night; but the moment he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said,—

“Jane, I congratulate you. You are going to be a very happy woman.”

Jane went to him at once, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are a good girl,” he answered, “and I take real satisfaction in believing you will be settled so happily. I have not the least doubt that you will do very well together. Your tempers are by no means unlike. You are both so yielding, that nothing will ever be decided; so easy, that every servant will manage to cheat you; and so liberal, that you will always run beyond your income.”

“I hope not. Any imprudence or thoughtlessness in money matters would be unforgivable in _me_.”

“Run beyond their income! My dear Mr. Bennet,” cried his wife, “what are you saying? Why, he has four or five thousand a year, and very likely more.” Then, turning to her daughter, “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so delighted! I know I shan’t sleep a wink all night. I always knew it would come to this. I told you it must be so at last. I was certain you could not be so beautiful for nothing! I remember, the very first time I saw him, when he came into Hertfordshire last year, I thought it was very likely you would be brought together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man that ever was seen!”

Wickham and Lydia were soon forgotten. Jane was her favourite child, beyond all comparison. At that moment she cared for no one else. Her younger sisters soon began to press her with hopes of other sources of happiness they might, in time, be able to enjoy.

Mary asked for the use of the library at Netherfield; and Kitty pleaded, with all her might, for a few balls there every winter.

From this time, Bingley was, of course, a daily visitor at Longbourn; he came often before breakfast, and always stayed until after supper; except when some barbarous neighbour—one whom he could never be made to detest enough—had given him an invitation to dinner, which he felt himself bound to accept.

Elizabeth now had little opportunity to talk with her sister; for while he was there, Jane had no attention to spare for anyone else: yet in those intervals of separation, which must sometimes occur, she found herself of considerable use to both. When Jane was absent, he always attached himself to Elizabeth, for the pleasure of talking about her; and when Bingley was gone, Jane constantly sought the same relief.

“He has made me so happy,” said she, one evening, “by telling me that he was quite unaware of my being in town last spring!”"}

{"request_id":"d2d86cfb8f38266ac612b08b","rewritten_text":"“Git up! What you ’bout?”

I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to figure out where I was. It was after sunrise, and I’d been asleep hard. Pap was standing over me, looking sour and sick. He said:

“What you doin’ with this gun?”

I figured he didn’t know anything about what he’d been doing, so I told him, “Somebody tried to get in, so I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you roust me out?”

“I tried, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t move you.”

“Well, all right. Don’t stand there talking all day. Get out and see if there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I went out along the riverbank. I saw bits of limbs and other stuff floating down, and some bark too. That meant the river had started to rise. I figured I’d have a good time now if I was over in town. The June rise always brought me luck. As soon as it starts here, cordwood comes floating down, along with pieces of log rafts—sometimes a dozen logs together. All you have to do is catch them and sell them to the wood yards and the sawmill.

I walked up the bank, keeping one eye out for Pap and the other on what the rise might bring. Then, all at once, a canoe came drifting in. It was a fine one, about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high like a duck. I dove headfirst off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and swam for the canoe. I expected someone might be in it, because people sometimes did that to trick you. When a man pulled a skiff out, they’d pop up and laugh at him. But that didn’t happen this time.

It was really a drift canoe. I climbed in and paddled it to shore. I thought, the old man will be glad when he sees this. It’s worth ten dollars. But when I got to shore, Pap wasn’t there yet. As I pushed the canoe into a small creek, like a narrow gully, covered over with vines and willows, I got another idea. I decided to hide it well. Instead of running off into the woods, I’d take the canoe down the river about fifty miles, find a place to camp, and stay there for good. Then I wouldn’t have to keep dealing with the hard walking.

It was pretty close to the shanty. I thought I could hear the old man coming the whole time, but I hid the canoe first. Then I stepped out and looked around through the willows. The old man was down the path a ways, aiming his gun at a bird."}

{"request_id":"c798ddc4fb2a305f6c000deb","rewritten_text":"It is a strange notion, yet everyone who vanishes is said to be seen in San Francisco. The city must be charming, and it must offer all the pleasures of the next world.”

“What do you suppose has happened to Basil?” asked Dorian, holding his Burgundy up to the light and wondering how he managed to speak of it so quietly.

“I can’t imagine. If Basil wants to keep out of sight, that’s not my concern. If he’s dead, I won’t trouble myself with it. Death is the only thing that ever frightens me. I hate it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked wearily.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, as he held the gilt trellis of an open vinaigrette box to his nostrils, “these days one may get through everything—save that. Death and vulgarity are the only two certainties in the nineteenth century that you can’t talk away. Come, let’s take our coffee in the music-room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The fellow my wife ran off with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I truly liked her. The place feels rather empty without her. Of course, married life is only a habit—an ugly one. Still, one grieves even for one’s worst habits. Perhaps one grieves for them most of all. They’re such a necessary part of one’s nature.”

Dorian said nothing. He rose from the table, went into the next room, and sat down at the piano, letting his fingers wander over the white and black ivory of the keys. When the coffee was brought in, he paused, looked across at Lord Henry, and said, “Harry, has it ever occurred to you that Basil was murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was well liked, and he always wore a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He wasn’t sharp enough to make enemies. True, he had a fine gift for painting. But a man may paint like Velasquez and still be as lifeless as possible. Basil was, in truth, rather dull. He interested me only once—years ago—when he told me he had a wild devotion for you, and that you were the guiding motive of his art.”

“I was fond of Basil,” said Dorian, with a touch of sadness. “But don’t people say he was murdered?”

“Oh, some of the papers say so. It doesn’t strike me as likely. I know there are dreadful quarters in Paris, but Basil wasn’t the kind of man to go there. He had no curiosity. That was his chief failing.”

“And what would you say, Harry, if I told you that I had murdered Basil?” asked the younger man."}

{"request_id":"e5f5f2c75fa448df3bbe4431","rewritten_text":"Of course, he was amusing, and all that, but I was really disappointed. When I asked him about the coat of mail, he only laughed and said it was far too cold to wear in England. Ah, here is Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I want you to tell the Duchess of Paisley’s fortune. Duchess, you must take your glove off. No, not the left hand—the other one.

“Dear Gladys, I don’t think this is quite right,” said the Duchess, slowly unfastening a rather dirty kid glove.

“Nothing interesting ever is,” said Lady Windermere. “That’s just how the world is. But I must introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favorite palm reader. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley. And if you say she has a bigger ‘mountain of the moon’ than I do, I’ll never believe in you again.”

“I’m sure, Gladys, there’s nothing like that in my hand,” said the Duchess seriously.

“Your Grace is right,” said Mr. Podgers, looking at the little fat hand with its short, square fingers. “The mountain of the moon isn’t developed. But the line of life is excellent. Please bend your wrist. Thank you. Three clear lines on the rascette! You’ll live to a great age, Duchess, and you’ll be extremely happy. Ambition—very moderate. The line of intellect—nothing exaggerated. The line of the heart—”

“Now, do be discreet, Mr. Podgers,” Lady Windermere called out.

“Nothing would please me more,” said Mr. Podgers, bowing, “if the Duchess had ever been, but I’m sorry to say I see strong, lasting affection mixed with a firm sense of duty.”

“Please go on, Mr. Podgers,” said the Duchess, looking pleased.

“Economy is one of Your Grace’s virtues,” Mr. Podgers continued, and Lady Windermere burst into laughter.

“Economy is a very good thing,” the Duchess said, pleased with herself. “When I married Paisley, he had eleven castles, and not a single house that was fit to live in.”

“And now he has twelve houses, and not a single castle,” Lady Windermere said.

“Well, my dear,” the Duchess began.

“Comfort,” said Mr. Podgers. “Modern improvements. Hot water in every bedroom. Your Grace is right. Comfort is the only thing our civilization can offer.”

“You’ve described the Duchess’s character wonderfully, Mr. Podgers. Now you must describe Lady Flora’s,” and, as the smiling hostess nodded, a tall girl with sandy Scotch hair stepped awkwardly out from behind the sofa and held out a long, bony hand with spatula-like fingers.

“Ah, a pianist!” said Mr. Podgers. “I see. An excellent pianist, but perhaps not quite a real musician.”"}

{"request_id":"dd56820045dca2a84df73d9a","rewritten_text":"Mr. Darcy spoke of his sister’s skill with warm approval.

“I am very glad to receive so favorable an account of her,” said Lady Catherine; “and do tell her for me, that she cannot expect to excel unless she practises a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he answered, “that she has no need of such counsel. She practises with great constancy.”

“Then so much the better. It cannot be urged too strongly; and when I next write to her, I shall insist that she neglect it on no account. I often tell young ladies that no excellence in music can be gained without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet more than once that she will never play really well unless she practises more; and though Mrs. Collins has no instrument, she is still welcome, as I have often said to her, to come to Rosings every day and play on the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. She would not be in anyone’s way there, you know.”

Mr. Darcy looked a little embarrassed by his aunt’s rudeness, and made no reply.

When coffee was finished, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth that she had promised to play for him, and she went at once to the instrument. He drew a chair close by. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, and then, as before, spoke to her other nephew; until the latter left her. With his usual deliberation he then walked toward the pianoforte and took his place so that he could command a full view of the fair performer’s face. Elizabeth understood what he was doing, and at the first convenient pause turned toward him with an arch smile and said,—

“You mean to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming in all this state to hear me. But I will not be alarmed, even if your sister _does_ play so well. There is a stubbornness in me that can never endure being frightened at the bidding of others. My courage always grows stronger with every attempt to intimidate me.”

“I shall not pretend that you are mistaken,” he replied, “for you could not truly suppose I meant to alarm you; and I have had the pleasure of knowing you long enough to be sure that you take great satisfaction in sometimes stating opinions which, in truth, are not your own.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at the likeness of herself, and said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, “Your cousin will give you a very charming idea of me, and teach you not to believe a word I say. I am particularly unfortunate in meeting with someone so well placed to uncover my real character, in a part of the world where I had hoped to pass myself off with at least some credit.”"}

{"request_id":"63112f3bb4311cb224c03ffc","rewritten_text":"The night was dark and stormy. Around the high throne, not a single star even seemed to tremble. Instead, loud thunder kept rumbling in the ears, and terrible lightning flashed through the cloudy sky in an angry mood, as if it mocked the power that the famous Franklin had tried to use to control its fear. Even the rough winds seemed to come out together from their hidden places, blowing and shouting as though they wanted to make the scene even wilder.

In a time like this—so dark, so miserable—I felt my spirit sink with sorrow for human suffering; but then, instead of that,

“My dearest friend, my counsellor, my comforter and guide— My joy in grief, my second bliss in joy,”

came to my side.

She moved like one of the bright beings people imagine in the sunny gardens of fancy’s Eden, the kind romantic young hearts love to picture. She stepped so softly that she made no sound at all. If not for the special thrill her kind touch gave me, she might have slipped away unnoticed, like other quiet beauties who are not looked for. A strange sadness sat on her face, like cold tears on the robe of December. She pointed outside at the fighting elements and told me to look at the two forces she had set before me.

This nightmare took up about ten pages of manuscript, and it ended with a sermon so harsh against non-Presbyterians that it won first prize. Everyone agreed it was the best work of the evening. When the mayor of the village handed the prize to the author, he gave a warm speech. He said it was far the most “eloquent” thing he had ever heard, and that Daniel Webster himself might be proud of it.

It may be noted, in passing, that the number of compositions that overused the word “beauteous,” and that talked about human experience as “life’s page,” was about the usual amount.

Now the master, calm and almost friendly, pushed his chair aside. He turned his back to the audience and began drawing a map of America on the blackboard, to keep the geography class busy. But he struggled with it because his hand was unsteady. A quiet ripple of laughter spread through the room. He knew what was happening, and tried to fix it. He wiped out the lines and redrew them, but he only made them worse, and the laughter grew louder. He focused hard on his work, as if determined not to be defeated by the amusement. He felt that everyone was watching him. He believed he was doing better, yet the laughter continued—and it even clearly increased."}

{"request_id":"7c6faceabcaaf48178f5f6c7","rewritten_text":"The exquisite gentlemen of the finest breeding wore small dangling trinkets that chimed as they moved languidly; their golden fetters rang like precious little bells; and between that ringing and the rustle of silk and brocade and fine linen, there was a flutter in the air that fanned Saint Antoine and his devouring hunger far away.

Dress was the one reliable talisman and charm used to keep everything in its proper place. Everyone was dressed for a Fancy Ball that was never meant to end. From the Palace of the Tuileries, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the Tribunals of Justice, and all society (except the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball descended to the Common Executioner—who, in keeping with the charm, was required to officiate “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe was a rarity—Monsieur Paris, as it was the episcopal style among his fellow Professors in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest, presided in that dainty outfit. And who among the company at Monseigneur’s reception in that seventeen hundred and eightieth year of our Lord could possibly doubt that a system rooted in a frizzled hangman, powdered, gold-laced, pumped, and white-silk stockinged, would see the very stars out!

After Monseigneur had relieved his four men of their burdens and taken his chocolate, he had the doors of the Holiest of Holiests thrown open, and he came out. Then what submission, what cringing and fawning, what servility, what abject humiliation! As for bowing down in body and spirit, nothing of that sort was left for Heaven—which may have been one of the reasons the worshippers of Monseigneur never bothered with it.

With a word of promise here and a smile there, a whisper to one happy slave and a wave of the hand to another, Monseigneur passed affably through his rooms to the remote region of the Circumference of Truth. There, Monseigneur turned and came back again, and in due course of time got himself shut up in his sanctuary by the chocolate sprites, and was seen no more.

When the show was over, the flutter in the air became a little storm, and the precious little bells went ringing downstairs. Soon there was only one person left from the whole crowd, and he, with his hat under his arm and his snuff-box in his hand, slowly made his way out, passing among the mirrors.

“I devote you,” said this person, stopping at the last door on his way and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

With that, he shook the snuff from his fingers as if he were shaking dust from his feet, and quietly walked downstairs."}
