{"request_id":"0000f552fd6802b22fef1e12","rewritten_text":"Could our lofty dreams have been meant to vanish so? Our name had been set “a little lower than the angels,” and, see now, we were no better than fleeting breath. We had styled ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and lo! we turned out to be a “quint-essence of dust.” We grieved that the pyramids endured longer than the embalmed body of their maker. And yet, on the road, the simple shepherd’s hut of straw we passed held within its very frame a rule of greater staying-power than the entire race of man. How can one square this bitter shift with our former hopes, with the seeming strength we once possessed?

Then, suddenly, an inward voice—plain and distinct—seemed to declare:—So from eternity it was decreed; the steeds that carry Time onward have this hour and its fulfilment bound upon them, since the void brought forth its burden. Would you try to read backward the unalterable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Omnipotent! eternal, unchanging Necessity! You, with busy fingers, sit ever weaving the unbreakable chain of events! I will not complain of thy doings. If my human mind cannot admit that whatever is, is right; still, since what is must be, I will take my place among the ruins and smile. Truly, we were not fashioned for enjoyment, but for submission—and for hope.

Will the reader grow weary, if I set down our long, drawn-out passage from Paris to Geneva? If, day by day, I should write—like a journal—the crowding miseries of our lot, could my hand find words, or language grant terms, to show the many shapes of our woe; the pressing and jostling of one dreadful occurrence upon another? Patience, O reader, whoever thou art, wherever thou dwellest—whether of a spiritual kind, or sprung from some pair that survived—your nature will still be human, your dwelling the earth. Here you will read the deeds of the extinct race, and you will wonder, as you look on what you find recorded, whether those who endured it were of frail flesh and tender organization like your own. Most certainly they were—so weep; for surely, being alone, you will be of a gentle temper: shed compassionate tears; yet, while you do, lend your attention to the tale, and learn the acts and sufferings of your forebears.

Still, the last events that marked our progress through France were so steeped in strange terror and dark misery that I cannot linger long over the telling. If I were to break down each incident, every small fragment of a second would carry an appalling story, and even the least word would chill the blood in your young veins. It is fitting that I raise for your instruction this monument to the race that has gone before; but not that I should drag you through the wards of an hospital, nor into the hidden rooms of the charnel-house."}

{"request_id":"b684f54f46d58cbd973b023d","rewritten_text":"“Next, we built a wire fence.”

“Wire fence?”

“Yes. You yourself dropped the hint about it, two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember—the time the Church tried to test its strength against us the first time, and then decided it was wise to wait for a more hopeful season. So how have you arranged the fence?”

“I start twelve immensely strong wires—bare, not insulated—from a big dynamo in the cave—dynamo with no brushes except a positive and a negative one—”

“Yes, that’s right.”

“The wires go out from the cave and fence in a circle of level ground a hundred yards across; they form twelve independent fences, ten feet apart—that is, twelve circles inside circles—and their ends come back into the cave again.”

“Right; go on.”

“The fences are fastened to heavy oaken posts only three feet apart, and those posts are sunk five feet into the ground.”

“That’s good and strong.”

“Yes. The wires have no ground connection outside the cave. They go out from the positive brush of the dynamo; there’s a ground connection through the negative brush; the other ends of each wire return to the cave, and each one is grounded independently.”

“No, no, that won’t do!”

“Why?”

“It’s too expensive—it wastes force for nothing. You don’t want any ground connection except the one through the negative brush. The other end of every wire has to be brought back into the cave and fastened independently, and without any ground connection. Now, then, look at the economy of it. A cavalry charge throws itself at the fence; you’re using no power, spending no money, because there’s only one ground connection until those horses hit the wire. The moment they touch it, they make a connection with the negative brush through the ground, and they drop dead. Don’t you see?—you’re using no energy until it’s needed; your lightning is there, ready like the load in a gun, but it isn’t costing you a cent until you fire it. Oh, yes—the single ground connection—”

“Of course! I don’t know how I overlooked that. It’s not only cheaper, but more effective than the other way, because if wires break or get tangled, no harm is done.”

“No, especially if we have a tell-tale in the cave and disconnect the broken wire. Well, go on. The gatlings?”

“Yes—that’s arranged. In the center of the inner circle, on a spacious platform six feet high, I’ve grouped a battery of thirteen gatling guns, and provided plenty of ammunition.”

“That’s it. They’ll cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, there’ll be music. The brow of the precipice over the cave—”

“I’ve got a wire fence there, and a gatling.”"}

{"request_id":"f81e0427c635ecc0933ef608","rewritten_text":"“Listen, then! You!” returned Monks. “His father fell ill in Rome, and was joined there by his wife—my mother—who had been separated from him for a long time. She left Paris and brought me with her, to look after his property, as far as I know; for she had no real affection for him, and he had none for her. He knew nothing of us, because his senses were gone, and he slept on until the next day, when he died. Among the papers in his desk were two, dated the night his illness first began, addressed to yourself”—he turned to Mr. Brownlow—“and enclosed in a few short lines to you, with a note on the outside of the package saying it was not to be forwarded until after he was dead. One of those papers was a letter to this girl, Agnes; the other was a will.

“What about the letter?” asked Mr. Brownlow.

“The letter?—A sheet of paper crossed and crossed again, with a confession written over and over, and prayers to God to help her. He had told the girl a story—that some secret mystery, to be explained one day, prevented him from marrying her just then—and so she went on trusting him patiently, until she trusted too far and lost what no one could ever give back. At that time she was only a few months from giving birth. He told her everything he had meant to do, to hide her shame if he had lived, and prayed her, if he died, not to curse his memory or think that the consequences of their sin would be visited on her or their young child; for all the guilt was his. He reminded her of the day he had given her the little locket and the ring with her Christian name engraved upon it, and a blank left for that which he hoped one day to bestow upon her—prayed her yet to keep it and wear it next her heart, as she had done before—and then he went on, wildly, in the same words, over and over again, as if he had lost his mind. I believe he had.

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, as Oliver’s tears fell fast.

Monks was silent.

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, speaking for him, “was in the same spirit as the letter. He talked about the miseries his wife had brought on him; about the rebellious disposition, vice, malice, and your premature bad passions—his only son—who had been trained to hate him; and he left you, and your mother, each an annuity of eight hundred pounds. He divided the bulk of his property into two equal portions—one for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, if it should be born alive, and ever come of age.”}"}

{"request_id":"9713a7878553a21ea8b588f4","rewritten_text":"Mr. Attorney-General had to tell the jury that the prisoner in front of them, though young, was already old in the treasonous practices that should cost him his life. He said this correspondence with the public enemy was not something that had started recently—today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. It was certain the prisoner had been traveling back and forth between France and England for longer than that, on secret business he could not explain honestly. If treasonous behavior had been the kind that could thrive, then the real wrongdoing behind his actions might have stayed hidden. But Providence had put it in the heart of a person who was fearless and above reproach to uncover what the prisoner was planning. Horrified by it, this person reported everything to his Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and to the most honorable Privy Council. That patriot would now be brought before the jury.

Mr. Attorney-General said the man’s position and attitude were, in general, sublime. He had been the prisoner’s friend, but at a time that was both promising and dangerous, he had recognized the prisoner’s dishonesty. He decided to destroy the traitor he could no longer protect in his own home, offering him up on the sacred altar of his country. If Britain made statues for public benefactors the way ancient Greece and Rome did, this shining citizen would surely have one. Since Britain did not do that, he probably would not.

He added that virtue, as the poets had said in many lines the jury knew by heart, was contagious. The jury’s faces showed a guilty awareness that they did not actually know those lines. He said especially that patriotism—the love of one’s country—spreads from person to person. The high example of this spotless, unimpeachable witness for the Crown, whom it was an honor to mention, though he did so in a way that was not worthy, had passed to the prisoner’s servant. It led the servant to decide, with a holy determination, to search the prisoner’s table drawers and pockets, and to hide away his papers.

Mr. Attorney-General said he was ready to hear that this admirable servant had been criticized, but that, in general, he preferred him to his own brothers and sisters. He honored him more than his own father and mother. He urged the jury, with confidence, to do the same. He said the testimony of these two witnesses, along with the documents showing what they discovered, would prove that the prisoner had been given lists of his Majesty’s forces and how they were arranged and prepared, both by sea and by land. He said this would leave no doubt that the prisoner had regularly passed such information to a hostile power."}

{"request_id":"f4375a54ee96c4733b5c15e4","rewritten_text":"One day, while I was occupied with my books and Mr. Pocket, a letter came by post, and the very outside of it set me in a great flutter; for although I had never before seen the handwriting in which it was addressed, I could tell whose hand it was. It did not open in any regular way—no “Dear Mr. Pip,” or “Dear Pip,” or “Dear Sir,” or “Dear Anything”—but went on thus:—

“I am to come to London the day after to-morrow by the midday coach. I believe it was settled you should meet me? At all events Miss Havisham has that impression, and I write in obedience to it. She sends you her regard.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

Had there been time, I might have ordered several suits of clothes for the occasion; but since there was none, I had to make do with what I already had. My appetite disappeared at once, and I could find no ease or rest until the day came. Yet even when it arrived, I was no better; I grew worse, and began prowling about the coach-office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. I knew, of course, that I was being perfectly unreasonable, but still I felt as though it would not be safe to let the coach-office out of my sight for more than five minutes at a time. In that state of folly I had already done the first half-hour of a watch that was to last four or five hours, when Wemmick ran into me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” said he; “how do you do? I shouldn’t have thought this was _your_ beat.”

I told him I was waiting to meet someone who was coming up by coach, and I asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both flourishing, thankye,” said Wemmick, “and particularly the Aged. He’s in wonderful feather. He’ll be eighty-two next birthday. I have a notion of firing eighty-two times, if the neighbourhood shouldn’t complain, and that cannon of mine should stand up to the strain. But this isn’t London talk. Where do you suppose I’m going?”

“To the office?” I said, for he was making straight for it.

“Next thing to it,” returned Wemmick. “I’m going to Newgate. We’re in a banker’s-parcel scrape just now, and I’ve been down the road taking a look at the scene of action, and so I must have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” answered Wemmick, very quietly. “But he’s accused of it. So might you or I be. Either of us might be accused of it, you know.”"}

{"request_id":"9de5036cb2c6ddbb093ce599","rewritten_text":"At that moment, his eyes—and mine as well—fell on a scrap of parchment, which I first took to be paper. It lay half buried in the sand, with one corner sticking up. Near where we found it, I noticed the remains of the hull of what looked like a ship’s longboat. The wreck seemed to have been there for a very long time, because you could hardly make out the shape of the boat timbers anymore.

“Well, Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Not long after that, we started back home and, along the way, met Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he begged me to let him take it to the fort. When I agreed, he immediately put it into his waistcoat pocket, but without the parchment that had been wrapped around it. I kept holding that parchment in my hand while he looked at the beetle. Maybe he feared I would change my mind, and thought it was safer to secure the prize right away. You know how excited he gets about anything connected to Natural History. At the same time, without realizing it, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket.

“You remember that when I went to the table to make a sketch of the beetle, I found no paper where it was usually kept. I checked the drawer, and there was none there either. I searched my pockets, hoping to find an old letter, and then my hand touched the parchment. That is why I’m explaining the exact way I came to have it; the circumstances made a strong impression on me.

“No doubt you’ll think I’m being fanciful, but I had already made a kind of connection. I had put together two links in a chain. There was a boat on a seacoast, and not far from the boat was a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn on it. You’ll probably ask, ‘Where is the connection?’ I answer that the skull, or death’s-head, is the well-known symbol of pirates. The death’s-head flag is raised in all their battles.

“I said the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment lasts a long time—almost forever. Things of little importance are rarely written on parchment, because for ordinary drawing or writing it isn’t nearly as suitable as paper. This made me think there was some meaning, some relevance, in the death’s-head. I also noticed the shape of the parchment. Even though one corner had been damaged by some accident, you could still tell it was originally oblong.”}"}

{"request_id":"6d7d455d582e8d8459c6c6d3","rewritten_text":"Mr. Darcy spoke with warm praise of his sister’s skill.

“I’m very glad to hear such a good report of her,” said Lady Catherine. “And please tell her for me that she can’t expect to excel unless she practises a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he replied, “that she doesn’t need advice like that. She practises very consistently.”

“Even better. It can never be done too much; and when I next write to her, I shall tell her not to neglect it for any reason. I often tell young ladies that no excellence in music can be achieved without constant practice. I’ve told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play really well unless she practises more; and although Mrs. Collins has no instrument, she’s very welcome, as I’ve often told her, to come to Rosings every day and play on the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. She wouldn’t be in anyone’s way in that part of the house.”

Mr. Darcy looked a little ashamed of his aunt’s bad manners and said nothing.

When the coffee was finished, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth of her promise to play for him, and she sat down at once at the instrument. He pulled a chair close to her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, and then, as before, spoke to her other nephew, until the latter walked away from her. With his usual deliberate care, he moved toward the pianoforte and positioned himself so that he could get a full view of the fair performer’s face. Elizabeth noticed what he was doing, and at the first convenient pause turned to him with an arch smile and said,—

“You mean to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming in all this formality just to hear me. But I won’t be intimidated, even if your sister does play so well. There’s a stubbornness in me that can never stand being frightened at the will of other people. My courage always grows with every attempt to intimidate me.”

“I won’t say you’re wrong,” he replied, “because you couldn’t really believe I would have any intention of alarming you; and I’ve had the pleasure of knowing you long enough to understand that you take great enjoyment in sometimes stating opinions that, in fact, aren’t your own.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this picture of herself, and said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, “Your cousin will give you a very flattering idea of me and teach you not to believe a word I say. I’m especially unlucky in meeting someone so capable of exposing my true character, in a part of the world where I’d hoped to pass myself off with at least some credibility.”"}

{"request_id":"ca2562b94289016f2f95ae52","rewritten_text":"After we saw our friend properly settled in his new office, we turned our attention to Windsor. Windsor was so close to London that leaving Raymond and Perdita did not feel like a painful separation. We said goodbye to them at the Protectoral Palace. It was very moving to watch my sister step into her role as if she truly belonged in the drama, and try to carry herself with the dignity her position required. Her pride and her humility were now in conflict more than ever. Her shyness was not something she pretended; it came from her fear of not being valued, and from the way she seemed to think the world did not truly notice her. Raymond had the same kind of attitude. But Perdita thought about other people more often than he did, and part of her bashfulness came from a wish to keep those around her from feeling inferior. That feeling never once crossed her own mind.

Because of how she was born and educated, Idris would probably have been better suited to formal ceremonies. Still, the ease with which she could do those things, because she was used to them, made them feel dull. Even with all the drawbacks, Perdita clearly enjoyed her situation. She was too full of new ideas to feel much pain when we left. She said goodbye to us warmly, promised to visit soon, and yet she did not regret the circumstances that caused our separation.

Raymond’s spirits were high. He did not know what to do with his new power. His head was full of plans, and he had not chosen any yet, but he promised himself, his friends, and the world that the start of his protectorship would be marked by an act of extraordinary glory. So we talked about them and tried to make sense of it all, as we returned to Windsor Castle with fewer people than before. We felt great relief at escaping political trouble, and we threw ourselves into our private life with even more energy. We did not lack for things to do. My own eagerness was now directed only toward intellectual work. I found that hard study was an excellent cure for the restless fever of the mind that, in idleness, would surely have taken hold of me. Perdita had let us take Clara back with us to Windsor, and she, along with Perdita and my two lovely infants, was a constant source of interest and amusement.

The only thing that disturbed our peace was Adrian’s health. It clearly was getting worse, and there were no signs that would have made us suspect his illness—unless, perhaps, his brighter eyes, lively look, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption. Still, he had no pain and no fear. He threw himself into books with great energy, and when he rested from study, he did so with the company he loved most: his sister and me."}

{"request_id":"36f7a5f87c94aa7d8a707470","rewritten_text":"Wake up later on and look around to see what caused it. You might even spot a steamboat coughing along upstream, so far off toward the other side that you couldn’t tell anything about her—only whether she was a stern-wheel or a side-wheel. Then, for about an hour, there would be nothing to hear and nothing to see, just solid loneliness. After that, you’d see a raft sliding by, way out there, and maybe a man on it chopping, because they’re always doing it on a raft. You’d see the axe flash and come down. You wouldn’t hear anything at first. You’d watch the axe rise again, and by the time it was above the man’s head you’d finally hear the k’chunk!—because it took all that time for the sound to travel over the water.

So we would spend the day drifting and lounging around, listening to the quiet. Once there was a thick fog, and the rafts and other things passing by were beating tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run over them. A scow or a raft would come by so close we could hear the people talking, cussing, and laughing—we could hear them clearly—but we couldn’t see any sign of them. It made you feel uneasy, like spirits carrying on out in the air. Jim said he believed it was spirits, but I said:

“No. Spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

The moment night came, we shoved off. When we got the raft out to about the middle, we left it alone and let it float wherever the current wanted. Then we lit the pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all kinds of things. We were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes would let us. The new clothes Buck’s folks made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and besides, I didn’t care much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we’d have the whole river to ourselves for the longest time. Over there were the banks and the islands, across the water. Maybe you’d see a spark—like a candle in a cabin window. And sometimes, out on the water, you could see one or two sparks on a raft or a scow. You might even hear a fiddle or a song coming from one of those boats. It’s lovely to live on a raft. Up in the sky there were stars scattered all over, and we used to lie on our backs and look up at them, talking about whether they were made or if they just happened. Jim said they were made, but I said they happened. I figured it would have taken too long to make that many."}

{"request_id":"a27c5b9a7136b728a8d33c91","rewritten_text":"His account was that, after leaving home and passing through Datchet, he was surprised to see smoke coming from the inn’s chimney. He thought he might find other people traveling with him, so he knocked and was let in. There was no one in the house except Lucy and her mother. Her mother had been left unable to use her limbs by rheumatism, and because of that, one by one, the rest of the people in the country had gone away, leaving Lucy and her mother alone.

Lucy begged the man to stay with her. In a week or two her mother would be better, and then they could set out together. But, she said, they would surely die if they were left helpless and alone. The man replied that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, and that, in his view, he could not stay.

As a last resort, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, to be delivered to her wherever he might meet us. He carried out this task at least, and Idris received the following letter with deep feeling:—

“HONOURED LADY,

“I am sure you will remember me and feel sorry for me, and I dare hope you will help me. What other hope do I have? Please forgive the way I write. I am so confused. A month ago my dear mother was left unable to use her limbs. She is already better, and in another month I am sure she will be able to travel, in the way you were kind enough to say you would arrange for us. But now everyone has gone—everyone. As they left, each person said that perhaps my mother would be better before we were completely deserted.

“Three days ago I went to Samuel Woods. He stayed until the last because of his newborn child, and since they have a large family, I thought I could persuade them to wait a little longer for us. But I found the house empty. I have not seen a single person since this good man came. What will become of us? My mother does not know our situation. She is so ill that I have hidden it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? I am sure we must perish miserably as we are. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road. And if, when she gets better, I were able to travel, I cannot even imagine how I would find the roads and make so many miles to the sea. You would all be in France by then, and the great ocean would be between us, which is so frightening even for sailors.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"b1e9f3795f928cfbea5a6639","rewritten_text":"Mr. Attorney-General had to tell the jury that the prisoner before them, though young in years, was old in the treasonable practices that had brought about the forfeiture of his life. That this correspondence with the public enemy was not correspondence from today, or yesterday, or even from last year, or from the year before that. That it was certain the prisoner had, for longer than that, been in the habit of going back and forth between France and England on secret business for which he could give no honest account. That if it were in the nature of traitorous ways to thrive (which, happily, they never did), the true wickedness and guilt of his business might have remained undiscovered. Providence, however, had put it into the heart of a person who was beyond fear and beyond reproach to uncover the nature of the prisoner’s schemes, and, struck with horror, to disclose them to his Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and the most honourable Privy Council. That this patriot would be produced before them. That his bearing and attitude were, on the whole, sublime. That he had been the prisoner’s friend, but at once, in a fortunate and an evil hour, detecting his infamy, he had resolved to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer cherish in his own bosom on the sacred altar of his country. That if statues were decreed in Britain, as in ancient Greece and Rome, to public benefactors, this shining citizen would surely have one. That, since such statues were not decreed, he probably would not. That virtue, as the poets had observed (in many passages which he knew the jury would have on the tip of their tongues word for word), was in a way contagious; especially the bright virtue known as patriotism, or love of country. That the lofty example of this spotless and unimpeachable witness for the Crown—whom, however unworthily, it was an honour to mention—had spread to the prisoner’s servant, and had stirred in him a holy determination to search his master’s table-drawers and pockets and to hide away his papers. That he (Mr. Attorney-General) was ready to hear some attempt to disparage this admirable servant; but that, in general, he preferred him to his (Mr. Attorney-General’s) brothers and sisters, and valued him more than his (Mr. Attorney-General’s) father and mother. That he called on the jury, with confidence, to do likewise. That the evidence of these two witnesses, together with the documents showing their discovery, would demonstrate that the prisoner had been furnished with lists of his Majesty’s forces and their disposition and preparation, both by sea and land, and would leave no doubt that he had habitually conveyed such information to a hostile power."}

{"request_id":"692942cfff02b66543abacbc","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten o’clock at night?”

“Yes, sir. Your honor told me to call you.”

“Oh! I remember. Very well, very well.”

After a few dull attempts to get to sleep again—which the man skillfully fought by stirring the fire nonstop for five minutes—he got up, tossed his hat on, and walked out. He turned into the Temple, and, having refreshed himself by pacing King’s Bench-walk and Paper-buildings twice, he went into the Stryver chambers.

The Stryver clerk, who never helped with these conferences, had gone home, and the Stryver principal opened the door. He had his slippers on, and a loose bed-gown, and his throat was bare for his comfort. He had that rather wild, strained, scorched look around the eyes, which you can see in all free drinkers of his class, from the portrait of Jeffries downward, and which can be traced, under various disguises of Art, through the portraits of every Drinking Age.

“You’re a little late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the usual time; it might be a quarter of an hour later.”

They went into a dingy room lined with books and scattered with papers, where a fire was blazing. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the wreck of papers a table shone, with plenty of wine on it, and brandy, and rum, and sugar, and lemons.

“I see you’ve had your bottle, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I think. I’ve been dining with the day’s client; or watching him dine—it’s all the same!”

“That was a rare point, Sydney, that you brought to bear on the identification. How did you come by it? When did it hit you?”

“I thought he was rather a handsome fellow, and I thought I’d be much the same kind of fellow if I’d had any luck.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until he shook his precocious paunch.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

Sullenly enough, the jackal loosened his dress, went into the adjoining room, and came back with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. He soaked the towels in the water, wrung them out only partly, folded them on his head in a way hideous to behold, sat down at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“Not much boiling down to be done tonight, Memory,” said Mr. Stryver cheerfully, as he looked through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets of them.”

“Give me the worst first.”

“There they are, Sydney. Fire away!”

The lion then settled himself on his back on a sofa to one side of the drinking-table, while the jackal sat at his own paper-strewn table on the other side, with the bottles and glasses ready to his hand."}

{"request_id":"2428ec65ec0e75c6b6bf1441","rewritten_text":"“Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,” the old lady called out when he came into the room, “why haven’t you come to see me at all this time?”

“My dear Lady Clem, I never seem to have a moment to myself,” said Lord Arthur, smiling.

“I suppose you mean you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton—picking up chiffons and talking nonsense. I can’t see why people make such a fuss about being married. In my day, we never dreamed of billing and cooing in public, or even in private.”

“I assure you I haven’t seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her milliners.”

“Exactly—that’s the only reason you come to visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder you men don’t take warning. On a fait des folies pour moi, and here I am, a poor rheumatic creature, with a false front and a bad temper. Why, if it weren’t for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me all the worst French novels she can get hold of, I don’t think I could get through the day. Doctors are no good at all, except to take fees. They can’t even cure my heartburn.”

“I’ve brought you something to ease that, Lady Clem,” said Lord Arthur gravely. “It’s a wonderful thing—an invention from America.”

“I don’t care for American inventions, Arthur. I’m quite sure I don’t. I’ve read a few American novels lately, and they were nothing but nonsense.”

“Oh, but there’s no nonsense in this, Lady Clem! I assure you it’s a perfect cure. You must promise to try it.” And Lord Arthur drew the little box from his pocket and handed it to her.

“Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it truly a present? That’s very kind of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks just like a bonbon. I’ll take it at once.”

“Good heavens, Lady Clem!” Lord Arthur cried, catching her hand. “You mustn’t do that. It’s homoeopathic medicine, and if you take it when you aren’t suffering heartburn, it may do you no end of harm. Wait until you have an attack, and then take it. You’ll be astonished by the result.”

“I’d rather take it now,” said Lady Clementina, holding the little transparent capsule up to the light, watching the floating bubble of liquid aconitine. “I’m sure it’s delicious. The truth is, though I dislike doctors, I do love medicines. Still, I’ll keep it for my next attack.”

“And when will that be?” Lord Arthur asked eagerly."}

{"request_id":"29c269004643835dc46456b8","rewritten_text":"But now she would rather it had not happened. She believed he had had too much of Mr. Weston’s good wine, and she was sure he would want to talk nonsense.

To keep him as restrained as she could, using her own manners, she was immediately preparing to speak with exquisite calmness and gravity about the weather and the night; but scarcely had she begun, scarcely had they passed the sweep-gate and joined the other carriage, than she found her topic cut off—her hand seized—her attention demanded—and Mr. Elton actually making violent love to her. Taking advantage of the precious opening, he declared sentiments that must already be well known, hoping—fearing—adoring—ready to die if she refused him; yet flattering himself that his ardent attachment, unequalled love, and unprecedented passion could not fail to have some effect. In short, he was very much resolved to be seriously accepted as soon as possible. It really was so. Without scruple—without apology—without much visible diffidence, Mr. Elton, the lover of Harriet, was presenting himself as her lover. She tried to stop him, but in vain; he kept going and said it all.

Angry as she was, the thought of the moment made her decide to restrain herself when she did speak. She felt that half of this folly must be drunkenness, and therefore could hope it would belong only to the passing hour. So, with a mixture of seriousness and playfulness—something she hoped would best fit his half-and-half state—she replied,

“I am very much astonished, Mr. Elton. This to me! You forget yourself—you take me for my friend. Any message to Miss Smith I shall be happy to deliver; but no more of this to me, if you please.”

“Miss Smith!—a message to Miss Smith!—What could she possibly mean!”—and he repeated her words with such confidence of accent, such boastful show of amazement, that she couldn’t help answering quickly,

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behavior! I can account for it only in one way: you are not yourself, or you could not speak either to me, or of Harriet, in such a manner. Command yourself enough to say no more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk wine enough only to lift his spirits, not at all to confuse his intellect. He knew perfectly well what he meant. After warmly protesting against her suspicion as most injurious, and lightly touching on his respect for Miss Smith as her friend—while admitting his surprise that Miss Smith should even be mentioned—he returned to the subject of his own passion, and was very urgent for a favorable answer."}

{"request_id":"1108d551d07bf847a9ace911","rewritten_text":"For a moment, I was so shocked that I couldn’t think clearly or accurately. I knew my design was different in the details, though the overall outline was similar. Soon I took a candle and sat at the other end of the room, then studied the parchment more closely. When I turned it over, I saw my own sketch on the back, exactly as I had made it.

At first, I was only surprised by how closely the outlines matched. I couldn’t ignore the strange coincidence that, without my knowing it, there was a skull on the other side of the parchment, directly beneath my figure of the _scarabæus_. Even more astonishing, the skull matched my drawing not just in outline, but in size. This coincidence stunned me completely for a time. That is what such coincidences usually do. The mind tries to connect everything, to build a chain of cause and effect. But when it can’t, it feels temporarily paralyzed.

Then, as the shock faded, a conviction began to form slowly, and it startled me even more than the coincidence itself. I started to remember clearly, positively, that when I made my sketch of the _scarabæus_, there had been no drawing on the parchment. I was sure of it. I remembered turning it over, first one side and then the other, looking for the cleanest spot. If the skull had been there at that time, of course I would have noticed it. This was a mystery I felt I couldn’t explain. Still, even then, I sensed—faintly, in the deepest and most hidden part of my mind—a kind of idea, like a glow-worm, about the truth that last night’s adventure had shown so clearly.

I stood up at once. I put the parchment away securely and stopped thinking about it until I was alone.

“When you had gone, and when Jupiter was fast asleep, I turned to a more careful investigation. First, I thought about how the parchment had come into my possession. The spot where we found the _scarabæus_ was on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island, and only a short distance above the high-water line. When I picked it up, it bit me sharply, and I had to drop it. Jupiter, as cautious as ever, before he seized the insect—after it flew toward him—looked around for a leaf, or something like that, to use as a way to hold it.”"}

{"request_id":"8bf6004d954302973830a7a4","rewritten_text":"Their arrival lit a kind of fire in Saint Antoine’s chest. It spread quickly as they moved along, stirring and flickering in the faces of people at nearly every door and window. Still, no one followed them, and when they entered the wine-shop, no man spoke. Every man’s eyes turned to them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

It may have been the cue for everyone to start talking. The room answered with a chorus of “Good day!”

“It is bad weather, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.

Then every man looked at his neighbor, and after that they all lowered their eyes and sat in silence. Only one man stood up and went out.

“My wife,” said Defarge, speaking to Madame Defarge, “I have traveled certain leagues with this good road-mender, called Jacques. I met him—by accident—about a day and a half’s journey from Paris. He is a good child, this road-mender, called Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man stood up and went out. Madame Defarge poured wine for the road-mender named Jacques. He took off his blue cap to the others, then drank. In the breast of his blouse he carried some coarse, dark bread. He ate it between sips, then sat munching and drinking near Madame Defarge’s counter. A third man stood up and went out.

Defarge took a drink of wine, but less than he gave the stranger, since it was not unusual for him to drink. He waited until the countryman had finished eating. He did not look at anyone, and no one looked at him now—not even Madame Defarge, who had picked up her knitting and kept working.

“Have you finished your meal, friend?” Defarge asked at the right moment.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Then come! You will see the room I told you you could use. It will suit you perfectly.”

They went out of the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, and from the staircase into a garret. It was the same garret where a white-haired man used to sit on a low bench, leaning forward and working hard, making shoes.

No white-haired man was there now. But the three men who had left the wine-shop one by one were there. And between them and the white-haired man far away was the one small link they had once seen him through, looking in through the cracks in the wall.

Defarge closed the door carefully and spoke in a low voice:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness encountered by appointment, by me, Jacques Four.”"}

{"request_id":"f9f7d3e32d5114ec031217b4","rewritten_text":"Many American ladies, when they leave their native country, fall into the habit of wearing an air of long-standing ill-health, believing it to be a kind of European polish; but Mrs. Otis had never made that mistake. She possessed a magnificent constitution, and an astonishing store of animal spirits. In fact, she was in many ways quite English, and served as a fine illustration of how we have everything in common with America these days—language, of course, excepted. Her eldest son, christened Washington by his parents in a burst of patriotism that he never stopped regretting, was fair-haired and rather good-looking. He had prepared himself for American diplomacy by taking the German at the Newport Casino for three seasons running, and even in London was known as an excellent dancer. Gardenias and the peerage were his only weak points. Otherwise, he was extremely sensible.

Miss Virginia E. Otis was a girl of fifteen—lithe and lovely as a fawn—with a frankness in her large blue eyes. She was a splendid amazon, and once raced old Lord Bilton on her pony twice round the park, winning by a length and a half, just ahead of the Achilles statue, to the immense delight of the young Duke of Cheshire, who proposed for her on the spot and was sent back to Eton that very night by his guardians, in floods of tears. After Virginia came the twins, usually dubbed “The Stars and Stripes,” because they were forever getting swished. They were delightful boys, and, with the exception of the worthy Minister, the only true republicans in the family.

Since Canterville Chase lay seven miles from Ascot, the nearest railway station, Mr. Otis had telegraphed for a waggonette to meet them, and they set off for their drive in high spirits. It was a beautiful July evening, and the air was delicately scented with pine-woods. Now and then they heard a wood pigeon brooding over its own sweet note, or caught sight, deep among the rustling fern, of the pheasant’s burnished breast. Little squirrels watched them from the beech-trees, and the rabbits darted away through the brushwood and over the mossy knolls, their white tails flashing in the air. Yet as they entered the avenue of Canterville Chase, the sky suddenly darkened with clouds; an odd stillness seemed to settle on the atmosphere, a great company of rooks swept silently over their heads, and before they reached the house, some heavy drops of rain had already fallen.

On the steps, ready to receive them, stood an old woman, neatly dressed in black silk, with a white cap and apron."}

{"request_id":"8a23fbe7bc7a428d10c460c6","rewritten_text":"And if he pressed me on why I wanted it, and on what grounds I believed I had any claim to it, I would have told him—though he cared little for such thin hopes—that I had loved Estella dearly and for a long time; and that even though I had lost her, and must go on living in grief, whatever touched her was still closer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. Seeing, too, that Mr. Jaggers remained quite motionless and silent, and seemed stubbornly unmoved by my appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I take you for a man with a kind heart. I’ve seen your comfortable home, and your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful ways that brighten your business life. I beg you to speak a word for me to Mr. Jaggers, and to make it plain to him that, taking all things into account, he ought to be more open with me!”

I had never witnessed two men regard one another so strangely as Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after that outburst. At first, a fear crossed my mind that Wemmick would be dismissed on the spot; but it faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers ease into something like a smile, and Wemmick grow more daring.

“What’s all this?” asked Mr. Jaggers. “You, with an old father—and you, with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” said Wemmick. “If I don’t bring ’em here, what’s the difference?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, putting his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this fellow must be the craftiest impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” answered Wemmick, becoming bolder and bolder. “I rather think you’re the other.”

Once more they exchanged those same odd looks, each still seeming to distrust the other, as if neither could quite believe he was being taken in.

“_You_ with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Provided it don’t get in the way of business,” returned Wemmick, “let it stand. And now, looking at you, sir, I shouldn’t be surprised if _you_ mean to scheme and contrive for a pleasant home of your own one of these days—when you’re done with all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded his head backward, two or three times, and even let out a sigh. “Pip,” said he, “we won’t talk about ‘poor dreams;’ you know more of that sort than I do, with my fresher experience. But now, about this other matter. I’ll lay a case before you. Mind— I admit nothing.”

He waited for me to say that I understood he had expressly meant that he admitted nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “put this case. Suppose that a woman, in the circumstances you’ve described, had kept her child hidden, and was forced to tell it to her legal adviser—who, in representing to her that he must know, with an eye to the latitude of his defence, how the matter stood regarding that child.”"}

{"request_id":"8a9239f7ea3a35266eedaaa6","rewritten_text":"Why, this hint might lead to a truly exciting bit of superstition. I suppose you will call the bug _scarabæus caput hominis_, or something like that—there are many similar names in the Natural Histories. But where are the _antennæ_ you mentioned?”

“The _antennæ_!” Legrand said, and he seemed to be getting unaccountably hot under the collar. “I’m sure you can see the _antennæ_. I made them as clear as they are in the original insect, and I think that should be enough.”

“Well, well,” I said, “maybe you have—but I still don’t see them.” Then I handed him the paper without any more comment. I didn’t want to upset him further. Still, I was very surprised by how things had turned. His bad temper confused me. And as for the drawing of the beetle, there were plainly _no antennæ_ at all. The picture looked very much like the usual drawings of a death’s-head.

He took the paper back in a very irritated way, and he was about to crumple it, as if he meant to throw it in the fire. Then, with a casual glance, he suddenly stopped and stared at the design. In an instant his face turned violently red, and then, a moment later, it became extremely pale. For several minutes he kept studying the drawing closely, sitting right where he was. At last he stood up, took a candle from the table, and went to sit on a sea-chest in the farthest corner of the room. He examined the paper again, turning it over and looking at it from every direction.

He said nothing, but his behavior greatly surprised me. Still, I thought it was safer not to make any remarks and worsen his growing mood. After a while he took a wallet from his coat pocket, put the paper carefully inside it, and then placed both in a writing-desk that he locked. He seemed calmer afterward, but his earlier excitement was gone. He didn’t seem so much angry as lost in thought. As the evening went on, he became more and more absorbed in his reverie, and nothing I said could pull him out of it.

I had planned to spend the night at the hut, as I often had before. But seeing my host like this, I decided it was best to leave. He didn’t try to persuade me to stay. When I went, he shook my hand with even more than his usual warmth.

About a month later—during the time when I hadn’t seen Legrand at all—I received a visit in Charleston from his man, Jupiter. I had never seen the old negro look so downhearted, and I feared that something serious had happened to my friend."}

{"request_id":"8cbe9f80a9adea71e6c56194","rewritten_text":"Knights and their horses, clad in heavy armor, couldn’t make much speed. Still, they’d do as well as they could; now that the ground was firm and there was neither snow nor mud, they might manage a seven-mile pace. They’d have to swap horses a time or two, and they ought to reach us around six o’clock, or just after. That would leave plenty of daylight, and they’d spot the white cloth I’d tie around my right arm, and then I’d take command. We’d close in on that prison and have the king out before long. It would look striking and picturesque enough, given the circumstances, though I would have preferred midday, if only because the whole business would have had a more theatrical air to it.

Now, to build up the strings for my bow, I figured I’d go and find some of the people I’d recognized earlier, and let them know me. That should help us out of our scrape, even without the knights. But I had to be careful—this was a touchy undertaking. I needed to dress in rich finery, and it wouldn’t do to dash and leap into it. No, I’d have to work up to it gradually: buying one outfit after another, in shops set well apart, and getting a finer piece each time, until I finally reached silk and velvet and was set for my plan. So I began.

But the whole scheme collapsed like a puff of smoke. The first corner I turned, I ran straight into one of our slaves, hanging about with a watchman. I cleared my throat at that instant, and he gave me a look so sharp it seemed to go straight through my bones. I take it he thought he’d heard that cough before. I immediately ducked into a shop and moved along the counter, checking prices and keeping an eye on things from the corner of my vision. Those fellows had paused; they were talking among themselves and peering in at the door. I decided I’d slip out the back way, if there was one, and I asked the shopwoman whether I might step out there and look for the escaped slave—supposed to be hiding somewhere back behind. I told her I was an officer in disguise, and that my partner was waiting at the door with one of the murderers under his charge. Would she be kind enough to go tell him he needn’t wait, but should head at once to the far end of the back alley, so he could be met and stopped when I went to roust him out.

She was practically bursting with eagerness to see one of those already famous murderers, and she set off on the errand right away."}

{"request_id":"7ff77c55047cf4e14b03dfa4","rewritten_text":"“‘We’ve been to your residence,’ said the first. ‘We weren’t fortunate enough to find you there, and we were told you were probably walking in this direction, so we followed in the hope of catching up. Will you please get into the carriage?’

“The way both of them spoke was commanding, and as they said it they moved so that I was positioned between them and the carriage door. They were armed. I was not.

“‘Gentlemen,’ said I, ‘pardon me; but I usually ask who it is that has the honour to seek my assistance, and what the matter is that I’m being summoned to address.’

“The second man answered. ‘Doctor, your clients are people of standing. As for the nature of the case, our confidence in your skill assures us that you’ll understand it for yourself better than we can describe it. That’s enough. Will you please get into the carriage?’

“I could do nothing but comply, and I got in in silence. They both got in after me—the last one springing in after putting up the steps. The carriage turned around and drove on at its former speed.

“I repeat this conversation exactly as it happened. I have no doubt it is, word for word, the same. I set down everything exactly as it took place, forcing my mind not to drift from the task. Where I make the broken marks that follow here, I stop for the time being, and put my paper back in its hiding-place.

*****

“The carriage left the streets behind, passed the North Barrier, and came out onto the country road. At two-thirds of a league from the Barrier—I didn’t measure the distance then, but later, when I traversed it—it turned off from the main avenue and soon stopped at a solitary house. We all three got out and walked, along a damp, soft footpath in a garden where a neglected fountain had overflowed, to the door of the house. It wasn’t opened right away in response to the ringing of the bell, and one of my two conductors struck the man who opened it across the face with his heavy riding glove.

“There was nothing in this action that particularly caught my attention, because I had seen common people struck more often than dogs. But the other of the two, also angry, struck the man in the same way with his arm; and the look and bearing of the brothers were so exactly alike that it was then I first realized they were twin brothers.

“From the moment we got down at the outer gate—which we found locked, and which one of the brothers had opened to let us in and then relocked—I had heard cries coming from an upper room.”"}

{"request_id":"f6496cd72466f11a6c705b11","rewritten_text":"“I’m going, Mr. Will—yes, I am,” the negro answered quickly. “I’m out to the end now.”

“Out to the end!” Legrand shouted. “Do you mean you’re out to the end of that branch?”

“Soon to the end, sir—o-o-o-o-oh! Lord, mercy! what is this thing up in the tree?”

“Well!” Legrand said, very pleased. “What is it?”

“It ain’t nothing but a skull. Somebody left it up there with its head in the tree, and the crows have eaten every bit of the meat off.”

“A skull, you say! All right—how is it attached to the branch? What keeps it there?”

“Sure enough, sir. I have to look. This is a strange thing, I swear—there’s a big nail in the skull that holds it to the tree.”

“Well, Jupiter, do exactly what I tell you. Do you hear me?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Listen, then. Find the skull’s left eye.”

“Hum! What? There ain’t no left eye at all.”

“Curse your foolishness! Do you know your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I know that. I know all about it. It’s my left hand that I chop the wood with.”

“Then of course you’re left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now, I suppose you can find the skull’s left eye—or where the left eye used to be. Have you found it?”

There was a long pause. At last the negro asked, “Is the skull’s left eye on the same side as the skull’s left hand, too? ’Cause the skull don’t have any hand at all. Never mind! I got the left eye now—here it is. What do I do with it?”

“Let the beetle drop through it, as far as the string will reach—but don’t let go of the string.”

“All done, Mr. Will. That’s easy enough. I’ll put the bug out through the hole. Watch out for it down there!”

During this talk, Jupiter’s body couldn’t be seen at all. But the beetle he had let down was now visible at the end of the string, shining like a globe of polished gold in the last rays of the setting sun. Those rays still faintly lit the hill where we stood. The scarab hung clear of any branches, and if it were allowed to fall, it would drop right at our feet. Legrand immediately took the scythe and cleared a circular patch, three or four yards across, directly under the insect. Then he told Jupiter to let go of the string and come down from the tree.”}"}

{"request_id":"1b4f88d3219359aa4e613da3","rewritten_text":"“What’s wrong?” Oliver demanded.

“Hush!” the Dodger replied. “Do you see that old man at the book stall?”

“The old gentleman across the street?” Oliver said. “Yes, I see him.”

“He’ll do,” said the Dodger.

“A good choice,” Master Charley Bates added.

Oliver looked from one boy to the other, shocked, but he wasn’t allowed to ask questions. The two boys moved quietly across the road and slipped close behind the old gentleman they had pointed out. Oliver followed a few steps behind them. Not knowing whether to come closer or back away, he just stood there, staring in silent amazement.

The old gentleman looked very respectable. He had a powdered head and wore gold spectacles. He was dressed in a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar, had white trousers, and kept a smart bamboo cane tucked under his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood there reading as if he were in his own study, in his favorite chair. It was easy to believe he thought he was there, too. From the way he was absorbed, it was clear he wasn’t seeing the book stall, the street, the boys, or anything else—only the book. He read straight through, turning the page when he reached the bottom, starting at the top line of the next page, and continuing with real interest and eagerness.

Oliver’s fear turned to horror as he watched from a few paces away, eyes wide open. He saw the Dodger reach into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief. Then he handed it to Charley Bates. After that, both boys ran away around the corner at full speed.

In an instant, the whole mystery of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewels, and the Jew came rushing into Oliver’s mind.

For a moment he stood frozen, his blood pounding with terror, feeling as if he were trapped in a burning fire. Then he got confused and frightened and ran as fast as he could, not even knowing what he was doing.

It all happened in a minute. The moment Oliver started running, the old gentleman reached into his pocket, realized the handkerchief was gone, and turned sharply around. Seeing the boy sprinting away, he naturally assumed the boy was the thief. He shouted, “Stop thief!” as loudly as he could, and ran after him with his book still in his hand."}

{"request_id":"ebbdce44611458f9c709e14","rewritten_text":"“Nothing but a tick.”

“Where’d you get him?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What’ll you take for him?”

“I don’t know. I don’t want to sell him.”

“All right. It’s a mighty small tick, anyway.”

“Oh, anybody can run a tick down that doesn’t belong to them. I’m satisfied with it. It’s a good enough tick for me.”

“Sho, there’s ticks a plenty. I could have a thousand of ’em if I wanted to.”

“Well, why don’t you? Because you know mighty well you can’t. This is a pretty early tick, I reckon. It’s the first one I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll give you my tooth for him.”

“Let’s see it.”

Tom got out a bit of paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry looked at it wistfully. The temptation was very strong. At last he said:

“Is it genuine?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the gap.

“Well, all right,” said Huckleberry. “It’s a trade.”

Tom put the tick in the percussion-cap box that had lately been the pinchbug’s prison, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer than before.

When Tom reached the little isolated frame schoolhouse, he strode in briskly, with the air of someone who had come with all honest speed. He hung his hat on a peg and flung himself into his seat with businesslike eagerness. The master, perched high in his great splint-bottom armchair, was dozing, lulled by the drowsy hum of study. The interruption woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that when his name was said in full, it meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to hide behind a lie, when he saw two long tails of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized with the electric sympathy of love; and that form was the only empty place on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. He instantly said:

“I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!”

The master’s pulse seemed to stop, and he stared helplessly. The buzz of study died away. The pupils wondered if this reckless boy had lost his mind. The master said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no mistaking the words.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astounding confession I have ever listened to. No mere ferule will answer for this offense. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm went to work until it was tired and the supply of switches had notably diminished. Then the order came:

“Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

The titter that rippled around the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but in truth it was caused more by his worshipful awe of his unknown idol and the dread pleasure of his great good fortune."}

{"request_id":"0f261e036c2e52cfd72988f2","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. I’ll be late for lunch if I linger any longer. Thank you for the information you gave me. I’ve always liked knowing everything about my new friends, and nothing at all about my old ones.”

“Where are you taking lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I’ve asked myself and Mr. Gray. He’s her newest _protégé_.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, that she needn’t trouble me with her charity appeals any more. I’m tired of them. The woman actually believes I have nothing better to do than write cheques for her foolish little fancies.”

“Very well, Uncle George. I’ll pass it on, though it won’t change a thing. People who are philanthropic lose all feeling for humanity. That’s their distinguishing trait.”

The old gentleman growled his approval and rang for his servant. Lord Henry went on past the low arcade into Burlington Street, then turned his steps toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the tale of Dorian Gray’s parentage. Even as crudely as it had been laid before him, it still stirred him with the hint of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a wild passion. A few reckless weeks of happiness cut short by a hideous, treacherous crime. Months of wordless agony, and then a child born in pain. The mother snatched away by death, the boy left to solitude and the rule of an old, loveless man. Yes; it was an absorbing background. It shaped the boy, made him, as it were, more perfect. For behind every exquisite thing that exists there is something tragic. Worlds must be in travail, so that the meanest flower may bloom.... And how delightful he had been at dinner the night before—how, with startled eyes and lips parted in frightened pleasure, he had sat opposite to him at the club, the red candle-shades turning the waking wonder of his face to a deeper rose. Speaking with him was like drawing music from an exquisite violin. He responded to every touch and every thrill of the bow.... There was something dreadfully captivating in the act of exerting influence. Nothing else was like it. To send one’s soul into some gracious form, and let it remain there for a moment; to have one’s own intellectual thoughts returned with all the added music of passion and youth; to pour one’s temperament into another, as though it were a subtle fluid or a strange perfume—there was a genuine joy in that, perhaps the most satisfying joy left to us in an age so narrow and vulgar as our own, an age grossly given over to the flesh in its pleasures, and grossly common in its aims.... This lad was a marvellous type as well—one whom, by such a curious turn, he had met in Basil’s studio, or at least could be made into a marvellous type."}

I picked up the ribbon at the foot of the lightning rod. It could not have belonged to either of the deceased. Now, if I’m wrong in my conclusion from this ribbon—that the Frenchman was a sailor belonging to a Maltese vessel—then I’ve still done no harm by saying what I did in the advertisement. If I’m mistaken, he will simply assume that I’ve been misled by some circumstance he won’t bother to look into. But if I’m right, then a great advantage is gained. Though he’s aware of the situation and innocent of the murder, the Frenchman will naturally hesitate before replying to the advertisement—before demanding the Ourang-Outang. He will reason like this:—‘I’m innocent; I’m poor; my Ourang-Outang is of great value—to someone in my circumstances it’s practically a fortune. Why should I give it up because of idle fears of danger? It’s right there within my reach. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne—at a vast distance from the scene of that slaughter. How could it ever be suspected that a brute animal did the deed? The police are to blame; they’ve failed to obtain the slightest clue. Even if they traced the animal, it would be impossible to prove that I knew about the murder, or to implicate me in guilt because of that knowledge. Above all, I am known. The advertiser identifies me as the owner of the beast. I don’t know how far his knowledge goes. If I avoid claiming property of such great value—property that it’s known I possess—I’ll at least make the animal liable to suspicion. It’s not my plan to draw attention either to myself or to the beast. I’ll answer the advertisement, get the Ourang-Outang, and keep it close until this matter has blown over.’”

At that moment, we heard a step on the stairs.

“Be ready,” said Dupin, “with your pistols, but don’t use them and don’t show them until you get a signal from me.”

The front door of the house had been left open, and the visitor had entered without ringing and gone several steps up the staircase. Now, however, he seemed to pause. Soon we heard him going back down. Dupin was moving quickly toward the door when we heard him coming up again. He didn’t turn back a second time; instead, he stepped up with determination and knocked on the door of our room.

“Come in,” said Dupin, in a cheerful, hearty tone.

A man entered. He was a sailor, clearly—a tall, thickset, muscular-looking person, with a certain daredevil expression on his face, not entirely unappealing."}

{"request_id":"41581a931bce3767ce63e864","rewritten_text":"On Saturday at noon I went to the well and stood there for a while, watching. Merlin was still at it with his smoke-powders—scratching at the air and muttering nonsense as fiercely as ever—yet he looked distinctly cast down, because, naturally, he hadn’t even managed to get a sweat going in that well yet. At last I said:

“Partner, what does the business look like by now?”

“See for yourself: I am even now trying the mightiest enchantment ever known to the princes of the occult arts in the Eastern lands. If it fails me, nothing else can help. Wait until I’m done.”

This time he sent up a smoke that darkened the whole region, and it must have made things awkward for the hermits, since the wind was their way; it rolled down over their dens in a thick, rolling fog. He poured out a torrent of words to go with it, and twisted his body and sawed the air with his hands in the strangest fashion. After twenty minutes he dropped down, panting and nearly spent. Then the abbot arrived with several hundred monks and nuns, and behind them came a crowd of pilgrims and a couple of acres of foundlings, all drawn by the astonishing smoke and all in a fine state of excitement. The abbot asked, with anxious urgency, whether there were any results. Merlin answered:

“If any work of mortal hands could break the spell that holds these waters, the attempt I’ve just made would have done it. It has failed; and so I now know that what I feared is indeed true. The sign of this failure is that the most powerful spirit known to the magicians of the East—whose name no one may speak and live—has laid his spell upon this well. No mortal breathes, nor ever will, who can uncover the secret of that spell; and without the secret, none can break it. The water will not flow again, Father. I’ve done what a man can. Let me go.”

Naturally, this set the abbot into a fair amount of consternation. He faced me, and you could see it plainly in his expression, saying:

“You’ve heard him. Is it true?”

“Some of it is.”

“Not all, then—not all! Which part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has put his spell upon the well.”

“Good heavens—then we’re ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? You mean, not certainly?”

“That’s the point.”

“And so you also mean that when he says none can break the spell—”

“Yes. When he says that, he’s saying what isn’t necessarily true. There are circumstances under which an attempt to break it might have some chance—only a small one, a trifling one—of succeeding.”"}

{"request_id":"d39bf4e4e317d9894fb3cc1e","rewritten_text":"I consider it one of the first refinements of polished societies.”

“Certainly, sir; and it has the added advantage of being fashionable even among the less polished societies of the world: every savage can dance.”

Sir William only smiled. “Your friend performs delightfully,” he continued after a pause, seeing Bingley join the group; “and I doubt not that you are yourself an adept in the science, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, indeed, and I took no small pleasure in the sight. Do you often dance at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Don’t you think it would be a proper compliment to the place?”

“It’s a compliment I never pay to any place if I can avoid it.”

“You have a house in town, I conclude?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once had thoughts of settling in town myself, for I’m fond of superior society; but I wasn’t quite certain that the air of London would agree with Lady Lucas.”

He paused, hoping for an answer; but his companion was not disposed to give one. At that instant Elizabeth moved toward them, and he was struck by the idea of doing something very gallant, so he called out to her,—

“My dear Miss Eliza, why aren’t you dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to present this young lady to you as a very desirable partner. You can’t refuse to dance, I’m sure, when so much beauty is before you.” And, taking her hand, he would have offered it to Mr. Darcy, who, though extremely surprised, was not unwilling to receive it, when she instantly drew back and said, with some discomposure to Sir William,—

“Indeed, sir, I have no intention at all of dancing. I beg you not to suppose that I came this way in order to ask for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with grave propriety, requested the honour of her hand, but in vain. Elizabeth was determined; nor did Sir William shake her resolve at all with his attempts at persuasion.

“You excel so much in the dance, Miss Eliza, that it’s cruel to deny me the happiness of seeing you; and though this gentleman dislikes the amusement in general, he can have no objection, I’m sure, to oblige us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He is, indeed; but considering the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we can’t be surprised at his willingness; for who would object to such a partner?”

Elizabeth looked archly and turned away. Her resistance did not harm her with the gentleman, and he was thinking of her with some complacency, when he was approached by Miss Bingley,—"}

{"request_id":"2ef515d6a42d51cb7ddbd802","rewritten_text":"“But,” I said, handing him back the slip, “I’m still just as much in the dark as before. Even if all the jewels of Golconda were waiting for me after I solved this riddle, I’m sure I still wouldn’t be able to earn them.”

“And yet,” Legrand replied, “the solution isn’t nearly as hard as you might think after a quick look at the characters. As you can easily guess, these characters form a cipher. They are meant to carry a message. But knowing what Kidd was like, I couldn’t believe he would bother with any of the more complicated kinds of secret writing. I decided right away it was a simple kind—simple enough, at least, that it would still be impossible for a sailor’s rough mind to solve without the key.”

“And you really solved it?”

“Of course. I’ve solved others that were ten thousand times more difficult. Circumstances, and a certain way of thinking, have made me interested in puzzles like this. It’s even possible to doubt that anyone could create a riddle that human skill couldn’t solve, if the right approach is used. Once I had the characters in a connected, readable form, I didn’t spend much time worrying about how hard it would be to understand what they meant.

“In any case of secret writing, the first question is always the language of the cipher. The rules for solving it—especially for simpler ciphers—depend on the style and habits of the language. Usually, the only option is to try every language the solver knows, guided by probabilities, until the correct one is found. But here, the signature removed all real difficulty. The joke on the word ‘Kidd’ works only in English. If not for that, I would have started by trying Spanish and French, since those are the languages a pirate from the Spanish Main would most likely use for a secret message. Since the signature pointed the way, I assumed the cipher was English.

“You’ll notice there are no spaces between the words. If there had been, the problem would have been much easier. In that situation, I would have compared and analyzed the shorter words first. And if a one-letter word appeared—something like ‘a’ or ‘I,’ for example—I would have felt the solution was basically certain. But because there were no divisions, my first step was to find the most common letters and also the least frequent ones.”"}

{"request_id":"dc7b6f317fe238daef0d371b","rewritten_text":"He shivered, then went back and closed the window behind him.

When he reached the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not even look at the dead man. He felt the secret to everything was not to understand what was happening. The friend who had painted the portrait that had led to all his misery was no longer in his life. That was enough.

Then he remembered the lamp. It was a strange one, made in Moorish style. It was dull silver, decorated with patterns of burnished steel, and set with rough turquoise stones. Maybe his servant would not notice it, and no one would ask questions. He hesitated, then turned back and took it from the table. He could not stop himself from looking at the dead thing. How still it was. How terrible the long hands looked, so white. It was like a horrible wax figure.

After he locked the door behind him, he moved quietly downstairs. The woodwork creaked, and it seemed to cry out as if it hurt. He stopped several times and waited. No—everything was quiet. It was only the sound of his own footsteps.

When he got to the library, he saw the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be hidden somewhere. He unlocked a secret press built into the wall paneling, a place where he kept his own unusual disguises, and put the bag and coat inside. He could burn them later. Then he took out his watch. It was twenty minutes to two.

He sat down and started to think. Every year—almost every month—men were strangled in England for what he had done. It felt like murder was in the air. As if some red star had come too close to the earth. Still, what proof was there against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. No one had seen him come back in. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.

Paris. Yes. Basil had gone to Paris, and he would take the midnight train, just as he planned. Because of his quiet, careful habits, it would be months before anyone became suspicious. Months. By then, everything could be destroyed.

A sudden thought came to him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went into the hall. He paused there, listening to the slow, heavy steps of the policeman outside on the pavement, and watching the flash of the bull’s-eye reflected in the window. He waited and held his breath.

After a few moments, he pulled back the latch and slipped out, closing the door very softly behind him. Then he began ringing the bell."}

{"request_id":"af5936dc40714b2e0cfdd686","rewritten_text":"Watching him in these moods, I often found myself drifting into the old philosophy of the Bi-Part Soul, and I amused myself with the fancy of a double Dupin—the creative one and the resolvent.

Let it not be supposed, from what I have just said, that I am laying out any mystery or writing a romance. What I described in the Frenchman was simply the result of an excited, or perhaps a diseased, intelligence. Still, an example of the character of his remarks at those moments will best convey the idea.

We were strolling one night down a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. Both of us, apparently lost in thought, had not spoken a single word for at least fifteen minutes. All at once Dupin broke in with these words:

“He’s a very small fellow, that’s true, and he’d do better at the _Théâtre des Variétés_.”

“There can be no doubt of that,” I replied, without meaning to, and only afterward—so absorbed had I been in my reflections—did I notice the extraordinary way the speaker had fallen into step with my thoughts. In an instant I snapped back to myself, and my astonishment was profound.

“Dupin,” I said gravely, “this is beyond my comprehension. I don’t hesitate to say that I’m amazed, and I can barely believe what I’m hearing. How could you possibly know I was thinking of ——?” I paused to make sure, beyond any doubt, that he really knew whom I was thinking about.

“—— of Chantilly,” he said. “Why do you pause? You were telling yourself that his diminutive figure didn’t suit tragedy.”

That was exactly what had been the subject of my reflections. Chantilly had once been a cobbler from the Rue St. Denis; after he became obsessed with the stage, he had tried to play Xerxes in Crébillon’s so-called tragedy, and he’d been notoriously mocked for it.

“Tell me, for Heaven’s sake,” I exclaimed, “the method—if there is a method—by which you’ve been able to read my soul in this matter.” In truth, I was even more startled than I was willing to admit.

“It was the fruiterer,” my friend replied, “who led you to the conclusion that the mender of soles wasn’t tall enough for Xerxes _et id genus omne_.”

“The fruiterer!—you astonish me—I don’t know any fruiterer at all.”

“The man who bumped into you as we entered the street—it might have been fifteen minutes ago.”

I now remembered that, as we passed from the Rue C—— into the thoroughfare where we were standing, a fruiterer carrying a large basket of apples on his head had nearly knocked me down by accident; but I still couldn’t understand what that had to do with Chantilly."}
