{"request_id":"e81eae044f177b1a136bcff9","rewritten_text":"The little man’s body was far broader than it should have been, making his whole figure look oddly round. His feet could not be seen at all. Still, a hard, suspicious-looking substance sometimes pushed out through a tear in the bottom of the car, or, more accurately, through the top of the hat. His hands were extremely large. His hair was very gray, gathered into a queue behind. His nose was very long, bent, and inflamed-looking. His eyes were full, bright, and sharp. Even though his chin and cheeks were wrinkled with age, they were broad, puffy, and doubled. Yet there was no sign of any ears anywhere on his head.

This strange little gentleman wore a loose surtout made of sky-blue satin, with tight breeches to match, held in place by silver buckles at the knees. His vest was made of bright yellow material. A white taffety cap sat tilted to one side of his head. To finish his outfit, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped around his throat and fell neatly onto his chest, tied into an elaborate bow-knot that was far too large.

As I said before, once he had come down to about one hundred feet above the ground, the little old man suddenly became frightened and seemed unwilling to get any closer to the earth. So he stopped at once. He did this by throwing out a quantity of sand from a canvas bag, which he lifted with great difficulty.

Then he hurried and fidgeted as he pulled a large morocco pocket-book from a side pocket in his surtout. He held it up suspiciously, stared at it with extreme surprise, and clearly seemed shocked by how heavy it was. At last he opened it. From inside, he drew a huge letter, sealed with red sealing wax and tied carefully with red tape, and dropped it right at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk.

His Excellency bent down to pick it up. But the aeronaut, still very upset and apparently having no more reason to stay in Rotterdam, began preparing to leave. Since he needed to throw out some ballast to rise again, he tossed out half a dozen bags one after another. He did this without bothering to empty them first. Unfortunately, every bag tumbled onto the burgomaster’s back, and rolled him over and over—no fewer than twenty-one times—in full view of every man in Rotterdam.

It should not be assumed, however, that the great Underduk let this disrespect pass without consequence."}

{"request_id":"b431f7bfbc66a22598cb5938","rewritten_text":"She and the children could stay quite comfortably.”

“Ah, Papa—that’s something you’ve never been able to do, and I don’t think you ever will. Isabella can’t bear to stay behind her husband.”

That was too true to argue with. Even though it was unwelcome, Mr. Woodhouse could only give a quiet, resigned sigh. And when Emma saw that his mood was affected by the idea of his daughter being so attached to her husband, she quickly changed the subject in a way that would lift his spirits.

“Harriet should spend as much time with us as she can while my brother and sister are here. I’m sure she’ll enjoy the children. We’re very proud of them, aren’t we, Papa? I wonder which one she’ll think is the handsomest—Henry or John?”

“Aye, I wonder which she’ll think. Poor little dears—how happy they’ll be to come. They really love being at Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they do, sir. I’m sure I don’t know anyone who wouldn’t.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John is very much like his mother. Henry is the eldest. He was named after me, not after his father. John, the second, is named after his father. Some people are surprised, I believe, that the eldest wasn’t named after him, but Isabella would have him called Henry, and I thought that was very sweet. And he’s a very clever boy, indeed. They’re all remarkably clever, and they have so many charming little habits. They’ll come and stand by my chair and say, ‘Grandpapa, can you give me a bit of string?’ Once Henry even asked me for a knife, but I told him knives are only made for grandpapas. I think their father is too rough with them far too often.”

“He seems rough to you,” Emma said, “only because you are so gentle yourself. But if you compared him with other fathers, you wouldn’t think him rough. He wants his boys to be active and strong. If they misbehave, he can give them a sharp word now and then, but he is an affectionate father—certainly Mr. John Knightley is an affectionate father. The children all love him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and throws them up to the ceiling in a very frightening way!”

“But they like it, Papa. There’s nothing they enjoy more. It’s such fun for them that, if their uncle didn’t set a rule about taking turns, whoever started would never let the other have a go.”

“Well, I can’t understand it.”

“That’s the way it is with all of us, Papa. One half of the world can’t understand the pleasures of the other.”"}

{"request_id":"7a20f8e6fb7b78f87aa4c679","rewritten_text":"Then they went past the lonely brickworks. The fog thinned there, and he could make out the odd, bottle-like kilns, their orange, fan-shaped tongues of flame. A dog barked as they passed, and, far off in the blackness, some stray sea-gull shrieked. The horse caught a rut, stumbled, then swung aside and broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled again along rough-set streets. Most of the windows were dark, yet now and then strange shadows cut themselves against a blind lit by lamplight. He studied them with a curious eye. They moved like grotesque marionettes and made gestures as if they were living. He loathed them. A heavy, dull fury sat in his chest. As they rounded a corner, a woman shouted something at them from an open doorway, and two men ran after the hansom for about a hundred yards. The driver lashed at them with his whip.

They say passion turns thought in a circle. Certainly, with hideous repetition, the bitten lips of Dorian Gray formed and re-formed those subtle words about soul and sense, until he had drawn from them the full expression—so it seemed—of his mood, and could, with intellectual assent, justify passions that, without such backing, would still have ruled his temper. From cell to cell of his brain crept that one idea; and the fierce wish to live—the most dreadful of all man’s cravings—surged into strength, quickening every quivering nerve and fibre. What ugliness had once disgusted him for making things real, became dear to him now for that very reason. Ugliness was the only reality. The coarse brawl, the filthy den, the blunt brutality of disordered life, the very foulness of thief and outcast—these struck him with a sharper, more intense immediacy than all the kindly forms of art, than the dreamy shadows of song. They were what he needed for forgetting. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the man pulled up with a jerk at the top of a dark lane. Over the low roofs and jagged chimney-stacks of the houses rose the black masts of ships. Bands of white mist clung to the yards like ghostly sails.

“Somewhere about here, sir, ain’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian started and looked round. “This will do,” he said; and after he had got out quickly and handed the driver the extra fare he’d promised, he walked fast toward the quay. Here and there a lantern shone at the stern of some great merchantman. The light trembled and shattered in the puddles. A red flare came from an outward-bound steamer that was coaling. The slimy pavement looked like wet mackintosh."}

{"request_id":"709f84e2a74e343cd5efd9ef","rewritten_text":"Shall I be borne aloft to the skies, on flow’ry beds of ease,

While others strive to seize the prize, and cut their way through blood-y seas?

He was looked upon as a remarkable reader. At church “sociables” he was always asked to recite poetry; and once he had finished, the ladies would raise their hands and let them drop helplessly into their laps, “wall” their eyes, and shake their heads, as though to say, “Words cannot express it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this mortal earth.”

After the hymn had been sung, the Rev. Mr. Sprague turned himself into a bulletin-board, and read off “notices” of meetings and societies and all such matters until it seemed the list might run on to the crack of doom—a peculiar habit still observed in America, even in cities, in spite of this present age of plentiful newspapers. The less there is to justify a time-honored custom, the more stubbornly it clings.

And now the minister prayed. It was a kind, hearty prayer, and it went into particulars: it pleaded for the church, and for the church’s little children; for the other churches in the village; for the village itself; for the county; for the State; for the State officers; for the United States; for the churches of the United States; for Congress; for the President; for the officers of the Government; for poor sailors, tossed by stormy seas; for the oppressed millions groaning beneath the heel of European monarchies and Oriental despotisms; for those who have the light and the good tidings, yet have not eyes to see nor ears to hear; for the heathen in the far islands of the sea; and it ended with a request that the words he was about to speak might find grace and favor, and be as seed sown in fertile ground, bringing forth in time a grateful harvest of good. Amen.

There was a rustle of dresses, and the congregation, standing, sat down. The boy whose story this book tells did not care for the prayer; he only endured it—if he did that much. He was restless from start to finish; he kept count of the prayer’s particulars, without meaning to—for he was not listening, yet he knew the old ground and the clergyman’s usual path through it—and when a small bit of new matter was slipped in, his ear caught it and his whole nature bristled at the intrusion; he judged additions to be unfair, and downright villainous. While the prayer was still going on, a fly settled on the back of the pew ahead of him and worried his spirit by calmly rubbing its hands together, embracing its head with its arms, and polishing it so vigorously that it seemed to almost separate from the body, and a slender thread of a neck showed itself; it scraped its wings with its hind legs and smoothed them back to its body as if they were coat-tails; it went through its entire toilet with the same quiet confidence as though it knew it was perfectly safe."}

{"request_id":"8e57e63961071f0fb423a615","rewritten_text":"“Is that all? It isn’t much at all! Many are under the Republic’s displeasure, and have to stare out through a little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?”

“I am he. Necessarily, being the last.”

It is Jarvis Lorry who has answered all the questions so far. It is Jarvis Lorry who has stepped down and stands with his hand on the coach door, replying to a group of officials. They walk around the carriage at their leisure and climb up onto the box at their leisure, to look at the little luggage it carries on the roof; the country people linger nearby, press closer to the coach doors, and stare in greedily; a small child, carried by its mother, has its short arm held out so it can touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the Guillotine.

“Behold your papers, Jarvis Lorry—countersigned.”

“One can depart, citizen?”

“One can depart. Forward, my postilions! A good journey!”

“I salute you, citizens—and the first danger is passed!”

These are again Jarvis Lorry’s words, as he clasps his hands and looks upward. Terror is in the carriage; there is weeping; there is the heavy breathing of the insensible traveler.

“Are we not going too slowly? Can’t they be made to go faster?” asks Lucie, clinging to the old man.

“It would seem like flight, my darling. I must not urge them too much; it would raise suspicion.”

“Look back, look back—see if we’re being followed!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, we are not being followed.”

Houses in twos and threes pass by us, solitary farms, ruined buildings, dye-works, tanneries, and the like; open country, avenues of leafless trees. The hard, uneven pavement is beneath us; the soft, deep mud lies on either side. Sometimes we veer into the edge mud to avoid the stones that clatter against us and shake the coach; sometimes we get stuck in ruts and sloughs there. The agony of our impatience becomes so intense that, in our wild alarm and hurry, we’re ready to get out and run—hide—do anything but stop.

Out of the open country, back among ruined buildings, solitary farms, dye-works, tanneries, and the like; cottages in twos and threes, avenues of leafless trees. Have these men tricked us and taken us back by another road? Isn’t this the same place twice over? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see if we’re being followed! Hush—the posting-house.

Leisurely, our four horses are taken out; leisurely, the coach stands in the little street, without horses and with no chance of ever moving again; leisurely, the new horses come into view, one by one; leisurely, the new postilions follow, sucking and braiding the lashes of their whips; leisurely, the old postilions count their money, make wrong additions, and end up with results that leave them dissatisfied."}

{"request_id":"95896dfacd67aa9d7b845bd4","rewritten_text":"“Well, everybody does it that way, Huck.”

“Tom, it don’t make no difference. I ain’t everybody, and I can’t _stand_ it. It’s miserable being tied up so. And the food comes too easy—I don’t have no appetite for vittles that way. I got to ask to go a-fishing; I got to ask to go in a-swimming—dern’d if I hain’t got to ask to do everything. And I’d have to talk so polite it wasn’t no comfort; I’d have to go up in the attic and tear out awhile every day just to get a taste in my mouth, or I’d a died, Tom. The widder wouldn’t let me smoke; she wouldn’t let me yell, she wouldn’t let me gape, nor stretch, nor scratch, before folks—” [Then with a spasm of special irritation and injury]—“And dad fetch it, she prayed all the time! I had to shove, Tom—I just had to. And besides, that school’s going to open, and I’d a had to go to it—well, I wouldn’t stand _that_, Tom. Looky-here, Tom, being rich ain’t what it’s cracked up to be. It’s just worry and worry, and sweat and sweat, and a-wishing you was dead all the time. Now these clothes suit me, and this bar’l suits me, and I ain’t ever going to shake ’em any more. Tom, I wouldn’t ever got into all this trouble if it hadn’t ’a’ been for that money; now you just take my share of it along with your’n, and gimme a ten-center sometimes—not many times, ’cause I don’t give a dern for a thing ’thout it’s tollable hard to git—and you go and beg off for me with the widder.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. ’Tain’t fair; and besides, if you’ll try this thing just a while longer you’ll come to like it.”

“Like it! Yes—the way I’d like a hot stove if I was to set on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in them cussed smothery houses. I like the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’ll stick to ’em, too. Blame it all! just as we’d got guns, and a cave, and all fixed to rob, here this dern foolishness has got to come up and spile it all!”

Tom saw his chance—

“Lookyhere, Huck, being rich ain’t going to keep me from turning robber.”

“No! Oh, good-licks; are you in real dead-wood earnest, Tom?”

“Just as dead earnest as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you into the gang if you ain’t respectable, you know.”

Huck’s joy was quenched.

“Can’t let me in, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"6905b16f7f02c0cc80c369af","rewritten_text":"“These thoughts soothed me, and in the afternoon I sank into a deep sleep; yet the fever in my blood would not let me have any gentle dreams. The dreadful spectacle of the day before kept returning, always before my eyes: the females were flying, and the furious Felix was wrenching me from my father’s feet. I woke worn out, and, finding it was already night, I slipped out from my hiding-place and went looking for food.

“When my hunger was satisfied, I took the well-known path that led to the cottage. Everything there seemed calm. I crawled into my hovel and waited in silent expectation for the usual hour when the family rose. That time came and went; the sun climbed high in the heavens, but the cottagers did not show themselves. I shook with violent fear, convinced that some dreadful misfortune had occurred. The cottage inside was dark, and I heard no movement; I cannot put into words the torment of that suspense.

“Soon two countrymen went by, but when they reached the cottage they stopped and began to talk, with violent gestures; I could not make out what they said, for they spoke the language of the country, which was different from that of my protectors. Not long after, Felix arrived with another man. I was startled, because I knew he had not left the cottage that morning, and I waited anxiously to learn from their conversation why these strange appearances had begun.

“‘Do you think,’ said his companion to him, ‘that you will be forced to pay three months’ rent and to give up the produce of your garden? I don’t want to gain any unfair advantage, so I ask you to take a few days to consider your decision.’

“‘It is quite useless,’ Felix answered; ‘we can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the gravest danger because of the terrible thing I have told you. My wife and my sister will never recover from the horror they have suffered. I beg you, do not argue with me any longer. Take your tenement and let me flee from this place.’

“Felix trembled violently as he spoke. He and his companion went into the cottage, stayed there for a few minutes, and then left. I never saw any member of the De Lacey family again.

“I spent the rest of the day in my hovel, sunk in a dull, utter despair. My protectors were gone, and they had snapped the only thread that kept me connected to the world. For the first time, the feelings of revenge and hatred filled my breast; I made no effort to restrain them, but let myself be carried along by the current, turning my thoughts toward injury and death.”"}

{"request_id":"c07ab15521ac19103b94ffd8","rewritten_text":"“Oh, your father, naturally, may spare you—if your mother can. A daughter is never of such consequence to a father. And if you can manage to remain another _month_ complete, I shall have it in my power to take one of you as far as London; for I mean to be there early in June, for a week. Since Dawson does not object to the barouche-box, there will be very comfortable room for one of you—and, if the weather should chance to be cool, I would not object to taking you both, for neither of you is large.”

“You are all kindness, madam; yet I think we must keep to our first plan.”

Lady Catherine looked as though she had resigned herself. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always say what I think, and I cannot bear the notion of two young women travelling post by themselves. It is quite improper. You must arrange for someone to go. I have the strongest dislike to that sort of thing. Young women ought always to be properly guarded and attended, according to their station. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I made a point of having two men-servants accompany her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley, and Lady Anne, could not possibly have appeared in any other way with propriety. I am exceedingly particular about such matters. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad it occurred to me to mention it; for it would truly be a discredit to _you_ to let them go alone.”

“My uncle is to send a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle—does he keep a man-servant? Then I am very pleased that you have someone who considers these things. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you give my name at the Bell, you will be taken care of.”

Lady Catherine had still many other questions to put to them about their journey; and as she did not answer them all herself, some attention was required—which Elizabeth thought fortunate for her; for, with her thoughts so taken up, she might otherwise have forgotten where she was. Reflection, she felt, must be kept for private hours: whenever she was alone, she indulged in it as her greatest relief; and not a day passed without a solitary walk, in which she could give way to all the pleasure of those disagreeable recollections.

Mr. Darcy’s letter, she was soon likely to know by heart. She examined every sentence; and her feelings toward its writer were at times very different. When she recalled the manner of his address, she was still full of indignation; but when she considered how unjustly she had condemned and reproached him, her anger turned upon herself, and his disappointed feelings became the subject of her compassion.”}"}

{"request_id":"70c2640f797465051a08077a","rewritten_text":"A little after noon, the boys borrowed a small skiff from a citizen who was away, and they set off right then. A few miles below “Cave Hollow,” Tom said:

“Now, look at this bluff. It all looks the same from the cave hollow—no houses, no wood-yards, just bushes that look alike. But do you see that white spot up there? That’s from a landslide. That’s one of my marks. We’ll go ashore now.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, where we’re standing, you could reach that hole I dug out with a fishing pole. See if you can find it.”

Huck looked around carefully, but he couldn’t find anything. Tom walked in with confidence into a thick clump of sumach bushes and said, “Here it is! Look, Huck. It’s the snuggiest hole in the whole country. You keep quiet about it. All along I’ve wanted to be a robber, but I knew I needed a place like this, and the hard part was finding where it was. We’ve got it now, and we’ll keep it secret. But we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers in, because of course there has to be a gang, or it wouldn’t have any style. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds great, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“It sure does, Tom. But who are we going to rob?”

“Almost anybody. We’ll stop people on the road—that’s mostly how it’s done.”

“And kill them?”

“Not always. We’ll lock them in the cave until they raise a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them get as much as they can from their friends, and if after a year they still haven’t raised it, then you kill them. That’s the usual way. But you don’t kill the women. You keep the women quiet, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and they’re terribly scared. You take their watches and other things, but you always take off your hat and act polite. Robbers are the most polite people, you’ll see that in any book. Well, the women start to like you, and after they’ve been in the cave for a week or two, they stop crying. After that, you couldn’t get them to leave. If you tried to drive them out, they’d just turn around and come back. That’s how it is in all the books.”

“That’s really great, Tom. I think it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s close to home, and there are circuses and all that.”

By then everything was ready, and the boys went into the hole, with Tom leading. They worked their way to the far end of the tunnel, then tied their spliced kite strings in place and moved on."}

{"request_id":"381b017880cf427abaf6d874","rewritten_text":"The loud voice—something we might call inorganic, because we could not connect it to any pipe or key—fell silent. The girl turned to help her elderly companion, and only then did she finally notice us.

It was her father. Since she was a child, she had guided his steps in the dark. They were Germans from Saxony. They had moved there only a few years earlier, and in that time they had formed new ties with the villagers around them. Around the time the pestilence began, a young German student joined them. Their story was easy to understand. He was noble, and he loved the beautiful daughter of the poor musician. He followed them when they fled persecution by his friends. But soon the great leveler came with an unblunted scythe, mowing down the youth along with the grass and the tall flowers of the field. She kept herself alive for her father’s sake. Because he was blind, she could keep up her lie. At first it was only an accident, but now they were alone—only survivors in that land. He did not know anything had changed. When he listened to her music, he believed the mute mountains, the silent lake, and the unconscious trees were still there. In truth, he was the only one who could hear her, and she was the only one who could see.

The very day we arrived, she had been struck by a sickness that showed itself in the usual way. She was filled with horror at the thought of leaving her aged, sightless father alone on the empty earth. But she did not have the courage to tell him the truth. Her desperation only made her push herself harder. At the usual hour for evening prayers, she led him to the chapel. Even though she trembled and cried for him, she played the hymn perfectly—on time, with no wrong notes—one that celebrated the creation of the decorated earth, soon to become her grave.

We came to her as if we were visitors from heaven. Her courage, which had been strained to the breaking point, and her firmness, barely held together, collapsed the moment she felt relief. With a shriek she ran toward us, threw her arms around Adrian’s knees, and, sobbing and crying in hysterical bursts, she managed only, “O save my father!” Then her grief poured out without restraint.

Poor girl. She and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, and which, in her last moments, she had pointed out to us. Her father, at last realizing she was in danger, could not see the changes in her face. Still, he stubbornly held her hand until death made it cold and stiff. He did not move or speak even then. Only twelve hours later, gentle death carried him to his endless rest. They lie under the sod, and the tree is their monument. The sacred place is still clear in my memory, though the craggy Jura and the far, immeasurable Alps pale it. The church spire they used to attend still rises above the surrounding trees. And even though her hand is cold, I still imagine the divine music they loved drifting around, comforting their gentle ghosts."}

{"request_id":"64ed50fbc48f98dcc03919a6","rewritten_text":"Weeks and weeks passed, and I became more and more absorbed in you. Then something new happened. I had drawn you as Paris in delicate armor, and as Adonis with a huntsman’s cloak and a gleaming boar-spear. Crowned with heavy lotus blossoms, you had sat on the prow of Adrian’s barge, looking out across the green, muddy Nile. You had leaned over the quiet pool of some Greek woodland and watched, in the water’s silent silver, the wonder of your own face. And it had all been exactly what art should be—unconscious, ideal, and distant.

One day—a day I sometimes think was fatal—I decided to paint a portrait of you exactly as you are, not in the costume of dead ages, but in your own clothes and in your own time. I can’t say whether it was the realism of the method, or simply the force of your own personality, presented to me so directly, without any haze or veil. But I know that as I worked, every flake and film of color seemed to show me my secret. I grew afraid that others would recognize my idolatry. I felt, Dorian, that I had said too much, that I had put too much of myself into it.

Then I resolved never to allow the picture to be exhibited. You were a little annoyed, but you didn’t understand what it meant to me. Harry, whom I told about it, laughed at me. I didn’t mind that. When the picture was finished, and I sat alone with it, I felt that I was right.... Well, after a few days the thing left my studio. And once I had gotten rid of the unbearable fascination of its presence, it seemed to me that I had been foolish to think I had seen anything in it beyond the fact that you were extremely good-looking and that I could paint. Even now I can’t help feeling that it’s a mistake to believe that the passion we feel in creating is ever truly shown in the work we create. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Form and color tell us only about form and color—that’s all. It often seems to me that art conceals the artist far more completely than it ever reveals him.

So when I received this offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the main piece in my exhibition. It never occurred to me that you would refuse. I see now that you were right. The picture cannot be shown. You must not be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have told you."}

{"request_id":"7cd5cf9ba5dd51c37796c7bd","rewritten_text":"“Mark me well: I have learned the tongue of despair. I know it word for word, for I am Despair—and a curious creature am I, laughing and triumphant Despair. Yet those words are not true; the sea may be dark, but it is not cruel. We lie down and close our eyes with a gentle good night, and when we rise, we are free. So come—no more delay, you slow one! See the pleasant draught! Look: I am a spirit of good, not some human maid who beckons you, and with winning tones—(oh, if only they could win you!)—she says, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I kept my gaze fixed on his face. His exquisite beauty, the heavenly compassion shining from his eyes, and his mild yet earnest look—half reproach, half astonishment—before he even answered, changed something in me: it loosened the tight, high-strung hardness of my despair, and left me with nothing but the softest grief. I noticed too that his eyes were wet, as he took both my hands. Then, sitting down close by, he said:

“This is a sorrowful deed you would draw me into, dearest friend, and your misery must be truly deep if it has filled you with such unhappy thoughts. You crave death, and yet you dread it; you want me to be your companion, though you shrink from the very thing you desire. But I have less courage than you, and even with you beside me I cannot bring myself to die. Hear me, and consider whether you ought to win me to your plan—though, with the overbearing eloquence of despair, you could make black death seem inviting, so that fair heaven itself would look like darkness. I beg you: take the words of one who has fed his own desperate thoughts, and longed with impatient hunger for death, but who has at last trampled the phantom underfoot and broken its sting. Come—since you have played Despair with me, I will play the part of Una with you, and lead you out, unhurt, from his dark cavern. Listen to me, and let yourself be softened by speech in which no selfish passion remains.

“We do not know what all this wide world signifies—how it mixes good and evil in such strange measure. Still, we have been placed here and commanded to live and hope. I cannot say what we are meant to hope for; but there is some good beyond us that we must seek, and that is our earthly work. If misfortune comes against us, we must stand against her; we must cast her aside and go on, still trying to discover what it is our nature to desire. Whether this promise of future good is meant as preparation for another existence, I cannot tell; or whether it is simply that, as workers in God’s vineyard, we must lend a hand to smooth the way for those who come after us.”"}

{"request_id":"f472213a2a12dfbb237dd6a1","rewritten_text":"The nephew glanced at him as he passed through, but it was no use, and he went on to the door.

“Good night!” said the uncle. “I look forward to seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well. Light Monsieur my nephew to his room there—and burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you like,” he added to himself, before he rang his small bell again and called his valet to his own bedroom.

When the valet came and went, Monsieur the Marquis paced back and forth in his loose robe, getting himself ready for sleep on that hot, still night. He rustled around the room, his soft slippers making no sound on the floor. He moved like a refined tiger—like some enchanted marquis in a story of shameless wickedness, whose change into a tiger was either just starting or just ending.

He crossed the room to the other end and back again, letting the scraps of the day’s journey come into his mind without being invited. He thought of the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the sun setting, the descent, the mill, the prison on the crag, the small village in the hollow, the peasants at the fountain, and the road mender with his blue cap pointing out the chain under the carriage. The fountain brought to mind the one in Paris, the small bundle on the step, the women bending over it, and the tall man with his arms raised, shouting, “Dead!”

“I’m calm now,” said Monsieur the Marquis. “I can go to bed.”

He left only one light burning on the big hearth. Then he let his thin gauze curtains fall around him, and he listened as the night broke its silence with a long sigh while he settled down to sleep.

For three heavy hours, the stone faces on the outer walls stared blindly into the black night. For three heavy hours, the horses in the stables rattled their racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound that had very little to do with the one men-poets usually give it. But these creatures are stubbornly unlikely to do what people expect.

For three heavy hours, the chateau’s stone faces—lion and human—stared blindly at the night. Dead darkness covered the whole landscape, and the darkness added its own quiet to the quiet of the dust on all the roads. The burial place had reached the point where its small mounds of poor grass looked like they were all the same. The figure on the Cross might as well have come down, for all anyone could see of it. In the village, the taxers and the taxed were asleep. They were probably dreaming of banquets, as the starving often do, and of comfort and rest, as the driven slave and the yoked ox may. The lean people slept deeply, and were fed and freed."}

{"request_id":"60303cdb5ecd1ec29e06f5e5","rewritten_text":"Not a word was spoken about it, however, until their visitor left for the night; but the moment he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said,--

“Jane, I congratulate you. You will be a very happy woman.”

Jane went to him at once, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are a good girl,” he answered, “and I feel great satisfaction in knowing you will be settled so happily. I have no doubt that you will get along very well together. Your tempers are not at all alike. You are both so agreeable that nothing will ever be decided; and you are so easygoing that every servant will take advantage of you; and you are so generous that you will always spend more than you earn.”

“I hope not. Any foolishness or carelessness with money would be unforgivable in _me_.”

“Spend more than you earn! My dear Mr. Bennet,” cried his wife, “what are you talking about? He has four or five thousand a year, and he may very likely have more.” Then, turning to her daughter, “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so happy! I know I won’t sleep a wink tonight. I knew it would turn out this way. I always said it would happen. I was sure you couldn’t be so beautiful for nothing! I remember that the moment I saw him, when he first came to Hertfordshire last year, I thought it was very likely that you would end up together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man anyone has ever seen!”

Wickham and Lydia were quickly forgotten. Jane was her favorite child, and nothing else mattered at that moment. Her younger sisters soon began to press her with ideas about the kinds of happiness she might be able to give them in the future.

Mary asked to use the library at Netherfield, and Kitty begged very hard for a few balls there every winter.

From then on, Bingley was, of course, a daily visitor at Longbourn. He often came before breakfast and always stayed until after supper, unless some barbarous neighbor—someone they could not possibly stand—had invited him to dinner, and he felt he had to accept.

Elizabeth now had very little time to talk with her sister. While he was there, Jane had no attention to spare for anyone else; but when they were apart, Jane found ways to be useful to both of them during those hours when separation would sometimes happen. When Jane was not there, he always stayed close to Elizabeth, enjoying the chance to talk about her. And when Bingley was gone, Jane often sought the same kind of relief.

“He has made me so happy,” Jane said one evening, “by telling me that he knew nothing at all about my being in town last spring!”"}

{"request_id":"0c87fe06ed7cf398c4c36035","rewritten_text":"“I’m with you. It’s the best way. Just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh, no, not like that. This is fine for small, trashy common matters—especially with girls, ’cause they’ll turn on you anyway, and chatter if they get their feelings hurt—but there ought to be something written down for a big business like this. And blood.”

Tom’s whole self seemed to cheer the notion. It was deep, and dark, and dreadful; the hour, the situation, the place around them all fit it perfectly. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, pulled a tiny bit of “red keel” from his pocket, set the moon to work on his writing, and with painful care scrawled the words, pressing each slow down-stroke by clamping his tongue between his teeth, then easing off the pressure on the up-strokes.

“‘Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.’”

Huckleberry was full of admiration for Tom’s knack at writing, and for the grandeur of his language. He immediately reached for a pin from his lapel, intending to prick his own flesh, but Tom cut in:

“Wait! Don’t you do that. A pin’s brass. It might have verdigris on it.”

“What’s verdigris?”

“Poison. That’s what it is. You swallow some of it once and you’ll find out.”

So Tom pulled the thread loose from one of his needles, and each boy pricked the ball of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After a lot of squeezing, Tom finally managed to sign his initials, using the ball of his little finger as a pen. Then he taught Huckleberry how to form an H and an F, and the oath was finished. They buried the shingle near the wall, with gloomy ceremonies and muttered spells, and the bonds meant to keep their tongues quiet were thought to be locked up, with the key tossed away.

A shape slipped through a gap at the far end of the ruined building, but they didn’t see it.

“Tom,” Huckleberry whispered, “does this stop us from ever talking—always?”

“Sure it does. It doesn’t matter what comes along—we’ve got to keep mum no matter what. We’d drop down dead—don’t you know that?”

“Yes, I guess that’s true.”

They kept whispering for a little while longer. Soon after, a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside—within ten feet of them. The boys clutched at each other at once, in pure terror.

“Which one of us does he mean?” Huckleberry blurted.

“I dono—peep through the crack. Quick!”

“No, _you_, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t _do_ it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"8b5bea3c412843516a4ad3c4","rewritten_text":"We both agreed on Adrian, and we loved her; but since she had not yet escaped childhood, she could not understand, the way I could, how great his gifts were. She also could not feel the same sympathy for his interests and opinions. I was always with him. There was a kind of sensitivity and sweetness in his nature that made our conversations feel gentle and almost unreal. Then he was cheerful, singing in his thoughts like a lark from a high, sky-blue tower. He would soar in his mind like an eagle, and he was as innocent as a dove with mild eyes. He could calm Perdita’s seriousness and take the pain out of the tormenting restlessness of my own nature. I began to look back on my restless desires and my painful struggles with other people as if they were only a troubled dream. I felt as changed as if I had been turned into someone else, with new senses and a different way of nerves working, so that the world I saw in the mirror of my mind looked different. But that was not true. I was still the same in strength, still hungry for sympathy, still longing for real, active effort. My manly virtues did not leave me. The witch Urania spared the locks of Sampson while he lay at her feet; yet everything in me was softened and made more human.

Adrian did not teach me only the cold truths of history and philosophy. While he used those lessons to help me control my own reckless and untrained spirit, he also showed me the living story of his own heart. He made me feel and understand its wonderful character.

The former queen of England had tried, even when her son was still a child, to plant bold and ambitious plans in his mind. She saw that he had genius and unusual talent, and she worked to develop those gifts so she could use them later to support her own goals. She encouraged his desire to learn and his impulsive courage. She even tolerated his wild love of freedom, hoping—because this often happens—that it would turn into a passion for command. She tried to raise him with resentment toward, and a wish to get revenge on, the people who had helped bring about his father’s abdication. She did not succeed in that.

Still, the stories she gave him—no matter how distorted—about a great and wise nation asserting its right to govern itself made him admire it. In his early years, he became a republican from principle. Even so, his mother did not give up. To her love of power and her proud sense of noble birth, she added firm ambition, patience, and self-control. She studied her son’s character closely. Through praise, blame, and urging, she tried to find the right way to reach him. Even if the “music” that followed her touch seemed wrong to her, she kept her hopes on his talents and believed that, in the end, she would win him over."}

{"request_id":"92f965894cef257b882697b0","rewritten_text":"But it is of little consequence.”

“I may as well ask,” she answered, “why, with such plain intent to offend and insult me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your judgment, and even against your nature. Was that not a ready pretext for rudeness, if I _was_ rude? Yet I have other grounds for complaint. You know I do. Had my own feelings not turned against you—had they been indifferent, or even inclined—do you suppose any consideration would persuade me to accept the man who has been the instrument of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a sister I love most dearly?”

As she spoke, Mr. Darcy flushed; but the feeling passed quickly, and he listened without trying to interrupt her while she went on, “I have every reason to think ill of you. No motive can make excusable the unjust and ungenerous part you played _there_. You cannot, you dare not deny that you were the chief—if not the only—means of setting them at odds, of exposing one to the world’s censure for caprice and instability, the other to its mockery for hopes disappointed, and of bringing them both into the keenest misery.”

She paused, and with no small indignation observed that he listened with an air that showed him wholly untouched by any remorse. He even regarded her with a smile that seemed meant to disbelieve her.

“Can you deny that you have done it?” she repeated.

With an air of studied calm he replied, “I have no wish to deny that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am glad of the result. Towards _him_ I have been kinder than towards myself.”

Elizabeth affected not to notice the politeness of the remark, but its meaning did not escape her, nor was it likely to soften her.

“But it is not only this matter,” she continued. “My dislike rests on more than what has just occurred. Long before it ever happened, my opinion of you was already formed. Your character was laid open in the account I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On that point, what have you to say? In what imagined act of friendship can you justify yourself here? Or by what misrepresentation can you expect to impose on others?”

“You show a lively concern for that gentleman’s affairs,” said Darcy, in a less steady voice, and with a deeper flush.

“Who, knowing what his misfortunes have been, could help feeling interest in him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated, with contempt. “Yes, his misfortunes have been very great indeed.”

“And those misfortunes, and your doing,” cried Elizabeth, with spirit; “You have brought him down to his present condition—comparative poverty.”"}

{"request_id":"3498a8c138d531bd97a7156f","rewritten_text":"The narrow streets and small courts finally opened into a large open space. Pens for animals were scattered around, along with other signs that this was a cattle market. When Sikes reached the spot, he slowed down. Nancy could not keep up anymore, not after the fast pace they had been walking. He turned to Oliver and roughly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Do you hear?” Sikes growled when Oliver hesitated and looked around.

They were tucked into a dark corner, away from the path of any passengers.

Oliver could see, all too clearly, that resisting would not help. He held out his hand, and Nancy grabbed it tightly.

“Give me the other,” said Sikes, taking Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog looked up and growled.

“Listen, boy!” Sikes said, pressing his other hand against Oliver’s throat. “If he says even a soft word, stop him. Understand?”

The dog growled again, and licked its lips as it stared at Oliver, as if it wanted to attach itself to his windpipe right away.

“He’s as willing as a Christian—strike me blind if he isn’t!” Sikes said, watching the animal with grim, fierce approval. “Now you know what to expect, so call out as fast as you like. The dog will end the game soon. Come on, young ’un!”

Bull’s-eye wagged his tail at this unusually kind-sounding talk, then gave another warning growl for Oliver’s benefit and led the way forward.

They were crossing Smithfield, though it could have been Grosvenor Square, for all Oliver knew. The night was dark and foggy. The shop lights could barely push through the thick mist, which seemed to grow heavier with every moment and hid the streets and houses in shadow. Everything looked strange to Oliver, and his uncertainty felt even worse.

They had gone only a few steps when a deep church bell rang out the hour. At the first strike, both of his handlers stopped and turned their heads toward the sound.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy said when the bell stopped.

“What’s the point of telling me that? I can hear it,” Sikes snapped.

“I wonder if they can hear it,” Nancy said.

“Of course they can,” Sikes replied. “It was Bartlemy time when I was sold, and there weren’t a penny trumpet at the fair that I couldn’t hear the squeaking of. After I was locked up for the night, the noise and shouting outside made the old jail so quiet that I could almost have beaten my brains out against the iron plates of the door.”"}

{"request_id":"387542bac4b1ace6ebecf0da","rewritten_text":"Men marry because they’re tired; women, because they’re curious—both end up disappointed.”

“I don’t think I’m likely to marry, Harry. I’m too much in love. That’s one of your aphorisms. I’m putting it into practice, the way I do everything you say.”

“Who are you in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a pause.

“With an actress,” Dorian Gray said, blushing.

Lord Henry shrugged. “That’s a rather commonplace début.”

“You wouldn’t say that if you’d seen her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“I’ve never heard of her.”

“No one has. People will, someday, though. She’s a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are a decorative sex. They never have anything to say, but they say it charmingly. Women represent the triumph of matter over mind, just as men represent the triumph of mind over morals.”

“Harry, how can you?”

“My dear Dorian, it’s quite true. I’m analysing women at the moment, so I ought to know. The subject isn’t as abstruse as I thought. I find that, in the end, there are only two kinds of women—the plain and the coloured. The plain women are very useful. If you want to build a reputation for respectability, you only have to take them down to supper. The other women are very charming. They make one mistake, though. They paint in order to try to look young. Our grandmothers painted in order to try to talk brilliantly. Rouge and esprit used to go together. That’s all over now. As long as a woman can look ten years younger than her own daughter, she’s perfectly satisfied. As for conversation, there are only five women in London worth talking to, and two of them can’t be admitted into decent society. Still—tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Ah! Harry, your views terrify me.”

“Never mind that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you come across her?”

“I’ll tell you, Harry, but you mustn’t be unsympathetic about it. After all, it never would have happened if I hadn’t met you. You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. For days after I met you, something seemed to throb in my veins. As I lounged in the park, or strolled down Piccadilly, I used to look at everyone who passed and wonder, with mad curiosity, what kind of lives they led. Some of them fascinated me. Others filled me with terror. There was an exquisite poison in the air. I had a passion for sensations...."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d2d784abfd902100eff4f000","rewritten_text":"He slipped out from the wainscoting under cover of stealth, an evil smile set on his cruel, wrinkled mouth, while the moon drew her face away behind a cloud as he glided past the great oriel window, where his own arms and those of his murdered wife were emblazoned in azure and gold. On and on he moved, like some malignant shadow; even the darkness seemed to recoil from him as he went. At one point he thought he heard a voice calling, and he halted—only to discover it was nothing more than the baying of a dog from the Red Farm. Then he resumed his course, muttering odd sixteenth-century curses, and now and again lifting the rusty dagger into the midnight air. At last he reached the bend in the passage that led to luckless Washington’s room. He paused there for a heartbeat, the wind stirring his long grey locks and twisting them into grotesque, fantastic folds around the nameless dread of the dead man’s shroud. Then the clock struck the quarter, and he felt that the moment had arrived. He gave a quiet chuckle to himself and turned the corner; but no sooner had he done so than, with a pitiful cry of terror, he stumbled back and pressed his pallid face into his long, bony hands. Directly before him stood a dreadful spectre, fixed and unmoving like a carved thing, and monstrous beyond any madman’s dream. Its head was bald and burnished; its face round, and thick, and white; and hideous laughter seemed to have twisted its features into an eternal grin. From its eyes streamed streaks of scarlet light; the mouth was a broad well of fire; and a hideous garment, akin to his own, wrapped the Titan shape in its silent snows. Across its breast hung a placard bearing strange writing in antique characters—some scroll of shame, some account of wild sins, some dreadful calendar of crime—and in its right hand it held aloft a falchion of gleaming steel.\n\nHaving never set eyes on a ghost before, he was naturally seized with fright; after a second, hurried look at the appalling phantom, he bolted back to his room, stumbling over his long winding-sheet as he hurried down the corridor, until at last he let the rusty dagger fall into the Minister’s jack-boots, where it was discovered the next morning by the butler. Once he was alone in his own apartment, he threw himself down on a small pallet-bed and buried his face beneath the clothes. After a time, though, the brave old Canterville spirit reasserted itself, and he resolved to go and speak to the other ghost as soon as daylight came. So, just as dawn began to touch the hills with silver, he made his way back toward the place where he had first laid eyes on the grisly phantom, thinking that, after all, two ghosts were better than one, and that with the help of his new companion he might safely take hold of the twins."}

{"request_id":"14b40d9b8311b25057d2d16c","rewritten_text":"Why, we might well be in for a rather stirring piece of superstition from this hint. I suppose you’ll name the bug _scarabæus caput hominis_, or something along those lines—there are plenty of similar headings in the Natural Histories. Still, where are the _antennæ_ you mentioned?”

“The _antennæ!_” Legrand said, and he appeared to be getting unaccountably hot under the collar at the very thought. “I’m sure you can see the _antennæ_. I made them as clear and separate as they are in the original insect, and I take that to be enough.”

“Well, well,” I replied, “maybe you have—only I can’t see them;” and I handed him the paper without any further comment, not wanting to set his temper off. Yet I was genuinely astonished at how things had turned. His ill humor left me at a loss; and as for the beetle’s drawing, there were plainly _no antennæ_ to be seen at all, and the whole _did_ resemble the usual death’s-head engravings.

He took the paper back in a very peevish manner, and seemed on the point of crumpling it—apparently to throw it into the fire—when a casual look at the design suddenly held him fast. In the next moment his face flushed violently red; and then, almost at once, it became excessively pale. For several minutes he kept studying the drawing closely, as he sat. At last he stood up, took a candle from the table, and went to sit himself upon a sea-chest in the farthest corner of the room. There too he examined the paper with anxious care, turning it this way and that. He said nothing, but his behavior greatly surprised me; still, I thought it safer not to inflame the growing gloom of his temper with any remark. Presently he drew a wallet from his coat pocket, put the paper carefully into it, and laid both into a writing-desk, which he locked. He then regained a steadier composure, though the first air of excitement had entirely vanished. Yet he was less sulky than absorbed. As the evening dragged on, he sank deeper and deeper into reverie, from which none of my attempts could draw him out.

I had meant to spend the night at the hut, as I often had before, but seeing my host in that state, I judged it right to take my leave. He did not urge me to stay; but when I went, he shook my hand with even more than his usual warmth.

It was about a month later—during which time I had seen nothing of Legrand—when I received a visit, in Charleston, from his man, Jupiter. I had never seen the good old negro look so cast down, and I feared that some serious misfortune had befallen my friend."}

{"request_id":"b3df23a23c2447580b56cb58","rewritten_text":"In my younger days, I never felt discontent. And if I was ever overcome by _ennui_, I could always be pulled back by the beauty of nature or by studying what is great and sublime in the works of human beings. But I am a blasted tree. The bolt has entered my soul, and I realized then that I would live long enough to show what I will soon stop being: a miserable sight of broken humanity, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent a long time in Oxford. We wandered through the surrounding area, trying to find every place that could be connected to the most inspiring period of English history. Our little trips of discovery were often delayed by the things we kept coming across. We visited the tomb of the famous Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment, my soul rose above my degrading, miserable fears, and I could think about the noble ideas of liberty and self-sacrifice that these sights stood for. For an instant, I dared to throw off my chains and look around with a free, proud spirit. But the iron had already sunk into my flesh, and I sank back again, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford with regret and went on to Matlock, where we stayed next. The countryside around this village looked even more like Switzerland. Still, everything was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the bright crown of distant white Alps that always rise behind the pine-covered mountains of my own country. We visited the amazing cave and the small natural history rooms, where the curiosities were arranged in the same way as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry said the name “Chamounix,” it made me tremble, and I hurried to leave Matlock, because that frightening scene was now tied to it.

From Derby, we kept traveling north. We spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. Now I could almost pretend I was among the Swiss mountains. The small patches of snow that still lingered on the north sides of the hills, the lakes, and the rush of the rocky streams were familiar sights, and they felt dear to me. We also met some people there, and they almost managed to trick me into being happy. Clerval’s joy was even greater than mine. His mind grew broader in the company of talented men, and he discovered in himself abilities and resources he would never have believed he had while he was around people he considered his inferiors."}

content.text: {"request_id":"46cab6c8659e52a89cb76747","rewritten_text":"Having seen our friend properly settled in his new office, we turned our attention to Windsor. The closeness of this place to London was such that it eased the idea of a painful separation when we left Raymond and Perdita. We said goodbye to them in the Protectoral Palace. It was quite moving to watch my sister step in, as if she were entering the spirit of the drama, and try to fill her role with the dignity it demanded. Her inner pride and her humility of manner were now more openly at odds. Her shyness wasn’t forced; it came from the fear of not being properly valued, that slight sense of being overlooked by the world—which also characterized Raymond. But Perdita thought more often of others than he did, and part of her bashfulness came from a wish to spare those around her any feeling of inferiority, a feeling that never once crossed her mind. Given the circumstances of her birth and upbringing, Idris would have been better suited to the set formulas of ceremony; yet the ease with which she carried out such actions, because it had become habit, made them feel tedious. Still, despite every drawback, Perdita clearly enjoyed her position. She was too full of new ideas to feel much pain when we departed. She said goodbye to us warmly, promised to visit soon, and yet she did not regret the circumstances that had caused our separation. Raymond’s spirits were boundless. He didn’t know what to do with his new authority; his head was full of plans, and he had not yet settled on any—still, he promised himself, his friends, and the world that the era of his protectorship would be marked by some act of surpassing glory. So we talked about them and moralized, as with fewer people we returned to Windsor Castle. We felt intense relief at escaping political turmoil, and we threw ourselves into our solitude with even greater enthusiasm. We didn’t lack for things to do; but my eager nature was now directed only toward intellectual effort. Hard study proved an excellent remedy for the fever of spirit that, in idleness, I would doubtless have been vulnerable to. Perdita had allowed us to take Clara back with us to Windsor; and she, along with my two lovely infants, was a constant source of interest and amusement.\n\nThe only thing that disturbed our peace was Adrian’s health. It clearly declined, without any symptoms that would have led us to suspect his illness—unless, perhaps, his brightened eyes, animated look, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption. Yet he had neither pain nor fear. He threw himself into books with real ardor, and when he rested from study, it was in the company he loved best: his sister’s and mine."}

{"request_id":"9fdde46d174ef3523f776fc5","rewritten_text":"“No, no—that’s tomorrow. And I especially wanted to see Knightley today, for that very reason. What a dreadful, scorching morning!—I even went over the fields too” (she spoke with an air of strong resentment), “which only made it worse. And then not to find him at home! I assure you, I’m not at all pleased. There was no apology, no message for me. The housekeeper said she knew nothing about my being expected. Very extraordinary!—And nobody knew at all which way he’d gone. Perhaps to Hartfield, perhaps to the Abbey Mill, perhaps into his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is not like our friend Knightley! Can you explain it?”

Emma amused herself by protesting that it was very extraordinary indeed, and that she had not a single word to say for him.

“I can’t imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, (feeling the indignity a wife ought to feel,) “I can’t imagine how he could do something like that to you, of all people in the world! The very last person you’d expect to be forgotten!—My dear Mr. E., he must have left you a message. He must have. Not even Knightley could be so eccentric;—and his servants forgot it. You can be sure that was the case: and it’s very likely to happen with the Donwell servants, who, as I’ve often noticed, are all extremely awkward and careless. I’m sure I wouldn’t have such a person as his Harry standing at our sideboard for any reason. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very little of her indeed.—She promised Wright a receipt, and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins,” continued Mr. Elton, “as I was getting near the house, and he told me I wouldn’t find his master at home, but I didn’t believe him. William seemed rather out of sorts. He didn’t know what had come over his master lately, he said, but he could hardly ever get a word out of him. I have nothing to do with William’s troubles, but it really is of the greatest importance that _I_ should see Knightley today; and it becomes, therefore, a matter of very serious inconvenience that I should have taken this hot walk for nothing.”

Emma felt she couldn’t do better than go home at once. In all probability she was being waited for there at this very moment; and Mr. Knightley might be kept from sinking deeper into his aggression toward Mr. Elton—if not toward William Larkins.

When she took her leave, she was pleased to find Miss Fairfax determined to accompany her out of the room, to go with her even downstairs; it gave her an opportunity she immediately made use of, to say,”"}

{"request_id":"c9202c2a5b319ec50b953243","rewritten_text":"One day, while I was busy with my books and Mr. Pocket, I received a note in the mail, and the plain outside of it sent me into a great flutter. Even though I had never seen the handwriting it was addressed in, I could tell whose hand it was. It didn’t start in any set way—no “Dear Mr. Pip,” or “Dear Pip,” or “Dear Sir,” or “Dear Anything”—but went like this:—

“I am to come to London the day after tomorrow by the midday coach. I believe it was settled that you should meet me. At all events, Miss Havisham has that impression, and I write in obedience to it. She sends you her regard.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

If there had been time, I probably would have ordered several suits of clothes for the occasion; but since there wasn’t, I had to make do with what I had. My appetite vanished at once, and I found no peace or rest until the day arrived. But even then it didn’t get any better. I was worse than ever, and started haunting the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. I knew perfectly well that I was being ridiculous, yet I still felt as if it wasn’t safe to let the coach office out of my sight for more than five minutes at a time. In that state of irrational worry, I managed the first half-hour of a watch that was supposed to last four or five hours, when Wemmick ran into me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How do you do? I wouldn’t have thought this was _your_ beat.”

I told him I was waiting to meet someone coming up by coach, and I asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both flourishing, thank you,” said Wemmick, “and especially the Aged. He’s in wonderful spirits. He’ll be eighty-two next birthday. I’ve got a notion of firing eighty-two times, if the neighborhood doesn’t complain, and if my cannon holds up under the pressure. But this isn’t London talk. Where do you think I’m going?”

“To the office?” I said, because he was heading that way.

“Next thing to it,” Wemmick replied. “I’m going to Newgate. We’re in a banker’s-parcel case just now, and I’ve been down the road taking a look at the scene of action, and I must have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” Wemmick answered, very dryly. “But he’s accused of it. So could you or I be. Either of us might be accused of it, you know.”"}

{"request_id":"cb04ef16e11b655954dad0b3","rewritten_text":"“Are you talking about—Mr. Knightley?”

“Of course I am. I can’t imagine anyone else—and I thought you knew. When we talked about him, it was as clear as possible.”

“Not quite,” Emma replied, forcing calm, “because everything you said then seemed to me to refer to a different person. I could almost say that you had named Mr. Frank Churchill. I’m sure the service Mr. Frank Churchill did for you—protecting you from the gypsies—was what you were talking about.”

“Oh! Miss Woodhouse, how you forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember perfectly well what I said on that occasion. I told you I didn’t wonder at your attachment; that, considering the service he had done for you, it was extremely natural. And you agreed with it, speaking very warmly about your sense of that service, and even mentioning what you felt when he stepped forward to rescue you. The impression of it is still strong in my memory.”

“Oh, dear,” Harriet cried, “now I remember what you mean; but I was thinking of something completely different at the time. It wasn’t the gypsies—it wasn’t Mr. Frank Churchill I meant. No!” (with some lift of feeling) “I was thinking of something far more precious—of Mr. Knightley coming to ask me to dance, when Mr. Elton wouldn’t stand up with me, and when there was no other partner in the room. That was the kind action; that was the noble benevolence and generosity; that was the service that made me begin to feel how far superior he was to every other person on earth.”

“Good God!” Emma cried. “This has been a most unfortunate—most deplorable mistake! What is to be done?”

“You wouldn’t have encouraged me, then, if you’d understood me. At least, however, I can’t be worse off than I would have been if the other had been the person; and now—it is possible—”

She paused for a few moments. Emma couldn’t speak.

“I don’t wonder, Miss Woodhouse,” she went on, “that you should feel such a great difference between the two, whether it’s about me or anyone else. You must think one five hundred million times more highly of me than the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that—supposing—that if—strange as it may seem—. But you know those were your own words, and that more wonderful things had happened: matches of far greater disparity than between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. So it seems as if something like this could have happened before—and if I should be so fortunate, beyond expression, as to—if Mr. Knightley really—if he doesn’t mind the disparity, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you won’t set yourself against it and try to put difficulties in the way.”"}

{"request_id":"68237adda8741cd5b0f11111","rewritten_text":"No, don’t bring it up by hand then. Not a bit of it!”

Joe put forward more gravy, and I was too uneasy to accept it.

“He was a world of trouble to you, ma’am,” Mrs. Hubble said, sympathizing with my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated. “Trouble?”—and then she launched into a dreadful roll-call of every illness I’d been blamed for, every stretch of sleeplessness I’d caused, every high place I’d tumbled from, and every low place I’d tumbled into, every injury I’d done myself, every time she’d wished me in my grave, and how stubbornly I’d refused to go there.

I dare say the Romans must have worried one another terribly with their noses. Maybe that’s why they turned out so restless. At any rate, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose so irritated me while she was listing my misdeeds that I felt like yanking it until he cried out. Still, nothing I’d endured so far could match the dreadful sensations that seized me when the pause came after my sister’s recital—during which everyone looked at me, as I felt keenly, with indignation and disgust.

“Yet,” said Mr. Pumblechook, steering the talk gently back to what they’d been discussing, “Pork—regarded as biled—is rich, too; ain’t it?”

“Have a little brandy, uncle,” my sister said.

Oh, heavens—so it had finally arrived! He’d taste it and say it was weak, he would, and then I was done for. I gripped the leg of the table under the cloth with both hands and waited for what would happen.

My sister went for the stone bottle, came back with it, and poured his brandy out—no one else took any. The poor man fidgeted with his glass, lifted it, held it up to the light, set it down again, and kept me in suspense. All the while, Mrs. Joe and Joe were briskly clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I couldn’t take my eyes off him. Always clinging to the table-leg with my hands and feet, I watched him toy with his glass, raise it, grin, throw his head back, and drink the brandy straight. The next moment the whole company was struck with utter consternation: he sprang to his feet, spun round several times in a dreadful, spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and bolted out the door. Through the window we could see him, violently plunging and spitting, making the most awful faces, and acting as though he’d lost his mind.

I held on tight as Mrs. Joe and Joe rushed after him."}

content.text: {"request_id":"cb767e7b8d8892d5ccf0301d","rewritten_text":"Raymond was thrilled by the strong feelings that came with his recovered health. He believed that, as a leading man among the Athenians, he held a position worthy of his ambition. And in his hope of conquering Constantinople, he expected an event that would stand out through the ages, an achievement unmatched in human history. He imagined that a city with deep historic meaning—whose beautiful setting was the wonder of the world—after many hundreds of years as a stronghold of the Moslems, would be freed from slavery and barbarism, and returned to a people known for genius, civilization, and a love of liberty. Perdita lay in his restored society, in his love, his hopes, and his fame, as a Sybarite rests on a luxurious couch. Every thought carried him away, and every feeling seemed to be warmed and comforted by something kind and soothing.\n\nWe arrived at Kishan on the 7th of July. The weather had been calm during our journey. Each day, before dawn, we left our camp for the night and watched the shadows pull back from hill and valley, while the sun’s golden light approached. The soldiers who traveled with us took real pleasure in the beautiful countryside, showing their excitement in a lively, national way. When the sun rose, it was greeted with triumphant music, and the birds, heard now and then, filled the gaps between the songs. At noon, we set up our tents in a shady valley or in a cool wood among the mountains. A stream running over pebbles made a gentle sound that helped us sleep. Our evening march was calmer than the restless feeling of the morning, and it was even more enjoyable. If the band played, they naturally chose tunes with less intense emotion. The music would move from the farewell of love or a lament for being away, and then end with a solemn hymn that matched the quiet beauty of evening and lifted the soul toward something grand and religious. Often, all sounds would stop so we could listen to the nightingale. Fireflies danced in bright rhythm, and the soft cooing of the aziolo seemed to promise fair weather for the travelers. If we passed through a valley, gentle shadows surrounded us, and the rocks showed beautiful colors. If we climbed among the mountains, Greece seemed like a living map spread out below us, with her famous peaks cutting through the sky, and her rivers running through the fertile land in silver lines. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travelers looked with amazement at this splendid landscape, so different from the plain colors and sad beauty of home. When we left Macedonia, the fertile but low plains of Thrace offered fewer sights, but the journey still stayed interesting. An advanced guard told us we were coming, and the local people quickly moved to show respect to Lord Raymond."}

{"request_id":"7a1863678ae992be5f13faa9","rewritten_text":"“Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—no, Sir Simon—are you hungry? I’ve got a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?”

“No, thank you. I don’t eat anything anymore; but it’s very kind of you all the same, and you’re much nicer than the rest of your horrid, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.”

“Stop!” Virginia cried, stamping her foot. “You’re the rude one, the horrid one, the vulgar one—and as for dishonesty, you know you stole the paints out of my box to try to spruce up that ridiculous bloodstain in the library. First you took all my reds, including the vermilion, and I couldn’t paint any more sunsets. Then you took the emerald-green and the chrome-yellow, and finally I had nothing left but indigo and Chinese white, so I could only do moonlight scenes—which are always depressing to look at, and not at all easy to paint. I never told on you, though I was very annoyed, and the whole thing was just ridiculous. Who ever heard of emerald-green blood?”

“Well, really,” said the Ghost, rather meekly. “What was I supposed to do? Getting real blood is very difficult these days, and since your brother started it all with his Paragon Detergent, I certainly saw no reason why I shouldn’t use your paints. As for color, that’s always a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, for instance—the bluest in England. But I know you Americans don’t care much for things like that.”

“You know nothing about it. The best thing you can do is emigrate and improve your mind. My father will be only too happy to give you a free passage, and although there’s a heavy duty on spirits of every kind, there won’t be any trouble with the Custom House, since the officers are all Democrats. Once you’re in New York, you’re sure to be a great success. I know lots of people there who would give a hundred thousand dollars just to have a grandfather—and much more than that for a family Ghost.”

“I don’t think I’d like America.”

“I suppose it’s because we have no ruins and no curiosities,” Virginia said, with a sharp edge.

“No ruins! No curiosities!” the Ghost answered. “You have your navy and your manners.”

“Good evening. I’ll go ask papa to give the twins an extra week’s holiday.”

“Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,” he cried. “I’m so lonely and so unhappy, and I really don’t know what to do. I want to go to sleep, and I can’t.”

“That’s quite absurd! You just have to go to bed and blow out the candle.”"}

{"request_id":"ff1dbbb9dc9d47fc013a71e3","rewritten_text":"He shivered, then went back, closing the window behind him.

Once he reached the door, he turned the key and opened it. He didn’t even look at the murdered man. He felt the secret to the whole thing was not to recognize what was happening. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait that had caused all his misery was gone from his life. That was enough.

Then he remembered the lamp. It was a rather curious one, made in Moorish style—dull silver, inlaid with arabesques of burnished steel, and studded with coarse turquoises. Maybe his servant wouldn’t notice it, and no one would ask questions. He hesitated for a moment, then turned back and took it from the table. He couldn’t help looking at the dead thing. How still it was! How horribly white the long hands looked! It was like some dreadful wax figure.

After locking the door behind him, he moved quietly downstairs. The woodwork creaked and seemed to cry out as if it were in pain. He stopped several times and waited. No—everything was still. It was only the sound of his own footsteps.

When he reached the library, he saw the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be hidden somewhere. He unlocked a secret press set into the wainscoting—a press where he kept his own strange disguises—and put them inside. He could burn them later. Then he took out his watch. It was twenty minutes to two.

He sat down and began to think. Every year—almost every month—men were strangled in England for what he had done. There had been a kind of murder-madness in the air. Some red star had come too close to the earth.... Still, what evidence was there against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. No one had seen him come back in. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.... Paris! Yes. Basil had gone to Paris, and by the midnight train, just as he’d planned. With his reserved, peculiar habits, it would be months before anyone became suspicious. Months! Everything could be destroyed long before then.

A sudden thought struck him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went out into the hall. He paused there, listening to the slow, heavy tread of the policeman outside on the pavement, and watching the flash of the bull’s-eye reflected in the window. He waited and held his breath.

After a few moments he drew back the latch and slipped out, shutting the door very gently behind him. Then he began ringing the bell."}
