{"request_id":"5561842fa2ad5a2dd1c99cc9","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced up and down the room, furious. I stood ready to take his complaints and answer them. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is completely ridiculous,” he said loudly. “If you were schoolboys, you couldn’t act more foolishly than this.”

“You don’t understand,” Raymond replied. “This is only part of a system—a plan of tyranny that I will never accept. Because I’m the Protector of England, am I supposed to be the only slave in its empire? They invade my privacy, judge my actions, and insult my friends. But I will get rid of the whole thing at once. Be witnesses,” he said, and he pulled the star—the insignia of his office—from his chest and threw it onto the table. “I renounce my office. I give up my power. Whoever wants it can take it!”

“Let him take it,” Adrian snapped. “Whoever thinks he can claim it, or whoever the world decides is your superior. There isn’t a man in England with enough arrogance to do that. Know yourself, Raymond, and your anger will fade, and your self-satisfaction will come back. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for our country’s prosperity—or our own—we prayed at the same time for the Protector’s life and well-being, because they were tied together. Your hours were spent for our benefit. Your ambition was to earn our approval. You decorated our towns with buildings, gave us useful institutions, and made the land more fertile. The powerful and unfair feared you, and the poor and oppressed rose up like flowers in the morning, bright under the sunshine of your protection.

“Can you really be surprised that we’re all shocked and grieving when it seems to have changed? But this angry mood is already passing. Go back to your duties. Your supporters will welcome you. Your enemies will be silenced. Our love, honor, and duty toward you will show themselves again. Control yourself, Raymond. The world will be yours.”

“All of that would make sense,” Raymond said bitterly, “if it were meant for someone else. Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the first peer of the land, might become its ruler. You, the good, the wise, the just, could rule everyone’s heart. But I see, too soon for my own happiness and too late for England’s good, that I took on a job I can’t handle. I can’t even rule myself. My passions control me; even my smallest impulse is my master. Do you think I gave up the Protectorate—yes, I have given it up—just out of anger? By the God who lives, I swear I will never take that trinket again. Never again will I burden myself with the weight of care and misery that it represents.”"}

{"request_id":"c44b589b579090cc03490593","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers let go of Lord Arthur’s right hand and took hold of his left instead, stooping so far to inspect it that the bright gold rims of his spectacles looked as if they might almost rest on the palm. For a moment his expression turned into a stark, white mask of terror, but he quickly regained his _sang-froid_, and, lifting his eyes to Lady Windermere, said with a smile that seemed forced, “It is the hand of a charming young man.

“Of course it is!” returned Lady Windermere. “But will he be a charming husband? That’s what I want to know.”

“All charming young men are,” said Mr. Podgers.

“I don’t think a husband ought to be too fascinating,” Lady Jedburgh murmured, thoughtful. “It’s so risky.”

“My dear child, they never are too fascinating,” Lady Windermere cried. “But what I want are details. Details are the only things that interest. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?”

“Well, within the next few months Lord Arthur will go a voyage—”

“Oh yes, his honeymoon, naturally!”

“And lose a relative.”

“Not his sister, I hope?” said Lady Jedburgh, in a tone full of pity.

“Certainly not his sister,” answered Mr. Podgers, with a slight deprecating sweep of his hand. “Only a distant relative.”

“Well, I’m dreadfully disappointed,” said Lady Windermere. “I have nothing at all to tell Sybil tomorrow. Nobody cares about distant relatives these days. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she’d better have a black silk with her; it always serves for church. And now, let’s go in to supper. They’re sure to have eaten everything, but perhaps we’ll find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but he’s so stirred up about politics at present that I never feel quite sure about him. I do wish General Boulanger would keep still. Duchess, you must be tired?”

“Not at all, dear Gladys,” replied the Duchess, waddling toward the door. “I’ve enjoyed myself immensely, and the cheiropodist—no, I mean the cheiromantist—is quite fascinating. Flora, where can my tortoise-shell fan be? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, how kind—I'm sure”; and at last the worthy woman managed to get downstairs without dropping her scent-bottle more than twice.

All the while Lord Arthur Savile had stayed standing by the fireplace, carrying the same dread in him, the same sickening certainty of evil to come. He gave his sister a sad smile as she passed him on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking lovely in her pink brocade and pearls, and he scarcely even heard Lady Windermere when she called to him to follow. He kept thinking of Sybil Merton, and the thought that anything might come between them brought tears to his eyes."}

{"request_id":"a81ef16b16d37d3daf1e8a74","rewritten_text":"Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had traveled so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle.

His face immediately turned to the darkest gloom, and he answered, “To find the one who ran away from me.”

“And was the man you were chasing traveling in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we must have seen him. The day before we picked you up, we saw some dogs pulling a sledge, with a man in it, across the ice.”

This made the stranger pay close attention. He asked many questions about the route the dæmon, as he called him, had taken. Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, “I’m sure I’ve made you curious, and I’ve made these good people curious too. But you’re kind enough not to ask.”

“Of course,” I said. “It would be very rude and inhuman of me to bother you with my own questions.”

“And yet you saved me from a strange and dangerous situation. You have kindly brought me back to life.”

Not long after that, he asked whether I thought the ice breaking up had destroyed the other sledge. I told him I couldn’t say for sure. The ice didn’t break until close to midnight, and the traveler might have reached safety before then, but I couldn’t know.

From that point on, a new energy seemed to return to the stranger’s failing body. He was very eager to stay on deck to watch for the sledge that had appeared before. But I persuaded him to remain in the cabin, because he was too weak to handle the cold air. I promised that someone would keep watch for him and let him know right away if anything new came into view.

This is my journal account of what has happened with this strange event up to today. The stranger has slowly started to get better, but he is still very quiet. He also seems uneasy whenever anyone other than me enters his cabin. Still, his manners are so kind and gentle that the sailors all take an interest in him, even though they have hardly spoken with him at all. As for me, I find myself growing to love him like a brother. His constant, deep grief moves me with real sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble person in better days, because even now, in wreck and ruin, he remains so attractive and pleasant.

In one of my letters, I wrote to you, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the wide ocean. Yet I have found a man who, before his spirit was crushed by misery, I would have been happy to have as the brother of my heart.”}"}

{"request_id":"9a842b78c242c9e63b120f27","rewritten_text":"Just as they were leaving the dining-room, midnight began to boom from the clock tower, and when the last stroke sounded they heard a crash and a sudden, shrill cry. A dreadful peal of thunder shook the house; an eerie strain of music drifted through the air. A panel at the top of the staircase flew back with a loud noise, and on the landing—looking very pale and white, with a small casket in her hand—Virginia stepped out. In an instant, they all rushed up to her. Mrs. Otis seized her passionately in her arms, the Duke overwhelmed her with violent kisses, and the twins spun around the group in a wild war-dance.

“Good heavens, child! Where have you been?” Mr. Otis demanded, rather angrily, convinced she must have been pulling some foolish trick on them. “Cecil and I have been riding all over the country looking for you, and your mother has been frightened to death. You must never play these practical jokes again.”

“Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!” the twins shrieked as they capered about.

“My own darling—thank God you are found. You must never leave my side again,” Mrs. Otis murmured, kissing the trembling child and smoothing the tangled gold of her hair.

“Papa,” Virginia said quietly, “I’ve been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for everything he’d done, and before he died he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.”

The whole family stared at her in mute amazement, but she was completely grave and serious. Then, turning around, she led them through the opening in the wainscoting into a narrow secret corridor, with Washington following and holding a lighted candle he had grabbed from the table. At last they reached a great oak door, studded with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it swung open on its heavy hinges, and they found themselves in a small, low room with a vaulted ceiling and one tiny grated window. Set into the wall was a huge iron ring, and chained to it was a gaunt skeleton stretched out at full length on the stone floor, as if it were trying to grasp—using its long, fleshless fingers—an old-fashioned trencher and ewer placed just out of reach. The jug had evidently once been filled with water, since the inside was covered with green mould. There was nothing on the trencher but a pile of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her little hands together, and began to pray silently, while the rest of the party watched in wonder at the terrible tragedy whose secret had now been revealed to them."}

{"request_id":"b19ef2164f8814155722874a","rewritten_text":"At the stairs where we had first taken him abroad, and ever since, I kept a watchful eye out for any sign that we were suspected. I saw nothing. We certainly were not, and at that moment we were no more attended or followed by any boat than we were suspected. Had a boat been waiting on us, I would have dashed to the shore and made her either go on or show plainly what she meant. As it was, we went on our way without any hint of interference.

He had his boat-cloak on, and, as I’ve said, he looked like a natural part of the scene. It was striking—though perhaps the miserable life he’d been living explained it—that he was the least uneasy of all of us. He wasn’t indifferent; he told me he hoped to live long enough to see his gentleman among the best of gentlemen in a foreign country. Still, he wasn’t the sort to be passive or resigned, as I understood it; he simply had no intention of meeting danger halfway. When danger came, he faced it, but it had to arrive before he would trouble himself.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it’s like to sit here along with my dear boy and have my smoke, after being shut up day by day between four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I know the pleasures of freedom,” I answered.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head gravely. “But you don’t know it like I do. You must’ve been under lock and key, dear boy, to know it as much as I do,—but I ain’t going to be low.”

It struck me as odd that, for any plan or controlling thought, he should have risked his freedom—and even his life. Yet I considered that perhaps freedom without danger was too far removed from the whole pattern of his existence to mean to him what it would mean to someone else. I was not far off, since after smoking a little he said—

“You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, on the other side of the world, I was always looking back to this side; and it got to feel flat there, even though I was growing rich. Everybody knew Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and Magwitch could go, and no one’s head would be troubled about him. They don’t feel that way about me here, dear boy—wouldn’t, leastwise, if they knew where I was.”

“If all goes well,” I said, “you’ll be perfectly free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he replied, drawing a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And you think so?”"}

{"request_id":"0169748305beddc59163c40e","rewritten_text":"“No!” the girl answered.

“Then tell me why.”

“For one reason,” the girl said, steady and resolute, “for one reason: the lady knows it, and she will stand by me in it—I have her promise. And for another reason besides: for all the bad life he has led, I’ve led a bad life too. There are many of us who have kept the same paths together, and I won’t turn on them—people who might, any of them, have turned on me, but didn’t, though they’re as bad as they are.”

“Then,” said the gentleman at once, as though that were the very point he’d been trying to reach, “put Monks into my hands, and leave him to me to manage.”

“What if he turns against the others?”

“I promise you,” he replied, “that if it comes to that—if the truth is forced out of him—then the matter will end there. There must be circumstances in Oliver’s little history that would be painful to drag before the public, and once the truth is drawn out, they shall go scot free.”

“And if it isn’t?” the girl suggested.

“Then,” the gentleman went on, “this Fagin shall not be brought to justice without your consent. In that event, I could lay out reasons, I think, that would lead you to agree.”

“Do I have the lady’s promise for that?” asked the girl.

“You do,” said Rose. “My true and faithful pledge.”

“Monks would never learn how you came to know what you know?” the girl asked after a short pause.

“Never,” answered the gentleman. “The right sort of intelligence must be brought to bear upon him, so that he could never even guess.”

“I’ve been a liar, and among liars from a little child,” said the girl after another interval of silence, “but I’ll take your word.”

Once she had received assurance from both that she might safely do so, she went on in a voice so low that it was often hard for the listener to make out even the meaning of what she said. She described, by name and situation, the public-house where she had been followed that night. From the way she sometimes paused, it seemed as if the gentleman were making quick notes of what she told him. After she had explained the place’s localities, the best spot from which to watch it without drawing notice, and the night and hour when Monks was most accustomed to go there, she stopped for a few moments, as if to fix his face and appearance more firmly in her mind.

“He is tall,” she said, “and strongly built, though not stout. He has a kind of furtive walk; and when he walks he keeps looking over his shoulder—first to one side, then to the other.”"}

{"request_id":"cfd08e1fc88ae06be21168a2","rewritten_text":"“I have to go, uncertain of what will happen to me; but I will return here, or follow your party, as soon as possible. One word, one look, will be enough to decide whether I enter your father’s house this evening—or never.”

Such a letter was not likely to be recovered from soon. Half an hour of solitude and reflection might have calmed her; but the ten minutes that had passed before she was interrupted—despite all the limits of her situation—could do nothing to bring her peace. Every moment only brought fresh agitation. It was overwhelming happiness. And before she had even moved beyond the first stage of full feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta all came in.

The sheer necessity of seeming like herself caused an immediate struggle; but after a while she could do no more. She stopped understanding a word they said, and had to plead indisposition and excuse herself. Then they could see she looked very ill, and were shocked and concerned, and would not move—would not stir—for anything in the world. This was dreadful. If only they had gone away and left her in quiet possession of that room, it might have cured her; but having them all standing and waiting around her was distracting, and in desperation she said she would go home.

“By all means, my dear,” cried Mrs Musgrove, “go home directly, and take care of yourself, so that you’ll be fit for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to doctor you, but I’m no doctor myself. Charles, ring and order a chair. She must not walk.”

But a chair would never do. Worse than everything! To lose the chance of saying two words to Captain Wentworth during her quiet, solitary walk up the town (and she felt almost certain she would meet him) was more than she could bear. The chair was earnestly protested against, and Mrs Musgrove—who was thinking only of one kind of illness—after assuring herself with some anxiety that there had been no fall in the matter; that Anne had not, at any time lately, slipped down and struck her head; that she was perfectly convinced there had been no fall—could part with her cheerfully and depend on finding her better at night.

Anxious not to miss any possible precaution, Anne struggled and said—

“I’m afraid, ma’am, that it isn’t quite understood. Please be so good as to mention to the other gentlemen that we hope to see your whole party this evening. I’m afraid there has been some mistake; and I want you particularly to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh! my dear, it is quite understood. I give you my word.”"}

{"request_id":"dc58bff189130df28e2e7ac6","rewritten_text":"“Now, in English, the letter that shows up most often is e. After that, the order of frequency runs like this: _a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z_. _E_ stands out so strongly that you hardly ever meet a sentence of any length in which it is not the dominant character.

“Having said that, we leave off at the very start with the groundwork for something beyond a mere guess. The table’s general usefulness is plain enough—but in this particular cipher we shall only need it in part. Since our leading character is 8, we begin by treating it as the _e_ of the natural alphabet. To test the idea, we should check whether the 8 appears frequently in pairs—for _e_ is doubled very often in English—such as in words like ‘meet,’ ‘.fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ &c. In the present case we find it doubled no fewer than five times, even though the cryptograph is short.

“Let us therefore take 8 as _e_. Now, among all _words_ in the language, ‘the’ is the most common; so we should look for repetitions of any three characters, in the same order of arrangement, with the last one being 8. If we locate such repeated letters, set up in that way, they will most likely stand for the word ‘the.’ On inspection, we find as many as seven such arrangements, the characters being ;48. We may accordingly suppose that ; stands for _t_, 4 stands for _h_, and 8 stands for _e_—a point now confirmed. Thus a major step is made.

“But once we have fixed a single word, we can fix a matter of far greater consequence: several beginnings and endings of other words. Take, for instance, the second-to-last occurrence, where the combination ;48 appears—not far from the end of the cipher. We know that the ; right after it begins a word, and among the six characters that follow this ‘the,’ we can account for no less than five. Let us write down those characters, using the letters we already know them to represent, and leave a blank for what we do not—

t eeth.

“From this we can at once throw out the ‘th,’ since it forms no part of the word that starts with the first t; for by trying the whole alphabet for a letter that could fit the gap, we see that no word can be formed in which this _th_ could belong. We are therefore reduced to

t ee,

and, going through the alphabet if need be as before, we reach the word ‘tree,’ as the only possible reading.”}"}

content.text: {"request_id":"9ae8b7e1e47e19dda9038ad7","rewritten_text":"Back in my day, in my own country, that money was gathered from imposts, and the citizen pictured the foreign importer as the one paying it—so it felt comforting to him to believe that; but in truth it was paid by the American people, and it was divided among them so evenly and exactly that the annual burden on the 100-millionaire and the annual burden on the poor day-laborer’s hungry child came out to the very same figure—each paid $6. I don’t see how anything could be more equal than that. Well, Scotland and Ireland were under Arthur’s tribute, and the combined populations of the British Isles came to something under 1,000,000. A mechanic’s average wage was 3 cents a day, after he’d paid for his own living. Using that, the national government’s yearly expenses worked out to $90,000, or roughly $250 a day. So, by swapping nickels for gold on a king’s-evil day, I didn’t end up hurting anyone or making anyone unhappy—I actually pleased everyone involved and, besides, cut four-fifths off that day’s national expense; a saving that would have been the same as $800,000 in my America. In making that substitution, I drew on wisdom from a very distant source—the kind I learned as a boy—because the true statesman doesn’t scorn any wisdom, no matter how humble its origin. When I was a child, I’d always saved my pennies and contributed buttons to the foreign missionary cause. Those buttons would do as well for the ignorant savage as the coin would; the coin, though, suited me better than the buttons. In the end, everyone was content and no one was harmed.\n\nMarinel took the patients as they arrived. He examined the candidate; if the man couldn’t meet the requirements, he was turned away, and if he could, he was sent on to the king. A priest spoke the words, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king pressed and stroked the ulcers while the reading went on; at last, the patient was approved, received his nickel—the king himself hanging it around his neck—and was dismissed. Would you think it cured? It certainly did. Any kind of ritual will work if the patient’s faith is firm. Up by Astolat there was a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who used to herd geese there—so the girl said—and they built the chapel on that spot and put up a picture showing the event; a picture you’d imagine would be risky for a sick person to get near. Yet, on the contrary, thousands of the lame and sick came each year, prayed before it, and left whole and sound; and even the healthy could look at it and live."}

{"request_id":"0428688d9e7cb77cb8639d16","rewritten_text":"But it’s really remarkable that she should always hear Jane better than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she won’t find her grandmama any less deaf than she was two years ago—which is saying a great deal at my mother’s age. And it really has been a full two years, you know, since she was here. We’ve never gone so long without seeing her, and as I was telling Mrs. Cole, we’ll hardly know how to make enough of her now.”

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax here soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Indeed!—that must be a very great pleasure.”

“Thank you. You’re very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone says the same kind things. I’m sure she’ll be as happy to see her friends at Highbury as they can be to see her. Yes—Friday or Saturday; she can’t say which, because Colonel Campbell will want the carriage himself one of those days. It’s so good of them to send her the whole way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes—Friday or Saturday next. That’s what she writes about. That’s the reason she’s writing out of the usual schedule, as we call it; because, in the normal course, we wouldn’t have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, that’s what I thought. I was afraid there might be little chance of my hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today.”

“So thoughtful of you! No, we wouldn’t have heard, if it hadn’t been for this particular circumstance—her coming here so soon. My mother is so delighted—for she’s to be three months with us at least. Three months, she says, positively, and I’m going to have the pleasure of reading to you. The situation is this: the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her father and mother to come over and see her right away. They hadn’t planned to go until the summer, but she’s so impatient to see them again—for before she married last October, she was never away from them for more than a week, which must make it very strange to be in different kingdoms, I was going to say, but really different countries. And so she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father, I declare I don’t know which it was, but we’ll see presently in Jane’s letter—writing in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, to urge their coming over directly. They’ll give them the meeting in Dublin, and take them back to their country seat, Baly-craig—a beautiful place, I imagine.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"8bcbf4ca8247ed5be95d8a7d","rewritten_text":"“April 7th. I got up early, and, to my great joy, I finally saw what there was no reason to doubt was the North Pole itself. It was there, beyond question, right under my feet. But I had already risen so far that I could not make out anything clearly. Still, if I judge by the numbers that show my different heights at different times—between 6 A.M. on April 2 and twenty minutes before 9 A.M. that same day, when the barometer began to fall—it seems reasonable to think that by 4 A.M. on April 7 the balloon had reached a height of at least 7,254 miles above the sea. That height sounds enormous, but the estimate I used was probably lower than the truth. In any case, I clearly saw the whole major diameter of the earth. The entire northern hemisphere lay beneath me like a map laid flat. Even the great circle of the equator formed the edge of my horizon. Your Excellencies can easily imagine that the parts within the Arctic Circle that had not been explored so far, though they were directly under me and therefore did not look stretched out, were still too small and too far away from where I was looking to allow any very accurate study. Even so, what I could see was strange and thrilling. Northward from that huge rim I mentioned—more or less the limit of human discovery in these regions—an unbroken, or almost unbroken, sheet of ice continues. At first, its surface is flattened. Farther on, it sinks into a flatter plane, and then, becoming clearly concave, it ends at the Pole in a circular center that is sharply defined. From the balloon, its apparent diameter made an angle of about sixty-five seconds. Its color was a dark gray that varied in intensity, and it was always darker than any other spot on the visible hemisphere. At times it deepened into the most complete and impenetrable blackness. Beyond that, there was little I could determine. By twelve o’clock the circular center had shrunk noticeably, and by seven P.M. I could no longer see it at all. The balloon passed over the western edge of the ice and then floated away quickly toward the equator.\n\n“April 8th. I noticed the earth’s apparent size had decreased, and its overall color and look had changed as well.”"}

{"request_id":"1dbfdd82419c45bf2d8bfc46","rewritten_text":"Emma did not regret being so condescending when she went to the Coles. The visit gave her many pleasant memories the next day. And anything she might have seemed to lose by staying quietly and with dignity was more than made up for by the excitement and popularity she received. She must have made the Coles very happy—good, deserving people who deserved to be pleased. And she left behind a name that would not be forgotten soon.

Perfect happiness, even when remembered, is rare. Still, there were two things that bothered her. First, she wondered if she had not gone against a woman’s duty by telling Frank Churchill her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings. It did not seem right, but the idea had been so strong that she could not stop herself. And the fact that he listened to everything she said made it feel like a compliment to her judgment. That, in turn, made it harder for her to be sure she should have kept quiet.

The second thing she regretted also involved Jane Fairfax. Emma had no doubt about this one. Jane truly and clearly regretted how much worse her own playing and singing were. She also sincerely regretted how idle she had been as a child, and then she sat down and practiced hard for an hour and a half.

After that, Harriet came in. If Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, Emma would have been comforted quickly.

“Oh! If I could only play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t put us in the same group, Harriet. My playing isn’t more like hers than a lamp is like sunshine.”

“Oh! dear—I think you play the best of the two. I think you play just as well as she does. I’m sure I’d rather hear you. Everyone said how well you played last night.”

“People who really knew anything about it would notice the difference. The truth is, Harriet, my playing is only good enough to be praised. Jane Fairfax’s is much better.”

“Well, I’ll always think you play just as well as she does, or that if there is any difference, nobody would ever notice it. Mr. Cole said how much taste you have. And Mr. Frank Churchill talked a lot about your taste, and he said he values taste more than skill.”

“Ah, but Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I saw that she had skill, but I didn’t know she had taste. Nobody ever talked about it. And I hate Italian singing. You can’t understand a word of it. Besides, if she plays so well, you know she has to, because she’ll have to teach.”}"}

{"request_id":"400cdc16be3a05fa2f21eec0","rewritten_text":"But don’t suppose that I felt it wasn’t an evil in itself.”

“Depend upon it, they were all quite at ease.”

“I may not like it the better for that, perhaps. With so many women and children on board, they have no _right_ to be comfortable.”

“My dear Frederick, you talk in the most idle fashion. Pray, what would become of us poor sailors’ wives—who are often eager to be taken to one port or another—after our husbands, if everyone had your way of thinking?”

“You see, my feelings didn’t stop me from taking Mrs Harville and all her family to Plymouth.”

“But I can’t bear to hear you speak as if you were some fine gentleman, and women were all fine ladies, instead of sensible creatures. None of us expects to be in smooth water every day of our lives.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “when he has a wife, he’ll change his tune. Once he’s married—if we’re lucky enough to live to another war—we shall see him do as you and I, and many others, have done. He’ll be very thankful to anyone who can bring his wife to him.”

“Ay, that he will.”

“Now I have done,” cried Captain Wentworth. “The moment married people start attacking me with,—‘Oh! you’ll feel quite differently when you are married.’ I can only answer, ‘No, I shan’t;’ and then they say again, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that’s the end of it.”

He rose and went away.

“What a fine traveller you must have been, ma’am!” said Mrs Musgrove to Mrs Croft.

“Pretty well, ma’am, in the fifteen years since I married; though many women have done more. I’ve crossed the Atlantic four times, and been once to the East Indies, and back again, and only once; besides having been in different places at home—Cork, and Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I never went beyond the Streights, and I never was in the West Indies. We don’t call Bermuda or Bahama, you know, the West Indies.”

Mrs Musgrove had nothing to object; she couldn’t accuse herself of ever having called them anything else in the whole course of her life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” Mrs Croft went on, “that nothing can surpass the accommodations of a man-of-war; I mean, of course, the higher rates. When you come to a frigate, you’re more shut in; though any reasonable woman may be perfectly happy in one. And I can safely say that the happiest part of my life has been spent on board a ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to be feared.”"}

{"request_id":"8c3fd830678b6725173c7010","rewritten_text":"The most exquisite gentlemen, bred to the finest degree, wore small pendant gewgaws that chimed as they drifted along in languor; those golden fetters rang out like tiny, treasured bells. Between that tinkling and the whisper of silk, brocade, and fine linen, the air seemed to flutter—fanning Saint Antoine and his devouring appetite far off in the distance.

Dress was the one sure talisman and charm for keeping everything in its proper place. Everyone was arrayed for a Fancy Ball that was never meant to end. From the Palace of the Tuileries, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the Tribunals of Justice, and all society (save the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball descended to the Common Executioner. In keeping with the charm, he was to appear “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—where the axe was a rarity—Monsieur Paris, as was the episcopal fashion among his fellow Professors in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest, presided in that dainty attire. And who among the company at Monseigneur’s reception, in that seventeen hundred and eightieth year of our Lord, could possibly doubt that a system planted in a frizzled hangman, powdered, gold-laced, pumped, and white-silk stockinged, would put the very stars to shame!

Having relieved his four men of their burdens and taken his chocolate, Monseigneur caused the doors of the Holiest of Holiests to be thrown open, and then he came forth. After that, what submission, what cringing and fawning, what servility, what abject humiliation! As for bowing down in body and spirit, Heaven was left nothing to receive—which may have been one of the reasons the worshippers of Monseigneur never bothered it.

With a word of promise here and a smile there, a whisper to one fortunate slave and a wave of the hand to another, Monseigneur moved pleasantly through his rooms toward the remote quarter of the Circumference of Truth. There he turned, came back again, and in due time, shut himself up in his sanctuary with the chocolate sprites, never to be seen again.

When the show was done, the flutter in the air swelled into a little storm, and the precious little bells began ringing downstairs. Soon there was only one person left of the whole crowd; with his hat under his arm and his snuff-box in his hand, he went on slowly, passing among the mirrors on his way out.

“I devote you,” said he, stopping at the last door on his route and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

With that, he shook the snuff from his fingers as though he were shaking dust from his feet, and walked quietly downstairs."}

{"request_id":"7a79ef3c34c54a836e8dd7f4","rewritten_text":"“Do you often come back?”

“I’ve never been here since.”

“Me neither.”

The moon began to rise, and I found myself thinking of the calm look on the white ceiling, which had already passed. The moon began to rise again, and I thought about the weight of my hand when I’d spoken the last words he had heard on earth.

Estella was the next to break the silence that followed between us.

“I’ve hoped and meant to come back very often, but I’ve been stopped by all sorts of circumstances. Poor, poor old place!”

The silvery mist caught the first rays of moonlight, and those same rays touched the tears that fell from her eyes. Not knowing that I saw them, and trying to keep herself from being overcome by them, she said quietly,—

“Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it ended up left in this condition?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The ground belongs to me. It’s the only possession I haven’t given up. Everything else has slipped away from me, little by little, but I’ve kept this. It was the only thing I resisted with any real determination during all those miserable years.”

“Is it going to be built on?”

“At last, it is. I came here to say goodbye to it before the change. And you,” she said, with a voice full of gentle interest toward a wanderer,—“you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And you’re doing well, I’m sure?”

“I work pretty hard to make a living, so—yes, I am doing well.”

“I’ve often thought of you,” Estella said.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. There was a long, hard time when I kept far from myself the memory of what I’d thrown away, when I was still ignorant of its value. But since my duty hasn’t been incompatible with admitting that memory, I’ve made room for it in my heart.”

“You’ve always had your place in my heart,” I answered.

And we were silent again until she spoke.

“I never imagined,” said Estella, “that I would be taking leave of you while taking leave of this spot. I’m very glad to do it.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? For me, parting is painful. For me, the memory of our last parting has always been mournful and painful.”

“But you told me,” Estella replied, very earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ And if you could say that to me then, you won’t hesitate to say it to me now—now, when suffering has been stronger than every other lesson, and has taught me to understand what your heart used to be. I’ve been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better shape.”"}

{"request_id":"2dd6a3e1891f5c0a4fa334ef","rewritten_text":"Yet even now I had not finished drinking the bitter potion. I still did not believe I had truly lost everything. I had not yet felt, in every heartbeat, in every nerve, in every thought, that I was alone—alone of my kind. I was not yet sure, in my bones, that I was the LAST MAN.

The day had turned cloudy, and at sunset a light rain began to fall. Even the sky seems to cry, I thought. If that is true, is it shameful for a human being to spend himself in tears? I remembered old stories, where people are said to dissolve away through crying, turning into fountains that pour and pour. I wished it were like that. Then my fate might be like the watery deaths of Adrian and Clara. But grief is strange. It makes a net you can trace, showing its pain in every change and every form. It clings to everything living. It feeds on every object. Like light, it fills the world, and like light, it gives everything its own colors.

I had wandered far from the place where I had been thrown, searching, when I came to one of those watch-towers that stand along the Italian shore at regular intervals. I was glad to find shelter. After staring so long at nature’s empty, bleak land, it felt good to see something made by human hands. So I went in and climbed the rough, winding stairs up to the guard-room. Fate had been kind to me, because there was little left to show what had once lived there. Two iron supports held up a few boards, and dried Indian corn leaves covered the bed. An open chest sat nearby, with some half-rotten biscuits inside, and it stirred up an appetite I did not even know I still had. 

Thirst also tormented me—sharp and burning—because of the sea-water I had drunk and the exhaustion of my body. Still, nature had given these needs pleasant feelings, so that I—yes, I—was refreshed and calmed as I ate this poor food and drank a little of the sour wine from a flask that was left behind in the abandoned place. Then I lay down on the bed, not too proud to rest there, like any shipwrecked man. The earthy smell of the dried leaves soothed me after the awful smell of seaweed. For a while, I forgot I was alone. I did not look back or forward. My senses went quiet, and I fell asleep. In my dreams I saw dear inland scenes again: hay-makers, and the shepherd’s whistle to his dog when he needed help driving the flock into the fold. I heard and saw the things from my boyhood mountain life that I had long forgotten."}

content.text: {"request_id":"78263bdf1aca091ae8a227bb","rewritten_text":"Raymond was thrilled by the intense sensations of regained health. He felt that, as general of the Athenians, he had earned a position worthy of his ambition; and in his hope of the conquest of Constantinople, he counted on an event that would stand as a milestone in the long waste of ages—an exploit without equal in the annals of mankind. A city with a grand historic legacy, whose site’s beauty was the wonder of the world, had for many hundreds of years been the stronghold of the Moslems; it should be rescued from slavery and barbarism, and restored to a people renowned for genius, civilization, and a spirit of liberty. Perdita lay in his restored society, on his love, his hopes, and his fame, just as a Sybarite reclines on a luxurious couch; every thought was carried away, and every emotion seemed bathed in a congenial, balmy element.\n\nWe arrived at Kishan on the 7th of July. The weather throughout our journey was calm and serene. Each day, before dawn, we left our night’s encampment and watched the shadows retreat from hill and valley, while the golden splendor of the sun’s approach filled the air. The soldiers accompanying us met the sight of beautiful nature with lively national enthusiasm. The rising of the star of day was greeted with triumphant music, and the birds—heard in bursts—filled the gaps between the melodies. At noon, we pitched our tents in some shady valley, or sheltered in an embowering wood among the mountains; a stream murmuring over pebbles lulled us into grateful sleep. Our evening march, calmer still, was even more delightful than the restless stir of spirit we felt in the morning. If the band played, they chose—almost without thinking—airs of restrained passion: the farewell of love, or the lament for absence, was followed and ended by some solemn hymn, which matched the tranquil loveliness of evening and lifted the soul toward grand, religious thoughts. Often all sound would fall away, so we could listen for the nightingale; while fireflies danced in bright, measured rhythm, and the soft cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travelers. Did we pass through a valley? Gentle shades surrounded us, and the rocks wore beautiful hues. If we crossed a mountain, Greece—a living map—lay spread beneath us, her famed peaks cleaving the sky; her rivers ran through the fertile land in silver lines. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travelers surveyed with ecstasy this splendid landscape, so different from the sober colors and melancholy grace of our own native scenery. When we left Macedonia, the fertile but low plains of Thrace offered fewer beauties, yet our journey remained interesting. An advanced guard gave word of our approach, and the local people quickly moved to honor Lord Raymond."}

{"request_id":"2c3f36e2141c6612bf3c4bdb","rewritten_text":"“Oh, bother my hat! I want Virginia!” cried the little Duke, laughing, and they galloped on to the railway station. There, Mr. Otis asked the station-master whether anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but he couldn’t get any news of her. The station-master, however, wired up and down the line and assured him that a strict watch would be kept, and after having bought a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper who was just putting up his shutters, Mr. Otis rode off to Bexley, a village about four miles away. He’d been told it was a well-known haunt of the gypsies, since there was a large common next to it. 

They woke up the rural policeman there, but got no information from him. After riding all over the common, they turned their horses’ heads homeward and reached the Chase about eleven o’clock, dead-tired and almost heart-broken. At the gate-house they found Washington and the twins waiting for them with lanterns, because the avenue was so dark. Not the slightest trace of Virginia had been discovered. The gypsies had been caught on Brockley meadows, but she wasn’t with them. They explained their sudden departure by saying they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and had left in a hurry for fear they’d be late. Indeed, they’d been quite distressed to hear about Virginia’s disappearance, since they were very grateful to Mr. Otis for letting them camp in his park, and four of their number had stayed behind to help with the search. The carp-pond had been dragged, and the whole Chase had been thoroughly searched, but with no result. 

It was clear that, at least for that night, Virginia was lost to them. In the deepest depression, Mr. Otis and the boys walked up to the house, with the groom following behind, leading the two horses and the pony. In the hall they found a group of frightened servants. In the library, lying on a sofa, was poor Mrs. Otis, almost beside herself with terror and anxiety, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted she should have something to eat and ordered supper for the whole party. It was a melancholy meal—hardly anyone spoke—and even the twins were awestruck and subdued, because they were very fond of their sister. 

When they’d finished, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke’s pleading, ordered them all to bed, saying nothing more could be done that night and that he would telegraph in the morning to Scotland Yard to have some detectives sent down immediately."}

{"request_id":"ec2a55471b7bd24747a9d9e5","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” Duff replied.

“And, translating the word yokel for the ladies, I take it you mean that this attempt was not made by a countryman?” asked Mr. Losberne, smiling.

“That’s it, master,” Blathers said. “This is all about the robbery, isn’t it?”

“All,” the doctor answered.

“Now, what’s this about that boy the servants keep talking about?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing at all,” the doctor replied. “One of the frightened servants decided he must have something to do with the attempt to break into the house, but that’s nonsense—pure absurdity.”

“Easy enough to dismiss, if it is,” Duff remarked.

“What he says is right,” Blathers agreed, nodding as if to confirm it, and idly playing with the handcuffs, as though they were castanets. “But who is the boy? What story does he tell about himself? Where did he come from? He didn’t just fall out of the clouds, did he, master?”

“Of course not,” the doctor said, glancing nervously at the two ladies. “I know his whole history, but we can talk about that later. First, you’d like to see where the thieves tried to get in, I suppose?”

“Certainly,” Mr. Blathers replied. “We should inspect the place first, then look at the servants afterward. That’s the usual way of doing things.”

Lights were brought in. Then Messrs. Blathers and Duff, with the native constable Brittles, Giles, and everyone else who was there, went into the small room at the end of the passage and looked out the window. After that, they walked around across the lawn and looked in through the window again. Then someone handed out a candle so they could inspect the shutter. After that, they used a lantern to trace the footsteps. Then they brought out a pitchfork to poke at the bushes. When all of that was done, with everyone watching in breathless excitement, they went back inside. Mr. Giles and Brittles were then made to act out, in a melodramatic way, their part in the adventures from the previous night. They did it about six times, contradicting each other in not more than one important detail the first time, and in no more than a dozen details the last.

Once that was finished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a long meeting together. It was, for secrecy and seriousness, about as far from a doctor’s discussion of the hardest medical question as you could get.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced in the next room, looking very uneasy. Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched him with anxious faces.

“Honestly,” he said, stopping after turning back and forth a great many times, “I hardly know what to do.”"}

{"request_id":"1298a429b9664a1c3e3b4bab","rewritten_text":"At the stairs where we had taken him abroad, and ever since, I had watched closely for any sign that we were being suspected. I had seen nothing. We certainly were not suspected, and at that time we were not being followed or watched by any boat either. If a boat had been waiting for us, I would have run to shore and made it go on, or else made its purpose clear. But we went on without any sign of being bothered.

He had his boat-cloak on, and, as I said, he looked like a natural part of the scene. It was strange, though maybe the miserable life he had lived explains it, that he was the least worried of all of us. He was not indifferent. He told me he hoped to live long enough to see his gentleman become one of the best gentlemen in a foreign country. He was not the kind of man who would give up or accept things quietly, as I understood it. But he also had no intention of meeting danger halfway. When danger came, he faced it, but only when it arrived.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it’s like to sit here with you, alonger my dear boy, and have my smoke, after being shut up day by day behind four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I know the joys of freedom,” I answered.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head seriously. “But you don’t know it as well as I do. You must have been locked up, dear boy, to know it as well as I do—but I ain’t going to be low.”

It struck me as strange that, if he really wanted to protect his freedom, he would risk it—and even his life. Still, I thought maybe freedom without danger meant less to him than it would to someone else, because danger had been part of his life for so long. I was not far off, since after smoking a little he said:

“You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, on the other side of the world, I was always looking back to this side. And it started to feel flat, even though I was getting rich. Everyone knew Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and go, and nobody’s mind would be troubled about him. But they don’t feel the same about me here, dear boy. They wouldn’t, at least, if they knew where I was.”

“If all goes well,” I said, “you’ll be free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he replied, letting out a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And you think so?”"}

{"request_id":"0825260f77fadcf3cad9ac92","rewritten_text":"Each person compares it, not to the voice of someone from any nation whose language he knows, but to the opposite. The Frenchman thinks it sounds like a Spaniard, and says he “might have distinguished some words had he been acquainted with the Spanish.” The Dutchman insists it was a Frenchman’s voice, but we are told that “not understanding French, this witness was examined through an interpreter.” The Englishman thinks it was a German’s voice, and adds that he “does not understand German.” The Spaniard is “sure” it belonged to an Englishman, but he “judges by the intonation,” and admits he has “no knowledge of the English.” The Italian believes it was a Russian’s voice, but he “has never conversed with a native of Russia.” A second Frenchman disagrees with the first and is certain the voice was Italian; yet, “not being cognizant of that tongue,” he, like the Spaniard, is “convinced by the intonation.”

Now, how strange and unusual must that voice really have been, if testimony like this could be drawn from it—if even the people who live in the five great divisions of Europe could recognize nothing familiar in its tones? You might say it could have been an Asian’s voice, or an African’s. Asians and Africans do not live in large numbers in Paris; but without denying that possibility, I will now point out three things. One witness calls the voice “harsh rather than shrill.” Two others say it was “quick and unequal.” No witness mentioned any words, or any sounds that even resembled words, that could be picked out.

“I know not,” continued Dupin, “what impression I may have made on your understanding so far, but I do not hesitate to say that even this part of the testimony—the part about the gruff and shrill voices—is enough by itself to create a suspicion. That suspicion should guide everything we do next in investigating this mystery. I said “legitimate deductions,” but I do not mean it in the simple way you might think. I mean that the deductions are the only proper ones, and that the suspicion arises inevitably from them, as the single result. What the suspicion is, however, I will not say yet. For now, just remember that, for me, it was strong enough to give my inquiries in the chamber a clear direction—a certain pull.

“Now let us move, in our minds, to this chamber. What should we look for first? The way the murderers got out. It is not too much to say that neither of us believes in supernatural events.”"}

{"request_id":"cb5556df5e74eec1242b1ed2","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had passed since my father’s return, and the seasons had almost completed their cycle. It was now the end of May; the woods were clothed in their freshest green, and the sweet smell of newly mown grass filled the fields. I thought that the warm air and the lovely face of Nature might help me find the right feelings to inspire him—to bring him gentle sensations, and prepare him for the calm peace and love I meant to win from him.

So I chose the evening of one of these days for my attempt. I invited him to walk with me, and led him to a nearby beech wood where the light shade sheltered us from the slanting, dazzling beams of the setting sun. After walking for some time in silence, I sat down with him on a mossy mound—It’s strange, but even now I can still see the place. The slender, smooth trunks were many of them wrapped with ivy, whose shining leaves of the darkest green stood out against the white bark and the light leaves of the young beech shoots growing from their parent trunks. The short grass was mixed with moss and partly covered by the dead leaves of last autumn, which the winds had driven here and there into little heaps. There were a few moss-covered stumps. The leaves were gently stirred by the breeze, and through their green canopy you could see the bright blue sky. As evening came on, the distant trunks were reddened by the sun, the wind died away entirely, and a few birds flew past us to their evening rest.

So it was here that we sat together, and when you hear everything that had happened—everything that tore our souls with such terrible force even in this peaceful spot, which, but for strange passions, might have been a paradise for us—you won’t be surprised that I remember it as I looked at it, hoping its calm might give me calm, and inspire me not only with courage but with persuasive words. I saw all these things and, in a kind of vacant way, noted them in my mind as I tried to arrange my thoughts in the right order for my attempt. My heart beat fast as I worked myself up to speak to him; I was determined not to be turned away, but I trembled to imagine what effect my words might have on him. At last, with great hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the affection—the excessive affection—that you had for me when you first returned—I hope will excuse me in your eyes for daring to speak to you, even though, with the tender affection of a daughter, I also speak with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”"}

{"request_id":"91816e029532d461999da7e4","rewritten_text":"It was early February; and Anne, after a month in Bath, found herself growing impatient for tidings from Uppercross and Lyme. She longed to know far more than Mary had managed to tell her. It had been three weeks since she had heard anything at all. She only knew that Henrietta was back at home again, and that Louisa, though thought to be mending quickly, was still in Lyme; and one evening, as she sat thinking of them all with great intensity, a letter—thicker than usual—came from Mary. To heighten her pleasure and astonishment, it came with the compliments of Admiral and Mrs Croft.

The Crofts must be in Bath! A detail that could not fail to interest her. They were the sort of people whose presence her heart turned toward without effort.

“What is this?” Sir Walter exclaimed. “The Crofts have come to Bath? The Crofts who take Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.”

“Oh! those letters are handy enough. They act as passports; they secure an introduction. I should have paid Admiral Croft a visit, though, in any case. I know what is owed to my tenant.”

Anne could not listen any longer; she could not even say how the Admiral’s complexion escaped notice—her own letter claimed her attention. It had been written several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

“I make no apology for my silence, because I know how little letters are valued in a place like Bath. You must be far too happy to think much of Uppercross, which, as you know, offers so little to write about. We have had a very dull Christmas; Mr and Mrs Musgrove have not given a single dinner party during the holidays. I do not count the Hayters as anyone. The holidays, however, are at last over: I believe no children ever had such long ones. I am sure I had not. The house was cleared yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to learn they have never gone home. Mrs Harville must be an odd mother to keep them so long. I cannot make sense of it. In my opinion, they are not at all nice children; yet Mrs Musgrove seems to like them as much as, if not more than, her own grandchildren.

“What dreadful weather we have had! It may not be felt in Bath, with your pleasant pavements; but in the country it matters. I have not had a soul call on me since the second week in January, except Charles Hayter, who had been coming much more often than was agreeable. Between ourselves, I think it a pity Henrietta had not stayed at Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her a little out of his way.”"}

{"request_id":"7687ac1bf3be0faa0dd3070f","rewritten_text":"After a while, twelve o’clock boomed from the tall tower at Westminster, and with every heavy ring of the bell the night seemed to shake. Then the railway lights went out. Only one lamp stayed on, shining alone like a big ruby on a giant mast, and the city’s noise faded.

At two o’clock he got up and walked toward Blackfriars. Everything looked unreal. It felt like a strange dream. The buildings across the river seemed to be made of darkness. It was as if silver and shadow had reshaped the whole world. St. Paul’s great dome loomed in the dim air like a bubble.

When he came near Cleopatra’s Needle, he saw a man leaning over the parapet. As he got closer, the man looked up, and the gaslight lit his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist. No one could mistake him: his fat, soft face, his gold-rimmed spectacles, his weak, sickly smile, and his sensual mouth.

Lord Arthur stopped. A bright idea flashed through him. He moved quietly up behind the man. In an instant he grabbed Mr. Podgers by the legs and threw him into the Thames. There was a rough curse, a heavy splash, and then everything went still. Lord Arthur looked anxiously over the water, but he could see nothing of the cheiromantist except a tall hat spinning in the moonlit current. After a time even that sank, and there was no sign of Mr. Podgers. Once, he thought he saw the thick, misshapen figure swimming toward the steps by the bridge, and a terrible feeling of failure hit him. But it was only a reflection, and when the moon came out from behind a cloud, it disappeared. At last he seemed to accept what destiny had decided. He let out a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name came to his lips.

“Have you dropped anything, sir?” a voice asked behind him.

He turned around and saw a policeman holding a bull’s-eye lantern.

“Nothing important, sergeant,” he said, smiling. Then he hailed a passing hansom, jumped in, and told the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

For the next few days he swung between hope and fear. Sometimes he almost expected Mr. Podgers to walk into the room. At other times he felt that Fate could not be so cruel to him. Twice he went to the cheiromantist’s address in West Moon Street, but he could not make himself ring the bell. He wanted certainty, and he was afraid of it.

In the end it arrived. He was sitting in the club’s smoking-room, drinking tea, and listening without much energy as Surbiton talked about the last comic song at the Gaiety. Then the waiter came in with the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"3097ce767b29109e93b9381c","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted she was a little taken aback by the match; yet she spoke less of her surprise than of her sincere wish for their happiness, and Elizabeth could not get her to treat it as unlikely. Kitty and Lydia had no particular envy for Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was only a clergyman; and the whole affair touched them in no other way than as fresh news to be passed around at Meryton.

Lady Lucas, however, could not help feeling pleased at being able to answer Mrs. Bennet with the consolation of a daughter settled well in marriage, and she paid a visit to Longbourn more often than usual to declare how delighted she was, though Mrs. Bennet’s sour looks and ill-natured remarks might have been enough to spoil any happiness.

Between Elizabeth and Charlotte there was a kind of restraint that kept them both silent on the subject; and Elizabeth felt convinced that no real confidence could ever exist between them again. Her disappointment in Charlotte only turned her thoughts with greater warmth toward her sister, whose integrity and delicacy she was sure could never be shaken; and for whose happiness she grew daily more uneasy, as Bingley had now been gone a week, and nothing was heard of his return.

Jane had written Caroline an early reply, and she was counting the days until she could reasonably expect to hear again. The promised letter of thanks from Mr. Collins reached them on Tuesday, addressed to their father, and composed with all the solemn gratitude that a twelve-month’s residence in the family might have inspired. Having discharged his conscience on that point, he went on, with many rapturous expressions, to tell them how happy he was to have won the affection of their amiable neighbour, Miss Lucas; and then he explained that it was only in order to enjoy her company that he had been so ready to agree to their kind wish of seeing him again at Longbourn, to which he hoped to be able to return on Monday fortnight. Lady Catherine, he added, so warmly approved of his marriage that she wished it to be carried out as soon as possible, which he trusted would be an argument not to be answered with his amiable Charlotte, to name an early day for making him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins’s coming back into Hertfordshire was no longer a matter of satisfaction to Mrs. Bennet. On the contrary, she was inclined to complain of it as much as her husband. It was very odd, she thought, that he should come to Longbourn rather than to Lucas Lodge; it was also extremely inconvenient and a great deal of trouble. She disliked having visitors in the house while her health was so poor, and lovers, above all others, were the most disagreeable."}

{"request_id":"841065130e2f260a9d5e7146","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I misunderstood you. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ so I assumed ‘anybody’ meant—well, anybody, that is, everybody.”

“It doth—anybody that is of lofty birth; and the better if he be royal.”

“That, it seems, might well be,” said the abbot. He thought this was his chance to smooth things over and prevent disaster. “It would not be likely that such a wonderful gift would be given to reveal the concerns of people who are less important than those born near the top of greatness. Our Arthur the king—”

“Would you know of him?” the enchanter cut in.

“Most gladly, yes, and with gratitude.”

Everyone was full of awe and interest again at once, those stubborn idiots. They watched the incantations closely and looked at me as if to say, “There now, what can you say to that?” Then the announcement came:

“The king is weary from the chase, and lies in his palace these two hours sleeping a dreamless sleep.”

“God’s blessing upon him!” said the abbot. He crossed himself. “May that sleep refresh his body and his soul.”

“And so it might be, if he were sleeping,” I said. “But the king is not sleeping. The king rides.”

Here was trouble again—a fight over who had authority. Nobody knew which of us to believe. I still had a little reputation left. The magician’s contempt flared, and he said:

“I have seen many wonderful soothsayers, prophets, and magicians in my life, but none before who could sit idle and watch what matters most without any incantation to help.”

“You’ve lived in the woods, and you lost a lot by it. I use incantations myself, as this good brotherhood knows—but only when it matters.”

When it comes to sarcasm, I think I know how to hold my own. That jab made the fellow squirm. The abbot asked about the queen and the court, and he got this answer:

“They be all on sleep, overcome by fatigue, just like the king.”

I said:

“That’s just another lie. Half of them are off with their amusements. The queen and the other half are not sleeping—they ride. Now maybe you can spread yourself a little and tell us where the king and queen and all the rest are going right now.”

“They sleep now, as I said; but on the morrow they will ride, because they go on a journey toward the sea.”

“And where will they be the day after tomorrow at vespers?”

“Far to the north of Camelot, and half their journey will be done.”

“That’s another lie, by the space of a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

{"request_id":"57835a7f482834f194808f92","rewritten_text":"In all of this there was something strange that drew me in and filled me with wonder. It was as if he had just woken from a long, dream-filled sleep. He felt, in a way, like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad, in that sweet imitation of an eastern tale. Diana was gone. His friends were changed or dead. And now, with his awakening, I was the only person he had left to love on earth.

How dear the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond felt to me now that I had such a beloved companion for my walks. I went with my father to every beautiful place we could find, whether on the islands or beside the waterfalls that hid behind trees. I explored every shaded path and every little valley tangled with thick undergrowth and fern. His conversation made my thoughts grow broader. I felt as if I had been made new, surrounded by the fresh energy of a new life. It seemed that, since his arrival, I had been carried from a small patch of earth into a world so wide it could stretch the imagination and the mind. Before, my life had been like a pleasant stream, quietly staying in its own fields, never meant to go far, and then disappearing without leaving a trace. Now it felt to me like a many-sided river flowing through a fertile, beautiful landscape—always changing, always lovely. But I did not know what desert it was heading toward, or the rocks that would tear its waters, or the ugly scene that would show up in its waves in a twisted way. Life was bright then. I began to learn to hope—and I also learned what brings a more bitter despair to the heart than hope destroyed.

Is it not strange that grief should come so quickly after such happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, but there was gall at the bottom of its long, sweet taste. My heart was full of deep affection, yet it was calm, even because of how full it was. I had no idea that misery could come from love. And this lesson—one that everyone must learn in the end—was taught to me in a way that few people are forced to experience. I still mourn those few short months of paradise. I disobeyed no command. I ate no apple. And yet I was driven out without mercy. My companion did it, and I was thrown down with him. But I am getting off track. Let sorrow arrive when it is meant to. At this point in my story, I can still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful closeness, and then my aunt fell ill. I spent a whole month in her room, nursing her, but her illness was deadly. She died, and for some time I was inconsolable. Death is so terrible for those who are still living. Even when affection does not hold you together, the chains of habit are so strong that the heart must suffer when they break."}

{"request_id":"b6ac1e8ef84f026c8cfd5283","rewritten_text":"“April 12th. Something unusual happened to the balloon’s direction. Even though I expected it, the change still filled me with clear, unmistakable joy. After we had been traveling on the old route for about the twentieth parallel of southern latitude, the balloon suddenly turned east at a sharp angle. From then on, it kept going through the day, staying almost exactly in the same plane as the lunar ellipse. The most noticeable effect was that the car shook a lot. This shaking came from the change in route and lasted, to a greater or lesser degree, for many hours.

“April 13th. I was again very frightened by the loud, crackling sound that had terrified me on the tenth. I thought about it for a long time, but I couldn’t reach any clear conclusion. The Earth looked much smaller now, and from the balloon it subtended an angle of a little more than twenty-five degrees. I couldn’t see the moon at all, because it was almost straight overhead. I kept traveling in the same plane of the ellipse, but I made little progress to the east.

“April 14th. The Earth’s apparent size dropped very fast. Today I became strongly convinced that the balloon was now moving along the line of apsides toward the point of perigee. In other words, it was following the direct path that would take it immediately to the moon at the part of its orbit closest to Earth. The moon was directly overhead, so I couldn’t see it. I had to work hard for a long time to condense the air.

“April 15th. I could no longer make out the outlines of continents and seas on the Earth in any clear way. Around twelve o’clock, I noticed that terrible sound again for the third time. This time it lasted for several moments, and it grew louder as it continued. At last, while I stood frozen with shock and fear, waiting for some kind of dreadful destruction, the car suddenly vibrated violently. A huge, blazing mass of material—something I couldn’t identify—came roaring and booming past the balloon, with a sound like a thousand thunders. Once my fear and astonishment eased, I had little trouble believing it was some great piece of volcanic matter thrown from the world I was rapidly approaching. It was probably one of those unusual substances sometimes found on Earth and called meteoric stones, simply because there isn’t a better name.

“April 16th. Today, as best I could, I looked up through the side windows one after another. To my great delight, I saw a very small part of the moon’s disk showing on all sides beyond the huge edge of the balloon.”"}

{"request_id":"0779637af262a33888a0bb9a","rewritten_text":"I now turn to my own story. In the first part of my life there is little worth setting down, and I shall be brief; yet I must be permitted to linger a little over my childhood, so it may be seen how, when one hope failed, all life became a blank; and how, when the only affection I was allowed to value was blasted, my very existence was extinguished with it.

I have already said that my aunt was very unlike my father. I believe that, without the faintest taint of a bad heart, she possessed the coldest nature that ever filled a human breast: she was wholly incapable of affection. She took me under her protection because she regarded it as her duty; but she had lived too long alone, undisturbed by the noise and chatter of children, to tolerate my disturbing her peace. She had never married; and for the last five years she had lived entirely by herself on an estate that had come to her through her mother, on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters, my father had expressed a wish that she should come and live with me at his family mansion, which stood in a beautiful district near Richmond in Yorkshire. She would not agree to this plan; but once she had put in order the affairs her brother’s departure had left to her care, she left England and took me with her to her Scottish estate.

The charge of me, first as a baby and afterwards until I had reached my eighth year, was entrusted to a servant of my mother’s, who had accompanied us in our retirement for that purpose. I was placed in a remote part of the house, and only saw my aunt at fixed times. These came twice each day: once about noon, when she came to my nursery, and once after her dinner, when I was brought to her. She never caressed me, and while I remained in the room she seemed to fear that I might annoy her with some childish whim. My good nurse, however, always prepared me with the greatest care before she would venture into the parlour; and the dread inspired by my aunt’s cold looks and her few, restrained words was so strong that I seldom broke the lessons I had been taught, nor did I betray the exemplary quiet in which I was trained during those brief visits.

In my good nurse’s keeping, I ran wild about our park and the neighboring fields. From my earliest years I showed the offspring of the deepest love, and with it the greatest sensibility of temperament. I cannot say with what fervor I loved everything, even the inanimate objects that surrounded me."}

{"request_id":"2e22e2058be3426c02383ba2","rewritten_text":"But enough of this. I will begin my story. This is my last task, and I hope I have enough strength to finish it. I do not record any crimes. My mistakes can easily be forgiven, because they did not come from evil intent. They came from poor judgment. I believe most people would agree that, with different choices and better wisdom, I could have avoided the misfortunes that now fall on me. My fate has been ruled by necessity—by a terrible necessity. It took hands stronger than mine, stronger than any human power, to break the thick, unbreakable chain that has held me. I once breathed only joy, always warmed by love and delight in goodness. Now it has brought me only to misery, which is ending, and will end, in death. But I am getting ahead of myself. My story is not finished yet. I will pause for a moment, wipe my dim eyes, and try to push away the heavy sadness I feel now, and instead focus on the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank. He had lost his father early and was raised by a weak mother, who gave him every indulgence she believed a wealthy nobleman should have. He was sent to Eton and then to college, and from childhood he was allowed to use large sums of money freely. So, from the earliest years, he enjoyed the independence that boys with these advantages usually gain at a public school.

Because of these circumstances, his passions found fertile ground. They could grow into either good things or bad ones, depending on what they were like. Since he was always allowed to act on his own, his character formed early and strongly. It showed itself in many ways, so that a sharp observer could see both the seeds of virtues and the seeds of misfortunes. His careless extravagance made him waste huge sums of money on passing whims. He called these whims “passions,” and he treated them as if their energy made them noble. At the same time, he often showed great generosity. He would work hard to meet other people’s needs, while his own desires were satisfied just as fully. He gave his money, but he did not sacrifice any of his own wishes to the gifts he made. He gave his time, which he did not value, and he gave his affections, which he was happy to put into action in any way.

I am not saying that, if his own desires had been forced to compete with those of others, he would have shown selfishness. But that test was never made. He was raised in prosperity and had all the advantages that came with it. Everyone loved him and wanted to please him."}

{"request_id":"0dfd8832cf70116b4c672191","rewritten_text":"From late reports out of Rotterdam, it would seem that the place is in a state of lively philosophical excitement. Indeed, there have been happenings there of such a character—so completely out of the ordinary, so wholly new, so at odds with what people had been expecting—that I cannot doubt that, before long, all Europe will be thrown into an uproar, all physics thrown into confusion, and reason and astronomy together will be at loggerheads.

It is said that on the—— day of—— (I cannot swear to the date), a vast crowd of persons, assembled for purposes not set down, gathered in the great square by the Exchange in the well-ordered city of Rotterdam. The weather was warm—more than usually so for the season—there was scarcely any air stirring; and the people were not in the least ill-tempered at being, now and then, lightly sprinkled with friendly showers of brief duration, which dropped from great white clouds that broke and shifted across the blue vault of the sky. Still, about noon, a small but notable stir made itself felt in the gathering: the clatter of ten thousand voices took over; and, almost at once, ten thousand faces were tilted upward toward the heavens, ten thousand pipes were lowered in unison from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a cry—fit to be likened to nothing but the roar of Niagara—rang out, long and loud and furious, through every quarter of Rotterdam.

The source of the commotion soon became plain enough. From behind the great bulk of one of those sharply outlined cloud-masses already mentioned, there was seen to drift slowly into an open patch of blue space a strange, mixed, yet apparently solid substance—so oddly shaped, so capriciously put together—that it could not, in any way, be understood, nor ever be admired enough by the stout burghers standing below with mouths agape. What could it be? In the name of all the vrows and devils in Rotterdam, what could it possibly mean? No one knew; no one could guess; no one—even Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, the burgomaster—had the least clue to unravel the matter. So, since nothing more sensible seemed available, each man to a man replaced his pipe carefully in the corner of his mouth, and with his right eye cocked upward toward the spectacle, puffed, paused, waddled about, and grunted in a way that was unmistakably significant; then he waddled back, grunted, paused, and at last puffed again.

Meanwhile, however, the object of all that curiosity, and the cause of all that smoke, came lower and lower toward the goodly city. In a few minutes it drew near enough to be read with certainty. It appeared to be—yes!—a kind of balloon; but surely no such balloon had ever been seen in Rotterdam before."}
