{"request_id":"8a6c0755665bcd775134c2a5","rewritten_text":"Smallpox!

I sprang straight to the king and spoke close to his ear:

“Out the door at once, sire—the woman is dying of that sickness that ruined the hem of Camelot two years back.”

He didn’t so much as move.

“By my word, I’ll stay—and I’ll lend a hand as well.”

I leaned in again, whispering:

“King, it can’t be. You must go.”

“You mean well, and you’re not speaking foolishly. Still, it would be a disgrace for a king to admit fear, and a disgrace for a knight with a belt to hold back his own hand when there are those who need help. No—I will not go. It’s you who must leave. The Church’s ban is not laid on me; it forbids you to be here, and if word reaches her of your trespass, she’ll deal with you harshly.”

It was a perilous position for him to take, one that might cost him his life, but there was no point arguing. Once he set his mind on his knightly honor being at stake, that was the end of discussion—he would remain, and nothing could turn him. I knew it, so I let the matter drop.

The woman spoke:

“Good sir, will you climb that ladder and bring me word of what you find? Don’t be afraid to tell it plain—there are seasons when even a mother’s heart can’t be broken any further, for it’s already been broken—long since.”

“Wait,” said the king, “and give the woman something to eat. I’ll go.” And he set down the knapsack.

I started to turn, but the king had already begun. He stopped, looked down at a man lying in a dim light, and only then seemed to notice us.

“Is that your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he asleep?”

“God be thanked for that mercy, yes—these three hours. Where do I pay for the full measure of my gratitude? My heart is bursting with it, for the sleep he’s having now.”

I said:

“We’ll be gentle. We won’t wake him.”

“Ah, no—you won’t,” she answered, “for he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes. What a triumph it is to know it! No one can harm him, no one can insult him again. He’s in heaven now, and happy; or if not, then he waits in hell and is content—because there he’ll find neither abbot nor bishop. We were boy and girl together; we were man and wife these five and twenty years, and never apart until today. Think how long it is to love and suffer side by side. This morning he was out of his mind, and in his fancy we were boy and girl again, roaming the bright fields; and so, in that innocent, glad talk, he wandered farther and farther—into those other places we don’t know—until he was shut away from mortal sight.”"}

{"request_id":"5f163848af9b0b95f6a7b6b1","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had secured a very fine house in Camden Place—high, stately, and exactly the sort of situation that suited a man of consequence; and there both he and Elizabeth were comfortably established, to their great satisfaction.

Anne entered with a heavy heart, expecting to be kept in confinement for many months, and inwardly asking herself, “Oh! when shall I be able to leave you again?” Yet the welcome she received was unexpectedly warm, and it did her good. Her father and sister were glad to see her, not only for her own sake, but because they wished to show her their house and furniture, and they met her with real kindness. That she should be the fourth at their dinner-table was remarked upon as an advantage.

Mrs Clay was exceedingly agreeable and always smiling, though her civilities and grins were, in a way, what one might expect. Anne had always thought that, on her arrival, they would act out what was proper; but the ease and consideration of the others had taken her by surprise. They were evidently in excellent spirits, and she was soon meant to hear the reasons. Still, they had no intention of listening to her. After a few compliments were laid out—regrets for her being so deeply missed in their old neighbourhood, which Anne could not honestly return—they made only some slight inquiries, and then the conversation had to be entirely their own. Uppercross interested them not at all, Kellynch scarcely more; it was all Bath.

They were pleased to assure her that Bath had fully met their hopes in every particular. Their house, they said, was unquestionably the best in Camden Place; their drawing-rooms had advantages that none of the others could match, whether they had seen them or heard of them, and the superiority held no less in the style of the fittings than in the taste of the furniture. Their acquaintance was in great demand. Everyone seemed eager to pay them visits. They had declined many introductions, and yet cards were still being left by people they did not know.

There was no end of enjoyment here. Could Anne doubt that her father and sister were happy? She might not doubt it, but she could not help sighing that her father should feel no loss in the change, should see nothing to regret in the duties and dignity of a resident landholder, should find so much to boast of in the small vanities of a town. She had to sigh, and smile, and wonder too, as Elizabeth threw open the folding-doors and, with lively triumph, moved from one drawing-room to the other, boasting of their space; even at the thought of that woman—who had once been mistress of Kellynch Hall—taking pride in the extent between two walls, perhaps no more than thirty feet apart.

But this was not everything that was meant to make them happy. They had Mr Elliot as well."}

{"request_id":"df97fe2656bd90829433216a","rewritten_text":"After they had all joined in general lamentations over the dreadful sequel of this event—which Elizabeth felt was nearly certain, and Miss Bennet could not claim was wholly impossible—the former kept the conversation going. “But tell me everything about it that I haven’t already heard. Give me further particulars. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they no reason to be afraid before the elopement took place? They must have seen them together—forever.”

“Colonel Forster admitted that he had often suspected some partiality, especially on Lydia’s side, but nothing that should have alarmed him. I am so grieved for him. His behavior was attentive and kind to the utmost. He was coming to us to assure us of his concern before he had any idea that they were not gone to Scotland; when that fear first became known, it only made him hurry his journey.”

“And was Denny convinced that Wickham would not marry? Did he know of their plan to run off? Had Colonel Forster seen Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when Denny was questioned by him, Denny denied knowing anything of their plan, and wouldn’t give his real opinion about it. He didn’t repeat his belief that they wouldn’t marry, and from that I’m inclined to hope he may have been misunderstood before.”

“And until Colonel Forster came himself, not one of you had any doubt that they were truly married, I suppose?”

“How could such an idea have entered our minds? I felt a little uneasy—a little afraid for my sister’s happiness with him in marriage, because I knew his conduct had not always been quite right. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only felt how imprudent the match must be. Kitty then admitted, with a very natural triumph at knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia’s last letter she had prepared her for such a step. She had known, it seems, that they had been in love with each other for many weeks.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I don’t believe so.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think badly of Wickham himself? Does he know his true character?”

“I must confess that he didn’t speak of Wickham as well as he used to. He believed him to be imprudent and extravagant; and since this sad affair has taken place, it’s said that he left Meryton in great debt: but I hope that may be false.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secret—if we had told what we knew about him—this could not have happened!”

“Perhaps it would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But to expose a person’s earlier faults, without knowing what their present feelings are, seemed unjustifiable.”"}

{"request_id":"5ad04ddc39307b4b37e32c2d","rewritten_text":"Other chances to make her observations would not fail to arise. Anne soon found herself in the company of all four together often enough to form an opinion, though she was too wise to admit it openly at home, where she knew it would satisfy neither husband nor wife. While she considered Louisa to be the favorite, she could not help thinking—so far as she dared judge from memory and experience—that Captain Wentworth was not in love with either. They were more in love with him; but that was not love. It was a kind of feverish admiration, and it might, probably must, end in love.

Charles Hayter seemed to be aware of being slighted, and yet Henrietta had sometimes the look of being split between them. Anne longed for the power to show them all what they were doing, and to point out the evils they were exposing themselves to. She did not believe any of them were acting with guile. It gave her the greatest comfort to think that Captain Wentworth was, at least, completely unaware of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph in his manner, and no pitiful kind of triumph either. He had, probably, never heard of any claims Charles Hayter might have, and had never thought of them. He was only wrong in accepting—accepting, she supposed, must be the word—the attention of two young women at once.

After a short struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to give up the field. Three days passed without his coming once to Uppercross, a very clear change. He had even refused one regular invitation to dinner; and when Mr Musgrove found him on the occasion with several large books in front of him, Mr and Mrs Musgrove were sure that nothing could be right, and talked, with grave faces, about his studying himself to death. Mary’s hope and belief was that he had received a positive dismissal from Henrietta, and her husband lived under the constant expectation of seeing him tomorrow. Anne could only feel that Charles Hayter was wise.

One morning, about this time, when Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth were out shooting together, the sisters in the Cottage were sitting quietly at their work when they were visited at the window by the sisters from the Mansion-house.

It was a very fine November day, and the Miss Musgroves came through the little grounds, stopping for no other reason than to say that they were going to take a long walk, and therefore concluded that Mary could not possibly want to go with them. When Mary immediately replied, with some jealousy at not being thought a good walker, “Oh, yes, I should like to join you very much; I am very fond of a long walk,” Anne felt, from the looks of the two girls, that it was precisely what they did not want. She admired again the kind of necessity that family habits seemed to create—how everything had to be shared, and everything had to be done together, even when it was undesired and inconvenient."}

{"request_id":"ff93169baadf969823f479ff","rewritten_text":"I have already said that he was a poet: at three-and-twenty he published his first poem, and it was received by the whole nation with warmth and rapture. His good star kept shining on him without pause; a reputation had never been won so swiftly, and it was universal. The crowd praised the very poems that had been the wonder of the sage in his closet; not a single dissenting voice was heard.

It was during this season, when his fame was at its height, that he came to know Elinor. She was a young heiress of uncommon beauty, living under the guardianship of another; from the first moment they were seen together, it seemed as though they had been made for one another. Elinor had not Woodville’s genius, yet she was generous and high-minded, and her youth—along with the affection it drew from everyone—lifted her above any thought beyond virtue and excellence. She was charming; her manners were open and unstudied; her deep blue eyes held a brightness that could only come from feeling joined to wisdom.

They were made for each other, and soon they loved. For the first time Woodville tasted the sweetness of love; and Elinor was transported by the thought of possessing the heart of one so beautiful and glorious among his fellows. Could anything other than unalloyed joy spring from such a union?

Woodville was a poet—every society sought him, and when he appeared all eyes fastened on him alone; yet he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a rich heiress. Her guardian did not show displeasure at their mutual attachment: Woodville’s merit was too conspicuous to be questioned because of his scanty means; but her father’s dying will would not permit her to marry until she reached her proper age, and her fortune depended on her keeping that command. She had just turned twenty, and she and her lover were therefore compelled to endure the postponement. Still they were always together, and their happiness seemed like Paradise: they studied side by side, laid plans for their future employments, and drank in love and delight from each other’s looks and words, scarcely murmuring at the delay that stood between them and their complete union. Woodville rose ever higher in renown; and Elinor grew more lovely and more wise under the instruction of her accomplished lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one: everything had been arranged for their marriage. How can I set down the catastrophe against so much joy?—for the earth would not be the earth it is, if it were not strewn with blight and sorrow, when such angelic creatures as these had been allowed to exist for one another; search the world over, and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have brought them. There must have been some overturning in the order of things, as it is established among us miserable dwellers on earth, to have admitted such consummate joy."}

{"request_id":"2f8e9755420d90d9c7e831f4","rewritten_text":"“Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,” the old lady called out when he came into the room. “Why haven’t you come to see me all this time?”

“My dear Lady Clem, I never get a moment to myself,” said Lord Arthur, smiling.

“I suppose you mean you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying chiffons and talking nonsense. I can’t understand why people make such a fuss about getting married. In my day, we never dreamed of flirting in public, or even in private.”

“I assure you I haven’t seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. From what I can tell, she’s completely taken up with her milliners.”

“Of course. That’s the only reason you come to visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder men don’t take warning. On a fait des folies pour moi, and here I am—a poor, rheumatic creature, with a false front and a bad temper. If it weren’t for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me the worst French novels she can find, I don’t think I could get through the day. Doctors are no help at all, except to take your money. They can’t even cure my heartburn.”

“I’ve brought you something to help with that, Lady Clem,” said Lord Arthur gravely. “It’s a wonderful thing, invented by an American.”

“I don’t think I like American inventions, Arthur. I’m sure I don’t. I read a few American novels lately, and they were full of nonsense.”

“Oh, but there’s no nonsense at all in this, Lady Clem! I promise it’s a perfect cure. You must promise to try it.” Then Lord Arthur took the little box from his pocket and handed it to her.

“Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it really a gift? That’s very kind of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a bonbon. I’ll take it right away.”

“Good heavens, Lady Clem!” Lord Arthur cried, grabbing her hand. “You mustn’t do that. It’s a homoeopathic medicine, and if you take it when you don’t have heartburn, it could do you a lot of harm. Wait until you have an attack, and take it then. You’ll be amazed by the result.”

“I’d like to take it now,” said Lady Clementina, holding the little transparent capsule up to the light. Inside was a floating bubble of liquid aconitine. “I’m sure it’s delicious. The truth is, even though I hate doctors, I love medicines. Still, I’ll save it for my next attack.”

“And when will that be?” Lord Arthur asked eagerly."}

{"request_id":"21ae537b5bafdfd0e9363f0d","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton paused in the street, not quite sure where to go. “At Tellson’s banking house at nine,” he said, wearing a thoughtful expression. “Should I show myself in the meantime? I think so. It’s best that these people know there’s a man like me here; it’s a sensible precaution, and it may be a necessary preparation. But—care, care, care! Let me think it through.”

As he checked his steps, which had begun to drift toward some destination, he turned a corner or two in the already darkening street and traced the idea in his mind to its possible consequences. His first impression was confirmed. “It is best,” he said at last, fully decided, “that these people should know there is such a man as I here.” Then he turned his face toward Saint Antoine.

Defarge had described himself that day as the keeper of a wine shop in the Saint Antoine suburb. For anyone who knew the city well, it wasn’t hard to find his house without asking questions. Once Carton had confirmed where it was, he came back out into the busier streets again, dined at a place of refreshment, and then fell into a deep, sound sleep after dinner. For the first time in many years, he had no strong drink. Since last night, he’d had nothing but a little light, thin wine; and last night he had let the brandy down slowly onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth, like a man done with it.

It was as late as seven o’clock when he woke, refreshed, and went back out into the streets. As he made his way toward Saint Antoine, he stopped at a shop window with a mirror and slightly rearranged his loose cravat, his coat collar, and his wild hair. Once that was done, he went straight to Defarge’s and went in.

There happened to be no customer in the shop except Jacques Three, with his restless fingers and his croaking voice. This man, whom Carton had seen on the jury, was standing at the little counter, drinking while he talked with the Defarges—husband and wife. The Vengeance took part in the conversation as if he were a regular member of the place.

When Carton walked in, took his seat, and asked (in very indifferent French) for a small measure of wine, Madame Defarge gave him a careless glance, then a sharper one, then an even sharper one, and finally came over to him herself. She asked what he had ordered.

He repeated what he had already said.

“English?” asked Madame Defarge, inquisitively lifting her dark eyebrows.

After looking at her, as though even the sound of a single French word took time for him to form, he answered in his earlier strong foreign accent."}

{"request_id":"0674092b7f20ed45bbc70e3b","rewritten_text":"A few days after that, Virginia and her curly-haired cavalier went riding out on Brockley meadows. In pushing through a hedge, she tore her habit so badly that, when she got home, she decided she would go up by the back staircase so she wouldn’t be seen. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber—whose door happened to be open—she thought she saw someone inside. Thinking it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes used to bring her work there, she looked in to ask her to mend her habit. To her immense surprise, it was the Canterville Ghost himself.

He was sitting by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees whirl through the air, while red leaves danced wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his whole posture showed extreme depression. In fact, he looked so miserable, so broken down, that little Virginia—whose first thought had been to run away and lock herself in her room—felt pity and decided to try to comfort him. Her footsteps were so light, and his melancholy so deep, that he didn’t notice her until she spoke.

“I’m so sorry for you,” she said. “But my brothers are going back to Eton tomorrow, and then, if you behave yourself, no one will bother you.”

“It’s ridiculous to ask me to behave myself,” he replied, turning in astonishment toward the pretty little girl who had dared to address him. “It’s absurd. I have to rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and walk about at night—if that’s what you mean. It’s my only reason for existing.”

“It’s no reason at all to exist,” Virginia said, “and you know you’ve been very wicked. Mrs. Umney told us, the very first day we arrived here, that you killed your wife.”

“Well, I’ll admit it,” the Ghost said petulantly. “But it was purely a family matter, and it concerned no one else.”

“It’s very wrong to kill anyone,” Virginia said. At times she had a sweet Puritan seriousness she’d picked up from some old New England ancestor.

“Oh, I hate the cheap severity of abstract ethics!” the Ghost snapped. “My wife was plain enough—she never had my ruffs properly starched, and she knew nothing about cookery. Why, there was a buck I shot in Hogley Woods—a magnificent pricket—and do you know how she had it sent up to the table? But it doesn’t matter now. It’s all over. And I don’t think it was very nice of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I did kill her.”"}

{"request_id":"7a586b8327cd5a5eabb953b7","rewritten_text":"His manner was stubborn to the extreme, and “dat deuced bug” were the only words that escaped his lips during the trip. For my part, I carried a couple of dark lanterns, while Legrand kept himself occupied with the _scarabæus_, which he had tied to the end of a short whip-cord; he swung it back and forth as he walked, turning it like a conjurer. When I noticed this last, clear sign of my friend’s disturbed state of mind, I could hardly keep from crying. Still, I thought it best to indulge his fancy—for now, at least—until I could take some more forceful measures with a better chance of success. Meanwhile, I tried, but in vain, to get him to talk about the purpose of the expedition. Once I had agreed to accompany him, he seemed unwilling to discuss anything of minor importance, and for every question I asked, the only answer he gave was, “we shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the head of the island in a skiff, and then, climbing the high ground along the shore of the mainland, we continued in a northwesterly direction through a stretch of country so wild and desolate that there was no sign of any human footstep. Legrand led the way with determination, stopping only for a moment now and then to consult what looked like certain landmarks of his own making from a previous occasion.

In this way we traveled for about two hours, and the sun was just setting when we entered a region far more bleak than anything we had seen yet. It was a kind of plateau near the top of an almost inaccessible hill—densely wooded from base to peak—and broken up by huge crags that seemed to rest loosely on the ground. In many places they were held from crashing down into the valleys below only by the trees they leaned against. Deep ravines running in different directions added an even harsher solemnity to the scene.

The natural platform we had climbed onto was thick with brambles. We soon found that we could not have pushed through them at all without the scythe. And at his master’s direction, Jupiter cleared a path to the base of an enormously tall tulip-tree. It stood on the level ground with eight or ten oaks, but it towered over them all—and over every other tree I had ever seen then—in the beauty of its foliage and shape, in the wide spread of its branches, and in the overall majesty of its appearance."}

{"request_id":"4cb6c42341845a8727291e82","rewritten_text":"It was long past noon when he woke. His valet had slipped into the room several times on tiptoe, just to see whether he was stirring, and had wondered why his young master slept so late. At last the bell sounded, and Victor came in quietly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray of old Sevres china. He drew back the olive-satin curtains, with their shimmering blue lining, that hung in front of the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said, smiling.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked, drowsy.

“One hour and a quarter, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up, sipped his tea, and began to sort through his letters. One of them was from Lord Henry and had been delivered by hand that morning. He hesitated for a moment, then set it aside. The others he opened without much interest. They held the usual assortment of cards—dinner invitations, tickets for private viewings, programs for charity concerts, and the like that are showered on fashionable young men every morning during the season. There was also a rather heavy bill for a chased silver Louis-Quinze toilet set he had not yet had the courage to send to his guardians. They were extremely old-fashioned and didn’t seem to understand that in our day, unnecessary things are the only necessities. Along with that were several very politely worded notes from money-lenders on Jermyn Street, offering to advance any sum at a moment’s notice, at the most reasonable rates of interest.

After about ten minutes, he got up and threw on an elaborate dressing gown of silk-embroidered cashmere wool. Then he went into the onyx-paved bathroom. The cool water refreshed him after his long sleep. It felt as though he had forgotten everything he had been through. A faint sense that he had taken part in some strange tragedy came back to him now and then, but it was only the unreal feeling of a dream.

The moment he was dressed, he went into the library and sat down to a light French breakfast laid out for him on a small round table near the open window. It was an exquisite day. The warm air seemed full of spices. A bee flew in and buzzed around the blue-dragon bowl in front of him, filled with sulphur-yellow roses. He felt completely happy.

Then his eyes fell on the screen he had placed in front of the portrait, and he started.

“Too cold for Monsieur?” asked his valet, setting an omelette on the table. “I shut the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I’m not cold,” he murmured."}

{"request_id":"363e7d1829e9ad1e0f8ffadc","rewritten_text":"Should I ask them? Or should I ask Miss Bates? She is even closer.—And I do not know whether Miss Bates might not understand the feelings of the rest of the people as well as anyone. I think we do need a bigger group to decide. What if I go and invite Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well—if you please,” said Mrs. Weston, sounding a little unsure, “if you think she will be any help.”

“You will get nothing useful from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She will be full of delight and gratitude, but she will tell you nothing. She won’t even listen to your questions. I see no point in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so amusing—so extremely amusing! I really enjoy hearing Miss Bates talk. And you don’t need to bring the whole family, you know.”

Then Mr. Weston joined them. When he heard what was being proposed, he fully agreed.

“Yes, do, Frank. Go and fetch Miss Bates, and let’s settle it right away. She will enjoy the plan, I’m sure, and I don’t know anyone better for showing us how to get rid of difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We’re being a little too careful. She is a constant lesson in how to be happy. But fetch them both. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady?”...

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I’ll think you a great blockhead, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I didn’t think of it at once. Of course, if you want it, I will try to persuade them both.” And he ran off.

Long before he came back, he returned with the aunt—short, neat, and brisk—and with her elegant niece. Mrs. Weston, being kind and good-tempered, and a good wife, had gone over the passage again. She now found the problems were much smaller than she had first thought—really, they were very trifling. With that, the question of what to do was settled. After that, everything else was smooth, at least in their minds. The small details—table and chair, lights and music, tea and supper—either arranged themselves, or were left as little matters that could be handled anytime between Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes. Everyone who was invited would certainly come. Frank had already written to Enscombe to suggest that he stay a few days longer than his fortnight, and that could not possibly be refused. And it would be a delightful dance.

When Miss Bates arrived, she agreed with them most warmly. As a counsellor, she was not needed, but as an approver—a much safer role—she was truly welcome. Her approval, both general and detailed, was constant and enthusiastic, and it could not help but please them. For another half-hour they all walked back and forth between the different rooms, some offering ideas, some paying attention, and all enjoying the happy prospect of what was coming."}

{"request_id":"c2b36345e1b78d3b57b578af","rewritten_text":"It was not every person who would have stood out in so considerate a manner as she did, and refused to accept Jane’s answer; yet she plainly insisted that she would not write any such denial yesterday, just as Jane wished. She would wait—and sure enough, by yesterday evening everything was settled, and Jane was to go. What a surprise to me! I had not the least notion!—Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and told her at once that, after thinking over the advantages of Mrs. Smallridge’s situation, she had resolved to accept it. “I did not know a word of it until it was all settled.”

“Did you spend the evening with Mrs. Elton?”

“Yes, all of us. Mrs. Elton would have us come. It was settled that way, upon the hill, while we were walking about with Mr. Knightley. ‘You must all spend your evening with us,’ said she—‘I positively must have you all come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was there too, then?”

“No, not Mr. Knightley; he refused it from the first. And though I thought he might come, because Mrs. Elton said she would not let him off, he did not. Still, my mother, and Jane, and I, were all there, and we had a very agreeable evening. Such kind friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse—one always finds them agreeable, though everybody seemed rather worn out after the morning’s party. Even pleasure, you know, is fatiguing; and I cannot say that any of them appeared to have enjoyed it very much. Still, I shall always think it a very pleasant party, and I feel extremely obliged to the kind friends who included me in it.”

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you were not aware of it, had been making up her mind all day?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the time may come, it must be unwelcome to her and all her friends—but I hope her engagement will have every alleviation that is possible. I mean, as to the character and manners of the family.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, there is everything in the world that can make her happy in it. Except the Sucklings and Bragges, there is not such another nursery establishment—so liberal and so elegant—in all Mrs. Elton’s acquaintance. Mrs. Smallridge is a most delightful woman!—a style of living almost equal to Maple Grove. And as for the children: except the little Sucklings and little Bragges, there are not such elegant, sweet children anywhere. Jane will be treated with such regard and kindness!—It will be nothing but pleasure, a life of pleasure. And her salary!—I really cannot venture to name her salary to you, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"99c14ff6b45b2ba9778e863b","rewritten_text":"I wrap him up in the paper and stuff each piece into his mouth—that was the way.

“And you think, then, that your master was really bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him sick?”

“I don’t think anything about it—I know. What makes him dream about the gold so much, if it wasn’t because he got bitten by the gold-bug? I heard about those gold-bugs before this.”

“But how do you know he dreams about gold?”

“How I know? Why, ’cause he talks about it in his sleep—that’s how I know.”

“Well, Jup, perhaps you are right; but to what fortunate circumstance am I to attribute the honor of a visit from you today?”

“What’s the matter, massa?”

“Did you bring any message from Mr. Legrand?”

“No, massa, I bring dis here pissel;” and here Jupiter handed me a note which read as follows:

“MY DEAR ——Why have I not seen you for so long a time? I hope you have not been so foolish as to take offense at any little _brusquerie_ of mine; but no, that is improbable. Since I saw you I have had great cause for anxiety. I have something to tell you, yet scarcely know how to tell it, or whether I should tell it at all.

“I have not been quite well for some days past, and poor old Jup annoys me, almost beyond endurance, by his well-meant attentions. Would you believe it?—he had prepared a huge stick the other day, with which to chastise me for giving him the slip and spending the day, _solus_, among the hills on the mainland. I verily believe that my ill looks alone saved me a flogging.

“I have made no addition to my cabinet since we met.

“If you can, in any way, make it convenient, come over with Jupiter. _Do_ come. I wish to see you tonight, upon business of importance. I assure you that it is of the _highest_ importance.

“Ever yours, “WILLIAM LEGRAND”.

There was something in the tone of this note that filled me with great uneasiness. Its whole style differed materially from that of Legrand. What could he be dreaming of? What new obsession had taken hold of his excitable mind? What “business of the highest importance” could he possibly need to handle? Jupiter’s account of him gave no good signs. I feared that the continued pressure of misfortune had, at last, fully unsettled the reason of my friend. Without hesitation, then, I prepared to accompany the negro.

Upon reaching the wharf, I noticed a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat in which we were to embark.

“What is the meaning of all this, Jup?”"}

{"request_id":"93501ac97c669b97db39e4ca","rewritten_text":"But there was no joy in the little town that calm Saturday afternoon. The Harpers, along with Aunt Polly’s family, were being put into mourning, with deep grief and many tears. The village felt unusually quiet, even though it was usually quiet enough. People moved around as if something was missing, and they spoke very little, but they sighed again and again. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children. They had no interest in their games, and slowly they stopped.

In the afternoon, Becky Thatcher found herself sitting and brooding in the empty schoolhouse yard. She felt very sad, but there was nothing there that could comfort her. She talked to herself.

“Oh, if I only had that brass andiron-knob again! But I don’t have anything now to remember him by.” She swallowed hard and held back a sob.

After a moment, she stopped and said to herself again:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for the whole world. But he’s gone now. I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

That thought broke her down. She walked away with tears running down her cheeks. Then a group of boys and girls came by—Tom’s and Joe’s playmates. They stood by the fence and talked in reverent voices about what Tom did the last time they saw him, and about what Joe said and did, with small details that now felt like terrible warnings. Each person pointed to the exact spot where the boys had stood when they were last seen, and then added something like, “And I was standing just like that—just as I am now. If you was him, I was as close as that. And he smiled, just like this. Then something seemed to go through me—awful, you know. I didn’t understand it then, but I can see it now!”

After that, they argued about who had seen the dead boys last while they were still alive. Many claimed that grim honor and offered proof, though it was more or less changed by the person telling it. When they finally decided who had seen the boys last and who had exchanged the last words with them, the lucky ones acted as if they were especially important. Everyone else stared at them and envied them. One poor boy, who had no other kind of glory to offer, said with clear pride in the memory:

“Well, Tom Sawyer beat me once.”

But that attempt at fame did not work. Most of the boys could say the same thing, so it made the distinction feel cheap. The group drifted away slowly, still remembering the lost heroes in hushed, awed voices."}

{"request_id":"64a7ab10d146ac428a3b2b2f","rewritten_text":"I know she would!”

The Widow Douglas’ splendid hospitality was a tempting lure. It, along with Tom’s arguments, soon won the day. So it was decided to tell nobody anything about the night’s plan. Presently Tom realized that maybe Huck might come this very night and give the signal. The thought drained a lot of the excitement from his anticipation. Still, he couldn’t bring himself to give up the fun at Widow Douglas’. And why should he? he reasoned—the signal hadn’t come the night before, so why would it be any more likely tonight? The certain fun of the evening outweighed the uncertain prize; and, like a boy, he decided to follow the stronger pull and not let himself think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town, the ferryboat stopped at the mouth of a wooded hollow and tied up. The crowd poured ashore, and soon the forest distances and jagged heights echoed far and near with shouting and laughter. Every way of getting hot and tired was tried out, and by and by the wanderers drifted back to camp with appetites that felt properly earned—then the destruction of the good things began. After the meal came a refreshing stretch of rest and conversation in the shade of spreading oaks. Soon someone shouted:

“Who’s ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. Bundles of candles were gathered, and right away there was a scramble up the hill. The cave’s mouth was up the hillside—an opening shaped like the letter A. Its massive wooden door stood unbarred. Inside was a small chamber, chilly as an icehouse, and lined by Nature with solid limestone that sweated cold. It was romantic and mysterious to stand in this deep gloom and look out over the green valley shining in the sun. But the impressiveness didn’t last long, and the roughhousing started again. The moment a candle was lit, everyone rushed toward the person holding it; there was a struggle and a brave defense, but the candle was soon knocked down or blown out, and then there was a happy uproar of laughter and a fresh chase.

But everything has an end. By and by the group began filing down the steep descent of the main avenue, the flickering line of lights dimly revealing the tall rock walls almost to where they met—sixty feet overhead. This main avenue was no more than eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps, other lofty but even narrower crevices branched off on either side—for McDougal’s cave was a vast labyrinth of crooked passageways that ran into each other and then out again, leading nowhere."}

{"request_id":"f4b33edc7ac80536aae00d18","rewritten_text":"“So what result, then, has followed? What impression have I made on your imagination?”

I felt my skin crawl as Dupin asked the question. “A madman,” I said. “Someone raving, escaped from a nearby _Maison de Santé_.”

“In some respects,” he replied, “your idea isn’t irrelevant. But the voices of madmen—even in their wildest attacks—are never a match for that particular voice heard on the stairs. Madmen belong to some nation, and even when their speech is incoherent, it still has the coherence of syllables. Besides, the hair of a madman isn’t like the tuft I’m holding in my hand. I’ve disentangled this little clump from the rigidly clenched fingers of Madame L’Espanaye. Tell me what you make of it.”

“Dupin!” I said, completely unnerved. “This hair is most unusual—this isn’t _human_ hair.”

“I haven’t claimed that it is,” he said. “But before we decide this point, I want you to look at the small sketch I’ve traced here on this paper. It’s a _fac-simile_ drawing of what, in one part of the testimony, is described as ‘dark bruises, and deep indentations of finger nails,’ on the throat of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye, and in another—by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne—as ‘a series of livid spots, evidently the impression of fingers.’

“You’ll see,” he continued, spreading the paper on the table between us, “that this drawing suggests a firm, fixed hold. There’s no _slipping_ anywhere. Each finger has kept—perhaps until the victim died—the terrible grip with which it originally dug in. Now try placing all your fingers at the same time into the impressions you see.”

I tried, but it was useless.

“We may not be giving this matter a fair test,” he said. “The paper is laid out on a flat surface, but the human throat is cylindrical. Here’s a piece of wood whose circumference is about the same as the throat. Wrap the drawing around it, and try again.”

I did, but the problem was even clearer than before. “This,” I said, “isn’t the mark of any human hand.”

“Now read,” Dupin replied, “this passage from Cuvier.”

It was a minute anatomical and generally descriptive account of the large, tawny Ourang-Outang of the East Indian islands. The enormous size, the prodigious strength and activity, the wild ferocity, and the imitative tendencies of these mammals were well known to everyone. I understood the full horror of the murder at once.

“The description of the digits,” I said, after I finished reading, “matches this drawing exactly.”"}

{"request_id":"b8fc40979c3cbd07f163aefa","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, horrified by Sikes’s crime, fell into a chain of reflection about whether an honest life wasn’t, after all, the best choice. Convinced that it was, he turned his back on the scenes of the past and resolved to set things right in some new sphere of action. He struggled hard and suffered a great deal for some time; but, with a contented temperament and a good purpose, he succeeded in the end. From being a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s boy, he is now the merriest young grazier in all Northamptonshire.

And now, the hand that writes these words hesitates as it nears the end of its task, and would weave, for a little longer, the thread of these adventures.

I would gladly linger a bit longer among those with whom I have moved for so long, and share their happiness by trying to depict it. I would show Rose Maylie in all the bloom and grace of early womanhood, casting a soft and gentle light along her secluded path—light that fell on everyone who walked it with her and shone into their hearts. I would paint the life and joy of the fireside circle and the lively summer group; I would follow her through the sultry fields at noon, and hear the low tones of her sweet voice on the moonlit evening walk. I would watch her in all her goodness and charity, and the smiling, tireless way she carries out domestic duties at home. I would paint her and her dead sister’s child happy in their love for one another, spending whole hours together imagining the friends they had so sadly lost. I would bring before me again those joyous little faces that clustered round her knee, and listen to their merry chatter. I would recall the sound of that clear laugh, and conjure up the sympathetic tear that glistened in the soft blue eye. These, and a thousand looks and smiles, and turns of thought and speech—I would gladly bring them all back.

How Mr. Brownlow went on, day after day, filling the mind of his adopted child with stores of knowledge, and becoming more and more attached to him as his nature developed and showed the thriving seeds of everything he hoped he would become—how he recognized in him new traits of his early friend, awakening in his own heart old memories, melancholy yet still sweet and soothing—how the two orphans, tried by adversity, remembered its lessons in mercy to others, in mutual love, and in fervent thanks to Him who had protected and preserved them—these are all matters that need not be told."}

{"request_id":"a7e21787ff179a6310a64047","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water left to see them through the feast. Presently Becky suggested that they should move on again. Tom fell silent for a moment, and then said:

“Becky, can you stand it if I tell you something?”

Becky’s cheeks went pale, though she believed she could manage it.

“Then, Becky, we’ve got to stay right here—where there’s water to drink. That little bit is our last candle!”

Becky broke down into tears and loud wailing. Tom did what he could to soothe her, but it did little good. At last Becky cried, “Tom!”

“Well, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and go looking!”

“Yes, they will—of course they will!”

“Maybe they’re hunting for us already, Tom.”

“Why, I reckon they might be. I hope they are.”

“When would they miss us, Tom?”

“When they get back to the boat, I reckon.”

“Tom, it could be dark by then—would they even notice we hadn’t come?”

“I don’t know. But in any case, your mother would miss you as soon as they got home.”

A look of fear spread over Becky’s face, and it snapped Tom back to himself; he saw he had made a mistake. The children grew quiet and began to think. Before long, another fresh wave of grief from Becky told Tom that what he had been thinking had struck her too—that the Sabbath morning might already be half gone before Mrs. Thatcher realized Becky wasn’t at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children stared at their small candle and watched it melt away, slow and merciless. They saw the wick stand alone at last; they saw the thin flame rise and fall, creep up the narrow column of smoke, hover at the top for a moment, and then—utter darkness took over, in all its terror!

How long afterward it was that Becky came to a sluggish awareness that she was crying in Tom’s arms, neither of them could say. What they did know was that, after what felt like a long stretch of time, both woke from a dead stupor of sleep and had to face their misery again. Tom said it might be Sunday now—maybe Monday. He tried to get Becky to speak, but her grief was too heavy; her hopes were gone. Tom said they must have been missed long ago, and that the search was probably already underway. He meant to shout, and perhaps someone would come. He tried it, but in the dark the far-off echoes sounded so dreadful that he stopped.

The hours dragged on, and hunger returned to torment them. A part of Tom’s half of the cake remained; they divided it and ate it. Still, they seemed hungrier than before."}

{"request_id":"f0c2a55900d68e33bd1a0fb2","rewritten_text":"They brought along a very nice-looking old gentleman and a very nice-looking younger one, with his right arm in a sling. And, my souls, how the people yelled and laughed, and kept it up. But I didn’t see anything funny about it, and I thought it would make the duke and the king look bad to watch. I figured they’d turn pale. But no—none of them turned pale. The duke didn’t show any suspicion at all. He just walked around with his eyes wide, acting happy and pleased, like a jug that’s spilling buttermilk. As for the king, he just stared and stared at the new arrivals, looking sad, like the thought of such frauds and rascals in the world gave him a stomachache right in his heart. He carried it off admirably. A lot of the important people gathered around the king so he could see they were on his side.

The old gentleman who had just arrived looked completely confused. Pretty soon he started to speak, and I could tell right away he sounded like an Englishman—not the king’s way, though the king’s was pretty good for an imitation. I can’t repeat the old man’s exact words, and I can’t copy his voice, but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

“This is a surprise to me. I wasn’t expecting it, and I’ll be honest—I’m not in a good position to answer it. My brother and I have had bad luck. He broke his arm, and our baggage was left behind at a town above here last night because of a mistake. I am Peter Wilks’ brother, Harvey, and this is his brother, William. William can’t hear or speak, and he can’t even make signs very well, because he only has one hand to use. We are who we say we are. In a day or two, when I get the baggage, I can prove it. Until then, I won’t say anything more. I’ll go to the hotel and wait.”

So Harvey and the new dummy started off. The king laughed and talked right away.

“Broke his arm—very likely, isn’t it?—and very convenient too, for a fraud who has to make signs and hasn’t learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s mighty good—and mighty clever—under the circumstances!”

He laughed again, and everyone else laughed too, except for three or four, maybe half a dozen. One of them was that doctor. Another was a sharp-looking man with an old-fashioned carpet-bag, who had just come off the steamboat. He was talking to the doctor in a low voice, looking toward the king now and then, nodding his head. That was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville. The others included a big, rough, husky man who had come along and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and who was listening to the king now as well."}

{"request_id":"59c2bc80a394866300e99707","rewritten_text":"The winters along the latitude of Sullivan’s Island are seldom very severe, and in the fall of the year it is a rare thing indeed for a fire to be considered necessary. About the middle of October, 18—, however, there occurred a day of remarkable chill. Just before sunset I made my way through the evergreens to my friend’s hut—a place I hadn’t visited for several weeks. At that time my home was in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and the means of getting there and back were far behind what they are today. When I reached the hut, I knocked, as I always did, and, getting no answer, searched for the key where I knew it was hidden. I unlocked the door and went in.

A fine fire was blazing on the hearth. It was a welcome novelty, and certainly not an ungrateful one. I shrugged off my overcoat, took an armchair by the crackling logs, and waited patiently for my hosts to arrive.

Soon after dark they came, and gave me a very warm welcome. Jupiter, grinning from ear to ear, bustled about to prepare some marsh-hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his moods—how else can I describe them?—of excitement. He had found an unknown bivalve, forming a new genus, and, even more than that, he had tracked down and secured, with Jupiter’s help, a _scarabæus_ that he believed to be totally new. Still, he wanted my opinion on it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, rubbing my hands over the blaze, and wishing the whole tribe of _scarabæi_ would go to the devil.

“Ah, if I’d only known you were here!” Legrand said. “But it’s been so long since I saw you, and how could I have guessed you’d come to visit me this very night of all nights? As I was coming home, I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, very foolishly, I lent him the bug. So you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I’ll send Jup down for it at sunrise. It’s the loveliest thing in creation!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Nothing of the sort! No—the bug. It’s a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of the back, and another, somewhat longer, at the other. The _antennæ_ are—”

“Dey aint no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin on you,” Jupiter cut in. “De bug is a goole bug—solid, ebery bit of him, inside and all, sep him wing. Neber feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”"}

{"request_id":"8463bdfeeb06eee3906b2eee","rewritten_text":"Those old, frail people were always seen by the public bowing, and it was widely believed that after they had bowed a customer out, they would keep bowing in the empty office until they bowed another customer in.

The barrister was sharp enough to see that the banker wouldn’t have gone so far in his opinion on anything less solid than moral certainty. Unprepared as he was for the big pill he had to swallow, he got it down. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, shaking his forensic forefinger at the Temple in general, once it was down, “my way out of this is to put you all in the wrong.”

It was a bit of the craft of an Old Bailey tactician, and it gave him real relief. “You won’t put me in the wrong, young lady,” said Mr. Stryver; “I’ll do that for you.”

So when Mr. Lorry called that night as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver, amid a pile of books and papers scattered for the purpose, seemed to have nothing on his mind at all about the subject of the morning. He even looked surprised to see Mr. Lorry, and was entirely absent-minded and preoccupied.

“Well!” said that good-natured messenger, after a full half-hour of fruitless attempts to bring him back to the point. “I’ve been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated, coldly. “Oh, of course! What was I thinking of!”

“And I have no doubt,” said Mr. Lorry, “that I was right in the conversation we had. My opinion is confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” Mr. Stryver replied, in the friendliest tone, “that I’m sorry for it on your account, and sorry for it on the poor father’s account. I know this must always be a painful subject for the family—let’s not say more about it.”

“I don’t understand you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I dare say not,” Stryver answered, nodding in a smoothing, final way; “no matter, no matter.”

“But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“No, it doesn’t. I assure you it doesn’t. Having supposed there was sense where there is no sense, and a worthy ambition where there is no worthy ambition, I’m well out of my mistake, and no harm is done. Young women have committed similar follies often before, and have repented them in poverty and obscurity often before. In an unselfish sense, I’m sorry the matter is dropped, because it would have been a bad thing for me in a worldly point of view; in a selfish sense, I’m glad it’s dropped, because it would have been a bad thing for me in a worldly point of view—it’s hardly necessary to say I could have gained nothing from it.”"}

{"request_id":"c20cf2f059b89078cdaa4328","rewritten_text":"“No, no—this is for to-morrow; and I had it in my mind, above all, to see Knightley to-day, for that very reason.—What a dreadful, broiling morning!—I even walked over the fields too—(with a tone of strong complaint,)—and that only made matters worse. And then, to find him not at home! I assure you I am by no means satisfied. There was not a word of apology, not a message for me. The housekeeper said she knew nothing of my being expected.—How very odd!—And not a soul could tell which way he had gone. Perhaps to Hartfield, perhaps to the Abbey Mill, perhaps into his woods.—Miss Woodhouse, this is quite unlike our friend Knightley!—Can you make it out?”

Emma found amusement in insisting that it was indeed most extraordinary, and that she had not a syllable to offer in his defence.

“I cannot conceive,” said Mrs. Elton, (with the proper sense of being wronged that a wife ought to feel,) “how he could treat you so, of all people in the world! The very last person one should think of as being forgotten!—My dear Mr. E., he must have left you some message; I am sure he must.—Not even Knightley could be so very eccentric;—and his servants have been careless about it. Depend upon it, that is what happened: and it is very likely with the Donwell servants, who, as I have often remarked, are all extremely awkward and remiss. I am sure I would not have such a creature as his Harry standing at our sideboard for any consideration. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright values her very little indeed.—She promised Wright a receipt, and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins,” continued Mr. Elton, “as I came near the house, and he told me I should not find his master at home; but I would not believe him. William looked quite out of sorts. He said he did not know what had come over his master of late, but that he could hardly ever get a word from him. I have nothing to do with William’s affairs, but it is really of the utmost consequence that _I_ should see Knightley to-day; and so it is a matter of very serious inconvenience that I should have taken this hot walk to no purpose.”

Emma thought she could do nothing better than go home at once. Most likely she was being waited for there at this very moment; and Mr. Knightley might be kept from sinking still deeper into his resentment against Mr. Elton, if not against William Larkins.

When she took her leave, she was glad to observe that Miss Fairfax was resolved to accompany her out of the room, and to go with her even downstairs; it gave her an opening which she instantly seized, to say,”"}

{"request_id":"755f8f7a567d9a29fa8412ef","rewritten_text":"And if he asked me why I wanted it, and why I thought I had any right to it, I would tell him—though he cared very little for dreams like that—that I had loved Estella dearly and for a long time. Even though I had lost her and had to live a bereaved life, anything connected to her was still closer to me and dearer than anything else in the world. Seeing that Mr. Jaggers stood quite still and silent, and apparently just as stubborn as ever, in response to my appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you to be a man with a gentle heart. I’ve seen your pleasant home, your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful ways you have of refreshing your business life. I beg you to say a word for me to Mr. Jaggers, and to make him understand that, considering all the circumstances, he ought to be more open with me!”

I have never seen two men look more strangely at one another than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after that. At first, I feared Wemmick would be dismissed from his employment on the spot; but that worry faded as I saw Mr. Jaggers relax into something like a smile, and Wemmick grow bolder.

“What’s all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You with an old father, and you with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick replied. “If I don’t bring ’em here, what does it matter?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, putting his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this man must be the most cunning impostor in all London.”

“Not a bit of it,” Wemmick shot back, getting bolder and bolder. “I think you’re the other one.”

Once again they exchanged those odd looks of theirs, each still apparently suspicious that the other was letting him in.

“_You_ with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Since it don’t interfere with business,” Wemmick answered, “let it be so. Now, I look at you, sir, and I wouldn’t be surprised if _you_ might be planning and scheming to have a pleasant home of your own one of these days, when you’re tired of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded his head two or three times, as if looking back on it, and actually let out a sigh. “Pip,” he said, “we won’t talk about ‘poor dreams.’ You know more about that sort of thing than I do, having had much fresher experience. But now about this other matter. I’ll put a case to you. Mind— I admit nothing.”

He waited for me to say that I understood he had expressly said he admitted nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “put this case. Put the case that a woman, under circumstances like the ones you’ve mentioned, held her child concealed, and was forced to tell her legal adviser about it—because he represented to her that he must know, with an eye to the latitude of his defence, how things stood regarding that child.”"}

{"request_id":"0ee511cab3f4f71789c0cec0","rewritten_text":"They know well enough how sharp a lad he is; he’ll be a lifer. They’ll see that the Artful gets nothing short of a lifer.”

“What do you mean by lagging and a lifer?” Mr. Bolter demanded. “What’s the point of speaking like that to me—why don’t yer say it plain, so I can make out what yer mean?”

Fagin was ready to put those puzzling phrases into the rougher tongue; and, once translated, Mr. Bolter would have been told that they amounted to that phrase, “transportation for life,” when the talk was cut short by Master Bates coming in, hands shoved into his breeches-pockets, his face twisted in a kind of half-comic misery.

“It’s all over, Fagin,” said Charley, once he and his new acquaintance had been introduced.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman that owns the box; two or three more’s on the way to ’dentify him; and the Artful’s booked for a passage out,” Master Bates replied. “I’ll need a proper suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband, to wisit him before he starts off on his travels. To think of Jack Dawkins—lummy Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—going abroad for a common twopenny-halfpenny sneeze-box! I never figured he’d do it under a gold watch, chain, and seals, at the very lowest. Oh, why couldn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his walables, and go out as a gentleman, not like some common prig, with no honour nor glory!”

With that burst of feeling for his unlucky mate, Master Bates settled himself in the nearest chair, looking full of chagrin and despair.

“What do you mean, talking about him having neither honour nor glory!” Fagin snapped, shooting an angry look at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the top-sawyer among you all? Is there one of you that could lay a hand on him, or get near him, on any scent? Eh?”

“Not one,” Master Bates answered, his voice thick with regret; “not one.”

“Then what are you going on about?” Fagin said, still angry; “what are you blubbering for?”

“’Cause it isn’t on the rec-ord, is it?” Charley said, smarting into open defiance of his old friend through the tide of his own regrets; “’cause it can’t be brought out in the ’dictment; ’cause nobody will ever know half of what he was. How’s he going to look in the Newgate Calendar? P’raps not be there at all. Oh, my eye, my eye—what a blow it is!”

“Ha! ha!” Fagin laughed, thrusting out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter, chuckling so hard it shook him as if he had the palsy. “See what a pride they take in their profession, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"e10ad771ef09fc0915118574","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was very upset about the second postponement of the marriage. Lady Julia, who had already ordered her wedding dress, did everything she could to make Sybil call off the match. But Sybil loved her mother too much to turn against her. She had put her whole life in Lord Arthur’s hands, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake her faith. 

As for Lord Arthur, it took him days to get over his terrible disappointment, and for a while his nerves were completely wrecked. Still, his good common sense soon returned. His practical mind did not keep him in doubt for long about what to do. Since poison had failed completely, he decided that dynamite, or some other kind of explosive, was the obvious thing to try.

So he went back through the list of friends and relatives he could reach, and after careful thought he decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean was a learned, well-cultured man who loved clocks. He had a remarkable collection of timepieces, from the fifteenth century up to the present day. Lord Arthur thought this hobby gave him a perfect chance to carry out his plan. Getting an explosive machine, however, was another matter. The London Directory did not help him at all. He also felt there was little point in going to Scotland Yard, because they never seemed to know anything about the dynamite faction’s movements until after an explosion had already happened, and even then they often knew very little.

Then he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with very revolutionary ideas. Lord Arthur had met him at Lady Windermere’s in the winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be writing a life of Peter the Great, and to have come to England to study documents about that Tsar’s residence here as a ship carpenter. But people generally suspected he was a Nihilist agent, and it was well known that the Russian Embassy did not approve of him being in London. Lord Arthur believed Rouvaloff was exactly the sort of person he needed. One morning, he drove to his lodgings in Bloomsbury to ask for advice and help.

“So you are taking up politics seriously?” Count Rouvaloff asked, after Lord Arthur explained what he wanted.

Lord Arthur hated any kind of swagger, so he had to admit that he had no interest at all in social questions. He only wanted the explosive machine for a private family matter, something that involved no one else but himself."}

{"request_id":"a2e431d4a9a9e0cca31b1564","rewritten_text":"“Now, in English, the letter that shows up most often is e. After that, the next most common letters come in this order: a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z. E is so dominant that you almost never see a sentence of any length where it is not the most common character.

“Here, then, we start laying the groundwork for something more than a guess. The table can be used in general, but in this cipher we will only need it a little. Since our most common character is 8, we will begin by treating it as the e of the natural alphabet. To check that idea, let’s see whether 8 appears often in pairs. In English, e is doubled very frequently, as in words like ‘meet,’ ‘fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and so on. In this case, we find 8 doubled at least five times, even though the cryptograph is short.

“Let us therefore assume that 8 stands for e. Now, among all the words in the language, ‘the’ is the most common. So we should look for repeats of any three characters in the same order, where the last one is 8. If we find such repeated letter patterns, they will most likely represent the word ‘the.’ When we inspect the cipher, we find no fewer than seven such arrangements, with the characters being ;48. So we can assume that ; represents t, 4 represents h, and 8 represents e—the last part is now strongly confirmed. That is a major step forward.

“But once we have established one word, we can also establish an important point: several beginnings and endings of other words. For example, look at the second-to-last time the combination ;48 appears, which is near the end of the cipher. We know that the ; right after it starts a word, and of the six characters that follow ‘the,’ we can identify five of them. Let’s write down those characters using the letters we know they stand for, leaving a space for the unknown—

t eeth.

“Now we can immediately rule out the ‘th,’ because it cannot be part of a word that starts with the first t. When we test the whole alphabet for a letter that could fit the missing spot, we find that no word can be formed where this th is included. So we narrow it down to

t ee,

and, going through the alphabet if we need to, we arrive at the word ‘tree’ as the only possible reading.”}"}

{"request_id":"df9bbd6a4e6aa468ea731889","rewritten_text":"In the morning, she was found dead in her bed, apparently having suffered no pain. Sir Mathew Reid had been sent for at once, but, of course, there was nothing to be done, and she was to be buried on the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before she died, she had made her will and left Lord Arthur her little house in Curzon Street, along with all her furniture, personal belongings, and pictures—except for her collection of miniatures, which was to go to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which Sybil Merton was to have. The property wasn’t worth much, but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, was extremely anxious for Lord Arthur to return as soon as possible, if he could, because there were many bills to be paid, and Lady Clementina had never kept any regular accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s kind remembrance of him, and he felt that Mr. Podgers had a great deal to answer for. His love for Sybil, however, dominated every other feeling, and the knowledge that he had done his duty gave him peace and comfort. When he arrived at Charing Cross, he felt perfectly happy.

The Mertons received him very kindly. Sybil made him promise that nothing would ever come between them again, and the marriage was set for the 7th of June. Life seemed bright and beautiful to him once more, and all his old joy returned.

One day, though, as he was going through the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil herself, burning packages of faded letters and emptying drawers of odd rubbish, the young girl suddenly gave a little cry of delight.

“What have you found, Sybil?” Lord Arthur asked, looking up from his work and smiling.

“This lovely little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. Isn’t it quaint and Dutch? Please—give it to me! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m over eighty.”

It was the box that had held the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, and a faint blush rose into his cheek. He had almost entirely forgotten what he had done, and it struck him as a strange coincidence that Sybil—who, for her sake, he had endured all that terrible anxiety—should be the first to remind him of it.

“Of course you can have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.”

“Oh, thank you, Arthur; and may I have the bonbon too? I had no idea Lady Clementina liked sweets. I thought she was far too intellectual.”

Lord Arthur went deadly pale, and a horrible thought crossed his mind."}

{"request_id":"7f1756c8da1722bb7bfcd854","rewritten_text":"The insect’s weight was astonishing, and, when I weighed everything, I could scarcely fault Jupiter for the opinion he formed about it; yet I could not, for the life of me, understand how Legrand came to agree with that same view.

“I sent for you,” he said, in a lofty, sweeping manner, once I had finished examining the beetle. “I sent for you so that I might have your counsel and your help in carrying forward the designs of Fate—and of the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I broke in, “you must be unwell. You’d do better to take a few precautions. Go to bed—you shall—and I’ll stay with you for a few days until you’ve shaken this off. You’re feverish, and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he replied.

I did, and, to be honest, I found not the smallest sign of fever.

“But you might be ill without having fever. Let me prescribe for you just this once. First of all, go to bed. Next—”

“You’re mistaken,” he cut in. “I’m as well as I can reasonably expect to be, given the agitation I’m under. If you truly want me well, you’ll help me put an end to this excitement.”

“And how am I to do that?”

“Very simply. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills, onto the mainland. On this trip we’ll need someone we can rely on. You’re the only person we can trust. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you see in me now will be just as thoroughly quieted.”

“I’m glad to help in any way I can,” I answered; “but are you saying that this infernal beetle has something to do with your journey into the hills?”

“It does.”

“Then, Legrand, I can’t take part in any such ridiculous business.”

“I’m sorry—terribly sorry,” he said, “but we’ll have to attempt it on our own.”

“Attempt it on your own! The man must be out of his mind!—but wait—how long do you mean to be gone?”

“Probably all night. We’ll set out at once, and we’ll be back, at the latest, by sunrise.”

“And will you promise me—on your honor—that once your little scheme is finished, and the bug matter (good God!) is settled to your satisfaction, you’ll return home and follow my advice without question, as you would that of a physician?”

“Yes; I promise. Now come—we have no time to waste.”

With a heavy heart, I went along with my friend. We set out at about four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and I. Jupiter brought the scythe and the spades, all of which he insisted on carrying himself—more, it seemed to me, out of fear of leaving any of the tools within his master’s reach than from any real excess of diligence or willingness to oblige."}

{"request_id":"8f6c9c742e8e7c84cc372bd5","rewritten_text":"When he reached the top of the staircase, he steadied himself and decided to let out his famous peal of demoniac laughter. He had found it useful on more than one occasion. People said it had turned Lord Raker’s wig grey in a single night, and it had certainly made three of Lady Canterville’s French governesses give up and warn their families before their month was over. So he let out his worst, most horrible laugh until the old vaulted roof rang again and again. But just as the terrible echo began to fade, a door opened and Mrs. Otis stepped out in a light blue dressing-gown.

“I’m afraid you’re not feeling well,” she said. “I’ve brought you a bottle of Dr. Dobell’s tincture. If it’s indigestion, you’ll find it an excellent remedy.”

The ghost glared at her in rage. He started right away to prepare to turn himself into a large black dog, which he was well known for doing. The family doctor always blamed that same talent for the permanent foolishness of Lord Canterville’s uncle, the Hon. Thomas Horton. But the sound of footsteps coming closer made him pause. He gave up his plan and instead became only faintly phosphorescent, then vanished with a deep churchyard groan, just as the twins came up to him.

When he got back to his room, he completely fell apart and was overwhelmed by violent agitation. The twins’ vulgar behavior and Mrs. Otis’s blunt, practical way of thinking were naturally very annoying. What truly upset him, though, was that he had not been able to wear the suit of mail. He had hoped that even modern Americans would be impressed by the sight of a Spectre In Armour, if only because of respect for their national poet Longfellow. He had spent many weary hours reading and enjoying Longfellow’s graceful, appealing poems while the Cantervilles were in town.

It was his own suit. He had worn it with great success at the Kenilworth tournament, and he had even received compliments on it from no less a person than the Virgin Queen herself. Yet the moment he put it on, the weight of the huge breastplate and steel casque overwhelmed him. He fell hard onto the stone pavement, hurt both knees badly, and bruised the knuckles of his right hand.

For several days afterward, he was extremely ill and hardly left his room at all, except to keep the bloodstain in proper repair. Eventually, with careful attention, he recovered. Then he decided to try again, this time to frighten the United States Minister and his family."}

{"request_id":"cd538e03bbf446386c2f0fee","rewritten_text":"The oaks about us were the haunt of a tribe of nightingales—there am I now; Idris, in the very bloom of youth, stands at my side—only remember, I am but twenty-two, and seventeen summers have scarcely gone by since my heart’s beloved. The river, swollen by autumn rains, has overflowed and drowned the low grounds; and Adrian, in his chosen boat, is engaged in the perilous sport of reaching for the highest bough from a submerged oak. Tell me, Adrian—are you weary of life, that you court danger so?—

He has won his prize, and he steers his boat through the flood; our eyes followed him with dread, yet the current bore him away from us. He was compelled to land far lower down, and make a long circuit before he could come back to us. “He is safe!” Idris called, as he sprang ashore, lifting the bough above his head as proof of success; “we’ll wait for him here.”

We were alone together; the sun had gone down; the nightingales began their song; the evening star shone clearly in the flood of light, still bright in the west. My angelic girl’s blue eyes were fixed on that gentle emblem of herself: “How the light seems to throb,” she said, “which is, as it were, the star’s own life. Its shifting brightness looks to me like a sign that its condition—like ours upon earth—is unsteady and changeful; it hesitates, I think, and it fears, and it loves.”

“Do not look at the star, dear, kind friend,” I cried; “do not read love in its trembling rays; do not gaze on distant worlds; do not speak of the mere fancy of a feeling. I have been silent for a long time—so long, indeed, that I have longed even to sickness to speak to you, and to lay my soul, my life, my whole self at your feet. Look not on the star, dear love; let that eternal spark plead for me. Let it be my witness and my advocate, silent as it shines—love is to me what light is to the star; and so long as that light is not blotted out by annihilation, so long shall I love you.”

That moment’s rapture must be veiled forever from the world’s cold gaze. Yet even now I feel her graceful form pressing against my heart, heavy with all its fullness—still do sight, and pulse, and breath grow sick and fail at the recollection of that first kiss. Slowly and in silence we went to meet Adrian, whom we heard drawing near.

I begged Adrian to come back to me after he had seen his sister home. And that very evening, as we walked along the moonlit paths of the forest, I poured out my whole heart—its agitation and its hope—to my friend. For a moment he seemed troubled. “I might have guessed this,” he said; “what conflict will now follow!”"}

{"request_id":"0c51329124ecf4e7717b52e8","rewritten_text":"“But the moment I saw you become the object of another’s love—when I pictured that you might be cherished in some way other than as a holy emblem of loveliness and excellence; or that you might come to love someone else with a fiercer devotion than the one you once gave me—then the fiend stirred within me. I drove away your lover, and from that hour I have known no peace. I have searched in vain for sleep or rest; my eyes would not close, and my blood has been in constant uproar. I woke into a new life, as if one who dies in hope might rise in Hell. I will not stain your imagination by recounting my struggles, my rage against myself, and my despair. Let a veil be drawn over the unspeakable sensations of a guilty father; the secrets of a heart so tortured must not be made common. Everything was turmoil, wrongdoing, remorse, and hatred—yet still the tenderest love. And what first hardened me into the resolve to master my passion and restore her father to my child was the sight of your bitter, compassionate sorrows. That is what brought me here: I told myself that if I could rouse again in my heart the grief I had felt at the loss of your mother, and the many memories of her that had been sleeping for seventeen years, then all love for her child would finally die out. In a burst of heroic determination I resolved to go alone; to leave you, the life of my life, and not to see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it would not work. I judged my strength too highly, or my love too lightly. I would surely have died if you had not hurried to me. Oh, if only I had truly been extinguished!”

“And now, Mathilda, I must make you my final confession. I have been wretchedly mistaken in thinking I could conquer my love for you; I never can. The sight of this house, these fields and woods where my first love lived seems only to have increased it. In my frenzy I even dared to say to myself—‘Diana died to give her birth; her mother’s spirit was carried into her body, and she ought to be Diana to me.’ With every attempt to cast it off, this love clings tighter: this guilty love is more unnatural than hate, it shrivels your hopes and leaves me ruined forever.

Better to have loved despair, and safer to have kissed her.

No time or distance can tear from my soul what is part of it. Since my arrival here, I have not for a single moment stopped feeling the Hell of passion that has been planted in me—to burn until everything is cold, stiff, and dead.”"}
