{"request_id":"07dcb8e103ed8a9bd32769d5","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I asked, “what’s the trouble now?—how’s your master?”

“Why, to tell the truth, massa, him not so very well as he might be.”

“Not well! I’m truly sorry to hear it. What’s he complaining of?”

“Dar! dat’s it!—he never ’plain of nothin’—but him berry sick for all dat.”

“_Very_ sick, Jupiter! Why didn’t you say so right away? Is he laid up in bed?”

“No, dat he ain’t!—he ain’t ’found nowhere—dat’s just where de shoe pinches; my mind is got to be berry heavy ’bout poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I’d like to understand what you mean. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what’s wrong?”

“Why, massa, ’tain’t worth while to get mad about de matter—Massa Will says noffin at all is de matter wid him; but then why should he go about looking dis here way, wid he head down and he soldiers up, and as white as a gose? And den he keeps a syphon all de time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a syphon wid de figgurs on de slate—de queerest figgurs I ebber did see. Ise gittin’ to be skeered, I tell you. I got to keep mighty tight eye ’pon him ’noovers. Todder day he give me slip ’fore de sun up and was gone de whole ob de blessed day. I had a big stick ready cut to give him deuced good beating when he did come—but Ise sich a fool dat I hadn’t de heart arter all—he look so berry poorly.”

“Eh?—what?—ah yes!—all things considered, I think you’d better not be too hard on the poor fellow. Don’t flog him, Jupiter—he can’t stand it very well; but can you make out what’s brought on this illness, or rather this change in his behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, massa, dey ain’t bin noffin unpleasant _since_ den—’twas _’fore_ den I’m feared—’twas de berry day you was dare.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, massa, I mean de bug—dare now.”

“The what?”

“De bug. I’m berry sartain Massa Will bin bit somewhere ’bout de head by dat goole-bug.”

“And what makes you think that, Jupiter?”

“Claws enuff, massa, and mouff too. I never did see sick a deuced bug—he kick and he bite ebery ting what come near him. Massa Will caught him fuss, but had for to let him go ’gin mighty quick, I tell you—den was de time he must ha’ got de bite. I didn’t like de look oh de bug mouff, myself, no how, so I wouldn’t take hold ob him wid my finger, but I caught him wid a piece ob paper dat I found.”}"}

{"request_id":"bdcd1ff05ae5913d52e5622f","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how strange and shadowy they were! In the soul there seemed to be something animal, while the body, in turn, could show flashes of spirituality. The senses might sharpen, and the intellect might sink. Who could say exactly where the pull of the flesh ended, or where the pull of the mind began? How thin and arbitrary were the definitions offered by ordinary psychologists! Still, how hard it was to choose between the competing claims of the different schools. Was the soul merely a shadow sitting within the house of sin? Or was the body truly contained in the soul, as Giordano Bruno had believed? The parting of spirit from matter was itself a mystery, and so too was their joining—spirit with matter.

He found himself wondering whether psychology could ever be made so exact a science that every small spring of life would be laid bare to us. As things stood, we were forever misreading ourselves and seldom understanding others. Experience held no ethical weight. It was only the name people gave to their errors. Moralists, for the most part, treated it as a kind of warning; they claimed it had a certain moral force in shaping character, praising it as what instructs us what to pursue and what to shun. Yet experience had no driving power. It was as inactive a cause as conscience itself. What it showed, in the end, was only this: that our future would repeat our past, and that the sin we had once committed with loathing we would do again, and with pleasure.

He was convinced that the experimental method was the sole route to any scientific account of the passions; and certainly Dorian Gray was a case well suited to him, one that seemed to promise abundant and fruitful findings. His sudden, mad love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological event of no small consequence. There was no denying that curiosity played a large part in it—curiosity and the hunger for fresh experiences—but it was not a simple passion; it was intricate, tangled, and many-layered. Whatever portion of it came from the purely sensuous instinct of boyhood had been reshaped by the imagination’s work, turned into something that appeared to the boy himself to be far from mere sense, and for that very reason became all the more perilous. It was the passions whose beginnings we manage to misjudge that ruled us most fiercely. Our feeblest motives were often the ones we knew best, the ones whose nature we were aware of. And it frequently happened that when we believed we were testing others, we were in truth testing ourselves.

While Lord Henry sat there, lost in thought, there came a knock at the door; his valet entered and reminded him that it was time to dress for dinner."}

{"request_id":"1461eab6d4948dead1c5b976","rewritten_text":"Country folk, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and every sort of wandering vagabond of the lowest sort were all jumbled together into one great mass; the drovers’ shrill whistles, the dogs barking, the oxen bellowing and plunging, the sheep bleating, the pigs grunting and squealing, the hawkers’ cries, and the shouts, oaths, and quarrels on every side; the clanging of bells and the roar of voices pouring out of every public-house; the crowding, shoving, driving, striking, whooping, and yelling; the hideous, discordant din rolling from every corner of the market; and the unwashed, unshaven, ragged, dirty figures constantly darting about, pushing in and out of the press, made it a scene so staggering and confusing that it fairly muddled the senses.

Mr. Sikes, dragging Oliver along, forced his way through the thickest part of the crowd, paying scarcely any heed to the sights and sounds that so amazed the boy. He gave a nod, twice or thrice, to a friend as he passed; and, turning aside from as many offers as he could to take a morning dram, kept on straight ahead, until they were clear of the uproar and had worked their way through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, young ’un!” said Sikes, glancing up at the clock on St. Andrew’s Church. “Hard upon seven! You must be off. Don’t hang back already, Lazy-legs!”

He drove the remark home with a jerk of his little companion’s wrist; Oliver, quickening his pace into something between a brisk walk and a run, tried to keep up with the house-breaker’s quick steps as best he could.

They kept on at that pace until they had gone past Hyde Park Corner and were making for Kensington; then Sikes eased his speed, until an empty cart some distance behind came up. Seeing “Hounslow” marked on it, he asked the driver, with as much politeness as he could manage, whether he would give them a lift as far as Isleworth.

“Get up,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes; he’s my boy,” answered Sikes, staring hard at Oliver, and slipping his hand, as if absent-minded, into the pocket where the pistol lay.

“Your father walks a bit too fast for you, doesn’t he, my man?” the driver asked, noticing Oliver was out of breath.

“Not at all,” said Sikes, cutting in. “He’s used to it. Here—take hold of my hand, Ned. In with you!”

So speaking to Oliver, he got him into the cart; and the driver, pointing to a heap of sacks, told him to lie down there and rest.

As they went by the different mile-stones, Oliver kept wondering, more and more, where his companion intended to take him. Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, Brentford—each was passed; yet they went on as steadily as though they had only just started their journey."}

{"request_id":"a5b47846d1f5912d238075db","rewritten_text":"Almost a year had gone by since my father came back, and the seasons were nearly through with their yearly round. It was now the close of May; the woods wore their freshest green, and the fields were filled with the sweet scent of newly cut grass. I believed that the mild air and the fair face of Nature might soften my mind and help me to awaken in him gentler feelings—peace, and love—so that I might gain from him the confidence I had resolved to win.

So I chose the evening of one of those days for my attempt. I asked him to walk with me, and I led him to a nearby beech wood, where the light shade kept us from the slanting, dazzling rays of the setting sun. After we had been walking for some time in silence, I sat myself down with him on a mossy little mound. Even now it seems to me I can see the very place: many of the slender, smooth trunks were twined with ivy, whose glossy leaves of the deepest green set off the pale bark, and the light leaves of the young beech shoots that sprang from their parent stems. The short grass was mixed with moss, and here and there it was partly covered by the dead leaves of the last autumn, blown by the winds into small heaps. There were a few moss-grown stumps scattered about. The breeze stirred the leaves softly, and through the green canopy the bright blue sky showed itself. As evening drew on, the far trunks took on a reddish tint from the sun, the wind fell entirely still, and only a few birds passed overhead on their way to their evening rest.

So it was that we sat together here; and when you consider all that had happened—everything terrible that had torn at our souls even in this quiet spot, which, but for strange passions, might have been a paradise—you will not be surprised that I remember it as I looked upon it, thinking that its calm might give me calm, and stir me not only to courage but to persuasive words. I saw these things, and in a kind of vacant way I took note of them, while I tried to set my thoughts in proper order for what I meant to do. My heart beat quickly as I gathered myself to speak to him; I was resolved not to be turned away, yet I could not help trembling at the thought of what my words might do to him. At last, with great hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the affection—the excessive affection—that you showed for me when you first returned, I hope will excuse me in your eyes if I venture to speak to you, though I do so with the tender affection of a daughter, yet also with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”"}

{"request_id":"03356bd89f987e5b6cfac5b5","rewritten_text":"“But,” said I, handing him the slip back, “I’m no clearer than I was before. If all the jewels of Golconda were waiting for me on the other side of this enigma, I’m sure I still couldn’t win them.”

“And yet,” Legrand replied, “the solution isn’t nearly as hard as you might think from that first quick look at the characters. Those characters, as anyone could guess, make up a cipher—that is, they carry a meaning; but, knowing Kidd, I couldn’t imagine him capable of devising any of the more recondite cryptographs. I decided at once it was of a plain sort—though, as it turned out, it was utterly beyond the sailor’s rough understanding without the key.”

“And you truly worked it out?”

“Of course. I’ve solved others that were ten thousand times more intricate. Circumstances, and a certain bent of mind, have drawn me to such puzzles, and it’s hard to doubt that human ingenuity can’t, with the right application, unravel an enigma of the same kind. Once I had set down connected, readable characters, I hardly gave a thought to the mere labor of extracting their import.

“In the present instance—indeed, in every case of secret writing—the first thing to consider is the language of the cipher; the methods of solution, particularly for the simpler ciphers, depend on—and are shaped by—the character of the idiom. In general, there’s nothing for it but to experiment (guided by probabilities) with every language known to the person attempting the deciphering, until the true one is found. But here, with the cipher in front of me, the signature removed nearly all the difficulty. The pun on the word ‘Kidd’ is only really felt in English. Had it not been for that, I would have started my trials with Spanish and French—the tongues in which a secret of this sort would most naturally have been written by a pirate of the Spanish Main. As it was, I took the cryptograph to be English.

“You’ll notice there are no breaks between the words. If there had been divisions, the job would have been much easier. Then I would have begun with a comparison and analysis of the shorter words, and if a one-letter word had turned up—as is quite likely, (a or I, for instance,)—I should have regarded the solution as essentially certain. But since there were no divisions, my first move was to determine the letters that appeared most often, as well as those that were least frequent.”"}

{"request_id":"64d36eb0f322249ffd80fdcb","rewritten_text":"He stood up and left the room with my nurse, and soon after my father entered.

At that moment, nothing could have made me happier than seeing my father. I reached out to him and cried, “Are you safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father reassured me that they were all well. He tried to lift my spirits by talking about things that mattered most to me, but he soon realized that a prison cannot be a place for cheerfulness. “What kind of place is this that you live in, my son?” he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and the miserable state of the room. “You came here hoping to find happiness, but it seems a terrible fate has followed you. And poor Clerval—”

Hearing the name of my unfortunate friend, who had been murdered, was more than I could bear in my weak condition. I began to cry.

“Alas! Yes, my father,” I answered. “Some terrible destiny hangs over me. I have to live long enough to carry it out, or I surely would have died on Henry’s coffin.”

We were not allowed to talk for long. My health was so fragile that every precaution was needed to keep me calm. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that I not wear myself out with too much effort. But my father’s presence felt to me like that of a good angel, and little by little my health improved.

As my sickness began to leave me, I fell into a dark, heavy sadness that nothing could shake. The image of Clerval stayed in front of me all the time—horrible and murdered. More than once, the distress caused by these thoughts made my friends fear that I might fall into a dangerous relapse. Oh, why did they keep me alive, when my life was so miserable and hated? It must be so I can fulfill my destiny, which is now coming to an end. Very soon, death will put an end to these pains and free me from the great weight of anguish that drags me down to the dust. And when I carry out the judgment of justice, I will also finally rest. At first, death still felt far away, even though I kept wishing for it. I often sat for hours without moving or speaking, hoping for some powerful change that would bury me and my destroyer under its ruins.

The time for the assizes was approaching. I had already been in prison for three months. Even though I was still weak and in constant danger of relapsing, I had to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court would meet. Mr. Kirwin took charge of everything, making sure witnesses were found and that my defense was prepared."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5ad0d19ce7aca7b426d53fbf","rewritten_text":"I’m also told by Mrs. Otis, who—if I may say so—is no small authority on Art, having had the privilege of spending several winters in Boston when she was a girl, that these gems are of considerable monetary value and, if they were offered for sale, would fetch a very high price. Given all that, Lord Canterville, I’m sure you’ll understand how impossible it would be for me to allow them to remain in the possession of any member of my family. Indeed, all such empty ornaments and toys, however appropriate or necessary they may be to the dignity of the British aristocracy, would be completely out of place among people raised on the strict—and I believe immortal—principles of republican simplicity. Perhaps I should add that Virginia is very anxious for you to let her keep the box as a memento of your unfortunate but misguided ancestor. Since it’s extremely old and, as a result, in pretty poor condition, you may decide to grant her request. For my part, I admit I’m rather surprised to see one of my children expressing sympathy for medievalism in any form, and I can only explain it by the fact that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from a trip to Athens.’\n\nLord Canterville listened very gravely to the worthy minister’s speech, tugging at his grey moustache now and then to hide an involuntary smile. When Mr. Otis finished, he shook his hand warmly and said, ‘My dear sir, your charming little daughter did Sir Simon, my unlucky ancestor, a very important service, and I and my family are greatly indebted to her for her remarkable courage and grit. The jewels are clearly hers, and, egad, I believe that if I were heartless enough to take them from her, the wicked old fellow would be out of his grave in a fortnight, making my life a misery. As for them being heirlooms, nothing is an heirloom unless it’s specifically named in a will or legal document, and the existence of these jewels has been entirely unknown. I assure you I have no more claim to them than your butler does. And when Miss Virginia grows up, I daresay she’ll be pleased to have pretty things to wear. Besides, Mr. Otis, you forget that you took the furniture and the ghost at a valuation, and anything that belonged to the ghost passed at once into your possession. Whatever activity Sir Simon may have shown in the corridor at night, in law he was really dead, and you acquired his property by purchase.’"}

Could not make out what was said, but believed the language to be Spanish. The condition of the room and of the bodies was described by this witness in the same way we described them yesterday.

“_Henri Duval_, a neighbor, and by trade a silversmith, states that he was one of the group who first entered the house. He confirms Musèt’s testimony in general. As soon as they forced their way in, they shut the door again to keep out the crowd, which gathered very quickly, even though it was late. The shrill voice, this witness thinks, was that of an Italian. He was certain it was not French. He could not be sure whether it was a man’s voice; it might have been a woman’s. He was not familiar with the Italian language. He could not distinguish the words, but was convinced by the speaker’s intonation that the person was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter. He had spoken with both often. He was sure the shrill voice was not either of the deceased.

“——_Odenheimer, restaurateur._ This witness offered his testimony. Not speaking French, he was questioned through an interpreter. He is a native of Amsterdam. He was passing the house at the time of the shrieks. They lasted for several minutes—probably ten. They were long and loud—very awful and distressing. He was one of those who entered the building. He confirmed the previous evidence in every respect except one. He was sure the shrill voice was that of a man—of a Frenchman. He could not distinguish the words that were spoken. They were loud and quick—uneven—apparently spoken in fear as well as in anger. The voice was harsh—not so much shrill as harsh. He could not call it a shrill voice. The rough voice said repeatedly ‘_sacré_,’ ‘_diable_,’ and once ‘_mon Dieu_.’

“_Jules Mignaud_, banker, of the firm of Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. Is the elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye had some property. She opened an account with his banking house in the spring of that year—(eight years earlier). She made frequent deposits in small amounts. She did not write checks for anything until the third day before her death, when she withdrew in person the sum of 4000 francs. This money was paid in gold, and a clerk went home with it.

“_Adolphe Le Bon_, clerk to Mignaud et Fils, states that on the day in question, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her residence with the 4000 francs, putting it into two bags. When the door was opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one of the bags from his hands, while the old lady took the other from him.”"}

{"request_id":"bab0e0d84f6057a6b1950dd8","rewritten_text":"The group was arranged on two benches next to each other. Anne sat among those in the front, and Mr. Elliot had managed it so well, with help from his friend Colonel Wallis, that he ended up with a seat beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins and the main focus of Colonel Wallis’s attention, was perfectly content.

Anne’s mind was in the best possible mood for the evening’s entertainment. It kept her busy in just the right way: she could enjoy the tender parts, the lively ones, the scientific explanations, and even the long, tiring sections. She had never liked a concert more—at least during the first act. Near the end of it, during the break after an Italian song, she explained the words to Mr. Elliot. They had the concert program between them.

“This,” she said, “is almost the meaning of the words—though I should say the sense, not that I can truly explain it. You can’t really talk about the meaning of an Italian love-song, but this is as close as I can get. I don’t pretend to understand the language. I’m a very poor Italian scholar.”

“Yes, yes, I see it. I can tell you know nothing about it. You only have enough knowledge of the language to translate, at once, these Italian lines that are turned around, rearranged, and shortened, into clear, easy, elegant English. You don’t need to say anything more about your ignorance. Here is full proof.”

“I won’t argue with such kindness,” Anne replied, “but I would be sorry to be tested by a real expert.”

“I haven’t had the pleasure of visiting Camden Place for so long,” Mr. Elliot answered, “without learning something about Miss Anne Elliot. And I truly believe she is too modest to notice, in the world at large, even half of her accomplishments—and too accomplished for modesty to come naturally to any other woman.”

“Shame on you! Shame on you! That’s far too much flattery. I forget what we have next,” she said, turning back to the program.

“Perhaps,” Mr. Elliot said quietly, “I have known your character longer than you realize.”

“Indeed? How could that be? You could only have known me since I came to Bath, unless you heard me spoken of earlier in my own family.”

“I knew you by reputation long before you came to Bath. I had heard you described by people who knew you well. I have known you by character for many years. Your appearance, your nature, your accomplishments, your manner—everything was already familiar to me.”

Mr. Elliot was not disappointed by the interest he had hoped to create. No one can resist the charm of such a mystery."}

{"request_id":"4986ef2be369e59b4ef63886","rewritten_text":"But in that bitter tirade about Chantilly, which appeared in yesterday’s “Musée,” the satirist, making some disgraceful allusions to the cobbler’s change of name after taking up the buskin, quoted a Latin line we have often discussed. I mean the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I told you that this was in reference to Orion, which had once been written Urion; and, from certain clues tied to that explanation, I knew you couldn’t have forgotten it. It was clear, then, that you wouldn’t fail to connect the two ideas of Orion and Chantilly. The fact that you did combine them, I saw in the expression of the smile that crossed your lips. You were thinking of the poor cobbler’s immolation. Up to that point, you had been stooping in your walk; but then I saw you straighten to your full height. I was sure, at that moment, that you were reflecting on Chantilly’s diminutive stature. And that’s when I interrupted your thoughts to say that, since he was in fact a very little man—that Chantilly—he’d do better at the Théâtre des Variétés.”

Not long after that, we were looking over an evening edition of the “Gazette des Tribunaux” when the following paragraphs caught our attention.

“Extraordinary Murders.—This morning, at about three o’clock, the residents of the Quartier St. Roch were woken from sleep by a series of terrifying shrieks, apparently coming from the fourth story of a house on the Rue Morgue, known to be occupied solely by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay—caused by a fruitless attempt to gain entry in the usual way—the gate was forced open with a crowbar, and eight or ten of the neighbors entered with two gendarmes. By then the cries had stopped; but as the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, two or more rough voices, arguing angrily, could be heard, and they seemed to come from the upper part of the house. When the second landing was reached, those sounds had also ceased, and everything was perfectly quiet. The party fanned out and hurried from room to room. When they arrived at a large back chamber on the fourth story (the door of which, found locked with the key inside, was forced open), a scene presented itself that struck everyone there with horror no less than with astonishment.

“The apartment was in the wildest disorder—the furniture broken and thrown about in every direction. There was only one bedstead; and from it the bed had been removed and thrown into the middle of the floor. On a chair lay a razor, smeared with blood.”"}

{"request_id":"b09b50320db65f545fd6647d","rewritten_text":"No note of condolence had been sent to Ireland. The omission fell back upon the person who had sinned; for when poor Lady Elliot died, no letter of condolence was received at Kellynch, and so there was far too much reason to fear that the Dalrymples regarded the relationship as ended. The point, then, was how to set this troublesome matter right and be taken up again as cousins; and it was a point which, in a more sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot considered trivial. “Family ties are always worth keeping, and good society is always worth seeking. Lady Dalrymple has taken a house, for three months, in Laura Place, and will be living handsomely. She was at Bath the year before, and Lady Russell had heard her spoken of as a charming woman. It is very desirable that the connexion should be renewed, if it can be done, without any breach of propriety on the part of the Elliots.”

Sir Walter, however, would manage matters in his own fashion, and at last wrote a very fine letter—full of explanation, regret, and entreaty—to his right honourable cousin. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot could find much to admire in it; but it served its purpose, and brought from the Dowager Viscountess only three lines of scrawl: “She was very much honoured, and should be happy in their acquaintance.” The labour was at an end; the pleasant part began. They called in Laura Place; they received the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and of the Honourable Miss Carteret, to be displayed wherever they might be most noticed; and “Our cousins in Laura Place”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret”—was repeated to everyone.

Anne felt mortified. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been agreeable, she would still have been ashamed of the commotion they caused; but they were nothing at all. There was no superiority of manner, no real accomplishment, no understanding. Lady Dalrymple had earned the reputation of “a charming woman” merely because she had a smile and a civil answer for everyone. Miss Carteret, who had even less to say, was so plain and so awkward that she would never have been tolerated in Camden Place, had it not been for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted she had expected something better; yet “it is an acquaintance worth having.” And when Anne ventured to give her opinion of them to Mr Elliot, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves, but still insisted that, as a family connexion, as good company, and as people who would gather good company about them, they had their value. Anne smiled and said,

“My notion of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of clever, well-informed people, who have a great deal to talk about; that is what I call good company.”"}

{"request_id":"8adcff1ec08d52221fd412ca","rewritten_text":"“I hope I’ll soon have the pleasure of introducing my son to you,” said Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, happy to think that this hope was meant as a special compliment to her, smiled very graciously.

“You’ve heard of a man named Frank Churchill, I suppose,” he went on. “You know he is my son, even though he doesn’t use my name.”

“Oh! Yes, and I’ll be very glad to meet him. I’m sure Mr. Elton won’t waste any time visiting him, and we’ll both be very pleased to see him at the Vicarage.”

“You’re very kind. I’m sure Frank will be extremely happy. He’s coming to town next week, if not sooner. We got word of it today in a letter. I found the letters this morning on my way, and when I saw my son’s handwriting, I assumed I could open it, even though it wasn’t addressed to me. It was addressed to Mrs. Weston. She is his main correspondent, I assure you. I hardly ever receive a letter.”

“And so you actually opened a letter that was meant for her! Oh, Mr. Weston—(laughing in a showy way) I have to protest. That’s a very dangerous example indeed. I beg you not to let your neighbors copy you. Really, if this is what I’m supposed to expect, married women will have to start standing up for themselves! Oh, Mr. Weston, I never would have believed it of you!”

“Ah, yes. Men are poor creatures. You should be careful, Mrs. Elton. This letter tells us—it's a short one, written in a hurry—only that they’re all coming up to town right away, because of Mrs. Churchill. She hasn’t been well all winter, and she thinks Enscombe is too cold for her. So they’re all moving south without delay.”

“Really!—from Yorkshire, I suppose. Is Enscombe in Yorkshire?”

“Yes. They’re about one hundred and ninety miles from London, which is quite a trip.”

“Yes, it’s certainly a long way. Sixty-five miles farther than it is from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance to people with a lot of money, Mr. Weston? You’d be amazed to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, sometimes rushes around. You can hardly believe me, but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back again with four horses.”

“The trouble with the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we understand it, hasn’t been able to leave the sofa for a whole week. In Frank’s last letter she complained that he was too weak to get into her conservatory without both his arm and his uncle’s.”"}

{"request_id":"75a4fc050f63341bb0b7b065","rewritten_text":"But my father was beside me to comfort me and to push away bitter memories with bright hopes. It seemed sweet to me to grieve, knowing that he might dry my tears.

Then again, he pulled my thoughts away from my sorrow by comparing it with his own despair when he lost my mother. Even then, I shuddered at the picture he painted of his passions. He had the imagination of a poet, and when he described the whirlwind that tore through his feelings, his words carried such force and life that I believed what he said even as I trembled. I wondered how he could ever again enter the ordinary offices of life after his wild thoughts had seemed to give him some kinship with the unearthly. The ideas he conveyed were so tremendous that it seemed as if the human heart were far too limited for their conception. His feelings appeared better suited to a spirit whose home is the earthquake and the volcano than to one confined to a mortal body and human features. But those were only memories; he had changed since then. He was now nothing but love, nothing but softness. And when I looked up at him in wonder as he spoke, the smile on his lips told me that his heart was filled with the gentlest passions.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father led me to pursue deeper studies than had occupied me before. My progress was his delight. He was with me throughout all my studies, assisting me or joining in every lesson. We saw a great deal of society, and no day passed without my father trying to make it richer with some new enjoyment. The tender attachment he had for me, and the love and reverence with which I returned it, cast a spell over every moment. The hours felt slow, because each minute was used. We lived more in one week than many do in the course of several months, and the variety and novelty of our pleasures gave everything a sharper zest.

We made excursions together again and again. Whether we went to see beautiful scenery, or to look at fine pictures, or sometimes for no other reason than to find amusement wherever it might arise, I was always happy when I was near my father. It was a matter of regret to me whenever a third person joined us; yet if I turned toward my father with a troubled look, his eyes would be fixed on me and shining with tenderness, and that instantly restored joy to my heart. Oh, hours of intense delight! Short as you were, you feel as long to me as a whole life when I look back on you through the mist of grief that rose immediately afterward, as if to shut you from my view."}

{"request_id":"bd1f6ff0878680460592be4c","rewritten_text":"“You haven’t stayed in Bath long enough,” said he, “to enjoy the evening gatherings there.”

“Oh! no. Their usual sort of company has nothing to recommend it to me. I’m no card-player.”

“You weren’t before, I know. You never cared for cards; but time brings many changes.”

“I’m not altered so much yet,” cried Anne, and stopped, afraid she scarcely knew how her words might be taken. After a pause, he spoke again, as though the thought had risen at once within him: “It is indeed a period! Eight years and a half is a period.”

Whether he meant to go on further was left for Anne to consider in a calmer hour; for even while she still heard what he had just said, Henrietta startled her into other matters, eager to take advantage of the leisure and get out, urging her companions to make no delay, lest someone else should enter.

They had to rise. Anne declared herself perfectly ready, and tried to appear so; yet she felt that if Henrietta had known the regret and reluctance of her heart in leaving that chair, and then preparing to leave the room, she would have found, in all Anne’s own feelings for her cousin, in the very security of his affection, enough to pity her.

Their preparations, however, were cut short. Disturbing sounds were heard; other visitors drew near, and the door was thrown open for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose arrival seemed to send a chill through everything. Anne felt an instant oppression, and wherever she looked she saw the same signs. The comfort, the ease, the liveliness of the room had vanished, replaced by cold composure, fixed silence, or dull talk, meant to match the heartless elegance of her father and sister. How mortifying to think it was truly so!

Her watchful jealousy was satisfied in one point. Captain Wentworth was received again by everyone, by Elizabeth even more kindly than before. She spoke to him once, and looked at him more than once. In fact, Elizabeth was working out a serious plan. The rest soon showed it. After wasting a few minutes on the proper trifles, she began to offer the invitation that would cover all the remaining obligations of the Musgroves. “To-morrow evening, to meet a few friends: no formal party.” Everything was said with great grace; the cards she had prepared—the “Miss Elliot at home”—were laid on the table with a courteous, comprehensive smile for all, and one smile and one card more pointedly for Captain Wentworth. The truth was that Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to know how important it was to have a man of such an air and appearance as his."}

{"request_id":"99d8b4f5882fe290be6fbb39","rewritten_text":"If not—if you would rather appeal to my patience, and to the mercy of those you have grievously wronged—then take your seat in that chair, in silence. It has been waiting for you these two full days.”

The monks muttered a few words that meant nothing, yet they still hesitated.

“You will be prompt,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and the other course is gone forever.”

The man held back a moment longer.

“I have no taste for negotiation,” said Mr. Brownlow, “and, since I stand up for the dearest interests of others, I have no right.”

“Is there—” Monks broke in, his voice faltering—“is there no middle way?”

“None.”

Monks stared at the old gentleman with a troubled look; but seeing nothing there except sternness and resolve, he went into the room, and, with a shrug, sat down.

“Lock the door on the outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and come when I ring.”

They obeyed, and the two were left alone.

“This is a pretty sort of treatment, sir,” said Monks, flinging down his hat and cloak, “for my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” Mr. Brownlow answered. “It is because the hopes and wishes of those early, bright years were bound up with him—and with that fair creature of his blood and kin, who returned to her God in youth, leaving me here a solitary, lonely man. It is because he knelt with me beside his only sister’s death-bed when he was still a boy, on the very morning that—Heaven willed otherwise—would have made her my young wife. It is because my heart, seared as it was, clung to him from that time through all his trials and mistakes, until he died. It is because old recollections and associations fill my breast, and even the sight of you brings back thoughts of him. It is for all these reasons that I am moved to deal with you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford—even now—and to blush for the unworthiness of you who bear the name.”

“What has the name to do with it?” asked the other, after weighing the words in half-silence and half-dogged astonishment. “What is the name to me?”

“Nothing,” said Mr. Brownlow. “Nothing to you. But it was hers; and even after all this time it brings back to me, an old man, the glow and quickening I once felt—only to have it spoken again by a stranger. I am truly glad you have changed it—very—very glad.”

“This is all very fine,” said Monks (to keep up his assumed character) after a long pause, in which he jerked himself back and forth in sullen defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face shaded by his hand."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e788f6d7979020914c26505e","rewritten_text":"For a moment I was so struck by amazement that I could not think with any exactness. I knew my design differed from this one in many details, though the general plan was undeniably similar. At once I took up a candle and, settling myself at the far end of the room, set about examining the parchment more carefully. When I turned it over, I saw my own sketch on the reverse, exactly as I had made it. My first reaction was nothing but astonishment at how remarkably the outlines matched—at the strange coincidence that, without my knowing it, there should be a skull on the other side of the parchment, lying immediately beneath my figure of the _scarabæus_, and that this skull should resemble my drawing not only in outline but in size as well. I can say the singularity of that coincidence fairly stunned me for a time. That is the usual effect of such things: the mind strains to link them into a connexion, a chain of cause and effect, and, failing to do so, falls into a kind of temporary paralysis. Yet once the stupor eased, a conviction began to dawn on me little by little—one that startled me even more than the coincidence itself. I started to remember, clearly and without doubt, that when I made my sketch of the _scarabæus_ there had been no drawing on the parchment. I was perfectly certain of it, because I recalled turning the sheet over and over, looking for the cleanest place. If the skull had been there then, of course I could not have failed to notice it. Here, indeed, was a mystery I felt I could not explain; but even at that early stage, there seemed to flicker—faintly, in the farthest and most hidden recesses of my mind—a sort of glow-worm notion of the truth that last night’s adventure had brought to such a magnificent demonstration. I stood up at once, put the parchment away securely, and dismissed any further thought until I should be alone.\n\n“When you had gone, and when Jupiter was fast asleep, I set myself to a more methodical investigation of the matter. First, I considered how the parchment had come into my hands. The spot where we found the _scarabæus_ was on the coast of the mainland, about a mile east of the island, and only a short distance above the high-water line. When I took hold of it, it gave me a sharp bite, so that I had to let it fall. Jupiter, with his usual caution, before seizing the insect—which had flown toward him—looked around for a leaf, or something of that sort, to take hold of it with.”"}

{"request_id":"32e5d44f10562599acbe328d","rewritten_text":"You see, I’d tucked my handkerchief into my helmet, along with a few other odds and ends; but it was the sort of helmet you can’t take off on your own. I hadn’t thought of that when I put it there, and honestly I didn’t even know. I figured it would be especially handy sitting right there. But now the idea of it being so close and so convenient—yet completely out of reach—made everything worse and harder to stand. Yes, the thing you can’t get is the thing you want most, that’s what everyone notices. Well, it took my attention off everything else, cleared it right away, and fixed it in my helmet; mile after mile it stayed there, with me imagining the handkerchief, picturing it. And it was bitter and maddening to have the salt sweat keep running into my eyes while I couldn’t reach it. It sounds small on paper, but it wasn’t small at all; it was the most genuine sort of misery. I wouldn’t say it if it weren’t true. 

I decided that next time I’d carry a reticule instead, whatever people might think. Sure, those iron fellows of the Round Table would probably call it scandalous and maybe raise Sheol about it, but for me—comfort first, and style after. So we jogged on, and now and then we hit a patch of dust; it would billow up in clouds, get into my nose, and make me sneeze and weep. And of course I said things I oughtn’t to have said—I won’t pretend otherwise. I’m not any better than the rest.

We couldn’t seem to run into anybody in this lonesome Britain, not even an ogre; and in the mood I was in then, it was a mercy for the ogre—that is, an ogre with a handkerchief. Most knights would’ve been thinking only about getting his armor back, but I managed to take his bandanna; he could keep his gear, for all of me.

Meanwhile, it was getting hotter and hotter in there. The sun kept beating down, warming the iron more and more all the time. When you’re hot like that, every little thing starts to irritate you. When I trotted, I rattled like a crate of dishes, and that got on my nerves; and I couldn’t stand the shield slatting and banging, now against my breast, now around my back. If I dropped into a walk, my joints creaked and screeched in that tiresome way a wheelbarrow does, and since we weren’t making any breeze at that pace, I felt like I’d be cooked in that stove. And besides, the quieter I went, the more the iron seemed to settle on me, until it felt like more and more tons, pressing down on me every minute."}

{"request_id":"f77feb623241bab404d041e1","rewritten_text":"“Are you talking about—Mr. Knightley?”

“To be sure I am. I could never imagine anyone else—and I thought you would know that. When we talked about him, it was as clear as I could make it.”

“Not quite,” Emma answered, keeping her voice steady. “Even though you said all that, it seemed to me you were talking about a different person. I could almost say you had actually named Mr. Frank Churchill. I’m sure you were speaking about the help Mr. Frank Churchill gave you when he protected you from the gipsies.”

“Oh! Miss Woodhouse, how you forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember perfectly what I said. I told you I didn’t doubt your feelings. And since he had done you that service, it was only natural. You agreed with me, and you spoke about it very warmly, saying how grateful you were for what he did. You even mentioned what you felt when he came forward to rescue you. The whole thing is still very strong in my memory.”

“Oh, dear,” Harriet said, “now I remember what you mean. But at the time, I was thinking of something else. It wasn’t the gipsies. It wasn’t Mr. Frank Churchill. No!” She lifted her voice a little. “I was thinking of something far more important—Mr. Knightley coming to ask me to dance, when Mr. Elton wouldn’t dance with me, and when there was no other partner in the room. That was the kind act. That was the noble, generous help. It was that service that made me start to feel how much better he was than anyone else on earth.”

“Good God!” Emma cried. “This is the most unfortunate—most dreadful—mistake. What can be done?”

“You wouldn’t have encouraged me, then, if you had understood what I meant. At least, though, I can’t be any worse off than I would have been if the other person had been the one. And now—it is possible—”

She paused. Emma couldn’t speak.

“I don’t doubt, Miss Woodhouse,” Harriet went on, “that you feel a big difference between the two, whether it’s about me or about anyone else. You must think one person is five hundred million times above me, and the other is not. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that if—if it turns out—strange as it may seem—”

She stopped again, and then continued. “You know those were your own words. And more surprising things have happened—matches with even greater differences than there is between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. So it seems possible that something like this could have happened before. And if I should be so lucky—beyond anything I can say—as to—if Mr. Knightley really—if he doesn’t mind the difference, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you won’t oppose it or try to create difficulties.”}"}

{"request_id":"64833add98a4790a5086f646","rewritten_text":"Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had come so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle.

His face instantly took on the look of the deepest gloom, and he replied, “To seek one who fled from me.”

“And did the man you were pursuing travel in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I suppose we’ve seen him. The day before we picked you up, we saw some dogs drawing a sledge, with a man in it, across the ice.”

This stirred the stranger’s attention, and he asked a whole series of questions about the route the dæmon, as he called him, had taken. Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, “I’ve no doubt excited your curiosity, as well as that of these good people; but you’re too considerate to ask questions.”

“Of course; it would be very impertinent and inhuman of me to trouble you with any curiosity of my own.”

“And yet you rescued me from a strange and dangerous situation; you’ve kindly brought me back to life.”

Soon after, he asked whether I thought the breaking up of the ice had destroyed the other sledge. I told him I couldn’t say for certain, because the ice hadn’t broken until near midnight, and the traveler might have reached a place of safety before then; but I couldn’t judge.

From that time on, a new spirit of life seemed to animate the stranger’s decaying body. He showed the greatest eagerness to be on deck to watch for the sledge that had appeared before; but I persuaded him to stay in the cabin, because he’s far too weak to endure the harshness of the air. I promised that someone would keep watch for him and give him immediate notice if any new object came into view.

Such is my journal of what has happened in this strange occurrence up to the present day. The stranger has gradually improved in health, but he is very quiet and seems uneasy whenever anyone other than myself enters his cabin. Still, his manners are so agreeable and gentle that the sailors are all interested in him, even though they’ve had very little chance to talk with him. As for me, I’ve begun to love him like a brother, and his constant, deep grief fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble creature in better days, since even now, in wreck, he remains so attractive and amiable.

I said in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the wide ocean; yet I have found a man who, before his spirit was broken by misery, I would have been happy to have as the brother of my heart.”"}

{"request_id":"7f08ca2cfe2f516500cecc92","rewritten_text":"“Just listen, then! You!” Monks replied. “When his father fell ill in Rome, he was joined there by his wife—my mother—after a long separation from him. She came from Paris and brought me along, to attend to his affairs, as far as I can tell; for she cared little for him, and he for her. He knew nothing of us, his senses having failed, and he slept on until the next day, when he died. Among the papers in his desk there were two, both dated the night his illness first began, and both addressed to yourself”; he turned to Mr. Brownlow; “and each enclosed in a few brief lines to you, with a note on the outside saying the package was not to be sent on until after he was dead. One was a letter to this girl, Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What about the letter?” asked Mr. Brownlow.

“The letter?—It was a page crossed and recrossed, again and again, with a penitent confession, and prayers to God for her help. He had kept up a story to the girl—that some secret matter, to be explained one day, had stopped him from marrying her at that time. So she went on, trusting him patiently, until she trusted too far and lost what no one could ever restore. At that point she was only a few months from her confinement. He told her everything he had intended, to spare her shame if he had lived, and if he died, he begged her not to curse his memory, nor to believe that the consequences of their sin would fall on her or on their young child; for the guilt was all his. He reminded her of the day he had given her the little locket and the ring, with her Christian name engraved upon it, and left a blank for the name he hoped one day to put there—prayed her still to keep it and wear it close to her heart, as she had done before—and then he kept going, wildly, repeating the same words over and over, as though he had lost his mind. I think he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, as Oliver’s tears came fast.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow went on, speaking for him, “was in the same tone as the letter. He spoke of the miseries his wife had brought him; of the stubborn bent, vice, malice, and early bad passions in you, his only son, whom he had trained to hate him. And he left you, and your mother, each an annuity of eight hundred pounds. He divided the rest of his property into two equal parts—one for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, if it should be born alive and live to come of age.”}"}

{"request_id":"90541193a15c90095b3465f9","rewritten_text":"He rose and left the room with my nurse, and after a moment my father entered.

At that instant nothing could have brought me more joy than seeing my father. I reached out to him and cried,

“Then you are safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father soothed me with assurances of their welfare, and tried—by dwelling on matters so dear to my heart—to lift my sinking spirits; yet he soon discovered that a prison cannot be a place of cheer. “What sort of dwelling is this for you, my son?” he said, casting a mournful look at the barred windows and the miserable state of the room. “You came to find happiness, but some fatality seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—”

The name of my unfortunate, murdered friend was more than my frail condition could bear; I burst into tears.

“Alas! Yes, my father,” I answered; “some destiny of the most dreadful kind hangs over me, and I must live to carry it out—or else I surely should have died upon Henry’s coffin.”

We were not permitted to talk for long, because my health was so precarious that every precaution was needed to keep me tranquil. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that my strength must not be worn down by too much effort. Still, my father’s presence felt to me like that of a kindly angel, and my health returned to me little by little.

As the sickness left me, I sank into a gloomy, black melancholy that nothing could dispel. The sight of Clerval remained before my eyes, ghastly and murdered. More than once, the agitation stirred up by these thoughts made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Alas! Why did they spare such a miserable and hated life for me? It must be so that I might fulfil my destiny, which is now drawing to its end. Soon—oh, very soon—death will put an end to these throbbings and free me from the heavy weight of anguish that drags me to the dust; and, in carrying out the sentence of justice, I shall also sink into rest. At that time the approach of death still seemed far off, though the wish was always present to my mind. Often I sat for hours, perfectly still and silent, longing for some great revolution that would bury both me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The time of the assizes drew near. I had already been three months in prison, and though I was still weak and in constant danger of relapsing, I was required to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court was to be held. Mr. Kirwin took it upon himself to see to every detail—collecting witnesses and arranging my defence.”}"}

{"request_id":"2ef2144405257a0304f2537d","rewritten_text":"“Now I hurry to the more moving part of my story. I will describe events that struck me with feelings which, from what I had been, have made me what I am.

“Spring advanced quickly; the weather turned fine, and the skies were cloudless. It surprised me that what had been desert and gloomy should now bloom with the most beautiful flowers and green growth. My senses were delighted and refreshed by a thousand delightful scents and a thousand sights of beauty.

“It was on one of these days, when my cottagers periodically rested from their labor—the old man played his guitar, and the children listened—that I noticed Felix’s face was melancholy beyond expression. He sighed often, and once his father paused in his music, and I guessed from his manner that he was asking about the cause of his son’s sorrow. Felix answered in a cheerful tone, and the old man was starting his music again when someone tapped at the door.

“It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a countryman who served as her guide. The lady wore a dark suit and was covered by a thick black veil. Agatha asked a question, and the stranger replied only by speaking, in a sweet accent, the name of Felix. Her voice was musical, but unlike that of either of my friends. At the sound of that word, Felix hurried to the lady. When she saw him, she lifted her veil, and I saw a face of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair was a shining raven black, and curiously braided; her eyes were dark, yet gentle, though full of life. Her features were evenly proportioned, and her complexion was wonderfully fair, each cheek touched with a lovely pink.

“Felix seemed completely overwhelmed with joy when he saw her; every trace of sorrow vanished from his face, and it instantly showed a kind of ecstatic happiness I could hardly have believed possible. His eyes sparkled as his cheeks flushed with pleasure; and at that moment I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed moved by different feelings. Wiping away a few tears from her lovely eyes, she held out her hand to Felix, who kissed it rapturously and called her—at least as I could make out—his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him, but she smiled. He helped her down from the horse, dismissed her guide, and led her into the cottage. Some conversation followed between him and his father. The young stranger then knelt at the old man’s feet and would have kissed his hand, but he lifted her and embraced her warmly.

“I soon realized that although the stranger spoke in clear, articulated sounds and seemed to have a language of her own, she was neither understood by the cottagers nor did she herself understand them.”"}

{"request_id":"5588d1f37424c181d8a0655c","rewritten_text":"Without the usual tools and resources, the analyst throws himself into the mindset of his opponent. He tries to understand how the other person thinks, and he often sees at a glance the only ways—sometimes in a way that is almost absurdly simple—by which he can trick someone into making a mistake or push them into miscalculating.

Whist has long been known for its effect on what people call the power to calculate. Even very intelligent men have been known to take real pleasure in it, while dismissing chess as too silly. There is probably nothing else that challenges the ability to analyze in quite the same way. The best chess-player in Christendom may be little more than the best chess-player, but skill at whist suggests a talent for succeeding in other, more important situations where one mind must deal with another. When I say skill, I mean the kind of mastery that includes understanding all the sources of real advantage. Those sources are many and varied, and they often hide in parts of thought that most people cannot reach. Paying close attention helps you remember clearly. So a player who concentrates well at chess will usually do well at whist, and the rules of Hoyle—based mainly on the game’s basic mechanics—are easy enough to understand.

So people often think that having a good memory and playing “by the book” is all that matters. But the analyst’s real skill shows up in areas beyond the simple rules. He makes, in silence, a whole series of observations and guesses. His companions may do the same, but the difference in what they learn does not come as much from whether their guesses are correct as from how good their observations are. The key is knowing what to watch.

Our player does not limit himself at all. Even though the game is the focus, he does not throw away deductions from things outside the game. He studies his partner’s face, comparing it carefully with each opponent’s. He looks at how the cards are sorted in each hand, sometimes counting trump card by card and honors by honors, based on the quick looks the players give to those cards. As the play goes on, he notices every change in expression, collecting information from differences in how certain someone looks, how surprised they seem, whether they show triumph, or whether they show frustration. From the way a person gathers up a trick, he judges whether that person can take another trick in the same suit. He also figures out what is being played through feints, by the way it is laid down on the table.

Even a casual or careless remark; an accidental dropping or turning of a card, along with the anxiety or carelessness about hiding it; the counting of tricks and the order they are arranged in—these, along with embarrassment, hesitation, eagerness, or nervous fear, all give him signs of what is really going on, as if he can see it intuitively."}

{"request_id":"febad1f4c65377d05ad79561","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?”

I says:

“Pap, and mam, and sis, and—”

Then I broke down. He says:

“Oh, dang it now, don’t go on so; we all has to have our troubles, and this’n ’ll turn out right. What’s wrong with ’em?”

“They’re—they’re—are you the watchman of the boat?”

“Yes,” he says, acting kind of pleased with himself. “I’m the captain and the owner and the mate and the pilot and watchman and head deck-hand; and sometimes I’m the freight and passengers. I ain’t as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be so blame’ generous and good to Tom, Dick and Harry as he is, nor throw money around the way he does; but I’ve told him a many a time ’t I wouldn’t trade places with him. For, says I, a sailor’s life’s the life for me, and I’m derned if I’d live two mile out o’ town, where there ain’t nothing ever goin’ on, not for all his spondulicks and as much more on top of it. Says I—”

I cut in and says:

“They’re in an awful peck of trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Why, pap and mam and sis and Miss Hooker; and if you’d take your ferry-boat and go up there—”

“Up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“What wreck?”

“Why, there ain’t but one.”

“What, you don’t mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good land! what are they doin’ there, for gracious sakes?”

“Well, they didn’t go there a-purpose.”

“I bet they didn’t! Why, great goodness, there ain’t no chance for ’em if they don’t git off mighty quick! Why, how in the nation did they ever get into such a scrape?”

“Easy enough. Miss Hooker was a-visiting up there to the town—”

“Yes, Booth’s Landing—go on.”

“She was a-visiting there at Booth’s Landing, and just on the edge of evening she started over with her nigger woman in the horse-ferry to stay all night at her friend’s house, Miss What-you-may-call-her—I disremember her name—and they lost their steering-oar, and swung around and went a-floating down, stern first, about two mile, and saddle-baggsed on the wreck. The ferryman and the nigger woman and the horses was all lost, but Miss Hooker she made a grab and got aboard the wreck. Well, about an hour after dark we come along down in our trading-scow, and it was so dark we didn’t notice the wreck till we was right on it; and so we saddle-baggsed too. But all of us was saved but Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the best cretur!—I most wish’t it had been me, I do.”

“My George! It’s the beatenest thing I ever struck.”"}

{"request_id":"ba551ae640af6fa487d0cb1b","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he burst out, “by the sun, and by the blue vault of heaven, and by the flame of love that consumes my heart: if you grant my request, then while they endure you shall never see me again. Go on to your home and begin your labours; I shall follow their course with unspeakable dread; and be assured that when you are prepared, I will come.”

Having said this, he suddenly left me, alarmed—perhaps—at any shift in my feelings. I watched him make his way down the mountain with a swifter pace than an eagle’s flight, and soon he was lost among the heaving folds of the sea of ice.

His account had filled the entire day, and the sun was already nearing the horizon when he took his leave. I knew I ought to hurry down toward the valley, for darkness would soon close around me; yet my spirit sank, and my steps dragged. The work of picking my way along the narrow mountain paths, and of planting my feet firmly as I went, held me back and troubled me, while I was still captive to the emotions that the events of the day had stirred. Long after night had set in, I reached the half-way resting-place and sat down beside the fountain. The stars appeared now and then as the clouds drifted aside; the dark pines rose before me, and here and there a shattered tree lay scattered on the ground. It was a spectacle of deep solemnity, and it stirred up strange thoughts within me. I wept bitterly, and with my hands clenched in anguish I cried, “O stars and clouds and winds—ye are all about to mock me. If you truly pity me, crush feeling and memory; let me be nothing. But if you do not, go—go—and leave me in darkness.”

These were wild and wretched thoughts; yet I cannot tell you how the everlasting flicker of the stars pressed upon me, nor how I listened to every gust of wind as though it were a dull, hideous siroc, coming to devour me.

Morning broke before I reached the village of Chamounix. I took no rest, but returned at once to Geneva. Even within my own breast I could not put my sensations into words; they bore down on me with the weight of a mountain, and their excess overwhelmed and extinguished my agony. So I went back home, and, entering the house, presented myself to the family. My gaunt and wild appearance struck them with intense alarm, yet I answered no question and scarcely spoke. I felt as though I were under a curse—as if I had no claim to their sympathy—as if I could never again enjoy their company.”"}

{"request_id":"db82a82fcd11161169eeb6ec","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is extraordinary! I have to see Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose from his seat and paced up and down the garden. After a while he came back. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is, to me, simply a motive in art. You might see nothing in him. I see everything in him. He is never more present in my work than when no image of him is there. He is, as I’ve said, a suggestion of a new manner. I find him in the curves of certain lines, in the loveliness and the subtleties of certain colors. That is all.”

“Then why won’t you exhibit his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I’ve put into it some expression of all this strange artistic idolatry—of which, of course, I’ve never cared to speak to him. He knows nothing about it. He shall never know anything about it. But the world might guess it, and I won’t lay my soul bare to their shallow prying eyes. My heart shall never be put under their microscope. There is too much of myself in the thing, Harry—too much of myself!”

“Poets aren’t as scrupulous as you are. They know how useful passion is for getting published. These days a broken heart will sell in many editions.”

“I hate them for it,” Hallward cried. “An artist should create beautiful things, but put nothing of his own life into them. We live in an age when men treat art as if it were meant to be a form of autobiography. We’ve lost the abstract sense of beauty. Someday I will show the world what it is; and for that reason the world shall never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you’re wrong, Basil, but I won’t argue with you. It’s only the intellectually lost who ever argue. Tell me—does Dorian Gray really like you?”

The painter thought for a few moments. “He likes me,” he answered after a pause; “I know he likes me. Of course I flatter him dreadfully. I find a strange pleasure in saying things to him that I know I’ll regret having said. As a rule, he’s charming to me, and we sit in the studio and talk about a thousand things. Now and then, though, he is horribly thoughtless, and seems to take real delight in hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I’ve given away my whole soul to someone who treats it like a flower to pin in his coat—a bit of decoration to charm his vanity, an ornament for a summer’s day.”"}

I had truly escaped narrowly. If the balloon had stayed in the cloud just a little longer—if I hadn’t been forced to deal with the problem of getting wet—I would have had to throw out the ballast, and that would have meant inevitable ruin. These dangers, though people don’t think about them much, may be the worst things you can face in a balloon. By this point, though, I had risen too high to feel much fear about it anymore.\n\n“I was now rising quickly, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of at least nine and a half miles. Breathing became very hard. My head also hurt badly. After I noticed moisture on my cheeks for some time, I finally realized it was blood, pouring out fast from the drums of my ears. My eyes also worried me. When I touched them, they seemed to bulge out of their sockets more than I could have expected. Everything in the basket, and even the balloon itself, looked distorted to my eyes. These signs were worse than I had expected, and they frightened me. At that moment, very foolishly and without thinking, I threw out three five-pound pieces of ballast from the car. The faster climb that followed pushed me too quickly, and without enough gradual change, into a very thin layer of air. The result nearly killed my trip—and me. I was suddenly seized by a spasm that lasted more than five minutes. Even after it eased, I could breathe only after long pauses, and even then only with gasps. All the while I kept bleeding heavily from my nose and ears, and even a little from my eyes. The pigeons seemed extremely upset and tried to get away. The cat mewed sadly, with her tongue hanging out, and staggered back and forth in the car as if she had been poisoned. Only then did I realize how reckless I had been in throwing out the ballast. My panic was intense. I expected nothing less than death, and death within a few minutes.”}]}"}

content.text: {"request_id":"49088181d54f890858eeac03","rewritten_text":"“They should interest you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his good name. You don’t want people talking about you as something vile and degraded. Of course, you have your position, your wealth, and all that sort of thing. But position and wealth aren’t everything. Mind you, I don’t believe these rumours at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I look at you. Sin is something that shows itself across a man’s face. It can’t be hidden. People sometimes talk about secret vices. There aren’t any. If a miserable man has a vice, it shows in the lines around his mouth, in the droop of his eyelids, in the way his hands are shaped, even. Someone—I'm not going to mention his name, but you know him—came to me last year to have his portrait painted. I had never seen him before, and at the time I hadn’t heard anything about him, though I’ve heard plenty since. He offered an extravagant price. I refused him. There was something about the shape of his fingers that I hated. I know now that I was right about what I suspected. His life is dreadful. But you, Dorian—with your pure, bright, innocent face, and your marvelous, untroubled youth—I can’t believe anything against you. And yet I see you so rarely, and you never come down to the studio anymore. When I’m away from you, and I hear all these hideous things people are whispering about you, I don’t know what to say. Why is it, Dorian, that a man like the Duke of Berwick leaves the room of a club as soon as you enter? Why is it that so many gentlemen in London will neither go to your house nor invite you to theirs? You used to be a friend of Lord Staveley. I met him at dinner last week. Your name came up in conversation, in connection with the miniatures you’ve lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said that you might have the most artistic tastes, but that you were a man no pure-minded girl should be allowed to know, and no chaste woman should ever sit in the same room with. I reminded him that I was your friend and asked him what he meant. He told me. He said it plainly, right in front of everyone. It was horrible! Why is your friendship so deadly to young men? There was that wretched boy in the Guards who committed suicide. You were his great friend. There was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with a tarnished name."}

{"request_id":"0d19459f7e1d84e4c43e46a9","rewritten_text":"“I have no nerves for that sort of thing.”

“But could you really be comfortable, spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes; you see his papa can, so why shouldn’t I? Jemima is so careful, and she could send us word every hour about how he is. I truly think Charles might as well have told his father that we would all come. I’m not more alarmed about little Charles now than he is. I was dreadfully frightened yesterday, but today is quite different.”

“Well, if you don’t think it too late to give notice for yourself, suppose you were to go too, along with your husband. Leave little Charles to my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot think it wrong while I remain with him.”

“Are you in earnest?” Mary cried, her eyes brightening. “Dear me! That’s a capital idea—an excellent one, indeed. I may as well go as not, for what good am I at home? It only worries me. You, who have not a mother’s feelings, are far the more proper person. You can make little Charles do anything; he always obeys you at a word. It will be much better than leaving him only with Jemima. Oh, I shall certainly go; I’m sure I ought to, if I can, quite as much as Charles, for they want me excessively to be acquainted with Captain Wentworth, and I don’t mind being left alone. What a splendid thought of yours, Anne. I’ll go and tell Charles, and get ready at once. You can send for us at a moment’s notice if anything happens; but I dare say there will be nothing to alarm you. I shouldn’t go, you may be sure, if I didn’t feel quite at ease about my dear child.”

The next moment she was tapping at her husband’s dressing-room door, and as Anne followed her upstairs, she caught the whole conversation. It began with Mary speaking in a tone of great triumph—

“I mean to go with you, Charles, for I’m no more use at home than you are. If I were to shut myself up forever with the child, I couldn’t persuade him to do anything he didn’t like. Anne will stay; Anne undertakes to stay at home and take care of him. It’s Anne’s own proposal, so I shall go with you, and it will be a great deal better, because I haven’t dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband replied. “I should be very glad to have you go; but it seems rather hard that she should be left at home by herself, to nurse our sick child.”"}

{"request_id":"d78e364d6c0785c0c367a062","rewritten_text":"“Mr Elliot looking up with so much respect.”

“Delightful indeed!” cried Mrs Clay, though she dared not lift her eyes to Anne. “Just like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I say father and son?”

“Oh! I put no restriction on anyone’s words. If you choose to think so! But, upon my word, I can hardly see that his attentions go beyond those of other men.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs Clay, raising her hands and eyes, and letting all the rest of her astonishment settle into a convenient silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you need not be so frightened about him. You know I invited him. I sent him away with smiles. And when I learned he was really going to his friends at Thornberry Park for the whole day to-morrow, I felt quite sorry for him.”

Anne watched the friend’s excellent performance, in managing to show so much pleasure—both in the expectation and in the actual arrival—of the very person whose presence must truly interfere with her chief purpose. It was impossible not to think that Mrs Clay must detest seeing Mr Elliot; yet she could assume an obliging, calm look, and seem perfectly content with having her attention to Sir Walter curtailed to half what it would otherwise have been.

For Anne herself, it was painful to have Mr Elliot enter the room; and still more so to have him come up and speak to her. She had long been accustomed to suspect that he could not always be quite sincere, but now she detected insincerity in everything. His careful deference to her father, set against his former manner, was hateful; and when she recalled his harsh behaviour towards Mrs Smith, she could scarcely endure the sight of his present smiles and gentle, well-turned sentiments.

She meant to avoid any change in her manners that might give him cause to remonstrate. Her great aim was to escape all inquiry and stir; yet she intended to be as plainly cool to him as her relationship would allow, and to draw back, as quietly as she could, the few steps of unnecessary intimacy she had been led into. Accordingly she was more guarded, and more reserved, than she had been the night before.

He tried to stir her curiosity again about how and where he might once have heard her praised, and wanted very much to be encouraged by further solicitation; but the spell was broken. He found that the warmth and animation of a public room were needed to inflame his modest cousin’s vanity; and, at least, he discovered that it could not be done now by any of the attempts he might make under the too-strong claims of the others.”"}

{"request_id":"ff9c5722ee3d5c9e91cadc77","rewritten_text":"“Oh, that’s nothing at all! It gives me pleasure. I don’t toil for money; I live wholly for my art.”

Lord Arthur set down £4, 2s. 6d. on the table, thanked the little German for his courtesy, and having managed to refuse an invitation to join some Anarchists for a meat-tea the next Saturday, he left the house and headed for the Park.

Over the next two days he was in a state of the utmost agitation, and on Friday, just after twelve, he drove down to the Buckingham to wait for word. All afternoon the heavy, unmoving hall-porter kept pinning up telegrams from different parts of the country—horse-race results, the outcomes of divorce cases, the state of the weather, and the like—while the tape continued to tick out tedious particulars about an all-night sitting in the House of Commons and a small scare on the Stock Exchange. At four o’clock the evening papers arrived, and Lord Arthur vanished into the library with the _Pall Mall_, the _St. James’s_, the _Globe_, and the _Echo_, to Colonel Goodchild’s great annoyance. Colonel Goodchild wanted to read the report of a speech he had given that morning at the Mansion House, on South African Missions and the wisdom of having black Bishops in every province, and, for reasons of his own, he had a marked dislike for the _Evening News_. None of the papers, though, mentioned Chichester in the slightest way, and Lord Arthur felt the attempt must have failed. It was a crushing disappointment, and for a while he was thoroughly shaken.

The next day he went to see Herr Winckelkopf, who was full of elaborate apologies and proposed to replace the clock for free, or else supply him with a case of nitro-glycerine bombs at cost. Lord Arthur, however, had lost faith in explosives, and Herr Winckelkopf himself admitted that everything was so adulterated these days that even dynamite could hardly be obtained in a clean, untainted state. Still, the little German—while conceding that something must have gone wrong with the mechanism—had not entirely given up hope that the clock might yet go off. He cited, as an example, a barometer he had once sent to the military Governor at Odessa: although it was meant to explode in ten days, it had not done so until nearly three months later. It was true that when it finally did go, it only managed to blow a housemaid to pieces, since the Governor had left town six weeks before; but it at least suggested that dynamite, as a destructive force, could be a formidable thing when kept under the control of machinery—if somewhat unreliable about its timing."}
