{"request_id":"cf04ad6b0ad7cee3274bca65","rewritten_text":"On the morning appointed for Admiral and Mrs Croft’s visit to see Kellynch Hall, Anne found it most natural to take her almost daily walk to Lady Russell’s, and to keep out of the way until everything was settled; and when she finally learned it was over, she found it most natural to be sorry she had missed the chance to see them.

This meeting of the two parties proved highly satisfactory, and settled the whole business at once. Each lady had already been well disposed toward an agreement, and therefore saw nothing but good manners in the other; and as for the gentlemen, there was such hearty good humor, such open, trusting generosity on the Admiral’s side, that it could not help but influence Sir Walter. He had also been flattered into his very best, most polished behavior by Mr Shepherd’s assurances that he was known—by report—to the Admiral as a model of good breeding.

The house and grounds, the furniture—everything—was approved. The Crofts were approved. The terms, the timing, every detail, and every person, were all right; and Mr Shepherd’s clerks were set to work, without any single preliminary disagreement to alter what “This indenture sheweth.”

Without hesitation, Sir Walter declared the Admiral to be the best-looking sailor he had ever met, and even went so far as to say that if his own man had been the one to arrange his hair, he should not be ashamed to be seen with him anywhere. The Admiral, with sympathetic warmth, remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we should soon come to a deal, my dear, in spite of what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but there seems to be no harm in him.”—a set of reciprocal compliments that would have been considered about equally matched.

The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas; and since Sir Walter proposed to move to Bath during the preceding month, there was no time to lose in making every dependent arrangement.

Lady Russell, convinced that Anne would not be allowed to be of any use, or any importance, in choosing the house they were going to secure, was very reluctant to have her sent away so soon. She wanted to make it possible for Anne to stay behind until she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas; but Lady Russell had her own commitments that would take her from Kellynch for several weeks, so she could not give the full invitation she wished. Anne, though dreading the possible heat of September in all the white glare of Bath, and grieving to give up the influence—so sweet and so sad—of the autumn months in the country, did not think that, everything considered, she wanted to remain."}

{"request_id":"c094bdcddedee9f7be497294","rewritten_text":"You can’t really know anything about me unless you’ve read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn’t matter. That book was written by Mr. Mark Twain, and he mostly told the truth. Sure, there were parts where he stretched things, but mostly it was the truth. That’s nothing. I’ve never met anyone who didn’t lie at least once, except maybe Aunt Polly, the widow, or possibly Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly—Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all in that book. It’s mostly true, with some exaggerations, like I said.

The story ends like this: Tom and I found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and it made us rich. We each got six thousand dollars, all in gold. It was an awful sight to see all that money piled up. Then Judge Thatcher took it and put it out at interest, and it paid us a dollar a day each, every day of the year. It was more money than anyone could say what to do with.

The Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she would civilize me, but living in her house all the time was hard. She was always so strict and proper, and everything felt dull and regular. I couldn’t stand it anymore, so I ran off. I put on my old rags again and went back to my sugar-hogshead, and I felt free and satisfied. But Tom Sawyer found me and told me he was going to start a band of robbers. He said I could join if I went back to the widow and acted respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, and she called me a lot of other names too, but she didn’t mean any harm. She dressed me in new clothes again, and I just kept sweating and sweating, feeling tight and uncomfortable. Then the whole routine started up again. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to be there on time. When you got to the table, you couldn’t just start eating right away. You had to wait while the widow bowed her head and grumbled a little about the food, even though there really wasn’t anything wrong with it. The only problem was that everything was cooked separately. In a barrel of odds and ends, it’s different. Things get mixed together, the juices trade places, and everything tastes better.

After supper she took out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers. I was eager to learn everything about him, but later she let it slip that Moses had been dead for a long time. After that, I didn’t care anymore, because I don’t believe in dead people."}

{"request_id":"ded4e652942d72e8e2a45b98","rewritten_text":"He never tried again. The boys lay there, counting out the dragging minutes until it felt to them as if time had to be finished and eternity was turning gray; and then they were relieved to see that the sun was finally going down.

One snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked about, and gave his partner a grim little smile. His comrade’s head was drooping on his knees, so Joe nudged him awake with his foot and said:

“Here! You’re the watchman, ain’t you! All right, though—nothing’s happened.”

“My! Have I been asleep?”

“Partly, partly. We’re nearly due to start moving, pard. What’ll we do with the small swag we’ve got left?”

“I don’t know—leave it here like we always do, I guess. No sense hauling it off till we head south. Six hundred and fifty in silver’s something to tote.”

“Well—fine. It won’t hurt to come back here once more.”

“No—but I’d say come in at night like we used to—it’s safer.”

“Yes, but see here; it may be a good while before I get the right chance for that job; accidents might happen; it ain’t exactly a good spot. We’ll just bury it regular—and bury it deep.”

“Good idea,” said the comrade. He crossed the room, knelt down, lifted one of the rear hearth-stones, and pulled out a bag that jingled in a way that felt downright pleasant. He took out twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, then handed the bag over. Injun Joe was already on his knees in the corner, digging with his bowie-knife.

In an instant the boys forgot every fear, every misery. They watched each motion with eyes full of satisfaction. Luck—its shine was beyond anything they could imagine! Six hundred dollars was enough to make half a dozen boys rich. This was treasure-hunting with the best possible luck—no annoying uncertainty about where to dig. They kept nudging one another, over and over—meaningful nudges, easy to read, because they were simply saying, “Oh, but ain’t you glad we’re here now!”

Joe’s knife struck something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What is it?” asked his comrade.

“Half-rotten plank—no, it’s a box, I reckon. Here—give me a hand and we’ll see what it’s for. Never mind, I’ve already broken through.”

He reached in and drew it out—

“Man, it’s money!”

The two men looked over the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were just as stirred up as the men, and just as pleased.

Joe’s comrade said, “We’ll be done with this quick. There’s an old rusty pick out among the weeds in the corner on the other side of the fireplace—I saw it a minute ago.”"}

{"request_id":"56642c061002e352513c9d60","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse—good-looking, quick-witted, and well-off—had a comfortable home and a cheerful temper, and it seemed as though she gathered together several of the finest advantages life can offer; she had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with scarcely anything to trouble or annoy her.

She was the younger of two daughters of a father whose affection was most warm and whose indulgence knew few bounds; and, as a result of her sister’s marriage, she had been mistress of his house from a very early age. Her mother had been gone so long that Emma could keep only a faint recollection of her caresses; her place was filled by an excellent woman, acting as governess, who fell little short of a mother in her tenderness.

For sixteen years Miss Taylor had been in Mr. Woodhouse’s family, less in the strict character of governess than as a friend—fond of both daughters, and especially attached to Emma. Between them, it was more like the closeness of sisters than anything else. Even before Miss Taylor had ceased to hold the mere title of governess, her gentle disposition had scarcely ever allowed her to lay down any real restraint; and with the shadow of authority long since gone, they had been living together as friend with friend, in the most mutual attachment, while Emma did exactly what she pleased—valuing Miss Taylor’s judgment highly, yet guided chiefly by her own.

Indeed, the true drawbacks of Emma’s situation were having rather too much her own way, and a tendency to think rather too well of herself; these were the disadvantages that might, one day, mingle with her many enjoyments. But the danger was at present so little perceived that it could not, by any means, take the rank of a misfortune with her.

Sorrow came—only a mild sorrow, and by no means accompanied by any unpleasant sense of wrong.—Miss Taylor married. It was Miss Taylor’s loss that first brought real grief. On the very day of this beloved friend’s wedding, Emma first found herself sitting in mournful thought about what might come next. When the ceremony was over and the wedding party had gone, her father and she were left to dine together, with no third person to brighten a long evening. After dinner, her father, as usual, settled himself to sleep; and then Emma had nothing to do but sit and consider what she had lost.

Everything promised happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of unexceptionable character, with an easy fortune, an age well suited, and agreeable manners; and there was even some comfort in reflecting on the self-denying, generous friendship with which she had always wished for and encouraged the match. Still, it was a black morning’s work for Emma. The absence of Miss Taylor would be felt every hour of every day. She went back over past kindnesses—the kindness and affection of sixteen years—how she had taught and played with her from the time she was five—how she had devoted all her powers to attach and amuse her in health—and how she had nursed her through the various illnesses of childhood."}

{"request_id":"00fcb35d9292cba1b90ecad3","rewritten_text":"“I need to step out for a moment to say this, Sir Walter,” Mr Shepherd began one morning at Kellynch Hall, as he set down the newspaper. “Right now is working very much in our favour. This peace will send all our rich naval officers back to land. They will all be looking for a home. It could not be a better time, Sir Walter, to choose tenants—proper, responsible ones. Many fortunes have been made during the war. If a rich admiral should come our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very lucky man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter answered. “That’s all I have to say about it. Kellynch Hall would be a prize indeed for him—perhaps the greatest prize of all, after all the others he may have taken before. Well, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, because he knew he had to, at the remark, and then went on—

“I would also suggest, Sir Walter, that in business, gentlemen in the navy are worth dealing with. I know something about how they do business. I can honestly say they have very generous ideas, and they are as likely to make good tenants as any group you could meet. So, Sir Walter, what I want to propose is this: if rumours should get out about your plans—which we have to consider possible, because it is so hard to keep one part of the world from watching and being curious about the other—then consequences will have their cost. I, John Shepherd, could hide any family matters I wanted, because nobody would bother to look closely at me. But Sir Walter Elliot is watched, and it may be hard to avoid notice. That is why I venture to say that, even with all our care, it would not surprise me if some rumour of the truth did reach people. And if that happens, as I was going to say, since applications will certainly follow, I think any from our wealthy naval commanders would be especially worth your attention. I would also add that I can come over at any time within two hours, so you won’t have the trouble of replying.”

Sir Walter only nodded. Soon after, though, as he rose and paced the room, he said with a touch of sarcasm—

“I suppose there are few among the gentlemen of the navy who would not be surprised to find themselves in a house like this.”

“They would look around, no doubt, and be grateful for their good fortune,” Mrs Clay said, because Mrs Clay was there. “My father brought me over, since nothing helps my health like a drive to Kellynch. But I agree with my father that a sailor might be a very desirable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"2ad71433e388c5b79ce81e09","rewritten_text":"At last it was settled that we should keep house together while I remained in the city; and, since my affairs in the world were a little less cramped than his, I was allowed to cover the cost of renting and fitting out, in a manner that matched the rather fantastic gloom of our shared temper, a timeworn and hideous mansion—one that had been left empty for years, abandoned to superstitions we never bothered to question, and leaning toward ruin in a secluded, desolate corner of the Faubourg St. Germain.

If the pattern of our life in that place had become known to the public, we would have been taken for madmen—though, perhaps, for madmen of a harmless sort. Our withdrawal was complete. We admitted no visitors. In fact, even the situation of our retreat had been kept carefully from my former acquaintances; and it had been many years since Dupin had stopped either knowing or being known in Paris. We lived as if within ourselves alone.

It was a whim of fancy in my friend (what else can I call it?) to love the night for its own sake; and into this _bizarrerie_, as into all his other notions, I slipped quietly, surrendering myself to his wild caprices with a full and easy _abandon_. The sable divinity would not always remain with us in person, yet we could mimic her presence. At the first dawn we shut every troublesome shutter of the old house, and set a couple of tapers burning—heavily perfumed, and throwing off nothing but the most ghastly, thin rays. With their help we then occupied our minds in dreams: reading, writing, or talking, until the clock warned us that the true Darkness was at hand. Then we went out together into the streets, arm in arm, carrying on the day’s talk or wandering far and wide until late, hunting through the city’s crowded lights and shadows for that infinity of mental excitement which only quiet observation can supply.

On such occasions I could not help noticing and admiring (though his rich ideality had already prepared me to expect it) a certain analytic power in Dupin. He seemed, too, to take a keen satisfaction in putting it to use—if not precisely in showing it—and he did not hesitate to own the pleasure he drew from it. With a low chuckling laugh he told me that most men, in regard to themselves, carried windows in their breasts, and that he was accustomed to follow such claims with direct and startling proofs of his intimate knowledge of my own. At those moments his bearing turned cold and abstract; his eyes went vacant in their expression; and while his voice, which was usually a rich tenor, rose into a treble, it would have sounded petulant—had it not been for the deliberate care and the perfectly clear distinctness of his enunciation."}

{"request_id":"9d61a0f79c994a34cb396908","rewritten_text":"About ten minutes later, the bell rang for tea, and since Virginia did not come down, Mrs. Otis sent one of the footmen upstairs to tell her. After a short time he returned and said he could not find Miss Virginia anywhere. Because she was in the habit of going out to the garden every evening to pick flowers for the dinner table, Mrs. Otis was not alarmed at first, but when six o’clock struck and Virginia still hadn’t appeared, she became truly agitated. She sent the boys out to look for her, while she and Mr. Otis searched every room in the house. At half-past six the boys came back and said they could find no trace of their sister anywhere. Everyone was now in the greatest state of excitement, and they didn’t know what to do, when Mr. Otis suddenly remembered that, a few days earlier, he had given a band of gypsies permission to camp in the park. He set off at once for Blackfell Hollow, accompanied by his eldest son and two of the farm servants. The little Duke of Cheshire, who was beside himself with anxiety, begged hard to be allowed to go too, but Mr. Otis wouldn’t let him, fearing there might be a scuffle.

When they arrived, however, they found the gypsies had already gone, and it was clear their departure had been sudden, since the fire was still burning and some plates lay on the grass. After sending Washington and the two men to scour the district, he hurried home and dispatched telegrams to all the police inspectors in the county, telling them to keep an eye out for a little girl who had been kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He then had his horse brought round, and, after insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, he rode off down the Ascot Road with a groom. He had hardly gone a couple of miles when he heard someone galloping after him. Looking back, he saw the little Duke coming up on his pony, his face very flushed and without a hat.

‘I’m awfully sorry, Mr. Otis,’ the boy gasped. ‘But I can’t eat any dinner as long as Virginia is lost. Please don’t be angry with me; if you’d let us be engaged last year, there would never have been all this trouble. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!’

The Minister couldn’t help smiling at the handsome young scapegrace, and he was deeply moved by the boy’s devotion to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted him kindly on the shoulders and said, ‘Well, Cecil, if you won’t go back, I suppose you must come with me, but I must get you a hat at Ascot.’"}

{"request_id":"18a2cfeb988909e5612cd222","rewritten_text":"By reports coming in from Rotterdam, it seems that city is in a state of intense, almost playful excitement. In fact, things have happened there that are so completely surprising—so new in every way—so different from what people expected that I have no doubt that, before long, all of Europe will be in an uproar, all of physics will be thrown into confusion, and reason and astronomy will be arguing with each other nonstop.

It seems that on the—— day of—— (I’m not sure of the date), a huge crowd of people gathered in the big square of the Exchange in the well-run city of Rotterdam. They had come for reasons that were not explained. The weather was warm, unusually warm for the season, and there was hardly any wind. The crowd didn’t seem annoyed that, from time to time, friendly showers of short duration fell on them. These came from large white clouds that moved in a restless pattern across the blue sky. Still, around noon, something changed. A small but noticeable agitation spread through the crowd: first came the clatter of ten thousand voices, and then, all at once, ten thousand faces were tilted upward. Ten thousand pipes were lowered at the same time from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a shout rose up—loud and fierce, like nothing but the roar of Niagara—and echoed through all of Rotterdam.

The source of the noise soon became clear. From behind the large, sharply outlined mass of cloud mentioned earlier, something slowly emerged into the open space of blue sky. It was a strange, mixed-looking, but apparently solid substance. Its shape was so odd and its parts were put together so whimsically that no one could make sense of it, and no one could stop staring at it. The sturdy citizens below stood with mouths open, unable to understand what they were seeing. What could it be? In the name of all the vrows and devils in Rotterdam, what could it possibly mean? No one knew. No one could guess. Not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, had the slightest clue to solve the mystery. So, since there was nothing more sensible to do, everyone—one by one—put his pipe back carefully in the corner of his mouth, then lifted his right eye toward the sky, puffed, paused, waddled around, and grunted in a meaningful way. Then they waddled back, grunted, paused again, and finally puffed once more.

Meanwhile, the object that caused all this curiosity and all this smoke drifted lower and lower toward the city. In just a few minutes it came close enough to be seen clearly. It looked like—yes!—it was definitely a balloon. But surely no balloon like that had ever been seen in Rotterdam before."}

content.text: {"request_id":"2c4172541730d39669fa7e9d","rewritten_text":"So then the ring-master made a little speech and said he hoped there wouldn’t be any disturbance. He told the man that if he promised he wouldn’t cause any more trouble, he’d let him ride—if he thought he could stay on the horse. So everybody laughed and said, all right, and the man got on. The minute he was on, the horse started ripping and tearing, jumping and cavorting around. Two circus men grabbed the bridle and hung on to it, trying to hold him, while the drunk man clung to his neck. Every jump sent the man’s heels flying into the air, and the whole crowd stood up shouting and laughing until tears rolled down their faces. And at last, sure enough, no matter what the circus men did, the horse broke loose. Off he went, like the very nation, running round and round the ring, with that sot sprawled on him and hanging to his neck. First one leg dangled down toward the ground on one side, and then the other leg on the other side, and the people went completely out of their minds. It wasn’t funny to me, though; I was shaking with fear at the danger he was in. But pretty soon he struggled up astride and grabbed the bridle, reeling this way and that. The next minute he sprang up, dropped the bridle, and stood there. The horse kept going like a house on fire too. He just stood up there, sailing around as easy and comfortable as if he’d never been drunk a day in his life. Then he started pulling off his clothes and tossing them aside. He shed them so fast and so many that they clogged the air, and in all he shed seventeen suits. And then there he was—slim and handsome—dressed in the gaudiest, prettiest outfit you’d ever seen. He went at that horse with his whip and made him perform like crazy. Finally he skipped off, made his bow, and danced away to the dressing-room, and everybody was howling with pleasure and astonishment.\n\nThen the ring-master saw how he’d been fooled, and he was the sickest ring-master you ever saw, I reckon. Why, it was one of his own men! He’d cooked up that whole joke in his own head and never let on to anybody. Well, I felt pretty sheepish about being taken in like that, but I wouldn’t have been in that ring-master’s place—not for a thousand dollars. I don’t know; maybe there are bolder circuses than that one, but I haven’t run into them yet. Anyway, it was plenty good enough for me. And wherever I come across it, it can have all of my custom every time."}

{"request_id":"90025decce14d2543fa168ad","rewritten_text":"The storm raged hard all night, but nothing unusual happened. The next morning, though, when they came down for breakfast, they found the terrible blood stain on the floor again. “I don’t think it can be the fault of the Paragon Detergent,” Washington said. “I’ve tried it on everything.” He then scrubbed the stain out a second time, but the next morning it was back again. The third morning it was there too, even though Mr. Otis had locked the library up at night himself, and kept the key upstairs.

Now the whole family was paying close attention. Mr. Otis began to suspect that he had been too certain when he denied that ghosts exist. Mrs. Otis said she planned to join the Psychical Society, and Washington started writing a long letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore about the Permanence of Sanguineous Stains when connected with Crime. That night, all doubts about whether phantoms exist in the real world were gone for good.

The day had been warm and sunny. In the cool of the evening, the whole family went out for a drive, and they didn’t get home until nine o’clock, when they had a light supper. No one talked about ghosts, so there weren’t even the usual conditions that often come before strange psychical events. As Mr. Otis later told me, they were only discussing the kind of things well-educated Americans talk about: how much better Miss Fanny Davenport was than Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; how hard it was to find green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy, even in the best English homes; the importance of Boston in the development of the world-soul; the benefits of the baggage check system when traveling by train; and how pleasant the New York accent sounds compared to the London drawl. Nothing supernatural was mentioned, and Sir Simon de Canterville was not brought up at all.

At eleven o’clock the family went to bed, and by half past all the lights were out. Sometime after that, Mr. Otis woke up because of a strange noise in the corridor outside his room. It sounded like metal clanking, and it seemed to be getting closer. He sat up at once, struck a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o’clock. He stayed calm and felt his pulse, which was not feverish at all. The noise continued, and now he could clearly hear footsteps. He put on his slippers, took a small oblong phial from his dressing-case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"7159e492401167c076f07611","rewritten_text":"The finest, best-bred gentlemen wore small hanging trinkets that jingled as they moved slowly. The gold-colored pieces rang like tiny bells. Between that ringing and the soft rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, the air seemed to flutter, fanning Saint Antoine and his hungry appetite far away.

For keeping everything in its proper place, dress was the one sure charm. Everyone was dressed for a Fancy Ball that was never meant to end. From the Palace of the Tuileries, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the chambers and the tribunals of justice, and through all of society (except the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball went on down to the Common Executioner. In keeping with the charm, he had to do his work dressed “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—though the axe was rare—Monsieur Paris, as was the usual way among his fellow professors in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest, presided in that neat outfit. And who, at Monseigneur’s reception in that seventeen hundred and eightieth year of our Lord, could possibly doubt that a system built on a frizzled hangman, powdered, in gold-laced clothes, with pumps and white-silk stockings, would drive the stars right out of the sky!

After Monseigneur had relieved his four men of their burdens and taken his chocolate, he had the doors of the Holiest of Holies thrown open, and he stepped out. Then came all the submission, the cringing and fawning, the servility, the complete humiliation. As for bowing down in body and spirit, there was nothing left for Heaven—perhaps one reason the people who worshipped Monseigneur never bothered with it.

With a word of promise here, a smile there, a whisper to one happy slave, and a wave of the hand to another, Monseigneur moved through his rooms toward the far-off region of the Circumference of Truth. Then he turned back, came again, and in time he was shut up in his sanctuary by the chocolate sprites, and was never seen again.

When the show was over, the flutter in the air turned into a small storm, and the little bells rang as they went downstairs. Soon there was only one person left from the whole crowd. He walked slowly out, with his hat under his arm and his snuff-box in his hand, passing among the mirrors.

“I devote you,” he said, stopping at the last door on his way out and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

Then he shook the snuff from his fingers, as if he were shaking dust from his feet, and quietly went downstairs."}

{"request_id":"e581b5b8681bcab4af5723ec","rewritten_text":"There comes a time in every properly raised boy’s life when he gets a wild urge to go somewhere and dig for hidden treasure. That desire suddenly hit Tom one day. He set out to find Joe Harper, but it didn’t work out. Next he went looking for Ben Rogers; Ben had gone fishing. Before long, Tom ran into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would go along. Tom brought him to a private spot and told him everything in confidence. Huck was willing. Huck was always willing to join any adventure that promised entertainment and didn’t require any capital, because he had a troublesome surplus of that kind of time that isn’t money. “Where’ll we dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, just about anywhere.”

“Why, is it hidden all around?”

“No, it isn’t. It’s hidden in very specific places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests under the end of a limb of an old dead tree, right where the shadow falls at midnight; but mostly under the floors in haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Why, robbers, of course—who’d you think? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it were mine, I wouldn’t hide it; I’d spend it and have a good time.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t do it that way. They always hide it and leave it there.”

“Don’t they come back for it anymore?”

“No, they think they will, but they usually forget the marks, or else they die. Either way, it sits there a long time and gets rusty; and then, sooner or later, somebody finds an old yellow paper that tells how to find the marks—a paper you have to cipher over for about a week, because it’s mostly signs and hy’roglyphics.”

“Hyro—which?”

“Hy’roglyphics—pictures and things, you know, that don’t seem to mean anything.”

“Do you have one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well then, how are you going to find the marks?”

“I don’t want any marks. They always bury it under a haunted house or on an island, or under a dead tree that has one limb sticking out. Well, we’ve tried Jackson’s Island a little, and we can try it again sometime; and there’s that old haunted house up the Still-House branch, and there are lots of dead-limb trees—dead loads of ’em.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“How could you say that? No!”

“Then how are you going to know which one to go for?”

“Go for all of ’em!”

“Tom, it’ll take all summer.”

“Well, what of it? Suppose you find a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest full of diamonds. How’s that?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s great. Plenty great enough for me. Just you give me the hundred dollars, and I don’t want no diamonds.”"}

{"request_id":"743ed6d1bf0aeb4f6db41157","rewritten_text":"The stars were still shining brightly when I woke. Taurus was high in the southern sky, and that meant it was midnight. I had been having troubled dreams. It seemed to me that I had been invited to Timon’s last feast. I arrived with a sharp hunger, the covers were lifted, and hot water was brought in, steaming in a way that never satisfied. Then I ran before the host’s anger, who had taken the form of Raymond. In my sick imagination, the things he threw at me were filled with foul, rotten-smelling vapors. His shape, twisted by a thousand distortions, grew into a huge phantom with the mark of pestilence on its brow. The shadow kept rising and rising, filling everything, as if it meant to break through the hard, unyielding ceiling that arched over and held the world inside.

The nightmare turned into real torture. With a strong effort, I forced myself awake and brought my thoughts back to reason. My first thought was Perdita. I had to return to her. I had to support her, taking whatever food I could from despair to keep her wounded heart going. I tried to bring her back from the wild excess of grief, using the strict rules of duty and the gentle comfort of regret.

The stars’ position was my only guide. I turned away from the terrible ruin of the Golden City, and after a great struggle, I managed to get myself out of it. Outside the walls, I met a group of soldiers. I borrowed a horse from one of them and hurried to my sister. In the short time I was gone, the plain looked different. The camp had been broken up. The remains of the army that had been dismissed were scattered in small groups. Every face was clouded, and every movement showed surprise and fear.

With a heavy heart, I entered the palace. I was afraid to move forward, afraid to speak, afraid to even look. In the middle of the hall sat Perdita. She was on the marble floor, her head resting on her chest, her hair loose and tangled, her fingers busy, twisting together. She was as pale as stone, and her face was pulled tight with pain. When she saw me, she looked up as if asking a question. The small look of hope in her eyes turned to misery. I couldn’t get the words out. I felt a horrible smile pull at my lips. She understood what I meant. Her head fell again, and her fingers kept working restlessly.

At last I found my voice, but it frightened her. The poor girl had already understood my look, and she would not, for anything, have wanted the story of her suffering to be shaped and confirmed by harsh, final words. It seemed, too, that she wanted to distract me from the subject. She rose from the floor and whispered, “Hush. After all this weeping, Clara is asleep. We must not disturb her.”"}

{"request_id":"02498494d8c43ae4a99957c1","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and apologised. He said, “Not at all,” and went on.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, so you can imagine she was treated like a great prize. Her half-brother had plenty of money again, but between old debts and fresh madness, he wasted it all most terribly once more. There were even bigger differences between him and her than there had been between him and his father. It is suspected that he held a deep, deadly grudge against her, believing she had influenced his father’s anger. Now, I come to the cruel part of the story—just stopping for a moment, my dear Handel, to say that a dinner napkin won’t fit into a tumbler.”

I have no idea why I was trying to pack mine into my tumbler. I only know that I found myself, with a stubborn determination that should have been used for something better, making the hardest effort to squeeze it into that space. Again I thanked him and apologised, and again he said, in the cheerfullest way, “Not at all, I’m sure!” and continued.

“Then a certain man appeared on the scene—at the races, at public balls, or anywhere else you like. He made love to Miss Havisham. I never saw him myself, because this was five-and-twenty years ago, before you and I were Handel, but I have heard my father say he was showy, the sort of man meant for that purpose. Still, my father insists—very strongly—that without ignorance or prejudice, you must not mistake him for a gentleman. He believes that no man who was not truly a gentleman at heart ever was, since the world began, a true gentleman in the way he behaved. He says no varnish can hide the grain of the wood; the more varnish you put on, the more the grain shows through. Well! This man followed Miss Havisham closely and claimed to be devoted to her. I think she hadn’t been very open to anyone at that time, but all the openness she had certainly came out then, and she passionately loved him. There’s no doubt she idolised him completely. He worked on her feelings in a careful, planned way, and he got large sums of money from her. He also persuaded her to buy her brother out of his share in the brewery—which her father had left him, though only weakly—at an enormous price, telling her that when he was her husband he would have to own and run it all. Your guardian wasn’t involved in Miss Havisham’s decisions at that time, and she was too proud and too in love to be guided by anyone.”}"}

{"request_id":"407517d2dd065c867d16f1da","rewritten_text":"Looking at him, you’d think Nemesis had stolen Pallas’s shield and shown him the Gorgon’s head. He seemed turned to stone, and his face was like marble in its melancholy. He had lived the delicate, luxurious life of a young man born to privilege and fortune—a life so exquisite because it was free from petty worries, with its beautiful, boyish carelessness; and now, for the first time, he became aware of the terrible mystery of Destiny, of the awful meaning of Doom.

How mad and monstrous it all seemed! Could it be that something written on his hand—in characters he couldn’t read himself, but that someone else could decipher—was some fearful secret of sin, some blood-red sign of crime? Was there no escape? Were we no better than chess pieces, moved by an unseen force, vessels the potter shapes at his will, for honor or for shame? His reason rebelled against it, and yet he felt that some tragedy was hanging over him, and that he had been suddenly called on to carry an unbearable burden. Actors are so lucky. They can choose whether they appear in tragedy or comedy, whether they will suffer or make merry, laugh or weep. But in real life it’s different. Most men and women are forced to play roles they’re not qualified for. Our Guildensterns perform Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets have to jest like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, but the play is badly cast.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers entered the room. When he saw Lord Arthur, he startled, and his coarse, fat face took on a sort of greenish-yellow color. The two men’s eyes met, and for a moment there was silence.

“The Duchess has left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and she’s asked me to bring it to her,” Mr. Podgers said at last. “Ah, I see it on the sofa. Good evening.”

“Mr. Podgers, I must insist that you give me a straightforward answer to a question I’m going to ask you.”

“Another time, Lord Arthur, but the Duchess is anxious. I’m afraid I have to go.”

“You won’t go. The Duchess isn’t in a hurry.”

“Ladies shouldn’t be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,” said Mr. Podgers, with his sickly smile. “The fair sex is apt to be impatient.”

Lord Arthur’s finely cut lips curled with petulant disdain. The poor Duchess seemed to him of very little importance at that moment. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers was standing and held out his hand.

“Tell me what you saw there,” he said. “Tell me the truth. I have to know it. I’m not a child.”"}

{"request_id":"64d415c3f5d9a7c28423e9a5","rewritten_text":"If not, then, since you are asking for my patience and for the mercy of the people you have hurt so deeply, sit down in that chair—quietly, without a word. It has been waiting for you for two full days.”

The monks muttered some words that no one could understand, but they still hesitated.

“You will be on time,” said Mr. Brownlow. “If I speak once, the other option will be gone forever.”

The man hesitated again.

“I have no desire to negotiate,” Mr. Brownlow said. “And because I am fighting for other people’s most important interests, I have no right to bargain.”

“Is there—” Monks began, his voice shaking. “Is there—no middle way?”

“None.”

Monks looked at the old gentleman with anxious eyes. But when he saw only strictness and determination in his face, he went into the room, shrugged his shoulders, and sat down.

“Lock the door from the outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants. “Come back when I ring.”

The men obeyed, and the two were left alone.

“This is how you treat me, sir,” said Monks, dropping his hat and cloak, “after my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” Mr. Brownlow replied. “It is because the hopes and wishes of those early, happy years were tied to him—and to that fine woman of his blood and family, who returned to God in her youth and left me here alone, a lonely man. It is because he knelt with me beside his only sisters’ death-bed when he was still a boy, on the morning that—if Heaven had willed it differently—would have made her my young wife. It is because my heart, hardened by pain, held on to him through all his trials and mistakes, until he died. It is because old memories and connections fill my mind, and even seeing you brings back thoughts of him. That is why I am choosing to treat you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford—even now—and why I blush for your unworthiness, since you carry the name.”

“What does the name have to do with it?” the other asked, after watching him in half-silence and half-stubborn confusion. “What is the name to me?”

“Nothing,” Mr. Brownlow answered. “Nothing to you. But it was hers. And even after all this time, it brings back to me—an old man—the warmth and excitement I once felt, only to have it spoken again by a stranger. I am very glad you changed it. Very glad.”

“This is all very impressive,” said Monks, keeping up his pretending name, after a long silence. During that silence he kept jerking himself back and forth in sullen defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face shaded by his hand.”}"}

{"request_id":"ba50a5eeee4c197ca77502d3","rewritten_text":"On the morning appointed for Admiral and Mrs Croft’s visit to Kellynch Hall, Anne found it perfectly natural to continue her almost daily walk to Lady Russell’s, keeping out of the way until everything should be finished; and then, when she discovered it was over, she felt it most natural to regret that she had not had the chance of seeing them.

This meeting of the two parties turned out extremely satisfactory, and settled the whole business at once. Each lady had already been disposed to agree, and therefore saw nothing in the other but good manners; while, as for the gentlemen, there was such hearty good humour, such an open, trusting liberality on the Admiral’s part, that it could not fail to affect Sir Walter. He had, besides, been flattered into his very best and most polished behaviour by Mr Shepherd’s assurances that he was, by report, known to the Admiral as a model of good breeding.

The house and grounds, the furniture—everything—was approved; the Crofts were approved; the terms, the time, every point, and every person, were right; and Mr Shepherd’s clerks were set to work, without any single preliminary disagreement to alter what “This indenture sheweth.”

Without the least hesitation, Sir Walter declared the Admiral the best-looking sailor he had ever met, and even went so far as to say that, if his own man had been the one to arrange his hair, he should not be ashamed to be seen with him anywhere. The Admiral, with sympathetic cordiality, remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we should soon come to a deal, my dear, in spite of what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but there seems to be no harm in him.”—so that the reciprocal compliments would have been judged about equal.

The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas; and as Sir Walter meant to remove to Bath during the preceding month, there was no time to lose in arranging every dependent matter.

Lady Russell, being persuaded that Anne would not be permitted to be of any use, or any consequence, in choosing the house they were about to secure, was very unwilling to have her sent away so soon. She wished to make it possible for Anne to stay behind until she could herself take her to Bath after Christmas; but as she had engagements of her own which must take her from Kellynch for several weeks, she could not give the full invitation she desired. Anne, though dreading the possible heats of September in all the white glare of Bath, and grieving to miss the influence so sweet and so sad of the autumnal months in the country, did not think, on the whole, that she ought to remain."}

{"request_id":"9a81a38a3300bc5b918df487","rewritten_text":"I wrapped him up in the paper and put the pieces in his mouth—that was the way.

“And you think, then, that your master was really bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him sick?”

“I don’t think about it—I know. Why would he dream about gold so much, if he wasn’t bitten by the gold bug? I heard about those gold bugs before this.”

“But how do you know he dreams about gold?”

“How do I know? Because he talks about it in his sleep—that’s how I know.”

“Well, Jup, perhaps you are right; but what lucky reason brings you here to visit me today?”

“What’s the matter, massa?”

“Did you bring any message from Mr. Legrand?”

“No, massa, I bring this here note;” and here Jupiter handed me a note that said:

“MY DEAR ——Why have I not seen you for so long? I hope you have not been so foolish as to take offense at any little _brusquerie_ of mine; but no, that is unlikely. Since I saw you, I have had great cause for anxiety. I have something to tell you, but I can hardly say it, and I don’t know whether I should tell it at all.

“I have not been quite well for some days now, and poor old Jup annoys me, almost beyond endurance, with his well-meant attentions. Would you believe it?—the other day he had prepared a huge stick to punish me for slipping away and spending the day, _solus_, among the hills on the mainland. I truly believe my bad looks alone saved me from being flogged.

“I have made no additions to my cabinet since we met.

“If you can, in any way, make it convenient, come over with Jupiter. _Do_ come. I want to see you tonight, on business of the _highest_ importance. I assure you it is of the _highest_ importance.

“Ever yours, “WILLIAM LEGRAND”.

“There was something in the tone of this note that made me feel very uneasy. Its style was quite different from Legrand’s usual way of writing. What could he be thinking about? What new idea had taken over his excitable mind? And what Jupiter said about him did not sound good. I feared that the steady pressure of bad luck had finally shaken my friend’s judgment. Without waiting, I decided to go with the negro.

“When we reached the wharf, I saw a scythe and three spades lying at the bottom of the boat we were going to take.

“What is the meaning of all this, Jup?”"}

{"request_id":"4a48ddc6608f889a6a9420a5","rewritten_text":"The two ladies were thrilled to see their dear friend again. It had been ages since they had met, and they kept asking what she had been doing with herself since they had last been together. They paid little attention to the rest of the family. They tried to avoid Mrs. Bennet as much as possible, said very little to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. Soon they were gone again. They stood up from their seats with sudden energy, which surprised their brother, and hurried away as if they were eager to get away from Mrs. Bennet’s polite attention.

The idea of the Netherfield ball pleased every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to treat it as a special compliment to her eldest daughter, and she was especially proud to receive an invitation from Mr. Bingley himself, not just a formal card. Jane imagined a happy evening with her two friends, along with her brother’s attention. Elizabeth felt pleased at the thought of dancing a lot with Mr. Wickham, and of seeing that Mr. Darcy’s looks and behavior seemed to confirm everything. Catherine and Lydia’s happiness depended less on any one event or any single person. Even though, like Elizabeth, they planned to dance half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was not the only partner who could satisfy them, and a ball was, after all, a ball. Mary could even tell her family that she had no real dislike of it.

“While I can have my mornings to myself,” she said, “that is enough. I don’t think it is a sacrifice to join in evening plans now and then. Society expects something from all of us, and I consider it a good thing for everyone to have breaks for recreation and fun.”

Elizabeth was in such a good mood that, even though she did not usually speak to Mr. Collins unless she had to, she could not help asking him whether he planned to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation. If he did, she wanted to know whether he would think it proper to join in the evening’s entertainment. She was surprised to find that he had no hesitation at all. He did not seem worried about being corrected, either by the Archbishop or by Lady Catherine de Bourgh, and he was even willing to dance.

“I assure you,” he said, “I am by no means of the opinion that a ball like this, given by a young man of good character to respectable people, could have any bad effect. I am also so far from objecting to dancing that I hope to be honored with the hands of all my fair cousins during the evening. And I take this chance to ask for yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the first two dances especially. I trust my cousin Jane will understand that this is for the right reason, and not because I mean any disrespect to her.”"}

{"request_id":"1a037dde46b13ae67e8ef3ac","rewritten_text":"Smallpox!

I rushed to the king and spoke quietly in his ear.

“Go out the door right now, sire. The woman is dying of the disease that struck Camelot two years ago.”

He didn’t move.

“I’ll stay,” he said, “and I’ll help as well.”

I whispered again. “King, you can’t do this. You must leave.”

“You mean well, and you’re not speaking foolishly. But it would be shameful for a king to admit fear, and shameful for a knight with a belt to hold back his hand when people need help. I won’t go. You must go instead. The Church’s ban isn’t on me, but it forbids you to be here. If she hears about your trespass, she will punish you severely.”

It was a dangerous position for him, one that could cost him his life, but there was no point arguing. If he believed his knightly honor was at stake, then that was the end of the discussion. He would stay, and nothing would change his mind. So I dropped the subject.

The woman spoke.

“Good sir, will you climb the ladder there and bring me word about what you find? Don’t be afraid to tell me. There may come a time when even a mother’s heart can’t break anymore—because it has already broken.”

“Wait,” the king said. “Give the woman something to eat. I’ll go.” Then he set down the knapsack.

I started to turn, but the king had already begun to move. He stopped and looked down at a man lying in a dim light. He hadn’t noticed us until now, and he hadn’t spoken.

“Is that your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he asleep?”

“Thank God, yes—that one mercy. For three hours.” Her voice shook as she added, “Where can I ever repay you for that? My heart is bursting with gratitude for the sleep he has now.”

I said, “We’ll be careful. We won’t wake him.”

“Oh, no,” she said. “You won’t. He’s dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes. What a victory it is to know it. No one can harm him now, and no one can insult him anymore. He is in heaven, and happy—or if he isn’t, then he’s in hell and content. In that place, he won’t find any abbot or bishop. We were boy and girl together. We were man and wife for twenty-five years, and we were never apart until today. Think how long it is to love and suffer side by side. This morning he was out of his mind, and in his thoughts we were boy and girl again, wandering in the happy fields. And so, in that innocent, joyful talk, he wandered farther and farther—into places we don’t know about—until he was shut away from the sight of mortal people.”"}

{"request_id":"03d1b5527c34ccdca331a373","rewritten_text":"In truth, he was dressed up as “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,”—one of his most striking impersonations, and one the Cantervilles had every reason to keep in mind, since it was the very first cause of their quarrel with their neighbour, Lord Rufford. It was a quarter past two in the morning, and, so far as he could judge, there was not a soul stirring. Yet as he wandered toward the library to see whether any trace of the blood-stain remained, two figures suddenly sprang at him from a dark corner; they flung their arms about above their heads and shrieked “BOO!” right into his ear.

Overcome with panic—quite natural enough under the circumstances—he made for the staircase, only to find Washington Otis waiting there with the big garden-syringe. Thus hemmed in on every side by his enemies, and driven nearly to bay, he disappeared into the great iron stove, which, happily for him, was not lit; and from there he had to pick his way home through the flues and chimneys, reaching his own room in a dreadful condition of dirt, confusion, and despair.

After that, he was never again seen on any midnight venture. The twins lay in wait for him on several nights, and scattered the passages with nutshells, to the intense annoyance of their parents and the servants, but all to no purpose. It was plain enough that his feelings had been so badly hurt that he would not show himself. Mr. Otis therefore went back to his great undertaking on the history of the Democratic Party, which he had been working at for some years; Mrs. Otis set about a splendid clam-bake that astonished the entire county; the boys took up lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games; and Virginia went riding along the lanes on her pony, with the young Duke of Cheshire at her side, he having come to spend the last week of his holidays at Canterville Chase. Everyone supposed the ghost had gone away, and, in fact, Mr. Otis wrote to Lord Canterville to say so; Lord Canterville, in reply, declared how delighted he was with the news, and sent his best congratulations to the Minister’s worthy wife.

The Otises, however, were mistaken, for the ghost was still in the house; and though he was now almost an invalid, he was by no means inclined to let the matter drop—especially once he learned that among the guests was the young Duke of Cheshire. His grand-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost, and the next morning he was found lying on the floor of the card-room in such a helpless state of paralysis that, though he lived to a great age, he could never afterward manage anything but “Double Sixes.”"}

{"request_id":"71bec474f85de34fd81265d2","rewritten_text":"He couldn’t help it. And it drove him crazy to see—at least, as he thought he saw—that Becky Thatcher never once suspected he was even in the land of the living. But she did see, nevertheless; and she knew she was winning her fight, too, and was glad to watch him suffer the way she had suffered.

Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom hinted at things he had to take care of—things that had to be done—and that time was running out. But it was useless—the girl kept chirping on. Tom thought, “Oh, come on—am I ever going to get rid of her?” At last he had to attend to those things, and she said, carelessly, that she’d be “around” when school let out. He hurried away, hating her for it.

“Any other boy!” Tom thought, grinding his teeth. “Any boy in the whole town but that Saint Louis smarty who thinks he dresses so fine and is aristocracy! Oh, sure—I beat you the first day you ever saw this town, mister, and I’ll beat you again! Just wait till I catch you out! I’ll just—”

And he went through the motions of beating an imaginary boy—pummeling the air, and kicking and stabbing. “Oh, you do, do you? You holler enough, do you? All right then—let that teach you!” And so the pretend beating was finished to his satisfaction.

Tom ran home at noon. His conscience couldn’t take any more of Amy’s grateful happiness, and his jealousy couldn’t bear any more of the other distress. Becky went back to inspecting her pictures with Alfred, but as the minutes dragged by and Tom didn’t come, her triumph began to fade and she lost interest; seriousness and absentmindedness followed, and then melancholy. Two or three times she perked up at a footstep, but it was only a false hope—no Tom came. At last she became completely miserable and wished she hadn’t pushed it so far. When poor Alfred, realizing he was losing her, didn’t know what else to do and kept blurting, “Oh, here’s a jolly one! look at this!” she finally lost patience and said, “Oh, don’t bother me! I don’t care for them!” Then she burst into tears, got up, and walked away.

Alfred fell in beside her, about to try to comfort her, but she said:

“Go away and leave me alone, can’t you! I hate you!”

So the boy stopped, wondering what he could have done—because she had said she’d look at pictures all through the nooning—and she kept walking on, crying. Then Alfred went on thinking in the empty schoolhouse. He felt humiliated and angry. He could easily see the truth: the girl had simply used him as a convenient way to vent her spite on Tom Sawyer."}

{"request_id":"2acf60b7f5ac261a159898bc","rewritten_text":"He climbed onto a fiery horse—the same one that had carried him forward to victory in Greece. He wore himself out with exhausting exercise, trying to dull the painful thoughts in his mind by focusing on physical sensation.

Slowly, he began to feel like himself again. In the end, it was as if he were waking from poison: he lifted his head out of the haze of fever and passion and into the quiet air of calm, clear thinking. He considered what should be done. First, he noticed how much time had passed, and how his actions had been driven more by madness than by any sensible impulse. A month had gone by, and during that time he had not seen Evadne. The strength of her hold on him—something tied to only a few of the lasting feelings in his heart—had faded a great deal. He was no longer her slave, no longer her lover. He would never see her again, and because his return was so complete, he would deserve Perdita’s trust.

But even as he decided this, his imagination brought up the miserable home of the Greek girl. She had refused to trade her situation for a life of even greater luxury, even though she could have. He pictured how splendid she had looked when he first met her. He remembered her life in Constantinople, surrounded by every kind of eastern wealth and display. Now he saw her in poverty, doing hard work every day, alone and abandoned, with a face worn down, faded, and hungry. Compassion filled his chest. He would see her again. He would come up with a plan to bring her back into society and restore her to the life and status she had lost. Then their separation would follow naturally.

He also thought about how, during this long month, he had avoided Perdita, pulling away from her as if she were stinging him with his own guilt. But now he was awake. All of this should be fixed. His future devotion would erase the memory of this one stain on the peace of their life. He felt more cheerful as he thought it through, and with sober determination he set out the course he would follow. He remembered that he had promised Perdita he would be there this very evening—the 19th of October, the anniversary of his election as Protector—at a festival held in his honor. This festival should be a good sign for the happiness of future years. First, he would go to see Evadne. He would not stay long. Still, he owed her some explanation, some compensation for his long absence and his silence. Then he would return to Perdita, to the world he had neglected, to the duties of society, to the pride of rank, and to the pleasures of power.

After the scene described in the previous pages, Perdita had expected Raymond to change completely in his manners and behavior. She hoped for easier conversation and a return to the warm, affectionate way of being together that had always been the joy of her life."}

{"request_id":"c1baea842f9ce35573a36d71","rewritten_text":"I would pretend to die; my satisfied heirs would fall upon my fortune, and I should buy my freedom. Yet my scheme must be set down with skill; I cannot be left without means—I must make sure of some money. Alas, what foul turns must I be pushed into? Otherwise my lot would have been a whole lifetime of deceit; and when the pang of having devised some fraud made me recoil from my design, I was drawn back, and confirmed in it, by the visit of some aunt or cousin, who would tell me that death is the end of all men. Then she would add that my father had surely lost his wits since my mother’s death; that he was out of his mind, and that I was lucky, for in one of his fits he might have killed me instead of ruining his own poor, deranged self. And all of this, of course, was delivered with delicacy; not spoken in plain terms, lest my feelings be wounded, but

Whispered so and so In dark hint soft and low

with eyes cast down and sympathetic smiles or little cries, and I sat listening with a steady face while every nerve shook. I, who dared not speak aye or no to such blasphemy. Oh, what a delectable life—so empty of guile! I, with a dove’s look and a fox’s heart; for I felt only the abasement of lying, not any holy stir of conscious innocence that could redeem it. I, who had dressed myself before in the bright garb of sincerity, must now borrow one of several colours; it might feel awkward at first, but practice would teach me to fold it neatly, to lie with grace. Yes, I might die my soul with falsehood until it had quite hidden its true hue. Oh, beloved father! Take the pure heart of your unhappy daughter; let me be joined to you unblemished as I was, or you will not recognize my changed face. As grief might alter Constance, so would deceit alter me, until in heaven you would say, “This is not my child.” My father, to be happy now and again when we meet, I must flee from all this life, which is mockery to one like me. In solitude alone shall I be myself; in solitude I shall be thine.

Alas! Even now I look back with loathing on the tricks and contrivances by which, after many painful struggles, I managed my escape. I could go into a long account of the steps I took—first to secure myself a small support for the rest of my life, and then to make sure they were convinced of my death. I might, but I will not."}

{"request_id":"7e06855f583b4a6e0382cf9e","rewritten_text":"Many American ladies, when they leave their native country, adopt the look of chronic ill-health, convinced it’s a kind of European refinement, but Mrs. Otis had never made that mistake. She had a magnificent constitution and a truly wonderful supply of animal spirits. In fact, in many ways she was quite English, and she was an excellent example of the fact that we really have everything in common with America these days—except, of course, the language.

Her eldest son, named Washington by his parents in a burst of patriotism that he never stopped regretting, was fair-haired and rather good-looking. He had prepared himself for American diplomacy by leading the German at the Newport Casino for three straight seasons, and even in London he was known as an excellent dancer. Gardenias and the peerage were his only weaknesses. Otherwise, he was extremely sensible.

Miss Virginia E. Otis was fifteen, lithe and lovely as a fawn, with a fine freedom in her large blue eyes. She was a wonderful amazon, and once raced old Lord Bilton on her pony twice around the park, winning by a length and a half just in front of the Achilles statue. The young Duke of Cheshire was delighted beyond measure; he proposed to her on the spot, and her guardians sent him back to Eton that very night in floods of tears. After Virginia came the twins, usually called “The Stars and Stripes,” because they were always getting swished. They were delightful boys, and—except for the worthy Minister—the only true republicans in the family.

Since Canterville Chase was seven miles from Ascot, the nearest railway station, Mr. Otis had telegraphed for a waggonette to meet them, and they set off on their drive in high spirits. It was a lovely July evening, and the air was delicate with the scent of the pine woods. Now and then they heard a wood pigeon brooding over its own sweet voice, or saw, deep in the rustling fern, the burnished breast of the pheasant. Little squirrels watched them from the beech trees as they passed, and rabbits darted away through the brushwood and over the mossy knolls, their white tails flashing in the air. But as they entered the avenue of Canterville Chase, the sky suddenly turned overcast with clouds. A strange stillness seemed to settle on the atmosphere; a great flight of rooks passed silently over their heads, and before they reached the house, some heavy drops of rain had already fallen.

Standing on the steps to receive them was an old woman, neatly dressed in black silk, with a white cap and apron."}

{"request_id":"b4a1b09ca5d06134aec0a681","rewritten_text":"“Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,” the old lady cried as he entered the room, “why haven’t you come to see me all this time?”

“My dear Lady Clem, I never have a moment to myself,” said Lord Arthur, smiling.

“I suppose you mean that you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying chiffons and talking nonsense? I can’t understand why people make such a fuss about getting married. In my day, we never dreamed of billing and cooing in public—or in private, for that matter.”

“I assure you I haven’t seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her milliners.”

“Of course; that’s the only reason you come to see an ugly old woman like myself. I wonder you men don’t take warning. On a fait des folies pour moi, and here I am—a poor rheumatic creature—with a false front and a bad temper. Why, if it weren’t for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me all the worst French novels she can find, I don’t think I could get through the day. Doctors are no use at all, except to get fees out of one. They can’t even cure my heartburn.”

“I’ve brought you a cure for that, Lady Clem,” said Lord Arthur gravely. “It’s a wonderful thing, invented by an American.”

“I don’t think I like American inventions, Arthur. I’m quite sure I don’t. I read some American novels lately, and they were quite nonsensical.”

“Oh, but there’s no nonsense at all about this, Lady Clem! I assure you it’s a perfect cure. You must promise to try it.” And Lord Arthur brought the little box out of his pocket and handed it to her.

“Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it really a present? That’s very sweet of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a bonbon. I’ll take it at once.”

“Good heavens! Lady Clem,” cried Lord Arthur, catching hold of her hand, “you mustn’t do anything of the kind. It’s homoeopathic medicine, and if you take it without having heartburn, it might do you no end of harm. Wait until you have an attack, and take it then. You’ll be astonished at the result.”

“I’d like to take it now,” said Lady Clementina, holding up to the light the little transparent capsule, with its floating bubble of liquid aconitine. “I’m sure it’s delicious. The fact is that, though I hate doctors, I love medicines. Still, I’ll keep it until my next attack.”

“And when will that be?” asked Lord Arthur eagerly."}

{"request_id":"11a10cc6f70f5ce222fc0d19","rewritten_text":"I do not understand why she wanted to be close to me. Still, if the same situation happened again, I am sure I would be fooled again. Caroline did not come back to see me until yesterday, and in the meantime I received not a note and not a word from her. When she finally did arrive, it was clear that she did not enjoy it. She made a small, formal apology for not calling sooner, said nothing at all about wanting to see me again, and she seemed so changed that, when she left, I decided to stop knowing her.

I feel sorry for her, even though I cannot help blaming her. She was wrong to single me out the way she did. I can say for certain that every step toward intimacy started with her. But I pity her because she must know she has been acting wrongly, and I am sure that her brother is the reason. I do not need to explain more. Even if we both know her anxiety is unnecessary, if she feels it, it can explain how she has behaved toward me. And however dear he is to his sister, any worry she has for him is natural and kind.

Still, I cannot help wondering why she has any such fears now. If he had cared about me at all, we would have met long ago. She knows I am in town, I am sure, because she said so herself. Yet the way she talks makes it seem as if she is trying to convince herself that he is really interested in Miss Darcy. I cannot understand that. If I were not afraid of judging too harshly, I might almost say that there is a strong look of dishonesty in all of this.

I will try to push away every painful thought and focus only on what will make me happy: your affection, and the steady kindness of my dear uncle and aunt. Please write to me again very soon. Miss Bingley mentioned that he might never return to Netherfield, and that they might give up the house, but she was not certain. We should not bring it up. I am very glad that you have such pleasant news from our friends at Hunsford. Please go and see them, with Sir William and Maria. I am sure you will be comfortable there.

“Yours, etc.”

This letter upset Elizabeth. But her spirits returned when she thought that Jane would not be fooled anymore, at least not by the sister. Any hope from the brother was now completely gone."}

{"request_id":"1aaf867053a3c488f4b4f686","rewritten_text":"It looked like a collection of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, giving the whole place the feel of a rather dull retirement. Wemmick’s house was a little wooden cottage set among plots of garden, and the top of it had been cut out and painted to look like a battery bristling with guns.

“My own doing,” said Wemmick. “Looks pretty, doesn’t it?”

I highly commended it, I think it was the smallest house I’d ever seen; with the strangest gothic windows (most of them were fake), and a gothic door almost too small to get into.

“That’s a real flagstaff,” said Wemmick. “And on Sundays I run up a real flag. Then look here. After I’ve crossed this bridge, I hoist it up—like this—and cut off the communication.”

The bridge was just a plank, spanning a chasm about four feet wide and two deep. Still, it was pleasant to watch the pride with which he lifted it and secured it; he smiled while doing it, with real relish rather than just mechanically.

“At nine o’clock every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun fires. There he is, you see! And when you hear him go, I think you’ll say he’s a Stinger.”

The piece of ordnance he referred to was mounted in a separate fortress made of lattice-work. It was protected from the weather by an ingenious little tarpaulin contrivance, like an umbrella.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of sight, so it doesn’t interfere with the idea of fortifications—for it’s a principle with me: if you have an idea, carry it out and keep it going—now, I don’t know whether that’s your opinion—”

I said, decisively.

“—At the back there’s a pig, and there are fowls and rabbits; then I knock together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers; and you’ll judge at supper what kind of salad I can raise. So, sir,” said Wemmick, smiling again, but seriously too as he shook his head, “if you can imagine the little place under siege, it would hold out a devil of a time when it comes to provisions.”

Then he led me to a bower about a dozen yards away, though you had to reach it by such clever twists of path that it took quite a while to get there; and in this retreat our glasses were already set out. Our punch was cooling in an ornamental lake, with the bower raised along its edge. This stretch of water—circular in shape, with an island in the middle that might have been the salad for supper—had a fountain in it. When you set a little mill going and took a cork out of a pipe, it played with such force that it made the back of your hand quite wet."}

{"request_id":"b36d26ef8c319a92ef06f338","rewritten_text":"For that reason, I decided to get off as soon as we reached the town and put myself out of his hearing. I carried out the plan successfully. My small portmanteau was in the boot under my feet; all I had to do was turn a hinge to get it out. I threw it down in front of me, climbed down after it, and ended up standing at the first lamp on the first stones of the town pavement. As for the convicts, they went on with the coach, and I knew exactly where they would be taken next—spirited off to the river. In my mind, I saw the boat with its convict crew waiting for them at the slime-washed stairs; I could hear the rough, “Give way, you!” again, like an order shouted to dogs; and again I saw the wicked Noah’s Ark lying out on the black water.

I couldn’t have said what I was afraid of, because my fear was completely undefined and vague, but it was fear all the same. As I walked on to the hotel, I felt a dread—far stronger than the simple apprehension of a painful or unpleasant recognition—making me tremble. I’m sure it didn’t have any clear shape, and that for a few minutes it was the old terror of childhood coming back.

The coffee-room at the Blue Boar was empty, and I had not only ordered my dinner there, but had already sat down to eat it before the waiter even realized who I was. The moment he apologized for forgetting me, he asked whether he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I said. “Certainly not.”

The waiter—he was the one who had brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was bound—seemed surprised, and took the first chance to slide a dirty old copy of a local newspaper so directly in front of me that I picked it up and read the paragraph:

Our readers will learn, not altogether without interest, in reference to the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young artificer in iron of this neighbourhood (what a theme, by the way, for the magic pen of our as yet not universally acknowledged townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!) that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and friend, was a highly respected individual not entirely unconnected with the corn and seed trade, and whose eminently convenient and commodious business premises are situate within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not wholly irrespective of our personal feelings that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is good to know that our town produced the founder of the latter’s fortunes."}

{"request_id":"18d90393e1180a3334bf9083","rewritten_text":"For years, Dorian Gray found himself unable to shake off the sway of that book. Or, perhaps it would be truer to say he never really tried to break its hold. From Paris he obtained no fewer than nine copies of the first edition, printed on large paper, and he had them bound in different colours, so they could match his shifting moods and the restless whims of a temperament over which, at times, he seemed to have almost completely lost command. The hero—the remarkable young Parisian in whom the romantic and the scientific temperaments were so oddly interwoven—came to him as a kind of shadowing likeness of himself. Indeed, the entire volume felt as though it held the history of his own life, set down before he had even lived it.

In one respect, though, he was luckier than the novel’s fantastic figure. He never learned—never, in fact, had any reason to learn—about that somewhat grotesque terror of mirrors, of polished metal, and of still water that struck the young Parisian so early in his life, and that was brought on by the sudden rotting of a beau who, once, had seemed so extraordinary. With something like a cruel delight—and in nearly every delight, and certainly in every pleasure, cruelty has its share—he would read the later portion of the book, with its genuinely tragic, though a touch too heavily stressed, account of the grief and despair of one who had lost, as he himself had, what others and the world had most dearly prized.

The extraordinary beauty that had captivated Basil Hallward, and many others besides, never seemed to leave him. Even those who had heard the worst things said about him—and from time to time strange rumours about his way of living slipped through London and became the talk of the clubs—could not bring themselves to believe anything that would stain his name when they saw him. He always carried the look of a man who had kept himself untouched by the world. When Dorian Gray entered, men who spoke in coarse terms would fall silent. There was something in the cleanness of his face that checked them. His very presence seemed to stir in them the memory of the innocence they had soiled. They could not understand how someone so captivating and graceful could have escaped the mark of an age at once sordid and sensual.

Often, when he returned from one of those secret, drawn-out absences that led his friends—or those who believed themselves to be his friends—to form such odd conjectures, he would slip up himself to the locked room. There he would open the door with the key that never left him, and stand, with a mirror, before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him—watching, in turn, the wicked, aging countenance on the canvas and the fair young face that met his gaze with laughter from the polished glass."}
