{"request_id":"326f6d2823594d4e3e1f25fc","rewritten_text":"Without giving herself any time to think, and barely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth, as soon as she finished this letter, grabbed the next one. She opened it with the greatest impatience and read on. It had been written a day after the first letter ended.

“By this time, my dearest sister, you have received my hurried letter. I hope this one is clearer, but I’m so confused that I can’t be sure I’m saying things in a sensible way. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to write, but I have bad news for you, and it can’t be delayed. Even though it would be foolish for Mr. Wickham to marry our poor Lydia, we are now desperate to know whether it has actually happened. There is too much reason to fear they have not gone to Scotland.

Colonel Forster came yesterday. He left Brighton the day before, not many hours after the express. Lydia had sent a short letter to Mrs. F., which made it seem like they were going to Gretna Green. But Denny said something that made them worry. He believed that W. never intended to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. He told Colonel F. this, and Colonel F. immediately became alarmed. He set off from B. to follow their route.

He was able to trace them easily to Clapham, but no farther. When they reached Clapham, they got into a hackney-coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. After that, all anyone knows is that they were seen continuing along the London road. I don’t know what to think.

After making every possible inquiry on that side of London, Colonel F. went on into Hertfordshire. He kept trying to find them at every turnpike and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but without success. No one had seen such people pass through. With the greatest kindness, he came on to Longbourn and tried to calm our fears in a way that reflects very well on his heart. I am truly sorry for him and Mrs. F., but no one can blame them.

Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother believe the worst, but I can’t think so badly of him. There are many reasons they might choose to marry privately in town instead of following their first plan. And even if he could somehow form such a plan against a young woman like Lydia, which is not likely, how could I believe she is so lost to everything? Impossible! Still, I’m sorry to say that Colonel F. doesn’t seem willing to rely on their marriage. When I told him my hopes, he shook his head and said he feared W. was not a man to be trusted.”"}

{"request_id":"f8606876aed85014cd541ae9","rewritten_text":"He made it clear to her that Frank admired her very much—he thought her extremely beautiful and charming. With so much to be said in his favor, she felt she shouldn’t judge him too harshly. As Mrs. Weston put it, “all young people would have their little whims.”

Among his new acquaintances in Surry, there was one person who did not feel so forgiving. In general, people in the parishes of Donwell and Highbury spoke about him with great honesty. They made allowances for the small mistakes of such a handsome young man—one who smiled so often and bowed so well. But there was one person whose judgment could not be softened by bows or smiles: Mr. Knightley. The story was told to him at Hartfield. For the moment, he was quiet, but Emma heard him almost at once say to himself, while he held a newspaper, “Hum! just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” She almost wanted to be offended, but a moment’s thought showed her he was only saying it to ease his own feelings, not to cause trouble. So she let it go.

Even though Mr. and Mrs. Weston had come this morning with news that was not entirely good, their visit was especially helpful in another way. Something happened while they were at Hartfield that made Emma want their advice, and—what was even better—she wanted exactly the advice they gave.

This was what happened:—The Coles had been settled in Highbury for some years, and they were good people. They were friendly, generous, and not at all showy. But they were of low origin, in trade, and only moderately well-bred. When they first moved into the country, they lived according to what they could afford. They kept to themselves, and they had only a small circle of acquaintances, and even that circle was not expensive. In the last year or two, though, they had gained a great deal of money. The house in town had brought in more profit, and their fortune had clearly improved. With their wealth, their ideas grew too. They wanted a larger house and more company. They added to their house, increased the number of servants, and raised their spending in every way. By now, in both money and the style of living, they were second only to the family at Hartfield. Their love of social life, and their new dining-room, made everyone expect that they would start hosting dinner parties. A few had already taken place, mostly among single men. Emma could hardly imagine that they would dare to invite the best and most regular families. That meant they would not invite Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. Nothing would make her go if they did. She also regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal mean less than she would have liked."}

{"request_id":"7eada23f6943d3b3a7f80f4e","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s final reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more packed than it usually was. Six Cabinet Ministers had arrived from the Speaker’s Levée in their stars and ribands; all the pretty women had turned out in their finest dresses; and at the far end of the picture-gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe—a heavy, Tartar-looking woman, with tiny black eyes and splendid emeralds—talking off-colour French at the top of her voice and laughing without restraint at everything that was said to her. Altogether it was a remarkable mixture of people. Handsome peeresses exchanged civilities with fierce Radicals; popular preachers brushed coat-tails with distinguished sceptics; a whole company of bishops kept trailing a stout prima-donna from room to room; on the staircase stood several Royal Academicians, disguised as artists; and it was even said that, at one time, the supper-room was crammed with geniuses. In truth, it was one of Lady Windermere’s best evenings, and the Princess remained until close on half-past eleven.

The moment she had gone, Lady Windermere went back to the picture-gallery, where a celebrated political economist was gravely laying out the scientific theory of music to an indignant virtuoso from Hungary, and she began to speak with the Duchess of Paisley. She looked wonderfully beautiful—her grand ivory throat, her large blue forget-me-not eyes, and her heavy coils of golden hair. Or rather, not that washed-out straw shade which nowadays steals the name of gold, but such gold as is spun into sunbeams or tucked away in strange amber; and it gave her face something of the look of a saint, with no small touch of the fascination of a sinner. She was, in a way, a curious study in psychology. From early on she had grasped the important truth that nothing resembles innocence so much as an indiscretion; and through a run of reckless escapades—half of them perfectly harmless—she had gathered all the advantages of a well-established personality. She had more than once changed her husband; indeed, Debrett credited her with three marriages; but since she had never changed her lover, the world had long since stopped talking scandal about her. She was now forty, childless, and possessed of that excessive passion for pleasure which is the secret of staying young.

Suddenly she swept her gaze eagerly round the room and said, in her clear contralto, “Where is my cheiromantist?”

“Your what, Gladys?” the Duchess cried, with an involuntary start.

“My cheiromantist, Duchess; I can’t get on without him at present.”

“Dear Gladys! you’re always so original,” the Duchess murmured, trying to recall what a cheiromantist really was—and hoping it wasn’t the same thing as a cheiropodist.

“He comes to see my hand twice a week, regularly,” Lady Windermere went on, “and he’s quite fascinating about it.”"}

{"request_id":"e0803da13a2ea780ff798c98","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had taken a very fine house in Camden Place—a lofty, dignified address, the kind that suits a man of consequence. Both he and Elizabeth were settled there, to everyone’s satisfaction.

Anne entered with a sinking heart, expecting to be shut up for many months, and anxiously thinking to herself, “Oh! when shall I leave you again?” Still, the welcome she received was unexpectedly warm, and it helped her. Her father and sister were glad to see her, not only for her sake, but because they wanted to show her the house and its furnishings; they met her with kindness. The fact that she was now the fourth person at their table, when they sat down to dinner, was treated as an advantage.

Mrs. Clay was very pleasant and very smiling, but her courtesies and smiles were more or less automatic. Anne had always expected that she would perform whatever was proper on her arrival, but the easy, accommodating attitude of the others was more than she had anticipated. They were clearly in excellent spirits, and she would soon hear the reasons. Yet they had no intention of listening to her. After a few compliments about how deeply they regretted her old neighbourhood, which Anne could not honestly return, they only asked a couple of faint questions before the conversation had to be entirely their own. Uppercross interested them hardly at all; Kellynch very little. It was all Bath.

They took pleasure in assuring her that Bath more than met their expectations in every respect. Their house, they said, was undoubtedly the best in Camden Place; their drawing-rooms had many clear advantages over any others they had either seen or heard of, and the superiority was just as strong in the style of the fittings and in the taste of the furniture. Their acquaintance was in great demand. Everyone wanted to visit them. They had turned down many introductions, and yet cards were still constantly being left by people they didn’t even know.

There was plenty to enjoy. Could Anne really be surprised that her father and sister were happy? She might not be surprised, but she had to sigh that her father felt no sense of humiliation in his change; that he saw nothing to regret in the duties and dignity of a resident landholder; that he found so much to be proud of in the small vanities of town life. And she had to sigh, and smile, and wonder too, as Elizabeth threw open the folding doors and walked with exultation from one drawing-room to the next, boasting of their space—at the thought that woman, who had once been mistress of Kellynch Hall, could now take pride in the extent of rooms between two walls, perhaps only thirty feet apart.

But this was not everything that made them happy. They had Mr. Elliot too."}

{"request_id":"64b37919b70900838c98bb40","rewritten_text":"After I had sent them in, I could not stay away from the places where they were, and I felt that they were more hopeful and less desperate when I was near. In my restless pain of mind, I would wander the streets in the evening, passing the offices and houses where I had left the petitions. Even now, the weary western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night—the stern, shut-up mansions and the long rows of lamps—still feel melancholy to me because of that.

The visits I could make him each day were now shorter, and he was kept under stricter watch. I thought, or feared, that they suspected I might try to poison him, so before I sat down at his bedside I asked to be searched. I told the officer who was always there that I was willing to do anything to prove that my intentions were honest. Nobody was cruel to him or to me. There was duty to be done, and it was done, but not harshly. The officer always assured me that he was worse, and that other sick prisoners in the room, and other prisoners who served as sick nurses—malefactors, but not without kindness, thank God—gave the same report.

As the days went on, I noticed more and more how he lay, calm and still, staring at the white ceiling, with a blank look on his face until some word of mine brightened it for a moment, and then it faded again. Sometimes he could hardly speak at all. Then he would answer me with small presses of my hand, and I learned to understand what he meant.

By the tenth day, I saw a bigger change in him than I had seen before. His eyes were turned toward the door, and they lit up when I came in.

“Dear boy,” he said, as I sat down by his bed, “I thought you was late. But I knew you couldn’t be that.”

“It is just the time,” I said. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always waits at the gate; don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. I don’t want to lose a moment.”

“Thank’ee, dear boy, thank’ee. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I held his hand in silence, because I could not forget that I had once meant to desert him.

“And what’s the best of all,” he said, “is that you’ve been more comfortable with me, since I was under a dark cloud, than when the sun was shining.”"}

{"request_id":"dec1f694f34014c5192945f8","rewritten_text":"She studied me closely for a moment, and then spoke in a low voice.

“What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I said, “that you won’t mix them up with the others. They may share the same blood, but, believe me, they are not the same in nature.”

Still watching me, Miss Havisham asked again, quietly and firmly.

“What do you want for them?”

“I’m not so clever as to hide things from you, even if I wanted to,” I answered, feeling my face grow warm. “I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you would spare the money to do my friend Herbert a lasting good in life—something that, because of the circumstances, must be done without his knowledge—I could show you how.”

“Why does it have to be done without his knowledge?” she asked. She rested her hands on her stick so she could look at me even more carefully.

“Because,” I said, “I started the work myself more than two years ago, without his knowledge. I don’t want it to be ruined by being found out. I can’t explain why I’m unable to finish it. It’s part of a secret that belongs to someone else, not to me.”

She slowly looked away from me and stared into the fire. She watched it for what seemed like a long time, in the quiet and in the dim light of the candles that were burning down. Then, when some of the red coals collapsed, she turned back toward me. At first her expression was empty, but then her attention sharpened. All this time Estella kept knitting. When Miss Havisham finally fixed her eyes on me again, she spoke as if nothing had interrupted our conversation.

“What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her now, and trying to control my shaking voice, “you know I love you. You know I have loved you for a long time, and with all my heart.”

She looked up at my face when I spoke to her. Her fingers kept working, and her expression stayed completely calm. I saw that Miss Havisham glanced from me to Estella, and then from Estella back to me.

“I should have said this sooner,” I continued, “but I made a long mistake. It made me hope that Miss Havisham meant for us to be together. When I thought you couldn’t help yourself, in a way, I held back. But I have to say it now.”

With her face still unmoved, and her hands still busy, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said, answering her. “I have no hope that I will ever be able to call you mine, Estella.”"}

{"request_id":"39247346defac1f6e71a38d4","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by the blue sky above, and by the fire of love burning in my heart, that if you grant my request, as long as they live you will never see me again. Go home and begin your work. I will watch how things go with unbearable worry. Don’t fear that I won’t come when you are ready—I will appear then.”

With that, he suddenly left me. He seemed afraid that my feelings might change. I watched him hurry down the mountain faster than an eagle could fly, and soon I lost sight of him among the shifting waves of the sea of ice.

His story took up the entire day, and the sun was already near the horizon when he left. I knew I should hurry down toward the valley, because darkness would soon surround me. But my heart was heavy, and my steps were slow. I had to work my way along the small paths of the mountain, carefully placing my feet, and that effort kept distracting me, even though I was still full of the emotions the day’s events had stirred in me. 

It was well into the night when I reached the halfway resting place. I sat down beside the fountain. The stars shone here and there as the clouds moved past them. Dark pines stood all around, and now and then a broken tree lay on the ground. The whole scene felt deeply solemn, and it brought strange thoughts to my mind. I cried bitterly. Clasping my hands in agony, I said, “Oh, stars and clouds and winds—you are all about to mock me. If you truly pity me, crush my feelings and my memories. Let me become nothing. But if you don’t, go—go—and leave me in darkness.”

These were wild and miserable thoughts, but I can’t explain to you how the endless twinkling of the stars weighed on me, or how I listened to every gust of wind as if it were a harsh, ugly sirocco, coming to destroy me.

Morning came before I reached the village of Chamounix. I didn’t rest at all. I went straight back to Geneva. Even inside my own heart, I couldn’t put my feelings into words. They pressed on me with the weight of a mountain, and the sheer force of them crushed my suffering beneath it. So I returned home and went into the house to face my family. My haggard, wild look made them fear for me, but I answered no questions and hardly spoke. I felt as if I were under some kind of curse—as if I had no right to ask for their sympathy—as if I would never again be able to enjoy their company."}

{"request_id":"961de04087b645822bd30fc4","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water to finish the feast with. After a while, Becky suggested that they move on again. Tom was quiet for a moment. Then he said:

“Becky, can you handle it if I tell you something?”

Becky’s face went pale, but she thought she could.

“Well, then, Becky, we have to stay here—where there’s water to drink. That little piece is our last candle!”

Becky broke into tears and loud, helpless wailing. Tom did what he could to comfort her, but it didn’t help much. At last Becky said:

“Tom!”

“Well, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and hunt for us!”

“Yes, they will! Of course they will!”

“Maybe they’re hunting for us right now, Tom.”

“Why, I guess maybe they are. I hope they are.”

“When would they miss us, Tom?”

“When they get back to the boat, I reckon.”

“Tom, it might be dark then—would they notice we hadn’t come?”

“I don’t know. But either way, your mother would miss you as soon as they got home.”

A frightened look crossed Becky’s face, and it snapped Tom back to his senses. He realized he’d made a mistake. Becky wasn’t supposed to go home that night! The children fell silent, each lost in thought. After a moment, Becky’s grief surged again, and Tom understood that what he’d been thinking had hit her too—that Sabbath morning might already be half over before Mrs. Thatcher discovered that Becky wasn’t at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children stared at their little bit of candle and watched it melt slowly and mercilessly away; saw the wick, finally standing alone; saw the weak flame rise and fall, climb the thin column of smoke, linger at the top for a moment, and then—total darkness took over, in all its horror!

How long afterward it was that Becky came to a slow awareness that she was crying in Tom’s arms, neither of them could say. All they knew was that, after what felt like a long stretch of time, both of them woke from a dead, numb sleep and started suffering again. Tom said it might be Sunday now—maybe Monday. He tried to get Becky to talk, but her sorrow was too heavy; all her hopes were gone. Tom said they must have been missed long ago, and no doubt the search was already underway. He tried to shout, and maybe someone would come. He did try it, but in the darkness the distant echoes sounded so dreadful that he stopped.

The hours dragged on, and hunger tormented them again. A portion of Tom’s half of the cake was left; they divided it and ate it. But they seemed hungrier than before."}

{"request_id":"221675c253aa7aad1e9c8aeb","rewritten_text":"And I don’t suddenly rush at him and risk making a clumsy mess of it. No, I move off to one side, and I build up to it slowly, so he never even suspects I’m going to hit him. Then, all at once, in a flash, he’s flat on his back, and he can’t figure out how it happened. That’s how I went for brother Dowley. I started talking in a lazy, easy way, like I was just passing the time. The oldest man in the world couldn’t have guessed where I was going to end up, just by looking at where I began.

“Boys, there are a lot of curious things about law, and custom, and the way people do things, when you really look at it. And there’s the way human opinion and human movement drift and change, too. There are written laws—they don’t last. But there are also unwritten laws—those are eternal. Take the unwritten law of wages. It says wages have to rise, little by little, straight through the centuries. Look at how it works. We know what wages are now, in one place and another. We average it out and call that today’s wages. We also know what wages were a hundred years ago, and what they were two hundred years ago. That’s as far back as we can go, but it’s enough to show the law of progress—the pace and rate of the steady increase. So even without any document, we can figure out pretty closely what wages were three, four, and five hundred years ago. So far, so good. Do we stop there? No. We stop looking backward and turn to the future and apply the same law.

“My friends, I can tell you what people’s wages will be at any date in the future you want to name, for hundreds and hundreds of years.”

“What, goodman, what!”

“Yes. In seven hundred years wages will be six times what they are now, in your region, and farm hands will be allowed 3 cents a day, and mechanics 6.”

“I would’t I might die now and live then!” Smug, the wheelwright, interrupted, with a bright, greedy look in his eye.

“And that isn’t all. They’ll get their meals too—though not much. Two hundred and fifty years after that—listen now—a mechanic’s wages will be—mind you, this is law, not guesswork—a mechanic’s wages will be twenty cents a day!”

Thinking, or imagining, that I was suspected of intending to carry poison to him, I asked to be searched before I sat down at his bedside, and told the officer who was always there that I was willing to do anything that would assure him of the single-mindedness of my intentions. Nobody was harsh with him or with me. There was duty to be done, and it was done, but not cruelly. The officer always gave me the same assurance: that he was worse, and that some other sick prisoners in the room, and some other prisoners who attended on them as sick nurses—malefactors, but not incapable of kindness, God be thanked!—were joining in the same report.

As the days went on, I noticed more and more that he would lie quietly, staring at the white ceiling, with an absence of light in his face until some word of mine brightened it for an instant, and then it would fade again. Sometimes he was almost, or quite, unable to speak; then he would answer me with slight pressure on my hand, and I came to understand his meaning very well.

The number of days had risen to ten, when I saw a greater change in him than I had yet. His eyes were turned toward the door, and they lit up as I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said, as I sat down by his bed, “I thought you was late. But I knowed you couldn’t be that.”

“It is just the time,” said I. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always waits at the gate; don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. Not to lose a moment of the time.”

“Thank’ee, dear boy, thank’ee. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I pressed his hand in silence, because I couldn’t forget that I had once meant to desert him.

“And what’s the best of all,” he said, “you’ve been more comfortable alonger me, since I was under a dark cloud, than when the sun shone.”"}

{"request_id":"62fac965dbbfa0af7bbfeaa6","rewritten_text":"“So I’m the proud owner of some knights,” I said, as we rode off. “Who would’ve thought I’d live to tally up assets of that sort? I don’t know what I’ll do with them—unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, if you please, sir—and their squires.”

“That’s a fine haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes—where do they live?”

“Ah, I didn’t catch you. I’ll tell you soon enough.” Then she fell to thinking, and in a soft voice, turning the words over with care: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; eh, right so; where do they hang out. Truly, the phrase has a pleasant and winning sound, and it’s prettily put together. I’ll say it again anon and anon in my idle hours, so I may, perhaps, learn it. Where do they hang out. There—it's already tripping off my tongue, and forasmuch as—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes; the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. A while back—you remember. Figuratively speaking, the game’s called.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Go on to the bat. I mean, get to work on your statistics, and don’t waste so much kindling trying to get your fire started. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will, and lightly will begin. So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I caught my mistake at once. I’d set her thoughts moving, and it was my own doing; she’d take thirty days to reach those facts. She usually started without any preface and ended without any result. If I interrupted her, she’d either continue on without noticing, or answer with a couple of words and then go back to say the sentence over again. So interruptions only did harm; and yet I had to interrupt—quite often, too—if I meant to save my life. A man would die if he let her monotony drip on him all day.

“Great Scott!” I said, in my distress. She simply went right back and began again:

“So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came to an abbey of monks, and there were well lodged. So on the morn they heard their masses in the abbey, and so they rode forth till they came to a great forest; then was Sir Gawaine aware in a valley by a turret, of twelve fair damsels, and two knights armed on great horses, and the damsels went to and fro by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"aeda5423a8c97f6770c20084","rewritten_text":"I went from shop to shop, buying whatever I needed to match the change in his appearance. Once that was done, I turned my attention to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but when he saw me come in, he stood up right away and positioned himself in front of his fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I answered. As I walked there, I had already decided what I was going to say.

“Don’t commit yourself,” Mr. Jaggers warned, “and don’t commit anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don’t tell me anything. I don’t want to know anything. I am not curious.”

Of course, I could tell he knew the man had arrived.

“I only want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to make sure that what I’ve been told is true. I don’t really expect it to be false, but I can at least check it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “When you said ‘told,’ did you mean ‘informed’?” he asked. He kept his head tilted to one side. He wasn’t looking at me; he was looking at the floor, as if he were listening to it. “Told sounds like it was spoken to him. You can’t have spoken communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I will say ‘informed,’ Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor, the one I didn’t even know about before.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers. “In New South Wales.”

“And only him?” I asked.

“And only him,” Mr. Jaggers said.

“I’m not so foolish, sir, as to think you’re responsible for my mistakes and wrong conclusions. Still, I always thought it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” Mr. Jaggers replied. He looked at me calmly, then took a bite of his forefinger. “I’m not responsible for that at all.”

“And yet it looked so much like it, sir,” I said, my heart heavy.

“Not a bit of evidence, Pip,” he said, shaking his head and gathering up his skirts. “Don’t trust how things look. Trust the evidence. That’s the best rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I sighed after standing quietly for a moment. “I’ve checked my information, and that’s the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having finally revealed himself,” Mr. Jaggers said, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly I have followed the facts in everything I’ve said to you. There has never been the slightest change from the strict line of fact. You know that, don’t you?”

“Quite, sir.”

“I told Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—that he must not expect me ever to stray from the strict line of fact.”}"}

{"request_id":"79f63e0fa5beb4332847e33e","rewritten_text":"“What’s wrong?” Oliver demanded.

“Hush!” answered the Dodger. “Do you spot that old gentleman at the book-stall?”

“The one across the way?” Oliver said. “Yes, I can see him.”

“He’ll do,” said the Dodger.

“A fine choice,” Master Charley Bates remarked.

Oliver stared from one to the other, utterly astonished; yet he wasn’t allowed to ask questions. The two boys slipped quietly across the road and crept close behind the old gentleman toward whom they’d directed his attention. Oliver followed a few paces, unsure whether to come on or fall back, and stood watching in silent amazement.

The old gentleman looked thoroughly respectable: a powdered head and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar, white trousers, and kept a smart bamboo cane tucked under his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood there reading with the same intensity as if he were settled in his own arm-chair. It was quite likely he imagined himself there, too; for his absorption showed that he saw nothing of the book-stall, the street, the boys, or anything else—only the book itself. He read straight through, turning over the leaf when he reached the bottom of a page, starting at the top line of the next, and carrying on with the greatest interest and eagerness.

Oliver’s dread and alarm were immediate as he stood a few paces off, staring with his eyes as wide as they could be, to watch the Dodger thrust his hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief. Then to see him pass it to Charley Bates, and at last to witness both of them darting away around the corner at full speed!

In an instant, the whole business of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewels, and the Jew himself, came crashing into the boy’s mind.

For a moment he stood frozen, the blood racing through his veins with terror, as though he were in a blazing fire; then, bewildered and frightened, he ran—without knowing what he was doing—making off as fast as his feet could carry him.

It was all over within a minute. The instant Oliver began to bolt, the old gentleman, reaching into his pocket and finding his handkerchief gone, wheeled sharply round. Seeing the boy tearing away at such a pace, he naturally took him for the thief; and, clutching his book, he shouted “Stop thief!” with all his might and chased after him."}

{"request_id":"aa18eb701f97ab63c98fe862","rewritten_text":"“They should interest you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his good name. You don’t want people to talk about you as if you were vile and ruined. Of course, you have your position, your wealth, and all that sort of thing. But position and wealth aren’t everything. Still, I don’t believe these rumors at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I look at you. Sin shows itself on a man’s face. It can’t be hidden. People sometimes talk about secret bad habits, but there’s no such thing. If a miserable man has a vice, it appears in the way his mouth looks, in the droop of his eyelids, and even in the shape of his hands.

Someone—I'm not going to say his name, but you know him—came to me last year to have his portrait painted. I had never met him before, and I hadn’t heard anything about him at the time, though I’ve heard plenty since. He offered an outrageous amount of money. I refused him. There was something about the shape of his fingers that I couldn’t stand. Now I know I was right about what I suspected. His life is dreadful. But you, Dorian, with your clean, bright, innocent face, and your wonderful, untroubled youth—I can’t believe anything bad about you.

And yet I see you so rarely, and you never come down to the studio anymore. When I’m away from you, and I hear all these awful things people are whispering about you, I don’t know what to say. Why does the Duke of Berwick leave a club room as soon as you walk in? Why do so many gentlemen in London refuse to visit your house or invite you to theirs? You used to be friends with Lord Staveley. I saw him at dinner last week. Your name came up in conversation, because of the miniatures you lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said you might have the most artistic tastes, but that you were a man no decent girl should be allowed to know, and no pure woman should sit in the same room with.

I told him I was your friend, and I asked what he meant. He told me. He said it plainly, right in front of everyone. It was terrible! Why is your friendship so dangerous for young men? There was that poor boy in the Guards who killed himself. You were his closest friend. Then there was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England because his name was stained."}

{"request_id":"e625c8b5f160fb2d22173c92","rewritten_text":"“Shucks, Tom,” I said, “I think you might tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, I don’t know. But he’s got to have it. All the nobility does.”

That was just his way. If it didn’t suit him to explain something to you, he wouldn’t do it. You could badger him for a week, and it wouldn’t make no difference.

He’d already gotten all that coat of arms business fixed, so now he started in to finish up the rest of that part of the work, which was to plan out a mournful inscription—said Jim got to have one, like they all did. He made up a lot, and wrote them out on paper, and read them off, like this:

1. Here a captive heart busted.

2. Here a poor prisoner, forsook by the world and friends, fretted out his sorrowful life.

3. Here a lonely heart broke, and a worn spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity.

4. Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV.

Tom’s voice trembled while he was reading them, and he most broke down. When he got done he couldn’t no way make up his mind which one for Jim to scratch on the wall—they was all so good—but at last he decided he would let him scratch them all on. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch that much stuff onto the logs with a nail, and he didn’t know how to make letters besides; but Tom said he would block them out for him, and then he wouldn’t have nothing to do but just follow the lines. Then pretty soon he said:

“Come to think, the logs aren’t going to do. They don’t have log walls in a dungeon. We got to dig the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll fetch a rock.”

Jim said the rock was worse than the logs; he said it would take him such a long time to dig them into a rock he wouldn’t ever get out. But Tom said he would let me help him do it. Then he took a look to see how me and Jim was getting along with the pens. It was the most tedious, hard work and slow, and it didn’t give my hands no chance to get well of the sores, and we didn’t seem to make no headway, hardly. So Tom said:

“I know how to fix it. We got to have a rock for the coat of arms and mournful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"165741461d063021f2c6138d","rewritten_text":"Just as they were leaving the dining room, midnight began to boom from the clock tower. When the last stroke sounded, they heard a crash and a sudden, sharp cry. Thunder rolled through the house, and something like strange, unearthly music drifted through the air. A panel at the top of the staircase flew open with a loud bang, and on the landing—very pale, almost white, with a small casket in her hand—Virginia stepped out. In an instant, everyone rushed to her. Mrs. Otis grabbed her tightly and held her close. The Duke covered her with fierce kisses, and the twins spun around the group in a wild, excited dance.

“Good heavens, child! Where have you been?” Mr. Otis said, sounding angry, as if he thought she had been pulling some foolish trick. “Cecil and I have been riding all over the country looking for you, and your mother has been terrified. You must never play these practical jokes again.”

“Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!” the twins shrieked as they danced around.

“My own darling, thank God you are safe,” Mrs. Otis murmured, kissing the trembling child and smoothing the tangled gold of her hair. 

“Papa,” Virginia said quietly, “I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for what he had done. Before he died, he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.”

The whole family stared at her in silent shock, but Virginia looked calm and serious. Then she turned and led them through the opening in the wainscoting into a narrow secret passage. Washington followed, carrying a lighted candle he had picked up from the table. At last, they reached a heavy oak door, covered with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, the door swung open on its heavy hinges, and they stepped into a small, low room with a vaulted ceiling and one tiny barred window. 

In the wall was a large iron ring, and chained to it was a gaunt skeleton stretched out on the stone floor. It seemed to be trying to reach, with its long, fleshless fingers, for an old-fashioned trencher and ewer placed just out of reach. The jug had clearly once held water, because the inside was coated with green mould. There was nothing on the trencher except a pile of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her hands, and began to pray silently. The rest of the group watched in wonder as the terrible secret of the tragedy was finally revealed to them."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3afd6d7aef37544f08505830","rewritten_text":"How long I stayed in that state, I can’t say. It must, however, have been no small amount of time, because when I partially regained the sense of being alive, I saw that day was breaking, the balloon hovering at an enormous height above a wilderness of ocean, and not a trace of land anywhere within the vast horizon. Yet when I came back to myself, my feelings were by no means as full of agony as I might have expected. In fact, there was a kind of budding madness in the calm way I began to survey my situation. I raised each of my hands to my eyes, one after the other, and wondered what could have caused my veins to swell and my fingernails to turn so horribly black. After that, I examined my head carefully, shaking it again and again and feeling it with minute attention, until I was satisfied it was not—something I’d half suspected—larger than my balloon. Then, in a knowing manner, I reached into both pockets of my breeches; finding that a set of tablets and a toothpick case were missing, I tried to account for their disappearance, and when I couldn’t, I felt an indescribable chagrin.\n\nIt now occurred to me that I was in great uneasiness in the joint of my left ankle, and a dim awareness of my condition began to come back into my mind. But, strangely enough, I was neither astonished nor horrified. If I felt any emotion at all, it was a kind of chuckling satisfaction at the cleverness I was about to show in getting myself out of this mess, and I never, for a moment, treated my ultimate safety as something in doubt. For a few minutes I remained wrapped in the deepest meditation. I distinctly remember repeatedly compressing my lips, putting my forefinger to the side of my nose, and making other gestures and grimaces that men make when they’re comfortable in their armchairs, meditating on matters of intricacy or importance. Once I thought I had gathered my thoughts enough, I now, with great caution and deliberation, put my hands behind my back and unfastened the large iron buckle that belonged to the waistband of my inexpressibles. This buckle had three teeth; because they were somewhat rusty, they turned with great difficulty on their axis. Still, after some trouble, I got them positioned at right angles to the body of the buckle, and I was glad to find they held there. Holding the instrument I’d obtained in my teeth, I then proceeded to untie the knot of my cravat. I had to pause several times before I could manage it, but at last I succeeded."}

{"request_id":"29c54710206f56bc2e5404d5","rewritten_text":"But no—there was something even more flashy than this. He would be a pirate! That was it! Now his future lay clear before him, bright with unimaginable splendor. How his name would fill the world and make people shudder! How gloriously he would plow through the dancing seas in his long, low, black-hulled racer, the Spirit of the Storm, with his grim flag flying at the bow! And at the height of his fame, how he would suddenly show up at the old village and stride into church—brown and weather-beaten—in his black velvet doublet and breeches, his big jack-boots, his crimson sash, his belt bristling with horse pistols, his crime-rusted cutlass at his side, his slouch hat with waving plumes, his black flag unfurled with the skull and crossbones on it, and listen with swelling ecstasy to the whispers: “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate!—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was decided; his career was set. He would run away from home and start it. He would begin the very next morning. So he had to start getting ready now. He would gather his supplies. He went to a rotten log nearby and began digging under one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he hit wood that sounded hollow. He put his hand there and recited the incantation with impressive seriousness:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped away the dirt and exposed a pine shingle. He lifted it and revealed a neat little treasure-house, its bottom and sides made of shingles. Inside lay a marble. Tom’s astonishment was limitless! He scratched his head, looking confused, and said:

“Well, that beats anything!”

Then he tossed the marble aside in a petulant mood and stood there thinking. The truth was that a superstition of his had failed—one that he and all his comrades had always treated as foolproof. If you buried a marble with certain necessary incantations, left it alone for a fortnight, and then opened the spot using the same incantation he’d just used, you’d find that all the marbles you’d ever lost had gathered themselves together there in the meantime, no matter how far apart they’d been. But now this thing had actually, undeniably failed. Tom’s whole foundation of faith shook to its core. He’d heard of it working plenty of times, but never of it failing before. It didn’t occur to him that he’d tried it several times himself, only he could never find the hiding places afterward. He puzzled over it for a while, and finally decided that some witch must have interfered and broken the charm."}

Mrs. Gardiner was standing a little behind; and when he paused, he asked her if she would do him the honor of introducing him to her friends. It was a moment of politeness she was completely unprepared for, and she could hardly keep from smiling at the fact that he was now trying to meet some of the very people against whom his pride had revolted—especially in his offer to herself. “What will be his surprise,” she thought, “when he learns who they are! He takes them for people of fashion now.”

The introduction, however, was made at once; and as she named their relationship to herself, she glanced at him to see how he handled it, expecting that he would quickly retreat from such disgraceful companions. That he was surprised by the connection was clear; still, he held his ground with fortitude. Instead of leaving, he turned back with them and joined in conversation with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth couldn’t help being pleased, couldn’t help feeling triumphant. It was comforting that he should know she had some relatives for whom there was no need to be ashamed. She listened with the greatest attention to everything that passed between them, and took pride in every expression, every sentence from her uncle, which showed his intelligence, his taste, or his good manners.

Soon the conversation turned to fishing; and she heard Mr. Darcy invite him, with the greatest civility, to fish there as often as he liked while he remained in the neighborhood. At the same time, he offered to supply him with fishing tackle and pointed out the parts of the stream where there was usually the best sport. Mrs. Gardiner, who was walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, gave her a look full of wonder. Elizabeth said nothing, but it pleased her greatly; the compliment had to be meant for her. Her astonishment, though, was intense, and she kept repeating to herself, “Why is he so different? What could have caused it? It can’t be for me, it can’t be for my sake that his manners have become so gentle. My reproaches at Hunsford couldn’t have brought about a change like this. It’s impossible that he still loves me.”

After they had walked some time in this way, the two ladies in front and the two gentlemen behind, when they resumed their places after descending to the riverbank to inspect some curious water-plant more closely, there was a small change. It began with Mrs. Gardiner, who, tired from the morning’s exercise, found Elizabeth’s arm insufficient for her support and therefore preferred her husband’s."}

{"request_id":"fc2184062da224552bc8ca69","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself; all the work of maintaining a slow, disappointing correspondence with Elizabeth fell on Anne.

Breakfast had barely ended when Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick joined them. They had arranged to take their last walk around Lyme together. They ought to be leaving for Uppercross by one, and in the meantime they were to be all together, outdoors as long as they could.

Anne noticed Captain Benwick coming close to her as soon as they were properly out in the street. The conversation the evening before had not discouraged him from seeking her again. They walked together for some time, talking as before about Mr. Scott and Lord Byron, and still as unable as before—unable as any other two readers—to judge the merits of either in exactly the same way, until something happened that caused almost everyone in their group to shift. Instead of Captain Benwick, Captain Harville was now walking beside her.

“Miss Elliot,” said he, speaking rather softly, “you’ve done a good deed by getting that poor fellow to talk so much. I only wish he could have company like that more often. I know it’s bad for him to be shut up as he is; but what can we do? We can’t separate.”

“No,” said Anne, “I can easily believe that would be impossible. But in time—perhaps. We know what time does in every kind of affliction. And you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend may yet be called a young mourner. Only last summer, I understand.”

“Ah, yes—true enough,” he said, with a deep sigh. “Only June.”

“And maybe not known to him so soon.”

“Not until the first week of August, when he came home from the Cape—just made into the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, dreading to hear about him. He did send letters, but the Grappler was under orders for Portsmouth. There the news had to follow him, but who was to tell it? Not I. I would as soon have been hauled up to the yard-arm. Nobody could do it, but that good fellow” (pointing to Captain Wentworth). “The Laconia had come into Plymouth the week before; there was no danger of her being sent to sea again. He had his chance for the rest, wrote for leave of absence, but without waiting for the return, traveled night and day until he reached Portsmouth. Then he rowed straight off to the Grappler and never left the poor fellow for a week. That’s what he did, and nobody else could have saved poor James. You may think, Miss Elliot, whether he is dear to us!”

Anne did think about it with complete certainty, and said as much in reply as her own feelings could manage, or as his seemed able to bear. But he was too deeply affected to bring the subject up again, and when he spoke once more, it was about something entirely different."}

{"request_id":"71f4b939dad9ddb3fa32466e","rewritten_text":"Her face changed, and she said no more.

Mrs. Gardiner stood a little behind her. When she paused, Mr. Gardiner asked her if she would do him the honor of introducing him to her friends. It was a polite gesture he had not prepared her for. She could hardly stop herself from smiling at the fact that he was now trying to meet some of the very people against whom his pride had once rebelled, even as he offered her his attention. “What will be his surprise,” she thought, “when he finds out who they are! He still thinks they are people of fashion.”

The introductions were made right away. As she named their relationship to herself, Elizabeth watched him out of the corner of her eye to see how he handled it. She expected him to pull away as quickly as he could from such embarrassing companions. That he was surprised by the connection was clear, but he managed it with steadiness. Instead of leaving, he turned back with them and joined Mr. Gardiner in conversation. Elizabeth could not help feeling pleased, could not help feeling triumphant. It was comforting to know that he had relations she did not have to be ashamed of. She listened carefully to everything they said and took pride in every remark from her uncle—every sign of his intelligence, his taste, or his good manners.

Soon the talk turned to fishing. Elizabeth heard Mr. Darcy invite him, with the greatest politeness, to fish there as often as he liked while he stayed nearby. At the same time, he offered to provide him with fishing tackle and pointed out the parts of the stream where there was usually the best sport. Mrs. Gardiner, who was walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, looked at her with clear surprise. Elizabeth said nothing, but it pleased her greatly. The compliment had to be meant for her.

Her astonishment, however, was intense. Again and again she repeated to herself, “Why has he changed so much? What could have caused it? It can’t be for me. It can’t be because of my sake that his manners have become so gentle. My remarks at Hunsford could not have brought about a change like this. It’s impossible that he still loves me.”

After they had been walking like this for some time, the two ladies in front and the two gentlemen behind resumed their places after they had gone down to the river’s edge to inspect a curious water-plant more closely. Then something small changed. It started with Mrs. Gardiner. Tired from the morning’s exercise, she found Elizabeth’s arm was not enough to support her, so she preferred her husband’s instead."}

{"request_id":"d235c4c69d76e307d60551b5","rewritten_text":"On that point, then, I will be completely silent. And you can be sure that no unfair criticism will ever leave my lips once we are married.”

It was absolutely necessary to interrupt him now.

“You are moving too fast, sir,” she said. “You forget that I have not answered yet. Let me do it right away. Thank you for the compliment you are giving me. I understand the honor of your proposal, but I cannot do anything other than refuse it.”

“I am not supposed to be learning,” replied Mr. Collins, making a formal gesture, “that it is common for young ladies to turn down the man they secretly plan to accept, when he first asks for their favor. And that sometimes they refuse him again a second time, or even a third. So I am not discouraged by what you have just said, and I will hope to bring you to the altar soon.”

“Really, sir,” Elizabeth said, “your hope is rather surprising after what I have just said. I assure you I am not one of those young ladies, if any such young ladies exist, who are bold enough to gamble their happiness on the chance that they will be asked a second time. I mean my refusal. You could not make me happy, and I am sure I am the last woman in the world who would make you happy. And if Lady Catherine were to know me, I believe she would find me, in every way, unfit for the position.”

“If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins, very gravely—“but I cannot imagine that her Ladyship would disapprove of you at all. And you may be certain that when I have the honor of seeing her again, I will speak of your modesty, your economy, and your other pleasant qualities in the highest terms.”

“Mr. Collins,” Elizabeth said, “praise of me is not needed. You should let me judge for myself, and you should believe what I say. I wish you to be very happy and very rich, and by refusing your hand, I will do everything I can to make sure you are not otherwise. In offering me your hand, you must have considered the delicacy of your feelings toward my family, and you may take possession of the Longbourn estate whenever it becomes yours, without any self-reproach. So this matter may be considered finally settled.”

As she spoke, she rose to leave the room, but Mr. Collins addressed her again.

“When I have the honor of speaking to you about this again,” he said, “I hope to receive a more favorable answer than the one you have given me now. I am not accusing you of cruelty at present, though, because I know it is the usual custom for your sex to reject a man on his first request. And perhaps you have even now said as much to encourage my suit, in a way that would still fit the true delicacy expected of women.”"}

{"request_id":"12f0e2ecabbbf6a638f7ee5b","rewritten_text":"If I can’t live on that, I won’t ask anyone to give me a lift. Is it satisfactory?”

There was a tremendous roar of applause, and out of it the king’s voice rose, saying:

“Take off his bonds and set him free! Pay him homage, high and low, rich and poor, for he has become the king’s right hand—clothed with power and authority, and seated on the highest step of the throne! Now sweep away this creeping night, and bring back the light and cheer, so that all the world may bless thee.”

But I said:

“It’s nothing if a common man is shamed before the world; but it would be an insult to the king if anyone who saw his minister naked should not also see him delivered from his shame. If I may ask that my clothes be brought back—”

“They won’t do,” the king cut in. “Fetch clothing of another kind; dress him like a prince!”

My plan worked. I wanted to keep things as they were until the eclipse was total; otherwise they would keep trying to get me to dismiss the darkness, and of course I couldn’t. Sending for the clothes bought me some time, but not enough. So I had to come up with another excuse. I said it would be natural for the king to change his mind and regret, at least to some extent, what he’d done in the heat of the moment; therefore I would let the darkness grow for a while, and if, at the end of a reasonable time, the king had kept his mind the same, then the darkness should be dismissed. Neither the king nor anyone else was happy with that arrangement, but I had to stick to it.

It grew darker and darker, blacker and blacker, while I wrestled with those awkward sixth-century clothes. At last it was pitch dark, and the crowd groaned with horror as they felt the cold, uncanny night breezes sweep through the place and saw the stars come out and twinkle in the sky. Finally the eclipse was total, and I was very glad of it, but everyone else was miserable—which was only natural. I said:

“The king, by his silence, still stands by the terms.” Then I lifted up my hands—held them just so for a moment—and then, with the most awful solemnity, I said, “Let the enchantment dissolve and pass harmless away!”

For a moment there was no response, in that deep darkness and that graveyard hush. But when the silver edge of the sun pushed itself out a moment or two later, the whole assembly erupted with a vast shout and came pouring down like a flood to smother me with blessings and gratitude; and Clarence was not the last of the crowd, of course.”}"}

{"request_id":"2721ed9389989cd2fef98151","rewritten_text":"“Story!”

He seemed determined to misunderstand the word she had just repeated, and then, with a quickness that betrayed him, he went on: “Yes—customers. In the banking trade we commonly name the connection we have our customers. He was a French gentleman; a scientific gentleman; a man of very fine education—a Doctor.”

“Not of Beauvais?”

“Why, yes, of Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he was a person of standing in Paris. I had the honour of knowing him there. Our dealings were business dealings, but kept confidential. At that time I was in our French House, and I had been—oh!—twenty years.”

“At that time—may I ask, at what time, sir?”

“I mean, miss, twenty years ago. He married—an English lady—and I served as one of the trustees. His affairs, as with those of many other French gentlemen and French families, were entirely managed by Tellson’s. In a like manner I am, or have been, trustee of one sort or another for scores of our customers. These are only business relations, miss; there’s no friendship in them, no special concern, nothing that can be called sentiment. I move from one to another in the course of my work, just as I move from one customer to another during the day; in short, I have no feelings—I’m nothing but a machine. To continue—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir; and I begin to think”—the oddly furrowed brow was fixed on him with a kind of earnestness—“that when I was left an orphan, my mother surviving my father by only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I’m nearly certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the small, hesitating hand that had come forward so trustingly to take his, and with some ceremony pressed it to his lips. Then he guided the young lady at once back to her chair. Keeping the chair-back steady with his left hand, and with his right he alternated between rubbing his chin, tugging his wig at the ears, or indicating what he meant, he stood looking down at her while she sat looking up.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how truly I spoke of myself just now, when I said I had no feelings, and that all the relations I keep with my fellow-creatures are mere business relations, when you consider that I have never seen you since. No—you have been the ward of Tellson’s House, and I have been occupied with the other business of Tellson’s House besides. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity for them. I spend my whole life, miss, turning an immense pecuniary Mangle.”"}

{"request_id":"ca826e1c8486a00f818f4655","rewritten_text":"When Tom woke up in the morning, he couldn’t help wondering where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked around. Then it all clicked. It was a cool gray dawn, and there was a wonderful feeling of rest and peace in the deep, steady calm and silence of the woods. Not a leaf moved; not a sound intruded on great Nature’s quiet thinking. Dewdrops beaded on the leaves and grasses. A white layer of ashes covered the fire, and a thin blue ribbon of smoke rose straight into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep.

Now, far out in the woods, a bird called; another answered; and soon the hammering of a woodpecker could be heard. Little by little, the cool dim gray of morning brightened, and little by little sounds multiplied and life showed itself. The wonder of Nature shaking off sleep and getting to work unfolded before the thoughtful boy. A small green worm crawled over a dewy leaf, lifting about two-thirds of its body into the air now and then and “sniffing around,” then going on again—because, Tom said, it was measuring. When the worm came toward him, he stayed as still as stone, his hopes rising and falling in turn as the creature kept coming closer or seemed ready to go somewhere else. And when, at last, it decided on a painful moment with its curved body held up, then came decisively down onto Tom’s leg and began to travel over him, his whole heart was glad—because that meant he was going to get a new suit of clothes, without any doubt a flashy pirate uniform.

Then, out of nowhere, a line of ants appeared and went about their work. One struggled bravely with a dead spider five times its size, carrying it straight up a tree trunk. A brown-spotted ladybug climbed to the dizzy height of a grass blade, and Tom leaned down close to it and said, “Lady-bug, lady-bug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children’s alone,” and she took off to go check on it. That didn’t surprise Tom, because he’d known for a long time that this insect was gullible about fires, and he’d tested her on her simplicity more than once. Next came a tumblebug, rolling along with steady effort, pushing its ball. Tom touched it, just to see it tuck its legs in against its body and pretend to be dead.

The birds were really going at it by then. A catbird—the Northern mocker—landed in a tree over Tom’s head and sang out her imitations of her neighbors with pure delight. Then a shrill jay swooped down: a flash of blue, and it stopped on a twig almost within the boy’s reach. It tilted its head to one side, eyeing the strangers with intense curiosity. A gray squirrel and a big “fox” kind of fellow came skittering along, sitting up at intervals to inspect and chatter at the boys, because the wild animals probably had never seen a human being before and barely knew whether they should be afraid."}

{"request_id":"a4e74aadcc7041a96c285098","rewritten_text":"“Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay,” was finally brought before the court.

His judges sat on the Bench in feathered hats; but the rough red cap and tricolored cockade were the headgear otherwise most commonly worn. Looking at the Jury and the restless crowd, he might have thought the usual order of things had been turned upside down, and that the criminals were putting the innocent on trial. The lowest, cruelest, and worst people in the city—never without their share of low, cruel, and bad—were the driving force of the whole scene: loudly commenting, applauding, disapproving, anticipating, and pushing the outcome forward, with no restraint. Most of the men were armed in one way or another; among the women, some wore knives, some daggers; some ate and drank as they watched, while many knitted. Among those knitting was one who kept a spare piece of knitting under her arm as she worked. She sat in the front row, beside a man he had never seen since his arrival at the Barrier, but whom he remembered at once as Defarge. He noticed that she leaned toward him once or twice to whisper, and that she seemed to be his wife; but what he noticed most about the two figures was that, though they were posted as close to himself as they could manage, they never looked toward him. They seemed to be waiting for something with stubborn determination, watching the Jury but nothing else.

Under the President sat Doctor Manette, in his usual quiet dress. As far as the prisoner could see, he and Mr. Lorry were the only men there who were not connected with the Tribunal, and who wore their ordinary clothes, without having put on the coarse garb of the Carmagnole.

Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, was accused by the public prosecutor as an emigrant, whose life was forfeit to the Republic under the decree that banished all emigrants on pain of death. It did not matter that the decree was dated since his return to France. The decree was there, and he was there; he had been taken in France, and his head was demanded.

“Take off his head!” the audience cried. “An enemy to the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to silence those cries, and asked the prisoner whether it was not true that he had lived many years in England.

Undoubtedly it was.

Then wasn’t he an emigrant? What did he call himself?

Not an emigrant, he hoped, in the sense and spirit of the law.

Why not? the President asked.

Because he had voluntarily given up a title that was distasteful to him, and a position that was distasteful to him, and had left his country—he said, before the word emigrant in the Tribunal’s current meaning was even used—to live by his own labor in England, rather than on the labor of the overburdened people of France."}

{"request_id":"6794a005c941c6266960fdda","rewritten_text":"And I don’t suddenly spring at him and risk turning it into a clumsy, half-finished mess; no, I move away over there to one side, and I work up on him slowly, so he never suspects I’m going to hit him at all. Then, little by little, all at once, he’s flat on his back, and he can’t, for the life of him, figure out how it all happened. That’s how I went for brother Dowley. I started talking lazily and comfortably, like I was just passing the time; and the oldest man in the world couldn’t have taken the bearings of where I began and guessed where I was going to end up:

“Boys, there are a lot of curious things about law, and custom, and usage, and all that kind of thing, once you really look at it; yes, and about the drift and progress of human opinion and movement, too. There are written laws—they perish; but there are also unwritten laws—_they_ are eternal. Take the unwritten law of wages: it says they’ve got to advance, little by little, straight through the centuries. And notice how it works. We know what wages are now, here and there and yonder; we take an average and say that’s what wages are today. We know what wages were a hundred years ago, and what they were two hundred years ago; that’s as far back as we can get, but it’s enough to show us the law of progress, the measure and rate of the steady increase. And so, without any document to help us, we can come pretty close to determining what wages were three, four, and five hundred years ago. All right, so far. Do we stop there? No. We stop looking backward; we turn around and apply the law to the future. My friends, I can tell you what people’s wages are going to be at any date in the future you want to know, for hundreds and hundreds of years.”

“What, goodman, what!”

“Yes. In seven hundred years wages will have risen to six times what they are now, here in your region, and farm hands will be allowed 3 cents a day, and mechanics 6.”

“I wouldn’t I might die now and live then!” Smug, the wheelwright, interrupted, with a fine, greedy glow in his eye.

“And that isn’t all; they’ll get their board too—such as it is: it won’t bloat them. Two hundred and fifty years later—pay attention now—a mechanic’s wages will be—mind you, this is law, not guesswork; a mechanic’s wages will then be _twenty_ cents a day!”

There was a general gasp of awed astonishment; Dickon the mason murmured, with raised eyes and hands:"}

{"request_id":"d0ae9f5c46b40d9ea9cd817f","rewritten_text":"WHEN the wedding took place, some three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a perfect crowd of smart people. The service was delivered in the most impressive way by the Dean of Chichester, and everyone agreed they had never seen a handsomer couple than the bride and bridegroom. They were more than handsome, though—they were happy. Not for a single moment did Lord Arthur regret everything he had suffered for Sybil’s sake, while she, on her side, gave him the best things a woman can give any man—worship, tenderness, and love. For them, romance wasn’t crushed by reality. They always felt young.

Some years afterwards, when two beautiful children had been born to them, Lady Windermere came down on a visit to Alton Priory, a lovely old place, the Duke’s wedding present to his son; and one afternoon, as she sat with Lady Arthur under a lime-tree in the garden, watching the little boy and girl as they played up and down the rose-walk like fitful sunbeams, she suddenly took her hostess’s hand in hers and said, ‘Are you happy, Sybil?’

‘Dear Lady Windermere, of course I am happy. Aren’t you?’

‘I have no time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the last person who is introduced to me, but, as a rule, the moment I get to know people I get tired of them.’

‘Don’t your lions satisfy you, Lady Windermere?’

‘Oh dear, no! Lions are only good for one season. The moment their manes are cut, they’re the dullest creatures going. Besides, they behave very badly if you’re really nice to them. Do you remember that horrid Mr. Podgers? He was a dreadful impostor. Of course, I didn’t mind that at all, and even when he wanted to borrow money I forgave him, but I couldn’t stand his making love to me. He’s really made me hate cheiromancy. I’m into telepathy now. It’s much more amusing.’

‘You mustn’t say anything against cheiromancy here, Lady Windermere; it’s the only subject Arthur doesn’t like people to joke about. I assure you he’s quite serious about it.’

‘You don’t mean to say that he believes in it, Sybil?’

‘Ask him, Lady Windermere—here he is’; and Lord Arthur came up the garden with a large bunch of yellow roses in his hand, his two children dancing round him.

‘Lord Arthur?’

‘Yes, Lady Windermere.’

‘You don’t mean to say that you believe in cheiromancy?’

‘Of course I do,’ said the young man, smiling.

‘But why?’

‘Because I owe to it all the happiness of my life,’ he murmured, sinking into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"a9fa437d149c42c74030f2fd","rewritten_text":"I have said that he was a poet. When he was twenty-three, he published his first poem, and the whole nation praised it with enthusiasm and delight. His good fortune kept shining on him. His reputation was made faster than anyone had ever managed before, and it was universal. People admired the same poems that amazed the wise man in his study. Not a single person disagreed.

It was during this time, at the height of his fame, that he met Elinor. She was a young heiress of striking beauty, living under the care of her guardian. From the moment they were seen together, it was clear they belonged with each other. Elinor did not have Woodville’s genius, but she was generous and noble. Her youth and the love she inspired everywhere made her feel lifted up by nothing except virtue and excellence. She was lovely. Her manners were open and simple. Her deep blue eyes seemed to glow with a kind of light that only comes from feeling guided by wisdom.

They were made for one another, and they soon loved. For the first time, Woodville felt the joy of love. Elinor was thrilled to have the heart of someone so beautiful and admired among his fellow men. What else could come from a union like that, except pure happiness?

Woodville was a poet. Every society wanted him, and when he appeared, everyone’s attention turned to him alone. But he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a rich heiress. Her guardian did not disapprove of their affection, because Woodville’s talent was too great to be dismissed because of his limited money. Still, her father’s will had one final condition: she was not allowed to marry until she was of age, and her fortune depended on her obeying it. She had just turned twenty, so she and her lover had to wait. They stayed together, and their happiness seemed like paradise. They studied together, made plans for their future, and drank in love and joy from each other’s eyes and words. They hardly complained about the delay, even though it meant waiting for their full union. Woodville kept rising in fame, and Elinor became even more lovely and wise from the lessons of her accomplished lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one, and everything was ready for their marriage. How can I describe the disaster that came after so much joy? The earth would not be the earth it is, full of blight and sorrow, if such angelic people had been allowed to find happiness with each other. Search the world over and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have brought them. Something would have had to change in the way things are set up for us miserable people on earth, to allow such complete joy."}

{"request_id":"c187097788fb79e8bb95a35d","rewritten_text":"But my father was right beside me, trying to comfort me and to push away painful memories with hopeful thoughts. I felt it was almost sweet to grieve, because it meant he might dry my tears.

Again, he pulled my mind away from my sorrow by comparing it to his own despair when he lost my mother. Even then, I could not help but shudder at the picture he painted of his feelings. He had the imagination of a poet, and when he described the storm of emotions that followed her death, his words felt so real that I believed them even while I trembled. I wondered how he could ever return to ordinary life after his wild thoughts seemed to connect him to something beyond the world. As he spoke, the ideas he carried were so powerful that it seemed the human heart could not hold them. His feelings seemed meant for a spirit that lives in earthquakes and volcanoes, not for someone trapped in a mortal body. But those were only memories. He had changed since then. Now he was all love and softness. When I looked at him in wonder as he spoke, the gentle smile on his lips told me that his heart was filled with the kindest passions.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London. My father brought me there so I could study more deeply than I had before. My progress made him happy. He stayed with me through all my studies and helped me, or joined me, in every lesson. We went out into society often, and no day passed without my father trying to add some new pleasure. The tender love he had for me, and the love and respect I gave back, made every moment feel special. Time seemed to stretch, because each minute was used. We lived more in one week than many people do in several months, and the variety and freshness of our pleasures made everything feel even better.

We took trips together again and again. Whether we went to see beautiful scenery, to look at fine paintings, or sometimes simply to find amusement wherever it appeared, I was always happy when I was near my father. I felt regret whenever a third person joined us. Still, if I turned toward him with a worried look, his eyes would meet mine, full of tenderness, and my joy would return at once. Oh, hours of intense delight! Even though they were short, they feel as long to me as a whole life when I look back on them through the mist of grief that rose right after, as if to block them from my view."}

{"request_id":"cb183e95ef3cf9b6bdb191e8","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him for a few moments in sheer astonishment, and then, noticing that he meant every word, wrote an address on a scrap of paper, put his initials to it, and passed it to him across the table.

“Scotland Yard would be glad of a great deal to know that address, my dear fellow.”

“They shan’t have it,” Lord Arthur declared, laughing; and after giving the young Russian a hearty shake of the hand, he hurried downstairs, checked the paper, and told the coachman to drive to Soho Square.

At once there, he dismissed him and wandered down Greek Street until he reached a place known as Bayle’s Court. He went beneath the archway and found himself in a rather odd cul-de-sac, apparently taken up by a French Laundry, for clothes-lines ran in a perfect tangle from house to house, and white linen fluttered in the morning air. He walked straight to the end and knocked at a small green house. After a short delay—during which every window in the court turned into a blurred crowd of watching faces—the door opened on a rough-looking foreigner, who asked, in very poor English, what Lord Arthur wanted. Lord Arthur handed him the paper Count Rouvaloff had given him. The man bowed at once, invited Lord Arthur into a very shabby front parlour on the ground floor, and, in a few minutes, Herr Winckelkopf—so he was called in England—came bustling in with a wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork in his left hand.

“Count Rouvaloff has given me an introduction to you,” said Lord Arthur, bowing. “I’m anxious to have a brief interview with you on a matter of business. My name is Smith—Mr. Robert Smith—and I want you to supply me with an explosive clock.”

“Delighted to make your acquaintance, Lord Arthur,” replied the genial little German, laughing. “Don’t look so frightened. It’s my duty to know everyone, and I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I hope her ladyship is quite well. Would you mind sitting with me while I finish my breakfast? There’s an excellent pâté, and my friends assure me that my Rhine wine is better than anything they get at the German Embassy.” Before Lord Arthur had fully recovered from the surprise of being recognised, he found himself seated in the back-room, sipping the most delicious Marcobrünner from a pale yellow hock-glass stamped with the Imperial monogram, and chatting in the most friendly fashion with the well-known conspirator.

“Explosive clocks,” said Herr Winckelkopf, “aren’t very suitable for foreign exportation; for even if they manage to get through the Custom House, the train service is so irregular that they usually go off before they’ve reached their proper destination.”"}
