{"request_id":"7d99a986bb667b7f1e1a263a","rewritten_text":"They were bringing along a very nice-looking old gentleman and a nice-looking younger one, with his right arm in a sling. And, my souls, how the people yelled and laughed, and kept it up. But I didn’t see any joke in it, and I figured it would strain the duke and the king to have to watch. I expected they’d turn pale. But no—none of them turned pale. The duke didn’t let on that he suspected anything; he just kept going on and on, happy and satisfied, like a jug that’s gurgling out buttermilk. As for the king, he just stared and stared down at the newcomers, looking so sorrowful, as if it gave him a stomachache right in his heart to think there could be such frauds and rascals in the world. Oh, he did it admirably. A lot of the important people gathered around the king so he could see they were on his side. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked completely baffled. Pretty soon he started to speak, and I could tell right away he pronounced like an Englishman—not the king’s way, though the king’s was pretty good as an imitation. I can’t give the old man’s exact words, and I can’t imitate him either, but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

“This is a surprise to me that I wasn’t expecting; and I’ll admit, candid and frank, I’m not very well prepared to answer it. My brother and I have had misfortunes. He’s broken his arm, and our baggage was put off at a town above here last night, by mistake. I am Peter Wilks’ brother, Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can’t hear or speak—and can’t even make signs that amount to much, since he’s only got one hand to work them with. We are who we say we are; and in a day or two, when I get the baggage, I can prove it. But until then I won’t say anything more—just go to the hotel and wait.”

So he and the new dummy started off. And the king laughed and talked on:

“Broke his arm—_very_ likely, isn’t it?—and very convenient, too, for a fraud who has to make signs and hasn’t learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s _mighty_ good—and mighty ingenious—under the _circumstances_!”

So he laughed again, and everyone else did too, except three or four, or maybe half a dozen. One of them was that doctor. Another was a sharp-looking gentleman with an old-fashioned carpet-bag, who had just come off the steamboat and was talking to him in a low voice, glancing toward the king now and then and nodding his head—it was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville. And another was a big, rough, husky fellow who came along and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king too."}

{"request_id":"b16c3a78fc9a0ca61858a605","rewritten_text":"No letter of condolence had been sent to Ireland. The neglect had been visited on the head of the sinner; for when poor Lady Elliot died herself, no letter of condolence was received at Kellynch, and, consequently, there was far too much reason to fear that the Dalrymples considered the relationship ended. The question was how to set this anxious business right, and be admitted as cousins again—and it was a question which, in a more sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot thought unimportant. “Family connections are always worth keeping, and good company is always worth seeking. Lady Dalrymple has taken a house for three months in Laura Place, and will be living in style. She was at Bath the year before, and Lady Russell has heard her spoken of as a charming woman. It’s very desirable that the connection should be renewed, if it can be done, without any compromise of propriety on the Elliots’ side.”

Sir Walter, however, would choose his own method, and at last wrote a very fine letter—full of explanation, regret, and entreaty—to his right-honourable cousin. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot could admire the letter; but it did what was needed, bringing three lines of scrawl from the Dowager Viscountess. “She was very much honoured, and should be happy in their acquaintance.” The hard part of the business was over; the pleasant part began. They visited in Laura Place. They had the Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple’s cards, and those of the Honourable Miss Carteret, to be arranged wherever they might be most visible: and “Our cousins in Laura Place”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret”—were talked about to everyone.

Anne was ashamed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been agreeable, she would still have been ashamed of the agitation they caused; but they were nothing. There was no superiority of manner, accomplishment, or understanding. Lady Dalrymple had earned the reputation of “a charming woman” only because she had a smile and a civil answer for everyone. Miss Carteret, with even less to say, was so plain and so awkward that she would never have been tolerated in Camden Place, except for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted she had expected something better; but still, “it’s an acquaintance worth having.” And when Anne ventured to share her opinion of them with Mr Elliot, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves, but still insisted that, as a family connection, as good company, and as people who would draw good company around them, they had their value. Anne smiled and said,

“My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of clever, well-informed people, who have a great deal of conversation; that is what I call good company.”"}

{"request_id":"02af32b89a6871a4c63da6de","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

Still nothing.

“What’s come over that boy, I wonder? You TOM!”

No answer.

The old lady drew her spectacles down and looked over them around the room; then she pushed them up and peered out beneath them. She hardly ever, if at all, looked _through_ them for something as small as a boy. They were her “state” pair, the pride of her heart, made for “style” rather than service—she might as well have seen through a couple of stove-lids. She looked puzzled for a moment, and then said, not with fury, but loud enough that the furniture could hear:

“Well, I’ll be bound, if I get hold of you I’ll—”

She didn’t get to finish, because at that point she bent down and jabbed the broom under the bed, needing breath to mark each punch. She brought up nothing but the cat.

“I never did see the beat of that boy!”

She went to the open door, stood there, and looked out over the tomato vines and the “jimpson” weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice at an angle meant for distance and called:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

A small sound came from behind her, and she spun just in time to grab a little boy by the slack of his roundabout and stop his dash.

“There! I might ’a’ thought of that closet. What you been doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What _is_ that truck?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I know. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve said if you didn’t leave that jam alone I’d skin you. Hand me that switch.”

The switch hung in the air—the danger was right there—

“My! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old lady snapped around and pulled her skirts out of harm’s way. The lad bolted at once, scrambled up the high board-fence, and vanished over it.

His aunt Polly stood there, startled for a beat, and then let out a gentle laugh.

“Hang the boy—can’t I never learn anything? Ain’t he played me tricks enough that I ought to be watching for him by now? But old fools is the biggest fools there is. Can’t teach an old dog new tricks, as the saying goes. Still, goodness—he never does it the same way two days running, and how’s a body supposed to know what’s coming? He ’pears to know just how long he can torment me before I get my dander up, and he knows if he can manage to put me off for a minute or make me laugh, then it’s all gone again and I can’t hit him a lick.”"}

{"request_id":"e9894fa59290d3b939a32989","rewritten_text":"You’ve raised an artificial soul and spirit in him, ma’am—something that doesn’t suit a person of his condition. As the board, Mrs. Sowerberry, who are practical philosophers, will tell you. What do paupers have to do with soul or spirit? It’s quite enough that we let them have living bodies. If you’d kept the boy on gruel, ma’am, this would never have happened.”

“Dear, dear!” ejaculated Mrs. Sowerberry, piously lifting her eyes to the kitchen ceiling. “This comes of being liberal!”

Mrs. Sowerberry’s “liberality” toward Oliver had consisted of giving him, in generous measure, all the dirty odds and ends that nobody else would eat; so there was a great deal of meekness and self-sacrifice in her choosing to stay under Mr. Bumble’s heavy accusation, of which, to do her justice, she was entirely innocent—in thought, word, or deed.

“Ah!” said Mr. Bumble, when the lady brought her eyes back down to earth. “The only thing that can be done now, that I know of, is to leave him in the cellar for a day or so, until he’s a little starved down. Then take him out and keep him on gruel all through his apprenticeship. He comes of a bad family, excitable natures, Mrs. Sowerberry! Both the nurse and the doctor said that his mother made her way here, against difficulties and pain that would have killed any well-disposed woman, weeks before.”

At this point in Mr. Bumble’s speech, Oliver—just hearing enough to know that something was being said about his mother—started kicking again with such force that every other sound was drowned out. Sowerberry returned at that moment. Once Oliver’s offense had been explained to him, with the exaggerations the ladies thought most likely to stir up his anger, he unlocked the cellar door in an instant and dragged his rebellious apprentice out by the collar.

Oliver’s clothes had been torn by the beating he’d received; his face was bruised and scratched; and his hair hung scattered over his forehead. The angry flush hadn’t gone away, though. When he was pulled from his prison, he scowled boldly at Noah and looked completely unshaken.

“Now, you’re a nice young fellow, aren’t you?” said Sowerberry, shaking Oliver and giving him a slap.

“He called my mother names,” Oliver replied.

“Well, what if he did, you little ungrateful wretch?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She deserved what he said—and worse.”

“She didn’t,” said Oliver.

“She did,” said Mrs. Sowerberry.

“It’s a lie!” said Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry burst into a flood of tears.

That flood of tears left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. If he’d hesitated for even a moment to punish Oliver most severely, it would have been clear to every experienced reader that he would have been—according to all the precedents in disputes of matrimony established—a brute, an unnatural husband, an insulting creature, a base imitation of a man, and various other agreeable characters too numerous to list within the limits of this chapter."}

{"request_id":"07b2f09395149dcfca8fb835","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself. All the work of keeping up a slow, disappointing correspondence with Elizabeth fell to Anne.

Breakfast had barely finished when Captain and Mrs Harville and Captain Benwick joined them. They had agreed to take their last walk around Lyme together. They were supposed to leave for Uppercross at one o’clock, and until then they would all be together, outside as long as they could.

As soon as they were properly out in the street, Anne noticed Captain Benwick coming close to her. The conversation they had had the previous evening did not make him less eager to speak with her again. They walked together for some time, talking as before about Mr Scott and Lord Byron, and still unable, as before, to agree exactly on the merits of either—at least, not in the same way. Then something happened that led to an almost general change among their group, and instead of Captain Benwick, Captain Harville was walking beside her.

“Miss Elliot,” said he, speaking more quietly, “you have done a good deed by getting that poor fellow to talk so much. I wish he could have company like that more often. I know it is bad for him to be shut up as he is, but what can we do? We can’t leave him.”

“No,” said Anne, “I can’t believe that would be possible. But in time, perhaps. We all know what time can do for every kind of suffering. And you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend may still be called a young mourner. Only last summer, I understand.”

“Yes, that’s true enough,” he said with a deep sigh. “Only June.”

“And maybe not known to him so soon.”

“Not until the first week of August,” he replied. “He came home from the Cape, and he was just made into the Grappler. I was in Plymouth, dreading to hear about him. He did send letters, but the Grappler was under orders for Portsmouth. There the news had to follow him, but who was supposed to tell it? Not I. I would as soon have been sent up to the yard-arm. Nobody could do it, except that good fellow” (pointing to Captain Wentworth). “The Laconia had come into Plymouth the week before, so there was no danger of her being sent out to sea again. He had his chance for the rest. He wrote for leave of absence, but without waiting for the reply, he traveled night and day until he reached Portsmouth. Then he rowed straight off to the Grappler and never left the poor fellow for a week. That’s what he did, and nobody else could have saved poor James. You may think, Miss Elliot, whether he is dear to us!”

Anne thought about it with complete certainty, and said as much as her own feelings could manage, and as his seemed able to bear. But he was too upset to bring the subject up again. When he spoke once more, it was about something entirely different."}

{"request_id":"30d51929c0abe20a82786f3b","rewritten_text":"But no—there was something even flashier than this. He would be a pirate! That was it. Now his future felt clear, and it seemed to shine with wonders he couldn’t even imagine. He could picture his name filling the world and making people tremble. He would sail across the seas in his long, low, black-hulled racer, the Spirit of the Storm, with his terrifying flag flying at the front. And at the height of his fame, he would suddenly show up at the old village and walk straight into church—brown from weather, wearing his black velvet doublet and trunks, his big jack-boots, his crimson sash, and a belt loaded with horse-pistols. His crime-rusted cutlass would hang at his side, and his slouch hat would have waving plumes. His black flag would be spread out, with the skull and crossbones on it. Then he would stand there, thrilled beyond measure, listening as people whispered, “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was decided. His career was set. He would run away from home and start it. He would begin the very next morning. So he had to get ready now. He gathered what he could. He went to a rotten log nearby and started digging under one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he hit wood that sounded hollow. He put his hand inside and said the words like a spell:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped away the dirt and uncovered a pine shingle. Under it was a small, neat hiding place, made of shingles for the bottom and sides. Inside lay a marble. Tom was completely amazed. He scratched his head, looking confused, and said,

“Well, that beats anything!”

Then he tossed the marble aside in a huff and stood thinking. The problem was that a superstition of his had failed—one he and all his friends had always believed was foolproof. If you buried a marble with the right incantations, left it alone for a fortnight, and then opened the hiding place using the same words, you would find that all the marbles you had ever lost had gathered there, no matter how far apart they had been. But this time, it had truly failed. Tom’s whole belief system shook. He had heard it work many times, but he had never heard of it not working before. It didn’t even occur to him that he had tried it himself several times, only to never find the hiding spots again afterward. He thought about it for a while, and in the end decided that some witch must have stepped in and broken the charm."}

content.text: {"request_id":"14adbe59a8a73a9118ba932d","rewritten_text":"How long I stayed in that condition I cannot say. Still, it must have been a fair stretch of time, because when I began to recover in part the feeling of being alive, I saw that day was breaking; the balloon hung at an astonishing height above a wilderness of ocean, and not a scrap of land could be found anywhere within the wide sweep of the horizon. Yet my sensations, once I came back to myself, were far from being all sharp agony, as one might have expected. In fact, there was a good deal of the beginnings of madness in the calm way I set about surveying my predicament. I drew each of my hands up to my eyes in turn, and wondered what could have caused the veins to swell and the nails to turn so horribly black. After that, I examined my head with care, shaking it again and again and feeling it with the closest attention, until I was satisfied it was not—though I had half suspected it might be—larger than my balloon. Then, with a sort of practiced air, I put my hands into both pockets of my breeches, found that a set of tablets and a toothpick case were missing, and, unable to account for their disappearance, felt an inexpressible annoyance. It struck me then that I was in great uneasiness at the joint of my left ankle, and a faint recollection of my situation began to come back. Oddly enough, though, I was neither startled nor stricken with horror. If I felt anything at all, it was a quiet chuckling pleasure at the cleverness I was about to show in getting myself out of this trouble, and I never once treated my final safety as something that might be in doubt. For a few minutes I fell into the deepest meditation. I clearly remember repeatedly pressing my lips together, touching my forefinger to the side of my nose, and using other gestures and grimaces that men make when they sit comfortably in their arm-chairs and think over matters of intricacy or consequence. Once I believed I had gathered my thoughts enough, I now, with the utmost caution and deliberation, put my hands behind my back and unfastened the large iron buckle that belonged to the waistband of my inexpressibles. This buckle had three teeth; being a little rusty, they turned with great reluctance on their axis. I managed, after some trouble, to bring them round so that they lay at right angles to the body of the buckle, and I was relieved to see them hold there. With the instrument thus secured, I kept it between my teeth and then set about untying the knot of my cravat. I had to pause and try again several times before I could manage the maneuver, but at last I succeeded."}

{"request_id":"504cb9fdf8199438377ecdae","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own amusement, never picked up any book except the Baronetage. There he found something to occupy an idle hour, and comfort in a time of distress. There his mind was stirred into admiration and respect as he contemplated the limited surviving remnants of the earliest patents. And there, whenever unpleasant feelings came from domestic matters, they naturally turned into pity and contempt as he leafed through the almost endless creations of the last century. Even if every other page were useless, he could still read his own history with an interest that never failed. This was the page where the favorite volume always opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

Precisely the same paragraph had originally stood exactly as the printer set it down; but Sir Walter had improved it, adding—so that he and his family would have the information—these words after the date of Mary’s birth: “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset,” and by inserting with the greatest accuracy the day of the month on which he had lost his wife.

Then came the history and rise of the ancient and respectable family, in the usual terms: how it had first been established in Cheshire; how it was mentioned in Dugdale; how it had served as high sheriff; how it had represented a borough in three successive parliaments; how it had shown loyalty and dignity of baronetcy in the first year of Charles II, with all the Marys and Elizabeths they had married. Altogether it made two fine duodecimo pages, and ended with the arms and motto:—“Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” and Sir Walter’s handwriting again in the final line:—

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character—vanity of person and of position. He had been remarkably handsome in his youth, and at fifty-four he was still a very fine man. Few women could think more highly of their personal appearance than he did, nor could the valet of any newly made lord be more pleased with the place he held in society. He believed the blessing of beauty was inferior only to the blessing of a baronetcy; and Sir Walter Elliot, who had both, was the constant object of his warmest respect and devotion.

His good looks and his rank had a strong claim on his attachment, since to them he must have owed a wife of a character far superior to anything he could have deserved on his own."}

{"request_id":"e0a20c9e6875ffbc19211e20","rewritten_text":"There was something striking in the growing brightness of Mr. Wopsle’s eye, and he appeared to be turning so many matters over in his mind, and to be so much at a loss, that I could not tell what he meant. I kept thinking of it long after he had gone up into the clouds in a large watch-case, and still I could not make it out. I was musing on it when I came out of the theatre an hour later, and there he was, waiting for me by the door.

“How do you do?” I said, taking his hand as we walked down the street together. “I saw that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he answered. “Yes, to be sure I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It is the strangest thing,” said Mr. Wopsle, slipping back into that same bewildered look; “and yet I could swear to him.”

Alarmed, I pressed Mr. Wopsle to explain what he meant.

“Whether I should have noticed him at first, if it hadn’t been for your being there,” he went on, still in his wandering manner, “I can’t say for certain; but I think I should.”

Without meaning to, I looked about me, as I had the habit of doing when I went home; for those mysterious words set a chill in me.

“Oh! He can’t be in sight,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He went out before I did. I saw him go.”

With the very grounds I had for suspecting, I even suspected that poor actor. I feared there might be some scheme to draw me into an admission. So I cast a glance at him as we went on together, but said nothing.

“I had a foolish notion that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw that you were quite unaware of him—sitting behind you there like a ghost.”

That first chill returned, but I was determined not to speak yet, because it was quite possible, from what he said, that he meant to have me connect those remarks with Provis. Still, I was perfectly certain and safe that Provis had not been there.

“I dare say you’re wondering at me, Mr. Pip; indeed, I see you are. But it is so very strange! You’ll hardly credit what I’m about to tell you. I could scarcely have believed it myself, if you had told me.”

“Indeed?” said I.

“No, indeed. Mr. Pip, you remember, in the old days, a certain Christmas Day, when you were still a child, and I dined at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to have a pair of handcuffs mended?”

“I remember it very well.”

“And you remember that there was a chase after two convicts, and that we joined in it, and that Gargery carried you on his back, and that I led the way, and you kept up with me as well as you could?”"}

{"request_id":"aa6367008f4dbdd2b50d69c2","rewritten_text":"It was a little past two o’clock when, after a sudden turn, I found myself near the lake by a cove where a small skiff was tied up. It wasn’t far from our house, and I saw my father and my aunt walking on the lawn. I jumped into the boat. I was used to doing things like this, so I pushed off from shore and rowed as fast as I could across the water.

When I came near, I was dressed in white. I was covered only by my tartan rachan, my hair falling over my shoulders and streaming behind me as I moved. It seemed to fly even faster than my boat could. My father had often told me that I looked more like a spirit than a human maid. I reached the shore, and he held the boat steady. I leapt out lightly, and in an instant I was in his arms.

And now I began to live. Everything around me had changed. What had felt dull and the same was now the brightest scene of joy and delight. The happiness I felt with my father was far more than I had dared to hope. We were together all the time, and our conversations never ran out. He had spent sixteen years away among nations that were almost unknown in Europe. He had traveled through Persia, Arabia, and the north of India, and he had moved among the people there with a freedom that few Europeans are allowed. He told me about their manners, shared stories, and described the scenery, and those things filled our days with pleasure—especially when we were tired of talking about our plans for the future.

The sound of love was new to me, so I listened with delight when he told me what he had felt about me during those long years when it seemed he had forgotten me. “At first,” he said, “I couldn’t bear to think of my poor little girl. But later, when the grief eased and hope came back, I could only think of her. In cities and deserts alike, her little fairy shape—just as I imagined it—kept appearing in my mind. The northern breeze, when it refreshed me, felt sweeter and softer, as if it carried some of your spirit with it. I often thought that I would return at once and take you with me to some fertile island, where we could live in peace forever. But when I came back, my hopes were crushed by so many fears. My impatience became unbearable. I couldn’t bear to imagine the sun shining and the moon rising over anything but your living face, not your grave. But no—it isn’t like that. I have my Mathilda. She is my comfort, and she is my hope.”"}

{"request_id":"ca468d97240352074a0d8afd","rewritten_text":"By late reports from Rotterdam, that city seems to be in a state of intense philosophical excitement. Indeed, phenomena have there occurred of such a nature—so completely unexpected, so entirely new, so utterly at odds with the opinions people held beforehand—that I have no doubt in my mind that, long before now, all Europe will be in an uproar, all physics in a ferment, and all reason and astronomy will be at each other’s throats.

It appears that on the—— day of—— (I’m not sure of the date), a vast crowd of people, for purposes not specifically mentioned, gathered in the great square of the Exchange in the well-run city of Rotterdam. The day was warm—unusually warm for the season—there was hardly any breath of air stirring; and the multitude were in no bad mood about being, from time to time, lightly sprinkled with friendly showers of brief duration that fell from large white masses of cloud, which flickered and shifted across the blue vault of the sky. Still, around noon, a slight but remarkable agitation became clear in the crowd: the clattering of ten thousand tongues was heard; and, an instant later, ten thousand faces were tilted upward toward the heavens, ten thousand pipes were lowered at the same time from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a shout—something like nothing but the roaring of Niagara—rang out, long, loud, and furious, through all the surrounding areas of Rotterdam.

The source of this commotion soon became obvious enough. From behind the huge bulk of one of those sharply defined masses of cloud already mentioned, there was seen slowly to emerge into an open stretch of blue space a strange, mixed, but apparently solid substance—shaped so oddly, put together so whimsically—that no one could make sense of it, and no one among the sturdy burghers standing below could stop staring. What could it be? In the name of all the vrows and devils in Rotterdam, what could it possibly mean? No one knew, no one could imagine; no one—even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—had the slightest clue for unraveling the mystery. So, since nothing more reasonable could be done, each person, one by one, carefully put his pipe back in the corner of his mouth, cocked his right eye upward at the phenomenon, puffed, paused, waddled around, and grunted meaningfully—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and finally—puffed again.

Meanwhile, though, the object of all that curiosity—and the cause of all that smoke—came lower and lower toward the good city. In just a few minutes it drew close enough to be seen clearly. It appeared to be—yes!—undoubtedly a species of balloon; but surely no such balloon had ever been seen in Rotterdam before."}

{"request_id":"0330b2410b10359fd74b843e","rewritten_text":"The stars still shone brightly when I woke, and Taurus high in the southern sky showed that it was midnight. I woke from disturbed dreams. It seemed to me that I had been invited to Timon’s last feast; I came with a sharp appetite. The covers were removed, hot water was brought up, and its steam rose in an unsatisfying haze, while I fled before the anger of the host, who took the form of Raymond. In my sick imagination, the vessels he hurled after me were filled with foul vapor, and my friend’s shape—warped by a thousand distortions—grew into a gigantic phantom, with the sign of pestilence stamped on its brow. The shadow kept rising and rising, filling everything, and then seeming to strain as if it would burst through the adamantine vault that arched over, holding up and enclosing the world. The nightmare became torture. With a strong effort, I shook off sleep and brought reason back to its usual work.

My first thought was Perdita. I had to return to her; I had to support her, drawing whatever food from despair might best sustain her wounded heart. I tried to bring her back from the wild excesses of grief, under the austere laws of duty, and with the gentle tenderness of regret.

The position of the stars was my only guide. I turned away from the terrible ruin of the Golden City, and, after great effort, managed to get myself out of its enclosure. I met a group of soldiers outside the walls; I borrowed a horse from one of them and hurried to my sister. In the short time I was gone, the plain looked different. The encampment had been broken up; the remains of the disbanded army were scattered in small groups here and there. Every face was clouded; every gesture said astonishment and dismay.

With a heavy heart, I entered the palace and stood there, afraid to move forward—to speak, to even look. In the middle of the hall was Perdita. She sat on the marble floor, her head fallen to her chest, her hair disheveled, her fingers busy, one within the other. She was pale as marble, and every feature was tightened by agony. She saw me and looked up, asking without words; that half glance of hope turned to misery. The words died before I could form them. I felt a ghastly smile pull at my lips. She understood my gesture; her head fell again, and her fingers kept working restlessly. At last I found my voice, but it frightened her. The poor girl had understood my look, and for all the world she would not have wanted the story of her heavy misery shaped and confirmed by harsh, irreversible words. No—she seemed to want to distract my thoughts from it. She rose from the floor and whispered, “Hush! After much weeping, Clara sleeps. We must not disturb her.”"}

{"request_id":"6d862c1404233133dd163c4d","rewritten_text":"“And do consider, ma’am,” said Oliver, with the tears pressing into his eyes in spite of every effort to keep them back. “Oh! think how young and how good she is, and how much pleasure and comfort she brings to everyone about her. I am sure—quite sure—no doubt at all—that, for your sake, who are so kind yourself; and for her own; and for the happiness she makes for all—she will not die. Heaven will never allow her to die so soon.”

“Hush!” said Mrs. Maylie, putting her hand on Oliver’s head. “You speak like a child, poor boy. Still, you remind me of my duty. I had forgotten it for a moment, Oliver, but I hope I may be forgiven; I am old, and I have seen enough of illness and death to know the agony of parting from those we love. I have seen enough, too, to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are spared to those that cherish them; but this ought to comfort us in our grief. Heaven is just; and such lessons, in a way, teach us there is a brighter world than this, and that the road to it is swift. God’s will be done! I love her—and He knows how truly!”

Oliver was startled to observe that, as Mrs. Maylie spoke these words, she checked her lamentations as if by a single effort; and, drawing herself up, she became composed and steady. He was even more astonished to learn that this steadiness did not fail her; for, amid all the care and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie remained ready and collected—carrying out every duty that had fallen to her, steadily, and, so far as anyone could see, even with cheerfulness. Yet Oliver was young, and did not understand what strong minds can endure when circumstances press hard. How could he, when those who possess such strength so rarely know their own power?

An anxious night passed. When morning came, Mrs. Maylie’s fears were only too well confirmed. Rose had entered the first stage of a high and dangerous fever.

“We must be active, Oliver, and not give way to useless grief,” said Mrs. Maylie, touching her finger to her lip as she looked straight into his face. “This letter must be sent, with the greatest speed, to Mr. Losberne. It must be taken to the market-town—which is no more than four miles away by the footpath across the field—and then, from there, dispatched by an express on horseback straight to Chertsey. The people at the inn will manage it; and I can rely on you to see that it is done, I know.”

Oliver had no answer to give, but he could not help showing how eager he was for it to be done at once."}

{"request_id":"e578b03e5b2b9e8f34ad6d4c","rewritten_text":"Other chances of observing her could not fail to present themselves. Anne was soon thrown into the company of all four together often enough to form an opinion, though she was too discreet to own it at home, where she knew it would satisfy neither husband nor wife; for though she judged Louisa to be the favourite, she could not help thinking—so far as she dared judge from what she remembered and had seen—that Captain Wentworth was not in love with either. They were, indeed, more in love with him; but that was not love. It was rather a little fever of admiration, which might, and probably must, turn into love. Charles Hayter appeared to be conscious of being slighted; and yet Henrietta had sometimes an air of being split between them. Anne longed for the power of making them all understand what they were doing, and of showing them the mischief they were laying themselves open to. She did not suppose any of them acted from guile. It was her greatest comfort to believe that Captain Wentworth was in no way aware of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph—no poor, pitiable triumph—in his manner. He had, most likely, never heard, and certainly never considered, any claims of Charles Hayter. His fault lay only in accepting—accepting must be the word—the attentions of two young women at once.

After a short struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to give up the contest. Three days went by without his coming once to Uppercross; a very decided alteration. He had even declined one of his usual invitations to dinner; and when Mr Musgrove found him on the occasion with several large books before him, Mr and Mrs Musgrove were persuaded that all could not be right, and talked gravely of his studying himself to death. Mary’s hope and belief was that he had received a plain dismissal from Henrietta; and her husband lived in a constant expectation of seeing him the next day. Anne could only think that Charles Hayter was wise.

One morning, about this time, when Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth were out shooting together, the sisters in the Cottage sat quietly at their work, and were visited at the window by the sisters from the Mansion-house.

It was a very fine November day, and the Miss Musgroves came through the little grounds, stopping for no other purpose than to say that they were going to take a long walk, and therefore concluded Mary could not care to go with them. When Mary, at once answering—somewhat with jealousy that she should not be thought a good walker—“Oh, yes, I should like to join you very much; I am very fond of a long walk,” Anne felt, from the looks of the two girls, that it was exactly what they did not wish. She admired again the kind of necessity which the family habits seemed to impose, of having everything communicated and everything done together, even when it was undesired and inconvenient."}

{"request_id":"c49328078c8371f2a70224d6","rewritten_text":"At last it was arranged that we should live together during my stay in the city. Since my circumstances in the world were somewhat less strained than his, I was allowed to cover the cost of renting and furnishing a place in a style that matched the rather fantastic gloom of our shared temperament: an old, time-worn, grotesque mansion, long abandoned—through superstitions we never bothered to question—and already leaning toward collapse in a secluded, desolate part of the Faubourg St. Germain.

If the routine of our life here had become known to the world, we would have been seen as madmen—though perhaps harmless ones. Our seclusion was complete. We admitted no visitors. In fact, the location of our retreat had been kept carefully secret even from my former associates; and it had been many years since Dupin had stopped knowing Paris, or being known there. We lived within ourselves alone.

It was a quirk of fancy in my friend (what else should I call it?) to be in love with the night for its own sake; and into this _bizarrerie_, as into all his other whims, I quietly fell, surrendering myself to his wild desires with complete _abandon_. The sable divinity would not remain with us all the time, but we could imitate her presence. At the first dawn of morning we shut all the messy shutters of our old building, and lit a couple of tapers—strongly perfumed—that cast only the ghastliest, faintest light. With their help we then occupied our minds with dreams: reading, writing, or talking, until the clock warned us that true Darkness was on its way. Then we would go out into the streets arm in arm, continuing the day’s topics or wandering far and wide until late, searching amid the city’s wild lights and shadows for that infinity of mental excitement that quiet observation can provide.

At such times I couldn’t help noticing and admiring (though, from his rich idealism, I had been prepared to expect it) Dupin’s particular analytic ability. He seemed, too, to take eager pleasure in using it—if not exactly in showing it—and he did not hesitate to admit the satisfaction he got from it. With a low chuckling laugh, he told me that most men, in his view, carried windows in their own chests, and that he liked to follow up such claims with direct and very startling proofs of his intimate knowledge of my own. His manner at those moments was cold and abstract; his eyes looked empty of expression; and while his voice was usually a rich tenor, it would rise into a treble that might have sounded petulant—except that the enunciation was so deliberate and so perfectly clear."}

{"request_id":"b0c29fa29556a4de19c1fd62","rewritten_text":"It was up to the young lady to say that she did not, in so many words, affirm that she would not; instead, she only made an emphatic, earnest plea to be “blessed” if she would. It was a polite, delicate way of dodging the request, showing that the young lady had the kind of natural good breeding that cannot bear to inflict on another person the pain of a direct, pointed refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned away from this young lady—bright and, if anything, gorgeously dressed in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers—and looked to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” said the Jew in a soothing tone, “what do you say?”

“That won’t do; so there’s no point trying it on, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” Mr. Sikes demanded, looking up in a surly way.

“What I mean, Bill,” the lady said, keeping her composure.

“Why, you’re just the right person for it,” Mr. Sikes reasoned. “Nobody around here knows anything about you.”

“And since I don’t want them to,” Nancy answered in the same steady manner, “it’s more no than yes with me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” said Nancy.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” said Sikes.

And Mr. Sikes was right. Through a mix of threats, promises, and bribes, the woman in question was finally persuaded to take on the job. She was not held back by the same concerns as her agreeable friend; for, having recently moved into the area of Field Lane from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, she had no fear of being recognized by any of her many acquaintances.

So, with a clean white apron tied over her gown, and her curl-papers tucked up under a straw bonnet—both items of clothing supplied from the Jew’s inexhaustible stock—Miss Nancy prepared to go out on her errand.

“Stop a minute, my dear,” said the Jew, producing a small, slightly covered basket. “Carry that in one hand. It looks more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door-key to carry in her other one, Fagin,” said Sikes. “It looks real and genuine like.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, it does,” the Jew agreed, slipping a large street-door key onto the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There. Very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” the Jew said, rubbing his hands.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried, bursting into tears, and clutching the little basket and the street-door key with an agony of distress. “What’s happened to him! Where have they taken him! Oh, please have pity—tell me what’s been done with the dear boy, gentlemen; do, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”"}

{"request_id":"759873e9e84d85e43700b0f0","rewritten_text":"Perdita’s name was never said, but I could not doubt that his love for her was what made him change his mind so often. And who was more deserving of love than my noble-minded sister? Who should have the hand of this self-important king more than she, whose look belonged to a queen among nations? Who loved him as he loved her—despite the disappointment that cooled her passion, while ambition kept fighting hard against it.

We went together to the House in the evening. Raymond knew that their plans and prospects would be discussed and decided in the debate that everyone expected, yet he was cheerful and careless. As we entered the coffee-room, a sound rose up—like the buzzing of ten thousand swarming bees—that stunned us. Groups of politicians stood together, their brows anxious, their voices loud or deep. The aristocratic party—the richest and most influential men in England—seemed less upset than the others, because the question was going to be discussed without their interference. Near the fire were Ryland and his supporters.

Ryland was a man of unknown or humble birth, but with immense wealth that he had inherited from his father, a manufacturer. As a young man, he had seen the king give up the throne, and the two houses of Lords and Commons join together. He had sympathized with these popular changes, and it had been his life’s work to strengthen and increase them. Since then, the power of the landed gentry had grown. At first, Ryland was not sorry to see Lord Raymond’s schemes, which pulled many of his opponents’ supporters away. But now it had gone too far. The poorer nobility welcomed the return of sovereignty, believing it would bring back the power and rights they had lost. In people’s minds, the half-forgotten spirit of royalty stirred again. They were willing slaves, self-made subjects, ready to bend their necks to the yoke. Some upright, strong men still remained—pillars of state—but the word republic had grown dull to ordinary ears. And many, as the event would show—whether it was a majority or not—still longed for the glitter and show of royalty. Ryland felt the need to resist. He claimed that only his own tolerance had allowed this party to grow, but he said the time for indulgence was over. With one motion of his arm, he would sweep away the cobwebs that blinded his countrymen.

When Raymond entered the coffee-room, his friends greeted him almost like a shout. They gathered around him, counted their numbers, and explained the reasons they were about to gain an addition of so many members—people who had not yet declared themselves."}

{"request_id":"f025e002c011868c8d2434ea","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, purely for his own amusement, would never take up any book except the Baronetage. There he found something to occupy an idle hour, and a kind of comfort in times of trouble; there his mind was stirred into admiration and respect by the sight of the scanty remains of the earliest patents; and there, whenever any unpleasant feeling rose out of domestic matters, it slipped away into pity and contempt as he turned over the almost endless productions of the last century. Even if every other leaf proved dull, he could still read his own story with an interest that never failed. That was the very page where the favourite volume always opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

The paragraph had stood in precisely that form as it came from the printer; yet Sir Walter had improved it, adding—both for his own information and that of his family—these words after the date of Mary’s birth: “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset,” and inserting with the greatest care the day of the month on which he had lost his wife.

After this came the usual account of the family’s antiquity and rise: how it was first established in Cheshire; how it was mentioned in Dugdale; how it had held the office of high sheriff; how it had returned members for a borough in three successive parliaments; how it had shown loyalty and dignity of baronetcy in the first year of Charles II, with all the Marys and Elizabeths they had married. Altogether it made up two neat duodecimo pages, and ended with the arms and motto:—“Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” and Sir Walter’s handwriting again at the close:—

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character—vanity of person and of station. He had been remarkably handsome in his youth, and at fifty-four was still a very fine-looking man. Few women could think more highly of their own appearance than he did; nor could the valet of any newly made lord be more pleased with the place he held in society. He ranked the blessing of beauty as next only to the blessing of a baronetcy; and the Sir Walter Elliot, who possessed both, was the constant object of his warmest respect and devotion.

His good looks and his rank gave him a further claim to attachment; for to them he must have owed a wife of a character far superior to anything his own merits could have warranted."}

I really must talk to him about buying a donkey. In the country, I think it’s almost a necessity; because no matter how many resources a woman has, it isn’t possible for her to be shut up at home all the time. And you know—long walks in summer mean dust, and in winter mean dirt.”

“You won’t find either between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and it’s perfectly dry right now. Come on a donkey, if you’d rather. You can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I’d like everything to be as much to your taste as possible.”

“That I’m sure you would. Indeed, I give you credit for it, my good friend. Under that particular kind of dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you’re a complete humorist.—Yes, believe me, Knightley, I’m fully aware of your attention to me throughout all of this plan. You’ve hit on exactly what will please me.”

Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding a table in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the party; and he knew that if either of them sat down outdoors to eat, it would inevitably make him ill. Mr. Woodhouse must not, under the flattering excuse of a morning drive and an hour or two spent at Donwell, be tempted away from his misery.

He was invited in good faith. There were no hidden horrors waiting to punish him for his easy trust. He did agree. He hadn’t been to Donwell for two years. “Some very fine morning, he, and Emma, and Harriet, could go very well; and he could sit still with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked about the gardens. He didn’t suppose they could be damp now, in the middle of the day. He should like to see the old house again very much, and would be very happy to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton, and any other of his neighbors.—He couldn’t see any objection at all to his, and Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there some very fine morning. He thought it very well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—very kind and sensible—much cleverer than dining out. He wasn’t fond of dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was fortunate in everyone’s ready agreement. The invitation was received everywhere so well that it seemed, as with Mrs. Elton, they were all taking the scheme as a special compliment to themselves. Emma and Harriet spoke of having very high expectations of pleasure from it; and Mr. Weston, without being asked, promised to get Frank to join them if possible—a proof of approval and gratitude that could have been spared. Mr. Knightley then had to say that he would be glad to see him; and Mr. Weston promised to waste no time in writing, and to spare no arguments to persuade him to come."}

{"request_id":"9671d90b650d07461ea2b0fa","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I think, sir,” said the spy, in the most grudging tone, turning to Mr. Lorry, “I may fairly appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness—ask you to put it to this other gentleman, so much younger than you—whether, under any circumstances, he can reconcile it with his position to play that Ace he has mentioned. I’ll own that I am a spy, and that it’s a station held in disrepute—though somebody must fill it; but this gentleman is not a spy. Why should he lower himself to become one?”

“I’ll play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, taking the answer upon himself, and glancing at his watch, “without the least hesitation, in only a few minutes.”

“I had hoped, gentlemen both,” the spy went on, still trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the talk, “that your regard for my sister—”

“I can show my respect for your sister no better than by at last freeing her from her brother,” said Sydney Carton.

“You don’t think so, sir?”

“I’ve made up my mind about it.”

The spy’s smoothness—oddly at odds with his showily rough appearance, and no doubt with his usual manner—met with such a check from the inscrutability of Carton, who was a puzzle even to wiser and better men, that it faltered and failed him. While he hesitated, Carton spoke again, falling back into his former look of studying the cards:

“And now, thinking it over, I’m under a strong impression that I have another good card here, one not yet named. That friend and fellow-sheep who spoke of himself as pasturing in the country prisons—who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” said the spy, promptly.

“French, is it?” Carton repeated, musing, and seeming not to notice him at all, though he echoed the word. “Well; he may be.”

“I assure you,” said the spy, “it’s French—though it isn’t of consequence.”

“Not of consequence,” Carton repeated in the same mechanical fashion—“not of consequence—No, it isn’t of consequence. No. Still, I know the face.”

“I don’t think so. I’m sure not. It can’t be,” said the spy.

“It-can’t-be,” Sydney Carton muttered, looking back on it, and idling his glass again (happily it was a small one). “Can’t be. He spoke good French. Yet, like a foreigner, I thought?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” cried Carton, slapping his open hand on the table, as a light broke in upon his mind. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had that fellow before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now, there you go too fast, sir,” said Barsad, with a smile that tipped his aquiline nose a little more to one side; “you really do give me an advantage over you.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"a01f11570477d4f73023db0c","rewritten_text":"“April 7th. I got up early, and, to my great joy, at last I saw what there could be no hesitation in believing was the northern Pole itself. It was there beyond doubt, immediately beneath my feet; but, alas, I had now risen to such a vast height that nothing could be discerned with any accuracy. Indeed, judging from the sequence of numbers showing my various altitudes at different times—between 6 A.M. on April 2 and twenty minutes before 9 A.M. that same day (when the barometer dropped)—it could fairly be inferred that the balloon had, by 4 A.M. on April 7, reached a height of not less than, certainly, 7,254 miles above the surface of the sea. That elevation may seem immense, but the estimate on which it is based likely gives a result far below the truth. In any case, I undoubtedly beheld the entire major diameter of the earth; the whole northern hemisphere lay beneath me like a chart projected orthographically, and the great circle of the equator itself formed the boundary line of my horizon. Your Excellencies may, however, easily imagine that the confined regions within the Arctic circle—though they were directly beneath me and therefore seen without any apparent foreshortening—were still, in themselves, comparatively too small, and too far from the point of view, to allow any very accurate examination. Still, what could be seen was singular and thrilling. Northward from that huge rim I mentioned—more or less the limit of human discovery in these regions—there continues an unbroken, or nearly unbroken, sheet of ice. In the first few degrees of its progress, its surface is very noticeably flattened; farther on it sinks into a plane, and finally, becoming somewhat concave, it ends at the Pole itself in a sharply defined circular center. Its apparent diameter, as seen from the balloon, subtended an angle of about sixty-five seconds, and its dusky color, varying in intensity, was at all times darker than any other spot on the visible hemisphere, and at times deepened into the most absolute and impenetrable blackness. Beyond that, little could be determined. By twelve o’clock the circular center had decreased materially in circumference, and by seven P.M. I lost sight of it entirely, as the balloon passed over the western edge of the ice and floated away rapidly in the direction of the equator.\n\n“April 8th. I noticed a clear decrease in the earth’s apparent diameter, along with a material change in its overall color and appearance.”"}

{"request_id":"df3db120a617cdf5e801702e","rewritten_text":"But in that harsh rant about Chantilly, printed in yesterday’s “Musée,” the satirist made some ugly references to how the cobbler changed his name when he took up the buskin. Then he quoted a Latin line we have talked about many times. I mean the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I told you that this line was meant to refer to Orion, which used to be written Urion. And because of the sharp hints in the way I explained it, I knew you couldn’t have forgotten. So it was obvious you would put together the two ideas of Orion and Chantilly. The fact that you did combine them was clear from the smile that crossed your lips. You were thinking about the poor cobbler’s destruction. Up to then, you had been walking with a slight bend in your posture, but now I saw you straighten up to your full height. At that moment, I was sure you were thinking about how small Chantilly is. Then I interrupted your thoughts to say that, since he really was a very little man, Chantilly would do better at the Théâtre des Variétés.”

Not long after that, we were looking through an evening edition of the “Gazette des Tribunaux” when the following paragraphs caught our attention.

“Extraordinary Murders.—This morning, at about three o’clock, the people of the Quartier St. Roch were woken from sleep by a series of terrifying screams. They seemed to be coming from the fourth floor of a house on the Rue Morgue, a place known to be occupied only by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay—caused by a failed attempt to get in the usual way—the gate was forced open with a crowbar. Eight or ten neighbors entered with two gendarmes. By then, the screams had stopped. But as the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, they could hear two or more rough voices arguing angrily, and it seemed the voices were coming from the top part of the house. When they reached the second landing, those sounds also stopped, and everything was perfectly quiet. The party searched room to room, moving quickly. When they arrived at a large back room on the fourth story—where the door was found locked, with the key still inside, so they had to force it open—they saw something that filled everyone there with horror as well as amazement.

“The room was in the wildest mess. The furniture was broken and thrown in every direction. There was only one bedstead, and the bed had been taken off and thrown into the middle of the floor. On a chair sat a razor covered in blood.”"}

{"request_id":"e8a88c5d9ba4bc4f65859b33","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse—handsome, clever, and rich—had a comfortable home and a cheerful disposition, and she seemed to bring together some of the best blessings life has to offer. She had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with very little to distress or upset her.

She was the younger of two daughters of a deeply affectionate, indulgent father; and, as a result of her sister’s marriage, she had been in charge of his household from a very early age. Her mother had died long enough ago that Emma could only remember her caresses vaguely; her place had been taken by an excellent woman as governess, who fell little short of a mother in affection.

For sixteen years, Miss Taylor had been in Mr. Woodhouse’s family—not so much as a governess as a friend. She was fond of both daughters, but especially of Emma. Between them, it was more like the closeness of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor had stopped holding the nominal office of governess, her gentle temperament had hardly allowed her to impose any real restraint; and with the shadow of authority long gone, they had been living together as friend and friend, mutually devoted, while Emma did exactly what she pleased. She held Miss Taylor’s judgment in high regard, but was guided chiefly by her own.

The real downsides of Emma’s situation, however, were having rather too much of her own way and a tendency to think a little too highly of herself. Those were the disadvantages that threatened to spoil some of her many enjoyments. The danger, though, was so completely unrecognized at present that it did not, by any means, count as a misfortune to her.

Sorrow came—a gentle sorrow—but not in the form of any unpleasant awareness. Miss Taylor married. It was Miss Taylor’s loss that first brought grief. On the wedding day of this beloved friend, Emma first found herself sitting in mournful thought about any future without her. After the ceremony was over and the wedding guests had gone, Emma and her father were left to dine together, with no prospect of a third person to make a long evening feel less empty. Her father, as usual, settled himself to sleep after dinner, and then Emma had only to sit and think about what she had lost.

The event promised happiness for her friend in every way. Mr. Weston was a man of unexceptionable character, with an easy fortune, a suitable age, and pleasant manners; and there was some comfort in knowing that Emma had always wished for and encouraged the match with self-denying, generous friendship. Still, it was a bleak morning’s work for Emma. The absence of Miss Taylor would be felt every hour of every day. She remembered the kindness of the past—the kindness and affection of sixteen years—how Miss Taylor had taught and played with her since she was five, how she had devoted all her abilities to attaching and entertaining her in good health, and how she had nursed her through the various illnesses of childhood."}

{"request_id":"450e5c48bd4612e3383c252c","rewritten_text":"Everything was settled in a friendly, satisfactory way, so the contract was formally agreed to with another small cup of the peppermint mixture. This was especially necessary because the lady’s spirits were fluttering and unsettled. While the mixture was being finished, she told Mr. Bumble that the old woman had died.

“Very good,” said Mr. Bumble, sipping his peppermint. “I’ll stop by Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to send it tomorrow morning. Was it that which frightened you, love?”

“It wasn’t anything in particular, dear,” the lady said, trying to avoid the question.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble pressed. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” the lady replied. “One of these days. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” Mr. Bumble exclaimed. “It wasn’t any impudence from any of those male paupers—”

“No, no, love!” the lady interrupted quickly.

“If I thought it was,” Mr. Bumble went on, “if I thought any of them had dared to look at that lovely face—”

“They wouldn’t have dared to do it, love,” the lady answered.

“They had better not!” Mr. Bumble said, clenching his fist. “Let me see any man, whether he’s from the parish or not, who would presume to do it, and I’ll tell him he won’t do it a second time!”

Without any fancy show of violence, this might not have sounded like the highest praise for the lady’s looks. But because Mr. Bumble backed up his threat with plenty of angry, warlike gestures, she felt very touched by it and insisted, with great admiration, that he was truly a dove.

The dove then pulled up his coat collar and put on his cocked hat. After sharing a long, affectionate embrace with his future partner, he faced the cold night air again. He only paused for a few minutes in the male paupers’ ward, where he let them have a bit of abuse, just to make sure he could do the job of workhouse-master with the right sharpness. Once he was satisfied he could handle it, Mr. Bumble left the building with a light heart and bright hopes of being promoted. Those thoughts kept him busy until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Now, Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out for tea and supper, and Noah Claypole was never the kind of person to take on more physical effort than was needed for eating and drinking. So the shop was not closed, even though it was past the usual time for shutting up. Mr. Bumble tapped his cane on the counter several times, but no one answered. Seeing a light through the glass window of the small back room, he decided to look in and see what was happening. When he saw what was happening, he was quite surprised."}

{"request_id":"cf51663f145c944ca29a52ed","rewritten_text":"“No bringing it up by hand, then. Not a bit of it!”

Joe offered me more gravy, and I was afraid to take it.

“He was nothing but trouble for you, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble, speaking with sympathy about my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated. “Trouble?” Then she launched into a terrifying list of everything I had done wrong: every illness I was said to have caused, every time I had kept her awake, every time I had fallen from high places, every time I had fallen into low places, every injury I had done to myself, every time she had wished I were in my grave, and how stubbornly I had refused to go there.

I think the Romans must have annoyed each other a great deal with their noses. Maybe that’s why they became so restless. In any case, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose annoyed me so much while she was listing my mistakes that I wanted to pull it until he screamed. But everything I had endured so far was nothing compared to the awful feelings that took over me when my sister finished and there was a pause. During that pause, everyone looked at me with anger and disgust, and I felt it painfully.

“Still,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently steering the group back to the subject they had drifted away from, “Pork—boiled—is rich, too; isn’t it?”

“Have some brandy, uncle,” my sister said.

Oh, heavens—so it had finally come. He would taste it and say it was weak, and then I was finished. I gripped the leg of the table under the cloth with both hands and waited for what would happen.

My sister went for the stone bottle, came back with it, and poured his brandy out. No one else took any. The poor man played with his glass—picked it up, held it to the light, set it down again—dragging out my misery. All the while, Mrs. Joe and Joe were busy clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I couldn’t take my eyes off him. Still gripping the table leg with my hands and feet, I watched him finger his glass, lift it, smile, throw his head back, and drink the brandy. Right after that, the whole group was seized with terrible alarm. He sprang to his feet, turned around several times in a shocking, spasmodic coughing dance, and rushed out through the door. Then he appeared at the window, violently coughing and spitting, making the most horrible faces, and acting as if he had lost his mind.

I held on tight while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to him."}

{"request_id":"35a5ff7515d44a5b36c85b34","rewritten_text":"On my return, I found the following letter from my father:—

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably been waiting impatiently for a letter that will set the date of your return to us; and at first I was tempted to write only a few lines, just mentioning the day on which I expected you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I can’t bring myself to do it. What would be your surprise, my son, if, when you expected a happy and joyful welcome, you were met instead with tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I tell you about our misfortune? Absence cannot have made you indifferent to our joys and griefs; and how could I inflict pain on my long-absent son? I want to prepare you for the dreadful news, but I know it’s impossible. Even now, your eyes skim over the page, searching for the words that will bring you these horrible tidings.

“William is dead!—that sweet child, whose smiles delighted and warmed my heart, who was so gentle, yet so full of life! Victor, he is murdered!

“I won’t try to comfort you; I’ll simply lay out the circumstances of what happened.

“Last Thursday (May 7th), I, my niece, and your two brothers went for a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and peaceful, and we stayed out longer than usual. It was already dusk before we thought of going back; and then we realized that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were missing. We sat down on a bench and waited until they returned. Soon after, Ernest came and asked whether we had seen his brother. He said that he had been playing with him, that William had run away to hide, and that he had searched for him in vain; afterward he waited a long time, but William never came back.

“This account alarmed us, and we kept searching for him until night fell. Then Elizabeth suggested that he might have returned home. He was not there. We went back again with torches; I couldn’t rest, because I kept thinking that my sweet boy had gotten lost and was exposed to all the damp and dew of the night. Elizabeth was in terrible anguish as well. About five in the morning I found my lovely boy—whom, the night before, I had seen healthy, blooming, and active—lying on the grass, pale and motionless; the mark of the murderer’s finger was on his neck.

“He was taken home, and the anguish visible in my face revealed the truth to Elizabeth. She was very insistent on seeing the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she wouldn’t listen. She went into the room where it lay, hurriedly examined the neck of the victim, and clasping her hands cried out, ‘O God!’"}

{"request_id":"1ad4f4cda0482c0ef78079e7","rewritten_text":"Of course, he was very amusing, and all that, but I was terribly disappointed. When I asked him about the coat of mail, he only laughed and said it was far too cold to wear in England. Ah—here is Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I want you to tell the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, you must take your glove off. No—not the left hand, the other one.”

“Dear Gladys, I really don’t think it’s quite right,” said the Duchess, weakly unfastening a rather soiled kid glove.

“Nothing interesting ever is,” said Lady Windermere: “_on a fait le monde ainsi_. But I must introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my pet cheiromantist. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley, and if you say she has a larger mountain of the moon than I have, I’ll never believe in you again.”

“I’m sure, Gladys, there’s nothing of the kind in my hand,” said the Duchess gravely.

“Your Grace is quite right,” said Mr. Podgers, looking at the little fat hand with its short square fingers. “The mountain of the moon isn’t developed. The line of life, however, is excellent. Kindly bend the wrist. Thank you. Three distinct lines on the _rascette_! You’ll live to a great age, Duchess, and be extremely happy. Ambition—very moderate; the line of intellect not exaggerated; the line of heart—”

“Now, do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers,” cried Lady Windermere.

“Nothing would give me greater pleasure,” said Mr. Podgers, bowing, “if the Duchess had ever been, but I’m sorry to say I see great permanence of affection, combined with a strong sense of duty.”

“Please go on, Mr. Podgers,” said the Duchess, looking quite pleased.

“Economy is not the least of your Grace’s virtues,” continued Mr. Podgers, and Lady Windermere burst into fits of laughter.

“Economy is a very good thing,” remarked the Duchess complacently. “When I married Paisley he had eleven castles, and not a single house fit to live in.”

“And now he has twelve houses, and not a single castle,” cried Lady Windermere.

“Well, my dear,” said the Duchess, “I like—”

“Comfort,” said Mr. Podgers. “And modern improvements. And hot water laid on in every bedroom. Your Grace is quite right. Comfort is the only thing our civilisation can give us.”

“You’ve told the Duchess’s character admirably, Mr. Podgers, and now you must tell Lady Flora’s”; and, in answer to a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall girl with sandy Scotch hair and high shoulder-blades stepped awkwardly out from behind the sofa and held out a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers.

“Ah, a pianist! I see,” said Mr. Podgers. “An excellent pianist, but perhaps hardly a musician.”"}

{"request_id":"a30a2d8a5ac6bb98278f21e6","rewritten_text":"“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at some length, “there’s no denying that, since the new way of feeding has been brought in, the coffins are a bit narrower and not so deep as they used to be; still, we must make some profit, Mr. Bumble. Well-seasoned timber is dear enough, sir, and every iron handle comes, by canal, straight from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” said Mr. Bumble, “every business has its drawbacks. A reasonable profit, of course, is to be expected.”

“Certainly, certainly,” returned the undertaker. “And if I don’t turn a profit on this or that particular item, why, I make it up in the long run, you understand—he! he! he!”

“Just so,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Yet I must add,” continued the undertaker, picking up the thread of talk the beadle had interrupted, “that I’m up against one serious disadvantage: the stout people are the first to go. Those who’ve had the better of it, and have paid rates for years, are the earliest to sink as soon as they’re brought into the house; and I can tell you, Mr. Bumble, that three or four inches beyond one’s estimate makes a tremendous difference to one’s profits—especially when a man has a family to support, sir.”

As Mr. Sowerberry said this, with the proper indignation of someone ill-used; and as Mr. Bumble felt it tended to cast a reflection on the parish’s honour, he thought it best to change the subject. Oliver Twist was uppermost in his mind, so he turned to him.

“By the bye,” said Mr. Bumble, “you don’t happen to know anyone who wants a boy, do you? A porochial ’prentis—at the moment he’s dead weight; a millstone, if you like, round the porochial throat. Liberal terms, Mr. Sowerberry—liberal terms?”

As he spoke, he lifted his cane to the board above him and gave three clear raps on the words “five pounds,” printed there in Roman capitals of enormous size.

“Gadso!” said the undertaker, catching Mr. Bumble by the gilt-edged lapel of his official coat. “That’s exactly what I wanted to speak to you about. You know—dear me—what a fine-looking button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it’s rather handsome,” said the beadle, looking down with pride at the large brass buttons that adorned his coat. “The die matches the porochial seal—the Good Samaritan healing the sick and bruised man. The board gave it me on Newyear’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember putting it on for the first time to attend the inquest on that reduced tradesman, who died in a doorway at midnight.”"}

{"request_id":"95dc5a6df7e0bedb2feab02a","rewritten_text":"“You haven’t been in Bath long enough,” he said, “to enjoy the evening parties here.”

“Oh! no. There’s nothing in the usual kind of them that interests me. I don’t play cards.”

“You didn’t used to,” he replied. “I know you didn’t care for cards before, but time changes a great deal.”

“I’m not changed that much yet,” cried Anne, stopping, because she feared she might be misunderstood. After a pause, he went on, as if the words came straight from what he felt. “It really is a long time! Eight and a half years is a long time.”

Whether he would have said more was left for Anne to think about later, in a calmer moment. Even while she still heard what he had just said, Henrietta called out to her, eager to use the moment’s leisure to go out. She urged her companions not to waste time, in case someone else came in.

They had to move. Anne said she was perfectly ready, and tried to look that way, but she felt that if Henrietta had known the regret and reluctance in her heart as she left that chair, and then prepared to leave the room, she would have understood it in everything she felt for her cousin. Even in the safety of his affection, she could not help but pity him.

But their plans were cut short. Scary sounds were heard, other visitors arrived, and the door was thrown open for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot. Their entrance seemed to bring a chill into the room. Anne felt it at once. Wherever she looked, she saw the same signs. The comfort, freedom, and lively spirit of the room were gone. Everything settled into cold politeness, stiff silence, or dull conversation meant to match the heartless elegance of her father and sister. It was humiliating to realize it.

Her jealous thoughts were satisfied in one respect. Captain Wentworth was recognized again by everyone, and Elizabeth was even more gracious than before. She spoke to him once, and then looked at him more than once. In fact, Elizabeth was working out a plan. The rest soon showed what it was. After wasting a few minutes on the usual empty talk, she began the invitation that would cover all the remaining obligations owed by the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends. No formal party.”

She said it very smoothly. The cards she had prepared—the “Miss Elliot at home”—were placed on the table with a polite, welcoming smile for everyone. She gave Captain Wentworth one more smile, and one more card. The truth was that Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to understand how important it was to have a man with his kind of presence and appearance."}
