{"request_id":"12d4045154bf75be4604bba5","rewritten_text":"But he had wronged no one, and he had jailed no one. So far was he from squeezing out the dues with any harsh hand, that he had surrendered them freely of his own accord; he had thrown himself among a world that offered him no special kindness, found his own private footing there, and earned his own daily bread. Monsieur Gabelle, acting on written directions, had managed the impoverished and entangled estate with the aim of sparing the people—giving them what little there was to give: such fuel as the heavy creditors would allow them in winter, and such produce as could be kept safe from the same grasp in summer. No doubt he had set down the matter as both plea and proof, for his own security, so that it could not help but look so now.

This was the kind of favoured, desperate resolve Charles Darnay had begun to form: that he would go to Paris.

Yes. As in the old tale of the mariner, the winds and currents had carried him under the pull of the Loadstone Rock; it was drawing him on, and he must go. Whatever rose in his thoughts only drove him forward—faster and faster, more and more surely—toward that dreadful attraction. The uneasiness he had kept hidden within him was that wicked purposes were being carried out in his own unhappy country by wicked instruments; and that he, who could not but know himself better than they, was not there, trying to put a stop to bloodshed and to uphold the claims of mercy and humanity. With that uneasiness half smothered and half reproaching him, he was led to the sharp comparison of himself with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so firm; and from that comparison (to his own hurt) there came at once Monseigneur’s sneers, which had stung him cruelly, and Stryver’s as well—above all, coarse and cutting, for old reasons. After these came Gabelle’s letter: the appeal of an innocent prisoner, facing death, to his justice, his honour, and his good name.

His resolution was fixed. He must go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was drawing him, and he must keep sailing until he struck. He knew of no rock, and he hardly saw any peril. The very intention with which he had done what he had done—even though he had left it unfinished—presented itself to him as something that, if he appeared in France to assert it, would be received with grateful recognition. Then that bright vision of doing good, which is so often the sanguine mirage of good minds, rose before him too; and he even imagined himself, in the illusion, with some influence to guide this Revolution, running so fearfully wild."}

{"request_id":"5aa53c3c2c7f76f7e7d0c1e3","rewritten_text":"He also had to think about Sybil’s father and mother, who were rather old-fashioned people and might object to the marriage if there was anything that looked like a scandal, though he felt sure that if he told them the full facts of the case, they would be the very first to understand the motives that had driven him. So he had every reason to decide in favor of poison. It was safe, reliable, and quiet, and it removed the need for any painful scenes, to which, like most Englishmen, he had a deep, rooted objection.

He knew absolutely nothing about the science of poisons, however, and since the waiter seemed unable to find anything in the library except Ruff’s Guide and Bailey’s Magazine, he examined the shelves himself. At last he came across a handsomely bound edition of the Pharmacopoeia, and a copy of Erskine’s Toxicology, edited by Sir Mathew Reid, the President of the Royal College of Physicians, and one of the oldest members of the Buckingham—having been elected by mistake for someone else. That contretemps enraged the Committee so much that when the real man came forward, they blackballed him unanimously. Lord Arthur was quite puzzled by the technical terms used in both books, and had begun to regret that he hadn’t paid more attention to his classics at Oxford, when, in the second volume of Erskine, he found a very interesting and thorough account of the properties of aconitine, written in fairly clear English. It seemed to him to be exactly the poison he wanted. It worked fast—almost immediate in its effect—was perfectly painless, and when taken in the form of a gelatine capsule, as Sir Mathew recommended, it was by no means unpleasant.

Accordingly, he made a note on his shirt cuff of the amount needed for a fatal dose, put the books back in their places, and strolled up St. James’s Street to Pestle and Humbey’s, the great chemists. Mr. Pestle, who always attended personally to the aristocracy, was rather surprised by the order and, in a very deferential manner, murmured something about needing a medical certificate. But as soon as Lord Arthur explained that it was for a large Norwegian mastiff he had to get rid of—since it showed signs of incipient rabies and had already bitten the coachman twice in the calf of the leg—he said he was perfectly satisfied. He complimented Lord Arthur on his wonderful knowledge of Toxicology and had the prescription made up immediately.

Lord Arthur put the capsule into a pretty little silver bonbonnière he’d seen in a shop window in Bond Street, threw away Pestle and Hambey’s ugly pill-box, and drove off at once to Lady Clementina’s."}

{"request_id":"946045dea9b9d70efecc4864","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and apologized. He said, “By no means,” and went on.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, and you can imagine she was being treated like a prize match. Her half-brother had plenty of money again, but between his debts and his new madness, he wasted it all most fearfully once more. There were stronger differences between him and her than there had been between him and his father, and it’s suspected that he carried a deep, mortal grudge against her for influencing the father’s anger. Now, I come to the cruel part of the story—simply pausing, my dear Handel, to point out that a dinner napkin won’t fit into a tumbler.”

Why I was trying to pack mine into my tumbler, I can’t say at all. I only know that I found myself, with a persistence that deserved a much better cause, making the most strenuous efforts to compress it within those limits. Again I thanked him and apologized, and again he said, in the cheeriest manner, “Not at all, I’m sure!” and continued.

“There appeared on the scene—say at the races, or the public balls, or anywhere else you like—a certain man who made love to Miss Havisham. I never saw him (this happened five-and-twenty years ago, before you and I were, Handel), but I’ve heard my father mention that he was showy, the kind of man for the job. But my father insists, with the strongest emphasis, that he must not be mistaken—without ignorance or prejudice—for a gentleman; because it’s a principle of his that no man who wasn’t a true gentleman at heart ever was, since the world began, a true gentleman in manner. He says no varnish can hide the grain of the wood; and the more varnish you put on, the more the grain will show. Well! This man pursued Miss Havisham closely and professed to be devoted to her. I believe she hadn’t shown much susceptibility up to that point; but all the susceptibility she had certainly came out then, and she passionately loved him. There’s no doubt she idolized him completely. He worked on her affection in that systematic way, getting large sums of money from her, and he persuaded her to buy her brother out of his share in the brewery (which had been left to him weakly by his father) at an enormous price, on the pretense that when he was her husband he would have to hold and manage it all. Your guardian wasn’t involved with Miss Havisham’s decisions at that time, and she was too proud and too much in love to be advised by anyone.”"}

{"request_id":"3b738528af937006ca33f7e6","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him for a few moments, amazed, and then, realizing that he was completely serious, wrote an address on a piece of paper, signed it with his initials, and slid it across the table to him.

“Scotland Yard would pay a lot to know that address, my dear fellow.”

“They won’t get it,” Lord Arthur said, laughing. After he warmly shook the young Russian’s hand, he hurried downstairs, checked the paper, and told the coachman to drive to Soho Square.

At Soho Square, he sent the coachman away and walked down Greek Street until he reached a place called Bayle’s Court. He went through the archway and found himself in a strange little dead-end street. It seemed to be used by a French laundry, because clothes-lines stretched from house to house, and white linen fluttered in the morning air. He walked all the way to the end and knocked on a small green house.

After a short wait—during which every window in the court turned into a blurry crowd of watching faces—the door opened. A rough-looking foreigner asked him, in very poor English, what he wanted. Lord Arthur handed over the paper Count Rouvaloff had given him. The man read it, bowed, and invited Lord Arthur into a very shabby front room on the ground floor. A few moments later, Herr Winckelkopf—what he was called in England—came bustling in. He had a wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork in his left hand.

“Count Rouvaloff has introduced me to you,” Lord Arthur said, bowing. “I’d like a short talk with you about business. My name is Smith—Mr. Robert Smith—and I need you to supply me with an explosive clock.”

“Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,” said the friendly little German, laughing. “Don’t look so worried. It’s my job to know everyone. I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I hope her ladyship is doing well. Would you mind sitting with me while I finish breakfast? There’s an excellent pâté, and my friends say my Rhine wine is better than anything they get at the German Embassy.”

Before Lord Arthur could fully get over the shock of being recognized, he found himself seated in the back room, sipping a delicious Marcobrünner from a pale yellow hock-glass marked with the Imperial monogram, and chatting in the most friendly way with the well-known conspirator.

“Explosive clocks,” said Herr Winckelkopf, “aren’t very good for sending abroad. Even if they manage to get through the Custom House, the train service is so unreliable that they usually go off before they reach the place they were meant to arrive.”"}

{"request_id":"e9eed38b3d79582cb422a728","rewritten_text":"Even reading about the luxury of the dead was wonderful.

Then he turned his attention to embroideries and to the tapestries that, in the cold rooms of northern Europe, did the same job frescoes would have done. As he looked into the subject—and he always had a rare ability to become completely absorbed in whatever he was doing—he felt almost sad when he thought about how time ruins beautiful and wonderful things. At least, he had escaped that. Summer came after summer, and the yellow jonquils bloomed and died again and again, while nights of horror repeated the story of their shame, but he stayed the same. No winter ever marred his face or spoiled his flowerlike beauty.

Material things were so different. Where had they gone? Where was the great crocus-colored robe, on which the gods fought the giants, made by brown girls for the pleasure of Athena? Where was the huge velarium Nero stretched across the Colosseum in Rome, that purple sail of the sky, showing the stars and Apollo driving a chariot pulled by white horses with gold reins? He longed to see the delicate table napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, covered with every kind of food and dish that could be wanted for a feast; the burial cloth of King Chilperic, with its three hundred golden bees; the strange robes that made the Bishop of Pontus so angry, and that were patterned with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—everything, in fact, that a painter can copy from nature”; and the coat Charles of Orleans once wore, with verses from a song embroidered on the sleeves. The song began “Madame, je suis tout joyeux,” and the music for the words was stitched in gold thread, with each note shaped like a square, and each note made with four pearls.

He read about the room prepared at the palace in Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, made in broidery, and blazoned with the king’s arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, whose wings were similarly ornamented with the arms of the queen, the whole worked in gold.” Catherine de Medicis had a mourning bed made for herself from black velvet dusted with crescents and suns. Its curtains were damask, with leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold and silver background, and the edges were fringed with pearl embroidery. It stood in a room lined with rows of the queen’s symbols, cut in black velvet on cloth of silver. Louis XIV. had gold-embroidered caryatids, fifteen feet tall, in his apartment."}

{"request_id":"26eb6840c4bdb3c176239ddc","rewritten_text":"You wouldn’t know anything about me unless you’d already read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that’s neither here nor there. That book was put together by Mr. Mark Twain, and for the most part he told the truth. Sure, there were bits he stretched, but mostly it was the truth. That’s nothing—people lie one way or another, and I’ve seen it; except maybe Aunt Polly, or the widow, or possibly Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly, she is—and Mary, and the Widow Douglas are the ones talked about in that book, which is mostly true, with a few stretches, like I said.

Now the way the story ends is this: Tom and me found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and that made us rich. We each got six thousand dollars—real gold. It was a terrible sight of money piled up. Well, Judge Thatcher took it and put it out on interest, and it paid us a dollar a day apiece, every day of the year—more than any person could say what to do with. The Widow Douglas took me for her son and said she’d civilize me, but living in her house all the time was hard going, what with how gloomy, regular, and proper she was in everything; so when I couldn’t stand it any longer, I slipped back into my old rags and my sugar-hogshead, and I was free and content. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and told me he was going to start a band of robbers, and I could join if I’d go back to the widow and act respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, and she gave me a heap of other names besides, but she didn’t mean any harm by it. She dressed me up in those new clothes again, and I just kept sweating and sweating, feeling all pinched and cramped. Then the same old business started up again. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to be there on time. When you got to the table, you couldn’t just start eating right away—you had to sit and wait while the widow bowed her head and grumbled a little over the food, though there wasn’t really anything wrong with it; nothing, except that everything was cooked by itself. In a barrel of odds and ends it’s different—things get mixed together, the juices kind of trade places, and the whole thing goes down better.

After supper she pulled out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was eager to learn all about him; but before long she let on that Moses had been dead for quite a long time. Then I didn’t care about him anymore, because I don’t put any faith in dead people."}

{"request_id":"d89a9ce0711b233a31b688ee","rewritten_text":"If I can’t live on that, then I won’t ask anyone to give me a lift. Is it satisfactory?”

There was a huge roar of applause, and from the middle of it the king’s voice rose, saying:

“Take off his bonds and set him free! Give him honor, high and low, rich and poor, because he has become the king’s right-hand man. He is clothed with power and authority, and his place is on the highest step of the throne! Now sweep away this creeping night and bring back light and cheer, so that the whole world may bless thee.”

But I said:

“It’s nothing if a common man is shamed in front of the world. But it would be an insult to the king if anyone who saw his minister naked did not also see him freed from his shame. If I may ask, let my clothes be brought back.”

“They won’t do,” the king interrupted. “Get him different clothes—clothe him like a prince!”

My plan worked. I wanted to keep things the way they were until the eclipse was completely over. Otherwise they would keep trying to get me to send the darkness away, and of course I couldn’t. Getting the clothes took some time, but not enough. So I had to make another excuse. I said it would be natural for the king to change his mind and regret, at least a little, what he had done in the heat of the moment. Therefore I would let the darkness last a while, and if, after a reasonable time, the king still kept the same decision, then the darkness could be dismissed. Neither the king nor anyone else liked that plan, but I had to stick to it.

The darkness kept growing darker and blacker as I struggled in those awkward clothes from the sixth century. At last it became pitch black, and the crowd groaned in horror as they felt the cold, strange night breezes blow through the place and saw the stars come out and twinkle in the sky. Finally the eclipse was total, and I was very glad of it, but everyone else was miserable, which was only to be expected. I said:

“The king, by his silence, still holds to the terms.” Then I raised my hands—held them there for a moment—and with the most solemn seriousness I said, “Let the enchantment dissolve and pass harmlessly away!”

For a moment there was no answer, in that deep darkness and that quiet, graveyard-like hush. But when the silver edge of the sun pushed out again, a moment or two later the whole crowd erupted with a huge shout. They rushed down like a flood to smother me with blessings and gratitude, and Clarence was not the last to join in, of course.”}"}

{"request_id":"228212c305c74fc4b2e94d0c","rewritten_text":"“It must have been about that same stretch of Mr. Elliot’s life,” said Anne, “the part of it that has always stirred my own particular curiosity. It must have been near the time he came to be known to my father and my sister. I never met him myself; I only heard of him; yet there was something in his behaviour toward my father and sister then, and afterwards in the circumstances of his marriage, that I could never quite bring to terms with the present day. It seemed to point to a different sort of man.”

“I understand it all, I understand it all,” cried Mrs. Smith. “He had been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I ever knew him, but I heard him talk of them again and again. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he chose not to go. I can set you right, perhaps, on matters you would hardly think to ask about; and as for his marriage, I knew everything at the time. I was privy to every turn of it—pros and cons alike; I was the friend to whom he laid out his hopes and plans. And though I had not known his wife before, her lower standing in society made that out of the question; still, I knew her all the rest of her life—at least until the last two years of it—and I can answer any question you may care to put.”

“Nay,” said Anne, “I have no special inquiry to make about her. I have always taken it that they were not a happy pair. But I should like to understand why, at that time of his life, he should have treated my father’s acquaintance so lightly, as he did. My father was certainly disposed to show him every kindness and proper attention. Why did Mr. Elliot step back?”

“Mr. Elliot,” replied Mrs. Smith, “at that period of his life, had one aim: to make his fortune, and by a quicker route than the law. He meant to secure it by marriage. He was resolved, at any rate, not to spoil it with an imprudent match; and I know it was his conviction—whether he was right or not, I cannot say—that your father and sister, with their civilities and invitations, were arranging a connection between the heir and the young lady, and that such a match could not possibly fit his notions of wealth and independence. That was why he drew back, I assure you. He told me the whole affair; there were no secrets between us. It was striking, too, that after you had just left me in Bath, my first and chief acquaintance on my marrying should be your cousin; and that, through him, I should be hearing of your father and sister without end.”"}

{"request_id":"a9888ebe08fe767298728817","rewritten_text":"This brief explanation from Mr. Knightley gave Emma real satisfaction. It belonged among the pleasant recollections of the ball; and the next morning she strolled about the lawn, lingering over it.—She was particularly pleased that matters had come to such a good understanding regarding the Eltons, and that their views of both husband and wife were so closely matched; and his praise of Harriet, together with his yielding to her in that point, was gratifying in a way that could not be mistaken. The Eltons’ impertinence, which for a few minutes had threatened to spoil the rest of her evening, had nevertheless been the very cause of some of its greatest comforts; and she looked forward to another happy consequence—the breaking of Harriet’s infatuation.—From Harriet’s way of speaking of what had occurred before they left the ballroom, Emma felt encouraged. It was as though her eyes had been opened at once, and she were now able to see that Mr. Elton was not the superior creature she had taken him for. The fever was gone, and Emma could scarcely fear that the pulse would be quickened again by any injurious civility. She relied on the Eltons’ ill-will to furnish all the further discipline of pointed neglect that might still be needed.—With Harriet reasoning, Frank Churchill not too deeply in love, and Mr. Knightley not disposed to quarrel with her, what a happy summer must be in store for her!

She was not to see Frank Churchill this morning. He had told her that he could not permit himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, since he was to be at home by the middle of the day. She did not regret it.

Having settled and reviewed everything, and put it all in order, she was just turning toward the house with spirits newly raised for the claims of the two little boys, as well as of their grandfather, when the great iron sweep-gate swung open and two persons entered whom she had least expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm—indeed Harriet!—In an instant she was sure that something extraordinary had taken place. Harriet looked pale and frightened, and he was trying to rouse her courage.—The iron gates and the front door were not more than twenty yards apart;—soon all three were in the hall, and Harriet at once sank into a chair and fainted away.

A young lady who faints must be brought round; questions must be put, and surprises explained. Such occurrences are certainly engaging, yet the suspense over them cannot last long. In a few minutes Emma learned the whole.

Miss Smith, and Miss Bickerton—another parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s, who had been at the ball as well—had gone out together and taken a road, the Richmond road; and though it looked public enough to be safe, it had carried them into alarm.—About half a mile beyond Highbury, after a sudden turn, and deeply shaded by elms on either side, it became for some distance very retired; and when the young ladies had gone some way into it, they suddenly perceived, at a little distance before them, on a broader patch of greensward beside the road, a party of gipsies."}

content.text: {"request_id":"59a9273902f8a4e5d753b485","rewritten_text":"In my day, in my own country, this money was collected from imposts, and the citizen imagined that the foreign importer paid it, and it made him comfortable to think so; whereas, in fact, it was paid by the American people, and was distributed among them so equally and exactly that the annual cost to the 100-millionaire and the annual cost to the day-laborer’s sucking child was precisely the same—each paid $6. Nothing could be more equal than that, I reckon. Well, Scotland and Ireland were tributary to Arthur, and the combined populations of the British Islands came to something less than 1,000,000. A mechanic’s average wage was 3 cents a day, when he paid his own keep. By that rule, the national government’s expenses were $90,000 a year, or about $250 a day. So, by substituting nickels for gold on a king’s-evil day, I not only harmed no one, dissatisfied no one, but pleased everyone involved and, besides, saved four-fifths of that day’s national expense—a saving that would have been the equivalent of $800,000 in my day in America. In making this substitution, I drew on the wisdom of a very remote source—the wisdom of my boyhood—for the true statesman does not despise any wisdom, no matter how humble its origin. In my boyhood, I had always saved my pennies and contributed buttons to the foreign missionary cause. The buttons would work on the ignorant savage as well as the coin; the coin would work better for me than the buttons. Everyone was happy, and nobody was hurt.\n\nMarinel took the patients as they came. He examined the candidate; if he couldn’t qualify, he was turned away; if he could, he was sent on to the king. A priest pronounced the words, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king stroked the ulcers while the reading continued; finally, the patient was approved, received his nickel—the king himself hanging it around his neck—and was dismissed. Would you think that would cure? It certainly did. Any kind of ritual will cure if the patient’s faith is strong. Up by Astolat there was a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who used to herd geese around there—the girl said so herself—and they built the chapel on that spot and hung a picture in it showing the occurrence—a picture you’d think would be dangerous for a sick person to approach. Yet, on the contrary, thousands of the lame and the sick came and prayed before it every year and went away whole and sound; and even the well could look at it and live."}

{"request_id":"edab86395d4b4231884aaabd","rewritten_text":"Yet he had one secret hidden from these dear friends—a secret he had nurtured since his earliest years. Even though he loved his fellow collegiates, he would not trust it to the delicacy or sympathy of anyone among them. He loved. He feared that the intensity of his passion might become the subject of their ridicule, and he could not bear for them to blaspheme it by treating as trivial and temporary what he felt was the life of his life.

There was a gentleman of small fortune who lived near his family mansion and had three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, but her beauty was only an addition to her other qualities—her understanding was clear and strong, and her disposition angelically gentle. She and my father had been playmates from infancy: Diana, even in childhood, had been a favorite with his mother. This partiality increased with the years of this beautiful and lively girl, and so during his school and college vacations they were perpetually together. Novels and all the various ways that youth in civilized life are led to learn about the existence of passions before they truly feel them had made a strong impression on him, since he was so unusually susceptible to every influence. At eleven years old, Diana was his favorite playmate, but he already spoke the language of love. Although she was nearly two years older than he was, the kind of education she had received made her more childish—at least in her knowledge and expression of feeling. She received his warm protestations with innocence and returned them without knowing what they meant. She had read no novels and associated only with her younger sisters; what could she know about the difference between love and friendship? And when the growth of her understanding revealed the true nature of their relationship to her, her affections were already committed to her friend. All she feared was that other attractions and fickleness might make him break his childish vows.

But their feelings became every day more ardent and tender. It was a passion that had grown with his growth; it had become entwined with every faculty and every sentiment, and it could be lost only with life. None knew of their love except their own two hearts. Yet in everything else—and even in this, though he dreaded the censure of his companions—for loving someone beneath him in fortune, nothing was ever able for a moment to shake his purpose of uniting himself with her as soon as he could gather enough courage to face those difficulties. He was determined to overcome them.

Diana was fully worthy of his deepest affection."}

{"request_id":"0d9f33d178244bac209143b2","rewritten_text":"On my return, I found the following letter from my father:—

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably been waiting with impatience for a note that would set the day of your return to us; at first I was inclined to send you only a few lines, just naming the time when I should expect you. But that would be a cruel sort of kindness, and I cannot bring myself to it. Imagine, my son, what your surprise would be: you come expecting a welcome full of joy and gladness, and instead you find tears and misery. Victor, how am I to tell you of our misfortune? Your absence cannot have made you indifferent to our joys and sorrows; and how could I inflict pain on my long-absent son? I mean to prepare you for the dreadful news, though I know it is impossible. Even now, I can see your eye darting over the page, hunting for the words meant to carry you the terrible tidings.

“William is dead!—that dear child, whose smiles warmed and delighted my heart, so gentle, and yet so full of life! Victor, he has been murdered!

“I will not try to comfort you; I will only set down the circumstances of what occurred.

“Last Thursday (May 7th), I, my niece, and your two brothers went out to take a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was mild and calm, and we lingered longer than usual. It was already getting dusk before we thought of turning back; and then we learned that William and Ernest, who had gone on ahead, were missing. We sat down on a bench and waited for them to return. Soon Ernest came back and asked whether we had seen his brother. He said that he had been playing with him; that William had run off to hide himself; that he searched for him in vain; and that after waiting a long time, William did not come back.

“This account alarmed us, and we kept on looking for him until night came. Then Elizabeth suggested that he might have returned home. He was not there. We went back again with torches; I could not rest, thinking of my sweet boy lost and left to the damp and dews of the night. Elizabeth was in the same distress. About five in the morning I found my lovely child—whom, the night before, I had seen blooming and active in health—lying on the grass, livid and motionless; the mark of the murderer’s hand was on his neck.

“He was taken home, and the anguish I could not hide showed Elizabeth the truth. She was very eager to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she would not be denied. She entered the room where it lay, hurriedly examined the neck of the victim, and clasping her hands cried out, ‘O God!’”"}

{"request_id":"3cfabcb194db0bf4b24ae80d","rewritten_text":"If not, and you’re asking for my patience, and for the mercy of the people you’ve deeply wronged, then sit down in that chair—silently. It has been waiting for you for two whole days.”

The monks muttered a few words that no one could make out, but they still hesitated.

“You will be prompt,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and the alternative is gone forever.”

The man still hesitated.

“I have no intention of negotiating,” said Mr. Brownlow. “And since I’m fighting for the dearest interests of others, I don’t have the right.”

“Is there—” Monks demanded, his voice faltering—“is there—no middle option?”

“None.”

Monks looked at the old gentleman with an anxious eye; but seeing only severity and determination in his face, he walked into the room. With a shrug, he sat down.

“Lock the door from the outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and come back when I ring.”

The men obeyed, and the two were left alone.

“This is pretty treatment, sir,” said Monks, throwing down his hat and cloak. “From my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” Mr. Brownlow replied. “It is because the hopes and wishes of those young and happy years were tied up with him—and with that fair creature of his blood and family who returned to her God in youth, leaving me here a solitary, lonely man. It is because he knelt with me beside his only sisters’ deathbed when he was still a boy, on the morning that—if Heaven had willed otherwise—would have made her my young wife. It is because my heart, scarred and hardened, clung to him from that time onward through all his trials and mistakes, until he died. It is because old memories and associations fill my heart, and even the sight of you brings back thoughts of him. It is because of all these things that I am moved to treat you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford—even now—and to blush for your unworthiness, you who bear the name.”

“What does the name have to do with it?” the other asked, after staring at him for a moment—half in silence, half in stubborn disbelief at his companion’s agitation. “What does the name mean to me?”

“Nothing,” said Mr. Brownlow. “Nothing to you. But it was hers—and even at this distance in time, it brings back to me, an old man, the glow and thrill I once felt, only to have it repeated now by a stranger. I’m very glad you’ve changed it—very—very.”

“This is all mighty fine,” said Monks—keeping up his assumed identity—after a long silence. During it, he jerked himself back and forth in sullen defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face shaded by his hand."}

{"request_id":"e1a35990b0e3d40c63b8ecc9","rewritten_text":"Moreover, this knot is one that only a few people besides sailors can tie, and it is something that belongs especially to the Maltese. I picked up the ribbon at the foot of the lightning-rod. It could not have belonged to either of the dead men. Now, even if I am wrong about what this ribbon suggests—that the Frenchman was a sailor from a Maltese ship—I have still done no harm by saying what I said in the advertisement. If I am mistaken, he will only think that I was led astray by some detail he will not bother to check. But if I am right, then a major advantage is gained. Even though the Frenchman knows nothing about the murder, he will naturally hesitate to answer the advertisement, and to demand the Ourang-Outang. He will think like this: ‘I am innocent. I am poor. My Ourang-Outang is worth a great deal to someone in my situation—a fortune by itself. So why would I give it up because of idle fears of danger? It is right here, within my reach. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne, far away from the place where that slaughter happened. How could anyone suspect that a wild animal did it? The police are to blame. They have not found the slightest clue. Even if they trace the animal, they still could not prove that I knew about the murder, or connect me to guilt because of that knowledge. Most of all, I am known. The advertiser names me as the owner of the beast. I do not know how far his information goes. If I avoid claiming something of such great value that everyone knows I have, then at least I will make the animal seem suspicious. It is not my plan to draw attention to myself or to the beast. I will answer the advertisement, get the Ourang-Outang, and keep it close until this whole matter has blown over.’”

At that moment, we heard a step on the stairs.

“Be ready,” said Dupin. “Have your pistols, but don’t use them and don’t show them until I give the signal.”

The front door of the house had been left open. The visitor came in without ringing and walked several steps up the staircase. Then, however, he seemed to pause. Soon we heard him going back down. Dupin moved quickly toward the door, but then we heard the man coming up again. He did not turn back a second time. Instead, he stepped forward with confidence and knocked on the door of our room.

“Come in,” said Dupin, in a cheerful, strong voice.

A man entered. He was clearly a sailor—a tall, thickset, muscular person, with a bold, dare-devil look on his face, though not entirely unpleasant."}

{"request_id":"4f5269cd9f35cc3bbe23e13e","rewritten_text":"It looked like a set of narrow back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, and it gave the feel of a quiet, rather boring retirement. Wemmick’s house was a small wooden cottage set among garden plots. The top of it had been cut out and painted to look like a battery, with guns.

“My own work,” said Wemmick. “Pretty, isn’t it?”

I agreed. I think it was the smallest house I had ever seen. It had the strangest Gothic windows—most of them were fake—and a Gothic front door that was almost too small to get inside.

“That’s a real flagstaff,” said Wemmick. “And on Sundays I raise a real flag. Now look here. After I cross this bridge, I lift it up—like this—and cut off the connection.”

The bridge was just a plank. It crossed a chasm about four feet wide and two feet deep. Still, it was pleasant to watch how proud he was as he lifted it and locked it in place. He smiled while doing it, enjoying himself rather than acting out a routine.

“At nine o’clock every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun fires. There it is, you see! And when you hear it go, I think you’ll say it’s a Stinger.”

The gun itself was mounted in a separate little fortress made of lattice work. It was protected from the weather by a clever tarpaulin cover, shaped like an umbrella.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of sight, so it doesn’t get in the way of the idea of fortifications. It’s a rule with me: if you have an idea, carry it out and keep it going. I don’t know if that’s your opinion—”

I said it was.

“—At the back there’s a pig, and there are fowls and rabbits. Then I put together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers. And at supper you can judge what kind of salad I can make. So, sir,” he said again, smiling but speaking seriously as he shook his head, “if you imagine the small place being besieged, it would hold out a devil of a time for supplies.”

Then he led me to a bower about a dozen yards away, though you had to reach it by winding paths that made the walk take a long time. In that retreat, our glasses were already set out. Our punch was cooling in an ornamental pool, and the bower sat above its edge. The water was round, with an island in the middle that could have been the salad for supper. He had built a fountain in it, and when you started a small mill and pulled a cork from a pipe, the water shot out so strongly that it soaked the back of your hand."}

{"request_id":"4c74aec3b3cd9f9a4b2ff74d","rewritten_text":"“Oh, your father can certainly spare you, if your mother can. Daughters never matter to a father as much as sons do. And if you stay another _month_ in full, I will be able to take one of you as far as London. I plan to go there early in June for a week. Since Dawson doesn’t object to the barouche-box, there will be very good room for one of you. And if the weather happens to be cool, I wouldn’t mind taking you both, since neither of you is very large.”

“You are very kind, madam; but I think we should stick to our original plan.”

Lady Catherine looked resigned. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always say what I think, and I cannot stand the idea of two young women travelling post by themselves. It’s highly improper. You must arrange for someone to go with them. I strongly dislike that kind of thing. Young women should always be properly protected and accompanied, according to their position in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I made sure she had two men-servants with her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley, and Lady Anne could not have appeared in any other way with propriety. I pay close attention to all these matters. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I’m glad it occurred to me to mention it, because it would really be a disgrace to _you_ to let them go alone.”

“My uncle will send a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle? Does he keep a man-servant? I’m very glad you have someone who thinks about these things. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you mention my name at the Bell, you’ll be taken care of.”

Lady Catherine had many more questions to ask about their journey. Since she didn’t answer all of them herself, Elizabeth thought it was lucky; otherwise, with her mind so busy, she might have forgotten where she was. She decided that she would save her thoughts for when she was alone. Whenever she had time by herself, she let them come, because it felt like the greatest relief. Not a day passed without her taking a solitary walk, where she could enjoy all the comfort of unpleasant memories.

She was soon going to know Mr. Darcy’s letter almost by heart. She studied every sentence, and her feelings about the man changed at times in very different ways. When she remembered the way he wrote to her, she was still full of anger. But when she thought about how unfairly she had judged him and spoken harshly to him, her anger turned back on herself, and his disappointment became something she felt sorry for.”}]}]}}"}

{"request_id":"3568b531a732c6efe4c51a97","rewritten_text":"I hurried to her and gathered her into my arms, showering her with caresses as I pleaded:

“Go on, darling—tell me! What is it?”

Her head went heavy against my chest, and she drew in a breath, almost too faint to hear:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Now then!” I called to Clarence. “Telephone the king’s homeopath and have him come at once!”

Within two minutes I was down on my knees beside the child’s crib, while Sandy sent servants scurrying here, there, and everywhere across the palace. I took in the whole matter at a glance—membranous croup. I leaned close and murmured:

“Wake up, sweetheart! Hello-Central.”

Her gentle eyes fluttered open, and she seemed to manage, in a weak voice:

“Papa.”

That at least was something. She wasn’t gone yet. I had sulphur brought for preparations, and I hauled out the croup-kettle myself; I don’t just sit and wait for doctors when Sandy or the child is ill. I knew how to nurse both of them, and I had done it before. This little one had spent much of its short life in my arms, and I could often coax away its troubles and get it to laugh through the tear-dews on its eye-lashes when even its mother couldn’t.

Sir Launcelot, dressed in his finest armor, came striding through the great hall toward the stock-board. He was president of the stock-board and held the Siege Perilous, which he had bought from Sir Galahad; for the stock-board was made up of the Knights of the Round Table, and they now used the Round Table for business. The seats there—well, you wouldn’t believe the sum, so it’s pointless to say. Sir Launcelot was a bear, and he’d staked a corner in one of the new lines, getting ready to squeeze the shorts today; but what did it matter? He was still the same old Launcelot, and when he glanced in as he passed the door and saw that his pet was sick, that was all it took. Let bulls and bears settle their own quarrel—he would come straight in and stand by little Hello-Central as long as he could. And that was exactly what he did. He tossed his helmet into the corner, and in half a minute he had a fresh wick in the alcohol lamp and was getting the croup-kettle going.

By then Sandy had thrown up a blanket canopy over the crib, and everything was set. Sir Launcelot got up steam; he and I loaded the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a touch of lactic acid, then filled it with water and set the steam-spout under the canopy. Everything was in proper order now, and we sat down on either side of the crib to keep watch."}

{"request_id":"3e5efcf0575d9e19ef97afd6","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was quite distressed by Lord Canterville’s refusal, and begged him to reconsider, but the good-natured peer was unshakably firm. In the end, he persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the present the ghost had given her. Then, in the spring of 1890, when the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s first drawing-room on the occasion of her marriage, her jewels became the universal subject of admiration. Virginia received the coronet, the reward for all good little American girls, and she married her boy-lover as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming, and they loved each other so much, that everyone was delighted with the match—except the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had tried to catch the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had thrown no fewer than three expensive dinner parties for that purpose, and, oddly enough, Mr. Otis himself. Mr. Otis was extremely fond of the young Duke personally, but in theory he objected to titles. As he put it, he was “not without apprehension lest, amid the enervating influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true principles of republican simplicity should be forgotten.” Those objections, however, were completely overruled. And I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter leaning on his arm, there was not a prouder man anywhere in all of England.

After the honeymoon ended, the Duke and Duchess went down to Canterville Chase. The day after they arrived, they took an afternoon walk over to the lonely churchyard by the pine woods. At first there had been a lot of trouble about the inscription on Sir Simon’s tombstone, but it was finally decided to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some lovely roses, which she scattered on the grave. After they had stood there for some time, they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. There the Duchess sat down on a fallen pillar, while her husband lay at her feet smoking a cigarette and looking up at her beautiful eyes. Suddenly he tossed his cigarette aside, took her hand, and said, “Virginia, a wife should have no secrets from her husband.”

“Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.”

“Yes, you do,” he replied, smiling. “You’ve never told me what happened to you when you were locked up with the ghost.”

“I have never told anyone, Cecil,” said Virginia gravely."}

{"request_id":"4b34418419c8aa7f78194022","rewritten_text":"“This must have been around the same time in Mr. Elliot’s life,” said Anne. “It’s always been the part I’ve been most curious about. It must have been about when he first became known to my father and my sister. I never met him myself; I only heard about him. Still, there was something in how he behaved toward my father and sister then, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, that I could never fully fit with the way things are now. It made him seem like a different kind of man.”

“I know it all, I know it all,” Mrs. Smith cried. “He had already been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I even knew him, but I heard him talk about them again and again. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he chose not to go. I can explain things to you on points you probably wouldn’t expect. And as for his marriage, I knew everything about it at the time. I was there for all the good and bad sides of it. I was the friend he trusted with his hopes and plans. And although I didn’t know his wife before, her lower position in society made that impossible. Still, I knew her well for the rest of her life, at least until the last two years of her life, and I can answer any question you want to ask.”

“Not really,” said Anne. “I don’t need to ask anything special about her. I’ve always understood they weren’t a happy couple. But I would like to know why, at that stage of his life, he would ignore my father’s acquaintance the way he did. My father was clearly ready to treat him with kindness and proper attention. Why did Mr. Elliot pull back?”

“Mr. Elliot,” Mrs. Smith replied, “at that time in his life, had one goal: to make his fortune, and to do it by a faster route than the law. He was determined to build it through marriage. He was determined, at least, not to ruin it with an unwise marriage. And I know it was his belief—whether it was right or not, I can’t say—that your father and sister, with all their politeness and invitations, were trying to set up a match between the heir and the young lady. He thought such a match couldn’t possibly fit what he wanted in terms of wealth and independence. That was why he drew back, I assure you. He told me the whole story. He kept nothing from me. It was strange that, after just leaving you with me in Bath, my first and main acquaintance after I married should be your cousin—and that through him I should keep hearing about your father and sister.”"}

{"request_id":"7b164006a6a543e6e9413de2","rewritten_text":"“Oh, bother my hat! I want Virginia!” the little Duke cried, laughing, and they rode hard on to the railway station. There, Mr. Otis asked the station-master whether anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but he could not get any news. The station-master did, however, send messages along the line and promised that a close watch would be kept for her. After that, Mr. Otis bought a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper who was just putting up his shutters, and then Mr. Otis rode off to Bexley, a village about four miles away. He had been told it was a well-known place for gypsies, because there was a large common there. 

They woke the rural policeman, but he had no information. After riding all over the common, they turned their horses back toward the Chase and arrived home at about eleven o’clock, completely worn out and almost heart-broken. At the gate-house, Washington and the twins were waiting for them with lanterns, since the avenue was very dark. No trace of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been caught on Brockley meadows, but Virginia was not with them. They said they had left suddenly because they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and had gone off in a hurry so they would not be late. They were also upset to hear that Virginia had disappeared. They were grateful to Mr. Otis for letting them camp in his park, and four of them had stayed behind to help search. 

The carp-pond had been dragged, and the whole Chase had been searched thoroughly, but nothing turned up. It was clear that, at least for that night, Virginia was lost to them. Mr. Otis and the boys went up to the house in deep depression, with the groom following behind, leading the two horses and the pony. In the hall they found a group of frightened servants. In the library, they saw poor Mrs. Otis lying on a sofa, almost beside herself with fear and worry, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau-de-cologne. 

Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she should eat something, and he ordered supper for the whole party. It was a sad meal. Hardly anyone spoke, and even the twins were quiet and subdued, because they were very fond of their sister. After they finished, Mr. Otis, even though the little Duke begged him not to, ordered them all to bed. He said nothing more could be done that night, and that in the morning he would telegraph Scotland Yard to have detectives sent down right away."}

{"request_id":"5591dac5d33988b947587bb3","rewritten_text":"The winters around Sullivan’s Island are usually mild, and in the fall it is rare for anyone to think they need a fire. But about the middle of October, 18—, there was one unusually cold day. Just before sunset, I picked my way through the evergreens to my friend’s hut. I hadn’t visited in several weeks. At that time I lived in Charleston, nine miles away from the island, and getting back and forth was much harder than it is now.

When I reached the hut, I knocked the way I always did. No one answered, so I found the key where I knew it was hidden, unlocked the door, and went in. A good fire was burning on the hearth. It was a welcome sight. I took off my overcoat, sat in an armchair near the crackling logs, and waited for my hosts.

Not long after dark, they arrived and greeted me warmly. Jupiter, smiling from ear to ear, hurried around to prepare some marsh-hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his moods—what else could I call them?—full of excitement. He had found an unknown bivalve, one that seemed to form a new genus. Even better, he had tracked down and secured, with Jupiter’s help, a scarabæus that he believed was completely new. Still, he wanted my opinion about it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, warming my hands by the fire, and wishing that whole tribe of scarabæi would go to the devil.

“Ah, if I had only known you were here!” Legrand said. “It’s been so long since I saw you, and how could I guess you would come to visit me on this particular night? On my way home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, very foolishly, I lent him the bug. So you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I’ll send Jup down for it at sunrise. It’s the loveliest thing in creation!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“No nonsense! No—the bug. It’s a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory nut. Near one end of its back it has two jet-black spots, and at the other end there’s another spot, a little longer. The antennæ are—”

“Dey aint no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin on you,” Jupiter interrupted. “De bug is a goole bug, solid, ebery bit of him, inside an’ all, sep him wing—neber feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”"}

{"request_id":"72157bef06feab7238a5fd19","rewritten_text":"So I went on for two years. Day after day, so many hundreds passed; they brought no visible change, yet a few of them worked slowly upon my mind as I drifted onward toward death. I began to study more; to share more readily the thoughts of others as they are set down in books; to read history, and to lose the individuality that had once belonged to me. Perhaps, as the sense of immediate suffering faded, I grew more human. Even solitude began to lose some of its charms: I found myself wishing again for sympathy—not that I was tempted to throw myself among the crowd, but that I wanted one friend to love me.

You may think, perhaps, that I was gradually becoming fit to return to society. I do not believe it. The sympathy I longed for would have to be so clean and so stripped of any sway from outward circumstances that, in the world, I could not help but be checked by the coarse materials that mingle, without fail, even with its best feelings. Believe me, I was then less prepared for any true communion with my fellow creatures than before. When I left them, they had tormented me, but in the same manner that pain and sickness torment—something foreign to the mind that irritates it, and that I wished to cast off. Now, though, I should have wanted sympathy; I would have tried to bind my soul to one of theirs, and I would have laid up for myself abundant draughts of disappointment and suffering; for I was as tender as the sensitive plant, all nerve. I did not crave sympathy and help in ambition or wisdom, but sweet and mutual affection—smiles to cheer me and gentle words of comfort. I wanted one heart into which I might pour out my complaints without restraint, and from which, by the heavenly nature of the soil, blessed fruit might grow from such bad seed.

But how could I find this? The love that is the very soul of friendship is a soft spirit, rarely met with unless two amiable creatures are joined from early youth, or unless they are bound together by mutual suffering and pursuits. It comes to some of the elect, unsought and unawares; it falls like gentle dew on chosen places that, though barren before, become fertile in all sweet plants under its kindly influence. Yet when it is desired, it flies; it mocks the prayers of its worshippers; it will grant, but it will not be sought.

I knew all this, and I did not go out to look for sympathy. Still, there on my solitary heath, under my lowly roof where everything around was desart, it came to me like a sunbeam in winter—meant to adorn while it helps to melt the drifted snow. Alas, the sun shone on blighted fruit; I did not revive in its radiance, for I was too utterly undone to feel its kindly power."}

{"request_id":"ec68d98dd87829985dfccbd1","rewritten_text":"The oaks around us are home to a tribe of nightingales. That is where I am now. Idris is beside me, in the best years of his youth. Remember, I am only twenty-two, and seventeen summers have barely passed since the beloved of my heart was first mine.

The river has swollen from autumn rains and has flooded the low land. Adrian, in his favorite boat, is doing a dangerous thing: he is trying to pluck the highest branch from an oak that is half submerged. “Are you tired of life, Adrian?” I asked. “Why do you play with danger like this?”

He has taken his prize. He steers his boat through the flood. Our eyes followed him with fear, but the current carried him away from us. He had to land much farther downstream, and then make a long detour before he could reach us again. “He’s safe!” Idris said as he jumped onto shore. He lifted the branch above his head to show he had succeeded. “We’ll wait for him here.”

Idris and I were alone together. The sun had set, and the nightingales began to sing. The evening star shone clearly, bright in the flood of light that still lingered in the west. My angelic girl’s blue eyes were fixed on that star. “How the light seems to beat,” she said. “That star’s life is in it. Its shifting brightness makes it seem like its state is the same as ours on earth—uncertain and changeable. It seems to fear, to love, and to waver.”

“Don’t look at the star, dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Don’t read love into its trembling light. Don’t stare at distant worlds. Don’t turn a feeling into something you imagine. I have been silent for a long time. Even to the point of sickness, I have wanted to speak to you. I want to give you my soul, my life, my whole self. Don’t look at the star, my love. Let that eternal spark speak for me. Let it be my witness and my advocate, silent as it shines. Love is to me what light is to the star. As long as it is not taken away, as long as it is not extinguished by nothingness, I will love you.”

That moment’s joy is forever hidden from the world’s cold eyes. Even now I still feel her graceful body pressed against my full heart. Even now, when I remember our first kiss, my sight, my pulse, and my breath all fail me.

Slowly and quietly, we went to meet Adrian, whom we could hear coming.

I asked Adrian to come back to me after he had taken his sister home. And that same evening, as we walked along the moonlit paths through the forest, I poured out my whole heart—its excitement and its hope—to my friend. For a moment he looked troubled. “I should have seen this,” he said. “Now there will be conflict, and—”"}

{"request_id":"488f6fc4e0d50765ccbfa5ac","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent by them to Adrian, who had been chosen arbiter; and they had made the journey from Paris to Calais, passing through empty towns and desolate fields, all the while feeding a fierce hatred toward one another; and now, with no restraint of party feeling, they urged their several cases.

By looking at the deputies one by one, and after a thorough inquiry, we learned the real state of affairs in Paris. Since parliament had named him Ryland’s deputy, all the surviving English had submitted to Adrian. He was our captain, to lead us from our native soil into unknown regions; our lawgiver and our preserver. At the first settling of our emigration plan, no lasting separation of our members had been intended, and the command of the whole body, rising by degrees in authority, reached its height in the Earl of Windsor. But unforeseen circumstances overturned our arrangements, and forced the greater part of our number to be parted from the supreme chief for nearly two months. They had crossed in two separate groups; and when they arrived in Paris, quarrelling sprang up between them.

They found Paris a desert. At the beginning, when the plague first showed itself, the return of travellers and merchants, along with communications by letter, kept us informed of the ravages disease was making on the continent. Yet as mortality increased, that intercourse dwindled and finally stopped. Even within England, communication from one part of the island to another grew slow and uncommon. No vessel ever pushed through the tide that lay between Calais and Dover; or if some miserable passenger, anxious to learn whether relatives still lived, put out from the French shore to come back among us, the greedy ocean would often swallow his small craft, or, after a day or two, he would be infected by the disorder and die before he could tell us the story of France’s desolation. Thus we were, to a great extent, ignorant of what was happening on the continent, and we still had a dim hope of finding many companions in its wide path. But the very causes that had so fearfully thinned the English nation gave the sister land even broader room for mischief. France was a blank; along the long road from Calais to Paris not a single human being was met. In Paris, however, there were a few—perhaps a hundred—who, resigned to what awaited them, drifted about the streets of the capital and gathered to talk of former days, with a liveliness, and even a kind of gaiety, that rarely deserts the individuals of this people.

The English took undisputed possession of Paris. Its tall houses and narrow streets lay lifeless. A few wan figures could be seen at the usual meeting-place at the Tuileries; they wondered why the islanders should come toward their ill-fated city—for in the extremity of misery, those afflicted always fancy that their share of the calamity is the bitterest; so that, while enduring intense pain, we would trade the particular torture we are writhing under for any other that might strike a different part of the body."}

{"request_id":"15b694428add710706d74749","rewritten_text":"This was invitation enough.

“Why, my dear, you must know that Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been taken by a young man with a large fortune from the north of England. He came down on Monday in a carriage with four horses to look at the place, and he was so pleased with it that he agreed with Mr. Morris right away. He plans to move in before Michaelmas, and some of his servants will be in the house by the end of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear, of course! A single man with a large fortune—four or five thousand a year. What a wonderful thing for our girls!”

“How so? How could it affect them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife replied, “how can you be so tiresome? You must know I’m thinking about him marrying one of them.”

“Is that his plan in settling here?”

“Plan? Nonsense. How can you talk like that? But it’s very possible he may fall in love with one of them, so you must visit him as soon as he arrives.”

“I don’t see any reason for that. You and the girls can go—or you can send them on their own, which might even be better. After all, you’re as handsome as any of them, so Mr. Bingley might prefer you most of all.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I admit I once had my share of beauty, but I don’t pretend to be anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown-up daughters, she should stop thinking about her own looks.”

“In that case, a woman usually doesn’t have much beauty to think about.”

“But, my dear, you really must go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes to the neighborhood.”

“I’m afraid I can’t promise that.”

“But think about your daughters. Just imagine what a good match it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, just for that reason. You know they usually don’t visit new people. In fact, you must go, because it will be impossible for us to visit him if you don’t.”

“You’re being too careful, surely. I’m sure Mr. Bingley will be very happy to see you, and I will send a few lines by you to let him know I fully approve of his marrying whichever girl he chooses—though I must add a good word for my little Lizzy.”

“I don’t want you to do that. Lizzy isn’t any better than the others. And I’m sure she isn’t half as handsome as Jane, nor half as good-tempered as Lydia.”"}

{"request_id":"6a0f5676a4ff15c84ad2174a","rewritten_text":"“No, no—that’s for tomorrow. I especially wanted to see Knightley today, for that very reason. What a dreadful, scorching morning! I even went across the fields too,” she added, sounding very put out, “and that only made it worse. And then he wasn’t at home! I assure you, I’m really not pleased. There was no apology, no message for me. The housekeeper said she had no idea I was expected. How strange! And nobody knew at all where he had gone. Maybe to Hartfield, maybe to the Abbey Mill, maybe into his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this isn’t like our friend Knightley. Can you explain it?”

Emma amused herself by saying, with protests, that it was indeed very extraordinary, and that she had nothing at all to say in his defense.

“I can’t imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, sounding indignant in the way a wife ought to, “I can’t imagine how he could do something like this to you, of all people in the world. You’re the very last person one would expect to be forgotten. My dear Mr. E., he must have left you a message. He must have. Not even Knightley could be so eccentric—and his servants forgot it. I’m sure that’s what happened. And it’s very likely with the Donwell servants, who, as I’ve often noticed, are all extremely awkward and careless. I’m sure I wouldn’t have someone like his Harry standing at our sideboard for any reason. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very little of her. She promised Wright a receipt and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins,” Mr. Elton went on, “as I was getting near the house, and he told me I wouldn’t find his master at home. But I didn’t believe him. William seemed rather annoyed. He said he didn’t know what had happened to his master lately, but he could hardly ever get him to speak. I don’t deal with William’s problems, but it really is very important that I should see Knightley today. So it’s a serious inconvenience that I’ve taken this hot walk for nothing.”

Emma felt she couldn’t do better than go home at once. She was probably being waited for there right now, and Mr. Knightley might be kept from getting even more aggressive toward Mr. Elton—if not toward William Larkins.

When she said goodbye, she was pleased to see Miss Fairfax determined to follow her out of the room and even downstairs. It gave her a chance, which she immediately used to say,”"}

Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get that headline out of the way! _Lively_ now! Come on—get out with your spring-line—what are you doing there? Go around that stump with the rope tied to it! Stand by that stage now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (he was trying the gauge-cocks).

Tom kept on whitewashing and didn’t pay any attention to the steamboat. Ben watched for a moment, then said, “_Hi-Yi!_ You’re up a stump, aren’t you!”

Tom didn’t answer. He looked over his last stroke like an artist, then made another careful, gentle sweep with his brush and checked the result again. Ben moved up beside him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he kept working. Ben said:

“Hello there, old chap. You’ve got to work, huh?”

Tom turned around suddenly. “Why, it’s you, Ben! I wasn’t even noticing.”

“Say—I’m going in for a swim. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d rather _work_—wouldn’t you? Sure you would!”

Tom studied him for a moment and asked, “What do you call work?”

“Why, isn’t _that_ work?”

Tom went back to whitewashing and answered without much care. “Maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh, come on now. You don’t mean to say you _like_ it?”

The brush kept moving.

“Like it? I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That made Ben look at it differently. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush back and forth neatly, then stepped back to see how it looked. He added a little here and there, checked it again, and Ben watched every move, getting more and more interested, more and more caught up in it. After a while Ben said:

“Say, Tom, let _me_ whitewash a little.”

Tom thought about it and seemed ready to agree, but then he changed his mind. “No—no. I don’t think it would work out, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly is really picky about this fence—right here on the street, you know. But if it were the back fence, I wouldn’t mind, and _she_ wouldn’t either. She’s very particular about this fence. It has to be done just right. I don’t think there’s one boy out of a thousand—maybe even two thousand—who can do it the way it has to be done.”

“No—is that so? Oh, come on. Let me just try. Just a little. I’d let _you_ if I were you, Tom.”

“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun, but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him. Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"50b25734bba68438101a7c38","rewritten_text":"So the ring-master made a little speech, saying he hoped there wouldn’t be any disturbance, and that if the fellow would promise he wouldn’t cause any more trouble, he’d let him ride—so long as he thought he could hold his seat on the horse. With that, everybody laughed and said all right, and the man climbed on. The instant he was mounted, the horse started to rip and tear, buck and jump and carry on, with two circus men gripping the bridle to keep him in check, while the drunk man clung to his neck, his heels flying up in the air with every leap. The whole crowd stood up, shouting and laughing until the tears ran down their faces. And sure enough, after all the circus men’s efforts, the horse finally broke free and away he went—like the very nation—round and round the ring, with that sot laid down on him and hanging to his neck. One leg dangled low on one side, then the other leg on the other side, and the people went wild. It wasn’t funny to me, though; I was shaking with worry at how much danger he was in. But pretty soon he managed to scramble up astride, grabbed the bridle, and reeled this way and that; then, in the next moment, he sprang up, let go of the bridle, and stood there. The horse kept going like a house afire. He just stood, sailing around as easy and comfortable as if he’d never been drunk a day in his life, and then he started stripping off his clothes and tossing them aside. He shed them so fast and so thick that it seemed to clog the air, and in all he got rid of seventeen suits. Then there he was—slim and handsome—wearing the gaudiest, prettiest outfit you ever saw, and he went to work on that horse with his whip, making him perform like he was put on rails. At last he skipped off, bowed, and danced away toward the dressing-room, while everyone was howling with pleasure and astonishment.\n\nThen the ring-master saw he’d been taken in, and he was the sickest ring-master you ever saw, I reckon. Why, it was one of his own men! He’d cooked up that whole bit from his own head and never let on to anybody. I’ll admit I felt pretty sheepish for getting fooled, but I wouldn’t have wanted to be in that ring-master’s place—not for a thousand dollars. I don’t know; maybe there are bigger circuses than that one, but I haven’t run into them yet. Anyways, it was good enough for me, and wherever I come across it again, it can have all of my custom every time."}

{"request_id":"fd30537a580278781c2bed14","rewritten_text":"The narrow streets and alleys, at last, opened into a large open space. Scattered around it were pens for animals and other signs of a cattle market. When Sikes reached this spot, he slowed down; the girl could barely keep going anymore, not at the fast pace they’d been walking. He turned to Oliver and roughly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Do you hear?” Sikes snarled as Oliver hesitated and looked around.

They were tucked into a dark corner, well out of the way of any passengers.

Oliver could see, all too clearly, that resisting would do no good. He held out his hand, and Nancy gripped it tightly in hers.

“Give me the other,” said Sikes, grabbing Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog looked up and growled.

“Look here, boy!” Sikes said, pressing his other hand to Oliver’s throat. “If he says even a soft word, hold him! You understand!”

The dog growled again, and licked its lips, staring at Oliver as if it couldn’t wait to clamp onto his windpipe.

“He’s as willing as a Christian—strike me blind if he isn’t!” Sikes said, watching the animal with grim, ferocious approval. “Now you know what you’ve got to expect, master, so call out as quick as you like; the dog will end that game soon enough. Come on, young ’un!”

Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail in response to this unusually affectionate way of speaking, and after another warning growl meant for Oliver, he led the way onward.

They were crossing Smithfield, though it might as well have been Grosvenor Square, for all Oliver knew. The night was dark and foggy. The lights in the shops could barely push through the thick mist, which seemed to grow heavier by the moment, swallowing the streets and houses in gloom. Everything looked unfamiliar to Oliver, and his uncertainty became even more miserable and depressing.

They had gone only a few paces when a deep church bell struck the hour. At the first stroke, both of his handlers stopped and turned their heads toward the direction the sound came from.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy said when the bell stopped.

“What’s the point of telling me that? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes snapped.

“I wonder if _they_ can hear it,” Nancy said.

“Of course they can,” Sikes replied. “It was Bartlemy time when I was shipped; and there weren’t a penny trumpet at the fair that I couldn’t hear the squeaking on. After I was locked up for the night, the noise and din outside made that old jail so quiet I could almost have beaten my brains out against the iron plates of the door.”"}

{"request_id":"76098e4fb5426848bc765bf4","rewritten_text":"At the sight of it, the Ourang-Outang burst straight through the chamber door, went down the stairs, and then—through an unfortunately open window—into the street.

The Frenchman followed in utter despair. The ape, razor still gripped in its hand, would sometimes halt to glance back and gesture wildly at its pursuer, until the latter had nearly caught up. Then it bolted again. So the pursuit went on for a long while. The streets were so still that it was nearly three o’clock in the morning. While running down an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive’s attention was caught by a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s room, on the fourth story of her house. It darted to the building, spotted the lightning rod, climbed it with incredible nimbleness, seized the shutter, which had been thrown wide back against the wall, and used it to swing itself directly onto the headboard of the bed. The whole maneuver took less than a minute. The Ourang-Outang kicked the shutter open again as it entered.

Meanwhile, the sailor was at once glad and troubled. He had strong hopes of getting the brute back now, since it could hardly slip out of the trap it had chosen, except by the rod—where it might be intercepted as it came down. Yet there was also real cause for alarm about what it might do inside the house. That thought kept him on the fugitive’s heels. A lightning rod can be climbed without much trouble, particularly by a sailor; but when he had reached the height of the window, far to his left, his progress stopped. All he could manage was to lean over and get a look into the room. At that sight he nearly lost his footing from sheer horror. It was then that those dreadful shrieks rose during the night, the very ones that had roused the sleepers of the Rue Morgue. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed in their night clothes, seemed to have been occupied arranging papers in the iron chest already mentioned, which had been wheeled into the middle of the room. It was open, and its contents lay beside it on the floor. The victims must have been seated with their backs toward the window; and, judging by the interval between the beast’s entry and the screams, it seems likely it was not noticed at once. The shutter’s sudden flapping would naturally have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor peered in, the huge creature had already seized Madame L’Espanaye by the hair—loose, as she had been combing it—and was brandishing the razor about her face, mimicking the movements of a barber."}
