{"request_id":"241373c975898371379030fd","rewritten_text":"And I call on you, spirits of the dead, and on you, wandering ministers of vengeance, to help me and guide me in my work. Let the cursed, hellish monster drink in deep agony. Let him feel the despair that torments me now.”

I began my words with solemn care and a kind of awe, almost certain that the shadows of my murdered friends were listening and approving my devotion. But as I finished, the furies took hold of me, and rage choked my speech.

In the silence of the night, I was answered by a loud, fiendish laugh. It echoed in my ears for a long time, heavy and mocking. The mountains seemed to repeat it, and I felt as if all of hell surrounded me just to laugh at me. I truly thought that in that moment I would lose my mind and destroy my miserable life—except that my vow was heard, and I was meant to live for vengeance. The laughter stopped. Then, from what seemed to be right beside my ear, a voice I knew well and hated spoke in a whisper you could hear: “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have decided to live, and I am satisfied.”

I rushed toward where the sound came from, but the devil slipped out of my reach. Then the moon rose and shone fully on his ghastly, twisted form as he fled with more speed than any mortal could have.

I followed him, and for many months this has been my task. With only a small clue to guide me, I traced his path along the bends of the Rhone, but it led nowhere. I reached the blue Mediterranean, and by some strange chance I saw the fiend enter by night and hide himself in a ship bound for the Black Sea. I took passage on the same ship, but he escaped—somehow I still do not know how.

Even in the wild lands of Tartary and Russia, though he keeps slipping away, I have kept on his trail. Sometimes the peasants, terrified by the sight of this horrible apparition, told me where he had gone. Other times, he himself left some sign to guide me, because he feared that if I lost all trace of him I would despair and die. Snow fell on my head, and on the white ground I saw the mark of his huge step. You who are just starting life, to whom worry is new and pain is still unknown—how could you understand what I have felt, and still feel? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were only the smallest of the sufferings I was forced to endure. I was cursed by some devil, and I carried my eternal hell with me. Still, a spirit of good followed me and guided my steps, and whenever I complained the most, it would suddenly pull me out of troubles that seemed impossible to escape. Sometimes, when hunger overcame my body and I sank into exhaustion, a meal would be prepared for me in the desert. It would restore my strength and give me new spirit."}

{"request_id":"38dc91856a15c24f8e209c7d","rewritten_text":"“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at length, “there’s no denying that, since the new system of feeding has come in, the coffins are narrower and shallower than they used to be; but we have to make some profit, Mr. Bumble. Well-seasoned timber is expensive, sir, and all the iron handles come by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” said Mr. Bumble, “every trade has its drawbacks. A fair profit, of course, is acceptable.”

“Of course, of course,” replied the undertaker. “And if I don’t make a profit on this or that particular item, I make it up in the long run, you see—he! he! he!”

“Just so,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Though I must say,” the undertaker went on, picking up the line of thought the beadle had interrupted, “that I have to deal with one very big disadvantage: all the stout people go first. The people who’ve been better off, and have paid rates for many years, are the first to sink as soon as they come into the house. And let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, that three or four inches over what you expect makes a huge difference to your profits—especially when you’ve got a family to support, sir.”

As Mr. Sowerberry said this, with the proper indignation of a man who’s been wronged, and as Mr. Bumble felt it tended to suggest something about the parish’s honor, he decided it was best to change the subject. Oliver Twist was uppermost in his mind, so he brought him up.

“By the way,” said Mr. Bumble, “do you know anyone who wants a boy? A parish apprentice—right now he’s dead weight, a millstone, as it were, around the parish’s throat. Liberal terms, Mr. Sowerberry—liberal terms?” As Mr. Bumble spoke, he lifted his cane to the board above him and gave three distinct raps on the words “five pounds,” printed there in Roman capitals of gigantic size.

“Gadso!” said the undertaker, grabbing Mr. Bumble by the gilt-edged lapel of his official coat. “That’s exactly what I wanted to talk to you about. You know—dear me, what an elegant button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it’s rather pretty,” said the beadle, looking down proudly at the large brass buttons that decorated his coat. “The design is the same as the parish seal—the Good Samaritan healing the sick and bruised man. The board gave it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember putting it on for the first time to attend the inquest on that reduced tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight.”"}

{"request_id":"df1579c58145e305d088962a","rewritten_text":"All this, and more—far more than I can easily set down—would I gladly lay before you. Yet, to keep it short, I must have my reward. I long to be back with my family and in my own home; and, as the price of any further communication from me—in return for the light I am able to shed upon many matters, both important branches of physical and metaphysical science—I must ask, through the good offices of your honorable body, a pardon for the crime I have committed in the death of the creditors when I left Rotterdam. Such, then, is the purpose of this paper. Its bearer, an inhabitant of the moon, whom I have persuaded, and properly instructed, to act as my messenger to the earth, will wait upon your Excellencies’ pleasure, and return to me with the pardon in question, should it be obtained in any way.

“I have the honor to be, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

When Professor Rub-a-dub had finished reading this most extraordinary document, it is said that, in the height of his astonishment, he let his pipe fall to the ground. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, having removed his spectacles, wiped them, and then—so completely did he forget both himself and his usual dignity—turned round three times upon his heel in the very quintessence of astonishment and admiration. There could be no question of it: the pardon must be secured. So, at least, swore Professor Rub-a-dub with a hearty oath; and so, in the end, thought the illustrious Von Underduk, as he took his brother in science by the arm. Without saying a word, he set off at once on his way home, to consider what steps ought to be taken. Yet when they reached the door of the burgomaster’s dwelling, the professor ventured to remark that, since the messenger had chosen to vanish—no doubt terrified out of his wits by the savage look of the burghers of Rotterdam—the pardon would be of little account, because no one but a man of the moon would undertake so immense a journey. The burgomaster agreed that this was true, and the matter was therefore concluded. Not so, however, with rumors and conjectures. Once the letter was published, it stirred up a whole crop of gossip and opinions. Some of the over-wise even made themselves ridiculous by denouncing the affair as a mere hoax. But hoax, with people of that sort, is, I take it, a catch-all name for anything beyond their understanding. As for me, I cannot see what grounds they have for such an accusation. Let us hear what they say:"}

Mrs. Elton, quite ready to take it as a compliment meant for her, smiled with the utmost graciousness.

“You have heard of a certain Frank Churchill, I presume,” he went on—“and you know him to be my son, though he does not go by my name.”

“Oh! yes, and I shall be very glad of the acquaintance. I am sure Mr. Elton will not delay in calling on him; and we shall both have great satisfaction in seeing him at the Vicarage.”

“You are very kind.—Frank will be exceedingly happy, I am sure.—He is to be in town next week, if not sooner. We have word of it in a letter received to-day. I came upon the letters this morning, and, seeing my son’s hand, I supposed I might open it—though it was not addressed to me—it was meant for Mrs. Weston. She is his chief correspondent, I assure you. I scarcely ever get a letter.”

“And so you actually opened what was meant for her! Oh! Mr. Weston—(laughing in a studied way) I must object to that. It is a very perilous precedent indeed!—Pray do not let your neighbours take your cue.—Upon my word, if this is what I am to expect, married women must begin to look to themselves!—Oh! Mr. Weston, I never could have thought it of you!”

“Aye, we men are poor creatures. You must look out for yourself, Mrs. Elton.—This letter tells us—though it is a short one—written in haste, only to give us notice—that they are all coming up to town at once, on Mrs. Churchill’s account. She has not been well all winter, and thinks Enscombe too cold for her—so they are to move southward without delay.”

“Indeed!—from Yorkshire, I suppose. Is Enscombe in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, they are about one hundred and ninety miles from London; it is a long journey.”

“Yes, upon my word, a very long one. Sixty-five miles farther than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance, Mr. Weston, to people of large fortune?—You would be astonished to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, will sometimes dart about. You can hardly believe me—but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back again with four horses.”

“The trouble of the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is, that Mrs. Churchill, _as_ _we_ _understand_, has not been able to leave the sofa for a week at a time. {"request_id":"549076708134d2f7c3d959cb","rewritten_text":"After everyone had shared their sorrow about the terrible outcome of this event—which Elizabeth thought was almost certain, and Miss Bennet couldn’t say was completely impossible—the first woman went on. “But tell me everything about it that I haven’t already heard. Give me more details. What did Colonel Forster say? Before the elopement happened, didn’t anyone have any reason to worry? They must have known they were together for good.”

“Colonel Forster admitted that he had often suspected some feelings, especially on Lydia’s side, but nothing that would make him fear the worst. I’m so sorry for him. His manner was attentive and kind. He was actually on his way to us to show how concerned he was, before he even knew that they weren’t going to Scotland. The moment that fear became public, it made him hurry his trip.”

“And was Denny sure that Wickham would not marry her? Did he know they planned to run off? Did Colonel Forster speak to Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when Denny was questioned by him, Denny denied knowing anything about their plan and wouldn’t give his real opinion. He didn’t repeat what he believed about them not marrying, and that makes me hope he may have been misunderstood before.”

“And until Colonel Forster arrived, none of you had any doubt that they were truly married?”

“How could such an idea even enter our minds? I felt a little uneasy, a little afraid for my sister’s happiness with him in marriage, because I knew his behavior had not always been completely right. My father and mother knew nothing of it. They only thought the match was foolish. Kitty then admitted, with a very natural sense of pride in knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia’s last letter she had warned her to expect something like this. It seems she had known for many weeks that Lydia and Wickham were in love with each other.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I don’t think so.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think badly of Wickham himself? Does he know what Wickham is really like?”

“I have to admit he didn’t speak of Wickham as well as he used to. He thought him imprudent and extravagant. And since this sad affair, it’s said that he left Meryton with a great deal of debt, though I hope that isn’t true.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secret, if we had told what we knew about him, this could not have happened!”

“Maybe it would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But to point out someone’s earlier faults, without knowing what their feelings are now, seems unfair.”"}

{"request_id":"a14626de81fd4edb50f2f269","rewritten_text":"But how could I, a poor, dazed village boy, avoid that wonderful inconsistency that even the best and wisest men fall into every day?

“It may be all quite true,” I said to Biddy, “but I admire her dreadfully.”

In short, when it came to that, I turned over on my face and got a good grip of the hair on each side of my head, and yanked it hard. All the while I knew how mad my heart was to be so mad and so completely misplaced; I was fully aware that it would have served my face right if I’d lifted it up by my hair and knocked it against the pebbles as punishment for being such an idiot.

Biddy was the wisest of girls, and she tried not to argue with me any more. She put her hand—comfortable, though roughened by work—on my hands, one after another, and gently pulled them out of my hair. Then she softly patted my shoulder in a soothing way, while my face was pressed against my sleeve and I cried a little—just as I had in the brewery yard—and I felt vaguely convinced that I was being badly treated by someone, or by everyone; I couldn’t say which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” said Biddy. “And that is, that you’ve felt you could trust me with your confidence, Pip. And I’m glad of another thing: that of course you know you can depend on me to keep it safe, and to deserve it as far as I can. If your first teacher—dear me, such a poor one, and so much in need of being taught herself—had been your teacher at the present time, she thinks she would know what lesson she’d set you. But it would be a hard one to learn, and you’ve already gone beyond her, so it’s no use now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank, and then, with a fresh and pleasant change of voice, asked, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, getting up, putting my arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I shall always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I never shall be, so that’s settled. And it’s not as if I have to tell you anything, because you already know everything I know—as I told you at home the other night.”

“Ah!” said Biddy, in a whisper, as she looked away at the ships. Then, with that same pleasant change of voice, she repeated, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon faded into summer evening, and it was very beautiful."}

{"request_id":"d8fb6dfc48b8dd678662bbf5","rewritten_text":"“One word more, Rose. Dearest Rose—one more!” Harry cried, throwing himself before her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as the world would call it—if some obscure and peaceful life had been my destiny—if I had been poor, sick, helpless—would you have turned from me then? Or has my likely rise to riches and honor given this hesitation its birth?”

“Don’t press me to answer,” Rose replied. “The question doesn’t arise, and never will. It’s unfair—almost unkind—to urge it.”

“If your answer is what I almost dare to hope,” Harry retorted, “it will cast a gleam of happiness on my lonely path and light the way ahead. It isn’t an idle thing to do, by speaking just a few brief words, for someone who loves you more than anything. Oh, Rose—in the name of my ardent and enduring attachment; in the name of all I have suffered for you, and all you doom me to endure—answer me this one question!”

“Then, if your lot had been cast differently,” Rose answered, “if you had been even a little, but not so far, above me; if I could have been a help and comfort to you in some humble scene of peace and retirement, and not a stain and burden in ambitious, distinguished crowds—I should have been spared this trial. I have every reason to be happy, very happy, now; but then, Harry, I admit I should have been happier.”

As she made this confession, busy memories of old hopes—cherished since she was a girl—came crowding into Rose’s mind; but they brought tears with them, as old hopes do when they return, dried up and ruined, and yet they also relieved her.

“I can’t help this weakness, and it only makes my purpose stronger,” Rose said, extending her hand. “I must leave you now, indeed.”

“I ask one promise,” Harry said. “Once, and only once more—say within a year, though it may be much sooner—I may speak to you again on this subject, for the last time.”

“Not to press me to change my right determination,” Rose replied, with a melancholy smile; “it will be useless.”

“No,” Harry said. “To hear you repeat it—if you will—finally repeat it! I will lay at your feet whatever station of fortune I may possess; and if you still hold to your present resolution, you will not seek, by word or deed, to change it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose rejoined. “It’s only one more pang, and by then I may be able to bear it better.”

She extended her hand again."}

content.text: {"request_id":"0d4d4f6b6501ebd2698ec4ff","rewritten_text":"I could still recall what it was like during our great civil war in the nineteenth century. In the North, a carpenter earned three dollars a day, reckoned in gold; in the South, he earned fifty—paid out in Confederate shinplasters that were supposed to be worth a dollar a bushel. In the North, a set of overalls cost three dollars, which was a day’s wages; in the South, it ran to seventy-five—two days’ wages. Everything else ran in the same way. So wages were twice as high in the North as in the South, since the one wage bought twice as much as the other.\n\nYes, I made a number of acquaintances in the hamlet, and what pleased me quite a bit was to see our new coins actually turning up in circulation—plenty of milrays, plenty of mills, lots of cents, a good many nickels, and some silver; all of it among the artisans and the common people generally. Yes, and even some gold—but that was at the bank, meaning the goldsmith’s. I went in while Marco, the son of Marco, was arguing with a shopkeeper about a quarter of a pound of salt, and I asked them to give me change for a twenty-dollar gold piece. They did—after they had worried it between their teeth, tapped it on the counter, tested it with acid, and then asked me where I’d gotten it, who I was, where I came from, where I was headed, when I expected to arrive, and probably a couple of hundred more questions besides. When they finally ran out of things to try, I kept right on supplying them with information on my own: I told them I owned a dog named Watch, that my first wife was a Free Will Baptist, that her grandfather was a Prohibitionist, that I used to know a man who had two thumbs on each hand and a wart on the inside of his upper lip, and that he died hoping for a glorious resurrection—on and on and on—until even that hungry little village questioner began to look satisfied, and a shade of relief came over him. Still, he had to treat a man with my financial standing, so he didn’t give me any backtalk, though I noticed he took it out on his underlings, which seemed perfectly natural enough. Yes, they changed my twenty, but I figured I’d strained the bank a bit, which was to be expected: it was like walking into a small village store in the nineteenth century and suddenly asking the proprietor to break a two-thousand-dollar bill for you. He might be able to do it, sure—but he’d also wonder how a small farmer happened to be carrying that kind of money in his pocket. That was probably the goldsmith’s thought as well; because he followed me to the door and stood there watching me go, staring with reverent admiration."}

{"request_id":"5ab17026031c31dce1cd087d","rewritten_text":"“‘We’ve gone to your place,’ said the first, ‘and, not finding you there, and having been told you were likely coming this way, we followed—hoping to catch up with you. Won’t you step into the carriage?’

“The tone of both was commanding, and as they spoke they shifted their positions so that I was set between them and the carriage door. They were armed. I was not.

“‘Gentlemen,’ said I, ‘excuse me; but I’m accustomed to asking who it is that seeks my services, and what sort of matter I’m being called upon to attend to.’

“The second speaker answered. ‘Doctor, your patients are persons of standing. As for the nature of the case, our trust in your ability means you’ll judge it for yourself better than we could lay it out. That’s enough. Will you please to enter the carriage?’

“I had no choice but to comply, and I got in, keeping silent. They followed in after me—the last one springing in after the steps were raised. The carriage swung round and went on at the same pace as before.

“I set down this exchange exactly as it happened. I’m sure it is, word for word, the very same. I note everything precisely as it occurred, keeping my thoughts from straying from the business in hand. Where I leave the broken marks that come next, I stop for the moment and tuck my paper away.

*****

“The carriage left the streets behind, passed the North Barrier, and came out upon the country road. At about two-thirds of a league from the Barrier—I didn’t measure it then, though later I did—it turned off from the main road and soon halted at a lone house. The three of us got down and walked, along a damp, yielding footpath through a garden where a neglected fountain had overflowed, to the door of the house. The bell was rung, but it wasn’t opened right away; then one of my two conductors, as soon as the man appeared, struck him across the face with his heavy riding glove.

“There was nothing in that act to single it out for my attention, since I had seen common people struck more often than dogs. Still, the other of the two, being just as provoked, struck the man in the same way with his arm. Their look and bearing were so closely alike that it was then, for the first time, that I realized they were twin brothers.

“From the moment we stepped out at the outer gate—which we found locked, and which one of the brothers had opened to let us in and then relocked—I had heard cries coming from an upper room.”"}

{"request_id":"3a30ed724f74db7595ebc000","rewritten_text":"This marriage is the right one. At first, I didn’t think so, but I admit it now. The gods made Sibyl Vane for you. Without her, you would have been incomplete.”

“Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray said, pressing his hand. “I knew you would understand me. Harry is so cynical that he scares me. But here is the orchestra. The music is awful, but it only lasts about five minutes. Then the curtain goes up, and you will see the girl I’m going to give my whole life to—the girl I’ve already given everything good in me.”

A quarter of an hour later, amid an extraordinary storm of applause, Sibyl Vane stepped onto the stage. Yes, she was lovely to look at—one of the loveliest people, Lord Henry thought, that he had ever seen. There was something gentle and timid in her graceful way of moving and in her startled eyes. A faint blush, like the shadow of a rose in a silver mirror, rose on her cheeks as she looked out at the crowded, excited audience. She stepped back a few paces, and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward jumped to his feet and started clapping. Dorian Gray sat completely still, as if he were dreaming, staring at her. Lord Henry leaned forward behind his glasses and murmured, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall of Capulet’s house. Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and the other friends. The band, as it was, played a few bars of music, and the dancing began. Through the crowd of awkward, shabby actors, Sibyl Vane moved as if she belonged to a better world. Her body swayed as she danced, like a plant swaying in water. The shape of her throat was like the curve of a white lily. Her hands looked as if they were made of cool ivory.

And yet she seemed strangely empty inside. When her eyes fell on Romeo, she showed no real joy. The few lines she had to say—

{"request_id":"5c6f983a29b66696d48d78fe","rewritten_text":"A little after noon, the boys borrowed a small skiff from a citizen who was away, and they set off right then. Several miles below “Cave Hollow,” Tom said:

“Now, look at this bluff—it all looks the same all the way down from the cave hollow. No houses, no wood-yards, just bushes that look alike. But do you see that white spot up there, where there’s been a landslide? That’s one of my marks. We’ll get ashore now.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, right where we’re standing, you could reach that hole I dug out with a fishing pole. See if you can find it.”

Huck searched the area and found nothing. Tom marched in proudly and pushed into a thick clump of sumach bushes.

“Here you are! Look at it, Huck—it’s the snuggiest hole in the whole country. You keep quiet about it. All along I’ve wanted to be a robber, but I knew I’d need something like this, and the hard part was finding where to stumble on it. We’ve got it now, and we’ll keep it secret. Only we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers in—because, of course, there has to be a Gang, or it wouldn’t have any style. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds splendid, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“Well, it does, Tom. And who are we going to rob?”

“Oh, just about anybody. We mostly waylay people—that’s the main way.”

“And kill them?”

“Not always. Lock them up in the cave until they raise a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them raise as much as they can from their friends, and after you’ve kept them a year, if they haven’t raised it, then you kill them. That’s the general plan. Only you don’t kill the women. You keep the women quiet, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and they’re terribly scared. You take their watches and things, but you always take your hat off and talk politely. There aren’t any robbers as polite as you’ll see in any book. Well, the women end up loving you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two, they stop crying. After that, you couldn’t get them to leave. If you drove them out, they’d just turn around and come right back. That’s how it is in all the books.”

“Why, it’s really great, Tom. I think it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s close to home, and there are circuses and all that.”

By then everything was ready, and the boys entered the hole, Tom leading. They worked their way to the far end of the tunnel, then tied their spliced kite strings in place and moved on."}

{"request_id":"58286d30fe02b67efaf96d65","rewritten_text":"“Now I hurry to the more important part of my story. I will describe events that deeply affected me, and that, in the end, helped shape who I am.

“Spring came on quickly. The weather turned pleasant, and the sky stayed clear. I was surprised that what had been desert and gloomy now seemed to burst into bloom, covered with the most beautiful flowers and green growth. My senses were delighted and refreshed by a thousand pleasant smells and a thousand sights of beauty.

“It was on one of those days, when my cottagers took their usual breaks from work. The old man played his guitar, and the children listened. That was when I noticed that Felix’s face was filled with sorrow beyond anything I had seen. He sighed again and again. Once, his father stopped playing, and from the way he looked, I guessed he was asking about the reason for his son’s sadness. Felix answered in a cheerful voice. The old man began playing again when someone tapped at the door.

“It was a lady riding on horseback, with a countryman guiding her. The lady wore a dark outfit and a thick black veil. Agatha asked a question, but the stranger only answered by speaking, in a gentle, sweet voice, the name ‘Felix.’ Her voice was musical, but it did not sound like either of my friends. When Felix heard that name, he hurried to the lady. When she saw him, she lifted her veil, and I saw a face of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair was a shining raven black, and it was braided in a special way. Her eyes were dark, yet kind, though full of life. Her features were well proportioned, and her skin was wonderfully fair, with each cheek touched by a soft pink.

“Felix looked completely taken with joy when he saw her. Every trace of sorrow left his face. In an instant, it showed a kind of ecstatic happiness that I could hardly have believed he was capable of. His eyes sparkled, and his cheeks flushed with pleasure. At that moment, I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed to be moved by different feelings. She wiped a few tears from her lovely eyes, then held out her hand to Felix. He kissed it eagerly and called her, as clearly as I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him, but she smiled. He helped her get down from the horse, sent her guide away, and led her into the cottage. Some conversation followed between Felix and his father. Then the young stranger knelt at the old man’s feet and would have kissed his hand, but he lifted her up and embraced her warmly.

“I soon realized that even though the stranger spoke in clear, understandable sounds and seemed to have her own language, neither the cottagers understood her, nor did she seem to understand them.”"}

{"request_id":"1d0d30d2b283f81d70dd6df4","rewritten_text":"Driving a peg into the ground with great care, right at the exact spot where the beetle had fallen, my friend now pulled a tape measure from his pocket. He fixed one end of it at that point on the trunk of the tree nearest the peg, then unrolled it until it reached the peg, and then unrolled it farther—along the line already set by the two points of the tree and the peg—for a distance of fifty feet—Jupiter clearing away the brambles with the scythe. At the spot thus reached, a second peg was driven, and around it, as a center, a rough circle about four feet across was drawn. Legrand then took up a spade himself, and handed one to Jupiter and one to me, begging us to start digging as quickly as possible.

To tell the truth, I never had much enthusiasm for this kind of activity, and at that moment I would gladly have refused; the night was coming on, and I felt very worn out by the work I’d already done. But I saw no way to get out of it, and I was afraid that refusing would upset my poor friend’s calm. If I could have counted on Jupiter’s help, I would have had no hesitation in trying to get the lunatic home by force; but I knew too well what the old negro was like to expect him to back me up, under any circumstances, in a personal fight against his master. I had no doubt that the man had been infected with some of the countless Southern superstitions about buried money, and that his fantasy had been confirmed by finding the scarabæus—or perhaps by Jupiter’s stubborn insistence that it was “a bug of real gold.” A mind already inclined to madness would be easily led by suggestions like that—especially if they matched the ideas it had been carrying around—and then I remembered what the poor fellow had said about the beetle being “the index of his fortune.” In the end, I was bitterly vexed and confused, but I decided to make a virtue of necessity: to dig with real energy, so I could convince the visionary, by direct proof, that the beliefs he held were wrong.

Once the lanterns were lit, we all threw ourselves into the work with a zeal that would have been worthy of a more rational cause; and as the light flared over our bodies and tools, I couldn’t help thinking how striking a group we must have looked, and how odd and suspicious our digging would have seemed to any stranger who might have happened upon us.

We dug steadily for two hours."}

May I ask who it’s meant for? If it’s for the police, or for anyone tied to Scotland Yard, I’m afraid I can’t help you. English detectives are really our best friends; I’ve always found that if we lean on their stupidity, we can carry out exactly what we please. I couldn’t spare even one of them.”

“I assure you,” said Lord Arthur, “it has nothing to do with the police at all. As a matter of fact, the clock is intended for the Dean of Chichester.”

“Good heavens! I had no idea you cared so much about religion, Lord Arthur. Very few young men feel that way these days.”

“I’m afraid you’re overestimating me, Herr Winckelkopf,” Lord Arthur said, blushing. “The truth is, I really know nothing about theology.”

“Then it’s purely a private affair?”

“Purely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf gave a shrug and left the room, coming back a few minutes later with a round cake of dynamite no bigger than a penny, along with a neat little French clock, topped by an ormolu figure of Liberty trampling on the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s expression brightened as soon as he saw it. “That’s exactly what I want,” he exclaimed. “Now tell me how it goes off.”

“Ah! there’s my secret,” replied Herr Winckelkopf, regarding his contrivance with a look of perfectly justified pride. “Tell me when you want it to explode, and I’ll set the machine for the moment.”

“Well, today is Tuesday, and if you could send it off right away—”

“That won’t be possible; I have a great deal of important work to do for some friends of mine in Moscow. Still, I might manage to send it tomorrow.”

“Oh, it will be plenty of time!” Lord Arthur said, courteous as ever. “If it’s delivered tomorrow night or Thursday morning. For the explosion itself—say Friday at noon, precisely. The Dean is always at home at that hour.”

“Friday, at noon,” Herr Winckelkopf repeated, and he jotted it down in a large ledger lying on a bureau near the fireplace.

“And now,” said Lord Arthur, rising from his seat, “pray let me know how much I owe you.”

“It’s such a small matter, Lord Arthur, that I don’t care to make a charge. The dynamite comes to seven and sixpence, the clock is three pounds ten, and the carriage about five shillings. I’m only too glad to oblige any friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.”

“But what about your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?”"}

{"request_id":"7b86ab92ceb32e355e5e4f8d","rewritten_text":"Wake up sooner or later and look around to see what caused it. Maybe you’d catch a steamboat coughing along upstream, so far off toward the other side that you couldn’t make out anything about her—only whether she was a stern-wheel or a side-wheel. Then for about an hour there’d be nothing to hear and nothing to see—just solid loneliness. Next you’d see a raft sliding by, way out yonder, and maybe some guy on it chopping, because they’re always doing it on a raft; you’d see the axe flash and come down—you wouldn’t hear a thing. You’d watch that axe go up again, and by the time it’s above the man’s head then you’d hear the _k’chunk!_—it took all that time for the sound to cross the water. So we’d spend the day drifting around, listening to the stillness.

Once there was a thick fog, and the rafts and all the other things going by were beating tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run over them. A scow or a raft would pass so close we could hear them talking and cussing and laughing—we heard them plain—but we couldn’t see any sign of them. It made you feel creepy, like spirits carrying on out there in the air. Jim said he believed it was spirits; but I said:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

The moment night came, we pushed off. When we got her out to about the middle, we left her alone and let her float wherever the current wanted. Then we lit the pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all kinds of things—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes would let us. The new clothes Buck’s folks made for me were too good to be comfortable, and besides, I didn’t care much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we’d have the whole river to ourselves for the longest time. Over there were the banks and the islands, across the water; and maybe a spark—like a candle in a cabin window. Sometimes on the water you could see a spark or two, on a raft or a scow, you know; and sometimes you could hear a fiddle or a song coming over from one of those crafts. It’s lovely to live on a raft. We had the sky right above us, all speckled with stars, and we’d lie on our backs and look up at them, talking about whether they were made or just happened. Jim said he thought they were made, but I said they just happened. I figured it would’ve taken too long to _make_ that many."}

{"request_id":"7617233a312fbea47632f5da","rewritten_text":"“And so I’m the proprietor of some knights,” I said as we rode off. “Who would ever have thought I’d live to list assets like that. I don’t know what I’ll do with them—unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, if you please, sir—and their squires.”

“It’s a good haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes—where do they live?”

“Ah, I didn’t understand you. I’ll tell you right away.” Then she said, thinking to herself, softly, turning the words over on her tongue with care: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; eh, right so; where do they hang out. Honestly, the phrase has a fine, charming sound, and it’s worded so prettily. I’ll repeat it again and again in my idle time, so I might learn it. Where do they hang out. There—already it trips off my tongue. And since—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes; the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. A while back, you remember. Figuratively speaking, the game’s called.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Go to bat. I mean, get to work on your statistics, and don’t burn so much kindling getting your fire started. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will, and lightly I’ll begin. So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I recognized my mistake at once. I’d set her going; it was my own fault. She’d take thirty days to get down to those facts. And she usually started without a preface and finished without a result. If you interrupted her, she’d either keep going without noticing, or answer with a couple of words and then go back and say the sentence again. So interruptions only did harm; and yet I had to interrupt—and interrupt pretty often, too—to save my life. A person would die if they let her monotony drip on them all day.

“Great Scott!” I said, in my distress. She went right back and began over again:

“So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came to an abbey of monks, and they were well lodged. So on the morning they heard their masses in the abbey, and then they rode forth until they came to a great forest; then was Sir Gawaine aware of a valley with a turret, of twelve fair damsels, and two knights armed on great horses, and the damsels went to and fro by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"7af5606bef26fe7dd8a4faed","rewritten_text":"Ten minutes later, with his face drained of color by terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House, pushing through the ring of fur-coated footmen around the broad striped awning, as if nothing he saw or heard could reach him. The night was bitterly cold; the gas-lamps about the square flared and fluttered in the sharp wind. Yet his hands burned with fever, and his forehead felt as though it were on fire. On and on he went, almost swaying along like a drunken man. A policeman glanced at him as he passed, and a beggar who had been lounging from an archway to beg for alms grew afraid, seeing a misery greater than his own. He paused beneath a lamp and stared at his hands. He believed he could already make out the stain of blood upon them, and a thin cry slipped from his trembling mouth.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had read there. Murder! The very night seemed to recognize it, and the desolate wind to carry the word into his ear. The dark corners of the streets were thick with it. It stared at him from the roofs of the houses.

First he reached the Park, whose gloomy woodland appeared to hold him in thrall. He sank wearily against the railings, cooling his brow on the wet metal, and strained to catch the trembling quiet of the trees. ‘Murder! murder!’ he kept repeating, as though saying it again and again might blunt the horror of the word. The sound of his own voice made him shiver, but he found himself almost wishing that Echo might hear and rouse the sleeping city from its dreams. A wild urge seized him to stop some ordinary passer-by and tell him everything.

Then he drifted across Oxford Street into narrow, shameful alleys. Two women with painted faces jeered at him as he went by. From a dark courtyard came the noise of oaths and blows, and then, with shrill screams, he saw—huddled on a damp door-step—the bent shapes of poverty and age. A strange pity took hold of him. Were these children of sin and misery, like him, already marked for their end? Were they, just as he was, nothing more than the puppets of some monstrous show?

Still, it was not the mystery, but the comedy of suffering that struck him—the sheer uselessness of it, the grotesque lack of any meaning. Everything felt so jumbled. Nothing seemed to fit together. He was astonished by the mismatch between the shallow optimism of the day and the real facts of existence. He was still very young.

After a while he found himself standing before Marylebone Church. The silent road stretched out like a long ribbon of polished silver, broken here and there by dark arabesques of moving shadows."}

{"request_id":"44de8005e9388614250f3c2d","rewritten_text":"“April 12th. A remarkable change happened in the balloon’s direction, and though I had fully expected it, it still gave me the clearest possible joy. After reaching, on its former course, about the twentieth parallel of southern latitude, it suddenly turned off at a sharp angle to the east, and so continued throughout the day, staying nearly—if not entirely—in the exact plane of the lunar ellipse. What stood out was that this change of route caused a very noticeable wobble in the car—a wobble that persisted, to a greater or lesser degree, for many hours.

“April 13th. I was again very alarmed by the loud, crackling noise that had terrified me on the tenth. I thought long and hard about it, but I couldn’t reach any satisfactory conclusion. The earth’s apparent diameter had decreased greatly; from the balloon it now subtended an angle of a little more than twenty-five degrees. I couldn’t see the moon at all, because it was nearly straight overhead. I still stayed in the plane of the ellipse, but I made little progress to the east.

“April 14th. The earth’s diameter decreased extremely fast. Today I became strongly convinced that the balloon was now actually running along the line of apsides toward the point of perigee—in other words, holding the direct course that would take it immediately to the moon at that part of its orbit where it is closest to the earth. The moon was directly overhead, and so it was hidden from my view. There was great and sustained labor required to condense the atmosphere.

“April 15th. I could no longer make out even the outlines of continents and seas on the earth with anything close to clarity. Around twelve o’clock, for the third time, I became aware of that terrifying sound that had so startled me before. This time, however, it lasted for several moments and kept growing louder as it continued. At last, while I stood stunned and terrified, waiting for I didn’t know what kind of hideous destruction, the car began to vibrate with extreme violence, and a gigantic, flaming mass of some material I couldn’t make out came roaring and booming past the balloon with a voice like a thousand thunders. Once my fears and astonishment had eased a little, I had little trouble believing it was some great volcanic fragment thrown from the world I was rapidly approaching—most likely one of those unusual substances sometimes found on the earth and called meteoric stones, simply because there’s no better name.

“April 16th. Today, looking upward as best I could through each of the side windows in turn, I saw—much to my delight—a very small portion of the moon’s disk protruding, as it were, on all sides beyond the huge circumference of the balloon.”"}

{"request_id":"5d7cbeaeec7b740f698e546f","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent by them to Adrian, who had been chosen as arbiter; and they had traveled from Paris to Calais, through empty towns and desolate countryside, all the while indulging their violent hatred for one another; and now they pleaded their separate cases with unrestrained party spirit.

By looking at the deputies one by one, and after a great deal of investigation, we learned the true state of affairs in Paris. Since Parliament had elected him Ryland’s deputy, all the surviving English had submitted to Adrian. He was our captain, to lead us from our native soil to unknown lands; our lawgiver and our preserver. When our emigration plan was first arranged, no continued separation of our members was intended, and the command of the whole body, rising gradually in power, reached its peak in the Earl of Windsor. But unforeseen circumstances changed our plans and forced the greater part of our numbers to be divided from the supreme chief for nearly two months. They had crossed over in two separate groups; and when they arrived in Paris, dissension broke out between them.

They found Paris deserted. When the plague first appeared, the return of travelers and merchants, and communications by letter, kept us regularly informed of how disease was ravaging the continent. But as mortality increased, that contact declined and finally stopped. Even within England itself, communication from one part of the island to the other became slow and rare. No vessel ever pushed through the flood that separated Calais from Dover; or if some sorrowful traveler, hoping to learn whether relatives on the French shore were alive or dead, sailed over and then tried to return among us, the greedy ocean often swallowed his small craft, or, after a day or two, he was infected by the disorder and died before he could tell us the tale of France’s desolation. So we were, to a great extent, ignorant of conditions on the continent, and we were not without some vague hope of finding many companions following the same trail. Yet the very causes that had so fearfully reduced the English nation gave even wider opportunity for harm in the sister land. France was a blank. Along the long road from Calais to Paris, not a single human being was found. In Paris there were a few—perhaps a hundred—who, resigned to their fate, drifted through the streets of the capital and gathered to talk about the past, with a liveliness and even a kind of cheerfulness that rarely leaves individuals of this nation.

The English took undisputed possession of Paris. Its tall houses and narrow streets were lifeless. A few pale figures could be seen at the usual meeting place at the Tuileries; they wondered why the islanders should approach their doomed city—for in the depth of misery, people always imagine that their own portion of the calamity is the bitterest, and, when enduring intense pain, we would trade the particular torture we are suffering for any other that might strike a different part of the body."}

{"request_id":"3d40431d07beee5014b3fbe5","rewritten_text":"“Look,” said Merlin, “there is the sword I spoke of.” With that, they saw a damsel moving across the lake. “What damsel is that?” said Arthur. “That is the Lady of the Lake,” said Merlin. “And within that lake there is a rock, and on it is as fine a place as any on earth. This damsel will come to you soon, and then you must speak kindly to her, for she will give you that sword.”

Soon afterward, the damsel came to Arthur and greeted him, and he greeted her in return. “Damsel,” said Arthur, “what sword is that that yonder arm holds up above the water? I wish it were mine, for I have no sword.” “Sir Arthur King,” said the damsel, “that sword is mine. And if you will give me a gift when I ask it, you shall have it.” “By my faith,” said Arthur, “I will give you whatever gift you ask.”

“Well,” said the damsel, “go into yonder barge and row yourself to the sword, and take it and the scabbard with you. I will ask for my gift when I see the right time.” So Sir Arthur and Merlin stepped down, and tied their horses to two trees, and then they went into the ship. When they came to the sword that the hand held, Sir Arthur took it up by the handles and took it with him. The arm and the hand went under the water, and so they reached the land and rode out.

Then Sir Arthur saw a rich pavilion. “What does yonder pavilion mean?” “It is the knight’s pavilion,” said Merlin. “It is the one you fought with last, Sir Pellinore, but he is gone—he is not there. He has been busy with one of your knights named Egglame, and they have fought together; but in the end Egglame fled, and otherwise he would have been dead. He has chased him all the way to Carlion, and we shall meet him soon on the highway.”

“That is well said,” Arthur replied. “Now I have a sword. Now I will wage battle with him and be avenged.”

“Sir,” said Merlin, “you shall not do that. The knight is weary of fighting and chasing, so you will have no honor in taking him on. Also, he will not easily be matched by any living knight. Therefore it is my counsel that you let him pass; he will do you good service in a short time, and his sons after his days. And you shall see that, in a short space, you will be glad to give him your sister to wed.”

“When I see him,” said Arthur, “I will do as you advise me.”"}

{"request_id":"a37c28571eee724d43cddd9c","rewritten_text":"“Just one word more, Rose. My dearest Rose—one more!” Harry cried, throwing himself in front of her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as the world might phrase it—if some obscure, quiet life had been what fate allotted me—if I had been poor, ill, helpless—would you have turned away from me then? Or does my likely rise to wealth and distinction give rise to this scruple?”

“Do not urge me to answer,” Rose replied. “The matter is not to be raised, and it never will be. It is unjust—almost cruel—to press it.”

“If your reply is what I can scarcely bring myself to hope,” Harry retorted, “it will cast a little gleam of happiness along my lonely road, and show me the way. It is no small thing to do, with only a few brief words, for one who loves you more than anything. Oh, Rose—in the name of my burning, lasting devotion; in the name of all I have endured for you, and all you mean to make me suffer—answer me this one question!”

“Then, if my fate had been set differently,” Rose rejoined, “if you had been even a little, but not so far, above me; if I could have been of use and comfort to you in some lowly scene of peace and retirement, and not a stain and hindrance in ambitious, distinguished circles—I should have been spared this trial. I have every reason to be content, very content, now; yet, Harry, I confess I should have been happier.”

As she spoke, Rose’s mind filled with busy recollections of old hopes, cherished in her girlhood; but they came back with tears, as old hopes do when they return, faded and ruined—and still they eased her.

“I cannot help this weakness, and it only strengthens my resolve,” said Rose, reaching out her hand. “I must leave you now, indeed.”

“I want one promise,” Harry said. “Only once more—once, and no more—say within a year, though it may be sooner—I may speak with you again on this subject, for the last time.”

“Not to press me to change my settled determination,” Rose answered, wearing a melancholy smile; “that would be pointless.”

“No,” said Harry. “To hear you repeat it—if you will—at last, repeat it. I will lay at your feet whatever rank or fortune I may come to possess; and if you still hold to your present resolution, you will not, by word or deed, try to alter it.”

“Then let it stand so,” Rose replied. “It is only one pang more, and by then I may be better able to bear it.”

She held out her hand once again."}

{"request_id":"07a6d6c799790f87a7bab262","rewritten_text":"At least he thought so. But who could really say? ... No. There had been nothing more. Out of vanity, he had spared her. In hypocrisy, he had worn the mask of goodness. For the sake of curiosity, he had tried to deny himself. He understood that now.

But this murder—would it haunt him for the rest of his life? Would he always be weighed down by his past? Would he really have to confess? Never. There was only one piece of evidence left against him. The picture itself—that was the evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it for so long? At first, it had given him pleasure to watch it change and grow old. Lately, he had felt no such pleasure. It had kept him awake at night. When he had been away, he’d been filled with terror that other eyes might look at it. It had brought melancholy into his passions. Even the memory of it had ruined many moments of joy. It had been like conscience to him. Yes, it had been conscience. He would destroy it.

He looked around and saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it again and again until there was no stain left on it. It was bright, and it gleamed. As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work—and everything that that meant. It would kill the past, and once that was dead, he would be free. It would kill this monstrous soul-life, and without its hideous warnings, he would be at peace. He grabbed the thing and stabbed the picture with it.

A cry was heard, and then a crash. The cry was so awful in its agony that the frightened servants woke and crept out of their rooms. Two gentlemen passing in the square below stopped and looked up at the great house. They went on until they met a policeman and brought him back. The man rang the bell several times, but there was no answer. Except for a light in one of the top windows, the house was completely dark. After a while, he left and stood in an adjoining portico, watching.

“Whose house is that, Constable?” asked the older of the two gentlemen.

“Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” the policeman answered.

They looked at each other as they walked away and sneered. One of them was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Inside, in the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed domestics were talking in low whispers to one another. Old Mrs. Leaf was crying and wringing her hands. Francis was as pale as death.

After about a quarter of an hour, he got the coachman and one of the footmen and crept upstairs."}

{"request_id":"30596cf2a04bf10c90fa210e","rewritten_text":"And then I repeated to myself that beautiful passage about Dante’s entrance into the earthly Paradise, and I thought it would be sweet to wander along those lovely banks and watch the car of light descend, bringing my long-lost parent back to me. While I waited there, full of expectation for that moment, I imagined how, among the lovely flowers that grew there, I would wind myself a chaplet and crown myself with joy. I would sing “Sul margine d’un rio,” my father’s favorite song, and my voice, gliding through the air that was perfectly still, would announce to him—wherever he sat, waiting for the moment of our reunion—that his daughter had come. Then the mark of misery would fade from my brow, and I would lift my eyes without fear to meet his, eyes that always shone with the gentle glow of innocent love. When I thought about the spellbinding look of those deep eyes, I wept, but softly, so my sobs wouldn’t disturb the fairy scene.

I was so completely caught up in this reverie that I kept walking, paying no attention to where my feet were taking me, until I actually bent down to gather a flower for my wreath on that bleak plain where no flower grew. Then I snapped out of my daydream and realized I didn’t know where I was.

The sun had set, and the rosy tint the clouds had caught from it as it descended was nearly gone. A wind swept across the plain. I looked around and saw nothing that could tell me where I was; I had lost my way, and I tried in vain to find my route. I kept wandering, and as darkness came on, every trace that might have guided me became indistinct. At last everything was swallowed by the deep obscurity of the blackest night. I grew tired, and I knew my servant would be sleeping that night in the neighboring village, so my absence wouldn’t alarm anyone. Since I was safe in this wild spot from any intruder, I decided to spend the night where I was. In fact, I was too weary to walk further. The air was cold, but I didn’t care about the discomfort. I told myself I was used to the weather after my two years of solitude, when no change of seasons had ever stopped my endless wandering.

I lay on the grass, surrounded by darkness so complete that not the slightest beam of light could reach me. There was no sound, because the deep night had lulled the insects to sleep—the only creatures that lived on that lonely patch of ground where no tree or shrub offered shelter to anything else. There was a wondrous silence in the air that calmed my senses, yet at the same time stirred my soul; my mind raced from image to image and seemed to grasp an eternity."}

{"request_id":"b6ba366170916903ebfbc14e","rewritten_text":"“Story!”

He seemed determined to misunderstand the word she had repeated, when he added, in a rush, “Yes, customers; in the banking business we usually call our connection our customers. He was a French gentleman; a scientific gentleman; a man of great learning—a Doctor.”

“Not of Beauvais?”

“Why, yes, of Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was well known in Paris. I had the honor of knowing him there. Our relationship was business, but confidential. At that time I was in our French House, and I had been—oh!—for twenty years.”

“At that time—I may ask, at what time, sir?”

“I’m speaking, miss, of twenty years ago. He married—an English lady—and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like the affairs of many other French gentlemen and French families, were entirely in Tellson’s hands. In a similar way I am, or I have been, trustee of one kind or another for scores of our customers. These are only business relations, miss; there’s no friendship in them, no particular interest, nothing like sentiment. I move from one to another, in the course of my business life, just as I move from one of our customers to another during the day; in short, I have no feelings; I’m nothing but a machine. To go on—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir; and I’m starting to think”—the oddly roughened brow was fixed on him with intense focus—“that when I was left an orphan because my mother survived my father by only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I’m almost sure it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the hesitant little hand that had advanced to take his with such trust, and he placed it, with great ceremony, against his lips. Then he guided the young lady straight back to her chair. Holding the chair-back with his left hand, and using his right in turn to rub his chin, tug his wig at the ears, or point as he spoke, he stood looking down at her while she sat looking up at him.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you’ll see how truly I spoke of myself just now, when I said I had no feelings, and that all the relationships I have with my fellow human beings are only business relations, when you consider that I have never seen you since. No—you’ve been Tellson’s ward ever since, and I’ve been busy with Tellson’s other business ever since. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity for them. I spend my whole life, miss, turning an immense pecuniary Mangle.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"3f699537937534f0e09ca18e","rewritten_text":"“But, as a matter of fact, if one ascends to any given height, the weighty portion of air that has been passed over in that further climb is by no means proportional to the extra elevation gained (as is plain from what has already been said); rather, it falls off in a ratio that keeps shrinking. So it follows that, however high we rise, we cannot—strictly speaking—reach a boundary beyond which no atmosphere exists. I maintained that it must be there, though it may be present in a state of infinite rarefaction.\n\n“On the other hand, I knew that there were arguments enough to show a real, definite limit to the atmosphere, after which there is absolutely no air. Yet there was a point that those who press for such a limit seemed to have overlooked; I could not offer a direct refutation of their view, but it struck me as deserving the most serious examination. When I compared the intervals between Encke’s comet returning to perihelion—allowing, in the most exact way possible, for every disturbance caused by the planets’ attractions—it turned out that the periods are steadily shortening. That is, the comet’s ellipse has a major axis that grows shorter, in a slow but perfectly regular decline. Now, this is exactly what should happen if we assume that the comet meets a resistance from an extremely rare ethereal medium filling the regions of its orbit. For it is clear that such a medium, by checking the comet’s speed, would strengthen its centripetal pull by weakening the centrifugal force. In other words, the sun’s attraction would be continually gaining power, and the comet would be drawn nearer with each revolution. Indeed, there is no other reasonable way to explain the change in question. But again:—the true diameter of the comet’s nebulosity is seen to contract quickly as it nears the sun, and to expand just as quickly as it moves away toward its aphelion. Was I not warranted, with M. Valz, in supposing that this apparent shrinking of volume comes from the compression of the same ethereal medium I mentioned earlier, which becomes only denser the nearer it is to the sun? The lenticular phenomenon, likewise known as the zodiacal light, also called for attention. This radiance, so conspicuous in the tropics and not to be mistaken for any meteoric glow, stretches from the horizon obliquely upward and generally keeps to the direction of the sun’s equator. It seemed to me clearly of the nature of a rare atmosphere spreading outward from the sun, at least beyond the orbit of Venus, and I believed it to extend indefinitely farther. In fact, I could not suppose this medium confined to the comet’s orbital path, or to the immediate vicinity of the sun.”"}

{"request_id":"176b096847076446bd50320e","rewritten_text":"The chain of necessity, which has so long been dragging misery after it, must surely have been snapped; and the malignant fate that rules over it would not suffer so much as a breach of her unalterable laws. Yet why should I fret at that? Misery has ever been my element, and nothing but what is miserable could ever draw near to me; had Woodville been happy, I should never have come to know him. And can I—who for many years have been fed on tears, and sustained beneath the dew of grief—stop now to tell a story of woe and death?

Woodville was compelled to go on a journey into the country, and was kept from day to day in an irksome absence from his lovely bride. He received a letter from her, saying she was slightly ill, but urging him to hasten to her; from his own eyes, she wrote, health would come, and that his company would be her surest medicine. He was detained three days longer, and then he made all haste to her. His heart, he could not tell why, foretold misfortune; he had heard nothing further from her. He feared she might be worse, and that fear made him restless and impatient for the instant when he should see her again, standing before him in health and beauty; for some sinister voice seemed always to murmur, “You will never more behold her as she was.”

When he reached her dwelling, everything was silent. He went through several rooms; in one he saw a servant weeping bitterly. He was so overcome with dread that he could scarcely bring himself to ask, “Is she dead?” and only then to listen to the dreadful reply, “Not yet.” Those words struck him with a force less terrible than what he had been bracing himself to hear; to learn that she still lived, and that hope was not yet extinguished, was some relief. He recalled the very terms of her letter, and gave way to a wild fancy—that his kisses, breathing warm love and life, might infuse new spirit into her; and that, with him at her side, she could not die; that his presence was the talisman of her existence.

He hurried to her sick room. She lay there with her cheeks burning from fever, yet her eyes were closed, and she seemed insensible. He drew her to him in his arms; he pressed breathless kisses upon her burning lips; he called to her in a voice subdued with anguish, using the tenderest names. “Return, Elinor; I am with you—your life, your love. Return, dearest one—you promised me this boon, that I should bring you health. Let your sweet spirit rise again; you cannot die near me. What is death? To see you no more? To be parted from what is a part of myself—without whom I have neither memory nor any future?”"}

{"request_id":"1f82be52604b6c00a172e28f","rewritten_text":"Smallpox!

I sprang to the king and said in his ear:

“Out the door at once, sire. The woman is dying of that disease that ruined the skirts of Camelot two years ago.”

He didn’t move.

“Truly, I shall stay—and help as well.”

I whispered again:

“King, it can’t be. You have to go.”

“You mean well, and you’re not speaking unwisely. But it would be shameful for a king to admit fear, and shameful for a belted knight to hold back his hand when there are people who need help. Peace—I won’t go. It’s you who must go. The Church’s ban isn’t on me, but it forbids you to be here, and she will deal with you harshly if she hears of your trespass.”

It was a desperate position for him to be in, and it might cost him his life, but there was no point arguing with him. If he thought his knightly honor was at stake here, then that was the end of the argument; he would stay, and nothing could stop it. I knew that. So I dropped the subject. The woman spoke:

“Good sir, will you climb the ladder there and bring me news of what you find? Don’t be afraid to report. There may come a time when even a mother’s heart can’t break anymore—already broken, as it is.”

“Stay,” said the king, “and give the woman something to eat. I will go.” And he set down the knapsack.

I turned to leave, but the king had already started. He stopped, looked down at a man lying in a dim light, and hadn’t noticed us until then or spoken.

“Is it your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he asleep?”

“God be thanked for that one mercy—yes. For three hours. Where can I ever repay the full measure of my gratitude? My heart is bursting with it for the sleep he’s sleeping now.”

I said, “We’ll be careful. We won’t wake him.”

“Ah, no—you won’t,” she said, “because he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes. What a triumph it is to know it! No one can harm him, no one can insult him anymore. He is in heaven now, and happy; or if not there, he waits in hell and is content—because in that place he’ll find neither abbot nor bishop. We were boy and girl together; we were man and wife for twenty-five years, and never separated until today. Think how long that is—to love and suffer together. This morning he was out of his mind, and in his fancy we were boy and girl again, wandering in the happy fields. And so, in that innocent, joyful conversation, he wandered farther and farther—still lightly talking—until he entered those other fields we don’t know about, and was shut away from mortal sight.”"}

{"request_id":"2302b7da27c84edb244c8a65","rewritten_text":"“Never!” the girl answered.

“Tell me why?”

“For one reason,” the girl replied firmly, “for one reason: the lady knows, and she will stand by me—I know she will, because I have her promise. And for this other reason as well: even though his life has been bad, I’ve lived badly too. There are many of us who have kept the same path together, and I won’t turn on them—people who might have turned on me, any of them—but didn’t, even though they’re bad.”

“Then,” the gentleman said quickly, as if this were the exact point he’d been trying to reach, “put Monks into my hands, and leave him to me to deal with.”

“What if he turns against the others?”

“I promise you that if that happens, and the truth is forced out of him, then the matter will end there. There must be circumstances in Oliver’s little history that would be painful to drag into public view, and once the truth is brought out, they shall go free.”

“And if it isn’t?” the girl suggested.

“Then,” the gentleman continued, “this Fagin won’t be brought to justice without your consent. In that case, I could show you reasons, I think, that would make you agree.”

“Do I have the lady’s promise for that?” the girl asked.

“You do,” Rose replied. “My true and faithful pledge.”

“Monks would never learn how you knew what you know?” the girl said after a short pause.

“Never,” the gentleman answered. “The information should be brought to bear on him in such a way that he could never even guess.”

“I’ve been a liar, and among liars since I was a child,” the girl said after another stretch of silence, “but I will take your word.”

After both of them assured her that she could do so safely, she went on in a voice so low that it was often hard for the listener to make out even what she meant. She described, by name and location, the public house where she had been followed that night. From the way she occasionally paused, it seemed as though the gentleman was making quick notes of what she was telling him. Once she had fully explained the layout of the place, the best spot from which to watch it without drawing attention, and the night and hour when Monks was most likely to go there, she seemed to stop and think for a few moments—trying to bring his face and appearance back more clearly.

“He’s tall,” the girl said. “A strongly built man, but not stout. He has a kind of furtive walk, and as he walks he keeps looking over his shoulder—first to one side, then to the other.”"}

{"request_id":"5132cc2b8cfb93e473c0b7d4","rewritten_text":"But there was no laughter to be found in the little town that same calm Saturday afternoon. The Harpers, along with Aunt Polly’s people, were being dressed in mourning, with heavy grief and a great deal of crying. An odd stillness lay over the village, though it was ordinarily quiet enough, if you asked me. The villagers went about their business with a kind of far-off look, speaking little; yet they sighed again and again. The Saturday holiday felt like a weight on the children. They had no spirit for their games, and little by little they let them drop.

In the afternoon Becky Thatcher drifted around the empty schoolhouse yard, looking downcast and feeling very low. Still, she found nothing there that could soothe her. At last she began to talk to herself:

“Oh, if I only had that brass andiron-knob back again! But I don’t have anything now to keep him in mind.” And she swallowed down a small sob.

Presently she paused, and said to herself:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for the whole world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

That thought broke her, and she wandered off, tears running down her cheeks. Then a whole cluster of boys and girls—Tom’s and Joe’s playmates—came along, and stopped to look over the paling fence, speaking in hushed, reverent tones about what Tom had done the last time they saw him, and about how Joe said this and that little matter (full of dreadful meaning, as they could plainly see now!). Each one pointed out the exact place where the lost lads had stood at the time, and then added something like, “and I was standing just so—just as I am now, and as if you was him—I was as close as that—and he smiled, just this way—and then it seemed like something went through me, like—awful, you know—and I didn’t think what it meant then, of course, but I can see it now!”

After that, there was a quarrel over who had seen the dead boys last while they were still alive, and many claimed that grim honor, bringing forward their proofs—more or less altered by the teller. And when, at last, it was decided who _had_ seen the departed last, and who had exchanged the final words with them, the fortunate ones took on a kind of sacred importance, and the rest stared at them and envied them. One poor fellow, having no other sort of greatness to offer, said with pretty plain pride in the recollection:

“Well, Tom Sawyer he licked me once.”

But that attempt at glory fell flat. Most of the boys could say the same thing, and so the distinction got cheapened too much. The group drifted away again, lingering on their memories of the lost heroes, speaking in awed voices."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a43999a997da80a0f1323879","rewritten_text":"“They ought to matter to you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his good name. You wouldn’t want people speaking of you as vile and fallen. Certainly, you have your position, your wealth, and all that sort of thing. Still, position and money aren’t everything. I must tell you plainly, I don’t believe these reports at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I look at you. Sin, once it’s there, shows itself across a man’s face. It can’t be hidden. People sometimes whisper about secret vices, but there’s no such thing. If a miserable fellow has a vice, it comes out in the very lines of his mouth, in the droop of his eyelids, in the way his hands are shaped. Someone—I'll not name him, but you know who I mean—came to me last year to have his portrait painted. I had never met him before, and at the time I’d heard nothing about him, though I’ve heard plenty since. He dangled an extravagant sum before me. I turned him away. There was something in the form of his fingers that I couldn’t stand. I see now that I was perfectly right about what I suspected. His life is dreadful. But you, Dorian—your pure, bright, innocent face, and your wonderful youth, so untroubled—I can’t bring myself to believe anything against you.\n\nAnd yet I hardly see you, and you never come down to the studio anymore. When I’m away from you, and I hear all these dreadful things people are murmuring about you, I don’t know what to think. Why is it, Dorian, that the Duke of Berwick leaves a club the moment you enter? Why do so many gentlemen in London neither visit your house nor invite you to theirs? You were once friendly with Lord Staveley. I dined with him last week, and your name came up—connected with the miniatures you’ve lent for the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said you might have the most artistic tastes, but that you were a man no pure-minded girl ought to be allowed to know, and no chaste woman should ever sit in the same room with. I reminded him that I was your friend, and I asked what he meant. He told me—told me openly, in front of everyone. It was dreadful! Why is your friendship so ruinous for young men? There was that wretched boy in the Guards who took his own life. You were his great friend. And there was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with a name that had been stained."}

{"request_id":"289cb11aa1a209866e202b6b","rewritten_text":"“You won’t, won’t you? Oh, you dear little flat!”

“Isn’t it wicked, is it, Oliver?” Charley Bates asked. “He’ll end up getting scragged, won’t he?”

“I can’t make sense of it,” Oliver answered.

“Something like that, old chap,” said Charley. As he spoke, Master Bates seized the end of his neckerchief, held it up straight in the air, then dropped his head onto his shoulder and snapped a strange little sound through his teeth—showing, with a lively bit of acting, that scragging and hanging were the very same thing.

“That’s what it means,” Charley said. “Just look at how he’s staring, Jack! I never saw such top-notch company as that boy; he’ll be the death of me, I swear.” Master Charley Bates laughed again, then went back to his pipe, tears in his eyes.

“You’ve been taught all wrong,” the Dodger told him, eyeing his boots with satisfaction after Oliver polished them. “Fagin will turn you into something, sure enough—unless you’re the first he ever had that didn’t turn out profitable. You’d best start right away, because you’ll be in the trade long before you think about it; and you’re wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates drove the point home with a handful of moral lectures of his own; once those ran out, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins launched into a bright, enthusiastic account of the many pleasures that came with the life they led, slipping in all sorts of hints for Oliver that the best thing he could do—without delay—was to win Fagin’s good will by the same means they themselves had used to get it.

“And always keep this in your pipe, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as the Jew was heard unlocking the door upstairs. “If you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the point of saying it like that?” Master Bates cut in. “He doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take pocket-handkechers and watches,” the Dodger went on, pitching his words down to Oliver’s level, “some other fellow will; and then the lads who lose ’em will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off too, and nobody’ll be any better for it—except the chaps who get ’em, and you’ve got as much right to them as they have.”

“Why, yes, why, yes!” said the Jew, who had come in unseen by Oliver. “It’s all in a nutshell, my dear—just take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the catechism of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands together with glee as he confirmed the Dodger’s argument in his own way, chuckling happily at his pupil’s skill.

The talk didn’t go any farther then, because the Jew had gone back home with Miss Betsy, and with a gentleman Oliver had never seen before—one the Dodger addressed as Tom Chitling. After lingering on the stairs to exchange a few gallantries with the lady, he now appeared."}
