content.text: {"request_id":"32af21f53685ccdd34f635c3","rewritten_text":"He chose Friday, the 17th of August, for his appearance, and spent most of that day going through his wardrobe, until he finally settled on a large, slouched hat with a red feather, a winding-sheet frilled at the wrists and neck, and a rusty dagger. Toward evening a violent storm of rain set in, and the wind was so strong that every window and door in the old house shook and rattled. In fact, it was exactly the kind of weather he loved. His plan was this: he would move quietly to Washington Otis’s room, gibber at him from the foot of the bed, and stab himself three times in the throat to the sound of slow music. He held Washington a special grudge, knowing full well that it was he who had the habit of removing the famous Canterville blood-stain with Pinkerton’s Paragon Detergent. After he had reduced the reckless, foolhardy youth to a state of abject terror, he would then go to the room occupied by the United States Minister and his wife, and there place a clammy hand on Mrs. Otis’s forehead while he hissed into her trembling husband’s ear the awful secrets of the charnel-house. As for little Virginia, he hadn’t fully decided. She had never insulted him in any way, and she was pretty and gentle. A few hollow groans from the wardrobe, he thought, would be more than enough; or, if that didn’t wake her, he might grab at the counterpane with palsy-twitching fingers. As for the twins, he was determined to teach them a lesson. The first thing to do, of course, was to sit on their chests to create the suffocating sensation of nightmare. Then, since their beds were close together, he would stand between them in the shape of a green, icy-cold corpse until they were paralyzed with fear. Finally, he would throw off the winding-sheet and crawl around the room with white, bleached bones and one rolling eyeball, playing the part of “Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide’s Skeleton”—a role in which he had more than once made a great impression, and which he considered every bit as good as his famous act of “Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.”\n\nAt ten-thirty he heard the family go to bed. For a while he was disturbed by wild shrieks of laughter from the twins, who, with the carefree cheer of schoolboys, were clearly entertaining themselves before turning in. But at a quarter past eleven everything was quiet, and when midnight sounded he slipped out. The owl beat against the window panes, the raven croaked from the old yew tree, and the wind wandered moaning around the house like a lost soul; yet the Otis family slept, unaware of their doom, and high above the rain and storm he could hear the steady snoring of the Minister for the United States."}

{"request_id":"512e6561c70bbee5590a67a6","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water left to finish the meal. After a while, Becky suggested they should move on again. Tom was quiet for a moment. Then he said, “Becky, can you stand it if I tell you something?”

Becky’s face went pale, but she thought she could handle it.

“Then we have to stay here,” Tom said. “We need the water to drink. That little candle piece is our last one!”

Becky broke down and cried out in loud, helpless wails. Tom did what he could to comfort her, but it didn’t help much. After a while Becky said, “Tom!”

“Well, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and come looking!”

“Yes, they will,” Tom said. “Of course they will!”

“Maybe they’re looking for us already, Tom.”

“Maybe they are,” Tom answered. “I hope they are.”

“When would they miss us?” Becky asked.

“When they get back to the boat,” Tom said.

“Tom, it might be dark by then. Would they notice we didn’t come?”

“I don’t know,” Tom said. “But your mother would miss you as soon as they got home.”

A frightened look crossed Becky’s face, and it made Tom realize he had made a serious mistake. Becky was not supposed to go home that night. The children fell silent, each lost in thought. Soon Becky’s grief surged again, and Tom could see that what he had been thinking had hit her too—that Sunday morning might already be half over before Mrs. Thatcher realized Becky wasn’t at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children stared at their small piece of candle and watched it melt slowly and without mercy. They saw the wick stand alone at last. They watched the weak flame rise and fall, climb the thin column of smoke, linger at the top for a moment, and then—total darkness took over.

How long later it was before Becky slowly came back to herself, crying in Tom’s arms, neither of them could say. All they knew was that after what felt like a long stretch of time, they both woke from a heavy, numb sleep and started suffering again. Tom said it might be Sunday now—or maybe Monday. He tried to get Becky to talk, but her pain was too much. Her hopes were gone.

Tom said they must have been missed long ago, and the search was probably already underway. He said he would shout, and maybe someone would come. He tried it, but in the dark the distant echoes sounded so terrible that he stopped.

The hours dragged on, and hunger began to torment them again. Some of Tom’s half of the cake was left, and they divided it and ate it. But even after that, they seemed hungrier than before."}

{"request_id":"e0a185b715ec08f565bad76a","rewritten_text":"But now she would rather it had not occurred. She was persuaded he had taken too freely of Mr. Weston’s excellent wine, and she felt certain he would be eager to talk nothing but nonsense.

With all the restraint she could manage through her own manner, she set herself at once to begin—speaking with the utmost composure and solemnity of the weather and the night; yet scarcely had she started, scarcely had they passed the sweep-gate and joined the other carriage, when her intended subject was broken in upon: her hand was seized, her attention claimed, and Mr. Elton actually made violent love to her. Taking advantage of the moment, he went on to declare sentiments that must already be well known; he hoped—feared—adoring—ready to die if she refused him; and yet he flattered himself that his ardent attachment, his unequalled love, and his unparalleled passion could not fail to have some effect. In short, he was very much resolved to be seriously accepted as soon as possible. And indeed it was so. Without scruple—without apology—without any great show of hesitation, Mr. Elton, the admirer of Harriet, was now professing himself her lover. She tried to stop him, but in vain; he would continue, and say it all.

Even though she was angry, the very thought of the moment made her determine, when she did speak, to keep herself in check. She felt that at least half of this folly must be drunkenness, and therefore might be confined to the passing hour. Accordingly, with a mixture of seriousness and playfulness—such, she hoped, as would best suit his half-sober, half-intoxicated condition—she answered,

“I am very much astonished, Mr. Elton. This to me! You forget yourself—you take me for my friend. Any message to Miss Smith I shall be glad to deliver; but no more of this to me, if you please.”

“Miss Smith!—message to Miss Smith!—What could she possibly mean!”—and he repeated her words with such confidence of accent, such self-satisfied pretence of astonishment, that she could not help replying at once,

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behaviour! I can account for it only in one way: you are not yourself, or you could not speak to me, or of Harriet, in such a manner. Command yourself enough to say no more, and I will endeavour to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk wine enough only to raise his spirits, not at all to confuse his understanding. He knew perfectly well what he meant. Having warmly protested against her suspicion as most injurious, and touched—only slightly—upon his respect for Miss Smith as her friend (while owning, with some wonder, that Miss Smith should be mentioned at all), he returned at once to the subject of his own passion, and pressed her for a favourable answer."}

{"request_id":"f6531355c6daf86997f0d10f","rewritten_text":"I want you to be permanently well settled in your connections, and for that reason it would be best to keep as few odd acquaintances as possible; so I say that if you are still in this country when Mr. Martin marries, I hope you won’t be drawn in by your closeness with the sisters—so as to become acquainted with his wife, who will probably be nothing more than some farmer’s daughter, with no education.”

“Certainly. Yes. I don’t suppose Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who hadn’t had some education—and been brought up very well. Still, I don’t mean to set my judgment against yours, and I’m sure I shall not want the acquaintance of his wife. I shall always have a great regard for the Miss Martins, particularly Elizabeth, and I should be very sorry to give them up, for they are quite as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, vulgar woman, then I had better not go to see her, if I can help it.”

Emma watched her as she spoke, and saw nothing that looked like any dangerous sign of love. The young man had been the first admirer, but she believed there was no other hold, and that on Harriet’s part there would be no serious trouble in resisting any friendly arrangement of her own.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day, while they were walking on the Donwell road. He was on foot, and after regarding her with the utmost respect, he looked with the most genuine satisfaction at her companion. Emma was glad of the chance to observe; and, walking a few yards ahead while they talked, she soon made her quick eye sufficiently acquainted with Mr. Robert Martin. He had a very neat appearance, and seemed like a sensible young man, but his person had no other advantage; and when she compared him with gentlemen, she felt he must lose all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s favor. Harriet was not unaware of his manner; she had, of her own accord, noticed her father’s gentleness with admiration as well as wonder. Mr. Martin looked as if he did not know what manner was.

They stayed together only a few minutes, for Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting; and then Harriet ran to her with a smiling face, and in a flutter of spirits which Miss Woodhouse hoped she would soon be able to settle.

“Only think of our actually running into him!—How very strange! He said it was quite an accident that he hadn’t gone round by Randalls. He didn’t think we ever walked this road. He thought we went towards Randalls most days.”"}

{"request_id":"8c6e15fb794c2dd5645ab081","rewritten_text":"This little explanation with Mr. Knightley gave Emma a great deal of pleasure. It was one of the pleasant memories of the ball, and the next morning she walked about the lawn to enjoy it.—She was especially glad that they had come to such a good understanding about the Eltons, and that their opinions of both husband and wife were so much alike; and his praise of Harriet, his willingness to support her, was particularly gratifying. The Eltons’ impertinence, which for a few minutes had threatened to ruin the rest of her evening, had also been the cause of some of its greatest satisfactions; and she looked forward to another happy result—the cure of Harriet’s infatuation.—From Harriet’s manner of speaking about the incident before they left the ballroom, Emma had strong hopes. It seemed as if her eyes had been suddenly opened, and she could now see that Mr. Elton was not the superior person she had believed him to be. The fever was over, and Emma could hardly fear that it would be quickened again by harmful politeness. She relied on the Eltons’ bad feelings to provide whatever further discipline of pointed neglect might still be needed.—With Harriet thinking more rationally, Frank Churchill not too deeply in love, and Mr. Knightley not inclined to quarrel with her, what a happy summer must be in store for Harriet!

She was not going to see Frank Churchill this morning. He had told her that he couldn’t allow himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, because he was to be at home by the middle of the day. She didn’t regret it.

Having arranged all these matters, checked them over, and put everything in order, she was just turning back toward the house with her spirits refreshed for the demands of the two little boys, as well as of their grandfather, when the great iron sweep-gate opened and two people entered whom she had never expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm—actually Harriet!—In a moment she was convinced that something extraordinary had happened. Harriet looked pale and frightened, and he was trying to cheer her.—The iron gates and the front door were not twenty yards apart;—soon all three were in the hall, and Harriet immediately sank into a chair and fainted away.

A young lady who faints must be brought round; questions must be asked, and surprises explained. Such events are very interesting, but the suspense can’t last long. In a few minutes Emma learned everything.

Miss Smith, and Miss Bickerton, another parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s, who had also been at the ball, had gone out together and taken a road—the Richmond road—which, though it looked public enough to be safe, had led them into alarm.—About half a mile beyond Highbury, making a sudden turn and deeply shaded by elms on both sides, it became for some distance very secluded; and when the young ladies had gone some way into it, they suddenly saw, at a short distance ahead, on a broader patch of greensward beside the road, a party of gipsies."}

{"request_id":"6525cda2464e15ba78e75607","rewritten_text":"Saturday noon I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning smoke-powders, clawing at the air, and muttering nonsense as hard as ever. But he looked very discouraged, because, of course, he hadn’t even managed to make the water in that well start moving yet. Finally I said:

“How is it going, partner? What does this thing promise by now?”

“Look,” he replied. “I’m working right now on the strongest enchantment known to the princes of the occult arts in the lands of the East. If it fails, nothing else can help. Wait until I finish.”

This time he raised a cloud of smoke that darkened the whole area. It must have made things uncomfortable for the hermits, because the wind carried it down over their dens, turning everything into thick, rolling fog. He kept talking as if he were filling the air with words, and he twisted his body and sawed at the air with his hands in a strange, dramatic way. After twenty minutes he dropped down, panting and nearly spent.

Then the abbot arrived, along with several hundred monks and nuns. Behind them came a crowd of pilgrims and even a couple of acres of foundlings, all drawn by the heavy smoke and all buzzing with excitement. The abbot asked anxiously if there were any results. Merlin said:

“If anything a mortal could do might break the spell that holds these waters, then what I have just tried would have done it. It failed. That means what I feared is true. The sign of this failure is that the most powerful spirit known to the magicians of the East has laid his spell on this well. No one may even speak his name and live. A mortal cannot breathe, and never will, who can uncover the secret of that spell. And without that secret, no one can break it. The water will not flow again, ever, Father. I have done what a man can. Let me go.”

Of course, this sent the abbot into real panic. He looked at me, and you could see it on his face. He said:

“You’ve heard him. Is it true?”

“Part of it is.”

“Not all of it? Not all? Then what part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has put his spell on the well.”

“God’s wounds, then we’re ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? You mean not certainly?”

“That’s right.”

“So when he says that none can break the spell—”

“Yes. When he says that, he’s saying something that isn’t necessarily true. There are conditions where an attempt to break it might have some chance—only a small one, a trifling one—of success.”}"}

{"request_id":"ee5d71cbf690e367a9bbb03c","rewritten_text":"At least, that was what he told himself. Yet who could be sure? ... No—there was nothing else. Through vanity he had spared her. With hypocrisy he had put on the mask of goodness. Out of sheer curiosity he had tried to deny himself. He understood it now.

But this murder—would it keep hunting him for the rest of his life? Would his past always weigh upon him? Would he truly have to confess? Never. There was only one remaining scrap of proof against him. The picture itself—that was the proof. He would destroy it. Why had he held onto it for so long? At first it had given him a kind of pleasure, watching it change and grow old. Lately, though, he had felt nothing of that sort. It had kept him awake at night. When he was away, he had been seized with terror that other eyes might fall upon it. It had poured melancholy over his desires. Even the recollection of it had spoiled many hours that might otherwise have been joyful. It had been like conscience to him. Yes, it was conscience. He would destroy it.

He turned his head and saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had scrubbed it again and again until no stain remained. It shone—bright and slick with light. As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work, and everything bound up with it. It would kill the past; and once the past was gone, he would be free. It would kill that monstrous soul-life, and with its dreadful warnings silenced, he would at last be at peace. He seized the thing and drove it into the picture.

A cry went up, and then a crash. The cry was so dreadful in its suffering that the frightened servants stirred and slipped out of their rooms. Two gentlemen passing in the square below stopped and looked up at the great house. They went on until they met a policeman, and brought him back. The man rang the bell again and again, but no one answered. Save for a light in one of the top windows, the house was wholly dark. After a while, he left and stood in a neighboring portico, watching.

“Whose place is that, Constable?” asked the elder of the two gentlemen.

“Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” replied the policeman.

They exchanged glances as they walked away, and sneered. One of them was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Within the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed domestics talked in low whispers. Old Mrs. Leaf was weeping and twisting her hands. Francis looked as white as death.

After about a quarter of an hour, he took the coachman and one of the footmen, and crept upstairs."}

{"request_id":"614939515e3d2c6a6f621562","rewritten_text":"During my younger years, discontent never entered my mind, and if I was ever overcome by _ennui_, the sight of what is beautiful in nature or the study of what is excellent and sublime in the works of human beings could always catch my heart and give elasticity to my spirits. But I am a blasted tree; the bolt has entered my soul. And I felt then that I would survive only to show what I shall soon cease to be—a miserable spectacle of wrecked humanity, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent a considerable time at Oxford, wandering through its surroundings and trying to identify every place that might connect to the most stirring period of English history. Our little journeys of discovery were often prolonged by the successive sights that presented themselves. We visited the tomb of the illustrious Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment, my soul rose above my degrading, miserable fears, to contemplate the divine ideas of liberty and self-sacrifice—ideas that these scenes were monuments to and reminders of. For an instant, I dared to throw off my chains and look around with a free, lofty spirit, but the iron had eaten into my flesh, and I sank again, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford with regret and went on to Matlock, which was our next place to rest. The countryside near this village resembled, even more closely, the scenery of Switzerland; but everything was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the crown of distant white Alps that always rise behind the pine-covered mountains of my native country. We visited the wondrous cave and the small natural history rooms, where the curiosities are arranged in the same way as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. The latter name made me tremble when Henry pronounced it, and I hurried to leave Matlock, since that terrible scene was thus linked to it.

From Derby, still traveling northward, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could now almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains. The small patches of snow that still lingered on the northern slopes of the mountains, the lakes, and the rushing of the rocky streams were all familiar and dear sights to me. Here, too, we made some acquaintances, who nearly managed to trick me into happiness. Clerval’s delight was, in proportion, even greater than mine; his mind expanded in the company of talented men, and he found in his own nature greater capacities and resources than he could have believed he possessed while he was with people of lesser ability."}

{"request_id":"9b9041922d5ff432fe96fae5","rewritten_text":"“I know she would!”

The Widow Douglas’ fine hospitality was a tempting lure. Between that and Tom’s urging, the matter was soon settled. So they decided to tell no one anything about the night’s plan. After a while Tom found himself wondering whether Huck might show up this very night and give the signal. The idea drained a good deal of the sparkle from his hopes. Still, he couldn’t bring himself to give up the fun at Widow Douglas’. And why should he? The signal hadn’t come the night before, so what made it any more likely to come tonight? The certain enjoyment of the evening beat the uncertain promise of a prize; and, in true boy fashion, he chose to follow the stronger pull and not let himself think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town, the ferryboat stopped at the mouth of a wooded hollow and made fast. The crowd poured ashore, and soon the forest distances and jagged heights rang with shouts and laughter. They tried every way they could think of to get hot and worn out, and by and by the rovers drifted back to camp with appetites that felt properly earned—then the spoiling of the good things began. After the meal came a pleasant stretch of resting and talking in the shade of spreading oaks. Presently someone called out:

“Who’s set for the cave?”

Everyone was. Bundles of candles were fetched, and at once there was a general scramble up the hill. The cave’s mouth sat higher on the slope—an opening shaped like the letter A. Its heavy oak door stood open, with no bar across it. Inside there was a small chamber, cold as an icehouse, and lined by Nature with solid limestone, slick and damp as if sweating with chill. It was romantic and mysterious to stand in that deep gloom and look out over the green valley shining in the sun. But the spell didn’t last; the play started up again. The instant a candle was lit, its owner was immediately surrounded; there was a scramble and a brave bit of resistance, yet the candle was soon knocked down or blown out, and then came a cheerful uproar of laughter and a fresh chase.

But everything ends. Soon the group began to file down the steep descent of the main avenue, the flickering lights only dimly showing the high rock walls up to where they met, some sixty feet overhead. This main passage was no more than eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps, other lofty but narrower crevices split off on either side—for McDougal’s cave was really a huge tangle of crooked corridors that kept joining and breaking apart again, leading nowhere."}

{"request_id":"d00be58b4990a1691613e552","rewritten_text":"“Now I examined the death’s-head with care. Its outer edges—the edges of the drawing nearest the edge of the vellum—were far clearer than the others. It was obvious that the action of the caloric had been imperfect or uneven. I immediately lit a fire and subjected every part of the parchment to a glowing heat. At first, the only result was that the faint lines in the skull grew stronger; but if I kept at the experiment, then, at the corner of the slip, diagonally opposite the spot where the death’s-head was drawn, there became visible the figure of what I at first took to be a goat. A closer look, though, convinced me it was meant to be a kid.”

“Ha! ha!” said I. “Surely I have no right to laugh at you—an amount of money like a million and a half is too serious a matter for mirth—but you’re not about to set up a third link in your chain. You won’t find any special connection between your pirates and a goat. Pirates, you know, have nothing to do with goats; they belong to the farming interest.”

“But I’ve just said the figure wasn’t that of a goat.”

“Well, then—a kid. Pretty much the same thing.”

“Pretty much, but not entirely,” said Legrand. “You may have heard of one Captain Kidd. I immediately took the animal’s figure as a kind of punning or hieroglyphical signature. I say signature, because its position on the vellum suggested that idea. The death’s-head at the corner diagonally opposite had, in the same way, the look of a stamp or seal. But I was deeply frustrated by the absence of everything else—of the body to my imagined instrument, of the text to go with my context.”

“I suppose you expected to find a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something like that. The fact is, I felt irresistibly struck by a presentiment of some vast good fortune about to happen. I can hardly say why. Maybe it was more desire than real belief—but do you know that Jupiter’s silly words, about the bug being solid gold, had a remarkable effect on my imagination? And then there was the whole series of accidents and coincidences—so extraordinary. Do you notice how it was just an accident that these events happened on the only day of the year that is cool enough for fire, and that without the fire, or without the dog’s intervention at the exact moment he appeared, I would never have noticed the death’s-head—and so would never have become the possessor of the treasure?”"}

{"request_id":"2fcd08faed2cacecf59eff5e","rewritten_text":"When the wedding happened about three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a crowd of smart, well-dressed people. The service was led in a very impressive way by the Dean of Chichester, and everyone agreed they had never seen a prettier couple than the bride and the bridegroom. They were not only handsome, though—they were happy. Lord Arthur never once regretted what he had gone through for Sybil’s sake, and Sybil, in return, gave him the best things a woman can give a man: worship, tenderness, and love. For them, romance was not destroyed by real life. They always felt young.

A few years later, after they had two beautiful children, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory, a lovely old place that the Duke had given as a wedding present to his son. One afternoon, she sat with Lady Arthur under a lime-tree in the garden, watching the little boy and girl play up and down the rose-walk, darting about like flashes of sunlight. Then she suddenly took her hostess’s hand and asked, “Are you happy, Sybil?”

“Dear Lady Windermere, of course I am happy. Aren’t you?”

“I don’t have time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the last person who is introduced to me, but once I get to know people, I usually get tired of them.”

“Don’t your lions satisfy you, Lady Windermere?”

“Oh, no! Lions are only good for one season. The moment their manes are cut, they become the dullest creatures you can imagine. And besides, they behave very badly if you are really kind to them. Do you remember that dreadful Mr. Podgers? He was a terrible fraud. Of course, I didn’t mind that at all, and even when he wanted to borrow money I forgave him, but I couldn’t stand him trying to make love to me. He has really made me hate cheiromancy. I’m into telepathy now. It’s much more fun.”

“You mustn’t say anything against cheiromancy here, Lady Windermere. It’s the only subject that Arthur doesn’t like people to tease him about. I can assure you he takes it very seriously.”

“You don’t mean to say he actually believes in it, Sybil?”

“Ask him, Lady Windermere. He’s here”; and Lord Arthur came over to them in the garden, holding a large bunch of yellow roses, with his two children running around him.

“Lord Arthur?”

“Yes, Lady Windermere.”

“So you mean to tell me you believe in cheiromancy?”

“Of course I do,” the young man said, smiling.

“But why?”

“Because it gave me all the happiness of my life,” he said softly, sinking into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"321614eb32d3d02dcfd08027","rewritten_text":"Dawn had come when I set the Manuscript aside. The rain had almost stopped. Everything looked gray and sad. The storm, worn out, was still making its last sounds, like it was trying to calm down. I went to the stranger’s room and listened at his door, which was slightly open. I could hear him talking, so I knocked. No one answered, but I kept hearing his voice. I leaned in and looked.

He lay on his back in bed, talking in broken bursts, but with energy. He kept moving his arms restlessly, as sick people do when they’re delirious. I slipped in quietly and bent over him. His mutterings and outbursts continued. I said only a single word, just to get his attention. The moment I spoke, his glassy eyes and ashy face lit up with joy—pleasure, gratitude, happiness, and relief.

“Oh, Sandy, you’ve finally come. How long I’ve waited for you! Sit by me—don’t go. Don’t leave me. Never leave me again, Sandy. Where is your hand? Give it to me, please. Let me hold it—there. Now everything is all right. Everything is peaceful, and I’m happy again. We’re happy again, aren’t we, Sandy? You look so dim and unclear. You’re only a mist, a cloud, but you’re here—and that’s enough. I have your hand. Don’t take it away. It will only be for a little while. I won’t need it long.

Was that the child? Hello—Central! She doesn’t answer. Maybe she’s asleep. Bring her when she wakes. Let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and tell her goodbye.

Sandy! Yes, you’re there. I lost track for a moment, and I thought you were gone.

How long have I been sick? It must be. It feels like months. And the dreams—such strange, terrible dreams, Sandy. Dreams that felt as real as life. Of course it’s delirium, but they were so real. I thought the king was dead. I thought you were in Gaul and couldn’t get home. I thought there was a revolution. In the wild confusion of those dreams, I believed Clarence and I, along with a few of my cadets, fought and wiped out all the chivalry of England.

But that wasn’t even the strangest part. It felt like I was a creature from some far age that hasn’t even been born yet—centuries from now. And that felt just as real as everything else. Yes, it was like I flew out of that future time back into this one, and then forward again. Then I was left here, a stranger and alone, in a strange England, with thirteen centuries of emptiness opening between me and you. Between me and my home and my friends. Between me and everything that matters to me—everything that could make life worth living.”"}

“My dear Lizzy,

I wish you joy. If you love Mr. Darcy half as well as I do my dear Wickham, you must be very happy. It is a great comfort to have you so rich; and when you have nothing else to do, I hope you will think of us. I am sure Wickham would like a place at court very much; and I do not think we shall have quite enough money to live on without some help. Any place would do, about three or four hundred a year; but, however, do not speak to Mr. Darcy about it, if you would rather not.

Yours, etc.

As it happened, Elizabeth would much rather not, and in her reply she tried to put an end to every request and expectation of that kind. Whatever relief she could manage—by what might be called economy in her own private expenses—she often sent them. It had always been clear to her that an income like theirs, under the direction of two people so extravagant in their wants and so careless about the future, must be very insufficient for their support; and whenever they changed their quarters, either Jane or she was sure to be asked for some small assistance toward paying their bills. Their way of living was unsettled to the extreme, even when the restoration of peace sent them back to a home. They were always moving from place to place in search of a cheap situation, and always spending more than they ought. His affection for her soon turned to indifference; hers lasted a little longer; and, despite her youth and her manners, she still held on to all the claims to reputation her marriage had given her. Though Darcy could never receive him at Pemberley, he nevertheless helped him further in his profession for Elizabeth’s sake. Lydia was sometimes a visitor there, when her husband went to enjoy himself in London or Bath; and with the Bingleys they both stayed so long so often, that even Bingley’s good humor was worn down, and he went so far as to talk about giving them a hint to leave.

Miss Bingley was very deeply mortified by Darcy’s marriage; but since she thought it best to keep the right of visiting at Pemberley, she dropped all her resentment. She was fonder than ever of Georgiana, almost as attentive to Darcy as before, and paid off every arrear of civility to Elizabeth.”}]}]}"}

{"request_id":"4e2aeba8fbba8ba2dbe3bf41","rewritten_text":"After they had all joined in those general lamentations over the dreadful sequel of the affair—which Elizabeth regarded as next to certain, and Miss Bennet could not quite bring herself to call wholly impossible—the former went on again. “But do tell me everything about it that I haven’t already heard. Give me the particulars. What did Colonel Forster say? Had no one any misgivings before the elopement actually occurred? They must have seen them together long enough to be sure of it.”

“Colonel Forster admitted that he had often suspected some partiality, particularly on Lydia’s side, but nothing that could alarm him. I am truly sorry for him. His conduct was as attentive and kind as possible. He was on his way to us, intending to show us how concerned he was, before he had the least notion that they were not gone to Scotland; and when that fear first became known, it only made him hurry forward.”

“And was Denny persuaded that Wickham would not marry? Did he understand that they meant to run off? Had Colonel Forster spoken with Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when Denny was questioned by him, Denny denied knowing anything of their plan, and would not give his real opinion of it. He did not repeat his belief that they would not marry, and for that reason I am inclined to think he may have been misunderstood before.”

“And until Colonel Forster came in person, none of you, I suppose, entertained any doubt that they were really married?”

“How could such an idea have found its way into our heads? I confess I felt a little uneasy—somewhat afraid for my sister’s happiness with him in marriage—because I knew his behaviour had not always been quite right. My father and mother knew nothing of it; they only saw how imprudent the match must be. Kitty then owned, with a very natural triumph at having learned more than the rest of us, that in Lydia’s last letter she had prepared her for such a step. It seems she had known for many weeks that they were in love with one another.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I don’t think so.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think ill of Wickham himself? Does he know his true character?”

“I must admit he did not speak of Wickham as he once did. He believed him imprudent and extravagant; and since this unhappy business has come to pass, it is said that he left Meryton with himself greatly in debt: but I hope that report is false.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secret—if we had told what we knew of him—this could not have happened!”

“Perhaps it might have been better,” returned her sister.

“But to lay bare the former faults of any person, without knowing what their present feelings are, seemed to me unjustifiable.”"}

{"request_id":"d0531f2c1430631a795f9cb7","rewritten_text":"During dinner, Mr. Bennet hardly spoke at all. But once the servants had left, he decided it was time to talk with his guest. He brought up a topic he expected would impress him, saying that he seemed very fortunate to have such a patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and her care for his comfort were, he said, truly remarkable. Mr. Bennet could not have chosen a better subject.

Mr. Collins praised her in an eloquent way. The topic made him even more solemn than usual. With a very serious expression, he declared that he had never in his life seen anyone of high rank behave as Lady Catherine did—her kindness and willingness to treat him as she had, he said, were exactly what he had experienced from her. He added that she had graciously approved of both sermons he had already had the honor of preaching before her. She had also asked him twice to dine at Rosings, and she had sent for him only the Saturday before, so he could take part in her evening game of quadrille.

Lady Catherine, Mr. Collins said, was thought by many people to be proud, but he had never seen anything in her except politeness. She always spoke to him as she would to any other gentleman. She never raised the slightest objection to him joining the neighborhood’s society, and she did not mind him leaving his parish now and then for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even advised him to marry as soon as he could, as long as he chose wisely. And once she had visited his modest parsonage, where she had approved of all the changes he had been making and had even suggested a few herself—some shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That all sounds very proper and kind,” said Mrs. Bennet. “I’m sure she’s a pleasant woman. It’s a shame that great ladies aren’t more like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden where my humble home stands is only separated from Rosings Park by a lane—Lady Catherine’s residence.”

“I thought you said she was a widow, sir. Does she have any family?”

“She has only one daughter, the heiress of Rosings, and she has a great deal of property.”

“Ah,” said Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she’s better off than many girls. And what kind of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is a most charming young lady, indeed. Lady Catherine herself says that, in true beauty, Miss de Bourgh is far superior to the handsomest girl of her whole group—because there is something in her features that shows she comes from distinguished birth.”"}

{"request_id":"f0b445c6cd19fdeefc8e4802","rewritten_text":"With everything thus settled in a friendly and satisfactory manner, the contract was formally ratified in yet another teacupful of the peppermint mixture; and this was made the more needful, owing to the fluttering and agitation of the lady’s spirits. As it was being poured out, she told Mr. Bumble of the old woman’s death.

“Very good,” said he, sipping his peppermint. “I’ll call at Sowerberry’s on my way home, and tell him to send tomorrow morning. Was it that as frightened you, love?”

“It wasn’t anything particular, dear,” answered the lady, with a careful evasion.

“It must have been something, love,” pressed Mr. Bumble. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” returned the lady; “one of these days. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” cried Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t any impudence from any of them male paupers as—”

“No, no, love!” the lady broke in, quickly.

“If I thought it was,” he went on; “if I thought as any one of ’em had dared to lift his wulgar eyes to that lovely countenance—”

“They wouldn’t have dared to do it, love,” said the lady.

“They had better not!” declared Mr. Bumble, tightening his fist. “Let me see any man, porochial or extra-porochial, as would presume to do it; and I can tell him that he wouldn’t do it a second time!”

Without any show of violence in his gestures, the remark might not have sounded like a very lofty compliment to the lady’s beauty; but, as Mr. Bumble backed his words with plenty of warlike motions, she was greatly moved by this proof of his devotion, and protested, with the highest admiration, that he was indeed a dove.

The dove then raised his coat-collar and set his cocked hat; and, after exchanging a long and affectionate embrace with his future partner, he faced the cold wind of the night again—only pausing for a few minutes in the male paupers’ ward, to scold them a little, so as to satisfy himself that he could carry out the workhouse-master’s office with the proper sharpness. Convinced of his fitness, Mr. Bumble left the building with a light heart and bright hopes of his coming promotion, which kept his mind busy until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Now, Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out to tea and supper, and Noah Claypole was never inclined to take on more physical exertion than was necessary for the convenient performance of eating and drinking; so the shop was not shut, though it was past the usual time for closing. Mr. Bumble tapped his cane on the counter several times, but getting no answer, and seeing a light shining through the glass-window of the little parlour at the back of the shop, he ventured to peep in and see what was going on; and when he saw what was going on, he was by no means a little surprised."}

{"request_id":"5e68ed56fd0d5719caa516ec","rewritten_text":"Dark and storm-tossed was the night. About the throne on high not a single star seemed to tremble; yet the deep, rolling thunder kept thudding upon the ear, while the dreadful lightning, in a fit of furious temper, flashed through the vaulted chambers of heaven, as though it scorned the authority exerted over its terrors by the illustrious Franklin! Even the boisterous winds, all of them, burst from their secret haunts and raged about, as if their help were meant to heighten the wildness of the scene.

At such a time—so black, so dismal—when human sympathy might have been expected to fail, my own spirit sighed; but instead of that,

‘My dearest friend, my counsellor, my comforter and guide— My joy in grief, my second bliss in joy,’ came to my side.

She moved like one of those bright beings painted in the sunny lanes of fancy’s Eden by the romantic and the young: a queen of beauty, unadorned except by her own surpassing loveliness. Her step was so gentle that it made no sound at all; and, had it not been for the magical thrill her kindly touch gave, she might, like other quiet beauties, have slipped away unnoticed—unsought. A peculiar sadness lay upon her face, as if icy tears had settled on the robe of December; and when she pointed outward to the battling elements, she bade me consider the two powers set before me.

This nightmare of a piece filled some ten pages of manuscript and ended with a sermon so ruinous to all hope among non-Presbyterians that it won the first prize. The whole thing was judged the finest work of the evening. When the mayor of the village presented the award to the author, he delivered a hearty speech, saying it was by far the most “eloquent” thing he had ever heard, and that Daniel Webster himself might well be proud of it.

It may be added, in passing, that the number of compositions in which the word “beauteous” was over-indulged, and human experience was spoken of as “life’s page,” stood at the usual average.

Now the master, softened almost to the edge of geniality, pushed his chair aside, turned his back on the audience, and began to draw a map of America on the blackboard, intending to exercise the geography class. But he managed it badly with his unsteady hand, and a smothered titter ran through the room. He knew what was happening and tried to set it right. He wiped out the lines and redrew them; yet he only made them more distorted, and the tittering grew louder. He fixed his whole attention on the work, as if resolved not to be beaten down by the laughter. He felt that everyone’s eyes were upon him; he told himself he was doing well, and still the tittering went on—indeed, it plainly increased."}

{"request_id":"43f0ebd898c4866bde7efcc9","rewritten_text":"“She would be such a delightful companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed with it all, but added,

“Our little friend Harriet Smith, however, is just such another pretty, kind young person. You will like Harriet. Emma could not have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I’m very happy to hear it—but only Jane Fairfax is known to be so very accomplished and superior!—and exactly Emma’s age.”

This topic was discussed very happily, and others followed in the same spirit, passing away with similar harmony; but the evening did not end without a small return of agitation. The gruel was served and gave them plenty to talk about—much praise and many comments—undoubted confidence in its wholesomeness for every constitution, and pretty severe Philippics against the many houses where it was never served in anything like tolerable form;—but, unfortunately, among the failures the daughter had to mention, the most recent, and therefore most prominent, was in her own cook at South End, a young woman hired for the time, who had never been able to understand what she meant by a basin of nice, smooth gruel—thin, but not too thin. No matter how often she had wished for it and ordered it, she had never been able to get anything tolerable. This was a dangerous opening.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and fixing his eyes on her with tender concern. The exclamation in Emma’s ear conveyed, “Ah! there is no end of the sad consequences of your going to South End. It does not bear talking about.” For a little while she hoped he would not bring it up, and that quiet rumination might be enough to restore his appetite for his own smooth gruel. After some minutes, however, he began,

“I shall always be very sorry that you went to the sea this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you be sorry, sir?—I assure you, it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides, if you must go to the sea, it had better not have been to South End. South End is an unhealthy place. Perry was surprised to hear you had fixed on South End.”

“I know there’s an idea like that among many people, but it’s quite a mistake, sir. We all had our health perfectly well there, and never found the least inconvenience from the mud; and Mr. Wingfield says it’s entirely wrong to suppose the place unhealthy. I’m sure you can rely on him, because he thoroughly understands the nature of the air, and his own brother and family have been there repeatedly.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere. Perry was a week at Cromer once, and he considers it the best of all the sea-bathing places.”"}

{"request_id":"1effd715d1cf7079f21301ff","rewritten_text":"“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” Then he shook his head and tapped it, showing that he felt he was lacking something in Joseph.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry, you must be exhausted. Sit down. Here is a chicken that has come from the Boar; here is a tongue that has come from the Boar; here are one or two little things that have come from the Boar, and I hope you won’t despise them. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, standing up again the moment after he sat down, “see before me the same one I used to play with in his happy infancy? And may I—may I—?”

This “may I” meant, of course, that he wanted to shake hands. I agreed, and he was very eager, and then he sat down again.

“Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink—thanks to Fortune—and may she always choose her favourites with the same good judgment! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, standing up again, “see before me One, and drink to One, without saying again—May I—may I—?”

I told him he could, and he shook hands with me again, then emptied his glass and turned it upside down. I did the same; and if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine could not have gone more straight to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook helped me to the liver wing, and to the best slice of tongue (none of those unusual No Thoroughfares of Pork now), and he took, in comparison, almost no care of himself at all. “Ah! poultry, poultry! You little thought,” said Mr. Pumblechook, speaking to the fowl in the dish, “when you were a young fledgling, what was waiting for you. You little thought you would be refreshment under this humble roof for one who—call it a weakness if you like,” said Mr. Pumblechook, standing up again, “but may I? may I—?”

Soon it was no longer necessary to repeat that he could, so he did it right away. I don’t know how he managed to do it so many times without cutting himself with my knife.

“And your sister,” he went on after a little steady eating, “who had the honour of bringing you up by hand! It’s a sad picture to think she can no longer fully understand the honour. May—”

I saw he was about to start again, and I stopped him.

“We’ll drink her health,” said I.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, quite limp with admiration, “that’s the way you know ’em, sir!” (I don’t know who Sir was, but it certainly wasn’t me, and there was no third person there); “that’s the way you know the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"4e7b0d3cfec76a93f7885657","rewritten_text":"We finally made the box lighter by taking out two thirds of what was inside. After some trouble, we were then able to lift it out of the hole. We put the items we removed down among the brambles, and we left the dog there to guard them. Jupiter gave him strict orders: under no circumstances was he to move from that spot, and he was not to open his mouth until we came back. Then we hurried home with the chest. We reached the hut safely, but only after a lot of hard work, at one o’clock in the morning. Even though we were exhausted, we couldn’t do anything else right away. We rested until two, ate supper, and then set off for the hills at once with three strong sacks, which, luckily, were already there.

A little before four we arrived at the pit. We divided the rest of the stolen goods among us as fairly as we could. Then we left the holes unfilled and went back to the hut for the second time, where we deposited our golden loads again. We did it just as the first faint light of dawn began to show over the treetops in the east.

By then we were completely worn out, but the excitement of what we had done kept us from resting. After an uneasy sleep of about three or four hours, we got up as if we had planned it together, to examine our treasure.

The chest had been filled to the brim. We spent the whole day, and most of the next night, going through everything carefully. There was no real order. Everything had been piled in without any arrangement. Once we sorted it all out, we realized we had even more wealth than we first thought. In coins, there was a little over four hundred and fifty thousand dollars, based on the value of the pieces as accurately as we could using the tables of the time. There was not a single piece of silver. All of it was gold from old times, and it varied a lot—French, Spanish, and German money, along with a few English guineas and some counters we had never seen before. There were also several very large and heavy coins, worn so badly that we couldn’t read their inscriptions. There was no American money.

We had more trouble estimating the value of the jewels. We found diamonds—some extremely large and fine—one hundred and ten in all, and none of them small. We found eighteen rubies, very bright; three hundred and ten emeralds, all beautiful; and twenty-one sapphires, along with an opal. These stones had all been broken out of their settings and thrown loose into the chest. The settings themselves, which we picked out from among the other gold, looked as if they had been smashed with hammers, as if someone wanted to prevent them from being identified."}

{"request_id":"a974e3cc3cf9c5735d1dcbc3","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” said he as we reached the base, “come here! Tell me—was the skull nailed to the limb with the face turned outward, or turned toward the limb?”

“De face was out, massa, so dat de crows could get at de eyes good, widout any trouble.”

“Well, then, was it this eye or that one through which you dropped the beetle?” Legrand asked, and he touched each of Jupiter’s eyes.

“’Twas dis eye, massa—de lef eye—jis as you tell me,” and Jupiter pointed to his right eye.

“That will do. We must try again.”

Here my friend, whose madness I now saw—at least, I thought I saw—some kind of method in, removed the peg that marked where the beetle had fallen. He moved it to a spot about three inches west of where it had been. Then he took the tape measure from the nearest point of the trunk to the peg, just as before, and extended the line straight out to a distance of fifty feet. This time, the spot was several yards away from where we had been digging.

We drew a new circle around the new position, a little larger than before, and started digging again with our spades. I was terribly tired, but I couldn’t quite explain why, and I no longer felt the same strong dislike for the work. Somehow I became deeply interested—almost excited. Maybe it was something in all the wild behavior of Legrand, some sign of planning or careful thought, that made me feel that way. I dug eagerly, and more than once I caught myself looking ahead with something close to expectation, as if I could already see the treasure that had driven my poor companion mad.

After we had been working for about an hour and a half, our digging was interrupted again by the dog’s violent howling. At first, his worry had clearly been caused by playfulness or moodiness, but now he sounded bitter and serious. When Jupiter tried again to muzzle him, the dog fought back fiercely. Then he leaped into the hole and clawed at the soil in a frenzy. In a few seconds he had uncovered a mass of human bones, enough to form two complete skeletons, mixed together, along with several metal buttons and what looked like the dust of decayed wool. One or two quick strokes of the spade turned up the blade of a large Spanish knife. As we dug farther, three or four loose pieces of gold and silver coin came to light as well."}

{"request_id":"eaf30229b2665d3098433f40","rewritten_text":"TEN minutes later, with his face drained of color by terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House, pushing through the crowd of fur-coated footmen gathered around the large striped awning, as if he neither saw nor heard anything. The night was bitterly cold, and the gas lamps around the square flared and flickered in the sharp wind; yet his hands were burning hot with fever, and his forehead felt like it was on fire. He kept going and going, almost staggering along like a drunk. A policeman glanced at him as he passed, and a beggar who had been slouching from an archway to ask for alms grew frightened, seeing misery greater than his own. Once he stopped beneath a lamp and stared at his hands. He thought he could already detect the stain of blood on them, and a faint cry broke from his trembling lips.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had seen there. Murder! Even the night seemed to know it, and the desolate wind to howl it into his ear. The dark corners of the streets were full of it. It grinned at him from the roofs of the houses.

First he came to the Park, whose gloomy woodland seemed to hold him in a strange fascination. He leaned wearily against the railings, cooling his brow on the wet metal, and listened to the trees’ trembling silence. “Murder! murder!” he kept repeating, as though saying it over and over could soften the horror of the word. The sound of his own voice made him shudder, yet he almost hoped that Echo might hear him and wake the sleeping city from its dreams. He felt a wild urge to stop any casual passer-by and tell them everything.

Then he drifted across Oxford Street into narrow, shameful alleys. Two women with painted faces mocked him as he went by. From a dark courtyard came the sound of oaths and blows, followed by shrill screams; and there, huddled on a damp doorstep, he saw the bent, crooked shapes of poverty and age. A strange pity washed over him. Were these children of sin and misery destined for their end, just as he was? Were they, like him, only puppets in some monstrous show?

And yet it wasn’t the mystery, but the comedy of suffering that struck him—its absolute uselessness, its grotesque lack of meaning. Everything seemed so incoherent. Everything seemed to be missing any real harmony. He was astonished by the clash between the shallow optimism of the day and the actual facts of existence. He was still very young.

After a while he found himself standing in front of Marylebone Church. The silent road looked like a long ribbon of polished silver, flecked here and there with the dark arabesques of moving shadows."}

{"request_id":"9eaa7aba6860518172846dc6","rewritten_text":"Mrs Clay’s feelings for the young man were stronger than her interest in other plans. For his sake, she gave up the chance to scheme longer for Sir Walter. Still, she has abilities as well as emotions. Now it is hard to say whether his cleverness or hers will win in the end. Even if he prevents her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he may still end up talking her into marrying Sir William, with flattery and gentle attention.

There is no doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and deeply upset by the loss of their companion, and by the discovery that they had been deceived. They could turn to their great cousins for comfort, but they must still feel that it is only half satisfying to flatter and follow other people, without ever being flattered and followed in return.

Anne, long before this, had understood what Lady Russell meant and had decided to love Captain Wentworth the way she should. Because of that, there was no other drawback to her happiness. The only thing that troubled her was the thought that she had no family connections to offer him—nothing that a sensible man would value. She felt her own lack of status very sharply. The difference in their fortunes did not bother her at all, and it did not make her regret anything. But the fact that she had no family to judge him properly, to offer respectability, harmony, and goodwill in return for all the worth and the warm welcome he received from his brothers and sisters, caused her real pain, even though everything else in her situation promised strong happiness. She had only two friends in the world to add to his list: Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. Captain Wentworth was, however, very willing to attach himself to both. Lady Russell, despite her earlier mistakes, was someone he could now truly value. He did not have to say that he believed she was right to separate them at first, but he was ready to say almost everything else in her favor. As for Mrs Smith, she had different reasons that made it easy for him to respect and keep her close.

Anne’s recent good offices were enough on their own to bring this about. And when Anne and Captain Wentworth married, it did not take away one friend from Mrs Smith; it actually gave her two. Mrs Smith was the first visitor to their home once their life became settled. Captain Wentworth, by helping her recover her husband’s property in the West Indies—through writing for her, acting on her behalf, and staying with her to deal with all the small problems that came up—paid back, fully and completely, the services she had given, and the services she had always meant to give, to his wife."}

{"request_id":"9739f609bc0f9e47c6e0d47f","rewritten_text":"“I wish we had a donkey. Then we could all ride on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and me—and my caro sposo walking alongside. I really need to talk to him about buying a donkey. In the country, I think it’s almost necessary. Even if a woman has plenty of resources, she can’t always stay shut up at home. And you know how it is: long walks in summer mean dust, and in winter they mean mud.”

“You won’t find either between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and right now it’s perfectly dry. If you want, you can come on a donkey. You can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I’d like everything to be as much to your taste as possible.”

“That I’m sure you would. And I truly give you credit for it, my good friend. Under that plain, blunt way of yours, I know you have the warmest heart. As I told Mr. E., you’re a real humorist. Yes, believe me, Knightley, I fully understand your attention to me in all of this plan. You’ve chosen exactly what will please me.”

Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding a table in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the outing. He knew that if any of them sat down outside to eat, it would almost certainly make him ill. Mr. Woodhouse must not, under the friendly excuse of a morning drive and a couple of hours at Donwell, be tempted away from his misery.

Mr. Woodhouse was invited in good faith. There were no hidden horrors waiting to punish him for trusting too easily. He did agree. He hadn’t been to Donwell for two years. “One fine morning,” he said, “he, Emma, and Harriet could go very well. He could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked around the gardens. He didn’t think they could be damp now, in the middle of the day. He would like to see the old house again very much, and he would be very happy to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton, and any other of his neighbors. He could see no objection at all to his going there, and Emma’s, and Harriet’s, on some very fine morning. He thought it was very thoughtful and sensible of Mr. Knightley to invite them—much better than dining out. He wasn’t fond of dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was lucky in how quickly everyone agreed. The invitation was received so warmly everywhere that it seemed, as if Mrs. Elton were doing, they were all treating the plan like a special compliment meant for them. Emma and Harriet said they expected a great deal of pleasure from it. And Mr. Weston, without being asked, promised to try to get Frank to join them if possible—an extra show of approval and gratitude that really wasn’t necessary. Mr. Knightley then had to say he would be glad to see him, and Mr. Weston promised to waste no time writing and using every argument to persuade him to come."}

{"request_id":"3ea6e7f5810ed8941ec5cbf5","rewritten_text":"She felt a strong pull toward the outer door; she wanted to know whether it rained. Why should she be made to suspect herself of some other motive? Captain Wentworth must be somewhere out of sight. She rose from her seat—she would go; one half of her ought not always to be so much wiser than the other, nor to keep suspecting it of being worse. She would find out if it rained. In the very moment, though, she was checked by Captain Wentworth’s entrance himself, coming in among a party of gentlemen and ladies—plainly his acquaintances—whom he must have joined a little below Milsom Street.

He was far more visibly struck and disconcerted by seeing her than she had ever noticed him to be; he looked quite red. For the first time since their renewed acquaintance, she felt that she was betraying the smaller share of feeling between them. She had the advantage over him in having prepared herself for the last few moments. The first, overwhelming, blinding, bewildering effects of a sudden surprise were past with her; yet she still had enough to feel. It was agitation, pain, pleasure—something poised between delight and misery.

He spoke to her, and then turned away. The tone of his manner was embarrassment. She could not call it cold, nor friendly, nor anything so plainly as embarrassed.

After a short interval, however, he came toward her again and spoke once more. Their mutual inquiries on common topics went on: neither of them, perhaps, much the wiser for what they learned, and Anne remained fully aware that he was less at ease than before. By dint of having been so much together, they had managed to talk with a fair show of indifference and calmness; but he could not keep it up now. Time had altered him, or Louisa had altered him. There was a consciousness of some sort or other. He looked very well—no sign of suffering in health or spirits—and he talked of Uppercross, of the Musgroves, even of Louisa; and when he named her, he gave her a brief look of his own arch meaning. Still, Captain Wentworth was not comfortable, not at ease, not able to pretend that he was.

It did not surprise Anne, but it did grieve her, to see that Elizabeth would not recognize him. She perceived that he saw Elizabeth, that Elizabeth saw him; there was a complete inward acknowledgment on both sides. She was sure he was ready to be received as an acquaintance, expecting it; and she had the pain of watching her sister turn away with the same unyielding coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot was growing very impatient, now drew up; the servant entered to announce it."}

{"request_id":"3246dcba3eb2660aec5f15a9","rewritten_text":"It’s a strange thing, but everyone who disappears is said to be seen in San Francisco. It must be a wonderful city, with all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you think happened to Basil?” Dorian asked. He held his Burgundy up to the light and wondered how he could talk about it so calmly.

“I have no idea at all. If Basil wants to hide, that’s not my business. If he’s dead, I don’t want to think about it. Death is the only thing that has ever truly frightened me. I hate it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked, sounding tired.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, lifting the gilt trellis of an open vinaigrette box and letting it pass near his nose, “these days you can survive almost anything—except that. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts in the nineteenth century that you can’t just explain away. Let’s have our coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran off with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria—I really did like her. The house feels lonely without her. Of course, marriage is only a habit, and a bad one. Still, you miss even your worst habits. Maybe you miss them the most. They’re such an important part of who you are.”

Dorian didn’t answer. He got up from the table, went into the next room, and sat at the piano. He let his fingers drift over the white and black keys. When the coffee arrived, he stopped playing and looked at Lord Henry. “Harry,” he said, “did it ever occur to you that Basil might have been murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was well liked, and he always wore a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He wasn’t clever enough to make enemies. Sure, he had real talent for painting. But a person can paint like Velasquez and still be completely dull. Basil was really rather dull. He only interested me once—years ago—when he told me he had a wild admiration for you, and that you were the main reason for his art.”

“I cared about Basil,” Dorian said, with a touch of sadness. “But don’t people say he was murdered?”

“Some of the papers do,” Lord Henry replied. “I don’t think it’s likely. I know there are terrible places in Paris, but Basil wasn’t the kind of man who would go there. He had no curiosity. That was his biggest fault.”

“What would you say, Harry,” Dorian asked, “if I told you that I murdered Basil?”"}

{"request_id":"54f3696755105a396ebdd0b4","rewritten_text":"He never tried again. The boys lay there, counting the dragging moments until it felt to them that time had to be over and eternity was turning gray; and then they were grateful to see that the sun was finally setting.

Now one snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, stared around, and gave his comrade a grim smile, whose head was drooping on his knees. He nudged him awake with his foot and said:

“Hey! You’re the watchman, aren’t you? All right, then—nothing’s happened.”

“Me! Have I been asleep?”

“Partly, partly. Almost time for us to move, pard. What are we going to do with the little swag we’ve got left?”

“I don’t know—leave it here like we always do, I guess. No point taking it with us until we start south. Six hundred and fifty in silver is something to carry.”

“Well—fine. It won’t matter if we come back here once more.”

“No—but I’d say come in at night like we used to. It’s better.”

“Yes, but look here; it might be a good while before I get the right chance for that job. Accidents could happen. It’s not exactly a good place. We’ll just bury it like we always do—and bury it deep.”

“Good idea,” said the comrade. He crossed the room, knelt down, lifted one of the hearth-stones in the back, and pulled out a bag that jingled pleasantly. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, then handed the bag to Injun Joe, who was on his knees in the corner now, digging with his bowie-knife.

The boys forgot every fear, every misery, in an instant. With gloating eyes they watched every movement. Luck!—the splendor of it was beyond imagination. Six hundred dollars was enough to make half a dozen boys rich. This was treasure-hunting under the best possible circumstances—no annoying uncertainty about where to dig. They nudged each other again and again—loud, clear nudges, because they only meant: “Oh, but aren’t you glad we’re here now!”

Joe’s knife struck something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What is it?” asked his comrade.

“A half-rotten plank—no, I think it’s a box. Here—help me out, and we’ll see what it’s for. Never mind, I’ve already broken a hole.”

He reached in and drew it out—

“Man, it’s money!”

The two men examined the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were just as excited as they were, and just as delighted.

Joe’s comrade said:

“We’ll make quick work of this. There’s an old rusty pick out among the weeds in the corner on the other side of the fireplace—I saw it a minute ago.”"}

{"request_id":"ce87f2b5f149c2f371e672b5","rewritten_text":"“Yes, it is—and I could’ve had it too, if I’d been big enough. I see him first. Who nailed him?”

“It was an old fellow, a stranger. He sold out his chance in him for forty dollars, because he’s got to go up the river and can’t wait. Think of that! You bet I’d wait, if it was seven years.”

“That’s me, every time,” I said. “But maybe his chance isn’t worth more than that, if he’ll sell it so cheap. Maybe something isn’t right.”

“But it is. It’s straight as a string. I can see the handbill myself. It tells everything about him, down to the details. It describes him like a picture and says the plantation he’s from is below New Orleans. No sir, no way—there’s no trouble about that speculation, you bet. Say, give me a chaw of tobacco, won’t you?”

I didn’t have any, so he left. I went to the raft and sat down in the wigwam to think. But I couldn’t come up with anything. I kept thinking until my head hurt, but I still couldn’t see any way out of the trouble. After all this long trip, and after everything we’d done for those scoundrels, it had all come to nothing. Everything was ruined, busted up, because they had the nerve to pull a trick like that on Jim and make him a slave again for the rest of his life—among strangers, too—for forty dirty dollars.

I told myself that it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave at home, where his family was, as long as he had to be a slave. So I thought I should write a letter to Tom Sawyer and tell him to tell Miss Watson where Jim was. But I gave up that idea for two reasons. First, she’d be mad and disgusted at his lying and leaving, and then she’d send him straight down the river again. Second, if she didn’t, everyone would naturally look down on an ungrateful Black man, and Jim would feel it all the time. He’d get ornery and ashamed. And then think about me. It would spread around that Huck Finn helped a Black man get his freedom. If I ever saw anyone from that town again, I’d be ready to crawl down and lick their boots for shame. That’s how it is: a person does something low and dirty, and then he doesn’t want to face the consequences. He thinks that if he can hide it long enough, it isn’t a disgrace. That was exactly my situation. The more I thought about it, the more my conscience started grinding me down, and the more wicked, low, and ornery I felt."}

{"request_id":"add5fce1291ddf11668f6d8e","rewritten_text":"“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! _lively_ now! Come—out with your spring-line—what are you doing there! Take a turn around that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).

Tom kept on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared for a moment, then said, “_Hi-Yi! You’re_ up a stump, ain’t you!”

No answer. Tom studied his last stroke with the eye of an artist, then gave his brush another gentle sweep and looked at the result again, just like before. Ben moved up alongside him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:

“Hello, old chap, you’ve got to work, huh?”

Tom turned suddenly and said, “Why, it’s you, Ben! I wasn’t noticing.”

“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d rather _work_—wouldn’t you? Sure you would!”

Tom looked at the boy for a moment and said, “What do you call work?”

“Why, isn’t _that_ work?”

Tom went back to whitewashing and answered carelessly, “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh, come now—you don’t mean to act like you _like_ it?”

The brush kept moving.

“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That put things in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to judge the effect—added a touch here and there—criticized the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. After a while he said:

“Say, Tom, let _me_ whitewash a little.”

Tom thought it over and was about to agree, but then he changed his mind:

“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t really do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind, and _she_ wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”

“No—is that so? Oh come on now—let me just try. Just a little—I’d let _you_, if you was me, Tom.”

“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid.”"}

{"request_id":"2c0a1f319c67285fe625f67d","rewritten_text":"In the center of this rift, I noticed a white spot, but at first I couldn’t make out what it was. I adjusted the telescope’s focus and looked again, and now I could see it clearly: a human skull.

“Once I made that discovery, I was so confident the mystery was solved that I thought the enigma was finished; for the phrase ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could only point to the skull’s position on the tree, while ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ allowed, in regard to searching for buried treasure, only one interpretation. I realized the plan was to drop a bullet from the skull’s left eye, and that a bee-line—meaning a straight line—drawn from the nearest point of the trunk through ‘the shot’ (that is, the spot where the bullet fell), and then extended out to a distance of fifty feet, would mark a definite point. Beneath that point, I thought it at least possible that something valuable was hidden.”

“All of this,” I said, “is exceedingly clear, and although it’s ingenious, it’s still simple and direct. When you left the Bishop’s Hotel, what happened then?”

“Well, after carefully taking the tree’s bearings, I headed home. The instant I left ‘the devil’s seat,’ though, the circular rift disappeared; no matter how I turned afterward, I couldn’t get so much as a glimpse of it again. The main ingenuity in the whole scheme, as I see it, is this: repeated experiments have convinced me it’s true—that the circular opening can be seen from no other place than the narrow ledge on the face of the rock.”

“In this trip to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel,’ I was accompanied by Jupiter, who, no doubt, had noticed for some weeks that my behavior had changed and made sure I wasn’t left alone. But the next day, I got up very early, managed to slip away from him, and went into the hills to find the tree. After a lot of effort, I found it. When I got home that night, my valet suggested I should be flogged. As for the rest of the adventure, I believe you know it as well as I do.”

“I suppose,” I said, “you missed the spot the first time you dug, because Jupiter was too careless to let the bug fall through the left eye of the skull instead of the right.”

“Exactly. That mistake changed the ‘shot’ by about two and a half inches—that is, the position of the peg nearest the tree. If the treasure had been beneath the ‘shot,’ the error wouldn’t have mattered much. But ‘the shot,’ along with the nearest point of the tree, were only two points used to establish a line of direction. Naturally, even a tiny error at the start grows as you extend the line, and by the time we’d gone fifty feet, it had thrown us completely off the trail.”"}
