{"request_id":"5ef59ad95e7fbc619a7e790e","rewritten_text":"He then bowed and left. At the time, he did not see anyone in the street. It’s a side street—very lonely.

“_William Bird_, tailor, testifies that he was one of the group that entered the house. He is an Englishman. He has lived in Paris for two years. He was among the first to go up the stairs. He heard the voices arguing. The rough voice was that of a Frenchman. He could make out several words, but can’t now remember them all. He distinctly heard ‘_sacré_’ and ‘_mon Dieu_.’ At the moment, there was a sound as if several people were struggling—a scraping and scuffling noise. The shrill voice was very loud—louder than the rough one. He is sure it was not the voice of an Englishman. It seemed to be a German’s voice. It might have been a woman’s voice. He does not understand German.

“Four of the witnesses named above, being recalled, testified that the door of the chamber where the body of Mademoiselle L. was found was locked from the inside when the group reached it. Everything was perfectly silent—no groans or noises of any kind. When the door was forced open, no person was seen. The windows, both in the back and the front room, were down and firmly fastened from within. A door between the two rooms was closed, but not locked. The door leading from the front room into the passage was locked, with the key on the inside. A small room at the front of the house, on the fourth story, at the end of the passage, was open, the door left ajar. This room was crowded with old beds, boxes, and the like. These were carefully removed and searched. There was not an inch of any part of the house that was not carefully searched. Sweeps were sent up and down the chimneys. The house was four stories high, with garrets (_mansardes_). A trapdoor on the roof was nailed down very securely—did not appear to have been opened for years. The time that passed between hearing the voices arguing and breaking open the room door was stated differently by the witnesses. Some said it was as short as three minutes—some as long as five. The door was opened with difficulty.

“_Alfonzo Garcio_, undertaker, testifies that he lives in the Rue Morgue. He is a native of Spain. He was one of the group that entered the house. He did not go up the stairs. He is nervous, and was afraid of the consequences of agitation. He heard the voices arguing. The rough voice was that of a Frenchman. He could not make out what was said. The shrill voice was that of an Englishman—he is sure of this.”"}

{"request_id":"b331355c24d83440c1c54a92","rewritten_text":"We proclaimed ourselves freemen so loudly and with such earnestness that we caught the attention of that liberty-sounding orator and his patriotic crowd; they gathered around us and adopted a very fixed, determined posture. The orator said:

“If, indeed, ye are freemen, ye have nought to fear—the God-given liberties of Britain are about ye for your shield and shelter! (Applause.) Ye shall soon see. Bring forth your proofs.”

“What proofs?”

“Proof that ye are freemen.”

Ah—I remembered. I came to myself, and said nothing. But the king flew into a storm and left:

“Thou'rt insane, man. It were better, and more in reason, that this thief and scoundrel here prove that we are _not_ freemen.”

You see, he knew his own laws the way other people so often know them—by words, not by results. They take a _meaning_, and it grows sharp and vivid the moment you try to apply it to yourself.

Every hand shook its head and looked disappointed; some turned away and lost interest. The orator spoke again—this time with the tone of business, not sentiment:

“If ye do not know your country's laws, it were time ye learned them. Ye are strangers to us; ye will not deny that. Ye may be freemen—we do not deny that; but ye may also be slaves. The law is plain: it doth not call on the claimant to prove ye are slaves; it requireth you to prove ye are not.”

I said:

“Dear sir, give us only time to send to Astolat; or give us only time to send to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Peace, good man, these are extraordinary requests, and you may not expect them to be granted. It would take much time, and would unwarrantably inconvenience your master—”

“_Master_, idiot!” the king raged. “I have no master; I myself am the m—”

“Silence, for God's sake!”

I got the words out in time to stop the king. We were already in enough trouble; it could not help us to let these people think we were raving mad.

There is no point in dragging out the particulars. The earl housed us and then sold us at auction. This same infernal law had been in force in my own South in my own time, more than thirteen hundred years later, and under it hundreds of freemen who could not prove they were freemen were sold into lifelong slavery, without the circumstance ever making any particular impression on me; but the minute law and the auction block came into my own experience, what had been merely improper before became suddenly hellish. That is how we are made.

Yes, we were sold at auction, like swine. In a large town with an active market we might have fetched a decent price; but this place was utterly stagnant, and so we were sold for a sum that makes me ashamed whenever I think of it."}

{"request_id":"adecb5d80412303a4914efad","rewritten_text":"A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired cavalier went riding on Brockley meadows. While she was pushing through a hedge, she tore her habit so badly that, when she got home, she decided to use the back staircase so no one would see her. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, the door was open, and she thought she saw someone inside. She assumed it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her work there, so she looked in to ask her to mend Virginia’s habit. To Virginia’s great surprise, it was the Canterville Ghost himself. He was sitting by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees blow through the air, while the red leaves danced wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his whole posture showed deep depression.

He looked so miserable, and so broken down, that Virginia—who had first thought of running away and locking herself in her room—felt sorry for him. She decided to try to comfort him. Her steps were so light, and his sadness so heavy, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

“I’m so sorry for you,” she said. “But my brothers are going back to Eton tomorrow. Then, if you behave yourself, no one will bother you.”

“It’s ridiculous to ask me to behave myself,” he replied, turning in astonishment toward the pretty little girl who had dared to speak to him. “It’s ridiculous. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and walk about at night—if that’s what you mean. That is the only reason I exist.”

“It isn’t any reason at all to exist,” Virginia said. “And you know you’ve been very wicked. Mrs. Umney told us, the very first day we arrived here, that you killed your wife.”

“Well, I admit it,” the Ghost said, sounding annoyed. “But it was a family matter, and it didn’t concern anyone else.”

“It’s very wrong to kill anyone,” Virginia answered. At times she had a calm, serious Puritan way of speaking, something she seemed to have picked up from an old New England ancestor.

“Oh, I hate the harsh, cheap way people talk about abstract ethics! My wife was plain enough. She never had my ruffs properly starched, and she knew nothing about cooking. And do you know what? There was a buck I shot in Hogley Woods—a magnificent pricket. She had it sent up to the table, and that’s the sort of thing she did. But it doesn’t matter now. It’s all over. Still, I don’t think it was very kind of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I killed her.”"}

{"request_id":"8fc3e815dee0c4ef9f756f04","rewritten_text":"But I must give you fair warning that I mean to tell Sybil everything. She’s coming to lunch with me tomorrow, to talk about bonnets; and if Mr. Podgers learns that you’ve got a bad temper, or a tendency to gout, or a wife who lives in Bayswater, I shall be sure to let her have the whole story.”

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. “I’m not afraid,” he replied. “Sybil knows me as well as I know her.”

“Ah, I’m sorry to hear you say that. The right foundation for marriage is a mutual misunderstanding. No, I’m not in the least cynical—I’ve only had experience, which is much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is dying to have his hand read. Don’t tell him that he’s engaged to one of the prettiest girls in London, because that appeared in the _Morning Post_ a month ago.”

“Dear Lady Windermere,” cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, “do let Mr. Podgers stay here a little longer. He’s just told me I ought to go on the stage, and I’m so taken with the idea.”

“If he’s told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly take him away. Come at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.”

“Well,” said Lady Jedburgh, drawing up her face in a small _moue_ as she rose from the sofa, “if I’m not to be allowed to go on the stage, then I must at least be permitted to sit in the audience.”

“Certainly; we’re all going to be part of the audience,” said Lady Windermere. “And now, Mr. Podgers, do be sure to tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is one of my special favourites.”

But the moment Mr. Podgers looked at Lord Arthur’s hand, he turned curiously pale and said nothing. A shiver seemed to run through him, and his thick, bushy eyebrows twitched in a convulsive, irritating way—just as they did when he was at a loss. Then great beads of perspiration sprang out on his yellow forehead, like a poisonous dew, and his fat fingers went cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur noticed every one of these odd signs of agitation, and for the first time in his life he felt fear himself. He wanted to bolt from the room, but he held back. It was better to learn the worst, whatever it might be, than to be left in such a dreadful uncertainty.

“I’m waiting, Mr. Podgers,” he said.

“We’re all waiting,” cried Lady Windermere, in her quick, impatient fashion; yet the cheiromantist gave no answer.

“I suppose Arthur is going on the stage,” said Lady Jedburgh, “and after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him so.”"}

{"request_id":"ebe93dc9a6a79dcac947ad1c","rewritten_text":"For years, Dorian Gray couldn’t escape the hold this book had on him. Or maybe it’s truer to say he never really tried to escape it. From Paris, he ordered at least nine large-paper copies of the first edition, and had each one bound in a different color, so they could match his changing moods and the shifting desires of a nature that, at times, seemed almost completely out of his control. The hero—the remarkable young Parisian, with romantic and scientific instincts mixed in such a strange way—began to feel like a kind of warning image of himself. In fact, the whole book seemed to him to be the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

In one respect, though, he was luckier than the novel’s strange hero. He never had to learn—he had no reason to learn—about the same ugly fear of mirrors, polished metal, and still water that struck the young Parisian so early in life. That fear came from the sudden decay of a once extraordinary beau. Dorian used to read the later part of the book with something like cruel pleasure, and in nearly every pleasure there is cruelty. He took in its truly tragic, though slightly exaggerated, account of the sorrow and despair of someone who had lost what he had valued most, while others still had it.

The wonderful beauty that had fascinated Basil Hallward, and many others besides, never seemed to leave him. Even those who had heard the worst things about him—and who, from time to time, passed along strange rumors about his life in London, becoming the talk of the clubs—couldn’t believe anything that would dishonor him when they saw him. He always had the look of someone who had stayed untouched by the world. Men who spoke in crude ways would fall silent as soon as Dorian Gray entered the room. Something in the clean purity of his face seemed to shame them. His very presence made them remember the innocence they had already ruined. They couldn’t understand how someone so charming and graceful could have avoided the stain of an age that was both sordid and sensual.

Often, when he returned home from one of those mysterious, long absences that made his friends—or people who thought they were his friends—make such strange guesses, he would slip upstairs himself to the locked room. He would open the door with the key that never left him, then stand with a mirror in front of the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him. He would look at the evil, aging face on the canvas, and then at the fair young face that smiled back at him from the polished glass."}

{"request_id":"b3962c585d7e54fd06ad657f","rewritten_text":"Men marry because they’re worn out; women, because they can’t help wondering—yet both end up disappointed.”

“I don’t suppose I’m likely to marry, Harry. I’m far too much in love. That’s one of your little sayings. I’m taking it to heart, just as I do with everything you tell me.”

“Who is it you’re in love with?” Lord Henry asked, after a pause.

“With an actress,” said Dorian Gray, his cheeks warming.

Lord Henry gave a shrug. “That’s a rather ordinary sort of début.”

“You wouldn’t say that if you’d seen her, Harry.”

“And who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“I’ve never heard of her.”

“No one has—at least not yet. People will know her someday, though. She’s a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are a decorative kind of sex. They never have anything to say, but they manage to say it so charmingly. Women stand for the victory of matter over mind, just as men stand for the victory of mind over morals.”

“Harry, how can you?”

“My dear Dorian, it’s perfectly true. I’m studying women at the moment, so I ought to know. The matter isn’t as difficult as I once imagined. In the end, there are only two sorts of women: the plain and the coloured. The plain ones are useful enough. If you want to build a reputation for respectability, you only need to take them down to supper. The other women are delightful. They do make one mistake, however. They paint in order to look younger. Our grandmothers painted to try to talk brilliantly. Rouge and esprit used to go together. That’s finished now. So long as a woman can appear ten years younger than her own daughter, she’s entirely content. As for conversation, there are only five women in London worth listening to, and two of them can’t be admitted into decent society. Still—tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Ah! Harry, your opinions frighten me.”

“Don’t worry about that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you meet her?”

“I’ll tell you, Harry, but you mustn’t be unkind about it. It never would have happened if I hadn’t met you. You stirred in me a wild hunger to know everything about life. For days after I met you, it felt as if something were beating and pulsing in my veins. When I lounged in the park, or wandered along Piccadilly, I would watch every passer-by and, with a reckless curiosity, ask myself what kind of lives they led. Some of them held me spellbound. Others filled me with dread. There was an exquisite poison in the air. I had a passion for sensations...."}

{"request_id":"255e7313bef30a34538c740a","rewritten_text":"“Story!”

He seemed determined to misunderstand the word she had repeated. Then, in a hurry, he added, “Yes, customers. In banking, we usually call our connection our customers. He was a French gentleman; a scientific gentleman; a man with a great education—a Doctor.”

“Not of Beauvais?”

“Why, yes, of Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he was well known in Paris. I had the honor of knowing him there. Our relationship was business, but confidential. At that time I worked in our French House, and I had been there—oh!—for twenty years.”

“At that time—may I ask, at what time, sir?”

“I mean, miss, twenty years ago. He married an English lady, and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like the affairs of many other French gentlemen and French families, were entirely handled by Tellson’s. In the same way, I am, or I have been, a trustee of one kind or another for dozens of our customers. These are only business relationships, miss. There is no friendship in them, no special interest, and nothing like sentiment. In my work, I move from one to another, the way I move from one customer to another during a normal day. In short, I have no feelings. I’m just a machine. To continue—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir; and I begin to think”—the woman’s forehead, oddly roughened, was fixed on him—“that when I was left an orphan, because my mother survived my father by only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I’m almost sure it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the small, hesitant hand that had reached out to take his. With great ceremony, he put it to his lips. Then he guided the young lady back to her chair. Holding the back of the chair with his left hand, and using his right hand in turn to rub his chin, tug his wig at the ears, or point as he spoke, he stood looking down at her while she sat looking up at him.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how truly I spoke of myself just now, when I said I had no feelings and that all my relationships with other people are only business. Think about this: I have never seen you since. No—you have been Tellson’s ward since then, and I have been busy with Tellson’s other business. Feelings! I have no time for them, no chance for them. I spend my whole life, miss, turning an enormous money Mangle.”"}

{"request_id":"edc54b5b0380c8144a63acef","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I see where I went wrong. I heard you say ‘anybody,’ and I took it that ‘anybody’ meant—well, anybody; that is, everybody.”

“It doth—anybody that is of lofty birth; and the better if he be royal.”

“That, it seemeth, might well be,” said the abbot, seizing his chance to smooth matters and head off disaster. “For it were not likely that so wondrous a gift as this would be granted for the uncovering of the affairs of lesser folk than those born near the very tops of greatness. Our Arthur the king—”

“Would you know of him?” the enchanter cut in.

“Most gladly, yea, and gratefully.”

Right away the whole crowd of incorrigible idiots was struck again with awe and curiosity. They watched the incantations with rapt attention, and then looked at me with a “There now—what do you say to that?” sort of air, until the announcement came:

“The king is weary with the chase, and lieth in his palace these two hours sleeping a dreamless sleep.”

“God’s benison upon him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May that sleep be for the refreshment of his body and his soul.”

“And so it might be, if he were sleeping,” I answered, “but the king is not sleeping—the king rides.”

Here was trouble again, a clash of authority. None of them knew which of us to trust; I still had a little credit left. The magician’s contempt was roused, and he said:

“Lo, I have seen many wonderful soothsayers and prophets and magicians in my life days, but none before that could sit idle and yet see to the heart of things, with never an incantation to lend a hand.”

“You have lived in the woods, and lost much by it. I use incantations myself, as this good brotherhood are aware—but only when the moment calls for it.”

When it comes to sparring with sarcasm, I reckon I know how to hold my own. That thrust made the fellow fidget. The abbot asked after the queen and the court, and received this:

“They be all on sleep, being overcome by fatigue, like as to the king.”

I said:

“That is only another falsehood. Half of them are about their amusements—the queen and the other half are not sleeping; they ride. Now perhaps you can stretch yourself a little and tell us where the king and queen and all the rest are riding to this very moment.”

“They sleep now, as I said; but on the morrow they will ride, for they go a journey toward the sea.”

“And where will they be the day after to-morrow at vespers?”

“Far to the north of Camelot, and half their journey will be done.”

“That is another lie, by the space of a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

{"request_id":"0063d0036603ff65de20b717","rewritten_text":"“And consider, ma’am,” said Oliver, as tears forced themselves into his eyes despite all his efforts to stop them. “Oh! consider how young and good she is, and what pleasure and comfort she brings to everyone around her. I’m sure—certain—quite certain—that, for your sake, since you are so good yourself; and for her own; and for the sake of all the happiness she makes possible, she will not die. Heaven will never allow her to die so young.”

“Hush!” said Mrs. Maylie, placing her hand on Oliver’s head. “You think like a child, poor boy. But you remind me of my duty, even so. I had forgotten it for a moment, Oliver, but I hope I may be forgiven, because I’m old, and I’ve seen enough illness and death to know the agony of being separated from the objects of our love. I’ve seen enough, too, to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are spared to those who love them; but that should give us comfort in our sorrow. Heaven is just, and these things teach us—powerfully—that there is a brighter world than this, and that the passage to it is swift. God’s will be done! I love her, and He knows how well!”

Oliver was surprised to see that, as Mrs. Maylie spoke those words, she checked her lamentations as if by a single effort; then, drawing herself up as she continued, she became composed and firm. He was even more astonished to find that this firmness held. Through all the care and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie remained ready and steady: carrying out every duty that had fallen to her, consistently, and—so far as anyone could see—almost cheerfully. But Oliver was young, and he didn’t know what strong minds can endure under trying circumstances. How could he, when those who possess such strength so seldom understand themselves?

An anxious night followed. When morning came, Mrs. Maylie’s predictions were only too well confirmed. Rose was in the first stage of a high and dangerous fever.

“We must be active, Oliver, and not give in to useless grief,” said Mrs. Maylie, pressing a finger to her lip as she looked steadily into his face. “This letter must be sent, with all possible speed, to Mr. Losberne. It must be carried to the market town—which is no more than four miles away, across the field by the footpath—and then dispatched, by an express on horseback, straight to Chertsey. The people at the inn will handle it, and I can trust you to make sure it gets done. I know I can.”

Oliver couldn’t find a reply, but he looked as if he wanted his anxiety to be gone at once."}

{"request_id":"66669d851249a5a75f8d7438","rewritten_text":"In the meantime, the force of gravity would keep weakening, in proportion to the squares of the distances. With a velocity that would accelerate enormously, I should finally reach those far-off regions where the earth’s pull would be replaced by the moon’s. Based on these ideas, I didn’t think it was worth bringing more provisions than would be enough for forty days.

“There was still, however, another difficulty, one that caused me some real unease. It has been observed that, in balloon ascents to any considerable height, besides the pain that comes with breathing, people often feel intense anxiety in the head and body. This is frequently accompanied by bleeding from the nose and other alarming symptoms, which become more and more troublesome the higher the altitude. This was a thought of a rather startling kind. Wasn’t it likely that these symptoms would keep increasing indefinitely—or at least continue until death ended them? In the end, I decided that it would not. Their cause, I believed, lay in the gradual removal of the usual atmospheric pressure acting on the body’s surface, leading to the distention of the superficial blood vessels—not in any direct breakdown of the animal system, as in the case of breathing difficulty, where the atmospheric density is chemically too low to properly refresh the blood in a ventricle of the heart. Unless that refreshing failed, I could see no reason, then, why life couldn’t be sustained even in a vacuum; for the expansion and compression of the chest—what we commonly call breathing—is an action that is purely muscular. It is the cause of respiration, not its effect. In short, I thought that as the body became accustomed to the lack of atmospheric pressure, the sensations of pain would gradually lessen. And while they lasted, I relied with confidence on the iron toughness of my constitution.

“Thus, may it please your Excellencies, I have laid out some of the considerations—though by no means all—that led me to form the plan of a lunar voyage. I will now go on to present the results of an attempt so seemingly audacious in its conception, and, in any case, so utterly without precedent in the annals of mankind.

“After reaching the altitude I mentioned—three miles and three-quarters—I threw a quantity of feathers out of the car and found that I still rose with enough speed. So there was no need to discharge any ballast. I was glad of that, because I wanted to keep with me as much weight as I could carry, for reasons that I will explain later.”"}

{"request_id":"bf9fc99cacb956ce98d09e9d","rewritten_text":"I walked with a quick pace, and we soon arrived at my college. Then I stopped to think, and the thought made me shiver: the creature I had left in my apartment might still be there, alive and moving around. I dreaded the moment I might have to see this monster, but I feared even more that Henry might see him. So I urged him to stay a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs, and I darted up toward my own room. My hand was already on the door’s lock before I caught myself. I paused, and a cold shiver ran through me. I threw the door open hard, the way children do when they expect a ghost to be waiting for them on the other side—but nothing was there. I stepped in cautiously: the apartment was empty, and my bedroom was free of its hideous guest as well. I could hardly believe that such a great good fortune could have fallen to me, but once I was certain my enemy had truly fled, I clapped my hands for joy and ran down to Clerval.

We went up into my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast; but I couldn’t contain myself. It wasn’t only joy that possessed me. I felt my skin tingle with an almost unbearable sensitivity, and my pulse hammered rapidly. I couldn’t stay in one place for a single instant; I jumped over the chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed out loud. At first, Clerval thought my unusual spirits were simply the result of joy at his arrival. But when he watched me more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes he couldn’t explain, and my loud, uncontrolled, heartless laughter frightened and astonished him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what is the matter? Don’t laugh like that. You’re terribly ill—what’s causing all this?”

“Don’t ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, because I thought I saw the dreaded specter glide into the room. “He can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined the monster had seized me; I fought furiously and then collapsed into a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A meeting he had expected with such joy had turned so strangely into bitterness. But I wasn’t there to witness his grief—I was lifeless, and I didn’t recover my senses for a long, long time.

This was the beginning of a nervous fever that kept me confined for several months. During all that time, Henry was my only nurse. Later I learned that, knowing my father’s advanced age and his inability to make such a long journey, and knowing how miserable my sickness would make Elizabeth, he spared them this grief by hiding how severe my disorder really was."}

{"request_id":"ded2920b70aaaeee2a8af4c2","rewritten_text":"The studio smelled strongly of roses. When the warm summer wind moved through the trees in the garden, the open door let in the heavy scent of lilac, or the lighter perfume of the pink-flowering thorn.

From where he lay on the corner of a divan covered with Persian saddle-bags, Lord Henry Wotton could just make out the honey-sweet, honey-colored blossoms of a laburnum. Its branches trembled, as if they could hardly hold so bright a beauty. Now and then, the strange shadows of birds flying past would flicker across the long tussore-silk curtains stretched in front of the big window, giving him a brief, almost Japanese feeling. It made him think of the pale, jade-faced painters in Tokyo, who try—through an art that cannot move—to show the feeling of speed and motion. Even the bees seemed to press on through the long grass that had not been cut, or to circle again and again around the dusty, golden horns of the climbing woodbine. Their constant sound made the quiet feel even heavier. The distant noise of London was like the steady drone of an organ far away.

In the middle of the room, fixed to an upright easel, stood a full-length portrait of a young man with extraordinary beauty. A little way in front of it sat the artist himself, Basil Hallward. Some years earlier, Basil had suddenly disappeared, which at the time caused a great deal of public excitement and led to many strange guesses.

As Basil looked at the graceful, handsome figure he had captured so well in his painting, a smile of pleasure crossed his face and seemed as if it might stay. Then he suddenly sat up. He shut his eyes and pressed his fingers against his eyelids, as though he were trying to hold inside his mind a strange dream he feared he might wake from.

“It is your best work, Basil, the best thing you have ever done,” said Lord Henry in a lazy tone. “You must send it next year to the Grosvenor. The Academy is too big and too common. Every time I’ve gone there, either there were so many people that I couldn’t see the pictures, which was awful, or there were so many pictures that I couldn’t see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is really the only place.”

“I don’t think I shall send it anywhere,” he replied, tossing his head back in the same odd way that used to make his friends laugh at him when he was at Oxford."}

{"request_id":"20128eaf215751d31cd6cfd2","rewritten_text":"After dinner, the whole gang went out to hunt for turtle eggs on the bar. They wandered around poking sticks into the sand, and when they found a soft spot, they dropped to their knees and dug with their hands. Sometimes they would pull fifty or sixty eggs out of a single hole. The eggs were perfectly round, white things, just a little smaller than an English walnut. That night they had a famous fried-egg feast, and another on Friday morning.

After breakfast, they ran out onto the bar, shouting and prancing, chasing each other in circles and shedding their clothes as they went until they were naked. Then they kept up the play, running farther and farther up the shoal water of the bar against the stiff current, which kept tripping their legs out from under them now and then and making it even more fun. Every so often they would huddle together and splash water in each other’s faces with their palms, moving closer while keeping their faces turned away to avoid the choking sprays. Finally they would grab and wrestle until the best man ducked his neighbor, and then they all went under in a tangle of white legs and arms, coming up at the same time, blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping for breath.

When they were good and worn out, they would run out and sprawl on the dry, hot sand, then lie there and cover themselves with it. After a while they’d break for the water again and go through the whole performance once more. Eventually it occurred to them that their naked skin looked pretty much like flesh-colored “tights,” so they drew a ring in the sand and put on a circus, with three clowns in it, since none of them would give up that proudest role to his neighbor.

Next they got their marbles and played “knucks,” “ringtaw,” and “keeps” until that stopped being fun. Then Joe and Huck went for another swim, but Tom wouldn’t—because when he kicked off his trousers he’d kicked his string of rattlesnake rattles off his ankle, and he couldn’t understand how he’d avoided cramps so long without the protection of that mysterious charm. He didn’t try again until he found it, and by then the other boys were tired and ready to rest. They drifted apart, dropped into the “dumps,” and lay there staring longingly across the wide river at the village, drowsing in the sun. Tom found himself writing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe; he scratched it out and got angry with himself for being weak. But he wrote it again anyway; he couldn’t help it. He erased it once more, and then pulled himself away from temptation by driving the other boys together and joining them."}

{"request_id":"5a7fbdddc5e6713f5cc0a6ef","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man, and when I got him up he seemed very nice and kind. I told him my brother and I had been over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and that we camped on a piece of raft we found. I also told him that about midnight he must have kicked his gun in his dreams, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted him to go over there and fix it, and we wanted him to say nothing about it and not let anyone know. We were planning to come home this evening and surprise the folks.

“Who are your folks?” he asked.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he said. After a minute he asked, “How did you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I said. “And it shot him.”

“A singular dream,” he said.

Then he lit up his lantern, got his saddle-bags, and we started. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like the look of it. He said it was big enough for one person, but it didn’t look safe for two. I told him, “You don’t need to be afraid, sir. It carried the three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Me and Sid, and—and—and the guns. That’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he said.

He put his foot on the side of the canoe and rocked it, then shook his head and said he thought he’d look around for a bigger one. But all the other canoes were locked and chained. So he took my canoe and told me to wait until he came back. He said I could look around some more, or maybe I should go down home and get everything ready for the surprise if I wanted to. I said I didn’t, so I told him how to find the raft, and then he went.

I got an idea pretty soon. I thought to myself, if he can’t fix that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, like they say, and if it takes him three or four days, what are we going to do? Just sit around there until he lets the cat out of the bag? No, sir. I knew what I’d do. I’d wait. And when he came back, if he said he had to go any farther, I’d go down there too, if I had to swim. Then we’d take him, tie him up, keep him, and push off down the river. After Tom was done with him, we’d give him what it was worth, or all we had, and then let him get ashore.

So I slipped into a lumber pile to get some sleep. The next time I woke up, the sun was way up over my head. I jumped up and ran to the doctor’s house, but they told me he’d left sometime during the night and hadn’t come back yet."}

{"request_id":"9ccc50b81a7654a9241aea20","rewritten_text":"_PS._—Pray, tell me about those bows. Jennings swears they’re all the rage.

Lord Arthur looked so grave and wretched over the letter that the Duchess burst into laughter.

‘My dear Arthur,’ she exclaimed, ‘I shall never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what am I to say about the clock? I think it’s a splendid contrivance, and I’d dearly like one for myself.’

‘I can’t say I care much for them,’ Lord Arthur replied, wearing a sad little smile; then, after kissing his mother, he left the room.

Upstairs, he threw himself on a sofa, and his eyes filled with tears. He had done his utmost to carry out this murder, yet on both occasions he had failed—through no fault of his own. He had tried to do what was right, but it felt as though Destiny herself had turned traitor. The whole business weighed on him: the emptiness of good intentions, the sheer pointlessness of trying to be “fine.” Perhaps it would be better to end the marriage altogether. Sybil would, of course, be made to suffer; still, suffering could not truly spoil a nature as noble as hers. As for himself—what did it matter? There’s always some war in which a man may die, some cause to which he can give his life; and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no terror either. Let Destiny take care of her own sentence. He would not lift a finger to help her.

At half-past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a set of young men, and he had to dine with them. Their petty talk and empty jests bored him, and the moment coffee was served he slipped away, making up some engagement to excuse himself. As he was leaving, the hall-porter handed him a letter. It was from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to call the next evening and inspect an explosive umbrella that would go off the instant it was opened. It was the newest thing, just received from Geneva. He tore the letter into scraps. He had resolved not to attempt any more experiments.

Then he drifted down to the Thames Embankment and sat there for hours by the river. The moon pushed through a mane of tawny clouds, as though it were a lion’s eye, while countless stars glittered across the dark vault, like gold dust scattered over a purple dome. Now and then a barge swung out into the muddy stream and floated off with the tide; and the railway signals shifted from green to scarlet as the trains ran shrieking across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"bd40c01f8b4cdc31f20ca36c","rewritten_text":"I have said that he was a poet: at the age of three and twenty, he first published a poem, and it was greeted by the whole nation with enthusiasm and delight. His good star shone on him without fail; a reputation had never been made so quickly—so universally. The crowd praised the very poems that had been the wonder of the sage in his closet; there was not a single dissenting voice.

It was at this time, at the height of his glory, that he became acquainted with Elinor. She was a young heiress of exquisite beauty, living under the care of her guardian; from the moment they were seen together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor did not have Woodville’s genius, but she was generous and noble, and her youth—and the love she inspired everywhere—lifted her above anything but virtue and excellence. She was lovely; her manners were open and simple; her deep blue eyes seemed to glow with a luster that could only come from feeling joined to wisdom.

They were made for one another, and they soon loved. For the first time, Woodville felt the delight of love; and Elinor was captivated by the chance to possess the heart of someone so beautiful and glorious among his fellow men. Could anything other than pure joy come from such a union?

Woodville was a poet—every society sought him, and when he appeared all eyes turned to him alone; but he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a rich heiress. Her guardian was not displeased with their mutual affection: Woodville’s merit was too outstanding to be dismissed because of his limited wealth. Yet her father’s dying will did not allow her to marry before she came of age, and her fortune depended on her obeying that command. She had just entered her twentieth year, and she and her lover had to accept this delay. Still, they were always together, and their happiness seemed like Paradise: they studied together, made plans for their future work, and drank in love and joy from each other’s eyes and words, hardly resenting the postponement of their full union. Woodville rose forever in glory, and Elinor became more lovely and wise under the lessons of her accomplished lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one: everything was ready for their union. How can I tell of the catastrophe when so much joy was in the air? But the earth would not be the earth it is, covered as it is with blight and sorrow, if such angelic creatures as these had been allowed to exist for one another. Search the world over, and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have brought them; there must have been a revolution in the order of things as it is established among us miserable earth-dwellers to allow such consummate joy."}

{"request_id":"3b3ee0d5cd328033c0a118e3","rewritten_text":"“Just a tick.”

“Where’d you find him?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What’ll you want for him?”

“I don’t know. I don’t want to part with him.”

“Fine. Still, it’s a pretty small tick, all the same.”

“Any fool can pick up a tick that don’t belong to him. I’m content with this one. It’s good enough for me.”

“Sho, there are ticks enough. If I felt like it, I could have a thousand.”

“Well, why don’t you then? You know as well as I do you can’t. This one’s pretty early, I figure. It’s the first I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I'll trade you my tooth for him.”

“Let me see it.”

Tom pulled out some paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry looked at it with longing. The urge was mighty strong. Finally he said:

“Is it genuine?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the empty spot.

“Well, all right,” said Huckleberry. “It’s a deal.”

Tom tucked the tick into the percussion-cap box that had only lately been the pinchbug’s jail, and the boys went their separate ways, both feeling richer than they had before.

When Tom got to the little, stand-alone frame schoolhouse, he went in with a brisk stride, acting like he’d come by nothing but plain, honest speed. He hung his hat on a peg and dropped into his seat with businesslike eagerness. The teacher sat up high in his big splint-bottom chair, dozing, soothed by the drowsy murmur of lessons. The interruption snapped him awake.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that when his name was said in full, it meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir—why are you late again, like you always are?”

Tom was ready to hide behind a lie, but then he saw two long ribbons of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized at once by the electric pull of love; and there, by that very sight, was the only empty place on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. Without missing a beat he blurted:

“_I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!_”

The master’s pulse seemed to freeze, and he stared as if he couldn’t help himself. The hum of study stopped. The pupils wondered whether the boy had gone out of his mind. The master said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no mistaking it.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astonishing confession I’ve ever heard. No ordinary switch will cover this. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm went to work until it was worn out and the supply of switches had clearly dwindled. Then came the next order:

“Now, sir, go sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

The little ripple of laughter that ran through the room did make the boy look a bit flustered, but it was mostly because, underneath, he was struck with reverent awe for his unknown idol—and with a dread kind of delight at how lucky he’d gotten."}

{"request_id":"e2efd908094ebb4e8f758b89","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was quite distressed by the second postponement of the marriage, and Lady Julia, who had already ordered her dress for the wedding, did everything she could to make Sybil call off the match. Deeply as Sybil loved her mother, she had given her whole life into Lord Arthur’s hands, and nothing Lady Julia could say could make her waver in her faith. As for Lord Arthur himself, it took him days to get over his terrible disappointment, and for a time his nerves were completely shattered. His excellent common sense, however, soon asserted itself, and his sound, practical mind did not leave him long in doubt about what to do. Since poison had proved a complete failure, dynamite—or some other kind of explosive—was obviously what he should try.

He therefore went back over the list of his friends and relatives, and, after careful consideration, decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean, a man of great culture and learning, was extremely fond of clocks, and he had a wonderful collection of timepieces, from the fifteenth century up to the present day. It seemed to Lord Arthur that this hobby of the good Dean’s offered an excellent opportunity for carrying out his plan. Getting hold of an explosive machine, of course, was another matter entirely. The London Directory gave him no information, and he felt there was little point in going to Scotland Yard about it, since they never seemed to know anything about the dynamite faction’s movements until after an explosion had already taken place, and not much even then.

Suddenly he thought of his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with very revolutionary leanings, whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s in the winter. Count Rouvaloff was supposed to be writing a life of Peter the Great, and to have come to England to study the documents connected with that Tsar’s residence in this country as a ship carpenter; but it was widely suspected that he was a Nihilist agent, and there was no doubt that the Russian Embassy did not look kindly on his presence in London. Lord Arthur felt he was exactly the man for the job, and drove down one morning to his lodgings in Bloomsbury to ask his advice and help.

“So you’re taking up politics seriously?” Count Rouvaloff said when Lord Arthur explained the purpose of his visit; but Lord Arthur, who hated any kind of swagger, felt obliged to admit that he had not the slightest interest in social questions and simply wanted the explosive machine for a purely family matter, in which no one was involved but himself."}

{"request_id":"916fec43ae15dddbdceb4473","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, gently resting his hand on the Doctor’s arm again, after a short pause on both sides, “what do you think caused this attack?”

“I believe,” Doctor Manette answered, “that the illness was brought on by a strong, unusual return of the thoughts and memories that first caused it. Certain painful associations were brought back very clearly, I think. It’s likely he had been living with a deep fear that those memories would return—perhaps under the right circumstances, perhaps on a particular occasion. He tried to prepare himself, but he failed. Maybe the effort to prepare only made him less able to handle it.”

“Would he remember what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry asked, hesitating naturally.

The Doctor looked around the room with sadness, shook his head, and said quietly, “Not at all.”

“Now, about the future,” Mr. Lorry suggested.

“As for the future,” the Doctor said, regaining some firmness, “I have real hope. Since it pleased Heaven, in its mercy, to restore him so quickly, I should have great hope. He gave in under the pressure of something complicated—something he had long dreaded and long vaguely expected, and fought against. Now that the cloud has burst and passed, and he has recovered, I should hope the worst is over.”

“Well, well! That’s good comfort. I’m thankful,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I’m thankful,” the Doctor repeated, bowing his head with reverence.

“There are two other points,” Mr. Lorry said, “that I want to understand. May I go on?”

“You can’t do your friend a better service,” the Doctor replied, and took his hand.

“Then first,” Mr. Lorry continued. “He’s the kind of person who studies, and he’s unusually energetic. He throws himself into learning professional knowledge, running experiments, and many other things. Does he do too much?”

“I don’t think so. It may be the nature of his mind to always feel he needs something to do. That could be partly natural, and partly the result of his suffering. The less it was filled with healthy things, the more it would be in danger of turning toward unhealthy ones. He may have noticed this in himself and learned the lesson.”

“Are you sure he isn’t under too much strain?”

“I’m quite sure of it.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt that could happen easily. There has been a heavy pressure in one direction, and it needs a counterweight.”

“Excuse me, as a man who’s used to business. If we assume for a moment that he _was_ overworked, would it show itself in some new return of this disorder?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"647ac2dcfe43f972bcb968f9","rewritten_text":"Even to read about the luxury of the dead was wonderful.\n\nThen he turned his attention to embroideries and to the tapestries that served the same purpose as frescoes in the cold rooms of northern Europe. As he examined the subject—and he always had an extraordinary gift for becoming completely absorbed, for the moment, in whatever he took up—he was almost saddened by the thought of how time ruins beautiful, wonderful things. At least, he had escaped that. Summer followed summer, and the yellow jonquils bloomed and died again and again, while nights of horror repeated the story of their shame, but he remained unchanged. No winter ever marred his face or stained his flowerlike bloom. How different it was with material things! Where had they gone? Where was the great crocus-colored robe, on which the gods fought the giants, that had been worked by brown girls for Athena’s pleasure? Where was the huge velarium Nero stretched across the Colosseum in Rome, that Titan sail of purple on which the starry sky was shown, with Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white, gilt-reined steeds? He longed to see the curious table napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, on which every kind of delicacy and dish that could be desired for a feast was displayed; the mortuary cloth of King Chilperic, with its three hundred golden bees; the fantastic robes that made the Bishop of Pontus so indignant, figured with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—all, in fact, that a painter can copy from nature”; and the coat Charles of Orleans once wore, whose sleeves were embroidered with the verses of a song that began “_Madame, je suis tout joyeux_,” with the musical accompaniment of the words stitched in gold thread, and each note—square in shape in those days—formed with four pearls. He read about the room prepared at the palace in Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, made in broidery, and blazoned with the king’s arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, whose wings were similarly ornamented with the arms of the queen, the whole worked in gold.” Catherine de Medicis had a mourning bed made for herself of black velvet powdered with crescents and suns. Its curtains were of damask, with leafy wreaths and garlands, set on a gold-and-silver ground, and fringed along the edges with embroideries of pearls; it stood in a room hung with rows of the queen’s devices in cut black velvet on cloth of silver. Louis XIV. had gold-embroidered caryatides fifteen feet high in his apartment."}

{"request_id":"d711898ecdaa5f1fd09beaee","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent by them to Adrian, who had been chosen as arbiter. They traveled from Paris to Calais, passing through empty towns and lonely countryside, all the while feeding their violent hatred for one another. Now they argued their separate cases with complete party spirit.

When we looked at the deputies one by one, and after a long investigation, we learned the real situation in Paris. Since Parliament had chosen him as Ryland’s deputy, all the surviving English had submitted to Adrian. He was our captain, to lead us from our home soil to unknown lands; he was our lawgiver and our protector. When we first planned our emigration, no lasting separation of our members was expected, and the command of the whole group, as its power grew step by step, reached its highest point in the Earl of Windsor. But unexpected events changed our plans and forced most of our people to be separated from the supreme chief for nearly two months. They had gone over in two separate groups, and when they arrived in Paris, conflict broke out between them.

They found Paris deserted. When the plague first appeared, the return of travelers and merchants, along with letters, kept us informed about how badly disease was striking the continent. But as the death rate rose, that contact slowed down and then stopped. Even within England, communication between one part of the island and another became slow and rare. No ship crossed the flood that separated Calais from Dover; or if some sad traveler tried to sail from the French shore back to us to learn whether relatives were alive or dead, the greedy ocean often swallowed his small boat, or after a day or two he caught the disease and died before he could tell us what had happened in France. So we were largely ignorant of conditions on the continent, and we still had some unclear hope of finding many companions there. But the same causes that had so severely reduced the English population gave even more room for harm in the sister country. France was a blank. Along the long road from Calais to Paris, not a single person was seen. In Paris there were a few—maybe a hundred—who, resigned to what was coming, moved through the streets of the capital and gathered to talk about the past, with a liveliness and even a kind of cheer that rarely leaves this nation’s people.

The English took control of Paris without resistance. Its tall houses and narrow streets were lifeless. A few pale figures could be seen at the usual place, the Tuileries. They wondered why the islanders would come toward their doomed city, because in the worst misery, people always imagine their own suffering is the bitterst. When we are enduring intense pain, we would trade the particular torture we are feeling for any other that might strike a different part of the body."}

{"request_id":"742b2652d16d04b1b0a08ad0","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis—at Lady Canterville’s pressing request—had agreed to let remain in her old post. When they stepped down, she curtsied low to each of them and, in a quaint, old-world way, said, “I bid you welcome to Canterville Chase.” After her, they went through the handsome Tudor hall into the library, a long, low chamber panelled in black oak, where at the far end stood a great stained-glass window. Tea had been laid out for them there; after they had taken off their wraps, they sat down and began to look about, while Mrs. Umney attended to them.

All at once Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red mark on the floor near the fireplace, and without the least idea what it meant, told Mrs. Umney, “I’m afraid something has been spilt there.”

“Yes, madam,” answered the old housekeeper in a low voice. “Blood has been spilt on that spot.”

“How dreadful,” cried Mrs. Otis. “I don’t care for blood-stains in a sitting-room. It ought to be taken care of at once.”

The old woman smiled and replied in the same subdued, shadowy tone: “It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, who was murdered on that very place by her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived on for nine years after her, and then vanished under circumstances most mysterious. His body has never been found, yet his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. The stain has been greatly admired by tourists and others, and it cannot be removed.”

“That’s all nonsense,” Washington Otis snapped. “Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will have it cleaned up in a jiffy,” and before the frightened housekeeper could get in a word, he dropped to his knees and began to scrub the floor with a small stick that looked like some sort of black cosmetic. In a few moments not the faintest trace of the blood-stain remained.

“I knew Pinkerton would manage it,” he declared, looking around at his delighted family; but no sooner had he spoken than a dreadful flash of lightning lit the gloomy room, followed by a violent peal of thunder that made them all jump to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What a monstrous climate!” said the American Minister, perfectly composed, as he lit a long cheroot. “I suppose the old country is so overrun that there isn’t decent weather enough for everyone. I’ve always thought emigration is the only remedy for England.”

“My dear Hiram,” Mrs. Otis cried, “what are we to do with a woman who faints?”

“Charge it to her like breakages,” the Minister replied. “She won’t faint after that.” And in a few moments, Mrs. Umney indeed came to."}

{"request_id":"356d4c48fb5f1645cfa383b4","rewritten_text":"Many American women, when they leave their home country, start to look as if they are always sick. They think this is a kind of European polish, but Mrs. Otis had never made that mistake. She had a strong constitution and a truly wonderful store of energy. In many ways, she was almost English, and she was a good example of how much America and England have in common these days—except, of course, for the language.

Her eldest son, named Washington by his parents in a burst of patriotism, was a fair-haired, good-looking young man. He regretted the name, though he had trained himself for American diplomacy by leading the German at the Newport Casino for three straight seasons. Even in London, he was known as an excellent dancer. Gardenias and the peerage were his only weaknesses. Otherwise, he was extremely sensible.

Miss Virginia E. Otis was fifteen, slim and lovely as a fawn, with a free, open look in her large blue eyes. She was a wonderful rider. Once, she raced old Lord Bilton on her pony twice around the park, winning by a length and a half, just in front of the Achilles statue. The young Duke of Cheshire was delighted and proposed to her on the spot. Her guardians sent him back to Eton that same night, in floods of tears. After Virginia came the twins, usually called “The Stars and Stripes,” because they were always getting into trouble. They were delightful boys, and, aside from the respectable Minister, they were the only true republicans in the family.

Since Canterville Chase was seven miles from Ascot, the nearest railway station, Mr. Otis had telegraphed for a waggonette to meet them. They set off for the drive in high spirits. It was a lovely July evening, and the air smelled faintly of pine. Now and then they heard a wood pigeon cooing over its own sweet voice, or they saw, deep in the rustling fern, the pheasant’s shining breast. Little squirrels watched them from the beech trees, and rabbits darted away through the brushwood and over the mossy knolls, their white tails flashing as they ran. But when they entered the avenue of Canterville Chase, the sky suddenly turned cloudy. The air seemed strangely quiet. A large flock of rooks passed silently overhead, and before they reached the house, some heavy drops of rain had already fallen.

Waiting on the steps to greet them was an old woman, dressed neatly in black silk, with a white cap and apron."}

{"request_id":"5353c072bd9b90cd38e0f224","rewritten_text":"“We have been to your home,” said the first. “We didn’t find you there. We were told you were probably walking this way, so we followed you, hoping to catch up. Will you please get into the carriage?”

“The way they spoke was forceful, and as they said it they both moved so that I was between them and the carriage door. They were armed. I was not.

“‘Gentlemen,’ I said, ‘please excuse me. I usually ask who is asking for my help, and what the matter is that brings me here.’

“The second man answered. ‘Doctor, your clients are people of standing. As for what the case is, we trust your skill to tell you what it is better than we could explain. That is enough. Will you please get into the carriage?’

“I had no choice but to obey, and I got in without speaking. They both got in after me—the last one jumped in after putting up the steps. The carriage turned around and drove on at the same speed as before.

“I repeat this conversation exactly as it happened. I have no doubt it is, word for word, the same. I describe everything exactly as it took place, making myself stay focused and not let my mind wander from the task. Where I put the marks that are missing here, I stop for the moment and put my paper back in its hiding place.

*****

“The carriage left the streets behind, passed the North Barrier, and came out onto the country road. About two-thirds of a league past the Barrier—at the time I did not measure it, but later I did—it left the main road and soon stopped at a lonely house. All three of us got out. We walked, along a damp, soft path through a garden where a neglected fountain had overflowed, to the door of the house. The door was not opened right away when the bell was rung. One of my two escorts struck the man who opened it across the face with his heavy riding glove.

“This didn’t catch my attention in a special way, because I had seen ordinary people struck more often than dogs. But the other brother, still angry, struck the man in the same way with his arm. Their faces and manner were so alike that I only then realized they were twin brothers.

“From the time we got out at the outer gate—which we found locked, and which one of the brothers had opened to let us in and then relocked—I had heard cries coming from an upper room.”"}

{"request_id":"8bfed9aa61ef30825ba25fb4","rewritten_text":"After I had sent them in, I found I could not stay away from the very places where they were lodged, and I had the sense that, when I stood near them, they looked more hopeful and less desperate. In that restless, tormenting state of mind I wandered the streets of an evening, going past those offices and houses where I had left the petitions. Even to this hour, the weary western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night—the stern, shut-up mansions in their rows, and the long lines of lamps—still weigh on me with melancholy, because of what I had tied to them.

The daily visits I could make him were cut down now, and he was kept under stricter watch. Thinking, or imagining, that I was suspected of intending to carry poison to him, I asked to be searched before I sat down at his bedside, and I told the officer who was always there that I was ready to do anything that might assure him of the single-mindedness of my purpose. Nobody was harsh with him or with me. There was work to be done, and it was done, but without cruelty. The officer would always tell me that he was worse, and that some other sick prisoners in the room, and some other prisoners who attended on them as sick nurses—(villains, to be sure, but not without kindness, thank God!)—were saying the same thing.

As the days went on, I saw more and more that he would lie quietly, staring at the white ceiling, with a blankness on his face until some word of mine lit it up for an instant, and then it would sink back again. At times he could hardly speak at all; then he would answer me with slight pressure of my hand, and I came to understand what he meant.

When the number of days had reached ten, I noticed a change in him greater than any I had yet seen. His eyes were fixed toward the door, and they brightened the moment I came in.

“Dear boy,” he said, as I sat down by his bed. “I thought you was late. But I knew you couldn’t be that.”

“It is just the time,” said I. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always waits at the gate; don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. Not to lose a moment of the time.”

“Thank’ee, dear boy, thank’ee. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I held his hand in silence, because I could not forget that I had once meant to desert him.

“And what’s the best of all,” he said, “you’ve been more comfortable alonger me, since I was under a dark cloud, than when the sun shone.”"}

{"request_id":"74ea828507bdfe2210d7425b","rewritten_text":"“Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay,” was finally brought before the court.

The judges sat on the bench wearing feathered hats, though most people else wore a rough red cap with a tricolored cockade. When Darnay looked at the jury and the angry crowd, it almost seemed as if the usual order had been flipped, and that criminals were judging honest men. The worst, most cruel people in the city—always ready in large numbers—ran the whole scene. They shouted comments, cheered, booed, guessed what would happen, and pushed the outcome along, with no one stopping them. Many of the men were armed in different ways. Among the women, some had knives, some had daggers. Some ate and drank while they watched, and many knitted. One of the women, with a spare piece of knitting under her arm as she worked, sat in the front row beside a man Darnay had never seen since his arrival at the Barrier. Darnay remembered that man at once: Defarge. Darnay noticed that she leaned close and whispered to him once or twice, and that she seemed to be his wife. What he noticed most, though, was that even though they were as close to him as they could be, they never looked at him. They acted as if they were waiting for something, stubbornly determined. They stared at the jury, but at nothing else. Under the President sat Doctor Manette, dressed as quietly as always. As far as the prisoner could tell, he and Mr. Lorry were the only men there who were not connected to the tribunal. They wore their usual clothes and had not put on the rough Carmagnole.

Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, was accused by the public prosecutor of being an emigrant. His life, the prosecutor said, was forfeit to the Republic under the decree that banished all emigrants on pain of death. It did not matter, the prosecutor argued, that the decree had been written long ago, before Darnay returned to France. The decree still existed, and Darnay was back in France. He had been taken in France, and they demanded his head.

“Take off his head!” the crowd shouted. “An enemy to the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to silence them and asked the prisoner whether it was true that he had lived in England for many years.

Undoubtedly it was.

Then was he not an emigrant? What did he call himself?

Not an emigrant, he said, in the sense and spirit of the law.

Why not? the President asked.

Because he had voluntarily given up a title he disliked, and a position he disliked. He had left his country—he added, before the word emigrant was used in the way the tribunal meant it—so he could live by his own work in England, instead of living off the work of the overburdened people of France."}

{"request_id":"a37d66bbda88d1a902c77cca","rewritten_text":"Sandy and I were back on the road again the next morning, bright and early. It felt so good to open up my lungs and take in whole, luscious barrels of the blessed God’s untainted, dew-made, woodland-scented air once more—after being stuck for two days and nights in the moral and physical stench of that intolerable old buzzard-roost. I mean, for me: of course the place was fine enough and agreeable for Sandy, since she’d been used to high life all her days.

Poor girl—her jaws had had a weary rest for a while now, and I was expecting to face the consequences. I was right, but she’d stood by me most helpfully in the castle, and had backed me up with gigantic, foolish things that were worth more for the moment than wisdoms twice their size. So I figured she’d earned the right to run her mill for a while, if she wanted to, and I didn’t feel a pang when she started it up:

“Now turn we unto Sir Marhaus that rode with the damsel of thirty winter of age southward—”

“Are you going to see if you can work up another half-stretch on the trail of the cowboys, Sandy?”

“Even so, fair my lord.”

“Go ahead, then. I won’t interrupt this time, if I can help it. Start over again—begin clean, shake out all your reefs, and I’ll load my pipe and pay close attention.”

“Now turn we unto Sir Marhaus that rode with the damsel of thirty winter of age southward. And so they came into a deep forest, and by fortune they were nighted, and rode along in a deep way, and at the last they came into a courtelage where abode the duke of South Marches, and there they asked harbour. And on the morn the duke sent unto Sir Marhaus, and bade him make him ready. And so Sir Marhaus arose and armed himself, and there was a mass sung before him, and he broke his fast, and so mounted on horseback in the court of the castle, there they should do the battle. So there was the duke already on horseback, clean armed, and his six sons with him, and each one had a spear in his hand, and so they encountered—whereas the duke and his two sons broke their spears upon him, but Sir Marhaus held up his spear and touched none of them. Then came the four sons in pairs, and two of them broke their spears, and so did the other two. And all this while Sir Marhaus didn’t touch them. Then Sir Marhaus ran to the duke and struck him with his spear, so that horse and man fell to the earth.”}"}

{"request_id":"455ddff5d775d0a6cc810f48","rewritten_text":"“Why, you don’t mean to say—” my sister began.

“Yes I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook; “but wait a bit. Go on, Joseph. Good for you! Go on!”

“What would respectable company say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?”

“Handsome would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well, then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That abject hypocrite, Pumblechook, nodded again and said, with a patronizing laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Good again! Follow her up, Joseph!”

“Then to wrap it up,” Joe said, delightedly handing the bag to my sister; “it’s five-and-twenty pounds.”

“It’s five-and-twenty pounds, Mum,” echoed the basest of swindlers, Pumblechook, rising to shake hands with her; “and it’s no more than your merits (as I said when my opinion was asked), and I wish you joy of the money!”

If the villain had stopped there, his case would have been bad enough, but he made his guilt even darker by taking me into custody, with a kind of patronage that made all his earlier criminality seem small by comparison.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, taking me by the arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those people who always see things through once they’ve started. This boy must be bound, right away. That’s _my_ way. Bound right away.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said (grasping the money), “we’re deeply obliged to you.”

“Don’t mind me, Mum,” returned that diabolical cornchandler. “A pleasure’s a pleasure for everyone. But this boy, you know—we have to have him bound. I said I’d see to it—to tell you the truth.”

The Justices were sitting in the Town Hall nearby, and we went at once to have me bound apprentice to Joe in the Magisterial presence. I say we went, but Pumblechook shoved me forward, just as if I’d picked a pocket or fired a shot that very moment; in fact, that was the general impression in Court—that I’d been caught red-handed. As Pumblechook pushed me through the crowd, I heard people say, “What’s he done?” and others, “He’s a young ’un, too, but he looks bad, doesn’t he?” One person, mild and benevolent in appearance, even handed me a tract with a woodcut of a malevolent young man fitted out with a perfect sausage-shop of fetters, and titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall was a strange place, I thought, with higher pews than a church—and people leaning over the pews to watch—and with the mighty Justices (one with a powdered head) leaning back in chairs, arms folded, or taking snuff, or nodding off, or writing, or reading the newspapers. And on the walls there were some shining black portraits, which my untrained eye took for a mix of hardbake and sticking-plaster."}

{"request_id":"c3fd32d3052ce9ab9abbb23c","rewritten_text":"Great God! Had I, even for a single moment, entertained what infernal purpose my villainous adversary might be harboring, I would sooner have banished myself forever from my native land and wandered the world as a friendless outcast than have agreed to such a wretched marriage. Yet, as though endowed with some spell, the monster kept me from seeing his true intentions; and when I believed I had only prepared my own death, I hurried on that of a victim far dearer.

As the appointed time for our wedding drew nearer, whether from cowardice or from some prophetic foreboding, I felt my heart sink within me. I hid these feelings behind an air of gaiety, which won smiles and gladness on my father’s face, though it scarcely deceived Elizabeth’s ever-alert, keener eye. She looked forward to our union with calm satisfaction, tempered with a little fear—fear taught by former misfortunes—that the happiness now seemed so sure and solid might soon vanish like a dream, leaving nothing behind but deep, lasting regret.

Preparations were set in motion for the event; congratulatory visits were received; and everyone wore a smiling countenance. I kept, as best I could, the anxiety that gnawed at my heart shut away within myself, and it entered with an air of seriousness into my father’s plans, even if those plans were meant only to serve as the ornaments of my tragedy. By my father’s efforts, a portion of Elizabeth’s inheritance was restored to her by the Austrian government. She had a small holding on the shores of Como. It was settled that, immediately after our marriage, we should go on to Villa Lavenza and spend our first days of happiness by the beautiful lake near which it stood.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to guard my own person in case the fiend should attack me openly. I carried pistols and a dagger constantly, and remained on guard against any trick or artifice; and by these means I won a greater measure of composure. Indeed, as the time approached, the threat began to seem more like a delusion—something not worth disturbing my peace—while the happiness I expected from my marriage appeared more and more certain, as the day for its solemnisation drew nearer and I heard it spoken of again and again as an event no accident could possibly prevent.

Elizabeth appeared content; my steady manner helped greatly to quiet her mind. But on the very day meant to fulfil my wishes and my fate, she was cast down, and a presentiment of evil lay upon her; and perhaps she also recalled the dreadful secret I had promised to disclose to her on the next day."}

{"request_id":"ebc088dd2aa046d48f2068e8","rewritten_text":"“Oh, your father, of course, may spare you—if your mother can. Daughters are never of so much consequence to a father. And if you will stay another _month_ complete, it will be in my power to take one of you as far as London, for I am going there early in June, for a week; and as Dawson does not object to the barouche-box, there will be very good room for one of you—and indeed, if the weather should happen to be cool, I should not object to taking you both, as neither of you is large.”

“You are all kindness, madam; but I believe we must stick to our original plan.”

Lady Catherine seemed resigned. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I cannot bear the idea of two young women travelling post by themselves. It is highly improper. You must arrange for someone to go with them. I have the greatest dislike in the world to that sort of thing. Young women should always be properly guarded and attended, according to their station in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I made a point of having two men-servants go with her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley, and Lady Anne could not have appeared with propriety in any other way. I am excessively attentive to all those things. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I’m glad it occurred to me to mention it; for it would really be discreditable to _you_ to let them go alone.”

“My uncle is to send a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a man-servant, does he? I’m very glad you have someone who thinks of those things. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you mention my name at the Bell, you will be taken care of.”

Lady Catherine had many other questions to ask about their journey; and as she did not answer them all herself, attention was necessary—which Elizabeth believed to be lucky for her; or, with a mind so occupied, she might have forgotten where she was. Reflection had to be saved for solitary hours: whenever she was alone, she gave way to it as the greatest relief; and not a day went by without a solitary walk, in which she could indulge in all the delight of unpleasant recollections.

Mr. Darcy’s letter she was soon in a fair way of knowing by heart. She studied every sentence; and her feelings toward its writer were at times very different. When she remembered the style of his address, she was still full of indignation; but when she considered how unjustly she had condemned and upbraided him, her anger turned against herself, and his disappointed feelings became the object of her compassion."}
