{"request_id":"2c9a1af1d39df0cbe898830f","rewritten_text":"Her situation was truly unusual and full of trouble. Even though she felt a strong, burning need to uncover the mystery surrounding Oliver’s past, she still had to respect the trust the miserable woman she had just spoken with had placed in her. The woman had trusted her as a young, innocent girl. Her words and her manner had moved Rose Maylie’s heart. Along with her love for her young charge, and just as real and intense, Rose also wanted to bring the outcast back to repentance and hope.

They planned to stay in London for only three days before leaving for several weeks on the distant coast. It was now midnight on the first night. What could she decide to do that would still be possible in forty-eight hours? And how could she delay the trip without raising suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them, and would be for the next two days. But Rose knew him well enough to expect his quick temper. She could already see how angry he would be, at the first burst of his indignation, when he learned that someone had helped with the plan to capture Oliver. For that reason, she could not trust him with the secret. Her arguments for the girl’s sake would not be supported by anyone experienced. These were all reasons to be extremely careful and cautious about telling Mrs. Maylie. Rose knew Mrs. Maylie’s first instinct would be to call a meeting with the doctor. As for getting legal advice, even if Rose had known how to do it, that also seemed out of the question for the same reason.

At one point, Rose thought about asking Harry for help. But then she remembered their last goodbye, and it felt wrong to call him back. As she kept thinking, tears came to her eyes. She worried that by now he might have learned to forget her, and might be happier away.

With all these thoughts pulling her in different directions—then pushing her back again whenever a new idea came to mind—Rose spent a sleepless, anxious night. The next day, after thinking even more, she reached a desperate decision: she would consult Harry.

“If it hurts him to come back here,” she thought, “it will hurt me too. But maybe he won’t come. He might write, or he might come himself and carefully avoid seeing me, the way he did when he left. I didn’t really think he would. Still, it’s better for both of us.”

At that point, Rose put down her pen and turned away, as if the paper that was supposed to carry her message should not have to see her cry."}

{"request_id":"65c9317f6600cfe6d88a75fb","rewritten_text":"Well, three or four months passed, and it was winter by then. I had been to school almost all the time. I could spell and read and write a little, and I could say the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five. I don’t think I could ever get any farther than that, even if I lived forever. I don’t really believe in math anyway.

At first I hated school, but after a while I could stand it. When I got unusually tired, I played hookey. The beating I got the next day helped me feel better and cheered me up. The longer I went, the easier it became. I was also getting used to the widow’s way of doing things, and it wasn’t as rough on me. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed felt too tight for me most of the time. Before the cold weather, though, I would slip out and sleep in the woods sometimes, and that gave me a break. I liked the old ways best, but I was starting to like the new ones a little too. The widow said I was coming along slowly but surely, and that I was doing very well. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast, I turned over the salt-cellar. I reached for it as fast as I could, trying to throw the salt over my left shoulder to avoid bad luck. But Miss Watson was quicker than me, and she stopped me. She said, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry. You’re always making a mess!” The widow defended me, but that wasn’t going to stop the bad luck. I knew that. After breakfast I went out feeling worried and shaky, wondering where the bad luck would land and what it would be. There are ways to avoid some kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of those. So I didn’t try to do anything. I just kept going, low-spirited and on guard.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile where you pass through the tall board fence. There was an inch of fresh snow on the ground, and I saw some tracks. They came up from the quarry, stopped near the stile for a while, and then went around the garden fence. It was strange that they didn’t go inside after standing there so long. I couldn’t figure it out. Somehow it felt very curious. I was going to follow, but first I bent down to look closely at the tracks."}

{"request_id":"d502d34505e8e40162003121","rewritten_text":"There comes a stretch in the life of every well-made boy when a wild itch hits him to go off somewhere and dig up hidden treasure. That same craving struck Tom one day, out of the blue. He went looking for Joe Harper, but it didn’t pan out. Then he tried Ben Rogers, only to find he’d gone fishing. Before long he ran across Huck Finn the Red-Handed, and Huck would listen. Tom led him off to a private spot and told him the whole thing in confidence. Huck was game—Huck was always ready to join any scheme that promised fun and didn’t demand any money, because he had an annoying abundance of that kind of time that isn’t money at all. “Where’re we digging?” Huck asked.

“Oh, just about anywhere.”

“Is it hid everywhere?”

“No, not everywhere. It’s tucked away in very particular places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests under the end of a limb of some old dead tree, right where the shadow lands at midnight; but mostly under the floors in haunted houses.”

“Who puts it there?”

“Why, robbers, of course—who else would you guess? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it were mine, I wouldn’t hide it. I’d spend it and have a good time.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t do it that way. They stash it and leave it sitting there.”

“Don’t they come back for it?”

“They think they will, but they usually forget the spots, or else they die. Either way, it sits a long time and gets rusty. Then some fellow finds an old yellow paper that tells how to find the marks—only it’s got to be ciphered over for about a week, because it’s mostly signs and hy’roglyphics.”

“Hyro—what?”

“Hy’roglyphics—pictures and such, you know, that don’t seem to mean anything.”

“You got one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well then, how’re you supposed to find the marks?”

“I don’t need any marks. They always bury it under a haunted house, or on an island, or under a dead tree with one limb sticking out. We’ve tried Jackson’s Island some already, and we can try it again another time; and there’s that old haunted house on the Still-House branch, and plenty of dead-limb trees—dead loads of ’em.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“How can you say that? No!”

“Then how’re you going to know which one to pick?”

“Pick all of ’em!”

“Tom, it’ll take all summer.”

“So what? Say you turn up a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it—rusty and gray—or a rotten chest full of diamonds. What do you think of that?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s great. Plenty great for me. Just you hand me the hundred dollars, and I don’t want no diamonds.”"}

{"request_id":"9689042acb73b3f1fd48338b","rewritten_text":"“I must beg leave to speak, Sir Walter,” said Mr Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, as he set down the newspaper, “that the present moment is greatly to our advantage. With this peace, all those rich naval officers will be obliged to come ashore. They will be in want of a home. Nothing could be better, Sir Walter, than the chance of choosing tenants—tenants of the most proper sort. Many a fine fortune has been gathered during the war. If a wealthy admiral should happen to come in our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” returned Sir Walter; “that is all I have to add. A prize indeed would Kellynch Hall be to him; the greatest prize of all, too—after all the others he may have taken before; eh, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, because he knew he must, at the turn of it, and then went on—

“I take the liberty to remark, Sir Walter, that in matters of business, gentlemen of the navy are not to be overlooked. I have learned something of the way they transact affairs; and I can freely own they have very liberal ideas, and are as likely to make good tenants as any set of people one could meet. So, Sir Walter, what I would venture to suggest is this: if, in consequence of any rumours getting abroad of your intention—which we must allow may be possible, for we know how hard it is to keep the doings and designs of one part of the world from the notice and curiosity of the other—then consequence has its price. I, John Shepherd, might keep any family concerns to myself, for nobody would trouble themselves to watch me; but Sir Walter Elliot has eyes upon him, and it may be difficult to slip them. Therefore I will say no more than this: it would not greatly surprise me if, for all our care, some report of the truth should reach people. And, supposing that to be the case—as I was about to observe—since applications will certainly follow, I should think that any from our wealthy naval commanders would be especially worth attending to; and I beg leave to add that two hours will bring me over at any time, to spare you the trouble of answering.”

Sir Walter only nodded. Yet soon after, as he rose and walked about the room, he observed with a touch of sarcasm—

“There are few, I imagine, among the gentlemen of the navy who would not be astonished to find themselves in a house of this kind.”

“They would look about them, no doubt, and thank their good fortune,” said Mrs Clay, for Mrs Clay was there: her father had driven her over, since nothing was of more service to Mrs Clay’s health than a drive to Kellynch. “But I entirely agree with my father that a sailor might be a very desirable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"8fe6cbed4b13b32d515e6284","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had taken a very fine house in Camden Place, in a high, respectable position—the kind of place that suits a man of importance. Both he and Elizabeth were now settled there, and they were very pleased with it.

Anne entered with a heavy heart, expecting to be kept there for many months. She found herself thinking, “Oh! when will I be able to leave you again?” Still, the welcome she received was more warm than she had expected, and it helped her. Her father and sister were glad to see her, partly because they wanted to show her their house and furniture, and they met her with kindness. When she sat down with them for dinner as their fourth, it was treated as a benefit.

Mrs Clay was very pleasant and always smiling, but her politeness and smiles seemed almost automatic. Anne had always expected that she would have to act the part of a proper visitor when she arrived, but the easy friendliness of the others surprised her. They were clearly in excellent spirits, and soon she would hear why. Yet they had no real interest in listening to her. After a few compliments about how much they regretted her old neighbourhood, which Anne could not honestly say she missed, they asked only a couple of weak questions before the conversation became entirely their own. Uppercross meant nothing to them, and Kellynch even less. It was all about Bath.

They were happy to tell her that Bath had met their expectations in every way. Their house, they said, was unquestionably the best in Camden Place. Their drawing-rooms had clear advantages over any others they had seen or heard of, and the difference was just as strong in the way everything was arranged as in the taste of the furniture. Their acquaintance was in great demand. Everyone wanted to visit them. They had refused many introductions, yet cards were still being left by people they did not even know.

There was plenty to enjoy. Could Anne really be surprised that her father and sister were happy? She might not be surprised, but she still had to sigh that her father felt no shame in his change. He saw nothing to regret in the duties and dignity of a resident landholder, and he found plenty to be proud of in the small, empty things a town offers. She had to sigh, and smile, and wonder too, as Elizabeth threw open the folding doors and walked with excitement from one drawing-room to the next, boasting about their space—especially the fact that this woman, who had once been mistress of Kellynch Hall, could now feel proud of the size of rooms between two walls, perhaps only thirty feet apart.

But this was not all that made them happy. They had Mr Elliot as well."}

{"request_id":"efc620bccda62a0a6d187f12","rewritten_text":"For that reason, I decided to get off as soon as we reached the town and move out of his hearing. I carried out the plan without trouble. My small portmanteau was in the boot under my feet. All I had to do was turn a hinge to get it out. I threw it down in front of me, climbed out after it, and ended up standing on the first lamp of the town pavement. As for the convicts, they rode on with the coach, and I knew exactly where they would be taken next, to the river. In my mind, I pictured the boat waiting for them at the slime-washed steps, and I could hear the rough “Give way, you!” again, like a command shouted at dogs. I saw the wicked Noah’s Ark again, sitting on the black water.

I couldn’t say what I was afraid of, because my fear didn’t have any clear shape. It was just a vague, heavy dread, but it was strong. As I walked to the hotel, I felt a kind of terror that went far beyond the normal worry of facing something unpleasant or embarrassing. I’m sure it didn’t come with any clear picture, only the return for a few minutes of the fear I had as a child.

The coffee-room at the Blue Boar was empty. I had not only ordered my dinner there, but had already sat down to eat it before the waiter even recognized me. The moment he apologized for forgetting, he asked if he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I said. “Certainly not.”

The waiter looked surprised. He was the same man who, on the day I was set to leave, had brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials. He quickly seized the first chance he had to slide a dirty old local newspaper right in front of me. I picked it up and read the paragraph:

Our readers will learn, not altogether without interest, in reference to the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young artificer in iron of this neighbourhood (what a theme, by the way, for the magic pen of our as yet not universally acknowledged townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!) that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and friend, was a highly respected individual not entirely unconnected with the corn and seed trade, and whose eminently convenient and commodious business premises are situate within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not wholly irrespective of our personal feelings that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is good to know that our town produced the founder of the latter’s fortunes."}

{"request_id":"5525b360aedca14dcda4c2cf","rewritten_text":"“Do you hear me? I know the language of despair. I’ve memorized it all, because I am Despair—strange, joyous, triumphant Despair. But those words are lies, because the wave may be dark, yet it isn’t bitter. We lie down and close our eyes with a gentle good night, and when we wake, we are free. So come—no more delay, you slow one! Look at the pleasant potion. See, I’m a spirit of good, not a human maid who invites you, and with winning words—oh, if only they could win you!—says, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I kept my eyes fixed on his face. His exquisite beauty, the heavenly compassion shining from his eyes, and his gentle but earnest look of reproach and wonder even before he answered all changed something in me: my high-strung feelings eased, the hard edge of despair fell away, and I was left only with the softest grief. I saw that his eyes were wet as well when he took both my hands. Then, sitting down near me, he said:

“This is a sad deed you would lead me into, dearest friend, and your sorrow must be truly deep to fill you with these unhappy thoughts. You long for death, yet you fear it, and you want me to be your companion. But I have less courage than you, and even with you beside me I still cannot dare to die. Listen to me, and then consider whether you should win me over to your plan—especially if, with the overbearing eloquence of despair, you could make black death so inviting that fair heaven itself would seem like darkness. Listen, I beg you, to the words of someone who has nurtured desperate thoughts and longed with impatient desire for death, but who has finally trampled the phantom underfoot and crushed its sting. Come—since you have played Despair with me, I will play the part of Una with you and bring you out unharmed from his dark cavern. Listen to me, and let yourself be softened by words in which no selfish passion lingers.

“We don’t know what this whole wide world means—its strange mix of good and evil. But we’ve been placed here and told to live and hope. I don’t know what we’re meant to hope for, but there is some good beyond us that we must seek, and that is our earthly task. If misfortune comes against us, we must fight her; we must cast her aside and still go on, to find out what it is our nature to desire. Whether this promise of future good is preparation for another existence, I can’t say; or whether it is simply that, as workers in God’s vineyard, we must lend a hand to smooth the way for those who come after us."}

{"request_id":"8d288513aadf91c4f75e58f3","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself; the whole burden of maintaining that slow, disappointing correspondence with Elizabeth fell to Anne.

Breakfast had scarcely ended when Captain and Mrs Harville and Captain Benwick joined them. They had agreed to take their last walk about Lyme together, and they ought to be starting for Uppercross by one; in the meantime they were to remain as long as they could out of doors, all in company.

Anne noticed Captain Benwick drawing close to her as soon as they were properly in the street. What they had talked of the previous evening did not seem to discourage him from seeking her again; and they walked together for some time, speaking as before of Mr Scott and Lord Byron, still as unable as ever—like any other two readers—to judge the merits of either in the same way, until something occurred that nearly changed the whole current of their party. Captain Harville then took Captain Benwick’s place beside her.

“Miss Elliot,” said he, in a lower voice, “you have done a good deed in getting that poor fellow to talk so much. I only wish he had such company more often. I know it is hard on him to be shut up as he is; but what are we to do? We cannot separate.”

“No,” said Anne, “I can well believe that would be impossible; yet in time—perhaps. We know what time does in every case of affliction. And you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend may yet be called a young mourner; only last summer, I understand.”

“Ay, that’s true enough,” (with a deep sigh) “only June.”

“And not known to him, perhaps, so soon.”

“Not till the first week of August. He came home from the Cape, just made into the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, fearing to hear of him. He wrote letters, but the Grappler was under orders for Portsmouth. There the news had to follow him, but who was to tell it? Not I. I would as soon have been hauled up to the yard-arm. Nobody could do it, but that good fellow” (pointing to Captain Wentworth). “The Laconia had come into Plymouth the week before; there was no risk of her being sent to sea again. He had his chance for the rest, wrote for leave of absence, but without waiting for the return, travelled night and day till he reached Portsmouth, rowed off to the Grappler at once, and never left the poor fellow for a week. That’s what he did, and nobody else could have saved poor James. You may judge, Miss Elliot, whether he is dear to us!”

Anne did consider the matter with complete certainty, and said as much as her own feelings could express, or as he seemed able to bear; but he was too much moved to take up the subject again. When he spoke once more, it was of something entirely different.”}"}

{"request_id":"0c9a8d3e129546e0a472f0f6","rewritten_text":"It is a strange thing, but everyone who disappears is said to be seen in San Francisco. It must be a delightful city, with all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you think has happened to Basil?” Dorian asked, holding up his Burgundy to the light, and wondering how he could possibly talk about it so calmly.

“I have no idea at all. If Basil wants to hide himself, it’s not my business. If he’s dead, I don’t want to think about him. Death is the only thing that ever terrifies me. I hate it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked wearily.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, moving the gilt trellis of an open vinaigrette box past his nostrils, “these days you can survive everything except that. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts in the nineteenth century that you can’t talk your way out of. Let’s have our coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran away with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house is rather lonely without her. Of course, married life is just a habit—a bad one. But you still miss even your worst habits. Maybe you miss them the most. They’re such an essential part of who you are.”

Dorian didn’t answer. He got up from the table, went into the next room, and sat down at the piano, letting his fingers drift over the white and black keys. When the coffee was brought in, he stopped and looked over at Lord Henry. “Harry,” he said, “did it ever occur to you that Basil was murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was well liked, and he always wore a Waterbury watch. Why would he be murdered? He wasn’t clever enough to make enemies. Of course, he had a wonderful gift for painting. But a man can paint like Velasquez and still be as dull as possible. Basil was really rather dull. He only interested me once—years ago—when he told me he had a wild adoration for you, and that you were the driving force of his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” Dorian said, with sadness in his voice. “But don’t people say he was murdered?”

“Oh, some of the papers do. It doesn’t seem at all likely to me. I know there are dreadful places in Paris, but Basil wasn’t the kind of man who would go there. He had no curiosity. That was his main flaw.”

“What would you say, Harry,” the younger man asked, “if I told you that I had murdered Basil?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"8fb421646c7a7fc641501e84","rewritten_text":"The storm battered on fiercely through the night, yet nothing especially worth remarking took place. In the morning, though, when they came down for breakfast, the dreadful smear of blood was there on the floor again. “I can’t believe it’s the Paragon Detergent’s doing,” Washington said; “I’ve tested it with everything.” So he scrubbed the mark out a second time, but on the following morning it reappeared. The third morning it was still present as well; for the library had been shut up at night by Mr. Otis himself, and the key had been carried upstairs. The entire household was now thoroughly stirred. Mr. Otis began to think he had been too certain in his denial of ghosts; Mrs. Otis declared she meant to join the Psychical Society; and Washington set about writing a long letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore on the Permanence of Sanguineous Stains when linked with Crime. That night, all lingering doubts about the real, external existence of phantasmata were done with forever.\n\nThe day turned out warm and bright, and in the cool of the evening the whole family went out for a drive. They did not get back until nine o’clock, when they had a light supper. The talk never once drifted toward ghosts, so there weren’t even those first conditions of eager expectation that so often come before psychical happenings. As I learned afterward from Mr. Otis, the matters discussed were simply the sort of everyday topics that well-bred Americans of the better sort talk over—Miss Fanny Davenport’s immense superiority to Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; how hard it was to get green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy, even in the best English homes; the importance of Boston in the shaping of the world-soul; the benefits of the baggage-check system for railway travel; and how much sweeter the New York accent is than the London drawl. Not a word was said of anything supernatural, and Sir Simon de Canterville was not mentioned in any way. At eleven the family went to bed, and by half-past all the lights were out. Some time later, Mr. Otis was roused by a peculiar noise in the corridor outside his room. It sounded like the clank of metal and seemed to be drawing nearer by the moment. He rose at once, struck a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o’clock. He remained perfectly composed and even felt his pulse, which was in no way feverish. The odd sound went on, and now he could hear footsteps plainly. He slipped on his slippers, took a small oblong phial from his dressing-case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"f2fdfea0057ef51215f64efb","rewritten_text":"“Next, we put up a wire fence.”

“Wire fence?”

“Yes. You yourself tossed out the idea a couple of years back—two or three, if I’m not mistaken.”

“Oh, I recall it—the time the Church tested its strength against us the first go-round, and then decided to wait for a more promising season. So, how have you laid out the fence?”

“I’ve started with twelve immensely strong wires—bare, not insulated—running from a big dynamo in the cave. The dynamo has no brushes besides a positive and a negative one—”

“Yes, that’s it.”

“The wires run out from the cave and form a circle of level ground a hundred yards across; they create twelve separate fences, ten feet apart—that is, twelve circles inside circles—and each wire’s end comes back into the cave.”

“Right; continue.”

“The fences are tied to heavy oaken posts spaced only three feet apart, and those posts are sunk five feet into the ground.”

“That’s solid.”

“Yes. Outside the cave, the wires have no ground connection. They leave from the dynamo’s positive brush; the ground connection is only through the negative brush; the other ends return to the cave, and each one is grounded on its own.”

“No, no—that won’t work!”

“Why?”

“Too costly—wastes force for nothing. You don’t want any ground connection except the one through the negative brush. The far end of every wire has to be brought back into the cave and fastened separately, and without any ground connection. Now, look at the economy of it. A cavalry charge slams into the fence; you’re using no power, spending no money, because there’s only one ground connection until the horses hit the wire. The instant they touch it, they complete a path to the negative brush through the ground, and they drop dead. Don’t you see?—you’re not using energy until it’s actually required; your lightning is waiting there, ready like the charge in a gun, but it costs you nothing until you pull the trigger. Oh, yes—the single ground connection—”

“Exactly! I don’t know how I missed that. It’s not just cheaper, it’s more effective than the other plan, because if wires break or tangle, nothing bad happens.”

“No, especially if we keep a tell-tale in the cave and disconnect the broken wire. All right, then—the gatlings?”

“Yes. In the middle of the inner circle, on a broad platform six feet high, I’ve arranged a battery of thirteen gatling guns, with plenty of ammunition.”

“That’s it. They’ll cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, there’ll be music. The cliff’s edge above the cave—”

“I’ve got a wire fence there too, and a gatling.”}"}

{"request_id":"7d8b5022334529f3f2a633e2","rewritten_text":"To look at a star by quick glances—to view it from the side, by turning toward it the outer portions of the retina (which are more susceptible to faint impressions of light than the inner parts)—is to see the star distinctly: it is to get the best sense of its brilliance, a brilliance that grows dim in direct proportion as we turn our vision fully upon it. In the latter case, more rays actually fall on the eye, but in the former there is a more refined capacity for understanding. By going too deep, we confuse and weaken thought; and it is even possible to make Venus herself disappear from the sky by a scrutiny that is too sustained, too concentrated, or too direct.

“As for these murders, let’s go over the facts ourselves before we form an opinion. An inquiry will be entertaining,” [I thought it was an odd word for what he meant, but I said nothing] “and besides, Le Bon once did me a service for which I’m not ungrateful. We’ll go and see the premises with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and I won’t have trouble getting the necessary permission.”

The permission was obtained, and we went at once to the Rue Morgue. It was one of those miserable thoroughfares that run between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We reached it late in the afternoon, since this part of town was far from where we lived. The house was easy to find, because many people were still standing across the street, staring up at the closed shutters with aimless curiosity. It was an ordinary Parisian house, with a gateway; on one side there was a glazed watch-box, with a sliding panel in the window, indicating a loge de concierge. Before going in, we walked up the street, turned down an alley, and then, turning again, passed behind the building—while Dupin, in the meantime, examined the whole neighborhood as well as the house, with a level of careful attention I couldn’t see any possible purpose for.

Walking back, we came again to the front of the dwelling, rang the bell, and, after showing our credentials, were admitted by the agents on duty. We went upstairs—into the chamber where the body of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been found, and where both of the deceased still lay. The room’s disorder had, as usual, been allowed to remain. I saw nothing beyond what had already been stated in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin scrutinized everything—not excluding the bodies of the victims. We then went into the other rooms and into the yard, with a gendarme accompanying us the whole time."}

{"request_id":"48ad6fd96c6be6fbb9b66ac4","rewritten_text":"If, however, you want one for home use, I can supply you with an excellent article, and I guarantee you’ll be satisfied with the result. May I ask who it’s intended for? If it’s for the police, or for anyone connected with Scotland Yard, I’m afraid I can’t do anything for you. The English detectives are really our best friends, and I’ve always found that by relying on their stupidity, we can do exactly what we like. I can’t spare one of them.”

“I assure you,” said Lord Arthur, “it has nothing to do with the police at all. In fact, the clock is meant for the Dean of Chichester.”

“Dear me! I had no idea you felt so strongly about religion, Lord Arthur. Few young men do nowadays.”

“I’m afraid you’re overrating me, Herr Winckelkopf,” said Lord Arthur, blushing. “The fact is, I really know nothing about theology.”

“Then it’s purely a private matter?”

“Purely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged, and left the room. A few minutes later he returned with a round cake of dynamite about the size of a penny, and a pretty little French clock, topped with an ormolu figure of Liberty trampling on the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face brightened when he saw it. “That’s exactly what I want,” he cried. “And now tell me how it goes off.”

“Ah! there’s my secret,” answered Herr Winckelkopf, regarding his invention with a look of pride that was entirely justified. “Let me know when you want it to explode, and I’ll set the machine for the moment.”

“Well, today is Tuesday, and if you could send it off right away—”

“That’s impossible; I have a great deal of important work to do for some friends of mine in Moscow. Still, I might send it off tomorrow.”

“Oh, it will be quite time enough!” Lord Arthur said politely. “If it’s delivered tomorrow night or Thursday morning. For the moment of the explosion—say Friday at noon exactly. The Dean is always at home at that hour.”

“Friday, at noon,” Herr Winckelkopf repeated, and he made a note of it in a large ledger lying on a bureau near the fireplace.

“And now,” said Lord Arthur, rising from his seat, “pray let me know how much I owe you.”

“It’s such a small matter, Lord Arthur, that I don’t care to make any charge. The dynamite comes to seven and sixpence, the clock will be three pounds ten, and the carriage about five shillings. I’m only too pleased to oblige any friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.”

“But what about your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?”"}

{"request_id":"ae15685109ff5c0cdf085709","rewritten_text":"The studio was heavy with the rich scent of roses, and when the warm summer breeze stirred among the trees in the garden, the open door let in the deep fragrance of lilac—or, even more delicately, the perfume of the pink-flowering thorn.

From the corner of the divan, where he lay amid Persian saddle-bags, smoking as was his habit, Lord Henry Wotton could just make out the gleam of the laburnum’s honey-sweet, honey-colored blossoms. Its trembling branches seemed barely able to hold the burden of a beauty so blazing as theirs. Now and then, the strange shadows of birds in flight would flicker across the long tussore-silk curtains stretched before the huge window, creating a brief, almost Japanese effect, and making him think of those pale, jade-faced painters from Tokyo who, through an art that is necessarily still, try to capture the feeling of speed and movement. The dull murmur of bees pushing through the long, uncut grass, or circling with monotonous insistence around the dusty gilt horns of the straggling woodbine, only made the quiet feel more oppressive. The dim roar of London was like the bourdon note of a distant organ.

In the middle of the room, bolted to an upright easel, stood the full-length portrait of a young man of extraordinary personal beauty. A little distance in front of it sat the artist himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance some years earlier had caused, at the time, such public excitement and led to so many strange speculations.

As the painter studied the gracious, handsome figure he had so skillfully mirrored in his art, a smile of pleasure crossed his face and seemed as if it might linger. But then he jerked upright, closed his eyes, and pressed his fingers to his lids, as though he were trying to trap in his mind some strange dream from which he feared he might wake.

“It is your best work, Basil—the best thing you have ever done,” Lord Henry said languidly. “You must send it next year to the Grosvenor. The Academy is too big and too vulgar. Every time I’ve gone there, there have been either so many people that I couldn’t see the pictures—which was dreadful—or so many pictures that I couldn’t see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is really the only place.”

“I don’t think I shall send it anywhere,” he replied, tossing his head back in that odd way that used to make his friends laugh at him at Oxford."}

{"request_id":"191b1a94db7f2fb98f40eca5","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten o’clock at night?”

“Yes, sir. Your honour told me to call you.”

“Oh! I remember. Very well, very well.”

After a few dull tries to fall asleep again, which the man skillfully stopped by stirring the fire nonstop for five minutes, he got up, tossed his hat on, and went out. He turned into the Temple. After walking twice along the pavements of King’s Bench-walk and Paper-buildings to wake himself up, he went into the Stryver chambers.

The Stryver clerk, who never took part in these meetings, had already gone home. The Stryver principal opened the door. He was wearing slippers, a loose bed-gown, and his throat was uncovered for comfort. His eyes had that wild, strained, scorched look you could see in all free drinkers of his kind, from the portrait of Jeffries down, and you could trace it, under different disguises of Art, through the portraits of every Drinking Age.

“You’re a little late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the usual time. It might be a quarter of an hour later.”

They went into a dingy room full of books and scattered with papers, where a fire was burning. A kettle steamed on the hob. In the middle of the mess of papers, a table glowed, with plenty of wine, brandy, and rum on it, along with sugar and lemons.

“So you’ve had your bottle, Sydney,” said Stryver.

“Two tonight, I think. I’ve been dining with the day’s client— or watching him dine. It’s all the same!”

“That was a fine point, Sydney, that you made for the identification. How did you come up with it? When did it hit you?”

“I thought he was a rather handsome fellow, and I thought I’d be much the same kind of fellow if I’d had any luck.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his early, overgrown belly shook.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

Sullenly, the jackal loosened his clothes, went into the next room, and came back with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. He soaked the towels in the water, wrung them out a bit, folded them on his head in a way that was hard to look at, sat down at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“Not much boiling down to do tonight, Memory,” said Mr. Stryver cheerfully, as he looked through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets.”

“Give me the worst first.”

“There they are, Sydney. Fire away!”

Then the lion lay back on a sofa on one side of the drinking table, while the jackal sat at his own table, covered with papers, on the other side, with the bottles and glasses right within reach."}

{"request_id":"35c9cfc27ff46fdfaa66401f","rewritten_text":"But I have to warn you in advance that I’m going to tell Sybil everything. She’s coming to lunch with me tomorrow, to talk about bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers finds out that you have a bad temper, or a tendency to gout, or a wife living in Bayswater, I will certainly let her know all about it.”

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. “I’m not afraid,” he answered. “Sybil knows me as well as I know her.”

“Ah! I’m a little sorry to hear you say that. The right foundation for marriage is a mutual misunderstanding. No, I’m not cynical at all—I’ve just had experience, which, as it happens, is very much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is dying to have his hand read. Don’t tell him that he’s engaged to one of the most beautiful girls in London, because that appeared in the _Morning Post_ a month ago.”

“Dear Lady Windermere,” cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, “do let Mr. Podgers stay here a little longer. He has just told me I should go on the stage, and I’m so interested.”

“If he’s told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I’ll certainly take him away. Come over at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.”

“Well,” said Lady Jedburgh, making a little moue as she rose from the sofa, “if I’m not allowed to go on the stage, then I must at least be allowed to be part of the audience.”

“Of course; we’re all going to be part of the audience,” said Lady Windermere. “And now, Mr. Podgers, be sure to tell us something nice. Lord Arthur is one of my special favorites.”

But when Mr. Podgers saw Lord Arthur’s hand, he turned curiously pale and said nothing. A shudder seemed to run through him, and his great bushy eyebrows twitched convulsively, in that odd, irritating way they did when he was puzzled. Then huge beads of perspiration broke out on his yellow forehead, like a poisonous dew, and his fat fingers grew cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur didn’t miss these strange signs of agitation, and for the first time in his life he felt fear himself. His instinct was to rush out of the room, but he held back. It was better to know the worst—whatever it was—than to be left in this hideous uncertainty.

“I’m waiting, Mr. Podgers,” he said.

“We’re all waiting,” cried Lady Windermere in her quick, impatient way, but the cheiromantist made no reply.

“I believe Arthur is going on the stage,” said Lady Jedburgh, “and that, after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him so.”"}

{"request_id":"f16662189ad8cd12a18667ce","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted she was a little surprised by the match, but she spoke less about her astonishment than about her sincere desire for their happiness; nor could Elizabeth get her to treat it as unlikely. Kitty and Lydia were far from envying Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was only a clergyman, and it affected them in no other way than as news to spread around Meryton.

Lady Lucas couldn’t help feeling triumphant at being able to answer Mrs. Bennet with the comfort of having a daughter who was well married, and she visited Longbourn more often than usual to say how happy she was, even though Mrs. Bennet’s sour looks and mean remarks might have been enough to drive happiness away.

Between Elizabeth and Charlotte there was a restraint that kept them both silent on the subject, and Elizabeth felt convinced that no real trust could ever exist between them again. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her turn with even greater affection to her sister, whose integrity and delicacy she was sure could never be shaken; and she grew daily more anxious for Charlotte’s happiness, as Bingley had now been gone a week and nothing was heard of his return.

Jane had sent Caroline an early reply to her letter, and she was counting the days until she could reasonably hope to hear again. The promised letter of thanks from Mr. Collins arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father, and written with all the solemn gratitude that a year spent in the family might have produced. After satisfying his conscience on that point, he went on, with many rapturous expressions, to tell them how happy he was to have won the affection of their amiable neighbor, Miss Lucas. He then explained that it was only with the intention of enjoying her company that he had been so ready to agree to their kind wish that he return to Longbourn, where he hoped to be able to come back on Monday fortnight. For Lady Catherine, he added, approved of his marriage so wholeheartedly that she wanted it to happen as soon as possible, which he trusted would be an unanswerable argument with his amiable Charlotte to set an early date and make him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire was no longer a matter of pleasure for Mrs. Bennet. On the contrary, she was just as inclined to complain about it as her husband. It was very strange that he should come to Longbourn instead of to Lucas Lodge; it was also very inconvenient and extremely troublesome. She hated having visitors in the house while her health was so uncertain, and lovers were, of all people, the most disagreeable."}

{"request_id":"3b81093132abeb7340ca3af7","rewritten_text":"Tom meant to scarify the cupboard with it, and was getting ready to move on to the bureau when he was interrupted and sent off to get dressed for Sunday-school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a bar of soap. He stepped out the door, set the basin on a small bench, dipped the soap into the water, and laid it aside. Then he rolled up his sleeves, poured the water onto the ground—carefully, as if he meant no harm—and went back into the kitchen to scrub his face with real diligence on the towel hung behind the door. But Mary took the towel away and said:

“Now ain’t you ashamed, Tom. You can’t be so bad. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom felt a bit thrown off. The basin was filled again, and this time he hovered over it a moment, collecting himself; he drew in a deep breath and started. When he came into the kitchen again, both eyes shut and reaching blindly for the towel, suds and water were dripping from his face in plain evidence. Yet when he stepped out, he still wasn’t right, because the clean part ended at his chin and jaws, like a mask; below that line, and all around his neck, there was a dark stretch of ground that hadn’t been washed. Mary took him in hand, and when she finished, he was a man and a brother, with no difference of color; his hair, soaked through, had been brushed neatly, and the short curls were arranged into a neat, balanced look. [He quietly smoothed the curls out again, with effort and trouble, and pressed his hair close to his head; he believed curls were too effeminate, and his own curls had filled his life with bitterness.] Then Mary brought out a suit of his clothes that had been worn only on Sundays for two years—what they simply called his “other clothes”—and that, we may say, tells you the size of his wardrobe. After he dressed himself, the girl “put him to rights”: she fastened his roundabout up to his chin, flipped his big shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and set his speckled straw hat on his head. He now looked much improved, though also very uncomfortable. He was as uncomfortable as he looked, too; there was a kind of tightness in wearing whole clothes and being clean that irritated him. He had hoped Mary would forget his shoes, but that hope failed—she rubbed them thoroughly with tallow, as was the custom, and brought them out. He snapped and complained that he was always being made to do things he didn’t want to do."}

{"request_id":"52ccfc636b5eee03e47a8b05","rewritten_text":"The group was split up and settled on two adjoining benches: Anne was among those seated in the front, and Mr. Elliot had managed so well—helped by his friend Colonel Wallis—that he ended up with a seat beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins and the main focus of Colonel Wallis’s gallantry, was perfectly content.

Anne’s mind was in an excellent state for the evening’s entertainment; it was just the right kind of occupation. She had feelings for the tender, spirits for the lively, attention for the scientific, and patience for the tedious—and she had never enjoyed a concert more, at least during the first act. Near the end of it, during the interval after an Italian song, she explained the words of the song to Mr. Elliot. They had a concert program between them.

“This,” she said, “is nearly the sense—or rather the meaning—of the words. Of course, you can’t really talk about the sense of an Italian love-song, but it’s as close to the meaning as I can give; I don’t pretend to understand the language. I’m a very poor Italian scholar.”

“Yes, yes, I see you are. I see you know nothing about it. You only have enough knowledge of the language to translate, at first glance, these inverted, transposed, shortened Italian lines into clear, understandable, elegant English. You don’t need to say anything more about your ignorance. Here’s complete proof.”

“I won’t argue with such kind politeness; but I’d be sorry to be examined by a true expert.”

“I haven’t had the pleasure of visiting Camden Place for so long,” he replied, “without learning something about Miss Anne Elliot. And I do consider her someone too modest for the world in general to realize half her accomplishments, and too highly accomplished for modesty to come naturally in any other woman.”

“For shame! For shame! This is far too much flattery. I forget what we’re supposed to have next,” she said, turning back to the program.

“Perhaps,” Mr. Elliot said quietly, “I’ve had a longer acquaintance with your character than you realize.”

“Indeed! How so? You could only have known it since I came to Bath—unless you might have heard me spoken of earlier in my own family.”

“I knew you by report long before you came to Bath. I’d heard you described by people who knew you intimately. I’ve been acquainted with you by character for many years. Your person, your disposition, your accomplishments, your manner—they were all present to me.”

Mr. Elliot was not disappointed in the interest he hoped to stir. No one can resist the charm of such a mystery."}

content.text: {"request_id":"cd2d9ea80f9b83d2df3dfd97","rewritten_text":"I got up early in the morning and, once again, tried to slip past the watchfulness of my creditors. Eagerly, I went to the bookseller’s stall and laid out the little ready money I had, buying volumes of Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. Once I got home safely with them, I devoted every spare moment to reading, and soon I felt I had gained enough proficiency in this kind of study to carry out my plan. During the time that followed, I made every effort to calm the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble. Eventually I succeeded—partly by selling enough of my household furniture to cover a portion of their claim, and partly by promising to pay the rest once I finished a small project I told them I had in mind. For that project, I asked for their help, and because they were ignorant men, I found it not too difficult to win them over to my purpose.\n\n“With everything thus arranged, I managed—using the help of my wife, and with the greatest secrecy and care—to dispose of whatever property I still had, and to borrow small sums under different pretexts, all without giving any thought to how I would repay them. With the money I gathered this way, I went on, at intervals, to buy cambric muslin, very fine, in pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a quantity of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and several other items needed to construct and equip a balloon of extraordinary size. I told my wife to assemble it as soon as possible and gave her all the necessary instructions about the exact method to follow. Meanwhile, I worked the twine into a net of sufficient dimensions; fitted it with a hoop and the required cords; bought a quadrant, a compass, a spyglass, a common barometer with some important modifications, and two astronomical instruments that were not so widely known. Then I took advantage of the cover of night to transport, to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam, five iron-bound casks meant to hold about fifty gallons each, along with one larger cask; six tinned ware tubes, three inches in diameter and ten feet long; a quantity of a particular metallic substance, or semi-metal, which I won’t name; and a dozen demijohns of a very common acid. The gas to be produced from these materials is a gas that no one else has ever generated—or at least, no one has ever used it for any similar purpose. I wouldn’t have any trouble disclosing the secret, except that it properly belongs to a citizen of Nantz in France, who communicated it to me conditionally.”"}

{"request_id":"2a6c0855aa425517c2c1d762","rewritten_text":"But there was no laughter in the little town that same calm Saturday afternoon. The Harpers, along with Aunt Polly’s family, were being put into mourning, with deep grief and many tears. An unusual quiet settled over the village, though it was usually quiet enough, if you’re being honest. The villagers went about their business with a distant, absent look, and talked very little; but they sighed often. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children. They had no heart for their games, and gradually gave them up.

In the afternoon, Becky Thatcher found herself hanging around the empty schoolhouse yard, feeling very down. But she found nothing there to comfort her. She talked to herself:

“Oh, if I only had that brass andiron-knob again! But I don’t have anything now to remember him by.” And she choked back a small sob.

After a moment, she stopped and said to herself:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over again, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for the whole world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

That thought broke her, and she wandered off with tears running down her cheeks. Then a whole group of boys and girls—Tom and Joe’s playmates—came by and stood looking over the paling fence, speaking in reverent tones about how Tom had done this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe had said this and that small detail (full of awful meaning, as they could see now!). Each person pointed out the exact spot where the lost boys had been standing at the time, and then added something like, “and I was standing just so—just like I am now, and as if you were him—I was as close as that—and he smiled, just this way—and then something seemed to go all over me, like—awful, you know—and I didn’t think what it meant, of course, but I can see now!”

Then there was an argument about who had seen the dead boys last in life, and many claimed that grim distinction, offering evidence that was more or less altered by the witness. And when it was finally decided who _did_ see the departed last and exchanged the last words with them, the lucky ones took on a kind of sacred importance, and everyone else stared at them and envied them. One poor fellow, who had no other kind of glory to offer, said with fairly obvious pride in the memory:

“Well, Tom Sawyer he beat me once.”

But that attempt at glory didn’t work. Most of the boys could say the same thing, and that made the distinction too cheap. The group drifted away again, still lingering on memories of the lost heroes, speaking in hushed, awed voices."}

{"request_id":"052cc4a96e7c7ea89b0fcded","rewritten_text":"“Yes—burglar’s tools. That seems to take a lot of pressure off you. But what made you change your mind? What did you think we’d found?”

Huck was in a tight spot—the questioning look was on him—he would have given anything for something that sounded like a plausible answer—nothing came to him. The questioning look kept boring deeper and deeper. He offered a senseless reply—there wasn’t time to think it through, so he took a shot and said it weakly:

“Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Poor Huck was too upset to smile, but the old man laughed loudly and happily, shook the details of his anatomy from head to foot, and ended by saying that a laugh like that was money in a man’s pocket, because it cut down the doctor’s bill like everything else. Then he added:

“Poor old chap—you’re pale and worn out—you’re not well at all, no wonder you’re a little flighty and off-balance. But you’ll get through it. Rest and sleep will set you right, I hope.”

Huck was irritated to realize he’d been such a fool and had shown such suspicious excitement. He had dropped the idea that the parcel brought from the tavern was the treasure as soon as he’d heard what was being said at the widow’s stile. He’d only thought it wasn’t the treasure—he hadn’t known it wasn’t—and so the thought of a captured bundle was too much for his self-control. Still, he felt glad the little episode had happened, because now he knew for sure that that bundle wasn’t the bundle, and his mind was at ease and he felt wonderfully comfortable. In fact, everything seemed to be drifting in exactly the right direction now: the treasure must still be in No. 2, the men would be captured and jailed that day, and he and Tom could take the gold that night without any trouble or fear of being interrupted.

Just as breakfast was finished, there was a knock at the door. Huck sprang up for a hiding place, because he had no desire to be connected in any way to what had happened. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas, and noticed that groups of citizens were climbing up the hill—to stare at the stile. So the news had spread. The Welshman had to tell the story of the night to the visitors. The widow’s gratitude for her rescue was plain to see.

“Don’t say a word about it, madam. There’s another you’re more indebted to than you are to me and my boys, maybe—but he won’t let me tell his name. We wouldn’t have been there but for him.”"}

{"request_id":"783d76600b31afb87f3bebb5","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

No answer.

“What’s happened to that boy, I wonder? You TOM!”

No answer.

The old lady pulled her spectacles down and looked around the room. Then she pushed them up and looked out over them. She almost never looked through them for something as small as a boy. They were her special pair, the pride of her heart. They were made for “style,” not for usefulness. She could have seen through a pair of stove lids just as well. She looked puzzled for a moment, and then she said, not angrily, but loud enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, I’ll be—if I get hold of you, I’ll—”

She didn’t finish, because she was already bending down and hitting under the bed with the broom, and she needed breath to go with the punches. She found nothing but the cat.

“I never did see the trick of that boy!”

She went to the open door, stood there, and looked out among the tomato vines and the “jimpson” weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice, aiming it for distance, and shouted:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

A small sound came from behind her, and she turned just in time to grab a little boy by the slack of his roundabout and stop him from running.

“There! I might’ve thought of that closet. What have you been doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What is that stuff?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I do. It’s jam—that’s what it is. I’ve told you forty times that if you don’t leave that jam alone, I’ll skin you. Hand me that switch.”

The switch hovered in the air—the danger was real.

“My! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old lady spun around and pulled her skirts back out of the way. The boy ran off at once, scrambled up the high board fence, and disappeared over it.

His aunt Polly stood there, surprised for a moment, and then she let out a gentle laugh.

“Good grief, can’t I ever learn anything? Hasn’t he played me tricks enough that I should be watching for him by now? But old fools are the biggest fools there are. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks, as the saying goes. Still, he never plays them the same way two days in a row. How is a person supposed to know what’s coming? He seems to know just how long he can torment me before I get mad, and he knows that if he can distract me for a minute or make me laugh, then I’m back to where I started and I can’t hit him a lick.”"}

{"request_id":"566a7c253b86487beb7bbe49","rewritten_text":"Biddy cried; the garden was growing darker, and the lane, and the stars beginning to show themselves, all swam before my eyes.

“Nothing ever found out, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what’s happened to Orlick?”

“I’d judge, from the look of his clothes, that he’s at work in the quarries.”

“Then you’ve seen him?—Why are you staring at that black tree down the lane?”

“I saw him there the night she died.”

“That wasn’t the last time either, Biddy?”

“No; I’ve seen him there since we’ve been walking here. —It’s no use,” said Biddy, laying her hand on my arm as I was ready to bolt out, “you know I wouldn’t deceive you; he wasn’t there a minute, and he’s gone.”

It set my anger at its height to learn she was still being followed by that man, and I felt a rooted dislike for him. I told her so, and said I’d spend any money and take any trouble to drive him out of that country. Little by little she brought me to calmer talk, and she told me how Joe loved me, and how Joe never complained of anything—she didn’t say, of me; she had no need to; I understood what she meant—always doing his duty in his own way of life, with a firm hand, a quiet tongue, and a kind heart.

“Indeed, you can’t say too much for him,” I answered; “and Biddy, we ought to speak of such things often, because I shall be coming down here frequently now. I’m not going to leave poor Joe by himself.”

Biddy didn’t say a word.

“Biddy, don’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Not to speak of your calling me Mr. Pip—which strikes me as poor manners, Biddy—what are you getting at?”

“What am I getting at?” Biddy asked, with a timid sort of air.

“Getting at?” I said, in a self-satisfied tone. “Now, don’t repeat me. You didn’t used to, Biddy.”

“Didn’t!” said Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Didn’t!”

Well! I thought I might as well surrender that point too. After one more silent turn in the garden, I took up my main argument again.

“Biddy,” said I, “I made a remark about my coming down here often to see Joe, and you met it with a marked silence. Do me the kindness, Biddy, and tell me why.”

“Are you quite sure, then, that you WILL come to see him often?” asked Biddy, stopping on the narrow path and looking at me beneath the stars with a clear, straightforward gaze."}

{"request_id":"440c16eeec50f381d457ddb5","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers let go of Lord Arthur’s right hand and took his left instead. He bent down so far to look at it that the gold rims of his spectacles almost touched the palm. For a moment his face looked like a blank white mask of fear, but then he quickly regained his sang-froid. Looking up at Lady Windermere, he said with a forced smile, “It is the hand of a charming young man.

“Of course it is,” Lady Windermere replied. “But will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know.”

“All charming young men are,” said Mr. Podgers.

“I don’t think a husband should be too fascinating,” Lady Jedburgh said thoughtfully. “It is so dangerous.”

“My dear child, they never are too fascinating,” Lady Windermere cried. “But what I want are details. Details are the only things that interest me. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?”

“Well, within the next few months Lord Arthur will go on a voyage—”

“Oh yes, his honeymoon, of course!”

“And lose a relative.”

“Not his sister, I hope?” Lady Jedburgh asked, sounding full of pity.

“Certainly not his sister,” Mr. Podgers answered, waving his hand as if to dismiss the idea. “A distant relative, only.”

“Well, I am terribly disappointed,” Lady Windermere said. “I have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives nowadays. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she had better have a black silk with her; it always works for church. And now let us go to supper. They are sure to have eaten everything, but we might find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but he is so upset about politics right now that I never feel completely sure about him. I do wish General Boulanger would keep quiet. Duchess, I’m sure you’re tired?”

“Not at all, dear Gladys,” the Duchess answered as she waddled toward the door. “I have enjoyed myself immensely, and the cheiropodist, I mean the cheiromantist, is most interesting. Flora, where can my tortoise-shell fan be? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, how kind. And at last she managed to get downstairs without dropping her scent-bottle more than twice.”

All this time Lord Arthur Savile had stayed standing by the fireplace, feeling the same dread and the same sickening sense that something evil was coming. He gave his sister a sad smile as she passed him on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking lovely in her pink brocade and pearls. He barely even heard Lady Windermere when she told him to follow her. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the idea that anything could come between them made his eyes fill with tears."}

{"request_id":"efa05b0f101105765dbd3d79","rewritten_text":"The two ladies were overjoyed to meet their dear friend again, and, after calling it quite a long while since they had last seen her, they kept asking what she had been doing with herself during their separation. The rest of the family interested them very little; they tried to avoid Mrs. Bennet as much as possible, said little to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. Before long they were off again, rising from their seats with a briskness that startled their brother, and hurrying away as though they were eager to get out of Mrs. Bennet’s civil attentions.

The Netherfield ball promised pleasure to every young woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to treat it as a compliment paid to her eldest daughter, and felt especially pleased to receive the invitation from Mr. Bingley himself, rather than from some formal card. Jane could already imagine a delightful evening with her two friends, along with the attentions of their brother; and Elizabeth, with real satisfaction, looked forward to dancing a great deal with Mr. Wickham, and to seeing in Mr. Darcy’s looks and conduct a further confirmation of everything she had observed. Catherine and Lydia’s expected happiness depended less on any one happening or any particular person; for though each of them, like Elizabeth, meant to spend half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was by no means the only partner who could please them, and, after all, a ball was a ball. Even Mary, she could assure her family, had no reluctance about it.

“While I may have my mornings to myself,” said she, “that is quite enough. I do not think it any great sacrifice to join now and then in evening engagements. Society has claims upon us all; and I am among those who believe intervals of rest and amusement are desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth’s spirits were so high that, though she did not often speak unnecessarily to Mr. Collins, she could not help asking whether he meant to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation, and, if he did, whether he would consider it proper to take part in the evening’s amusements. She was somewhat astonished to find that he had not the slightest hesitation on the matter, and was far from fearing any rebuke—whether from the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh—when he ventured to dance.

“I am by no means of opinion,” said he, “that a ball of this sort, given by a young man of character to respectable people, can have any evil tendency; and I am so far from objecting to dancing, that I shall hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins during the course of the evening. I take this opportunity, therefore, of requesting yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the first two dances especially; a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will understand to arise from the right motive, and not from any want of respect for her.”"}

{"request_id":"f9829ffe20dc1015e9824598","rewritten_text":"So the ring-master made a little speech. He said he hoped there wouldn’t be any disturbance, and that if the man promised he wouldn’t cause any more trouble, the ring-master would let him ride, as long as he thought he could stay on the horse. Everyone laughed and said, “All right,” and the man got on. The second he was on, the horse started ripping and tearing, jumping and running around, with two circus men gripping the bridle and trying to hold him. The drunk man hung onto his neck, his heels flying into the air with every jump. The whole crowd stood up, shouting and laughing until tears rolled down their faces. 

At last, sure enough, no matter what the circus men did, the horse broke free. Off he went, running around the ring like crazy, while the drunk man lay on him and clung to his neck. First one leg dangled closer to the ground on one side, and then the other leg on the other side. The people were wild with excitement. It wasn’t funny to me, though. I was shaking with fear for his safety. But pretty soon he struggled up into the saddle, grabbed the bridle, and wobbled this way and that. The next minute he sprang up, dropped the bridle, and stood there. The horse kept going just as fast, like it was on fire. He stood up there, moving around with the ease and comfort of someone who had never been drunk in his life. Then he started pulling off his clothes and throwing them aside. He shed them so quickly and so many that it seemed to clog the air, and in all he got rid of seventeen suits. 

Then he was slim and handsome, dressed in the gaudiest, prettiest outfit you could imagine. He took up his whip and went to work on that horse, making him perform so well that he finally skipped off. Then the man left the ring, made his bow, and danced off to the dressing room. Everyone was howling with pleasure and astonishment.

Then the ring-master realized he had been fooled, and he was the sickest ring-master you ever saw, I reckon. It turned out it was one of his own men. The joke had been planned by him, right from the start, and he never let on to anyone. I felt pretty foolish for falling for it, but I wouldn’t have wanted to be in that ring-master’s place, not for a thousand dollars. I don’t know—maybe there were bigger, better circuses than that one, but I haven’t found any yet. Anyway, it was good enough for me. And wherever I run across it, it can have all of my custom every time."}

{"request_id":"a4c76fb4b0e29c97664c4686","rewritten_text":"I walked along with a brisk step, and we soon reached my college. Then, as I reflected, the idea struck me with such force that I shivered: the creature I had left in my apartment might still be there—alive, moving about. I dreaded the thought of seeing this monster, yet I feared even more that Henry might catch sight of him. So I begged him to wait a few minutes at the foot of the stairs, and I hurried up to my own room. My hand was already on the door’s lock before I managed to check myself. I stopped; a cold trembling ran through me. I flung the door open with sudden violence, much as children do when they expect a spectre to be waiting on the other side, but nothing showed itself. I stepped in cautiously: the apartment was empty, and even my bedroom had been cleared of its hideous lodger. I could scarcely credit that such a great good fortune had fallen to me; yet once I was certain my enemy had truly gone, I clapped for joy and hurried down to Clerval.

We went up into my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast, but I could not steady myself. It was not mere happiness that seized me; I felt my skin prickle with an over-sensitiveness, and my pulse hammered quickly. I could not stay in one spot for a moment—I sprang over the chairs, clapped my hands, and burst into loud laughter. At first Clerval took my unusual spirits for nothing more than joy at my arrival; but when he watched me more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes he could not explain. My loud, unrestrained, heartless laughter both frightened and astonished him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what is it? Don’t laugh like that. You can’t be well—what is the reason for all this?”

“Don’t ask me,” I exclaimed, covering my eyes with my hands, for I thought I saw the dreaded spectre glide into the room. “He can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!” I believed the monster had seized me; I fought wildly and then fell into a fit.

Poor Clerval—what must his feelings have been? A meeting he had looked forward to with such delight had turned, so strangely, to bitterness. But I was not there to witness his grief, for I was lifeless, and I did not recover my senses for a long, long time.

This was the beginning of a nervous fever that kept me confined for several months. During all that time Henry was my only nurse. I later learned that, knowing my father’s advanced age and his inability to endure so long a journey, and considering how miserable my illness would make Elizabeth, he spared them this sorrow by hiding how severe my disorder really was."}

{"request_id":"e94808c8bfb80cdee2b4c882","rewritten_text":"What outcome, then, has followed? What sort of impression have I left on your mind?”

As Dupin put the question to me, I felt my skin crawl. “A madman,” I answered, “must have done it—some raving lunatic, escaped from a nearby _Maison de Santé._”

“In a few ways,” he returned, “your notion isn’t without weight. Still, the voices of the insane, even at their wildest moments, never match that particular voice heard on the stairs. Madmen belong to a nation; and though their speech may be incoherent in words, it always keeps the coherence of syllables. Besides, the hair of a madman is not the sort I’m holding in my hand right now. I’ve separated this small tuft from the rigidly clenched fingers of Madame L’Espanaye. Tell me what you make of it.”

“Dupin!” I said, thoroughly shaken. “This hair is extraordinary—there’s nothing _human_ about it.”

“I haven’t claimed that it is,” he said. “But before we settle the point, I want you to look at the little sketch I’ve traced here on this paper. It’s a _fac-simile_ of what, in one part of the testimony, is described as ‘dark bruises, and deep indentations of finger nails,’ upon the throat of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye, and, in another account (by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne), as a ‘series of livid spots, evidently the impression of fingers.’”

“You’ll see,” my friend went on, laying the sheet out on the table between us, “that the drawing conveys a firm, fixed hold. There’s no sign of any _slipping_. Each finger has kept—perhaps right up to the victim’s death—the dreadful grip with which it first sank in. Now try it: place all your fingers at once into the corresponding impressions you can see.”

I tried, but in vain.

“Perhaps we aren’t testing it properly,” he said. “The paper lies on a flat surface; yet the human throat is cylindrical. Here’s a piece of wood whose circumference is about the same as the throat. Wrap the drawing around it, then attempt the experiment again.”

I did so, but the trouble was even clearer than before. “This,” I said, “is no mark of a human hand.”

“Now read,” replied Dupin, “the passage from Cuvier.”

It was a brief but minute anatomical and descriptive account of the large fulvous Ourang-Outang of the East Indian islands. Everyone knows, in general, the creature’s enormous size, its prodigious strength and activity, its savage ferocity, and its imitative habits. I grasped at once the full horror of the murder.

“The description of the digits,” I said, finishing the reading, “matches this drawing exactly.”"}

{"request_id":"348b1b1160253a26eec9e8fe","rewritten_text":"I am not dining at home, so I won’t need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” the man said, and left the room.

“Now, Alan, don’t waste a moment. This chest is so heavy! I’ll carry it for you. You take the other things.” He spoke fast and in a commanding way. Campbell felt pushed and controlled by him. They left the room together.

When they reached the top landing, Dorian took out the key and put it in the lock. He turned it, then stopped. A worried look crossed his face. He shuddered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he whispered.

“It means nothing to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell said coldly.

Dorian opened the door halfway. As he did, he saw his portrait’s face staring out in the sunlight, sneering. On the floor in front of it, the torn curtain lay in pieces. He remembered that the night before he had forgotten—forgotten, for the first time in his life—to hide the deadly painting. He was about to rush forward, when he pulled back again, shaking.

What was that disgusting red liquid shining on one of the hands, wet and slick, as if the canvas had sweated blood? It was awful. For the moment, it felt even worse than the silent thing he knew was stretched across the table—the thing whose twisted, misshapen shadow on the spotted carpet told him it hadn’t moved. It was still there, exactly as he had left it.

He took a deep breath, opened the door a little wider, and walked in quickly with his eyes half-closed and his head turned away. He told himself he would not look at the dead man even once. Then, bending down, he grabbed the gold-and-purple cloth and threw it right over the picture.

He stopped there, afraid to turn around. His eyes stayed on the patterns in front of him. He heard Campbell bringing in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other things he needed for his terrible work. He started to wonder whether he and Basil Hallward had ever met, and, if they had, what they would have thought of each other.

“Leave me now,” a stern voice said behind him.

Dorian turned and hurried out. He could only think that the dead man had been pushed back into the chair, and that Campbell was staring at a shiny yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was long after seven when Campbell returned to the library. He looked pale, but completely calm. “I’ve done what you asked me to do,” he muttered."}

content.text: {"request_id":"57858955f6be185ec9fe2ee4","rewritten_text":"Morning had arrived, and I set the Manuscript aside. The rain had nearly stopped; everything lay gray and heavy, while the spent storm, worn out, kept sighing and sobbing as it tried to settle into rest. I went to the stranger’s room and stood listening at his door, which was left a little open. I could hear his voice, so I knocked. No one answered, yet the voice kept going. I leaned in and peeped. The man lay on his back in bed, speaking in broken bursts but with energy, and he kept punctuating his words with his arms, which he flung about restlessly, like sick men do when delirium takes them. I slipped in quietly and bent over him. His mutterings and outbursts continued. I said only a single word, just to draw his attention. In an instant his glassy eyes and ashen face brightened with pleasure, gratitude, joy, and welcome.\n\n“Oh, Sandy, you’ve come at last—how I’ve been longing for you! Sit by me—don’t go—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where is your hand?—give it here, my dear, let me hold it—there—now everything is right, all is peace, and I’m happy again—_we_ are happy again, aren’t we, Sandy? You look so dim, so shadowy; you’re only a mist, a cloud, yet you’re _here_, and that alone is blessedness. And I have your hand—don’t take it away; it’s only for a little while—I shan’t need it long.... Was that the child?... Hello-Central!... she doesn’t answer. Maybe she’s asleep? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and tell her good-bye.... Sandy! Yes, you’re there. I drifted for a moment, and I thought you were gone.... How long have I been ill? It must be—months, it feels like. And those dreams! Such strange, dreadful dreams, Sandy! Dreams that seemed as real as life—of course delirium, but _so_ real! I truly thought the king was dead; I thought you were in Gaul and couldn’t manage to get home; I thought there’d been a revolution. In the wild frenzy of it all, I believed Clarence and I, with a small crew of my cadets, fought and wiped out the whole chivalry of England! Yet that wasn’t even the strangest part. I felt like some creature from a far-off age not yet born—centuries ahead—and even that was as real as the rest. Yes, it seemed I’d flown back from that time into this one, and then forward again, and I was left here—alone, a stranger, and forlorn in that strange England—while an abyss of thirteen centuries yawned between me and you; between me and my home and my friends; between me and everything that’s dear to me, everything that could make life worth living.”"}
