{"request_id":"e78c2758ecdf910958e4e8a6","rewritten_text":"I would pretend to die; my satisfied heirs would take hold of my wealth, and I would buy my freedom. But then my plan had to be carried out with skill; I couldn’t be left with nothing. I had to make sure I had some money. Alas—what disgusting twists must I be driven to? Otherwise, I would have had a whole lifetime of falsehood as my lot. And when the guilt of being the one who devised any trick made me recoil from my scheme, I was irresistibly pulled back and confirmed in it by the visit of some aunt or cousin, who would tell me that death is the end of all men. Then they would add that my father had surely lost his mind since my mother’s death; that he was mad, and that I was fortunate, because in one of his fits he might have killed me instead of destroying his own broken self.

And all of this, of course, was delivered with care; not said in blunt terms, because my feelings might be hurt—but

Whispered so and so In dark hint soft and low

with eyes cast down, and sympathetic smiles or little whimpers; and I sat there with a calm face while every nerve trembled. I, who dared not say yes or no to any of this blasphemy. Oh, what a delicious life—so full of guilelessness! Me, with a dove’s look and a fox’s heart. For I felt only the humiliation of lying, not any sacred sense of innocence that could redeem it. I, who had dressed myself before in the bright clothing of sincerity, now had to borrow different colors. It might feel awkward at first, but practice would let me fold it into elegant shapes; I could lie with grace. Yes, I might die with my soul still wrapped in falsehood until I had completely hidden its true color.

Oh, beloved father! Accept the pure heart of your unhappy daughter; let me join you unspoiled as I was, or you won’t recognize my changed appearance. As grief might change Constance, so would deceit change me, until in heaven you would say, “This is not my child.” My father, to be happy both now and when we meet again, I must flee from all this life, which is mockery to someone like me. In solitude only shall I be myself; in solitude I shall be thine.

Alas! Even now I look back with disgust on the tricks and schemes by which, after many painful struggles, I managed to make my escape. I could go into a long account of the methods I used—first to secure myself a small support for the rest of my life, and afterward to ensure that people were convinced I was dead. I might, but I won’t."}

{"request_id":"c48cec22662ccee11e872fc2","rewritten_text":"She had left everything behind her—save only the memory that such things had ever existed.

Anne had not gone into Kellynch at all since she left Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need for it; and whenever it had been possible for her to visit the Hall, she had contrived to slip away from the chance and avoid it. Her first return was simply to take up again her place in the Lodge’s modern, elegant apartments, and to delight the mistress’s eyes.

Lady Russell’s joy in seeing her was tempered with some anxiety. She knew who had been coming to Uppercross. Yet, happily, either Anne had improved in fulness and appearance, or Lady Russell chose to believe she had; and when Anne received her compliments on the occasion, she found it amusing to connect them, in her own mind, with her cousin’s silent admiration, while hoping she might be granted a second season of youth and beauty.

As soon as they began to talk, Anne perceived a change in her thoughts. The matters that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch—those she had felt slighted in, and had been obliged to suppress among the Musgroves—had now fallen into the background. Lately she had even lost sight of her father and sister and Bath. Uppercross had swallowed up all those concerns; and when Lady Russell returned to their earlier hopes and fears, speaking of her satisfaction in the house in Camden Place, which had been taken, and of her regret that Mrs Clay was still with them, Anne would have been ashamed to have it known how much more she was thinking of Lyme and Louisa Musgrove, and of everyone she knew there. The home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick were far more engaging to her than her father’s house in Camden Place, or her sister’s closeness with Mrs Clay. In fact, she had to force herself to show something like equal care for Lady Russell on subjects that, by their very nature, ought first to claim her attention.

At the beginning there was a slight awkwardness in their conversation on another topic. They must speak of the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had not been there five minutes the day before, when a complete account of the whole affair had already been poured into her; still, it had to be discussed—she must ask questions, she must express regret for the imprudence, lament the outcome, and both must mention Captain Wentworth’s name. Anne felt she did not manage it as well as Lady Russell. She could not bring herself to say the name and then meet Lady Russell’s eye directly, until she had adopted the expedient of telling her, in a few words, what she thought of the attachment between him and Louisa."}

{"request_id":"b5791bfb86af5968f45ecf60","rewritten_text":"“Next, we built a wire fence.”

“Wire fence?”

“Yes. You suggested it yourself, two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember. The time the Church tried to fight us the first time, and then decided to wait for a better moment. So how did you set up the fence?”

“I start with twelve extremely strong wires—bare, not insulated—running from a big dynamo in the cave. The dynamo has no brushes except one positive and one negative.”

“Yes, that’s right.”

“The wires leave the cave and form a circle of level ground about a hundred yards across. They make twelve separate fences, ten feet apart—that is, twelve circles inside circles—and each wire end comes back into the cave.”

“Right. Keep going.”

“The fences are tied to heavy oak posts, spaced three feet apart, and each post is sunk five feet into the ground.”

“That’s good and strong.”

“Yes. Outside the cave, the wires have no ground connection. They go out from the positive brush of the dynamo. There is a ground connection only through the negative brush. The other ends of the wires return to the cave, and each one is grounded on its own.”

“No, no, that won’t do!”

“Why?”

“It’s too expensive. It wastes power for no reason. You don’t want any ground connection except the one through the negative brush. The other end of every wire has to be brought back into the cave and fastened separately, and without any ground connection. Now, look at the economy of it. A cavalry charge slams into the fence. You’re using no power and spending no money, because there’s only one ground connection until the horses hit the wire. The moment they touch it, they complete the circuit to the negative brush through the ground, and they drop dead. Don’t you see? You’re not using energy until it’s actually needed. Your lightning is there and ready, like the load in a gun, but it doesn’t cost you a cent until you fire it. Oh, yes—the single ground connection—”

“Of course! I don’t know how I missed that. It’s not only cheaper, but it works better than the other way. If wires break or tangle, no harm is done.”

“No, especially if we have a warning system in the cave and disconnect the broken wire. All right, then. The gatling guns?”

“Yes. That’s arranged too. In the center of the inner circle, on a platform six feet high, I’ve grouped thirteen gatling guns and stocked plenty of ammunition.”

“That’s it. They’ll cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, there’ll be music. The edge of the cliff above the cave—”

“I’ve got a wire fence there, and a gatling gun.”}"}

{"request_id":"5e3b4ba5484bac466ede5767","rewritten_text":"I don’t want to get mixed up in anything like that, I tell myself.

When I went downstairs in the morning, the parlor was shut up, and the watchers were gone. There wasn’t anyone around except the family, Widow Bartley, and our people. I watched their faces to see if anything had happened, but I couldn’t tell.

About the middle of the day, the undertaker came with his man. They set the coffin in the middle of the room on a couple of chairs, then lined up all our chairs in rows. They borrowed more chairs from the neighbors until the hall, the parlor, and the dining room were full. I could see the coffin lid was the same way it had been before, but I didn’t dare to look under it while people were there.

Then people started coming in. The men and the girls took seats in the front row at the head of the coffin. For about half an hour, everyone moved around slowly in a single line, looking down at the dead man’s face for a minute. Some people cried and dropped a tear. Everything was very still and solemn, except the girls and the men holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, keeping their heads bent, and sobbing a little. There wasn’t any sound except feet scraping on the floor and people blowing their noses. At a funeral, people blow their noses more than they do anywhere else, except church.

When the room was packed, the undertaker slid around in his black gloves, using his gentle, soothing way of doing things. He put the final touches on everything, made sure people and objects were arranged neatly, and made no more noise than a cat. He didn’t talk. He just moved people around, squeezed in the late arrivals, opened up paths for people to get through, and did it all with nods and hand signals. Then he stood by the wall. He was the softest, smoothest, stealthiest man I ever saw, and he didn’t have any more smile than a ham.

They had borrowed a melodeum, and it was a sick one. When everything was ready, a young woman sat down and played it. It sounded sharp and squeaky, like it was choking. Everyone joined in and sang. In my opinion, Peter was the only one who had a good thing going. Then Reverend Hobson came forward, slow and solemn, and started to speak. Right away, the most outrageous noise broke out in the cellar that I ever heard. It was only one dog, but it made a terrible racket, and it kept going the whole time. The parson had to stand there over the coffin and wait. You couldn’t hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"6d3b09a3aaf12da5bfdedd7a","rewritten_text":"I can’t describe the overwhelming joy with which I turned from political fights at home, and from the physical hardships of far-off countries, to my own dear home—the chosen place of goodness and love; to peace, and the exchange of every sacred sympathy. If I had never left Windsor, these feelings wouldn’t have been so intense; but in Greece I had been the victim of fear and terrible change. In Greece, after a stretch of anxiety and sorrow, I had watched two leave—whose very names were symbols of greatness and virtue. Yet none of those miseries could ever intrude on the domestic circle left to me, while, secluded in our beloved forest, we spent our lives in tranquillity.

Some small change, indeed, the passing years brought with it here; and time, as it always does, left the marks of mortality on our pleasures and expectations. Idris—the most affectionate wife, sister, and friend—was a tender, loving mother. Her feelings were not like those of many, a mere pastime; it was a passion. We had had three children; one, the second in age, died while I was in Greece. That loss crushed the triumphant, rapturous emotions of motherhood and replaced them with grief and fear. Before it happened, the little beings she had borne—the young heirs of her brief life—seemed to have a sure lease on existence; now she dreaded that the pitiless destroyer might snatch away her remaining darlings, just as it had taken their brother. The slightest illness brought on waves of terror. She was miserable if she was even briefly away from them. She had gathered her treasure of happiness in their fragile lives and kept it under constant watch, afraid that the insidious thief might steal those precious gems again, as before.

Fortunately, she had little reason to fear. Alfred, now nine years old, was an upright, manly little boy, with a radiant brow, soft eyes, and a gentle but independent temperament. Our youngest was still an infant; yet his downy cheek was sprinkled with the roses of health, and his tireless liveliness filled our halls with innocent laughter.

Clara had passed the age when, through her quiet ignorance, she was the source of Idris’s fears. Clara was dear to her, and to everyone. There was so much intelligence joined to innocence, sensibility joined to restraint, and seriousness joined to perfect good humor; a beauty so transcendent, paired with such endearing simplicity, that she seemed like a pearl set in the shrine of all our possessions—a treasure of wonder and excellence.

At the beginning of winter, our Alfred, now nine years old, first went to school at Eton. To him, it seemed like the first real step toward manhood, and he was accordingly pleased. Studying and playing together helped bring out the best in his character—his steady perseverance, his generosity, and his well-governed firmness."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b51e58add2f8aedbd3043290","rewritten_text":"“The stupor and surprise that filled my mind at this extraordinary shift in events was, perhaps after all, the part of the adventure least open to explanation. For the upheaval itself was not only natural and inevitable, but had long been anticipated as something to expect whenever I reached that exact point in my voyage where the planet’s pull would be replaced by the satellite’s pull—or, more precisely, where the balloon’s gravity toward the earth would be weaker than its gravity toward the moon. To be sure, I had woken from a deep sleep, with all my senses in confusion, to stare at a very startling phenomenon—one that, although I had expected it, I had not expected in that moment. The change itself must, of course, have happened gradually and without difficulty, and it is by no means clear that, even if I had been awake at the time, I would have noticed any sign of an inversion from anything internal—any inconvenience or disarrangement, either in my person or in my apparatus.\n\n“It is almost needless to say that, once I came to my senses and emerged from the terror that had seized every faculty of my soul, my attention was directed first of all to the general physical appearance of the moon. It lay beneath me like a chart—and although I judged it to be still at a considerable distance, the grooves of its surface were defined to my vision with a striking, altogether unaccountable clarity. The complete absence of ocean or sea, and indeed of any lake or river, or any body of water at all, struck me at first glance as the most extraordinary feature in its geological condition. Yet, strangely enough, I saw vast level regions of a clearly alluvial character, even though by far the greater portion of the hemisphere in view was covered with countless volcanic mountains—conical in shape, and looking more like artificial structures than natural protrusions. The highest of them does not exceed three and three-quarter miles in perpendicular height; but a map of the volcanic districts of the Campi Phlegraei would give your Excellencies a better idea of their overall surface than any poor description I might attempt. Most of these mountains were in a state of active eruption, and they made me understand, in the most frightening way, the force of their fury through the repeated thunder of the so-called meteoric stones—stones that now rushed upward by the balloon with increasing frequency, each surge more appalling than the last.”"}

{"request_id":"8059cc0da999bff030e29185","rewritten_text":"On this point, then, I shall be entirely silent; and you may be assured that no ungenerous reproach will ever leave my lips, once we are married.”

It was quite necessary to interrupt him at once.

“You are too quick, sir,” she exclaimed. “You forget that I have made no reply. Allow me to answer without any further delay. Accept my thanks for the compliment you have paid me. I feel the honour of your proposals very strongly, but I cannot do otherwise than decline them.”

“I am not to be taught now,” returned Mr. Collins, with a stiff gesture of the hand, “that it is customary for young ladies to refuse the addresses of the man whom they secretly intend to accept, when he first asks for their favour; and that sometimes the refusal is repeated a second time, or even a third. I am, therefore, by no means disheartened by what you have just said, and I shall hope to bring you to the altar before long.”

“Upon my word, sir,” cried Elizabeth, “your expectation is rather extraordinary after my declaration. I assure you I am not among those young ladies (if any such there be) who are bold enough to stake their happiness on the possibility of being asked again. I am perfectly in earnest in my refusal. You could not make me happy, and I am persuaded I am the very last woman in the world who would make you so. Indeed, were your friend Lady Catherine to know me, I believe she would find me, in every respect, ill fitted for the situation.”

“If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins, very gravely—“but I cannot suppose that her Ladyship would in the least disapprove of you. And you may be sure that when I have the honour of seeing her again, I shall speak of your modesty, economy, and other amiable qualities in the highest terms.”

“Indeed, Mr. Collins, praise of me is quite unnecessary. You must allow me to judge for myself, and grant me the compliment of believing what I say. I wish you to be very happy and very rich; and, by declining your hand, I do all I can to prevent your being otherwise. In offering me, you must have considered the delicacy of your feelings with regard to my family, and you may take possession of the Longbourn estate whenever it falls to you, without any self-reproach. This business may, therefore, be regarded as finally settled.”

And rising as she spoke, she would have left the room, had not Mr. Collins then addressed her—

“When I have the honour of speaking to you again on this subject, I shall hope to receive a more favourable answer than the one you have now given me; though I am far from charging you with cruelty at present, because I know it to be the established custom of your sex to reject a man on his first application, and perhaps you have even now said as much as would encourage my suit, in a way consistent with the true delicacy of the female character.”"}

{"request_id":"8fd5745c747050a928fd1dd7","rewritten_text":"He bowed and left. At the time, he did not see anyone in the street. It was a side street, very lonely.

“William Bird, a tailor, says he was one of the people who entered the house. He is an Englishman. He has lived in Paris for two years. He was among the first to go up the stairs. He heard voices arguing. The rough, gruff voice was that of a Frenchman. He could catch a few words, but he cannot remember them all now. He clearly heard ‘sacré’ and ‘mon Dieu.’ At the same moment, there was a sound like several people struggling—scraping and scuffling. The shrill voice was very loud, louder than the gruff one. He is sure it was not the voice of an Englishman. It seemed to be German. It might have been a woman’s voice. He does not understand German.

“Four of the witnesses named above were called back, and they said that when the group reached the chamber where the body of Mademoiselle L. was found, the door to that room was locked from the inside. Everything was completely silent—there were no groans or any other sounds. When they forced the door open, no one was seen. The windows in both the back and front rooms were down and firmly fastened from inside. The door between the two rooms was closed, but it was not locked. The door that led from the front room into the passage was locked, and the key was on the inside. A small room at the front of the house, on the fourth story, at the end of the passage, was open, with the door left slightly ajar. That room was crowded with old beds, boxes, and similar things. They removed these items carefully and searched them. There was not an inch of any part of the house that was not carefully searched. They sent sweepers up and down the chimneys. The house had four stories, with garrets (mansardes). A trapdoor on the roof was nailed down very securely and did not seem to have been opened for years. The time between hearing the voices arguing and breaking open the room door was described differently by the witnesses. Some said it was as short as three minutes; some said as long as five. The door was opened with difficulty.

“Alfonzo Garcio, an undertaker, says he lives in the Rue Morgue. He is from Spain. He was one of the people who entered the house. He did not go up the stairs. He was nervous and feared what might happen because of the agitation. He heard the voices arguing. The gruff voice was that of a Frenchman. He could not make out what was being said. The shrill voice was that of an Englishman, and he is sure of this.”"}

{"request_id":"78f7d42f9a62a2f53f3f233c","rewritten_text":"He also had to think about Sybil’s father and mother. They were very old-fashioned people, and they might object to the marriage if there were any hint of scandal. Still, he felt sure that if he told them the full facts of the case, they would be the first to understand the reasons that had pushed him to act. So he had every reason to choose poison. It was safe, reliable, and quiet. It also meant there would be no need for painful scenes, which, like most Englishmen, he strongly disliked.

He knew absolutely nothing about the science of poisons. Since the waiter seemed unable to find anything in the library except Ruff’s Guide and Bailey’s Magazine, he looked through the shelves himself. At last he found a well-bound copy of the Pharmacopoeia, and a copy of Erskine’s Toxicology, edited by Sir Mathew Reid, the President of the Royal College of Physicians. Reid was also one of the oldest members of the Buckingham, though he had been elected by mistake for someone else—a contretemps that enraged the committee so much that when the real man appeared, they black-balled him unanimously. Lord Arthur was confused by the technical terms in both books. He had even started to regret that he had not paid more attention to his classics at Oxford, when, in the second volume of Erskine, he found a clear and detailed account of the properties of aconitine. It seemed exactly like the poison he needed. It worked fast—almost immediately—was completely painless, and when taken in the form of a gelatine capsule, as Sir Mathew recommended, it was not unpleasant at all.

He then made a note, on his shirt-cuff, of the amount needed for a fatal dose. He put the books back where he found them and walked up St. James’s Street to Pestle and Humbey’s, the chemists. Mr. Pestle, who always dealt with the aristocracy in person, was surprised by the order. In a very deferential way, he hinted that a medical certificate was required. But the moment Lord Arthur explained that it was for a large Norwegian mastiff he needed to get rid of—because it showed signs of rabies and had already bitten the coachman twice in the calf of the leg—Mr. Pestle said he was completely satisfied. He praised Lord Arthur’s knowledge of Toxicology and had the prescription made up at once.

Lord Arthur put the capsule into a small, pretty silver bonbonnière he had seen in a shop window in Bond Street. He threw away Pestle and Hambey’s ugly pill-box and drove straight to Lady Clementina’s."}

{"request_id":"895c642bdbe78c9dc932fe53","rewritten_text":"At the sight of it, Jupiter’s joy could barely be held back, but his master’s face showed extreme disappointment. Still, he urged us to keep working, and the words were barely out of his mouth when I tripped and fell forward, catching my boot toe on a large iron ring half buried in the loose earth.

We now worked with real effort, and I never went ten minutes without feeling intense excitement. In that time we had managed to uncover an oblong wooden chest. Its perfect preservation and remarkable hardness showed that it had clearly been subjected to some mineralizing process—perhaps that of the bi-chloride of mercury. The box was three and a half feet long, three feet wide, and two and a half feet deep. It was held firmly in place by bands of wrought iron, riveted on, forming a kind of open trelliswork over the whole. On each side of the chest, near the top, were three iron rings—six in all—by which six people could get a solid grip. All our combined efforts only managed to shift the coffer slightly in its bed. We immediately saw that removing so heavy a thing was impossible. Luckily, the only fastenings on the lid were two sliding bolts. We pulled them back, trembling and panting with anxious urgency. In an instant, a treasure of incalculable value lay gleaming before us. As the lantern rays fell into the pit, a flash of light shot upward—glow and glare—from a confused heap of gold and jewels, so dazzling it made our eyes ache.

I won’t pretend to describe what I felt as I stared. Amazement, of course, dominated everything. Legrand looked worn out by excitement and said very little. For several minutes, Jupiter’s face wore a deadly pallor—about as deadly as any negro’s features can take on. He seemed stunned, struck as if by lightning. Then he dropped to his knees in the pit and, burying his bare arms up to the elbows in gold, left them there as though he were enjoying the luxury of a bath. At last, with a deep sigh, he exclaimed, as if speaking to himself:

“An dis all cum ob de goole-bug! de putty goole-bug! de poor little goole-bug, what I boosed in dat sabage kind ob style! Aint you shamed ob yourself, nigger?—answer me dat!”

Eventually, it became necessary for me to rouse both master and valet to the practical need of removing the treasure. It was getting late, and we had to push ourselves so we could get everything secured before daylight. It was hard to say what should be done, and a great deal of time was spent deliberating, because everyone’s thoughts were so tangled."}

{"request_id":"eab3ee2233955dd4aa895f87","rewritten_text":"In the meantime, the pull of gravity would keep waning without pause, falling off in proportion to the squares of the distances; and so, with an astonishingly increasing speed, I should finally reach those far-off regions where the earth’s attraction would give way to that of the moon. Following these thoughts, I saw no real advantage in loading myself with more supplies than would last for forty days.

“There remained, however, one further obstacle, which caused me some uneasiness. It has been remarked that, in balloon ascents to any considerable height, besides the pain that attends respiration, there is often a strong distress felt in the head and throughout the body—frequently with bleeding from the nose and other symptoms of a threatening sort—growing more troublesome the higher one goes. The reflection was of a somewhat startling character. Was it not likely that such symptoms would continue to intensify without limit, or at least only stop when death put an end to them? At last I could not believe it. Their source, I thought, lay in the gradual removal of the usual atmospheric pressure acting on the surface of the body, and the resulting distention of the superficial blood-vessels; it was not, as in the case of difficulty in breathing, a matter of any positive derangement of the animal system, where the chemical deficiency of atmospheric density prevents the proper renewal of blood in a ventricle of the heart. Unless that renewal failed, I could see no reason why life could not be maintained even in a vacuum; for the expansion and compression of the chest—what is commonly called breathing—is an operation purely muscular, and the cause, not the effect, of respiration. In short, I imagined that, as the body became accustomed to the absence of atmospheric pressure, the sensations of pain would lessen little by little; and while they lasted, I trusted in the iron hardiness of my constitution to carry me through.

“Thus, may it please your Excellencies, I have set down some of the considerations—though by no means all—which brought me to form the plan of a lunar voyage. I shall now go on to present the outcome of an attempt so wildly daring in its conception, and, in any case, so entirely without precedent in the records of mankind.

“After I had reached the altitude I mentioned—three miles and three-quarters—I threw out from the car a quantity of feathers, and I found that I still rose with enough speed; there was therefore no need to discharge any ballast. I was pleased by this, because I wanted to keep with me as much weight as I could manage, for reasons that I will explain later.”"}

{"request_id":"377a964bca4d0db6284be7da","rewritten_text":"She left everything behind her, except for the memory that such things had existed.

Anne had not gone into Kellynch since she left Lady Russell’s house in September. She did not need to, and whenever it was possible for her to go to the Hall, she managed to avoid it and get away. Her first return was simply to take up her place again in the modern, elegant rooms of the Lodge, and to please the eyes of its mistress.

There was some worry mixed with Lady Russell’s happiness when she met Anne. Lady Russell knew who had been visiting Uppercross. But, luckily, either Anne really looked fuller and healthier, or Lady Russell only imagined it; and when Anne accepted her compliments, she found it amusing to connect them with her cousin’s quiet admiration, and to hope that she might be given a second spring of youth and beauty.

As soon as they began to talk, Anne could tell that her mind had changed. The matters that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch—things she had felt slighted about, and had been forced to hold back among the Musgroves—now seemed less important. She had even lost sight, lately, of her father and sister and Bath. Those concerns had been pushed aside by everything happening in Uppercross. So when Lady Russell returned to their old hopes and fears, and spoke about her satisfaction that the house in Camden Place had been taken, and her regret that Mrs Clay was still living with them, Anne would have been embarrassed if anyone knew how much more she was thinking about Lyme and Louisa Musgrove, and everyone she knew there. She found the home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick far more interesting than her father’s house in Camden Place, or her sister’s closeness with Mrs Clay. She even had to force herself to show something like equal care for Lady Russell, and to talk with the right attention about topics that, by their nature, should have come first.

At first there was a little awkwardness in their conversation about another subject. They had to talk about the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had arrived only the day before, and within five minutes she had already heard the full story. Still, it had to be discussed; Anne had to ask questions; Lady Russell had to regret the imprudence, mourn the outcome, and both of them had to mention Captain Wentworth’s name. Anne felt she did not do it as well as Lady Russell. She could not say his name and look straight at Lady Russell’s eyes at the same time, until she used a simple solution: she told Lady Russell, briefly, what she thought about the attachment between him and Louisa."}

{"request_id":"f4759f08a271f1f56d663873","rewritten_text":"For years, Dorian Gray couldn’t shake off the influence of this book. Or maybe it would be more accurate to say that he never really tried to free himself from it. From Paris he had procured no fewer than nine large-paper copies of the first edition, each bound in a different color, so they could match his shifting moods and the changing whims of a nature over which, at times, he seemed to have almost completely lost control. The hero—the wonderful young Parisian in whom the romantic and the scientific temperaments were so strangely blended—became for him a kind of prefiguring image of himself. In fact, the whole book seemed to him to contain the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

In one respect, he was luckier than the novel’s fantastic hero. He never knew—never, indeed, had any reason to know—that grotesque dread of mirrors, of polished metal surfaces, and of still water that struck the young Parisian so early in his life, and that was brought on by the sudden decay of a beau who had once, apparently, been so remarkable. With an almost cruel joy—and perhaps in nearly every joy, and certainly in every pleasure, cruelty has its place—he used to read the later part of the book, with its truly tragic, though somewhat overemphasized, account of the sorrow and despair of someone who had lost, himself, what in others and in the world he had most dearly valued.

The wonderful beauty that had fascinated Basil Hallward, and many others besides him, never seemed to leave him. Even those who had heard the worst things about him—and from time to time strange rumors about his way of life slipped through London and became the talk of the clubs—couldn’t believe anything that would dishonor him when they saw him. He always had the look of someone who had kept himself untainted by the world. Men who spoke crudely would fall silent when Dorian Gray entered the room. There was something in the purity of his face that rebuked them. His very presence seemed to bring back to them the memory of the innocence they had tarnished. They wondered how someone so charming and graceful could have escaped the stain of an age that was at once sordid and sensual.

Often, when he returned home from one of those mysterious and prolonged absences that made his friends— or those who thought they were his friends—so full of strange conjecture, he would creep upstairs himself to the locked room. He would open the door with the key that never left him now, and stand there, with a mirror, in front of the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him—looking at the evil, aging face on the canvas, and then at the fair young face that laughed back at him from the polished glass."}

content.text: {"request_id":"269c588089192b002096ee05","rewritten_text":"We both agreed on Adrian with love, even though she—still not yet escaped from childhood—couldn’t fully appreciate, as I did, the extent of his merits, nor feel the same sympathy in his pursuits and opinions. I was forever with him. There was a sensibility and sweetness in his nature that gave our conversations a tender, almost otherworldly tone. Then he was as cheerful as a lark, singing from its sky-high tower—soaring in thought like an eagle, innocent as the mild-eyed dove. He could calm Perdita’s seriousness and take the sting from the torturing restlessness of my own nature. I looked back on my restless desires and painful struggles with my fellow beings as if they were only a troubled dream, and I felt myself as changed as though I had been transformed into another form—one with a fresh set of senses and a different mechanism of nerves, so that the apparent universe reflected differently in the mirror of my mind. But it wasn’t that way. I remained the same in strength, the same in my earnest craving for sympathy, the same in my yearning for active exertion. My manly virtues didn’t desert me; the witch Urania spared the locks of Sampson while he lay at her feet. Yet everything was softened and made more human. Nor did Adrian teach me only the cold truths of history and philosophy. At the same time that he taught me, through them, to restrain my own reckless and uncultured spirit, he opened my eyes to the living page of his own heart, and made me feel and understand its wondrous character.\n\nThe ex-queen of England had, even during her son’s infancy, tried to plant daring and ambitious designs in his mind. She saw that he had genius and extraordinary talent, and she cultivated those gifts so she could later use them to advance her own plans. She encouraged his hunger for knowledge and his impetuous courage; she even tolerated his untamed love of freedom, hoping—though it so often happens—that it would turn into a passion for command. She tried to raise him with resentment toward, and a desire to get revenge on, those who had been responsible for his father’s abdication. In this, she didn’t succeed. Still, the accounts she provided—however distorted—of a great and wise nation asserting its right to govern itself stirred his admiration. In his early days, he became a republican from principle. Yet his mother didn’t give up. To her love of rule and her proud sense of birth she added determined ambition, patience, and self-control. She devoted herself to studying her son’s disposition. Through praise, censure, and exhortation, she tried to strike the right chords; and though the melody that followed her touch seemed discordant to her, she held on to her hopes, trusting that, at last, she would win him."}

{"request_id":"360b75a18a94f96b5d2b55d9","rewritten_text":"Those old, infirm fellows were always seen by the public bowing, and it was commonly held that once they had bowed a customer out, they would keep on bowing in the empty office until another customer came in.

The barrister was sharp enough to see that the banker would not have gone so far in his judgment on anything less secure than moral certainty. Though he was not ready for the big draught he had to swallow, he managed to get it down. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, wagging his forensic forefinger toward the Temple at large, when it was swallowed, “my way out of this is to put you all in the wrong.”

It was a touch of the Old Bailey tactician’s craft, and it gave him real relief. “You shall not put me in the wrong, young lady,” said Mr. Stryver; “I’ll do that for you.”

So, when Mr. Lorry came that night as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver—amid a heap of books and papers scattered for the purpose—seemed to have nothing on his mind at all like the business of the morning. He even looked surprised to see Mr. Lorry, and was plainly absent and preoccupied.

“Well!” said the kindly messenger, after a full half-hour of fruitless efforts to bring him back to the subject. “I’ve been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” repeated Mr. Stryver, with a chill. “Oh, to be sure! What should I be thinking of!”

“And I have no doubt,” said Mr. Lorry, “that I was right in the conversation we had. My opinion is confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” returned Mr. Stryver, in the friendliest tone, “that I’m sorry for it on your account, and sorry for it on the poor father’s account. I know this must always be a painful matter for the family; let us say no more about it.”

“I don’t understand you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I dare say not,” rejoined Stryver, nodding in a smoothing, final fashion; “never mind, never mind.”

“But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry pressed.

“No, it doesn’t; I assure you it doesn’t. Having supposed there was sense where there is no sense, and a proper ambition where there is no proper ambition, I’m well out of my mistake, and no harm is done. Young women have fallen into like follies often enough before, and have repented of them in poverty and obscurity often enough before. In one light, I’m sorry the matter is dropped, because it would have been a bad thing for me in a worldly point of view; in another, I’m glad it’s dropped, because it would have been a bad thing for me in a worldly point of view—though it hardly needs saying that I could have gained nothing by it.”}"}

{"request_id":"804c0670b4a89174b35fe682","rewritten_text":"But enough of this. I will begin my tale: it is my last task, and I hope I have the strength to carry it through. I record no crimes. My faults can easily be pardoned; they did not come from evil intent, but from a lack of judgment. And I believe few would deny that, with different conduct and greater wisdom, I could have avoided the misfortunes that have made me their victim. My fate has been ruled by necessity—hideous necessity. It demanded hands stronger than mine; stronger, I believe, than any human power, to break the thick, adamantine chain that has bound me. Once I breathed nothing but joy, always warmed by love and delight in goodness—now I am brought only to misery, and it is now about to end, in death. But I lose myself; my tale is still untold. I will pause for a few moments, wipe my dim eyes, and try to let the present, obscure but heavy feeling of unhappiness fade into the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank. He had lost his father early and was raised by a weak mother, with all the indulgence she believed due to a nobleman of wealth. He was sent to Eton and afterward to college, and from childhood he was allowed the free use of large sums of money; so, from his earliest youth, he enjoyed the independence that a boy with these advantages always comes to acquire at a public school.

Under these circumstances his passions found deep ground where they could take root and flourish, either as flowers or weeds, depending on what they were. Because he was always permitted to act for himself, his character became strongly and early marked, showing a varied surface on which a quick observer might see the seeds of virtues and of misfortunes. His careless extravagance—making him squander immense sums of money to satisfy passing whims, which, because of their apparent energy, he dignified with the name of passions—often showed itself in boundless generosity. Yet while he earnestly concerned himself with the needs of others, his own desires were gratified to the fullest extent. He gave his money, but none of his own wishes were sacrificed to his gifts; he gave his time, which he did not value, and his affections, which he was happy to have called into action.

I do not claim that, if his own desires had been set against those of others, he would have shown undue selfishness—but that test was never made. He was raised in prosperity and surrounded by all its advantages; everyone loved him and wanted to please him."}

{"request_id":"74e55a2d51be67aa1347b7da","rewritten_text":"After supper, the whole crew spilled out to the bar to look for turtle eggs. They wandered around with sticks, prodding the sand, and whenever they struck a yielding spot they dropped to their knees and dug with their bare hands. At times they hauled fifty or sixty eggs from a single hole. The eggs were perfectly round, white as anything, just a bit smaller than an English walnut. That night they had a celebrated fried-egg feast, and again on Friday morning.

After breakfast they went out yelling and prancing across the bar, circling each other and shedding their clothes as they went, until they were completely naked; then the play carried them farther up the shoal water of the bar, right against the stiff current, which kept knocking their legs out from under them now and then and made it all the more hilarious. Now and then they would huddle together and splash water in each other’s faces with their palms, edging closer with their faces turned aside to dodge the choking sprays, until it came to grabbing and wrestling—until the best man ducked his neighbor—and then they all went under in a tangle of white legs and arms. When they came up, they were blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping for breath all at once.

Once they were properly worn out, they ran back and sprawled on the dry, hot sand, then lay there and covered themselves with it. After a while they broke for the water again and went through the same business over. At last it struck them that their bare skin looked remarkably like flesh-colored “tights,” so they drew a ring in the sand and put on a circus, with three clowns in it—since none of them would give up that proud spot to his neighbor.

Then they took up their marbles and played “knucks,” “ringtaw,” and “keeps” until that game lost its charm. Joe and Huck went for another swim, but Tom wouldn’t, because when he kicked off his trousers he’d also kicked loose his string of rattlesnake rattles off his ankle; he kept wondering how he’d managed to avoid cramps so long without the protection of that mysterious charm. He didn’t try again until he’d found the rattles, and by then the other boys were worn out and ready to rest. They drifted off one by one, dropped into the “dumps,” and stared longingly across the broad river toward the village, lying drowsy in the sun. Tom caught himself writing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe; he scratched it out and felt annoyed at his own weakness. Still, he wrote it again—he couldn’t help it. He erased it once more, and then tried to break the temptation by herding the other boys together and joining them."}

content.text: {"request_id":"860bcf5131c0e9b613a4f2ee","rewritten_text":"“April 19th. This morning, to my great delight, about nine o’clock, the moon’s surface being frightfully close, and my fears stirred to the highest pitch, the pump of my condenser at last showed unmistakable signs that the atmosphere had altered. By ten, I had good reason to think its density had risen considerably. By eleven, scarcely any work was needed at the apparatus; and at twelve o’clock, with some hesitation, I went so far as to unscrew the tourniquet. Finding no harm in having done so, I at length threw open the gum-elastic chamber and unfastened it from around the car. As might be expected, spasms and a violent headache followed at once from so sudden and hazardous an experiment. Yet, since these and the other troubles of breathing were by no means so severe as to put my life in jeopardy, I resolved to bear them as best I could, considering that I should leave them behind me moment by moment as I neared the denser layers close to the moon. Still, the descent itself remained extraordinarily headlong; and it soon became painfully clear that, though I had probably not been mistaken in expecting an atmosphere whose density would rise in proportion to the satellite’s mass, I had erred in supposing that this density—even at the surface—was sufficient to carry the great weight lodged in the car of my balloon. That it ought to have been so, and in the same degree as on the earth, the actual gravity of bodies at either planet ought to correspond to the ratio of atmospheric condensation. But that it was not so, my sudden fall proved beyond doubt; why it was otherwise, I can only account for by those possible geological disturbances I mentioned earlier. In any case, I was now close to the planet and dropping with the most dreadful force. I therefore lost no time in throwing overboard, first my ballast, then my water-kegs, then my condensing apparatus and gum-elastic chamber, and at last every item inside the car. It availed me nothing, however; I continued to fall with dreadful speed, and was now less than half a mile from the surface. As a final expedient, having disposed of my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car loose from the balloon itself—its weight was no small matter—and, gripping the net-work with both hands, I had barely time to notice that the whole country, as far as the eye could reach, was dotted thickly with tiny dwellings, before I tumbled headlong into the very heart of a city of the strangest appearance, and straight into the midst of a vast crowd of ugly little people. Not one of them spoke a single syllable, nor did any of them trouble themselves to offer me the least help; they simply stood, like a bundle of idiots, grinning in a ridiculous fashion, and staring at me and my balloon askance, with their arms planted akimbo.”"}

{"request_id":"7bf3732a4570bbc1631917cd","rewritten_text":"Then I went over in my own mind that beautiful passage about Dante’s coming into the earthly Paradise, and I fancied it would be sweet if, when I strayed along those fair banks, I might watch the car of light descend—bringing my long-lost parent back to me. While I waited there, full of expectation for that instant, I thought of how, from the lovely flowers that grew in that place, I would braid myself a chaplet and crown my brow with joy. I would sing “sul margine d’un rio,” my father’s own favourite song; and my voice, gliding through the air that held no wind, would tell him—wherever he sat in some bower, still waiting for the moment of our meeting—that his daughter had arrived. Then the mark of misery would have faded from my face, and I would lift my eyes without fear to meet his, which would always shine with the gentle radiance of innocent love. When I considered the spell of those deep eyes, I wept, but softly, so that my sobs might not disturb the fairy scene.

So wholly taken up in that reverie, I wandered on without paying attention to where my feet were taking me, until I actually bent down to pick a flower for my wreath on that bleak plain where no flower grew. Then I woke from my daydream and found that I did not know where I was.

The sun had already set, and the rose-coloured tint that the clouds had caught from it as it sank was nearly gone. A wind swept over the plain; I looked about and saw nothing that could tell me my situation. I had lost my way, and all my efforts to recover my path were useless. I kept walking, and as darkness gathered it blurred every trace by which I might have been guided. At last everything was swallowed in the deep obscurity of the blackest night. I grew weary, and remembered that my servant was to sleep that night in the neighbouring village, so that my absence would not raise any alarm; and, believing myself safe in this wild place from any intruder, I resolved to pass the night where I lay. In truth, I was too tired to go farther. The air was cold, yet I scarcely cared for bodily discomfort, thinking myself well used to the weather through my two years of solitude, when no change of seasons ever checked my wandering.

I stretched myself on the grass, surrounded by darkness so complete that not the faintest beam of light could enter. There was no sound, for the deep night had lulled the insects to rest, and the only living things in that lonely spot were those that could find no shelter in tree or shrub. There was a wondrous silence in the air: it soothed my senses, yet at the same time quickened my soul. My thoughts darted from picture to picture, and seemed to seize upon an eternity."}

{"request_id":"6fe573f09b2f6b2dfe092dfa","rewritten_text":"The congratulatory letter Elizabeth received from Lydia, on the occasion of her marriage, made it plain to her that, at least by Lydia’s own wife, if not by Lydia himself, such a hope was being cherished. The note ran to this effect:--

“My dear Lizzy,

I wish you joy. If you love Mr. Darcy half as well as I love my dear Wickham, you must be exceedingly happy. It is a great comfort to have you so well off; and when you have nothing else to occupy you, I hope you will remember us. I am sure Wickham would be very glad of a place at court; and I do not think we shall manage to live without some help, even with what we have. Any situation of about three or four hundred a year would do; but, whatever you do, do not mention it to Mr. Darcy, if you would rather not.

Yours,” etc.

As it turned out, Elizabeth would far rather not, and in her reply she tried to put an end to every entreaty and expectation of that sort. Still, whatever relief she could manage—by what might be called economy in her own private expenses—she often contrived to send. It had always been clear to her that an income like theirs, under the direction of two people so extravagant in their wants and so careless of what lay ahead, must be far from enough for their support; and whenever they shifted their quarters, either Jane or herself were sure to be asked for some small assistance toward paying their bills. Their way of living, even after the restoration of peace sent them back to a home, remained in the most unsettled state. They were forever changing places in search of a cheap situation, and just as constantly spending more than they ought. His affection for her soon cooled into indifference: hers endured a little longer; and, despite her youth and her manners, she kept all the claims to reputation which her marriage had brought her. Though Darcy could never admit _him_ at Pemberley, yet, for Elizabeth’s sake, he continued to help him in his profession. Lydia was sometimes a visitor there, when her husband had gone to enjoy himself in London or Bath; and with the Bingleys they both stayed so long at a time, that even Bingley’s good humour was worn down, and he went so far as to _talk_ of giving them a hint to be gone.

Miss Bingley was very much mortified by Darcy’s marriage; but as she judged it best to keep the privilege of visiting at Pemberley, she let her resentment drop. She became fonder than ever of Georgiana, almost as attentive to Darcy as before, and paid off every arrear of civility to Elizabeth."}

{"request_id":"78bf0da5d6c4e0bd0465f9bf","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton halted in the street, undecided as to where he ought to go. “At Tellson’s banking-house at nine,” he said, wearing a thoughtful look. “Shall I show myself in the meantime? I think I should. It’s important that these people should understand there’s a man like me about; it’s a prudent precaution, and might well be a necessary step. But—steady, steady, steady! I must work it out.”

Feeling his feet, which had begun to drift toward some purpose, he turned once or twice in the already deepening dark and followed the idea in his mind through to what it might lead to. His first notion held true. “It is best,” he said at last, having settled it, “that these people should know there is such a man as I here.” With that, he turned his face toward Saint Antoine.

That day Defarge had spoken of himself as the keeper of a wine-shop in the Saint Antoine quarter. For anyone who knew the city, it was no great matter to locate his place without asking questions. Once he had made sure of where it stood, Carton slipped back out of the nearer streets again, dined at a place of refreshment, and after dinner fell into a sound sleep. For the first time in many years, he took no strong drink. Since last night he had had nothing but a little light, thin wine; and last night he had let the brandy go down on Mr. Lorry’s hearth, slowly, as though he were done with it.

He did not wake until nearly seven o’clock, feeling refreshed, and went out once more into the streets. As he made his way toward Saint Antoine, he paused at a shop-window with a mirror in it, and slightly rearranged the untidy set of his loose cravat, his coat-collar, and his wild hair. When that was done, he went straight to Defarge’s and went in.

There happened to be no customer in the shop, only Jacques Three, with his restless fingers and his croaking voice. Carton had seen this man upon the Jury; now he stood at the little counter, drinking, in talk with the Defarges—husband and wife. The Vengeance took part in the conversation as if it were a regular fixture of the place.

When Carton entered, took his seat, and asked (in very indifferent French) for a small measure of wine, Madame Defarge gave him a careless glance at first, and then a sharper one, and then another still sharper, before coming up to him and asking what he had ordered.

He repeated what he had already said.

“English?” asked Madame Defarge, inquisitively lifting her dark eyebrows.

After studying her for a moment, as though even a single French word were slow to find its way into his mind, he answered in the same strong foreign accent as before."}

{"request_id":"62eaafbe8385f0208e8b5f42","rewritten_text":"Ten minutes later, with his face drained of color from terror and his eyes full of grief, Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House. He pushed through the crowd of fur-coated footmen gathered around the large striped awning, as if he did not see or hear anything. The night was bitterly cold. Gas lamps around the square flared and flickered in the sharp wind, but his hands were burning hot with fever, and his forehead felt like it was on fire. He kept going and going, almost staggering along like a drunk. A policeman watched him as he passed. A beggar, who had been slouching from an archway to ask for alms, became afraid when he saw a misery even worse than his own.

Once, he stopped under a lamp and stared at his hands. He thought he could already see the stain of blood on them, and a faint cry escaped his trembling lips.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had seen in his hand. Murder! The night itself seemed to know it, and the empty wind sounded the word in his ear. The dark corners of the streets were filled with it. It seemed to grin at him from the roofs of the houses.

First, he came to the Park, where the gloomy trees and woodland held him as if by force. He leaned wearily against the railings, pressing his brow to the wet metal to cool it, and listened to the shaky silence of the trees. “Murder! murder!” he kept repeating, as though saying it again and again could lessen the horror of the word. Hearing his own voice made him shudder, but he almost hoped that Echo might hear him and wake the sleeping city from its dreams. He felt a wild urge to stop any casual passer-by and tell them everything.

Then he wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, shameful alleys. Two women with painted faces mocked him as he went by. From a dark courtyard came the sound of curses and blows, followed by sharp screams. Huddled on a damp doorstep, he saw bent, broken figures of poverty and age. A strange pity came over him. Were these children of sin and misery already meant for their end, just as he was meant for his? Were they, like him, only puppets in some monstrous show?

Still, it was not the mystery that struck him, but the comedy of suffering—its total uselessness, its grotesque lack of meaning. Everything felt wrong and out of place. Nothing seemed to fit together. He was shocked by the mismatch between the cheerful optimism of the day and the real facts of life. He was still very young.

After a while, he found himself standing in front of Marylebone Church. The road was silent and stretched out like a long ribbon of polished silver, broken here and there by dark shapes of moving shadows."}

{"request_id":"ca173427d6d560ab37c55d5a","rewritten_text":"On that point, then, I shall be completely silent; and you can be sure that no ungenerous reproach will ever leave my lips once we are married.”

It was absolutely necessary to interrupt him now.

“You’re moving too fast, sir,” she cried. “You forget that I haven’t answered yet. Let me do it without wasting any more time. Accept my thanks for the compliment you’re paying me. I’m fully aware of the honor of your proposals, but I cannot do anything other than decline them.”

“I’m not supposed to be learning,” replied Mr. Collins, with a formal wave of the hand, “that it’s customary for young ladies to refuse the man they secretly intend to accept, when he first asks for their favor; and that sometimes the refusal is repeated a second time, or even a third. So what you’ve just said doesn’t discourage me at all, and I shall hope to lead you to the altar before long.”

“Upon my word, sir,” cried Elizabeth, “your hope is rather extraordinary after my declaration. I assure you I’m not one of those young ladies—if any such young ladies exist—who are bold enough to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second time. I mean my refusal entirely. You could not make me happy, and I’m convinced I’m the last woman in the world who would make you happy. And if your friend Lady Catherine were to know me, I’m persuaded she would find me, in every respect, ill qualified for the position.”

“If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins, very gravely—“but I can’t imagine that her Ladyship would disapprove of you at all. And you may be certain that when I have the honor of seeing her again, I shall speak in the highest terms of your modesty, economy, and other amiable qualities.”

“Indeed, Mr. Collins, praise of me will be unnecessary. You must allow me to judge for myself, and do me the compliment of believing what I say. I wish you every happiness and every bit of wealth; and by refusing your hand, I will do everything I can to prevent you from being otherwise. In making me the offer, you must have been satisfied that your feelings were guided by proper consideration for my family, and you may take possession of the Longbourn estate whenever it falls to you, without any self-reproach. This matter, then, may be considered finally settled.” And as she spoke, she would have left the room, had not Mr. Collins addressed her—

“When I have the honor of speaking to you again on this subject, I shall hope to receive a more favorable answer than the one you’ve given me now; though I’m far from accusing you of cruelty at present, because I know it to be the established custom of your sex to reject a man on his first application. And perhaps you have even now said as much to encourage my suit as would be consistent with the true delicacy of the female character.”"}

{"request_id":"db9346908093ddd8e4056615","rewritten_text":"“Oh, that’s nothing at all! It’s a pleasure for me. I don’t work for money; I live entirely for my art.”

Lord Arthur set £4, 2s. 6d. on the table, thanked the little German for his kindness, and, having managed to decline an invitation to meet some Anarchists at a meat-tea the following Saturday, left the house and headed for the Park.

For the next two days he was in a state of intense excitement, and on Friday at twelve o’clock he drove down to the Buckingham to wait for news. All afternoon the stolid hall-porter kept posting up telegrams from different parts of the country, listing the results of horse races, the verdicts in divorce cases, the state of the weather, and similar items, while the tape ticked out tedious details about an all-night sitting in the House of Commons and a small panic on the Stock Exchange. At four o’clock the evening papers arrived, and Lord Arthur disappeared into the library with the _Pall Mall_, the _St. James’s_, the _Globe_, and the _Echo_, to the immense outrage of Colonel Goodchild, who wanted to read the reports of a speech he had delivered that morning at the Mansion House—about South African Missions, and the advisability of having black bishops in every province—and for some reason or other had a strong prejudice against the _Evening News_. None of the papers, however, mentioned even the slightest thing about Chichester, and Lord Arthur felt the attempt must have failed. It was a terrible blow to him, and for a time he was completely thrown.

Herr Winckelkopf, whom he went to see the next day, was full of elaborate apologies and offered to provide him with another clock free of charge, or with a case of nitro-glycerine bombs at cost price. But he had lost all faith in explosives, and Herr Winckelkopf himself admitted that everything is so adulterated these days that even dynamite can hardly be obtained in a pure form. The little German, though, while conceding that something must have gone wrong with the machinery, still had hope that the clock might yet go off. He pointed to the case of a barometer he had once sent to the military governor at Odessa: although it was set to explode in ten days, it hadn’t gone off for something like three months. It was true that when it finally did, it only succeeded in blowing a housemaid to atoms, since the governor had left town six weeks earlier—but at least it showed that dynamite, as a destructive force, could be a powerful agent when controlled by machinery, even if it was a somewhat unreliable one."}

{"request_id":"4a53efdec21677a5e81254d2","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I said, “what’s wrong now? How is your master?”

“To tell the truth, massa, he ain’t doing so well as he ought to.”

“Not well! I’m truly sorry to hear that. What is he complaining about?”

“Dar! That’s it—he never complains about anything. But he’s been very sick, for all that.”

“Very sick, Jupiter. Why didn’t you say so right away? Is he stuck in bed?”

“No, he ain’t! He ain’t in bed anywhere. That’s just where the trouble is. My mind won’t stop worrying about poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I’d like to understand what you mean. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what’s wrong?”

“Why, massa, it ain’t worth getting mad about it. Massa Will won’t say anything at all. But then why is he going around this way, with his head down, and acting like he’s fighting himself? And he’s as white as a goose. Then he keeps a siphon going all the time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“A siphon, massa, with the numbers on the slate. The strangest numbers I ever saw. I’m getting scared, I tell you. I’ve had to keep a very close eye on him. The day before yesterday he slipped out before sunrise and was gone the whole blessed day. I had a big stick ready to give him a proper beating, but I’m such a fool that I couldn’t bring myself to do it. He looked so very sick.”

“Eh? What? Yes—on the whole, I think you’d better not be too hard on him. Don’t flog him, Jupiter. He can’t really handle it. But can you think of what caused this illness, or this change in his behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, massa, nothing unpleasant has happened since then. I’m afraid it was before then—on the very day you were there.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“I mean the bug. I’m sure Massa Will got bitten somewhere on his head by that goole-bug.”

“And what makes you think that, Jupiter?”

“Claws enough, massa, and mouth enough. I never saw a sick bug before. He kicked and he bit anything that came near him. Massa Will tried to catch him, but he had to let him go again very quickly, I tell you—because that was the time he must have gotten the bite. I didn’t like the look of the bug’s mouth at all, so I wouldn’t grab him with my finger. But I caught him with a piece of paper I found.”"}

{"request_id":"4afaeae7d60c3134d9128479","rewritten_text":"There was something striking about the way Mr. Wopsle’s eyes kept getting brighter, and it looked as if he was turning things over in his mind. He also seemed more and more confused, and I couldn’t tell what he meant. I kept thinking about it long after he had gone up into the clouds in a large watch-case, and even then I still couldn’t make it out. I was still thinking about it when I came out of the theatre an hour later, and I found him waiting for me near the door.

“How do you do?” I said, shaking his hand as we walked down the street together. “I saw that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he answered. “Yes, of course I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It’s the strangest thing,” Mr. Wopsle said, slipping back into that faraway look. “And yet I could swear it was him.”

I became worried and asked Mr. Wopsle to explain what he meant.

“Maybe I wouldn’t have noticed him at first if you hadn’t been there,” he went on, still speaking in that same lost way. “I can’t be sure, but I think I would have.”

Without meaning to, I looked around me the way I always did when I was on my way home. Those strange words made me feel uneasy.

“Oh! He can’t be in sight,” Mr. Wopsle said. “He left before I went up. I saw him go.”

Because I had reason to be suspicious, I even began to suspect the poor actor. I thought he might be trying to trick me into admitting something. So as we walked on, I kept glancing at him, but I said nothing.

“I had a foolish idea that he must be with you, Mr. Pip,” Mr. Wopsle said. “Until I saw that you didn’t seem to know he was there. He was sitting behind you like a ghost.”

That same uneasy feeling came back to me, but I decided not to speak yet. It was possible, after all, that he was trying to get me to connect what he was saying with Provis. Still, I was certain and safe that Provis had not been there.

“I suppose you’re wondering about me, Mr. Pip,” he said. “Yes, I can see you are. But it’s so strange. You’ll hardly believe what I’m about to tell you. I could hardly believe it myself if you told me.”

“Indeed?” I said.

“No, indeed. Mr. Pip, you remember, when you were a child, a certain Christmas Day long ago. I dined at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to get a pair of handcuffs mended?”

“I remember it very well.”

“And you remember there was a chase after two convicts, and that we joined in it. Gargery carried you on his back, and I took the lead, and you kept up with me as best you could?”"}

{"request_id":"7468bf67c4f43cee7072bae6","rewritten_text":"His account was that, while traveling from his home and passing through Datchet, he was startled to see smoke coming from the inn’s chimney. Thinking he might find fellow travelers for his journey gathered there, he knocked and was let in. There was no one in the house except Lucy and her mother. Her mother had been left unable to use her limbs by an attack of rheumatism, and so, one by one, all the remaining inhabitants of the country had set out, leaving them alone. Lucy urged the man to stay with her. In a week or two her mother would be better, and then they could set out; but they would surely die if they were left helpless and abandoned like this.

The man said that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, and that, in his view, it was impossible for him to remain. As a last resort, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, to be delivered to her wherever he might meet us. At least he carried out that errand, and Idris received, with emotion, the following letter:—

“HONOURED LADY,

“I am sure you will remember me and pity me, and I dare to hope that you will help me. What other hope do I have? Please forgive the way I write—I am so overwhelmed. A month ago my dear mother was deprived of the use of her limbs. She is already better, and in another month I am sure I will be able to travel, in the way you were so kind as to say you would arrange for us. But now everyone has gone—everyone. As they left, each one said that perhaps my mother would be better before we were completely deserted.

“Three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who, because of his newborn child, stayed as long as he could. And since they have a large family, I thought I could persuade them to wait a little longer for us; but I found the house deserted. I have not seen a soul since this good man came. What will become of us? My mother does not know our situation; she is so ill that I have hidden it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? I am sure we must perish miserably as we are. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road. And if, when she gets better, I were able to do it, I cannot even guess how I would find the roads and make so many miles to the sea. You would all be in France by then, and the great ocean would be between us—which is so terrifying even for sailors.”"}

{"request_id":"f2b76109553356095bfc6abb","rewritten_text":"It looked like a jumble of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, giving the whole place the air of a rather sleepy retirement. Wemmick’s home was a modest wooden cottage set among little plots of garden, and the top of it had been cut away and painted to resemble a battery, complete with guns.

“My own handiwork,” said Wemmick. “Pretty, isn’t it?”

I praised it, I suppose, because it was the tiniest house I’d ever seen; it had those odd gothic windows—most of them sham, no doubt—and a gothic door so narrow it was almost too small to get through.

“That’s a proper flagstaff,” Wemmick went on, “and on Sundays I hoist a real flag. Then, after I’ve crossed this bridge, I raise it—like that—and cut off the connection.”

The bridge was just a plank spanning a gap about four feet across and two deep. Still, it was pleasant to watch the satisfaction with which he lifted it and secured it; he smiled while doing it, with genuine relish rather than doing it by mere habit.

“At nine o’clock every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun fires. There you see him! And when you hear it go, I think you’ll say it’s a Stinger.”

The ordnance he meant was set up in a separate little fortress made of lattice-work. A clever contrivance—something like an umbrella—kept it sheltered from the weather.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of sight, so it doesn’t spoil the notion of fortifications—for it’s a rule with me: if you’ve got an idea, carry it out and keep it going—though I don’t know if that’s your view—”

“I’m of that opinion,” I said.

“—At the back there’s a pig, and there are fowls and rabbits; then I knock together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers; and you’ll judge at supper what kind of salad I can manage. So, sir,” he added, still smiling, though now with a seriousness that matched his shaking of the head, “if you imagine the small place besieged, it would hold out a devil of a time for provisions.”

After that, he led me to a bower some dozen yards away, though you had to reach it by such clever twists of path that it took quite a while to get there; and in that retreat our glasses were already laid out. Our punch was cooling in an ornamental pool, and the bower rose from its edge. The water was circular—there was even an island in the middle, which might have served as the salad for supper—and he had built a fountain in it that, once you started a little mill and pulled a cork from a pipe, would play with such force that it made the back of your hand quite wet."}

{"request_id":"02c78a017450ceb5bde9c2c2","rewritten_text":"Gazing at him, one might have thought that Nemesis had stolen Pallas’s shield and displayed the Gorgon’s head. He looked as though he had been turned to stone; his features were like marble, wearing a melancholy that would not lift. He had led the delicate, luxurious life of a young man born to rank and means—a life made exquisite by its freedom from mean anxieties, by its bright, boyish carelessness; and now, for the first time, he seemed to grasp the dreadful mystery of Destiny, the grim import of Doom.

How wild and monstrous it all felt! Could it be that something written on his hand—in characters he himself could not read, though another might decipher—was some dreadful secret of sin, some blood-red mark of wrongdoing? Was there truly no way out? Were we no better than chessmen, moved by a power we cannot see, vessels shaped by the potter for honour or for shame? His reason rose up in revolt, and yet he could not shake the sense that some tragedy hung over him, and that he had been suddenly summoned to carry an unbearable weight. Actors, at least, are blessed with choice: they may decide whether to appear in tragedy or comedy, whether to endure suffering or to make merry, to laugh or to weep. But in real life it is otherwise. Most men and women are compelled to play roles for which they have never been fitted. Our Guildensterns perform Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets must turn and jest like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, certainly—but the play has been cast badly.

At once Mr. Podgers came into the room. The moment he saw Lord Arthur, he flinched; his coarse, heavy face took on a greenish-yellow look. The two men’s eyes met, and for a heartbeat there was silence.

‘The Duchess has left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and she’s asked me to take it to her,’ Mr. Podgers said at last. ‘Ah—there it is on the sofa. Good evening.’

‘Mr. Podgers, I must insist that you give me a plain answer to the question I’m about to ask you.’

‘Not now, Lord Arthur—but the Duchess is uneasy. I’m afraid I must go.’

‘You shall not go. The Duchess is in no hurry.’

‘Ladies shouldn’t be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,’ said Mr. Podgers, with that sickly smile of his. ‘The fair sex is apt to be impatient.’

Lord Arthur’s well-cut lips tightened into a look of petulant contempt. The poor Duchess seemed to him of scarcely any consequence at that moment. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and thrust out his hand.

‘Tell me what you saw there,’ he said. ‘Tell me the truth. I have to know it. I’m not a child.’"}

{"request_id":"f3ccf93239ad424ca1f4acbe","rewritten_text":"He climbed onto a fiery horse—the same one that had carried him forward to victory in Greece. He wore himself out with numbing exercise, trying to drown the pangs of a troubled mind in the sensations of his body.

He slowly regained himself; and at last, as if recovering from poison, he lifted his head out of the haze of fever and passion into the quiet air of calm reflection. He thought about what was best to do. First, he was struck by how much time had passed since his actions had been governed less by any reasonable impulse than by madness. A month had gone by, and during that time he had not seen Evadne. Her power—tied to only a few of the lasting emotions in his heart—had greatly faded. He was no longer her slave—no longer her lover. He would never see her again, and by the completeness of his return, he would deserve Perdita’s trust.

Yet, even as he decided this, his imagination conjured the miserable home of the Greek girl. A home she had refused to trade, out of noble and principled conviction, for one with greater luxury. He pictured the splendor of her situation and appearance when he first came to know her; he remembered her life in Constantinople, surrounded by every circumstance of eastern magnificence. He thought of her present poverty, her daily work, her lonely condition, her faded, famine-struck face. Compassion swelled in his chest. He would see her once more; he would devise some plan to restore her to society and to the privileges of her rank. Their separation would then follow, as a matter of course.

Again he thought about how, during this long month, he had avoided Perdita—fleeing from her as if she were the stings of his own conscience. But he was awake now. All of this should be put right; and his future devotion would erase the memory of this one blot on the serenity of their life. He felt cheerful as he considered it, and with sober resolve he laid out the course of action he would follow. He remembered that he had promised Perdita to be present this very evening—the 19th of October, the anniversary of his election as Protector—at a festival held in his honor. This festival should be a good sign for the happiness of future years. First, he would go by and see Evadne; he would not stay long. But he owed her some explanation, some compensation for his long absence without word. Then, to Perdita, to the forgotten world, to the duties of society, to the splendor of rank, to the enjoyment of power.

After the scene described in the preceding pages, Perdita had been considering a complete change in Raymond’s manners and behavior. She expected more freedom in their communication and a return to the affectionate habits that had made up the joy of her life."}
