{"request_id":"e09175d9de5641de34fcf7e1","rewritten_text":"With a pounding heart and a fearful sense of not knowing why, I dismissed the servant and locked my door. Then I sat down to read my father’s letter. These were the words it contained.

“My dear Child

“I have betrayed your confidence; I have tried to poison your mind, and I have made your innocent heart familiar with the looks and language of unlawful and monstrous passion. I must atone for these crimes, and I must try, in some measure, to match my punishment to my guilt. You, I doubt not, are ready for what I am about to tell you: we must separate and be divided forever.

“I deprive you of your parent and only friend. You are cast out, shelterless into the world: your hopes are shattered; the peace and security of your pure mind are destroyed; memory will bring you frightful images of guilt, and the anguish of innocent love betrayed. Yet I—who bring all this misery upon you; I—who cast you forth and, without remorse, have stamped the seal of distrust and agony on the heart and brow of my own child, who with devilish levity has tried to steal away her loveliness and replace it with the foul deformity of sin—I, in the overflowing anguish of my heart, beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must, and you do, abhor me: but forgive me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts follow me into my banishment with unrelenting anger. I must never see you again; never hear your voice again; but the gentle whisperings of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning of my disordered brain and heart. I am sure I would feel it even in my grave. And I dare enforce this request by telling you how miserably I was led into this net of fiery anguish, and all my struggles to free myself. Indeed, if your soul were less pure and bright, I would not try to clear myself to you; I would fear that if I led you to regard me with less abhorrence, you might hate vice less. But in speaking to you, it feels as though I am appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness, and I must try to earn it—or I must despair. I urge you, therefore, to listen to my words, and if, by the sharp agony and remorse that tears the brain as madness perhaps you may think, the good guilt may be in any degree lessened, though I dare not, that I have some claim to your compassion.

“I ask you to remember, if you can, our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from a weary wandering of sixteen years, during which, though I had faced many dangers and misfortunes, my affections had been entirely empty."}

{"request_id":"e319381a6e9bf2089d74575c","rewritten_text":"And he always acted like Peter wrote him those things, but that was a lie. He got every last one of them out of that young fool we canoed up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane went and brought the letter her father had left behind. The king read it out loud and cried over it. The letter gave the girls the house they lived in and three thousand dollars in gold. It also gave the tannery, which was doing well, along with some other houses and land worth about seven thousand dollars, plus three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William. It even said where the six thousand dollars in cash was hidden in the cellar. So these two frauds said they would go get it and make everything neat and proper, and they told me to come with a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag, they dumped it out on the floor. It was a fine sight—those bright yellow coins everywhere. The way the king’s eyes lit up! He slapped the duke on the shoulder and said:

“Oh, this ain’t great or anything? Oh no, I don’t think so. Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, don’t it?”

The duke agreed. They grabbed the yellow coins, rubbed them between their fingers, and let them clatter down on the floor. Then the king said:

“It ain’t any use talking. Being brothers to a rich dead man and the representatives of foreign heirs who are left—that’s the line for you and me, Bilge. This is what comes from trusting in Providence. It’s the best way in the long run. I’ve tried them all, and there isn’t a better way.”

Most people would have been satisfied with the pile and taken it on trust, but no—they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came up four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king said:

“Darn him. I wonder what he did with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?”

They worried about it for a while and searched everywhere. Then the duke said:

“Well, he was a pretty sick man, and he probably made a mistake. That’s what I think. The best thing is to let it go and keep quiet about it. We can spare it.”

“Oh, sure, we can spare it. I don’t care about that. It’s the counting I’m thinking about. We want to be real square and honest and above-board here. We want to carry this money upstairs and count it in front of everybody, so nothing looks suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

{"request_id":"2ffaf6112cdaffd242fe0565","rewritten_text":"No letter of condolence had been sent to Ireland. This neglect was blamed on the person who had done wrong. When poor Lady Elliot died, no letter of condolence was received at Kellynch, and so there was every reason to believe that the Dalrymples thought the family connection was over. The question was how to fix this awkward situation and be accepted as cousins again. Both Lady Russell and Mr Elliot felt that this was not a small matter.

“Family ties are always worth keeping,” Lady Russell said. “Good company is always worth seeking. Lady Dalrymple has taken a house for three months in Laura Place, and she will be living in style. She was in Bath the year before, and Lady Russell has heard her described as a charming woman. It would be very desirable to renew the connection, if it can be done, without the Elliots having to compromise what is proper.”

Sir Walter, however, would choose his own way. In the end, he wrote a fine letter full of explanation, regret, and pleading to his right honorable cousin. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot liked the letter, but it did what was needed. It brought three lines of writing from the Dowager Viscountess: “She was very much honoured, and should be happy in their acquaintance.” The hard part was done, and now came the pleasant part. They visited in Laura Place, and they had the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret, to be shown wherever they would be seen most. Everyone talked about “Our cousins in Laura Place”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret.”

Anne felt embarrassed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been very agreeable, she would still have been ashamed of the excitement they caused, but they were not agreeable at all. There was no real superiority in their manners, their accomplishments, or their understanding. Lady Dalrymple had earned the name of “a charming woman” only because she smiled and gave a polite answer to everyone. Miss Carteret had even less to say. She was plain and awkward, and she would never have been accepted in Camden Place if it were not for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted she had expected something better, but she still said, “It is an acquaintance worth having.” When Anne tried to share her opinion with Mr Elliot, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves. Still, he insisted that, as a family connection, as good company, and as people who could bring good company around them, they had value. Anne smiled and said,

“My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of clever, well-informed people, who have a great deal of conversation. That is what I call good company.”"}

{"request_id":"a7264c50710a3f140aeb2b35","rewritten_text":"He was delivered to you. You see, I’ve been told the details. Is that right?”

“That is true,” said Defarge. He had been warned to answer, and to do it briefly, after his wife accidentally brushed his elbow while she knitted and sang.

“It was to you,” the spy said, “that his daughter came. And it was from your care that his daughter took him away, with a neat brown gentleman. What is he called?—with a little wig—Lorry, from the bank of Tellson and Company, who took him over to England.”

“That is true,” Defarge repeated.

“Very interesting memories!” the spy said. “I’ve known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Yes?” said Defarge.

“You don’t hear much about them anymore?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“Indeed,” madame said, without looking away from her work and her small song, “we never hear about them. We got the news that they arrived safely, and maybe another letter, or maybe two. But after that, they just went on with their lives—ours too—and we never kept in touch.”

“Exactly, madame,” the spy replied. “She is going to be married.”

“Going?” madame repeated. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. It seems to me you English are cold.”

“Oh! You know I’m English,” the spy said.

“I can tell your tongue is,” madame answered. “And I suppose the man is, too.”

He didn’t take it as a compliment. Still, he tried to laugh it off. After he finished his cognac, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is going to be married. But not to an Englishman. She will marry a man who, like her, is French by birth. And speaking of Gaspard—ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel—there’s something strange about this. She is going to marry the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, for whom Gaspard was raised to such a great height, in other words, the present Marquis. But in England he lives without being known as a marquis. There he is simply Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is the name of his mother’s family.”

Madame Defarge kept knitting, but the news clearly affected her husband. No matter what he did behind the little counter—whether he tried to strike a light or light his pipe—he was still troubled, and his hand was not steady. The spy would not have been a spy if he hadn’t noticed it, and if he hadn’t kept it in his mind.

After making at least this one point, whatever it might be worth, and with no customers coming in to help Defarge, Mr. Barsad paid for what he had drunk and left. Before he went, he said, in a polite way, that he looked forward to seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

{"request_id":"d08bb675c5a6e549cd2e7b22","rewritten_text":"Weeks and weeks passed, and I became more and more absorbed in you. Then something new happened. I had drawn you as Paris in delicate armor, and as Adonis wearing a hunter’s cloak and holding a polished boar-spear. With heavy lotus blossoms on your head, you sat on the prow of Adrian’s barge, looking out over the green, muddy Nile. In another scene, you leaned over the quiet pool of a Greek woodland and watched, in the water’s silent silver, the wonder of your own face. It was exactly what art should be—unconscious, perfect, and far away.

Then, one day—one I sometimes call fatal—I decided to paint a portrait of you the way you really are. I wanted it to be in your own clothes and your own time, not in the costumes of long-dead ages. I don’t know whether it was the realism of my method, or simply the strength of your own personality, but you seemed to come to me directly, without any mist or veil. As I worked, I felt that every tiny bit of color was giving away my secret. I became afraid that other people would see my worship of you. I felt, Dorian, that I had said too much—that I had put too much of myself into the painting.

That was when I decided I would never let the picture be shown. You were a little annoyed, but you didn’t understand what it meant to me. Harry, who I told about it, laughed at me. I didn’t mind that. When the painting was finished, and I was alone with it, I felt sure I was right. Then, after a few days, the picture left my studio. Once I had gotten rid of the unbearable pull it had on me, it seemed to me that I had been foolish to think I had seen anything in it at all—except that you were extremely good-looking, and that I could paint.

Even now, I can’t help thinking that the passion you feel while creating is never truly shown in the work you make. Art is always more distant and abstract than we imagine. Form and color only tell us about form and color. That is all. It often seems to me that art hides the artist more completely than it ever reveals him. So when I received an offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the main piece in my exhibition. It never occurred to me that you would refuse. I understand now that you were right. The picture cannot be shown.

You must not be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have told you."}

{"request_id":"b429b99d95aa1914496d532e","rewritten_text":"I see it as one of the first improvements in well-mannered society.”

“Of course, sir; and it also has the advantage of being popular even among the less refined societies in the world. Any savage can dance.”

Sir William only smiled. “Your friend dances wonderfully,” he said after a pause, as he saw Bingley join the group. “And I have no doubt that you know the art yourself, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, I did, and it gave me a great deal of pleasure to watch. Do you dance often at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Then don’t you think it would be a nice compliment to the place?”

“It’s a compliment I never give to any place, if I can help it.”

“You have a house in town, I suppose?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once thought of living in town myself, because I enjoy better society. But I wasn’t sure the air of London would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, waiting for an answer, but his companion did not seem willing to give one. At that moment Elizabeth walked toward them, and he suddenly had the idea of doing something very gallant. He called out to her—

“My dear Miss Eliza, why aren’t you dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must let me introduce this young lady to you as a very desirable partner. You can’t refuse to dance when there is so much beauty in front of you.”

Then, taking her hand, he would have offered it to Mr. Darcy. Mr. Darcy, though very surprised, was not unwilling to accept it, when Elizabeth immediately pulled back and said, with some embarrassment, to Sir William—

“Indeed, sir, I have no intention of dancing. I beg you not to think I came over here just to ask for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with proper seriousness, asked for the honor of her hand, but it was no use. Elizabeth was determined, and Sir William did not manage to change her mind with his attempts to persuade her.

“You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it would be cruel to deny me the happiness of seeing you. And although this gentleman dislikes the amusement in general, I’m sure he won’t mind doing us the favor for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is nothing but politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He is, indeed. But with such an invitation, my dear Miss Eliza, we can’t really blame him for being willing. Who could refuse a partner like that?”

Elizabeth looked slyly at him and turned away. Her refusal did not upset the gentleman, and he was pleased to think of her, when Miss Bingley approached and spoke to him—"}

{"request_id":"06903993b89ddcea35925584","rewritten_text":"Raymond strode angrily back and forth across the room. I stood ready to take in his reproaches and answer them. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is infinitely ridiculous,” he cried. “If you were schoolboys, you couldn’t behave more irrationally.”

“You don’t understand,” said Raymond. “This is only part of a system—a scheme of tyranny that I will never submit to. Because I am Protector of England, am I supposed to be the only slave in its empire? My privacy invaded, my actions censored, my friends insulted? But I’ll get rid of the whole thing at once. Be you witnesses,” and he pulled the star, the insignia of his office, from his breast and threw it on the table. “I renounce my office, I abdicate my power—whoever wants it can take it!”—-

“Let him assume it,” Adrian exclaimed, “who can declare himself, or whom the world will declare to be your superior. There is no man in England with the right kind of presumption. Know yourself, Raymond, and your outrage will fade; your self-satisfaction will come back. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country—or our own—we prayed at the same time for the life and welfare of the Protector, as inseparably tied to it. Your hours were devoted to our benefit; your ambition was to earn our approval. You decorated our towns with buildings, you gave us useful institutions, you made the soil fertile. The powerful and unjust cowered at the steps of your judgment-seat, and the poor and oppressed rose like flowers awakened by morning under the sunshine of your protection.

“Can you blame us for being horrified and mourning when this seems to have changed? But come—this bitter mood has already passed. Resume your duties; your supporters will hail you; your enemies will be silenced. Our love, honor, and duty will be shown to you again. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world will be subject to you.”

“All of that would be very good sense, if it were addressed to someone else,” Raymond replied, darkly. “Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the first peer of the land, may become its sovereign. You—the good, the wise, the just—may rule all hearts. But I see, too soon for my own happiness and too late for England’s good, that I took on a task I’m not fit for. I can’t rule myself. My passions are my masters; even my smallest impulse is my tyrant. Do you think I renounced the Protectorate—yes, I have renounced it—in a fit of temper? By the God who lives, I swear I’ll never take up that trinket again; never again burden myself with the weight of care and misery, of which that is the visible sign.”"}

{"request_id":"8455898cb9d7c45ec0d8b568","rewritten_text":"Those old, weak people were always seen by the public bowing. People believed that after they bowed a customer out, they would keep bowing in the empty office until they had another customer to bow in.

The barrister could tell that the banker would not have gone so far in his opinion unless he was sure of it in a moral sense. Even though he was not ready for the big pill he had to swallow, he managed to get it down. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, shaking his finger like a lawyer, pointing toward the Temple in general, “my way out of this is to put you all in the wrong.”

It was a trick of an Old Bailey tactician, and it gave him real relief. “You won’t put me in the wrong, young lady,” said Mr. Stryver. “I’ll do that for you.”

So when Mr. Lorry came that night, as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver—surrounded by a pile of books and papers left out for the purpose—seemed to have nothing on his mind at all about the matter from the morning. He even looked surprised to see Mr. Lorry, and he was clearly absent-minded and preoccupied.

“Well!” said that friendly messenger after trying for a full half hour to get him to focus on the subject. “I’ve been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated, coldly. “Oh, of course! What was I thinking of!”

“And I have no doubt,” said Mr. Lorry, “that I was right in the conversation we had. My opinion is confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” Mr. Stryver answered, in the friendliest tone, “that I’m sorry for it—for your sake, and for the poor father’s sake. I know this must always be a painful subject for the family. Let’s not talk about it anymore.”

“I don’t understand you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I dare say you don’t,” Stryver replied, nodding in a smooth, final way. “No matter, no matter.”

“But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“No, it doesn’t,” said Stryver. “I assure you it doesn’t. I thought there was sense where there is no sense, and a proper ambition where there isn’t one, and I’m glad I was wrong. No harm is done. Young women have made similar mistakes before, and they have often regretted them later, in poverty and obscurity, just as often. In one way, I’m sorry the matter is dropped, because it would have been a bad thing for me in a worldly sense. In another way, I’m glad it’s dropped, because it would have been a bad thing for me in a worldly sense too. And it hardly needs saying that I could have gained nothing from it.”"}

{"request_id":"cbfaad013b3f5044ab41fa8f","rewritten_text":"“But I may ask you two questions, may I?”

“You may ask,” said Monks, with some show of surprise; “but whether I answer or not is another question.”

“—Which makes three,” observed Mr. Bumble, trying to sound facetious.

“Is that what you expected to get from me?” demanded the matron.

“It is,” replied Monks. “The other question?”

“What do you propose to do with it? Can it be used against me?”

“Never,” rejoined Monks; “nor against me either. Listen—don’t take a step forward, or your life won’t be worth a bulrush.”

With that, he suddenly shoved the table aside, and yanked an iron ring set into the boarding. He threw back a large trapdoor that opened right at Mr. Bumble’s feet, forcing that gentleman to stumble back several paces in a rush of panic.

“Look down,” said Monks, lowering the lantern into the dark opening. “Don’t be afraid of me. I could have let you down quietly enough when you were sitting over it, if that had been my plan.”

Encouraged, the matron stepped closer to the edge; and even Mr. Bumble himself, driven by curiosity, did the same. The muddy water, swollen by the heavy rain, was surging rapidly below; and every other sound was swallowed by the noise of it splashing and churning against the green, slimy piles. There had once been a water-mill beneath. The tide, foaming and snapping around the few rotten stakes and fragments of machinery still left there, seemed to dart onward with fresh force once it was freed from obstacles that had tried in vain to stop its headlong rush.

“If you threw a man’s body down there, where would it be tomorrow morning?” said Monks, swinging the lantern back and forth in the dark well.

“Twelve miles down the river—and cut to pieces besides,” replied Bumble, recoiling at the thought.

Monks took the small packet from his breast, where he had shoved it in a hurry. Tying it to a lead weight that had been part of some pulley and was lying on the floor, he dropped it into the stream. It fell straight and true, like a shot; it split the water with a splash so faint it was almost nothing, and then it was gone.

The three of them stared into each other’s faces and seemed to breathe more freely.

“There!” said Monks, shutting the trapdoor, which fell heavily back into place. “If the sea ever gives up its dead, as the books say it will, it will keep its gold and silver to itself—and that trash with it. We have nothing more to say, and we can break up our little party.”

“By all means,” said Mr. Bumble, with eager readiness.

“You’ll keep a quiet tongue in your head, won’t you?” Monks said, fixing him with a threatening look."}

{"request_id":"1dcc812f28b7e8ad875879f1","rewritten_text":"His attitude was stubborn to the extreme, and during the whole trip the only words that came out of his mouth were “dat deuced bug.” As for me, I carried a couple of dark lanterns. Legrand, meanwhile, kept himself busy with the _scarabæus_, which he had tied to the end of a short piece of whip-cord. He kept twirling it back and forth as he walked, like a conjurer performing a trick. When I noticed that plain sign that my friend’s mind was not right, I could hardly keep from crying. Still, I thought it was better to go along with his ideas for now, at least until I could try something more forceful and hope it would work.

In the meantime, I tried in vain to get him to talk about the purpose of the expedition. Since he had agreed to let me come with him, I expected him to answer at least some of my questions, but he would not discuss anything of minor importance. Every time I asked, the only reply I got was, “we shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the top of the island in a skiff. Then we climbed up into the high ground on the main land and headed northwest. We went through a stretch of country so wild and empty that there was no sign of any human footstep. Legrand led the way with confidence, stopping now and then for a moment to check what looked like landmarks he had planned for himself on a previous trip.

We traveled like this for about two hours. The sun was just setting when we entered an even more miserable region than anything we had seen before. It was a kind of plateau near the top of a hill that was almost impossible to reach. The whole place was thickly wooded from the bottom to the very top, and it was broken up by huge rocks that seemed to be resting loosely on the ground. In many places, they did not fall into the valleys below only because the trees held them up. Deep ravines ran in different directions, making the scene feel even more grim and serious.

The platform we had climbed onto was covered in brambles. We soon found that we could not push through them without the scythe. At Legrand’s direction, Jupiter cleared a path for us to the base of an enormous tulip-tree. It stood on level ground with eight or ten oaks around it, but it was far taller and more impressive than all of them. Its foliage and shape were beautiful, its branches spread wide, and the whole tree looked majestic in a way I had never seen before."}

{"request_id":"50f58413fb1bf370739ae7e9","rewritten_text":"While these things were happening in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old room—the same one from which Oliver had been taken out by the girl. He stared at a dull, smoky fire and worried over it. On his knee he held a pair of bellows, as if he had been trying to get the fire burning better, but he had slipped into deep thought. With his arms folded on them and his chin resting on his thumbs, he kept his eyes fixed on the rusty bars.

Behind him, at a table, sat the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling. They were all focused on a game of whist. The Artful was playing dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The Artful’s face was always sharp and intelligent, and watching the game made it even more interesting. He studied Mr. Chitling’s hand closely, and whenever it seemed useful, he gave it serious looks. He then adjusted his own play based on what he saw in his neighbor’s cards. Since it was a cold night, the Dodger wore his hat indoors, as he often did. He also kept a clay pipe in his mouth, taking it out only briefly when he needed to ask for more gin-and-water from a quart pot on the table, which was kept ready for everyone.

Master Bates watched the game too, but he was more easily excited than his friend. It showed in how often he went back to the gin-and-water. He also made jokes and said things that had nothing to do with the game, which was not fitting for a serious player. The Artful, because he and Bates were so close, more than once spoke to him seriously about these habits. Master Bates took the complaints very well. He would just tell his friend to be “blowed,” or suggest he put his head in a sack, or answer with some other quick joke like that. Mr. Chitling seemed especially impressed by it. It was also strange that Mr. Chitling and his partner always lost. Yet instead of getting angry, Master Bates seemed to enjoy it most of all. He laughed loudly after every deal and said he had never seen such a fun game in all his life.

“That’s two doubles and the rub,” said Mr. Chitling, with a long face, as he pulled half-a-crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never see such a feller as you, Jack; you win everything."}

{"request_id":"1f3c9d4c4999ddae7f3dfecf","rewritten_text":"“I must leave, though I cannot tell what will become of me; but I shall come back here, or else join your party, as soon as I possibly can. One word, one look, will decide whether I enter your father’s house this evening—or whether I never do.”

Such a letter was not likely to be recovered from quickly. Half an hour of solitude and thought might have soothed her; but the ten minutes that had passed before she was interrupted—under all the limits of her situation—could do nothing to calm her. Each moment only brought fresh agitation. It was an overpowering happiness. And before she had even reached the first stage of full feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta were all in.

The sheer need to appear like herself caused an immediate struggle; but after a while she could do no more. She could not make out a word of what they said, and was forced to plead indisposition and excuse herself. Then they saw how very ill she looked, and were shocked and alarmed, and would not move without her for anything in the world. It was dreadful. If only they had gone away and left her to the quiet possession of that room, it might have been her cure; but having them all standing about and waiting for her was maddening, and in her distress she said she would go home.

“By all means, my dear,” cried Mrs Musgrove, “go home at once, and take care of yourself, so that you may be fit for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to attend you, but I am no doctor. Charles, ring for a chair. She must not walk.”

But a chair would never do. Worse than everything! To lose the chance of exchanging two words with Captain Wentworth during her quiet, solitary walk up the town (and she felt almost sure she would meet him) was more than she could bear. The chair was protested against with all earnestness; and Mrs Musgrove, thinking only of one kind of illness, after assuring herself with some anxiety that there had been no fall—that Anne had not, at any time lately, slipped down and struck her head—was perfectly convinced there had been no fall; and she could part with her readily, depending on finding her better by night.

With anxious care not to omit any possible precaution, Anne struggled and said—

“I am afraid, ma’am, that it is not quite understood. Pray, be so good as to tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your whole party this evening. I fear there has been some mistake; and I wish you particularly to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh! my dear, it is quite understood; I give you my word.”"}

{"request_id":"b532ebda5a6247930ead3dfd","rewritten_text":"Had she known that her sister was trying to pull her away from the hopes and realities of a life like this, what would she have felt? Only her mother could have understood it, and her mother might have felt almost the same. Lydia’s going to Brighton was the only thing that comforted her, in spite of the sad belief that her husband never meant to go there himself.

But they did not know anything about what had happened, and their excitement kept going, with hardly any break, right up to the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now going to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since she had been in his company so often after her return, her agitation had mostly settled down. The feelings from her earlier partiality were gone too. She had even learned to notice, in the very gentleness that had first pleased her, a kind of pretending and a sameness that soon made her tired and disgusted. And now, in the way he behaved toward her, she found a new reason to dislike him. The interest he soon showed in starting those attentions again that had marked the beginning of their acquaintance could only, after everything that had happened since, make her even more annoyed. She stopped caring about him altogether when she realized he had chosen her as the target of such empty, silly flirting. Even while she kept her feelings under control, she could not help noticing the insult in his belief that no matter how long his attentions had been away, or for whatever reason, her vanity would still be pleased and her preference would be secured again at any time.

On the very last day the regiment stayed in Meryton, he dined with the other officers at Longbourn. Elizabeth was so willing to stay on good terms with him that, when he asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she told him that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both spent three weeks at Rosings. Then she asked him if he knew the colonel.

He looked surprised, annoyed, and alarmed. But after a moment, he remembered, smiled again, and said that he had seen him often before. Then, after remarking that he was a very gentlemanlike man, he asked her what she thought of him. Her answer was strongly in his favor. With an air of indifference, he soon added, “How long did you say he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves with knowing him.”

“Indeed!” Wickham said, with a look that did not escape her. “And may I ask—” He stopped himself, then continued in a lighter tone, “Is it in manners that he improves?”"}

{"request_id":"333d8b42689545d89ea2aca8","rewritten_text":"Could not tell whether the sound belonged to a man or to a woman. Could not catch what was being said, though he believed it was Spanish. The condition of the room and of the bodies, this witness said, matched what we had described yesterday.

“_Henri Duval_, a neighbor, and by trade a silversmith, states that he was among the first to enter the house. In general, he confirms Musèt’s account. As soon as they forced their way in, they shut the door again, to keep the crowd out; the people gathered very quickly, despite how late it was. The sharp voice, this witness thinks, was Italian. He was certain it was not French. He could not be sure whether it was a man’s voice—it might have been a woman’s. He did not know Italian. He could not make out the words, but the intonation convinced him the speaker was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter, and had spoken with both often. He was sure the shrill voice was neither of the two deceased.

“——_Odenheimer, restaurateur._ This witness offered his testimony. Not speaking French, he was questioned through an interpreter. He is a native of Amsterdam. He was passing the house when the cries began. They went on for several minutes—probably ten. They were long and loud—very dreadful and distressing. He was one of those who entered the building. He corroborated the earlier evidence in every respect, except that he was sure the shrill voice belonged to a man—a Frenchman. He could not distinguish the words that were uttered. They were loud and quick—uneven—spoken, it seemed, in fear as well as in anger. The voice was harsh—not so much shrill as harsh. He could not really call it a shrill voice. The rough voice kept repeating ‘_sacré_,’ ‘_diable_,’ and once ‘_mon Dieu_.’

“_Jules Mignaud_, banker, of the firm of Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye had some property. She had opened an account with his banking house in the spring of that year—(eight years earlier). She made frequent deposits in small sums. She had not drawn anything out until the third day before her death, when she took out, in person, the sum of 4000 francs. That amount was paid in gold, and a clerk went home with the money.

“_Adolphe Le Bon_, clerk to Mignaud et Fils, deposes that on the day in question, about noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her residence with the 4000 francs, which he had put into two bags. When the door was opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one of the bags from his hands, while the old lady took the other from him.”"}

{"request_id":"19580ab37e892c9ad23de362","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

No answer.

“What’s happened to that boy, I wonder? You TOM!”

No answer.

The old lady pulled her spectacles down and looked over them around the room; then she put them up and looked out beneath them. She seldom, if ever, looked through them for something as small as a boy. They were her everyday pair, the pride of her heart, made for “style,” not for usefulness—she could have seen through a pair of stove-lids just as well. She looked puzzled for a moment, and then said, not fiercely, but still loud enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, I’ll be—if I get hold of you, I’ll—”

She didn’t finish, because by then she was bending down and punching under the bed with the broom, and she needed breath to punctuate the punches. She found nothing but the cat.

“I never did see the beat of that boy!”

She went to the open door, stood in it, and looked out among the tomato vines and the “jimpson” weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice at an angle meant for distance and shouted:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

There was a slight sound behind her, and she turned just in time to grab a small boy by the slack of his roundabout and stop him from running.

“There! I might’ve thought of that closet. What have you been doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What is that truck?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I know. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve said that if you didn’t leave that jam alone, I’d skin you. Hand me that switch.”

The switch hovered in the air—the danger was desperate—

“My! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old lady spun around and yanked her skirts out of danger. The boy bolted at once, scrambled up the high board fence, and disappeared over it.

His aunt Polly stood there, surprised for a moment, and then broke into a gentle laugh.

“Hang the boy—can’t I never learn anything? Hasn’t he played me tricks enough that I should be watching for him by now? But old fools are the biggest fools there is. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks, as the saying goes. But goodness, he never plays them the same way two days in a row, and how is a person supposed to know what’s coming? He seems to know just how long he can torment me before I get mad, and he knows if he can manage to distract me for a minute or make me laugh, then it’s all gone again and I can’t hit him a lick.”"}

{"request_id":"b04c7087fca58e9316a3f276","rewritten_text":"The tight lanes and courts, after a time, opened out into a broad, open space; here and there, pens for beasts lay scattered about, along with other signs that a cattle-market was in progress. When Sikes and the others reached this place, he slowed his steps, for the girl could not keep up any longer with the brisk pace they had been making. He wheeled on Oliver and, in a rough tone, ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Do you hear?” Sikes snarled as Oliver hesitated and glanced around.

They had drawn up in a dark nook, well away from the path of any passengers.

Oliver could see—too clearly—that resistance would be useless. He offered his hand, and Nancy clutched it hard in hers.

“Give me the other,” said Sikes, catching Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog lifted its head and growled.

“Look here, boy!” Sikes said, pressing his other hand to Oliver’s throat. “If he says so much as a soft word, hold him! D’ye mind!”

The dog growled again, and, licking its lips, stared at Oliver as though it meant to fasten itself to his windpipe without delay.

“He’s as ready as a Christian—strike me blind if he ain’t!” Sikes declared, watching the animal with a grim, savage satisfaction. “Now, you know what you’ve got to expect, master, so call away as quick as you like; the dog will soon end that little game. Come on, young ’un!”

Bull’s-Eye wagged its tail at this unusually kind way of speaking, and after another warning growl meant for Oliver, it went on ahead.

They were crossing Smithfield, though it might as well have been Grosvenor Square, for all Oliver knew. The night was dark and foggy. The shop-lights could scarcely force their way through the thick mist, which seemed to grow heavier every moment, wrapping the streets and houses in gloom; the place looked stranger still to Oliver, and his uncertainty became all the more wretched and depressing.

They had gone only a few paces when a deep church-bell struck the hour. At the first peal, both of his conductors halted and turned their heads toward the direction the sound came from.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy said when the bell stopped.

“What’s the use of telling me that; I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes answered.

“I wonder whether _they_ can hear it,” Nancy said.

“Why, of course they can,” Sikes replied. “It was Bartlemy time when I was put out; and there weren’t a penny trumpet at the fair that I couldn’t hear the squeaking of. After I was locked up for the night, the noise and clatter outside made the old jail so still that I could almost have beaten my brains out against the iron plates of the door.”"}

{"request_id":"c0bfef20f2e93c1b25501db5","rewritten_text":"“Unless you call Miss Havisham a he. And I doubt even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, up town?” said Joe.

“Is there any Miss Havisham down town?” my sister shot back.

“She wants this boy to go and play there. And of course he’s going. And he’d better play there,” my sister said, shaking her head at me as encouragement to be extremely light and playful, “or I’ll work him.”

I had heard about Miss Havisham up town—everybody for miles around had heard about Miss Havisham up town—as an immensely rich and grim woman who lived in a large, dismal house barricaded against robbers, and who lived a life of seclusion.

“Well, of course!” Joe said, astounded. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“Noodle!” my sister cried. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Which some individual,” Joe hinted politely again, “mentioned that she wanted him to go and play there.”

“And couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knows of a boy to go and play there? Isn’t it just barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook might be a tenant of hers, and that he may sometimes—we won’t say quarterly or half-yearly, because that would be asking too much of you—but sometimes—go there to pay his rent? And couldn’t she then ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, being always considerate and thoughtful for us—though you may not think it, Joseph,” she said in the deepest reproachful tone, as if he were the most callous of nephews, “then mention this boy, standing Prancing here”—which I solemnly declare I was not doing—“that I have forever been a willing slave to?”

“Good again!” Uncle Pumblechook cried. “Well put! Nicely said! Good indeed! Now, Joseph, you know the situation.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister said, still reproachful, while Joe apologized by wiping the back of his hand across and across his nose, “you don’t yet—though you may not think it—you don’t know the situation. You may think you do, but you don’t, Joseph. Because you don’t know that Uncle Pumblechook, being sensible that for anything we can tell, this boy’s fortune may be made by going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, and to keep him tonight, and to take him with his own hands to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And Lor-a-mussy me!” my sister cried, throwing off her bonnet in sudden desperation. “Here I am standing talking to mere Mooncalfs, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, and the mare catching cold at the door, and the boy all grimed with crock and dirt from the hair of his head to the sole of his foot!”"}

{"request_id":"08f02c0a3c286857e8622a52","rewritten_text":"You see, I had my handkerchief in my helmet, along with some other things; but it was the kind of helmet you can’t take off by yourself. I hadn’t thought of that when I put it there, and honestly I didn’t even know it. I assumed it would be especially convenient right there. So now, the fact that it was there—so handy and so close by, yet completely out of reach—made everything worse and harder to bear. Yes, the thing you can’t get is the thing you want most, mainly; everyone has noticed that. Well, it took my mind off everything else, cleared it completely, and centered it in my helmet. Mile after mile, it stayed there, imagining the handkerchief, picturing the handkerchief. And it was bitter and aggravating to have the salt sweat keep trickling down into my eyes while I couldn’t get at it. It sounds like a small thing on paper, but it wasn’t a small thing at all; it was the most real kind of misery. I wouldn’t say it if it weren’t true. I decided that next time I’d carry a reticule, no matter what it looked like, and let people say what they wanted. Of course those iron men of the Round Table would think it was scandalous, and maybe raise Sheol about it, but as for me—give me comfort first, and style afterward.

So we jogged along, and now and then we hit a stretch of dust. It would tumble up in clouds, get into my nose, and make me sneeze and cry; and of course I said things I shouldn’t have said—I won’t deny that. I’m not better than anyone else.

We couldn’t seem to meet anybody in this lonely Britain, not even an ogre; and in the mood I was in then, it was better for the ogre—that is, an ogre with a handkerchief. Most knights would have thought only about getting his armor, but I got his bandanna instead. He could keep his hardware, for all of me.

Meanwhile, it was getting hotter and hotter in there. You see, the sun kept beating down and warming up the iron more and more all the time. And when you’re hot like that, every little thing irritates you. When I trotted, I rattled like a crate of dishes, and that annoyed me; and on top of that, I couldn’t stand the shield slatting and banging—now against my breast, now around my back. If I dropped into a walk, my joints creaked and screeched in that wearisome way a wheelbarrow does, and since we weren’t creating any breeze at that pace, I was close to getting fried in that stove. Besides, the quieter I went, the heavier the iron seemed to settle on me, and the more and more tons I felt like I weighed every minute."}

{"request_id":"ba9a9224f74ff58b9b48e755","rewritten_text":"The storm raged fiercely all that night, but nothing of particular note happened. The next morning, though, when they came down to breakfast, they found the terrible stain of blood on the floor again. “I don’t think it can be the fault of the Paragon Detergent,” said Washington. “I’ve tried it with everything. It must be the ghost.” He rubbed out the stain a second time, but on the second morning it was there again. On the third morning it was still there, even though the library had been locked up at night by Mr. Otis himself, and the key had been carried upstairs.

The whole family were now fully invested in the matter. Mr. Otis began to suspect that he had been too rigid in his denial of ghosts; Mrs. Otis said she intended to join the Psychical Society; and Washington prepared a long letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore about the Permanence of Sanguineous Stains when connected with Crime. That night, all doubts about the objective existence of phantoms were removed for good.

The day had been warm and sunny, and in the cool of the evening the whole family went out for a drive. They didn’t get home until nine o’clock, when they had a light supper. The conversation never turned to ghosts, so there weren’t even those basic conditions of expectation that so often come before psychical phenomena appear. The topics they discussed, as Mr. Otis later told me, were simply the kind of everyday talk that cultured Americans of the better sort have—Miss Fanny Davenport’s immense superiority over Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; how hard it was to get green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy, even in the best English houses; the importance of Boston in the development of the world-soul; the advantages of the baggage-check system for railway travel; and how sweet the New York accent sounded compared with the London drawl. Not a word was said about anything supernatural, and Sir Simon de Canterville was not mentioned at all. At eleven o’clock the family went to bed, and by half past all the lights were out.

Some time later, Mr. Otis was awakened by a strange noise in the corridor outside his room. It sounded like the clank of metal and seemed to be getting closer every moment. He sat up at once, struck a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o’clock. He was completely calm and felt his pulse, which was not feverish in the least. The noise continued, and with it he heard footsteps clearly. He put on his slippers, took a small oblong phial from his dressing-case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"2f135438c042ecb853fe71ee","rewritten_text":"Knights in heavy armor, with horses, could not move very fast. They would go as quickly as they could, and since the ground was in good shape and there was no snow or mud, they should manage about a seven-mile pace. They would have to switch horses a couple of times. They would arrive around six o’clock, or a little after. It would still be light enough. They would see the white cloth I would tie around my right arm, and I would take command. We would surround that prison and get the king out in no time. It would look impressive and picturesque, considering everything, even though I would have preferred midday, because it would be more theatrical that way.

Now, to increase the strength of my bow, I decided to find some of the people I had recognized before and let them know who I was. That would help us get out of our trouble, without relying on the knights. But I had to be careful, because it was risky. I needed to dress in fine, rich clothes, and I couldn’t just run and jump into them. No, I would have to work up to it step by step, buying one outfit after another in shops that were far apart, getting a little finer quality each time, until I finally reached silk and velvet and was ready for my plan. So I started.

But the plan fell apart at once. The first corner I turned, I ran straight into one of our slaves, who was hanging around with a watchman. I coughed at that exact moment, and he gave me a look so sharp it felt like it went straight into my bones. I figured he thought he had heard that cough before. I turned right away into a shop and moved along the counter, checking prices and watching from the corner of my eye. Those people had stopped. They were talking together and looking in at the door. I decided I would leave through the back, if there was one. I asked the shopwoman if I could step out there and look for the escaped slave, who was believed to be hiding somewhere behind. I told her I was an officer in disguise, and that my partner was by the door with one of the murderers in charge. I asked her to go tell him he didn’t need to wait, but should go at once to the far end of the back alley, so she could be ready to head him off when I dragged him out.

She was eager to see one of those already famous murderers, and she set off on the errand immediately."}

{"request_id":"a53aff1d58c756e9ef52c6fe","rewritten_text":"The two ladies were delighted to see their dear friend again. It had been an age since they had met, and they kept asking what she had been doing with herself since their separation. They paid little attention to the rest of the family; they tried to avoid Mrs. Bennet as much as possible, said little to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. Before long, they were gone again. They rose from their seats with a burst of energy that surprised their brother, and hurried off as if they were eager to get away from Mrs. Bennet’s polite attention.

The prospect of the Netherfield ball was extremely pleasing to every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to treat it as a compliment to her eldest daughter, and she was especially flattered to receive the invitation from Mr. Bingley himself, rather than a formal card. Jane imagined a happy evening in the company of her two friends, along with their brother’s attentions; and Elizabeth, with real pleasure, looked forward to dancing a great deal with Mr. Wickham, and to seeing a confirmation of everything in Mr. Darcy’s look and behavior. The happiness Catherine and Lydia anticipated depended less on any single event or any particular person. Even though each of them, like Elizabeth, intended to dance half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was by no means the only partner who could satisfy them, and in any case, a ball was a ball. And even Mary could reassure her family that she had no reluctance about it.

“While I can have my mornings to myself,” she said, “it is enough. I don’t think it’s a sacrifice to join in evening plans now and then. Society has claims on all of us; and I consider myself one of those who believe intervals of recreation and amusement are desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth’s spirits were so high on the occasion that, although she didn’t often speak unnecessarily to Mr. Collins, she couldn’t help asking him whether he intended to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation, and if he did, whether he would think it proper to take part in the evening’s entertainment. She was rather surprised to find that he had no hesitation at all on the matter, and was far from fearing a rebuke—either from the Archbishop or from Lady Catherine de Bourgh—once he ventured to dance.

“I am by no means of the opinion,” said he, “that a ball of this kind, given by a young man of character to respectable people, can have any evil tendency. And I am so far from objecting to dancing myself that I shall hope to be honored with the hands of all my fair cousins during the course of the evening. I take this opportunity, therefore, of requesting yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the first two dances especially—a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to the right cause, and not to any disrespect for her.”"}

{"request_id":"c1d5a3ea22b4842db19ddb6b","rewritten_text":"Thus I passed two years. Day after day, so many hundreds went by; they brought no outward changes, but a few slowly began to work on my mind as I drifted toward death. I started to study more; to sympathize more with the thoughts of others as they were expressed in books; to read history, and to lose my individuality among the crowd that had existed before me. In this way, perhaps, as the sensation of immediate suffering faded, I became more human.

Solitude also lost some of its appeal. I began again to wish for sympathy—not because I was ever tempted to seek the crowd, but because I wanted one friend to love me. You might say, perhaps, that I was gradually becoming fit to return to society. I don’t think so. The sympathy I desired had to be so pure, so stripped of any influence from outward circumstances, that in the world I could not fail to be blocked by the coarse materials that constantly mingle even with its best feelings. Believe me, I was then less suited for any communion with my fellow creatures than before. When I left them, they tormented me—but it was the way pain and sickness can torment: something extraneous to the mind that grates on it, and that I wanted to cast off. Now, though, I would have wanted sympathy; I would have wanted to bind my soul to one of theirs, and I would have prepared myself for plenty of disappointment and suffering, for I was tender as a sensitive plant—every nerve. I didn’t want sympathy and help in ambition or wisdom, but sweet and mutual affection: smiles to lift me and gentle words of comfort. I wanted one heart into which I could pour out my complaints without restraint, and from which, by the heavenly nature of the soil, blessed fruit might grow from such bad seed.

But how could I find this? The love that is the soul of friendship is a soft spirit, seldom found except when two amiable creatures are joined from early youth, or when they are bound by mutual suffering and shared pursuits. It comes to some of the elect, unsought and unaware; it falls like gentle dew on chosen places that, however barren they were before, become fertile for all sweet plants under its kindly influence. Yet when it is desired, it flies. It mocks the prayers of those who long for it; it will give, but it will not be sought.

I knew all this, and I didn’t go looking for sympathy. But there, on my solitary heath, under my humble roof where everything around was desart, it came to me like a sunbeam in winter—something that adorns while it helps to melt the drifted snow. Alas, the sun shone on blighted fruit. I didn’t revive under its radiance, because I was too utterly undone to feel its kindly power."}

{"request_id":"82ce69142aa470703115783a","rewritten_text":"“Well, everybody does it that way, Huck.”

“Tom, it don’t make no difference. I ain’t everybody, and I can’t _stand_ it. It’s awful being tied up so. And food comes too easy—I don’t take any interest in eating that way. I got to ask to go fishing; I got to ask to go swimming—damn if I haven’t got to ask to do everything. And I’d have to talk so nice it wasn’t no comfort. I’d have to go up in the attic and tear out awhile every day just to get a taste in my mouth, or I’d a died, Tom. The widow wouldn’t let me smoke; she wouldn’t let me yell, she wouldn’t let me gape, nor stretch, nor scratch in front of people—” [Then with a spasm of special irritation and injury]—“And dad would fetch it, she prayed all the time! I never see such a woman! I _had_ to shove, Tom—I just had to. And besides, that school’s going to open, and I’d have had to go to it—well, I wouldn’t stand _that_, Tom. Look here, Tom, being rich ain’t what it’s cracked up to be. It’s just worry and worry, and sweat and sweat, and wishing you was dead all the time. Now these clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I ain’t ever going to shake ’em off again. Tom, I wouldn’t ever got into all this trouble if it hadn’t been for that money; now you just take my share of it along with yours, and give me a ten-cent piece sometimes—not many times, because I don’t give a damn for a thing unless it’s tolerably hard to get—and you go and talk the widow out of it for me.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. It ain’t fair; and besides, if you try this thing just a little longer, you’ll come to like it.”

“Like it! Yes—the way I’d like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in them cursed stuffy houses. I like the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’ll stick with ’em, too. Blame it all! just as we’d got guns, and a cave, and everything all set up for robbing—here this damn foolishness has got to come along and spoil it all!”

Tom saw his chance—

“Look here, Huck, being rich isn’t going to stop me from turning robber.”

“No! Oh, good grief; are you in real dead-wood earnest, Tom?”

“Just as dead earnest as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you into the gang if you ain’t respectable, you know.”

Huck’s joy was cut short.

“Can’t let me in, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"cf8dc8ae1d6ceb4a45049ab0","rewritten_text":"“Yes—burglars’ tools. That seems to explain a lot. But what made you change your mind? What did you think we’d find?”

Huck was trapped by the man’s questioning look. He would have given anything for an answer that sounded believable, but nothing came to him. The look kept pressing on him, deeper and deeper. He had no time to think it through, so he took a guess and said it weakly:

“Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Huck was too upset to smile, but the old man laughed loudly and happily. He shook himself from head to foot, then said that a laugh like that was good for a man’s pocket, because it cut down the doctor’s bill—like everything else. After that, he added:

“Poor old chap—you’re pale and worn out. You’re not well at all. No wonder you’re a little jumpy and out of sorts. But you’ll get better. Rest and sleep should set you right, I hope.”

Huck felt irritated that he had been such a fool and had shown suspicious excitement. He had already dropped the idea that the parcel brought from the tavern was the treasure as soon as he heard what people were saying at the widow’s stile. He had only thought it wasn’t the treasure, though—he hadn’t known it wasn’t—and that made the idea of a captured bundle too much for his self-control. Still, he felt better that the whole thing had happened. Now he knew for sure that that bundle wasn’t the one, and his mind was finally at rest. Everything seemed to be moving the right way again. The treasure must still be in No. 2. The men would be caught and jailed that day. Then he and Tom could take the gold that night without any trouble and without fear of being interrupted.

Just as breakfast was finished, there was a knock at the door. Huck sprang up to find a hiding place, because he didn’t want to be connected to what had happened. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas. He also noticed groups of citizens climbing up the hill to stare at the stile. So the news had spread. The Welshman had to tell the story of the night to the visitors, and the widow’s gratitude for being saved was plain to see.

“Don’t say a word about it, madam. There’s another you’re more grateful to than you are to me and my boys, maybe, but he won’t let me tell his name. We wouldn’t have been there if it weren’t for him.”"}

{"request_id":"d7b62bb12cd6affc419a7930","rewritten_text":"At the sight of it, the Ourang-Outang sprang immediately through the chamber door, down the stairs, and then—through an unfortunately open window—into the street.

The Frenchman followed in despair. The ape, razor still in hand, would occasionally stop to look back and gesture wildly at its pursuer, until the latter had nearly caught up. Then it bolted again. In this way the chase went on for a long time. The streets were profoundly quiet, since it was nearly three o’clock in the morning. As it ran down an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive’s attention was caught by a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s chamber, on the fourth story of her house. It rushed to the building, saw the lightning rod, climbed up with unbelievable agility, caught hold of the shutter—thrown fully back against the wall—and used it to swing itself directly onto the headboard of the bed. The whole feat took less than a minute. The Ourang-Outang kicked the shutter open again as it entered the room.

Meanwhile, the sailor was both relieved and confused. He had strong hopes of recapturing the brute now, since it could hardly escape the trap it had entered except by the rod, where it might be intercepted as it came down. On the other hand, there was plenty to fear about what it might do inside the house. That thought pushed him to keep following the fugitive. Climbing a lightning rod is not difficult, especially for a sailor; but when he reached the height of the window, which lay far to his left, his progress stopped. All he could do was lean over far enough to get a look into the room. At that glimpse, he nearly lost his grip from sheer horror. It was then that those dreadful shrieks rose during the night, the ones that had jolted the people of the Rue Morgue awake. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed in their nightclothes, seemed to have been busy arranging some papers in the iron chest already mentioned, which had been wheeled into the middle of the room. It was open, and its contents lay beside it on the floor. The victims must have been sitting with their backs toward the window; and, from the time that passed between the beast’s entry and the screams, it seems likely it wasn’t noticed right away. The shutter slamming shut would naturally have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor looked in, the gigantic animal had seized Madame L’Espanaye by the hair—loose, since she had been combing it—and was brandishing the razor near her face, mimicking the motions of a barber."}

{"request_id":"37def0f9c6c3131a47b354ec","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis—at Lady Canterville’s earnest request—had agreed to keep in her former position. As they stepped down, she gave each of them a low curtsey and said, in a quaint, old-fashioned way, “I bid you welcome to Canterville Chase.” After her, they walked through the fine Tudor hall into the library, a long, low room paneled in black oak, with a large stained-glass window at the far end. Tea had been laid out there for them, and after they took off their wraps, they sat down and began to look around while Mrs. Umney attended to them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor just by the fireplace and, without realizing what it meant, said to Mrs. Umney, “I’m afraid something has been spilled there.”

“Yes, madam,” the old housekeeper replied in a low voice. “Blood has been spilled on that spot.”

“How dreadful,” Mrs. Otis exclaimed. “I don’t at all like blood stains in a sitting room. It has to be removed at once.”

The old woman smiled and answered in the same low, mysterious tone, “It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, who was murdered right here by her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived through her by nine years and then disappeared suddenly under very mysterious circumstances. His body has never been found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. The bloodstain has been admired by tourists and others, and it cannot be removed.”

“That’s all nonsense,” Washington Otis snapped. “Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it up in no time.” Before the terrified housekeeper could stop him, he dropped to his knees and began rapidly scrubbing the floor with a small stick that looked like a black cosmetic. In a few moments, not a trace of the bloodstain could be seen.

“I knew Pinkerton would do it,” he said triumphantly, looking around at his admiring family. But no sooner had he spoken than a terrible flash of lightning lit up the gloomy room, followed by a fearful crash of thunder that made them all jump to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What a monstrous climate!” the American Minister said calmly as he lit a long cheroot. “I guess the old country is so overpopulated that they don’t have decent weather for everyone. I’ve always believed emigration is the only solution for England.”

“My dear Hiram,” Mrs. Otis cried, “what can we do with a woman who faints?”

“Charge it to her like breakages,” the Minister answered. “She won’t faint after that.” And within moments, Mrs. Umney certainly came around."}

{"request_id":"2aa89ea67084f46e59b94e36","rewritten_text":"Great God! If, for even a moment, I had guessed the hellish plan of my cruel enemy, I would have banished myself from my native country forever and wandered the world as a lonely outcast rather than agree to this wretched marriage. But it was as if the monster had used magic to blind me to his true intentions. When I believed I was only preparing my own death, I hurried the death of someone far dearer to me.

As the day of our marriage came closer, whether out of fear or because I sensed something was coming, my heart sank. I hid what I felt behind an act of cheerful excitement. It made my father smile and look pleased, but it hardly fooled Elizabeth, who watched me closely. She expected our union to bring calm, steady happiness, though it was mixed with a little fear. Past troubles had taught her that what now seemed certain and real might quickly fade into nothing, leaving no trace except deep, lasting regret.

Plans were made for the wedding. People came to offer congratulations, and everyone looked as if they were happy. I kept my anxiety locked away as best I could, even though it was eating at me. I also let it show, in a way that seemed sincere, in the plans my father made—plans that might only serve as decorations for my tragedy. Through my father’s efforts, part of Elizabeth’s inheritance was restored to her by the Austrian government. She had a small property on the shores of Como. It was decided that right after our marriage we would go to Villa Lavenza and spend our first days of happiness by the beautiful lake near it.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to protect myself in case the fiend attacked me openly. I carried pistols and a dagger with me at all times. I stayed alert for any trick or deception, and these steps helped me feel calmer. As the wedding date drew near, the threat seemed less like something real and more like a delusion that should not disturb my peace. The happiness I hoped for in my marriage felt more and more certain as the day for the ceremony approached. People kept talking about it as an event that no accident could possibly stop.

Elizabeth appeared happy, and my calm manner helped her feel at ease. But on the day that was meant to fulfill my wishes and my fate, she was sad. A sense of evil filled her, and perhaps she was also thinking about the terrible secret I had promised to tell her the next day."}

{"request_id":"e9d52a5e02fde38d79d96213","rewritten_text":"I ran to her and lifted her into my arms, showering her with caresses as I begged:

“Speak, darling—speak! What is it?”

Her head went heavy against my chest, and she gasped, almost too faint to hear:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Quick!” I shouted to Clarence. “Call the king’s homeopath—get him here!”

Within two minutes I was kneeling by the child’s crib, and Sandy was sending servants here, there, and everywhere, all through the palace. I took in the situation at a glance—membranous croup. I leaned down and whispered:

“Wake up, sweetheart. Hello-Central.”

She opened her soft eyes, sluggishly, and seemed to manage:

“Papa.”

That was a comfort. She wasn’t dead yet. I had sulphur prepared; I even got up and took care of the croup-kettle myself. I don’t sit back and wait for doctors when Sandy or the child is sick. I knew how to nurse both of them, and I had experience. This little one had spent much of its short life in my arms, and I often could calm its troubles and make it laugh through the tear-wet shine in its eyelashes—when even its mother couldn’t.

Sir Launcelot, in his finest armor, strode into the great hall on his way to the stock-board. He was president of the stock-board and occupied the Siege Perilous, which he had bought from Sir Galahad. The stock-board was made up of the Knights of the Round Table, and they used the Round Table for business now. Seats there—well, you’d never believe the number, so it’s pointless to say it. Sir Launcelot was a bear, and he’d staked out a corner in one of the new lines, and was just getting ready to squeeze the shorts today. But what did that matter? He was still the same old Launcelot, and when he glanced in as he passed the door and saw that his pet was sick, that was all it took. Let the bulls and bears fight it out however they wanted—he would come right in here and stand by little Hello-Central as long as he could. And that’s exactly what he did. He tossed his helmet into the corner, and in half a minute he had a fresh wick in the alcohol lamp and was firing up the croup-kettle.

By then Sandy had built a blanket canopy over the crib, and everything was ready.

Sir Launcelot got the steam going. He and I loaded the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a touch of lactic acid, then filled it with water and set the steam-spout under the canopy. Everything was set properly now, and we sat down on either side of the crib to keep watch."}

{"request_id":"2cfe0bf0aa7e15b5308caeb2","rewritten_text":"You’ve raised an artificial soul and spirit in him, ma’am—hardly the sort of thing that suits a boy in his state. The board, Mrs. Sowerberry, who are practical philosophers, will tell you as much. What business have paupers with soul or spirit? It’s quite sufficient that we allow them living bodies. Had you kept the boy on gruel, ma’am, this never would have come about.”

“Dear, dear!” cried Mrs. Sowerberry, with pious eyes turned up toward the kitchen ceiling. “This is what comes of being liberal!”

Mrs. Sowerberry’s liberality toward Oliver had amounted to giving him, in abundance, all the dirty odds and ends that no one else would touch; and so there was no small share of meekness and self-sacrifice in her, in choosing to stand under Mr. Bumble’s heavy accusation, though, to do her justice, she was entirely innocent—neither in thought, word, nor deed.

“Ah!” said Mr. Bumble, once the lady let her gaze fall back to earth. “The only thing I can see to do now is to leave him in the cellar for a day or so, until he’s starved down a bit; then take him out and keep him on gruel through the whole apprenticeship. He comes of a bad family, Mrs. Sowerberry—excitable natures! Both the nurse and the doctor said that his mother made her way here, against difficulties and pain that would have killed any woman of good disposition, weeks before.”

At this point in Mr. Bumble’s speech, Oliver—just hearing enough to know that his mother was being spoken of—began kicking again with such force that every other sound was swallowed up. Sowerberry returned at that moment. When Oliver’s offence had been explained to him, with the sort of exaggerations the ladies thought most likely to stir his anger, he unlocked the cellar-door in an instant and dragged the rebellious apprentice out by the collar.

Oliver’s clothes were torn from the beating he had received; his face was bruised and scratched; and his hair lay scattered over his forehead. The angry flush, however, had not left him. When he was hauled from his prison, he scowled straight at Noah, and looked in no way daunted.

“Now, you’re a fine young fellow, aren’t you?” said Sowerberry, giving Oliver a shake and a box on the ear.

“He called my mother names,” answered Oliver.

“Well, what if he did, you little ungrateful wretch?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She deserved what he said—and more.”

“She didn’t,” said Oliver.

“She did,” said Mrs. Sowerberry.

“It’s a lie!” said Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry broke into a flood of tears.

That flood of tears left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. Had he delayed for even a moment before punishing Oliver most severely, it would have been plain to every seasoned reader that he would, by all the established precedents in disputes of matrimony, have been a brute—an unnatural husband—an insulting creature—a base imitation of a man—and a number of other agreeable descriptions too many to list within the limits of this chapter."}

{"request_id":"3a19e3018a75e4235f343899","rewritten_text":"When Tom woke up in the morning, he couldn’t help wondering where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked around. Then it all made sense. It was a cool gray dawn, and the woods felt calm and restful, with a deep quiet that seemed to fill everything. Not a leaf moved. Not a sound broke in on Nature’s steady thinking. Dew drops clung to the leaves and grass. A thin layer of white ash covered the fire, and a little blue ribbon of smoke rose straight into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep.

Far off in the woods, a bird called, and another answered. Soon a woodpecker began hammering. Little by little, the morning light grew brighter and clearer, and more sounds came, until life really showed itself. Tom watched it all with the quiet wonder of a boy who was thinking. A small green worm crawled over a wet, dewy leaf. It lifted about two-thirds of its body into the air now and then, “sniffing around,” and then crawled on again. Tom said it was measuring. When the worm came closer to him, Tom stayed as still as a stone. His hopes rose and fell as the worm kept moving toward him or seemed ready to go somewhere else. At last, it paused with its curved body raised in the air, then came down firmly on Tom’s leg and started crawling over him. His whole heart felt glad, because that meant he was going to get a new suit of clothes—no doubt about it—a bright, pirate-style uniform.

Then a line of ants appeared, as if from nowhere, and went to work. One ant struggled hard with a dead spider that was five times its size, carrying it straight up a tree trunk. A brown-spotted ladybug climbed to the top of a tall blade of grass. Tom leaned close and said, “Lady-bug, lady-bug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children’s alone.” The ladybug took off and flew away to check on it. That didn’t surprise Tom, because he already knew this insect believed stories about fires, and he had tested that idea more than once. Next came a tumblebug, pushing its ball along with steady effort. Tom touched it, and the creature pulled its legs in against its body and pretended to be dead.

By this time, the birds were almost everywhere. A catbird, the Northern mocker, landed in a tree above Tom’s head and sang her neighbors’ sounds with pure joy. Then a shrill jay swooped down, flashed blue, and stopped on a twig within the boy’s reach. It tilted its head to one side, stared at the strangers with intense curiosity, and seemed to study them. A gray squirrel and a larger “fox” squirrel skittered along too, stopping now and then to look and chatter. The wild animals probably had never seen a human being before, and they didn’t know whether to be afraid."}

{"request_id":"aafd61e81d389ceb484fa57e","rewritten_text":"Moreover, this knot is one that very few besides sailors can make, and it is peculiar to the Maltese. I picked up the ribbon at the foot of the lightning-rod. It could not have belonged to either of the dead men. Now, if I am mistaken in the inference I draw from this ribbon—that the Frenchman was a sailor attached to a Maltese vessel—then, at any rate, I have done no harm in saying what I put in the advertisement. If I am wrong, he will only think that I have been led astray by some circumstance he will not trouble himself to look into. But if I am right, a great advantage is secured. Though he is aware of nothing of the murder, the Frenchman will naturally pause before replying to the advertisement—before demanding the Ourang-Outang. He will argue to himself thus:—‘I am innocent; I am poor; my Ourang-Outang is of immense value—to someone in my position, a fortune in its own right—so why throw it away through idle fears of danger? It lies here within my reach. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne—at a great remove from the scene of that slaughter. How could it ever be suspected that a brute beast committed the deed? The police are to blame; they have not obtained the smallest clue. Even if they were to trace the animal, it would be impossible to show that I knew of the murder, or to connect me with guilt on the ground of such knowledge. Above all, I am known. The advertiser points to me as the owner of the beast. I cannot tell how far his information goes. If I were to avoid claiming a property of such value—one that is known I possess—I would at least make the animal liable to suspicion. It is not my plan to draw attention either to myself or to the beast. I will answer the advertisement, take the Ourang-Outang, and keep it close until this business has blown over.’”

At that instant we heard a step on the stairs.

“Be ready,” said Dupin, “with your pistols; but neither use them nor show them until you have a signal from me.”

The front door of the house had been left open, and the visitor had come in without ringing, and gone forward several paces upon the staircase. Now, however, he seemed to waver. Soon we heard him descending. Dupin moved quickly toward the door, when we heard him again coming up. He did not go back a second time, but stepped forward with decision and knocked at the door of our chamber.

“Come in,” said Dupin, in a cheerful, hearty voice.

A man entered. He was a sailor, evidently—a tall, thick-set, muscular-looking fellow, with a certain dare-devil cast to his face, though not altogether unpleasing."}
