{"request_id":"14025cbd15c94d471aaf3c1d","rewritten_text":"I walked quickly, and we soon reached my college. Then I stopped and thought, and the thought made me shiver: the creature I had left in my apartment might still be there, alive, moving around. I dreaded seeing this monster, but I feared even more that Henry might see him. So I asked him to wait a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs, and I hurried up to my room. My hand was already on the door lock before I caught myself. I paused, and a cold shiver ran through me. I threw the door open hard, the way children do when they expect a ghost to be waiting for them on the other side. But nothing was there. I stepped in carefully. The apartment was empty, and my bedroom was also free of its hideous visitor. I could hardly believe such good luck, but once I was sure my enemy had truly gone, I clapped with joy and ran down to Clerval.

We went into my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast, but I couldn’t calm down. It wasn’t only happiness. I felt my skin tingle as if I were too sensitive, and my pulse raced. I couldn’t stay in one place for even a moment. I jumped over the chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed out loud. At first, Clerval thought my excitement was just from joy at his arrival. But when he watched me more closely, he saw a wild look in my eyes that he couldn’t explain. My loud, uncontrolled laughter frightened and shocked him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what is wrong? Don’t laugh like that. You’re not well. What’s causing all this?”

“Don’t ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, because I thought I saw the dreaded spectre slip into the room. “He can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined the monster had grabbed me. I fought wildly and then fell into a fit.

Poor Clerval—what must he have felt? The meeting he had expected with such joy had turned so suddenly into bitterness. But I wasn’t there to see his grief. I was unconscious, and I didn’t regain my senses for a long, long time.

This was the start of a nervous fever that kept me sick for several months. During all that time Henry was my only nurse. Later I learned that, because he knew my father was old and not fit for such a long trip, and because he also knew how much my sickness would hurt Elizabeth, he spared them this pain by hiding how bad my condition really was."}

{"request_id":"cd00447cb4ba2d82015b644e","rewritten_text":"He mounted a fiery horse—the same one that had carried him on to victory in Greece—and, by throwing himself into deadening exertion, he dulled the sharpness of a troubled mind by giving himself over to mere animal sensation.

He recovered himself slowly; and at last, as though emerging from the effects of poison, he raised his head out of the vapours of fever and passion into the quiet air of sober reflection. He began to consider what ought to be done. The first thing that struck him was the length of time that had passed, since it was madness, not any reasonable impulse, that had governed his actions. A month had gone by, and during it he had not seen Evadne. Her influence—tied to only a few of the lasting feelings in his heart—had greatly withered. He was no longer her slave—no longer her lover: he would never see her again, and, by the completeness of his return, would deserve Perdita’s confidence.

Yet, even as he resolved this, his thoughts conjured the wretched dwelling of the Greek girl. A home she had refused to trade, from noble and lofty principle, for one of greater luxury. He recalled the splendour of her situation and appearance when he first came to know her; he recalled her life at Constantinople, attended by every circumstance of eastern magnificence; and then her present penury, her daily labour, her lonely condition, her faded, famine-struck cheek. Compassion swelled within him. He would see her once more; he would devise some plan to restore her to society, and to the comforts of her station; their separation would then follow, as a matter of course.

Again he considered how, throughout this long month, he had kept away from Perdita, slipping from her as if from the stings of his own conscience. But he was awake now; all this must be put right; and a future devotion would blot out the memory of this one stain upon the serenity of their life. He grew cheerful at the thought, and with sober resolve laid out the course he meant to follow. He remembered that he had promised Perdita to be present this very evening—the 19th of October, the anniversary of his election as Protector—at a festival held in his honour. Surely such a festival ought to be a good omen for the happiness of coming years. First, he would call on Evadne; he would not linger; but he owed her some account, some compensation for his long absence without word. Then, to Perdita, to the world he had neglected, to the duties of society, the splendour of rank, and the enjoyment of power.

After the scene set down in the pages before, Perdita had expected an entire change in Raymond’s manners and conduct. She looked for freer communication, and a return to those habits of affectionate intercourse that had been the delight of her life."}

{"request_id":"5e28f938accc8a1424577964","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was very upset about Lord Canterville’s refusal. He begged the peer to change his mind, but Lord Canterville was kind but firm. In the end, he persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the present the ghost had given her. Then, in the spring of 1890, when the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s first drawing-room because of her marriage, her jewels became the subject of everyone’s admiration. Virginia received the coronet, which is the reward for all good little American girls, and she married her young lover as soon as he was old enough. They were both so charming, and they loved each other so much, that almost everyone was happy about the match. The only exception was the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had tried to get the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters. She had even given three expensive dinner parties to make it happen, and, oddly enough, Mr. Otis was among the guests. Mr. Otis liked the young Duke very much, but in theory he still disliked titles. As he put it himself, he was “not without apprehension lest, amid the enervating influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true principles of republican simplicity should be forgotten.” Still, his objections were completely ignored. I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter leaning on his arm, he was the proudest man in all of England.

After the honeymoon ended, the Duke and Duchess went to Canterville Chase. The day after they arrived, they walked in the afternoon to the lonely churchyard near the pine woods. At first there had been a lot of trouble about what to put on Sir Simon’s tombstone. In the end, they decided to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess brought some lovely roses, and she laid them on the grave. After they had stood there for a while, they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. The Duchess sat down on a fallen pillar. Her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and looking up at her beautiful eyes. Suddenly he threw his cigarette away, took her hand, and said, “Virginia, a wife should have no secrets from her husband.”

“Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.”

“Yes, you have,” he said, smiling. “You have never told me what happened to you when you were locked up with the ghost.”

“I have never told any one, Cecil,” Virginia answered seriously."}

{"request_id":"1c57e28902b9b092963c265b","rewritten_text":"She would make such a charming companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed with all of it, though he added,

“Our little friend Harriet Smith, however, is just as pretty a sort of young person. You will find Harriet delightful. Emma could hardly have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am very glad to hear it—but only Jane Fairfax is known to be so very accomplished and superior!—and she is exactly Emma’s age.”

This subject was talked over with great pleasure, and other remarks of the same kind followed, passing away with much the same ease; yet the evening did not end without a small return of uneasiness. The gruel was brought in and furnished plenty to say—general praise and many observations—about the undoubted wholesomeness of it for every constitution, along with rather sharp remarks on the many houses where it was never served in a way that was tolerable; but, among the instances the daughter had to mention, the latest—and therefore the most noticeable—was in her own cook at South End, a young woman taken on for the time, who could never make sense of what she meant by a basin of nice smooth gruel, thin, but not too thin. However often she had asked for it and ordered it, she had never been able to get anything fit to be called tolerable. That was a dangerous opening.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with tender concern. The words in Emma’s ear conveyed, “Ah! there’s no end to the sad consequences of your going to South End. It really should not be talked of.” For a little while she hoped he would not return to it, and that his quiet reflection might be enough to bring him back to the comfort of his own smooth gruel. After some minutes, though, he began,

“I shall always be very sorry that you went to the sea this autumn, instead of staying here.”

“But why should you be sorry, sir?—I assure you, it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides, if you were determined to go to the sea, it would have been better not to have been to South End. South End is an unhealthy place. Perry was quite surprised to hear you had chosen South End.”

“I know there’s such an opinion among many people, but it’s quite a mistake, sir.—We were all in perfect health there, and never felt the least inconvenience from the mud; and Mr. Wingfield says it is entirely wrong to think the place unhealthy; and I’m sure he can be relied on, for he understands the nature of the air thoroughly, and his own brother and family have been there again and again.”

“You ought to have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere.—Perry was a week at Cromer once, and he thinks it the very best of all the sea-bathing places.”"}

{"request_id":"7a9303d2a95846fc3513f8dd","rewritten_text":"Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not destroyed by spirits. The people who carried out the crime were real, and they escaped in a real, physical way. So how did they get away? There is only one sensible way to reason this out, and it must lead us to a clear answer. Let us look, step by step, at every possible way out.

It is clear that the assassins were in the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye was found, or at least in the room next to it, when the group went up the stairs. That means we only need to search for exits from these two rooms. The police have examined the floors, the ceilings, and the walls in every direction. No secret openings could have escaped their attention. Still, I did not rely only on their eyes. I checked myself. There were, then, no secret exits.

Both doors that led from the rooms into the hallway were locked from the inside, with the keys kept inside as well. So we turn to the chimneys. They are fairly normal in width for about eight or ten feet above the hearths, but they cannot fit the body of a large cat anywhere along their length. Since escape through the ways we have already considered is impossible, we are left with only the windows. From the front room, no one could have escaped without being seen by the crowd in the street. The murderers must, then, have gone through the windows of the back room.

Now that we have reached this conclusion so clearly, it is not our job, as thinkers, to throw it out just because it seems impossible. We only need to show that these “impossibilities” are not actually impossible.

“There are two windows in the room. One of them is not blocked by furniture, and you can see it fully. The lower part of the other is hidden from view by the heavy bedstead pushed right up against it. The first window was found locked from the inside. It resisted the strongest efforts of the people who tried to lift it. A large hole had been drilled into the left side of its frame, and a very thick nail was fitted into that hole, almost up to the top. When the other window was checked, a similar nail was found fitted in the same way. A strong attempt to lift that sash also failed. The police were now fully convinced that no one had escaped through those windows. And so, they thought it was unnecessary to remove the nails and open the windows.

“My own examination was more careful, for the reason I just mentioned—because this was the place where I knew that every apparent impossibility had to be proven, in reality, not to be one.”"}

{"request_id":"e15764dbc6a2eeff2ae88196","rewritten_text":"“Why, you can’t mean to say—” my sister began.

“Yes I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook; “but just hold on. Joseph—go on. Well done! Go on!”

“What would respectable company think,” Joe continued, “of twenty pounds?”

“Handsome would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well, then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That abject hypocrite, Pumblechook, nodded once more, and with a patronizing chuckle said, “It’s more than that, Mum. Good again! Follow her up, Joseph!”

“Then to settle it,” Joe said, pleased as anything, as he handed the bag to my sister; “it’s five-and-twenty pounds.”

“It’s five-and-twenty pounds, Mum,” the basest of swindlers echoed, rising to shake her hand; “and it’s no more than your merits (as I said when my opinion was asked), and I wish you joy of the money!”

Had the villain stopped there, his wickedness would already have been bad enough; but he deepened his guilt by taking me into custody, with a show of patronage that made all his earlier villainy seem small.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, taking me by the arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those that always see things through once they’ve been started. This boy must be bound—no delay. That’s _my_ way. Bound out of hand.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said, clutching the money, “we’re truly in your debt.”

“Don’t mind me, Mum,” returned that diabolical cornchandler. “A pleasure’s a pleasure, wherever you find it. But this boy—you know—we’ve got to have him bound. I said I’d look after it—tell you the truth.”

The Justices were sitting in the Town Hall close by, so we went straight over to have me bound apprentice to Joe in the Magisterial presence. I say we went over, but in truth Pumblechook shoved me along, as if I’d just then lifted a pocket or fired a shot; and in fact the general notion in Court was that I’d been caught red-handed. As Pumblechook pushed me through the crowd, I heard people say, “What’s he done?” and others, “He’s a young ’un too, but he looks bad, don’t he?” One mild, kindly-looking person even pressed a tract into my hand, with a woodcut of a spiteful young man fitted out with a complete sausage-shop of fetters, and the title TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall struck me as a strange place. There were higher pews than in a church, and people leaned over them to watch. The Justices—one with a powdered head—sat back in chairs with arms folded, or took snuff, or nodded off, or wrote, or read the newspapers. On the walls hung some bright black portraits, which my untrained eye took for a mash of hardbake and sticking-plaster."}

{"request_id":"f6d1fe585e6187312af934b3","rewritten_text":"I ran to her and lifted her into my arms. I covered her with kisses and caresses, and begged her:

“Please, darling—tell me what’s wrong. Speak!”

Her head went heavy against my chest. She gasped, almost too softly to hear:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Now!” I shouted to Clarence. “Call the king’s homeopath and have him come right away!”

Within two minutes, I was kneeling beside the child’s crib. Sandy was sending servants everywhere across the palace. I understood what was happening at once: membranous croup. I leaned close and whispered, “Wake up, sweetheart. Hello-Central.”

Her eyes opened slowly, and she seemed to struggle to say, “Papa.”

That was a relief. She was still far from dead. I had sulphur prepared, and I got the croup-kettle going myself. I don’t just sit and wait for doctors while Sandy or the child is sick. I knew how to care for both of them, and I had done it before. This little one had spent much of its short life in my arms, and I often managed to calm it and make it laugh again through the tears on its eyelashes—when even its mother couldn’t.

Sir Launcelot came striding through the great hall in his finest armor, on his way to the stock-board. He was president of it, and he sat in the Siege Perilous, which he had bought from Sir Galahad. The stock-board was made up of the Knights of the Round Table, and they used the Round Table for business now. The seats were worth a fortune—so much that you wouldn’t believe the number, and it wouldn’t help to say it. Sir Launcelot was a bear, and he had a place in one of the new lines; he was getting ready to squeeze the shorts today. But what did that matter? He was still the same old Launcelot. When he glanced in as he passed the door and saw that his pet was sick, that was all he needed. Let the bulls and bears fight it out without him—he came straight in and stood by little Hello-Central as long as he could. That’s exactly what he did. He tossed his helmet into the corner, and in half a minute he had a new wick in the alcohol lamp and was firing up the croup-kettle.

By then, Sandy had set up a blanket canopy over the crib, and everything was ready. Sir Launcelot got the steam going. He and I filled the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a touch of lactic acid, then filled it with water and placed the steam-spout under the canopy. Everything was set. We sat on either side of the crib to keep watch."}

{"request_id":"ae82d07b82b6d83a889e301d","rewritten_text":"She now felt a strong urge to go to the outer door; she wanted to see whether it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of some other motive? Captain Wentworth must be out of sight. She rose from her seat—she would go; one half of her shouldn’t always be so much wiser than the other half, or always suspecting it of being worse than it was. She would find out if it rained. But she was sent back at once by Captain Wentworth’s entrance himself, among a party of gentlemen and ladies—evidently people he knew—whom he must have joined a little below Milsom Street.

He was more visibly struck and confused by seeing her than she had ever noticed before; he looked quite red. For the first time, since their renewed acquaintance, she felt that she was betraying the least sensibility of the two. She had the advantage over him in the preparation of the last few moments. All the overpowering, blinding, bewildering first effects of strong surprise were over for her. Still, she had enough to feel. It was agitation, pain, pleasure—something caught between delight and misery.

He spoke to her, and then turned away. The tone of his manner was embarrassment. She couldn’t call it cold, or friendly, or anything so clearly as embarrassed.

After a short interval, however, he came toward her again and spoke once more. Their mutual inquiries on common subjects passed; neither of them, probably, learned much from what they heard, and Anne continued to be fully aware that he was less at ease than before. By dint of being together so much, they had managed to speak to each other with a considerable show of indifference and calmness; but he couldn’t do it now. Time had changed him, or Louisa had changed him. There was some kind of awareness in him. He looked very well—not as if he had been suffering in health or spirits—and he talked of Uppercross, of the Musgroves, even of Louisa, and had even a brief moment of his own arch significance as he mentioned her; yet still it was Captain Wentworth who was not comfortable, not at ease, not able to pretend that he was.

It didn’t surprise Anne, but it grieved her, to see that Elizabeth wouldn’t recognize him. She could tell that he saw Elizabeth, that Elizabeth saw him, and that there was complete internal recognition on both sides. She was convinced he was ready to be acknowledged as an acquaintance, expecting it; and she had the pain of watching her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot was growing very impatient, now drew up; the servant came in to announce it."}

{"request_id":"2e3fe7a5be77df5ab229e44b","rewritten_text":"But now she wished it had not happened. She thought he had drunk too much of Mr. Weston’s fine wine, and she was sure he would soon be talking nonsense.

To keep him under control as much as she could, she immediately tried to speak with perfect calm and seriousness about the weather and the night. But almost at once, before she had even finished starting, they had passed through the sweep-gate and joined the other carriage, and then her plan was ruined. Her hand was seized, her attention was demanded, and Mr. Elton actually began making violent love to her. He took advantage of the moment, saying things that must already be well known. He hoped, feared, adored her, and declared that he was ready to die if she refused him. Yet he also seemed to believe that his strong attachment, his unmatched love, and his extraordinary passion could not fail to have some effect. In short, he was determined to be accepted seriously as soon as possible. That was exactly what he was doing. Without any scruple, without apology, and with little visible hesitation, Mr. Elton—the man who loved Harriet—was now speaking as if he were her lover.

She tried to stop him, but it was no use. He kept going and said everything he wanted to say. Even though she was angry, the thought of the moment made her decide to hold herself back when she finally spoke. She felt that at least half of his foolishness must be caused by drunkenness, and that she could hope it would pass with the hour. So, mixing seriousness with a bit of playfulness, the way she thought would suit his half-sober, half-drunk state, she answered,

“I am very much astonished, Mr. Elton. This to me! You forget yourself. You take me for my friend. If you have any message to Miss Smith, I will be happy to deliver it; but please, no more of this to me.”

“Miss Smith!—a message to Miss Smith!—What could she possibly mean!” He repeated her words with such confidence, and with such showy pretending surprise, that she could not help replying quickly,

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behavior! I can explain it only in one way: you are not yourself, or you could not speak to me, or about Harriet, in such a way. Command yourself enough to say no more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk enough wine to lift his spirits, not enough to confuse his mind. He understood exactly what he meant. After warmly protesting against her suspicion, saying it was the most harmful thing she could believe, and after touching lightly on his respect for Miss Smith as her friend—though admitting he was surprised that Miss Smith was even mentioned—he returned at once to his own feelings. He was very urgent for a favorable answer."}

{"request_id":"c776d4f8c4a223a488195648","rewritten_text":"My heart was pounding, and I felt afraid, though I did not know why. I sent the servant away, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were the words it contained.

“My dear Child,

“I have betrayed your trust. I tried to poison your mind, and I have made your innocent heart learn the look and the words of unlawful, monstrous passion. I must make up for these crimes, and I must try to match my punishment to my guilt. You are, I doubt not, ready for what I am about to tell you. We must separate, and be divided forever.

“I take away your parent and your only friend. You are left with no shelter in the world. Your hopes are destroyed. The peace and safety of your pure mind are gone. When you remember, you will see terrible images of guilt, and you will suffer the pain of innocent love betrayed. Yet I am the one who brings all this misery on you. I am the one who casts you out, and without mercy puts the seal of distrust and agony on the heart and brow of my own child. With devilish carelessness, I tried to steal away her beauty and replace it with the ugly shape of sin. In the deep anguish of my heart, I beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity. You must, and you do, hate me. But forgive me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts follow me into my exile with unrelenting anger. I must never see you again. I must never hear your voice again. Still, the gentle whispers of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning of my confused mind and heart. I am sure I would feel it even in my grave. And I dare to ask this of you by telling you how badly I was tricked into this net of burning anguish, and how I struggled to free myself. In truth, if your soul were less pure and bright, I would not try to defend myself to you. I would be afraid that if I made you think of me with less hatred, you might hate vice less. But when I speak to you, it feels as if I am appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness. I must try to earn it, or I must despair. So I urge you to listen to my words. And if, by some sharp agony and remorse that tears the mind apart like madness, my guilt can be lessened in any way, then perhaps you will think I deserve some compassion.

“I ask you to remember our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned after sixteen years of weary wandering. During that time, even though I faced many dangers and misfortunes, my feelings were completely empty."}

{"request_id":"7aa91bfb46a7895d61cadd0d","rewritten_text":"After a while, twelve o’clock boomed from the tall tower at Westminster, and with each strike of the deep, resonant bell the night seemed to shudder. Then the railway lights went out; only one solitary lamp remained, shining like a large ruby on a giant mast, and the roar of the city faded.

At two o’clock he got up and strolled toward Blackfriars. Everything looked unreal. Everything felt like some strange dream. The houses across the river seemed built out of darkness. It was as if silver and shadow had remade the world. The huge dome of St. Paul’s loomed like a bubble in the dim air.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle, he saw a man leaning over the parapet. When he came closer, the man looked up, and the gaslight fell full on his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist. No one could mistake the fat, flabby face, the gold-rimmed spectacles, the sickly, weak smile, the sensual mouth.

Lord Arthur stopped. A brilliant idea flashed through him, and he moved quietly up behind. In an instant he had seized Mr. Podgers by the legs and thrown him into the Thames. There was a coarse oath, a heavy splash, and then everything went still. Lord Arthur looked anxiously over, but he could see nothing of the cheiromantist except a tall hat, spinning in an eddy of moonlit water. After a time even that sank, and no trace of Mr. Podgers was visible. Once he thought he caught sight of the bulky, misshapen figure striking out for the staircase by the bridge, and a horrible feeling of failure swept over him, but it turned out to be only a reflection. When the moon slipped out from behind a cloud, it was gone. At last it seemed he had accepted the decree of destiny. He let out a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name came to his lips.

“Have you dropped anything, sir?” a voice said behind him suddenly.

He turned around and saw a policeman holding a bull’s-eye lantern.

“Nothing of importance, sergeant,” he replied, smiling. Then, hailing a passing hansom, he jumped in and told the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

For the next few days he swung between hope and fear. There were moments when he almost expected Mr. Podgers to walk into the room, and yet at other times he felt that Fate couldn’t be so unjust to him. Twice he went to the cheiromantist’s address in West Moon Street, but he couldn’t bring himself to ring the bell. He wanted certainty, and he was afraid of it.

Finally it came. He was sitting in the club’s smoking-room, having tea, listening rather dully to Surbiton’s account of the last comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter came in with the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"ede3578341021d4a9718f6aa","rewritten_text":"Then I repeated to myself that beautiful passage about Dante’s arrival in the earthly Paradise. I thought it would be wonderful if, when I wandered along those lovely banks, I could watch the car of light come down and bring my long-lost parent back to me. While I waited for that moment, I imagined how I would make a wreath from the beautiful flowers there and crown myself with joy. I would sing “sul margine d’un rio,” my father’s favorite song, and my voice would glide through the still, windless air to tell him—wherever he sat in his quiet place—that his daughter had arrived. Then the mark of misery would fade from my brow, and I would look up without fear to meet his eyes, which would always shine with the gentle light of innocent love. When I thought about the spell of those deep eyes, I cried, but softly, so my sobs would not disturb the magical scene.

I was so lost in this daydream that I kept walking without paying attention to where I was going. I only realized it when I bent down to pick a flower for my wreath on that bleak plain, where no flower grew. Then I woke from my dream and found that I did not know where I was.

The sun had set, and the pink glow that the clouds had caught from it as it went down was almost gone. A wind swept across the plain. I looked around and saw nothing that could tell me where I was. I had gotten lost, and I tried in vain to find my way back. I kept walking, but as darkness came, everything that might have guided me became harder to see. At last the night grew so dark that everything was hidden. I felt tired, and I knew my servant would be sleeping that night in the nearby village, so my absence would not worry anyone. Since I was safe in this wild place from any intruder, I decided to spend the night where I was. In fact, I was too tired to walk farther. The air was cold, but I did not care much about it. I told myself I was used to the weather after my two years of solitude, when no change of seasons ever stopped my endless wandering.

I lay on the grass, surrounded by darkness so complete that not even the smallest light could reach me. There was no sound, because the deep night had put the insects to sleep, and the only living things were those that could survive on that lonely spot where no tree or shrub offered shelter. The silence was so strange and wonderful that it calmed my senses, yet it also stirred my soul. My thoughts raced from one image to the next, and it felt as if my mind could grasp an eternity."}

“My dear Child

“I have betrayed your confidence; I have tried to corrupt your mind, and I have brought your innocent heart to know the looks and language of unlawful and monstrous passion. I must atone for these crimes, and I must, as far as I can, measure my punishment against my guilt. You are, I doubt not, ready for what I am about to tell you; we must separate and be divided for ever.

“I deprive you of your parent and only friend. You are turned out upon the world without shelter: your hopes are shattered; the peace and security of your pure mind are destroyed; memory will return to you with frightful pictures of guilt, and with the torment of innocent love betrayed. Yet I—who bring all this misery upon you; I—who cast you off and, with remorseless levity, have set the seal of distrust and agony upon the heart and brow of my own child, who has sought, with devilish lightness, to steal away her loveliness and put in its place the foul deformity of sin; I, in the overflowing anguish of my heart, beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must, and you do, abhor me: but pardon me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts pursue me in my banishment with unrelenting anger. I must never more see you; never more hear your voice; yet the gentle whisperings of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning of my disordered brain and heart. I am sure I should feel it even in my grave. And I dare press this request by telling you how miserably I was drawn into this net of fiery anguish, and by describing all my efforts to free myself. Indeed, if your soul were less pure and bright, I would not try to clear myself to you; I should fear that, if I made you regard me with less abhorrence, you might hate vice less. But in speaking to you, I feel as though I were appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot go away without your forgiveness, and I must strive to obtain it—or I must despair. I conjure you, therefore, to listen to my words; and if, by the good guilt, anything may be lessened by sharp agony and by remorse that tears the brain as madness perhaps you may think, though I dare not say it, that I have some claim to your compassion.

“I entreat you to recall our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had come after a weary wandering of sixteen years, during which, though I had passed through many dangers and misfortunes, my affections had been a complete blank."}

{"request_id":"58305c1d6ec29b898292fa79","rewritten_text":"To look at a star by quick glances, or to see it from the side by turning your eye so that the outer parts of the retina take in the light, is to see the star clearly. This gives you the best sense of its brightness, and that brightness fades the more directly you look at it. In the second case, more rays actually enter the eye, but in the first you have a more careful way of understanding what you see. If you stare too deeply, you confuse and weaken your thoughts. It is even possible to make Venus disappear from the sky if you look at it too steadily, too intensely, or too directly.

“As for these murders, let’s examine things for ourselves before we decide what we think. An inquiry will be entertaining,” [I thought it was a strange word to use, but I said nothing] “and, besides, Le Bon once did me a favor that I’m not going to forget. We’ll go and see the place with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, so getting the permission won’t be hard.”

The permission was obtained, and we went at once to the Rue Morgue. It was one of those miserable streets that lies between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, since this part of town was far from where we lived. We found the house easily, because many people were still standing across the way, staring up at the closed shutters with empty curiosity. The building was an ordinary Parisian house, with a gateway. On one side there was a glazed watch-box, and in the window a sliding panel showed that there was a loge de concierge. Before we went in, we walked up the street, turned down an alley, and then, turning again, went around behind the building. All the while, Dupin studied the whole neighborhood and the house itself with such careful attention that I could not see what purpose it could serve.

We retraced our steps, came back to the front, rang the bell, and, after showing our credentials, were admitted by the agents on duty. We went upstairs into the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been found, and where both bodies still lay. The room’s disorder had, as usual, been allowed to remain. I saw nothing beyond what had already been reported in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin examined everything, not leaving out the bodies of the victims. Then we went into the other rooms and into the yard, with a gendarme accompanying us the whole time."}

{"request_id":"3b567144423405ac395d5b8f","rewritten_text":"“And think about it, ma’am,” Oliver said, with tears filling his eyes even though he tried to stop them. “Oh, think how young and good she is, and how much pleasure and comfort she brings to everyone around her. I’m sure—absolutely sure—that, for your sake, since you are so kind yourself; and for her sake; and for everyone she makes happy, she will not die. Heaven will not allow her to die so young.”

“Hush!” Mrs. Maylie said, putting her hand on Oliver’s head. “You talk like a child, poor boy. Still, you remind me of my duty. I had forgotten it for a moment, Oliver, but I hope you will forgive me. I am old, and I have seen enough illness and death to know the pain of being separated from the people we love. I have also seen enough to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are spared. But this should comfort us in our sorrow, because Heaven is fair. These things teach us, in a powerful way, that there is a better world than this—and that the road to it is short. God’s will be done! I love her, and He knows how well.”

Oliver was surprised to see that, as Mrs. Maylie spoke those words, she stopped her crying as if she had forced herself to do it. She straightened up and became calm and steady. He was even more astonished to learn that this steadiness lasted. Through all the care and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie remained ready and composed, doing every duty that fell to her, steadily—and, from the outside, even cheerfully. But Oliver was young, and he did not understand what strong minds can handle in hard times. How could he, when those people so rarely even understand their own strength?

An anxious night passed. When morning came, Mrs. Maylie’s fears were confirmed. Rose was in the first stage of a high and dangerous fever.

“We must act, Oliver, and not give in to useless grief,” Mrs. Maylie said. She put a finger to her lip and looked straight at him. “This letter must be sent as quickly as possible to Mr. Losberne. It has to be carried to the market town, which is only about four miles away. You can take the footpath across the field, and then it must be sent on by an express on horseback straight to Chertsey. The people at the inn will handle it from there, and I can trust you to make sure it gets done. I know I can.”

Oliver had no answer. He only looked as if he wanted his anxiety to be gone at once."}

{"request_id":"6c674d23ecbe7ed0b2ea2b88","rewritten_text":"She studied me closely for a moment, and then said quietly,—

“What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I said, “that you won’t mix them up with the others. They may share the same blood, but, believe me, they’re not of the same nature.”

Still looking at me closely, Miss Havisham repeated,—

“What do you want for them?”

“You see, I’m not so clever,” I answered, aware that I was blushing a little. “I can’t hide from you, even if I wanted to, that I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you’d spare the money to do my friend Herbert a lasting service in life—something that, by its very nature, must be done without his knowledge—I could show you how.”

“Why must it be done without his knowledge?” she asked, resting her hands on her stick so she could look at me even more carefully.

“Because,” I said, “I started the service myself more than two years ago, without his knowledge, and I don’t want to be betrayed. I can’t explain why I’ve failed to finish it. It’s part of a secret that belongs to someone else, not me.”

She slowly pulled her eyes away from me and turned them to the fire. After watching it for what seemed like a long time in the silence, and by the light of the candles burning down, she was stirred by the collapse of some of the red coals. She looked back toward me—first blankly, then with attention that steadily sharpened. All this time Estella kept knitting. When Miss Havisham finally fixed her attention on me, she said, as if there had been no break in our conversation,—

“What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her now, and trying to control my trembling voice, “you know I love you. You know I’ve loved you for a long time, and with all my heart.”

She lifted her eyes to my face as I spoke, and her fingers kept working. She looked at me with an expressionless face. I saw that Miss Havisham glanced from me to her, and from her back to me.

“I should have said this sooner, but for my long mistake. It made me hope that Miss Havisham meant us for one another. While I thought you couldn’t help yourself, in a way, I held back from saying it. But I have to say it now.”

With her unmoved expression still in place, and her fingers still going, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said in response to that gesture. “I have no hope that I will ever call you mine, Estella.”"}

{"request_id":"c36579e28eb74717df228b7c","rewritten_text":"I want you to be permanently well connected, and for that reason it would be best to have as few odd acquaintances as possible. So I say this: if you are still in this country when Mr. Martin marries, I hope you won’t be pulled in by your closeness to the sisters—so that you end up meeting his wife. She will probably be nothing more than some farmer’s daughter, with no education.

“Of course. Yes. I don’t think Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who hadn’t had some education, and been very well brought up. Still, I don’t mean to argue against your opinion. I’m sure I won’t want to know his wife. I will always have a great regard for the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and I would be very sorry to give them up, because they are just as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, vulgar woman, then I had better not visit her, if I can avoid it.”

Emma watched her as she spoke and saw nothing that looked like love. The young man had been the first admirer, but she believed there was no other reason for Harriet to be taken with him, and that nothing serious would get in the way of any friendly arrangement Harriet might want.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day while they were walking on the Donwell road. He was on foot. After looking at her very respectfully, he seemed genuinely pleased with her companion. Emma was glad to have the chance to study him. As she walked a few steps ahead while they talked, her quick eyes soon learned what Mr. Robert Martin was like. He looked neat and like a sensible young man, but he had no other real advantage. When she compared him with other gentlemen, she felt he would lose the ground he had gained in Harriet’s favor. Harriet noticed his manner too. She had already seen her father’s gentleness and admired it with both wonder and approval. Mr. Martin looked as if he didn’t really know what to do with his manners.

They stayed together only a few minutes, because Miss Woodhouse couldn’t be kept waiting. Then Harriet ran to her with a smiling face, full of excitement, which Miss Woodhouse hoped she would calm down soon.

“Just think of it—we actually met him! How strange! He said it was a lucky thing he hadn’t gone by Randalls. He didn’t think we ever walk this road. He thought we walk toward Randalls most days.”"}

{"request_id":"71e271d2878a8d847118cbcc","rewritten_text":"I don’t want to get mixed up in any such business as that, I says to myself.

When I come down the stairs in the morning, the parlor was shut up tight, and the watchers was gone. There weren’t nobody about except the family, the widow Bartley, and our tribe. I kept my eyes on their faces to see if anything had been going on, but I couldn’t make out.

About the middle of the day the undertaker showed up with his man, and they set the coffin down in the middle of the room on a couple of chairs. Then they lined up all our chairs in rows, and borrowed more from the neighbors till the hall and the parlor and the dining-room was full. I could see the coffin lid was just as it had been before, but I didn’t dare to go look under it, with folks standing around.

After that, people started coming in, and the beats and the girls took seats in the front row right at the head of the coffin. For about half an hour folks filed past slow in a single line, looking down at the dead man’s face a minute at a time; some dropped a tear. Everything stayed very still and solemn, except the girls and the beats holding their handkerchiefs to their eyes, keeping their heads bowed, and giving a little sob. There wasn’t any other sound besides the scraping of feet on the floor and people blowing their noses—because at a funeral folks blow them more than they do anywhere else, save church.

When the place was packed, the undertaker slid around in his black gloves with his soft, soothing ways, putting on the last touches and getting everything shipshape and comfortable, and making no more noise than a cat. He didn’t speak; he just shifted people around, squeezed in the late ones, opened up little passages, and did it all with nods and signs with his hands. Then he stood over against the wall. He was the softest, glidingest, stealthiest man I ever saw; and there wasn’t any more smile on him than there is on a ham.

They had borrowed a melodeum—an ill one; and once everything was ready, a young woman sat down and worked it. It was pretty screechy and colicky, and everybody joined in and sang, and Peter was the only one that had a good thing, as far as I could tell. Then Reverend Hobson opened up, slow and solemn, and started talking; and right off the most outrageous row broke out down in the cellar that I ever heard. It was only one dog, but he made a powerful racket, and he kept at it the whole time. The parson had to stand there over the coffin and wait—you couldn’t hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"a2183aa7b767cf002af8781c","rewritten_text":"There was something wonderfully satisfying about tidying up and then taking a quiet pause before going on with life again, and in our village on Saturday nights it made Joe bold enough to linger half an hour longer on Saturdays than he did at other times. When that half-hour was up, and the rum and water ran out together, Joe rose to go and took me by the hand.

“Hold on a half moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the odd man. “I believe I’ve got a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket; and if I have, the boy shall have it.”

He fished it out from a handful of small change, tucked it into some crumpled paper, and handed it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Mind—your own.”

I thanked him, staring at him well past what good manners would allow, and kept a firm grip on Joe. He said good-night to Joe, and good-night to Mr. Wopsle as well (who went out with us), and to me he gave nothing but a look from his aiming eye—no, not exactly a look, because he shut it up; still, wonders can be done with an eye by hiding it.

On the way home, if I’d been in the mood to talk, the conversation would have been entirely on my side, for Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe went all the way home with his mouth wide open, trying to blow the rum out with as much air as he could manage. But I was so dazed by the sudden return of my old wrongdoing and my old acquaintance that I couldn’t think of anything else.

When we presented ourselves in the kitchen, my sister wasn’t in a particularly ill temper, and that unusual calm encouraged Joe to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll warrant,” said Mrs. Joe, with triumph, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see it.”

I took it from the paper, and it turned out to be a good one. “But what’s this?” said Mrs. Joe, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two One-Pound notes?”

Nothing less than two thick, hot, sweltering one-pound notes, as if they’d been on the friendliest terms with every cattle-market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat again and ran with them to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat down on my usual stool and stared vacantly at my sister, feeling pretty certain the man wouldn’t be there.

At last Joe came back, saying the man had gone, but that Joe had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

{"request_id":"932cca793559e4092bd45760","rewritten_text":"“Just a tick.”

“Where’d you get him?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What’ll you take for him?”

“I don’t know. I don’t want to sell him.”

“All right. Anyway, it’s a pretty small tick.”

“Oh, anyone can catch a tick that doesn’t belong to them. I’m happy with it. It’s good enough for me.”

“Sure, there are plenty of ticks. I could have a thousand if I wanted.”

“Well, why don’t you? You know you can’t. This is an early tick, I think. It’s the first one I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll trade you my tooth for him.”

“Let me see it.”

Tom pulled out some paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry looked at it with longing. The temptation was very strong. Finally he said:

“Is it real?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the empty spot.

“Well, all right,” Huckleberry said. “It’s a trade.”

Tom put the tick into the percussion-cap box that had recently been the pinchbug’s prison, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer than before.

When Tom got to the little, isolated frame schoolhouse, he walked in quickly, acting like he’d come with nothing but honest business. He hung his hat on a peg and sat down at once, eager and ready to work. The teacher sat up high in his big splint-bottom chair, dozing off, lulled by the sleepy hum of lessons. The interruption woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that when his full name was said, it meant trouble.

“Yes, sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, like always?”

Tom was about to make up a lie, but then he saw two long tails of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized with the quick feeling of love; and that was the only empty spot on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. He immediately said:

“I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!”

The teacher’s pulse seemed to stop. He stared, helpless. The quiet buzz of study died away. The students wondered if the boy had lost his mind. The teacher said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no doubt about what he’d said.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most unbelievable confession I’ve ever heard. No ordinary punishment will cover this. Take off your jacket.”

The teacher’s arm worked until it was tired, and the switches were clearly running low. Then he ordered:

“Now, sir, go sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

The little ripple of laughter around the room made the boy seem embarrassed, but it was really because he was overwhelmed by his worshipful awe of his secret idol and the happy thrill of getting such a good outcome."}

{"request_id":"b6fb36f6aff980d21095ea9d","rewritten_text":"I then went from shop to shop, making whatever purchases were necessary to account for the change in his appearance. Once that was done, I turned my face, on my own business, toward Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but the moment he saw me enter, he stood up at once and positioned himself before the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I answered. I had been thinking carefully about what I was going to say as I came along.

“Don’t commit yourself,” Mr. Jaggers warned, “and don’t commit anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don’t tell me anything. I don’t want to know anything. I’m not curious.”

Of course I could see he knew the man had arrived.

“I only want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to make sure that what I’ve been told is true. I don’t have any hope that it’s untrue, but at least I can verify it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head to one side. He wasn’t looking at me; he was looking at the floor in a listening way. “Told would suggest verbal communication. You can’t have verbal communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I’ll say ‘informed,’ Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I’ve been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor, one who has been unknown to me until now.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And only him?” I asked.

“And only him,” Mr. Jaggers replied.

“I’m not so unreasonable, sir, as to think you’re in any way responsible for my mistakes and wrong conclusions; but I always assumed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” Mr. Jaggers answered, turning his eyes on me coolly, and taking a bite at his forefinger. “I’m not responsible for that at all.”

“And yet it looked so much like it, sir,” I pleaded, my heart sinking.

“Not a particle of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his skirts. “Don’t take anything from how it looks. Take everything from evidence. That’s the best rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I said at last, with a sigh, after standing silent for a little while. “I’ve verified my information, and that’s the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having at last disclosed himself,” Mr. Jaggers went on, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, throughout my communication with you, I have always stuck to the strict line of fact. There has never been the least deviation from it. You know that, don’t you?”

“Quite, sir.”

“I communicated to Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—the caution that he must never expect me to deviate from the strict line of fact.”}"}

{"request_id":"da65b06ac6858d31983361d3","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?” Oliver demanded.

“Hush!” the Dodger replied. “Do you see that old fellow at the book-stall?”

“The old gentleman across the way?” Oliver said. “Yes, I see him.”

“He’ll do,” said the Dodger.

“A fine choice,” Master Charley Bates observed.

Oliver looked from one to the other, utterly astonished, but he wasn’t allowed to ask questions. The two boys moved stealthily across the road and slipped close behind the old gentleman toward whom his attention had been directed. Oliver followed a few paces behind them; not knowing whether to step forward or back, he stood watching in silent amazement.

The old gentleman was a very respectable-looking man, with a powdered head and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar, white trousers, and carried a smart bamboo cane under his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood there reading as intensely as if he were in his own study, in his elbow-chair. It was very possible he imagined himself there, too; his deep focus made it clear he wasn’t seeing the book-stall, the street, the boys, or anything at all—except the book itself. He read straight through, turning the page when he reached the bottom, starting at the top line of the next, and continuing steadily on with the greatest interest and eagerness.

What horror and alarm seized Oliver as he stood a few paces away, watching with his eyes wide open as they could possibly be—seeing the Dodger plunge his hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief! Seeing him pass it to Charley Bates. And then, finally, watching them both run away around the corner at full speed!

In an instant, the whole mystery of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewels, and the Jew came rushing into the boy’s mind.

For a moment he stood frozen, his blood tingling through his veins with terror, as if he were trapped in a burning fire. Then, confused and frightened, he ran—without even knowing what he was doing—straight off as fast as he could put his feet to the ground.

It all happened in the space of a minute. The moment Oliver started to run, the old gentleman put his hand to his pocket, found it empty, and spun around sharply. Seeing the boy sprinting away at such a pace, he naturally assumed him to be the thief. Shouting “Stop thief!” with all his might, he took off after him, book in hand."}

{"request_id":"964655a8eb0560d8ba56fc48","rewritten_text":"About ten minutes later, the bell rang for tea. Since Virginia did not come down, Mrs. Otis sent one of the footmen upstairs to find her. After a short time he returned and said he could not find Miss Virginia anywhere. Because Virginia was used to going out to the garden every evening to pick flowers for the dinner table, Mrs. Otis was not worried at first. But when six o’clock came and Virginia still had not appeared, she became truly upset. She sent the boys out to look for her, while she and Mr. Otis searched every room in the house. At half-past six the boys came back and said they could find no sign of their sister anywhere. Everyone was now in a state of panic and did not know what to do, until Mr. Otis suddenly remembered that, a few days earlier, he had allowed a group of gypsies to camp in the park. He set off at once for Blackfell Hollow, taking his eldest son and two farm servants with him.

The little Duke of Cheshire was beside himself with worry and begged to be allowed to go too, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing there might be a fight. When they arrived, however, they found that the gypsies had already left. It was clear their departure had been sudden, because the fire was still burning and some plates were still lying on the grass. Mr. Otis sent Washington and the two men out to search the area, then hurried home. He sent telegrams to all the police inspectors in the county, telling them to watch for a little girl who might have been kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He then had his horse brought round. After insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, he rode off down the Ascot Road with a groom.

He had only gone a couple of miles when he heard someone galloping after him. He turned and saw the little Duke coming up on his pony, his face very flushed and without a hat. “I’m awfully sorry, Mr. Otis,” the boy gasped. “But I can’t eat any dinner while Virginia is lost. Please don’t be angry with me. If you had let us be engaged last year, none of this would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!”

The Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young scapegrace. He was also deeply moved by how devoted the boy was to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted him gently on the shoulders and said, “Well, Cecil, if you won’t go back, I suppose you must come with me. But I’ll have to get you a hat at Ascot.”"}

{"request_id":"28f148f669778c2d693b6aeb","rewritten_text":"This marriage is absolutely right. I didn’t think so at first, but I’ll admit it now. The gods made Sibyl Vane for you. Without her, you would have been incomplete.”

“Thanks, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, pressing his hand. “I knew you’d understand me. Harry is so cynical—he terrifies me. But here is the orchestra. It’s dreadful, really, but it only lasts about five minutes. Then the curtain rises, and you’ll see the girl I’m going to give all my life to—the girl I’ve already given everything good in me to.”

A quarter of an hour later, amid an extraordinary surge of applause, Sibyl Vane stepped onto the stage. Yes, she was lovely to look at—one of the loveliest creatures, Lord Henry thought, that he had ever seen. There was something of a fawn in her shy grace and startled eyes. A faint blush, like the shadow of a rose in a silver mirror, touched her cheeks as she glanced at the crowded, enthusiastic audience. She stepped back a few paces, and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward sprang to his feet and began applauding. Dorian Gray sat completely still, as if in a dream, staring at her. Lord Henry leaned in behind his glasses and murmured, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall of Capulet’s house, and Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and his other friends. The band—such as it was—struck up a few bars of music, and the dance began. Through the crowd of awkward, shabby actors, Sibyl Vane moved like a creature from a finer world. Her body swayed as she danced, like a plant swaying in water. The curves of her throat were the curves of a white lily. Her hands seemed made of cool ivory.

And yet she was strangely listless. When her eyes rested on Romeo, she showed no sign of joy. The few lines she had to speak—

Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much, 
Which mannerly devotion shows in this; 
For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch, 
And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss—

and the brief exchange that followed were delivered in a completely artificial way. Her voice was exquisite, but in terms of tone it was absolutely false. The color was wrong. It drained all life from the verse. It made the passion unreal.

Dorian Gray went pale as he watched her. He was both puzzled and anxious. None of his friends dared say anything to him. To them, she seemed utterly incompetent."}

{"request_id":"096a29dac2eaba4b08647a7b","rewritten_text":"After dinner, the whole gang went out on the bar to hunt for turtle eggs. They poked sticks into the sand, and when they found a soft spot, they dropped to their knees and dug with their hands. Sometimes they pulled fifty or sixty eggs from one hole. The eggs were perfectly round and white, a little smaller than an English walnut. That night they had a big fried-egg feast, and another one on Friday morning.

After breakfast, they ran out onto the bar shouting and prancing, chasing each other in circles and throwing off their clothes as they went. Soon they were naked, and they kept playing, running farther up the shoal water of the bar, right against the strong current. The current would trip their legs now and then, which made it even funnier. Every so often they would huddle together and splash water in each other’s faces with their palms, moving closer while keeping their faces turned away to avoid the harsh sprays. Then they would grab and wrestle until the best man ducked his neighbor, and after that they all went under in a tangle of white legs and arms. When they came up, they were blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping for breath all at once.

When they were worn out, they ran back out onto the dry, hot sand and sprawled there. They covered themselves with sand, then later broke for the water again and did the whole thing over. At last they realized their naked skin looked a lot like flesh-colored “tights.” So they drew a ring in the sand and put on a circus, with three clowns in it, because none of them would give up that proud role to anyone else.

After that, they got their marbles and played “knucks,” “ringtaw,” and “keeps” until it stopped being fun. Then Joe and Huck went for another swim, but Tom wouldn’t, because when he kicked off his trousers he had also kicked his string of rattlesnake rattles off his ankle. He wondered how he had managed to avoid cramps for so long without the protection of that strange charm. He didn’t try again until he found the rattles. By then the other boys were tired and ready to rest. They drifted apart, went into the “dumps,” and stared longingly across the wide river at the village, sleeping in the sun. Tom found himself writing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe. He scratched it out and got angry at himself for being weak, but he wrote it again anyway. He erased it once more, then tried to break the temptation by calling the other boys together and joining them."}

{"request_id":"5f21fa68e5705e0861d80eb4","rewritten_text":"She left it all behind her, except for the memory that such things had ever been.

Anne had never gone into Kellynch since she left Lady Russell’s house in September. It hadn’t been necessary, and on the few occasions when it was possible for her to go to the Hall, she managed to avoid it and get away. Her first return was simply to take up her place again in the modern, elegant apartments of the Lodge, and to delight the eyes of its mistress.

There was some anxiety mixed with Lady Russell’s joy when she met her. She knew who had been visiting Uppercross. But happily, either Anne had improved—plumper and better-looking—or Lady Russell was imagining it; and when Anne received her compliments, she found it amusing to connect them with her cousin’s silent admiration, and to hope she might be blessed with a second spring of youth and beauty.

When they began to talk, Anne soon noticed a change in her mind. The subjects that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch—those she had felt slighted about, and had been forced to suppress among the Musgroves—were now of only secondary interest. She had recently even lost sight of her father and sister and Bath. Their concerns had been pushed aside by those of Uppercross; and when Lady Russell returned to their earlier hopes and fears, and spoke of her satisfaction with the house in Camden Place, which had been taken, and her regret that Mrs Clay was still with them, Anne would have been ashamed to have it known how much more she was thinking of Lyme and Louisa Musgrove, and of everyone she knew there. How much more interesting to her was the home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick than her own father’s house in Camden Place, or her own sister’s closeness with Mrs Clay. She was even forced to make an effort to meet Lady Russell with anything like equal concern, on topics that, by their very nature, had the first claim on her.

At first there was a little awkwardness in their conversation about another subject. They had to talk about the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell hadn’t been there five minutes the day before when a full account of everything had burst on her; but it still had to be discussed, she had to ask questions, she had to regret the imprudence, mourn the outcome, and Captain Wentworth’s name had to be mentioned by both. Anne was aware she wasn’t doing it as well as Lady Russell. She couldn’t say the name and look straight into Lady Russell’s eyes until she had adopted the expedient of telling her, briefly, what she thought about the attachment between him and Louisa."}

{"request_id":"6358e53c833fa7694e9e995f","rewritten_text":"“I agree. It’s the best thing. Just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh no, not like that. This is good enough for small, ordinary things, especially with girls, because they always turn on you and then they run their mouths if they get mad. But for something big like this, there ought to be writing. And blood.”

Tom’s whole body seemed to approve of the idea. It felt deep, dark, and awful. The hour, the situation, and the place all fit it. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, took a small piece of “red keel” from his pocket, held it up to the moon, and carefully wrote the words. He pressed his tongue between his teeth to make each slow stroke, then eased up on the upstrokes.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry was full of admiration for Tom’s skill in writing and for how grand the words sounded. He immediately took a pin from his lapel and started to prick his own flesh, but Tom stopped him.

“Wait! Don’t do that. A pin is brass. It might have verdigris on it.”

“What’s verdigris?”

“It’s poison. That’s what it is. If you swallow it once, you’ll see.”

So Tom pulled the thread out from one of his needles. Then each boy pricked the ball of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After many squeezes, Tom finally managed to sign his initials, using the ball of his little finger as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to make an H and an F, and the oath was finished. They buried the shingle near the wall, with gloomy ceremonies and strange chants. The fetters that were supposed to bind their tongues were treated as locked, and the key was thrown away.

A figure crept through a gap at the other end of the ruined building, but they didn’t notice it.

“Tom,” Huckleberry whispered, “does this stop us from ever telling—always?”

“Of course it does. It doesn’t matter what happens. We have to keep quiet. We’d drop down dead—don’t you know that?”

“Yes, I guess that’s true.”

They kept whispering for a little while. Then, just outside—within ten feet of them—a dog let out a long, mournful howl. The boys grabbed each other suddenly, shaking with terror.

“Which one of us does he mean?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don’t know—look through the crack. Quick!”

“No, you, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t do it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"c220f4327dadb737132909ad","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” he said as we reached its base, “come here! Was the skull nailed to the limb with the face outward, or with the face turned toward it?”

“De face was out, massa, so dat de crows could get at de eyes good, widout any trouble.”

“Well, then, was it this eye or that one through which you dropped the beetle?” Here Legrand touched each of Jupiter’s eyes.

“’Twas dis eye, massa—de lef eye—jis as you tell me,” and then it was his right eye that the negro indicated.

“That will do—we must try it again.”

Here my friend, whose madness I now saw—at least, I thought I saw—some signs of method, removed the peg that marked where the beetle had fallen, and set it down about three inches to the west of its former position. Taking, as before, the tape measure from the nearest point of the trunk to the peg, and then extending the line straight out to fifty feet, we indicated a new spot, removed by several yards from where we had been digging.

Around this new position we drew a circle, somewhat larger than before, and started digging again with the spades. I was dreadfully tired, but, without really understanding what had caused the shift in my thoughts, I no longer felt any strong aversion to the labor. I had become, quite inexplicably, deeply interested—indeed, even excited. Perhaps there was something in all the extravagant behavior of Legrand—some hint of forethought, some deliberation—that impressed me. I dug eagerly, and now and then I caught myself actually looking, with something very close to expectation, for the supposed treasure—the vision of which had driven my unfortunate companion mad. At a time when these kinds of thoughts most fully possessed me, and when we had been working perhaps an hour and a half, we were interrupted again by the dog’s violent howling. At first his uneasiness, it seemed, had been nothing more than playfulness or whim, but now he took on a bitter, serious tone. When Jupiter tried again to muzzle him, he fought furiously, and then, leaping into the hole, tore up the earth frantically with his claws. In a few seconds he had uncovered a mass of human bones, forming two complete skeletons, intermingled with several buttons of metal, and what appeared to be the dust of decayed wool. One or two strokes of a spade lifted the blade of a large Spanish knife, and as we dug farther, three or four loose pieces of gold and silver coin came to light."}

{"request_id":"751e02ef44179944869b965b","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. I’ll be late for lunch if I stay any longer. Thanks for telling me what I wanted to know. I always like to know everything about my new friends, and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I’ve asked myself and Mr. Gray. He’s her newest protégé.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, not to bother me with her charity appeals anymore. I’m tired of them. She really seems to think I have nothing to do but write cheques for her silly causes.”

“All right, Uncle George. I’ll tell her, but it won’t change anything. People who are always talking about philanthropy lose all sense of humanity. That’s what makes them different.”

The old gentleman growled in approval and rang the bell for his servant. Lord Henry walked up through the low arcade into Burlington Street, then turned toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s parentage. Even though it was told to him in a rough way, it still stirred him. It suggested a strange kind of romance, almost modern. A beautiful woman risking everything for a wild passion. A few reckless weeks of happiness cut short by a horrible, treacherous crime. Months of silent suffering, and then a child born in pain. The mother taken by death, the boy left alone under the control of an old man who had no love for him. Yes; it was an interesting background. It shaped the boy and, in a way, made him even more perfect. Behind every beautiful thing there was something tragic. Whole worlds had to be in turmoil so that even the smallest flower could bloom.... And how charming the boy had been at dinner the night before. With startled eyes and parted lips, he had sat opposite him at the club, looking frightened and pleased at the same time, while the red candle shades made the wonder on his face seem even richer. Talking to him was like playing an exquisite violin. The boy responded to every touch and every change in the music. There was something terribly gripping about the act of influencing someone. No other activity was like it. To put your own soul into some graceful form and let it stay there for a moment. To hear your own ideas reflected back to you, with the added music of passion and youth. To pass your own temperament into another person, as if it were a subtle fluid or a strange perfume. There was real joy in that—maybe the greatest joy left to us in an age as limited and vulgar as our own, an age that is grossly focused on the body in its pleasures and grossly ordinary in its goals.... This was a remarkable type, too, this lad whom he had met in Basil’s studio by such a strange chance, or at least could be made into a remarkable type."}

{"request_id":"899ccf7198a5ca873ea69519","rewritten_text":"“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” With that, he shook his head and tapped it, as if to show how he felt himself lacking in Joseph.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry, you must be worn out. Sit down. Here is a chicken had round from the Boar, here is a tongue had round from the Boar, here’s one or two little things had round from the Boar, that I hope you won’t despise. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again the very instant after he had sat down, “see afore me the same fellow I used to sport with in his days of happy infancy? And may I—_may_ I—?”

This May I—what he meant was might he shake hands—so I consented; he was all warmth about it, and then sat down again.

“Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink—thanks to Fortune—and may she always choose her favourites with equal judgment! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “see afore me One—and likewise drink to One—without once more saying—May I—_may_ I—?”

I told him he might, and he shook hands with me again, and emptied his glass and turned it upside down. I did the same; and if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine could not have gone more straight to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook took me to the liver wing, and to the best slice of tongue (none of those out-of-the-way No Thoroughfares of Pork now), and, as far as I could see, took comparatively no care of himself at all. “Ah! poultry, poultry! You little thought,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the fowl in the dish, “when you were a young fledgling, what was laid up for you. You little thought you were to be refreshment beneath this humble roof for one as—call it a weakness, if you like,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “but may I? _may_ I—?”

Before long it began to feel needless to repeat the form of asking, so he did it at once. How he managed to do it so often without cutting himself with my knife, I can’t say.

“And your sister,” he went on, after a little steady eating, “who had the honour of bringing you up by hand! It’s a sad picture to think she’s no longer able to understand the honour in full. May—”

I saw he was about to press on again, and I stopped him.

“We’ll drink her health,” said I.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, quite limp with admiration, “that’s the way you know ’em, sir!” (I don’t know who Sir was, but it certainly wasn’t I, and there was no third person there); “that’s the way you know the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"ef8413d1c0d1b45e50c00c5a","rewritten_text":"He bowed once more and went on his way. At that moment he saw no one in the street. It is a side lane—extremely lonely.

“_William Bird_, tailor, states that he was among the group that entered the house. He is an Englishman. Has lived in Paris for two years. Was among the first to climb the stairs. Heard the voices arguing. The rough voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could catch a few words, though he cannot now recall them all. He distinctly heard ‘_sacré_’ and ‘_mon Dieu_.’ At the same time there was a noise, as though several people were grappling together—a scraping and scuffling sound. The sharp voice was very loud—louder than the rough one. He is certain it was not the voice of an Englishman. It seemed to be German. It might have been a woman’s voice. He does not understand German.

“Four of the witnesses named above, being brought back, declared that the door of the chamber where the body of Mademoiselle L. was found was locked from the inside when the party reached it. Everything was perfectly still—no groans, no noises of any sort. When the door was forced, no person was seen. The windows, both in the back and in the front room, were lowered and tightly fastened from within. A door between the two rooms was shut, but not locked. The door from the front room into the passage was locked, with the key left on the inside. A small room at the front of the house, on the fourth story, at the end of the passage, was open, the door standing ajar. That room was full of old beds, boxes, and the like. These were taken out and searched with care. There was not an inch of any part of the house that was not examined in the same way. Men were sent up and down the chimneys. The house had four stories, with garrets (_mansardes_). A trap-door on the roof was nailed down very securely—there was no sign that it had been opened for years. The interval between the hearing of the voices in contention and the breaking open of the room door was given differently by the witnesses. Some put it as brief as three minutes—others as long as five. The door was opened with difficulty.

“_Alfonzo Garcio_, undertaker, deposes that he lives in the Rue Morgue. Is a native of Spain. Was one of the party who entered the house. Did not go up the stairs. Is nervous, and was uneasy about what might follow from such agitation. Heard the voices in contention. The gruff voice was that of a Frenchman. Could not make out what was being said. The shrill voice was that of an Englishman—he is sure of it.”"}
