{"request_id":"0971872029d22027340750d0","rewritten_text":"The chain of necessity that keeps bringing misery must have been broken, and the malignant fate that rules it would not allow this breach of her eternal laws. But why should I resent that? Misery was my element, and only what was miserable could draw near to me; if Woodville had been happy, I should never have known him. And can I—who for many years have been sustained by tears, and nourished by the dew of grief—stop now to tell a tale of woe and death?

Woodville was forced to make a journey into the country, and he was kept away day after day in an exhausting absence from his lovely bride. He received a letter from her saying she was only slightly ill, but urging him to hurry to her; she told him that from his eyes she would receive health, and that his company would be her surest medicine. He was detained three days longer, and then he rushed to her. His heart, he could not say why, foretold misfortune. He had not heard from her again; he feared she might be worse, and that fear made him impatient and restless for the moment when he could see her once more, standing before him in health and beauty. Still, a sinister voice seemed always to whisper to him, “You will never more behold her as she was.”

When he arrived at her home, everything was silent. He moved through several rooms; in one he saw a servant weeping bitterly. He was so overcome with fear that he could hardly bring himself to ask, “Is she dead?” and he only listened to the terrible answer, “Not yet.” Those astonishing words struck him as less dreadful than what he had expected. To learn that she was still alive—and that he might still hope—was some relief. He remembered the words of her letter, and he let himself fall into a wild idea: that his kisses, breathing warm love and life, would infuse new spirit into her; and that with him near her, she could not die—that his presence was a charm for her life.

He hurried to her sick room. She lay there, her cheeks burning with fever, yet her eyes were closed and she seemed senseless. He wrapped her in his arms; he pressed breathless kisses on her burning lips. He called to her in a voice of restrained anguish, using the tenderest names: “Return, Elinor; I am with you; your life, your love. Return, dearest one—you promised me this boon, that I should bring you health. Let your sweet spirit revive; you cannot die near me. What is death? To see you no more? To be parted from what is a part of myself—without whom I have no memory and no future?”"}

{"request_id":"78b8df7252036fa4b0ddccce","rewritten_text":"They know how clever he is. He’ll be in prison for life. They’ll make the Artful nothing less than a lifer.”

“What do you mean by lagging and a lifer?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “Why talk like that to me? Why don’t you say it in a way I can understand?”

Fagin was about to translate those strange words into plain language. Once he did, Mr. Bolter would have been told that they meant “transportation for life.” But before the explanation could be finished, Master Bates came in. He had his hands in his breeches pockets, and his face was twisted into a look of half-comical misery.

“It’s all up, Fagin,” Charley said, once he and his new companion had been introduced.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman who owns the box. Two or three more are coming to identify him, and the Artful is booked to leave on a passage out,” Master Bates replied. “I’ll need a full suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband, so I can visit him before he sets off. Think of Jack Dawkins—lummy Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—going abroad in a cheap little two-penny-halfpenny sneeze-box! I never thought he’d do it, not under a gold watch, chain, and seals, at the very least. Why didn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his valuables, and go out as a gentleman, instead of like a common fool, with no honor and no glory!”

With that outburst of sympathy for his unfortunate friend, Master Bates sat down in the nearest chair, looking both annoyed and hopeless.

“What do you mean, talking about him having no honor or glory?” Fagin snapped, glaring at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the best one among you all? Is there one of you who could match him, or even get close to him, on any job? Eh?”

“Not one,” Master Bates answered, his voice rough with regret. “Not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” Fagin demanded, still angry. “Why are you blubbering?”

“Because it isn’t on the record, is it?” Charley said, furious at his old friend. “Because it can’t come out in the indictment. Because nobody will ever know half of what he was. How will he look in the Newgate Calendar? Maybe he won’t even be there. Oh, my eye, my eye—what a blow it is!”

“Ha! ha!” Fagin laughed, throwing out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter. He chuckled so hard it shook him, as if he had the palsy. “Look at the pride they take in their profession, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"f5ffe7ba587c0d28b395ea90","rewritten_text":"“Shucks, Tom,” I says, “I reckon you could tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, _I_ don’t know. But he’s got to have it. All the nobility does.”

That was just the way he carried on. If it didn’t suit him to explain something to you, he wouldn’t. You could pester him for a week and it wouldn’t make no difference.

He’d already got all that coat of arms business squared away, so now he went on to finish the rest of that work—planning out a mournful inscription, the kind Jim was supposed to have, same as they all done. He made up a bunch, wrote them out on paper, and read them off, like so:

1. _Here a captive heart busted._

2. _Here a poor prisoner, forsook by the world and friends, fretted out his sorrowful life._

3. _Here a lonely heart broke, and a worn spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity._

4. _Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV._

Tom’s voice shook while he was reading them, and he pretty near fell apart. When he was done he couldn’t make up his mind which one Jim ought to scratch on the wall—because they were all so good—but in the end he decided he’d let him scratch all of them on. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch that much stuff onto the logs with a nail, and he didn’t know how to make letters besides; but Tom said he’d block them out for him, and then Jim wouldn’t have anything to do but follow the lines. Then pretty soon Tom says:

“Come to think, the logs ain’t going to do it. There ain’t log walls in a dungeon. We got to dig the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll fetch a rock.”

Jim said a rock was worse than the logs; he said it would take him such a pison long time to dig those words into a rock he’d never get out. But Tom said he’d let me help him with it. Then he looked over to see how me and Jim was getting along with the pens. It was awful tedious and hard, and slow, and it didn’t give my hands any chance to heal up the sores—we didn’t seem to make no headway at all. So Tom says:

“I know how to fix it. We got to have a rock for the coat of arms and mournful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"d67e978e724ad89892b5be89","rewritten_text":"“Good heavens!” the Duchess said to herself. “So he really is one of those people who reads your hands. How awful. I hope he’s a foreigner, at least. Then it wouldn’t feel quite so bad.”

“I must introduce him to you.”

“Introduce him!” the Duchess cried. “You mean to say he’s here?” She started looking around for a small tortoiseshell fan and a very worn lace shawl, ready to leave at once.

“Of course he’s here. I wouldn’t think of having a party without him. He tells me I have a very psychic hand. And he says that if my thumb had been even a little shorter, I would be a confirmed pessimist and would have gone into a convent.”

“Oh, I see!” the Duchess said, feeling much more relieved. “So he tells fortunes, I suppose?”

“And misfortunes, too,” Lady Windermere replied. “A lot of them. Next year, for instance, I’m in great danger, both by land and sea. So I’m going to live in a balloon, and I’ll draw up my dinner in a basket every evening. It’s all written on my little finger, or on the palm of my hand—I can’t remember which.”

“But surely that’s tempting Providence, Gladys.”

“My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their hands read once a month, so you know what not to do. Of course, people do it anyway, but it’s so pleasant to be warned. Now, if someone doesn’t go and fetch Mr. Podgers at once, I’ll have to go myself.”

“Let me go, Lady Windermere,” said a tall, handsome young man standing nearby. He had been listening with an amused smile.

“Thank you, Lord Arthur,” she said, “but I’m afraid you wouldn’t recognize him.”

“If he’s as wonderful as you say, Lady Windermere, I couldn’t possibly miss him. Tell me what he’s like, and I’ll bring him to you right away.”

“Well, he isn’t like a palm-reader at all. I mean he isn’t mysterious, or full of secret meanings, or romantic-looking. He’s a small, stout man with a funny bald head and big gold-rimmed spectacles. He looks something like a family doctor or a country attorney. I’m really sorry, but it’s not my fault. People are so annoying. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look exactly like pianists. And last season I invited a dreadful conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up so many people, and who always wore a coat of mail and carried a dagger up his shirt-sleeve. Do you know that when he arrived, he looked just like a nice old clergyman, and he cracked jokes all evening?”"}

{"request_id":"fe53155ed66c4877dc05c073","rewritten_text":"“She would be such a delightful companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed, but added,

“Our little friend Harriet Smith is just as pretty and kind as any young person. You will like Harriet. Emma could not have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am very happy to hear it,” said Emma, “but only Jane Fairfax is known to be so accomplished and superior—and she is exactly Emma’s age.”

They talked about it very pleasantly, and the conversation moved on to other similar topics, all with the same easy harmony. Still, the evening did not end without a small return of worry. The gruel was brought in, and it gave them plenty to say—everyone praised it, made comments, and agreed it was wholesome for every kind of person. They also made sharp remarks about the many houses where it was never served in a way that was at all tolerable. Unfortunately, among the failures Emma had to mention, the most recent—and therefore the most important—was in her own cook at South End. A young woman had been hired there for the time, and she never seemed to understand what Emma meant by a basin of nice, smooth gruel: thin, but not too thin. No matter how often Emma had asked for it and ordered it, the cook had never been able to make it come out right. This was a dangerous opening.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with gentle concern. The sound he made in Emma’s ear said, “Ah, there is no end to the sad results of your going to South End. It shouldn’t be talked about.” For a little while, Emma hoped he would not bring it up, and that his quiet worry might be enough to let him enjoy his own smooth gruel again. After a few minutes, however, he began,

“I shall always be very sorry that you went to the sea this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you be sorry, sir?” Emma asked. “I assure you it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides,” Mr. Woodhouse continued, “if you had to go to the sea, it should not have been to South End. South End is an unhealthy place. Perry was surprised to hear you had chosen South End.”

“I know many people think that,” Emma replied, “but it is quite a mistake. We were all perfectly healthy there, and we never had the least trouble from the mud. And Mr. Wingfield says it is entirely wrong to suppose the place is unhealthy. I am sure you can trust him, because he understands the air so well, and his own brother and family have been there again and again.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere,” said Mr. Woodhouse. “Perry was there for a week once, and he thinks it is the best place of all for sea-bathing.”"}

{"request_id":"f788fadd430805a3fdad1f35","rewritten_text":"“I’m very ignorant, and it worries me—just a little.”

“Then tell me what it is.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative, and she is an orphan too, just as I am. I love her very dearly. She is five years younger than I, and she lives in a farmer’s house in the southern country. Poverty has kept us apart, and she knows nothing of my fate—for I cannot write; and even if I could, how would I manage to tell her? It is better this way.”

“Yes, yes—better as it is.”

“What I have been thinking while we came along, and what I’m still thinking now as I look into your kind, strong face—one that gives me so much support—is this: if the Republic truly does good for the poor, and they grow less hungry, and in every way suffer less, she may live a long time. She may even live to be old.”

“And then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you think—” the uncomplaining eyes, full of endurance, fill with tears, and the lips part a little more and tremble—“that it will seem long to me, while I wait for her in the better land, where I trust both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”

“It cannot be, my child; there is no Time there, and no trouble there.”

“You comfort me so much! I’m so ignorant. Am I to kiss you now? Has the moment come?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips; he kisses hers; and they solemnly bless one another. His spare hand does not shake when he lets it go; nothing harsher than a sweet, steady brightness is on the patient face. She goes on before him—she is gone; the knitting-women count Twenty-Two.

“I am the Resurrection and the Life, saith the Lord: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die.”

The murmuring of many voices, the turning up of many faces, the crowding of many footsteps at the edge of the throng, until it swells forward in one great mass, like a single heave of water—everything flashes away. Twenty-Three.

{"request_id":"464ccdf6c2a7e72e7010d474","rewritten_text":"Yet, despite all that, the boy only sank deeper into gloom—growing more and more melancholy, wan, and cast down. She tried hot baths, sitz baths, shower baths, and even plunges. Still he stayed as cheerless as a hearse. Next she began to “doctor” the water with a thin oatmeal diet and blister-plasters. She measured his “capacity” the way one would judge a jug, and every day she filled him up with quack cure-alls.

By this time Tom had grown indifferent to persecution. That stage alarmed the old lady and set her heart in consternation. Indifference, she decided, had to be checked at any cost. Then she heard of Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a great quantity at once. When she tasted it, she felt nothing but gratitude; it was, as she put it, fire in liquid form. She abandoned the water treatment and everything else, and pinned her hopes entirely on Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and waited with the keenest anxiety to see what would happen. Her worries were soothed at once, her soul settled again; for the “indifference” had been broken. The boy couldn’t have shown a more eager, hearty interest if she’d actually lit a fire under him.

Tom decided it was time to wake up. This kind of life might have seemed romantic enough for his ruined condition, but it was beginning to feel short on sentiment and long on distracting variety. So he weighed different schemes for relief, and finally settled on pretending to be fond of Pain-killer. He asked for it so often he became a nuisance, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop bothering her. If it had been Sid, she would have been delighted without a trace of doubt; but with Tom, she watched the bottle in secret. She saw that the medicine truly did lessen, yet it never occurred to her that the boy was using it to patch up a split in the sitting-room floor.

One day Tom was in the middle of dosing the crack when his aunt’s yellow cat wandered in, purring and eyeing the teaspoon with greedy interest, begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you want it, Peter.”

But Peter made it plain that he did want it.

“You’d better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“Now that you’ve asked, I’ll give it to you, because there ain’t anything mean about me; but if you find you don’t like it, you mustn’t blame anybody but your own self.”

Peter agreed. So Tom pried his mouth open and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter sprang a couple of yards into the air, then let out a war-whoop and ran round and round the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flower-pots, and making a general mess."}

{"request_id":"718be21b9a2ec40188273976","rewritten_text":"His face, badly sunburned, was more than half hidden by whiskers and a _mustache_. He had with him a huge oak cudgel, but otherwise seemed to be unarmed. He bowed awkwardly and greeted us with “good evening,” in French accents that, though a bit Neufchâtel-like, were still clear enough to suggest a Parisian origin.

“Sit down, my friend,” said Dupin. “I suppose you’ve come about the Ourang-Outang. Honestly, I almost envy you for having him—a remarkably fine animal, and no doubt very valuable. How old do you think he is?”

The sailor drew a long breath, with the look of a man relieved of some unbearable burden, and then answered in a confident tone:

“I can’t really say—but he can’t be more than four or five years old. Do you have him here?”

“Oh no. We didn’t have any way to keep him here. He’s at a livery stable in the Rue Dubourg, just around the corner. You can get him in the morning. Of course you’re prepared to identify the property?”

“Of course I am, sir.”

“I’ll be sorry to part with him,” said Dupin.

“I don’t mean you should go to all this trouble for nothing, sir,” the man replied. “You couldn’t expect that. I’m very willing to pay a reward for finding the animal—that is, anything reasonable.”

“Well,” my friend answered, “that’s all very fair, of course. Let me think! What should I have? Oh! I’ll tell you. My reward will be this: you will give me all the information you can about these murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin spoke the last words in a very low voice, and very quietly. Just as quietly, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he drew a pistol from his bosom and set it on the table without the slightest flurry.

The sailor’s face flushed, as if he were struggling for breath. He sprang to his feet and grabbed his cudgel, but the next moment he sank back into his seat, trembling violently, with the expression of death itself. He didn’t say a word. I pitied him from the bottom of my heart.

“My friend,” said Dupin, in a kind tone, “you’re frightening yourself unnecessarily—you really are. We mean you no harm at all. I give you my word as an honorable gentleman, and as a Frenchman, that we intend you no injury. I know perfectly well that you’re innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue. Still, it won’t do to deny that you’re in some measure implicated in them.”"}

{"request_id":"bd0f467a7761f2560a619d6e","rewritten_text":"It was the beginning of February, and Anne, having been in Bath for a month, was growing very eager for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted to hear much more than Mary had told her. It had been three weeks since she had heard anything at all. She only knew that Henrietta was back at home again, and that Louisa, though thought to be recovering quickly, was still in Lyme. One evening, she was thinking of them all very intensely when a thicker letter than usual from Mary was delivered to her; and, to heighten her pleasure and surprise, it came with the compliments of Admiral and Mrs. Croft.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was a circumstance to interest her. They were people her heart turned to very naturally.

“What is this?” cried Sir Walter. “The Crofts have arrived in Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.”

“Oh! those letters are convenient passports. They secure an introduction. I should have visited Admiral Croft, however, at any rate. I know what is due to my tenant.”

Anne could listen no longer; she could not even have said how the poor Admiral’s complexion escaped her notice—her letter took her attention completely. It had been begun several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

“I make no apology for my silence, because I know how little people think of letters in such a place as Bath. You must be a great deal too happy to care about Uppercross, which, as you well know, offers very little to write about. We have had a very dull Christmas; Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove have not had a single dinner party all the holidays. I don’t count the Hayters as anybody. The holidays, however, are over at last: I believe no children ever had such long ones. I am sure I did not. The house was cleared yesterday, except of the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to hear they have never gone home. Mrs. Harville must be an odd mother to keep them so long. I don’t understand it. They are not at all nice children, in my opinion; but Mrs. Musgrove seems to like them quite as well, if not better, than her grandchildren.

“What dreadful weather we have had! It may not be felt in Bath, with your nice pavements; but in the country it matters. I have not had a single person call on me since the second week in January, except Charles Hayter, who has been calling much more often than was welcome. Between ourselves, I think it a great pity Henrietta did not remain at Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her a little out of his way.”"}

{"request_id":"9a006344e4ca8aa05344ea9f","rewritten_text":"“So, now, let’s know all about it.”

“Well, you see, it was like this. Old Missus—Miss Watson—she picks on me all the time and treats me pretty rough, but she always said she wouldn’t sell me down to Orleans. Still, I noticed there was a slave trader hanging around the place a lot lately, and I started getting uneasy. Well, one night I slipped out to the door pretty late, and it wasn’t quite shut. I heard Missus telling the widow she was going to sell me down to Orleans. She didn’t want to, but she could get eight hundred dollars for me, and it was such a big pile of money she couldn’t resist. The widow tried to get her to promise she wouldn’t do it, but I didn’t wait to hear the rest. I took off fast, I can tell you.

“I got out and headed down the hill. I was going to steal a skiff along the shore somewhere above town, but people were still moving around, so I hid in the old tumble-down cooper shop on the bank and waited for everyone to go away. I stayed there all night. There was somebody around all the time. Sometime around six in the morning the skiffs started passing, and about eight or nine every skiff that went by was talking about how your father came over to town and said you’d been killed. Those last skiffs were full of ladies and gentlemen going over to see the place. Sometimes they’d pull up at the shore and take a rest before they started across, so from all the talk I learned everything about the killing. I’m mighty sorry you’re killed, Huck, but I ain’t no more.

“I lay there under the shavings all day. I was hungry, but I wasn’t scared, because I knew old Missus and the widow were going to start off to the camp meeting right after breakfast and be gone all day. They know I go off with the cattle at daylight, so they wouldn’t expect to see me around the place, and they wouldn’t miss me until after dark in the evening. The other servants wouldn’t miss me either, because they’d slip out and take a holiday as soon as the old folks were out of the way.

“Well, when it got dark I went out up the river road and walked about two miles or more to where there weren’t any houses. I’d already decided what I was going to do. You see, if I kept trying to get away on foot, the dogs would track me. And if I stole a skiff to cross, they’d notice that skiff was missing, you see, and they’d know where I landed on the other side and where to pick up my trail."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b3c265af518190fe0d861955","rewritten_text":"The mental traits spoken of as analytical are, by their very nature, scarcely open to being analyzed. We come to know them chiefly through what they produce. Among other things, we observe that, when a person indulges them immoderately, they become for their owner a wellspring of the keenest pleasure. Just as the robust man rejoices in his bodily powers, taking delight in exercises that set his muscles working, so the analyst exults in that moral labor which _disentangles_. He finds satisfaction even in the smallest employments, so long as his gift can be brought to bear. He is drawn to riddles, conundrums, and hieroglyphics, and in solving each he shows a degree of _acumen_ that seems, to ordinary understanding, almost uncanny. His outcomes—shaped by the very soul and substance of method—carry, in truth, the look of something like intuition.\n\nThe power of re-solution may be greatly sharpened by mathematical study, and especially by the highest branch of it which, unfairly and merely because it works backward, has been dubbed, as if _par excellence_, analysis. Still, to calculate is not, in itself, to analyze. A chess-player, for instance, can do one thing without the other. It follows that chess, in the way it affects mental character, is widely misread. I am not setting out to write a treatise; I am only introducing a somewhat singular narrative with remarks offered at random. I will therefore take the liberty of saying that the higher faculties of the reflective mind are more distinctly and more profitably engaged by the plain, unassuming game of draughts than by all the elaborate, empty play of chess. In the latter, where the pieces move in different and _bizarre_ ways and carry various, shifting values, what is merely complicated is taken for what is profound (a mistake not uncommon). Here the _attention_ is brought powerfully into action. If it slips for even a moment, an oversight follows, and injury or defeat is the result. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but also intricate, the likelihood of such oversights is increased; and in nine cases out of ten it is the more concentrating, rather than the more keenly acute, player who wins. In draughts, however, where the moves are _unique_ and allow little variation, the chances of inadvertence are reduced, and with attention left comparatively idle, the advantage each side gains comes from superior _acumen_. To make it less abstract, suppose a game of draughts reduced to four kings, where, naturally, no oversight is to be expected. Then, with the players otherwise equal, it is plain that victory can be decided only by some _recherché_ maneuver—the product of a vigorous exertion of the intellect."}

{"request_id":"fe2004c0950169e44d484bf6","rewritten_text":"“April 12th. A remarkable change occurred in the balloon’s direction, and though I had fully expected it, nothing could have given me more certain pleasure. After reaching, along its former path, about the twentieth parallel of southern latitude, it suddenly swung off at a sharp angle toward the east, and so went on through the day, keeping nearly—if not entirely—in the same plane as the lunar ellipse. Worth noting, the car showed a very noticeable trembling as a result of this altered route; the motion continued, in greater or lesser degree, for many hours.

“April 13th. I was again greatly alarmed by the loud, crackling noise that had frightened me on the tenth. I thought it over at length, yet could reach no satisfying conclusion. The earth’s apparent size kept shrinking; from the balloon it now subtended an angle a little over twenty-five degrees. The moon could not be seen at all, since it lay almost in my zenith. I remained in the ellipse’s plane, but I made little headway to the east.

“April 14th. The earth’s diameter diminished with extraordinary speed. Today I became strongly convinced that the balloon was now actually running along the line of apsides toward the point of perigee—in other words, maintaining the direct course that would carry it at once to the moon at that portion of its orbit nearest the earth. The moon was directly overhead and therefore out of my sight. There was great and prolonged labor required for the condensation of the atmosphere.

“April 15th. Even the outlines of continents and seas could no longer be traced on the earth with anything like distinctness. About twelve o’clock I became aware, for the third time, of that dreadful sound which had so startled me before. This time, however, it lasted for some moments and grew louder as it continued. At last, while I stood, dazed and terrified, waiting—though for what I could not say—the car shook with extreme violence, and a vast, blazing mass of some substance, which I could not make out, swept past the balloon with a voice like a thousand thunders, roaring and booming overhead. When my fears and astonishment had somewhat settled, I found little difficulty in believing it to be some great volcanic fragment hurled from the world I was approaching so rapidly, and, most likely, one of those peculiar materials sometimes gathered on the earth and called meteoric stones for want of a better name.

“April 16th. Today, looking upward as best I could through each of the side windows in turn, I saw, to my great delight, a very small part of the moon’s disk protruding, as it were, on every side beyond the enormous rim of the balloon.”"}

{"request_id":"d9597aa4efc95ff5653b6061","rewritten_text":"About ten minutes later the bell rang for tea, and as Virginia still did not come down, Mrs. Otis sent one of the footmen upstairs to find out what was the matter. After a short while he returned and reported that he could not discover Miss Virginia anywhere. Since she was accustomed every evening to go out into the garden to gather flowers for the dinner-table, Mrs. Otis was not much alarmed at first; but when six o’clock struck and Virginia had not shown herself, her uneasiness turned to real agitation. She sent the boys out at once to search for her, while she and Mr. Otis went through every room in the house. At half-past six the boys came back, saying they could find no trace of their sister. Everyone was now in the utmost excitement, not knowing what to do, when Mr. Otis suddenly recalled that, only a few days earlier, he had allowed a band of gypsies to camp in the park. He therefore set off immediately for Blackfell Hollow, with his eldest son and two of the farm-servants.

The little Duke of Cheshire, who was beside himself with anxiety, pleaded hard to be allowed to go as well, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing there might be a scuffle. When they arrived, however, they found the gypsies had already gone, and it was plain their departure had been sudden, for the fire was still burning and some plates lay on the grass. After sending Washington and the two men to scour the surrounding district, he hurried home and dispatched telegrams to every police inspector in the county, instructing them to keep an eye out for a little girl who had been kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He then had his horse brought round, and, after insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, rode off along the Ascot Road with a groom.

He had scarcely gone a couple of miles when he heard someone galloping after him. Turning his head, he saw the little Duke coming up on his pony, his face very flushed and without a hat. ‘I’m awfully sorry, Mr. Otis,’ the boy panted, ‘but I can’t eat any dinner while Virginia is lost. Please don’t be angry with me; if you’d let us be engaged last year, none of this trouble would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!’

The Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young scapegrace, and was deeply moved by his devotion to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted him gently on the shoulders and said, ‘Well, Cecil, if you won’t go back I suppose you must come with me, but I must get you a hat at Ascot.’"}

{"request_id":"c8741193932fd184e4123307","rewritten_text":"At the stairs where we had taken him abroad, and ever since, I had watched warily for any sign that we were suspected. I saw none. We certainly weren’t, and at that time we were certainly not being attended or followed by any boat. If we had been met by any boat, I would have run to shore and told it to go on, or made its purpose clear. But we kept our course without any sign of being bothered.

He had his boat-cloak on, and, as I’ve said, he looked like a natural part of the scene. It was remarkable—though perhaps the miserable life he’d led explains it—that he was the least anxious of all of us. He wasn’t indifferent; he told me he hoped to live long enough to see his gentleman become one of the best gentlemen in a foreign country. He wasn’t disposed to be passive or resigned, as I understood it; but he had no intention of meeting danger halfway. When danger came for him, he faced it, but it had to arrive before he would trouble himself.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it is to sit here alonger my dear boy and have my smoke, arter having been day by day betwixt four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I know the delights of freedom,” I answered.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head gravely. “But you don’t know it equal to me. You must have been under lock and key, dear boy, to know it equal to me—but I ain’t a-going to be low.”

It struck me as inconsistent that, for any plan to work, he should have risked his freedom—and even his life. But I thought maybe freedom without danger was too far removed from the habits of his whole existence for it to feel to him the way it would to another man. I wasn’t far off, since he said, after smoking a little—

“You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, t’other side the world, I was always a looking to this side; and it come flat to be there, for all I was a growing rich. Everybody knowed Magwitch, and Magwitch could come, and Magwitch could go, and nobody’s head would be troubled about him. They ain’t so easy concerning me here, dear boy—wouldn’t be, leastwise, if they knowed where I was.”

“If all goes well,” I said, “you’ll be perfectly free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he replied, drawing a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And think so?”"}

{"request_id":"9e0882c762124ad004858adc","rewritten_text":"“Get up! What are you up to?”

I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to figure out where I was. It was after sunrise, and I’d been sound asleep. Pap was standing over me, looking sour and sick, too. He said:

“What were you doing with this gun?”

I figured he didn’t know anything about what he’d been doing, so I said:

“Somebody tried to get in, so I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me up?”

“I tried, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t move you.”

“Well, all right. Don’t stand there talking all day—get out and see if there’s a fish on the line for breakfast. I’ll be along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I headed out along the riverbank. I noticed bits of limbs and other things floating down, and a scattering of bark, so I knew the river had started to rise. I figured I’d have a great time now if I was over in town. The June rise used to always be good luck for me—because as soon as the water starts rising here comes cordwood floating down, and pieces of log rafts, sometimes a dozen logs together. All you have to do is catch them and sell them to the wood yards and the sawmill.

I walked up the bank with one eye out for Pap and the other watching what the rise might bring in. Then, all at once, a canoe came drifting in—what a beauty, too, about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high like a duck. I launched myself headfirst off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and paddled hard for the canoe. I expected someone might be lying in it to fool people, because sometimes when a man pulled a skiff out, they’d pop up and laugh at him. But that wasn’t what happened this time. It was a real drift-canoe, and I climbed in and paddled it ashore.

I thought, the old man will be glad when he sees this—it’s worth ten dollars. But when I got to shore, Pap wasn’t in sight yet. As I was pushing the canoe into a little creek like a narrow gully, all tangled with vines and willows, another idea hit me: I figured I’d hide it well. Then, instead of running off into the woods when I got away, I’d go down the river about fifty miles and camp in one place for good, so I wouldn’t have to keep dealing with the rough time of walking on foot.

It was pretty close to the shanty, and I thought I could hear the old man coming the whole time. But I got the canoe hidden, then stepped out and looked around through the willows—and there was the old man down the path a ways, aiming his gun at a bird, drawing a bead."}

{"request_id":"fd9225d9b0acb52238681a7d","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him for a few moments in amazement, and then, seeing that he was quite serious, wrote an address on a piece of paper, initialed it, and handed it to him across the table.

“Scotland Yard would give a good deal to know this address, my dear fellow.”

“They shan’t have it,” cried Lord Arthur, laughing; and after warmly shaking the young Russian’s hand, he hurried downstairs, examined the paper, and told the coachman to drive to Soho Square.

When they arrived, he dismissed him and strolled down Greek Street until he reached a place called Bayle’s Court. He went under the archway and found himself in a curious cul-de-sac, apparently occupied by a French Laundry, with a perfect network of clothes-lines stretched from house to house and a flutter of white linen in the morning air. He walked all the way to the end and knocked at a small green house. After a delay—during which every window in the court turned into a blurred mass of faces peering out—the door opened. A rather rough-looking foreigner asked him, in very bad English, what his business was. Lord Arthur handed him the paper Count Rouvaloff had given him. The man bowed when he saw it and invited Lord Arthur into a very shabby front parlour on the ground floor. In a few moments, Herr Winckelkopf—what he was called in England—bustled into the room, with a very wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork in his left hand.

“Count Rouvaloff has given me an introduction to you,” said Lord Arthur, bowing. “And I’m anxious to have a short interview with you about a matter of business. My name is Smith, Mr. Robert Smith, and I want you to supply me with an explosive clock.”

“Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,” said the genial little German, laughing. “Don’t look so alarmed. It’s my duty to know everyone, and I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I hope her ladyship is quite well. Would you mind sitting with me while I finish my breakfast? There’s an excellent pâté, and my friends are kind enough to say that my Rhine wine is better than any they get at the German Embassy.” Before Lord Arthur had fully recovered from the shock of being recognized, he found himself seated in the back room, sipping the most delicious Marcobrünner from a pale yellow hock-glass marked with the Imperial monogram, and chatting in the friendliest possible way with the famous conspirator.

“Explosive clocks,” said Herr Winckelkopf, “aren’t very good for foreign export. Even if they manage to get through the Custom House, the train service is so irregular that they usually go off before they’ve reached their proper destination.”"}

{"request_id":"a524f37a58449f608fbd4caa","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, shocked by Sikes’s crime, began to think about whether an honest life might not, after all, be the best choice. When he decided that it was, he turned away from the past and resolved to change his life in a new way. He worked hard and suffered for a long time, but because he had a calm, steady nature and a good purpose, he finally succeeded. From being a farm worker and a carrier’s boy, he is now the happiest young grazier in all Northamptonshire.

And now, the hand that writes these words hesitates as it comes near the end of its task, and it would keep going a little longer, weaving the thread of these adventures.

I would like to stay longer with some of the people among whom I have lived for so long, and share their happiness by trying to describe it. I would show Rose Maylie in the full bloom and grace of early womanhood, bringing soft, gentle light to the quiet path of her life—light that would fall on everyone who walked that way, and shine into their hearts. I would describe the warmth and joy of the fire-side circle, and the lively summer gatherings. I would follow her through the hot fields at noon, and hear the low, sweet sound of her voice during the evening walk under the moon. I would watch her as she shows kindness and charity wherever she goes, and as she carries out her home duties with a steady, smiling spirit. I would show her, and her dead sister’s child, happy in their love for each other, spending long hours imagining the friends they had lost so sadly. I would bring back those cheerful little faces that gathered around her knee, and listen to their happy chatter. I would remember the clear sound of her laugh, and picture the sympathetic tear that shone in her soft blue eyes. These, and a thousand looks and smiles, and the ways of thinking and speaking that went with them—I would like to recall them all.

As for how Mr. Brownlow went on, day after day, teaching his adopted child and filling his mind with knowledge, and how he became more and more attached to him as the boy’s character grew and showed the good seeds of everything he hoped he would become—how he noticed in him new traits of his old friend, bringing back memories in his own heart, sad but also comforting—how the two orphans, tested by adversity, remembered its lessons in mercy to others, in mutual love, and in deep thanks to Him who had protected and preserved them—these are things that do not need to be told."}

{"request_id":"27ff7ceb0eaf6e6c3aac4fb7","rewritten_text":"All of it carried a kind of strangeness that drew me in and held me spellbound. He seemed, as it were, to have just been roused from his long, visionary sleep; and he felt something like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad, in that gentle imitation of an eastern tale. Diana was gone; his friends were altered or dead; and with his awakening I became everything he had left to love upon the earth.

How dear to me were the waters, the mountains, and the woods of Loch Lomond now that I had such a beloved companion for my wanderings. I went with my father to every delightful place—whether on the islands, or along the sides of tree-sheltered waterfalls; by every shady path, every dingle tangled with underwood and fern. His conversation widened my thoughts. I felt as though I were made new, with all the freshness and vigor of a newly born being about me: it was as if, since his arrival, I had been carried from a narrow patch of earth into a universe boundless to imagination and understanding. My life before had been like a pleasant country rill, never meant to stray beyond its own native banks, but to run its course quietly and then be absorbed, leaving no trace. Now it seemed to me a many-channeled river, moving through a fertile and lovely landscape—always shifting, always fair. Alas, I did not know what desert lay ahead, what rocks would rend its waters, and what hideous spectacle would be thrown back, in a more distorted fashion, upon its waves. Life was bright then; I began to learn to hope—and what brings a sharper despair to the heart than hope when it is destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should come so swiftly after such heavenly happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, yet gall waited at the bottom of its long-drawn sweetness. My heart was full of deep affection, but it was calm, precisely because it was so full. I had never imagined that misery could spring from love; and this lesson—one that all at last must learn—was taught me in a way that few are forced to endure. I lament now, and must always lament, those few short months of blissful Paradise. I broke no command; I ate no apple; and still I was driven from it without mercy. Alas! my companion did, and I was hurled down with him. But I stray from my account—let sorrow arrive when its appointed time comes; at this point in my story I may still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful companionship, when my aunt fell ill. I spent a whole month in her chamber, nursing her, yet her sickness was mortal, and she died, leaving me for some time inconsolable. Death is so dreadful to the living; the chains of habit are so strong even when affection does not bind them, that the heart must be tormented when they snap."}

{"request_id":"d9b4f2a67160fffaf5cebc87","rewritten_text":"There was a wonderful feeling of tidying up and then taking a quiet pause before going on with life again, in our village on Saturday nights. It made Joe dare to stay out half an hour longer on Saturdays than he did at other times. When that half-hour was up, and the rum and water ran out together, Joe stood up to go and took me by the hand.

“Wait just half a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the strange man. “I think I’ve got a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if I do, the boy gets it.”

He dug it out from a handful of small change, folded it up in some crumpled paper, and handed it to me. “It’s yours!” he said. “Mind—your own.”

I thanked him, staring at him well beyond what good manners would allow, and holding tight to Joe. He said good-night to Joe, and good-night to Mr. Wopsle (who went out with us), and to me he gave only a look from his aiming eye—no, not a look, because he shut it up; but wonders can be done with an eye when you hide it.

On the way home, if I’d been in the mood to talk, the conversation would have been all on my side, because Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe went all the way home with his mouth wide open, trying to rinse the rum out with as much air as possible. But I was so stunned by the sudden return of my old wrongdoing and my old acquaintance that I couldn’t think of anything else.

When we presented ourselves in the kitchen, my sister wasn’t in a particularly bad temper, and Joe was encouraged by that unusual fact to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll bet,” said Mrs. Joe triumphantly. “Or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s look at it.”

I took it out of the paper, and it turned out to be a good one. “But what’s this?” said Mrs. Joe, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two two-pound notes?”

Nothing less than two thick, sweaty one-pound notes, as if they’d been on the closest terms with every cattle-market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat again and ran to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat down on my usual stool and stared vacantly at my sister, pretty sure the man wouldn’t be there.

Presently, Joe came back, saying the man was gone, but that Joe had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

“But could you really be comfortable, spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes. You see his father can do it, so why shouldn’t I? Jemima is so careful, and she could send us word every hour about how he is. I really think Charles might as well have told his father that we would all come. I’m not more worried about little Charles now than Charles is. I was terribly worried yesterday, but today is different.”

“Well, if you don’t think it’s too late to give notice for yourself, suppose you go too, along with your husband. Leave little Charles to my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove can’t think it wrong as long as I stay with him.”

“Are you serious?” Mary cried, her eyes brightening. “Dear me! That’s a very good idea—an excellent one, indeed. I might as well go as not, because I’m no use at home, am I? It only makes me more restless. You, who don’t have a mother’s feelings, are much more suited for this. You can make little Charles do anything; he always listens to you when you speak. It will be much better than leaving him only with Jemima. Oh, I will certainly go. I’m sure I ought to, if I can, just as much as Charles, because they want me to meet Captain Wentworth, and I don’t mind being left alone. What a wonderful thought, Anne. I’ll go tell Charles and get ready right away. You can send for us at any moment if anything goes wrong, but I don’t think there will be anything to worry you. I wouldn’t go at all if I didn’t feel fairly at ease about my dear child.”

The next moment she was tapping at her husband’s dressing-room door. As Anne followed her upstairs, she arrived in time to hear the whole conversation. It began with Mary speaking in a tone full of excitement.

“I mean to go with you, Charles, because I’m no more use at home than you are. If I were to shut myself up forever with the child, I wouldn’t be able to make him do anything he doesn’t want. Anne will stay. Anne will take care of him at home. It’s Anne’s own idea, so I’ll go with you, which will be much better, because I haven’t dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband answered. “I would be glad for you to go, but it seems rather unfair that she should be left at home by herself to nurse our sick child.”"}

{"request_id":"d66cc4040cccd87b4da0c9f5","rewritten_text":"Dear me, she was a master at talking. It would not do for me to point out that it was very late, that I was a tired man, and that I was so sleepy. I wished I had gone to bed when I had the chance. Now I had to stick it out—there was no other way. So she kept tinkling on and on, in the otherwise deep and ghostly hush of the sleeping castle, until, sooner or later, there came—like something rising from far beneath us—a distant sound, like a muffled shriek, with an expression of agony in it that made my skin crawl. The queen stopped, and her eyes brightened with pleasure; she tilted her graceful head the way a bird does when it listens. The sound worked its way up through the stillness again.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is truly a stubborn soul, and it endureth long. It is many hours now.”

“Endureth what?”

“The rack. Come—ye shall see a blithe sight. If he yield not his secret now, ye shall see him torn asunder.”

What a smooth, wicked hellion she was—and how calm and serene, even as the cords all down my legs began to ache in sympathy with that man’s pain. With mailed guards bearing flaring torches, we marched along echoing corridors and down stone stairways that were dank and dripping, smelling of mold and the ages of imprisoned night—a cold, uncanny journey, and a long one, and the sorceress’s talk about the sufferer and his crime did nothing to make it shorter or cheerier. He had been accused by an anonymous informer of killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said,

“Anonymous testimony isn’t the right thing, Your Highness. It would be fairer to confront the accused with the accuser.”

“I hadn’t thought of that, since it seemed of little consequence. But if I wanted to, I couldn’t, because the accuser came masked by night, told the forester, and straightway got him taken away again—so the forester knoweth him not.”

“Then is this Unknown the only person who saw the stag killed?”

“Marry, no man saw the killing, but this Unknown saw this hardy wretch near to the spot where the stag lay, and came with right loyal zeal and betrayed him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag, too? Isn’t it possible he did the killing himself? His loyal zeal—while masked—looks just a shade suspicious. But what is your highness’s plan for racking the prisoner? Where is the profit?”

“He will not confess, else—and then his soul would be lost. For his crime his life is forfeited by the law—and of a surety will I see that he payeth it!—but it would be peril to my own soul to let him die unconfessed and unabsolved.”"}

{"request_id":"628d34252d2c99838cff5b2d","rewritten_text":"“What’s wrong?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“Ten o’clock—at night?”

“Yes, sir. Your honour told me to come and fetch you.”

“Oh! I see. Very good, very good.”

After a few lifeless attempts to get back to sleep—efforts the man skillfully thwarted by keeping the fire stirred for five minutes—he rose, flung his hat on, and went out. He turned into the Temple, and, having set himself right again by pacing twice along the King’s Bench-walk and the Paper-buildings, he made for the Stryver rooms.

The Stryver clerk, who never took part in these meetings, had already gone home, and the Stryver principal opened the door. He was in his slippers, with a loose bed-gown on, and his throat was uncovered for his comfort. There was that rather wild, strained, scorched look about the eyes—something to be seen in all the free livers of his set, from Jeffries’ portrait down—and it could be traced, under all manner of artistic disguises, through the portraits of every Drinking Age.

“You’re a bit late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the usual time; perhaps a quarter of an hour later.”

They went into a dingy room, lined with books and strewn with papers, where a fire was burning. A kettle hissed on the hob, and amid the ruin of papers a table gleamed, well supplied with wine, and brandy, and rum, and sugar, and lemons.

“I take it you’ve had your bottle, Sydney,” said Stryver.

“Two tonight, I suppose. I’ve been dining with the day’s client—or else watching him dine; it’s much the same!”

“That was a fine stroke, Sydney, the way you handled the identification. How did it come to you? When did it first occur?”

“I figured he was a pretty handsome sort, and I thought I’d be much the same kind of fellow if I’d had any luck.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his precocious paunch shook.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

With a sullen air, the jackal loosened his dress, went into the adjoining room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. He soaked the towels, wrung them out only partly, laid them on his head in a fashion hideous to look at, sat down at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“Not much boiling down to do tonight, Memory,” Mr. Stryver said cheerfully, as he leafed through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets of them.”

“Give me the worst first.”

“There you are, Sydney. Fire away!”

The lion settled himself on his back on a sofa at one side of the drinking-table, while the jackal took his place at his own paper-covered table on the other side, with the bottles and glasses set within easy reach."}

{"request_id":"38350597f090005633e8f83d","rewritten_text":"I can’t fully describe the joy I felt when I left behind the noisy fights of politics at home, and the physical suffering I had seen in faraway places, and turned instead to my own dear home—the place chosen for goodness and love. I felt peace there, and the chance to share every sacred feeling with others. If I had never left Windsor, these emotions wouldn’t have been so strong. But in Greece I had been trapped by fear and by terrible change. In Greece, after a time of worry and sorrow, I watched two people leave—people whose names alone stood for greatness and virtue. Still, none of those troubles could reach the family life I had left behind. While we lived quietly in our beloved forest, shut away from the world, we were safe.

Of course, time brought small changes, as it always does. It left signs of how mortal we are on our pleasures and hopes. Idris—my most loving wife, sister, and friend—was a tender, affectionate mother. Her love was not like a casual hobby for her, as it is for many. It was a true passion. We had three children. One of them, the second oldest, died while I was in Greece. That loss crushed the proud joy of motherhood and filled me and her with grief and fear. Before that tragedy, the little ones she had borne—the young heirs of her brief life—seemed to have a secure future. Now she feared that the cruel destroyer might take her remaining children, just as it had taken their brother.

The smallest illness brought her terror. She was miserable whenever she was away from them. Her happiness was built on their fragile lives, and she kept watch constantly, afraid that the same thief might steal those precious treasures again. Luckily, she had little reason to fear. Alfred was now nine years old. He was upright and strong in spirit, with a bright forehead, soft eyes, and a gentle but independent nature. Our youngest was still an infant, but his cheeks were smooth and healthy, touched with the pink of good health, and his constant energy filled our halls with innocent laughter.

Clara had passed the age when her quiet ignorance would have caused Idris to worry. Clara was loved by Idris, and by everyone. She had so much intelligence mixed with innocence, so much feeling mixed with restraint, and such seriousness joined to perfect good humor. Her beauty was extraordinary, and it came with such simple, lovable ways that she seemed like a pearl kept in the heart of our home—a treasure of wonder and excellence.

At the start of winter, Alfred, now nine, went to school at Eton for the first time. To him, it felt like the first real step toward manhood, and he was pleased. Studying and playing with others helped bring out the best in him. He became steady and persistent, generous, and firm in a way that was well controlled."}

{"request_id":"510e28baad02dd6ec9f3c569","rewritten_text":"For that reason, I decided to step down the moment we reached the town and to place myself beyond his reach of hearing. I carried it out without a hitch. My small portmanteau lay in the boot beneath my feet; all I had to do was work a hinge and it would come free. I let it fall in front of me, climbed down after it, and found myself standing on the first stones of the town pavement, at the first lamp. As for the convicts, they rode on with the coach, and I could tell at what point they would be taken off toward the river. In my mind I pictured the boat with its convict crew waiting for them at the slime-smeared steps; I could hear again the rough “Give way, you!”—as if it were an order to dogs; and once more I saw the wicked Noah’s Ark lying out on the black water.

I couldn’t have said exactly what I feared, because my fear had no clear object at all—only a dim, undefined dread—but I was seized by a great terror. When I walked on to the hotel, I felt a kind of dread that went far beyond the ordinary uneasiness of facing some painful or unpleasant recognition; it made me shake. I’m sure it had no definite outline, and that for a few minutes it was nothing more than the old terror of childhood coming back to life.

The coffee-room at the Blue Boar was empty, and I had not only ordered my dinner there, but had taken my seat with it before the waiter even knew me. The moment he had apologised for his lapse of memory, he asked whether he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” said I, “certainly not.”

The waiter—he it was who had brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day when I was bound—looked taken aback, and seized the first opening to slide a dirty, old copy of a local newspaper straight in my path. I picked it up and read the paragraph he had placed before me:—

Our readers will learn, not altogether without interest, in reference to the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young artificer in iron of this neighbourhood (what a theme, by the way, for the magic pen of our as yet not universally acknowledged townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!) that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and friend, was a highly respected individual not entirely unconnected with the corn and seed trade, and whose eminently convenient and commodious business premises are situate within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not wholly irrespective of our personal feelings that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is good to know that our town produced the founder of the latter’s fortunes."}

Her eyes brightened with pleasure, and she tilted her graceful head the way a bird does when it listens. The sound pushed its way back through the silence.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is truly a stubborn soul, and it endureth long. It is many hours now.”

“Endureth what?”

“The rack. Come—ye shall see a blithe sight. If he will not yield his secret now, ye shall see him torn asunder.”

What a smooth, cruel little devil she was. And yet she looked so calm and peaceful, even as the cords down my legs began to hurt in sympathy with the man’s pain. Mailed guards led us, torches flaring as we marched through echoing corridors and down stone stairs that were damp and dripping. The air smelled of mold and of old, trapped night. It was a cold, strange journey, and a long one, and it was not made shorter or more pleasant by the sorceress’s talk, which was all about this sufferer and his crime. He had been accused by an anonymous informer of killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

“Anonymous testimony isn’t the right thing, Your Highness. It would be fairer to confront the accused with the accuser.”

“I hadn’t thought of that, since it seemed to matter little. But if I wanted to, I couldn’t. The accuser came masked at night, told the forester, and then had him taken away at once. So the forester does not know him.”

“Then is this Unknown the only person who saw the stag killed?”

“Marry, no man saw the killing. But this Unknown saw that hardy fellow near where the stag lay, and came with loyal zeal to betray him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag too? Isn’t it possible he killed it himself? His loyal zeal—while wearing a mask—looks a little suspicious. But what does Your Highness plan to gain by racking the prisoner?”

“He will not confess, else; and then his soul would be lost. By law, his life is forfeit for his crime, and I will see that he pays it. But it would be dangerous to my own soul to let him die without confession and without absolution.”"}

{"request_id":"a5b63b62022e8395e7cbb0e6","rewritten_text":"You will be glad to hear that nothing terrible has happened as I began this journey, even though you worried so much about it. I arrived here yesterday, and my first duty is to tell my dear sister that I am safe and that I feel more and more confident about the success of what I am doing.

I am already far north of London. As I walk through the streets of Petersburgh, a cold northern wind touches my cheeks. It steadies my nerves and makes me feel happy. Do you know that feeling? This breeze has come from the far regions I am moving toward, and it gives me a preview of those freezing places. Because of this promising wind, my daydreams grow stronger and clearer. I cannot convince myself that the pole is only a place of ice and emptiness. Instead, it always appears to me as a land of beauty and joy. There, Margaret, the sun stays in view all the time. Its bright disk sits just above the horizon and spreads a constant, dazzling light. There, with your permission, my sister, I will trust what earlier sailors said—there, snow and frost are gone. And if we sail over a calm sea, we may be carried to a land that is more wonderful and beautiful than anything anyone has found so far on the habitable earth. Its plants and features may be unlike anything else, just as the wonders of the sky must be unlike anything in those still unknown regions. What could we not expect in a country of endless daylight? I may discover the strange power that draws the compass needle, and I may also be able to make a thousand observations of the heavens that would only make sense after this one voyage, so that their apparent oddities stay consistent forever. I will satisfy my eager curiosity by seeing part of the world no one has visited before, and I may walk on land that no human foot has ever touched. These are the reasons that pull me forward, and they are enough to drive away all fear of danger or death. They make me start this hard journey with the same joy a child feels when he sets off in a small boat with friends on an expedition to explore his home river.

But even if all my guesses are wrong, you still cannot deny the great benefit I will bring to all people, even for the last generation. I will either find a route near the pole to reach those countries that now take so many months to get to, or I will learn the secret of magnetism—something that, if it is possible at all, can only be discovered through an undertaking like mine.

These thoughts have calmed the worry I felt when I began my letter. I feel my heart warm with excitement, as if it lifts me toward heaven. Nothing helps the mind as much as a steady purpose—something the soul can fix its attention on, like a clear point for the mind to look at."}

{"request_id":"8c866a99045304b2bcbd81f6","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed to keep on in her old job, at Lady Canterville’s firm request. When they stepped out, Mrs. Umney bowed low to each of them and said, in a quaint, old-fashioned way, “I bid you welcome to Canterville Chase.” After her, they walked through the Tudor hall and into the library, a long, low room with black oak paneling. At the far end was a large stained-glass window. Tea was already laid out for them. After they took off their wraps, they sat down and began to look around, while Mrs. Umney served them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor near the fireplace. Without thinking about what it meant, she said to Mrs. Umney, “I’m afraid something has been spilled there.”

“Yes, madam,” the old housekeeper answered in a low voice. “Blood has been spilled on that spot.”

“How awful,” Mrs. Otis said. “I don’t want blood stains in a sitting-room. It has to be cleaned right away.”

The old woman smiled and replied in the same quiet, mysterious tone, “It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, who was murdered right there by her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived for nine years after her death, and then disappeared under very strange circumstances. His body was never found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. The stain has been admired by tourists and others, and it cannot be removed.”

“That’s nonsense,” Washington Otis snapped. “Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will take care of it in no time.” Before the frightened housekeeper could stop him, he dropped to his knees and quickly scrubbed the floor with a small stick that looked like a black cosmetic. In a few moments, the blood stain was gone.

“I knew Pinkerton would do it,” he said triumphantly, looking around at his impressed family. But the moment he finished speaking, a terrible flash of lightning lit up the dark room. A fearful crash of thunder followed, and they all jumped up. Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What a dreadful climate,” the American Minister said calmly as he lit a long cheroot. “I guess the old country is so crowded that they don’t have decent weather for everyone. I’ve always believed that emigration is the only answer for England.”

“My dear Hiram,” Mrs. Otis cried, “what can we do with a woman who faints?”

“Treat it like a breakage,” the Minister replied. “She won’t faint after that.” In a few moments, Mrs. Umney did come around."}

{"request_id":"d1ee493366256b8eadab3511","rewritten_text":"At dinner, Mr. Bennet hardly said a word; but once the servants had withdrawn, he judged it the right moment to speak with his visitor, and so he began a topic on which he expected him to shine—remarking that he seemed extremely fortunate in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes, and her care for his comfort, struck him as especially noteworthy. Mr. Bennet could not have picked a better subject. Mr. Collins grew eloquent in praising her. The matter put him into a more than ordinary gravity of manner, and with a most consequential air he declared that he had never, in all his life, seen such conduct in any person of rank—so much affability and condescension as he had personally experienced from Lady Catherine. She had been gracious enough to approve of both sermons he had already had the honour of delivering before her. She had also asked him twice to dine at Rosings, and had sent for him only the Saturday before, so that he might make up her party for quadrille in the evening. Lady Catherine was thought proud by many people, he knew, but he had never observed anything in her except affability. She had always spoken to him as she would to any other gentleman; she raised not the slightest objection to his mixing with the neighbourhood, nor to his leaving his parish now and then for a week or two to see his relations. She had even condescended to advise him to marry as soon as he could, as long as he chose with discretion; and she had once paid him a visit at his modest parsonage, where she had approved every alteration he had been making, and had even deigned to suggest a few herself—some shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That’s all very proper and civil, I’m sure,” said Mrs. Bennet. “And I dare say she’s a very agreeable woman. It’s a pity that great ladies in general aren’t more like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden where my humble home stands is separated from Rosings Park by nothing more than a lane—her Ladyship’s residence.”

“I thought you said she was a widow, sir. Has she any family?”

“She has only one daughter—the heiress of Rosings, and possessed of very extensive property.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she’s better off than many girls. And what kind of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is, indeed, a most charming young lady. Lady Catherine herself says that, in point of true beauty, Miss de Bourgh is far superior to the handsomest of her sex; for there is something in her features that marks her as a young woman of distinguished birth.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"682fabb9514daeb02319fac2","rewritten_text":"In truth, he had been completely unaware of any influence he might have had. He followed her into the shrubbery without any plan to try anything. He had come, driven by anxiety to see how she handled Frank Churchill’s engagement, with no selfish motive at all—indeed, with no clear motive beyond wanting, if she gave him the chance, to calm her or offer advice. What happened next was simply the result of the moment and of what he heard right then. Her confident assurance that she felt no interest in Frank Churchill—her heart being entirely free of him—gave rise to the hope that, over time, he might win her affection himself. But at that instant, he did not even think in terms of time; in the rush of eagerness over good judgment, he only wanted to be told that she would not forbid him to try to win her. The hopes that opened up to him gradually were even more thrilling. The affection he had been asking to be allowed to create was already his. Within half an hour, he had gone from being deeply distressed to something so close to perfect happiness that it could not be called anything else.\n\n_Her_ change matched his. This same half-hour gave each of them the precious certainty of being loved, and removed from each the same ignorance, jealousy, or distrust. On his side, there had been jealousy for a long time, starting with Frank Churchill’s arrival—or even with the expectation of it. He had been in love with Emma and jealous of Frank Churchill from about the same period, and one feeling likely helped him understand the other. It was his jealousy of Frank Churchill that made him leave the country. The Box Hill party decided him to go away. He wanted to protect himself from having to witness again those attentions that were allowed and encouraged. He had gone to learn to be indifferent. But he had gone to the wrong place. There was too much domestic happiness in his brother’s house; the women there wore too pleasant a face; Isabella was too much like Emma, differing only in those obvious, lesser faults that always made the other seem brighter to him, even if he had had more time to do something about it. Still, he stayed on, day after day, until this very morning’s post brought him the story of Jane Fairfax. Then, with the gladness he had every right to feel—gladness he did not hesitate to admit, since he had never believed Frank Churchill deserved Emma—he found that there was so much real concern for her, so much sharp anxiety on her behalf, that he could not stay any longer. He rode home through the rain, and after dinner he went straight to see how this best and sweetest of all creatures, faultless despite all her faults, handled the discovery."}

{"request_id":"6c9a6a3412604a54a20c2563","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” said he, as we reached the base, “come here! Tell me—was the skull fixed to the limb with the face turned outward, or turned toward the limb?”

“De face was out, massa, so de crows could get at de eyes good, widout any trouble.”

“Then which eye was it—this one or that one—through which you let the beetle drop?” Here Legrand touched each of Jupiter’s eyes in turn.

“’Twas dis eye, massa—de lef eye—jis as you tell me,” and at that the negro pointed out his right eye.

“That will do. We’ll have to try it again.”

Here my friend—whose madness I had begun to see, or thought I saw, showed some sort of method—pulled out the peg that marked where the beetle had fallen, and set it down about three inches farther west than before. Then, taking the tape measure from the nearest point of the trunk to the peg as we had done earlier, and carrying the line straight on for fifty feet, we were led to a spot that lay several yards away from where we’d been digging.

A circle, a bit larger than the last, was drawn around this new place, and we started in again with the spades. I was terribly tired, yet, without quite knowing what had brought about the shift in my thoughts, I no longer felt any strong dislike for the work. I had become, in the strangest way, absorbed—indeed, even stirred. Maybe it was something in all the wildness of Legrand—some hint of forethought, some deliberation—that carried me along. I dug with eagerness, and now and then I caught myself actually staring, with an expression very like expectation, for the imagined treasure—the very vision that had driven my poor companion out of his mind. At a time when these fancies held me most completely, and after we had been at it perhaps an hour and a half, we were cut off again by the dog’s violent howling. At first his distress had clearly been nothing more than play or whim, but now it took on a harsh, serious note. When Jupiter tried once more to put a muzzle on him, the dog fought back fiercely, and, springing into the hole, clawed at the earth with frantic energy. In a few seconds he had uncovered a mass of human bones, making up two full skeletons, tangled together, along with several buttons of metal and what looked like the dust of decayed wool. One or two quick strokes of a spade brought up the blade of a large Spanish knife, and as we dug farther, three or four loose pieces of gold and silver coin came to light."}

{"request_id":"0851110f9363b2b7f4dd3f82","rewritten_text":"Biddy cried; the darkening garden, the lane, and the stars that were beginning to show were blurred in my own sight.

“Nothing was ever discovered, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what has become of Orlick?”

“I’d say, from the color of his clothes, that he’s working in the quarries.”

“Then you’ve seen him?—Why are you staring at that dark tree in the lane?”

“I saw him there, on the night she died.”

“That wasn’t the last time either, Biddy?”

“No; I’ve seen him there since we’ve been walking here. —It’s no use,” said Biddy, laying her hand on my arm as I was about to run out. “You know I wouldn’t deceive you; he wasn’t there for a minute, and he’s gone.”

It flared my anger to realize that this man was still pursuing her, and I felt a deep, stubborn hatred toward him. I told her so, and told her that I would spend any money or take any trouble to drive him out of that country. Bit by bit, she brought the conversation back to calmer ground, and she told me how Joe loved me, and how Joe never complained about anything—she didn’t say anything about me; she didn’t need to; I understood what she meant. He always did his duty in his own way of life, with a firm hand, a quiet tongue, and a gentle heart.

“Indeed, it would be hard to say too much for him,” I said. “And, Biddy, we’ll have to talk about these things often, because I’ll be down here a great deal now. I’m not going to leave poor Joe alone.”

Biddy didn’t say a single word.

“Biddy, don’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Not to mention your calling me Mr. Pip—which, to me, sounds like bad taste, Biddy—what do you mean?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked, timidly.

“Biddy,” I said, in a self-righteous way, “I need to know what you mean by this.”

“By this?” said Biddy.

“Now, don’t echo,” I snapped. “You didn’t used to, Biddy.”

“Used not!” said Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Used!”

Well! I figured I’d have to give up that point too. After another silent turn in the garden, I fell back on my main argument.

“Biddy,” I said, “I made a remark about how often I come down here to see Joe, and you responded with a very noticeable silence. Please, Biddy, tell me why.”

“Are you quite sure, then, that you WILL come to see him often?” Biddy asked, stopping in the narrow garden path and looking at me under the stars with a clear, honest gaze."}
