{"request_id":"04bc26877935b55beb0127f5","rewritten_text":"“Is that all? Why, it’s hardly much at all! Many are under the Republic’s displeasure, and must keep their eyes on that small window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?”

“I am he. Of course—since I’m the last.”

It is Jarvis Lorry who has answered all the questions that came before. It is Jarvis Lorry who has stepped down and now stands with his hand on the coach door, answering a knot of officials. They stroll around the carriage at their ease, and at their ease climb up to the box, to see what scanty luggage it carries up on the roof; the country folk linger about, draw nearer to the coach doors, and stare in with hungry eyes. A little child, borne by its mother, has its short arm held out so that it may touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry—countersigned.”

“One may go, citizen?”

“One may go. Forward, my postilions! A good journey!”

“I salute you, citizens—and the first danger is past!”

Once more those are Jarvis Lorry’s words, as he clasps his hands and looks upward. In the carriage there is terror; there is weeping; there is the heavy breathing of the insensible passenger.

“Are we not moving too slowly? Can’t they be made to go faster?” Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

“It would look like flight, my dear. I mustn’t press them too hard; it might awaken suspicion.”

“Look back, look back—see whether we’re being followed!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, we are not pursued.”

Houses in twos and threes pass by us, solitary farms, ruinous buildings, dye-works, tanneries, and the like; open country, and avenues of leafless trees. The hard, uneven pavement is beneath us, while soft, deep mud lies on either side. Now and then we veer into the bordering mud to dodge the stones that clatter and rattle us; now and then we get caught in ruts and sloughs there. Then the torment of our impatience becomes so sharp that, in our wild alarm and hurry, we are for getting out and running—hiding—doing anything but stopping.

From the open country we come again among ruinous buildings, solitary farms, dye-works, tanneries, and the like; cottages in twos and threes, avenues of leafless trees. Have these men tricked us and brought us back by another road? Isn’t it the very same place twice over? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see if we are pursued! Hush! the posting-house.

Leisurely, our four horses are taken out; leisurely, the coach stands in the little street, stripped of its horses and with no prospect of ever moving again; leisurely, the new horses come into view, one after another; leisurely, the new postilions follow, drawing and plaiting the lashes of their whips; leisurely, the old postilions count their money, make wrong sums, and reach results that leave them dissatisfied."}

{"request_id":"ef41d5444e67c46102ed56c5","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton paused in the street, unsure where to go. “At Tellson’s banking house at nine,” he said, looking as if he were thinking. “Should I show myself in the meantime? I think I should. It’s important that these people know there’s a man like me here. It’s a sensible precaution, and it may be necessary. But—care, care, care! I need to think it through.”

He checked his steps, which had started to lead him toward some purpose, then turned down a couple of streets that were already growing darker. He followed the idea in his mind and considered what it might lead to. His first thought was right. “It’s best,” he decided at last, “that these people should know there is such a man as I here.” Then he turned his face toward Saint Antoine.

That day, Defarge had said he was the owner of a wine shop in the Saint Antoine suburb. If you knew the city, it was easy to find his house without asking questions. Once Carton knew where it was, he went back out into the nearby streets and ate dinner at a place where people could refresh themselves. After dinner, he fell into a deep sleep. For the first time in many years, he didn’t have any strong drink. Since last night, he’d had only a little light, thin wine. And last night he had set the brandy down on Mr. Lorry’s hearth slowly, as if he were done with it.

He woke up refreshed at about seven o’clock and went back out into the streets. As he walked toward Saint Antoine, he stopped at a shop window with a mirror. He adjusted his loose cravat, his coat collar, and his wild hair, making them look slightly more disordered. Then he went straight to Defarge’s and went inside.

There was no customer in the shop, only Jacques Three, with his restless fingers and his croaking voice. Carton had seen him at the Jury. Now he stood at the small counter, drinking while he talked with the Defarges—husband and wife. The Vengeance took part in the conversation as if it were a normal member of the place.

When Carton came in, he took a seat and asked, in very indifferent French, for a small measure of wine. Madame Defarge gave him a casual look at first, then a sharper one, then an even sharper one. After that, she came over to him and asked what he had ordered.

He repeated what he had already said.

“English?” Madame Defarge asked, lifting her dark eyebrows.

He looked at her as if even a single French word took time to form in his mind, and then answered in the same strong foreign accent as before."}

{"request_id":"2ad1304bdea501b708dda1c3","rewritten_text":"The following day the ghost was faint with weariness. The dreadful excitement of the past four weeks was at last beginning to tell upon him; his nerves were utterly in pieces, and he started at the smallest sound. For five days he kept to his room, and then, after much turning over the matter, decided to abandon the whole business of the blood-stain on the library floor. If the Otis family did not want it, then, plainly, they did not deserve it. They seemed to him to live on a low, material level, and to be quite unable to grasp the symbolic force of sensuous appearances. The matter of phantasmal manifestations, and the shaping of astral bodies, was another question altogether—indeed, something beyond his own control. His duty, solemn and fixed, was to show himself in the corridor once a week, and to gibber from the great oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of each month; and he could not see how he might, with any propriety, slip out of such obligations.

It was true enough that his life had been wicked, yet he was, on the other hand, scrupulous in everything connected with the supernatural. Accordingly, for the next three Saturdays, he went through the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every precaution so that he should neither be heard nor seen. He took off his boots, stepped as lightly as he could on the old worm-eaten boards, drew a heavy black velvet cloak about him, and made sure to apply the Rising Sun Lubricator when it came to oiling his chains. I must admit it was no small struggle for him to bring himself to adopt this last safeguard. Still, one night—while the family were at dinner—he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and made off with the bottle. At first he felt a little ashamed of himself, but later he was sensible enough to recognize that there was a great deal to be said for the invention, and that, to a certain extent, it served his turn.

Yet even so, he was not left in peace. Strings were constantly stretched across the corridor; he caught his foot on them in the dark, and on one occasion, when he was dressed for the part of “Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,” he came down hard after stepping on a butter-slide. The twins had laid it from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber up to the top of the oak staircase. This fresh affront so inflamed him that he resolved to make one last attempt to assert his dignity and social standing, and he determined to call upon the impertinent young Etonians the next night in his famous character of “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.”

He had not worn that disguise for more than seventy years; in truth, not since it had so frightened pretty Lady Barbara Modish. By means of it she had broken off her engagement with the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather, and fled to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton, declaring that nothing in the world would ever persuade her to marry into a family that permitted so dreadful a phantom to pace the terrace at twilight."}

{"request_id":"d6a2c481e233138c9eae7261","rewritten_text":"It was in Warwick Castle that I came across the curious stranger I’m going to talk about. He drew me in for three reasons: his candid simplicity, his marvelous familiarity with ancient armor, and the calm, restful feeling of his company—for he did all the talking. We fell into step together, as modest people do, at the back of the group being led through, and he immediately began saying things that genuinely interested me. As he spoke—softly, pleasantly, smoothly—he seemed to drift, almost without my noticing, out of this world and out of its time, and into some far-off era and an old, forgotten country. Slowly he wove such a spell around me that I felt as if I were moving among the specters and shadows and dust and mold of a gray antiquity, holding conversation with something from it! Just as I would talk about my closest personal friends or enemies, or my most familiar neighbors, he spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other great names of the Round Table—and how old, old, unspeakably old, and faded, and dry, and musty, and ancient he seemed to become as he went on.

At last he turned to me and said, as casually as one might mention the weather—or any other ordinary subject—

“Do you know about the transmigration of souls? Do you know about the transposition of epochs—and bodies?”

I told him I hadn’t heard of it. He was so little concerned—just as people are when they talk about the weather—that he didn’t seem to notice whether I answered him or not. There was a brief half-moment of silence, immediately broken by the droning voice of the paid cicerone:

“Ancient hauberk, dating from the sixth century, time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; observe the round hole through the chain-mail in the left breast; can’t be accounted for; supposed to have been made with a bullet since the invention of firearms—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My acquaintance smiled—not a modern smile, but one that must have gone out of common use many, many centuries ago—and muttered, as if to himself:

“Wit ye well, I saw it done.” Then, after a pause, he added: “I did it myself.”

By the time I had recovered from the electric shock of that remark, he was gone.

All that evening I sat by my fire at the Warwick Arms, sunk in a dream of the olden time, while the rain hammered at the windows and the wind roared around the eaves and corners. From time to time I dipped into old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, feeding on its rich feast of prodigies and adventures, breathing in the fragrance of its obsolete names, and dreaming again."}

{"request_id":"dc90f2d2949a62a467cedbb1","rewritten_text":"“I hope I shall soon have the pleasure of introducing my son to you,” said Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, very willing to assume that this hope was meant as a compliment to her, smiled most graciously.

“You have heard of a certain Frank Churchill, I presume,” he continued—“and you know him to be my son, even though he doesn’t bear my name.”

“Oh! yes, and I shall be very happy to make his acquaintance. I’m sure Mr. Elton will waste no time in calling on him; and we shall both have great pleasure in seeing him at the Vicarage.”

“You are very kind.—Frank will be extremely happy, I’m sure.—He’s to be in town next week, if not sooner. We’ve had notice of it in a letter today. I came across the letters this morning, and seeing my son’s handwriting, I presumed to open it—though it wasn’t addressed to me—it was addressed to Mrs. Weston. She is his main correspondent, I assure you. I hardly ever get a letter.”

“And so you actually opened what was meant for her! Oh, Mr. Weston—(laughing in a showy way) I must protest against that.—It’s a most dangerous precedent indeed!—I beg you won’t let your neighbors follow your example.—Upon my word, if this is what I’m to expect, married women will have to start looking after themselves!—Oh, Mr. Weston, I couldn’t have believed it of you!”

“Aye, we men are poor creatures. You must take care of yourself, Mrs. Elton.—This letter tells us—it’s a short letter—written in a hurry, just to give us notice—it says that they’re all coming up to town at once, on Mrs. Churchill’s account—she hasn’t been well all winter, and thinks Enscombe too cold for her—so they’re all to move south without delay.”

“Indeed!—from Yorkshire, I think. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, they are about one hundred and ninety miles from London—a considerable journey.”

“Yes, upon my word, very considerable. Sixty-five miles farther than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance, Mr. Weston, to people of large fortune?—You’d be amazed to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, sometimes flies about. You would hardly believe me—but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back again with four horses.”

“The trouble with the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, _as_ _we_ _understand_, hasn’t been able to leave the sofa for a week at a time. In Frank’s last letter she complained, he said, of being too weak to get into her conservatory without both his arm and his uncle’s!”}"}

{"request_id":"fd208e7ac3753755d62c7d87","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had passed since my father returned, and the seasons were almost through their cycle. It was now the end of May. The woods were at their greenest, and the fields smelled sweet from the new grass that had been cut. I hoped that the warm air and the beautiful face of Nature would help me. I wanted them to soften him, and to bring him a gentle feeling of peace and love, before I tried to win his confidence.

So I chose one of these evenings for my attempt. I asked him to walk with me, and I led him to a nearby beech wood, where the light shade kept us from the slanting, dazzling rays of the setting sun. After we had walked in silence for some time, I sat down with him on a mossy hillock. Even now, I can still picture the place. Many of the slim, smooth trunks were wrapped with ivy. Its leaves were a deep, shining green, which made a strong contrast against the white bark and the pale new leaves of the young beech shoots growing from the older trunks. The short grass was mixed with moss, and it was partly covered by dead leaves from last autumn. Those leaves, blown by the wind, had gathered here and there into small piles. There were a few moss-covered stumps around us. The breeze moved the leaves gently, and through the green cover you could see the bright blue sky. As evening came, the distant trunks turned red in the last sunlight. The wind finally stopped, and a few birds flew past us on their way to settle for the night.

We sat there together. And if you knew everything that had happened—everything terrible that had torn at our souls even in this quiet spot, which might have been a paradise for us if not for strange passions—you would not be surprised that I remember it with the hope that its calm could give me calm too. I wanted it to help me, not only with courage, but with words that could persuade him. I noticed all these things in a blank, careful way as I tried to put my thoughts in the right order for what I meant to say. My heart beat fast as I worked myself up to speak. I was determined not to be turned away, but I still trembled at the thought of how my words might affect him. At last, after a long pause, I began:

“Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the affection—the excessive affection—that you showed me when you first returned, I hope will excuse me in your eyes for daring to speak to you. Even though I speak with a daughter’s tender love, I also speak with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”"}

{"request_id":"3682849c2bd65e2126a206f1","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers let go of Lord Arthur’s right hand and took hold of his left instead, bending so low to examine it that the gold rims of his spectacles seemed almost to touch the palm. For a moment his face turned into a pale mask of horror, but he quickly regained his sang-froid, and looking up at Lady Windermere, said with a forced smile, “It is the hand of a charming young man.

“Of course it is!” Lady Windermere replied. “But will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know.”

“All charming young men are,” said Mr. Podgers.

“I don’t think a husband should be too fascinating,” Lady Jedburgh murmured, thoughtful. “It’s so dangerous.”

“My dear child, they never are too fascinating,” cried Lady Windermere. “But what I want are details. Details are the only things that interest me. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?”

“Well, within the next few months Lord Arthur will go on a voyage—”

“Oh yes, his honeymoon, of course!”

“And lose a relative.”

“Not his sister, I hope?” Lady Jedburgh asked, in a voice full of pity.

“Certainly not his sister,” Mr. Podgers answered, waving a hand dismissively. “A distant relative, merely.”

“Well, I’m dreadfully disappointed,” Lady Windermere said. “I have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives nowadays. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she’d better have a black silk with her; it always works for church, you know. And now let’s go to supper. They’re sure to have eaten everything, but we might find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup once, but he’s so agitated about politics at present that I never feel quite certain about him. I do wish General Boulanger would keep quiet. Duchess, I’m sure you’re tired?”

“Not at all, dear Gladys,” the Duchess answered, waddling toward the door. “I’ve enjoyed myself immensely, and the cheiropodist—I mean the cheiromantist—is most interesting. Flora, where can my tortoiseshell fan be? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, that’s very kind. I’m sure”; and the worthy woman finally managed to get downstairs without dropping her scent-bottle more than twice.”

All this time Lord Arthur Savile had remained standing by the fireplace, with the same feeling of dread over him, the same sickening sense of coming evil. He smiled sadly at his sister as she swept past him on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking lovely in her pink brocade and pearls, and he hardly heard Lady Windermere when she called to him to follow her. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the idea that anything could come between them made his eyes fill with tears."}

{"request_id":"ece14b5ab620e2ea29fbedb8","rewritten_text":"I know she would!”

The Widow Douglas’ wonderful hospitality was a tempting lure. Tom’s arguments soon won the day. So they decided to tell no one anything about the plan for the night. Then Tom suddenly wondered if Huck might come that very night and give the signal. The thought drained a lot of the excitement from him. Still, he couldn’t bring himself to give up the fun at Widow Douglas’. And why should he? He told himself that since the signal hadn’t come the night before, it probably wouldn’t come tonight either. The certain fun of the evening mattered more than the uncertain chance of finding money. Like a boy, he chose to follow the stronger pull and not think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town, the ferryboat stopped at the mouth of a wooded hollow and tied up. The crowd poured ashore, and soon the forest paths and rocky heights echoed with shouts and laughter. They tried every way they could to get hot and tired, and then, little by little, the men and boys drifted back to camp with appetites that felt well earned. After that, the good food and treats began to disappear. After the meal, everyone rested and chatted in the shade of spreading oaks. Soon someone called out:

“Who’s ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. Bundles of candles were gathered up, and right away people scrambled up the hill. The cave entrance was on the hillside, shaped like the letter A. Its heavy wooden door stood open, with no bars on it. Inside was a small chamber, cold as an icehouse, with walls of solid limestone that looked wet and cold, as if it were sweating. It was romantic and mysterious to stand in the deep dark and look out over the green valley shining in the sun. But the mood didn’t last. Soon the playing started again. The moment a candle was lit, the person holding it was immediately surrounded. There was a struggle and a brave defense, but the candle was soon knocked down or blown out, and then everyone laughed loudly and chased each other again.

But everything ends. After a while, the group moved in a line down the steep descent of the main passage. The flickering lights only dimly showed the high rock walls, almost up to where they met about sixty feet overhead. This main passage was only about eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps, other tall but narrower openings branched off to either side. McDougal’s cave was really a huge maze of crooked hallways that connected and split again and again, leading nowhere."}

{"request_id":"bc0839717a254048c7752c6b","rewritten_text":"“But when I saw you become the object of another’s love; when I imagined that you might be loved in a way other than as a sacred type and image of loveliness and excellence; or that you might love someone else with a more ardent affection than the one you bore to me, then the fiend awoke within me. I dismissed your lover; and from that moment I have known no peace. I have sought in vain for sleep and rest. My eyelids would not close, and my blood has been in constant turmoil. I woke to a new life, as one who dies in hope might wake in Hell. I will not sully your imagination by recounting my battles, my self-anger, and my despair. Let a veil be drawn over the unimaginable sensations of a guilty father; the secrets of so agonized a heart must not be made vulgar. Everything was uproar, crime, remorse, and hate—yet still the tenderest love. And what first drove me to the firm resolve of conquering my passion and restoring her father to my child was the sight of your bitter, sympathizing sorrows. It was this that led me here: I thought that if I could again awaken in my heart the grief I had felt at the loss of your mother, and the many associations with her memory that had been laid to sleep for seventeen years, then all love for her child would become extinct. In a fit of heroism I decided to go alone; to leave you, the life of my life, and not to see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it would not work. I judged my fortitude too highly, or my love too low. I would certainly have died if you had not hurried to me. If only I had truly been extinguished!

“And now, Mathilda, I must make you my last confession. I have been miserably mistaken in imagining that I could conquer my love for you; I never can. The sight of this house, these fields and woods that my first love once inhabited seems only to have increased it. In my madness I dared to tell myself—Diana died to give her birth; her mother’s spirit was transferred into her body, and she ought to be Diana to me. With every effort to cast it off, this love clings closer; this guilty love is more unnatural than hate, that withers your hopes and destroys me forever.

Better to have loved despair, and safer to have kissed her.

No time or space can tear from my soul what makes up part of it. Since my arrival here I have not for a moment ceased to feel the hell of passion that has been planted in me to burn until everything is cold, stiff, and dead.”"}

{"request_id":"ba0cf36608a7aeaffad83ab9","rewritten_text":"“Shucks, Tom,” I said. “I think you might tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, I don’t know. But he’s got to have it. All the nobility does.”

That was just the way he was. If he didn’t feel like explaining something to you, he wouldn’t. You could ask him for a week, and it wouldn’t make any difference.

He’d already gotten the coat of arms part figured out, so now he started finishing the rest of that work. That meant planning a mournful inscription—Jim was supposed to have one, like they all did. He made up a lot, wrote them out on paper, and read them off.

“Here a captive heart busted.”

“Here a poor prisoner, forsook by the world and friends, fretted out his sorrowful life.”

“Here a lonely heart broke, and a worn spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity.”

“Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV.”

Tom’s voice shook while he read them, and he broke down completely when he finished. After that, he couldn’t decide which one Jim should scratch onto the wall, because they were all so good. In the end, he decided Jim would scratch all of them on.

Jim said it would take him a year to scratch that much stuff onto the logs with a nail, and he didn’t know how to make letters. But Tom said he would block the letters out for him, and then Jim wouldn’t have to do anything except follow the lines.

Then Tom said, “Come to think of it, the logs aren’t going to work. There aren’t log walls in a dungeon. We have to dig the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll fetch a rock.”

Jim said a rock would be worse than the logs. He said it would take him so long to dig the words into a rock that he’d never get out. But Tom said he would let me help him do it.

Tom looked at how me and Jim were getting on with the pens. The work was slow and tedious, and it didn’t help my hands heal the sores. We didn’t seem to be making much progress at all. So Tom said, “I know how to fix it. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the mournful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"118b21195449cd8cec614faa","rewritten_text":"He couldn’t help it. And it drove him wild to think—at least as he believed—that Becky Thatcher never once suspected he was even in the world of the living. Still, she did see him; and she knew she was carrying her point, too, and was pleased to watch him suffer the way she had suffered.

Amy’s cheerful chatter soon became unbearable. Tom let fall hints about things he had to take care of—matters that must be done—and that time was slipping away. But it was all to no purpose; the girl kept chirping on. Tom thought, “Oh, bother her—ain’t I ever going to be rid of her?” At last he had to attend to those very things, and she said, with a kind of innocent ease, that she’d be “around” when school let out. He hurried off, furious with her for it.

“Any other boy!” Tom thought, grinding his teeth. “Any boy in the whole town but that Saint Louis smart aleck who thinks he dresses so fine and is some kind of aristocrat! Oh, sure—I licked you the first day you ever set foot here, and I’ll lick you again! Just you wait till I catch you out! I’ll just—”

He then went through the business of beating an imaginary boy, pounding the air and making kicks and savage jabs. “Oh, you do, do you? You holler enough, do you? Well then—let that teach you!” And with that, the pretend thrashing was finished to his liking.

Tom slipped home at noon. His conscience couldn’t stand any more of Amy’s thankful happiness, and his jealousy couldn’t bear the other girl’s pain any longer. Becky went back to studying pictures with Alfred; but as the minutes dragged and Tom didn’t come, her triumph started to dim and she lost interest. Then came heaviness and absent-mindedness, and after that melancholy. Two or three times she perked up at the sound of footsteps, but each time it was only a false hope—no Tom arrived. At last she became thoroughly miserable and wished she hadn’t pushed it so far. When poor Alfred, realizing he was losing her, kept blurting, “Oh, here’s a jolly one! just look at this!” she snapped at him, “Oh, don’t bother me! I don’t care for them!” and burst into tears, then rose and walked away.

Alfred drifted alongside, intending to comfort her, but she said:

“Go on away and leave me alone, can’t you! I hate you!”

So the boy stopped, wondering what he could have done—since she had said she’d be looking at pictures clear through the nooning—and she went on, crying. Then Alfred sat there, thinking, in the empty schoolhouse. He felt ashamed and angry. He could see his way to the truth easily enough: the girl had simply used him as a handy target for her spite against Tom Sawyer."}

{"request_id":"b4e0059a103860cf7830ca4f","rewritten_text":"His understanding and temper, though not like hers, would still have met every wish of hers. Such a match must have benefited them both: with her ease and liveliness, his mind might be softened, his manners improved; and from his judgment, his information, and his knowledge of the world, she would gain something of far greater consequence.

But no marriage of that sort could now show the admiring crowd what true conjugal happiness really is. A union of another character—one that would rule out the possibility of the former—was soon to be formed within their family.

She could not picture how Wickham and Lydia were to be supported in any tolerable independence. Yet she could readily imagine how little lasting happiness could belong to a pair brought together only because their passions were stronger than their virtue.

Mr. Gardiner wrote again to his brother without delay. To Mr. Bennet’s acknowledgments he answered briefly, assuring him of his readiness to promote the welfare of any of his family; and he ended with earnest requests that the matter might never be mentioned to him again. The chief purpose of his letter was to let them know that Mr. Wickham had resolved to quit the militia.

“It was greatly my wish that he should do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. And I think you will agree with me that removing him from that corps is highly advisable, both for his sake and for my niece’s. Mr. Wickham means to enter the Regulars; and among his former friends there are still some who can and will help him in the army. He has the promise of an ensigncy in General----’s regiment, which is now quartered in the north. It is an advantage to have it so far from this part of the kingdom. He promises fairly; and I hope that, among different people, each having a character to keep up, they will both be more prudent. I have written to Colonel Forster to acquaint him with our present arrangements, and to ask that he will satisfy the several creditors of Mr. Wickham in and near Brighton with assurances of speedy payment, for which I have pledged myself. And will you take the trouble of carrying similar assurances to his creditors at Meryton, of whom I shall add a list, according to his information? He has stated all his debts; I hope at least he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be finished in a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and I learn from Mrs. Gardiner that my niece is very eager to see you all before she leaves the south.”"}

{"request_id":"6261c728b9fd02b91995ab5a","rewritten_text":"The next day the ghost felt very weak and tired. The frightening excitement of the last four weeks was starting to catch up with him. His nerves were completely wrecked, and he jumped at even the smallest sound. For five days he stayed in his room, and then, at last, he decided to stop worrying about the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family didn’t want it, then they clearly didn’t deserve it. They seemed to live on a low, practical level, and he believed they were too shallow to understand the symbolic meaning of sensuous things.

The matter of ghostly visions and the making of astral bodies was different, of course, and not really his choice. It was his duty to appear in the corridor once a week, and to make his loud, gibbering display from the large oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of every month. He couldn’t see any honorable way to escape those obligations. It was true that his life had been very evil, but he was also very careful about anything connected with the supernatural.

So, for the next three Saturdays, he went through the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every precaution so that he would not be heard or seen. He took off his boots, stepped as lightly as he could on the old boards that were eaten up by worms, and wore a large black velvet cloak. He was also careful to use the Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I have to admit it wasn’t easy for him to get himself to use that last kind of protection. Still, one night, while the family were at dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and stole the bottle. At first he felt a little ashamed, but soon he understood that the invention had a lot going for it, and it did help him, to a certain extent.

Even so, he wasn’t left alone. Strings were stretched across the corridor again and again, and he kept tripping over them in the dark. On one occasion, while he was getting ready for his part as “Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,” he fell hard because he stepped on a butter-slide. The twins had made it from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber all the way to the top of the oak staircase. This insult made him so angry that he decided to make one last attempt to prove his dignity and his social standing. The next night he planned to visit the rude young Etonians in his famous disguise as “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.”

He hadn’t worn that costume for more than seventy years. In fact, it was the first time since he had frightened pretty Lady Barbara Modish with it. She had broken off her engagement to the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather, then ran away to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton. She said nothing in the world would make her marry into a family that let such a horrible phantom walk up and down the terrace at twilight."}

{"request_id":"1c43226bfca6e01a3daf1ce2","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I think, sir,” the spy said, in the most unpleasant way, turning to Mr. Lorry, “I can appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness. Ask him, if he can, whether there is any situation in which he could accept his place and play that Ace you mentioned. I admit that I am a spy, and people treat that as a shameful job—though someone has to do it. But this gentleman is not a spy. Why should he lower himself to become one?”

“I’ll play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, taking the answer for himself. He glanced at his watch. “In just a few minutes, without any hesitation.”

“I hoped, gentlemen both,” said the spy, always trying to pull Mr. Lorry into the conversation, “that your respect for my sister—”

“I can’t show my respect for your sister better than by finally freeing her from her brother,” Sydney Carton said.

“You don’t think so, sir?”

“I’ve already decided.”

The spy’s smooth manner—especially since his clothes were rough and showy—didn’t fit with what he was doing. It was thrown off by the way Carton answered, so calm and unreadable that even wiser and better men than the spy found him a mystery. The spy faltered. While he hesitated, Carton spoke again, as if he were simply looking at the cards.

“And now, thinking again, I’m sure I have another good card here—one I haven’t counted yet. That friend and fellow-sheep who said he had been pasturing in the country prisons. Who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” the spy said quickly.

“French, is it?” Carton repeated, thinking, and acting as though he didn’t even notice the spy. “Well; he might be.”

“I assure you,” said the spy, “it’s French. But it doesn’t matter.”

“It doesn’t matter,” Carton repeated in the same automatic tone. “It doesn’t matter. No. Still, I know his face.”

“I don’t think so. I’m sure you don’t. It can’t be,” said the spy.

“It can’t be,” Sydney Carton muttered, looking back on it, and idly turning his glass again. “Can’t be. He spoke good French. But, like a foreigner, I thought—”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” Carton cried, slapping his open hand on the table as the answer suddenly came clear to him. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had him before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now, there you are, sir,” said Barsad, smiling. His smile made his aquiline nose tilt even more to one side. “You’re being too quick. You really do give me an advantage over you.”"}

{"request_id":"51ba1c0f54f01987557593ec","rewritten_text":"Mrs Clay’s feelings had carried her beyond her own interest, and, for the young man’s sake, she had given up the chance of plotting longer in Sir Walter’s favour. Yet she has talents as well as attachments; and it remains uncertain whether his craft or hers will at last prevail—whether, after he has managed to keep her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he may not still be persuaded, coaxed, and fondly treated into making her the wife of Sir William.

There can be no doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were both startled and deeply vexed by the loss of their companion, and by the discovery of the deception practised upon them. They had, to be sure, their great cousins to turn to for comfort; but they must still feel, for a long time, that to praise and follow others, while one is not praised and followed in return, can amount to no more than a kind of half-enjoyment.

Anne, long before, had understood Lady Russell’s intention well enough to be in earnest about loving Captain Wentworth as she ought; and there was no other drawback to the happiness of her prospects than the thought that she could offer him no relations—nothing that a man of sense would value. There she felt her own inferiority most sharply. The mismatch in their fortunes gave her not a moment’s regret; it was not that. But having no family to receive and judge him properly, no respectable, harmonious, well-disposed connections to offer in return for all the worth and the ready welcome which met her in his brothers and sisters—this was a pain as lively as her mind could well feel, even amid circumstances otherwise rich in felicity. She had only two friends in the world to add to his list: Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. Still, he was disposed to attach himself closely to both. Lady Russell, despite all her earlier offences, he could now prize from his heart. Though he did not feel bound to declare that he believed her right in originally separating them, he was willing to say almost everything else in her favour; and as for Mrs Smith, she had claims of several sorts that made her worth recommending at once and securing permanently.

Anne’s recent good offices had been enough in themselves; and their marriage, far from costing her one friend, actually gave her two. She was the first visitor in their settled life; and Captain Wentworth, by putting her in the way of recovering her husband’s property in the West Indies—by writing for her, acting for her, and carrying her through all the small troubles of the business with the energy and steadiness of a bold man and a resolute friend—fully repaid the services she had rendered, or ever meant to render, to his wife."}

{"request_id":"3c75e511f081803daf243361","rewritten_text":"Great God! If, for even an instant, I had considered the hellish intent of my fiendish adversary, I would rather have banished myself forever from my native country and wandered the earth as a friendless outcast than have agreed to this miserable marriage. But it was as if the monster had magic powers; he blinded me to his true intentions. And when I believed I had only prepared my own death, I hurried that of a far dearer victim.

As the time fixed for our marriage drew nearer, whether from cowardice or from some prophetic feeling, I felt my heart sink within me. Still, I hid my feelings behind an outward show of cheerfulness. It brought smiles and joy to my father’s face, though it hardly deceived Elizabeth’s ever-watchful, sharper eye. She looked forward to our union with calm contentment, mixed with a little fear—fear shaped by past misfortunes—that what now seemed like certain, tangible happiness might soon vanish into an airy dream and leave behind nothing but deep, everlasting regret.

Preparations were made for the event; congratulatory visits were received; and everyone wore a smiling expression. I shut up, as best I could, the anxiety that preyed on my mind, and it entered into my father’s plans with an air of earnestness, even if those plans were only meant to serve as the decorations of my tragedy. Through my father’s efforts, part of Elizabeth’s inheritance was restored to her by the Austrian government. A small property on the shores of Como belonged to her. It was agreed that, immediately after our union, we would go to Villa Lavenza and spend our first days of happiness beside the beautiful lake near which it stood.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to defend myself in case the fiend should openly attack me. I carried pistols and a dagger constantly, and I stayed on guard to prevent any trickery. By these means I gained a greater measure of calm. In fact, as the time approached, the threat seemed more like a delusion—something not worth disturbing my peace—while the happiness I hoped for in my marriage appeared more and more certain as the day for its solemnization drew closer. I heard it spoken of again and again as an event that no accident could possibly prevent.

Elizabeth seemed happy, and my steady, composed manner helped calm her mind. But on the day that was meant to fulfill my wishes and my destiny, she was melancholy, and a presentiment of evil weighed on her. Perhaps she also thought of the dreadful secret I had promised to reveal to her the following day."}

{"request_id":"30d3e11c7293ba797ad25caf","rewritten_text":"He sprang up and caught her roughly by the arm. “Take me to him. Which one is he? Point him out. I must see him!” he cried; but just then the Duke of Berwick’s four-in-hand slid between them, and once it had cleared the space, the carriage had swept out of the park.

“He is gone,” Sibyl said, with a sad little murmur. “I only wish you had seen him.”

“I wish I had, for by all that’s holy, if he ever does you wrong, I’ll kill him.”

She stared at him in alarm. He repeated himself, and the words seemed to cut the air like a blade. Those nearby began to stare. A lady close by gave a little titter.

“Come away, Jim; come away,” she whispered. He followed her stubbornly as she pushed through the crowd. He felt pleased with what he had said.

When they reached the Achilles Statue, she turned back. Compassion showed in her eyes, which quickly turned to laughter. She shook her head at him. “You’re a fool, Jim—an utter fool. Just a bad-tempered boy, that’s all. How can you say such dreadful things? You don’t know what you’re talking about. You’re only jealous and mean. Oh, I do wish you’d fall in love. Love makes people good, and what you said was wicked.”

“I’m sixteen,” he answered, “and I know my own mind. Mother is no help to you. She doesn’t know how to manage you. I only wish now I weren’t going to Australia at all. I’ve half a mind to throw the whole business up. I would, if my papers hadn’t been signed.”

“Oh, don’t be so solemn, Jim. You’re like one of the heroes from those silly melodramas Mother used to be so taken with. I’m not going to quarrel with you. I’ve seen him, and—oh!—to see him is perfect happiness. We won’t fight. I know you’d never hurt anyone I care for. Would you?”

“Not while you love him, I suppose,” came the sulky reply.

“I’ll love him forever!” she exclaimed.

“And he?”

“Forever, too!”

“He’d better.”

She recoiled from him, then laughed and laid her hand on his arm. He was only a boy.

At the Marble Arch they hailed an omnibus, which set them down near their poor little home in the Euston Road. It was after five o’clock, and Sibyl had to lie down for a couple of hours before she could act. Jim insisted she should do it. He said he’d rather be parted from her when their mother wasn’t there. Mother would be sure to make a scene, and he loathed scenes of any sort."}

{"request_id":"daa46abc73c0fc6975d12585","rewritten_text":"“Unless you mean Miss Havisham as a he. And I doubt even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, up town?” Joe asked.

“Is there any Miss Havisham down town?” my sister shot back.

“She wants this boy to go and play there. And of course he will. And he’d better play there,” my sister said, shaking her head at me as if to encourage me to be light and playful, “or I’ll work him.”

I had heard about Miss Havisham up town. Everyone for miles around had heard about her. She was an extremely rich, grim woman who lived in a large, gloomy house, shut up tight against robbers, and who kept to herself.

“Well, of course!” Joe said, clearly shocked. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“Noodle!” my sister cried. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Someone,” Joe suggested politely again, “said she wants him to go and play there.”

“And why can’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knows a boy who could go and play there? Isn’t it just possible that Uncle Pumblechook is one of her tenants, and that sometimes—though we won’t say every quarter or every half-year, because that would be asking too much of you—but sometimes he goes there to pay his rent? And then couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knows a boy to go and play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, who is always kind and thoughtful for us—though you may not think it, Joseph,” she said with the deepest reproach, as if he were the most heartless nephew, “then mention this boy, standing here prancing”—which I solemnly declare I was not doing—“that I have been a willing slave to?”

“Good again!” Uncle Pumblechook cried. “Well said! Nicely put! That’s right! Now, Joseph, you know the situation.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister said, still sounding reproachful, while Joe apologized by wiping the back of his hand across and across his nose. “You don’t yet—though you may not think it—know the situation. You may think you do, but you don’t, Joseph. You see, Uncle Pumblechook knows that, as far as we can tell, this boy’s future might be made by going to Miss Havisham’s. So he has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, to keep him there tonight, and then to take him with his own hands to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And Lor-a-mussy me!” my sister cried, suddenly desperate, throwing off her bonnet. “Here I am talking to mere Mooncalfs, while Uncle Pumblechook is waiting, the mare is catching cold at the door, and the boy is covered in grime—crock and dirt—from the hair on his head to the sole of his foot!”"}

{"request_id":"8c28afbaa8107e7bb9c8e5cd","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I said, “what’s the matter now?—how is your master?”

“Why, to tell the truth, sir, he ain’t so very well as he ought to be.”

“Not well! I’m truly sorry to hear it. What is he complaining of?”

“Dar! That’s it—he never ’plains of anything at all, but he’s mighty sick for all that.”

“Very sick, Jupiter—why didn’t you say so at once? Is he confined to bed?”

“No, sir, he ain’t!—he ain’t found anywhere—this is where the shoe pinches; my mind has got to be very heavy about poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I’d like to understand what you’re talking about. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what’s wrong?”

“Why, sir, it ain’t worth getting mad about the matter—Massa Will says nothing at all is the matter with him; but then why does he go about looking this way, with his head down and he’s all soldiered up, and as white as a goose? And then he keeps a siphon all the time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a siphon with the figures on the slate—those queerest figures I ever did see. I’m getting scared, I tell you. I’ve got to keep a mighty tight eye on him. The day before yesterday he slipped me before sunrise and was gone the whole blessed day. I had a big stick ready, cut out to give him a deuced good beating when he did come—but I’m such a fool that I didn’t have the heart for it; he looked so very poorly.”

“Eh?—what?—ah yes!—on the whole, I think you’d better not be too severe with the poor fellow. Don’t flog him, Jupiter—he can’t very well stand it. But can you form no idea of what has caused this illness, or rather this change in his conduct? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, sir, there ain’t been nothing unpleasant since then—only it was before then that I’m afraid—on the very day you were there.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, sir, I mean the bug—there now.”

“The what?”

“The bug. I’m very sure Massa Will got bitten somewhere about the head by that goole-bug.”

“And what makes you think that, Jupiter?”

“Claws enough, sir, and mouth too. I never did see a sick bug—he kicked and he bit everything that came near him. Massa Will caught him at first, but had to let him go again mighty quick, I tell you—because that was the time he must have got the bite. I didn’t like the look of the bug’s mouth myself, no how, so I wouldn’t take hold of him with my finger; but I caught him with a piece of paper that I found.”}"}

{"request_id":"e16d8f3873471885e4f152cb","rewritten_text":"At last it was arranged that we would live together while I was in the city. Since my money situation was a little easier than his, I was allowed to pay for the rent and to furnish the place in a style that matched the strange, gloomy mood we shared. We moved into an old mansion, worn with age and full of odd, grotesque details. It had been empty for a long time, abandoned because of superstitions that we never bothered to question. The building was falling apart, and it stood in a quiet, lonely part of the Faubourg St. Germain.

If anyone had known what our daily life was like there, they would have called us madmen, though maybe harmless ones. We kept to ourselves completely. We did not allow visitors. In fact, even the location of our retreat was kept secret from my old friends and associates, and it had been many years since Dupin had stopped knowing Paris or being known there. We lived only within our own world.

It was a strange idea of my friend—what else could I call it?—to love the night for its own sake. I fell into this odd habit, just as I did with all his other whims, and I gave myself up to them with total abandon. The dark, shadowy presence we wanted could not stay with us all the time, but we could pretend it was there. At the first dawn we shut all the messy shutters on the old building. Then we lit a couple of strongly perfumed tapers, which cast only the most sickly, weak light. With that dim glow, we spent our time in dreams—reading, writing, or talking—until the clock warned us that true Darkness was coming. Then we went out into the streets arm in arm, keeping up the topics of the day or wandering far and wide until late at night. In the busy city, with its wild lights and shadows, we searched for that kind of mental excitement that comes from quiet observation.

During those times I could not help noticing and admiring, even though I had expected it from his strong imagination, Dupin’s unusual skill at analysis. He seemed eager to use it, if not exactly to show it off, and he did not hesitate to admit that he enjoyed the pleasure it gave him. With a low chuckling laugh, he told me that most men, as far as he was concerned, carried “windows” in their own hearts, and he would follow that claim with direct, very startling proof of how well he knew things about me. When he spoke like that, his manner turned cold and distant. His eyes looked empty, and his voice, which was usually a rich tenor, rose into a higher pitch. It might have sounded petulant, but it never did, because he spoke with careful control and clear, distinct words."}

{"request_id":"e42d78bee5c015bb37602053","rewritten_text":"He let her understand, in the plainest way, that Frank held her in the highest esteem—thinking her exceedingly beautiful and exceedingly engaging; and, considering all that could be said in his favour, she felt she ought not to judge him too severely. As Mrs. Weston remarked, “every young person has their little fancies.”

Among his new acquaintances in Surry, however, there was one person who was not disposed to be so indulgent. In general, throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury, he was spoken of with remarkable openness; allowances were readily made for the small excesses of so fine-looking a young man—one who smiled so often and bowed so well; yet there was a temper among them that no bows or smiles could soften, owing to the strength of its censure—Mr. Knightley. The matter was related to him at Hartfield; for the moment he was silent, but Emma heard him almost at once, while he held a newspaper in his hand, say to himself, “Hum! just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” She had half a mind to take offence; but a moment’s reflection showed her it was only meant to ease his own feelings, and not to provoke her; so she let it go.

Though, in one respect, the bearers of not-so-pleasant news—Mr. and Mrs. Weston’s visit this morning—was in another particularly well-timed. Something happened while they were at Hartfield that made Emma feel she needed their counsel; and, what was even better, she wanted exactly the advice they gave.

The circumstance was this:—The Coles had been settled in Highbury for some years, and were very decent people—friendly, liberal, and without pretension; but then, on the other hand, they were of low origin, in trade, and only moderately genteel. When they first came into the neighbourhood, they lived within their means, quietly, keeping little company, and that little without much expense; but the last year or two had brought them a very considerable increase of fortune—the house in town had turned a better profit, and their circumstances in general had prospered. With their wealth, their notions grew bolder; their wish for a larger house, and their inclination for more company. They enlarged their house, increased their number of servants, and raised their expenses of every kind; and by this time, in both fortune and manner of living, they stood next only to the family at Hartfield. Their fondness for society, and their new dining-room, had prepared everyone for their giving dinner-parties; and a few gatherings, chiefly among the single men, had already occurred. The principal and most regular families Emma could hardly suppose they would venture to ask—neither Donwell, nor Hartfield, nor Randalls. Nothing could persuade her to go, if they did; and she regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal carry less meaning than she could wish."}

{"request_id":"6f0b5ec235c73ec4ea092325","rewritten_text":"In fact, he was dressed as “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,” which was one of his best impersonations. The Cantervilles had every reason to remember it, because it was the real start of their fight with their neighbor, Lord Rufford. It was a little after two in the morning, and, as far as he could tell, no one was moving. Still, as he walked toward the library to look for any traces of the bloodstain, two figures suddenly burst out of a dark corner. They waved their arms wildly over their heads and shrieked “BOO!” right into his ear.

He panicked, as anyone would in that situation. He ran for the stairs, but Washington Otis was already there, holding a big garden syringe. With his enemies all around him and nowhere to go, he slipped into the large iron stove. Luckily for him, it was not lit. He then had to work his way home through the flues and chimneys, and when he finally reached his own room, he was in a terrible mess—dirty, disordered, and full of despair.

After that, he was not seen again on any night-time adventure. The twins waited for him on several occasions and, every night, scattered nutshells in the passages, which annoyed their parents and the servants a great deal. But it did not help. It was clear that his feelings were hurt enough that he would not show himself again. Mr. Otis therefore went back to his big project on the history of the Democratic Party, which he had been working on for years. Mrs. Otis planned a wonderful clam-bake that amazed the whole county. The boys took up lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games. Virginia rode around the lanes on her pony, with the young Duke of Cheshire beside her. He had come to spend the last week of his holidays at Canterville Chase.

Everyone assumed the ghost had gone away. In fact, Mr. Otis wrote a letter to Lord Canterville to say so. Lord Canterville replied with great pleasure and sent his best congratulations to the Minister’s wife.

The Otises were wrong, though. The ghost was still in the house. Even though he was now almost an invalid, he was not ready to let things end—especially once he heard that one of the guests was the young Duke of Cheshire. The Duke’s grand-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once bet a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost. The next morning, Carbury was found lying on the floor of the card-room in such a helpless state that, even though he lived to a great age, he could never speak again except to say, “Double Sixes.”"}

{"request_id":"b8e159f91118a2175b5977a9","rewritten_text":"It was well beyond noon when he woke. His valet had slipped in more than once, moving on tiptoe, to see whether his young master had stirred, and he had been puzzled by what kept him asleep so late. At last the bell rang, and Victor entered quietly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters, all carried on a small tray of old Sevres china. He drew back the olive-satin curtains, whose blue lining caught the light with a faint shimmer, that hung before the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept very well this morning,” he said, smiling.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked, still drowsy.

“One hour and a quarter, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up, took a sip of tea, and began to sort through his letters. One had come from Lord Henry, delivered by hand that morning. He paused, then set it aside. The rest he opened with a kind of indifference. They were the usual assortment—cards, invitations to dinner, tickets for private views, notices of charity concerts, and all the other things that are sent to fashionable young men every morning during the season. There was also a rather heavy bill for a chased silver Louis-Quinze toilet-set, which he had not yet found the nerve to forward to his guardians. They were extremely old-fashioned, and could not see that we live in an age where unnecessary things are the only necessities. Along with that were several messages from the money-lenders of Jermyn Street, written with the utmost courtesy, offering to advance any sum at a moment’s notice and on the most reasonable terms of interest.

After about ten minutes he rose, slipped into an elaborate dressing-gown of silk-embroidered cashmere wool, and went into the onyx-paved bathroom. The cool water revived him after his long sleep. It was as though he had forgotten everything he had been through. Now and then a vague feeling returned—that he had somehow taken part in some strange tragedy—but it came with the same unreality as a dream.

Once he was dressed, he went into the library and sat down to a light French breakfast laid out for him on a small round table near the open window. It was an exquisite day. The warm air seemed thick with spices. A bee wandered in and buzzed around the blue-dragon bowl before him, filled with sulphur-yellow roses. He felt perfectly content.

Then his gaze caught the screen he had placed in front of the portrait, and he started.

“Too cold for Monsieur?” asked his valet, setting an omelette on the table. “I shut the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I am not cold,” he murmured."}

{"request_id":"ee03639ae4414a637ba54714","rewritten_text":"Col. Grangerford was a gentleman, you see. He was a gentleman in every way, and so was his family. He was well born, as people say, and that mattered as much for a man as it did for a horse, the Widow Douglas liked to say. Nobody in our town ever argued with her, either, because she was considered one of the top families. Pap always said the same thing, too, even if he wasn’t any better than a mudcat himself.

Col. Grangerford was very tall and very thin. His complexion was dark and pale, with no red anywhere. Every morning he was clean-shaven across his thin face. His lips were thin, his nostrils were thin, and he had a high nose. He had heavy eyebrows and the blackest eyes, set so deep that they looked like they were staring at you from caverns, as you might imagine. His forehead was high. His hair was black and straight, and it fell down to his shoulders. His hands were long and thin. Every day of his life he put on a clean shirt and a full suit from head to foot made of linen so white it hurt your eyes to look at it. On Sundays he wore a blue tail-coat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane with a silver head.

There was nothing silly about him at all, and he was never loud. He was as kind as he could be, and you could feel it, so you trusted him. Sometimes he smiled, and it was nice to see. But when he stood up straight like a flagpole, and the lightning seemed to flicker out from under his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree first and figure out what was wrong afterward. He never had to tell anyone to mind their manners, because everyone was always well behaved when he was around. People loved having him there, too. He was like sunshine most of the time—at least, he made it seem like good weather. When he turned into a cloud, though, it got terribly dark for about half a minute, and that was enough. Nothing bad would happen again for a week.

When he and the old lady came down in the morning, the whole family got up from their chairs to greet them and didn’t sit back down until they had sat down. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard where the decanter was. They mixed a glass of bitters, handed it to him, and he held it while Tom’s and Bob’s were mixed. After that, they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam.” They bowed a little themselves and said, “Thank you,” and then all three drank. Bob and Tom poured a spoonful of water onto the sugar and the tiny bit of whisky or apple brandy at the bottom of their glasses, and then they gave it to me and Buck. We drank to the old people, too."}

{"request_id":"24bd1a599ea1e22d1a67ac95","rewritten_text":"“Look,” said Merlin. “There is the sword I told you about.” As they watched, they saw a young woman walking on the lake. “Who is that?” Arthur asked. “That is the Lady of the Lake,” Merlin said. “Inside this lake there is a rock, and on it there is a fine place, as good as any on earth. She will come to you soon, and then you must speak kindly to her. She will give you that sword.”

Soon after, the young woman came to Arthur and greeted him, and he greeted her in return. “Lady,” Arthur said, “what sword is that, the one your arm is holding above the water? I wish it were mine. I have no sword.”

“Sir Arthur King,” she replied, “that sword is mine. If you promise to give me a gift whenever I ask, I will give it to you.”

“By my faith,” Arthur said, “I will give you whatever gift you ask for.”

“Then,” said the young woman, “go into that barge and row yourself to the sword. Take it, and take the scabbard too. I will ask for my gift when I have the right moment.”

So Sir Arthur and Merlin stepped into the ship. They tied their horses to two trees, then went aboard. When they reached the sword that the hand was holding, Sir Arthur picked it up by the handles and took it with him. The arm and hand went back under the water. Then they returned to land and rode out.

After that, Sir Arthur saw a rich pavilion. “What does that pavilion mean?” he asked.

“It is the knight’s pavilion,” Merlin said. “You fought there last, Sir Pellinore, but he is gone. He is not there. He has been dealing with one of your knights named Egglame. They fought together, but in the end Egglame fled. Otherwise he would have been dead. Egglame has chased him all the way to Carlion, and we will meet him soon on the road.”

“That is good,” Arthur said. “Now I have a sword. Now I will fight him and get revenge.”

“Sir,” Merlin said, “you must not do that. The knight is tired from fighting and chasing, so you will gain no honor by getting involved with him. Also, he will not be easily matched by any living knight. So my advice is to let him pass. He will do you good service soon, and his sons will serve you after his days. And you will see that, in a short time, you will be glad to give your sister to him to marry.”

“When I meet him,” Arthur said, “I will do as you advise me.”"}

{"request_id":"7cc8d0868f82cc25b2d149fb","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” Duff replied.

“And, translating the word yokel for the ladies’ benefit, I take it you mean that this attempt wasn’t made by a countryman?” said Mr. Losberne, smiling.

“That’s it, master,” Blathers answered. “This is all about the robbery, isn’t it?”

“All,” the doctor replied.

“Now, what’s this about that boy—about the one the servants are talking about?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing at all,” the doctor said. “One of the frightened servants got it into his head that he had something to do with this attempt to break into the house; but it’s nonsense—pure absurdity.”

“Very easily dealt with, if it is,” Duff remarked.

“What he says is perfectly right,” Blathers observed, nodding as if to confirm it, and idly playing with the handcuffs, as though they were a pair of castanets. “Who is the boy? What story does he tell about himself? Where did he come from? He didn’t just drop out of the clouds, did he, master?”

“Of course not,” the doctor replied, casting a nervous glance at the two ladies. “I know his whole history, but we can talk about that later. First, you’d like to see the place where the thieves made their attempt, I suppose?”

“Certainly,” Mr. Blathers said. “We’d better inspect the premises first, and then question the servants. That’s the usual way of doing business.”

Lights were then brought in. Messrs. Blathers and Duff, accompanied by the native constable Brittles, Giles, and everyone else in short, went into the small room at the end of the passage and looked out through the window; then they went around by way of the lawn and looked in through the window; after that, a candle was handed out so they could inspect the shutter; then a lantern to trace the footsteps; and after that, a pitchfork to poke the bushes. When all this was done, amid the breathless interest of everyone watching, they went back in. Mr. Giles and Brittles were then put through a melodramatic retelling of their part in the previous night’s adventures: they performed it some six times, contradicting each other in not more than one important respect the first time, and in not more than a dozen the last. Once that was finished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a long council together—one that, for secrecy and solemnity, would make a consultation of great doctors on the knottiest point in medicine seem like a child’s game.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced up and down in the next room in a state of deep unease, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with anxious faces.

“Upon my word,” he said, stopping after a great many very rapid turns, “I hardly know what to do.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"36a05b260204f4a39c0bc3fa","rewritten_text":"The mental traits discussed as the analytical are, in themselves, only slightly open to analysis. We understand them mainly through their effects. Among other things, we know that they are always, for the person who has them in an excessive degree, a source of the liveliest enjoyment. Just as the strong man takes pride in his physical ability—delighting in exercises that bring his muscles into action—so the analyst takes pride in that moral activity which disentangles. He finds pleasure even in the most trivial tasks, so long as his talent can be brought to bear. He likes enigmas, conundrums, and hieroglyphics; in solving each, he shows a level of acumen that seems supernatural to ordinary understanding. His results, produced by the very soul and essence of method, truly have the whole look of intuition.\n\nThe faculty of re-solution may well be strengthened by mathematical study, and especially by that highest branch of it which, unjustly, and merely because its operations run backward, has been called—so to speak—analysis par excellence. Still, to calculate is not, by itself, to analyze. A chess player, for example, can do one without the other. It follows that chess, in its effects on mental character, is greatly misunderstood. I am not writing a treatise now, but simply prefacing a somewhat peculiar narrative with observations drawn very much at random; I will therefore take the opportunity to claim that the higher powers of the reflective intellect are more decidedly and more usefully exercised by the unshowy game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In the latter, where the pieces have different and bizarre moves, with various and changeable values, what is merely complex is mistaken (a not uncommon mistake) for what is profound. Here attention is called powerfully into play. If it slips for even an instant, an oversight is made that leads to injury or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but also intricate, the chances of such oversights are multiplied; and in nine cases out of ten it is the more concentrative rather than the more acute player who wins. In draughts, by contrast, where the moves are unique and have little variation, the likelihood of inadvertence is reduced, and because mere attention is left comparatively idle, the advantages gained by either side come from superior acumen. To make this less abstract, let us suppose a game of draughts in which the pieces are reduced to four kings, and where, of course, no oversight is to be expected. It is clear that here victory can be decided (since the players are equally matched) only by some recherché move—the result of a strong exertion of the intellect."}

{"request_id":"0c4e0e91ce57cdf43ab63db8","rewritten_text":"Watching him in such moods, I would often fall into a meditative turn over the old notion of the Bi-Part Soul, and I would amuse myself with the conceit of a double Dupin—the one inventive, the other quick to resolve.

Nor let it be imagined, from what I have just set down, that I am laying out any mystery, or composing any romance. What I have said of the Frenchman was simply the outcome of an excited—perhaps even a disordered—intelligence. Yet, as to the nature of his remarks at those moments, an example will serve best to show the point.

We were walking one night along a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. Both of us, as it seemed, were taken up with our thoughts; for at least fifteen minutes neither of us had spoken a single syllable. Then, all at once, Dupin burst out with these words:

“He is a very little fellow, that’s true, and would do better for the _Théâtre des Variétés_.”

“There can be no doubt of that,” I answered, before I had even noticed—so deep was I in my own reverie—the odd way in which the speaker had fallen in with my meditations. In the next instant, however, I checked myself, and my astonishment was profound.

“Dupin,” said I, gravely, “this is beyond my understanding. I do not hesitate to say that I am amazed, and can scarcely bring myself to believe my senses. How could you possibly know that I was thinking of ——?” I paused, to be sure—beyond any doubt—that he truly knew whom I had in mind.

“—— of Chantilly,” said he. “Why do you stop? You were just remarking to yourself that his small figure did not suit tragedy.”

That, in truth, was exactly what had been occupying my thoughts. Chantilly had once been a cobbler of the Rue St. Denis; having grown stage-mad, he had tried to take the _rôle_ of Xerxes in Crébillon’s so-called tragedy, and had been notoriously Pasquinaded for his pains.

“Tell me, for Heaven’s sake,” I cried, “the method—if there is any method—by which you have managed to sound my mind in this matter.” Indeed, I was more shaken than I cared to admit.

“It was the fruiterer,” replied my friend, “who led you to the conclusion that the mender of soles was not tall enough for Xerxes _et id genus omne_.”

“The fruiterer!—you surprise me—I know of no fruiterer at all.”

“The man who brushed against you as we entered the street—it can’t have been more than fifteen minutes ago.”

I remembered then that, as we passed from the Rue C—— into the very thoroughfare where we were standing, a fruiterer with a large basket of apples balanced on his head had nearly knocked me down by accident; but I could not see how that had anything to do with Chantilly."}

{"request_id":"722f62cc061a5ba2d89c889e","rewritten_text":"Her predicament was, in truth, unlike any ordinary trial and full of perplexity. Though she burned with the keenest longing to pierce the mystery that shrouded Oliver’s past, she could not help but treat as sacred the trust which the wretched woman she had just spoken with had placed in her—trust given to her as a young, artless girl. Her words and manner had gone straight to Rose Maylie’s heart; and, blended with her affection for her young charge, and no less fervent in its sincerity, was her earnest desire to bring the outcast back toward repentance and hope.

They meant to stay in London only three days before setting out, for some weeks, to a far part of the coast. It was now midnight of the first day. What plan could she settle upon that might be carried out within forty-eight hours? Or how could she delay the journey without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them, and would remain so for the next two days; yet Rose knew too well the impetuous temper of the excellent gentleman, and she saw too clearly the anger with which, at the first burst of his indignation, he would view the very means of Oliver’s recapture, to entrust him with the secret—especially when her plea in the girl’s behalf could not be supported by any seasoned person. All this called for the utmost caution and the most careful circumspection in what she communicated to Mrs. Maylie, whose first impulse would surely be to call a consultation with the worthy doctor. As for turning to any legal adviser, even had she known how to do so, it was hardly to be considered for the same reason. Once the idea came to her of seeking help from Harry; but at once she remembered their last parting, and it seemed to her unworthy to summon him back—when, as the tears rose to her eyes and she followed the thought further—he might already have learned to forget her, and to be happier away.

Bothered by these shifting reflections—now leaning toward one course, now recoiling from it, and then from all again as each new consideration presented itself—Rose spent a sleepless, troubled night. After thinking it over again the next day, she reached a desperate decision: she would consult Harry.

“If it hurts him,” she told herself, “to return here, then it will hurt me too! But perhaps he won’t come. He may write, or he may come and yet, with studied care, avoid meeting me—as he did when he left. I hardly expected he would; still, it is better for both of us.” With that, Rose let the pen fall and turned aside, as though the very paper that was to serve as her message ought not to witness her tears."}

{"request_id":"bde794a0ddc249e104d9069b","rewritten_text":"Among the public buildings in a certain town—one I will not name, for reasons I won’t bother to explain—there is one old and common place found in nearly every town, large or small: a workhouse. In that workhouse, Oliver Twist was born. It happened on a day and date I don’t need to repeat, since it can’t matter to the reader at this point. What does matter is the death that is mentioned at the start of this chapter.

For a long time after Oliver was brought into the world of sorrow and trouble, the parish surgeon could not say for sure whether the child would live long enough to have any name at all. If he had not, then these memoirs would never have been written. And if they had been, they would have been only a couple of pages long, and would have been the shortest and truest biography ever seen.

I don’t mean to claim that being born in a workhouse is the best or most enviable thing that can happen to anyone. But in Oliver’s case, it was the best outcome that could possibly have happened. The truth is, there was real trouble getting Oliver to start breathing. It was a difficult process, but it is something custom has made necessary for us to live. For a while he lay gasping on a small flock mattress, balanced between this world and the next, with the next world clearly winning.

If, during that short time, Oliver had been surrounded by careful grandmothers, anxious aunts, experienced nurses, and doctors who knew exactly what to do, he would almost certainly have died right away. But no one like that was there. Instead, there was only a pauper old woman, made a little confused by an unusual amount of beer, and a parish surgeon who handled these things for pay. Oliver and Nature fought it out between them. After a few struggles, Oliver finally breathed, sneezed, and then made it clear to everyone in the workhouse that the parish now had a new burden. He did this by crying as loudly as could reasonably be expected from a newborn boy who did not yet have that very useful part, and he kept crying for longer than three minutes and a quarter."}
