{"request_id":"4f92cd559f3f933bf9b47b8d","rewritten_text":"Tom managed to scarify the cupboard with it, and was getting ready to start on the bureau when he was called away to dress for Sunday-school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a piece of soap. He went outside the door, set the basin on a little bench, dipped the soap in the water, and laid it down. Then he rolled up his sleeves, poured the water onto the ground—gently—and went back into the kitchen to wipe his face carefully on the towel behind the door. But Mary took the towel away and said:

“Now ain’t you ashamed, Tom. You can’t be so bad. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom was a little thrown off. The basin was refilled, and this time he stood over it for a moment, gathering himself. He took a big breath and started. When he came back into the kitchen, both eyes shut and feeling around for the towel with his hands, suds and water were dripping off his face in an honorable display. But when he stepped away from the towel, he still wasn’t satisfactory: the clean part stopped short at his chin and his jaws, like a mask. Below that line, and all around his neck, there was a dark stretch of unwashed ground that spread downward in front and backward. Mary took him in hand, and when she was finished with him he was a man and a brother, with no difference in color, his saturated hair neatly brushed, its short curls shaped into a neat, symmetrical overall effect. [He privately smoothed out the curls with effort and difficulty, pressing his hair close to his head; he believed curls were effeminate, and his own hair filled his life with bitterness.] Then Mary brought out a suit of his clothes that had been worn only on Sundays for two years—they were simply called his “other clothes”—and that’s how we know the size of his wardrobe. After he dressed himself, the girl “put him to rights”: she buttoned his neat roundabout up to his chin, flipped his big shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and topped him with his speckled straw hat.

He looked much better now, though also very uncomfortable. He was just as uncomfortable as he looked, because there was a kind of restraint in having whole clothes and being clean that irritated him. He’d hoped Mary would forget his shoes, but that hope was crushed; she coated them thoroughly with tallow, as was the custom, and brought them out. He lost his temper and said he was always being made to do things he didn’t want to do."}

{"request_id":"527bc5f74ce98799b180c5f7","rewritten_text":"I want to see you permanently well connected, and for that reason it would be best to have as few odd acquaintances as possible. So I say that if you should still be in this country when Mr. Martin marries, I hope you won’t be pulled in by your closeness with the sisters—especially not to become acquainted with his wife, who will probably be some plain farmer’s daughter, with no education.”

“Of course. Yes. I don’t mean to say that I think Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who hadn’t had some education—and been very well brought up. Still, I’m not trying to set my opinion against yours, and I’m sure I won’t want to know his wife. I’ll always have a great regard for the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and I’d be very sorry to give them up, because they’re just as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, vulgar woman, then certainly I’d better not visit her, if I can help it.”

Emma watched her as she spoke, and saw no alarming signs of love. The young man had been Harriet’s first admirer, but Emma trusted there was no other hold on her, and that there would be no serious difficulty on Harriet’s side in opposing any friendly arrangement of her own.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day, as they were walking on the Donwell road. He was on foot, and after looking at her with the utmost respect, he looked with the most genuine satisfaction at her companion. Emma was not sorry to have the chance to study him; and as she walked a few yards ahead while they talked, her quick eye soon became familiar enough with Mr. Robert Martin. He looked very neat, and he seemed like a sensible young man, but his appearance had no other advantage; and when she compared him with gentlemen, she thought he would lose all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s favor. Harriet was not unaware of his manner; she had noticed her father’s gentleness with admiration as well as wonder. Mr. Martin looked as if he didn’t really know what to do with his manners.

They stayed together only a few minutes, because Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting; and then Harriet came running to her with a smiling face, in a flutter of spirits that Miss Woodhouse hoped she would settle down very soon.

“Just think of it—we happened to meet him! How strange! He said it was quite a chance that he hadn’t gone round by Randalls. He didn’t think we ever walked this road. He thought we walked toward Randalls most days.”"}

{"request_id":"c592614671d2e23824151d5c","rewritten_text":"Without giving herself any time to reflect, and scarcely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth, the moment she had finished this letter, snatched up the next; and opening it with the utmost impatience, read on: it had been written a day after the close of the first.

“By this time, my dearest sister, you have received my hurried letter; I hope this may be more intelligible, though I am not so much pressed for time as my head is so bewildered that I cannot answer for being coherent. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what I should write, but I have bad news for you, and it cannot be put off. Imprudent as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now anxious to be assured it has actually taken place, for there is too much reason to fear they have not gone on to Scotland. Colonel Forster came yesterday, having left Brighton the day before, not many hours after the express.

Though Lydia’s short letter to Mrs. F. had led them to understand that they were going to Gretna Green, something was dropped by Denny, expressing his belief that W. never intended to go there, nor to marry Lydia at all; which was repeated to Colonel F., who, instantly alarmed, set out from B., meaning to trace their route. He traced them with ease as far as Clapham, but no farther; for on entering that place, they took themselves into a hackney-coach, and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. After that, all that is known is that they were seen to keep on along the London road.

I know not what to think. After making every inquiry possible on that side of London, Colonel F. went on into Hertfordshire, anxiously renewing his search at every turnpike, and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but without success—no such people had been seen to pass through. With the kindest concern he came on to Longbourn, and relieved our fears in a way that does him and Mrs. F. the highest credit. I am truly grieved for him and Mrs. F.; but no one can lay blame on them.

Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother believe the worst, but I cannot bring myself to think so ill of him. Many circumstances might make it more suitable for them to be married privately in town than to pursue their first plan; and even if _he_ could entertain such a design against a young woman of Lydia’s connections—which is not likely—how can I suppose her so lost to everything? Impossible! I grieve, however, to learn that Colonel F. is not disposed to rely on their marriage: when I spoke of my hopes, he shook his head and said he feared W. was not a man to be trusted.”"}

{"request_id":"b51eb0a0302d7cc79e8d665e","rewritten_text":"“Not at all,” Duff answered.

“And, to put the word yokel in plain terms for the ladies, I take it you mean that this attempt wasn’t made by some country fellow?” said Mr. Losberne, smiling.

“That’s it, master,” Blathers replied. “It’s all about the robbery, isn’t it?”

“Everything,” the doctor said.

“Then what’s this about a boy—this here boy—servants have been talking of?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing whatever,” the doctor returned. “One of the frightened servants fancied to himself that he had some part in the attempt to force his way into the house; but it’s nonsense—pure absurdity.”

“Easy enough disposed of, if that’s the case,” Duff remarked.

“What he says is perfectly right,” Blathers observed, nodding as though to confirm it, and idly turning the handcuffs about in his hands, as if they were castanets. “But who is the boy? What story does he tell about himself? Where did he come from? He didn’t just drop out of the clouds, did he, master?”

“Certainly not,” the doctor said, casting a quick, nervous look toward the two ladies. “I’m acquainted with his whole background; but we can speak of that presently. First, I suppose you’d like to see the spot where the thieves made their attempt?”

“By all means,” Mr. Blathers answered. “We’d better examine the premises first, and then the servants. That’s the proper order of business.”

Lights were then brought in. Messrs. Blathers and Duff, with the native constable Brittles, Giles, and everyone else in short, went into the little room at the end of the passage and peered out at the window; then they went round by way of the lawn and looked in at the window there; after that, a candle was handed out so they might inspect the shutter; then a lantern, to trace the footsteps; and then a pitchfork, to poke about in the bushes. When all this was done, amid the breathless attention of everyone present, they returned again; and Mr. Giles and Brittles were made to go through a melodramatic account of their part in the adventures of the previous night—doing it some six times, contradicting each other in no more than one important point the first time, and in no more than a dozen the last. Once that was finished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a long council together—one, for secrecy and solemnity, that would make a consultation of doctors on the most intricate question in medicine seem like a child’s game.

In the meantime, the doctor paced the next room in a state of great uneasiness, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched him with anxious faces.

“Upon my word,” he said, stopping after turning about with great rapidity for a long while, “I hardly know what to do.”"}

{"request_id":"7baec7d05f1a69ae356ed5fb","rewritten_text":"With everything arranged amicably and to everyone’s satisfaction, the contract was solemnly ratified with another cupful of the peppermint mixture—something made all the more necessary by the fluttering, agitated state of the lady’s spirits. As the drink was being finished, she told Mr. Bumble that the old woman had died.

“Very good,” said he, sipping his peppermint. “I’ll call at Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to send tomorrow morning. Was it that which frightened you, love?”

“It wasn’t anything particular, dear,” the lady said, trying to dodge the question.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble pressed. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” she replied. “One of these days. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” Mr. Bumble exclaimed. “It wasn’t any impudence from any of those male paupers—”

“No, no, love!” the lady interrupted quickly.

“If I thought it was,” he went on, “if I thought any one of them had dared to lift his vulgar eyes to that lovely face—”

“They wouldn’t have dared to do it, love,” she answered.

“They’d better not!” Mr. Bumble said, clenching his fist. “Let me see any man, parish or non-parish, who would presume to do it—and I’ll tell him he won’t do it a second time!”

Without any fancy show of violence in his gestures, it might not have sounded like the highest compliment to the lady’s looks; but because Mr. Bumble backed the threat with plenty of warlike motions, she was deeply moved by what she took as proof of his devotion. With great admiration, she insisted that he was indeed a dove.

The dove then raised his coat collar and put on his cocked hat. After exchanging a long, affectionate embrace with his future partner, he braved the cold night air again—only pausing for a few minutes in the male paupers’ ward to scold them a little, just to satisfy himself that he could carry out the workhouse-master’s job with the right kind of sharpness. Convinced of his qualifications, Mr. Bumble left the building with a light heart and bright visions of his coming promotion, which kept his mind occupied until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Now, Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out for tea and supper, and Noah Claypole was never inclined to take on more physical effort than was necessary for the convenient performance of the two functions of eating and drinking. So the shop wasn’t closed, even though it was past the usual time for shutting up. Mr. Bumble tapped his cane on the counter several times, but getting no response, and seeing a light shining through the glass window of the small parlor at the back of the shop, he had the nerve to peek in and see what was going on. And when he saw what was going on, he was far from unsurprised."}

{"request_id":"334a2ea2233cc697f8d8d9c1","rewritten_text":"“Never!” the girl answered.

“Tell me why?”

“For one reason,” the girl said firmly, “because the lady knows it and will stand by me. I know she will, because I have her promise. And there’s another reason too. Even though he has lived a bad life, I have lived a bad one as well. There are many of us who have stayed on the same path together, and I won’t turn on them. People who might have turned on me—any of them—didn’t, even though they were just as bad.”

“Then,” the gentleman said quickly, as if this was the exact point he had been trying to reach, “put Monks into my hands, and leave him to me to deal with.”

“What if he turns against the others?”

“I promise you that if he does, and the truth is forced out of him, then the matter will end there. There must be things in Oliver’s little history that would be painful to bring into public view, and once the truth is brought out, they will all be left alone.”

“And if it isn’t?” the girl asked.

“Then,” the gentleman continued, “this Fagin will not be brought to justice without your consent. If that happens, I can show you reasons, I think, that would make you agree.”

“Do I have the lady’s promise for that?” the girl asked.

“You do,” Rose replied. “My true and faithful pledge.”

“Monks would never learn how you knew what you know?” the girl said after a short pause.

“Never,” the gentleman answered. “The information should be used in a way that he could never even guess.”

“I’ve been a liar, and I’ve been among liars since I was a child,” the girl said after another silence, “but I will take your word.”

After both of them assured her that she could do so safely, she spoke in a very low voice. It was often hard for the listener to catch even what she meant as she named, one by one, the public-house where she had been followed that night. From the way she sometimes paused, it seemed the gentleman was making quick notes of what she told him. When she had explained the place fully—the best spot to watch it without drawing attention, and the night and hour when Monks was most likely to go there—she stopped for a few moments, as if trying to bring his face and appearance back more clearly.

“He is tall,” the girl said. “He’s strongly built, but not fat. He walks in a way that makes you notice him, and as he walks he keeps looking over his shoulder, first to one side and then to the other.”"}

{"request_id":"8a6002df831adb8bff403eca","rewritten_text":"Sandy and I were back on the road the next morning, fresh and early. It felt wonderful to draw in air and fill one’s lungs with whole, luscious barrels-ful of the blessed God’s pure, dew-borne, woodland-scented breath again, after being cramped in body and mind for two days and nights in the moral and physical stink of that wretched old buzzard-roost! I mean, for me; of course the place suited Sandy well enough, since she’d been raised on high life all her days.

Poor girl—her jaws had had a weary spell of rest for a while, and I expected to pay for it in the end. I was right, though she’d stood by me most loyally in the castle, and had propped me up with vast, ridiculous foolishnesses that were worth more for the moment than wisdoms twice their size. So I figured she’d earned the right to run her mill for a bit, if she wanted, and I didn’t feel so much as a pang when she started:

“Now turn we unto Sir Marhaus that rode with the damsel of thirty winter of age southward—”

“Are you going to see if you can work up another half-stretch on the trail of the cowboys, Sandy?”

“Even so, fair my lord.”

“Go on, then. I won’t interrupt this time, if I can manage it. Begin over again; start fair, and shake out all your reefs, and I’ll load my pipe and give it my best attention.”

“Now turn we unto Sir Marhaus that rode with the damsel of thirty winter of age southward. And so they came into a deep forest, and by fortune they were nighted, and rode along in a deep way, and at the last they came into a courtelage where abode the duke of South Marches, and there they asked harbour. And on the morn the duke sent unto Sir Marhaus, and bad him make him ready. And so Sir Marhaus arose and armed him, and there was a mass sung afore him, and he brake his fast, and so mounted on horseback in the court of the castle, there they should do the battle. So the duke was already on horseback, clean armed, with his six sons beside him, and each had a spear in his hand; and thus they encountered it, where the duke and his two sons brake their spears upon him, but Sir Marhaus held up his spear and touched none of them. Then came the four sons, two and two, and two of them brake their spears, and so did the other two. And all this while Sir Marhaus touched them not. Then Sir Marhaus ran to the duke and smote him with his spear, so that horse and man fell to the earth.”}"}

{"request_id":"08d1a65adb755f03721f852c","rewritten_text":"His body was short, but he stood with remarkable uprightness, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He began his lecture with a recap of the history of chemistry and the various improvements made by different learned men, pronouncing with real fervor the names of the most distinguished discoverers. He then gave a quick overview of the science as it stood at present and explained many of its basic terms. After a few preparatory experiments, he ended with a praise of modern chemistry—words I will never forget:

“The ancient teachers of this science,” said he, “promised the impossible and delivered nothing. The modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be transmuted and that the elixir of life is a chimera. Yet these philosophers, whose hands seem made only to dabble in dirt, and whose eyes are meant to pore over the microscope or crucible, have truly performed miracles. They go into the hidden recesses of nature and show how she works in her hiding-places. They rise into the heavens; they have discovered how the blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new powers—almost unlimited. They can command the thunders of heaven, imitate an earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with shadows of its own.”

Those were the professor’s words—no, let me say the words of fate—spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as though my soul were wrestling with a tangible enemy; one by one, the different keys were turned that made up the mechanism of my being. Chord after chord was struck, and soon my mind was filled with a single thought, a single idea, a single purpose. “So much has been done,” exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein; “more, far more, will I accomplish. Walking in the path already marked, I will blaze a new way, explore unknown powers, and unfold to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.”

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner self was in a state of rebellion and turmoil; I felt that order would come from it, but I had no power to bring it about. Gradually, after the morning’s dawn, sleep finally came. I woke, and the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. What remained was only a resolution: to return to my old studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural talent. That same day I went to see M. Waldman. In private, his manners were even gentler and more appealing than in public; there was a certain dignity in his bearing during his lecture, but in his own home it was replaced by the greatest affability and kindness."}

{"request_id":"a1e47ab8689739f1cf7687ad","rewritten_text":"The studio was steeped in the luscious perfume of roses, and when the light summer breeze wandered among the garden trees, the open door let in the heavy fragrance of lilac, or else the finer, more delicate scent of the pink-flowering thorn.

From the corner of the divan, where Persian saddle-bags lay beside him and where he reclined smoking—always as he liked to do—Lord Henry Wotton could just make out the gleam of laburnum blossoms, sweet as honey and golden in colour. Their trembling boughs seemed scarcely strong enough to carry a beauty so flame-like. Now and then, the strange shadows of birds wheeling in flight would skim across the long tussore-silk curtains drawn before the great window, giving him a brief, almost Japanese impression; and it made him think of those pale, jade-faced painters in Tokyo, who, by means of an art that must remain still, try to suggest the feeling of speed and movement. The bees, pushing through the long grass that had not been cut, or circling with stubborn monotony round the dusty gilt horns of the straggling woodbine, only served to press the quiet down more heavily. Even the dim roar of London sounded to him like the bourdon note from some distant organ.

In the middle of the room, fixed to an upright easel, stood the full-length portrait of a young man of extraordinary personal beauty; and a little way in front of it sat the artist himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance some years earlier had caused, at the time, such public excitement and had led to so many odd guesses.

As the painter regarded the gracious, well-formed figure he had so deftly reproduced in his art, a look of satisfaction crossed his face and seemed as if it might stay. Then he abruptly sprang up; shutting his eyes, he pressed his fingers to his lids, as though he were trying to keep inside his mind some strange dream from which he feared he might wake.

“It’s your finest work, Basil—your best yet,” said Lord Henry, in a languid tone. “You ought to send it next year to the Grosvenor. The Academy is far too big and far too common. Every time I’ve gone there, either there were so many people I couldn’t properly see the pictures—which was bad enough—or there were so many pictures I couldn’t properly see the people—which was worse. The Grosvenor is really the only place.”

“I don’t suppose I’ll send it anywhere,” he replied, throwing his head back in that peculiar way that had once made his friends laugh at him at Oxford."}

{"request_id":"8f1f34af5372574dfb52ccfe","rewritten_text":"But enough of this. I shall begin my story: it is my last duty, and I pray I have strength enough to carry it through. I set down no crimes; whatever faults I have can readily be forgiven. They did not spring from wicked intent, but from a lack of judgment; and I think few would deny that, with a different course and wiser understanding, I might have escaped the misfortunes that now pursue me. My lot has been ruled by necessity—by a dreadful necessity. It demanded hands stronger than mine; stronger, I believe, than any human power, to break the thick, adamantine chain that has held me. Once I breathed nothing but joy, always warmed by love and delight in goodness—now it is misery alone, and it is about to end, in death. Yet I lose myself; my tale is still untold. I will stop for a few moments, wipe my dim eyes, and try to let the present, dim and heavy unhappiness fade into the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank. He had lost his father early, and was brought up by a weak mother, with every indulgence she believed proper for a gentleman of wealth. He was sent to Eton and afterward to college; and from childhood he was allowed the free use of large sums of money, so that, from his earliest years, he enjoyed that independence which a boy with such advantages at a public school will always come to possess.

Under these conditions his passions found rich ground to take root and grow, whether as flowers or weeds, according to what they truly were. Because he was always permitted to act for himself, his character was marked early and deeply, and showed a shifting surface on which a sharp observer might discern the seeds of virtues and of misfortunes. His careless extravagance—making him throw away immense sums to satisfy passing whims, which, by their show of force, he called by the grand name of passions—often appeared as boundless generosity. Still, while he earnestly attended to the needs of others, his own desires were indulged to the fullest. He gave his money, but he sacrificed none of his own wishes to those gifts; he gave his time, which he did not value, and his affections, which he was glad to have stirred into action in any way.

I do not claim that, had his own desires been set against those of others, he would have shown an undue selfishness; but that test was never put to him. He was raised in prosperity and surrounded by all its advantages; everyone loved him and wanted to gratify him."}

{"request_id":"f81a9d4ab22b325c2cdf830f","rewritten_text":"On Saturday noon I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning smoke-powders, pawing at the air, and muttering nonsense as hard as ever, but he looked pretty down-hearted—of course, he hadn’t even managed to start a sweat in that well yet. Finally I said:

“Partner, how is it looking by now? What does it promise?”

“Look—right now I’m testing the most powerful enchantment known to the princes of the occult arts in the lands of the East. If it fails me, nothing else can help. Peace until I’m finished.”

This time he raised a smoke that darkened the whole area, and it must have made things uncomfortable for the hermits, since the wind was their way; it rolled down over their dens in a thick, billowy fog. He poured out volumes of speech to match, contorted his body, and sawed the air with his hands in the most extraordinary way. After twenty minutes he dropped down panting and nearly spent.

Now the abbot arrived, along with several hundred monks and nuns, and behind them a crowd of pilgrims and a couple of acres of foundlings—drawn by the tremendous smoke—and all in a state of intense excitement. The abbot asked anxiously for results. Merlin said:

“If any work a mortal could do might break the spell that binds these waters, then what I’ve just tried would have done it. It has failed; which means what I feared is true. The sign of that failure is that the most potent spirit known to the magicians of the East—whose name no one may speak and live—has laid his spell on this well. No mortal can breathe and ever will who can penetrate the secret of that spell, and without that secret none can break it. The water will not flow again, Father. I’ve done what a man can. Let me go.”

Of course this threw the abbot into serious consternation. He turned to me, and you could see it on his face, and said:

“You’ve heard him. Is it true?”

“Part of it is.”

“Not all, then—not all! What part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has put his spell on the well.”

“God’s wounds—then we’re ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? You mean, not certainly?”

“That’s it.”

“So when he says none can break the spell—”

“Yes. When he says that, he’s saying something that isn’t necessarily true. There are conditions under which an attempt to break it might have some chance—some small chance, some trifling chance—of success.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"868242924e1f3601d894baa3","rewritten_text":"The mental traits people call “analytical” are, by themselves, not very easy to break down and explain. We understand them mainly by what they do. We also know that, when someone has them too strongly, they become a steady source of the most intense pleasure. Just as a strong man enjoys his physical power and takes delight in exercises that make his muscles work, the analyst takes pride in that moral activity that “untangles.” He enjoys even small, ordinary tasks as long as they let him use his talent. He likes puzzles, riddles, and even hieroglyphs, and in solving each one he shows a sharpness that seems almost beyond normal understanding. His results come from the very core of his method, and they often feel like intuition.\n\nThe ability to solve again and again may be strengthened by studying mathematics, especially its highest branch, which has been unfairly named “analysis,” as if that word were the best and most special one. Still, to calculate is not the same as to analyze. A chess player, for instance, can do one without the other. That is why chess is often misunderstood in how it shapes the mind. I am not writing a formal treatise; I am only setting up a somewhat unusual story with observations that come to mind at random. So I will say this: the higher powers of careful thinking are more clearly and more usefully challenged by the quiet, unshowy game of draughts than by all the elaborate, empty tricks of chess. In chess, the pieces move in different and strange ways, and they have different, shifting values. Because of that, what is merely complicated is mistaken for what is truly deep. Here, attention is pushed hard into action. If it slips for even a moment, a mistake follows, and that mistake can lead to injury or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only many but also hard to untangle, the chances of such errors grow. In nine cases out of ten, the player who wins is the one who can concentrate more, not necessarily the one who is the most sharp. In draughts, however, the moves are unique and have little variation, so the chances of careless mistakes are smaller. With attention left comparatively free, the advantage goes to the player with better real understanding. To make this less abstract, imagine a game of draughts where the pieces are reduced to four kings, so that no oversight can really happen. Then, with both players equal, it is clear that the winner must be decided by some rare, carefully chosen move—something that requires real effort from the mind."}

{"request_id":"ed78d050853b1f743a7749ef","rewritten_text":"“Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—no, Sir Simon—are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?”

“No, thank you. I don’t eat anything anymore. Still, it’s very kind of you, and you’re much nicer than the rest of your awful, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.”

“Stop!” Virginia shouted, stamping her foot. “You’re the rude one—horrid and vulgar. And as for dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to try to fix up that ridiculous blood stain in the library. First you took all my reds, including vermilion, so I couldn’t paint any more sunsets. Then you took the emerald green and the chrome yellow, and in the end I had nothing left but indigo and Chinese white. That meant I could only paint moonlight scenes, and they’re always depressing to look at, and they’re not easy to paint at all. I never told on you, even though I was very annoyed. It was all so ridiculous—who ever heard of emerald green blood?”

“Well, really,” the Ghost said, sounding rather timid. “What was I supposed to do? Getting real blood is very hard these days. And since your brother started it all with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason why I shouldn’t use your paints. As for color, that’s a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, for instance—the bluest in England. But I know Americans don’t care much about things like that.”

“You know nothing about it. The best thing you can do is move to another country and improve your mind. My father will be more than happy to give you free passage. And even though there’s a heavy tax on spirits of every kind, there won’t be any trouble at the Custom House, because the officers are all Democrats. Once you’re in New York, you’ll be a huge success. I know plenty of people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars just to have a grandfather, and much more than that to have a family ghost.”

“I don’t think I would like America.”

“I guess it’s because we don’t have any ruins or interesting old things,” Virginia said with a sharp, mocking tone.

“No ruins! No curiosities!” the Ghost replied. “You have your navy and your manners.”

“Good evening. I’m going to ask papa to give the twins an extra week off.”

“Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,” he cried. “I’m so lonely and so unhappy. I don’t know what to do. I want to go to sleep, and I can’t.”

“That’s ridiculous. You just have to go to bed and blow out the candle.”"}

{"request_id":"9b7cf90109b1e3284efa8be6","rewritten_text":"After a while, twelve o’clock thundered out from the high tower at Westminster, and with every heavy, ringing blow of the bell the night seemed to shudder. Then the railway lights died down; only one lone lamp remained, burning on like a great ruby atop a towering mast, and the din of the city thinned away.

At two o’clock he rose and wandered toward Blackfriars. Everything looked unreal—so unreal, it might as well have been a dream. The buildings across the river appeared to have been made of darkness. One might have thought that silver and shadow had remade the world. St. Paul’s vast dome loomed up like a bubble in the dim air.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle, he noticed a man leaning over the parapet; and when he drew closer, the fellow looked up, the gas-light falling straight on his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist! No one could fail to recognize the fat, flabby countenance, the gold-rimmed spectacles, the sickly, weakly smile, the sensual mouth.

Lord Arthur halted. A bright notion struck him, and he slipped quietly behind. In an instant he had seized Mr. Podgers by the legs and hurled him into the Thames. There was a coarse oath, a heavy splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur peered anxiously over, but could make out nothing of the cheiromantist except a tall hat, spinning in an eddy of moonlit water. After a time even that sank, and no trace of Mr. Podgers could be seen. Once he fancied he caught sight of the bulky, misshapen form making for the stairway by the bridge, and a dreadful sense of failure seized him; but it proved only to be a reflection, and when the moon slipped out from behind a cloud it vanished. At last he seemed to grasp the decree of destiny. He let out a deep breath of relief, and Sybil’s name came to his lips.

“Have you dropped anything, sir?” a voice asked behind him suddenly.

He wheeled round and saw a policeman holding a bull’s-eye lantern.

“Nothing of consequence, sergeant,” he replied, smiling; and hailing a passing hansom, he jumped in and told the driver to go to Belgrave Square.

For the next few days he swung between hope and dread. There were times when he nearly expected Mr. Podgers to come walking into the room, and yet at other moments he felt that Fate could not be so cruel to him. Twice he went to the cheiromantist’s place in West Moon Street, but he could not summon the courage to ring the bell. He craved certainty, and feared it at the same time.

At last it arrived. He was seated in the club’s smoking-room, taking tea and listening—rather listlessly—to Surbiton’s account of the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter entered with the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"8bc8d99940e4be4bf4f5dd33","rewritten_text":"Not a word, however, passed his lips in reference to it until their visitor took his leave for the night; but the moment he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said,—

“Jane, I congratulate you. You will be a very happy woman.”

Jane went to him at once, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are a good girl,” he replied, “and I take real pleasure in believing you will be so happily settled. I have no doubt you will do very well together. Your tempers are by no means unlike. You are both so agreeable that nothing will ever be decided; so easygoing that every servant will cheat you; and so generous that you will always end up exceeding your income.”

“I hope not so. Any imprudence or thoughtlessness in money matters would be unforgivable in _me_.”

“Exceed their income! My dear Mr. Bennet,” cried his wife, “what are you talking about? Why, he has four or five thousand a year, and very likely more.” Then, turning to her daughter, “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so happy! I’m sure I won’t get a wink of sleep tonight. I knew how it would turn out. I always said it must be so at last. I was sure you couldn’t be so beautiful for nothing! I remember, the moment I saw him when he first came into Hertfordshire last year, I thought it was likely you would end up together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man that ever was seen!”

Wickham and Lydia were all forgotten. Jane was beyond competition her favorite child. At that moment she cared about nothing else. Her younger sisters soon began to press her with ideas of future happiness—things she might one day be able to provide.

Mary petitioned for the use of the library at Netherfield; and Kitty begged very hard for a few balls there every winter.

From this time, Bingley was, of course, a daily visitor at Longbourn; he came frequently before breakfast and always stayed until after supper—unless some barbarous neighbor, whom he could not possibly detest enough, had given him an invitation to dinner, which he felt obliged to accept.

Elizabeth now had very little time to talk with her sister; for while he was there, Jane had no attention to spare for anyone else. But she found herself considerably useful to both of them during those hours of separation that must sometimes occur. In Jane’s absence, he always attached himself to Elizabeth for the pleasure of talking about her; and when Bingley was gone, Jane constantly sought the same kind of relief.

“He has made me so happy,” said she one evening, “by telling me that he was completely unaware of my being in town last spring!”"}

{"request_id":"b3bec2ae108e911da33416fd","rewritten_text":"We proclaimed ourselves freemen so loudly and so earnestly that we caught the attention of that liberty-mouthing orator and his patriotic crowd. They gathered around us and took on a very determined attitude. The orator said:

“If, indeed, you are freemen, you have nothing to fear—the God-given liberties of Britain are around you as your shield and shelter! (Applause.) You’ll see soon. Bring forth your proofs.”

“What proofs?”

“Proof that you are freemen.”

Ah—I remembered. I came to myself; I said nothing. But the king stormed out:

“You’re insane, man. It would be better, and more reasonable, for this thief and scoundrel here to prove that we are not freemen.”

You see, he knew his own laws the way other people often know them—by words, not by results. They take a meaning and make it feel very vivid when you apply it to yourself.

Everyone shook their heads and looked disappointed; some turned away, no longer interested. The orator said—this time in the tone of business, not sentiment:

“If you don’t know your country’s laws, then it’s time you learned them. You’re strangers to us; you won’t deny that. You may be freemen—we don’t deny that—but you may also be slaves. The law is clear: it does not require the claimant to prove you are slaves; it requires you to prove you are not.”

I said:

“Dear sir, give us only time to send to Astolat; or give us only time to send to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Peace, good man. These are extraordinary requests, and you can’t hope they’ll be granted. It would take too much time, and it would unreasonably inconvenience your master—”

“_Master_, idiot!” the king stormed. “I have no master—I myself am the m—”

“Silence, for God’s sake!”

I got the words out in time to stop the king. We were in trouble enough already; it wouldn’t help us to give these people the idea that we were lunatics.

There’s no point in dragging out the details. The earl put us up and sold us at auction. This same infernal law had existed in our own South in my own time, more than thirteen hundred years later, and under it hundreds of freemen who couldn’t prove they were freemen were sold into lifelong slavery, without the circumstance making any particular impression on me; but the moment the minute law and the auction block came into my personal experience, something that had only been improper before became suddenly hellish. That’s how we’re made.

Yes, we were sold at auction, like swine. In a big town with an active market we would have brought a good price; but this place was utterly stagnant, and so we sold for a sum that makes me ashamed every time I think of it."}

{"request_id":"f6f018860805b4dc312de93b","rewritten_text":"Mrs. Clay’s feelings had overwhelmed her interest, and she had given up, for the young man’s sake, the chance to scheme longer for Sir Walter. She has abilities, though, as well as feelings; and it is now a doubtful question whether his cunning or hers will finally carry the day—whether, after preventing her from being Sir Walter’s wife, he may not at last be persuaded, coaxed, and coddled into making her the wife of Sir William.

There can be no doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and mortified by the loss of their companion, and by the discovery of their deception in her. They had their great cousins to turn to for comfort, to be sure, but they must still feel for a long time that to flatter and follow others, without being flattered and followed in return, is only a kind of half-enjoyment.

Anne, satisfied very early on of what Lady Russell meant—namely, that she should love Captain Wentworth as she ought—had no other bitterness mixed into the happiness of her prospects than what came from the awareness that she had no relations to offer him that a sensible man would value. There she felt her own inferiority very sharply. The mismatch in their fortunes meant nothing; it gave her not a moment’s regret. But to have no family to receive and properly judge him, no respectability, no harmony, no goodwill to offer in return for all the worth and the prompt welcome that met her in his brothers and sisters—this was a source of pain as lively as her mind could well feel, even under circumstances of otherwise strong felicity. She had only two friends in the world to add to his list: Lady Russell and Mrs. Smith. To them, however, he was very disposed to attach himself. Lady Russell, despite all her earlier wrongdoings, he could now value from his heart. While he was not required to say that he believed her to have been right in originally separating them, he was ready to say almost everything else in her favor. And as for Mrs. Smith, she had claims of various kinds that recommended her quickly and permanently.

Her recent good offices to Anne had been enough on their own, and their marriage, instead of costing her one friend, secured her two. She was their earliest visitor in their settled life. And Captain Wentworth, by putting her in the way of recovering her husband’s property in the West Indies—by writing for her, acting for her, and seeing her through all the small difficulties of the case with the energy and determination of a fearless man and a steadfast friend—fully repaid the services she had rendered, or ever meant to render, to his wife."}

{"request_id":"d99fad4db62be6dd602de716","rewritten_text":"The next day was set for the event, so that our honor would not be harmed by delay. The next day Drummle showed up with a polite little confession in Estella’s hand. He had the “honour” of dancing with her several times. That left me with no real choice but to regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and, overall, to reject the idea that I could be found anywhere. Drummle and I then sat facing each other, snorting, for an hour. Meanwhile, the Grove kept contradicting itself, and at last it was announced that the promotion of good feeling had moved forward at an astonishing speed.

I say this lightly, but it was not a small thing for me. I cannot properly explain the pain I felt at the thought of Estella showing any kindness to such a contemptible, clumsy, sulky fool, far below the average. Even now, I believe my suffering came from the pure generosity and unselfish love I felt for her. I could not bear the idea of her lowering herself to that kind of dog. Of course, I would have been miserable no matter who she chose; but if she had chosen someone more worthy, my distress would have been different in kind and in degree.

It was not hard for me to learn what was happening, and I soon found out that Drummle had started following her closely, and that she let him. After a little while, he was always chasing her. He and I crossed paths every day. He kept at it in a dull, stubborn way, and Estella kept him there—sometimes encouraging him, sometimes discouraging him, sometimes almost flattering him, sometimes openly despising him, sometimes acting as if she knew him very well, and sometimes barely remembering who he was.

The Spider—Mr. Jaggers’s name for him—was used to waiting in ambush, and he had the patience of his kind. He also had a thick confidence in his money and in his family’s importance, which sometimes did him good service, almost in place of real focus and steady purpose. So the Spider, watching Estella with stubborn persistence, outlasted many brighter insects. He would often hold back until the exact right moment, then suddenly drop in.

At one Assembly Ball in Richmond—there were Assembly Balls in most places then—Estella had outshone every other beauty. Yet this clumsy Drummle hovered around her so constantly, and she tolerated it so much, that I decided to speak to her about him. I took the next chance, when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home. She was sitting apart among some flowers, ready to leave."}

{"request_id":"0cae50d772a7ff7f5f50d307","rewritten_text":"“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” Then he shook his head and tapped it, showing how he felt Joseph was lacking.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry, you must be exhausted. Sit down. Here is a chicken that was had from the Boar, here is a tongue that was had from the Boar, here’s one or two little things that were had from the Boar—things I hope you won’t despise. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again the moment after he had sat down, “see before me the man I used to joke with in his days of happy infancy? And may I—may I—?”

This “May I” meant might he shake hands. I agreed, and he was fervent, and then sat down again.

“Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink—thanks to Fortune—and may she always pick out her favorites with equal judgment! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “see before me One—and likewise drink to One—without expressing again—May I—_may_ I—?”

I told him he could, and he shook hands with me again, emptied his glass, and turned it upside down. I did the same; and if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine couldn’t have gone more directly to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook walked me to the liver wing, and to the best slice of tongue (none of those out-of-the-way No Thoroughfares of Pork now), and took, comparatively speaking, no care of himself at all. “Ah! poultry, poultry! You little thought,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the fowl in the dish, “when you were a young fledgling, what was in store for you. You little thought you were to be refreshment beneath this humble roof for one as—call it a weakness, if you will,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “but may I? _may_ I—?”

It started to feel unnecessary to repeat the form of asking permission, so he did it at once. I don’t know how he managed to do it so often without cutting himself with my knife.

“And your sister,” he went on, after a little steady eating, “who had the honor of bringing you up by hand! It’s a sad picture to think she’s no longer able to fully understand the honor. May—”

I saw he was about to come at me again, and I stopped him.

“We’ll drink her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, quite limp with admiration, “that’s the way you know ’em, sir!” (I don’t know who Sir was, but it certainly wasn’t me, and there was no third person present); “that’s the way you know the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"e0ad5441a7854a78006ead09","rewritten_text":"Right in front of him, in the weak moonlight, he saw an old man with a frightening look. His eyes burned red, like coals. Long grey hair hung over his shoulders in tangled, matted locks. His clothes were cut in an old-fashioned style, but they were dirty and torn. Heavy manacles and rusty chains hung from his wrists and ankles.

“My dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I really must insist that you oil those chains. I’ve brought you a small bottle of the Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator for that purpose. They say it works completely the first time you use it, and there are several testimonials on the label from some of our most important local divines. I’ll leave it here for you by the bedroom candles, and I’ll be glad to get you more if you need it.” With that, the United States Minister set the bottle down on a marble table, shut his door, and went to bed.

For a moment, the Canterville ghost stood perfectly still, filled with natural anger. Then he grabbed the bottle and smashed it hard on the polished floor. He ran down the corridor, groaning in a hollow way and casting out a sickly green light. But just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open. Two small figures in white robes appeared, and a large pillow shot past his head. Clearly, there was no time to waste. He quickly used the Fourth Dimension of Space to escape, vanished through the wall paneling, and the house fell silent.

When he reached a small secret room in the left wing, he leaned against a patch of moonlight to catch his breath and start thinking clearly about what had happened. In his long, uninterrupted career of three hundred years, he had never been insulted so badly. He remembered the Dowager Duchess, whom he had scared into a fit while she stood before the mirror in her lace and diamonds. He remembered the four housemaids, who had broken down into hysterics simply because he grinned at them through the curtains of one of the spare bedrooms. He remembered the parish rector, whose candle he had blown out one night when he came home late from the library, and who had been under Sir William Gull’s care ever since, a true martyr to nervous troubles. And he remembered old Madame de Tremouillac, who, after waking up early one morning and seeing a skeleton sitting in an armchair by the fire reading her diary, had been stuck in bed for six weeks with brain fever. After she recovered, she returned to the Church and cut ties with that notorious skeptic, Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"751705d145f2b1c9aa309305","rewritten_text":"Each man likens it—not to the utterance of some particular person from any nation whose language he knows—but to the opposite. The Frenchman thinks it was the voice of a Spaniard, and “might have distinguished some words had he been acquainted with the Spanish.” The Dutchman insists it was that of a Frenchman; yet we are told that “not understanding French this witness was examined through an interpreter.” The Englishman takes it for the voice of a German, and “does not understand German.” The Spaniard “is sure” it belonged to an Englishman, but “judges by the intonation” alone, “as he has no knowledge of the English.” The Italian believes it to be the voice of a Russian, though “has never conversed with a native of Russia.” A second Frenchman, moreover, disagrees with the first and is certain the voice was Italian; but, “not being cognizant of that tongue,” he, like the Spaniard, is “convinced by the intonation.” 

Now, how odd indeed must that voice have been, if testimony like this could be drawn from it—so that, even in its tones, the inhabitants of the five great divisions of Europe could recognise nothing familiar! You may say it might have been the voice of an Asiatic—of an African. Neither Asiatics nor Africans are plentiful in Paris; but without denying the inference, I will only ask you to notice three points. One witness calls it “harsh rather than shrill.” Two others describe it as “quick and unequal.” No witness mentions any words, or any sounds that resemble words, as being distinguishable.

“I know not,” continued Dupin, “what impression I may have made, up to this point, on your own understanding; but I do not hesitate to say that even legitimate deductions from this portion of the testimony—the portion about the gruff and shrill voices—are enough, of themselves, to raise a suspicion that ought to guide every step of further inquiry into the mystery. I said ‘legitimate deductions;’ but I mean something more than that. I intended to suggest that the deductions are the _only_ proper ones, and that the suspicion springs _inevitably_ from them, as the single outcome. What the suspicion is, however, I will not tell you yet. I only want you to keep in mind that, for me, it was strong enough to give my inquiries in the chamber a definite shape—a certain direction.

“Let us now, in imagination, place ourselves in this chamber. What shall we look for first? The means of egress used by the murderers. It is not too much to say that neither of us believes in præternatural events.”"}

{"request_id":"dcb9dc30d0e14432cae4e9ad","rewritten_text":"She was to be placed among those who truly loved her, and who had more judgment than she possessed; secure enough to guard her from harm, and yet provided with enough to keep her cheerful. She would never be drawn into temptation, nor left so that temptation might come and find her out. She would be both respectable and content; and Emma confessed her to be the luckiest creature in the world for having formed so steady and persevering an attachment in such a man;—or, if not quite the luckiest, at least to have yielded only to her own feelings.

Harriet, necessarily pulled away by her duties with the Martins, was less and less often at Hartfield; and that was not to be regretted. The closeness between her and Emma must gradually lessen; their friendship was to take on a quieter, more settled kind of goodwill; and, happily, what ought to be, and must be, seemed already to be beginning—slowly, naturally, and without violence.

Before the end of September, Emma took Harriet to church, and saw her hand given to Robert Martin with so complete a satisfaction that no recollection—however it might connect itself with Mr. Elton as he stood before them—could disturb it. Perhaps, indeed, at that time she scarcely saw Mr. Elton at all; but she could not help thinking of the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might next be hers. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the newest pair among the three engaged, were the first to be married.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury, and was brought back to the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Mr. Churchills were also in town; and they were only waiting for November.

The intervening month was the one fixed on, as far as Emma and Mr. Knightley could manage it. They had resolved that their marriage should be completed while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so that they might have their fortnight’s absence on a tour to the seaside, which was the plan. John and Isabella, and every other friend, agreed in approving it. But Mr. Woodhouse—how was Mr. Woodhouse to be brought to consent?—he, who had never yet spoken of their marriage except as something distant.

At first, when the subject was raised, he was so wretched that they were nearly without hope. A second mention, however, caused him less pain. He began to believe it was to be, and that he could not prevent it—a hopeful movement of the mind toward resignation. Yet even then he was not happy. Indeed, he seemed so much the contrary, that Emma’s courage failed. She could not bear to see him suffering, or to know him imagining himself neglected; and though her reason almost agreed with the assurances of both Mr. Knightleys, that once the event was over his distress would soon be over too, she still faltered—she could not go on."}

{"request_id":"60898ae0ee7efe3a191587b8","rewritten_text":"Well, three or four months went by, and it was well into winter now. I’d been to school most of the time, and I could spell and read and write a little, and I could say the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five. I don’t think I could ever get any farther than that, even if I lived forever. I don’t put much faith in mathematics anyway.

At first I hated school, but after a while I got to where I could stand it. Whenever I got unusually tired, I played hooky, and the hiding I got the next day did me good and cheered me up. So the longer I went to school, the easier it got. I was getting used to the widow’s ways, too, and they weren’t so rough on me. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed pulled on me pretty hard most of the time, but before the cold weather I used to slip out and sleep in the woods sometimes, and that was a relief. I liked the old ways best, but I was starting to like the new ones a little too. The widow said I was coming along slow but sure, and doing very satisfactory. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning I happened to tip over the salt-cellar at breakfast. I reached for it as fast as I could, to throw it over my left shoulder and keep off the bad luck, but Miss Watson was already there and stopped me. She said, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; you’re always making a mess!” The widow spoke up for me, but that wasn’t going to keep off the bad luck, I knew that well enough. After breakfast I went out feeling worried and shaky, wondering where it was going to land on me and what it was going to be. There are ways to ward off some kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of those kinds, so I never tried to do anything. I just kept going, low-spirited and on the lookout.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile where you go through the high board fence. There was an inch of new snow on the ground, and I saw somebody’s tracks. They had come up from the quarry and stood around the stile for a while, and then went on around the garden fence. It was strange they hadn’t come in after standing there so long. I couldn’t figure it out. Somehow it felt very curious. I was going to follow them, but I bent down to look at the tracks first."}

{"request_id":"5159225bbfdf978ae0d6457a","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s last reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more crowded than usual. Six Cabinet Ministers had arrived from the Speaker’s Levée, wearing their stars and ribands, and all the pretty women were dressed in their finest clothes. At the end of the picture-gallery stood the Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a heavy, Tartar-looking woman with tiny black eyes and wonderful emeralds. She was talking bad French loudly and laughing too much at everything people said to her. It was, without doubt, a strange mix of people. Beautiful peeresses chatted easily with loud Radicals, popular preachers brushed past eminent sceptics, and a group of bishops kept moving from room to room, following a stout prima-donna. On the staircase stood several Royal Academicians, disguised as artists, and it was said that at one time the supper-room was packed with geniuses. In fact, it was one of Lady Windermere’s best nights, and the Princess stayed until nearly half past eleven.

The moment the Princess left, Lady Windermere went back to the picture-gallery. There, a celebrated political economist was solemnly explaining the scientific theory of music to an angry virtuoso from Hungary, and Lady Windermere began talking to the Duchess of Paisley. She looked wonderfully beautiful, with her grand ivory throat, her large blue forget-me-not eyes, and her heavy coils of golden hair. Or perhaps not—she wasn’t that pale straw color that people call gold these days. Her hair was real gold, like gold woven into sunlight or hidden in amber. It gave her face the look of a saint, with just enough of the pull of a sinner. She was a fascinating study of psychology. Early in life she had learned an important truth: nothing looks so innocent as an indiscretion. Through a series of reckless adventures—many of them harmless—she had gained all the benefits of having a reputation. She had changed her husband more than once; Debrett even credits her with three marriages. But since she had never changed her lover, the world had long stopped talking about her as a scandal. Now she was forty, had no children, and had that strong passion for pleasure that is the secret of staying young.

Suddenly she looked around the room eagerly and said, in her clear contralto voice, “Where is my cheiromantist?”

“Your what, Gladys?” the Duchess asked, startled before she could help it.

“My cheiromantist, Duchess. I can’t live without him right now.”

“Dear Gladys! You’re always so original,” the Duchess murmured, trying to remember what a cheiromantist really was, and hoping it wasn’t the same thing as a cheiropodist.

“He comes to see my hand twice a week, regularly,” Lady Windermere went on. “And he’s very interesting about it.”"}

{"request_id":"a7a5b3c87665b0765c82b2ed","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats. Every now and then you’d see one poke his nose out of a hole in the corner. She told me she had to keep things ready to throw at them when she was by herself, or they wouldn’t leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot, and said she was a pretty steady shot with it generally, but she’d wrenched her arm a day or two back and didn’t know whether she could throw true now. Still, she kept her eyes open for a chance, and straightway she struck at a rat; but she missed him clean, and she cried out, “Ouch!”—it hurt her arm so. Then she told me to go for the next one.

I wanted to be making off before the old man came back, but I didn’t show it. I took the thing, and the first rat that showed itself I let fly at, and if he’d stayed where he was he’d have been a pretty sick rat. She said it was first-rate, and she figured I’d have the next one too. She went and got the lump of lead again, brought it back, and along with it a hank of yarn she wanted me to help her with. I held my two hands up, and she laid the hank over them, then carried on talking about her and her husband’s affairs. But she stopped short to say:

“Mind the rats. You’d best have the lead in your lap, ready.”

So at that very moment she dropped the lump into my lap, and I clapped my legs together on it, and she went right on talking. Only about a minute passed. Then she took the hank away, looked me straight in the face, and in a very pleasant voice asked:

“Now then, what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what is it, mum?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—or what is it?”

I thought I must have been shaking like a leaf. I didn’t know what to do. But I managed to say, “Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, mum. If I’m in the way, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay just where you are. I ain’t going to hurt you, and I ain’t going to tell on you neither. You just tell me your secret, and trust me. I’ll keep it; and what’s more, I’ll help you. So will my old man, if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway ’prentice—that’s all. It ain’t nothing. There ain’t no harm in it. You’ve been treated bad, and you decided to cut. Bless you, child—I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"0c143db9be48dc6be68e2cbf","rewritten_text":"In the morning, she was found dead in her bed, and it seemed she had suffered no pain. Sir Mathew Reid was sent for right away, but there was nothing anyone could do. She was to be buried on the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before she died, she made her will. She left Lord Arthur her small house in Curzon Street, along with all her furniture, personal belongings, and pictures. The only exceptions were her collection of miniatures, which were to go to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which Sybil Merton was to have. The property itself was not worth much, but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, was very worried that Lord Arthur should come back as soon as possible, if he could. There were many bills to pay, and Lady Clementina had never kept careful accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s thoughtful kindness toward him, and he felt that Mr. Podgers had a lot to answer for. Still, his love for Sybil was stronger than anything else. The fact that he believed he had done his duty gave him peace and comfort. When he reached Charing Cross, he felt completely happy.

The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise that nothing would ever come between them again, and they set the wedding for the 7th of June. To him, life felt bright and wonderful again, and all his old happiness returned.

But one day, while he was going through the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil herself—burning old packets of faded letters and emptying drawers of odd rubbish—Sybil suddenly let out a little cry of delight.

“What have you found, Sybil?” Lord Arthur asked. He looked up from what he was doing and smiled.

“This lovely little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. Isn’t it quaint and Dutch? Please, give it to me! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m over eighty.”

It was the box that had held the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, and a faint blush rose in his cheeks. He had almost forgotten what he had done. It felt like a strange coincidence that Sybil—who he had done all that terrible worrying for—should be the first to bring it back to his mind.

“Of course you can have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.”

“Oh, thank you, Arthur. And may I have the bonbon too? I didn’t know Lady Clementina liked sweets. I thought she was far too intellectual.”

Lord Arthur went deadly pale, and a terrible thought crossed his mind."}

{"request_id":"e8a741efb061be81be00e8b3","rewritten_text":"He made it clear to her that Frank admired her greatly—he thought her very beautiful and very charming; and with so much to be said in his favor, she found she couldn’t judge him too harshly. As Mrs. Weston observed, “all young people would have their little whims.”

There was one person among his new acquaintances in Surry who was not so forgiving. In general, he was judged, throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury, with great candor; allowances were made for the little excesses of such a handsome young man—one who smiled so often and bowed so well; but there was one spirit among them that could not be softened by bows or smiles—Mr. Knightley. The situation was explained to him at Hartfield. For the moment, he was silent; but Emma heard him almost immediately afterward, speaking to himself over a newspaper he held in his hand: “Hum! just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” She had half a mind to be offended; but a moment’s observation convinced her he said it only to ease his own feelings, not to provoke anyone; and so she let it go.

Although in one respect the bearers of not-good news—Mr. and Mrs. Weston’s visit this morning—was in another way especially well-timed. Something happened while they were at Hartfield that made Emma want their advice; and, even more fortunately, she wanted exactly the advice they gave.

This was what happened:—The Coles had been settled in Highbury for some years, and they were very good people—friendly, generous, and unpretending; but, on the other hand, they were of low origin, in trade, and only moderately genteel. When they first came into the country, they lived according to their income, quietly, keeping little company, and that little without expense; but in the last year or two they had gained a considerable increase of means—the house in town had brought in better profits, and their fortune in general had smiled on them. With their wealth, their expectations grew; their lack of a larger house, and their desire for more company. They added to their house, to the number of servants, and to their expenses of every kind; and by now, in both fortune and style of living, they were second only to the family at Hartfield. Their love of society, and their new dining-room, prepared everyone for their hosting dinner-parties; and a few gatherings, mostly among the single men, had already taken place. The regular and best families Emma could hardly imagine they would presume to invite—neither Donwell, nor Hartfield, nor Randalls. Nothing should tempt her to go, if they did; and she regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal carry less meaning than she would have liked."}

{"request_id":"73a6e02b09eecd4782b04b1c","rewritten_text":"“So I’m the owner of some knights,” I said, as we rode off. “Who would ever think I’d live to list assets like that. I don’t know what I’ll do with them—unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, please you, sir, and their squires.”

“It’s a good haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes. Where do they live?”

“Ah, I didn’t understand you. I’ll tell you right away.” Then she paused, thinking, and said the words softly, as if tasting them: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; eh, right so; where do they hang out. Honestly, that phrase has a nice, charming sound, and it’s worded so prettily. I’ll repeat it again and again in my idle moments, and maybe I’ll learn it. Where do they hang out. There—it's already tripping off my tongue. And since—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes; the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. A while back, remember? Figuratively speaking, the game’s called.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Get to the bat. I mean, get to work on your statistics, and don’t waste so much kindling trying to get your fire started. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will. And lightly I’ll begin. So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I realized my mistake right away. I’d started her on it, and that was my fault. It would take her thirty days to get to the facts. She usually started without any introduction and ended without any result. If I interrupted her, she would either keep going without noticing, or answer with a couple of words and then go back and say the sentence again. So interruptions only did harm. Still, I had to interrupt, and pretty often, too, just to save my life. A person would die if they let her monotony drip on them all day.

“Great Scott!” I said, in panic. She immediately began over again:

“So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came to an abbey of monks, and they were well lodged. So on the morning they heard their masses in the abbey, and then they rode forth until they came to a great forest; and then Sir Gawaine noticed, in a valley by a turret, twelve fair damsels, and two knights armed on great horses, and the damsels went to and fro by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"14cbfcdf84fcb54ea2ce3256","rewritten_text":"No bringing it up by hand, then. Not a bit of it!”

Joe offered me more gravy, which I was afraid to take.

“He was a world of trouble to you, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble, sympathizing with my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated. “Trouble?” Then she launched into a terrifying list of every illness I’d been guilty of, every act of sleeplessness I’d committed, every high place I’d tumbled from, every low place I’d tumbled into, every injury I’d done myself, every time she’d wished me in my grave—and how stubbornly I’d refused to go there.

I think the Romans must have aggravated one another a great deal with their noses. Maybe that’s why they became so restless. In any case, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose so aggravated me during the recital of my misdeeds that I wanted to pull it until he howled. But everything I’d endured up to then was nothing compared with the awful feelings that took hold of me when the pause came after my sister finished—during which pause everyone looked at me (as I felt painfully aware) with indignation and disgust.

“Yet,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently steering the conversation back to the subject they’d drifted from, “Pork—regarded as biled—is rich, too; ain’t it?”

“Have a little brandy, uncle,” my sister said.

Oh, heavens—it had finally come! He’d find it was weak, he’d say it was weak, and I was finished! I gripped the leg of the table under the cloth with both hands and waited for what would happen.

My sister went for the stone bottle, came back with it, and poured his brandy out—no one else took any. The poor man fidgeted with his glass, picked it up, looked at it in the light, set it down again, and dragged out my misery. All the while, Mrs. Joe and Joe were briskly clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I couldn’t take my eyes off him. Always holding tight to the table leg with my hands and feet, I watched the miserable man finger his glass playfully, lift it, smile, throw his head back, and drink the brandy straight down. Immediately afterward, the whole company was seized with unspeakable alarm, because he sprang to his feet, turned around several times in an appalling, spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and rushed out the door. Then he became visible through the window, violently plunging and coughing up everything, making the most hideous faces, and acting as if he’d completely lost his mind.

I held on tight while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to him."}

{"request_id":"5cf65dbd26eb11ca8d494939","rewritten_text":"The day went by much as the one before it had. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley had spent several hours of the morning with the invalid, who continued, though only slowly, to get better; and in the evening Elizabeth joined their party in the drawing-room. The loo table, however, was not to be seen. Mr. Darcy was at his writing, and Miss Bingley, seated close by, watched the progress of his letter, while repeatedly diverting his attention with messages to her sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were engaged at piquet, and Mrs. Hurst sat by, observing their play.

Elizabeth took up some needlework, and found herself entertained enough by what passed between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s constant praises—of his hand-writing, of the evenness of his lines, of the length of his letter—delivered with a perfect air of indifference to the effect they produced, made a sort of dialogue, and matched exactly her own estimate of each point.

“How pleased Miss Darcy must be to receive such a letter!”

He offered no reply.

“You write astonishingly fast.”

“You’re mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must have occasion to put down in the course of a year! Letters of business, too! I should think them dreadful.”

“Then it is lucky, at least, that they fall to my share rather than to yours.”

“Pray, tell your sister that I long to see her.”

“I have already told her once, at your request.”

“I’m afraid you don’t like your pen. Let me fix it for you. I mend pens remarkably well.”

“Thank you—but I always mend my own.”

“How do you manage to write so evenly?”

He was silent.

“Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her improvement on the harp, and do let her know that I am quite carried away by her pretty little design for a table; I think it infinitely better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“Will you allow me to postpone your raptures until I write again? At present I have not space enough to do them justice.”

“Oh, it matters nothing. I shall see her in January. But do you always send her such charming long letters, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are generally long; but whether they are always charming, that is not for me to decide.”

“It is a maxim with me that anyone who can write a long letter with ease cannot write badly.”

“That won’t do as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” cried her brother; “because he does not write with ease. He thinks too much about words of four syllables. Don’t you, Darcy?”

“My manner of writing is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” said Miss Bingley, “Charles writes in the most careless fashion imaginable.”"}

Even before I opened it, the outside of the envelope made me feel wildly nervous. I had never seen the handwriting before, but I knew whose it was. The note did not start in any usual way, like “Dear Mr. Pip,” or “Dear Pip,” or “Dear Sir,” or anything like that. Instead, it said:—

“I am to come to London the day after to-morrow by the midday coach. I believe it was settled you should meet me. At all events, Miss Havisham has that impression, and I write to you because of it. She sends you her regard.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

If I had had time, I would probably have bought several new suits of clothes for the occasion. But since I didn’t, I had to make do with what I already owned. My appetite disappeared at once, and I couldn’t find any peace or rest until the day finally came. But even when it arrived, I was no better. I became so restless that I kept going to the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. I knew, in a sensible way, that I understood this perfectly well, yet I still felt it was not safe to let the coach office out of my sight for more than five minutes. In that state of irrational worry, I had already spent the first half-hour of a watch that was supposed to last four or five hours when Wemmick ran into me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How do you do? I wouldn’t have thought this was your job.”

I told him I was waiting to meet someone who was coming by coach, and I asked how things were at the Castle and with the Aged.

“Both are doing well, thank you,” Wemmick said. “And especially the Aged. He’s in wonderful spirits. He’ll be eighty-two next birthday. I’m thinking of firing my cannon eighty-two times, if the neighborhood doesn’t complain, and if that cannon of mine can handle the strain. But this isn’t London talk. Where do you think I’m going?”

“To the office?” I said, because he was heading that way.

“Next thing to it,” Wemmick replied. “I’m going to Newgate. We’re in a banker’s-parcel situation right now, and I’ve been down the road to take a look at what’s going on. After that, I had to have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” Wemmick answered, very dryly. “But he’s accused of it. So could you or I be. Either of us might be accused of it, you know.”"}
