{"request_id":"82f3c84f748f662e6480bfff","rewritten_text":"Shall I speak to them? Or to Miss Bates?—She is still the nearer one. And I cannot help thinking that Miss Bates may be just as likely as anyone to catch the temper of the rest of the people. Still, we do want a larger council. Why not go and ask Miss Bates to come in with us?”

“Well—if you please,” said Mrs. Weston, with a little hesitation, “if you believe she will be of any service.”

“You’ll get nothing worth the trouble from Miss Bates,” Emma replied. “She’ll be all smiles and gratitude, but she won’t tell you anything. She won’t even listen to your questions. I see no use in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so entertaining—so very entertaining! I do enjoy hearing Miss Bates talk. And you needn’t bring the whole family, you know.”

At this moment Mr. Weston joined them; and when he heard what was proposed, he gave it his full approval.

“Aye, do, Frank.—Go and fetch Miss Bates, and let us settle it at once. She’ll be pleased with the plan, I’m sure; and I don’t know a better person for showing us how to get rid of difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We’re getting a little too particular. She’s a standing example of how to be happy. But fetch them both—invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady?”...

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall think you a great blockhead, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I didn’t at once remember. Undoubtedly, if you wish it, I will try to persuade them both.” And off he ran.

Long before he came back, bringing the short, neat, brisk-moving aunt, and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston—sweet-tempered as she was, and a good wife besides—had gone over the passage again, and found the troubles in it far less than she had first imagined; indeed, they were very trifling. So the question of decision was at an end. As for everything else, at least in their thoughts, it was perfectly smooth. The smaller arrangements—table and chair, lights and music, tea and supper—either arranged themselves, or were left as mere trifles to be settled at any time between Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes. Everyone invited was certainly to come; Frank had already written to Enscombe to propose staying a few days beyond his fortnight, which could not possibly be refused. And it would be a delightful dance.

Most cordially, when Miss Bates arrived, did she agree that it must be so. As a counsellor she was not needed; but as an approver—(a far safer part)—she was truly welcome. Her approval, at once general and minute, warm and unceasing, could not fail to please; and for another half-hour they were all walking from room to room, some suggesting, some attending, and all in happy expectation of what was to come."}

{"request_id":"13dae401779241be6b35bf53","rewritten_text":"He was handed over to you. You understand, then—am I right in saying I’m acquainted with the circumstances?”

“Indeed, that is so,” said Defarge. He had been told to answer, in that brief, accidental moment when his wife’s elbow brushed him while she knitted and hummed her little song, but always to keep it short.

“It was to you,” the spy went on, “that his daughter came; and it was from your attention that his daughter took him away, with a tidy brown monsieur beside her. What is he called?—with a small wig—Lorry—of the bank of Tellson and Company—across to England.”

“Such is the fact,” Defarge repeated.

“Very striking recollections!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter, in England.”

“Yes?” said Defarge.

“You don’t hear much of them these days?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“Not at all,” madame put in, lifting her eyes from her work and her faint song. “We get word of their safe arrival, and maybe another letter—or perhaps two; but after that they’ve gone on, step by step, along their lives—ours as well—and we’ve kept up no correspondence.”

“Just so, madame,” replied the spy. “She’s to be married.”

“To be married?” madame echoed. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. You English seem so cold, that’s what I think.”

“Oh! You know I’m English.”

“I see your tongue is,” returned madame; “and I suppose the man is, too.”

He didn’t take the remark as a compliment; still, he made the best of it and brushed it off with a laugh. After finishing his cognac, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is to be married. But not to an Englishman; to one who, like herself, is French by birth. And as for Gaspard (ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel!), it’s a curious thing that she’s going to marry the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis—who was raised by Gaspard to that lofty height of so many feet; in other words, the present Marquis. Yet he lives unknown in England; he isn’t a marquis there—he’s Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is the name of his mother’s family.”

Madame Defarge continued knitting without pause, but the news showed itself plainly in her husband. Whatever he tried to do behind the little counter—striking a light, lighting his pipe—he was still disturbed, and his hand would not be steady. The spy would have been no spy if he hadn’t noticed it, or if he hadn’t kept it in mind.

Having made, at least, this one point—whatever it might come to—and with no customers arriving to give him any other opening, Mr. Barsad paid for what he’d had, and took his leave. Before going, he took the occasion, in a polite sort of way, to say that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

{"request_id":"eeb67ce3ba204a18573484e4","rewritten_text":"Thus I spent two years. Day after day, so many hundreds of days passed; nothing obvious changed on the outside, but a few things slowly worked on my mind as I drifted closer to death. I began to study more. I began to understand others more, through the thoughts they expressed in books. I read history, and in doing so I lost the sense of being only myself, the individuality I had once had. Perhaps, as the feeling of immediate suffering faded, I became more human. Even solitude began to lose some of its appeal. I started to wish again for sympathy. Not because I wanted to join the crowd, but because I wanted one friend to love me.

You might say that I was gradually becoming ready to return to society. I do not think so. The sympathy I wanted had to be pure, free from the pull of outside circumstances. In the world, I could not help running into the rough, everyday things that mix even with the best feelings. Believe me, at that time I was less fit for any real closeness with my fellow people than before. When I left them, they had tormented me in the same way that pain and sickness can torment—something outside the mind that hurts it, and that I wanted to throw off. But now I would have wanted sympathy. I would have wanted to tie my soul to someone else’s, and I would have had to prepare myself for disappointment and suffering. I was as delicate as a sensitive plant, all nerve. I did not want sympathy and help for ambition or wisdom. I wanted sweet, mutual affection—smiles to lift me and gentle words of comfort. I wanted one heart where I could pour out my complaints without restraint, and where, if the soil were heavenly, good fruit might grow even from such bad seed.

But how could I find this? The love that is the soul of friendship is a soft spirit, rarely found unless two kind people are joined from early youth, or unless they are bound together by shared suffering and shared pursuits. It comes to a few, chosen ones, without being asked for or even noticed. It falls like gentle dew on places that had been barren before, and then those places become fertile for all sweet plants. But when it is desired, it flies. It mocks the prayers of those who long for it. It will give, but it will not be sought.

I knew all this, and I did not go looking for sympathy. Yet there, on my lonely heath, under my humble roof, with nothing around me but desert, it came to me like a winter sunbeam—something that brightens and helps dissolve the snow that has piled up. Alas, the sun shone on blighted fruit. I did not come back to life under its light, because I was too completely broken to feel any kindness in it."}

{"request_id":"fbe7cb9b3f6ef6f0b70e8f09","rewritten_text":"Without giving herself time to think, and scarcely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth, having finished this letter, immediately grabbed the other one. She opened it with the utmost impatience and read as follows: it had been written a day later than the end of the first.

“By this time, my dearest sister, you have received my hurried letter; I hope this one is clearer, but though I’m not short on time, my head is so confused that I can’t answer for being coherent. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what I would write, but I have bad news for you, and it cannot be delayed. As imprudent as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now anxious to be sure it has taken place, for there is far too much reason to fear they are not gone to Scotland.

Colonel Forster came yesterday. He left Brighton the day before, not many hours after the express. Although Lydia’s short letter to Mrs. F. made it clear they were going to Gretna Green, something Denny said led them to believe W. never intended to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. He repeated this to Colonel F., who, instantly alarmed, set off from B. intending to trace their route. He traced them easily as far as Clapham, but no farther; for when they entered that place, they got into a hackney-coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom.

All that is known after this is that they were seen to continue along the London road. I don’t know what to think. After making every possible inquiry on that side of London, Colonel F. went on into Hertfordshire, anxiously renewing his search at every turnpike and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but without success—no such people had been seen to pass through.

With the kindest concern he came on to Longbourn and broke his fears to us in a way that reflects most creditably on his heart. I am sincerely grieved for him and Mrs. F.; but no one can blame them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother believe the worst, but I can’t think so badly of him. Many circumstances might make it more suitable for them to be married privately in town than to follow their first plan; and even if he could form such a design against a young woman of Lydia’s connections—which is not likely—can I suppose her so lost to everything? Impossible! I grieve, however, to find that Colonel F. is not disposed to rely on their marriage: when I expressed my hopes, he shook his head and said he feared W. was not a man to be trusted."}

{"request_id":"10019773af0f4b5e97a9def8","rewritten_text":"In the middle of the rift, I saw a white spot, but at first I couldn’t tell what it was. I adjusted the telescope’s focus and looked again. This time I could make out that it was a human skull.

“Once I found that,” I said, “I felt sure the puzzle was solved. The phrase ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could only mean where the skull was on the tree. And ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ could mean only one thing, if we’re talking about finding buried treasure. I realized the plan was to drop a bullet from the skull’s left eye. Then, if you draw a straight line—a bee-line—from the nearest point of the trunk through ‘the shot’ (the spot where the bullet fell), and extend that line for fifty feet, it should point to a specific place. Beneath that point, I thought, it was at least possible that something valuable was hidden.”

“All of this,” I said, “is very clear. Even though it’s clever, it’s still simple and direct. When you left the Bishop’s Hotel, what happened next?”

“First,” he replied, “I carefully took the tree’s bearings and then started back home. But the moment I left ‘the devil’s seat,’ the circular rift disappeared. No matter how I turned afterward, I couldn’t see it again. The main clever part of the whole thing, as far as I can tell, is this: after repeated tests, I’m convinced the circular opening can be seen from no other place than the narrow ledge on the rock’s face.”

“In that trip to the Bishop’s Hotel, I had Jupiter with me. He must have noticed, for weeks, that I’d been acting strangely, and he made sure I wasn’t left alone. But the next day, I got up very early and managed to get away from him. I went into the hills to look for the tree. After a lot of work, I found it. When I got home that night, my valet suggested I should be flogged. As for the rest of the story, I think you know it as well as I do.”

“I take it,” I said, “that you missed the spot the first time you tried digging, because Jupiter was careless and let the bug fall through the right eye instead of the left eye of the skull.”

“That’s exactly right,” he said. “That mistake changed the ‘shot’ by about two and a half inches—that is, it shifted the peg nearest the tree. If the treasure had been directly under the shot, the error wouldn’t have mattered much. But the ‘shot,’ along with the nearest point of the tree, were only two points used to set the direction of a line. Even a small error at the start grows as you extend the line. By the time we had gone fifty feet, it had thrown us completely off the trail.”"}

{"request_id":"e84907deaf5a989c00be15ed","rewritten_text":"She and the children might stay very comfortably.”

“Ah! papa—that is exactly what you have never managed to do, and I don’t believe you ever will. Isabella cannot bear to remain behind her husband.”

This was too true to be contradicted. Though it was unwelcome, Mr. Woodhouse could only give a resigned little sigh; and the moment Emma noticed how much his spirits were affected by his daughter’s attachment to her husband, she steered the conversation into a channel that would lift them.

“Harriet must give us as much of her company as she can while my brother and sister are here. I’m sure she’ll be delighted with the children. We are very proud of them, aren’t we, papa? I wonder which she’ll think the handsomest—Henry or John?”

“Aye, I wonder which she will. Poor little dears—how happy they’ll be to come. They’re very fond of being at Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they are, sir. I’m sure I don’t know anyone who isn’t.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John is very much like his mother. Henry is the eldest; he was named after me, not after his father. John, the second, is named after his father. Some people, I believe, are surprised the eldest wasn’t; but Isabella would have him called Henry, which I always thought very pretty of her. And he is a very clever boy, indeed. They are all remarkably clever, and they have so many engaging ways. They’ll come and stand by my chair, and say, ‘Grandpapa, can you give me a bit of string?’—and once Henry asked me for a knife; but I told him knives were only made for grandpapas. I think their father is too rough with them far too often.”

“He seems rough to you,” said Emma, “only because you are so very gentle yourself; but if you compared him with other fathers, you wouldn’t think him rough. He wants his boys to be active and hardy; and if they misbehave, he can give them a sharp word now and then; but he is an affectionate father—at least, Mr. John Knightley is an affectionate father. The children are all fond of him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and tosses them up to the ceiling in the most dreadful fashion!”

“But they like it, papa; there’s nothing they enjoy more. It’s such pleasure to them that, if their uncle didn’t insist on taking turns, whoever began would never give way to the other.”

“Well, I can’t make sense of it.”

“That’s just the way with us all, papa. One half of the world can’t understand the pleasures of the other.”"}

{"request_id":"0d99b1133e5be286ad73b776","rewritten_text":"In my day, in my own country, this money was collected from imposts. The citizen believed that the foreign importer paid it, and that belief made him feel comfortable. In truth, though, it was paid by the American people, and it was divided among them so evenly and exactly that the yearly cost to the 100-millionaire and the yearly cost to the day laborer’s sucking child was the same—each paid $6. I don’t see how anything could be more equal than that.

Well, Scotland and Ireland were under Arthur’s rule, and the combined population of the British Isles was a little under 1,000,000. A mechanic’s average wage was 3 cents a day, after he paid for his own living. Using that rule, the national government’s expenses came to $90,000 a year, or about $250 a day. So, by replacing nickels for gold on a king’s-evil day, I didn’t harm anyone, didn’t upset anyone, and yet pleased everyone involved. I also saved four-fifths of that day’s national expense. In my day in America, that saving would have been the equivalent of $800,000.

When I made that substitution, I drew on wisdom from a very distant source—the wisdom of my boyhood. A true statesman doesn’t ignore any wisdom, no matter how humble its origin. As a boy, I had always saved my pennies and contributed buttons to the foreign missionary cause. The buttons would work just as well for the ignorant savage as the coin would; the coin would work better for me than the buttons. Everyone was happy, and nobody was hurt.

Marinel took the patients as they arrived. He examined the candidate. If the person couldn’t qualify, he was turned away. If the person could qualify, he was sent on to the king. A priest then said, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” While the reading continued, the king pressed and stroked the ulcers. Finally, the patient was approved, received his nickel—the king even hung it around his neck himself—and was dismissed. Would you think that would cure them? It certainly did. Any kind of show or ritual will cure if the patient’s faith is strong.

Up by Astolat there was a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who used to herd geese there. The girl said so herself, and they built the chapel on that spot and hung a picture inside showing the event. You might think it would be dangerous for a sick person to go near it. Yet, on the contrary, thousands of lame and sick people came every year, prayed before it, and left whole and well. Even people who were healthy could look at it and live."}

{"request_id":"baa01f268264e6af9ddda35a","rewritten_text":"“Do you come back here often?”

“I’ve never been here at all since.”

“Neither have I.”

The moon began to climb, and I found myself thinking of the calm look of the white ceiling—now gone. The moon began to rise again, and I remembered the weight of his last words upon my hand, when I had spoken them and he had heard them on earth.

Estella was the next to break the quiet that followed between us.

“I’ve hoped and meant to return again and again, but I’ve been kept away by all sorts of circumstances. Poor, poor old place!”

The silvery mist caught the first moonlight, and the same light fell on the tears that slipped from her eyes. She did not know I saw them, and, trying to master herself, she said softly,—

“Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it came to be left in this state?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The ground is mine. It’s the only thing I’ve never surrendered. Everything else has slipped from me, little by little, but I’ve held on to this. It was the one stubborn resistance I made in all those miserable years.”

“Is it meant to be built on?”

“At last, it is. I came here to bid it farewell before the change. And you,” she added, with a voice that held a tender interest for a wanderer,—“you’re still living abroad?”

“Still.”

“And you do well, I’m sure?”

“I work pretty hard to make a living, and so—yes—I do well.”

“I’ve often thought of you,” Estella said.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. There was a long, hard stretch when I kept myself far from the memory of what I had thrown away, before I knew its true value. But since my duty hasn’t made it impossible to admit that remembrance, I’ve let it have a place in my heart.”

“You’ve always kept your place in my heart,” I answered.

Then we were silent once more, until she spoke again.

“I never imagined,” said Estella, “that I should be taking leave of you when I take leave of this spot. I’m glad to do it.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? For me, parting is painful. The memory of our last parting has always been mournful and painful.”

“But you told me,” Estella replied, very earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ And if you could say that to me then, you won’t hesitate to say it now—now, when suffering has been stronger than every other lesson, and has taught me what your heart used to be. I’ve been bent and broken, but—I hope—into something better.”"}

{"request_id":"fbbab90e5f393b100d0894c3","rewritten_text":"A little after noon the boys took a small skiff from a citizen who happened to be away, and pushed off right away. After they’d gone several miles below “Cave Hollow,” Tom said:

“Now, look at this bluff—down from the cave hollow it all seems the same, mile after mile. No houses, no wood-yards, just bushes that look alike. But see that white spot up yonder, where there’s been a landslide? That’s one of my marks. We’ll land here.”

They came ashore.

“Now, Huck, right where we’re standing you ought to be able to reach that hole I dug out with a fishing-pole. See if you can spot it.”

Huck searched around and couldn’t find a thing. Tom, feeling pleased with himself, marched straight into a thick clump of sumach bushes and said:

“There you are! Look here, Huck; it’s the snuggiest hole in the whole country. Keep it quiet, that’s all. I’ve been wanting to be a robber all along, but I knew I’d need a place like this—and the trouble was finding it. Well, we’ve found it, and we’ll keep it secret. Only we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers in, because, of course, there has to be a Gang, or it wouldn’t have any style to it. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds splendid, don’t it, Huck?”

“It sure does, Tom. But who are we going to rob?”

“Almost anybody. We’ll waylay folks—that’s the main thing.”

“And kill them?”

“Not always. We’ll lock them up in the cave until they raise a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them scrape together all they can, off their friends; and if, after you’ve kept them a year, it still isn’t raised, then you kill them. That’s the usual way. Only you don’t kill the women. You keep the women shut up, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and they’re terribly scared. You take their watches and things, but you always take your hat off and act polite. There ain’t anybody as polite as robbers—you’ll see that in any book. Well, the women start to like you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two they stop crying, and then you couldn’t get them to leave. If you drove them out, they’d just turn around and come back. That’s how it is in all the books.”

“Why, that’s real bully, Tom. I reckon it’s better’n being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s close to home and there’s circuses and all that.”

By then everything was ready, and the boys went into the hole, Tom leading. They worked their way to the far end of the tunnel, then tied their spliced kite-strings fast and went on."}

{"request_id":"c794ed58821247b0dd5c3bdd","rewritten_text":"But he had oppressed no one, imprisoned no one. He was so far from having harshly collected what was owed that he had given up his dues of his own free will, thrown himself into a world with no favors in it, secured his own private place there, and earned his own bread. Monsieur Gabelle had held the impoverished, entangled estate under written instructions, meant to spare the people—meant to give them whatever little there was to give: such fuel as the heavy creditors would allow them in the winter, and such produce as could be saved from the same grip in the summer. No doubt he had set it down in his plea and proof, for his own safety, so that it could not but seem true now.

This was the kind of advantage that fed the desperate decision Charles Darnay had begun to make: that he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the mariner in the old story, the winds and streams had driven him within the pull of the Loadstone Rock, and it was drawing him in, and he had to go. Everything that rose in his mind carried him forward—faster and faster, more and more steadily—toward the terrible attraction. His buried uneasiness had been that bad aims were being carried out in his own unhappy country by bad instruments, and that the man who could not fail to know he was better than they were was not there, trying to stop bloodshed and assert the claims of mercy and humanity. With that uneasiness half smothered and half reproaching him, he had been pushed into a sharp comparison of himself with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so strong. From that comparison—injurious to himself—there had immediately come Monseigneur’s sneers, which stung him bitterly, and Stryver’s, which above all were coarse and hard to bear, for old reasons. After that came Gabelle’s letter: the appeal of an innocent prisoner, facing death, to his justice, honor, and good name.

His resolution was made. He had to go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was drawing him, and he had to keep sailing on until he struck. He knew of no rock; he saw hardly any danger. The intention with which he had done what he had done—even though he had left it incomplete—presented itself to him in a way that, when he appeared in France to assert it, would be gratefully recognized. Then that glorious vision of doing good, which is so often the sanguine mirage of so many good minds, rose before him, and he even saw himself under the illusion that he might have some influence to guide this raging Revolution, running so wildly."}

{"request_id":"54d606b0462a1e4dc7f91f44","rewritten_text":"“Lo,” said Merlin, “yonder is the sword I told you of.” With that, they beheld a damsel moving upon the lake. “What damsel is that?” asked Arthur. “That is the Lady of the lake,” said Merlin; “and within that lake there is a rock, and in it a place as fair as any upon earth—well appointed to the eye. This damsel will come to you anon, and then you shall speak kindly to her, and she will give you that sword.” 

Anon the damsel came to Arthur and greeted him, and he greeted her in turn. “Damsel,” said Arthur, “what sword is it that yonder arm holds up above the water? I would it were mine, for I have no sword.” “Sir Arthur King,” said the damsel, “that sword is mine; and if you will grant me a gift when I ask it, you shall have it.” 

“By my faith,” said Arthur, “I will give you whatever gift you ask.” “Well,” said the damsel, “go you into yonder barge and row yourself to the sword, and take it with the scabbard; and I will ask my gift when I see my time.” 

So Sir Arthur and Merlin stepped down, and tied their horses to two trees, and went into the ship. When they came to the sword that the hand held, Sir Arthur took it up by the handles and took it with him. Then the arm and hand went under the water; and so they came to land and rode forth. 

Afterward Sir Arthur saw a rich pavilion. “What means that pavilion yonder?” “It is the knight’s pavilion,” said Merlin, “the one you fought with last, Sir Pellinore; but he is out—he is not there. He has business with a knight of yours, that is called Egglame, and they have fought together; yet at the last Egglame fled, and else he had been dead. He has chased him even to Carlion, and we shall meet him anon upon the highway.” 

“That is well said,” replied Arthur. “Now have I a sword; now will I wage battle with him, and be avenged.” “Sir,” said Merlin, “you shall not do so. The knight is weary of fighting and chasing, so you shall have no honor to be at work with him; and he will not lightly be matched by any living knight. Therefore it is my counsel, let him pass—he shall do you good service in short time, and his sons after his days. Also, you shall see that day in short space, when you shall be glad to give him your sister to wed.” 

“When I see him,” said Arthur, “I will do as you advise me.”"}

{"request_id":"d3a856630038fe6db902dcba","rewritten_text":"Yet he kept one secret from these dear friends—something he had carried and tended since his earliest years. Though he truly loved his fellow collegiates, he would not entrust it to the delicacy or sympathy of any one of them. He loved; he feared. He feared that the force of his passion might become sport for their ridicule, and he could not endure the thought that they might profane it by treating as trifling and fleeting what, to him, was the very substance of his life.

Near his family mansion there lived a gentleman of small means with three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, yet her beauty was only an added grace to her other gifts: her understanding was clear and firm, and her temper was angelically mild. She and my father had been playmates from infancy. Diana—so even in childhood had she been a particular favourite with his mother—grew more and more dear as the years went on; and so, during his school and college vacations, they were almost always together. Novels, and the many ways by which young people in civilized society are brought to a knowledge of passions before they truly feel them, had made a strong impression on him, for he was unusually open to every influence. At eleven, Diana was already his favourite companion, though he spoke the language of love. Though she was nearly two years older than he, the kind of education she had received left her, at least in her knowledge and expression of feeling, more childish. She took his warm protestations with innocence, and answered them without knowing what they meant. She had read no novels and kept to her younger sisters; what could she know of the difference between love and friendship? And when her understanding finally revealed the real nature of their intimacy, her affections were already claimed by her friend; all she worried about was that other attractions or a changeable heart might cause him to break the vows of his childhood.

Still, day by day they grew more ardent and more tender. It was a passion that had grown alongside his own growth; it had woven itself into every faculty and every sentiment, and could be lost only with life itself. No one knew of their love except their two hearts. Yet in everything else—and even in this, though he dreaded the judgment of his companions—he remained fixed in his purpose of joining himself to her as soon as he could gather courage enough to face the obstacles before him. For he was determined to overcome those difficulties, even though he loved someone of less fortune than his own.

Diana was fully worthy of his deepest affection."}

{"request_id":"baf1baadb635430c0043ed4c","rewritten_text":"But don’t imagine that I didn’t feel it was evil in itself.”

“Depend on it, they were all perfectly comfortable.”

“I might not like them any better for that, perhaps. Such a number of women and children have no _right_ to be comfortable on board.”

“My dear Frederick, you’re talking quite idly. Pray, what would become of us poor sailors’ wives, who often want to be taken to one port or another after our husbands, if everyone had your feelings?”

“My feelings, you see, didn’t stop me from taking Mrs Harville and all her family to Plymouth.”

“But I hate to hear you talk like a fine gentleman—talking as if women were all fine ladies, instead of rational creatures. None of us expect to be in smooth water all our days.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “when he has got a wife, he’ll sing a different tune. When he’s married, if we’re lucky enough to live to another war, we shall see him do as you and I, and a great many others, have done. We shall have him very thankful to anyone who will bring him his wife.”

“Ay, that we shall.”

“Now I’m done,” cried Captain Wentworth. “Once married people start attacking me with—‘Oh, you’ll think very differently when you’re married.’ I can only say, ‘No, I won’t;’ and then they say again, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that’s the end of it.”

He got up and moved away.

“What a great traveller you must have been, ma’am!” said Mrs Musgrove to Mrs Croft.

“Pretty well, ma’am, in the fifteen years of my marriage; though many women have done more. I’ve crossed the Atlantic four times, and I’ve been once to the East Indies and back again—only once. Besides that, I’ve been in different places at home: Cork, and Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I never went beyond the Streights, and I never was in the West Indies. We don’t call Bermuda or Bahama the West Indies, you know.”

Mrs Musgrove had not a word to say in disagreement; she couldn’t accuse herself of ever calling them anything else in the whole course of her life.

“And I do assure you, ma’am,” Mrs Croft went on, “that nothing can exceed the accommodations of a man-of-war; I mean, you know, the higher rates. When you come to a frigate, of course, you’re more confined; though any reasonable woman may be perfectly happy in one of them. And I can safely say that the happiest part of my life has been spent on board a ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to be feared.”"}

{"request_id":"74ef9eaee23afb92724cfb2f","rewritten_text":"Shall I call on them? Or Miss Bates? She is still closer.—And I don’t know whether Miss Bates isn’t as likely to understand the inclinations of the rest of the people as anyone else. I think we do want a larger council. Suppose I go and invite Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well—if you please,” said Mrs. Weston, rather hesitating, “if you think she will be of any use.”

“You’ll get nothing to the purpose from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She’ll be all delight and gratitude, but she won’t tell you anything. She won’t even listen to your questions. I see no advantage in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so amusing, so extremely amusing! I’m very fond of hearing Miss Bates talk. And I needn’t bring the whole family, you know.”

Here Mr. Weston joined them, and, on hearing what was proposed, gave it his decided approval.

“Aye, do, Frank.—Go and fetch Miss Bates, and let us end the matter at once. She will enjoy the scheme, I’m sure; and I don’t know a more proper person for showing us how to do away with difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We are growing a little too nice. She is a standing lesson in how to be happy. But fetch them both. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady?”...

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I’ll think you a great blockhead, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I didn’t immediately recollect. Undoubtedly, if you wish it, I will try to persuade them both.” And off he ran.

Long before he reappeared, bringing the short, neat, brisk-moving aunt, and her elegant niece,—Mrs. Weston, like a sweet-tempered woman and a good wife, had examined the passage again, and found the evils of it much less than she had supposed before—indeed, very trifling; and here the difficulties of decision ended. Everything else, at least in speculation, was perfectly smooth. All the minor arrangements—table and chair, lights and music, tea and supper—either took care of themselves, or were left as mere trifles to be settled at any time between Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes.—Everyone invited was certainly to come; Frank had already written to Enscombe to propose staying a few days beyond his fortnight, which could not possibly be refused. And it was going to be a delightful dance.

Most cordially, when Miss Bates arrived, did she agree that it must. As a counsellor she was not wanted; but as an approver, (a much safer role,) she was truly welcome. Her approval, at once general and minute, warm and incessant, could not but please; and for another half-hour they were all walking to and fro between the different rooms—some suggesting, some attending, and all in happy enjoyment of what lay ahead."}

{"request_id":"dac61ad2a7fe36d65704360e","rewritten_text":"The powerful voice—something we might call inorganic, since we could in no way connect it to the workings of a pipe or a key—fell silent, and the girl, turning to help her elderly companion, finally noticed us.

It was her father; and since childhood she had guided his darkened steps. They were Germans from Saxony, and, having emigrated there only a few years earlier, had formed new ties with the villagers around them. Around the time the pestilence broke out, a young German student had joined them. Their story was easy to piece together. He was a nobleman who loved the fair daughter of the poor musician, and he followed them in their flight from the persecution of his friends; but soon the mighty leveler came with an unblunted scythe to mow down, along with the grass, the tall flowers of the field. The youth was an early victim. She kept herself alive for her father’s sake. His blindness allowed her to keep up a delusion—at first, born of accident—and now, as the only two survivors left in the land, he remained unaware of the change. He did not know that when he listened to his child’s music, the mute mountains, the senseless lake, and the unconscious trees—except for himself—were her only listeners.

The very day we arrived, she had been attacked by a sickness that showed itself in the usual way. She was paralyzed with horror at the thought of leaving her aged, sightless father alone on the empty earth; but she lacked the courage to tell the truth. And the very excess of her desperation drove her into extraordinary effort. At the usual hour for vespers, she led him to the chapel; and, though she trembled and wept for him, she played the hymn meant to celebrate the creation of the adorned earth—without fault in timing or any mistake in note—soon to be her tomb.

We came to her as if from heaven itself. Her intense courage, her firmness barely held together, vanished the moment she saw relief. With a shriek she rushed toward us, threw her arms around Adrian’s knees, and, saying only, “O save my father!” while sobs and hysterical cries poured out of her, she finally opened the long-closed floodgates of her grief.

Poor girl!—she and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, and which, in her dying moments, she had pointed out to us. Her father, at last aware of his daughter’s danger, could not see the changes in her dear face; he stubbornly held her hand until it grew cold and stiff with death. He did not move or speak even then, until twelve hours later, kindly death carried him to his endless rest. They lie beneath the sod, the tree their monument. The sacred spot is still clear in my memory, pale beside the craggy Jura and the far, immeasurable Alps; the church spire they used to attend still points above the surrounding trees. And though her hand is cold, I still think the sounds of the divine music they loved drift around, comforting their gentle ghosts."}

{"request_id":"f2e70010faf1d68ab99fdab1","rewritten_text":"He was delivered to you. You see, I’m informed of the circumstances?”

“Such is the fact, certainly,” said Defarge. He had been told, in an accidental brush of his wife’s elbow as she knitted and hummed her little song, that he would do best to answer—always briefly.

“It was to you,” said the spy, “that his daughter came; and it was from your care that his daughter took him, accompanied by a neat brown monsieur. What’s his name—wearing a little wig—Lorry, from the bank of Tellson and Company—over to England.”

“Such is the fact,” Defarge repeated.

“Very interesting memories!” said the spy. “I’ve known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Yes?” said Defarge.

“You don’t hear much about them now?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“In effect,” madame broke in, looking up from her work and her little song, “we never hear about them. We received the news of their safe arrival, and perhaps another letter—or perhaps two; but since then, they’ve gradually gone on with their lives—us with ours—and we’ve had no correspondence.”

“Precisely so, madame,” the spy replied. “She’s going to be married.”

“Going?” madame echoed. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. It seems to me the English are cold.”

“Oh! You know I’m English.”

“I see your tongue is,” madame returned; “and I suppose the man is, too.”

He didn’t take the identification as a compliment, but he made the best of it and brushed it off with a laugh. After sipping his cognac to the end, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is going to be married. But not to an Englishman; to someone who, like herself, is French by birth. And speaking of Gaspard—ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel—there’s something curious about it: she’s going to marry the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, for whom Gaspard was raised to that height of so many feet—in other words, the present Marquis. But he lives unknown in England; he isn’t a marquis there. He’s Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is the name of his mother’s family.”

Madame Defarge kept knitting steadily, but the information had a clear effect on her husband. No matter what he did behind the little counter—whether striking a light, or lighting his pipe—he was troubled, and his hand wasn’t steady. The spy would have been no spy if he hadn’t noticed it, or if he hadn’t stored it away in his mind.

Having made, at least, this one hit—whatever it might prove to be worth—and with no customers coming in to help him with anything else, Mr. Barsad paid for what he’d drunk and took his leave. Before departing, he took the opportunity, in a polite manner, to say that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3848a08eaa2cf7e46f3d48dd","rewritten_text":"No one could fancy the full sublimity that such a spectacle might show itself, if it were to occur in the thick darkness of night. Hell, indeed, might well serve as the proper comparison. Even so, my hair rose upon my head as I stared far off into the yawning abysses, letting my mind run down, as it were, and pace about in those strange vaulted chambers—through the ruddy gulfs and the red, ghastly chasms of that hideous, unfathomable fire. I had, in truth, made a narrow escape. If the balloon had stayed a little longer within the cloud—if, that is, I had not been forced by the annoyance of getting wet to throw out the ballast—then inevitable ruin would have followed. Such dangers, though often overlooked, may be the very greatest that balloons have to meet. By this time, however, I had risen so high that I could no longer be much troubled on that score.\n\n“I was now climbing rapidly, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of not less than nine and a half miles. I found it hard to draw my breath. My head, too, ached violently; and after some time I noticed a dampness on my cheeks, and at last learned it was blood, oozing steadily from the drums of my ears. My eyes likewise troubled me greatly. When I passed my hand over them, they seemed to have pushed out of their sockets to a noticeable degree; and everything in the car, and even the balloon itself, looked distorted through my sight. These signs were more severe than I had expected, and they set me alarmed. At this moment, in a very foolish way, and without thinking, I threw out three five-pound pieces of ballast from the car. The quicker ascent that followed carried me too fast, and without proper easing, into a very rarefied layer of the air; and the consequence had nearly proved fatal to my journey and to myself. I was suddenly seized by a spasm that lasted more than five minutes; and even after it eased, I could draw breath only at long intervals, and with a kind of gasping, while I continued to bleed freely from the nose and ears, and even a little from the eyes. The pigeons seemed in the utmost distress and struggled to get away; while the cat mewed in a piteous tone, with her tongue hanging out, and staggered from side to side in the car as if poisoned. Only then, too late, did I recognize how rash I had been in casting out the ballast, and my agitation was extreme. I expected nothing less than death—death within a few minutes.”"}

Lord Arthur looked so serious and miserable over the letter that the Duchess burst into laughter.

“My dear Arthur,” she said, laughing, “I’ll never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what am I supposed to say about the clock? I think it’s a capital invention, and I’d like one for myself.”

“I don’t think much of them,” Lord Arthur said, wearing a sad smile. After kissing his mother, he left the room.

When he went upstairs, he threw himself onto a sofa, and his eyes filled with tears. He had done his best to carry out this murder, but on both occasions he had failed, and not through any fault of his own. He had tried to do his duty, yet it felt as though Destiny herself had turned traitor. He was weighed down by the emptiness of good intentions, by the pointlessness of trying to be fine. Maybe it would be better to end the marriage altogether. Sybil would suffer, of course, but suffering couldn’t truly ruin a nature as noble as hers. As for himself—what did it matter? There’s always some war in which a man can die, some cause to which a man can give his life, and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no terror. Let Destiny work out his doom. He wouldn’t lift a hand to help her.

At half past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a party of young men, and he had to dine with them. Their petty talk and idle jokes bored him, and the moment coffee was brought he left them, making up some engagement so he could get away. As he was going out, the hall-porter handed him a letter. It was from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to call the next evening and look at an explosive umbrella that went off as soon as it was opened. It was the very latest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. He tore the letter into fragments. He’d decided he wouldn’t try any more experiments.

Then he wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat by the river for hours. The moon pushed through a mane of tawny clouds, as if it were a lion’s eye, and countless stars glittered across the dark vault, like gold dust scattered over a purple dome. Now and then a barge swung out into the muddy stream and drifted away with the tide, while the railway signals changed from green to scarlet as the trains shrieked across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"af12cfe27b062b845900ebbe","rewritten_text":"There was something so remarkable in the growing glare of Mr. Wopsle’s eye, and he seemed to be turning so many things over in his mind that he grew more and more confused, and I couldn’t make out what he meant. I sat thinking about it long after he had gone up into the clouds in a large watch-case, and still I couldn’t make it out. I was still thinking about it when I came out of the theatre an hour later and found him waiting for me near the door.

“How do you do?” I said, shaking hands with him as we walked down the street together. “I saw that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he answered. “Yes, of course I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It is the strangest thing,” said Mr. Wopsle, slipping back into his lost look; “and yet I could swear to him.”

Alarmed, I urged Mr. Wopsle to explain what he meant.

“Whether I should have noticed him at first but for your being there,” he went on, still in that same lost way, “I can’t be sure; but I think I should have.”

Without meaning to, I looked around me, the way I was used to look around when I went home; these mysterious words gave me a chill.

“Oh! He can’t be in sight,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He went out before I did. I saw him go.”

With the reason I had for being suspicious, I even suspected this poor actor. I mistrusted some plan to trap me into admitting something. So as we walked on together, I glanced at him, but I said nothing.

“I had a ridiculous notion that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw that you were completely unaware of him—sitting behind you there like a ghost.”

My earlier chill crept over me again, but I was determined not to speak yet, because it was still possible, based on his words, that he might be trying to get me to connect these references with Provis. Of course, I was perfectly sure and safe that Provis hadn’t been there.

“I suppose you’re wondering about me, Mr. Pip; I can see you are,” said Mr. Wopsle. “But it’s so very strange! You’ll hardly believe what I’m about to tell you. I could hardly believe it myself, if you told me.”

“Indeed?” I said.

“No, indeed. Mr. Pip, you remember, in the old days, a certain Christmas Day, when you were still quite a child, and I dined at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to get a pair of handcuffs mended?”

“I remember it very well.”

“And you remember there was a chase after two convicts, and that we joined in it, and that Gargery carried you on his back, and that I took the lead, and you kept up with me as best you could?”"}

“Tell me what it is.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative and an orphan, just like me, whom I love very dearly. She is five years younger than I am, and she lives in a farmer’s house in the south country. “What I’ve been thinking as we came along, and what I’m still thinking now as I look into your kind, strong face—which gives me so much support—is this: if the Republic truly does good for the poor, and they come to be less hungry, and in every way suffer less, she may live a long time. “What then, my gentle sister?”

{"request_id":"75b1756ef5de5f35cae8f474","rewritten_text":"“I hurry now to the more stirring portion of my narrative. I will set down occurrences that made a deep impression on me—impressions that, as I look back, have shaped what I have become.

“Spring moved on apace; the weather turned fair, and the sky remained clear of clouds. I was struck by the change: what had lately been desert and cheerless now seemed to burst into bloom, covered with the fairest flowers and rich verdure. My senses were gratified and refreshed by a thousand delightful scents and a thousand pleasing sights.

“It was on one of those days, when my cottagers, at intervals, rested from their labour—the old man playing on his guitar while the children listened—that I noticed Felix’s face was weighed down with a melancholy beyond measure. He sighed again and again; and once his father paused in his music, I judged from his manner that he was asking after the cause of his son’s sorrow. Felix answered in a cheerful tone, and the old man was beginning his playing once more when someone tapped at the door.

“It was a lady on horseback, with a countryman to guide her. She wore a dark suit and was wrapped in a thick black veil. Agatha put a question; the stranger answered only by speaking, in a sweet accent, the name of Felix. Her voice was musical, yet it did not resemble that of either of my friends. At the sound of that name, Felix hurried forward to her; and when she saw him, she lifted her veil, so that I beheld a countenance of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair was a shining raven black, curiously braided; her eyes were dark, but gentle, though full of life. Her features were of regular proportion, and her complexion wonderfully fair, with each cheek touched by a tender pink.

“Felix appeared transported with joy at the sight of her; every trace of sorrow vanished from his face, and it at once showed a kind of rapturous delight that I could scarcely have imagined possible. His eyes brightened, his cheek reddened with pleasure; and in that instant I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. Yet she seemed moved by other feelings as well. Wiping away a few tears from her lovely eyes, she extended her hand to Felix, who kissed it with ardent eagerness and called her—so far as I could make out—his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him, but only smiled. He helped her to dismount, dismissed her guide, and led her into the cottage. Some conversation followed between him and his father; and the young stranger, kneeling at the old man’s feet, would have kissed his hand, but he raised her and embraced her with affectionate warmth.

“I soon perceived that, though the stranger uttered distinct sounds and appeared to have a language of her own, she was neither understood by the cottagers, nor did she herself understand them.”"}

{"request_id":"35dbbb20c734980726fc0b14","rewritten_text":"Re-reading his letter and replying to it had such a softening effect that it was especially necessary to steady her with a few decisive words. She was so worried about the idea of making him unhappy, and cared so much about what his mother and sisters would think and say, and was so anxious that they shouldn’t see her as ungrateful, that Emma believed that if the young man had happened to come by at that moment, he would still have been accepted after all.

But the letter was written, sealed, and sent. The business was finished, and Harriet was safe. She was rather low all evening, but Emma could make room for her kind regrets, and sometimes eased them by talking about her own affection, sometimes by bringing up the idea of Mr. Elton.

“I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” Harriet said, in a tone that sounded quite sorrowful.

“Nor, if you were, could I ever bear to be separated from you, my Harriet. You’re far too necessary at Hartfield to be spared to Abbey-Mill.”

“And I’m sure I should never want to go there; I’m never happy anywhere except at Hartfield.”

After some time, Harriet said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what had happened. I’m sure Miss Nash would be too—for Miss Nash thinks her own sister very well married, and it’s only a linen-draper.”

“One should feel sorry to see more pride or refinement in the teacher of a school, Harriet. I dare say Miss Nash would envy you the chance to be married. Even this ‘conquest’ would probably look valuable to her. As for anything better for you, I suppose she’s completely in the dark. The attentions of a certain person can hardly be among the gossip of Highbury yet. Up to now, I think you and I are the only ones whose looks and manners have made it clear what he means.”

Harriet blushed and smiled, and said something about being surprised that people liked her so much. The idea of Mr. Elton was certainly cheering; but after a while, she became tender-hearted again toward the man who had been rejected, Mr. Martin.

“Now he has got my letter,” she said softly. “I wonder what they’re all doing—whether his sisters know. If he’s unhappy, they’ll be unhappy too. I hope it won’t trouble him so much.”

“Let’s think about those among our absent friends who are more cheerfully occupied,” Emma cried. “At this moment, perhaps, Mr. Elton is showing your picture to his mother and sisters, telling them how much more beautiful the original is—and after being asked for it five or six times, he’s letting them hear your name, your own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"fbb89021d81df0b7e5f7f77a","rewritten_text":"“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at length, “you can’t deny that since the new way of feeding was introduced, the coffins have become narrower and shallower than they used to be. But we still have to make some profit, Mr. Bumble. Well-seasoned timber is expensive, sir, and all the iron handles are shipped in by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” said Mr. Bumble, “every trade has its downsides. A fair profit is, of course, allowed.”

“Of course, of course,” replied the undertaker. “And if I don’t make profit on one item or another, I make it up in the long run, you see—he! he! he!”

“Just so,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Still,” the undertaker went on, picking up the point the beadle had interrupted, “I have to deal with one big disadvantage. The stout people go first. The people who have been better off, and have paid rates for many years, are the first to sink once they come into the house. And let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, that being even three or four inches off your estimate can make a big difference to your profits—especially when you have a family to support, sir.”

As Mr. Sowerberry said this, with the proper anger of a man who feels he has been treated unfairly, and as Mr. Bumble felt it sounded like a criticism of the parish’s honor, Mr. Bumble decided it was best to change the subject. Oliver Twist was on his mind, so he brought him up.

“By the bye,” said Mr. Bumble, “do you know anyone who wants a boy? A parish apprentice—he’s just dead weight at the moment. Like a millstone around the parish’s neck, as you might say. Liberal terms, Mr. Sowerberry—liberal terms?”

As he spoke, he lifted his cane to the board above him and tapped three times on the words “five pounds,” printed in huge Roman capitals.

“Gadso!” said the undertaker, grabbing Mr. Bumble by the gilt-edged lapel of his official coat. “That’s exactly what I wanted to talk to you about. You know—dear me, what an elegant button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it’s rather fine,” said the beadle, looking proudly down at the large brass buttons on his coat. “The design is the same as the parish seal—the Good Samaritan healing the sick and bruised man. The board gave it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember putting it on for the first time to attend the inquest on that poor tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight.”"}

{"request_id":"afa2e95bdc88e429351948a9","rewritten_text":"On the morning set for Admiral and Mrs Croft to see Kellynch Hall, Anne felt it was only natural to take her usual walk to Lady Russell’s and stay out of the way until everything was finished. Then, when she learned how it had gone, she found herself sorry she had missed the chance to see them.

This meeting between the two groups went very well, and it settled the whole matter at once. Each lady had already been willing to agree, so she saw nothing but good manners in the other. As for the gentlemen, there was such hearty good humor, and such open, trusting generosity on the Admiral’s side, that it could not help but affect Sir Walter. He had also been flattered into his best, most polished behavior by Mr Shepherd’s assurances that he was known, by reputation, to the Admiral, as a model of good breeding.

The house, grounds, furniture, and everything about them were approved. The Crofts were approved too. Terms, timing, and every detail were right, and Mr Shepherd’s clerks were set to work, with no earlier disagreement at all to change what the indenture said.

Without hesitation, Sir Walter declared that the Admiral was the best-looking sailor he had ever met. He even went so far as to say that if his own man had been the one to arrange the Admiral’s hair, he would not be ashamed to be seen with him anywhere. The Admiral, in the same friendly spirit, told his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we should soon come to a deal, my dear, in spite of what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but there seems to be no harm in him.” Their compliments were meant to be about equally matched.

The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas. And since Sir Walter planned to move to Bath during the month before, there was no time to lose in arranging everything that depended on the move.

Lady Russell was sure Anne would not be allowed to matter in the choice of the house they were going to secure, so she was reluctant to have her sent away so soon. She wanted to keep it possible for Anne to stay behind until she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas. But Lady Russell had her own commitments that would take her from Kellynch for several weeks, so she could not give the full invitation she wanted. Anne, though she dreaded the hot weather of September in the bright glare of Bath, and was sad to give up the gentle influence of the autumn months in the country, still did not think that, considering everything, she should stay."}

{"request_id":"e49b3f365c60e5bb7384b779","rewritten_text":"You don’t know anything about me unless you’ve read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that doesn’t matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mostly. There were parts he stretched, but mostly he told the truth. That’s nothing. I’ve never seen anybody lie once or twice without it being Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly, she is—and Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all talked about in that book, which is mostly a true book, with some stretches, like I said before.

Now the way the book ends is this: Tom and me found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars apiece—pure gold. It was an awful sight of money when it was piled up. Well, Judge Thatcher took it and put it out at interest, and it brought us a dollar a day each, every day all year long—more than a person could ever say what to do with. The Widow Douglas took me for her son and said she was going to civilize me; but living in her house all the time was rough, considering how gloomy, regular, and decent she was in all her ways. So when I couldn’t stand it anymore, I took off. I got back into my old rags and my sugar-hogshead, and I was free and satisfied. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and said he was going to start a band of robbers, and I could join if I went back to the widow and acted respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, and she called me a lot of other names too, but she never meant any harm by it. She put me in those new clothes again, and I couldn’t do anything but sweat and sweat and feel all cramped up. Then the whole thing started up again. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to be there on time. When you got to the table, you couldn’t just start eating right away—you had to wait for the widow to bow her head and grumble a little over the food, even though there really wasn’t anything wrong with it—nothing except that everything was cooked separately. In a barrel of odds and ends it’s different; things get mixed together, the juices kind of trade places, and the food comes out better.

After supper she brought out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was eager to find out everything about him. But after a while she let it slip that Moses had been dead for a long time, so then I didn’t care anymore, because I don’t put any faith in dead people."}

{"request_id":"b9e0590971504b53181cfa5e","rewritten_text":"_PS._—Do tell me about the bows. Jennings says they’re the latest fashion.

Lord Arthur looked so serious and miserable about the letter that the Duchess burst into laughter.

“My dear Arthur,” she said, laughing, “I’ll never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what should I say about the clock? I think it’s a wonderful invention, and I’d like one for myself.”

“I don’t think much of them,” Lord Arthur replied, with a sad smile. After he kissed his mother, he left the room.

When he went upstairs, he threw himself onto a sofa, and tears filled his eyes. He had done his best to carry out this murder, but on both occasions he had failed, and not because of anything he did wrong. He had tried to do his duty, yet it felt as if Destiny herself had turned against him. He was weighed down by the emptiness of good intentions, and by how pointless it was to try to be “fine.” Maybe it would be better to end the marriage altogether. Sybil would be hurt, of course, but suffering couldn’t truly ruin a nature as noble as hers. As for himself, what did it matter? There’s always some war where a man can die, some cause where he can give his life. And since life held no pleasure for him, death held no fear. Let Destiny carry out his doom. He wouldn’t move to stop her.

At half past seven he got dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and Lord Arthur had to dine with them. Their small talk and silly jokes bored him, and the moment coffee was served he left, saying he had some engagement so he could get away. As he was heading out, the hall-porter handed him a letter. It was from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to call the next evening and look at an explosive umbrella that would go off as soon as it was opened. It was the newest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. Lord Arthur tore the letter into pieces. He had decided not to try any more experiments.

Then he walked down to the Thames Embankment and sat by the river for hours. The moon pushed through a mane of tawny clouds, as if it were a lion’s eye, and countless stars glittered across the dark sky, like gold dust scattered over a purple dome. From time to time a barge swung out into the muddy water and drifted away with the tide. The railway signals changed from green to scarlet as the trains roared across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"d9ef57e6767a71ec380ee03f","rewritten_text":"“I only wish we had a donkey. Then we could all go together on donkeys, Jane, Miss Bates, and me—while my caro sposo walks alongside. I really ought to speak with him about getting a donkey. In country life, I take it to be almost a necessity; for, no matter how many comforts a woman may have, she can’t always be shut up at home;—and you know how very long walks are—there’s dust in summer, and in winter there’s dirt.”

“You won’t meet with either between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and it’s perfectly dry at present. If you like, come on a donkey. You may borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I should like everything to be as much to your liking as possible.”

“That I’m sure you would. Indeed, I do you justice, my dear friend. Beneath that particular kind of dry, blunt way, I know you have the warmest heart. As I told Mr. E., you are a complete humourist.—Yes, believe me, Knightley, I’m perfectly aware of how attentive you’ve been to me throughout all of this plan. You’ve chosen exactly what will please me.”

Mr. Knightley had another motive for steering clear of a table in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the party; and he knew that if either of them sat down out of doors to eat, it would almost certainly make him unwell. Mr. Woodhouse must not, under the flattering pretext of a morning drive and an hour or two spent at Donwell, be drawn away from his misery.

He was asked in good faith. There were no hidden terrors meant to reproach him for being so easily persuaded. He did agree. He hadn’t been at Donwell for two years. “Some very fine morning, he, and Emma, and Harriet, could go very well; and he could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked about the gardens. He didn’t think they could be damp now, in the middle of the day. He should be delighted to see the old house again, and would be very glad to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton, and any other of his neighbours.—He could see no objection at all to his, and Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there some very fine morning. He thought it very well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—so kind and sensible—far better than dining out.—He wasn’t fond of dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was lucky in having everyone’s ready assent. The invitation was taken up so readily everywhere, that it seemed as though, like Mrs. Elton, they were all treating the scheme as a special compliment to themselves. Emma and Harriet declared they expected the greatest pleasure from it; and Mr. Weston, without being asked, promised to try to get Frank to come along, if possible—a mark of approval and gratitude that might well have been spared. Mr. Knightley then found it necessary to say that he would be glad to see him; and Mr. Weston undertook to write at once, and spare no arguments to bring him."}

{"request_id":"8fb2090b82b4fb8884ab449c","rewritten_text":"Biddy cried. In my own eyes, the darkening garden, the lane, and the stars that were starting to show all blurred together.

“Nothing was ever found, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what has happened to Orlick?”

“I’d guess, from the color of his clothes, that he’s working in the quarries.”

“So you’ve seen him, then? Why are you staring at that dark tree in the lane?”

“I saw him there the night she died.”

“That wasn’t the last time either, Biddy?”

“No. I’ve seen him there since we’ve been walking here. It’s no use,” said Biddy, putting her hand on my arm as I tried to run out. “You know I wouldn’t lie to you. He wasn’t there for even a minute, and he’s gone.”

It made me as angry as I could be to learn that this man was still after her. I felt a strong hatred for him. I told her so, and I told her I would spend any money or take any trouble to drive him out of that country. Little by little, she calmed me down and talked more calmly. She told me how Joe loved me, and how Joe never complained about anything. She didn’t say anything about me, because she didn’t need to; I understood what she meant. Joe always did his duty in his own way, with a firm hand, a quiet voice, and a gentle heart.

“Truly,” I said, “it would be hard to say too much about him. And, Biddy, we should talk about these things often, because I’ll be coming down here a lot now. I’m not going to leave poor Joe alone.”

Biddy didn’t say a word.

“Biddy, don’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Not to mention the fact that you call me Mr. Pip, which sounds to me like bad manners, Biddy—what do you mean by this?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked, timidly.

“By this?” I said. “Now don’t repeat me. You didn’t used to echo, Biddy.”

“Used not!” Biddy said. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Used!”

Well! I thought I might as well give up that point too. After another quiet turn in the garden, I went back to my main question.

“Biddy,” I said, “I made a remark about coming down here often to see Joe, and you answered it with a very noticeable silence. Please tell me why.”

“Are you sure, then, that you WILL come to see him often?” Biddy asked. She stopped on the narrow path in the garden and looked at me clearly and honestly under the stars."}

{"request_id":"9d63e1e5843208bc33816856","rewritten_text":"Now that he had no work to keep him busy, he pressed the knuckles of his right hand into the hollow of his left, then the knuckles of his left into the hollow of his right. After that, he ran his hand across his bearded chin, and then did the same kind of thing again, switching back and forth in a steady rhythm, without stopping for even a moment. Trying to bring him back from the wandering life he always slipped into after he spoke was like trying to wake someone very weak from a faint, or like trying to hold on to a dying man’s spirit, hoping for some last clear sign.

“Did you ask me for my name?”

“Yes, I did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a tired sound that was not a sigh and not a groan, he bent down to work again, until the silence was broken once more.

“You are not a shoemaker by trade?” said Mr. Lorry, staring at him.

His hollow, worn eyes shifted to Defarge, as if he wanted to pass the question to him. But since no help came, his gaze returned to Mr. Lorry.

“Not a shoemaker by trade? No. I was not a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He trailed off, even for minutes, while he kept making those careful, measured movements with his hands. His eyes slowly came back at last to the face they had left. When they landed there, he startled, then went on again, like someone who has just woken up and returns to what he was thinking about last night.

“I asked permission to teach myself, and I got it only after a long time, and with a lot of trouble. And I’ve been making shoes ever since.”

As he held out his hand for the shoe that had been taken from him, Mr. Lorry said, still watching him closely:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing about me?”

The shoe fell to the ground. He sat there, staring at Mr. Lorry.

“Monsieur Manette,” Mr. Lorry said, putting his hand on Defarge’s arm; “do you remember nothing about this man? Look at him. Look at me. Is there no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no old time coming back to you, Monsieur Manette?”

While the prisoner of many years stared, first at Mr. Lorry and then at Defarge, faint signs of an intelligence that had once been active slowly pushed through the dark fog on his forehead. Then the signs faded again, grew weaker, and disappeared. Still, they had been there."}

{"request_id":"727a5e7deff297f1ea806cc6","rewritten_text":"But in that sharp _tirade_ against Chantilly, which had appeared in yesterday’s ‘_Musée_,’ the satirist, with some shameful insinuations about the cobbler’s change of name when he took up the buskin, quoted a Latin line that we have often discussed. I mean the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I told you, you remember, that it was meant to point to Orion, once written Urion; and, from the particular turns of phrase tied to that explanation, I knew you could not possibly have forgotten it. It was plain, then, that you would bring together the two notions of Orion and Chantilly. That you did so, I judged from the sort of smile that flickered across your lips. You were thinking of the cobbler’s miserable sacrifice. Up to then you had been bending in your walk; but now I saw you straighten to your full height. I was convinced, at that moment, that you were reflecting on Chantilly’s small, diminutive stature. And it was at this point that I cut short your thoughts to say that, since he was indeed a very little fellow—that Chantilly—he would be better suited to the _Théâtre des Variétés_.”

Not long afterward, we were going through an evening issue of the “Gazette des Tribunaux,” when the following paragraphs caught our notice.

“_Extraordinary Murders_.—This morning, about three o’clock, the residents of the Quartier St. Roch were roused from sleep by a run of dreadful shrieks, apparently coming from the fourth story of a house in the Rue Morgue, which is known to be occupied solely by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay—caused by a fruitless attempt to gain entry by the usual means—the gate was forced open with a crowbar, and eight or ten of the neighbors went in, with two _gendarmes_. By then the cries had stopped; but as the group hurried up the first flight of stairs, two or more rough voices, raised in angry dispute, could be heard, and seemed to come from the upper part of the house. When the second landing was reached, those sounds had also ended, and everything was perfectly still. The party fanned out and searched room after room. At last, arriving at a large back chamber on the fourth story—(the door of which, found locked with the key inside, was forced)—they were met by a scene that struck everyone present with horror no less than with astonishment.

“The place was in the wildest confusion—the furniture smashed and scattered in every direction. There was only one bedstead; and from it the bed had been taken and flung into the middle of the floor. On a chair lay a razor, smeared with blood.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"b11ee32ab2009f45d1051c32","rewritten_text":"No one could fancy the kind of sublimity that might be shown by a similar event unfolding in the darkness of the night. Hell itself could have seemed like a fitting image. Even so, my hair stood on end as I stared far down into the yawning abysses, letting my imagination run wild—almost as if it descended into those strange vaulted halls, and the ruddy gulfs, and the red, ghastly chasms of hideous, unfathomable fire. I had indeed made a narrow escape. If the balloon had stayed in the cloud only a little longer—if it hadn’t been the inconvenience of getting wet that pushed me to dump the ballast—then inevitable ruin would have followed. Such dangers, though often overlooked, may be the greatest ones balloons have to face. By this point, though, I had risen too high to be uneasy about that anymore.\n\n“I was now rising rapidly, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of no less than nine and a half miles. I began to have a hard time drawing breath. My head also hurt intensely; and after feeling for some time a dampness on my cheeks, I finally realized it was blood, oozing quite fast from the drums of my ears. My eyes, too, filled me with uneasiness. When I passed my hand over them, they seemed to have pushed out of their sockets to a noticeable degree; and all objects in the car—and even the balloon itself—appeared distorted in my vision. These symptoms were more than I had expected, and they frightened me. At this moment, very imprudently, and without thinking, I threw three five-pound pieces of ballast out of the car. The faster climb that followed carried me too quickly, and without enough gradual change, into a highly rarefied layer of the atmosphere; the result nearly proved fatal to my expedition and to myself. I was suddenly seized by a spasm that lasted more than five minutes. Even after it eased, I could only catch my breath at long intervals, and in gasps—bleeding all the while copiously from my nose and ears, and even slightly from my eyes. The pigeons seemed extremely distressed and struggled to escape; while the cat mewed pitifully, with her tongue hanging out, staggering back and forth in the car as if poisoned. Only now, too late, did I realize how reckless I had been in dumping the ballast, and my agitation was intense. I expected nothing less than death—death within a few minutes.”"}
