content.text: {"request_id":"c0580956e9062137b3eb451e","rewritten_text":"Raymond was stirred by the sharp, exhilarating return of health; he believed that, as commander among the Athenians, he had secured a place worthy of his ambition; and, in his expectation of the conquest of Constantinople, he looked for an event that would stand out like a milestone in the long ruin of ages—an achievement without equal in the history of mankind. He imagined a city of vast and venerable associations, whose site’s beauty had long been the wonder of the world, rescued after many hundreds of years from the Moslems’ stronghold, freed from slavery and barbarism, and restored to a people renowned for genius, civilization, and a love of liberty. Perdita lay in his restored society, in his affection, his hopes, and his reputation, much as a Sybarite reclines on a luxurious couch; every thought carried him away, and every feeling seemed to be steeped in a kindred, gentle warmth.\n\nWe reached Kishan on the 7th of July. Throughout our journey the weather stayed calm. Each morning, before dawn, we left our night encampment, and observed how the shadows withdrew from hill and valley, while the sun’s first golden blaze drew near. The soldiers who accompanied us met the sight of beautiful country with lively national enthusiasm. When the star of day rose, it was greeted with triumphant music; and whenever the birds were heard in fragments, they filled the pauses between the notes. At noon we pitched our tents in some shaded valley, or sheltered in the green embrace of woods among the mountains, where a stream murmuring over pebbles lulled us into grateful sleep. Our evening march, quieter still, was even more pleasing than the restless stir of spirit we had felt in the morning. If the band played, they could not help choosing tunes of tempered feeling; the parting of love, or a lament for absence, was followed and ended by some grave hymn, which matched the peaceful loveliness of evening and lifted the mind toward lofty, religious thoughts. Often every sound fell away, so we might listen to the nightingale; then the fire-flies danced in bright order, and the soft cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to travellers. Did we pass through a valley? Gentle shades gathered around us, and the rocks wore beautiful tints. If we climbed among the mountains, Greece—like a living map—lay spread beneath us, her famous pinnacles cleaving the sky, while her rivers ran in silver threads across the fertile ground. Almost afraid to draw breath, we English travellers gazed with rapture on this splendid landscape, so unlike the sober colors and melancholy grace of our own native scenery. When we left Macedonia, the fertile but low plains of Thrace offered fewer attractions, though the journey remained engaging. An advanced guard gave notice of our approach, and the local people were soon moving to pay honour to Lord Raymond."}

{"request_id":"c0c39e17f6aba3c5a0288853","rewritten_text":"You have to learn some of my philosophy. Think only of the past, because remembering it is what gives you pleasure.”

“I can’t give you credit for any philosophy like that. Your retrospection must be so completely free of blame that the comfort it brings isn’t philosophy at all, but—what’s much better—ignorance. With me, it’s not like that. Painful memories keep intruding; they can’t be pushed away, and they ought not to be. I’ve been selfish all my life in practice, even if not in principle. As a child, I was taught what was right, but I wasn’t taught to correct my temper. I was given good principles, but I was left to follow them out of pride and conceit. Unfortunately, as an only son—for many years an only child—I was spoiled by my parents. They were good themselves, especially my father, who was particularly benevolent and kind, but they allowed, encouraged, and almost taught me to be selfish and overbearing: to care for no one beyond my own family circle, to think poorly of everyone else in the world, and even to wish that I could think their sense and worth were inferior to my own. That was who I was, from eight to eight-and-twenty; and I might still have been that way, if not for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth. What do I not owe you? You taught me a lesson—hard at first, but most beneficial. Because of you, I was properly humbled. I came to you without any certainty of how I would be received. You showed me how inadequate all my pretensions were to please a woman who was truly worth being pleased.”

“Did you then persuade yourself that I would?”

“Indeed I did. What will you think of my vanity? I believed you were wishing and expecting my addresses.”

“My manners must have been at fault, but not intentionally, I assure you. I never meant to deceive you, though my spirits might often have led me astray. How could you not have hated me after that evening!”

“Hate you! I was angry, perhaps, at first, but my anger soon began to take the right direction.”

“I’m almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. You blamed me for coming?”

“No, indeed. I felt nothing but surprise.”

“Your surprise couldn’t be greater than mine at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I didn’t deserve any extraordinary politeness, and I confess I didn’t expect to receive more than what I was due.”

“My purpose then,” Darcy replied, “was to show you, through every civility I could manage, that I was not so petty as to resent the past. And I hoped to win your forgiveness, to reduce your bad opinion, by letting you see that your criticisms had been taken to heart.”"}

{"request_id":"65915808bb131af7c11e7f2b","rewritten_text":"He stood up and left the room with my nurse, and in a moment my father entered.

Nothing at this moment could have given me greater pleasure than my father’s arrival. I reached out my hand to him and cried,

“Are you then safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father soothed me with assurances that they were well, and tried—by dwelling on matters so dear to my heart—to lift my spirits, which were sinking. But he soon realized that a prison can’t be a place of cheer. “What kind of place is this that you live in, my son?” he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and the miserable state of the room. “You traveled to find happiness, but it seems a fatality follows you. And poor Clerval—”

The name of my unfortunate, murdered friend was more than I could bear in my weakened condition; I burst into tears.

“Alas! Yes, my father,” I answered. “Some destiny of the most horrible kind hangs over me, and I must live to carry it out—or surely I should have died on the coffin of Henry.”

We weren’t allowed to talk for long, because my health was so precarious that every precaution was needed to keep me calm. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that my strength not be drained by too much exertion. But my father’s presence felt to me like that of a good angel, and I gradually regained my health.

As my sickness left me, I fell into a gloomy, black melancholy that nothing could dispel. The image of Clerval was always before me—ghastly and murdered. More than once, the agitation these thoughts stirred in me made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Alas! Why did they preserve such a miserable, detested life for me? It must be so that I can fulfill my destiny, which is now drawing to a close. Soon—oh, very soon—death will extinguish these throbbings and relieve me from the immense weight of anguish that drags me to the dust; and in carrying out the award of justice, I will also sink to rest. At that time, death still seemed far off, even though the wish was always in my mind. I often sat for hours, motionless and silent, longing for some great revolution that would bury both me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The season of the assizes approached. I had already been three months in prison, and although I was still weak and in constant danger of relapsing, I was required to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court was held. Mr. Kirwin took it upon himself to handle every detail of collecting witnesses and arranging my defense."}

{"request_id":"d3912ddd7b8eda1f2f8e621c","rewritten_text":"Once that was done, I unfastened a few more of the loops from the rim, brought in a further section of the cloth, and then connected the loosened loops to their proper buttons. In this way, I could slide the entire upper part of the bag between the net-work and the hoop. It was clear that the hoop would now drop down inside the car, while the car’s own weight, along with everything inside it, would be supported only by the buttons. At first, this might seem like too little support, but it really was not. The buttons were very strong, and they were also so close together that any one button carried only a small share of the total weight. In fact, even if the car and its contents had been three times heavier than they were, I would not have been worried at all. 

I lifted the hoop again, placing it back inside the gum-elastic covering, and propped it up to nearly its former height using three light poles set up for that purpose. This was done, of course, to keep the bag stretched tight at the top and to hold the lower part of the net-work in the right position. The only remaining step was to close the opening of the enclosure. I did this by gathering the folds of the material together and twisting them tightly on the inside with a stationary tourniquet.

“In the sides of the covering, now fitted around the car, three circular panes of thick but clear glass had been inserted. Through them, I could see in every horizontal direction without difficulty. In the cloth that formed the bottom, there was also a fourth window of the same kind, aligned with a small opening in the floor of the car itself. This let me look straight down. But I could not place any similar opening overhead, because of the special way the top part had to be closed and the wrinkles that would form in the cloth. So I did not expect to see anything directly above me, at the zenith. That was not very important anyway, because even if I had been able to put a window at the top, the balloon would have blocked my view and made it useless.

“About a foot below one of the side windows was a circular opening, eight inches across, fitted with a brass rim. The rim’s inner edge matched the windings of a screw. The large tube of the condenser was screwed into this rim, while the main body of the machine was, of course, inside the chamber of gum-elastic.”"}

{"request_id":"8e671634867c489962c8efc3","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man—an awfully nice, kind-looking old man, at least the way he seemed when I got him up. I told him me and my brother had been over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and we’d camped on a bit of a raft we’d found. And about midnight, I said, he must’ve kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted him to come over there and fix it, and we didn’t want him saying a word about it or letting anybody know, because we meant to be home this evening and surprise the folks.

“Who are your folks?” he asks.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. Then, after a minute, he says:

“How’d you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I says, “and it shot him.”

“A singular dream,” he says.

So he lit up his lantern, grabbed his saddle-bags, and we set out. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like the look of it. He said it was big enough for one, but it didn’t look pretty safe for two. I says:

“Oh, you needn’t be afeard, sir. She carried the three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and _the guns;_ that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

Still, he put his foot on the gunnel, rocked her, and shook his head, saying he reckoned he’d go look for a bigger one. But all the others were locked up and chained, so he took my canoe instead. He told me to wait till he came back, or I could go hunt around further, or maybe I better go down home and get everything ready for the surprise if I wanted. But I told him I wouldn’t, so I explained to him how to find the raft, and then he started off.

I got an idea pretty soon. I says to myself, if he can’t fix that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, as the saying goes—if it takes him three or four days—what are we going to do? Just sit there and wait till he lets the cat out of the bag? No, sir; I knew what _I’ll_ do. I’ll wait, and when he comes back, if he says he’s got to go any more, I’ll go down there too, if I have to swim. Then we’ll take and tie him up, keep him, and shove out down the river. And when Tom’s done with him, we’ll give him what it’s worth—or all we’ve got—and then let him get ashore.

So I slipped into a lumber-pile to get some sleep. Next time I woke up, the sun was way up over my head. I jumped out and ran for the doctor’s house, but they told me he’d gone away in the night some time or other, and he hadn’t come back yet."}

{"request_id":"4ba39dac9edde3419b11deef","rewritten_text":"Ye spirits of storm, receive me! Ye powers of destruction, open wide your arms and hold me forever. If a kinder power has not already decided on a different end, then after long suffering I may finally get my reward, and again feel my heart beating close to the heart of another, like my own.

Tiber, the road laid out by nature herself as it cuts through her continent, lay at my feet, and many boats were tied along the banks. With only a few books, some supplies, and my dog, I would board one of them and let the current carry me down into the sea. Then, staying near the shore, I would sail along the beautiful coasts and sunny headlands of the blue Mediterranean, pass Naples, go along Calabria, and face the twin dangers of Scylla and Charybdis. After that, with no fear at all—since what did I have to lose?—I would skim across the ocean toward Malta and the farther Cyclades.

I would avoid Constantinople, because the towers and harbors I already knew there belonged to a different kind of life than the one I have now. I would sail along Asia Minor and Syria, and after passing the Nile, with its seven mouths, I would steer north again until I could no longer see forgotten Carthage and deserted Libya, and then I would reach the Pillars of Hercules. And then, no matter where I end up, the wet caves and silent depths of the ocean may be my home—before I finish this long journey, or before the arrow of disease finds my heart while I drift alone on the rough Mediterranean. Or, if I stop somewhere along the way, I might find what I’m looking for: a companion. If not, then even to endless time, old and gray-headed, with youth already in the grave among those I love, the lone wanderer will still unfurl his sail, grip the tiller, and, still obeying the winds of heaven, keep circling promontory after promontory, anchoring in bay after bay, still cutting through an ocean with no seed, leaving behind the green land of my native Europe and sailing down the tawny coast of Africa, after surviving the fierce seas of the Cape. Then I may moor my worn skiff in a sheltered inlet, shaded by fragrant groves on the far Indian Ocean islands.

These are wild dreams. But since, a week ago, they first came over me while I stood on the height of St. Peter’s, they have taken over my imagination. I have chosen my boat and packed my small supplies. I have picked out a few books—the main ones are Homer and Shakespeare. And the libraries of the world are open to me, so in any port I can restock. I don’t expect things to get better. Still, the endless sameness of the present is unbearable to me."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c30b1d9f18a606d7c2469710","rewritten_text":"“April 7th. I rose early, and, to my great delight, at last saw what could admit of no doubt—nothing less than the northern Pole itself. It lay there, beyond question, directly under my feet; yet, having climbed to so enormous a height, I could discern nothing with any certainty. Indeed, judging from the sequence of figures that marked my different altitudes at various times—between six A.M. on the second of April and twenty minutes before nine A.M. of the same day (when the barometer fell)—one might fairly conclude that, by four o’clock in the morning of April the seventh, the balloon had attained a height of at least 7,254 miles above the surface of the sea. Such an elevation may seem staggering, but the estimate on which it rests almost certainly falls short of the truth. At all events, I unquestionably beheld the whole of the earth’s greatest diameter; the entire northern hemisphere lay beneath me like a map projected orthographically, and the great circle of the equator itself traced the very edge of my horizon. Your Excellencies will, however, easily understand that the limited tracts hitherto unexplored within the Arctic circle—though situated straight beneath me and therefore seen without any appearance of being foreshortened—were still, in themselves, comparatively too small, and too far from the point of view, to allow any close or accurate inspection. Still, what I could make out was of a singular and stirring character. Northward from that vast rim just mentioned—which, with slight qualification, may be taken as the boundary of human discovery in these parts—there runs one continuous, or nearly continuous, expanse of ice. In the first few degrees of its course its surface is very noticeably flattened; farther on it sinks into a plane, and finally, becoming somewhat concave, it ends at the Pole in a circular centre, sharply defined. Its apparent diameter, as seen from the balloon, subtended an angle of about sixty-five seconds; and its dusky tint, varying in strength, was at all times darker than any other spot on the visible hemisphere, and at intervals deepened into the most absolute and impenetrable blackness. Beyond this, little could be determined. By twelve o’clock the circular centre had sensibly diminished in circumference, and by seven P.M. I lost sight of it altogether; the balloon passing over the western edge of the ice and drifting away swiftly toward the equator.\n\n“April 8th. I observed a marked decrease in the earth’s apparent diameter, along with a material change in its general color and aspect.”"}

{"request_id":"78b9062389c2f8f9e9572d8c","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, laying his hand once more, gently, on the Doctor’s arm, after a brief pause from both of them, “to what, then, would you attribute this attack?”

“I think,” replied Doctor Manette, “that there was a powerful and extraordinary return of the train of thought and recollection which first brought on the illness. Certain intense associations—of the most painful kind—were, I believe, brought back with vivid force. It is likely that there had been a long-standing dread in his mind, that those associations would be recalled—perhaps under particular circumstances—perhaps on some specific occasion. He tried in vain to brace himself; and maybe the very attempt to brace himself only left him less able to withstand it.”

“Would he remember what occurred during the relapse?” asked Mr. Lorry, pausing in his question.

The Doctor looked about the room in a desolate way, shook his head, and answered, in a low voice, “Not at all.”

“Now, regarding what lies ahead,” Mr. Lorry suggested.

“As for the future,” said the Doctor, regaining steadiness, “I have every reason to hope. Since it pleased Heaven, in its mercy, to restore him so soon, I should have great hope. He, having yielded under the pressure of some complicated thing—long dreaded, long vaguely foreseen, and long struggled against—and then recovering after the cloud had burst and passed, I should hope that the worst is over.”

“Well, well! That is good comfort. I’m thankful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I’m thankful!” echoed the Doctor, bowing his head with reverence.

“There are two other matters,” said Mr. Lorry, “on which I am anxious to be instructed. May I go on?”

“You cannot do your friend a better service.” The Doctor took his hand.

“Then to the first. He is given to study, and unusually active; he throws himself with great ardour into the gaining of professional knowledge, into the conducting of experiments, into many things. Now—does he do too much?”

“I don’t think so. It may be the temper of his mind to be always in some singular need of occupation. That may be partly natural to it, and partly the consequence of affliction. The less it was taken up with wholesome things, the more it would be in danger of turning toward the unhealthy. He may have noticed it in himself, and found the truth.”

“Are you certain he is not under too great a strain?”

“I think I am quite sure of it.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt whether that could easily be. There has been a violent stress in one direction, and it requires a counterweight.”

“Pardon me, as a man of business who persists. Suppose, for the moment, that he _was_ overworked; would it not show itself in some fresh return of this disorder?”"}

{"request_id":"0857a64e0710ac67c62fd73d","rewritten_text":"“So what result has followed, then? What impression have I made on your imagination?”

As Dupin asked me the question, I felt my skin crawl. “A madman,” I said. “Someone raving, escaped from a nearby Maison de Santé.”

“In some ways,” he answered, “your idea isn’t wrong. But the voices of madmen, even when they’re at their wildest, never match that particular voice heard on the stairs. Madmen belong to some nation, and even when their words are a mess, their speech still has a clear pattern of syllables. And besides, the hair of a madman isn’t like the hair I’m holding in my hand right now. I pulled this small tuft free from the fingers of Madame L’Espanaye, which were clenched so tightly. Tell me what you think of it.”

“Dupin!” I said, completely shaken. “This hair is very unusual. It isn’t human hair.”

“I haven’t claimed that it is,” he replied. “But before we decide, I want you to look at the small sketch I’ve drawn here on this paper. It’s a fac-simile of what one part of the testimony describes as ‘dark bruises, and deep indentations of finger nails’ on Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat, and what another part describes, by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne, as ‘a series of livid spots, evidently the impression of fingers.’”

“You’ll see,” Dupin continued, spreading the paper on the table between us, “that the drawing shows a firm, steady grip. There’s no sign of slipping. Each finger seems to have kept the terrible hold it first made—perhaps right up until the victim died. Now try placing all your fingers at once into the impressions you see there.”

I tried, but I couldn’t do it.

“We may not be testing this in the right way,” he said. “The paper lies flat, but a human throat is round. Here is a piece of wood with a circumference about the same as the throat. Wrap the drawing around it, then try again.”

I did, but the problem was even clearer than before. “This,” I said, “is not the mark of a human hand.”

“Now read,” Dupin replied, “this passage from Cuvier.”

It was a detailed anatomical description of the large, tawny Ourang-Outang from the East Indian islands. Everyone knows the creature’s huge size, its extraordinary strength and energy, its wild ferocity, and its ability to imitate. I understood the full horror of the murder at once.

“The description of the digits,” I said after I finished reading, “matches this drawing exactly.”"}

{"request_id":"37b047da8bc3b4bce0fb239a","rewritten_text":"Emma did not feel any remorse for her condescending manner in going to the Coles. The visit left her with many agreeable recollections the following day; and whatever she might be thought to have sacrificed by keeping herself in dignified seclusion, was more than made up to her by the brilliance of her popularity. She must have pleased the Coles—fine, deserving people, who ought to be made happy!—and she would leave behind a name that would not soon fade.

Perfect happiness, even when recalled, is not something one often meets; and there were two matters on which she was not entirely at ease. She wondered whether she had not overstepped a woman’s duty by passing on to Frank Churchill her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings. It was hardly proper; yet the notion had taken such hold of her that it would slip out, and his readiness to submit to everything she told him was, in a way, a compliment to her discernment—so that it was hard for her to be fully certain she ought to have kept her silence.

The other point of regret also concerned Jane Fairfax; and there she had no doubt. She regretted, plainly and without any qualification, the inferiority of her own playing and singing. She truly mourned the idleness of her childhood, and then sat down and practised with vigour for an hour and a half.

She was then interrupted by Harriet’s coming in; and if Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, she might soon have been comforted.

“Oh! if I could only play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t put us together, Harriet. My playing isn’t any more like hers than a lamp is like sunshine.”

“Oh! dear—I think you play the best of the two. I’m sure you play quite as well as she does. I know I’d rather hear you. Everybody last night said how well you played.”

“Those who understood anything about it must have noticed the difference. The truth is, Harriet, that my playing is just good enough to be praised, but Jane Fairfax’s goes much farther.”

“Well, I shall always think you play quite as well as she does, or that if there is any difference, no one would ever be able to tell. Mr. Cole said how much taste you had; and Mr. Frank Churchill talked a great deal about your taste, and said he valued taste far more than execution.”

“Ah! but Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I saw she had execution, but I didn’t know she had any taste. No one ever spoke of it. And I hate Italian singing—it’s impossible to make out a word of it. Besides, if she plays so very well, you know, it’s no more than she’s required to do, because she’ll have to teach.”}"}

{"request_id":"e67d07c3e56aca8271f19b35","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so thoroughly content with what had passed that he troubled himself no more about it, nor once again annoyed his dear sister Elizabeth by bringing the matter up; and she was glad to feel that she had said enough to keep him quiet.

The day of his and Lydia’s departure soon arrived; and Mrs. Bennet had to endure a separation which, since her husband by no means shared her plan of having them all go to Newcastle, was likely to last at least a twelvemonth.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when shall we meet again?”

“Oh, Lord! I don’t know. Perhaps not for these two or three years.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women never have much time to write. My sisters may write to _me_. They will have nothing else to do.”

Mr. Wickham’s parting words were far more tender than his wife’s. He smiled, looked very handsome, and said a great many flattering things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet as soon as they were out of the house. “He simpers, and smirks, and makes love to us all. I am prodigiously proud of him. I defy even Sir William Lucas himself to produce a better son-in-law.”

The loss of her daughter left Mrs. Bennet dull for several days.

“I often think,” said she, “that nothing is so dreadful as being separated from one’s friends. Without them one feels so forlorn.”

“This is the natural result, you see, madam, of marrying off a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It ought to make you more content that your other four are still single.”

“It is no such thing. Lydia does not leave me because she is married; she goes only because her husband’s regiment happens to be so far away. If it had been nearer, she would not have gone so soon.”

Yet the languid state into which this event threw her was soon eased, and her thoughts opened again to the stir of expectation, by a piece of news that had just begun to be talked of. The Netherfield housekeeper had received orders to get ready for the arrival of her master, who was to come down in a day or two, to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was all in a flutter. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head, now one way and now the other.

“Well, well, and so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” (for Mrs. Philips was the first to tell her). “Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, though. He is nothing to us, you know, and I am sure I never want to see him again. But, if he chooses it, he is very welcome to come to Netherfield.”"}

{"request_id":"4061d17b718f582535a96fdb","rewritten_text":"“Good heavens!” the Duchess said to herself. “So he really is some kind of hand-reader after all. How dreadful. I hope, at least, that he’s a foreigner. Then it wouldn’t be quite so bad.”

“I must certainly introduce him to you.”

“Introduce him!” the Duchess cried. “You don’t mean to say he’s here?” She started looking around for a small tortoiseshell fan and a very tattered lace shawl, ready to leave at a moment’s notice.

“Of course he’s here. I wouldn’t dream of throwing a party without him. He tells me I have a pure psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even a little shorter, I’d have been a confirmed pessimist and gone into a convent.”

“Oh, I see!” said the Duchess, feeling a great deal more relieved. “He tells fortunes, I suppose?”

“And misfortunes, too,” Lady Windermere answered. “Any number of them. Next year, for instance, I’m in serious danger—by land and sea—so I’m going to live in a balloon, and have my dinner drawn up in a basket every evening. It’s all written down on my little finger, or on the palm of my hand—I can’t remember which.”

“But surely that’s tempting Providence, Gladys.”

“My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their hands read once a month, so you know what not to do. Of course, one does it all the same, but it’s so pleasant to be warned. Now, if someone doesn’t go and fetch Mr. Podgers at once, I’ll have to go myself.”

“Let me go, Lady Windermere,” said a tall, handsome young man standing nearby, listening with an amused smile.

“Thank you so much, Lord Arthur; but I’m afraid you wouldn’t recognize him.”

“If he’s as wonderful as you say, Lady Windermere, I couldn’t possibly miss him. Tell me what he’s like, and I’ll bring him to you right away.”

“Well, he isn’t anything like a fortune-teller. I mean he isn’t mysterious, or esoteric, or romantic-looking. He’s a small, stout man with a funny bald head and big gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country attorney. I’m really sorry, but it isn’t my fault. People are so annoying. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look exactly like pianists; and I remember last season asking a dreadful conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up so many people, and always wore a coat of mail and carried a dagger up his shirt-sleeve. And when he came, do you know what he looked like? A nice old clergyman—and he cracked jokes all evening.”"}

{"request_id":"5dd8b7835dba2bdaec6b7f94","rewritten_text":"There was something wonderful about tidying up and then stopping for a quiet moment before starting life again. In our village, on Saturday nights, that feeling made Joe stay out about half an hour longer than he did on other nights. When the half hour was up, and the rum and water ran out at the same time, Joe stood up to go and took me by the hand.

“Wait just half a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the strange man. “I think I’ve got a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket. If I do, the boy gets it.”

He searched through his small pile of change, found it, folded it up in some crumpled paper, and handed it to me. “It’s yours,” he said. “Just remember—your own.”

I thanked him, staring at him in a way that was far beyond good manners, while I held on tightly to Joe. He said good-night to Joe, and good-night to Mr. Wopsle too, who went out with us. Then he only gave me a look with his steady aiming eye—no, not exactly a look, because he shut it away. Still, you could tell wonders could be done with an eye by hiding it.

On the way home, if I had felt like talking, I would have had all the talking to myself. Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe walked all the way home with his mouth wide open, trying to rinse the rum out with as much air as he could. But I was so stunned by this sudden return of my old mistake and my old acquaintance that I couldn’t think of anything else.

When we got into the kitchen, my sister wasn’t in a very bad mood. That made Joe feel bold enough to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll bet,” said Mrs. Joe, pleased with herself. “If he didn’t mean it, he wouldn’t have given it to the boy. Let’s see it.”

I took it out of the paper, and it turned out to be a good one. “But what is this?” Mrs. Joe said, dropping the shilling and picking up the paper again. “Two one-pound notes?”

They were nothing less than two thick, hot-looking one-pound notes, as if they had been on the closest terms with every cattle market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat again and ran to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat on my usual stool and stared at my sister, feeling sure the man wouldn’t be there.

Soon Joe came back. He said the man had gone, but that Joe had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

{"request_id":"1f7147f006b47784edd88e53","rewritten_text":"When I stopped crying, reason and memory came back to me. Then I began to think more calmly about what had happened and about what I had to do. Only a few hours had passed, but a huge change had taken place in my life. What would normally take years had already been decided since that morning. My father felt dead to me. For a moment it seemed as if, with his white hair, he was lying in his coffin, and I—youth turning into age—was crying over his timely death. But it was not like that. I was still young, far too young. And he was not dead to everyone. It was only me who was most miserable: I must never see him or speak to him again. I must run from him with even more urgency than from my worst enemy. Whether in solitude or in a city, I must never look at him again.

That thought filled me with such pain that I could hardly breathe. It took over my mind, and for a while I could not follow any other thoughts. After that, I decided I would live in the bleakest isolation. I would go back to the Continent and become a nun—not because of religion. I was not Catholic. I wanted to be shut out from the world forever. There I could find solitude where I could cry, and the voices of life would never reach me.

But my father—my beloved and most wretched father—would he die? Would he never overcome the fierce passion that now ruled him without mercy? Could it be that, many years from now, when age had cooled the burning feelings he has now, he might become a father to me again? This thought smoothed my face. I could feel it, and I cried because I felt it: a faint, half-sad smile pulled at my lips, showing my suffering. I dared to hope again for my future. Time would pass, and it would feel lighter because of hope. Even if the years passed heavily, they would still pass—and I would not have lost my father forever. Let him spend another sixteen years wandering in loneliness. Let him shout his wild complaints again to the vast woods and the terrifying waterfalls of another country. Let him face terrible danger and hardships that break the soul. Let the hot southern sun burn his passion-worn cheeks again, and let the cold night rains fall on him and chill his blood.

To this life, miserable father, I give you to it! Go! Let your days be spent among savages, and your nights beneath the open sky. Let your limbs wear out and your heart grow cold, and let all youth die inside you!"}

{"request_id":"0efa8ccd713725bdd9e23bb6","rewritten_text":"Were our proud dreams meant to fade like this? Our name had been written “a little lower than the angels,” and now we were no better than something brief and fragile. We had called ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and yet we were only “the quint-essence of dust.” We were bitter that the pyramids had lasted longer than the embalmed body of their builder. Even the small shepherd’s hut of straw we passed on the road had, in its simple structure, a kind of lasting power greater than the whole human race. How could we accept this painful change from our earlier hopes, from the strength we seemed to have?

Then an internal voice, clear and unmistakable, seemed to speak:—So it was decided from eternity. The horses that carry Time forward are bound to this hour and its ending, because the void brought forth its burden. Would you try to read backward the unchangeable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Omnipotent! eternal, unchanging Necessity! You sit with busy hands, weaving the unbreakable chain of events. I will not complain about what you do. If my human mind cannot accept that everything that is, is right, then I will still accept this: what is, must be. I will sit among the ruins and smile. We were not born to enjoy; we were born to submit and to hope.

Will the reader grow tired if I describe our long journey from Paris to Geneva in detail? If, day by day, I wrote down the many miseries of our life as a journal, could my hand, or my language, find words for the full range of our suffering—how one dreadful event crowded in on the next? Be patient, reader, whoever you are, wherever you live, whether you belong to some spiritual race or you come from some surviving pair. Your nature will still be human, and your home will still be the earth. Here you will read about the deeds of a people long gone, and you will wonder whether those who suffered what you now read were made of the same frail flesh and soft organization as you. That is true—so weep. You are alone, and you will be gentle; you will shed tears of compassion. Still, pay attention to the story and learn the acts and sufferings of those who came before.

But the last events that marked our progress through France were so full of strange horror and dark misery that I cannot linger on them. If I broke down each incident, every small moment would hold a terrible tale, and even the smallest word would make the blood in your young veins run cold. It is right that I should raise this monument for the instruction of those who are gone, but it is not right to drag you through the wards of a hospital or into the hidden rooms of the charnel-house."}

{"request_id":"175fabb1f7f8058f5cd9f8b4","rewritten_text":"His account was this: that, while travelling from his home and passing through Datchet, he was startled to see smoke rising from the inn’s chimney; thinking he might find fellow-travellers for his journey gathered there, he knocked, and was admitted. There was no one in the house except Lucy and her mother. The latter had been struck by rheumatism and had lost the use of her limbs, and so, one after another, all the remaining inhabitants of the country had gone on, leaving them behind. Lucy begged the man to remain with her; in a week or two her mother would be better, and then they could set out together; yet, she said, they must surely perish if they were left in such helplessness and loneliness. The man replied that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, and that, in his judgment, he could not stay. As a last resort, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, to be delivered to her wherever he might meet us. He carried out this errand at least, and Idris received, with feeling, the letter that followed:—

“HONOURED LADY,

“I am persuaded you will remember me and have pity on me, and I venture to hope you will help me; what other hope is there for me? Forgive the way I write—I am so bewildered. A month ago my dear mother was deprived of the use of her limbs. She is already better, and in another month I am sure I shall be able to travel, as you were so kind as to say you would arrange for us. But now everyone has gone—everyone—as they left, each one said that perhaps my mother would be better before we were quite deserted. Yet three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who, because of his new-born child, stayed to the last; and, as they had a large family, I thought I might persuade them to wait a little longer for us. Instead, I found the house empty. I have not seen a living soul since, until this good man came. —What will become of us? My mother does not know our condition; she is so ill that I have kept it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? I am sure we must perish miserably as we are. If I were to try to move my mother now, she would die on the road; and if, when she is better, I were able, I cannot tell how I should find the roads, and make so many miles to the sea—by then you would all be in France, and the great ocean would lie between us, which is dreadful even to sailors.”"}

{"request_id":"6c2e534ce0eb05bd9ca6b738","rewritten_text":"Shall I be carried up to the skies, on flowery beds of comfort, while others fight to win the prize and sail through blood-y seas?

He was known as a wonderful reader. At church “sociables,” he was always asked to read poetry. When he finished, the ladies would lift their hands, let them fall helplessly into their laps, and “wall” their eyes, shaking their heads as if to say, “Words cannot express it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this mortal earth.”

After the hymn, Rev. Mr. Sprague turned himself into a bulletin-board and read out “notices” about meetings, societies, and other things, until it felt as if the list would go on until the end of the world. It was a strange custom, and it still exists in America, even in cities, even in this age when newspapers are everywhere. Often, the less there is to justify a traditional custom, the harder it is to get rid of it.

Then the minister prayed. It was a good, generous prayer, full of details. He prayed for the church and for the little children in it; for the other churches in the village; for the village itself; for the county; for the State; for the officers of the State; for the United States; for the churches of the United States; for Congress; for the President; for the officers of the government; for poor sailors, tossed by stormy seas; for oppressed millions suffering under European monarchies and Oriental despots; for those who have the light and the good news but still do not have eyes to see or ears to hear; for the heathen in far islands of the sea. He ended with a request that the words he was about to speak might find grace and favor, and be like seed planted in fertile ground, producing a grateful harvest of good in time. Amen.

There was a rustling of dresses, and the congregation sat down. The boy whose story this book tells did not like the prayer. He only endured it, if he even did that much. He was restless the whole time. He kept track of the details of the prayer without meaning to, because he was not really listening. He knew the usual ground and the clergyman’s regular route through it. When a small new detail was added, his ear caught it at once, and his whole nature pushed back. He thought the additions were unfair and scoundrelly.

During the prayer, a fly landed on the back of the pew in front of him and tormented his spirit by calmly rubbing its hands together, holding its head with its arms, and polishing itself so vigorously that it seemed to almost separate from its body, leaving a thin thread of a neck visible. It scraped its wings with its hind legs and smoothed them back onto its body as if they were coat-tails. It went through its whole grooming routine as calmly as if it knew it was completely safe."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5b5216fe17444d31f12cdf19","rewritten_text":"He had, in truth, been entirely unaware of any power of his own. He had followed her into the shrubbery without the least intention of trying anything. Driven by anxiety to learn how she took Frank Churchill’s engagement, he had no selfish aim—indeed, no aim at all—only a desire, if she gave him the chance, to soothe or advise her.—What followed was simply the work of the moment, the immediate consequence of what he heard, acting upon his feelings. Her delightful assurance of being wholly indifferent to Frank Churchill—her heart entirely disengaged from him—had first awakened the hope that, in time, he might win her affection;—yet it was not a hope for the present. In the brief rush of eagerness over judgment, he had only wanted to be told that she would not forbid his attempt to attach her.—The stronger hopes that opened gradually were all the more thrilling.—The affection he had been asking permission to form, if he could, was already his!—Within half an hour, he had moved from a mind thoroughly distressed to a state so near perfect happiness that no other name could fit it.\n\n_Her_ change matched his. This same half-hour had given each of them the precious certainty of being loved, and had cleared from each the same measure of ignorance, jealousy, or distrust. On his side, there had been a jealousy long established—dating back to Frank Churchill’s arrival, or even to the expectation of it. He had loved Emma, and been jealous of Frank Churchill, from about the same time; one feeling may well have helped to explain the other. It was his jealousy of Frank Churchill that had carried him away from the country. The Box Hill party had decided him to go. He meant to keep himself from seeing again those attentions, so freely allowed and encouraged. He had gone to learn indifference. But he had gone to the wrong place. There was too much domestic happiness in his brother’s home; woman there wore too pleasing a shape; Isabella was too much like Emma—differing only in those conspicuous, inferior points that always made the other appear the brighter, even though there would have been plenty to do, had his time been longer. Still, he stayed on, steadily, day after day—until the post this very morning brought him the story of Jane Fairfax. Then, with the gladness that must be felt—indeed, which he did not hesitate to feel, having never believed Frank Churchill deserving of Emma—there was so much tender solicitude, so much sharp anxiety for her, that he could not remain. He rode home through the rain; and after dinner he walked straight in, to see how this sweetest and best of all creatures, faultless even with all her faults, bore the discovery."}

{"request_id":"d86ee9bb5c5fccec6f5e0eb6","rewritten_text":"Her situation was, indeed, one of no ordinary trial and difficulty. While she felt the most eager, burning desire to uncover the mystery that surrounded Oliver’s history, she could not help but treat as sacred the confidence the miserable woman she had just spoken with had placed in her—as a young, innocent girl. Her words and manner had touched Rose Maylie’s heart; and, mixed with her love for her young charge, and scarcely less intense in its truth and fervor, was her heartfelt wish to bring the outcast back to repentance and hope.

They planned to stay in London only three days before leaving for some weeks to a distant part of the coast. It was now midnight of the first day. What course of action could she decide on that could be carried out in forty-eight hours? Or how could she delay the journey without raising suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them, and would be for the next two days; but Rose knew the excellent gentleman’s impulsiveness too well, and she could see too clearly the anger with which, in the first burst of his indignation, he would regard the very person who had been used to secure Oliver’s recapture, to trust him with the secret—especially when her arguments on the girl’s behalf could not be supported by anyone experienced. These were all reasons for the greatest caution and the most careful restraint in communicating it to Mrs. Maylie, whose first impulse would inevitably be to call a meeting with the respectable doctor about it. As for turning to any legal adviser, even if she had known how to do so, it was hardly worth considering for the same reason. Once the idea came to her of seeking help from Harry; but that brought back the memory of their last parting, and it seemed wrong to call him back—Rose’s thoughts turned, and as the tears rose to her eyes, she told herself that by now he might have learned to forget her, and to be happier away.

Disturbed by these shifting thoughts—leaning toward one course, then another, and then pulling back from all of them as each new consideration presented itself—Rose spent a sleepless, anxious night. After thinking it over again the next day, she reached a desperate conclusion: she would consult Harry.

“If it hurts him,” she thought, “to come back here, it will hurt me even more! But maybe he won’t come. He might write, or he might come himself, and carefully avoid meeting me—he did when he left. I hardly thought he would; but it’s better for us both.” And at that, Rose set down the pen and turned away, as though the very paper that was meant to be her messenger should not have to see her weep."}

{"request_id":"a8cff365d086a2d32df07230","rewritten_text":"“Mr. Elliot looked up with so much respect.”

“Quite delightful!” cried Mrs. Clay, though she did not dare to look at Anne. “It’s exactly like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not say father and son?”

“Oh! I don’t forbid anyone from saying what they like. If you have those ideas! But, honestly, I can’t see that his attention is any more than what other men show.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs. Clay. She raised her hands and eyes, and then kept the rest of her surprise to herself in a convenient silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you don’t need to be so worried about him. You know I invited him. I sent him away with smiles. And when I learned he was really going to his friends at Thornberry Park for the whole day tomorrow, I felt sorry for him.”

Anne admired how well her friend acted. She could show so much pleasure, both in the expectation and in the actual arrival of the very person whose presence would truly interfere with her main goal. It was impossible not to think that Mrs. Clay must hate seeing Mr. Elliot. Still, she could put on a friendly, calm expression and seem perfectly satisfied with having to spend only half as much time with Sir Walter as she would have otherwise.

For Anne, it was very upsetting to watch Mr. Elliot enter the room. It was also painful to have him come up to her and speak. She had been used to the idea that he could not always be completely sincere, but now she saw insincerity in everything. His careful respect for her father, compared with what he had said before, was disgusting. And when she remembered how cruel he had been to Mrs. Smith, she could hardly bear to look at his present smiles and gentle manner, or to hear his practiced kind words.

She meant to avoid any change in her manners that might make him feel the need to correct her. Her main goal was to avoid any questions or attention. Still, she planned to be as clearly cool to him as she could, while keeping their relationship. She also meant to quietly step back, as much as she could, from the few moments of unnecessary closeness that had been slowly drawn out of her. So she was more guarded and more cool than she had been the night before.

He wanted to spark her curiosity again about how and where he had heard her praised before. He wanted very much to be encouraged with more attention. But the charm was gone. He found that the lively warmth of a public room was what helped kindle his modest cousin’s vanity. He also found that, at least now, he could not do it with any of the attempts he might make, given how strongly the others demanded attention."}

{"request_id":"83c5eea80399081b36561361","rewritten_text":"It was at this moment that his eyes, and mine as well, fell on the scrap of parchment, which I then took to be paper. It lay half buried in the sand, with a corner sticking up. Near where we found it, I noticed the remains of the hull of what appeared to have been a ship’s longboat. The wreck seemed to have been there for a very long time; the resemblance to boat timbers could scarcely be traced.

“Well, Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Soon afterward we turned to go home, and on the way we met Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he begged me to let him take it to the fort. Once I agreed, he immediately shoved it into his waistcoat pocket—without the parchment it had been wrapped in, which I kept holding in my hand during his inspection. Maybe he feared I’d change my mind, and thought it best to secure the prize right away. You know how enthusiastic he is about anything connected with Natural History. At the same time, without realizing it, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket.

“You remember that when I went to the table to make a sketch of the beetle, I found no paper where it was usually kept. I checked the drawer, and there was none. I searched my pockets, hoping to find an old letter, when my hand came across the parchment. So I’m laying out the exact way it came into my possession; the circumstances struck me with a particular force.

“No doubt you’ll think me fanciful—but I had already made a kind of connection. I had put together two links in a great chain. There was a boat lying on a seacoast, and not far from it was a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn on it. You’ll, of course, ask, ‘Where is the connection?’ I answer that the skull, the death’s head, is the well-known emblem of the pirate. The death’s-head flag is raised in all their engagements.

“I’ve said the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment is durable—almost imperishable. Things of little importance are rarely committed to parchment; for the ordinary purposes of drawing or writing, it isn’t nearly as suitable as paper. That thought suggested some meaning—some relevance—in the death’s-head. I also didn’t fail to notice the shape of the parchment. Even though one of its corners had been destroyed by some accident, it could be seen that the original form was oblong.”"}

{"request_id":"90b58f65a43f33ba850cb43b","rewritten_text":"“I’m not eating at home, so I won’t need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” the man said, and left the room.

“Now, Alan, there’s no time to waste. Look how heavy this chest is! I’ll carry it for you. You take the other things.” He spoke fast, with an air of command. Campbell felt himself overpowered by him. They went out together.

At the top landing, Dorian drew out the key and turned it in the lock. Then he paused, and something troubled crossed his face. He shuddered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he whispered.

“It’s nothing to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell said, cold as ever.

Dorian eased the door half open. In that moment he saw his portrait’s face, leering in the sunlight. On the floor before it lay the torn curtain. He recalled that the night before, for the first time in his life, he had failed to hide the fatal canvas; he had been on the verge of rushing forward, when he had drawn back again, shuddering.

What was that loathsome red dew, shining—wet and slick—on one of the hands, as though the picture had sweated blood? How dreadful it was!—worse, it seemed to him then, than the silent thing he knew was stretched across the table, the thing whose grotesque, misshapen shadow on the spotted carpet told him it had not moved, but remained where he had left it.

He drew in a deep breath, opened the door a little wider, and, with his eyes half shut and his head turned away, hurried inside, resolved that he would not look at the dead man even once. Then, bending down, he seized the gold-and-purple hanging and flung it straight over the picture.

He stopped there, afraid to turn around, and his gaze fixed itself on the intricacies of the pattern in front of him. He heard Campbell come in with the heavy chest, the irons, and the other items he had required for his dreadful work. He found himself wondering whether he and Basil Hallward had ever met, and, if they had, what they might have thought of one another.

“Leave me now,” said a stern voice behind him.

Dorian turned and hurried out, only half aware that the dead man had been pushed back into the chair and that Campbell was staring into a glistening yellow face. As he went down the stairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was long after seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale, yet utterly composed. “I’ve done what you asked me to do,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"8fa9e799c2fb50c40afcbf5f","rewritten_text":"It was well past noon when he woke up. His valet had quietly tiptoed into the room several times to check whether he was moving, and he kept wondering why his young master slept so late. At last the bell rang. Victor came in softly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray made of old Sevres china. He then pulled back the olive-satin curtains, with their shimmering blue lining, that hung in front of the three tall windows.

“Monsieur slept well this morning,” Victor said, smiling.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked, still sleepy.

“One hour and a quarter, Monsieur.”

How late it was. He sat up, took a sip of tea, and began sorting through his letters. One of them was from Lord Henry and had been delivered by hand that morning. He paused, then set it aside. The rest he opened without much interest. They were the usual mix: cards, invitations to dinner, tickets for private viewings, programs for charity concerts, and all the other things that fashionable young men receive every morning during the season. There was also a rather large bill for a chased silver Louis-Quinze toilet set that he still hadn’t had the nerve to send to his guardians. They were very old-fashioned and didn’t understand that in this age, unnecessary things are the only necessities. In addition, there were several polite notes from money-lenders on Jermyn Street offering to advance any amount of money at a moment’s notice, with the most reasonable interest rates.

After about ten minutes, he got up. He slipped into an elaborate silk-embroidered dressing gown made of cashmere wool, then went into the bathroom paved in onyx. The cool water refreshed him after his long sleep. For a while, it felt as if he had forgotten everything he had been through. Now and then, he had a vague sense that he had taken part in some strange tragedy, but it also felt unreal, like something from a dream.

Once he was dressed, he went into the library and sat down to a light French breakfast set out for him on a small round table near the open window. It was a beautiful day. The warm air seemed full of spices. A bee flew in and buzzed around the blue-dragon bowl in front of him, which was filled with sulphur-yellow roses. He felt completely happy.

Then his eyes fell on the screen he had placed in front of the portrait, and he startled.

“Too cold for Monsieur?” his valet asked, setting an omelette on the table. “I shut the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “No,” he murmured. “I’m not cold.”"}

{"request_id":"57c2247ca2c5387fd7d30647","rewritten_text":"All this, and more—much more—I would gladly lay out in detail. But to be brief, I need my reward. I am longing to return to my family and to my home; and as the price of any further communication from me—in light of what I can offer, which may shed understanding on many very important branches of physical and metaphysical science—I must ask, through the influence of your honorable body, for a pardon for the crime I committed in the death of the creditors when I left Rotterdam. This, then, is the purpose of the present paper. Its bearer, an inhabitant of the moon, whom I have persuaded and properly instructed to act as my messenger to the earth, will wait for your Excellencies’ pleasure, and return to me with the pardon in question, if it can be obtained in any way.

“I have the honor to be, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

After reading this extremely extraordinary document, Professor Rub-a-dub, it is said, dropped his pipe to the ground in the height of his surprise. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, having taken off his spectacles, wiped them, and then—so far did he forget both himself and his dignity—turned around three times on his heel in the purest essence of astonishment and admiration. There was no doubt about it—the pardon should be obtained. So at least swore, with a round oath, Professor Rub-a-dub; and so, in the end, thought the illustrious Von Underduk, as he took his brother in science by the arm. Without saying a word, he began to make his way home as best he could, to consider what measures should be taken. When he reached, however, the door of the burgomaster’s dwelling, the professor ventured to suggest that since the messenger had chosen to disappear—no doubt frightened to death by the savage appearance of the burghers of Rotterdam—the pardon would be of little use, because no one but a man of the moon would undertake a journey so vast a distance. The burgomaster agreed that this was true, and the matter was therefore over.

Not so, however, with rumors and speculation. Since the letter had been published, it sparked all kinds of gossip and opinions. Some of the over-wise even made themselves ridiculous by dismissing the whole affair as a hoax. But hoax, for people of that sort, is, I believe, a general term for anything beyond their understanding. As for me, I cannot imagine what grounds they have for making such an accusation. Let us see what they say:"}

{"request_id":"9dbf027faa4212c18b8afea1","rewritten_text":"His figure was small, yet he stood with an extraordinary straightness, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He opened his discourse with a brief review of the history of chemistry and the improvements introduced by learned men, uttering with great warmth the names of the most celebrated discoverers. He then gave a quick survey of the science as it stood at present, and explained several of its first principles and common terms. After a few preliminary experiments, he ended with a glowing tribute to modern chemistry—words which I shall never forget:

“The ancient teachers of this science,” said he, “promised impossibilities and accomplished nothing. The modern masters promise very little; they are aware that metals cannot be transmuted, and that the elixir of life is a mere chimera. Yet these philosophers—whose hands seem made only to dabble in dirt, and whose eyes are meant to pore over the microscope or the crucible—have truly wrought miracles. They press into the hidden recesses of nature and show how she operates in her secret places. They rise into the heavens; they have learned how the blood circulates, and what is the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new powers, almost without limit; they can command the thunders of heaven, imitate the earthquake, and even mock the unseen world with shadows of its own.”

Such were the professor’s words—no, rather such were the words of fate, spoken to ruin me. As he continued, it seemed to me that my soul was wrestling with a tangible foe; key after key was turned, each one fitting the mechanism of my being; note after note was struck, and soon my mind was filled with a single thought, a single idea, a single resolve. “So much has been done,” cried the soul of Frankenstein; “more, far more, will I accomplish. Following the path already traced, I will strike out a new course, seek out unknown powers, and lay before the world the deepest mysteries of creation.”

I did not close my eyes that night. My inward life was in a state of rebellion and agitation; I felt that order would come from it, but I had no strength to bring it about. By degrees, after the morning had dawned, sleep at last overtook me. When I awoke, the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. There was nothing left but to resolve to return to my earlier studies and to devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural aptitude. On the same day I went to call upon M. Waldman. In private his manners were even gentler and more engaging than in public; for though a certain dignity marked his bearing during his lecture, at home it gave way to the greatest affability and kindness."}

{"request_id":"b46b35df784c6c75216b96d7","rewritten_text":"And if he asked me why I wanted it, and why I thought I had any right to it, I would tell him—though he cared very little for such small hopes—that I had loved Estella dearly for a long time. Even though I had lost her and would have to live as a grieving man, anything connected to her was still closer and more important to me than anything else in the world. Seeing that Mr. Jaggers stayed perfectly still and silent, and seemed unmoved by my plea, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you’re a man with a gentle heart. I’ve seen your comfortable home, your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful ways you have of making your work feel brighter. I beg you to say something to Mr. Jaggers for me, and to tell him that, given all the circumstances, he should be more open with me.”

I had never seen two men stare at each other so strangely as Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after that. At first, I worried that Wemmick would be fired at once. But that fear faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers relax into something like a smile, and when Wemmick grew more confident.

“What is all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You, with an old father? You, with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick answered. “If I don’t bring them here, what difference does it make?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, putting his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this man must be the cleverest impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” Wemmick replied, getting bolder and bolder. “I think you’re the impostor.”

They exchanged those same odd looks again, both still seeming to doubt that the other was really accepting him.

“You, with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Only if it doesn’t get in the way of business,” Wemmick said. “Let it be so. And now, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if you’re planning to have a pleasant home of your own one of these days, when you’re tired of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded his head two or three times, as if looking back on it, and even let out a sigh. “Pip,” he said, “we won’t talk about ‘poor dreams.’ You know more about that sort of thing than I do, since you have had fresher experience. But now, about this other matter. I’ll put a case to you. Mind— I admit nothing.”

He waited for me to say that I understood he had clearly meant that he admitted nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “put this case. Imagine that a woman, under the kind of circumstances you’ve described, kept her child hidden, and had to tell her legal adviser about it. She did so because he told her that, for the sake of the range of his defense, he needed to know how the situation really stood with that child.”"}

Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and her consideration for his comfort struck him as truly remarkable. Mr. Bennet could not have chosen better. Mr. Collins was eloquent in praising her. The subject put him into more than his usual solemn mood; and with an air of the utmost importance, he protested that he had never in his life witnessed such conduct in a person of rank—such affability and condescension—as he had personally experienced from Lady Catherine. She had been gracious enough to approve both sermons he had already had the honor of preaching before her. She had also asked him twice to dine at Rosings, and had sent for him only the Saturday before, so he could take his place in her evening quadrille. Many people, he knew, considered Lady Catherine proud, but he had never seen anything in her except affability. She had always spoken to him as she would to any other gentleman; she had raised not the slightest objection to his joining the neighborhood’s society, nor to his leaving his parish now and then for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even condescended to advise him to marry as soon as he could, as long as he chose with discretion. And once she had visited his humble parsonage, where she had approved everything he had been doing to make alterations, and had even deigned to suggest a few herself—some shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That’s all very proper and civil, I’m sure,” said Mrs. Bennet. “And I dare say she’s a very agreeable woman. It’s a pity that great ladies in general aren’t more like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden where my humble home stands is separated from Rosings Park by only a lane—her Ladyship’s residence.”

“I thought you said she was a widow, sir. Does she have any family?”

“She has one only daughter—the heiress of Rosings—and of very extensive property.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she’s better off than many girls. And what kind of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is a most charming young lady, indeed. Lady Catherine herself says that, in terms of true beauty, Miss de Bourgh is far superior to the handsomest woman of her sex; because there’s something in her features that marks her as a young woman of distinguished birth.”"}

{"request_id":"8ca3b2352da94aa47b1ae606","rewritten_text":"But I have to warn you first: I will tell Sybil everything. She’s coming to lunch with me tomorrow to talk about bonnets. And if Mr. Podgers finds out that you have a bad temper, or a tendency to gout, or a wife living in Bayswater, I will certainly tell her all about it.”

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. “I’m not afraid,” he said. “Sybil knows me as well as I know her.”

“Ah, I’m sorry to hear you say that,” the Marchioness of Jedburgh replied. “The best foundation for marriage is a mutual misunderstanding. No, I’m not cynical. I just have experience, which is basically the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is dying to have his hand read. Don’t tell him that he’s engaged to one of the most beautiful girls in London, because that was printed in the _Morning Post_ a month ago.”

“Dear Lady Windermere,” cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, “please let Mr. Podgers stay here a little longer. He just told me I should go on the stage, and I’m so interested.”

“If he told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I will take him away for sure,” said Lady Windermere. “Come here right now, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.”

“Well,” said Lady Jedburgh, making a small pout as she stood up from the sofa, “if I can’t be allowed to go on the stage, then I should at least be allowed to be part of the audience.”

“Of course,” said Lady Windermere. “We’re all going to be part of the audience. Now, Mr. Podgers, be sure to tell us something nice. Lord Arthur is one of my favorites.”

But the moment Mr. Podgers saw Lord Arthur’s hand, he turned strangely pale and said nothing. A shiver seemed to run through him, and his thick, bushy eyebrows twitched in a nervous, irritating way, the way they did when he was confused. Then huge drops of sweat appeared on his yellow forehead, like a poisonous mist, and his fat fingers went cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur noticed every one of these signs of distress. For the first time in his life, he felt fear. He wanted to rush out of the room, but he held back. It was better to find out the worst, whatever it was, than to be stuck in this awful uncertainty.

“I’m waiting, Mr. Podgers,” he said.

“We’re all waiting,” Lady Windermere said quickly and impatiently, but the cheiromantist still didn’t answer.

“I think Arthur is going on the stage,” said Lady Jedburgh. “And after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him so.”"}

{"request_id":"45ee74d771bb63706658c68c","rewritten_text":"All of this, and more—much more—I would gladly explain. But to keep it brief, I need my reward. I long to return to my family and my home. And as the price for any further messages from me—because I can share what I know about many important parts of physical and metaphysical science—I ask, through the influence of your honorable body, for a pardon for the crime I committed when the creditors died after my departure from Rotterdam. That is the purpose of this paper. The person who will carry it is a resident of the moon. I have persuaded and instructed him to act as my messenger to Earth. He will wait for your Excellencies’ decision, and then return to me with the pardon, if it can be obtained in any way.

“I have the honor to be, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

After reading this extraordinary document, Professor Rub-a-dub, it is said, dropped his pipe to the ground from sheer surprise. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk took off his spectacles, wiped them, and put them in his pocket. Then, forgetting both himself and his dignity, he turned around three times on his heel, in the height of astonishment and admiration. There was no doubt about it—the pardon should be obtained. That was what Professor Rub-a-dub swore to with a loud oath, and what the distinguished Von Underduk finally decided as well. He took his brother in science by the arm, said nothing, and started making his way home to think through what should be done.

When they reached the door of the burgomaster’s house, however, the professor suggested that the pardon might not help much. The messenger had disappeared, and the professor assumed he had done so because he was frightened to death by the savage look of the people of Rotterdam. If that was the case, then the pardon would be useless, because only someone from the moon would agree to travel such a huge distance. The burgomaster agreed with this point, and the matter was settled.

Rumors and speculation were not so easily ended. Since the letter had been published, it led to all kinds of gossip and opinions. Some of the overly clever people made themselves look foolish by calling the whole thing a hoax. But for people like that, I believe “hoax” is just a general word for anything beyond their understanding. As for me, I cannot see what facts they used to support their accusation. Let’s see what they say:"}

{"request_id":"da38170f2d07bfa134775ab7","rewritten_text":"In fact, he was dressed as “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,” one of his most remarkable impersonations—one the Cantervilles had every reason to remember, since it was the real spark for their quarrel with their neighbor, Lord Rufford. It was about a quarter past two in the morning, and, as far as he could tell, no one was moving. Still, as he strolled toward the library to check whether any traces remained of the bloodstain, two figures suddenly sprang out at him from a dark corner. They flailed their arms wildly above their heads and shrieked “BOO!” right into his ear.

Overcome by panic—which, given the circumstances, was only natural—he bolted for the staircase, but Washington Otis was waiting there with the big garden syringe. Hemmed in by his enemies on every side, driven almost to the edge, he disappeared into the large iron stove, which, fortunately for him, was not lit. From there he had to make his way home through the flues and chimneys, arriving in his own room in a terrible state of dirt, chaos, and despair.

After that, he was not seen again on any night-time expedition. The twins lay in wait for him on several occasions and every night scattered the passages with nutshells, to the great annoyance of their parents and the servants, but it made no difference. It was clear that his feelings were so badly hurt that he wouldn’t show up again. Mr. Otis therefore resumed his major work on the history of the Democratic Party, which he had been working on for some years; Mrs. Otis organized a wonderful clam-bake that amazed the whole county; the boys took up lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games; and Virginia rode around the lanes on her pony, accompanied by the young Duke of Cheshire, who had come to spend the last week of his holidays at Canterville Chase. Everyone assumed the ghost had gone away. In fact, Mr. Otis wrote a letter to Lord Canterville saying as much. In reply, Lord Canterville expressed his great pleasure at the news and sent his best congratulations to the Minister’s worthy wife.

The Otises, however, were being fooled, because the ghost was still in the house. Though now almost an invalid, he was in no mood to let things rest—especially once he heard that among the guests was the young Duke of Cheshire. His grand-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once bet a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost. The next morning, he was found lying on the floor of the card room in such a helpless paralytic state that, though he lived to a great age, he was never able to say anything again except “Double Sixes.”"}
