{"request_id":"4177fbf0f5e09105fccfcd7c","rewritten_text":"Far off, the flickering line of gas-lamps bent away into the distance, and just beyond a small, walled-in house a lone hansom waited, the driver asleep within. He set off briskly toward Portland Place, glancing over his shoulder now and then, as if he were afraid someone might be trailing him. At the corner of Rich Street two men stood reading a small notice pinned to a hoarding. A strange prickle of curiosity seized him, and he crossed over.

As he drew near, the word “Murder,” printed in bold black letters, caught his eye. He gave a start, and a hot flush spread up into his cheek. It was an advertisement offering a reward for any information that would lead to the arrest of a man of medium height, between thirty and forty years old, wearing a billy-cock hat, a black coat, and check trousers, with a scar on his right cheek. He read it again and again, unable to stop himself, and found his thoughts turning to whether the poor wretch would ever be caught, and how he had come by that scar. Maybe, some day, his own name would be pasted up on the walls of London. Maybe, too, a price would be put on his head.

The idea sickened him with sheer horror. He wheeled about and hurried on into the night.

Where he went, he could scarcely say. He had only a hazy recollection of threading through a maze of mean houses, of getting swallowed up in a tangle of gloomy streets, and it was bright dawn before he finally emerged in Piccadilly Circus. As he wandered back toward Belgrave Square, he met the great waggons bound for Covent Garden. The carters, in their white smocks, with sunburnt faces and thick, curly hair, marched on with steady purpose, cracking their whips and calling to one another now and then; on the back of a huge grey horse, the leader of a clattering team, sat a chubby boy with a battered hat and a bunch of primroses, gripping the mane tightly with his small hands and laughing. The towering heaps of vegetables looked like blocks of jade against the morning sky—like masses of green jade set against the pink petals of some extraordinary rose. Lord Arthur felt oddly stirred, though he could not have said why. There was something in the dawn’s delicate beauty that struck him as inexpressibly pathetic, and he thought of all the days that break in loveliness and then fall into storm. Even these rustics, with their rough, good-natured voices and their easy, careless ways, seemed to him to show him a strange London: one free of the sin of night and the smoke of day, a pale, ghostly city, a desolate place of tombs. He wondered what they made of it, and whether they knew anything of its splendour and its shame—of its fierce, blazing-coloured joys, and of everything it both creates and ruins from morning to night."}

{"request_id":"1186d4aae3fa3a04b7c5f7b2","rewritten_text":"You will be glad to hear that no disaster has marked the start of an enterprise you have viewed with such dark forebodings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first task is to reassure my dear sister of my well-being and of my growing confidence in the success of what I’m setting out to do.

I’m already far north of London, and as I walk through the streets of Petersburgh, I feel a cold northern breeze touch my cheeks. It steadies my nerves and fills me with delight. Do you understand that feeling? This breeze, coming from the regions I’m moving toward, gives me a preview of those icy climates. Encouraged by this promising wind, my daydreams become more intense and vivid. I try in vain to convince myself that the pole is the place of frost and desolation; it always appears in my imagination as a region of beauty and joy. There, Margaret, the sun is always visible—its broad disk just skimming the horizon and spreading a constant brilliance. There—if you’ll allow me, my sister, I’ll trust in the navigators who came before—snow and frost are gone. And sailing over a calm sea, we may be carried to a land that surpasses every region discovered so far in wonders and beauty on the habitable globe. Its features and products may have no equal, just as the phenomena of the heavenly bodies undoubtedly do in those undiscovered places. What could we not expect in a country of endless light? I may there uncover the remarkable power that draws the needle and be able to regulate a thousand celestial observations that, with only this voyage, would make their apparent irregularities consistent forever. I will satisfy my intense curiosity by seeing a part of the world never before visited, and I may walk on land never before marked by the foot of man. These are my reasons for being drawn in, and they’re enough to overcome every fear of danger or death and to make me begin this difficult voyage with the same joy a child feels when he sets off in a small boat with his holiday friends on an expedition of discovery up his home river.

But even if all these guesses are wrong, you can’t deny the priceless benefit I will bring to all mankind, even to the last generation, by finding a passage near the pole to those countries that, for now, require so many months to reach—or by uncovering the secret of magnetism, which, if it’s possible at all, can only be learned through an undertaking like mine.

These thoughts have driven away the agitation I felt when I started my letter, and I feel my heart warm with an enthusiasm that lifts me toward heaven. Nothing helps to calm the mind so much as a steady purpose—a point on which the soul can fix its intellectual gaze."}

{"request_id":"695f71f2c6ce05d873528d09","rewritten_text":"“These were the events that preyed on Felix’s heart and made him, when I first saw him, the most miserable member of his family. He could have endured poverty, and while that hardship had been the reward of his virtue, he took pride in it; but the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were misfortunes far more bitter and beyond repair. The Arabian’s arrival now poured new life into his soul.

“When word reached Leghorn that Felix had been stripped of his wealth and rank, the merchant ordered his daughter to stop thinking about her lover and to prepare to return to her native country. Safie’s generous nature was outraged by this command. She tried to argue with her father, but he stormed out, repeating his tyrannical order.

“A few days later, the Turk entered his daughter’s apartment and told her, in a hurry, that he had reason to believe his stay in Leghorn had been discovered and that he should be handed over to the French government without delay. He had therefore hired a vessel to take him to Constantinople, where he would sail in only a few hours. He planned to leave his daughter in the care of a trusted servant, while he followed later at his leisure with most of his property, which had not yet arrived in Leghorn.

“When she was alone, Safie decided, in her own mind, what course of action she should take in this emergency. Living in Turkey was unbearable to her; her religion and her feelings were both strongly opposed to it. From some papers of her father that came into her hands, she learned that her lover had been exiled and discovered the name of the place where he was then living. She hesitated for a while, but in the end she made her decision. She took with her a few jewels that belonged to her and a sum of money, left Italy with an attendant—a native of Leghorn who understood the common language of Turkey—and set out for Germany.

“She arrived safely at a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage, but her attendant soon fell dangerously ill. Safie nursed her with the most devoted affection, yet the poor girl died, leaving the Arabian alone—unable to speak the language of the country and completely ignorant of the world’s customs. Still, she fell into good hands. The Italian had mentioned the name of the place they were traveling to, and after her death the woman of the house where they had lived made sure that Safie reached her lover’s cottage safely.”"}

{"request_id":"6c5e0bc5109a360950ae433f","rewritten_text":"“Listen, then! You!” Monks replied. “His father fell ill in Rome, and then he was joined by his wife—my mother—who had been separated from him for a long time. She left Paris and brought me with her, so she could look after his property. From what I know, neither of them had much affection for the other. His father knew nothing about us, because his senses were gone, and he slept until the next day, when he died. Among the papers in his desk were two, dated the night his illness first began, and they were addressed to you.” He turned to Mr. Brownlow. “They were also enclosed in a few short lines to you, and the cover said the package was not to be sent on until after he was dead. One paper was a letter to this girl, Agnes. The other was a will.

“What about the letter?” Mr. Brownlow asked.

“The letter? It was a sheet of paper covered and covered again with writing—full of a confession and prayers to God to help her. He had told the girl a story, saying that some secret mystery—something he would explain one day—was the reason he could not marry her yet. So she kept waiting for him, trusting him patiently, until she trusted too much and lost what no one could ever give back. At that time she was only a few months away from giving birth. He told her everything he had meant to do, to hide her shame, if he had lived. And if he died, he asked her not to curse his memory, or believe that the consequences of their sin would fall on her or on their young child. He said all the guilt was his. He reminded her of the day he gave her the little locket and the ring with her Christian name engraved on it, and he left a blank space for the name he hoped one day to put there—he prayed she would keep it and wear it close to her heart, the way she had before. Then he kept going, wildly, repeating the same words over and over, as if he had lost his mind. I think he had.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow said, as Oliver’s tears fell fast.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued, speaking for him, “was written in the same spirit as the letter. He talked about the misery his wife had brought him. He blamed you, his only son, for your rebellious nature, your vice, your malice, and your early bad passions—because you were trained to hate him. He left you, and your mother, each an annuity of eight hundred pounds. He divided the rest of his property into two equal parts: one for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, if it was born alive and ever reached adulthood.”"}

{"request_id":"da4ad88b41ab24d461fe0a72","rewritten_text":"Emma was never, by any later discovery, made to withdraw her harsh opinion of Mrs. Elton. What she had observed the first time had been pretty much right. As Mrs. Elton presented herself to her on this second interview, so she appeared whenever they met again—self-important, forward, familiar, ignorant, and ill-bred. She had a little beauty and a little accomplishment, but so scanty a share of judgment that Emma believed her to imagine she was bringing superior knowledge of the world to enliven and improve a country neighbourhood; and she even supposed Miss Hawkins to have held a place in society that Mrs. Elton’s consequence alone could outdo.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton differed in his thoughts from his wife. He seemed not only content with her, but proud of her. He had the look of congratulating himself on having brought such a woman to Highbury, as if not even Miss Woodhouse could match her; and most of the new acquaintance, disposed to praise or not accustomed to judge, fell in with Miss Bates’s good humour, or took it for granted that the bride must be as clever and as agreeable as she claimed to be. Thus Mrs. Elton’s commendations passed from one person to another as they ought to, without any check from Miss Woodhouse, who continued with ready good grace her first contribution, and talked of her being “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one respect, Mrs. Elton became even worse than she had seemed at first. Her feelings shifted towards Emma.—Offended, most likely, by the slight encouragement her proposals of intimacy received, she drew back in her turn and grew gradually colder and more distant; and though the change was agreeable in its effect, the ill-will that caused it could only be increasing Emma’s dislike. Their manners, too—Mrs. Elton’s and Mr. Elton’s—were disagreeable towards Harriet. They were sneering and careless. Emma hoped it would soon bring Harriet’s cure about; but the very temper that could lead to such conduct lowered them both in her estimation.—There was no doubting that poor Harriet’s attachment had been offered up as a kind of conjugal indiscretion, and that her own part in the affair, given under the least favourable colouring to her and the most soothing to him, had in all likelihood been supplied as well. Harriet, of course, was the object of their joint dislike.—When they had nothing else to say, it was always easy to begin by abusing Miss Woodhouse; and the enmity they dared not show in open disrespect to her found a wider outlet in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.

Mrs. Elton took a strong fancy to Jane Fairfax; and from the very beginning. Not only when a state of rivalry with one young lady might be thought to make the other more desirable, but from the first moment itself; and she was not content merely to express a natural and reasonable admiration—but without being asked, without excuse, without any claim or privilege, she must be eager to assist and befriend her.—Before Emma had lost her confidence, and about the third time of their meeting, she heard the whole of Mrs. Elton’s knight-errantry on the subject."}

{"request_id":"c045a15da9be186d8c3d620f","rewritten_text":"We shouted so loudly and so sincerely that we were free men that we caught the attention of that liberty-speaking orator and his patriotic crowd. They gathered around us and took on a very determined look. The orator said:

“If you really are free men, then you have nothing to fear. The God-given liberties of Britain are all around you, like a shield and shelter! (Applause.) You’ll see soon. Bring out your proof.”

“What proof?”

“Proof that you are free men.”

Ah—I remembered. I came to my senses, and I said nothing. But the king stormed out.

“You’re insane, man. It would be better, and more reasonable, for this thief and scoundrel to prove that we are not free men.”

You see, he knew his own laws the way other people often know laws: by words, not by results. They take a meaning and make it feel very real once you try to apply it to yourself.

Everyone shook their heads and looked disappointed. Some turned away and lost interest. The orator said again, this time in a practical tone, not a sentimental one:

“If you don’t know your country’s laws, then it’s time you learned them. You are strangers to us, and you won’t deny that. You might be free men—we’re not denying that—but you might also be slaves. The law is clear. It does not require the person making the claim to prove you are slaves. It requires you to prove you are not.”

I said, “Sir, just give us time to send to Astolat, or give us time to send to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Peace, good man. These are unusual requests, and you can’t expect them to be granted. It would take too much time, and it would seriously inconvenience your master.”

“Master,” the king snapped, “you idiot! I have no master. I am the m—”

“Silence, for God’s sake!”

I managed to get the words out in time to stop the king. We were already in enough trouble. It wouldn’t help us to give these people the idea that we were crazy.

There’s no point in dragging out every detail. The earl arranged for us to be put up for auction and sold. This same awful law had existed in my own South in my own time, more than thirteen hundred years later, and under it hundreds of free men who couldn’t prove they were free were sold into lifelong slavery, and it didn’t make much of an impression on me. But the moment the exact law and the auction block became part of my own life, something that had only seemed wrong before turned suddenly into something truly hellish. That’s how it works.

Yes, we were sold at auction, like pigs. In a big town with a busy market we would have fetched a good price, but this place was completely dead, so we sold for an amount that makes me ashamed every time I think about it."}

{"request_id":"6c6c5e01eaafa086d124fb81","rewritten_text":"When Emma read over her letter again, and then wrote her reply, it made her feel softer. Because of that, she had to steady herself with a few firm words. She was very worried about the idea of making him unhappy, and she kept thinking about what his mother and sisters would think and say. She was also afraid they would think she was ungrateful. So Emma believed that if the young man had happened to come by at that moment, he would still have been accepted.

But the letter was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was finished, and Harriet was safe. Harriet was rather low all evening, but Emma could understand her gentle regrets. Sometimes she eased them by talking about her own affection, and sometimes she brought up the idea of Mr. Elton.

“I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” Harriet said, in a rather sad tone.

“Nor, if you were, could I ever bear to be separated from you, my Harriet. You are far too important at Hartfield to be spared to Abbey-Mill.”

“And I’m sure I would never want to go there,” Harriet replied. “I’m never happy anywhere except at Hartfield.”

After some time, Harriet said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what happened. I’m sure Miss Nash would be surprised too. Miss Nash thinks her own sister is very well married, and it’s only a linen-draper.”

“One should feel sorry to see more pride or refinement in a schoolteacher, Harriet,” Emma said. “I dare say Miss Nash would envy you the chance to be married. Even this match would look valuable to her. As for anything better for you, I suppose she has no idea. The attention of a certain person can hardly be part of the gossip in Highbury yet. So far, I think you and I are the only ones whose eyes and manners have made it clear.”

Harriet blushed and smiled, and said something about being surprised that people liked her so much. The thought of Mr. Elton was certainly cheering, but after a while she became tender-hearted again toward the man who had been rejected, Mr. Martin.

“Now he has got my letter,” Harriet said softly. “I wonder what they are all doing. Do his sisters know? If he is unhappy, they will be unhappy too. I hope it won’t trouble him too much.”

“Let’s think about those among our friends who are away and are being kept busy in a happier way,” Emma said. “At this moment, perhaps, Mr. Elton is showing your picture to his mother and sisters. He is telling them how much more beautiful the original is, and after being asked for it five or six times, he keeps letting them hear your name—your own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"3a4392c39f7b4abd0377eec0","rewritten_text":"It was in Warwick Castle that I met the strange man I’m going to tell you about. He drew me in for three reasons: he was openly simple, he knew ancient armor in a way that was truly impressive, and his presence felt calm and easy—because he did all the talking. We ended up together, like quiet people do, at the back of the group being led through, and he immediately started saying things that held my attention.

As he spoke, softly and smoothly, he seemed to slip away from the present, almost without me noticing, and drift into a far-off time and a long-forgotten country. Slowly, he cast a spell over me. It felt as if I was walking among the ghosts, shadows, dust, and mold of a gray, ancient age, having conversations with something left over from it. He talked about Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other great names of the Round Table, just as naturally as I might talk about my closest friends or enemies, or the people I see every day. And as he went on, it became clear how old—so old it was almost beyond words—how faded, dry, musty, and ancient he thought these things were.

Then he turned to me and said, in the same casual way someone might talk about the weather or any other ordinary subject—

“Do you know about the transmigration of souls? And do you know about the transposition of epochs—and bodies?”

I told him I hadn’t heard of it. He seemed no more interested than someone talking about the weather, and he didn’t even seem to notice whether I answered him or not. For a moment there was silence, and then it was broken by the dull, practiced voice of the guide.

“Ancient hauberk, date of the sixth century, time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; observe the round hole through the chain-mail in the left breast; can’t be explained; thought to have been made with a bullet after firearms were invented—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My new acquaintance smiled—not like a modern smile, but one that must have disappeared from common use many, many centuries ago—and muttered as if to himself, “Wit ye well, I saw it done.” Then, after a pause, he added, “I did it myself.”

When I finally recovered from the shock of that statement, he was already gone.

That whole evening I sat by the fire at the Warwick Arms, lost in a dream of the old days while rain hammered the windows and the wind roared around the eaves and corners. From time to time I opened old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, let myself feed on its rich store of wonders and adventures, breathed in the smell of its outdated names, and dreamed again."}

{"request_id":"210d8cc57acc3458bc1a1fce","rewritten_text":"I am also told by Mrs. Otis, who, I should say, is an authority on Art. She spent several winters in Boston when she was young, and she believes these gems are worth a great deal of money. If they were offered for sale, they would bring a very high price. Given all that, Lord Canterville, I think you will understand that it would be impossible for me to let any member of my family keep them. In fact, all these silly ornaments and toys, even if they suit the dignity of the British aristocracy, would be completely out of place with people who were raised on the strict—and I believe immortal—principles of republican simplicity.

Perhaps I should add that Virginia is very anxious for you to let her keep the box as a reminder of your unfortunate but misguided ancestor. Since it is extremely old and, as a result, in pretty poor condition, you may decide to grant her request. As for me, I admit I am surprised to hear one of my children show sympathy for anything medieval. I can only explain it by the fact that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from a trip to Athens.

Lord Canterville listened very seriously to the worthy minister’s speech, tugging at his grey moustache now and then to hide an involuntary smile. When Mr. Otis finished, he shook his hand warmly and said, “My dear sir, your charming little daughter did my unlucky ancestor, Sir Simon, a great service. My family and I are deeply grateful to her for her wonderful courage and spirit. The jewels are clearly hers. And, egad, if I were cruel enough to take them from her, that wicked old fellow would be out of his grave in a fortnight, causing me the devil of a life.

As for them being heirlooms, nothing is an heirloom unless it is named in a will or a legal document. The truth is that no one even knew these jewels existed. I can assure you I have no more right to them than your butler does. And when Miss Virginia grows up, I’m sure she will enjoy having pretty things to wear.

Also, you forget, Mr. Otis, that you bought the furniture and the ghost at a valuation. Anything that belonged to the ghost passed to you at once. Whatever Sir Simon may have done in the corridor at night, in law he was truly dead, and you acquired his property by purchase.”"}

{"request_id":"36cf5a2940a0f9fdde77a772","rewritten_text":"The congratulatory letter Elizabeth received from Lydia about her marriage told her that, at least by Lydia’s wife, and perhaps by Lydia herself, such a hope was being held. The letter said this:—

“My dear Lizzy,

I wish you joy. If you love Mr. Darcy half as well as I love my dear Wickham, you must be very happy. It is a great comfort to have you so rich; and when you have nothing else to do, I hope you will think of us. I am sure Wickham would like a place at court very much, and I do not think we will have quite enough money to live on without some help. Any place would do, as long as it pays about three or four hundred a year; but, whatever you do, don’t speak to Mr. Darcy about it, if you would rather not.

Yours, etc.

As it happened, Elizabeth would much rather not, so in her reply she tried to end every request and expectation of that kind. Still, whenever she could, she offered whatever relief she could manage by being careful with her own private spending. She had always known that their income would not be enough, given how extravagant their needs were and how little they thought about the future. Every time they moved to new quarters, either Jane or Elizabeth was sure to be asked for a little help to pay their bills. Even after peace was restored and they could finally settle at home, their life was still unsettled. They were always searching for a cheap place to live, and they were always spending more than they should. His affection for her soon turned into indifference; hers lasted a little longer. Even so, despite her youth and her manners, she kept all the claims to reputation that her marriage had given her. Darcy could never receive him at Pemberley, but for Elizabeth’s sake he still helped him in his profession.

Lydia sometimes visited Pemberley when her husband was away enjoying himself in London or Bath. With the Bingleys, they stayed there so long that even Bingley’s good humor was worn down, and he went so far as to talk about giving them a hint to leave.

Miss Bingley was very upset by Darcy’s marriage. But since she thought it best to keep the right to visit Pemberley, she dropped her resentment. She became even more fond of Georgiana, was almost as attentive to Darcy as before, and paid Elizabeth back for every bit of civility she owed her.”}]}]}"}

{"request_id":"8e1dc056217e74aa861a716c","rewritten_text":"Yet he had one secret he kept from these dear friends. It was a secret he had carried since his earliest years. Even though he loved his fellow students, he would not trust this secret to their care or their sympathy. He loved, but he feared that the strength of his feelings would become a joke to them. He also could not bear the idea that they might treat what he felt was the real meaning of his life as something small and temporary.

Near his family mansion lived a gentleman of modest means. He had three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, but her beauty was only one part of her. She also had a clear, strong mind, and her nature was as gentle as an angel. She and my father had been playmates since they were children. Diana, even when she was young, had been his mother’s favorite. That preference grew over the years, and during his school and college breaks they were almost always together. Books and the many ways that young people in civilized life are taught about passions before they truly feel them had made a deep impression on him, because he was unusually sensitive to every kind of experience. At eleven, Diana was his favorite playmate, and yet he already spoke the language of love.

She was nearly two years older than he was, but her education had made her more childish, at least when it came to understanding and expressing feelings. She received his warm promises with innocence, and she did not know what they meant. She had not read novels and spent her time only with her younger sisters. What could she know about the difference between love and friendship? And when her understanding finally showed her what this relationship really was, her feelings were already tied to her friend. All she feared was that other attractions or his own changeable nature might make him break the vows of their childhood.

Still, their bond grew stronger every day, becoming more ardent and tender. It was a passion that had grown as he grew. It had become part of every part of him—his thoughts, his feelings, and his deepest sentiments—and it could only be lost with life itself. No one knew about their love except their two hearts. And yet, in everything else, and even in this, he feared what his companions might say. He knew that loving someone of lower fortune than his own would invite their judgment. But nothing could shake his plan to marry her as soon as he could find the courage to face those difficulties, and he was determined to overcome them.

Diana was fully worthy of his deepest affection."}

{"request_id":"6f8facae67b023a89bcc3e67","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats. Every so often you’d see one stick its nose out of a hole in the corner. She said she had to keep things ready to throw at them when she was alone, or they wouldn’t leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot, and said she was a good shot with it generally, but she’d wrenched her arm a day or two ago and didn’t know whether she could throw straight now. Still, she watched for a chance, and then she went for a rat—she banged at it—but she missed him badly, and she said, “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so much. Then she told me to try for the next one.

I wanted to get away before the old man came back, but of course I didn’t let on. I took the lead, and the first rat that showed its nose—I let it have it. If it had stayed where it was, it would’ve been a decent sick rat. She said that was first-rate and figured I’d get the next one too. She went and got the lump of lead again, brought it back, and also brought a hank of yarn she wanted me to help her with. I held up my two hands, and she put the hank over them, then kept talking about her and her husband’s business. But she stopped to say:

“Keep your eye on the rats. You’d better have the lead in your lap, ready.”

So she dropped the lump into my lap right then, and I clapped my legs together over it, and she went on talking. Only about a minute. Then she took the hank away, looked me straight in the face, and in a very pleasant voice said:

“Come on now—what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob?—or what is it?”

I think I shook like a leaf. I didn’t know what to do. But I said, “Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m in the way here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay where you are. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you either. You just tell me your secret, and trust me. I’ll keep it—and what’s more, I’ll help you. So will my old man, if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway apprentice—that’s all. It isn’t anything. There’s no harm in it. You’ve been treated badly, and you decided to cut out. Bless you, child—I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"2d85a9cca098390d9970cba1","rewritten_text":"She studied me closely for a moment, and then spoke in a low voice,—

“What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I said, “that you won’t mix them up with the others. They may share the same blood, but, trust me, they are not of the same sort.”

Still regarding me with that same keen attention, Miss Havisham repeated,—

“What do you want for them?”

“I’m not so clever, you see,” I answered, feeling my cheeks warm a little, “that I could keep anything from you, even if I wished to. I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you’ll spare the money to give my friend Herbert a lasting benefit in life—one that, by the very nature of it, must be done without his knowing—I can show you how.”

“Why must it be done without his knowledge?” she asked, resting her hands on her stick so she could look at me even more intently.

“Because,” said I, “I started that service myself, more than two years ago, without his knowledge, and I don’t want it to be turned against me. I can’t explain why I’ve failed to carry it through. It’s part of a secret that belongs to someone else, not to me.”

She slowly let her gaze slip away from me and fixed it on the fire. After watching it for what seemed a long while—through the hush and by the light of candles that were burning down—she was stirred when some of the red coals collapsed. Then she looked back toward me again—first without expression, and then with attention that steadily sharpened. All the while, Estella kept knitting. When Miss Havisham finally settled her focus on me, she said, as though there had been no pause in our talk,—

“What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her and struggling to steady my voice, “you know I love you. You know I have loved you for a long time, and with all my heart.”

She lifted her eyes to my face as I spoke, and her fingers continued at their work; she regarded me with an expression that never changed. I noticed Miss Havisham glance from me to her, and from her back to me.

“I ought to have said it sooner, but for my long error. It made me hope that Miss Havisham meant us for one another. While I believed you couldn’t help yourself, as it were, I held back. But I must say it now.”

With her unmoved look preserved, and her hands still busy, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I replied to that motion. “I have no hope that I shall ever be able to call you mine, Estella.”"}

{"request_id":"6c430ec288c2757bedecd22b","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, and by the blue sky of heaven, and by the fire of love that burns in my heart, that if you grant my prayer, while they exist you shall never see me again. Go on to your home and begin your work; I shall watch their progress with unbearable anxiety; and don’t fear that when you are ready I won’t appear.”

With that, he suddenly left me, frightened—perhaps—of any change in my feelings. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle’s flight, and soon he was lost among the rolling waves of the sea of ice.

His story had taken up the whole day, and the sun was already near the horizon when he departed. I knew I should hurry down toward the valley, because darkness would soon surround me; but my heart was heavy, and my steps were slow. The work of winding through the mountain’s narrow paths and planting my feet firmly as I went left me perplexed, because I was still caught up in the emotions the day’s events had stirred. Long after night had fallen, I reached the halfway resting-place and sat down beside the fountain. The stars shone here and there as the clouds passed over them; dark pines rose before me, and now and then a broken tree lay on the ground. It was a scene of profound solemnity, and it stirred strange thoughts in me. I wept bitterly, and with my hands clasped in agony I cried, “Oh, stars and clouds and winds—you’re all about to mock me. If you truly pity me, crush feeling and memory; let me become nothing. But if you don’t, go, go, and leave me in darkness.”

These were wild and miserable thoughts, but I can’t tell you how the endless twinkling of the stars weighed on me, and how I listened to every blast of wind as if it were a dull, ugly sirocco on its way to consume me.

Morning came before I reached the village of Chamounix. I took no rest, but returned at once to Geneva. Even in my own heart I couldn’t put my feelings into words—they pressed on me with the weight of a mountain, and their sheer force crushed my agony beneath them. So I went back home, entered the house, and presented myself to the family. My haggard, wild appearance caused intense alarm, but I answered no questions and scarcely spoke. I felt as if I were under a curse—as if I had no right to ask for their sympathy—as if I would never again be able to enjoy their company.”"}

{"request_id":"482e3f1af6642cb82fec6a24","rewritten_text":"Far away, the line of gas lamps flickered in the dark. Outside a small walled-in house, a single hansom cab sat waiting, with the driver asleep inside. He walked quickly toward Portland Place, glancing around now and then, as if he was afraid someone was following him.

At the corner of Rich Street, two men stood reading a small notice pinned to a board. A strange feeling of curiosity came over him, so he crossed the street. As he got closer, the word “Murder,” printed in black letters, caught his eye. He stopped short, and a deep flush rose into his cheeks.

The notice was an advertisement offering a reward for any information that would lead to the arrest of a man of medium height, between thirty and forty years old, wearing a billy-cock hat, a black coat, and check trousers, with a scar on his right cheek. He read it again and again. He wondered whether the poor man would ever be caught, and how he had gotten that scar. Maybe, one day, his own name would be posted on the walls of London. Maybe, one day, a price would be put on his head too.

The thought filled him with horror. He turned sharply and hurried on into the night.

Where he went, he barely knew. He only had a vague memory of wandering through a maze of dirty houses, getting lost in a huge tangle of dark streets. By the time he finally found his way, it was bright dawn, and he was in Piccadilly Circus. As he walked home toward Belgrave Square, he met the big wagons heading to Covent Garden. The men driving them wore white smocks; their faces were sunburnt, and their coarse, curly hair showed as they walked firmly along, cracking their whips and calling to each other now and then. On the back of a large grey horse, the leader of a noisy team, sat a chubby boy with a battered hat. He held the horse’s mane tightly with his small hands, a bunch of primroses tucked in his hat, and he laughed.

The piles of vegetables looked like blocks of green jade against the morning sky, like green jade against the pink petals of some amazing rose. Lord Arthur felt strangely moved, though he could not say why. There was something about the dawn’s gentle beauty that seemed deeply sad to him. He thought about days that break in beauty and then end in storm. Even these country workers, with their rough but friendly voices and their relaxed ways, made him think: what a strange London they must see. A London without the sin of night and the smoke of day—a pale, ghost-like city, a lonely town of tombs. He wondered what they thought of it, and whether they knew anything about its splendor and its shame, its fierce, fiery joys, and the terrible hunger of it—everything it makes and ruins from morning to night."}

{"request_id":"cfb5d021306a4d51a9ebd6e1","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man—an awfully nice, kind-looking old man when I got him up. I told him me and my brother was over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and we camped on a piece of a raft we found. And about midnight, he must’ve kicked his gun in his dreams, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted him to go over there and fix it, and not say nothing about it, and not let anybody know, because we wanted to come home this evening and surprise the folks.

“Who is your folks?” he says.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. And after a minute, he says:

“How’d you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I says, “and it shot him.”

“Singular dream,” he says.

So he lit up his lantern, and got his saddle-bags, and we started. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like the look of her. He said she was big enough for one, but didn’t look pretty safe for two. I says:

“Oh, you needn’t be afeard, sir. She carried the three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and the guns—that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

But he put his foot on the gunnel, rocked her, and shook his head, and said he reckoned he’d look around for a bigger one. But all the others was locked and chained. So he took my canoe, and told me to wait till he came back, or I could hunt around further, or maybe I better go down home and get them ready for the surprise if I wanted to. But I said I didn’t. So I told him just how to find the raft, and then he started.

I struck an idea pretty soon. I says to myself, suppose’n he can’t fix that leg just in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, as the saying is—suppose’n it takes him three or four days? What are we going to do—lay around there till he lets the cat out of the bag? No, sir; I know what I’ll do. I’ll wait, and when he comes back if he says he’s got to go any more, I’ll get down there too, if I swim. And we’ll take and tie him, and keep him, and shove out down the river. And when Tom’s done with him, we’ll give him what it’s worth—or all we got—and then let him get ashore.

So then I crept into a lumber-pile to get some sleep. And the next time I woke up, the sun was way up over my head. I shot out and went for the doctor’s house, but they told me he’d gone away in the night some time or other, and he wasn’t back yet."}

{"request_id":"39bbc5ece3993ef5460deb36","rewritten_text":"Then they passed by lonely brickworks. The fog was thinner here, and he could make out the strange, bottle-shaped kilns, their orange, fanlike tongues of fire. A dog barked as they went by, and far off in the darkness some wandering sea-gull screamed. The horse caught in a rut, stumbled, then veered aside and broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled again over rough-paved streets. Most of the windows were dark, but now and then fantastic shadows were cut out against a blind lit by lamplight. He watched them with interest. They moved like monstrous marionettes and made gestures like living things. He hated them. A dull rage sat in his chest. As they turned a corner, a woman yelled something at them from an open doorway, and two men ran after the hansom for about a hundred yards. The driver lashed at them with his whip.

They say passion makes you think in circles. Certainly, with hideous repetition, the bitten lips of Dorian Gray shaped and reshaped those subtle words about soul and sense, until he had found in them the full expression—so it seemed—of his mood, and could justify, with intellectual approval, passions that, without such justification, would still have ruled his temper. From cell to cell of his mind crept the single thought; and the wild desire to live, the most terrible of all human appetites, surged into strength, quickening every trembling nerve and fiber. What ugliness had once disgusted him with because it made things real became dear to him now for that very reason. Ugliness was the only reality. The coarse brawl, the loathsome den, the crude violence of disordered life, the sheer filth of thief and outcast—these were more vivid, more intensely real in the force of their impression, than all the graceful forms of art, than the dreamy shadows of song. They were what he needed for forgetfulness. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the man pulled up with a sharp jerk at the top of a dark lane. Over the low roofs and jagged chimney-stacks of the houses rose the black masts of ships. Wreaths of white mist clung to the yards like ghostly sails.

“Somewhere around here, sir, ain’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian started and looked around. “This will do,” he said, and after getting out quickly and handing the driver the extra fare he had promised, he walked fast toward the quay. Here and there a lantern glimmered at the stern of some huge merchantman. The light trembled and broke apart in the puddles. A red glare came from an outward-bound steamer that was coaling. The slimy pavement looked like a wet mackintosh."}

{"request_id":"afa57a2fb3dd78d2ed753d9a","rewritten_text":"The day went by much the same as the day before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent several hours of the morning with the invalid, who continued, though slowly, to improve; and in the evening Elizabeth joined their group in the drawing-room. The loo table, however, was not there. Mr. Darcy was writing, and Miss Bingley, seated near him, watched the progress of his letter, repeatedly trying to draw his attention away by sending messages to her sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst sat observing their game.

Elizabeth picked up some needlework and was entertained enough by watching what passed between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s constant praise—of his handwriting, of the evenness of his lines, of the length of his letter—delivered with perfect unconcern at how it was received, made a curious kind of conversation, and matched exactly her own opinion of each.

“How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!”

He did not answer.

“You write remarkably fast.”

“You’re mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must have to write over the course of a year! Business letters, too! How dreadful I should think them!”

“Then it’s fortunate that they fall to my lot instead of yours.”

“Please tell your sister that I long to see her.”

“I’ve already told her once, at your request.”

“I’m afraid you don’t like your pen. Let me fix it for you. I mend pens remarkably well.”

“Thank you—but I always mend my own.”

“How do you manage to write so evenly?”

He was silent.

“Tell your sister I’m delighted to hear of her improvement on the harp, and please let her know that I’m quite in raptures with her beautiful little design for a table, and that I think it infinitely better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“Will you let me postpone your raptures until I write again? Right now I don’t have room to do them justice.”

“Oh, it doesn’t matter. I’ll see her in January. But do you always write such charming long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

“They’re generally long; but whether they’re always charming, that isn’t for me to decide.”

“It’s a rule with me that a person who can write a long letter with ease can’t write badly.”

“That won’t do as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” her brother cried, “because he does not write with ease. He studies too much for words of four syllables. Don’t you, Darcy?”

“My way of writing is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” Miss Bingley exclaimed, “Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable.”"}

{"request_id":"df0f7fde44447d776d646745","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, struck with horror at Sikes’s wickedness, fell to thinking whether, after all, an upright life might not be the better choice. Convinced that it was, he turned away from the old scenes, resolved to set himself to some fresh work. He laboured long and endured much for a time; yet, with a steady temper and a sincere intention, he came at last to success. And so, from being a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s lad, he is now the merriest young grazier in all Northamptonshire.

And now the hand that writes these lines hesitates as it nears the end of its duty, and would gladly spin the thread of these adventures a little farther.

I would like to linger still among some of those with whom I have so long been moving, and to share their happiness by trying to set it forth. I would show Rose Maylie in the full bloom and quiet grace of early womanhood, casting along her secluded path a gentle, kindly light—soft to all who walk with her, and shining into their hearts. I would portray the life and gladness of the fireside circle and the bright summer company; I would follow her through the sultry fields at noon, and catch the low, tender notes of her voice on the moonlit evening walk; I would observe her in all her goodness and charity abroad, and the cheerful, untiring performance of domestic duties at home. I would paint her, and her dead sister’s child, content in their love for one another, spending long hours together in imagining the friends they had so sadly lost; I would bring again before me those happy little faces that gathered round her knee, and hear their merry chatter. I would recall the sound of that clear laugh, and call up the sympathetic tear that shone in the soft blue eye. These, and a thousand looks and smiles, and turns of thought and speech—I would fain have them all back again.

As for how Mr. Brownlow went on, day after day, laying up in the mind of his adopted child stores of knowledge, and growing more and more attached to him as his character unfolded—showing the thriving seeds of everything he hoped to make of him—how he traced in him new marks of the early friend, stirring in his own breast old recollections, melancholy yet gentle and soothing—how the two orphans, tried by adversity, remembered its lessons in mercy toward others, in mutual love, and in fervent thanks to Him who had guarded and preserved them—these are matters that need not be set down."}

{"request_id":"119dd3f22946e5739aeb8fe4","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, nearly everyone told him he was making a most senseless choice, since there was no question at all that the house was haunted. In fact, Lord Canterville himself—scrupulously exact in matters of honour—had considered it only right to bring the matter up to Mr. Otis when they met to settle the terms.

‘We haven’t ourselves cared to live there,’ said Lord Canterville, ‘since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was scared into a fit—one from which she never truly recovered—when two skeleton hands were laid on her shoulders while she was dressing for dinner. And I must tell you, Mr. Otis, that the ghost has been seen by several members of my family who are still living, as well as by the rector of the parish, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the Duchess’s unfortunate mishap, none of our younger servants would remain with us, and Lady Canterville has often had hardly any sleep at night, owing to the strange sounds that come from the corridor and the library.’

‘My Lord,’ replied the Minister, ‘I’ll take the furniture and the ghost at a valuation. I come from a modern country, where we have everything that money can buy; and with all our lively young fellows painting the Old World red, and whisking away your finest actresses and prima-donnas, I’m sure that if there were such a thing as a ghost in Europe, we’d have it back home in no time—either in one of our public museums or on the road as a spectacle.’

‘I daresay the ghost is real,’ said Lord Canterville, smiling, ‘even if it has managed to ignore the invitations of your enterprising showmen. It has been a known thing for three centuries—since 1584, to be exact—and it always shows itself before the death of any member of our family.’

‘Why, the family doctor does the same, Lord Canterville, for that matter. But there’s no such thing as a ghost, sir, and I don’t expect the laws of Nature to be set aside for the British aristocracy.’

‘You’re certainly very sensible in America,’ answered Lord Canterville, who didn’t quite catch what Mr. Otis meant by his last remark; ‘and if you don’t mind a ghost in the house, then it’s perfectly fine. Only remember—I did warn you.’

A few weeks later, the purchase was finished, and when the season ended the Minister and his family went down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, who, as Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street, had once been a celebrated New York belle, was now a striking, middle-aged woman, with bright eyes and a magnificent profile.’"}

{"request_id":"dea9b0a0738c4dc3d312a7bd","rewritten_text":"Emma did not regret her condescension in going to the Coles. The visit gave her many pleasant memories the next day; and whatever she might be thought to have lost by keeping herself at a dignified distance, would be more than repaid by the brilliance of her popularity. She must have delighted the Coles—worthy people, who deserved to be made happy!—and left behind a name that would not soon fade.

Perfect happiness, even in memory, is not common; and there were two things about it that made her feel uneasy. She wondered whether she had not crossed the duty of one woman toward another by telling Frank Churchill her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings. It hardly seemed right; but the idea had been so strong that it slipped her, and his readiness to accept everything she told him was a compliment to her insight—something that made it hard for her to be completely sure she should have kept quiet.

The other cause for regret also concerned Jane Fairfax; and there she had no doubt. She truly, clearly regretted the inferiority of her own playing and singing. She grieved most sincerely over the idleness of her childhood—and then sat down and practiced vigorously for an hour and a half.

She was then interrupted by Harriet coming in; and if Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, she might soon have been comforted.

“Oh! if I could only play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t put us in the same category, Harriet. My playing isn’t any more like hers than a lamp is like sunshine.”

“Oh! dear—I think you play the best of the two. I think you play just as well as she does. I’m sure I’d much rather hear you. Everyone last night said how well you played.”

“Those who knew anything about it would have noticed the difference. The truth is, Harriet, that my playing is just good enough to be praised, but Jane Fairfax’s is far beyond that.”

“Well, I’ll always think you play quite as well as she does, or that if there is any difference, nobody would ever be able to tell. Mr. Cole said how much taste you have; and Mr. Frank Churchill talked a great deal about your taste, and he values taste much more than execution.”

“Ah! but Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I saw she had execution, but I didn’t know she had any taste. Nobody talked about it. And I hate Italian singing.—You can’t understand a word of it. Besides, if she plays so very well, you know, it’s no more than she’s required to do, because she’ll have to teach.”}"}

{"request_id":"4039f591d588dfc11d6dc94d","rewritten_text":"In the morning she was discovered dead in her bed, apparently without having felt any pain. Sir Mathew Reid was sent for immediately, though, naturally, there was nothing to be done; she was to be buried on the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before her death she had drawn up her will, leaving Lord Arthur her small house in Curzon Street, together with all her furniture, personal belongings, and pictures—save for her set of miniatures, which were to go to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which Sybil Merton was to receive. The estate itself was not worth much, but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, was intensely anxious for Lord Arthur to come back at once, if he could, since there were many bills to settle, and Lady Clementina had never kept any proper accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s thoughtful remembrance of him, and he felt that Mr. Podgers had a great deal to answer for. Yet his love for Sybil ruled everything else, and the knowledge that he had done his duty brought him peace and comfort. When he reached Charing Cross, he felt entirely happy.

The Mertons welcomed him with great kindness. Sybil made him promise that nothing would ever come between them again, and the marriage was set for the 7th of June. Life appeared to him bright and beautiful once more, and all his old joy returned.

One day, though, while he was going through the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil herself—burning bundles of faded letters and emptying drawers of odd scraps—the young girl suddenly gave a little cry of pleasure.

‘What have you found, Sybil?’ Lord Arthur asked, looking up from what he was doing, and smiling.

‘This lovely little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. Isn’t it quaint and Dutch? Do let me have it! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m past eighty.’

It was the box that had held the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, and a faint flush rose in his face. He had nearly forgotten what he had done, and it struck him as a strange coincidence that Sybil—who, for her sake, he had endured all that dreadful strain—should be the first to bring it back to his mind.

‘Of course you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.’

‘Oh! thank you, Arthur; and may I have the bonbon too? I had no idea Lady Clementina cared for sweets. I thought she was far too intellectual.’

Lord Arthur went deathly pale, and a dreadful thought flashed through his mind."}

“And you think, then, that your master was truly bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him ill?”

“I do n’t think noffin about it—I know it. What makes him dream ’bout de goole so much, if ’taint because he got bit by de goole-bug? Ise heard ’bout dem goole-bugs afore dis.”

“But how do you know he dreams about gold?”

“How I know? Why ’cause he talks about it in he sleep—that’s how I know.”

“Well, Jup, perhaps you are right; but to what lucky circumstance am I to owe the honor of a visit from you to-day?”

“What de matter, massa?”

“Did you bring any message from Mr. Legrand?”

“No, massa, I bring dis here pissel;” and here Jupiter handed me a note, which ran thus:

“MY DEAR ——Why have I not seen you for so long a time? I hope you have not been so foolish as to take offence at any little _brusquerie_ of mine; but no, that is improbable. Since I saw you I have had great cause for anxiety. I have something to tell you, yet scarcely know how to tell it, or whether I should tell it at all.

“I have not been quite well for some days past, and poor old Jup annoys me, almost beyond endurance, by his well-meant attentions. Would you believe it?—he had prepared a huge stick, the other day, with which to chastise me for giving him the slip, and spending the day, _solus_, among the hills on the main land. I verily believe that my ill looks alone saved me a flogging.

“I have made no addition to my cabinet since we met.

“If you can, in any way, make it convenient, come over with Jupiter. _Do_ come. I wish to see you to-_night_, upon business of importance. I assure you that it is of the _highest_ importance.

“Ever yours, “WILLIAM LEGRAND”.

“There was something in the tone of this note that set me uneasy. Its whole manner differed materially from Legrand’s. What could he be thinking of? What fresh notion had taken hold of his excitable head? And what “business of the highest importance” could he possibly have to manage? Jupiter’s account of him gave no comfort. I feared that the steady pressure of misfortune had, at last, fairly shaken my friend’s mind. Without a moment’s hesitation, then, I set about to go with the negro.

“On reaching the wharf, I saw a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat we were to embark in.

“‘What’s the meaning of all this, Jup?’”"}

{"request_id":"531f4bd996025cecc9b773b6","rewritten_text":"While these matters were going on in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old den—the very one from which Oliver had been taken away by the girl—sitting and brooding over a lifeless, smoky fire. On his knee he had a pair of bellows, which he seemed to be trying to coax into a brighter, more cheerful blaze; yet his mind had gone elsewhere. With his arms folded over them and his chin resting on his thumbs, he stared, in a far-off way, at the rusty bars.

Behind him, at a table, were the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, all absorbed in a game of whist. The Artful played dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The face of the first-named gentleman—always sharp and shrewd—took on even more interest as he watched the game closely, and studied Mr. Chitling’s hand; whenever the moment called for it, he fixed earnest looks upon it, and from those observations he managed his own play with careful judgment. Since it was a cold night, the Dodger kept his hat on, as he often did even indoors. He also had a clay pipe clenched between his teeth, taking it out only for a short spell when he thought it time to ask for a fresh drink from the quart pot on the table, which stood ready, filled with gin-and-water for the company.

Master Bates, too, followed the play; but being more hot-blooded than his accomplished companion, it was plain he reached for the gin-and-water more often, and filled the pauses with plenty of jokes and off-topic remarks—utterly out of place for a serious rubber. The Artful, relying on their close friendship, had more than once taken the chance to speak to him gravely about these missteps; yet Master Bates took every remonstrance in the best possible spirit, only asking his friend to be “blowed,” or to put his head in a sack, or answering with some other neatly turned bit of wit of the same sort. The effect of it was such that Mr. Chitling could hardly contain his admiration. It was also notable that Mr. Chitling and his partner always lost; but instead of vexing Master Bates, the fact only seemed to heighten his enjoyment, for he roared with laughter at the end of every deal and swore he had never in all his born days seen such a jolly game.

“That’s two doubles and the rub,” said Mr. Chitling, with a very long face, as he drew half-a-crown from his waistcoat-pocket. “I never see such a feller as you, Jack; you win everything."}

{"request_id":"eb9d69828151171d6d622f00","rewritten_text":"With nothing left to do to keep him steady, he set the knuckles of his right hand into the hollow of his left, then the knuckles of his left into the hollow of his right; after that he drew a hand over his bearded chin, and went on making the same measured changes, without the least pause. To drag him back from the wandering state into which he always slipped after he had spoken was like trying to rouse some very feeble creature out of a swoon, or to hold the spirit of a man who is dying fast, in the hope that something might yet be disclosed.

“Did you ask me for my name?”

“Certainly I did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a tired sound that was neither sigh nor groan, he bent himself to his work again, until the quiet was broken once more.

“You are not a shoemaker by trade?” said Mr. Lorry, staring at him.

His gaunt eyes swung to Defarge, as though he meant to pass the question on to him; but finding no help there, they returned to the man who had asked, and they searched for the ground.

“I am not a shoemaker by trade? No, I was not a shoemaker by trade. I-I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked leave to—”

He trailed off, even for minutes, continuing those steady alternations of his hands all the while. At last his eyes drifted back, slowly, to the face they had left; when they settled on it, he started, and went on as a sleeper does when he has just awakened, falling back upon a matter from last night.

“I asked leave to teach myself, and I got it after a long while, with great difficulty; and I have been making shoes ever since.”

As he held out his hand for the shoe that had been taken from him, Mr. Lorry said, still fixing his gaze upon him:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing of me?”

The shoe fell to the ground, and he sat staring straight at the questioner.

“Monsieur Manette”; Mr. Lorry laid his hand upon Defarge’s arm; “do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Is there no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no old time coming back into your mind, Monsieur Manette?”

While the prisoner of many years sat staring, now at Mr. Lorry and now at Defarge, some long obliterated marks of an intelligence that had once been keen and active began, little by little, to force themselves through the black mist that had settled over him. They were clouded again; they grew fainter; they vanished; yet they had been there."}

{"request_id":"d7ec601b4bba96b731ef92be","rewritten_text":"The great voice—what we might call inorganic, since no pipe or key could be made to account for it—fell silent in its sonorous strength; and the girl, turning to offer help to her elderly companion, at last noticed us.

It was her father. And she, from childhood onward, had been the guide of his dimmed steps. They were Germans from Saxony, and, having emigrated there only a few years before, had formed fresh connections with the villagers round about. Not long after the pestilence began, a young German student joined them. Their plain story was not hard to read: he was a gentleman who loved the fair daughter of the poor musician, and he followed them in their flight from the persecutions of his friends; but soon the mighty leveller came with an unsharpened scythe—mowing down, with the grass, the tall flowers of the field. The youth was taken early. She kept herself alive for her father’s sake. His blindness allowed her to keep up a delusion; at first it was only the child of accident, and now, as solitary beings, the two remained—sole survivors in the land. He did not know that, when he listened to her music, the mute mountains, the senseless lake, and the unconscious trees, save himself, were her only listeners.

The very day we arrived, she had been struck by a sickness that showed itself in symptoms. She was seized with horror at the thought of leaving her aged, sightless father alone upon the empty earth; yet she lacked the courage to tell the truth, and the very excess of her despair drove her to extraordinary exertions. At the usual hour for vespers, she led him to the chapel; and though she trembled and wept for his sake, she played the hymn—written to celebrate the creation of the adorned earth—without a fault in time or a mistake in note, soon to be her own requiem.

We came to her as if from heaven itself. Her strained courage, her firmness barely held together, broke and slipped away at the sight of relief. With a shriek she sprang toward us, threw her arms about Adrian’s knees, and, uttering nothing but, “O save my father!” with sobs and frantic cries, she let loose the long-closed floodgates of her misery.

Poor girl!—she and her father now lie side by side beneath the high walnut-tree where her lover rests, and which, in her last moments, she had pointed out to us. Her father, at last realizing her peril, could not see the changes in her dear face; still he stubbornly kept hold of her hand until death chilled it and made it stiff. Even then he did not stir or speak until, twelve hours later, kindly death carried him to his unbroken repose. They lie beneath the sod; the tree is their monument. The sacred place is clear in my memory, though it is pale beside the craggy Jura and the far, immeasurable Alps; the church spire they had frequented still rises above the sheltering trees; and though her hand is cold, I still fancy the sounds of the divine music they loved wandering about, comforting their gentle ghosts."}

{"request_id":"ac8d4577fc3b70aec227bf43","rewritten_text":"When we got back to the raft, he counted what he had collected and found it came to eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He had also taken a three-gallon jug of whisky, which he found under a wagon when he was heading home through the woods. The king said it was worth more than any day he’d ever spent in the missionary work. He said it wasn’t worth talking, because heathens didn’t amount to much compared to pirates, who could work a camp meeting.

The duke thought he’d been doing pretty well until the king showed up, and then he didn’t feel that way anymore. He had set up and printed two small jobs for farmers in the printing office—horse bills—and he took four dollars for them. He also got ten dollars’ worth of advertisements for the paper. He said he would put them in for four dollars if they paid in advance, and they agreed. The paper cost two dollars a year, but he brought in three subscriptions at half a dollar each, as long as they paid him up front. They were going to pay him in cordwood and onions as usual, but he said he had just bought the business and cut the price as low as he could afford, and he was going to run it for cash. He also set up a little piece of poetry he wrote himself, out of his own head—three verses, kind of sweet and sad. It was called “Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart.” He left it all set and ready to print in the paper and didn’t charge anything for it. In the end, he took in nine dollars and a half, and he said he’d done a pretty fair day’s work.

Then he showed us another small job he’d printed and hadn’t charged for, because it was for us. It had a picture of a runaway man with a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, and “$200 reward” under it. The text was all about Jim and described him exactly. It said he ran away from St. Jacques’ plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, last winter, and was likely headed north. It said that whoever caught him and sent him back would get the reward and the expenses.

“Now,” says the duke, “after tonight we can run during the day if we want to. Whenever we see someone coming, we can tie Jim hand and foot with a rope, put him in the wigwam, and show this handbill. We’ll say we captured him up the river, and we were too poor to travel on a steamboat, so we got this little raft on credit from our friends and are going down to get the reward.”"}

{"request_id":"b45aad3a650bcdccd09ae9bd","rewritten_text":"And Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the castle, met Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay. The four knights fought fiercely, and they broke their spears against their hands. Then Sir Pertolope came from the castle, and he met Sir Lionel. There, Sir Pertolope, the green knight, struck down Sir Lionel, the brother of Sir Launcelot. All of this was watched and recorded by noble heralds, who carried the news and named the men involved.

Then Sir Bleobaris broke his spear on Sir Gareth, but when he struck, Sir Bleobaris fell to the earth. When Sir Galihodin saw that, he told Sir Gareth to keep him, and Sir Gareth struck Sir Galihodin down to the earth. Then Sir Galihud took up a spear to avenge his brother, and Sir Gareth met him in the same way. Sir Dinadan and his brother La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore le Disirous, and Sir Dodinas le Savage all came on, and Sir Gareth knocked them all down with one spear.

When King Aswisance of Ireland saw how Sir Gareth fought, he was amazed. At one moment Sir Gareth seemed green, and at another, when he came again, he seemed blue. So with every charge he rode back and forth, his color changed, and no king or knight could recognize him quickly. Then Sir Agwisance, King of Ireland, met Sir Gareth, and Sir Gareth struck him from his horse, saddle and all. After that, King Carados of Scotland came, and Sir Gareth struck him down, horse and man. In the same way, he served King Uriens of the land of Gore.

Then Sir Bagdemagus arrived, and Sir Gareth struck him down, horse and man, to the earth. Bagdemagus’s son Meliganus broke a spear on Sir Gareth mightily and like a true knight. Then Sir Galahault, the noble prince, cried out, “Knight with the many colors, well have you proved your justice. Now be ready, so that I may joust with you.” Sir Gareth heard him, took up a great spear, and they met. There the prince broke his spear, but Sir Gareth struck him on the left side of the helm. The prince reeled this way and that, and he would have fallen had not his men caught him.

“Truly,” said King Arthur, “the knight with the many colors is a good knight.” So the king called to him, Sir Launcelot, and asked him to fight that knight. “Sir,” said Launcelot, “I could just as well keep from him in my heart, because he has had enough trouble today. When a good knight does so well on one day, it is not a good knight’s part to stop him from his honor—especially when he sees that a knight has done such great work. Perhaps, said Sir Launcelot, his quarrel is here today, and perhaps he is the best loved by this lady among all who are here. I can see that he pushes himself and forces himself to do great deeds. Therefore, as for me, this day he shall have the honor. Even if it were in my power to stop him, I would not.”"}

{"request_id":"5b1a301a8999c1722826e883","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s last reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more crowded than usual. Six Cabinet Ministers had come over from the Speaker’s Levée in their stars and ribands, all the pretty women wore their smartest dresses, and at the end of the picture-gallery stood the Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe—a heavy, Tartar-looking lady—with tiny black eyes and wonderful emeralds, talking bad French at the top of her voice and laughing immoderately at everything that was said to her. It was certainly a wonderful mix of people. Gorgeous peeresses chatted affably with violent Radicals; popular preachers brushed coat-tails with eminent sceptics; a perfect group of bishops kept following a stout prima-donna from room to room. On the staircase stood several Royal Academicians, disguised as artists, and it was said that at one time the supper-room was absolutely crammed with geniuses. In fact, it was one of Lady Windermere’s best nights, and the Princess stayed until nearly half past eleven.

The moment she had gone, Lady Windermere returned to the picture-gallery, where a celebrated political economist was solemnly explaining the scientific theory of music to an indignant virtuoso from Hungary, and she began to talk to the Duchess of Paisley. She looked wonderfully beautiful, with her grand ivory throat, her large blue forget-me-not eyes, and her heavy coils of golden hair. Or perhaps they were—not that pale straw color that nowadays steals the gracious name of gold, but such gold as is woven into sunbeams or hidden in strange amber; and it gave her face something of the frame of a saint, with no small touch of the fascination of a sinner. She was a curious study in psychology. Early in life she had discovered the important truth that nothing looks so much like innocence as an indiscretion; and through a series of reckless escapades—half of them quite harmless—she had acquired all the privileges of a personality. She had more than once changed her husband; indeed, Debrett credits her with three marriages. But since she had never changed her lover, the world had long ago stopped talking scandal about her. She was now forty years old, childless, and with that intense passion for pleasure which is the secret of staying young.

Suddenly she looked eagerly around the room and said, in her clear contralto voice, “Where is my cheiromantist?”

“Your what, Gladys?” exclaimed the Duchess, giving an involuntary start.

“My cheiromantist, Duchess; I can’t live without him at present.”

“Dear Gladys! you’re always so original,” murmured the Duchess, trying to remember what a cheiromantist really was—and hoping it wasn’t the same thing as a cheiropodist.

“He comes to see my hand twice a week, regularly,” continued Lady Windermere. “And he’s most interesting about it.”"}

{"request_id":"cc84bdec23079446feebabb1","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own entertainment, never picked up any book except the Baronetage. There he could pass an idle hour, and find comfort when things at home went badly. Looking at the early patents, he felt his mind stirred with admiration and respect, because they showed only a small, surviving beginning. As he turned through the almost endless records of the last century, any unpleasant feelings that came from domestic matters would naturally turn into pity and contempt. And even if every other page failed him, he could still read his own family history with an interest that never stopped. This was the page where his favorite volume always opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

The paragraph had originally been printed exactly like that, but Sir Walter had improved it. For the information of himself and his family, he added, after the date of Mary’s birth, the words: “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset,” and he also inserted the exact day of the month when he had lost his wife.

After that came the usual account of the family’s history and rise—how it was first established in Cheshire; how it was mentioned in Dugdale; how they served as high sheriff; how they represented a borough in three straight parliaments; how they showed loyalty and dignity as baronets in the first year of Charles II; and how, through all those generations, they married Marys and Elizabeths. Altogether it filled two neat duodecimo pages, and ended with the arms and motto: “Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” followed by Sir Walter’s handwriting again at the end:

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the start and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character—vanity about his looks and his position. In his youth he had been remarkably handsome, and at fifty-four he was still a very fine-looking man. Few women could think more highly of their appearance than he did, and no valet of a newly made lord could be more pleased with the place he held in society. He believed that the blessing of beauty was only less important than the blessing of a baronetcy. Sir Walter Elliot, who had both, was the constant object of his own warm respect and devotion.

His good looks and his rank gave him another reason to be attached to himself, because they must have earned him a wife of a character far superior to anything he could claim on his own."}
