{"request_id":"f1f221a9db9abda0f2684867","rewritten_text":"“Just one more word, Rose. My dearest Rose—just one more!” Harry cried, throwing himself in front of her. “If I had been less—if I had been less lucky, as the world would say—if my life had been meant to be quiet and ordinary; if I had been poor, sick, helpless—would you have turned away from me then? Or does the fact that I may soon become rich and respected make you hesitate now?”

“Don’t ask me to answer,” Rose said. “This question doesn’t matter, and it never will. It’s unfair, almost cruel, to keep pushing it.”

“If your answer is what I almost dare to hope,” Harry replied, “it will bring a little light to my lonely path and show me the way forward. It isn’t nothing to do this, to give a few simple words to someone who loves you more than anything. Oh, Rose—in the name of my deep and lasting love; in the name of everything I have suffered for you, and everything you force me to face—answer me this one question!”

“Then if your life had been different,” Rose answered, “if you had been only a little, but not so far, above me; if I could have been a comfort to you in some quiet, humble life, instead of being a burden in ambitious, well-known crowds—you would have been spared this trial. I have every reason to be happy now, very happy. But, Harry, I admit I would have been happier.”

As she said this, old hopes she had held onto since she was a girl came rushing back into Rose’s mind. They brought tears with them, the way old hopes always do when they return broken and faded—and yet they also helped her.

“I can’t help this weakness, and it only makes my decision stronger,” Rose said, reaching out her hand. “I really must leave you now.”

“I only ask for one promise,” Harry said. “Just once more—only once—say within a year, though it could be sooner—I may speak to you about this subject one last time.”

“Not to ask me to change my decision,” Rose replied, with a sad smile. “That would be pointless.”

“No,” Harry said. “To hear you say it again—if you will—your final answer. I will put whatever I have, in money or position, at your feet. And if you still hold to your choice, you won’t try, with words or actions, to change it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose said. “It will be one more painful moment, and by then I may be able to bear it better.”

She reached out her hand again."}

{"request_id":"2f141a720ae265821023436a","rewritten_text":"“Good heavens!” the Duchess said to herself. “So he really is a sort of cheiropodist after all. How dreadful. I do hope he’s a foreigner, at any rate. Then it wouldn’t be quite so bad.”

“I must certainly introduce him to you.”

“Introduce him!” the Duchess exclaimed. “You don’t mean to tell me he’s here?” And she immediately began to hunt for a small tortoise-shell fan and a very shabby lace shawl, as if she might have to be off at once.

“Of course he’s here; I wouldn’t dream of giving a party without him. He tells me I have a pure psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even a little shorter, I should have been a confirmed pessimist and gone into a convent.”

“Oh, I see!” said the Duchess, feeling considerably relieved. “He tells fortunes, then?”

“And misfortunes as well,” Lady Windermere replied. “Any number of them. Next year, for instance, I’m in great danger, both by land and sea; so I’m going to live in a balloon, and have my dinner drawn up in a basket every evening. It’s all written down on my little finger—or on the palm of my hand, I forget which.”

“But surely that’s tempting Providence, Gladys.”

“My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone ought to have their hands read once a month, just to know what not to do. Of course one does it all the same, but it’s so pleasant to be warned. Now, if someone doesn’t go and fetch Mr. Podgers at once, I shall have to go myself.”

“Let me go, Lady Windermere,” said a tall, handsome young man who was standing by, listening with an amused smile.

“Thank you so much, Lord Arthur; but I’m afraid you wouldn’t recognise him.”

“If he’s as wonderful as you say, Lady Windermere, I couldn’t very well miss him. Tell me what he’s like, and I’ll bring him to you at once.”

“Well, he isn’t at all like a cheiromantist. I mean he isn’t mysterious, or esoteric, or romantic-looking. He’s a little, stout man with a funny bald head and big gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country attorney. I’m truly sorry, but it isn’t my fault. People are so provoking. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look exactly like pianists; and last season I asked a most dreadful conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up so many people, and who always wore a coat of mail and carried a dagger up his shirt-sleeve. And when he arrived, do you know he looked just like a nice old clergyman, and cracked jokes all evening?”"}

{"request_id":"a3b067cce901f991a9db0df0","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I misunderstood you. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ so I assumed ‘anybody’ included—well, anybody; that is, everybody.”

“It doth—anybody that is of lofty birth; and the better if he be royal.”

“That, it seems to me, might well be,” said the abbot, who saw his chance to smooth things over and avert disaster. “For it were not likely that so wonderful a gift as this would be conferred for the revelation of the concerns of lesser beings than such as be born near to the summits of greatness. Our Arthur the king—”

“Would you know of him?” broke in the enchanter.

“Most gladly, yes—and gratefully.”

Everybody was full of awe and interest again right away, those incorrigible idiots. They watched the incantations with rapt attention, and looked at me with a “There, now—what can you say to that?” kind of expression when the announcement came:

“The king is weary with the chase, and lies in his palace these two hours sleeping a dreamless sleep.”

“God’s benison upon him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May that sleep be for the refreshment of his body and his soul.”

“And so it might be, if he were sleeping,” I said, “but the king is not sleeping—the king rides.”

Here was trouble again—a conflict of authority. Nobody knew which of us to believe; I still had some reputation left. The magician’s scorn was stirred, and he said:

“Lo, I have seen many wonderful soothsayers and prophets and magicians in my life days, but none before that could sit idle and see to the heart of things with never an incantation to help.”

“You have lived in the woods, and lost much by it. I use incantations myself, as this good brotherhood are aware—but only on occasions of moment.”

When it comes to sarcasming, I reckon I know how to keep my end up. That jab made this fellow squirm. The abbot asked after the queen and the court, and got this information:

“They be all on sleep, being overcome by fatigue, like as to the king.”

I said:

“That is merely another lie. Half of them are about their amusements—the queen and the other half are not sleeping; they ride. Now perhaps you can spread yourself a little and tell us where the king and queen and all that are this moment riding with them are going?”

“They sleep now, as I said; but on the morrow they will ride, for they go a journey toward the sea.”

“And where will they be the day after to-morrow at vespers?”

“Far to the north of Camelot, and half their journey will be done.”

“That is another lie, by the space of a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

{"request_id":"d7c1be6ee14d9391bd386e68","rewritten_text":"I saw several funerals. They were attended by only a few mourners, and the people watching treated them like bad signs of the worst kind. Some stared at the processions with eager, wild curiosity. Others ran away in fear. Some cried out loud.

After he had helped the sick right away, Adrian’s main goal was to hide the plague’s symptoms and how it was spreading from the people of London. He understood that fear and gloomy thoughts could help the disease. When people gave in to despair and kept worrying, the body became more likely to catch infection. So there were no disturbing sights to be seen. Most shops stayed open, and the streets still had some traffic. Even so, London looked changed to me, since I had not seen it since the outbreak began. There were no carriages. Grass had grown high in the streets. The houses looked empty and worn down. Most shutters were closed. And the people I passed had a pale, frightened stare that felt nothing like the usual, practical way Londoners carried themselves. My own carriage drew attention as it rattled toward the Protectoral Palace, and the fashionable streets leading to it looked even more empty and bleak. 

Adrian’s waiting room was crowded. It was his time to see visitors. I did not want to interrupt his work, so I stayed and watched people come in and go out. They were mostly from the middle and lower classes, whose money ran out when trade stopped. There was also the restless drive to make money in every form, which was so common in our country. The newcomers looked anxious, sometimes even terrified, which stood in sharp contrast to the calm, resigned, and even pleased faces of those who had already been heard. I could tell how my friend was affecting them by the way they moved faster and looked happier. At two o’clock the door closed, and no one else was admitted. Those who were turned away left in a sour or sorrowful mood, and then I went into the audience chamber.

I was surprised by how much Adrian’s health had improved. He was no longer bent over like an over-cared-for spring flower that grows too fast and ends up weighed down by its own blossoms. His eyes were bright, his face calm, and there was a focused strength in his whole manner that was nothing like his earlier weakness. He sat at a table with several secretaries, who were arranging petitions and recording the notes from that day’s meetings. Two or three petitioners were still waiting. I admired his fairness and patience. For those who had the means to live outside London, he told them to leave at once, and he made sure they had the resources to do so."}

{"request_id":"76548b11323fdaf73c96b385","rewritten_text":"“Oh, that’s nothing at all. It’s a pleasure for me. I don’t do this for money. I live for my art.”

Lord Arthur put £4, 2s. 6d. on the table, thanked the little German for his kindness, and after managing to refuse an invitation to meet some Anarchists at a meat-tea the next Saturday, he left the house and went to the Park.

For the next two days he was in a state of intense excitement. On Friday, at twelve o’clock, he drove down to the Buckingham to wait for news. All afternoon the serious hall-porter kept posting telegrams from different parts of the country: the results of horse races, the outcomes of divorce cases, the weather, and similar items. Meanwhile, the tape kept clicking out dull details about an all-night sitting in the House of Commons, and a small panic on the Stock Exchange. At four o’clock the evening papers arrived, and Lord Arthur went into the library with the Pall Mall, the St. James’s, the Globe, and the Echo, to Colonel Goodchild’s great anger. Colonel Goodchild wanted to read reports of a speech he had given that morning at the Mansion House about South African Missions, and whether black bishops should be in every province. For some reason, he also had a strong dislike for the Evening News. None of the papers mentioned Chichester at all, though, and Lord Arthur felt sure the attempt had failed. It was a terrible blow, and for a while he was completely shaken.

The next day he went to see Herr Winckelkopf, who was full of careful apologies. Herr Winckelkopf offered to replace the clock for free, or to sell him a case of nitro-glycerine bombs at cost. But Lord Arthur had lost faith in explosives. Herr Winckelkopf agreed that things were so mixed and adulterated these days that even dynamite was hard to get in a truly pure form. Still, the little German said that even if something had gone wrong with the machinery, there was hope the clock might still work. He pointed to a time when he had sent a barometer to the military governor at Odessa. It was set to go off in ten days, but it did not explode for about three months. When it finally did, it only managed to blow a housemaid to pieces, because the governor had left town six weeks earlier. Even so, it showed that dynamite, when controlled by machinery, could be a powerful destructive force—though it was, in a way, rather unreliable about the timing."}

{"request_id":"c815836182ff2618150dd7fa","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced the room in angry strides. I stood prepared to take in his reproaches and answer them. Adrian rested against the wall. “This is utterly ridiculous,” he burst out; “if you were school-boys, you could not behave more irrationally.”

“You do not understand,” said Raymond. “This is only one part of a system—a contrivance of tyranny to which I will never submit. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the only slave in its empire? My privacy invaded, my actions watched and censured, my friends insulted? But I’ll be rid of the whole at once.—Be you witnesses,” and he drew the star, the insignia of his office, from his breast and flung it upon the table. “I renounce my office, I abdicate my power—let whoever will assume it!”—-

“Let him assume it,” Adrian cried, “who can claim it for himself, or whom the world will declare to be your superior. There does not exist in England the man with sufficient presumption. Know yourself, Raymond, and your indignation will quiet; your former self-satisfaction will return. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country, or our own, we prayed at the same time for the life and welfare of the Protector, as inseparably bound up with it. Your hours were spent for our good; your ambition aimed at earning our approval. You adorned our towns with buildings, you gave us useful establishments, you made the soil yield in abundant fertility. The powerful and unjust shrank from the steps of your judgment-seat, and the poor and oppressed rose like flowers awakened by morning under the sunshine of your protection.

“Can you wonder, then, that we are all stricken with grief and dismay when this seems altered? But, come—this bitter mood is already over. Take up your functions again; your partizans will greet you; your enemies will be silenced; our love, honour, and duty will be shown to you once more. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world will be subject to you.”

“All this would be very good sense, if it were spoken to someone else,” Raymond answered, darkly. “Take the lesson to yourself, and you, the first peer of the land, may become its sovereign. You, the good, the wise, the just, may rule all hearts. But I see—too soon for my own happiness, too late for England’s good—that I have undertaken a task I cannot carry. I cannot govern myself. My passions are my masters; my smallest impulse is my tyrant. Do you think that I renounced the Protectorate—(and I have renounced it)—in a fit of spleen? By the God who lives, I swear I will never take up that bauble again; never again to burden myself with the weight of care and misery, of which that is the visible sign.”"}

{"request_id":"2a25c2b3cd0986f66f3fd54e","rewritten_text":"I don’t want to get mixed up in any business like that, I tell myself.

When I went downstairs in the morning, the parlor was shut up, and the watchers were gone. There wasn’t anybody around except the family, Widow Bartley, and our people. I watched their faces to see if anything had been going on, but I couldn’t tell.

Toward the middle of the day, the undertaker came with his man. They set the coffin in the middle of the room on a couple of chairs, then arranged all our chairs in rows. They borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, the parlor, and the dining room were full. I could see the coffin lid was the same way it had been before, but I didn’t dare go look underneath it with people standing around.

Then the people started to come in. The beats and the girls took seats in the front row at the head of the coffin. For half an hour, people filed around slowly in a single line, looking down at the dead man’s face for a minute. Some people shed a tear, and everything was very still and solemn. Only the girls and the beats held their handkerchiefs to their eyes, kept their heads bent, and sobbed a little. There wasn’t any other sound except the scraping of feet on the floor and people blowing their noses—because at a funeral they blow their noses more than they do anywhere else, except church.

When the place was packed, the undertaker slid around in his black gloves with his soft, soothing ways, putting on the last touches and getting everything shipshape and comfortable, making no more noise than a cat. He never spoke. He moved people around, squeezed in the late arrivals, opened up passageways, and did it all with nods and signs with his hands. Then he took his place against the wall. He was the softest, glidingest, stealthiest man I ever saw, and there wasn’t any more smile on him than there is on a ham.

They had borrowed a melodeum—a sick one. When everything was ready, a young woman sat down and played it. It was pretty screechy and colicky, and everybody joined in and sang, and Peter was the only one that had a good thing, in my opinion. Then Reverend Hobson opened up, slow and solemn, and started talking. Right away, the most outrageous row broke out in the cellar—something like a body ever heard. It was only one dog, but he made a powerful racket, and he kept it up the whole time. The parson had to stand there over the coffin and wait. You couldn’t hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"f545e260c3b25fc7a69e2cc1","rewritten_text":"Tom tried to use it to scarify the cupboard, and he was getting ready to start on the bureau when he was called away to get dressed for Sunday-school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a bar of soap. He went outside the door, set the basin on a small bench, dipped the soap into the water, and laid it down. Then he rolled up his sleeves, poured the water onto the ground carefully, and went back into the kitchen to wash his face. He scrubbed at it hard, using the towel that hung behind the door. But Mary took the towel away and said,

“Now, ain’t you ashamed, Tom. You mustn’t be so bad. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom felt a little embarrassed. The basin was filled again, and this time he stood over it for a moment, gathering himself. He took a big breath and started. When he went back into the kitchen, both eyes shut and reaching for the towel with his hands, suds and water were dripping from his face. When he came out again, he still wasn’t clean enough. The soap had only reached up to his chin and jaws, like a mask; below that line, his neck and the area around it were still dark and dirty, with no water on them. Mary took him in hand, and when she was finished he looked like a man and a brother, with no difference in color. His hair was soaked but brushed neatly, and the short curls were shaped into a neat, even style. [He quietly fixed the curls himself, with effort and difficulty, and pressed his hair close to his head. He thought curls looked effeminate, and his own hair always made him bitter.] Then Mary brought out a suit of his clothes that had only been worn on Sundays for two years. They were simply called his “other clothes,” and that’s how we know what his wardrobe looked like.

After Tom dressed himself, Mary “put him to rights.” She fastened his roundabout up to his chin, turned his large shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and set his speckled straw hat on his head. Now he looked much better, but also very uncomfortable. He was as uncomfortable as he looked, because he hated the feeling of being forced into clean clothes and keeping himself neat. He hoped Mary would forget his shoes, but that hope didn’t last. She rubbed them thoroughly with tallow, as was the custom, and brought them out. He lost his temper and said he was always being made to do things he didn’t want to do."}

{"request_id":"614c62a21bde086f8cc875f0","rewritten_text":"The young people were all eager to see Lyme. Captain Wentworth even talked about going again himself. It was only seventeen miles from Uppercross, and although it was November, the weather was not bad at all. Louisa, who was the most eager of the eager, had decided to go. She wanted to do what she liked, and she also felt proud of being able to stick to her own plan. Because of this, she pushed aside all her father and mother’s wishes to wait until summer. So they were going to Lyme—Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth.

At first, the plan had been to leave in the morning and come back the same night. But Mr Musgrove would not agree, mainly for the sake of his horses. When they thought it through more sensibly, it was clear that a day in the middle of November would not give them much time to see a new place. After allowing seven hours for traveling there and back, there would be little left for anything else. So they would stay the night, and they would not be expected back until the next day’s dinner. Everyone felt this was a real improvement.

They met at the Great House for breakfast a little earlier than usual, and they left very punctually. Still, it was well past noon before the two carriages came down the long hill into Lyme. Mr Musgrove’s coach carried the four ladies, and Charles’s curricle carried Captain Wentworth. Once they reached the town, they had to go down even farther, into the steeper street itself. It was clear that they would have only a short time to look around before the light and warmth of the day were gone.

After they had found places to stay and ordered dinner at one of the inns, the next thing to do was to walk straight down to the sea. They had arrived too late in the year for any of the usual fun or variety that Lyme, as a public place, might offer. The rooms were shut up, most of the lodgers had already left, and there were hardly any families there except the residents. Since there is nothing especially impressive about the buildings themselves, what a visitor would notice most is the town’s remarkable setting: the main street seems to hurry right toward the water. The walk to the Cobb goes along a pleasant little bay, which in season is lively with bathing machines and people. The Cobb itself has its old attractions and its newer improvements, and there is also a beautiful line of cliffs stretching to the east of the town. Any stranger who does not see the charms of the area around Lyme would have to be very strange indeed, because it would surely make them want to know the place better."}

{"request_id":"ba209d70eaca74a12ce42d51","rewritten_text":"Well, three or four months went by, and winter was well set in by then. I’d been at school nearly all the time, and I could spell and read and write a little, and I could say the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five; beyond that, I don’t reckon I’d ever get, even if I lived forever. I don’t put much faith in mathematics, anyway.

At first I hated school, but after a while I got to where I could bear it. Whenever I got unusually tired, I’d play hookey, and the punishment I got the next day did me good and put me in a better humor. The longer I kept going, the easier it became. I was getting used to the widow’s ways, too, and they weren’t so sharp on me. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed held me pretty tight most of the time, but before the cold weather I’d slip out and sleep in the woods sometimes, and that was a kind of rest. I liked the old ways best, but I was starting to like the new ones some, too. The widow said I was coming along slow but sure, and doing very satisfactory. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning, at breakfast, I turned over the salt-cellar. I reached for it as quick as I could, to throw some of the salt over my left shoulder and ward off the bad luck, but Miss Watson was already there and beat me to it. She says, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; you’re always making a mess!” The widow spoke up for me, but that wasn’t going to stop the bad luck, I knew that well enough. I went out after breakfast feeling worried and shaky, wondering where it was going to land on me and what it was going to be. There are ways to keep off certain kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of those, so I didn’t try to do anything—just drifted along low-spirited, and on the lookout.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile where you pass through the high board fence. There was an inch of fresh snow on the ground, and I saw somebody’s tracks. They’d come up from the quarry and lingered around the stile a while, and then went on around the garden fence. It struck me as odd they hadn’t gone in after standing there so long. I couldn’t make it make sense. It was curious, somehow. I was going to follow them, but I bent down first to look closely at the tracks."}

{"request_id":"d4704eb75ef7137627c8fe6a","rewritten_text":"Yet, despite all of that, the boy grew more and more sad, pale, and worn down. She tried hot baths, sitz baths, shower baths, and plunges. The boy stayed as gloomy as a funeral cart. Then she started helping the water along with a thin oatmeal diet and blister plasters. She measured his “capacity” the way you would measure a jug, and every day she filled him up with quack cures.

By this time, Tom had become indifferent to being persecuted. This made the old lady panic. She decided that this indifference had to be broken, no matter what it took. Then she heard about Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a lot of it at once. She tasted it and felt instantly grateful. It was, she thought, just fire in liquid form. She stopped the water treatments and everything else, and put all her trust in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and watched with deep anxiety to see what would happen. Her worries settled at once, and her mind was at peace again, because the “indifference” had been broken. The boy couldn’t have shown a wilder, happier interest if she had lit a fire under him.

Tom decided it was time to wake up. This kind of life might be romantic enough for his ruined condition, but it was starting to feel like too little feeling and too much constant distraction. So he thought through different plans for relief, and finally settled on pretending to be fond of Pain-killer. He asked for it so often that he became a nuisance, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop bothering her. If it had been Sid, she would have been delighted without any doubts, but because it was Tom, she watched the bottle in secret. She saw that the medicine did seem to go down, but it never occurred to her that the boy was using it to patch a crack in the sitting-room floor.

One day Tom was in the middle of filling the crack when his aunt’s yellow cat came along. It purred, watched the teaspoon greedily, and begged for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you really want it, Peter.”

But Peter made it clear that he did want it.

“You’d better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“Now that you’ve asked, I’ll give it to you, because I’m not mean. But if you don’t like it, you can’t blame anyone but yourself.”

Peter agreed. So Tom pried his mouth open and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter jumped a couple of yards into the air, then let out a war-whoop and ran around the room in circles, crashing into furniture, knocking over flower-pots, and causing all kinds of chaos."}

{"request_id":"35a520efa9738ef1edb8fb88","rewritten_text":"The nephew glanced at him, in vain, as he went on past him toward the door.

“Good night!” said the uncle. “I count on the pleasure of seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Light Monsieur my nephew to his chamber there—and burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you please,” he added to himself, before he rang his little bell once more and called his valet to his own bedroom.

The valet came and went, and then Monsieur the Marquis paced his way in his loose chamber-robe, preparing himself, as gently as he could, for sleep in that hot, motionless night. With his softly-slippered feet making no sound on the floor, he rustled about like a refined tiger:—he looked like some bewitched marquis of the impenitently wicked sort, in tales, whose shifting into tiger-shape was either just beginning or just ending.

He crossed from one end of his voluptuous room to the other, again and again catching at the scraps of the day’s journey that drifted into his mind unbidden—the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the sun going down, the descent, the mill, the prison perched on the crag, the small village in the hollow, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender with his blue cap pointing out the chain beneath the carriage. The fountain brought up the Paris fountain; then the little bundle on the step; the women leaning over it; and the tall man with his arms raised, crying, “Dead!”

“I’m cool again,” said Monsieur the Marquis. “Now I may go to bed.”

So, leaving only a single light burning on the great hearth, he let his thin gauze curtains fall about him, and listened as the night broke its silence with a long sigh while he settled himself to sleep.

For three heavy hours the stone faces on the outer walls stared, blind, into the black night; for three heavy hours the horses in the stables rattled at their racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound that bore very little resemblance to the owl-noise men-poets assign it. Yet it is the stubborn habit of such creatures to say almost nothing of what is expected of them.

For three heavy hours the chateau’s stone faces—lion and man—stared blindly at the night. Dead darkness lay over everything, dead darkness adding its own hush to the hush of the dust on all the roads. The burial-place had reached the point where its little heaps of poor grass were no longer distinguishable from one another; the figure on the Cross might as well have come down, for all that could be seen of it. In the village, taxers and the taxed were fast asleep. Perhaps they dreamed of banquets, as the starving do, and of ease and rest, as the driven slave and the yoked ox may; and so the lean inhabitants slept soundly, and were fed and freed."}

{"request_id":"b87b06c00df32799d16d6f80","rewritten_text":"“Well, everybody does it that way, Huck.”

“Tom, it doesn’t make any difference. I’m not everybody, and I can’t stand it. It’s awful to be stuck up like that. And food comes too easy—I don’t care about eating that way. I have to ask to go fishing. I have to ask to go swimming. I even have to ask to do everything. And I had to talk so politely that it wasn’t any comfort. I had to go up in the attic every day and tear things up just to get some taste in my mouth, or I’d have died, Tom. The widow wouldn’t let me smoke. She wouldn’t let me yell, or stare, or stretch, or scratch in front of people—” [Then, with a sudden burst of special irritation and hurt]—“And Dad would come along and she’d pray the whole time! I had to shove, Tom. I just had to. And besides, school’s going to open, and I would have had to go. Well, I wouldn’t stand that, Tom. Look here, Tom—being rich isn’t what people say it is. It’s just worry and worry, and sweating and sweating, and wishing you were dead all the time. Now these clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I’m never going to get rid of them again. Tom, I wouldn’t have gotten into all this trouble if it hadn’t been for that money. Now you just take my share of it along with yours, and give me a ten-cent piece sometimes—not very often, because I don’t care about anything unless it’s tolerable to get—and you go and talk to the widow for me.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. It isn’t fair. And besides, if you try this thing just a little longer, you’ll start to like it.”

“Like it? Yes—the way I’d like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those cursed stuffy houses. I like the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’ll stick with them too. Blame it all! Just when we’d gotten guns and a cave, and everything set up so we could rob—then this stupid nonsense has to come along and ruin it all!”

Tom saw his chance—

“Look here, Huck, being rich isn’t going to stop me from turning robber.”

“No! Oh, good-licks. Are you serious, Tom?”

“Just as serious as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you into the gang if you aren’t respectable, you know.”

Huck’s joy was cut short.

“Can’t let me in, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"0a4e21668412e0954d5feee8","rewritten_text":"Emma was not later forced, by any new discovery, to take back her harsh opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her judgment had been pretty accurate. As Mrs. Elton seemed to her in this second interview, so she seemed whenever they met again—self-important, presumptuous, familiar, ignorant, and badly bred. She had a little beauty and a little accomplishment, but so little judgment that Emma believed she thought herself bringing superior knowledge of the world to enliven and improve a country neighborhood; and she concluded that Miss Hawkins must have held a place in society that Mrs. Elton’s importance could only surpass.

There was no reason to suppose Mr. Elton thought any differently from his wife. He did not seem merely happy with her, but proud. He had the air of congratulating himself on having brought such a woman to Highbury—so much so that even Miss Woodhouse could not equal her; and most of her new acquaintances, either inclined to praise or not in the habit of judging, followed Miss Bates’s good will, or simply assumed that the bride must be as clever and as agreeable as she claimed. As a result, everyone was very well satisfied; so that Mrs. Elton’s praise passed from one mouth to another as it should, unimpeded by Miss Woodhouse, who readily continued her first contribution and talked, with good grace, about how “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed” Mrs. Elton was.

In one respect, Mrs. Elton grew even worse than she had seemed at first. Her feelings changed toward Emma. Offended, probably, by the little encouragement her proposals of intimacy received, she pulled back in her turn and gradually became much more cold and distant; and though the effect was agreeable, the ill will that caused it necessarily increased Emma’s dislike. Her manners, too—and Mr. Elton’s—were unpleasant toward Harriet. They were sneering and careless. Emma hoped it would quickly work Harriet’s cure; but the feelings that could lead to such behavior weighed on them both very heavily. It was not to be doubted that poor Harriet’s attachment had been an offering to conjugal openness, and that her own part in the story, presented in the least favorable light to her and the most soothing to him, had likely been given as well. She was, of course, the object of their shared dislike. When they had nothing else to say, it would always be easy to start by criticizing Miss Woodhouse; and the enmity they could not show in open disrespect to her found a wider outlet in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.

Mrs. Elton took a strong fancy to Jane Fairfax—and from the very beginning. Not only when a state of war with one young lady might be expected to make the other seem more desirable, but from the first. And she was not content merely to express a natural and reasonable admiration—without being asked, without pleading, without any claim of privilege, she had to offer help and friendship. Before Emma had lost her confidence, and about the third time of their meeting, she heard all of Mrs. Elton’s knight-errantry on the subject."}

{"request_id":"da4ab8be2da733a40c66cf6c","rewritten_text":"If I can’t manage on that, I won’t ask anyone to give me a lift. Is it satisfactory?”

There came a tremendous roar of applause, and from the middle of it the king’s voice rose, saying:

“Loose him from his bonds, and set him free! and let high and low, rich and poor, do him homage, for he has become the king’s right hand—clothed with power and authority, and seated on the highest step of the throne! Now sweep away this creeping night, and bring back light and cheer, so that all the world may bless thee.”

But I answered:

“That a common man should be shamed before the world is nothing; yet it would be dishonor to the king, if anyone who saw his minister naked were not also to see him delivered from his shame. If I might request that my clothes be brought back—”

“They are not fit,” the king cut in. “Go fetch raiment of another sort; clothe him like a prince!”

My plan worked. I meant to keep things as they were until the eclipse was fully over; otherwise they’d keep trying to get me to dismiss the darkness, and of course I couldn’t. Getting the clothes sent for bought me some time, but not enough. So I had to invent another excuse. I said it would be only natural for the king to change his mind and repent, at least in part, for what he’d done in the heat of the moment; therefore I would allow the darkness to linger a while, and if, by the end of a reasonable stretch, the king still held to the same mind, then the darkness should be dismissed. Neither the king nor anyone else liked that arrangement, but I had to stand by it.

It kept growing darker and darker, blacker and blacker, while I wrestled with those awkward sixth-century clothes. At last it became pitch dark, and the crowd groaned with horror as they felt the cold, uncanny night breezes sweep through the place and saw the stars come out and twinkle overhead. At last the eclipse was total, and I was glad of it, though everyone else was miserable—which was only to be expected. I said:

“The king, by his silence, still holds to the terms.” Then I raised my hands—kept them just so for a moment—and then, with the most dreadful solemnity, I declared: “Let the enchantment dissolve and pass harmless away!”

For a moment there was no answer, in that deep darkness and graveyard hush. But when the silver rim of the sun pushed itself out, a moment or two later, the whole gathering burst loose with a vast shout and came pouring down like a flood to smother me with blessings and gratitude; and Clarence was not the last of the rush, not by any means.”"}

{"request_id":"e9e28d62d8d39ce03c937081","rewritten_text":"I take it to be among the earliest improvements of well-bred, polished communities.”

“Undoubtedly, sir; and it has the further merit of being fashionable even among the less refined societies in the world—every savage can dance.”

Sir William only smiled. “Your friend performs to delight,” he went on, after a pause, as he saw Bingley join the circle; “and I have no doubt you yourself are skilled in the art, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, indeed; and I confess I derived no small pleasure from the sight. Do you dance often at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Then you do not think it would be a proper compliment to the place?”

“It is a compliment I never offer to any place, if I can possibly help it.”

“You have a house in town, I conclude?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once entertained the notion of settling in town myself, for I am fond of superior company; but I could not be sure that the air of London would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, expecting an answer; but his companion showed no inclination to give one. At that instant Elizabeth came toward them, and he was struck by the idea of doing something very gallant, so he called out to her,—

“My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to introduce this young lady to you as a very desirable partner. You cannot refuse to dance, I am sure, with so much beauty before you.” Taking her hand, he would have placed it in Mr. Darcy’s, who, though greatly astonished, was not unwilling to accept it, when she instantly drew back and said, with some embarrassment to Sir William,—

“Indeed, sir, I have not the least intention of dancing. I beg you not to think I moved this way in order to solicit a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with grave propriety, requested the honour of her hand, but in vain. Elizabeth remained firm; nor did Sir William, by any attempt at persuasion, succeed in shaking her resolve.

“You dance so remarkably well, Miss Eliza,” said he, “that it is cruel to deny me the happiness of seeing you; and though this gentleman dislikes the amusement in general, he can have no objection, I am sure, to oblige us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He is, indeed; but, my dear Miss Eliza, with such an inducement, we cannot be surprised at his readiness; for who could refuse a partner like this?”

Elizabeth glanced with an air, and turned away. Her refusal had not displeased the gentleman; he was even thinking of her with some satisfaction, when Miss Bingley accosted him,—"}

{"request_id":"d90605daadc236409ba1e7bd","rewritten_text":"The chain of events that always brings misery must have been broken, and the cruel fate that rules it would not allow this break in her eternal laws. But why should I complain? Misery was my nature, and only something miserable could draw me near. If Woodville had been happy, I would never have known him. And can I, who for many years have been fed by tears and kept alive by the dew of grief, stop now and tell a story of sorrow and death?

Woodville had to travel into the country, and he was kept away from his lovely bride day after day, in a way that felt unbearable. He received a letter from her saying she was only slightly ill, but urging him to come quickly. She told him that her health would return from the look in his eyes, and that his company would be the best medicine. He was delayed three more days, and then he hurried to her. His heart, for reasons he could not explain, warned him of trouble. He had not heard from her again. He feared she might be worse, and that fear made him restless and impatient, because he could not wait to see her again—healthy and beautiful, as she had been. Still, a dark voice seemed to whisper to him again and again, “You will never see her as she was.”

When he reached her home, everything was silent. He moved through several rooms. In one, he found a servant crying bitterly. He was so frightened he could hardly ask, “Is she dead?” Then he only heard the terrible answer, “Not yet.” Those words hit him as less frightening than what he had expected. Knowing she was still alive, and that he might still hope, eased him a little. He remembered what her letter had said. He let himself believe wildly that his kisses, full of warm love and life, could bring her back. He told himself that she could not die while he was near her, and that his presence was like a charm that kept her alive.

He rushed to her sick room. She lay there with her cheeks burning from fever, but her eyes were closed, and she seemed unaware. He held her in his arms. He pressed breathless kisses on her burning lips. In a voice filled with restrained anguish, he called her by the gentlest names. “Come back, Elinor. I am here with you. Your life, your love. Come back. My dearest one, you promised me this gift—that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit return. You cannot die near me. What is death? To never see you again? To be separated from what is part of myself—without whom I have no memory and no future?”"}

{"request_id":"0bcf92189b310c5dc74ea1c5","rewritten_text":"I am very ignorant, and it worries me—just a little.”

“Tell me what it is.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative, and she is an orphan too, like me. I love her very much. She is five years younger than I am, and she lives in a farmer’s house in the south country. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing about my fate—because I cannot write. And even if I could, how would I tell her? It is better this way.”

“Yes, yes. Better this way.”

“What I have been thinking as we came along, and what I am still thinking now as I look at your kind, strong face—which gives me so much support—is this: if the Republic really does good for the poor, and they are less hungry and suffer less in every way, then she may live a long time. She may even live to be old.”

“Then what, my gentle sister?”

“Do you think,” the quiet eyes that hold so much endurance fill with tears, and her lips part a little more and tremble, “that it will feel long to me while I wait for her in the better land, where I trust both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”

“It cannot be, my child. There is no Time there, and no trouble there.”

“You comfort me so much. I am so ignorant. Am I to kiss you now? Has the moment come?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips; he kisses hers. They bless each other solemnly. His spare hand does not shake when he lets go. On her patient face there is nothing worse than a sweet, steady brightness. She goes next before him—she is gone; the knitting-women count Twenty-Two.

“I am the Resurrection and the Life, says the Lord: whoever believes in me, even if he is dead, will live. And whoever lives and believes in me will never die.”

The murmuring of many voices, the lifting of many faces, the crowd pressing forward with many footsteps at the edge, until it swells ahead in one great mass, like a single heave of water—all of it flashes away. Twenty-Three.

*****

That night, people in the city said that his face was the most peaceful they had ever seen. Many also said he looked sublime and prophetic.

One of the most remarkable women who suffered under the same axe had asked, not long before, at the foot of the same scaffold, to be allowed to write down the thoughts that were inspiring her. If he had spoken his own thoughts, and if they were truly prophetic, they would have been these:

“I see Barsad, and Cly, Defarge, The Vengeance, the Juryman, the Judge—long lines of the new oppressors who rise after the old ones are destroyed, perishing by this instrument of retribution, before it stops being used.”"}

{"request_id":"12bb9d305b1616e878543a9b","rewritten_text":"I then went from shop to shop, buying whatever was needed to bring about the change in his appearance. Once that was done, I turned my thoughts, on my own business, toward Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk; but the moment he saw me come in, he rose at once and took his place before the fire.

“Now, Pip,” said he, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I answered. As I had been walking, I had decided what I meant to say.

“Don’t commit yourself,” Mr. Jaggers warned, “and don’t commit anyone. Mind you—anyone. Don’t tell me anything. I don’t want to know anything. I’m not curious.”

Of course I understood that he already knew the man had arrived.

“I only want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to satisfy myself that what I’ve been told is true. I don’t expect it to be false, but I can at least check it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head to one side. He wasn’t looking at me; he was looking, as if listening, at the floor. “Told suggests a man speaking to you. You can’t have verbal communication with someone in New South Wales, you know.”

“I’ll say ‘informed,’ Mr. Jaggers.”

“Right.”

“I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor—unknown to me until now.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And only he?” I asked.

“And only he,” Mr. Jaggers replied.

“I’m not so unreasonable, sir, as to think you in any way responsible for my errors and wrong conclusions; still, I had always supposed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” returned Mr. Jaggers, fixing his eyes on me with a cool look, and biting his forefinger as he spoke. “I’m not in the least responsible for that.”

“And yet it looked so like it, sir,” I urged, my heart cast down.

“Not a particle of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his skirts. “Take nothing on its looks; take everything on evidence. That’s the best rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I said at last, with a sigh, after standing silent for a little while. “I’ve verified my information, and that’s the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having at last made himself known,” Mr. Jaggers went on, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, in all my dealings with you, I have kept to the straight line of fact. There has never been the smallest deviation from it. You know that, don’t you?”

“Quite so, sir.”

“I told Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—that he must not expect me ever to swerve from the strict line of fact.”"}

{"request_id":"c2b1ffc27673b6c25825aa51","rewritten_text":"It was only proper for the young lady to admit that she did not, in so many words, declare she would not; rather, she let it be known—earnestly and with emphasis—that she wished to be “blessed” if she were to do so. It was a courteous, careful sidestep of the request, and it made clear that the young lady had that instinctive good breeding which cannot bear to burden another creature with the sharp misery of a direct, pointed refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned away from this young lady—bright, if not to say splendidly dressed—in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers, and looked to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” said the Jew, in a soothing tone, “what do _you_ say?”

“That won’t do; so there’s no point in trying it on, Fagin,” answered Nancy.

“What are you getting at?” demanded Mr. Sikes, glancing up with a surly air.

“What I say, Bill,” replied the lady, keeping herself steady.

“Why, you’re just the right sort for it,” argued Mr. Sikes. “Nobody around here knows a thing about you.”

“And I don’t want them to,” Nancy returned, equally composed; “it’s more no than yes with me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” said Nancy.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” said Sikes.

And Mr. Sikes proved to be right. By trading on alternate threats, promises, and bribes, the lady in question was finally worn down into agreeing to take on the job. She was not, however, held back by the same scruples as her agreeable friend; for, having only lately moved into the Field Lane area from the more distant, yet still genteel, suburb of Ratcliffe, she had no such fear of running into recognition among her many acquaintances.

So, with a clean white apron tied over her gown, and her curl-papers tucked up beneath a straw bonnet—both items supplied from the Jew’s inexhaustible store—Miss Nancy readied herself to set out on her errand.

“Hold on a minute, my dear,” said the Jew, drawing out a small, covered basket. “Put that in one hand. It’ll look more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door-key to carry in her t’other one, Fagin,” said Sikes. “It looks proper and genivine like.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, it does,” said the Jew, slipping a large street-door key onto the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There—very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” he said, rubbing his hands.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” cried Nancy, breaking into tears, as she clutched the basket and the street-door key, wringing them in a paroxysm of distress. “What’s happened to him! Where have they taken him! Oh, have pity—tell me what’s been done with the dear boy, gentlemen; do, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”"}

{"request_id":"1636c3567ecd12c645df5456","rewritten_text":"This small explanation from Mr. Knightley gave Emma a great deal of pleasure. It was one of the nicest things she remembered from the ball. The next morning she walked around the lawn to enjoy it.—She was especially glad that they had reached such a good understanding about the Eltons, and that their opinions of both Mr. and Mrs. Elton were so much the same. Mr. Knightley’s praise of Harriet, and his willingness to support her, was particularly satisfying. The Eltons’ rudeness, which for a few minutes had threatened to spoil the rest of her evening, had actually led to some of its best moments. And she was looking forward to another happy result—the end of Harriet’s infatuation.—From the way Harriet had spoken about what happened before they left the ballroom, Emma felt very hopeful. It was as if Harriet’s eyes had been suddenly opened, and she could now see that Mr. Elton was not the superior person she had always believed him to be. The excitement had passed, and Emma could hardly fear that his quickened attention would return through any harmful politeness. She expected the Eltons’ bad feelings to provide all the lessons she might still need, through careful, pointed neglect.—If Harriet could stay sensible, if Frank Churchill were not too much in love, and if Mr. Knightley did not want to quarrel with her, what a happy summer Harriet must have ahead of her!

Emma was not going to see Frank Churchill this morning. He had told her he could not stop at Hartfield, because he had to be at home by the middle of the day. She did not regret it.

After she had arranged everything, checked it all, and put matters in order, she was just turning toward the house, with her spirits lifted for the demands of the two little boys and their grandfather, when the great iron sweep-gate opened. Two people entered whom she had never expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm—actually Harriet! For a moment Emma could tell that something unusual had happened. Harriet looked pale and frightened, and Frank was trying to comfort her. The iron gates and the front door were not more than twenty yards apart, and soon all three were in the hall. Harriet immediately sank into a chair and fainted.

A young lady who faints must be brought round. Questions must be asked, and the surprises must be explained. Such events are interesting, but the suspense cannot last long. In a few minutes Emma learned everything.

Miss Smith, and Miss Bickerton, another girl boarding at Mrs. Goddard’s, who had also been at the ball, had gone out together and taken the Richmond road. It looked public enough to be safe, but it led them into trouble. About half a mile beyond Highbury, after a sudden turn, and sheltered for a long stretch by elms on both sides, the road became very quiet. When the young ladies had gone some distance into it, they suddenly saw, not far ahead, a group of gipsies on a wider patch of green beside the road."}

{"request_id":"b73dc30e3f0975cdd703d994","rewritten_text":"“Unless you mean to call Miss Havisham a he. And I don’t suppose even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, up town?” Joe asked.

“Is there any Miss Havisham down town?” my sister shot back.

“She wants this boy to go and play there. Naturally he’s going. And he’d better play there,” my sister said, shaking her head at me as if to spur me on to be as light and spry as possible, “or I’ll work him.”

I’d heard tell of Miss Havisham up town—everybody within miles had heard of Miss Havisham up town—an enormously rich, stern woman who kept to herself in a great, cheerless house barred against robbers.

“Well, I declare!” Joe exclaimed, plainly taken aback. “I wonder how she ever came to know Pip!”

“Noodle!” my sister cried. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Some person,” Joe suggested again, with his usual politeness, “must have said she wanted him to go and play there.”

“And can’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knows a boy fit for such a place? Isn’t it just possible that Uncle Pumblechook is a tenant of hers, and that he sometimes—though we won’t say quarterly or half-yearly, because that would ask too much of you—but sometimes goes there to pay his rent? And then can’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knows a boy to go and play there? And can’t Uncle Pumblechook, always thoughtful and considerate for us—though you may not think it, Joseph,” she added in the deepest reproachful tone, as though he were the most heartless nephew alive—“then mention this boy, standing Prancing here”—which I solemnly insist I wasn’t doing—“as one who has been a willing slave to her forever?”

“Good again!” Uncle Pumblechook cried. “Well said! Neatly put! Capital! Now Joseph, you understand the matter.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister answered, still reproachful, while Joe, with an apologetic air, wiped the back of his hand across and across his nose, “you don’t yet—though you may not think it—know the matter. You may fancy you do, but you don’t, Joseph. Because you don’t know that Uncle Pumblechook, seeing as how, for all we can tell, this boy’s fortune may hinge on his going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, to keep him there tonight, and to take him himself to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And Lor-a-mussy me!” my sister burst out, flinging off her bonnet in sudden despair. “Here I am, standing and talking to mere Mooncalfs, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, and the mare taking cold at the door, and the boy all grimed with crock and dirt from the hair of his head down to the sole of his foot!”"}

{"request_id":"55b87a4e04128fb6fa4eebf8","rewritten_text":"Mr. Elliot looked up with so much respect.”

“Quite delightful!” cried Mrs. Clay, though she didn’t dare to turn her eyes toward Anne. “Exactly like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not say father and son?”

“Oh! I’m putting no limits on anyone’s words. If you have such ideas! But, upon my word, I can hardly see that his attentions are any more than those of other men.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs. Clay, lifting her hands and eyes, and letting all the rest of her astonishment settle into a convenient silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you needn’t be so alarmed about him. You know I invited him. I sent him away with smiles. When I learned he was really going to his friends at Thornberry Park for the whole day tomorrow, I felt sorry for him.”

Anne admired how well her friend could act—how she managed to show such pleasure, both in the expectation and in the actual arrival of the very person whose presence must truly interfere with her main objective. It was impossible not to think that Mrs. Clay must hate seeing Mr. Elliot; and yet she could adopt the most obliging, calm expression and look perfectly satisfied with the reduced freedom of devoting herself only half as much to Sir Walter as she otherwise would have.

For Anne herself, it was most distressing to watch Mr. Elliot enter the room; and it was even more painful to have him come up to her and speak. She had been used to the feeling that he couldn’t always be entirely sincere, but now she saw insincerity in everything. His attentive deference to her father, set against his former words, was disgusting; and when she remembered his cruel conduct toward Mrs. Smith, she could hardly bear to see his present smiles and gentle manner, or even to hear his rehearsed good sentiments.

She meant to avoid any change in her manners that might give him reason to remonstrate. Her great aim was to escape all inquiry or attention; but she intended to be as clearly cool to him as could be reconciled with their relationship, and to step back—quietly, as far as she could—from the few degrees of unnecessary intimacy she had been gradually drawn into. Accordingly, she was more guarded and more reserved than she had been the night before.

He wanted to spark her curiosity again about how and where he might have heard her praised before; he wanted very much to be encouraged by more solicitation. But the spell was broken. He found that the warmth and liveliness of a public room were needed to feed his modest cousin’s vanity; he found, at least, that it couldn’t be done now by any of the attempts he might make under the too-strong claims of the others."}

{"request_id":"88564dd7280af79d980eeda4","rewritten_text":"The moment it was seen, the Ourang-Outang burst through the chamber door, ran down the stairs, and then—through an open window—got into the street.

The Frenchman followed in despair. The ape still held the razor and would sometimes stop to look back at him and wave its arms, until he was almost close enough to catch it. Then it ran off again. The chase went on like this for a long time. The streets were completely silent, since it was nearly three in the morning.

As it ran down an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the ape noticed a light coming from an open window in Madame L’Espanaye’s room, on the fourth floor. It rushed to the building, climbed up the lightning rod with unbelievable skill, grabbed the shutter, which had been pushed fully back against the wall, and used it to swing itself straight onto the bed’s headboard. The whole trick took less than a minute. As soon as it entered, the Ourang-Outang kicked the shutter open again.

Meanwhile, the sailor felt both hopeful and confused. He thought he might be able to catch the animal now, because it seemed trapped in the room it had chosen. It could only get away by using the lightning rod, and he might intercept it as it came down. But he also had good reason to worry about what the ape might do inside the house. That fear made him keep following.

Climbing a lightning rod is not hard, especially for a sailor. But when he reached the height of the window, which was far to his left, he could go no farther. All he could do was lean over and look into the room. When he saw what was inside, he nearly lost his grip from sheer horror.

That was when the terrible screams began, the ones that had woken the people in the Rue Morgue. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, still in their night clothes, seemed to have been busy arranging papers in the iron chest mentioned earlier. The chest had been wheeled into the middle of the room. It was open, and its contents were lying on the floor beside it. The victims must have been sitting with their backs to the window. And because of the time between the ape entering and the screams starting, it seems likely they did not notice the animal right away. The shutter slamming shut would naturally have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor looked in, the huge animal had grabbed Madame L’Espanaye by the hair—her hair was loose because she had been combing it—and was waving the razor near her face, copying the movements of a barber."}

{"request_id":"f00110a59d4ab547ddf7eb49","rewritten_text":"This was invitation enough.

“Why, my dear, you must understand it. Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been taken by a young man with a very large fortune from the north of England. He arrived on Monday in a chaise and four to look at the place, and was so taken with it that he agreed with Mr. Morris at once. He means to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the close of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married, or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear—of course! A single man of large fortune; four or five thousand a year. What a splendid prospect for our girls!”

“How so? In what way can it matter to them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” returned his wife, “how can you be so tiresome? You ought to know I’m thinking of his marrying one of them.”

“Is that what he’s aiming at, settling here?”

“Aim? Nonsense—how can you talk like that! Still, it’s very possible he may fall in love with one of them, so you must call on him as soon as he arrives.”

“I can see no need for that. You and the girls can go—or you can send them on their own, which might be even better; for since you’re as pretty as any of them, Mr. Bingley may well prefer you above the rest.”

“My dear, you do me a kindness. I admit I’ve had my share of beauty, but I don’t pretend to be remarkable now. When a woman has five grown-up daughters, she ought to stop worrying about her own looks.”

“In that sort of situation, a woman doesn’t usually have much beauty left to consider.”

“But you must, my dear, go and see Mr. Bingley the moment he comes into the neighbourhood.”

“I’m afraid I can’t promise that.”

“Just think of your daughters. Consider what an advantage it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are resolved to go, simply for that reason; for, as you know, they don’t pay visits to new arrivals in general. Indeed, you must go, because it will be impossible for us to visit him if you don’t.”

“You’re being far too particular. I dare say Mr. Bingley will be pleased to see you; and I will send a few lines by you to let him know how heartily I approve of his marrying whichever girl he chooses—though I must add a good word for my little Lizzy.”

“I don’t want you to do anything of that sort. Lizzy isn’t any better than the others, and I’m sure she isn’t half as handsome as Jane, nor half so good-tempered as Lydia.”"}

{"request_id":"fbf7e05e584a932c8e04a46e","rewritten_text":"You must take in some of my way of thinking. Only look back on the past, since remembering it brings you pleasure.”

“I can’t grant you credit for philosophy of that sort. Your backward-looking thoughts must be so entirely free of blame that the satisfaction they give you isn’t philosophy at all, but—something far better—mere ignorance. With me, it’s not like that. Painful recollections press in, ones I cannot, and ought not, try to drive away. I’ve been selfish all my life in practice, though not in principle. As a child I was taught what was right, yet I wasn’t taught to govern my temper. I was handed good principles, but I was left to follow them with pride and conceit. Worse still, being an only son—indeed, for many years an only child—I was spoiled by my parents. They were good themselves, (my father especially, all kindness and good nature,) yet they let me be, encouraged me, almost trained me to be selfish and overbearing: to care for no one beyond my own family circle; to think meanly of everyone else in the world; and even to wish that I could think just as meanly of their understanding and worth compared with my own. That was how I was, from eight to eight-and-twenty; and I might still have been so, if not for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth. What do I not owe you? You gave me a lesson—hard at first, but of the greatest use. Through you I was brought down properly. I came to you with no confidence at all in how I’d be received. You showed me how empty all my pretensions were, when it came to pleasing a woman who was truly meant to be pleased.”

“Then did you persuade yourself that I would?”

“Honestly, I did. What do you think of my vanity? I thought you were wishing and expecting my addresses.”

“My manners must have been at fault, though not on purpose, I assure you. I never meant to deceive you, but my spirits might easily have led me astray. How you must have hated me after that evening!”

“Hate you! I was angry, perhaps, at first, but my anger soon found its proper direction.”

“I’m almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. You blamed me for coming?”

“No, indeed—I felt nothing but surprise.”

“Your surprise couldn’t be greater than mine was, in being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no extraordinary politeness, and I admit I didn’t expect to receive more than my due.”

“My purpose then,” Darcy replied, “was to show you, by every civility I could manage, that I was not so low as to resent what was past; and I hoped to win your forgiveness, to soften your poor opinion, by letting you see that your reproofs had been taken to heart.”}"}

{"request_id":"4e76f3a95da95a1771ed514d","rewritten_text":"“Do you hear me? I know the language of despair. I have it memorized, because I am Despair—and I am a strange thing: joyful, triumphant Despair. But those words are not true. The wave may be dark, but it is not bitter. We lie down and close our eyes for a gentle good night, and when we wake, we are free. So come—no more delay, you slow one! Look at this pleasant potion. See, I am a spirit of good, not a human maid who calls you in. With words that would persuade you—oh, if only they could—she says, ‘Come and drink.’”

As I spoke, I stared at his face. His beauty was striking, and the compassion in his eyes shone through. Even before he answered, his quiet, sincere look—half regret, half amazement—changed my own tight, strained feelings. It took away the hard edge of despair and left only the gentlest kind of grief. I saw that his eyes were wet too. When he took both my hands, he sat down near me and said:

“This is a sad plan you are trying to lead me into, my dearest friend. Your pain must be very deep if it has brought you to these thoughts. You want death, but you fear it, and you still want me to be with you. But I have less courage than you. Even if I am with you, I cannot dare to die. Listen to me, and then think carefully about whether you should try to win me over to your plan. Even if, with the forceful speech of despair, you could make black death seem inviting—so that fair heaven itself would look like darkness—listen to the words of someone who has fed desperate thoughts and longed, with impatient desire, for death, but who has finally crushed that phantom and broken its power.

“Come, since you have played Despair with me, I will play the part of Una with you, and I will bring you out safely from his dark cave. Listen to me, and let yourself be softened by words that carry no selfish feeling.

“We do not know what this wide world really means. It is a strange mix of good and evil. But we have been placed here, and we have been told to live and to hope. I do not know exactly what we should hope for, but there is some good beyond us that we must search for. That is our work here on earth. If misfortune comes against us, we must fight it. We must push it aside and keep going, still trying to reach what it is in our nature to desire. I do not know whether this promise of future good is meant to prepare us for another life, or whether it simply means that, as workers in God’s vineyard, we must help smooth the way for those who come after us.”"}

{"request_id":"0787af823a4fb6c169a03a0c","rewritten_text":"And he always acted like Peter wrote him those things, but that was a lie. He got every blessed one of them out of that young flathead we canoed up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane went and fetched the letter her father had left behind, and the king read it out loud and cried over it. It gave the girls the dwelling-house and three thousand dollars in gold. It gave the tannery (which was doing a good business), along with some other houses and land worth about seven thousand, and three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William, and it told where the six thousand in cash was hidden down in the cellar. So these two frauds said they’d go and fetch it up, get everything square and above-board, and told me to come with a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag, they spilled it out on the floor, and it was a lovely sight—every one of those yellow boys. My, the way the king’s eyes did shine! He slaps the duke on the shoulder and says:

“Oh, this ain’t bully or anything! Oh, no, I reckon not! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, don’t it?”

The duke agreed. They pawed the yellow boys, sifted them through their fingers, and let them jingle down on the floor; and the king says:

“It ain’t no use talking. Being brothers to a rich dead man and representatives of foreign heirs that’s got left is the line for you and me, Bilge. This is what comes of trusting in Providence. It’s the best way in the long run. I’ve tried them all, and there ain’t no better way.”

Most everybody would’ve been satisfied with the pile and taken it on trust, but no—they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came out four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king says:

“Darn him. I wonder what he done with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?”

They worried over that for a while and ransacked all around for it. Then the duke says:

“Well, he was a pretty sick man, and likely he made a mistake. That’s probably the way of it. The best way’s to let it go and keep quiet about it. We can spare it.”

“Oh, shucks, yes, we can spare it. I don’t care nothin’ about that—it’s the count I’m thinking about. We want to be awful square and open and above-board here, you know. We want to lug this here money upstairs and count it before everybody, then there ain’t nothin’ suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

{"request_id":"124042166bf84c1ca44e43b1","rewritten_text":"But he had oppressed no one and imprisoned no one. He was so far from demanding payment harshly that he had given up what was owed to him of his own choice. He threw himself into a world that offered him no special help, found his own place there, and earned his own bread. Monsieur Gabelle had been holding the poor, troubled estate under written instructions meant to protect the people: to give them whatever little could be given—fuel that the heavy creditors would allow them to have in winter, and whatever produce could be saved from the same tight grip in summer. No doubt he had also stated and proved the same point in his defense, for his own safety, so that it could now seem unavoidable.

This helped shape the desperate decision Charles Darnay had already started to make: that he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the mariner in an old story, the winds and currents had carried him into the pull of the Loadstone Rock. It was drawing him in, and he had to go. Everything that came to his mind pushed him forward, faster and faster, more and more steadily, toward the terrible attraction. His hidden uneasiness was that bad plans were being carried out in his own unhappy country by bad people, and that the man who knew he was better than they were was not there, trying to stop the bloodshed and to stand up for mercy and humanity. With that uneasiness half silenced and half accusing him, he was led to compare himself to the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so strong. That comparison, which hurt him, was followed at once by Monseigneur’s sneers, which stung him bitterly, and then by Stryver’s, which were worse of all—coarse and especially painful for old reasons. After that came Gabelle’s letter: the plea of an innocent prisoner, facing death, asking for justice, honor, and a good name.

His decision was final. He had to go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was pulling him, and he would keep sailing until he struck. He knew of no rock, and he saw hardly any danger. Even though he had left what he had done unfinished, the purpose behind it still showed itself to him in a way that, in France, would be welcomed when he went there to claim it. Then that bright vision of doing good—so often the hopeful illusion of good-minded people—rose before him. He even imagined himself, under some guiding influence, able to steer this raging Revolution, which was running so wildly out of control."}

{"request_id":"2518d8eee4a1fdda8d66b173","rewritten_text":"The oaks around us were home to a tribe of nightingales—there I am now; Idris, in the prime of youth, is at my side—remember, I am only twenty-two, and seventeen summers have scarcely passed over the beloved of my heart. The river, swollen by autumn rains, has flooded the lowlands, and Adrian, in his favorite boat, is engaged in the dangerous pastime of plucking the topmost bough from a submerged oak. Are you weary of life, O Adrian, that you play with danger like this?—

He has won his prize, and he pilots his boat through the flood; our eyes followed him with fear, but the current carried him away from us. He was forced to land far downstream and make a long circuit before he could join us. “He is safe!” Idris said as he leapt ashore, waving the bough over his head as proof of success. “We’ll wait for him here.”

We were alone together; the sun had set; the nightingales began to sing; the evening star shone clearly in the flood of light, which still lingered in the west. The blue eyes of my angelic girl were fixed on this sweet emblem of herself. “How the light palpitates,” she said, “which is that star’s life. Its shifting brilliance seems to say that its condition, even like ours on earth, is wavering and changeable; it fears, I think, and it loves.”

“Don’t look at the star, dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Don’t read love in its trembling rays; don’t look at distant worlds; don’t speak of the mere imagination of a feeling. I have been silent for a long time—so long, even to sickness, have I wanted to speak to you and lay my soul, my life, my entire being at your feet. Don’t look at the star, dear love, or let that eternal spark plead for me; let it be my witness and my advocate, silent as it shines. Love is to me what light is to the star; as long as it is not eclipsed by annihilation, so long shall I love you.”

The joy of that moment must be forever hidden from the world’s cold gaze. Even now I can feel her graceful form pressed against my full, overflowing heart—still do sight, and pulse, and breath grow sick and fail at the memory of that first kiss. Slowly and quietly we went to meet Adrian, whom we heard approaching.

I urged Adrian to return to me after he had brought his sister home. And that same evening, walking along the moonlit paths of the forest, I poured out my whole heart—its rush of feeling and its hope—to my friend. For a moment he looked disturbed. “I might have foreseen this,” he said. “What conflict will now ensue!”"}
