{"request_id":"8c503f62cbebcb761743a75a","rewritten_text":"“Do you often come back?”

“I have never been here since.”

“Nor I.”

The moon began to rise, and I thought about the calm look of the white ceiling, which was gone now. The moon began to rise again, and I remembered the pressure of his hand when I spoke the last words he ever heard on earth.

Estella was the next one to break the silence between us.

“I have often hoped and planned to come back, but many things kept me away. Poor, poor old place!”

The silvery mist caught the first light of the moon, and the same light fell on the tears that were running down her face. She did not know I saw them, and she tried to control herself. Then she said quietly,—

“Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it ended up like this?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The ground belongs to me. It is the only thing I have not given up. Everything else has slipped away from me, little by little, but I have kept this. It was the only thing I fought for, in all those miserable years.”

“Is it going to be built on?”

“At last, it is. I came here to say goodbye to it before it changes. And you,” she asked, with a gentle interest in her voice, as if speaking to a traveler,—“you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And do well, I hope?”

“I work hard enough to make a living, so yes—I do well.”

“I have often thought of you,” Estella said.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. There was a long, hard time when I kept myself from remembering what I had thrown away, before I knew how much it was worth. But since my duty has not stopped me from admitting that memory, I have made room for it in my heart.”

“You have always had your place in my heart,” I answered.

Then we were silent again until she spoke.

“I never thought,” Estella said, “that I would be saying goodbye to you while I was saying goodbye to this place. I am glad to do it.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? For me, parting is painful. The memory of our last goodbye has always been sad and painful for me.”

“But you told me,” Estella replied, very earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ And if you could say that to me then, you will not hesitate to say it to me now—now, when suffering has been stronger than everything else, and has taught me what your heart used to be. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into something better.”"}

{"request_id":"92cfed5bd711f7cc31b6f063","rewritten_text":"These thoughts finally calmed me, and in the afternoon I fell into a deep sleep. But my fever would not let me have peaceful dreams. The terrible scene from the day before kept replaying in my mind: the women flying away, and Felix, furious, ripping me from my father’s feet. When I woke, I was worn out. It was already night, so I slipped out from where I had been hiding and went looking for food.

“Once I had eaten, I followed the familiar path that led to the cottage. Everything there seemed calm. I crawled into my hovel and waited in silence for the usual time when the family would get up. That time came and went. The sun rose high in the sky, but the cottagers did not appear. I shook with fear, sure that something dreadful had happened. Inside the cottage was dark, and I heard no movement. I cannot explain how painful that waiting was.

“Not long after, two countrymen passed by. They stopped near the cottage and began talking, with loud, forceful gestures. I could not understand them, because they spoke the language of the country, not the language my protectors used. Soon after that, Felix arrived with another man. I was shocked, because I knew Felix had not left the cottage that morning. I waited anxiously, hoping to learn from their conversation why things were so strange.

“‘Do you think,’ his companion asked, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and lose the produce from your garden? I don’t want to take advantage of you unfairly. So please take a few days to think about what you decide.’

“‘It’s completely useless,’ Felix answered. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of what happened, and I told you about it. My wife and my sister will never get over the horror. Please don’t keep arguing with me. Take your property and let me escape from this place.’

“Felix trembled as he said this. He and his companion went into the cottage. They stayed there for a few minutes, then left. I never saw any of the De Lacey family again.

“I spent the rest of the day in my hovel, in complete and numb despair. My protectors had gone, and they had broken the only connection I had to the world. For the first time, feelings of revenge and hatred filled my chest. I did not try to control them. Instead, I let myself be carried along, and I turned my thoughts toward harm and death.”"}

{"request_id":"839bcbc5cd8399f060147c3d","rewritten_text":"“These were the troubles that gnawed at Felix’s heart and made him, when I first met him, the most wretched member of his family. He might have borne poverty; and though that hardship had been the reward of his virtue, he took pride in it. Yet the Turk’s ingratitude, and the loss of his beloved Safie, were sorrows far sharper and beyond repair. The Arabian’s arrival, however, breathed fresh life into his soul.

“When word reached Leghorn that Felix had been stripped of his wealth and station, the merchant ordered his daughter to think of her lover no more and to prepare to go back to her native land. Safie’s generous spirit was stung by the command. She tried to argue with her father, but he left her in anger, repeating his harsh, tyrannical decree.

“A few days later, the Turk entered his daughter’s room and told her, in a hurried tone, that he had reason to believe his stay at Leghorn had been discovered, and that he must soon be handed over to the French government. He had therefore hired a vessel to take him to Constantinople, where he meant to sail within a few hours. He planned to leave his daughter in the keeping of a trusted servant, while he followed later at his ease with the larger portion of his property, which had not yet reached Leghorn.

“Left to herself, Safie resolved in her own mind what course of action she ought to take in this crisis. A life in Turkey repelled her; her religion and her heart were equally opposed to it. From certain papers of her father that came into her hands, she learned of her lover’s exile and discovered the name of the place where he was then living. She hesitated for a time, but at last she made up her mind. She took with her a few jewels that belonged to her and a sum of money, then left Italy with an attendant—a woman from Leghorn who could speak the common language of Turkey—and set out for Germany.

“She reached safely a town some twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage, but there her attendant fell gravely ill. Safie tended her with the utmost devotion; yet the poor girl died, and the Arabian was left alone—ignorant of the tongue of the country and wholly unacquainted with the ways of the world. Still, she came into good hands. The Italian had already named the place they were bound for, and after her death the mistress of the house where they had lodged took care that Safie should be brought safely to the cottage of her lover.”"}

{"request_id":"c91d716e9a4c8af51cc76989","rewritten_text":"It is not everyone who would have handled it the way she did—standing up for herself in such a kind way, and refusing to accept Jane’s answer. But she was absolutely clear that she would not write any such denial yesterday, as Jane wished; she would wait. And sure enough, yesterday evening it was all settled that Jane should go. Quite a surprise to me! I had no idea at all. Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and told her at once that, after thinking through the advantages of Mrs. Smallridge’s situation, she had decided to accept it. “I didn’t know a word of it until everything was settled.”

“You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton?”

“Yes, all of us. Mrs. Elton insisted that we come. It was decided up on the hill while we were walking about with Mr. Knightley. ‘You must all spend your evening with us,’ she said—‘I positively must have you all come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was there too, was he?”

“No, not Mr. Knightley. He refused it from the first. And though I thought he might come, because Mrs. Elton said she wouldn’t let him off, he didn’t. But my mother, and Jane, and I were all there, and we had a very agreeable evening. Such kind friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse—you always find them agreeable, even if everyone seemed rather worn out after the morning’s party. Even pleasure, you know, is tiring, and I can’t say any of them seemed to have enjoyed it very much. Still, I shall always think it a very pleasant party, and I feel extremely grateful to the kind friends who included me in it.”

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you weren’t aware of it, had been making up her mind all day?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the time may come, it must be unwelcome to her and all her friends—but I hope her engagement will have every alleviation that’s possible. I mean, as far as the character and manners of the family go.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, there is everything in the world that can make her happy in it. Except the Sucklings and Bragges, there isn’t such another nursery establishment—so liberal and so elegant—in all of Mrs. Elton’s acquaintance. Mrs. Smallridge is a most delightful woman. The style of living is almost equal to Maple Grove. And as for the children—except the little Sucklings and the little Bragges—there aren’t such elegant, sweet children anywhere. Jane will be treated with such regard and kindness. It will be nothing but pleasure—a life of pleasure. And her salary! I really can’t bring myself to name her salary to you, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"0ecdf47da9fe35239b9bc3bb","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so completely satisfied with this conversation that he never again bothered himself, or provoked his dear sister Elizabeth, by bringing up the subject; and she was pleased to discover that she had said enough to keep him quiet.

The day of his and Lydia’s departure soon arrived; and Mrs. Bennet was forced to accept a separation, which, since her husband by no means agreed with her plan of having them all go to Newcastle, was likely to last at least a year.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when shall we meet again?”

“Oh, Lord! I don’t know. Not for these two or three years, perhaps.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women never have much time for writing. My sisters may write to me. They have nothing else to do.”

Mr. Wickham’s goodbyes were far more affectionate than his wife’s. He smiled, looked handsome, and said many flattering things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet as soon as they were out of the house, “as ever I saw. He simpers, and smirks, and makes love to us all. I’m prodigiously proud of him. I defy even Sir William Lucas himself to produce a more valuable son-in-law.”

The loss of her daughter left Mrs. Bennet very dull for several days.

“I often think,” said she, “that there is nothing so bad as parting with one’s friends. You feel so forlorn without them.”

“This is the consequence, you see, madam, of marrying a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It ought to make you more satisfied that your other four are still single.”

“It is no such thing. Lydia isn’t leaving me because she’s married, but only because her husband’s regiment happens to be stationed so far away. If it had been nearer, she wouldn’t have gone so soon.”

But the listless state this event left her in was soon relieved, and her mind opened again to the agitation of hope, by a piece of news that then began to circulate. The housekeeper at Netherfield had received orders to prepare for the arrival of her master, who was coming down in a day or two to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was quite restless. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head in turn.

“Well, well, and so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” (for Mrs. Philips was the one who first brought her the news). “Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, though. He is nothing to us, you know, and I’m sure I never want to see him again. But, however, he is very welcome to come to Netherfield, if he likes it."}

{"request_id":"04b06c068156769c1e415986","rewritten_text":"The day went by much the same as the day before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent part of the morning with the invalid. He was still slowly getting better, and in the evening Elizabeth joined their group in the drawing-room. The loo table, however, was not there. Mr. Darcy was writing. Miss Bingley sat near him and watched his letter as he worked, often distracting him by sending messages to her sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst watched their game.

Elizabeth picked up some needlework and was entertained by what happened between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s constant praise—about his handwriting, the neatness of his lines, and how long his letter was—came with such complete calm, as if she expected no special reaction, that it turned into a strange kind of conversation. It matched her own opinion of him perfectly.

“Miss Darcy will be so happy to receive a letter like this!”

He did not answer.

“You write very fast.”

“You’re mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must have to write in a year! Business letters, too. I should think they would be dreadful.”

“Then it’s lucky that they fall to my responsibility instead of yours.”

“Please tell your sister that I can’t wait to see her.”

“I’ve already told her that once, at your request.”

“I’m afraid you don’t like your pen. Let me fix it for you. I repair pens remarkably well.”

“Thank you—but I always repair my own.”

“How do you manage to write so neatly?”

He stayed silent.

“Tell your sister I’m delighted to hear she’s improved on the harp. And please let her know I’m completely thrilled with her beautiful little design for a table. I think it’s infinitely better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“May I ask you to hold off on your excitement until I write again? Right now I don’t have space to do it justice.”

“Oh, it doesn’t matter. I’ll see her in January. But do you always write such charming long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

“They’re usually long. As for whether they’re always charming, that’s not for me to decide.”

“It’s a rule for me: if someone can write a long letter easily, they can’t write badly.”

“That won’t do as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” her brother said. “He doesn’t write with ease. He thinks too much about every word, even words of four syllables. Don’t you, Darcy?”

“My writing style is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” Miss Bingley said, “Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable.”"}

{"request_id":"1ba379f1cf2a561a03251a12","rewritten_text":"Emma did not have to change her opinion of Mrs. Elton after anything she later learned. Her first judgment had been pretty accurate. The way Mrs. Elton seemed to her in this second visit was the same way she seemed whenever they met again: self-important, presumptuous, too familiar, ignorant, and badly brought up. Mrs. Elton had a little beauty and a little accomplishment, but so little judgment that Emma believed she thought she knew more about the world than everyone else. She imagined herself improving and brightening a country neighborhood. Emma also thought Miss Hawkins must have had a place in society that only Mrs. Elton’s status could possibly surpass.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton felt any differently from his wife. He did not just seem happy with her; he seemed proud. He had the look of someone congratulating himself for bringing such a woman to Highbury, a woman even Miss Woodhouse could not match. Most of the people who were now meeting her were either ready to praise her or not used to judging for themselves. They followed Miss Bates’s friendly attitude, or simply assumed that the bride must be as clever and as pleasant as she claimed to be. Because of this, Mrs. Elton’s praise moved from one person’s mouth to another, just as it should, without being interrupted by Miss Woodhouse. Miss Woodhouse, in fact, kept up her first kind contribution and talked easily about how “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed” Mrs. Elton was.

In one way, Mrs. Elton became even worse than she had seemed at first. Her feelings toward Emma changed. She was probably offended by the small amount of encouragement she got when she tried to become more intimate. So she pulled back, and gradually became much colder and more distant. The result was pleasant for Emma, but the bad feeling that caused it could only make Emma dislike her more. Their manners were also unpleasant toward Harriet. Mrs. Elton and Mr. Elton were sneering and careless. Emma hoped it would quickly help cure Harriet, but the kind of behavior that could produce such treatment showed how much they disliked her, and it made both of them seem even worse. It was not in doubt that Harriet’s attachment had been offered as a kind of openness in marriage, and that their story about it—presented in the least favorable way to Harriet and the most comforting way to him—had likely included Harriet’s own part as well. Harriet, of course, was the target of their shared dislike. When they had nothing else to say, it was always easy to start criticizing Miss Woodhouse. And since they could not show their hostility toward her openly, they let it out more freely by treating Harriet with contempt.

Mrs. Elton soon took a strong fancy to Jane Fairfax, and she did so from the beginning. Not only because a rivalry with one young woman might make her want to support another, but from the very first. She was not content with simply showing a natural, reasonable admiration. Without being asked, without making any request, and without any special right or permission, she felt she must help and befriend her. Before Emma had lost Mrs. Elton’s confidence, and about the third time they met, Emma heard all of Mrs. Elton’s “knight-errantry” on the subject."}

{"request_id":"44e676f18b55a1f0e4286ccb","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and a cheerful nature, seemed to have many of the best things life can offer. She had lived almost twenty-one years with very little that could upset or annoy her.

She was the younger of two daughters of a loving, indulgent father. Because of her sister’s marriage, she had been in charge of his household from an early age. Her mother had died long enough ago that Emma could only remember her in a vague way. An excellent woman had taken her place as governess, and she was nearly like a mother to Emma in her affection.

For sixteen years, Miss Taylor had been part of Mr. Woodhouse’s family. She was less a strict governess than a friend, and she was especially fond of Emma. Between them, it was more like the closeness of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor stopped being a governess in name, her gentle temper made it hard for her to impose any real control. Now that the idea of authority was long gone, they lived together as friends who were strongly attached to each other, and Emma did what she pleased. She valued Miss Taylor’s judgment, but she mostly followed her own.

In truth, the real problems in Emma’s situation were that she had too much freedom and that she tended to think very highly of herself. Those were the disadvantages that could spoil her many pleasures. For now, though, the danger was so easy to ignore that it did not feel like a misfortune to her.

Then sorrow came—quiet sorrow, not the kind that made her feel openly unhappy. Miss Taylor married. It was Miss Taylor’s loss that first brought grief. On the day of this beloved friend’s wedding, Emma first found herself thinking sadly about what might come next. After the ceremony was over and the wedding guests had left, Emma and her father were left to dine together, with no hope of a third person to make a long evening pleasant. After dinner, her father settled down to sleep as usual, and Emma had only her thoughts to keep her company.

The marriage promised happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of good character, with an easy income, a suitable age, and pleasant manners. Emma also felt some comfort in knowing that she had always wanted and encouraged the match with her selfless, generous friendship. Still, it was a dark day for Emma. She would feel Miss Taylor’s absence every hour, every day. She remembered the kindness of the past—the kindness and affection of sixteen years—how Miss Taylor had taught her and played with her since Emma was five, how she had used all her strength to keep Emma happy and entertained when she was well, and how she had cared for her through the illnesses of childhood."}

{"request_id":"e9fa23bf948e162c1766b469","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was considerably upset by Lord Canterville’s refusal, and urged him to reconsider, but the good-humoured peer remained quite resolute. At last he persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the present the ghost had given her; and when, in the spring of 1890, the young Duchess of Cheshire was introduced at the Queen’s first drawing-room on the occasion of her marriage, her jewels became the universal subject of admiration. Virginia received the coronet—the reward, as it were, for all good little American girls—and she married her boy-lover as soon as he came of age. They were both so delightful, and they loved one another so deeply, that nearly everyone was pleased with the match, save for the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had been trying to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had given no fewer than three costly dinner-parties for the purpose—oddly enough, including Mr. Otis’s. Mr. Otis was personally very fond of the young Duke, but in principle he objected to titles, and, in his own words, ‘was not without apprehension lest, amid the enervating influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true principles of republican simplicity should be forgotten.’ Those objections, however, were entirely set aside; and I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter leaning on his arm, there was not a prouder man anywhere in all England.

After the honeymoon had ended, the Duke and Duchess went down to Canterville Chase, and the day after their arrival they took an afternoon walk over to the lonely churchyard by the pine-woods. At first there had been some trouble about what should be written on Sir Simon’s tombstone, but it was finally decided to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some lovely roses, which she scattered on the grave; and after they had stood there for a while, they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. There the Duchess sat down on a fallen pillar, while her husband lay at her feet smoking a cigarette and gazing up into her beautiful eyes. Suddenly he tossed his cigarette aside, took her hand, and said, ‘Virginia, a wife should have no secrets from her husband.’

‘Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.’

‘Yes, you have,’ he replied, smiling; ‘you have never told me what happened to you when you were shut up with the ghost.’

‘I have never told anyone, Cecil,’ said Virginia gravely."}

content.text: {"request_id":"9036f3d7c73ac5b43aaddae7","rewritten_text":"In fact, he had been completely unaware of any influence of his own. He had followed her into the shrubbery without any intention of trying to do anything. He had come, driven by anxiety to see how she handled Frank Churchill’s engagement, with no selfish motive at all—indeed, with no motive in particular—except to try, if she gave him an opening, to soothe or advise her.—What happened next was simply the work of the moment, the immediate effect of what he heard on his feelings. Her delightful certainty of being entirely indifferent to Frank Churchill, her heart completely disengaged from him, had sparked the hope that, over time, he might win her affection himself;—but it was not a hope for the present. In the brief rush of eagerness overpowering judgment, he had only wanted to be told that she would not forbid his attempt to attach her.—The stronger hopes that gradually opened up were all the more enchanting.—The affection he had been asking permission to create, if he could, was already his!—Within half an hour, he had gone from a state of mind that was thoroughly distressed to something so close to perfect happiness that it could have no other name.\n\n_Her_ change matched his. This same half-hour had given each of them the precious certainty of being loved, and had cleared from each the same degree of ignorance, jealousy, or distrust.—On his side, there had been a long-standing jealousy, dating back to Frank Churchill’s arrival—or even the expectation of it. He had been in love with Emma, and jealous of Frank Churchill, from about the same period; one feeling had probably helped him understand the other. It was his jealousy of Frank Churchill that had pulled him away from the country.—The Box Hill party had decided him to go. He would protect himself from having to witness again those attentions that were allowed and encouraged. He had gone to learn to be indifferent.—But he had gone to the wrong place. There was too much domestic happiness in his brother’s house; the women there wore too amiable a face; Isabella was too much like Emma—differing only in those striking, inferior qualities that always made the other seem brighter by comparison, even though there would have been plenty to do, had his time been longer. He stayed on, though, vigorously, day after day—until this very morning’s post brought him the story of Jane Fairfax. Then, with the gladness that had to be felt—indeed, which he did not hesitate to feel, since he had never believed Frank Churchill deserved Emma at all—there was so much tender concern, so much sharp anxiety for her, that he could not stay any longer. He rode home through the rain; and after dinner he walked straight up, to see how this sweetest and best of all creatures—faultless despite all her faults—handled the discovery."}

{"request_id":"44b6d5e7578804c75160e103","rewritten_text":"“I examined the death’s-head anew, with close attention. Its outer margins—those portions of the drawing lying nearest the edge of the vellum—stood out much more clearly than the rest. It was plain that the action of the caloric had been either imperfect or uneven. I promptly set a fire, and warmed every part of the parchment with a steady glow. At first, the only result was to make the faint lines of the skull more pronounced; but, if I persisted with the trial, then—at the corner of the slip, diagonally across from the place where the death’s-head was drawn—there came into view the shape of what I took, at first, for a goat. A nearer look, though, convinced me it was meant to be a kid.”

“Ha! ha!” said I. “Why, certainly I have no business laughing at you; a million and a half of money is far too grave a thing for mirth. Still, you’re not going to forge a third link in your chain—you won’t discover any special tie between your pirates and a goat. Pirates, you know, have nothing to do with goats; they belong to the farming interest.”

“But I’ve just said the figure wasn’t a goat.”

“Well—then a kid. Pretty much the same business.”

“Pretty much, but not quite,” said Legrand. “You may have heard of one Captain Kidd. I took the animal’s figure at once as a kind of pun, or hieroglyphical signature. I call it a signature because its position on the vellum suggested the notion. The death’s-head at the corner diagonally opposite had, in the same way, the look of a stamp, or seal. Yet I was vexed by the lack of everything else—of the body to match my imagined instrument—of the text to supply my context.”

“I suppose you expected to find a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something of that sort. The truth is, I felt an irresistible presentiment of some great good fortune hanging over me. I can hardly say why. Perhaps it was more a longing than a real belief;—but you know, Jupiter’s foolish talk about the bug being of solid gold had a striking effect on my imagination. And then there was the whole chain of accidents and coincidences—so extraordinary. Do you notice how it was mere chance that these events should have fallen on the one day of the year that is, or may be, cool enough for fire, and that, without the fire—or without the dog’s intervention at the exact moment when he appeared—I should never have noticed the death’s-head, and so never have become the owner of the treasure?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"d604a3eff2c83237efa63ea0","rewritten_text":"Col. Grangerford was a gentleman, you see. He was a gentleman from head to toe, and so was his family. He was well born, as the saying goes, and that’s worth as much in a man as it is in a horse, so the Widow Douglas said, and nobody ever denied that she was among the first aristocracy in our town; and pap said it too, though he wasn’t any more quality than a mudcat himself. Col. Grangerford was very tall and very slim, with a darkish-pale complexion—there wasn’t a sign of red in it anywhere. He was clean-shaven every morning all over his thin face, and he had the thinnest kind of lips, and the thinnest kind of nostrils, and a high nose, and heavy eyebrows, and the blackest kind of eyes, sunk so deep back that they seemed like they were looking out of caverns at you, as you might say. His forehead was high, and his hair was black and straight and hung down to his shoulders. His hands were long and thin, and every day of his life he put on a clean shirt and a full suit from head to foot made out of linen so white it hurt your eyes to look at it; and on Sundays he wore a blue tail-coat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane with a silver head on it. There wasn’t any frivolousness about him, not a bit, and he wasn’t ever loud. He was as kind as he could be—you could feel that, you know, and so you had confidence. Sometimes he smiled, and it was good to see; but when he straightened himself up like a liberty pole, and the lightning started flickering out from under his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree first and find out what the matter was afterward. He never had to tell anybody to mind their manners—everybody was always well-mannered where he was. Everybody loved to have him around, too; he was sunshine most always—I mean he made it seem like good weather. When he turned into a cloudbank it was awful dark for half a minute, and that was enough; there wouldn’t be nothing go wrong again for a week.\n\nWhen he and the old lady came down in the morning, all the family got up out of their chairs and gave them good-day, and didn’t sit down again until they had sat down. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard where the decanter was, mixed a glass of bitters, and handed it to him. He held it in his hand and waited until Tom’s and Bob’s was mixed, and then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam;” and they bowed the least bit in the world and said thank you. Then they drank, all three. Bob and Tom poured a spoonful of water on the sugar and the tiniest bit of whisky or apple brandy at the bottom of their tumblers, and gave it to me and Buck, and we drank to the old people too."}

{"request_id":"331fb48f35469640e3038a08","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, gently laying his hand on the Doctor’s arm again, after a short silence from both sides, “what would you say caused this attack?”

“I believe,” returned Doctor Manette, “that there was a strong and extraordinary revival of the train of thought and remembrance that was the first cause of the illness. Some intense associations of the most distressing kind were vividly brought back, I think. It’s probable that there had long been a dread in his mind—that those associations would be recalled—say, under certain circumstances—say, on a particular occasion. He tried to prepare himself in vain; perhaps the effort to prepare made him less able to bear it.”

“Would he remember what happened during the relapse?” asked Mr. Lorry, with natural hesitation.

The Doctor looked desolately around the room, shook his head, and answered, in a low voice, “Not at all.”

“Now, about the future,” Mr. Lorry suggested.

“As for the future,” said the Doctor, regaining firmness, “I have great hope. Since it pleased Heaven, in its mercy, to restore him so soon, I have great hope. He, yielding under the pressure of a complicated something—long dreaded, long vaguely foreseen, and long fought against—and recovering after the cloud had burst and passed, I should hope that the worst is over.”

“Well, well! That’s good comfort. I’m thankful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I’m thankful!” repeated the Doctor, bowing his head with reverence.

“There are two other points,” said Mr. Lorry, “on which I’m anxious to be instructed. May I go on?”

“You can’t do your friend a better service.” The Doctor took his hand.

“To the first, then. He’s studious by habit, and unusually energetic; he applies himself with great ardour to acquiring professional knowledge, to conducting experiments, to many things. Now—does he do too much?”

“I don’t think so. It may be the nature of his mind to always be in need of occupation. That could be partly natural to him, and partly the result of affliction. The less it was occupied with healthy things, the more it would be in danger of turning toward the unhealthy. He may have noticed it in himself and made that discovery.”

“You’re sure he isn’t under too much strain?”

“I think I’m quite sure of it.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt if that could easily be. There has been a violent stress in one direction, and it needs a counterweight.”

“Excuse me, as a persistent man of business. Suppose, for a moment, that he _was_ overworked; would it show itself in some renewed outbreak of this disorder?”"}

{"request_id":"c8712be03ca6da888d9949c6","rewritten_text":"A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired cavalier went out riding over Brockley meadows. In forcing their way through a hedge, she tore her habit so badly that, when she came back home, she decided to take the back staircase, so she would not be seen. As she passed the Tapestry Chamber—whose door happened to be open—she thought she caught sight of someone within. Believing it to be her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her work there, she peeped in to ask that her habit be mended. To her utter astonishment, it was the Canterville Ghost himself. He sat by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees whirl and fly through the air, while the red leaves danced furiously down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his whole posture spoke of the deepest depression. Indeed, he looked so forlorn, and so much out of repair, that little Virginia—whose first impulse had been to run away and lock herself in her room—felt pity and resolved to try to comfort him. Her step was so light, and his misery so heavy, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

“I am so sorry for you,” she said. “But my brothers are going back to Eton to-morrow; and then, if you behave yourself, no one will annoy you.”

“It is absurd to ask me to behave myself,” he replied, turning his head in astonishment toward the pretty little girl who had dared to address him. “Quite absurd. I must rattle my chains, and groan through keyholes, and pace about at night—if that is what you mean. It is my only business in existing.”

“It is no business at all to exist for that,” said Virginia, with at times a sweet Puritan seriousness she had caught from some old New England ancestor. “And you know you have been very wicked. Mrs. Umney told us, the very first day we arrived here, that you had killed your wife.”

“Well,” said the Ghost, with petulance, “I do allow it. But it was a purely family affair, and it concerned no one else.”

“It is very wrong to kill anyone,” Virginia insisted.

“Oh, I detest the cheap severity of abstract ethics!” he cried. “My wife was plain enough—she never had my ruffs properly starched, and she knew nothing about cookery. Why, there was a buck I shot in Hogley Woods—a magnificent pricket—and do you know how she had it sent up to table? But it is all over now, and I don’t think it was very kind of her brothers to starve me to death, though I did kill her.”"}

“I think, sir,” said the spy, in the meanest manner, as he turned to Mr. Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your years and benevolence to put it to this other gentleman—so much your junior—whether, under any circumstances, he can reconcile it to his station to play that Ace of which he has spoken. I admit that I am a spy, and that it is considered a discreditable station—though it must be filled by somebody; but this gentleman is no spy. Why should he demean himself into becoming one?”

“I’ll play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, taking the answer on himself, and looking at his watch, “without any scruple, in a very few minutes.”

“I should have hoped, gentlemen both,” said the spy, always trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the discussion, “that your respect for my sister—”

“I couldn’t show my respect for your sister better than by finally relieving her of her brother,” said Sydney Carton.

“You don’t think so, sir?”

“I’ve made up my mind about it.”

The spy’s smooth manner—curiously at odds with his ostentatiously rough dress, and probably with his usual behavior—received such a blow from the inscrutability of Carton, who was a mystery to wiser and more honest men than he, that it faltered and failed him. While he was at a loss, Carton said, resuming his earlier air of studying the cards:

“And indeed, now that I think again, I have a strong impression that I have another good card here, not yet counted. That friend and fellow-sheep who spoke of himself as pasturing in the country prisons—who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” said the spy quickly.

“French, is he?” repeated Carton, musing, and not seeming to notice him at all, though he echoed the word. “Well; he may be.”

“I assure you,” said the spy, “though it’s not important.”

“Not important,” repeated Carton in the same mechanical way—“not important—No, it’s not important. No. Still, I know the face.”

“I don’t think so. I’m sure I don’t. It can’t be,” said the spy.

“It-can’t-be,” muttered Sydney Carton, looking back on it, and idling his glass again (which fortunately was a small one). “Can’t be. Spoke good French. Yet, like a foreigner, I thought?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” cried Carton, slapping his open hand on the table as a clear light broke in his mind. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had that man before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now, there you are, sir,” said Barsad, with a smile that made his aquiline nose tilt even more to one side; “there you really give me an advantage over you.”"}

{"request_id":"eaafa81c5fe84d03552c54c4","rewritten_text":"Countrymen, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and vagabonds of every low sort were all mixed together into one mass. The drovers whistled, dogs barked, and the oxen bellowed and surged forward; sheep bleated, pigs grunted and squeaked; hawkers cried out; on every side there were shouts, oaths, and quarrels. Bells rang and voices roared from every public-house. The crowd pressed in, shoved, drove, struck, and kept up a constant whooping and yelling. From every corner of the market came a hideous, discordant din, and through it all ran unwashed, unshaven, squalid, dirty figures, constantly darting to and fro, bursting into the throng and breaking out of it again—making a stunning, bewildering scene that left the senses completely confused.

Mr. Sikes, dragging Oliver after him, elbowed his way through the thickest part of the crowd, paying very little attention to the sights and sounds that so astonished the boy. He nodded two or three times to a passing friend; and, resisting as many invitations as he could to stop for a morning drink, he kept moving steadily onward until they were clear of the chaos and had made their way through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, young ’un!” said Sikes, looking up at the clock on St. Andrew’s Church. “It’s hard on seven—so you’ve got to step out. Don’t fall behind already, Lazy-legs!”

He punctuated this with a jerk on his little companion’s wrist. Oliver quickened his pace into a kind of trot—somewhere between a fast walk and a run—and kept up with the house-breaker’s rapid strides as best he could.

They kept going at that pace until they had passed Hyde Park Corner and were on their way to Kensington. Then Sikes slowed down until an empty cart a short distance behind caught up. Seeing “Hounslow” written on it, he asked the driver, as politely as he could manage, whether he would give them a lift as far as Isleworth.

“Jump up,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes; he’s my boy,” Sikes answered, staring hard at Oliver, and slipping his hand absently into the pocket where the pistol was.

“Your father walks rather too quick for you, doesn’t he, my man?” the driver asked, noticing Oliver was out of breath.

“Not a bit of it,” Sikes cut in. “He’s used to it. Here—take hold of my hand, Ned. Get in with you!”

With that, he addressed Oliver and helped him into the cart. The driver pointed to a heap of sacks and told him to lie down there and rest.

As they passed the different mile-stones, Oliver wondered more and more where his companion meant to take him. Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, Brentford—all were passed, and still they went on as steadily as if they had only just started their journey."}

{"request_id":"f4c95e961e612aa23a7221bc","rewritten_text":"Should I be carried up to the skies, on flowery beds of ease,

While others fight to win the prize, and sail through blood-y seas?

He was regarded as a wonderful reader. At church “sociables” he was always called on to read poetry; and when he finished, the ladies would lift up their hands and let them fall helplessly into their laps, and “wall” their eyes, and shake their heads, as much as to say, “Words cannot express it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this mortal earth.”

After the hymn had been sung, the Rev. Mr. Sprague turned himself into a bulletin-board, and read off “notices” of meetings and societies and things until it seemed the list would stretch out to the crack of doom—a queer custom that is still kept up in America, even in cities, out here in this age of abundant newspapers. Often, the less there is to justify a traditional custom, the harder it is to get rid of it.

And now the minister prayed. It was a good, generous prayer, and it went into details: it pleaded for the church, and the little children of the church; for the other churches of the village; for the village itself; for the county; for the State; for the State officers; for the United States; for the churches of the United States; for Congress; for the President; for the officers of the Government; for poor sailors, tossed by stormy seas; for the oppressed millions groaning under the heel of European monarchies and Oriental despotisms; for those who have the light and the good tidings, and yet have not eyes to see nor ears to hear; for the heathen in the far islands of the sea; and it closed with a supplication that the words he was about to speak might find grace and favor, and be as seed sown in fertile ground, yielding in time a grateful harvest of good. Amen.

There was a rustling of dresses, and the standing congregation sat down. The boy whose history this book tells did not enjoy the prayer; he only endured it—if he even did that much. He was restless all through it; he kept tally of the details of the prayer, without meaning to—for he wasn’t listening, but he knew the ground of it, and the clergyman’s regular route over it—and when a little trifle of new matter was slipped in, his ear caught it and his whole nature resented it; he thought the additions unfair, and downright scoundrelly. In the middle of the prayer a fly had landed on the back of the pew in front of him and tortured his spirit by calmly rubbing its hands together, embracing its head with its arms, and polishing it so vigorously that it seemed to almost separate from the body, and the slender thread of a neck was exposed to view; scraping its wings with its hind legs and smoothing them back to its body as if they were coat-tails; going through its whole grooming as tranquilly as if it knew it was perfectly safe."}

{"request_id":"0f696628d1bad106f9d6433f","rewritten_text":"I will now tell my own story. In the early part of my life there is not much to say, so I will be brief. Still, I need to spend a little time on my childhood, because it should be clear how, when one hope failed, life became empty, and how, when the only affection I was allowed to hold onto was taken away, my life ended with it.

I have already said that my aunt was nothing like my father. I believe she had the coldest heart a person can have, with no trace of cruelty or bad feeling—she simply could not feel affection. She took me under her protection because she thought it was her duty. But she had lived alone for so long, undisturbed by the noise and chatter of children, that she could not bear for me to disturb her peace. She had never married. For the last five years she had lived by herself on an estate that had come to her from her mother, on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland.

In his letters, my father had asked that she come live with me at his family home, a large mansion in the beautiful countryside near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused. But once she had dealt with the matters her brother’s leaving had put in her hands, she left England and took me with her to her Scottish estate.

When I was a baby, and later until I turned eight, my care was handled by a servant from my mother’s household. This servant had come with us when we withdrew to live there. I was placed in a quiet, remote part of the house, and I only saw my aunt at set times. She came to me twice a day. Once, around noon, she visited my nursery. The second time was after her dinner, when she took me to her. She never hugged or comforted me, and whenever I was in the room she seemed to worry that I might annoy her with some childish act. My nurse always prepared me carefully before she would bring me into the parlour. The fear I felt from my aunt’s cold looks and her few, careful words was so strong that I rarely broke the rules, and I was never caught failing to be as quiet and well-behaved as I was taught to be during those short visits.

With my nurse’s care, I ran freely around the park and the nearby fields. From my earliest years, I showed the deepest love, and it made me very sensitive. I cannot even say how strongly I loved everything, even the lifeless things around me."}

Ah—there’s Mr. Podgers! Mr. Podgers, I want you to read the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, you must take your glove off. No, not the left—the other one.”

“Dear Gladys, I don’t really think it’s quite proper,” said the Duchess, weakly unfastening a kid glove that was rather grimy.

“Nothing interesting ever is,” said Lady Windermere: “_on a fait le monde ainsi_. Still, I must introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my pet cheiromantist. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley; and if you tell me she has a larger mountain of the moon than I do, I shall never believe a word you say again.”

“I’m sure, Gladys, nothing of that sort is in my hand,” the Duchess replied, solemnly.

“Your Grace is quite right,” said Mr. Podgers, looking down at the little, fat hand with its short, square fingers; “the mountain of the moon isn’t developed. The line of life, however, is excellent. If you please, bend the wrist. Thank you. Three distinct lines on the _rascette_! You’ll live to a great age, Duchess, and be exceedingly happy. Ambition—very moderate; the line of intellect—nothing overstated; the line of heart—”

“Now, do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers,” Lady Windermere called out.

“Nothing would give me more satisfaction,” said Mr. Podgers, bowing, “if the Duchess had ever been otherwise; but I’m afraid I perceive a strong permanence of affection, joined with a firm sense of duty.”

“Pray continue, Mr. Podgers,” said the Duchess, looking quite pleased.

“Economy is by no means the least of Your Grace’s virtues,” Mr. Podgers went on, and Lady Windermere burst into laughter.

“Economy is a very fine thing,” the Duchess said, pleased with herself; “when I married Paisley he had eleven castles, and not a single house fit to live in.”

“And now he has twelve houses, and not a single castle,” Lady Windermere retorted.

“Well, my dear,” said the Duchess, “I like—”

“Comfort,” said Mr. Podgers. “Modern improvements. Hot water laid on in every bedroom. Your Grace is quite right. Comfort is the only thing our civilisation can offer.”

“You’ve described the Duchess’s character beautifully, Mr. Podgers; and now you must tell Lady Flora’s,” and, at a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall girl with sandy Scotch hair and high shoulder-blades stepped awkwardly out from behind the sofa, holding out a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers.

“Ah—so a pianist! I see,” said Mr. Podgers. “An excellent pianist, certainly, though perhaps hardly a musician.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"d64684de27233b67fd2bd594","rewritten_text":"We both agreed in loving Adrian: yet though she had not escaped childhood, she could not grasp, as I did, the full measure of his merits, nor share the same sympathy in his pursuits and opinions. I was forever with him. There was a sensibility and sweetness in his temper that lent our talk a tender, almost unearthly music. And then he was as gay as a lark, singing from its skyward height—thoughtful as an eagle, innocent as the mild-eyed dove. He could quiet the seriousness of Perdita, and draw the sting from the tormenting activity of my nature. I began to look back on my restless desires and my painful struggles with my fellow beings as though they were only the stuff of a troubled dream, and I felt myself altered as if I had passed into another shape, with a new set of senses and nerves that changed how the apparent universe was reflected in the mind’s mirror. Yet it was not so: I remained the same in strength, in my earnest craving for sympathy, in my longing for active exertion. My manly virtues did not desert me; for Urania spared the locks of Sampson while he lay at her feet, though everything was softened and made more human. Nor did Adrian teach me only the cold truths of history and philosophy. While he trained me, through those lessons, to master my own reckless and uncultivated spirit, he also turned my gaze to the living page of his own heart, so that I could feel and understand its wondrous character.\n\nThe ex-queen of England, even in her son’s earliest years, had tried to plant daring and ambitious designs in his mind. She saw that he was endowed with genius and uncommon talent, and she cultivated these qualities so they could later be used to advance her own purposes. She encouraged his hunger for knowledge and his impetuous courage; she even put up with his untamed love of freedom, hoping—what so often happens—that it would grow into a passion for command. She sought to raise him with resentment toward, and a desire to revenge himself upon, those who had helped bring about his father’s abdication. In that aim she failed. Still, the accounts she provided him—however skewed—of a great and wise nation asserting its right to govern itself stirred his admiration; in his early days he became a republican from principle. Yet his mother did not give up. To her love of rule and her proud sense of birth she added determined ambition, patience, and self-command. She set herself to study the turn of her son’s disposition. By means of praise, censure, and exhortation she tried to strike the right chords; and though the music that followed her touch seemed discordant to her, she held fast to her hopes in his talents, convinced that she would at last win him."}

{"request_id":"35f5e65122ecf06828e42945","rewritten_text":"She would be placed among those who loved her, and who had better judgment than she did; safe enough to avoid danger, and cheerful enough to enjoy herself. She would never be led into temptation, nor left to discover it on her own. She would be respectable and happy; and Emma admitted her to be the luckiest creature in the world for having created such steady, persevering affection in a man like him;—or, if not quite the luckiest, for yielding only to her own feelings.

Harriet, necessarily pulled away by her obligations to the Martins, was less and less often at Hartfield; and that was not something to regret. The closeness between her and Emma had to fade; their friendship would have to shift into a calmer kind of goodwill; and, fortunately, what ought to be, and must be, seemed already to be beginning—slowly, naturally.

Before the end of September, Emma took Harriet to church, and saw her hand given to Robert Martin with such complete satisfaction that even any memories connected with Mr. Elton, standing there before them, could not spoil it. Perhaps, indeed, at that time she scarcely saw Mr. Elton at all—but as the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might next be hers. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the newest couple engaged of the three, were the first to be married.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury, and was back in the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Mr. Churchills were also in town; they were only waiting for November.

The month in between was the one fixed on, as far as Emma and Mr. Knightley dared. They had decided that their marriage should be settled while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so they could have their planned fortnight away on a seaside trip. John and Isabella, and every other friend, agreed that this was the right plan. But how was Mr. Woodhouse to be persuaded to consent?—he, who had never mentioned their marriage except as a distant event.

When the subject was first brought up, he was so miserable that they were almost without hope. A second mention, however, caused less pain. He began to think it was going to happen, and that he could not stop it—a promising step of the mind on its way toward resignation. Still, though, he was not happy. Indeed, he seemed so much otherwise that Emma’s courage failed. She could not bear to see him suffering, or to know him imagining himself neglected; and though her understanding nearly agreed with the assurance from both Mr. Knightleys that once the event was over, his distress would soon end too, she hesitated—she could not go on."}

{"request_id":"fcd1ae23e776abf0a2bff0ec","rewritten_text":"The insect’s weight was truly remarkable, and, when I considered everything, I could hardly blame Jupiter for his opinion about it; but I couldn’t, for the life of me, figure out what Legrand’s agreement with that opinion meant.

“I sent for you,” he said, in a grand, showy tone, after I finished examining the beetle. “I sent for you so I could have your counsel and your help in carrying forward the plans of Fate—and of the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I interrupted, “you’re certainly unwell. You’d better take some precautions. You should go to bed, and I’ll stay with you for a few days until you recover. You’re feverish, and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I did, and to be honest I found not the slightest sign of fever.

“But you could still be sick without having a fever. Let me prescribe for you—just this once. First, go to bed. Next—”

“You’re wrong,” he cut in. “I’m as well as I can expect to be, given the excitement I’m under. If you truly want me well, you’ll relieve this excitement.”

“And how is that supposed to happen?”

“Very simply. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills, on the mainland. In this expedition, we’ll need the help of someone we can trust. You’re the only person we can rely on. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you’re seeing in me will be just as quickly settled.”

“I’m eager to help you in any way,” I said. “But are you saying that this infernal beetle has anything to do with your trip into the hills?”

“It does.”

“Then, Legrand, I can’t take part in anything so absurd.”

“I’m sorry—very sorry—because we’ll have to try it on our own.”

“Try it on your own! The man is surely mad!—but wait—how long do you plan to be gone?”

“Probably all night. We’ll leave right away, and we’ll be back, at the latest, by sunrise.”

“And will you promise me—on your honor—that once your little stunt is over, and the bug business (good God!) is settled to your satisfaction, you’ll return home and follow my advice without question, as if it were your physician’s?”

“Yes; I promise. Now let’s go—we don’t have time to waste.”

With a heavy heart, I accompanied my friend. We set out at about four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and I. Jupiter brought the scythe and the spades, insisting on carrying all of them himself—more, it seemed to me, out of fear of leaving either tool within reach of his master than from any excess of industry or willingness to help."}

{"request_id":"5fc2c04cc6d9e6462c4e66d2","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats. Every so often, you’d see one stick its nose out from a hole in the corner. She told me she had to keep things ready to throw at them when she was alone, or they wouldn’t leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot. She said she was a good shot with it, usually, but she’d hurt her arm a day or two ago and didn’t know if she could throw straight now. Still, she watched for a chance, and then she struck at a rat. She missed it badly and cried out, “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so much.

Then she told me to try for the next one. I wanted to get away before the old man came back, but I didn’t let on. I took the lead, and the first rat that showed its nose, I threw at it. If it had stayed where it was, it would have been a pretty sick rat. She said that was excellent and that she thought I’d hit the next one too.

She went and got the lump of lead again, brought it back, and also brought a hank of yarn. She wanted me to help her with it. I held up my two hands, and she put the yarn over them while she kept talking about her and her husband’s business. But then she stopped and said, “Keep your eye on the rats. You’d better have the lead in your lap, ready.”

Right then she dropped the lump into my lap. I pressed my legs together over it, and she went on talking. Only about a minute later, she took the yarn off my hands and looked straight at me. In a very kind voice she asked, “Come now. What’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—what is it?”

I think I shook like a leaf. I didn’t know what to do. Then I said, “Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m in the way, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay where you are. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you either. You just tell me your secret, and trust me. I’ll keep it. And I’ll help you, too. My old man will help you if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway apprentice. That’s all. It isn’t anything. There’s no harm in it. You’ve been treated badly, and you decided to leave. Bless you, child. I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"22684167cc731dc09831d83d","rewritten_text":"As they were just leaving the dining-room, the clock tower began to boom at midnight, and when the final stroke rang out they were met by a crash and a sudden, piercing cry. The house shuddered under a dreadful peal of thunder; through the air drifted a thread of unearthly music; and with a loud report a panel at the top of the staircase sprang back. On the landing, looking very faint and chalk-pale, Virginia stepped out with a small casket in her hand. In the next instant everyone surged up to her. Mrs. Otis drew her close with fierce tenderness, the Duke overwhelmed her with violent kisses, and the twins whirled around the group in a frantic war-dance.

‘Good heavens, child—where have you been?’ Mr. Otis demanded, somewhat sharply, convinced she must have been up to some foolish trick. ‘Cecil and I have been riding all over the country to find you, and your mother has been terrified out of her wits. You must never play these practical jokes again.’

‘Only on the Ghost! Only on the Ghost!’ the twins shrieked, capering as they spoke.

‘My own darling—thank God you’re safe; you must never leave my side again,’ Mrs. Otis breathed, kissing the trembling child and smoothing the tangled gold of her hair.

‘Papa,’ Virginia said quietly, ‘I’ve been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for everything he’d done, and before he died he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.’

The entire family stared at her in stunned silence, yet she remained perfectly grave and steady. Then, turning about, she guided them through the opening in the wainscoting into a narrow secret passage, with Washington following and carrying a lighted candle he had snatched from the table. At last they reached a heavy oak door, bristling with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it swung inward on its weighty hinges, and they found themselves in a small, low chamber with a vaulted ceiling and a single tiny grated window. Set into the wall was a great iron ring, and chained to it lay a gaunt skeleton, stretched out full length on the stone floor, as though it were straining to seize an old-fashioned trencher and ewer placed just beyond the reach of its long, fleshless fingers. The jug had evidently once held water, for its interior was coated with green mould. There was nothing on the trencher but a heap of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her little hands, and began to pray in silence, while the rest of the company watched in astonishment at the dreadful tragedy whose secret had at last been revealed to them."}

“_Henri Duval_, a neighbor, and by trade a silversmith, states that he was one of the group that first entered the house. He confirms Musèt’s testimony in general. As soon as they forced their way in, they shut the door again to keep the crowd out. The crowd gathered very quickly, even though it was late. The witness thinks the shrill voice was Italian. He was sure it was not French. He could not be certain whether it was a man’s voice; it might have been a woman’s. He did not know Italian. He could not make out the words, but he was convinced from the way the speaker sounded that the person was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter and had spoken with both often. He was sure the shrill voice was not either of the two deceased.

“——_Odenheimer, restaurateur._ This witness offered his testimony. He does not speak French, so an interpreter questioned him. He is from Amsterdam. He was passing the house when the shrieks began. They lasted for several minutes—probably ten. They were long and loud, very awful and upsetting. He was one of the people who entered the building. He confirmed the earlier evidence in every way except one. He was sure the shrill voice was a man’s voice—a Frenchman’s. He could not make out the words. The voice was loud and fast, uneven, and it sounded as if the speaker was afraid as well as angry. The voice was harsh. It was not so much shrill as harsh. He could not really call it a shrill voice. The rough voice said again and again ‘_sacré_,’ ‘_diable_,’ and once ‘_mon Dieu_.’

“_Jules Mignaud_, a banker with the firm of Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the older Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye had some property. She opened an account with his bank in the spring of that year—eight years earlier. She made frequent deposits in small amounts. She did not write checks for anything until the third day before her death, when she took out, in person, 4000 francs. She paid this amount in gold, and a clerk went home with the money.

“_Adolphe Le Bon_, clerk to Mignaud et Fils, states that on the day in question, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her home with the 4000 francs, carrying it in two bags. When the door was opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one of the bags from his hands, while the old lady took the other.”"}

{"request_id":"71afe2fd1eec9746b684042e","rewritten_text":"Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had gone so far over the ice in so odd a contrivance.

At once his face settled into the deepest gloom, and he answered, “To find the one who fled from me.”

“And does the fellow you were chasing go in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we must have already seen him; the day before we took you up, we noticed dogs hauling a sledge, with a man aboard, crossing the ice.”

The stranger grew alert at this, and he pressed me with a host of questions about the course the dæmon, as he called him, had taken. Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, “I dare say I’ve stirred your curiosity, and that of these good people as well; but you’re too kind to pry.”

“Of course; it would be both very rude and inhuman for me to trouble you with any curiosity of my own.”

“And yet you rescued me from a strange and dangerous plight, and you’ve restored me to life with kindness.”

Not long after, he asked whether I thought the breaking of the ice had destroyed the other sledge. I told him I could not say for certain, since the ice did not give way until close to midnight, and the traveller might have reached a safe place before then; but beyond that I could not judge.

From that point, a fresh spark of life seemed to quicken the stranger’s wasting body. He showed the greatest eagerness to be on deck, watching for the sledge that had appeared before; but I persuaded him to stay in the cabin, for he was far too weak to endure the sharpness of the air. I promised that someone would keep watch for him and let him know at once if anything new came into view.

This is my journal of what has occurred with regard to this strange business up to the present day. The stranger has gradually grown better, though he remains very quiet, and looks uneasy whenever anyone other than myself enters his cabin. Still, his manners are so agreeable and gentle that the sailors take an interest in him, even though they have had hardly any chance to speak with him. As for me, I find myself beginning to love him like a brother; his constant, deep sorrow moves me with sympathy and pity. He must once have been a noble creature, for even now, in wreck, he is so engaging and amiable.

In one of my letters I told you, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the wide ocean; yet I have found a man who, before his spirit was broken by misery, I would have been glad to have had as the brother of my heart.”"}

{"request_id":"84bb4c4d3bd9cb73d9f7fce1","rewritten_text":"Were our proud dreams meant to fade like this? Our name had been written “a little lower than the angels,” and, look at us—we were no better than something as brief as a moment. We had called ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and now—look—we were a “quint-essence of dust.” We resented that the pyramids had outlasted the embalmed body of their builder. And yet, the straw shepherd’s hut we passed along the road held, in its very structure, the principle of a longer life than the entire human race. How can I reconcile this painful shift with the aspirations we once had, with the powers we seemed to possess?

Suddenly, an internal voice—clear and unmistakable—seemed to say:—So it was decreed from eternity. The steeds that carry Time onward are bound to this hour and to this fulfillment, since the void brought forth its burden. Would you try to read backward the unchangeable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Omnipotent! eternal, unchanging Necessity! You sit with busy fingers, always weaving the indissoluble chain of events. I will not complain about your actions. If my human mind cannot accept that everything that is, is right, still, since what is must be, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly, we were not born to enjoy, but to submit—and to hope.

Will the reader grow tired if I describe in detail our long, drawn-out journey from Paris to Geneva? If, day by day, I were to record, in the form of a journal, the crushing miseries of our fate, could my hand write—or language find words—to express the variety of our suffering? Could I capture the frantic rush and the crowding of one deplorable event onto the next? Patience, oh reader—whoever you are, wherever you live, whether of a spiritual race or descended from some surviving pair—your nature will be human, your home the earth. Here you will read of the deeds of the extinct race, and you will wonder, as you read, whether those who endured what you find recorded were made of the same frail flesh and soft organization as you. It is true—they were. So weep therefore; for surely, being alone, you will be gentle in disposition. Shed compassionate tears; but while you do, lend your attention to the tale and learn the deeds and sufferings of your predecessors.

Yet the last events that marked our progress through France were so full of strange horror and grim misery that I cannot linger too long on the narration. If I were to break down each incident, every small fragment of a second would contain a harrowing story, and the very smallest word would turn your young blood cold. It is right that I should raise, for your instruction, a monument to the race that has passed away; but it is not right that I should drag you through the wards of a hospital, nor into the secret rooms of the charnel-house."}

{"request_id":"e04443678e0456e8fbf9b516","rewritten_text":"“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! _lively_ now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you hanging back for there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).

Tom kept on whitewashing—paid no mind to the steamboat. Ben watched for a moment, then said, “_Hi-Yi! You’re_ up a stump, ain’t you!”

No answer. Tom checked his last stroke with the eye of an artist, then gave his brush another careful sweep and looked over the result again, same as before. Ben drifted up alongside him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stayed with his work. Ben said:

“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”

Tom spun around quick and said, “Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”

“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d rather _work_—wouldn’t you? Sure you would!”

Tom studied the boy a bit, then asked, “What do you call work?”

“Why, ain’t _that_ work?”

Tom went back to his whitewashing and answered kind of careless. “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh, come now—you don’t mean to say you _like_ it?”

The brush kept moving.

“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I shouldn’t like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That put the whole thing in a different light. Ben quit nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to judge the look—put in a touch here and there—then criticized the effect again—Ben keeping his eyes on every move, getting more and more curious, more and more taken up with it. After a bit he said:

“Say, Tom, let _me_ whitewash a little.”

Tom thought it over, and was about to agree; but then he changed his mind. “No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind, and _she_ wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”

“No—is that so? Oh come now—let me just try. Only just a little—I’d let _you_, if you was me, Tom.”

“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid.”"}

{"request_id":"d1355e195c1f5cf68e6bb49c","rewritten_text":"“Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay,” was at length brought before the court.

His judges sat upon the Bench in feathered hats; yet the rough red cap and tricoloured cockade were the head-dress that otherwise prevailed. When he looked toward the Jury and the uproarious crowd, he might well have thought the common order of things had been turned about, and that the guilty were judging the upright. The lowest, cruellest, and most wretched rabble of the city—never short of its share of low, cruel, and vile—were the ones directing the whole scene: loudly commenting, applauding, condemning, foreseeing, and driving on the outcome, with no restraint. Many of the men were armed in one way or another; among the women, some had knives, some daggers; some ate and drank while they watched, and many knitted. Of those knitters, one had a spare bit of knitting tucked under her arm as she worked. She sat in the front row, beside a man whom he had never seen since his arrival at the Barrier, though he remembered him at once as Defarge. He observed that she leaned close and whispered to him once or twice, and that she seemed to be his wife; but what struck him most about the two figures was that, though they were posted as near to himself as they could manage, they never once turned their eyes toward him. They appeared to be waiting for something with stubborn resolve, and their gaze went to the Jury, but to nothing else. Beneath the President sat Doctor Manette, in his usual quiet dress. So far as the prisoner could tell, he and Mr. Lorry were the only men there who were not tied to the Tribunal, and who wore their ordinary clothes, without putting on the coarse garb of the Carmagnole.

Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, was charged by the public prosecutor as an emigrant, whose life was forfeit to the Republic under the decree that banished all emigrants on pain of Death. It mattered nothing that the decree bore date since his return to France. The decree stood there, and he stood there; he had been taken in France, and his head was demanded.

“Take off his head!” the audience cried. “An enemy to the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to silence those cries, and asked the prisoner whether it was true that he had lived for many years in England.

Undoubtedly it was.

Then was he not an emigrant? What did he call himself?

Not an emigrant, he hoped, in the sense and spirit of the law.

Why not? the President pressed.

Because he had willingly given up a title that was distasteful to him, and a position that was distasteful to him, and had left his country—he added, before the word emigrant in the Tribunal’s present meaning came into use—to earn his living by his own industry in England, rather than by the industry of the overburdened people of France."}

{"request_id":"58c84be2341c11db9455dac7","rewritten_text":"And I don’t suddenly spring at him and run the risk of turning it into some clumsy, half-done affair; no, I slip off to one side, out yonder, and I work up on him little by little, so he never even thinks I’m about to strike him. Then, little by little, all at once—like a flash—he’s flat on his back, and he can’t make out, for the life of him, how it came about. That’s how I went for brother Dowley. I began talking slow and easy, as if I were only passing the time; and the oldest man in the world couldn’t have taken the bearings of where I started and guessed where I meant to end up:

“Boys, there are a heap of curious things about law, and custom, and usage, and that whole sort of business, once you start looking into it; yes, and about the drift and progress of human opinion and motion, too. There are written laws—they fade away; but there are also unwritten laws—_they_ endure. Consider the unwritten law of wages: it says they’ve got to climb, little by little, straight through the centuries. And watch how it plays out. We know what wages are now, in one place and another; we take an average and call that the wages of today. We know what wages were a hundred years back, and what they were two hundred years ago; that’s as far as we can reach, but it’s enough to show us the law of progress, the pace and measure of the steady increase. So, even without any paper to point the way, we can get pretty close to what wages were three, four, five hundred years ago. All right so far. Do we stop there? No—we turn around and apply the same law to what’s coming. My friends, I can tell you what people’s wages will be at any date in the future you care to name, for hundreds upon hundreds of years.”

“What, goodman, what!”

“Yes. In seven hundred years wages will have climbed to six times what they are now, right here in your district, and farm hands will be allowed 3 cents a day, and mechanics 6.”

“I wouldn’t I might die now and live then!” Smug, the wheelwright, cut in, with a bright, greedy sort of glow in his eye.

“And that’s not the whole of it; they’ll get their board as well—such as it is: it won’t swell them. Two hundred and fifty years after that—listen now—a mechanic’s wages will be—mark you, this is law, not guesswork; a mechanic’s wages will then be _twenty_ cents a day!”

There was a general gasp of awed astonishment; Dickon the mason murmured, with his eyes and hands raised:"}
