{"request_id":"ad3c11617050ce00f2552ca1","rewritten_text":"“But,” I said, handing him the slip back, “I’m just as much in the dark as ever. If all the jewels of Golconda were waiting for me once I solved this riddle, I’m sure I still wouldn’t be able to earn them.”

“And yet,” Legrand said, “the solution is by no means as difficult as you might think from that first quick look at the characters. Those characters, as anyone could guess, form a cipher—that is, they carry meaning. But given what is known of Kidd, I couldn’t imagine him capable of constructing any of the more complex cryptographs. I decided right away that it was a simple kind—simple, however, as it turns out, for the crude mind of the sailor, it would be absolutely impossible to crack without the key.”

“And you really solved it?”

“Of course. I’ve solved others that were ten thousand times more abstruse. Circumstances, and a certain bias of mind, have led me to take an interest in puzzles like these, and it’s hard to believe that human ingenuity could create an enigma of the sort that human ingenuity, with the right approach, couldn’t resolve. In fact, once I had established connected, readable characters, I hardly gave a thought to the mere difficulty of working out their meaning.

“In the present case—indeed, in all cases of secret writing—the first question is the language of the cipher. The principles of solving, especially for the simpler ciphers, depend on the genius of the particular idiom and are shaped by it. In general, there’s no choice but to experiment—guided by probabilities—with every language known to the person trying to solve it, until the correct one is found. But with the cipher in front of us, all difficulty was removed by the signature. The pun on the word ‘Kidd’ is only really noticeable in English. Without that clue, I would have started my attempts with Spanish and French, since those are the languages in which a secret like this would most naturally have been written by a pirate from the Spanish Main. As it was, I assumed the cryptograph was English.

“You’ll notice there are no divisions between the words. If there had been, the task would have been comparatively easy. In that situation, I would have begun with a comparison and analysis of the shorter words, and if a word of a single letter appeared—as is most likely, (a or I, for example,)—I would have considered the solution essentially certain. But since there are no divisions, my first step was to determine the most common letters, as well as the least frequent.”"}

{"request_id":"dd359565b0913279d7b3a7fa","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how mysterious they were! There was animal instinct in the soul, and the body had its moments of spirituality. The senses could sharpen, and the intellect could sink. Who could say where the impulse of the flesh ended, or where the impulse of the mind began? How shallow were the arbitrary definitions offered by ordinary psychologists! And yet how hard it was to choose between the claims of the different schools. Was the soul a shadow sitting in the house of sin? Or was the body truly in the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? The separation of spirit from matter was a mystery, and so was the union of spirit with matter.

He began to wonder whether we could ever make psychology so absolute a science that each small spring of life would be laid bare to us. As it was, we always misunderstood ourselves and rarely understood others. Experience had no ethical value. It was only the name men gave to their mistakes. Moralists, as a rule, had treated it as a kind of warning; they had claimed for it a certain ethical power in shaping character; they praised it as something that teaches us what to follow and shows us what to avoid. But experience had no motive force. It was as little an active cause as conscience itself. All it really proved was that our future would be the same as our past—that the sin we had once committed, with loathing, we would do again many times, and with joy.

It was clear to him that the experimental method was the only method by which one could reach any scientific analysis of the passions; and certainly Dorian Gray was a subject made for his purposes, one that seemed to promise rich and fruitful results. His sudden, mad love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological phenomenon of no small interest. There was no doubt that curiosity had a great deal to do with it—curiosity and the desire for new experiences—but it was not a simple passion; it was a very complex one. What in it had been the purely sensuous instinct of boyhood had been reshaped by the workings of the imagination, turned into something that seemed to the boy himself remote from sense, and for that very reason more dangerous. It was the passions about which we deceive ourselves regarding their origin that tyrannized us most strongly. Our weakest motives were often the ones we were aware of least. It often happened that when we thought we were experimenting on others, we were really experimenting on ourselves.

While Lord Henry sat dreaming over these thoughts, there came a knock at the door, and his valet entered to remind him that it was time to dress for dinner."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c3117c698f884e4209e4b251","rewritten_text":"For a moment I was so stunned that I couldn’t think clearly enough to be accurate. I knew that my design was very different in the details from this—though there was a certain similarity in the overall outline. Soon after, I took a candle and, sitting at the other end of the room, began to examine the parchment more closely. When I turned it over, I saw my own sketch on the reverse, exactly as I had made it. My first reaction, then, was just surprise at the truly remarkable similarity of the outline—the singular coincidence that, unknown to me, there should have been a skull on the other side of the parchment, immediately beneath my figure of the _scarabæus_, and that this skull, not only in outline but in size, should so closely resemble my drawing. I can say that the strangeness of this coincidence left me completely stunned for a time. That’s the usual effect of coincidences like this. The mind tries to connect things—to establish a chain of cause and effect—and, unable to do so, it suffers a kind of temporary paralysis. But when I recovered from that shock, a conviction began to dawn on me gradually, and it startled me even more than the coincidence itself. I began to remember, clearly and positively, that there had been no drawing on the parchment when I made my sketch of the _scarabæus_. I was perfectly certain of it. I remembered turning it over first one way and then the other, looking for the cleanest spot. If the skull had been there then, of course I couldn’t have failed to notice it. Here was indeed a mystery I felt I couldn’t explain; yet even at that early moment, there seemed to flicker—faintly, in the most distant and hidden chambers of my mind—a kind of glow-worm idea of the truth that last night’s adventure brought to such a magnificent demonstration. I got up at once, put the parchment away securely, and dismissed any further thought until I should be alone.\n\n“When you had gone, and when Jupiter was fast asleep, I turned to a more methodical investigation of the matter. First, I considered how the parchment had come into my possession. The spot where we found the _scarabæus_ was on the coast of the mainland, about a mile east of the island, and only a short distance above the high-water mark. When I picked it up, it gave me a sharp bite, which made me drop it. Jupiter, with his usual caution, before seizing the insect—which had flown toward him—looked around for a leaf, or something like that, to hold it by.”"}

{"request_id":"2ecbf50f25d310114bc4469c","rewritten_text":"His temper was stubborn to the last degree, and “dat deuced bug” was the only phrase that managed to slip from his lips all the way. As for me, I carried a pair of dark lanterns, while Legrand busied himself with the _scarabæus_, which he had fastened to the end of a short whip-cord; he kept rolling it from side to side, turning it as he walked, with the practiced air of a conjurer. When I took note of this last, plain proof of my friend’s wandering mind, I could hardly keep back my tears. Still, I judged it wiser to indulge his whim—for the moment at least—until I might try some sterner measures with a better prospect of success. In the meantime I made efforts, but to no effect, to draw him out about the purpose of our expedition. Once I had consented to accompany him, he seemed unwilling to talk on any matter of lesser consequence, and to every question I put to him he vouchsafed no answer beyond “we shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the island’s upper end in a skiff, and then, climbing the high ground along the main shore, we went on in a northwesterly course through a stretch of country so wild and desolate that not a single sign of a human footstep could be found. Legrand took the lead with confidence; he would stop for no more than a moment at a time, now and then, to consult certain landmarks of his own contriving, as though he had marked them out on a former occasion.

Thus we traveled for about two hours, and the sun was just sinking when we entered a region far more cheerless than anything we had yet encountered. It was a kind of table-land near the top of an almost inaccessible hill, thickly wooded from the lowest growth to the highest, and broken up by enormous crags that seemed to rest loosely on the ground; in many places they were kept from sliding down into the valleys below only because the trees leaned against them. Deep ravines, running in different directions, lent the whole scene an air of even harsher solemnity.

The natural platform we had scrambled up to was choked with brambles, and we soon found that we could not have forced our way through them without the scythe. At Legrand’s bidding, Jupiter set about clearing a passage to the base of a tulip-tree of prodigious height, which stood—together with some eight or ten oaks—on the level ground, and far outshone them all, and every other tree I had ever seen then, in the beauty of its foliage and shape, in the wide sweep of its branches, and in the general grandeur of its appearance."}

He looked turned to stone, his face cold and pale like marble, full of sadness. He had lived the careful, comfortable life of a young man born into money and good position—a life free from ugly worries, with an easy, carefree spirit. But now, for the first time, he truly understood the terrible mystery of Destiny, and the frightening meaning of Doom.

How wild and monstrous it all felt! Could it be that something was written on his hand—words he couldn’t read himself, but that someone else could understand—some secret of sin, some blood-red sign of crime? Was there really no way out? Were we nothing more than chess pieces, moved by a power we can’t see, tools shaped by a potter for honor or shame? His mind fought against the idea, and yet he felt that some tragedy was hanging over him, and that he had suddenly been forced to carry an unbearable burden. Actors are lucky. They can choose whether to take part in a tragedy or a comedy, whether to suffer or to enjoy themselves, whether to laugh or to cry. But in real life it’s different. Most men and women are made to play roles they never trained for. Our Guildensterns perform Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets have to joke like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, but the play has been cast badly.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers came into the room. The moment he saw Lord Arthur, he startled, and his thick, heavy face turned a greenish-yellow. The two men looked at each other, and for a moment there was silence.

“The Duchess left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and asked me to bring it to her,” Mr. Podgers said at last. “Ah, I see it on the sofa. Good evening.”

“Mr. Podgers, I insist that you give me a clear answer to the question I’m about to ask you.”

“Not now, Lord Arthur, but the Duchess is worried. I’m afraid I have to go.”

“You won’t go. The Duchess isn’t in a hurry.”

“Ladies shouldn’t be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,” Mr. Podgers said, with a sickly smile. “The fair sex tends to get impatient.”

Lord Arthur’s well-shaped lips curled with irritated contempt. At that moment, the poor Duchess seemed almost meaningless to him. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and held out his hand.

“Tell me what you saw there,” he said. “Tell me the truth. I have to know. I’m not a child.”"}

{"request_id":"a3526a2faf40df7a120f2445","rewritten_text":"“You haven’t been in Bath long enough,” he said, “to enjoy the evening parties here.”

“Oh! no. The usual kind of them has nothing for me. I’m no card-player.”

“You weren’t formerly, I know. You didn’t used to like cards; but time changes a great deal.”

“I’m not changed that much yet,” cried Anne, stopping, afraid she hardly knew what she might be taken to mean. After waiting a few moments, he said—almost as if the words came straight from the feeling itself—“It is, indeed, a period! Eight and a half years is a period.”

Whether he would have gone further was left for Anne to consider in a calmer hour; for even while she still heard the sounds he had made, Henrietta startled her into other thoughts. Henrietta was eager to take advantage of the present leisure to get out, urging her companions not to waste time, lest someone else should come in.

They had to move. Anne talked as if she were perfectly ready, and tried to look it; but she felt that if Henrietta had known the regret and reluctance in her heart as she left that chair, and prepared to leave the room, she would have found, in all her own feelings toward her cousin, in the very security of his affection—something to pity her.

Their preparations, however, were cut short. Alarming sounds were heard; other visitors approached, and the door was thrown open for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose entrance seemed to bring a general chill. Anne felt an instant pressure, and wherever she looked she saw the same signs. The comfort, freedom, and liveliness of the room were gone, replaced by cold composure, determined silence, or dull, empty talk—meant to match the heartless elegance of her father and sister. How mortifying it was to feel that it was truly so!

Her jealous eye was satisfied on one point. Captain Wentworth was acknowledged again by everyone, by Elizabeth more graciously than before. She even spoke to him once, and looked at him more than once. In fact, Elizabeth was working through a serious plan. The rest would explain it. After wasting a few minutes on the proper little nothings, she began to extend the invitation that would cover all the remaining obligations of the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends: no formal party.” She said it all very gracefully, and the cards she had prepared—the “Miss Elliot at home”—were laid on the table, with a courteous, all-encompassing smile for everyone, and one smile and one card more decidedly for Captain Wentworth. The truth was that Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to understand how important it was to have a man of such an air and appearance as his."}

{"request_id":"303989140b1bc9bab3afd994","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how strange and hard to understand they were. People seemed to carry animal instincts in the soul, while the body could also show moments of something almost spiritual. The senses could sharpen, and the mind could fall apart. Who could say exactly where physical urges ended and mental urges began? How thin and uncertain were the definitions made by ordinary psychologists! Still, it was hard to choose between the different schools of thought. Was the soul like a shadow living inside a house of sin? Or was the body truly inside the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? Separating spirit from matter was a mystery, and joining spirit with matter was also a mystery.

He started to wonder if we could ever make psychology so exact that every small part of life would be laid bare for us. As things stood, we always misunderstood ourselves and rarely understood other people. Experience had no real moral value. It was only the name people gave to their mistakes. Moralists usually treated it as a kind of warning. They said it could shape character in a useful way, and they praised it for teaching us what to do and what to avoid. But experience did not create any real force. It was as inactive as conscience itself. What it showed, in the end, was only this: that our future would repeat our past. The sin we had once committed with disgust, we would do again and again—with joy.

He believed it was clear that the experimental method was the only way to reach any scientific understanding of the passions. And Dorian Gray was the kind of subject that suited him, promising rich and useful results. Dorian’s sudden, mad love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological event of real interest. There was no doubt that curiosity played a big part, along with the desire for new experiences. Still, it was not a simple feeling. It was a complicated passion. What was purely the sensuous instinct of boyhood had been reshaped by imagination. It became something that seemed, even to the boy himself, far removed from ordinary sense—and for that very reason it was more dangerous. The passions that most strongly control us are the ones we fool ourselves about, the ones we do not truly understand at their source. Our weakest motives are often the ones we can name and recognize. And it often happened that when we thought we were testing other people, we were really testing ourselves.

While Lord Henry sat lost in these thoughts, there was a knock at the door. His valet came in and reminded him that it was time to dress for dinner."}

{"request_id":"2e9fc201ee0fb49728cbf42b","rewritten_text":"Wake up sooner or later, then look around to see what started it—maybe you’d catch a steamboat coughing along upstream, so far off toward the other side you couldn’t make out much about her, only whether she was a stern-wheel or a side-wheel. After that, for about an hour, there’d be nothing to hear and nothing to see—just plain, solid lonesomeness. Then you’d spot a raft sliding by, way off yonder, and maybe some fellow on it chopping, because that’s what they’re always doing on a raft. You’d see the axe flash and come down—you don’t hear a thing—then you watch it rise again, and by the time it’s above the man’s head you finally hear the _k’chunk!_—like it took all that time for the sound to cross the water. So we’d spend the day drifting and loafing, listening to the quiet. Once there was a thick fog, and the rafts and all that traffic going by was beating tin pans, so the steamboats wouldn’t run into them. A scow or a raft would pass so close we could hear the talk and the cussing and the laughing—heard it plain enough—but we couldn’t see so much as a shape. It made you feel all creepy, like spirits carrying on out there in the air. Jim said he thought it was spirits; but I told him:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

The minute night came, we shoved off. When we got her out to about the middle, we left her to it and let her float wherever the current wanted. Then we lit the pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about every kind of thing—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes would let us. The new clothes Buck’s folks made for me were too fine to be comfortable, and besides I never did care much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we’d have the whole river to ourselves for the longest stretch. Over there were the banks and the islands, across the water; and maybe a spark—like a candle in a cabin window. And sometimes on the water you could see a spark or two, on a raft or a scow, you know. Maybe you’d even hear a fiddle or a song drifting over from one of those boats. It’s a fine thing to live on a raft. We’d stare up at the sky, all speckled with stars, and lie on our backs looking at them, talking about whether they were made or if they just happened. Jim said they were made, but I said they happened. I figured it would’ve taken too long to _make_ that many."}

{"request_id":"033229341f5eb8f6c44519e8","rewritten_text":"His understanding and temper, though not like her own, would have satisfied all her wishes. It was a union that must have benefited both of them: with her ease and liveliness, his mind might have been softened, his manners improved; and from his judgment, his information, and his knowledge of the world, she would have gained something of far greater importance.

But no such happy marriage could now teach the admiring crowd what real marital contentment looked like. A different kind of union—one that would rule out the other—was soon to be formed within their family.

She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would be supported in tolerable independence. But she could easily guess how little lasting happiness could belong to a couple brought together only because their passions were stronger than their virtue.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote again to his brother. To Mr. Bennet’s acknowledgments he replied briefly, with assurances of his eagerness to promote the welfare of any of his family; and he ended with requests that the subject might never be mentioned to him again. The main purpose of his letter was to let them know that Mr. Wickham had resolved to quit the militia.

“It was greatly my wish that he should do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. And I think you will agree with me that removing him from that corps is highly advisable, both for his sake and for my niece’s. It is Mr. Wickham’s intention to go into the Regulars; and among his former friends there are still some who are able and willing to help him in the army. He has the promise of an ensigncy in General----’s regiment, which is now stationed in the north. It is an advantage to have it so far from this part of the kingdom. He promises fairly; and I hope that, among different people—where each of them will have a character to protect—they will both be more prudent. I have written to Colonel Forster to inform him of our present arrangements, and to ask that he satisfy the various creditors of Mr. Wickham in and near Brighton with assurances of speedy payment, for which I have pledged myself. And will you take the trouble of carrying similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton, of whom I shall add a list, according to his information? He has declared all his debts; I hope at least he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be completed in a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and I understand from Mrs. Gardiner that my niece is very eager to see you all before she leaves the south.”"}

{"request_id":"61818b3e198e9170a3602da3","rewritten_text":"Then they passed lonely brickworks. The fog was thinner here, and he could make out the strange, bottle-shaped kilns, with their orange, fanlike flames. A dog barked as they went by, and in the distance, somewhere in the dark, a wandering sea-gull screamed. The horse caught its hoof in a rut, stumbled, then swung aside and broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled over rough, paved streets again. Most of the windows were dark, but now and then strange shadows showed up against a blind lit by a lamp. He watched them with interest. They moved like huge puppets, and they made gestures that looked like living people. He hated them. A dull anger filled his chest. As they turned a corner, a woman shouted something at them from an open door, and two men ran after the hansom for about a hundred yards. The driver lashed at them with his whip.

People say that passion makes you think in circles. That seemed true here. With horrible repetition, the bitten lips of Dorian Gray formed and reshaped those careful words about the soul and the mind, until he felt he had found the full meaning of his mood in them. He also used his own intellectual approval to justify passions that, without that kind of justification, would still have ruled his temper. One thought crept from one part of his brain to another: the wild desire to live, the most terrible appetite a man can have. It grew stronger and pushed into every nerve and fiber. What had once disgusted him—ugliness, because it made everything real—became precious to him now for that same reason. Ugliness was the only real thing. The rough fighting, the filthy den, the crude violence of a life that had fallen apart, the very ugliness of thieves and outcasts—all of it felt more vivid, more real in the moment, than all the graceful forms of art or the dreamy shadows of songs. It was what he needed to forget. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the man pulled up hard at the top of a dark lane. Above the low roofs and jagged chimney stacks, the black masts of ships rose into view. Thick white mist clung to the yards like ghostly sails.

“Somewhere about here, sir, ain’t it?” he asked in a hoarse voice through the trap.

Dorian started and looked around. “This will do,” he said. Then, getting out quickly and giving the driver the extra money he had promised, he walked fast toward the quay. Here and there, lanterns glimmered on the sterns of big merchant ships. The light shook and broke apart in the puddles. A red glow came from a steamer that was out at sea, coaling. The slimy pavement looked like wet rubber."}

{"request_id":"388b5205d8d945d0edeb3df2","rewritten_text":"And Mrs Musgrove took the first chance to be alone with Anne. “Oh! Miss Anne, I can’t help wishing Mrs Charles had a little of your way with those children. They are completely different with you. But, really, they are so spoiled in general. It’s a pity you can’t show your sister how to manage them. They are fine, healthy children, as good as you could wish for, poor little dears, and they are not unfairly treated; but Mrs Charles doesn’t know how they should be handled. Bless me! They can be so troublesome sometimes. I can assure you, Miss Anne, it makes me wish I didn’t have to see them at our house as often as I otherwise would. I think Mrs Charles isn’t very pleased that I don’t invite them more often, but you know it’s very bad to have children in your home when you’re always forced to stop them every moment—‘don’t do this’ and ‘don’t do that’—or else you can only keep them in tolerable order by giving them more cake than is good for them.”

She also had something to say on this matter from Mary. “Mrs Musgrove thinks all her servants are so steady that it would be treason to question it. But I’m sure, without exaggerating, that her upper house-maid and her laundry-maid are not doing their work. They spend all day wandering around the village. I run into them wherever I go, and I can honestly say I never go into my nursery twice without seeing something of them. If Jemima weren’t the most trustworthy, steady creature in the world, it would be enough to spoil her. She tells me they are always trying to get her to go for a walk with them.”

And on Mrs Musgrove’s side, she said, “I make it a rule never to interfere in any of my daughter-in-law’s business, because I know it wouldn’t do. But I’ll tell you, Miss Anne, because you might be able to put things right. I don’t have a very good opinion of Mrs Charles’s nursery-maid. I hear strange stories about her. She’s always out and about. And from what I know myself, I can say she dresses so well that she could ruin any servants she comes near. Mrs Charles speaks highly of her, I know, but I’m only giving you this hint so you can keep an eye on things. If you notice anything wrong, you won’t need to be afraid to mention it.”

Again, Mary complained that Mrs Musgrove was often not willing to give her the place she deserved when they dined at the Great House with other families. Mary said she could see no reason why she should be treated as if she were so much at home that she should lose her position."}

{"request_id":"b91de3c835f8a68c9d52ef12","rewritten_text":"She would be placed among people who loved her, and who had better judgment than she did. She would be safe, and still have enough to keep her cheerful. She would never be led into temptation, and she would not be left alone long enough for temptation to find her. She would be respectable and happy. Emma admitted that she was the luckiest creature in the world for creating such a steady, lasting affection in a man like him—or, if she was not quite the luckiest, then at least she had only had to trust her own feelings.

Harriet, pulled away more and more by her duties with the Martins, was less and less often at Hartfield. That was not something to regret. Their closeness had to fade; their friendship would need to become a calmer kind of goodwill. Fortunately, what should happen, and must happen, seemed to be starting already, in the slow and natural way it always does.

Before the end of September, Emma took Harriet to church. She saw Harriet’s hand given to Robert Martin with such complete satisfaction that nothing, not even anything she remembered about Mr. Elton standing there before them, could spoil it. Perhaps, at that time, Emma hardly saw Mr. Elton at all—except as the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might soon be given to herself. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the newest couple among the three who were engaged, were the first to be married.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury. She was now back in the comfort of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Mr. Churchills were also in town, and they were only waiting for November.

The month in between was the one Emma and Mr. Knightley had chosen, as far as they could manage. They decided their marriage should be finished while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so they could have their planned two-week trip to the seaside. John and Isabella, and every other friend, agreed that this was the right plan. But how could Mr. Woodhouse be persuaded to say yes? He had never even mentioned their marriage except as something far in the future.

When they first brought it up, he was so miserable that they almost gave up hope. A second mention caused him less pain. He began to believe it would happen, and that he could not stop it. That was a hopeful step of the mind, moving toward resignation. Still, he was not happy. In fact, he seemed so different from before that Emma’s courage failed. She could not bear to see him suffering, or to know that he was imagining himself neglected. Even though her better judgment almost agreed with the Mr. Knightleys’ promise that once the wedding was over his distress would soon end, she hesitated. She could not go on."}

{"request_id":"67b7c94b2590c8599c547f73","rewritten_text":"“I examined the death’s-head carefully. The outer edges—meaning the edges of the drawing that were closest to the edge of the vellum—were much clearer than the rest. It was obvious that the heat had not worked evenly. So I immediately lit a fire and warmed every part of the parchment until it glowed. At first, all that happened was that the faint lines of the skull became darker. But when I kept going with the experiment, a new figure appeared in the corner of the slip, diagonally opposite the place where the death’s-head was drawn. At first I thought it was a goat. A closer look showed me it was meant to be a kid.”

“Ha! ha!” I said. “Of course I don’t have any right to laugh at you. A million and a half of money is too serious to treat like a joke. But you’re not going to set up a third link in your chain. You won’t find any special connection between your pirates and a goat. Pirates, you know, have nothing to do with goats. Goats belong to the farming business.”

“But I just said the figure wasn’t a goat.”

“Well, then a kid—pretty much the same thing.”

“Pretty much, but not entirely,” said Legrand. “You may have heard of Captain Kidd. I immediately took the animal’s figure as a kind of pun or a hieroglyphic signature. I say ‘signature’ because its position on the vellum suggested that idea. The death’s-head in the corner diagonally opposite also seemed to act like a stamp or a seal. But I was very frustrated by the lack of anything else—by the missing body of what I had imagined my instrument would be, and by the missing text to go with it.”

“I suppose you expected to find a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something like that. The truth is, I felt an irresistible sense that great good fortune was about to happen. I can’t really say why. Maybe it was more a wish than a real belief. But do you know that Jupiter’s silly words about the bug being made of solid gold had a strange effect on my imagination? And then there were all the accidents and coincidences. They were so unusual. Don’t you see how it was just chance that these events happened on the only day of the year that is cool enough for a fire, and that without the fire—or without the dog showing up at exactly the right moment—I would never have noticed the death’s-head, and so I would never have become the owner of the treasure?”"}

{"request_id":"7ec0b5b8a320f1a80fdf3f1b","rewritten_text":"In the thin, wan moonlight, right before him, there stood an old man of dreadful appearance. His eyes burned like red coals; long grey hair hung in tangled, matted masses over his shoulders; his clothes, cut in an old-fashioned style, were filthy and torn, and from his wrists and ankles there dangled heavy manacles and rusty gyves.

“Dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I must really insist that you oil those chains, and I’ve brought you for the purpose a small bottle of the Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. It’s said to be entirely efficacious with a single application, and the wrapper carries several testimonials to that effect from some of our most distinguished native divines. I’ll leave it here for you by the bedroom candles, and I’ll be glad to provide more if you should need it.” With that, the United States Minister set the bottle down on a marble table, shut his door, and went off to bed.

For a moment the Canterville ghost remained perfectly still, stung with natural indignation; then, flinging the bottle hard onto the polished floor, he bolted down the corridor, letting out hollow groans and casting a sickly green light behind him. But just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open—two little figures in white robes appeared, and a large pillow shot past his head! Evidently there was no time to spare, so, scrambling to use the Fourth Dimension of Space as his escape, he slipped through the wainscoting, and the house fell quiet.

When he got to a small secret chamber in the left wing, he braced himself against a moonbeam to catch his breath and began to take stock of his situation. Never, in his three hundred years of a brilliant, unbroken career, had he been treated so rudely. He recalled the Dowager Duchess, whom he had frightened into a fit while she stood before the glass in her lace and diamonds; the four housemaids, who had broken into hysterics simply because he grinned at them through the curtains of one of the spare bedrooms; the rector of the parish, whose candle he had blown out one night when he came late from the library, and who had been under Sir William Gull’s care ever since—a complete martyr to nervous disorders; and old Madame de Tremouillac, who, having woken one morning early to find a skeleton seated in an arm-chair by the fire reading her diary, had been confined to her bed for six weeks with brain fever, and, after her recovery, had grown reconciled to the Church and severed her ties with that notorious sceptic Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"7cfbbb3120d570fc9e5ade29","rewritten_text":"Every well-made boy eventually gets a wild urge to go somewhere and dig up hidden treasure. That urge hit Tom one day. He went out looking for Joe Harper, but he didn’t find him. Then he went after Ben Rogers, only to learn that Ben had gone fishing. After that, Tom soon ran into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would go along. Tom took him to a private spot and told him everything in confidence. Huck was willing. Huck was always willing to join in any plan that was fun and didn’t cost money, because he had far too much of that kind of time that isn’t money.

“Where are we going to dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, just about anywhere.”

“Is it hidden everywhere?”

“No, not everywhere. It’s hidden in very specific places, Huck. Sometimes on islands. Sometimes in rotten chests under the end of a limb on an old dead tree, right where the shadow falls at midnight. But most of the time it’s under the floor in haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Robbers, of course. Who else would it be? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it were mine, I wouldn’t hide it. I’d spend it and have a good time.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t do it that way. They hide it and leave it there.”

“Don’t they come back for it?”

“No. They think they will, but they usually forget the marks, or else they die. Either way, the treasure sits there a long time and gets rusty. Then one day someone finds an old yellow paper that explains how to find the marks. That paper has to be decoded for about a week, because it’s mostly signs and hy’roglyphics.”

“Hyro—what?”

“Hy’roglyphics. Pictures and things. You know, stuff that doesn’t seem to mean anything.”

“Do you have one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Then how are you going to find the marks?”

“I don’t need any marks. They always bury it under a haunted house, or on an island, or under a dead tree with one limb sticking out. We tried Jackson’s Island once, but we can try it again later. There’s also that old haunted house on the Still-House branch, and there are lots of dead-limb trees. Dead ones, too.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“How could you say that? No!”

“Then how will you know which one to pick?”

“We’ll go for all of them.”

“Tom, that’ll take all summer.”

“So what? If you find a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest full of diamonds, what’s wrong with that?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s great. Plenty great for me. Just give me the hundred dollars, and I don’t want any diamonds.”"}

{"request_id":"75d204919480260f0fd81778","rewritten_text":"They know what a clever lad he is; he’ll be a lifer. They’ll make the Artful nothing less than a lifer.”

“What do you mean by lagging and a lifer?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “What’s the point of talking like that to me? Why don’t you speak so I can understand you?”

Fagin was about to translate those mysterious phrases into plain language; and once it was translated, Mr. Bolter would have been told that they meant that combination of words, “transportation for life,” when the conversation was cut short by the entrance of Master Bates, with his hands in his breeches pockets and his face twisted into a look of half-comical misery.

“It’s all up, Fagin,” said Charley, once he and his new companion had been introduced to each other.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman who owns the box; two or three more are coming to identify him; and the Artful’s been booked for a passage out,” replied Master Bates. “I’ll need a full suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband to visit him in before he sets out on his travels. To think of Jack Dawkins—lummy Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—going abroad for a common two-penny-halfpenny sneeze-box! I never thought he’d do it under a gold watch, chain, and seals, at the very lowest. Oh, why didn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his valuables, and go out as a gentleman—rather than like some common little nobody, with no honor and no glory!”

With that outpouring of feeling for his unfortunate friend, Master Bates sat down in the nearest chair, looking chagrined and utterly downcast.

“What do you mean, talking about him having neither honor nor glory!” Fagin snapped, flashing an angry look at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the best of you all? Is there one of you that could match him or come near him on any trail? Eh?”

“Not one,” Master Bates replied, his voice rough with regret; “not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” Fagin shot back, furious. “What are you blubbering for?”

“’Cause it isn’t on the record, is it?” said Charley, stung into perfect defiance of his respected friend by the flood of his regrets. “’Cause it can’t come out in the indictment; ’cause nobody will ever know half of what he was. How will he stand in the Newgate Calendar? Maybe he won’t even be there. Oh, my eye, my eye—what a blow it is!”

“Ha! ha!” cried Fagin, thrusting out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter as he burst into chuckling that shook him as though he had the palsy. “Look at the pride they take in their profession, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"8d503c4e6d25b7456a883e41","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone told him he was making a very foolish choice, because there was no doubt at all that the place was haunted. In fact, Lord Canterville himself—an unusually scrupulous man—had felt it was his duty to mention the matter to Mr. Otis when they met to discuss the terms.

“We haven’t cared to live here ourselves,” said Lord Canterville. “Not since my great-aunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was frightened into a fit—one she never really recovered from—when two skeleton hands were placed on her shoulders while she was dressing for dinner. And I feel I must tell you, Mr. Otis, that the ghost has been seen by several living members of my family, as well as by the rector of the parish, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, who is a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the duchess’s unfortunate accident, none of our younger servants would stay with us, and Lady Canterville often got very little sleep at night because of the mysterious noises coming from the corridor and the library.”

“My Lord,” replied the Minister, “I’ll take the furniture and the ghost at a valuation. I come from a modern country, where we have everything that money can buy. And with all our energetic young men painting the Old World red, and stealing away your best actresses and prima donnas, I figure that if there were such a thing as a ghost in Europe, we’d have it back home in no time—either in one of our public museums or on the road as a show.”

“I’m afraid the ghost does exist,” said Lord Canterville, smiling, “though it may have resisted the pitches of your enterprising impresarios. It has been known for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and it always shows itself before the death of any member of our family.”

“Well, so does the family doctor, for that matter, Lord Canterville. But there’s no such thing as a ghost, sir, and I don’t think the laws of Nature are going to be suspended for the British aristocracy.”

“You’re certainly very natural in America,” Lord Canterville answered, not quite understanding Mr. Otis’s last remark. “And if you don’t mind a ghost in the house, then it’s fine. Just remember—I warned you.”

A few weeks later, the purchase was finalized, and at the end of the season the Minister and his family went down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, who—back when she was Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street—had been a celebrated New York belle, was now a very handsome, middle-aged woman, with fine eyes and a superb profile."}

{"request_id":"eb4338b6d5d7362823454db9","rewritten_text":"Not everyone would have handled it the way she did—refusing to accept Jane’s answer in such a gentle way. But she clearly said she would not write any denial yesterday, the way Jane asked. She would wait, and sure enough, by yesterday evening it was settled that Jane would go. I was truly surprised. I had no idea at all. Jane then took Mrs. Elton aside and told her right away that, after thinking through the advantages of Mrs. Smallridge’s situation, she had decided to accept it. “I didn’t know a word of it until everything was already settled.”

“Did you spend the evening with Mrs. Elton?”

“Yes, all of us. Mrs. Elton wanted us to come. It was decided on the hill while we were walking around with Mr. Knightley. ‘You must all spend your evening with us,’ she said. ‘I positively must have you all come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was there too, was he?”

“No, not Mr. Knightley. He refused from the start. Even so, I thought he might come, because Mrs. Elton said she wouldn’t let him off, but he didn’t. Still, my mother, Jane, and I were all there, and we had a very pleasant evening. You know, Miss Woodhouse, you always find kind friends agreeable, even if everyone seemed rather tired after the morning’s party. Pleasure, you know, can be tiring too, and I can’t say any of them looked like they enjoyed it very much. Still, I will always think it was a very pleasant party, and I feel extremely grateful to the kind friends who included me.”

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you weren’t aware of it, had been deciding all day?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the time comes, it must be hard for her and for all her friends. But I hope her engagement will have every comfort it possibly can. I mean, in terms of the family’s character and manners.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, there is everything in the world that can make her happy there. Except for the Sucklings and the Bragges, there isn’t another nursery setup like it—so generous and so elegant—in all of Mrs. Elton’s circle. Mrs. Smallridge is a truly delightful woman. The way they live is almost as good as Maple Grove. And as for the children—except for the little Sucklings and the little Bragges—there aren’t any children anywhere who are more elegant or sweeter. Jane will be treated with so much respect and kindness. It will be nothing but pleasure—a life of pleasure. And her salary—well, I really can’t bring myself to tell you her salary, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"de017f46094db9cb8d6a349b","rewritten_text":"The following day was fixed for the business (so that our honour should not suffer from delay), and on that day Drummle turned up with a civil little confession in Estella’s hand—that she had had the honour of dancing with him several times. That left me nothing to do but regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and, in the end, to reject, as impossible, the notion that I might be found anywhere. Drummle and I then sat facing one another, snorting, for an hour, while the Grove kept up indiscriminate contradiction, and at last it was announced that the promotion of good feeling had gone forward at an astonishing pace.

I say this lightly, but it was no light matter to me. I cannot properly put into words the pain it gave me to think that Estella should show any kindness to such a contemptible, clumsy, sulky booby—so far beneath the ordinary. Even to this day, I believe the only reason I could not bear the thought of her stooping to that hound was some pure fire of generosity and disinterestedness in my love for her. Of course I should have been miserable no matter who she favoured; yet a more worthy object would have caused a different sort and degree of distress.

It was not hard for me to learn it, and I soon did learn that Drummle had started to keep close to her, and that she let him. After a little while he was always after her, and he and I kept crossing paths every day. He persisted in his dull, stubborn way, and Estella held him there—sometimes with encouragement, sometimes with discouragement; now almost flattering him, now openly despising him; now knowing him well, now scarcely remembering who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had called him, was used to lying in wait, though, and had the patience of his kind. On top of that, he had a blockhead confidence in his money and in his family greatness, which at times served him almost instead of concentration and steady purpose. So the Spider, watching Estella doggedly, outlasted many brighter insects, and would often uncoil himself and drop at just the right moment.

At a particular Assembly Ball in Richmond (back then there were Assembly Balls in most places), where Estella had outshone every other beauty, this blundering Drummle hovered about her so persistently, and with so much patience on her part, that I decided to speak to her about him. I seized the next opening—when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home, and was sitting apart among some flowers, ready to go."}

{"request_id":"aa3d724c4d58cc93ac35e28b","rewritten_text":"Mr. Darcy spoke with warm praise of his sister’s skill.

“I’m very glad to hear such a good report about her,” said Lady Catherine. “Please tell her for me that she can’t expect to be excellent unless she practices a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he answered, “that she doesn’t need advice like that. She practices very regularly.”

“Even better. She can never practice too much. And when I write to her next, I will tell her not to neglect it for any reason. I often tell young ladies that you can’t learn to play music well without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play really well unless she practices more. And even though Mrs. Collins has no instrument, she is welcome, as I have often told her, to come to Rosings every day and play the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. She won’t be in anyone’s way there, you know.”

Mr. Darcy looked a little ashamed of his aunt’s rude manner, and said nothing.

When the coffee was finished, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth that she had promised to play for him. She sat down at once at the instrument. He pulled a chair close to her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, and then, as before, talked to her other nephew. The latter walked away from her, and with his usual careful slowness went toward the pianoforte. He positioned himself so that he could see Elizabeth’s face clearly. Elizabeth noticed what he was doing. At the first convenient pause, she turned to him with a teasing smile and said,—

“You mean to scare me, Mr. Darcy, by coming in all this grand way just to hear me. But I won’t be frightened, even if your sister does play so well. There is a stubbornness in me that never can stand being frightened just because someone else wants it. My courage always grows every time someone tries to intimidate me.”

“I won’t say you’re wrong,” he replied, “because you couldn’t really believe I would try to alarm you. I’ve known you long enough to understand that you enjoy sometimes stating opinions that aren’t really your own.”

Elizabeth laughed warmly at this picture of herself, and then said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, “Your cousin will give you a very nice idea of me, and teach you not to believe a word I say. I’m especially unlucky to meet someone who is so good at showing my true character, in a place where I had hoped to pass myself off with at least some credit.”"}

{"request_id":"91cc83f2e7d1694b222714ca","rewritten_text":"But no—there was something even flashier than that. He would be a pirate! That was the whole point! _now_ his future stood out before him, bright with an almost unbelievable magnificence. How his name would ring through the world and make people tremble! How proudly he would cut across the laughing seas, in his long, low, black-hulled racer, the Spirit of the Storm, with his grim flag flying at the bow! And at the height of his renown, how he would suddenly show up at the old village and stride straight into church—brown, weather-worn, and swaggering—in his black velvet doublet and trunks, his big jack-boots, his crimson sash, his belt bristling with horse-pistols, his crime-rusted cutlass at his side, and his slouch hat with its plumes tossing in the air; his black flag would be unfurled too, with the skull and crossbones on it, and he would drink in, with swelling delight, the murmured words, “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate!—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was settled; his career was fixed. He would slip away from home and take it up. He would begin the very next morning. So now he had to get ready. He gathered what he could and went to a rotten log nearby, starting to dig under one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he struck wood that sounded hollow. He put his hand into the opening and recited the words in a showy, solemn way:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped off the dirt and uncovered a pine shingle. He lifted it and revealed a neat little hiding-place, built of shingles for its bottom and sides. Inside lay a marble. Tom’s amazement knew no bounds. He scratched his head, looking thoroughly puzzled, and said:

“Well, that beats anything!”

Then he flung the marble aside with irritation and stood there thinking hard. The trouble was that one of his superstitions had failed—one that he and all his mates had always treated as certain. If you buried a marble with the right incantations, left it alone for a fortnight, and then opened the spot using the same words, you’d find that every marble you’d ever lost had gathered itself there in the meantime, no matter how far apart they’d been scattered. But this time the thing had actually, beyond question, gone wrong. Tom’s whole confidence was shaken to the core. He’d heard of it working, plenty of times, but never of it failing. It didn’t even occur to him that he’d tried it himself several times before—only he’d never been able to locate the hiding-places again. He worried over it for a while, and at last decided that some witch must have stepped in and snapped the charm."}

{"request_id":"75200041fcccb62077d2d4cd","rewritten_text":"I’m not dining at home, so I won’t need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” the man said, and left the room.

“Now, Alan, there’s no moment to waste. How heavy this chest is! I’ll take it for you. You bring the other things.” He spoke quickly, with an authoritative edge. Campbell felt overpowered by him. They left the room together.

When they reached the top landing, Dorian took out the key and turned it in the lock. Then he stopped, and a troubled look came over his face. He shuddered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he murmured.

“It means nothing to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell said coldly.

Dorian opened the door halfway. As he did, he saw his portrait’s face leering in the sunlight. On the floor in front of it, the torn curtain lay in pieces. He remembered that the night before he had forgotten—forgotten, for the first time in his life, to hide the fatal canvas—and he was about to rush forward when he pulled back with a shudder.

What was that loathsome red dew that gleamed, wet and shining, on one of the hands, as though the canvas had sweated blood? How horrible it was!—horrible, it seemed to him in that moment, even more horrible than the silent thing he knew was stretched across the table, the thing whose grotesque, misshapen shadow on the spotted carpet showed him it hadn’t moved, but was still there, exactly as he had left it.

He drew a deep breath, opened the door a little wider, and, with half-closed eyes and his head turned away, stepped quickly inside, determined he wouldn’t look even once at the dead man. Then, bending down and picking up the gold-and-purple hanging, he flung it right over the picture.

There he stopped, afraid to turn around, and his eyes fixed on the intricate pattern in front of him. He heard Campbell bringing in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other things he needed for his dreadful work. He began to wonder whether he and Basil Hallward had ever met, and, if they had, what they would have thought of each other.

“Leave me now,” said a stern voice behind him.

He turned and hurried out, only vaguely aware that the dead man had been pushed back into the chair and that Campbell was staring into a glistening yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was long after seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale, but completely calm. “I’ve done what you asked me to do,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"9b62e5d5798237fd6bf44979","rewritten_text":"Now that he had no work to hold, he set the knuckles of his right hand into the hollow of his left, then the knuckles of his left into the hollow of his right, then dragged a hand across his bearded chin—then did it all again in steady, regular changes, with not a moment’s pause. The effort of bringing him back from the vagrancy he always fell into after he had spoken was like trying to rouse some very weak person from a swoon, or like trying, in the hope of some disclosure, to keep the spirit of a man who was dying fast from slipping away.

“Did you ask me for my name?”

“Of course I did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a weary sound that wasn’t a sigh and wasn’t a groan, he bent to work again, until the silence was broken once more.

“You’re not a shoemaker by trade?” said Mr. Lorry, staring at him.

His haggard eyes shifted to Defarge, as if he meant to pass the question to him; but since no help came from that direction, they returned to the man who had asked, searching for the ground.

“I’m not a shoemaker by trade? No, I wasn’t a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He trailed off, even for minutes, repeating those measured movements with his hands the whole time. His eyes slowly came back at last to the face they had wandered from; when they landed on it, he startled, and resumed in the way a sleeper does when he suddenly wakes, falling back on a subject from last night.

“I asked permission to teach myself, and I got it only after a long time, with a great deal of difficulty—and I’ve been making shoes ever since.”

As he held out his hand for the shoe that had been taken from him, Mr. Lorry said, still staring straight into his face:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing about me?”

The shoe fell to the ground, and he sat staring fixedly at the questioner.

“Monsieur Manette”; Mr. Lorry placed his hand on Defarge’s arm; “do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Is there no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no old time rising in your mind, Monsieur Manette?”

As the captive of many years sat staring, now at Mr. Lorry and now at Defarge, some long-buried marks of an intelligence that had once been actively intent gradually pushed their way through the black mist that had settled over him. They were clouded over again; they grew fainter; they vanished—but they had been there."}

{"request_id":"40553e18fe4093e958026145","rewritten_text":"To look at a star by quick, oblique glances—to catch it, as it were, in a sideward view, by directing toward it the outer parts of the _retina_ (which are more prone to faint impressions of light than the inner portions)—is to see the star clearly; it is to gain the truest sense of its brilliance, a brilliance that fades in exact proportion as we bring our sight _fully_ to bear upon it. In the latter case, more rays actually strike the eye, yet in the former there is a finer, more discriminating power of perception. If one goes too far into excessive depth, one only muddles and weakens thought; and it is even possible to make Venus itself disappear from the sky by an inspection that is too steady, too concentrated, or too direct.

“As for these murders, let’s begin by examining things for ourselves, before we settle on any opinion. The inquiry will be diverting,” [I found it a strange word for the matter, but I said nothing] “and, besides, Le Bon has once done me a service for which I’m not ungrateful. We’ll go and look at the scene with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and I won’t have trouble getting the proper permission.”

The permission was secured, and we set out at once for the Rue Morgue. It is one of those wretched streets that run between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We reached it late in the afternoon, since this part of town lay far from where we lived. The place was easy to find: across the way, many people were still staring up at the closed shutters, driven by a curiosity with no clear object. The building was a typical Parisian one, with a gateway; on one side there was a glazed watch-box, and in the window a sliding panel marked a _loge de concierge_. Before entering, we walked up the street, turned into an alley, and then, turning again, passed behind the building—while Dupin, in the meantime, studied the entire neighborhood as well as the house, with a minuteness of attention I could not see any reason for.

We retraced our steps to the front, rang, and, after showing our credentials, were admitted by the officers on duty. We went upstairs into the chamber where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been found, where both of the dead still lay. The room’s disorder had, as usual, been left to stand. I noticed nothing beyond what had already been reported in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin, however, examined everything—nothing excluded, not even the bodies of the victims. We then moved into the other rooms and into the yard, with a _gendarme_ accompanying us the whole time."}

{"request_id":"683fc4be41d84775079658c7","rewritten_text":"Their coming kindled something like a fire in Saint Antoine’s breast, spreading quickly as they moved, so that faces at nearly every door and window seemed to flare and flicker with it. Still, no one followed them, and when they entered the wine-shop not a soul spoke; yet every man’s eyes turned on them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

It may well have been the cue to loosen the general tongue. The words brought back a ready chorus of “Good day!”

“It’s bad weather, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.

At that, each man glanced at his neighbor, then let his eyes fall and sat in silence. All except one man, who rose and went out.

“My wife,” said Defarge, speaking aloud to Madame Defarge, “I’ve travelled certain leagues with this good mender of roads, called Jacques. I met him—by accident—some day and a half’s journey out of Paris. He’s a good child, this mender of roads, called Jacques. Give him something to drink!”

A second man rose and went out. Madame Defarge set wine before the mender of roads called Jacques; he doffed his blue cap to the company and drank. In the breast of his blouse he carried some coarse dark bread; he ate between whiles, then sat munching and drinking near Madame Defarge’s counter. A third man rose and went out.

Defarge took a draught of wine to refresh himself, but he drank less than was offered the stranger, since it was no rarity for him. He stood waiting until the countryman had finished his breakfast. He did not look at anyone there, and no one looked at him now—not even Madame Defarge, who had taken up her knitting and kept at her work.

“Have you done with your meal, friend?” he asked, at the proper time.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Then come! You shall see the room I told you you might take. It will suit you to a marvel.”

From the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep stair, from the stair into a garret—once the garret where a white-haired man had sat on a low bench, bending forward and very busy, making shoes.

That white-haired man was gone now; but the three men were there who had left the wine-shop one by one. And between those three and the white-haired man far off lay the single small link they had once glimpsed at him through the cracks in the wall.

Defarge shut the door with care and spoke in a low voice:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness encountered by appointment, by me, Jacques Four.”"}

{"request_id":"e0bf00a9bddcc93997ef6f30","rewritten_text":"But it is of little importance.”

“I might as well ask,” she replied, “why, when you clearly meant to offend and insult me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your judgment, and even against your character. Was that not an excuse for being rude, if I was rude? But I have other reasons to be angry. You know I do. If my own feelings had not already turned against you—if they had been indifferent, or even kind—do you think anything would have persuaded me to accept the man who has been the cause of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a sister I love most?”

As she said this, Mr. Darcy blushed; but the feeling passed quickly. He listened without trying to interrupt her while she went on.

“I have every reason in the world to think badly of you. Nothing can excuse the unfair and unkind part you played there. You cannot deny that you were the main cause, if not the only one, of driving them apart. You exposed one to the world’s criticism for being fickle and unstable. You exposed the other to the world’s mockery for hopes that were disappointed. And you brought them both into the worst kind of misery.”

She paused, and with real anger she noticed that he was listening in a way that showed he felt no remorse at all. He even looked at her with a smile that seemed meant to show disbelief.

“Can you deny that you did it?” she asked again.

With an air of calm, he then answered, “I have no wish to deny that I did everything I could to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am pleased with my success. Toward him I have been kinder than I have been to myself.”

Elizabeth pretended not to notice the polite remark, but she did not miss its meaning, and it was not likely to make her more willing to forgive him.

“But it is not only this matter,” she continued. “My dislike is based on more than what happened then. Long before it took place, my opinion of you was already formed. Your character was made clear to me in the story I heard months ago from Mr. Wickham. What can you say about that? How can you defend yourself here, in any imagined act of friendship? Or how can you mislead other people here?”

“You seem very eager to hear about that gentleman’s concerns,” Darcy said, in a less steady tone, and with a deeper blush.

“Who could avoid feeling interested in him,” Elizabeth replied, “when he has suffered so much?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated, with contempt. “Yes, his misfortunes have been very great indeed.”

“And the harm you caused him,” Elizabeth cried, with force. “You have brought him down to his present condition—relative poverty.”"}

{"request_id":"9cc52c6724a1053221547050","rewritten_text":"You must learn some of my philosophy. Think only of the past, because remembering it gives you pleasure.”

“I can’t give you credit for a philosophy like that. Your habit of looking back must be so free of blame that the comfort you feel from it isn’t really philosophy at all, but something better—ignorance. But it isn’t like that for me. Painful memories keep coming back, and they can’t, and shouldn’t, be pushed away. I have been selfish all my life in practice, even if not in principle. As a child, I was taught what was right, but I wasn’t taught to control my temper. I was given good principles, yet I was allowed to follow them with pride and arrogance. I was an only son—an only child for many years—and my parents spoiled me. They were good people themselves, especially my father, who was kind and pleasant, but they let me become selfish and overbearing. They encouraged it, and in a way they even taught it: to care only about my own family, to think badly of everyone else, and to want to believe that their sense and worth were less than mine. That was who I was, from the age of eight to twenty-eight. I might still be that way, if not for you, my dearest, loveliest Elizabeth. What do I not owe you? You taught me a lesson—hard at first, but very helpful. Because of you, I was truly humbled. I came to you without any confidence that you would receive me well. You showed me how little all my efforts and hopes meant when it came to pleasing a woman who is truly worth being pleased.”

“Did you really think then that I would be persuaded?”

“Of course I did. What do you think of my vanity? I believed you were hoping for, and expecting, my proposal.”

“My manners must have been at fault, but not on purpose, I assure you. I never meant to deceive you, but my feelings might have led me the wrong way. How could you not have hated me after that evening!”

“Hate you! I was angry at first, perhaps, but my anger soon found the right direction.”

“I’m almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. You blamed me for coming?”

“No, indeed. I felt nothing but surprise.”

“Your surprise couldn’t be greater than mine was, when you noticed me. My conscience told me I didn’t deserve any special politeness, and I admit I didn’t expect to receive more than what I was owed.”

“My purpose then,” Darcy replied, “was to show you, through every bit of civility I could manage, that I wasn’t so small-minded as to resent what happened in the past. I hoped to win your forgiveness, and to reduce your bad opinion of me, by showing you that your criticisms had been taken to heart.”}"}

{"request_id":"4716b7be4a0def14595ef37c","rewritten_text":"WHEN the wedding happened—some three weeks later—St. Peter’s was packed to the rafters with a perfect crowd of clever, well-dressed people. The service was delivered in the most striking fashion by the Dean of Chichester, and everyone agreed they had never seen a finer-looking pair than the bride and bridegroom. They were not merely handsome, though; they were content. Not once did Lord Arthur look back with regret for all he had endured for Sybil’s sake, while she, for her part, gave him the best a woman can offer any man—adoration, tenderness, and love. For them, romance was not crushed by reality. They always felt young.

Some years on, after two beautiful children had been born to them, Lady Windermere paid a visit to Alton Priory, that charming old place which had been the Duke’s wedding gift to his son. One afternoon, as she sat with Lady Arthur beneath a lime-tree in the garden, keeping an eye on the little boy and girl as they ran along the rose-walk like restless streaks of sunlight, she suddenly took her hostess’s hand and said, ‘Are you happy, Sybil?’

‘Dear Lady Windermere, naturally I’m happy. Aren’t you?’

‘I’ve no time to be happy, Sybil. I always take a liking to the last person introduced to me; but, as a rule, once I’ve got to know people, I grow tired of them.’

‘Don’t your lions please you, Lady Windermere?’

‘Oh, not at all! Lions are only good for one season. Once their manes are clipped, they’re the dullest creatures going. And besides, they behave dreadfully if you’re really kind to them. Do you remember that dreadful Mr. Podgers? He was a shocking impostor. I didn’t mind that, of course, and even when he wanted to borrow money I forgave him—but I couldn’t bear his making love to me. He’s really made me loathe cheiromancy. I’m for telepathy now. It’s far more entertaining.’

‘You mustn’t say anything against cheiromancy here, Lady Windermere; it’s the one topic Arthur doesn’t like people to tease about. I can assure you he takes it very seriously.’

‘You don’t mean to tell me he believes in it, Sybil?’

‘Ask him, Lady Windermere—here he is’; and Lord Arthur came up the garden with a big bunch of yellow roses in his hand, while his two children danced round him.

‘Lord Arthur?’

‘Yes, Lady Windermere.’

‘You don’t mean to say you believe in cheiromancy?’

‘Of course I do,’ said the young man, smiling.

‘But why?’

‘Because I owe to it all the happiness of my life,’ he said softly, sinking into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"edef25075f68ec81cb78502d","rewritten_text":"She now felt a strong urge to go to the outer door, just to see whether it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of having some other motive? Captain Wentworth had to be out of sight. She rose from her seat and decided she would go; one part of her should not always be so much wiser than the other, or always suspect the other of being worse. She would see if it rained. But before she could, Captain Wentworth himself appeared at the entrance, coming in among a group of gentlemen and ladies who were clearly his acquaintances, and who must have joined him a little below Milsom Street.

He seemed far more struck and confused by seeing her than she had ever noticed him to be. He looked quite red. For the first time since their renewed acquaintance, she felt that she was betraying the least sensibility of the two. She had the advantage over him in how she had prepared herself for the last few moments. The overwhelming, blinding, bewildering shock of strong surprise was already past for her. Still, she had enough to feel. It was agitation, pain, pleasure—something caught between delight and misery.

He spoke to her, and then turned away. His manner showed embarrassment. She could not call it cold, or friendly, or anything so clearly as embarrassed.

After a short interval, though, he came back toward her and spoke again. They exchanged mutual enquiries on common topics, and neither of them was probably much wiser for what they heard. Anne could still tell that he was less at ease than before. Because they had been together so much, they had learned to speak to each other with a fair show of indifference and calmness, but he could not manage it now. Time had changed him, or Louisa had changed him. There was a kind of awareness in him. He looked very well, not as if he had been suffering in health or spirits, and he talked of Uppercross, of the Musgroves, and even of Louisa. When he named her, he even gave a brief look full of his own arch meaning; yet even so, Captain Wentworth was not comfortable, not at ease, and not able to pretend that he was.

It did not surprise Anne, but it did grieve her, to see that Elizabeth would not recognize him. She could see that he saw Elizabeth, that Elizabeth saw him, and that there was complete recognition between them. She was sure he was ready to be acknowledged as an acquaintance, expecting it. And she had the pain of watching her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot was growing very impatient, now drew up. The servant came in to announce it."}

{"request_id":"7071c487fd1dbec91b54ccfa","rewritten_text":"FOUR days after these strange events, a funeral began at Canterville Chase at about eleven o’clock at night. The hearse was pulled by eight black horses, and each one wore a large tuft of nodding ostrich feathers on its head. The coffin was covered with a rich purple cloth, embroidered in gold with the Canterville coat-of-arms. Alongside the hearse and the coaches, the servants walked with torches that were burning, and the whole procession looked truly impressive.

Lord Canterville was the main mourner. He had come all the way from Wales just to attend the funeral, and he sat in the first carriage with little Virginia. Next came the United States Minister and his wife, then Washington and the three boys. In the last carriage rode Mrs. Umney. People generally agreed that, since she had been frightened by the ghost for more than fifty years, she had every right to see the end of him.

A deep grave had been dug in the corner of the churchyard, right under the old yew tree. The service was carried out in a very solemn way by the Rev. Augustus Dampier. When the ceremony ended, the servants, following an old custom in the Canterville family, put out their torches. As the coffin was lowered into the grave, Virginia stepped forward and placed on it a large cross made of white and pink almond blossoms. At that moment, the moon slipped out from behind a cloud and lit up the small churchyard with its quiet silver light, and from a distant grove a nightingale began to sing. She remembered the ghost’s description of the Garden of Death. Her eyes filled with tears, and during the drive home she could hardly say a word.

The next morning, before Lord Canterville went up to town, Mr. Otis met him to talk about the jewels the ghost had given to Virginia. They were truly magnificent, especially a ruby necklace with an old Venetian setting. It was an excellent example of sixteenth-century work, and because the jewels were so valuable, Mr. Otis felt very uneasy about letting his daughter accept them.

“My lord,” he said, “I know that in this country mortmain applies to small things as well as land. And it seems clear to me that these jewels are, or should be, part of your family’s inheritance. I must ask you, then, to take them to London with you, and to treat them simply as property that has been returned to you under certain strange conditions. As for my daughter, she is only a child, and I’m glad to say she has, as yet, very little interest in such ornaments of idle luxury.”"}

{"request_id":"2575dcb9263281b3cbc07f8b","rewritten_text":"But my father stood by me, to comfort me and to chase away the sharpness of old recollections with brighter hopes; it seemed to me a kind of sweetness to mourn, since it might be the means of drying my tears.

Again, he turned my thoughts from my sorrow by setting it beside his own despair, when he had lost my mother. Even then I could not help shuddering at the scene he painted of his feelings: he had the imagination of a poet, and when he described the whirlwind that tore through him at that time, his words carried such a living force that I believed even while I trembled. I kept asking myself how he could ever return to the common business of life, now that those wild thoughts appeared to have drawn him into kinship with things beyond the earth; for while he spoke, the ideas he conveyed were so vast that it seemed the human heart was far too narrow for their grasp. His emotions looked as though they belonged rather to a spirit whose dwelling is the earthquake and the volcano than to one shut within a mortal frame and human features. Yet these were only memories; he had altered since then. He was now nothing but love, all gentleness; and when I lifted my eyes in wonder at him as he spoke, the smile upon his lips told me that his heart was taken up by the mildest passions.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father led me to pursue studies deeper than those that had previously occupied me. My progress was his pleasure; he was with me through every study, helping me or joining in each lesson. We went into society often, and not a single day passed without his trying to brighten it with some fresh enjoyment. The tender attachment he showed me, and the love and reverence with which I answered it, lent a charm to every moment. The hours seemed to drag, for each minute was put to use; we lived in one week more than many do in the stretch of several months, and the variety and novelty of our pleasures gave them a lively relish.

We made excursions together without end. Whether it was to look upon beautiful country, or to see fine paintings, or sometimes with no particular aim beyond whatever amusement might present itself, I was always glad when I was near my father. I regretted it whenever a third person joined us; still, if I glanced at him with a troubled expression, his eyes, fixed on me and shining with tenderness, would at once bring back joy to my heart. O hours of keen delight! Though brief, they are as long to me as a whole life, when I look back upon them through the mist of grief that rose immediately afterward, as if to bar them from my sight."}
