{"request_id":"dea2e8cb80534ad68fee434c","rewritten_text":"“Now, in English, the letter that occurs most frequently is e. After that, the order of succession is as follows: _a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z_. _E_ predominates so remarkably that you rarely see a sentence of any length in which it is not the prevailing character.

“Here, then, we leave, right at the beginning, the groundwork for something more than a mere guess. The general use that can be made of the table is obvious—but, in this particular cipher, we will only need it very partially. Since our predominant character is 8, we will start by assuming it is the _e_ of the natural alphabet. To check whether that assumption holds, let’s see if the 8 appears often in pairs—for _e_ is doubled with great frequency in English—in words such as ‘meet,’ ‘.fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and so on. In the present instance, we see it doubled no fewer than five times, even though the cryptograph is brief.

“Let us assume, then, that 8 stands for _e_. Now, among all _words_ in the language, ‘the’ is the most common; so let’s see whether there are any repetitions of any three characters, in the same order of collocation, with the last of them being 8. If we find repetitions of letters arranged this way, they will most likely represent the word ‘the.’ Upon inspection, we find no fewer than seven such arrangements, with the characters being ;48. We may therefore assume that ; represents _t_, 4 represents _h_, and 8 represents _e_—the last of which is now well confirmed. Thus a great step has been taken.

“But, having established a single word, we are now able to establish a vastly important point: namely, several beginnings and endings of other words. Let’s refer, for example, to the second-to-last instance in which the combination ;48 occurs—not far from the end of the cipher. We know that the ; immediately following is the start of a word, and, of the six characters that come after this ‘the,’ we are aware of no fewer than five. Let us write these characters down, using the letters we know them to represent, leaving a space for what we don’t know—

t eeth.

“Here we can immediately discard the ‘th,’ since it forms no part of the word that begins with the first t; because, by testing the entire alphabet for a letter that could fit the gap, we find that no word can be formed in which this _th_ can be part. We are thus narrowed into

t ee,

and, going through the alphabet, if necessary, as before, we arrive at the word ‘tree,’ as the only possible reading.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"d003a55143d5c8b28ea94468","rewritten_text":"The bewilderment and astonishment that seized my mind at this remarkable shift in the whole state of things was, perhaps, after all, the portion of the adventure least open to explanation. For the bouleversement itself was not only natural and unavoidable, but had long been actually foreseen as something to be expected whenever I should reach that precise stage of my voyage where the pull of the planet would give way to the pull of the satellite—or, to speak more exactly, where the balloon’s gravitation toward the earth should prove weaker than its gravitation toward the moon. Of course, I had risen from a sound sleep, with every sense in confusion, to observe a phenomenon so startling; and yet, though it was expected, it was not expected in the very instant. The change must, no doubt, have occurred in an easy and gradual fashion, and it is by no means certain that, even if I had been awake at the moment, I would have recognized it from any inward sign—any inconvenience or disorder, either in my own person or in my apparatus.\n\n“It is scarcely necessary to add that, once I came to a proper understanding of my situation, and had escaped the terror that had taken hold of every faculty of my soul, my attention was first of all fixed on the moon’s general physical aspect. It lay beneath me like a chart; and though I still reckoned it at a considerable distance, the markings of its surface stood out to my sight with a vividness that was both striking and wholly inexplicable. The total lack of ocean or sea—and, indeed, of any lake or river, or any body of water whatever—struck me, at first glance, as the most extraordinary feature in its geological condition. Still, to my surprise, I saw broad level tracts of a decidedly alluvial nature, while the greater part of the hemisphere before me was covered with countless volcanic mountains, conical in form, and looking more like artificial projections than natural elevations. The tallest of them does not rise above three and three-quarter miles in perpendicular height; but a map of the volcanic districts of the Campi Phlegraei would show your Excellencies their general surface far better than any unworthy account I might attempt. Most of these mountains were in a state of evident eruption, and they made me dreadfully aware of their rage and force through the repeated thunders of the so-called meteoric stones, which now shot upward by the balloon with an ever-increasing frequency, more and more alarming.”"}

{"request_id":"591b5272e4be1df719599385","rewritten_text":"The winters along the latitude of Sullivan’s Island are usually mild, and in the autumn it is a rare thing indeed to think a fire is truly needed. Yet about the middle of October, 18—, there came a day of unusual cold. Just before sunset I picked my way through the evergreens to my friend’s hut, which I had not seen for several weeks—at that time I lived in Charleston, nine miles away from the island, and the means of going and coming were nothing like what they are now. When I reached the hut, I knocked, as I always did, and, getting no answer, went looking for the key I knew was hidden away; I unlocked the door and stepped inside. A bright fire was burning on the hearth. It was a welcome sight, and not at all an unwelcome one. I shrugged off my overcoat, settled into an arm-chair beside the crackling logs, and waited quietly for my hosts.

Not long after dark they came in, and greeted me with the warmest friendliness. Jupiter, smiling from ear to ear, hurried about to get some marsh-hens ready for supper. Legrand was in one of his moods—what else could I call them?—of high spirits. He had turned up an unknown bivalve, one that he said formed a new genus; and, beyond that, he had tracked down and secured, with Jupiter’s help, a _scarabæus_ that he believed to be entirely new, though he wanted my judgment on it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, warming my hands at the blaze, and wishing the whole tribe of _scarabæi_ were off to the devil.

“Ah, if I’d only known you were here!” Legrand replied. “But it’s been so long since I saw you, and how could I guess you’d come to visit me on this very night of all nights? On my way back I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and—very foolishly—I lent him the bug. So you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I’ll send Jup down for it at sunrise. It’s the loveliest thing in creation!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Absurd! No—sunrise is for the bug. It’s a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory-nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of the back, and another—somewhat longer—at the other. The _antennæ_ are—”

“Dey aint no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin on you,” Jupiter cut in; “de bug is a goole bug, solid, ebery bit of him, inside and all, sep him wing—neber feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”"}

{"request_id":"99536b39fa3a2ab0c37e24c6","rewritten_text":"“But may I trouble you with two questions?” “May I?”

“You may ask,” said Monks, showing a bit of surprise; “but whether I choose to answer is a different matter.”

“—That makes three,” put in Mr. Bumble, trying to sound witty.

“Is that what you meant to get out of me?” demanded the matron.

“It is,” said Monks. “And the other question?”

“What do you plan to do with it? Will you use it against me?”

“Never,” Monks returned. “Nor against me either. Now listen—don’t take one step nearer, or your life won’t be worth a bulrush.”

With that, he suddenly shoved the table aside, and, reaching for an iron ring set into the boarding, he yanked it; a large trap-door swung back, opening right by Mr. Bumble’s feet, and sent that gentleman stumbling several paces backward in a rush.

“Look down,” said Monks, lowering the lantern into the pit. “Don’t be afraid of me. If I’d wanted to drop you quietly while you were sitting over it, I could have done so.”

Encouraged by this, the matron edged up to the brink; and even Mr. Bumble, driven by curiosity, followed suit. The muddy water, swollen by the heavy rain, was surging swiftly below, and every other sound was swallowed by the noise of it splashing and churning against the green, slimy piles. There had once been a water-mill there; the tide, foaming and worrying at the few rotten stakes and the broken bits of machinery still left, seemed to dart forward with fresh force once freed from the obstacles that had tried in vain to stop its headlong rush.

“If you threw a man’s body down there,” said Monks, swinging the lantern to and fro in the dark well, “where would it be tomorrow morning?”

“Twelve miles down the river—and cut to pieces besides,” Bumble answered, backing away at the thought.

Monks took the small packet from his breast, where he had thrust it in haste; then he tied it to a leaden weight that had belonged to some pulley and lay on the floor, and dropped it into the stream. It sank straight and true, with scarcely a splash; then it was gone.

The three stared at one another’s faces, as if they could breathe easier.

“There!” said Monks, shutting the trap-door, which fell heavily back into place. “If the sea ever gives up its dead, as the books claim, it will keep its gold and silver to itself—and that rubbish with it. We’ve nothing more to say, and we may break up our pleasant little gathering.”

“By all means,” said Mr. Bumble at once, with eager readiness.

“And you’ll keep a quiet tongue in your head,” Monks added, fixing him with a threatening look."}

{"request_id":"7b4ba8f0006c5cf79502f949","rewritten_text":"But how could I, a poor, dazed village boy, avoid the kind of contradiction that even the best and wisest men fall into every day?

“It may be all true,” I told Biddy, “but I can’t help admiring her so much.”

So when it came to that, I turned over onto my face. I grabbed the hair on both sides of my head and pulled it hard. All the while I knew my heart was acting wildly and wrongly, and I was fully aware that I deserved it. If I had lifted my face by my hair and knocked it against the pebbles, that would have been a fair punishment for being such an idiot.

Biddy was the wisest girl, and she didn’t try to argue with me anymore. She put her rough, work-worn hand on my hands, one after another, and gently pulled them out of my hair. Then she patted my shoulder softly, in a way meant to calm me. With my face pressed against my sleeve, I cried a little—just like I had in the brewery yard—and I felt, in a vague way, that I was being treated badly by someone, or by everyone. I couldn’t tell which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” Biddy said. “You’ve been able to trust me, Pip. And I’m glad of another thing: you know you can always rely on me to keep your confidence, and to deserve it as much as I can. If your first teacher—dear me, what a poor teacher she was, and how much she still needed to be taught herself—had been your teacher right now, she would think she knew what lesson she would give you. But it would be a hard lesson to learn, and you’ve already moved past her. There’s no point in it now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy stood up from the bank. Then, with a fresh and pleasant change in her voice, she asked, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, as I got up. I put my arm around her neck and kissed her. “I’ll always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” Biddy said.

“You know I never will be,” I answered, “so that’s settled. And it’s not even like I have to tell you anything, because you already know everything I know. As I told you the other night at home.”

“Ah!” Biddy said, almost in a whisper, as she looked away at the ships. Then, with the same pleasant change of voice as before, she asked again, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon slowly faded into summer evening, and it was beautiful."}

{"request_id":"ab8012752252f4ccf3d84e5e","rewritten_text":"“Git up! What you ’bout?”

I opened my eyes and took a look around, trying to figure out where I was. It was after sun-up, and I’d been dead asleep. Pap was standing over me, looking sour and sick, same as anything. He says:

“What you doin’ with this gun?”

I figured he didn’t have a clue about what he’d been up to, so I says:

“Somebody tried to get in, so I was laying for him.”

“Why didn’t you roust me out?”

“Well, I tried to, but I couldn’t; I couldn’t budge you.”

“Well, all right. Don’t stand there palavering all day—get out with you and see if there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I slipped out up the river-bank. I saw bits of limbs and other stuff floating down, and a sprinkling of bark, so I knew the river had started to rise. I figured I’d be having fine times now if I was over in town. The June rise used to be good luck for me—once it starts here, cordwood comes floating down, and chunks of log rafts, sometimes a dozen logs together. All you had to do was catch ’em and sell them to the wood-yards and the sawmill.

I went along the bank with one eye on where Pap might be and the other on what the rise might bring. Then, all at once, here comes a canoe—real pretty, too—about thirteen or fourteen foot long, riding high like a duck. I launched head-first off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and paddled straight for it. I just figured there’d be somebody in it, because folks often did that to make a fool of you; when a man had hauled a skiff out most of the way, they’d pop up and laugh at him. But this time it wasn’t like that. It was a drift-canoe for sure, and I climbed in and paddled her ashore. I thought, the old man’ll be glad when he sees it—she’s worth ten dollars. But when I got to shore, Pap wasn’t anywhere in sight. And as I was pushing her into a little creek, like a gully, all tangled over with vines and willows, I got another notion: I’d hide her good. Then, instead of heading for the woods when I run off, I’d go down the river about fifty mile and camp in one place for good, so I wouldn’t have to keep tramping on foot.

It was pretty close to the shanty, and I thought I could hear the old man coming the whole time, but I got the canoe stowed. Then I stepped out and looked around through a bunch of willows, and there was the old man down the path a ways, drawing a bead on a bird with his gun."}

{"request_id":"f295a98b8b27ff4f1ba5f73d","rewritten_text":"“Why, you don’t mean to say—” my sister began.

“Yes I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook. “But wait a bit. Go on, Joseph. Good for you! Go on!”

“What would respectable people say,” Joe went on, “about twenty pounds?”

“Handsome would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well, then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That miserable hypocrite, Pumblechook, nodded again and said, with a smug laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Good again! Follow her up, Joseph!”

“Then to finish it,” Joe said happily, handing the bag to my sister, “it’s twenty-five pounds.”

“It’s twenty-five pounds, Mum,” Pumblechook echoed, rising to shake her hand. “And it’s no more than your merits, as I said when my opinion was asked. I wish you joy of the money!”

If the villain had stopped there, his behavior would already have been bad enough. But he made his guilt even worse by taking me into custody, with a kind of proud, bossy authority that made all his earlier wrongdoing seem small.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” Pumblechook said, taking me by the arm just above the elbow, “I’m one of those people who always see things through once they’ve started. This boy must be bound, right away. That’s my way. Bound right away.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said, holding the money. “We’re very grateful to you.”

“Don’t worry about me, Mum,” said that evil cornchandler. “A pleasure is a pleasure for anyone. But this boy—you know we have to have him bound. I said I’d take care of it. To tell you the truth, I said I’d see to it.”

The Justices were sitting in the Town Hall nearby, so we went at once to have me bound as an apprentice to Joe, in front of the Justices. I say we went, but Pumblechook shoved me forward, as if I had just stolen something or shot a man. In fact, that was the general feeling in Court. People were saying as he pushed me through the crowd, “What’s he done?” and others, “He’s young, too, but he looks bad, doesn’t he?” One man, mild and kind-looking, even handed me a tract with a picture of a wicked young man in a cell, surrounded by a perfect sausage-shop of iron fetters, titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall was a strange place, I thought. It had higher pews than a church, and people leaned over the pews to watch. There were serious Justices—one with a powdered wig—sitting back in chairs with folded arms, or taking snuff, or falling asleep, or writing, or reading the newspapers. On the walls there were some shiny black portraits, which my untrained eye thought looked like hardbake and sticking-plaster put together."}

{"request_id":"dfe6a12c9766ab2fd45b071c","rewritten_text":"While these things were happening in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old den—the same one from which the girl had removed Oliver—brooding over a dull, smoky fire. He held a pair of bellows on his knee, apparently trying to get it going again with a bit more cheer, but he had slipped into deep thought. With his arms folded over them and his chin resting on his thumbs, he stared, absent-mindedly, at the rusty bars.

Behind him, at a table, sat the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, all focused on a game of whist. The Artful was playing dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The first gentleman’s face—always unusually intelligent—took on even more interest as he watched the game closely, studying Mr. Chitling’s hand. From time to time, whenever it seemed useful, he sent him earnest looks, carefully adjusting his own play based on what he observed in his neighbor’s cards. Since it was a cold night, the Dodger wore his hat, as he often did indoors. He also kept a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly when he thought it necessary to ask for a refill from the quart pot on the table, which stood ready with gin-and-water for the company.

Master Bates was attentive too, but because he was more excitable than his accomplished friend, it was noticeable that he went back to the gin-and-water more often, and that he also indulged in plenty of jokes and irrelevant remarks—utterly inappropriate for a serious game. Indeed, the Artful, assuming their close friendship, more than once took the chance to speak gravely to him about these improprieties. Master Bates took the remonstrances in extremely good part, only asking his friend to be “blowed,” or to put his head in a sack, or answering with some other neatly turned bit of humor of the same kind; and the way he did it earned him considerable admiration in Mr. Chitling’s mind. It was striking that Mr. Chitling and his partner always lost. Yet instead of making Master Bates angry, it seemed only to amuse him more—he laughed uproariously at the end of every deal and insisted he had never seen such a jolly game in all his born days.

“That’s two doubles and the rub,” said Mr. Chitling, with a very long face, as he drew half-a-crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never see such a feller as you, Jack; you win everything.”"}

{"request_id":"b6748fecdffe42c2a7779d6b","rewritten_text":"Indeed, I had no fear for her. She was the kind of woman people call notable, and she could handle things in the world without my help. To be honest, I think she always saw me as a lazy boy, a useless extra, good for nothing except building castles in the air. She was probably relieved to be rid of me.

It was a dark night when I said goodbye. I took with me, as aides-de-camp, the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble. We carried the balloon, along with the car and all the equipment, by a roundabout route to the station where the other items had been stored. When we got there, we found everything safe and untouched, and I went straight to work.

“It was the first of April. As I said, the night was dark, with no stars to be seen. Rain fell in short bursts, and it made us miserable. My biggest worry was the balloon. Even though it was protected by varnish, it was starting to get heavy from the moisture, and the powder could also be damaged. So I kept the three duns busy, working hard: they pounded ice around the central cask and stirred the acid in the others. They did not stop asking me what I planned to do with all this equipment. They complained bitterly about the terrible work I was making them do. They could not understand, they said, how it could help anything to get soaked just to take part in such awful, strange rituals. I began to feel uneasy. I truly believed the idiots thought I had made a deal with the devil, and that what I was doing now was no better than it should be. I was afraid they would abandon me altogether.

I managed, though, to calm them by promising to pay every debt in full as soon as I could finish this job. Of course, they took my words in their own way. They probably imagined that, at the very least, I would end up with a lot of ready money. If I paid them what I owed, and a little extra for their trouble, they probably did not care much what happened to my soul or my body.

“After about four and a half hours, I found the balloon inflated enough. I attached the car, and put all my tools inside it. I made sure not to forget the condensing apparatus, a large supply of water, and plenty of provisions, including pemmican, which has a lot of nourishment packed into a small amount.”"}

{"request_id":"4ac1920dc083c0f33d4713e4","rewritten_text":"His face, baked by the sun, was more than half concealed beneath a thick growth of whiskers and a _mustachio._ He carried with him a huge oaken cudgel, though he seemed otherwise to have no weapons. He bowed in a clumsy fashion and greeted us with “good evening,” speaking French with accents that, though a bit tinged with Neufchatel, were still plain enough to point to Paris.

“Take a seat, my friend,” said Dupin. “I take it you’ve come about the Ourang-Outang. Upon my word, I almost envy you for having him; a splendid creature, and no doubt a very valuable one. How old do you think he is?”

The sailor drew in a long breath, as though freed from some unbearable weight, and then answered with confidence:

“I can’t say for certain—but he can’t be more than four or five years old. Have you got him here?”

“Oh no; we had no arrangements for keeping him here. He’s at a livery stable in the Rue Dubourg, just around the corner. You can fetch him in the morning. Of course you’re ready to identify the property?”

“Certainly, sir.”

“I shall be sorry to let him go,” said Dupin.

“I don’t mean you should go to all this trouble for nothing, sir,” the man returned. “I couldn’t ask it. I’m quite willing to pay a reward for finding the animal—that is, anything reasonable.”

“Well,” said my friend, “that’s all very fair, to be sure. Let me consider—what should I ask? Ah! I’ll tell you. My reward will be this: you will give me all the information you can about these murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin spoke the last words in a very low voice, and very quietly. In the same quiet manner he went to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he drew a pistol from his bosom and set it on the table, without the slightest agitation.

The sailor’s face reddened, as if he were fighting for breath. He sprang up and seized his cudgel, but the next instant he sank back into his chair, shaking violently, with the very look of death. He said nothing. I felt for him sincerely.

“My friend,” said Dupin, in a gentle tone, “you’re frightening yourself unnecessarily—you really are. We mean you no harm at all. I pledge you the honor of a gentleman, and of a Frenchman, that we intend you no injury. I know perfectly well that you are innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue. Still, it won’t do to deny that you are, in some measure, implicated in them.”"}

{"request_id":"f5d9ceb96fef680f7c647f00","rewritten_text":"You see, I had my handkerchief in my helmet, along with a few other things. But it was the kind of helmet you can’t take off by yourself. I hadn’t thought about that when I put it there, and I didn’t even know it. I just assumed it would be especially convenient right there. Now, though, the idea of it being there—so close, so useful—yet impossible to reach, made everything worse and harder to bear. Yes, the thing you can’t get is usually the thing you want most. Everyone notices that.

Well, it took my mind off everything else. It pulled my thoughts straight into my helmet, and mile after mile I kept imagining the handkerchief, picturing it again and again. Meanwhile the salt sweat kept running into my eyes, and I couldn’t get to it. It sounds like a small problem on paper, but it wasn’t small at all. It was the most real kind of misery. I wouldn’t say it if it weren’t true. I decided that next time I would bring a reticule, no matter what anyone thought. Of course those iron men of the Round Table would probably call it scandalous and maybe start talking about Sheol, but for me, comfort comes first, and style comes later.

So we jogged along. Every now and then we hit a stretch of dust, and it would rise in clouds, get into my nose, and make me sneeze and cry. And of course I said things I shouldn’t have said—I won’t deny that. I’m not better than anyone.

We couldn’t seem to meet anyone in this lonely Britain, not even an ogre. And in the mood I was in then, it was better for the ogre—an ogre with a handkerchief. Most knights would have thought only about getting his armor, but I managed to take his bandanna instead. He could keep his gear, for all of me.

In the meantime, it kept getting hotter and hotter inside. The sun was beating down and warming the iron more and more all the time. When you’re hot like that, even small things start to irritate you. When I trotted, I rattled like a crate of dishes, and that annoyed me. I also couldn’t stand the shield slatting and banging—first against my breast, then around my back. If I slowed down into a walk, my joints creaked and screeched in that tiresome way a wheelbarrow does. And since we weren’t making any breeze at that pace, I felt like I’d get fried in a stove. Besides, the quieter I went, the more the iron seemed to settle on me, and the more and more tons it felt like I weighed every minute."}

{"request_id":"0193b8fc24f269aed9a8df32","rewritten_text":"“I need to step out for a moment to observe, Sir Walter,” said Mr Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, as he set down the newspaper, “that the current situation is working very much in our favour. This peace will send all our rich naval officers ashore. They’ll all be looking for a home. Could there be a better time, Sir Walter, to have a choice of tenants—very responsible ones. Many a noble fortune has been made during the war. If a wealthy admiral were to come our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very lucky man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter replied; “that’s all I have to say on it. What a prize Kellynch Hall would be to him—rather the greatest prize of all, considering how many he may have taken already; eh, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he must, at the joke, and then added—

“I would presume to observe, Sir Walter, that, in matters of business, gentlemen of the navy are well worth dealing with. I’ve learned something about the way they do business, and I’m free to admit they have very liberal ideas, and are as likely to make desirable tenants as any group of people one could meet. So, Sir Walter, what I would venture to suggest is this: if, as a result of any rumours getting out about your intentions—which we have to consider a possible thing, because it’s so hard to keep the actions and plans of one part of the world from the notice and curiosity of the other—then consequence has its price. I, John Shepherd, might conceal whatever family matters I chose, because nobody would think it worth their while to watch me; but Sir Walter Elliot has eyes on him, and it may be very difficult to avoid them. Therefore, I’ll say this much: it won’t greatly surprise me if, despite all our caution, some rumour of the truth should get abroad. And if that happens—since applications will unquestionably follow—I think any from our wealthy naval commanders would be particularly worth attending to. And I beg leave to add that two hours will bring me over at any time, to save you the trouble of replying.”

Sir Walter only nodded. But soon afterwards, as he rose and paced the room, he remarked with a touch of sarcasm—

“There are few, I imagine, among the gentlemen of the navy who wouldn’t be surprised to find themselves in a house like this.”

“They would look around them, no doubt, and bless their good fortune,” said Mrs Clay, for Mrs Clay was there: her father had driven her over, since nothing was of more use to Mrs Clay’s health than a drive to Kellynch. “But I quite agree with my father in thinking a sailor might be a very desirable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"af0fa36da2ee4e8ed5da2ec4","rewritten_text":"I got up early in the morning and again tried to slip past the watchfulness of my creditors. Eagerly, I went to the bookseller’s stall and laid out the little cash I had on hand to buy some books on Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. Once I got home safely, I spent every spare moment reading them. Before long, I felt I had learned enough to carry out my plan.

During that time, I also worked hard to calm down the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble. I finally managed it. Partly I raised money by selling some of my household furniture to cover part of what they were owed. Partly I promised to pay the rest once I finished a small project I told them I was working on, and I asked for their help in doing it. Since they were not very knowledgeable men, I had little difficulty turning them to my purpose.

With everything arranged, I then planned—quietly and with the help of my wife—to get rid of whatever property I still had. I also borrowed small amounts of money under different excuses, and I paid no attention at all to how I would repay it later. With the money I gathered, I bought, in stages, cambric muslin, very fine cloth, cut into pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a supply of caoutchouc varnish; a large deep wicker basket made to order; and several other items needed to build and equip a balloon of extraordinary size. I told my wife to put it together as soon as possible and gave her clear instructions on exactly how to proceed.

Meanwhile, I worked the twine into a net large enough for the job. I fitted it with a hoop and the cords it needed. I bought a quadrant, a compass, a spy-glass, and a common barometer, with some important modifications. I also acquired two astronomical instruments that were not as well known. Then, whenever I could, I carried by night to a secluded place east of Rotterdam: five iron-bound casks, each meant to hold about fifty gallons, plus one larger cask; six tinned ware tubes, three inches across and ten feet long; a quantity of a particular metallic substance, or semi-metal, which I will not name; and a dozen demijohns of a very common acid.

The gas made from these materials is a gas that no one else has ever produced, at least not for any similar purpose. I would not have trouble explaining the secret, except that it properly belongs to a citizen of Nantz in France, who shared it with me on the condition that I use it."}

{"request_id":"0e236eb394305323ace291f8","rewritten_text":"Yet despite all that, the boy grew more and more melancholy, pale, and dejected. She added hot baths, sitz baths, shower baths, and plunges. The boy stayed as grim as a hearse. She started to help the water along with a thin oatmeal diet and blister plasters. She calculated his capacity the way you would a jug’s, and filled him up every day with quack cure-alls.

Tom had become indifferent to persecution by this point. This stage filled the old lady’s heart with consternation. That indifference had to be broken up at any cost. Now she heard about Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a lot at once. She tasted it and felt instantly grateful. It was simply fire in liquid form. She dropped the water treatment and everything else, and put all her faith in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and watched with the deepest anxiety to see what would happen. Her troubles were instantly at rest, her soul at peace again; for the “indifference” had been broken up. The boy couldn’t have shown a wilder, heartier interest if she’d built a fire under him.

Tom felt it was time to wake up. This kind of life might be romantic enough, given his ruined condition, but it was starting to have too little feeling and too much distracting variety. So he thought through different plans for relief, and finally settled on pretending to be fond of Pain-killer. He asked for it so often he became a nuisance, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop bothering her. If it had been Sid, she would have had no reason to temper her delight; but because it was Tom, she watched the bottle in secret. She found that the medicine did, in fact, reduce, but it never occurred to her that the boy was using it to patch the crack in the sitting-room floor.

One day Tom was in the middle of dosing the crack when his aunt’s yellow cat came along, purring, eyeing the teaspoon greedily, and begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you want it, Peter.”

But Peter made it clear that he did want it.

“You’d better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“Now that you’ve asked for it, I’ll give it to you, because there ain’t anything mean about me; but if you find you don’t like it, you mustn’t blame anybody but your own self.”

Peter agreed. So Tom pried his mouth open and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter sprang a couple of yards into the air, then let out a war-whoop and took off around the room, running in circles, crashing into furniture, knocking over flower-pots, and causing general havoc."}

{"request_id":"c5128e2f0f6c71585234e50c","rewritten_text":"His understanding and temper, though not like hers, would still have met all her wishes. It would have been a marriage that benefited both of them. With her ease and lively spirit, his mind might have become gentler, and his manners could have improved. And from his judgment, his knowledge, and his experience of the world, she would have gained something even more important.

But no such happy marriage could now show the crowd what real marital happiness was. A different kind of union—one that would make the other impossible—was soon to be formed in their family.

She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would be supported in a tolerable independence. But she could easily guess how little lasting happiness could belong to a couple brought together only because their passions were stronger than their virtue.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote again to his brother. He answered Mr. Bennet’s acknowledgments briefly, assuring him that he was eager to promote the welfare of any of his family. He then ended by asking, very earnestly, that the subject might never be mentioned to him again. The main purpose of his letter was to tell them that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

“It was greatly my wish that he should do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. I think you will agree with me that leaving that corps is highly advisable, both for his sake and for my niece’s. Mr. Wickham intends to join the Regulars. Among his old friends, there are still some who can and will help him in the army. He has been promised an ensigncy in General----’s regiment, which is now stationed in the north. It is an advantage that it is so far from this part of the kingdom. He promises fairly, and I hope that, among different people, where each of them has a character to protect, they will both be more careful. I have written to Colonel Forster to tell him about our present plans, and to ask him to satisfy the different creditors of Mr. Wickham in and near Brighton, with assurances of prompt payment. I have pledged myself for this. And will you take the trouble of giving similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton? I will attach a list, based on the information he has given. He has reported all his debts; I hope at least he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be finished in a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are invited to Longbourn first. And I understand from Mrs. Gardiner that my niece is very eager to see you all before she leaves the south.”"}

{"request_id":"088d1cf74005835ba3262934","rewritten_text":"Had she known that her sister meant to wrench her away from prospects and realities of so particular a kind, what feelings might she have had? Only her mother could have understood them, and even she would probably have felt much the same. Lydia’s going to Brighton was all that could still comfort her against the melancholy certainty that her husband never intended to go there himself.

But they were wholly unaware of what had occurred; and their transports went on, with scarcely any break, right up to the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now to meet Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since her return she had been much in his company, so that agitation had pretty well subsided; the fluttering of former partiality was gone entirely. She had even learned to read, in the very softness that had at first charmed her, a studied sameness—something meant to please, yet fitted to disgust and weary. In his conduct toward herself, too, she found a new cause of offence; for the readiness he soon showed to resume those attentions which had distinguished the beginning of their acquaintance could only, after what had since taken place, serve to irritate her. She cared no longer for him when she saw herself chosen as the mark of such empty and trifling gallantry; and though she kept her feelings down, she could not help perceiving the rebuke implied in his belief that, however long his attentions had been withheld, and for whatever reason, her vanity would still be flattered, and her preference secured, whenever he chose to renew them.

On the very last day that the regiment remained in Meryton, he dined, with the other officers, at Longbourn; and so little was Elizabeth disposed to part from him in ill-humour, that when he asked how her time had been spent at Hunsford, she told him that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both passed three weeks at Rosings, and asked whether he knew the former.

He started, and looked surprised, displeased, and alarmed; but after a brief recollection, and with a smile returning, he answered that he had seen him often before. Then, having remarked that he was a very gentlemanlike man, he asked her how she had liked him. Her reply was warmly favourable. With an air of indifference, he soon added, “How long did you say that he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him frequently?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves on acquaintance.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, with a look that did not escape her. “And pray may I ask—” but stopping himself, he continued in a lighter tone, “Is it in address that he improves?”"}

{"request_id":"70276986566be6b76c9aa7b1","rewritten_text":"They was bringing along a very fine-looking old gentleman, and a very fine-looking younger one too, with his right arm in a sling. And, my souls, how the crowd yelled and carried on—laughing and keeping it up. Still, I didn’t see any real joke in it, and I figured it would put the duke and the king out some to have to look at it. I thought they’d go pale. But no—none of them went pale. The duke never showed the least sign that he suspected anything; he just kept wandering around, cooing and acting pleased, as happy and satisfied as a jug that’s spilling out buttermilk. As for the king, he just stared and stared down at the new arrivals, looking so sorrowful, like the thought of such frauds and rascals in the world gave him a stomach-ache right in his own heart. Oh, he played it admirable. A good many of the leading folks gathered close to the king, so he could see they were on his side. The old gentleman who’d just come looked as if he was puzzled clear through. Pretty soon he started to talk, and I could tell at once he pronounced himself like an Englishman—though it wasn’t the king’s way, even if the king’s imitation was pretty good. I can’t set down the old gent’s exact words, and I can’t copy his voice, but he turned to the crowd and said something pretty much like this:

“This is a surprise to me that I wasn’t expecting; and I’ll admit, candid and plain, I’m not in the best shape to meet it and answer it. For my brother and me have had misfortunes. He’s broke his arm, and our baggage got left off at a town above here last night, by mistake. I am Peter Wilks’ brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can’t hear nor speak—and can’t even make signs to amount to much, seeing as he’s only got one hand to work them with. We are who we say we are; and in a day or two, when I get the baggage, I can prove it. But until then I won’t say anything more—only go to the hotel and wait.”

So he and the new dummy started off. The king laughed and blustered out:

“Broke his arm—_very_ likely, _ain’t_ it?—and mighty convenient, too, for a fraud that has to make signs and hasn’t learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s _mighty_ fine—and mighty clever—under the _circumstances_!”

He laughed again, and everybody else did too, except three or four—maybe half a dozen. Among them was that doctor. Another was a sharp-looking gentleman with a carpet-bag of the old-fashioned sort, made out of carpet-stuff, who’d just come off the steamboat and was talking to him in a low voice, looking toward the king now and then and nodding his head. That was Levi Bell, the lawyer that had gone up to Louisville. And there was also a big rough husky who’d come along and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now."}

{"request_id":"d1d8d3537396066634670965","rewritten_text":"Their arrival kindled a kind of fire in Saint Antoine’s breast, spreading quickly as they came, stirring and flickering in flames of faces at nearly every door and window. Still, no one followed them, and when they entered the wine-shop no man spoke, though the eyes of every man there were fixed on them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

It may have been the cue to loosen the general tongue. It brought an answering chorus of “Good day!”

“The weather is bad, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.

At that, every man looked at his neighbor, then all lowered their eyes and sat in silence. Except for one man, who rose and went out.

“My wife,” said Defarge aloud, addressing Madame Defarge, “I’ve traveled certain leagues with this good road-mender, called Jacques. I met him—by accident—day and a half’s journey out of Paris. He’s a good child, this road-mender, called Jacques. Give him something to drink!”

A second man rose and went out. Madame Defarge set wine before the road-mender called Jacques, who tipped his blue cap to the company and drank. In the breast of his blouse he carried some coarse dark bread; he ate it in between, and sat munching and drinking near Madame Defarge’s counter. A third man rose and went out.

Defarge refreshed himself with a draught of wine, but he took less than was offered to the stranger, since he was a man for whom such things were no rarity. He stood waiting until the countryman had finished his breakfast. He did not look at anyone present, and no one looked at him now—not even Madame Defarge, who had taken up her knitting and was working.

“Have you finished your meal, friend?” he asked, at the right moment.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Then come! You’ll see the room I told you you could use. It will suit you wonderfully.”

From the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, from the staircase into a garret—once the garret where a white-haired man had sat on a low bench, stooping forward and very busy, making shoes.

No white-haired man was there now; but the three men were there who had gone out of the wine-shop one by one. And between them and the white-haired man far off was the one small link they had once seen him through, peering in at him through the cracks in the wall.

Defarge closed the door carefully and spoke in a low voice:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness encountered by appointment, by me, Jacques Four.”"}

{"request_id":"e7114c3a64e3fd3e79b23e07","rewritten_text":"“You won’t, won’t you? Oh, you precious little flat!”

“Is it naughty, isn’t it, Oliver?” Charley Bates asked. “He’ll end up getting scragged, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that means,” Oliver said.

“Something like that, old fellow,” Charley replied. As he spoke, Master Bates grabbed the end of his neckerchief. He held it up in the air, then dropped his head onto his shoulder and jerked his head in a strange way, making a curious sound with his teeth. It was a lively show that made it clear that scragging and hanging were the same thing.

“That’s what it means,” Charley said. “Look how he stares, Jack! I’ve never seen such good company as that boy. He’ll be the death of me, I just know it.” Master Charley Bates laughed again, then went back to his pipe, tears in his eyes.

“You were brought up badly,” the Dodger said, looking at Oliver’s polished boots with satisfaction. “Fagin will turn you into something, but if he doesn’t, you’ll be the first person he ever had who turned out useless. You’d better start right away, because you’ll be in the trade long before you think about it. And you’re wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates added his own moral warnings. When those were done, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins went on to describe, in glowing terms, all the pleasures that came with the life they lived. They kept slipping in hints to Oliver that the best thing he could do was to get Fagin’s favor as soon as possible, using the same methods they had used to win it.

“And always put this in your pipe, Nolly,” the Dodger said, as the Jew was heard unlocking the door upstairs. “If you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the point of talking like that?” Master Bates interrupted. “He doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take pocket-handkechers and watches,” the Dodger said, making his words match Oliver’s understanding, “some other fellow will. Then the guys who lose them will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off too. And nobody will be any better, except the people who get them—and you’ve got just as much right to them as they have.”

“Of course, of course!” the Jew said. He had come in without Oliver noticing. “It all comes down to a nutshell, my dear. Take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the whole lesson of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands together with delight as he agreed with the Dodger’s reasoning, and he chuckled happily at how well his pupil understood.

The talk didn’t go any further then, because the Jew went back home with Miss Betsy, and with a gentleman Oliver had never seen before. The Dodger called him Tom Chitling. After lingering on the stairs to exchange a few polite flirtations with the lady, he finally appeared."}

{"request_id":"6298c0ac7465b28a3824aa95","rewritten_text":"Watching him in these moods, I often found myself thinking about an old idea called the Bi-Part Soul. I would even amuse myself with the thought of a double Dupin: one part creative, the other part able to solve things.

Don’t think, though, that what I’ve just said is me explaining a mystery or writing a romance. Everything I described about the Frenchman was simply the result of an excited mind, or maybe a sick one. Still, the best way to understand what his remarks were like at those moments is to give an example.

One night we walked together down a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. Both of us seemed lost in thought, and for at least fifteen minutes neither of us said a word. Then Dupin suddenly spoke.

“He is a very little fellow, that’s true, and he’d do better at the Théâtre des Variétés.”

“There can be no doubt of that,” I answered, without thinking. At first I didn’t notice anything strange about how he had suddenly joined my thoughts. I had been so absorbed in reflection. But then, right away, I caught myself, and my surprise was intense.

“Dupin,” I said seriously, “this is beyond me. I don’t hesitate to say I’m amazed. I can hardly believe what I’m hearing. How could you possibly know I was thinking of—?” I stopped to make sure, as clearly as I could, that he really knew who I meant.

“—Chantilly,” he said. “Why do you pause? You were telling yourself that his small size made him unsuitable for tragedy.”

That was exactly what I had been thinking about. Chantilly had once been a cobbler from the Rue St. Denis. After he became obsessed with the stage, he tried to play Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy. He was mocked for it, and everyone made fun of him.

“Tell me, for Heaven’s sake,” I cried, “the method—if there is any method—by which you were able to read my mind in this matter.” In truth, I was even more shocked than I wanted to admit.

“It was the fruiterer,” my friend replied. “He led you to the conclusion that the man who mends soles wasn’t tall enough for Xerxes, and for that sort of role.”

“The fruiterer! You surprise me. I don’t know any fruiterer at all.”

“The man who bumped into you when we entered the street,” Dupin said. “It might have been fifteen minutes ago.”

Now I remembered it. As we moved from the Rue C—— into the street where we were standing, a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples on his head had nearly knocked me down by accident. But I still couldn’t understand what that had to do with Chantilly."}

{"request_id":"15b5dcb9ac5260df3f9579c2","rewritten_text":"It was at Warwick Castle that I first ran into the odd stranger I’m about to tell you of. Three things drew me to him: a plain, openhearted straightforwardness; a remarkable ease with ancient armor; and the calm comfort of his presence—because he did all the talking. We drifted together, as quiet folk do, at the back of the little group being led through, and he immediately began saying things that caught my attention. As he spoke on, in a soft, pleasant, flowing way, it was as though he slipped, little by little, out of this world and its time, and into some far-off age and a country long since forgotten; and so, almost without my noticing, he spun a spell around me until I felt myself moving among the specters and shadows, the dust and mildew of a gray antiquity, conversing with a relic of it. Just as I might speak of my closest friends or foes, or the neighbors I know best, he spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other great names of the Round Table—and how old, old, unspeakably old, and worn, faded, dry, and musty and timeworn he seemed to grow as he went on.

At last he turned to me, speaking as casually as one might mention the weather, or any other everyday matter—

“Do you know about the transmigration of souls? Do you know about the transposition of epochs—and bodies?”

I told him I hadn’t heard of it. He showed so little interest—much as people do when they talk about the weather—that he didn’t seem to notice whether I answered him or not. There was a brief half-moment of silence, promptly broken by the droning voice of the paid cicerone:

“Ancient hauberk, date of the sixth century, time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; observe the round hole through the chain-mail in the left breast; can’t be accounted for; supposed to have been done with a bullet since invention of firearms—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My acquaintance smiled—not with any modern sort of smile, but one that must have fallen out of common use many, many centuries ago—and muttered, as if to himself:

“Wit ye well, _I saw it done_.” Then, after a pause, he added: “I did it myself.”

Before I could recover from the electric shock of that remark, he was gone.

That whole evening I sat by the fire at the Warwick Arms, sunk in a dream of those earlier days, while rain struck the windows and the wind battered the eaves and corners. Now and then I dipped into old Sir Thomas Malory’s spellbinding book, taking my fill from its rich table of marvels and adventures, breathing in the perfume of its obsolete names, and dreaming again."}

{"request_id":"e5a83861ff3f13fa82140815","rewritten_text":"It was the beginning of February. Anne, after spending a month in Bath, was growing very eager for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted to know much more than Mary had told her. It had been three weeks since she had heard anything at all. She only knew that Henrietta was back at home, and that Louisa, though thought to be recovering quickly, was still in Lyme. One evening, while she was thinking of them all very intensely, Mary’s letter arrived—thicker than usual. To make the pleasure and surprise even greater, it came with Admiral and Mrs. Croft’s compliments.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was something that interested her. They were people her heart naturally warmed to.

“What is this?” Sir Walter exclaimed. “The Crofts have come to Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.”

“Oh! Those letters are convenient passports. They get you an introduction. I would have visited Admiral Croft anyway. I know what I owe my tenant.”

Anne could not listen any longer. She could not even say how the Admiral’s complexion escaped notice; her own letter took over her attention. It had been written several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

“I make no apology for my silence, because I know how little people care about letters in a place like Bath. You must be much too happy to think about Uppercross, which, as you know, gives you very little to write about. We have had a very dull Christmas. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove have not had a single dinner party during the holidays. I do not count the Hayters as anyone. The holidays are over at last. I believe no children ever had such long ones. I am sure I did not.

“The house was cleared yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to hear they have never gone home. Mrs. Harville must be an odd mother to keep them so long. I do not understand it. In my opinion, the children are not at all nice; but Mrs. Musgrove seems to like them just as much, if not more, than her grandchildren.

“What dreadful weather we have had! It may not be felt in Bath, with your nice pavements, but in the country it matters a great deal. I have not had anyone call on me since the second week in January, except Charles Hayter, who has been calling much more often than was welcome. Between ourselves, I think it a pity Henrietta did not stay at Lyme as long as Louisa did. It would have kept her a little out of his way.”"}

{"request_id":"16647ed0827ba6e52e8a040f","rewritten_text":"And he always acted like Peter had written him those things; only that was a lie—he’d hauled every blessed one of them out of that young flathead we’d canoed up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane went and got the letter her father had left behind, and the king read it aloud and carried on, crying over it. It gave the girls the dwelling-house and three thousand dollars in gold; it gave the tanyard (which was turning a good profit), along with some other houses and land worth about seven thousand, and three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William, and it even said where the six thousand in cash was tucked away in the cellar. So those two frauds said they’d go fetch it up and make everything neat and above-board, and they told me to come along with a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag they dumped it out on the floor, and there it was—a fine sight, all them yellow boys. Lord, the way the king’s eyes lit up! He pats the duke on the shoulder and says:

“Oh, this ain’t bully nor nothin’! Oh, no, I reckon not! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, don’t it?”

The duke agreed. They pawed at the yellow boys, sifted them through their fingers, and let them clink and jingle down on the floor; and the king says:

“It ain’t no use talkin’; bein’ brothers to a rich dead man and representatives of foreign heirs that’s got left is the line for you and me, Bilge. This here comes of trustin’ to Providence. It’s the best way, in the long run. I’ve tried ’em all, and there ain’t no better way.”

Most folks would’ve been satisfied with the pile and taken it on trust, but no—they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came up four hundred and fifteen dollars short. Says the king:

“Dern him, I wonder what he done with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?”

They fretted over it for a spell and tore the place apart, looking everywhere. Then the duke says:

“Well, he was a pretty sick man, and likely he made a mistake—I reckon that’s how it is. The best way’s to let it go and keep quiet about it. We can spare it.”

“Oh, shucks, yes, we can spare it. I don’t care nothin’ about that—it’s the count I’m thinkin’ about. We want to be awful square and open and above-board here, you know. We want to lug this here money upstairs and count it before everybody—then there ain’t nothin’ suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thous’n dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

{"request_id":"deda9706bf783ed162f6bedf","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so pleased with their conversation that he never brought it up again, and he did not bother or upset his dear sister Elizabeth by talking about it. Elizabeth was glad, because she felt she had said enough to keep him quiet.

The day when he and Lydia were going to leave soon arrived. Mrs. Bennet had to accept the separation, and since her husband had no interest in the plan of having all of them go to Newcastle, it was likely to last at least a year.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when shall we meet again?”

“Oh, Lord! I don’t know. Maybe not for two or three years.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women don’t have much time for writing. My sisters can write to me. They will have nothing else to do.”

Mr. Wickham’s goodbyes were much warmer than his wife’s. He smiled, looked handsome, and said many sweet things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet as soon as they were out of the house. “He flirts and acts silly, and makes love to all of us. I’m extremely proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas to produce a better son-in-law.”

After her daughter left, Mrs. Bennet felt very dull for several days.

“I often think,” she said, “that nothing is as hard as being separated from your friends. Without them, you feel so lonely.”

“This is what happens, you see, madam, when you marry a daughter,” Elizabeth replied. “It should make you feel better about the other four, since they are still single.”

“It’s not like that. Lydia isn’t leaving me because she is married. She is leaving only because her husband’s regiment is so far away. If it were nearer, she wouldn’t have gone so soon.”

Still, the gloomy mood this caused her did not last long. Her mind soon opened again to the feeling of hope, stirred by some new news that was starting to spread. The housekeeper at Netherfield had been told to get ready for the arrival of her master. He was coming down in a day or two to stay there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet became restless at once. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head in turn.

“Well, well, so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” (Mrs. Philips had first told her). “Well, that’s good news. Not that I care much, though. He has nothing to do with us, you know, and I’m sure I never want to see him again. But if he wants to come to Netherfield, he’s very welcome to do so.”"}

{"request_id":"e50ed746376b4de659049b7f","rewritten_text":"Men marry because they are tired; women, because they are curious. Either way, they end up disappointed.

“I don’t think I’m likely to marry, Harry. I’m too much in love. That’s one of your sayings. I’m following it, just like I follow everything you say.”

“Who are you in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a pause.

“With an actress,” Dorian Gray said, blushing.

Lord Henry shrugged. “That’s a pretty ordinary beginning.”

“You wouldn’t say that if you’d seen her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“I’ve never heard of her.”

“No one has. But people will know her someday. She’s a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are meant to be decorative. They never have anything important to say, but they say it in a charming way. Women show how matter wins over the mind, just as men show how the mind wins over morals.”

“Harry, how can you?”

“My dear Dorian, it’s true. I’m thinking about women right now, so I should know. It isn’t as complicated as I first thought. In the end, there are only two kinds of women: plain ones and colored ones. Plain women are useful. If you want to build a reputation for respectability, you only need to take them to supper. The other women are very charming. But they make one mistake. They paint their faces to look younger. Our grandmothers painted to sound brilliant. Rouge and esprit used to go together. That’s all changed now. As long as a woman can look ten years younger than her own daughter, she’s satisfied. And when it comes to conversation, there are only five women in London worth listening to, and two of them can’t be allowed into decent society. Still, tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Ah, Harry, your opinions frighten me.”

“Don’t worry about that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you meet her?”

“I’ll tell you, Harry, but you must promise not to be unkind about it. After all, it wouldn’t have happened if I hadn’t met you. You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. For days after I met you, something seemed to pulse in my veins. When I sat around in the park or walked down Piccadilly, I would look at everyone who passed and wonder, with a crazy curiosity, what kind of lives they lived. Some of them fascinated me. Others filled me with fear. There was an exquisite poison in the air. I had a passion for sensations...."}

{"request_id":"3c3b1bc635d49cc5e93d6ebb","rewritten_text":"I now turn to my own story. In the early part of my life there is little to tell, and I will be brief; but I must be allowed to dwell a little on the years of my childhood, so it may be clear how, when one hope failed, all life became a blank—and how, when the only affection I was allowed to cherish was taken from me, my existence was extinguished with it.

I have said that my aunt was very unlike my father. I believe that, without the slightest hint of a bad heart, she had the coldest nature that ever filled a human breast: she was completely incapable of affection. She took me under her protection because she thought it was her duty; but she had lived too long alone, undisturbed by the noise and chatter of children, to tolerate me disturbing her peace. She had never married; and for the last five years she had lived entirely by herself on an estate that had passed to her through her mother, on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters, my father had expressed a wish that she should live with me at his family mansion, which stood in a beautiful part of the country near Richmond in Yorkshire. She would not agree to this, but once she had arranged the affairs that her brother’s departure had left in her care, she left England and took me with her to her Scottish estate.

The care of me, first as a baby and later until I reached my eighth year, fell to a servant of my mother’s, who had accompanied us in our retirement for that purpose. I was placed in a remote part of the house, and I only saw my aunt at set times. These came twice a day: once around noon, when she came to my nursery, and once after her dinner, when I was taken to her. She never caressed me, and while I stayed in the room she seemed to fear that I might annoy her with some childish whim. My good nurse always prepared me with the greatest care before she would take me into the parlour—and the fear my aunt’s cold looks and few, tightly controlled words inspired was so strong that I seldom failed to follow her lessons, or betrayed the exemplary quiet I was taught to maintain during those brief visits.

Under my good nurse’s care, I ran wild about our park and the neighboring fields. From my earliest years, I showed the deepest love, and with it the greatest sensitivity of temperament. I cannot say with what passion I loved everything, even the inanimate objects that surrounded me."}

{"request_id":"6d4842257a4d83907864a25c","rewritten_text":"Had she known that her sister meant to tear her away from prospects and realities like these, what would her feelings have been? Only her mother could have understood them, and she might have felt nearly the same. Lydia’s going to Brighton was all that consoled her for the melancholy certainty that her husband never intended to go there himself.

But they were completely unaware of what had happened; and their excitement continued, with hardly any break, right up to the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now going to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since she had been in his company so often after her return, her agitation had mostly settled; the earlier agitation from partiality was entirely gone. She had even learned to recognize, in the very gentleness that had first delighted her, an affectation and a sameness that disgusted and tired her. What he did toward her now was also a fresh source of displeasure; for the inclination he soon showed to renew those attentions that had marked the beginning of their acquaintance could only, after everything that had happened since, provoke her. She lost all concern for him when she found herself chosen as the target of such idle, frivolous gallantry; and while she kept it firmly under control, she couldn’t help feeling the rebuke in his belief that, no matter how long—no matter for whatever reason—his attentions had been withdrawn, her vanity would be pleased and her preference secured at any time by their renewal.

On the very last day the regiment remained in Meryton, he dined, with other officers, at Longbourn; and so little was Elizabeth inclined to part from him in anything but good humor that, when he asked how her time had passed at Hunsford, she told him that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both spent three weeks at Rosings, and asked if he knew the former.

He looked surprised, displeased, and alarmed; but after a moment’s recollection, and with a returning smile, he replied that he had seen him often before. Then, after remarking that he was a very gentlemanlike man, he asked her how she had liked him. Her answer was warmly in his favor. With an air of indifference, he soon afterward added, “How long did you say that he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him frequently?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves with acquaintance.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, with a look that didn’t escape her. “And may I ask—” but stopping himself, he continued in a lighter tone, “Is it in address that he improves?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"0e5b092fc9f64c159697b33c","rewritten_text":"I am also told by Mrs. Otis—who, I should add, is no small authority on matters of Art, having once had the chance to spend a few winters in Boston—that these gems are worth a great deal of money, and that if they were put up for sale they would command a handsome sum. Given that, Lord Canterville, I trust you will see how utterly impossible it would be for me to let any member of my family keep them; indeed, all such empty baubles and toys, however well they might suit the standing of the British aristocracy, would be quite out of place with people raised on the stern—and, as I believe, immortal—rules of republican plainness. I ought perhaps to add that Virginia is very keen for you to let her keep the box as a memento of your unfortunate, though misguided, ancestor. Since it is extremely old and therefore in a poor state of repair, you may think it best to grant her request. For my part, I admit I’m rather astonished to hear one of my own children show sympathy for anything medieval, in any shape; I can only make sense of it by remembering that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs not long after Mrs. Otis came back from a journey to Athens.\n\nLord Canterville listened with great seriousness to the respectable Minister’s remarks, tugging at his grey moustache from time to time to conceal an involuntary smile; and when Mr. Otis finished, he took him warmly by the hand and said, ‘My dear sir, your charming little daughter did my unlucky ancestor, Sir Simon, a very real service, and I and my household owe her a great deal for her extraordinary courage and spirit. The jewels are plainly hers; and, egad, if I were cruel enough to snatch them from her, that wicked old fellow would be out of his grave in a fortnight, giving me the devil of a time. As for calling them heirlooms, nothing deserves that name unless it is set down in a will or some legal paper, and the fact of these jewels has never been known. I can assure you I have no more right to them than your butler has; and when Miss Virginia grows up, I daresay she’ll be glad to have pretty things to wear. Besides, Mr. Otis, you seem to forget that you took the furniture and the ghost at a valuation, and whatever belonged to the ghost passed straight into your hands—because, however lively Sir Simon may have been in the corridor at night, in law he was truly dead, and you bought his property.’"}

{"request_id":"c260c5ff4fdf2160ac668708","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, nearly everyone told him he was making a big mistake, because there was no doubt at all that the house was haunted. In fact, Lord Canterville himself, a man known for being very proper and careful about honor, felt he had to warn Mr. Otis when they met to talk about the deal.

“We haven’t lived there ourselves,” said Lord Canterville. “Not since my great-aunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was so frightened that she had a fit. She never really recovered. It happened when two skeleton hands were placed on her shoulders while she was getting dressed for dinner. I should tell you, Mr. Otis, that the ghost has been seen by several members of my family who are still alive. It has also been seen by the rector of the parish, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, who is a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After what happened to the Duchess, none of our younger servants would stay with us. Lady Canterville also often got very little sleep at night because of the strange noises coming from the corridor and the library.”

“My Lord,” the Minister replied, “I will buy the furniture and the ghost at a fair price. I come from a modern country, where we can get anything money can buy. And with all our energetic young men painting the Old World red, and taking your best actresses and famous performers, I think that if there were such a thing as a ghost in Europe, we would have it back home in no time. We’d put it in a public museum, or we’d turn it into a show on the road.”

“I’m afraid the ghost is real,” said Lord Canterville, smiling. “It may have refused the offers of your bold showmen, but it has been known for three hundred years. In fact, since 1584. It always appears before the death of someone in our family.”

“Well, the family doctor shows up too, Lord Canterville,” Mr. Otis said. “But there is no such thing as a ghost. And I don’t think the laws of nature are going to be changed just for the British aristocracy.”

“You are certainly very sensible in America,” Lord Canterville answered. He did not fully understand what Mr. Otis meant, but he went on. “And if you don’t mind a ghost in the house, then it’s fine. Just remember—I warned you.”

A few weeks later, the purchase was finished. At the end of the season, the Minister and his family went down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, who had been Miss Lucretia R. Tappan from West 53rd Street and was once a famous New York beauty, was now a very handsome, middle-aged woman with fine eyes and an excellent profile.”}"}

{"request_id":"f4a6ecefac16805e9b0a936e","rewritten_text":"“But I can ask you two questions. May I?”

“You may ask,” said Monks, sounding surprised. “But whether I answer is a different matter.”

“—That makes three,” said Mr. Bumble, trying to be clever.

“Is that what you expected to get from me?” the matron demanded.

“It is,” Monks replied. “Now, the other question.”

“What are you planning to do with it? Can it be used against me?”

“Never,” Monks said. “Not against me either. Listen—don’t take a step forward, or your life won’t be worth a bulrush.”

With that, he suddenly pushed the table aside. Then he pulled an iron ring built into the boarding, and he threw open a large trap-door that dropped right at Mr. Bumble’s feet. Mr. Bumble stumbled back several paces, very quickly and clumsily.

“Look down,” Monks said, lowering the lantern into the dark space below. “Don’t be afraid of me. If I wanted to, I could have let you down quietly while you were sitting over it.”

The matron, reassured, stepped closer to the edge. Even Mr. Bumble, driven by curiosity, moved in the same direction. The water below was muddy and rising fast from the heavy rain. It rushed along noisily, splashing and swirling around the green, slimy piles, and it swallowed up every other sound. There had once been a water-mill there. The tide, foaming and snapping around the few rotten stakes and the broken bits of machinery still left behind, seemed to surge forward with new energy now that nothing was stopping it.

“If you threw a man’s body down there,” Monks said, swinging the lantern back and forth in the well, “where would it be tomorrow morning?”

“About twelve miles down the river—and cut to pieces besides,” Bumble answered, backing away at the thought.

Monks took the small packet from his breast, where he had shoved it in quickly. He tied it to a heavy lead weight that had been part of some pulley and was lying on the floor, then dropped it into the stream. It fell straight down, true as a die, made only a faint splash, and was gone.

The three of them stared at each other’s faces, and they seemed to breathe easier.

“There!” Monks said, shutting the trap-door. It fell heavily back into place. “If the sea ever gives up its dead, like the books say it will, it will keep its gold and silver for itself—and that junk too. We have nothing more to say, and we can end our little gathering.”

“By all means,” Mr. Bumble said at once, eager to agree.

“You’ll keep a quiet tongue in your head, won’t you?” Monks said, looking at him with a threatening expression."}

{"request_id":"f8f005d6b99634c9f79170b2","rewritten_text":"“Do you mean—Mr. Knightley?”

“To be sure I do. I could never have imagined anyone else—and that is why I thought you understood. When we spoke of him, it was as plain as possible.”

“Not quite,” returned Emma, keeping her composure with an effort; “for all that you then said, it seemed to me to point to someone different. I could almost say that you had _named_ Mr. Frank Churchill. I am certain that what was said of the service Mr. Frank Churchill rendered you—protecting you from the gipsies—was what you referred to.”

“Oh! Miss Woodhouse, how you do forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember perfectly well the substance of what I told you. I said I did not wonder at your attachment; that, considering the service he had done you, it was perfectly natural. You agreed to it, speaking very warmly of your sense of that service, and even mentioning the feelings you had when he came forward to your rescue. The whole impression of it is still strong in my mind.”

“Oh, dear,” cried Harriet, “now I remember what you mean; but I was thinking of something quite different then. It was not the gipsies—it was not Mr. Frank Churchill I meant. No! (with some spirit) I was thinking of a far more precious circumstance—of Mr. Knightley’s coming to ask me to dance, when Mr. Elton would not rise with me, and when there was no other partner in the room. That was the kindness; that was the noble benevolence and generosity; that was the service which first made me feel how much superior he was to every other creature upon earth.”

“Good God!” cried Emma. “This is the most unfortunate—most deplorable mistake!—What is to be done?”

“You would not have encouraged me, then, if you had understood me. At least, however, I cannot be any worse off than I should have been, if the other had been the person; and now—it _is_ possible—”

She stopped for a few moments. Emma could not answer.

“I do not wonder, Miss Woodhouse,” she went on, “that you should feel such a difference between the two, whether in regard to me or to anyone else. You must think one five hundred million times more highly of me than the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that—supposing—that if—strange as it may seem—. You know those were your own words, and that _more_ wonderful things than this have happened: matches of far greater disparity than there is between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. So it seems as if something like this might have occurred before; and if I should be so fortunate—beyond all expression—as to—if Mr. Knightley should really—if _he_ does not mind the disparity, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you will not set yourself against it, nor try to raise difficulties.”"}
