{"request_id":"7223f82ec9ad1dfc5c790a02","rewritten_text":"“I don’t have the nerves for that kind of thing.”

“But could you be comfortable yourself, spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes; you see his papa can, and why shouldn’t I? Jemima is so careful, and she could send us word every hour about how he is. I really think Charles might as well have told his father that we would all come. I’m not more alarmed about little Charles now than he is. I was dreadfully alarmed yesterday, but the situation is very different today.”

“Well, if you don’t think it’s too late to give notice for yourself, suppose you were to go as well as your husband. Leave little Charles to my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove can’t think it wrong while I stay with him.”

“Are you serious?” Mary cried, her eyes brightening. “Dear me! That’s a very good idea—an excellent one, truly. Of course, I might as well go as not, because I’m of no use at home—am I? It only wears me down. You, who don’t have a mother’s feelings, are a much better choice. You can get little Charles to do anything; he always listens to you at a word. It will be a great deal better than leaving him only with Jemima. Oh, I shall certainly go; I’m sure I ought to, if I can, just as much as Charles, because they want me to be introduced to Captain Wentworth, and I don’t mind being left alone. What a wonderful thought of yours, indeed, Anne. I’ll go tell Charles and get ready right away. You can send for us at a moment’s notice if anything is wrong, but I dare say there will be nothing to alarm you. I wouldn’t go, you can be sure, if I didn’t feel fairly at ease about my dear child.”

The next moment she was tapping at her husband’s dressing-room door, and as Anne followed her upstairs, she arrived in time to hear the whole conversation. It began with Mary saying, in a tone of great excitement—

“I mean to go with you, Charles, because I’m no more use at home than you are. If I were to shut myself up forever with the child, I wouldn’t be able to persuade him to do anything he didn’t like. Anne will stay; Anne will take care of him at home. It’s Anne’s own idea, so I’ll go with you, which will be much better, because I haven’t dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband answered, “and I should be very glad to have you go; but it seems rather hard that she should be left at home by herself, to nurse our sick child.”"}

{"request_id":"e260fe24357dec325bb149d1","rewritten_text":"“Yes—burglar’s tools. That seems to take a great deal off your mind. But what made you change your tune? What did you suppose we’d turned up?”

Huck was in a tight spot—the questioning look was fixed on him—he would have given anything for something that sounded like a sensible answer—nothing came to him. The inquiring gaze kept boring deeper and deeper; a foolish reply slipped out—there wasn’t time to measure it, so, taking a chance, he said it, weakly:

“Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Poor Huck was too upset to grin, but the old man burst into loud, hearty laughter, shook himself from head to foot as if the whole thing were a joke, and wound up by declaring that such laughter was money in a man’s pocket, because it cut down the doctor’s bill, same as anything. Then he added:

“Poor old fellow—you’re pale and worn out—you ain’t well at all; no wonder you’re a little flighty and out of sorts. But you’ll pull through. Rest and sleep will set you right, I hope.”

Huck was annoyed that he’d been such a fool and shown such a suspicious excitement, for the moment he’d heard what was being said at the widow’s stile he had dropped the notion that the parcel brought from the tavern was the treasure. He had only meant that it wasn’t the treasure—he hadn’t known it wasn’t—and so the idea of a captured bundle had been too much for his self-control. Still, on the whole, he felt glad the little business had happened, because now he knew for certain that that bundle was not the bundle, and his mind was at ease and comfortable. In fact, everything seemed to be drifting the right way again: the treasure must still be in No. 2, the men would be caught and locked up that day, and he and Tom could take the gold that night without any trouble or fear of being interrupted.

When breakfast was finished, there came a knock at the door. Huck sprang for a hiding-place, because he had no wish to be linked, even in the slightest, with what had happened. The Welshman admitted several ladies and gentlemen, among them the Widow Douglas, and Huck saw groups of citizens climbing the hill to stare at the stile. So the word had spread. The Welshman had to tell the visitors the story of the night. The widow’s gratitude for her rescue was plain enough.

“Don’t say a word about it, madam. There’s another that you’re more beholden to than you are to me and my boys, perhaps—but he won’t have me mention his name. We wouldn’t have been there but for him.”"}

{"request_id":"9f6dc1881b034d8070cd1109","rewritten_text":"These thoughts calmed me, and in the afternoon I sank into a deep sleep; but the fever in my blood would not let me have peaceful dreams. The horrible scene from the day before kept replaying itself before my eyes forever: the females were flying, and Felix, enraged, was tearing me from my father’s feet. I woke utterly worn out, and since it was already night, I slipped out from my hiding place and went looking for food.

“When my hunger was satisfied, I followed the well-known path that led to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I crept into my hovel and waited in silent expectation for the usual hour when the family got up. That hour passed, the sun climbed high in the sky, but the cottagers did not appear. I shook violently with fear, convinced that some dreadful misfortune had happened. The inside of the cottage was dark, and I heard no movement; I can’t describe the agony of that suspense.

“Soon two countrymen passed by, but when they reached the cottage they stopped and began talking, using violent gestures. I didn’t understand what they said, because they spoke the language of the country, which was different from that of my protectors. Not long after, Felix came along with another man. I was startled, because I knew he hadn’t left the cottage that morning, and I waited anxiously to learn from their conversation what these unusual events meant.

“‘Do you think,’ his companion asked him, ‘that you’ll have to pay three months’ rent and lose the produce from your garden? I don’t want to take any unfair advantage, so I ask you to take a few days to think over your decision.’

“‘It’s completely useless,’ Felix replied. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of the dreadful thing I’ve told you. My wife and my sister will never recover from their horror. I beg you not to argue with me anymore. Take possession of your property and let me flee this place.’

“Felix trembled violently as he said this. He and his companion went into the cottage, stayed there for a few minutes, and then left. I never saw any of the De Lacey family again.

“I spent the rest of the day in my hovel in total, numb despair. My protectors were gone, and they had broken the only connection that kept me in the world. For the first time, feelings of revenge and hatred filled my chest, and I didn’t try to control them. Instead, letting myself be carried along by the current, I turned my mind toward injury and death."}

{"request_id":"58c9f95664a231f763525443","rewritten_text":"On my return, I found the following letter from my father:—

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably been waiting impatiently for a letter that tells you the date of your return to us. At first, I was tempted to write only a few lines, just to say the day I expected you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I cannot do it. What would be your surprise, my son, if you were expecting a happy, joyful welcome and instead found tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I tell you about our misfortune? Being away cannot have made you cold to our joys and sorrows. How could I cause pain to my son who has been away so long? I want to prepare you for the terrible news, but I know it is impossible. Even now, your eyes are moving over the page, looking for the words that will bring you these horrible facts.

“William is dead!—that sweet child, whose smile warmed and delighted my heart. He is murdered, Victor—so gentle, yet so full of life!

“I will not try to comfort you. I will simply explain what happened.

“Last Thursday, May 7th, I, my niece, and your two brothers went for a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and calm, so we stayed out longer than usual. It was already getting dark before we thought of going back. Then we realized that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were not to be found. So we sat down on a bench and waited for them to return.

“Soon Ernest came back. He asked whether we had seen his brother. He said that William had been playing with him, that William had run off to hide, and that he had searched for him in vain. He waited a long time, but William did not come back.

“This made us worry, and we kept looking for him until night fell. Then Elizabeth suggested that he might have returned home. He was not there. We went back again with torches. I could not rest, because I kept thinking that my dear boy had gotten lost and was exposed all night to the cold damp and dew. Elizabeth was in terrible distress too. About five in the morning I found my lovely boy. The night before, I had seen him healthy and active, full of life, and now he lay on the grass, pale and motionless. There was a mark on his neck, the sign of the murderer’s hand.

“He was taken home, and the anguish on my face told Elizabeth what had happened. She was very determined to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she would not listen. She went into the room where it lay, quickly examined the neck of the victim, and then, clasping her hands, she cried out, ‘O God!’”"}

{"request_id":"0fa8bb0840cd362469570e49","rewritten_text":"At the heart of that cleft I noticed a pale mark, though at first I couldn’t tell what it was. I adjusted the telescope’s focus, looked again, and this time recognized it as a human skull.

“On the strength of that discovery I grew so confident that I thought the riddle solved; for the words ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could only point to where the skull sat upon the tree, while ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ allowed, likewise, just one meaning—namely, a search for buried treasure. I saw that the plan was to drop a bullet from the skull’s left eye, and that a bee-line—meaning a straight line—drawn from the nearest point of the trunk through ‘the shot’ (the spot where the bullet struck), and then carried out for fifty feet, would mark a definite place; and beneath that place, I thought it at least possible that something of value was hidden.”

“All this,” I said, “is remarkably plain, and though it’s clever, it’s still straightforward and stated without ambiguity. When you left the Bishop’s Hotel, what happened next?”

“Why, after I’d taken the tree’s bearings with care, I made for home. The moment I stepped away from ‘the devil’s seat,’ though, the circular rift disappeared; no matter how I turned afterward, I couldn’t catch so much as a glimpse of it again. The chief ingenuity, as I see it, lies in the fact—repeated trials have convinced me it’s true—that this circular opening can be seen from no other vantage than the narrow ledge on the rock’s face.”

“In that trip to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel’ I had Jupiter with me, who, no doubt, had noticed for weeks the change in my manner and took pains not to leave me by myself. But the following day I rose very early, managed to slip away from him, and went into the hills to look for the tree. After a great deal of labor I found it. When I returned home that night, my valet suggested I should be flogged. As for the rest of the affair, I take it you know it as well as I do.”

“I take it,” said I, “that you missed the spot the first time you tried digging—owing to Jupiter’s blunder in letting the bug fall through the right eye instead of through the left.”

“Exactly. That slip altered the ‘shot’ by roughly two and a half inches—that is, the position of the peg nearest the tree. And if the treasure had been beneath the ‘shot,’ the error would have mattered little; but ‘the shot,’ along with the nearest point of the tree, were only two points used to set the line of direction. Naturally, even a small beginning error grows as you extend the line, and by the time we’d gone fifty feet, it had thrown us completely off the trail.”"}

{"request_id":"1fac283c189f8a927356f363","rewritten_text":"Such were the events that weighed on Felix’s heart and made him, when I first saw him, the most miserable person in his family. He could have lived with poverty, and even though it was hard, he took pride in it; but the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were troubles that cut deeper and could not be undone. Then the Arabian’s arrival brought new life back into his soul.

“When news reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and rank, the merchant told his daughter to stop thinking about her lover and to prepare to return to her native country. Safie’s generous nature was outraged by this order. She tried to argue with her father, but he left her angrily, repeating his harsh command.

“A few days later, the Turk went into his daughter’s room and told her quickly that he had reason to believe his stay in Leghorn had been discovered. He said he would have to be turned over to the French government at once. He had therefore hired a ship to take him to Constantinople, and he would sail in just a few hours. He planned to leave his daughter in the care of a trusted servant, while he followed later with most of his property, which had not yet arrived in Leghorn.

“Left alone, Safie decided what she would do in this emergency. Living in Turkey was unbearable to her. Her religion and her feelings both made her reject it. From some papers her father had left behind and that she managed to get, she learned that her lover had been exiled, and she found out the name of the place where he was living then. She hesitated for a while, but in the end she made up her mind. She took a few jewels that belonged to her and some money, left Italy with an attendant from Leghorn, and went to Germany. The attendant understood the common language of Turkey.

“She reached safely a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage, but her attendant soon became dangerously ill. Safie cared for her with deep devotion, but the poor girl died. The Arabian was left alone, unable to speak the language there and completely unaware of the ways of the world. Still, she was taken in by good people. The Italian had already told them the name of the place they were going, and after her attendant died, the woman of the house where they had been staying made sure that Safie arrived safely at the cottage of her lover.”}"}

{"request_id":"263e1e2a68aa32d96e6d4c58","rewritten_text":"Among the other public buildings in a certain town—which, for many reasons, it would be wise not to name, and which I will not give a fictitious title—there is one anciently common to most towns, large or small: a workhouse. And in that workhouse he was born, on a day and date I don’t need to repeat, since it can’t possibly matter to the reader at this point in the story. This is the mortality whose name is placed at the start of this chapter.

For a long time after he was brought into this world of sorrow and trouble by the parish surgeon, it was far from certain whether the child would survive long enough to have any name at all. If he had not, it is more than likely these memoirs would never have been written; and if they had, then, being limited to a couple of pages, they would have had the priceless distinction of being the most concise and faithful example of biography ever found in the literature of any age or country.

I’m not saying that being born in a workhouse is, in itself, the most fortunate and enviable thing that can happen to a human being. But in this particular case, it was the best thing that could possibly have happened to Oliver Twist. The truth is that there was considerable difficulty in getting Oliver to do the work of breathing—a troublesome practice, though custom has made it necessary for our comfortable existence. For some time he lay gasping on a small flock mattress, balanced rather unevenly between this world and the next, with the scales clearly tipping toward the latter.

Now, if during that brief period Oliver had been surrounded by careful grandmothers, worried aunts, experienced nurses, and doctors of deep wisdom, he would most certainly and without question have been killed quickly. But there was no one there except a pauper old woman, made rather hazy by an unusual allowance of beer, and a parish surgeon who handled such matters on contract. Oliver and Nature fought it out between them. The outcome was that, after a few struggles, Oliver breathed, sneezed, and then began to announce to the workhouse inmates that a new burden had been placed on the parish—by crying as loudly as could reasonably be expected from a male infant who had not yet been given that very useful appendage, and for a much longer time than three minutes and a quarter."}

{"request_id":"ccf6eab1a98dec2dc08b651e","rewritten_text":"The nephew looked at him, in vain, as he passed on to the door.

“Good night!” said the uncle. “I look forward to seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Light Monsieur my nephew to his chamber there—and burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you please,” he added to himself, before ringing his little bell again and summoning his valet to his own bedroom.

The valet came and went, and then Monsieur the Marquis paced his room in his loose chamber-robe, preparing himself gently for sleep on that hot, still night. Rustling around, his soft, slippered feet making no sound on the floor, he moved like a refined tiger: like some enchanted marquis of the impenitently wicked kind in stories, whose periodic change into tiger form was either just starting or just ending.

He crossed from one end of his voluptuous bedroom to the other, looking again at the scraps of the day’s journey that kept coming unbidden into his mind—the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the sun setting, the descent, the mill, the prison on the crag, the little village in the hollow, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender with his blue cap pointing out the chain beneath the carriage. That fountain brought to mind the Paris fountain, the small bundle lying on the step, the women bending over it, and the tall man with his arms raised, crying, “Dead!”

“I’m cool now,” said Monsieur the Marquis. “I can go to bed.”

So, leaving only one light burning on the large hearth, he let his thin gauze curtains fall around him, and listened as the night broke its silence with a long sigh while he settled down to sleep.

For three heavy hours, the stone faces on the outer walls stared blindly at the black night. For three heavy hours, the horses in the stables rattled their racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound that had very little resemblance to the one men-poets conventionally assign to owls. But it is the stubborn habit of creatures like that to rarely say what people have written down for them.

For three heavy hours, the chateau’s stone faces—lion and human—stared blindly at the night. Dead darkness lay over the whole landscape; dead darkness added its own hush to the hush of dust on all the roads. The burial ground had reached the point where its little heaps of poor grass were no longer distinguishable from one another; the figure on the Cross might as well have come down, for all that could be seen of it. In the village, the taxers and the taxed were fast asleep. Perhaps they dreamed of banquets, as the starving usually do, and of comfort and rest, as the driven slave and the yoked ox may—its lean inhabitants slept soundly, and were fed and freed."}

{"request_id":"5a8135acbb6986ee1550dd8e","rewritten_text":"If, however, you want one for use at home, I can provide you with an excellent article, and I guarantee you will be satisfied with the result. Who is it intended for? If it is for the police, or for anyone connected with Scotland Yard, I’m afraid I can’t help you. English detectives are really our best friends. I’ve always found that if we rely on their stupidity, we can do exactly what we like. I can’t spare any of them.”

“I assure you,” said Lord Arthur, “it has nothing to do with the police. In fact, the clock is meant for the Dean of Chichester.”

“Good heavens! I had no idea you felt so strongly about religion, Lord Arthur. Few young men feel that way these days.”

“I’m afraid you’re overestimating me, Herr Winckelkopf,” Lord Arthur said, blushing. “The truth is, I know nothing about theology.”

“So it’s purely a private matter?”

“Purely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged, left the room, and returned a few minutes later with a round cake of dynamite, no bigger than a penny, and a small French clock. On top of the clock was an ormolu figure of Liberty, trampling on the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face brightened when he saw it. “That’s exactly what I want,” he said. “Now tell me how it works—how does it go off?”

“Ah, there’s my secret,” Herr Winckelkopf replied, looking at his invention with justified pride. “Tell me when you want it to explode, and I will set the machine for that moment.”

“Well, today is Tuesday. If you could send it off right away—”

“That isn’t possible. I have a great deal of important work to do for some friends of mine in Moscow. Still, I might send it tomorrow.”

“Oh, it will be plenty of time,” Lord Arthur said politely. “If it’s delivered tomorrow night or Thursday morning. For the explosion, set it for Friday at noon exactly. The Dean is always at home at that hour.”

“Friday, at noon,” Herr Winckelkopf repeated. He made a note of it in a large ledger on a bureau near the fireplace.

“And now,” said Lord Arthur, standing up, “please tell me how much I owe you.”

“It’s such a small matter, Lord Arthur, that I don’t even want to charge you. The dynamite costs seven shillings and sixpence, the clock is three pounds ten, and the carriage is about five shillings. I’m only too happy to help any friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.”

“But what about your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?”"}

{"request_id":"856b5e82a8fc1acba5b3d984","rewritten_text":"It was only fair to say that the young lady did not clearly promise that she would not do it. Instead, she made a strong, serious wish to be “blessed” if she agreed. It was a polite, careful way of dodging the request, and it showed that she had good manners—she couldn’t bear to cause another person the hurt of a direct, blunt refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned away from this young lady, who was dressed brightly, almost gaudily, in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers, and looked to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” the Jew said in a calm, soothing voice, “what do you say?”

“That won’t do, so there’s no point in trying it on, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” Mr. Sikes asked, looking up in a sour mood.

“What I mean, Bill,” the lady answered, keeping her composure.

“Why, you’re exactly the right person,” Mr. Sikes argued. “Nobody around here knows you.”

“And I don’t want them to,” Nancy said, still steady. “For me it’s more no than yes, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” Nancy said.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” Sikes insisted.

And Mr. Sikes was right. After a back-and-forth of threats, promises, and bribes, the woman in question was finally persuaded to take on the job. She wasn’t held back by the same worries as her friend. Since she had only recently moved into the area near Field Lane, from the more distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, she didn’t fear being recognized by any of her many acquaintances.

So, with a clean white apron tied over her gown, and her curl-papers tucked up under a straw bonnet—both items of clothing taken from the Jew’s endless supply—Miss Nancy got ready to go out on her errand.

“Stop a minute, my dear,” the Jew said, pulling out a small basket that was partly covered. “Carry that in one hand. It looks more respectable.”

“Give her a door-key to carry in her other one, Fagin,” Sikes said. “It looks real and genivine like.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, it does,” the Jew agreed, and he slipped a large street-door key onto the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There. Very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” The Jew rubbed his hands together.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried, bursting into tears. She clutched the little basket and the street-door key, wringing them in distress. “What has happened to him? Where have they taken him? Oh, please have pity—tell me what’s been done with the dear boy, gentlemen. Do, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”"}

{"request_id":"6ea0937c2e1ac8f1942c2fe3","rewritten_text":"He never tried again. The boys lay there, counting the slow, dragging minutes until it felt to them like time was almost over and eternity was turning gray. Then they were relieved to see that the sun was finally setting.

One snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked around, and gave his partner a grim smile. He nudged him awake with his foot and said:

“Hey! You’re the watchman, aren’t you? All right, then—nothing’s happened.”

“Good grief. Have I been asleep?”

“Yeah, a little, a little. It’s almost time for us to move, pal. What are we going to do with the little bit of swag we’ve got left?”

“I don’t know. Leave it here like we always do, I guess. No point taking it until we start south. Six hundred and fifty in silver is something to carry.”

“Well—fine. It won’t hurt to come back here again.”

“No, but I’d say come at night like we used to. It’s better.”

“Sure, but look here. It might be a long time before I get the right chance to do that job. Accidents could happen. It’s not exactly a safe place. We’ll just bury it like we always do—and bury it deep.”

“Good idea,” said his partner. He walked across the room, knelt down, lifted one of the hearth-stones in the back, and pulled out a bag that jingled nicely. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, then handed the bag to him. Injun Joe was on his knees in the corner, digging with his bowie-knife.

The boys forgot every fear and every misery in an instant. They watched every move with greedy excitement. Luck—its shine was beyond anything they could imagine. Six hundred dollars was enough to make half a dozen boys rich. This was treasure hunting under the best possible conditions. There wouldn’t be any annoying uncertainty about where to dig. They kept nudging each other, over and over—clear, excited nudges that only meant one thing: “Ain’t you glad we’re here now!”

Joe’s knife hit something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What is it?” his partner asked.

“Half-rotten plank—no, it’s a box, I think. Here, help me. Let’s see what it’s for. Never mind—I’ve already made a hole.”

He reached in and pulled it out—

“Man, it’s money!”

The two men looked through the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were just as excited as the men, and just as happy.

Joe’s partner said, “We’ll get this done fast. There’s an old rusty pick out in the weeds in the corner on the other side of the fireplace. I saw it a minute ago.”"}

{"request_id":"1c4a99daecda391c86d37b8c","rewritten_text":"In all this there was a strangeness that drew me in and enchanted me. It was as if he had just awakened from his long, visionary sleep, and he felt something like one of the seven sleepers—or like Nourjahad—in that sweet imitation of an eastern tale: Diana was gone; his friends were changed or dead; and now, in his awakening, I was all he had left to love on earth.

How dear to me were the waters, the mountains, and the woods of Loch Lomond now that I had such a beloved companion for my rambles. I visited every delightful spot with my father—on the islands, or beside tree-sheltered waterfalls; every shady path, every little dingle tangled with undergrowth and fern. His conversation broadened my thoughts. I felt as if I had been remade, surrounded by the freshness and life of a new being. It was as though, since his arrival, I had been transported from a narrow patch of earth into a universe boundless to imagination and understanding. My life before had been like a pleasing country rill—never meant to leave its native fields, but to do its work quietly, then be absorbed and leave no trace. Now it seemed to me like a varied river flowing through a fertile, lovely landscape—always changing, always beautiful. Alas, I did not know what desert it was about to reach; what rocks would tear its waters; and what hideous scene would be reflected, in a more distorted way, in its waves. Life was then brilliant. I began to learn to hope—and what brings a more bitter despair to the heart than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should follow so quickly on such divine happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, but there was gall at the bottom of its long, drawn sweetness. My heart was full of deep affection, yet it was calm from the very depth and fullness of it. I had no idea that misery could arise from love, and this lesson—that all at last must learn—was taught me in a way that few are forced to receive. I lament now, and must always lament, those few short months of blissful paradise. I disobeyed no command; I ate no apple; and yet I was ruthlessly driven out of it. Alas! my companion did, and I was thrown down in his fall. But I’m straying from the point—let sorrow come when it is due; at this stage of my story I can still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful companionship when my aunt fell ill. I spent a whole month in her chamber nursing her, but her disease was mortal, and she died, leaving me for some time inconsolable. Death is so dreadful to the living. The chains of habit are so strong, even when affection does not bind them, that the heart must be agonized when they break."}

{"request_id":"90aeeabe6512dc1b7816554e","rewritten_text":"In the meantime, the pull of gravity would keep getting weaker, following the rule that it drops with the square of the distance. With that, my speed would increase greatly, until I finally reached those far regions where the Earth’s attraction would be weaker than the Moon’s. Based on these ideas, I did not think it was worth bringing more supplies than I would need for forty days.

“There was still, however, another problem, and it made me uneasy. People have noticed that when balloons rise to great heights, they do not only feel pain when they breathe. They also often feel a strong discomfort in the head and body, sometimes with bleeding from the nose and other frightening symptoms. These symptoms get worse the higher the balloon goes. That thought was unsettling. Would these symptoms keep increasing without limit, or at least continue until death? I finally decided that they would not. I believed the cause was the steady loss of normal air pressure on the body’s surface, which makes the small blood vessels swell. It was not, as with trouble breathing, caused by the air being too thin in a chemical sense to refresh the blood in the heart. So, unless the blood could not be renewed for some other reason, I saw no why life could not continue even in a vacuum. Breathing, after all, is mainly a muscular action—the expansion and contraction of the chest—and it is the cause of respiration, not the result.

“In short, I thought that as the body became used to the lack of air pressure, the pain would slowly lessen. While the pain lasted, I trusted in the toughness of my constitution.

“Thus, may it please your Excellencies, I have explained some of the reasons—though not all—that led me to plan a voyage to the Moon. I will now tell you the outcome of an attempt that seems so daring in its design, and in any case so completely without precedent in the history of mankind.

“After I reached the height I mentioned—three miles and three-quarters—I threw a quantity of feathers out of the car. I found that I was still rising quickly enough, so there was no need to release any ballast. I was glad of that, because I wanted to keep as much weight with me as I could carry, for reasons I will explain later."}

{"request_id":"bb944934123c78971c916d28","rewritten_text":"Right in front of him, in the thin, wan moonlight, he saw an old man with a truly terrible presence. His eyes burned like red coals; long grey hair fell over his shoulders in tangled, matted coils. His clothes, cut in an old-fashioned style, were filthy and torn, and heavy manacles and rusty gyves hung from his wrists and ankles.

‘My dear sir,’ said Mr. Otis, ‘I really must insist that you oil those chains. I’ve brought you a small bottle of the Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator for that purpose. It’s said to be completely effective with just one application, and there are several testimonials on the wrapper from some of our most eminent native divines. I’ll leave it here for you by the bedroom candles, and I’ll be glad to supply more if you need it.’ With those words, the United States Minister set the bottle down on a marble table, shut his door, and retired to bed.

For a moment the Canterville ghost stood completely still, burning with natural indignation; then, with a violent motion, he dashed the bottle onto the polished floor, fled down the corridor, groaning hollowly and casting out a ghastly green light. Just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, though, a door was flung open—two little figures in white robes appeared, and a large pillow whizzed past his head! Evidently there was no time to waste. He quickly adopted the Fourth Dimension of Space as a way to escape, vanished through the wainscoting, and the house fell silent.

When he reached a small secret chamber in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and began trying to make sense of his situation. Never, in his brilliant and uninterrupted career of three hundred years, had he been treated with such blatant disrespect. He thought of the Dowager Duchess, whom he had frightened into a fit while she stood before the mirror in her lace and diamonds; of the four housemaids, who had burst into hysterics when he only grinned at them through the curtains of one of the spare bedrooms; of the rector of the parish, whose candle he had blown out one late night as he came back from the library, and who had been under Sir William Gull’s care ever since—a perfect martyr to nervous disorders; and of old Madame de Tremouillac, who, having woken up early one morning and found a skeleton seated in an arm-chair by the fire reading her diary, had been confined to her bed for six weeks with an attack of brain fever, and, after her recovery, had reconciled herself to the Church and cut ties with that notorious skeptic Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"a209e60527cd2767be3bb435","rewritten_text":"“What’s the trouble?”

I said:

“Pap, and mam, and sis, and—”

Then I broke down. He said:

“Oh, dang it now, don’t take on so; we all has to have our troubles, and this’n ’ll come out all right. What’s the matter with ’em?”

“They’re—they’re—are you the watchman of the boat?”

“Yes,” he said, kind of pretty well satisfied like. “I’m the captain and the owner and the mate and the pilot and watchman and head deck-hand; and sometimes I’m the freight and passengers. I ain’t as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be so blame’ generous and good to Tom, Dick and Harry as what he is, and slam around money the way he does; but I’ve told him a many a time ’t I wouldn’t trade places with him; for, says I, a sailor’s life’s the life for me, and I’m derned if I’d live two mile out o’ town, where there ain’t nothing ever goin’ on, not for all his spondulicks and as much more on top of it. Says I—”

I cut in and said:

“They’re in an awful peck of trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Why, pap and mam and sis and Miss Hooker; and if you’d take your ferry-boat and go up there—”

“Up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“What wreck?”

“Why, there ain’t but one.”

“What, you don’t mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good land! what are they doin’ there, for gracious sakes?”

“Well, they didn’t go there a-purpose.”

“I bet they didn’t! Why, great goodness, there ain’t no chance for ’em if they don’t git off mighty quick! Why, how in the nation did they ever git into such a scrape?”

“Easy enough. Miss Hooker was a-visiting up there to the town—”

“Yes, Booth’s Landing—go on.”

“She was a-visiting there at Booth’s Landing, and just in the edge of the evening she started over with her nigger woman in the horse-ferry to stay all night at her friend’s house, Miss What-you-may-call-her—I disremember her name—and they lost their steering-oar, and swung around and went a-floating down, stern first, about two mile, and saddle-bagged on the wreck, and the ferryman and the nigger woman and the horses was all lost, but Miss Hooker she made a grab and got aboard the wreck. Well, about an hour after dark we come along down in our trading-scow, and it was so dark we didn’t notice the wreck till we was right on it; and so we saddle-bagged; but all of us was saved but Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the best cretur!—I most wish’t it had been me, I do.”

“My George! It’s the beatenest thing I ever struck.”"}

{"request_id":"155f7b8270c92f470d762d84","rewritten_text":"“This must have been around that same period in Mr. Elliot’s life,” said Anne, “the time that has always sparked my particular curiosity. It must have been about when he first became known to my father and my sister. I never met him myself; I only heard about him. Still, there was something in his behavior toward my father and sister then, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, that I could never quite bring myself to reconcile with the way things are now. It felt like it pointed to a different kind of man.”

“I know it all, I know it all,” cried Mrs. Smith. “He had already been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I ever met him, but I heard him talk about them constantly. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he chose not to go. I can probably satisfy you on points you wouldn’t expect. And as for his marriage—I knew everything about it at the time. I was privy to every advantage and every drawback; I was the friend he confided in about his hopes and plans. And although I didn’t know his wife before, her lower position in society made that impossible, yet I knew her all her life afterward—at least until the last two years of her life—and I can answer any question you want to ask.”

“No,” said Anne, “I don’t have any particular questions I need to ask about her. I’ve always understood they weren’t a happy couple. But I would like to know why, at that stage of his life, he should have brushed off my father’s acquaintance the way he did. My father was certainly disposed to give him the kind and proper attention. Why did Mr. Elliot pull back?”

“Mr. Elliot,” replied Mrs. Smith, “at that period of his life, had one goal: to make his fortune, and by a quicker route than the law. He was determined to build it through marriage. He was determined—not to ruin it with an imprudent marriage. And I know it was his belief (whether he was right or not, I can’t say) that your father and sister, with their politeness and invitations, were trying to arrange a match between the heir and the young lady. In his view, such a match could never fit his ideas of wealth and independence. That was why he drew back, I assure you. He told me the whole story. He kept nothing from me. It was strange that, after just leaving you behind me in Bath, my first and principal acquaintance through marriage should have been your cousin—and that, through him, I should be continually hearing about your father and sister.”"}

{"request_id":"a21ae5c83a49d0f8377df14b","rewritten_text":"His face was badly sunburned, and more than half of it was hidden by his whiskers and thick mustache. He carried a huge wooden cudgel, but otherwise he seemed to have no weapons. He bowed awkwardly and greeted us with “good evening,” speaking French with a noticeable accent. It sounded a bit like Neufchâtel, but it was still clearly French, and even hinted at Paris.

“Sit down, my friend,” said Dupin. “I assume you came about the Ourang-Outang. Honestly, I almost envy you. What a fine animal—and no doubt a valuable one. How old do you think he is?”

The sailor took a long breath, looking like a man who had finally been freed from something unbearable. Then he answered with confidence.

“I can’t really say—but he can’t be more than four or five years old. Do you have him here?”

“Oh no. We didn’t have any place to keep him here. He’s at a livery stable on the Rue Dubourg, just around the corner. You can pick him up in the morning. Of course you’re ready to prove you own him.”

“Of course I am, sir.”

“I’ll be sorry to let him go,” said Dupin.

“I don’t mean you should go to all this trouble for nothing, sir,” the man replied. “I wouldn’t expect that. I’m very willing to pay a reward for finding the animal—anything reasonable.”

“Well,” my friend said, “that’s fair enough. Let me think. What should I ask for? Oh! I’ll tell you. My reward will be this: you will give me all the information you can about the murders on the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin spoke the last words very softly, and very calmly. Without changing his tone, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he took a pistol from inside his coat and set it on the table, without any sign of hurry.

The sailor’s face turned red, as if he were struggling to breathe. He sprang up and grabbed his cudgel, but the next moment he collapsed back into his seat, shaking violently, with an expression like death itself. He did not say a word. I felt real pity for him.

“My friend,” said Dupin, in a gentle voice, “you’re frightening yourself for no reason. We mean you no harm. I give you my word as a gentleman—and as a Frenchman—that we intend you no injury. I know very well that you are innocent of the atrocities on the Rue Morgue. Still, it won’t do to pretend you’re not in some way involved.”}"}

{"request_id":"9b5911c3eef7e75b5b670210","rewritten_text":"She and the children could stay very comfortably.”

“Ah! Papa—that’s exactly what you’ve never been able to manage, and I don’t think you ever will. Isabella can’t bear to stay behind her husband.”

That was too true to argue with. As unwelcome as it was, Mr. Woodhouse could only give a resigned sigh; and the moment Emma saw his spirits affected by the thought of his daughter’s attachment to her husband, she steered the conversation into a direction that would lift them.

“Harriet must give us as much of her company as she can while my brother and sister are here. I’m sure she’ll be pleased with the children. We’re very proud of the children, aren’t we, Papa? I wonder which she’ll think is the handsomest—Henry or John?”

“I wonder which she’ll think so, too. Poor little dears—how happy they’ll be to come. They’re very fond of being at Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they are, sir. I’m sure I don’t know who wouldn’t be.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John is very much like his mother. Henry is the eldest; he was named after me, not after his father. John, the second, is named after his father. Some people are surprised, I believe, that the eldest wasn’t, but Isabella would have him called Henry, which I always thought was very pretty of her. And he’s a very clever boy, indeed. They’re all remarkably clever, and they have so many charming little ways. They’ll come and stand by my chair and say, ‘Grandpapa, can you give me a bit of string?’ And once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives are only made for grandpapas. I think their father is too rough with them very often.”

“He seems rough to you,” said Emma, “because you’re so gentle yourself; but if you could compare him with other fathers, you wouldn’t think him rough. He wants his boys to be active and tough; and if they misbehave, he can give them a sharp word now and then; but he’s an affectionate father—certainly Mr. John Knightley is an affectionate father. The children are all fond of him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and tosses them up to the ceiling in such a terrifying way!”

“But they like it, Papa; there’s nothing they like more. It’s such fun for them that if their uncle didn’t lay down the rule about taking turns, whoever started would never give in to the other.”

“Well, I can’t make sense of it.”

“That’s true for all of us, Papa. One half of the world can’t understand the pleasures of the other.”"}

{"request_id":"18e5d60b32ea7918f74ffe27","rewritten_text":"Dark and stormy was the night. Around the throne above, not a single star flickered; yet the deep, heavy thunder kept vibrating in my ears. Meanwhile, terrifying lightning flashed in an angry mood through the clouded chambers of heaven, as if it scorned the power exerted over its terror by the great Franklin. Even the loud, unruly winds, all at once, burst from their mysterious homes and howled about, as though their help could only add to the wildness of the scene.

At such a time—so dark, so bleak—for human sympathy, my very spirit sighed; but instead of that,

‘My dearest friend, my counsellor, my comforter and guide— My joy in grief, my second bliss in joy,’ came to my side.

She moved like one of those bright beings pictured in the sunny paths of fancy’s Eden by the romantic and young: a queen of beauty, unadorned except for her own transcendent loveliness. So gentle was her step that it made no sound at all; and, but for the magical thrill her warm touch gave, she would have slipped away unnoticed—uninvited. A strange sadness rested on her face, like icy tears on the robe of December, as she pointed to the elements battling outside and told me to contemplate the two beings presented.

This nightmare filled about ten pages of manuscript and ended with a sermon so destructive of hope for non-Presbyterians that it won the first prize. The piece was considered the finest work of the evening. When the mayor of the village presented the award to its author, he gave a warm speech, saying it was by far the most “eloquent” thing he had ever heard, and that Daniel Webster himself might well be proud of it.

It may be noted, in passing, that the number of compositions in which the word “beauteous” was overused, and human experience was referred to as “life’s page,” was about the usual average.

Now the master, softened almost to the edge of geniality, pushed his chair aside, turned his back to the audience, and began drawing a map of America on the blackboard, to keep the geography class occupied. But he made a miserable job of it with his unsteady hand, and a muffled titter ran through the room. He knew what was happening and tried to correct it. He wiped out the lines and redrew them, but he only distorted them even more, and the tittering grew louder. He threw himself entirely into his work, as if determined not to be beaten down by the laughter. He felt that everyone’s eyes were fixed on him; he imagined he was doing well, and yet the tittering continued—it even clearly increased."}

{"request_id":"ef5ba866f659f4cf90344251","rewritten_text":"Knights and horses in heavy armor couldn’t travel very fast. They would make the best time they could, and now that the ground was in good condition—no snow, no mud—they would probably manage a seven-mile pace. They’d have to switch horses a couple of times; they’d arrive around six, or a little after. It would still be light enough. They would see the white cloth I would tie around my right arm, and I would take command. We would surround that prison and get the king out in no time. It would be showy and picturesque enough, all things considered, though I would have preferred midday, because the more theatrical side of the whole thing would be better then.

Now, then, to increase the strings to my bow, I thought I’d look up some of the people I’d recognized before and make myself known. That would help us out of our scrape, without the knights. But I had to proceed cautiously, because it was a risky business. I needed to get into sumptuous clothes, and it wouldn’t do to run and jump into them. No—I’d have to work up to it gradually, buying suit after suit from shops far apart, getting a little finer piece each time, until I finally reached silk and velvet and was ready for my plan. So I started.

But the scheme fell apart like scat. The first corner I turned, I ran straight into one of our slaves, snooping around with a watchman. I coughed at the moment, and he gave me a sudden look that went right through me. I figure he thought he’d heard that cough before. I turned immediately into a shop and worked my way along the counter, pricing things and watching out of the corner of my eye. Those people had stopped and were talking together, looking in at the door. I decided I’d get out the back way, if there was one, and I asked the shopwoman if I could step out there and look for the escaped slave, who was believed to be hiding back there somewhere. I told her I was an officer in disguise, and that my partner was yonder at the door with one of the murderers in charge. Would she be kind enough to go tell him he didn’t need to wait, but should go at once to the far end of the back alley and be ready to head him off when I rousted him out?

She was burning with eagerness to see one of those already celebrated murderers, and she set off on the errand at once."}

{"request_id":"b7113a72d77c4141fc5f2d63","rewritten_text":"The next day was set for the production (so that our honor wouldn’t suffer from delay), and the next day Drummle showed up with a polite little admission in Estella’s hand—that she had had the honor of dancing with him several times. That left me with no real choice but to regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and, on the whole, to reject as untenable the idea that I could be found anywhere. Drummle and I then sat facing each other, snorting for an hour, while the Grove kept up indiscriminate contradiction, and at last it was declared that the promotion of good feeling had gone forward at an astonishing pace.

I say this lightly, but it wasn’t a light thing for me. I can’t adequately describe the pain it caused me to think that Estella might show any favor to such a contemptible, clumsy, sulky fool—so far below the average. Even now, I believe it was due to some pure fire of generosity and disinterestedness in my love for her that I couldn’t bear the thought of her stooping to that hound. No doubt I would have been miserable no matter who she favored; but a worthier object would have caused a different kind and degree of distress.

It was easy enough for me to find out, and I soon did find out, that Drummle had begun to follow her closely, and that she let him. After a little while, he was always in pursuit of her, and he and I crossed paths every day. He kept at it in a dull, persistent way, and Estella kept him at it—now with encouragement, now with discouragement, now almost flattering him, now openly despising him, now knowing him very well, now scarcely remembering who he was.

The Spider—what Mr. Jaggers called him—was used to lying in wait, though, and had the patience of his kind. On top of that, he had a thick-headed confidence in his money and in his family’s greatness, which sometimes worked in his favor—almost in place of concentration and determined purpose. So the Spider, doggedly watching Estella, outlasted many brighter insects, and would often uncoil himself and drop at exactly the right moment.

At a certain Assembly Ball in Richmond (back then, there were Assembly Balls in most places), where Estella had outshone every other beauty, this blundering Drummle hovered around her so persistently, and with so much tolerance on her part, that I decided to speak to her about him. I took the next opportunity—when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home, and was sitting apart among some flowers, ready to leave."}

{"request_id":"91374c6638e0cb8e47faead2","rewritten_text":"He was short, but he stood very straight, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He began his talk by reviewing the history of chemistry and the improvements different learned men had made, speaking with great energy the names of the most famous discoverers. Then he gave a quick look at the current state of the science and explained many of its basic terms. After a few preliminary experiments, he ended with a strong praise of modern chemistry. The words were so memorable that I will never forget them:

“The ancient teachers of this science,” he said, “promised the impossible and achieved nothing. The modern masters promise very little. They know that metals cannot be turned into other substances, and that the elixir of life is only a fantasy. But these philosophers—whose hands seem made only to handle dirt, and whose eyes are meant to study the microscope or the crucible—have truly performed miracles. They dig into the hidden parts of nature and show how she works in her secret places. They rise into the heavens. They have learned how the blood circulates and what the air we breathe is like. They have gained new powers, almost without limit. They can command the thunder of the sky, imitate an earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with shadows of its own.”

Those were the professor’s words—no, the words of fate itself—spoken in a way that was meant to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as if my soul were wrestling with a real enemy. One by one, the different keys that made up the mechanism of my life were turned. Note after note was struck, and soon my mind was filled with a single thought, a single idea, a single goal. “So much has been done,” I heard the soul of Frankenstein exclaim; “more, far more, will I accomplish. Following the path already laid out, I will find a new way. I will explore unknown powers and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.”

That night I did not close my eyes. Inside me, everything was in revolt and confusion. I could feel that order would come out of it, but I had no power to bring it about. Little by little, after morning dawn, sleep finally came. When I woke, the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. What remained was only a firm decision: to return to my old studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural talent. On the same day I went to see M. Waldman. In private, his manners were even gentler and more appealing than in public. There was a dignity in his face during his lectures, but in his own home that dignity was replaced by the greatest friendliness and kindness.”}"}

{"request_id":"992703217387175d74248696","rewritten_text":"But don’t think that I didn’t feel it was evil in itself.”

“Be sure of it, they were all perfectly comfortable.”

“I may not like it any better for that. With so many women and children on board, they have no right to be comfortable.”

“My dear Frederick, you’re talking in a careless way. What would happen to poor sailors’ wives, who often need to be taken to one port or another after their husbands, if everyone had your feelings?”

“You see, my feelings didn’t stop me from taking Mrs Harville and all her family to Plymouth.”

“But I can’t stand hearing you talk like a gentleman, as if women were all fine ladies instead of sensible people. None of us expects to have smooth sailing every day.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “when he has a wife, he’ll change his mind. If we’re lucky enough to live to another war, we’ll see him do what you and I, and many others, have done. He’ll be very grateful to anyone who can bring his wife to him.”

“Yes, he will.”

“Now I’m done,” Captain Wentworth cried. “Once married people start telling me, ‘Oh, you’ll feel differently when you’re married,’ I can only say, ‘No, I won’t.’ Then they say again, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that’s the end of it.”

He stood up and walked away.

“What a great traveler you must have been, ma’am!” Mrs Musgrove said to Mrs Croft.

“Pretty well, ma’am, in the fifteen years since I married, though many women have done more. I crossed the Atlantic four times, and I went once to the East Indies and came back again, and only once. Besides that, I’ve been in different places at home: Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I never went beyond the Straits, and I never was in the West Indies. You know we don’t call Bermuda or Bahama the West Indies.”

Mrs Musgrove had nothing to say against it. She couldn’t accuse herself of ever calling them anything else in all her life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” Mrs Croft went on, “that nothing can be better than the accommodations on a man-of-war. I mean the higher rates. When you move to a frigate, you’re more cramped, though any sensible woman can be perfectly happy in one. And I can safely say that the happiest part of my life has been spent on board a ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to be afraid of.”}"}

{"request_id":"52268bfd7cf64d1923b998fc","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is amazing! I have to see Dorian Gray.”

Hallward stood up and walked back and forth in the garden. After a while, he returned. “Harry,” he said, “to me, Dorian Gray is only a reason to make art. You might see nothing at all in him. I see everything. He is most alive in my work when there is no picture of him there. As I said, he is a sign of a new style. I see it in the shape of certain lines, in the beauty and small details of certain colors. That’s all.”

“Then why don’t you show his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I put into it some expression of all this strange worship of art. Of course, I’ve never told him about it. He doesn’t know anything. He will never know anything. But the world might guess, and I won’t expose my soul to their shallow curiosity. They will never put my heart under a microscope. There’s too much of me in it, Harry—too much of me!”

“Poets aren’t as careful as you are. They know how useful strong feelings are for getting published. These days, a broken heart can sell in many editions.”

“I hate that,” Hallward cried. “An artist should make beautiful things, but should put nothing of his own life into them. We live in an age where people treat art like it’s supposed to be a kind of autobiography. We’ve lost the pure sense of beauty. One day I’ll show the world what it really is. And for that reason, the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you’re wrong, Basil, but I won’t argue. Only people who are lost in their thinking argue like that. Tell me, is Dorian Gray very fond of you?”

The painter thought for a moment. “He likes me,” he answered after a pause. “I know he likes me. Of course I flatter him terribly. I get a strange pleasure from telling him things I know I’ll regret later. Most of the time, he is charming to me, and we sit in the studio talking about a thousand things. But sometimes, he is horribly careless, and it seems like he truly enjoys hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I’ve given my whole soul to someone who treats it like a flower to pin on his coat—just decoration to please his vanity, an ornament for a summer day.”"}

{"request_id":"9fbc4f2b8c6e694fd62639c7","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was considerably upset by the second postponement of the marriage, and Lady Julia—who had already had her wedding dress made—did everything she could to get Sybil to call the match off. Yet, as much as Sybil loved her mother, she had given her whole life into Lord Arthur’s keeping, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake her confidence. As for Lord Arthur, the blow took him days to get over; for a while his nerves were so thoroughly disordered that he could hardly think straight. His good common sense, however, soon reasserted itself, and his steady, practical judgment did not keep him long from deciding what to do. Since poison had turned out to be a complete failure, dynamite—or some other kind of explosive—was plainly what ought to be tried next.

Accordingly, he went back over the list of friends and relatives, and after careful thought decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean, a man of much learning and refinement, was passionately fond of clocks, and kept an extraordinary collection of timepieces, from the fifteenth century right up to the present day; and it struck Lord Arthur that this particular hobby of the good Dean’s would give him an excellent opening for carrying out his plan. Getting hold of an explosive machine, of course, was another question entirely. The London Directory offered him nothing, and he felt there was little point in asking Scotland Yard, since they never seemed to know anything about the dynamite crowd’s movements until after an explosion had already occurred—and not much even then.

Then, all at once, he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with strongly revolutionary leanings, whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s that winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be writing a life of Peter the Great, and to have come to England to study the documents connected with that Tsar’s residence here as a ship carpenter; but it was widely believed that he was a Nihilist agent, and there was no question that the Russian Embassy viewed his presence in London with little goodwill. Lord Arthur felt Rouvaloff was precisely the sort of man he needed, and one morning he drove down to his rooms in Bloomsbury to seek his counsel and help.

“Then you’re taking politics seriously?” Count Rouvaloff asked, after Lord Arthur explained the purpose of his errand. But Lord Arthur, who despised any show of swagger, found himself obliged to tell him that he had not the least interest in public questions at all; he only wanted an explosive machine for a matter of family concern, in which no one else was involved but himself."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ace183032d4bcf6844dc7674","rewritten_text":"Up with the morning light, and again scheming to slip past the watchfulness of my creditors, I hurried to the bookseller’s stall and spread out the small amount of ready money I had, using it to buy a few volumes on Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. Once I got home safely with them, I threw myself into their study, and before long I had made myself so far proficient in these subjects that I judged it enough to carry out my plan. During the pauses of this time, I spared no effort to soothe the three creditors who had been giving me such trouble. At last I managed it—partly by selling enough of my household furniture to cover a moiety of their demand, and partly by promising to pay the remainder once I had finished a little project I told them I had in mind, and for which I asked their help. Since they were simple-minded men, I found it no great task to bring them round to my purpose.\n\n“Matters being thus arranged, I then contrived, with the assistance of my wife, and with the utmost secrecy and care, to dispose of whatever property I still had, and to raise, in small sums, under various pretences, and with no regard at all for how I might repay, a considerable quantity of ready money. With what came in, I set about procuring, from time to time, cambric muslin—very fine—cut in pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a supply of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and several other items needed for the construction and fitting-out of a balloon of extraordinary size. I told my wife to get it assembled as quickly as possible, and I gave her full instructions as to the exact method to follow. Meanwhile, I worked the twine into a net of the proper dimensions; fitted it with a hoop and the necessary cords; bought a quadrant, a compass, a spy-glass, and a common barometer with certain important alterations, along with two astronomical instruments not so widely known. After that, I took chances to convey by night, to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam, five iron-bound casks meant to hold about fifty gallons each, and one larger besides; six tinned ware tubes, three inches across and ten feet long; a quantity of a particular metallic substance, or semi-metal, which I will not name; and a dozen demijohns of a very ordinary acid. The gas to be produced from these materials is a gas never yet made by anyone else—or, at least, never used for any like purpose. I would not hesitate to set out the secret, but it properly belongs to a citizen of Nantz in France, who communicated it to me conditionally.”"}

{"request_id":"0277963b8c03d8044f8cb0bc","rewritten_text":"Countrymen, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and vagabonds of every kind were all mixed together in one crowd. Drovers whistled, dogs barked, and oxen bellowed and surged forward. Sheep bleated, pigs grunted and squeaked, hawkers shouted, and all around there were cries, threats, and fights. Bells rang and voices roared from every public-house. People shoved and pushed and drove each other along, yelling and screaming. The noise was ugly and rough, coming from every corner of the market, and there were dirty, unwashed, unshaven figures running back and forth, pushing into the crowd and bursting out of it again and again. It was a scene so loud and confusing that it left the senses completely thrown off.

Mr. Sikes, dragging Oliver behind him, forced his way through the thickest part of the crowd. He paid almost no attention to the sights and sounds that amazed the boy. He nodded a couple of times to a friend as he passed, and he refused as many chances as he could to stop for a morning drink. Then he kept going until they were out of the worst of the chaos, and had made their way through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, young ’un!” said Sikes, looking up at the clock on St. Andrew’s Church. “It’s hard on seven. You’ve got to move. Don’t fall behind already, Lazy-legs!”

As he said this, Sikes jerked Oliver’s wrist. Oliver hurried his pace into a fast trot, somewhere between walking and running, and tried to keep up with the quick steps of the house-breaker.

They kept this pace until they had passed Hyde Park Corner and were on their way to Kensington. Then Sikes slowed down. An empty cart that had been some distance behind caught up. Seeing “Hounslow” written on it, he asked the driver, as politely as he could manage, whether he would give them a lift as far as Isleworth.

“Jump up,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes; he’s my boy,” Sikes answered, staring hard at Oliver. At the same time, he put his hand absentmindedly into the pocket where the pistol was.

“Your father walks a bit too fast for you, doesn’t he?” the driver asked, noticing Oliver was out of breath.

“Not at all,” Sikes cut in. “He’s used to it. Here, take hold of my hand, Ned. Get in with you!”

With that, he spoke to Oliver and helped him climb into the cart. The driver pointed to a pile of sacks and told Oliver to lie down there and rest.

As they passed the mile-stones, Oliver kept wondering, more and more, where Sikes planned to take him. They went by Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford, and still they traveled on at the same steady pace, as if they had only just started their journey."}

{"request_id":"2f39333ae835578ddb8b3024","rewritten_text":"I thanked him, and offered my apologies. He answered, “By no means,” and went on.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, so you may imagine she was treated as a prize match. Her half-brother, too, had plenty of money again; yet between debts and fresh outbreaks of madness, he squandered it most terribly once more. There were sharper grounds of difference between him and her than there had ever been between him and his father, and it is thought that he nursed a deep, deadly resentment against her for having, as he believed, fanned the father’s anger. Now I come to the cruel part of the tale,—only pausing, my dear Handel, to note that a dinner-napkin won’t fit into a tumbler.”

Why I was trying to cram mine into my tumbler, I can’t say at all. I only know that I found myself, with a persistence that deserved a better cause, making the most strenuous efforts to squeeze it within those limits. Once more I thanked him and apologised, and once more he replied, in the cheeriest tone, “Not at all, I’m sure!” and continued.

“On the scene there appeared—at the races, or at the public balls, or wherever else you please—a certain man who paid court to Miss Havisham. I never set eyes on him (this was five-and-twenty years ago, before you and I were, Handel), but I’ve heard my father speak of him as a showy sort, and just the sort of fellow for the job. Still, my father insists—without any allowance for ignorance or prejudice—that he must not be mistaken for a gentleman; for it is one of his principles that no man who is not a true gentleman at heart ever was, or ever could be, a true gentleman in manner. He says no varnish can conceal the grain of the wood; and the more varnish you lay on, the more the grain shows itself. Well! This man kept close to Miss Havisham and professed himself devoted to her. I don’t think she had shown much readiness for such things up to then; but every bit of susceptibility she had certainly came out then, and she loved him passionately. There’s no question she idolised him completely. He worked upon her feelings in that methodical fashion, drawing large sums of money from her, and he persuaded her to buy her brother out of his share in the brewery (which had been left him, weakly, by his father) at an enormous price, on the pretext that when he became her husband he would have to own and manage the whole concern. Your guardian was not, at that time, among Miss Havisham’s advisers, and she was too proud and too much in love to take counsel from anyone.”"}
